### Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscripts, most diligently corrected; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions issued during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating the material treated below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers has written on any theme may be surveyed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily apparent to the reader which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture. An edition of the greatest accuracy, and one easily preferable to all others if the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reissued works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the modest price, and especially this collection—single, systematic, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but for the first time gathered in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,000 francs; 130 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.**

# In the Year of Our Lord 999

## Richer, Monk of Saint-Remigius Outside the Walls of Reims

### Notice Concerning Richer and His Chronicle

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores, vol. III.)*

[Col. 0009]

[Col. 0009A] It is only rarely granted to history, as a matter of such great advantage, that a man connected by some relationship with both the fall of ancient kings and the rise of a new kind of men, and capable of writing history, should commit these events to writing. Yet this distinction was granted to Richer, born in the last days of the Carolingians and under Hugh, first of the kings who even today flourish in Gaul.

As we learn from his own testimony, Richer was a monk of Saint-Remigius outside the walls of Reims [Note: [Col. 0009C] Prologue of the work and Book IV, 50.]. His father was Rodulf, a soldier and adviser of Louis IV, the king from overseas. His father was “serviceable in counsel, exceedingly rich in eloquence and boldness alike; hence the king was very accustomed to him and very frequently consulted him.” Among other things that he accomplished, in 949 he proposed to the king’s council the plan for capturing Laon, and himself successfully carried it out as commander [Col. 0009B] [Note: [Col. 0009C] II, 87–91.]. In 956 he also captured by night Mount Castrilocus, the chief town of Hainaut, as the avenger of Queen Gerberga, and compelled Ragener, who had inflicted injuries upon the queen, to make satisfaction to her after taking away his wife and children [Note: [Col. 0009C] III, 6–10.].

Born of such a father and raised under King Lothair, who, the last of the Carolingians, maintained royal dignity with no little success amid civil and foreign wars, Richer may naturally be expected to have been inflamed by devotion to the royal lineage and love of his homeland, and to have acquired at home his first knowledge of public affairs and the art of war.

In the final years of Archbishop Odelric [Note: [Col. 0009C] Certainly not before the year 966, for he seems not to have known Flodoard. See the Prologue.], or, as I rather believe, under Archbishop Adalbero, he entered the monastery of Saint-Remigius. There, under the discipline of Abbot Rodulf, he was instructed in letters by the outstanding teacher Gerbert, turned his attention to the liberal arts [Col. 0009C], and, taught various branches of philosophy and steeped in the classical Roman writers—philosophers, poets, historians, and cosmographers—as might be expected of a monk, he also devoted himself to reading the holy Fathers and the ecclesiastical canons [Note: [Col. 0009C] Jerome and Sulpicius are mentioned in I, 3; in III, [Col. 0010C] 46 ff., he lists the classical authors used by Gerbert.].

At that time the city of Reims [Col. 0010A] was, among the cities of Gaul, anciently renowned and distinguished by the primacy of its bishop; it had been ennobled by the administration of Adalbero and was thereby powerful not less through example than through teaching in the formation of the minds and character of the young. Richer therefore won the friendship of Gerbert through his goodness and intelligence—“a man,” in his own words, “of great talent and marvelous eloquence, by which all Gaul shone resplendently, quivering as though by the light of a lamp.”

Since Gerbert was among the intimate advisers of Archbishop Adalbero, and through journeys, letters, and teaching was linked by personal familiarity with the greatest men in Gaul, Germany, and Italy, he gave the young man an excellent opportunity to learn and understand the affairs of his own time.

Amid the disturbances, however, that accompanied the fall of the Carolingians and the beginnings of the new kingdom, Richer devoted himself to the medical art [Col. 0010B]. The zeal with which he embraced it may be inferred from the many descriptions of diseases inserted in his work [Note: [Col. 0010C] For example, I, 11, 13, 18, 49, 56, 65; II, 37, 46, 59, 99, 103; III, 13, 96, 109; IV, 5, 24, 50 ff., 94.].

In March 991, summoned by a letter and a delegation from his friend Heribrand, a physician and cleric of Chartres, he went to Chartres. There, in the company of a man of great generosity and learning, he studied more diligently the Aphorisms of Hippocrates and the book On the Agreement of Hippocrates, Galen, and Surianus. He described the hardships of this journey in Book IV, chapter 50.

Shortly afterward, when Arnulf, the successor of Adalbero, had been deposed and Gerbert, through the favor of Kings Hugh and Robert, his pupil, had assumed the archbishopric of Reims, Richer was commissioned to compose a history of the Gauls. He says that he undertook this task “because of the great usefulness it appeared to offer and the abundance of its material, with that effort of mind by which he was drawn along through the remarkable kindness of the one giving the command” [Note: [Col. 0010C] Prologue.], and completed it in three years.

Thus, in the years 995 and 996, he composed the letters prefixed to the work, Book I, and chapters 1–78 of Book II, in which the history is brought down to the year 948. He seems to have added the remaining chapters of Book II and Books III and IV, which encompass the history of the years 948–995, in the years 996–998, and at that time also revised the entire work and put the final hand to it [Note: [Col. 0011C] I infer this from the fact that the first part of the work was written in brown ink, while the remainder, beginning with chapter 79 of Book II, was written in a darker ink, as were the corrections and additions to the first part. The same difference in ink is visible in the historical notices added by Richer on the final pages of the codex: especially the years 995 and 996 are written in brown ink, faint and barely legible, of the kind found in the first part of the work, while the remainder, covering the years 996–998, is written in darker ink, of the kind used for the rest of the work and for the corrections.].

He himself reveals the plan and method of the work in his preface as follows:

> “It has been specifically proposed to recall in writing the wars waged by the Gauls, their various disturbances, and the different circumstances of their affairs. If matters concerning others are also brought forward, this should be thought to have happened because of incidental circumstances that could not be avoided.”

He began the work at the point where Hincmar had brought his Annals to an end [Note: [Col. 0011D] Prologue.]. Although he proposed to carry the book forward for more than a hundred years, following the example of Julius Caesar he began with a division of the world and a description of Gaul and the peoples inhabiting it [Note: [Col. 0011D] Book I, 1–3.].

He presents the history of Kings Odo and Charles IV down to the year 920 [Col. 0011B] [Note: [Col. 0011D] I, 4–19.] from sources inaccessible to us, except for Flodoard’s History of Reims, from which he borrowed only a little. He composed the history of Charles IV, Robert, Rodulf, Louis, and the beginnings of Lothair—from the year 920 to the year 965—from Flodoard’s Annals [Note: [Col. 0011D] I, 19 through III, 21.] and sources unknown to us [Note: [Col. 0011D] Prologue.]. Finally, he wrote the reigns of Lothair [Note: [Col. 0011D] III, 22–109.], Louis V, Hugh, and Robert [Note: [Col. 0011D] Book IV], from the year 969 to 995, without the assistance of any historian, though he used certain documents from the archive of Saint-Remigius [Note: [Col. 0011D] III, 29, 30.] and Gerbert’s account of the council of Reims and the synod of Mouzon [Note: [Col. 0011D] IV, 73.].

With what judgment and reliability he did this will become apparent when his sources are compared with the histories that still survive.

Since Richer had proposed to write not annals but a history of the Gauls, he used Flodoard’s book but “arranged not the same words, but different words in place of different words, in a wholly different structure of expression” [Note: [Col. 0011D] Prologue. For example, in I, 49, Flodoard’s passage reads: “Count Warnarius was captured and killed there after the horse on which he was sitting had been killed.” Richer expresses it thus: “Count Warnerius died there, pierced by ten wounds, after the horse on which he was riding had been killed.” In I, 51, “the king was wounded between the shoulders,” where Flodoard writes, “the king was wounded there.”], and thought that the reader had been sufficiently served if he had arranged everything plausibly [Note: [Col. 0011D] A word of ambiguous meaning, used by Richer himself.] and clearly, briefly and concisely.

Certainly no one will fail to notice, and Richer cannot be blamed for it, that he omitted much of what Flodoard reported and often arranged the rest so that the sequence of events could be understood much better [Col. 0012A] [Note: [Col. 0012C] For example, II, 27, 43.]. By adding material of his own, he arranged everything so that it became an entirely new and plausible narrative.

He deserves not merely indulgence but congratulations because, in proportion to the varied abundance of his learning, he expanded matters that Flodoard had sometimes touched upon only in a word. Thus even that part of the work which flowed from Flodoard alone in a certain sense fills the role of a continuous commentary [Note: [Col. 0012C] For example, in I, 64, the use of commendation is explained; in I, 60–61, the Consecration; in I, 62, the capture of Laon; in II, 45, the siege of Reims.].

He may be forgiven for occasionally failing to understand Flodoard correctly [Note: [Col. 0012C] For example, in I, 50, where he writes that the Normans, returning from battle, entered the island, whereas Flodoard relates this of the Normans of Rouen; in the same place he says that King Rodulf captured the island, though this should be attributed to Count Heribert while the king was staying in the district of Beauvais; in II, 82, he confuses the synods of Saint Vincent at Laon and at Trier.].

Yet he must be censured sharply because, sometimes departing from Flodoard, he reports in descriptions of wars either very large numbers [Note: [Col. 0012D] For example, I, 62: 8,000; I, 44: he first wrote 5,000, then 6,000, and finally 10,000.] or numbers of combatants and slain far greater than those known from Flodoard’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0012D] I, 49: Flodoard has more than 800, Richer 960; I, 51: Flodoard 1,100, Richer 8,000; II, 85: Richer says more than 560 slain, Flodoard 400 in the History of Reims and 40 in the Annals.].

He attributes an undeserved victory to the Gauls [Note: [Col. 0012D] I, 49: the victory over the Normans, the burning of the camp, and the killing of 3,000 Normans contradict Flodoard.]. Indeed, he says that Flodoard wrote that eleven thousand were killed on Robert’s side and seven thousand one hundred and eighteen on Charles’s side [Col. 0012B] [Note: [Col. 0012D] I, 46.], whereas all manuscripts and editions of Flodoard [Note: [Col. 0012D] Year 923. A second edition of Flodoard, or perhaps another work of his unknown to us, cannot at all be taken into account here, as what follows demonstrates.] read only these words: “Many falling on both sides.”

Although this is plainly contrary to the truth and cannot be concealed by any excuse, the fault will nevertheless seem slight if one considers another passage, in which he allowed himself to be carried away by partisan zeal and vanity into a license wholly unworthy of a candid man, such as a writer of histories ought to be.

When he was revising the completed work, he did not blush to alter that part of Book I dealing with the affairs of Charles and the Belgians and their leader Gislebert, writing Germany in place of Belgica and Henry in place of Gislebert, so as to pretend that Germany had at that time been subject to Charles. Since this was accepted by Ekkehard of Urauge, who had read our author, and contradicted all the other evidence, it cast at least a doubt into the minds of historians down to our own time, and could be explained only when an authentic copy was discovered.

Having found Richer excessively devoted to his homeland beyond what can be tolerated, and devoted to empty glory—the kind that even provoked the indignation of peoples in Napoleon’s bulletins [Note: [Col. 0012D] Bulletins.] [Col. 0013A]—we may judge that the entire work must be read cautiously and that no passage should be used without first carefully examining its foundations. In doing so, we shall not seem to assert anything beyond what is just and true.

I readily admit that even in the first books, apart from what rests on Flodoard’s authority, there are many matters peculiar to Richer to which it is permissible to give credence. These appear to include the history of King Odo, especially the account of the victory at Mount Panchei [Note: [Col. 0013C] I, 4–13.], although it is not mentioned in the Annals of Vedastinus, Abbo, or Regino; in the history of Charles and Rodulf, the notices concerning Belgian affairs [Note: [Col. 0013C] I, 20, 23, 24, 34, 35–41.], derived from an ancient source but noted above as adulterated; the accounts of Haganon, the capture of Charles [Note: [Col. 0013C] I, 14–16, 21, 22.], the affairs of the Normans [Note: [Col. 0013D] I, 28–33.], and a few other matters [Note: [Col. 0013D] For example, I, 63.]; and much [Col. 0013B] [Note: [Col. 0013D] For example, II, 1–5, 16–20, 30–35, 51–59, 87–90, 93, 94; at the beginning of Lothair’s reign, III, 6–10.] in the history of Louis IV, whose adviser we have said Richer’s father was and whose final years Richer himself may have witnessed as a boy.

In this part of the work, therefore, one should proceed as follows: after using Flodoard, one must first determine what is owed to him or should be regarded merely as his commentary; then the reliability of the remaining material must be investigated, with due regard for the author’s loquacity and excessive devotion to his homeland.

Although by this method the authority of some things that flowed from sources unknown to us is also weakened [Note: [Col. 0013D] For example, in II, 30 ff., Richer’s authority alone is sufficient for us to attribute the killing of William, duke of the Normans, to Otto the Great.], you will nevertheless find that they contribute greatly to an understanding of the history of the tenth century.

The second part of the work, comprising chapters 22–110 of Book III and Book IV, will win the author particular praise, since he wrote candidly, clearly, and accurately about his own time and about matters that he had himself experienced or [Col. 0013C] learned from Gerbert, the instigator of the work.

It is also to his credit that he preserved his devotion to the Carolingians even after their destruction. Although, following Adalbero and Gerbert, he acknowledged the authority of the new kings [Note: [Col. 0013D] He also seems to have known Robert, Gerbert’s pupil; he praises him in IV, 13.] and transferred to Charles, beginning with Hugh’s coronation, the term “tyrant,” which he had previously used to designate the rebels and deserters [Note: [Col. 0013D] I, 46.] of Charles and Louis [Note: [Col. 0013D] For example, II, 27.], he nevertheless concealed the justice of Charles’s cause not at all [Note: [Col. 0013D] IV, 39.] and condemned the treachery of Adalbero, bishop of Laon, in the narrative itself as sharply as possible.

In writing about the councils at Saint-Basolus and at Mouzon, he agrees with Gerbert in general. He reports certain matters omitted by Gerbert [Note: [Col. 0013D] The speech of Bishop Guido, IV, 63.], yet, as the purpose of the work required, he presented everything thoughtfully and concisely.

The proceedings inserted by both men differ in only a few words of no importance; where the authority of one should prevail is not clear.

The work, therefore, weighed in the balance, reveals an author who is benevolent, serious, perceptive, equipped with varied forms of learning, accustomed to investigate the causes of events, well informed about the people and matters relevant to the history of his own time, and who had learned to write history from the example of the Romans.

Among writers of his own age he is especially distinguished by his knowledge of the art of war [Note: [Col. 0013D] Compare the descriptions of battles and military machines in I, 8 ff.; II, 10, 35, 45; III, 8, 103–107; IV, 17, 19, 22.] and of the places [Note: [Col. 0013D] For example, III, 101: the location of Verdun.] where events occurred, and he devoted himself to describing them [Col. 0014B].

His errors should be attributed to excessive devotion to the glory of his homeland and to vanity [Note: [Col. 0014C] He also committed other errors because he had not considered the matter carefully; for example, in I, 3, he makes Charles two years old when his father died; in I, 12, he makes him fifteen in the year 893; in III, 109, he does not calculate Lothair’s years accurately.].

In general, the order follows the course of time, though it is sometimes disrupted by the effort to connect events. His style is clear and concise, and is pleasing for its vigor and simplicity.

Richer, having carried the work down to June of the year 995, brought his writing to an end, though he recorded the principal events of the years 996, 997, and 998, so that it is clear that he also turned his attention to composing these sections.

At the time when Gerbert was advanced to the see of Ravenna and, in the following year, raised to the summit of the Roman pontificate, it may be questioned whether Richer sent him the work. Certainly the autograph book is not arranged in such a way that I would readily believe it was delivered into the hands of an archbishop or supreme pontiff; whether it was copied, however, we do not know.

Nothing further is known about Richer, except that an old inscription records that, through his scholarly efforts, a copy of the Salic Law, now preserved in the Royal Library of Paris under the number 4789, was brought into the library of Saint-Remigius at Reims [Note: [Col. 0014D] “The book of Saint-Remigius, through the efforts … of Richer …”].

The autograph history was brought, perhaps among the first books, in the eleventh century into the library of the monastery of Saint Michael at Bamberg, founded by the Emperor Henry II. It is listed, together with other books known to Gerbert and Richer, in the catalogue of Ruotger, compiled between 1112 and 1123 [Note: [Col. 0014D] Schannat, Vindemiae, I, 52.].

Between the years 1098 and 1101 it was copied by Ekkehard of Urauge [Note: [Col. 0014D] Compare Arch. VII, 470–471. Ekkehard, contrary to his usual practice as demonstrated in his copying of other writers, uses Richer’s text quite freely. He presents not only different words and sentences but twice—namely, in the histories of Haganon and Gislebert—a wholly different narrative, though with an intention and in words that agree as closely as possible with Richer. One might therefore conjecture that he used another edition of the work, but no trace of another manuscript survives.

Our manuscript was already preserved in the metropolitan church of Bamberg before the year 1611. It must have been transferred there in earlier centuries, perhaps after the great devastation of the monastery of Saint Michael in 1453, since in the older catalogue of the metropolitan library, belonging to the twelfth or thirteenth century and published by the distinguished Jaeck in Oken’s Isis in 1829, pp. 1237–1238, no mention of Richer is made.

Trithemius had our manuscript and Ekkehard before his eyes. I do not fear that anyone will think that the story of the witch and Rantheus’s mare, inserted by him into the history of Haganon, was taken from Richer; it is as foreign to Richer’s manner of writing as to his mind, which was scarcely subject to superstition. Such things could suit Flodoard.

Hugh of Flavigny, in his Chronicle published by Labbeus I, p. 157, [Col. 0016D] took the capture of Charles and Gerbert’s debate with Othric either from our author or from another writer who had copied him. Conversely, Hugh of Fleury knew our author not at all, and the Deeds of the Bishops of Reims cited by him presented a history of Arnulf and Gerbert very different from the one read here.].

Four hundred years later it was copied by Trithemius [Col. 0015A] [Note: [Col. 0016D] In the Chronicle of Hirsau and in the book On the Origin of the Franks, published by Schardius.]. It was then transferred to the chapter library and, in 1611, bound into a manuscript whose margins had unfortunately been trimmed. Finally, in our own century, it was brought into the public library of Bamberg.

When, accompanied by our colleague Boehmer, I examined its treasures in August 1833, a book was presented to us among the historical manuscripts, much of it difficult to read. On its front, in a recent hand, among other things, was written: “The four books of the History of Richer, monk of Siena, of the Order of Saint Benedict. (Achery, Spicilegium, vols. II–III, does not agree.)” On the first folio, in a sixteenth-century hand, was also written: “History of Richer the monk.”

At first glance, having perceived the antiquity of the work, and then, even in the opening lines, with immense joy, I recognized a hitherto unpublished tenth-century writer, whose name alone had been transmitted by Trithemius [Col. 0015B]. I easily obtained permission to copy him from the distinguished Jaeck, who directs the extremely rich library with great benefit to scholarship and supports our studies with the greatest goodwill toward German affairs.

The book now emerges from the darkness in which it had been concealed for more than eight hundred years, and will itself claim its place among the principal historians of the Middle Ages.

To speak more fully about the manuscript from which it has come to us: as its script itself shows—the specimens of which we append—it was written at the end of the tenth century, namely in the years 996–998.

The parchment is for the most part palimpsest; its format varies according to the different quires, but in general it is what is called quarto oblong, or octavo. Six quires are marked with numbers. The first consists of folios 1–8, with a slip [2b] inserted, bearing at its head the inscription “Ant[idotum] Philonium for catarrh”; the second of folios 9 and 12–16, with 10 and 11 inserted; the third of folios 17–22; the fourth of folios 23–28, 30, and 32, with 29 and 31 inserted; the fifth of folios 33 and 38–44, with 34–37 inserted; the sixth of folios 45, 46, 48, 52, and 54–57, with 47, 49–51, and 53 inserted.

The script is larger in the first part of the work and diminishes from folio 9 onward. On some pages, especially pages 49 and 50, it is extremely small; on others it is so faded through the injury of time that it can be read only with difficulty.

As the work itself reveals, it is Richer’s autograph, completed and revised entirely in his own hand. This is evident from many words and sentences erased in the same ink in which they had been begun, with other words and sentences substituted in the same sequence of writing.

Since the text to be published below will provide examples of this, it will suffice to note here that, in revising the work, the author also altered many matters of greater importance, erasing words, sentences, and even pages, and replacing them with others.

This occurred especially in the first quire [Col. 0016A], whose faded ink differs greatly from the darker ink of the author revising his work: folios 2, 5, 6, 7, and 8 also show this, and there the name of Henry, duke of Saxony, was substituted for the name of Gislebert, count of Belgica.

In the second quire he altered much on folios 9 and 10, and inserted folios 10 and 11, both extensively corrected and written in darker ink. In the fourth quire he erased the beginning of the second page of folio 33, inserted folios 34–37, and altered a little on folio 38.

Finally, in the sixth quire, by inserting folios 49–50 and slip 51, he added the account of his journey from Reims to Chartres and the history of the synod held in the monastery of Saint-Basolus; he also inserted slip 53 and added six lines to the account of the battle fought between Conan and Fulk.

Thus it truly appears that, if the autograph of any author has ever been left to us, Richer’s autograph has been.

The book ends on line eight of page 55 verso. Most of the page, together with page 56, was left blank; on page 56 verso, letters of Gerbert were written in an entirely different hand. Page 57 is blank; page 57 verso, again in Richer’s principal hand, contains the main points of a continuation of the history written at a different time.

It remains to say briefly something about the plan and method of the edition.

After transcribing the work with as much diligence as possible, I judged that the text should be reproduced as it was last approved by the author, with the first reading added wherever the faded appearance of the script permitted this. The earlier readings often proved highly useful for establishing the true sense.

I introduced divisions into chapters that originated with the author himself but were sometimes omitted, wherever they appeared necessary according to his own meaning. I retained the headings placed in the margin and added numbers.

Where passages were obscure or damaged by the loss of one or another letter, I supplied a probable conjecture. I touched the punctuation only rarely, when the connection of the sentences most clearly required it.

In this matter, Richer and Gerbert seem to have followed nearly the same practice, the division of the words being adapted to the modulation of the voice.

Finally, since Richer is greatly illuminated by Gerbert’s history of the councils at Saint-Basolus, Mouzon, and Coucy, I have included these minor works on the basis of manuscripts from the end of the tenth and the eleventh centuries, namely:

1. The Lyon manuscript among the Vossian manuscripts, in quarto, no. 54, formerly belonging to the monastery of Micy, from which the council of Reims, together with Gerbert’s letters to Widerod, bishop of Strasbourg, and to Siguin, archbishop, and King Hugh’s letter to Pope John, was published at Frankfurt in 1600 in octavo. These materials were copied by our colleague Boehmer and me.

2. The Wolfenbüttel manuscript among the Helmstedt manuscripts, no. 32, in folio [Col. 0017A], formerly belonging to Saint-Remigius at Reims [Note: [Col. 0017A] Marlot writes in his History of the Metropolitan Church of Reims II, 45, that he possessed an autograph, though mutilated, in which chapters 25–40 were missing; hence he transcribed only a few passages, pp. 45–46. The manuscript of the Barberini Library mentioned in our Annals is on paper and was copied from Chesne’s smaller manuscript.], from which Flacius’s defective edition of the council at Saint-Basolus derived. I have decided to report it as an appendix after it was again collated by D. Waitz with the printed editions.

I have added from the Wolfenbüttel manuscript, folios 169–170, a letter of Pope Gregory V to Archbishop Willigis, in which he informs him of the decrees of the synod of Pavia concerning Arnulf.

I am convinced that these documents, exceptionally suitable for illuminating the history of the tenth century, proceeding from eminent men and either restored to their integrity through the authority of excellent manuscripts or brought to light for the first time, will accompany Richer’s unpublished books very appropriately. (You will find below, under Gregory V and Gerbert, the letter of Gregory V and the Council of Mouzon about which Pertz speaks here.)

**The editor of Patrology.**

# Richer’s Four Books of Histories

## Author’s Prologue

[Col. 0017B] To the lord and most blessed Father Gerbert, archbishop of Reims: Richer, monk.

The authority of your rule, most holy Father Gerbert [Note: [Col. 0017] Manuscript G.], gave me the occasion to record in a volume the encounters of the Gauls. Since this offers the greatest usefulness and presents a manifold abundance of material [Note: [Col. 0017] The letter X has faded away.], I embrace it with that effort of mind by which I am drawn along through the marvelous kindness of the one giving the command.

I thought that the beginning of this undertaking should be taken from what lies near at hand [Note: [Col. 0017] “I wanted to begin from the author,” altered above to “should be taken.”], since [Note: [Col. 0017] The letter *m* has faded.] the late Hincmar, eighth in the pontificate before you [Note: [Col. 0017] First hand: “Hincmar, seventh metropolitan of Reims before you.”], appended in his annals a very full account of events that had taken place long before.

The farther back the reader goes through his records from the beginning of our little work, the earlier material he will find. I say this so that the frequent repetition of the Carolingians and others in both works may not disturb the order of either work [Col. 0017C]. For where the order of events is not observed, error confuses the mind struggling to understand, just as much as it misleads one who departs from the sequence of order.

Thus, since the names of Charles and Louis often appear here and there, the prudent reader will carefully distinguish kings who bear the same name by reference to the time of the authors [Col. 0018B].

It has been specifically proposed to recall in writing the wars frequently waged by the Gauls, their various disturbances, and the different circumstances of their affairs. If matters concerning others are also brought forward, this should be thought to have happened because of incidental circumstances that could not be avoided [Note: [Col. 0017] *per* in manuscript 1.].

But [Note: [Col. 0017] In the second hand—that is, the correcting hand—“But until I shall have arranged [them].”] if I am accused of ignorance concerning an unknown antiquity, I do not deny that I have taken some material from a little book by Flodoard, a priest of Reims. Yet the work itself most clearly demonstrates that I have arranged not the same words, but different words in place of different words, in a wholly different structure of expression [Note: [Col. 0017] *ordinationis* corrected to *orationis*.].

I believe that the reader has been sufficiently served if I have arranged everything plausibly, clearly, briefly, and concisely. For in speaking, refusing to overflow, I shall dispatch very much in compressed form.

I shall begin the whole narrative by briefly dividing the world and distributing Gaul into its parts, since it is my intention to describe the customs and actions of its peoples [Col. 0018C].

# Book One

## 1. The Division of the World

[Col. 0017C] The region of the world that makes itself suitable for human beings is said by the cosmographers to be divided into three parts [Note: [Col. 0017C] Compare Orosius, Book I, chapter 2]: Asia, namely, Africa, and Europe.

Of these, the first, extending from the north through the eastern region as far as the south, is bounded externally by the Ocean [Col. 0018C]; internally it is separated from Europe by the Rhipaean Mountains, the navel of the earth, the Tanais, Maeotis, and the Mediterranean Sea.

From the navel of the earth as far as the south, it is separated from Africa by the river Nile.

The Mediterranean, lying between Africa and Europe, distinguishes them, while externally they are surrounded by the Ocean from south to north [Col. 0019A] [Note: *interjectus* in the manuscript.].

Internally, the Nile separates one of them from Asia, while the Mediterranean, the Tanais, and Maeotis, as has been said, separate the other.

Although each of these regions has its own divisions, I have decided to divide one part of Europe, which is called Gaul from its whiteness [Note: [Col. 0019C] Namely, from Greek γάλα, “milk.”], because its people bear the mark of a whiter appearance, into its own constituent parts.

## 2. The division of this Gaul into regions

[Note: [Col. 0019] Chapter 2. 3. Ekkehard copied this out in his history of Pippin and Carloman, mayors of the royal palace.]

Gaul, then, is itself divided into three distinct regions: Belgica, Celtica, and Aquitania. The first of these, Belgica, extends from the Rhine—which separates Germany from the Ocean—up to the River Marne. It is fertile in many peoples and received its name from *germinando*, “springing forth.” On either side it is bounded: here by the Pennine Alps, there by the sea, whose surrounding waters make Britain an island.

Celtica stretches lengthwise from the Marne to the Garonne. Its sides are bounded by the British Ocean and the island of Britain. Whatever extends from the Garonne to the Pyrenees is called Aquitania; on one side it borders the Rhône and Saône, and on the other the Mediterranean.

[Note: [Col. 0019] “But” here: on this side the Marne, on that the Garonne, is the earlier reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0019] The words “to the Hiberus, which gave its name to the region of Hiberia, and onward to the Ocean” have been deleted.]

[Note: [Col. 0019] “Here”: the province of Lugdunensis; “and there”: deleted in the first copy.]

Thus the whole extent of Gaul is enclosed on the east by the Rhine, on the west by the Pyrenees,

[Note: [Col. 0019] “Hiberus” in the first copy.]

on the north by the British Sea, and on the south by the Mediterranean.

## 3. The character of the Gauls

All the peoples of Gaul are therefore greatly stirred by their inborn boldness and cannot endure accusations. If provoked, they exult in slaughter and, rendered more savage, attack with excessive severity. Once something has been accepted and approved by argument, they are scarcely accustomed to refute it.

Hence Jerome says (*Epistle* 60, against Vigilantius):

[Note: [Col. 0019] The phrase “the voice” is cut off.]

[Col. 0020A] “Gaul alone,” he says, “has had no monsters, but has always shone with prudent and most eloquent men.”

Besides these qualities, the Belgians are especially distinguished in arranging affairs, and are not inferior in strength or boldness. They pursue the greatest enterprises more by intelligence than by force. If they fail through intelligence in what they seek, they use force boldly. They are also exceedingly frugal in food and drink.

The Celts and Aquitanians, on the other hand, are very capable both in counsel and in boldness, and are useful in seditious affairs. The Celts, however, are more prudent, while the Aquitanians act impulsively and are carried to an excessive appetite for food. This is so innate in them that they do not desire anything contrary to their nature.

Hence Sulpicius also says (*Dialogues* I, 4):

> “Gluttony among the Greeks is appetite; among the Gauls it is nature.”

[Note: [Col. 0019] The word is cut off.]

Although all these peoples are naturally fierce, history records that in ancient times they fared prosperously in nearly every respect, even while they were pagans.

[Note: [Col. 0019] The phrase “in nearly every respect” is cut off; I restored the passage by using the place in which Ekkehard employed it.]

[Col. 0020B]

[Note: [Col. 0019] The syllables *um pa* are cut off.]

Afterward, baptized by Saint Remigius, they are said always to have shone forth with pre-eminent and illustrious victory.

[Note: [Col. 0019] The words *a s. R.* are cut off.]

[Note: [Col. 0019] The word *adprime* is cut off.]

[Note: [Col. 0019] The words *a semper, lustri* are cut off.]

[Note: [Col. 0019] The word *emicuisse* is cut off.]

Their first Christian king is likewise said to have been Clovis. From him onward, through successive periods, the commonwealth is known to have been governed by distinguished emperors, down to Charles, with whom we shall begin our history.

## 4. How, because of the king’s childhood and the dissension of the princes, pirates invaded Gaul

[Note: [Col. 0019] “Gaul” has been supplied conjecturally.]

He had as his father King Carloman.

[Note: [Col. 0019] The first copy reads: “he had as father King Louis …, but as paternal grandfather …”]

[Col. 0019C]

Rather, he had Louis the Stammerer as his father, and was born after Louis’s death.

At this point it seemed appropriate to insert a notice concerning the war waged in the year 880 by Louis the Younger against Louis and Carloman, the sons of Louis the Stammerer. Our Boehmer copied it from a royal manuscript in Munich, among the Augustan manuscripts numbered 151, a ninth-century quarto containing canons and decretals. It appears there on the final folio, 74:

> “When we were beside the River Aisne, in the village of Ritest [today Rethel], on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, on the vigil of Saint Praejectus the martyr, after the ninth hour of the day, suddenly a star of extraordinary size and brilliance appeared. It surpassed the measure of a star, yet did not attain the magnitude of the sun. As we watched it, it seemed at one moment to grow beyond measure with flaming rays, and at another to fail through excessive pallor. Thus, changing with incredible speed, it moved toward the west; finally, before it entered among the hidden mountain places and removed the obstacle of its setting from our sight, it completely vanished.
>
> “Nor can it be conjectured that this sign of the star was displayed without cause. When the brilliant power of certain men then held sway, through sins meriting this it failed to a lasting end, and so vanished that it is not even worthily retained in memory.”

[Note: [Col. 0019D] The words *e haud legitur*—“e is not read”—are supplied as a note.]

[Col. 0020D] Another version:

> “When Louis thought that he was prospering, and in the western kingdom—which he had then seized unlawfully, and in which sacrilege, murders, rapes, arsons, and other unheard-of crimes had been perpetrated through his invasion—was lifted up in spirit by these most empty successes, the diligence of the princes who then governed that kingdom drove him back beyond their borders.
>
> “On that return, having lost hope of invading the kingdom (880), he encountered the Northmen. Having engaged them in battle, he lost his dear son [Hugh], and was so exhausted by the hardships of the journey home that he and his men scarcely returned to their own country. Then, in his own kingdom, numerous obstacles began to rage against him. Surrounded everywhere by indescribable calamities and harassed by the attacks of the Northmen, he was seized by fever and breathed his last (882).”

[Col. 0020C]

His paternal grandfather was Louis, surnamed the Stammerer, and his great-grandfather was Charles the Bald, the distinguished emperor of the Germans and Gauls. He lost his father when he was still two years old, his mother surviving for scarcely four years thereafter.

[Note: [Col. 0019] The first copy reads, “his mother having died shortly beforehand.”]

[Col. 0020C]

Because of his childhood, the princes of the kingdoms, driven by excessive desire for power, competed to outstrip one another, and each prolonged the disorder as he was able. No one sought the king’s advancement,

[Note: [Col. 0021] The first copy reads “the king’s interests.”]

nor anyone the protection of the kingdom. Acquiring what belonged to another was the highest aim of each; no one seemed to advance his own affairs unless he added something belonging to another.

Thus universal concord fell into the most complete discord. Here plunder, there fires, there seizures of property broke out. While these things were being carried on with extreme violence, the pirates who inhabited the province of Rouen—which is part of Celtic Gaul—were stirred to acts of savagery.

This people had departed long before from more distant islands of the northern Ocean. Wandering across the seas, they reached this principal region of Gaul in a fleet. They often attacked it with arms, and often also, defeated by the rulers of the land, fell in battle.

Since they repeatedly stirred up conflict among themselves, it seemed to the leading men of Gaul that this province should be granted to them as a gift from the kings, but on the condition that, completely abandoning idolatry, they should faithfully devote themselves to the Christian religion and should faithfully serve the kings of Gaul by land and sea.

The metropolis of this province is known to be Rouen, extending its authority over only six cities: Bayeux, Avranches, Évreux, Séez, Coutances, and Lisieux.

[Note: [Col. 0021D] Today: Bayeux, Avranches, Évreux, Séez, near Alençon, Coutances, and Lisieux.]

It is therefore clear that this province had formerly been possessed by pirates. But now, driven by their ancestral savagery, they attempted to plot against the quarreling princes. Accordingly, they began to harass Brittany Minor—which is adjacent to Gaul and under arms—with raids and incursions.

Finding an opportunity, they completely broke their agreement and advanced farther into Gaul. Roaming everywhere, they spread far and wide, carrying off a considerable amount of booty: women, children, livestock, and other goods. With all this they withdrew to the banks of the Seine, at the place now called Givold’s Ditch.

[Note: [Col. 0021D] Compare Prudentius’s *Annals*, year 856.]

Having attempted the same thing repeatedly, they nearly overran the whole part of Celtic Gaul lying between the rivers Seine and Loire, which is also called Neustria. They intended to break into the interior regions of Gaul and either drive their peoples from their borders or impose the heaviest tribute upon them. They hastened to do this before the princes could be recalled to agreement, being entirely confident that, amid such dissension, they would carry away the wealth of Gaul.

Their attack was led, it was said, by Catillus. The princes, overwhelmed by such barbarian disgrace, earnestly sought peace among themselves through envoys.

Not long afterward, under the law of hostages, they assembled to deliberate together. At this meeting, following the counsel of wise men and keeping faith with their agreement, they returned to the greatest concord, prepared to avenge the insults inflicted by the barbarians.

And because Charles was scarcely three years old,

[Note: [Col. 0021D] Charles was born in September 879, and below, in chapter 12, is said to have been fifteen in the year 893.]

they deliberated on creating a king—not as deserters, but as men indignant against their adversaries.

## 5. The king’s lineage and fortune

[Note: [Col. 0021] The letter *a* is deleted.]

[Note: [Col. 0021] The words “of the Lord’s incarnation” are cut off.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 888, in February, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March,

[Note: [Col. 0021] “In the year” and “of the Lord’s incarnation” are cut off.]

[Note: [Col. 0021] The date is cut off.]

[Note: [Col. 0022D] Since only the sixteenth day before the Kalends, the ninth day before the Kalends, the second day before the Kalends, the second day before the Ides, or the Nones of March can be reckoned here, I chose the first of these—that is, 15 February—because Wido departed for Italy immediately after Odo’s election and was elected there before 21 February.]

on the fifth day of the week, by common decree they created Odo, a military man and energetic leader, king in the basilica of Saint . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0021] The word is omitted.]

[Note: [Col. 0022D] According to the *Annals of Saint-Vaast*, Odo was crowned in the palace at Compiègne, thus in the chapel of the Blessed Virgin Mary.]

His father was Robert, of the equestrian order; his paternal grandfather was Witichin, a German immigrant. Once created king, he conducted everything vigorously and usefully, except that amid military turmoil he rarely had the power to settle disputes.

[Note: [Col. 0021] The deleted text explained this as due to the soldiers’ sometimes refusing to submit even to a moderate authority.]

For he defeated the pirates in pitched battle within Neustria seven times and drove them into flight nine times.

[Note: [Col. 0021] The deleted reading says, “Indeed, he completely expelled them from the borders of Gaul.”]

And this continued for almost five years, from 889.

[Note: [Col. 0021] From the *Annals of Fulda*.]

After their repulse, a severe famine followed, since the land remained uncultivated for three years. A measure of grain which, multiplied sixteen times, made a *modius*, was now selling for ten *dragmas*. A chicken likewise cost four *dragmas*, a sheep three ounces, and a cow fetched a *jabus*.

[Note: [Col. 0022D] A *jabus* is eleven-twelfths.]

There was no purchase of wine, since the vineyards had everywhere been cut down and scarcely any wine could be obtained.

Meanwhile the king built fortifications in places that offered access to invading pirates, and stationed troops in them. He himself withdrew with the army into the regions of Aquitania, declaring that he would not return until the aforementioned measure of grain sold for two *dragmas*, a chicken for one denarius, a sheep likewise for two *dragmas*, and a cow for three ounces.

[Note: [Col. 0021] The word “coastal” has been deleted.]

## 6. (890.) The pirates attack and devastate Brittany

Meanwhile, while the king was administering the commonwealth at the city of Anicium,

[Note: [Col. 0022D] Le Puy, near the sources of the Loire.]

the pirates, driven from the borders of Neustria, learned that he had withdrawn into the interior of Aquitania.

[Note: [Col. 0021] The first copy reads “had retreated.”]

They therefore gathered and prepared a fleet, and suddenly invaded Brittany. The Bretons, terrified by the barbarians’ sudden assault, were slaughtered as the latter raged. Each person was content merely to save his life. No one sought to rescue his possessions; they were concerned only with life.

Thus, abandoning almost everything they possessed, the pirates carried off whatever they found scattered about. They transported away everything of value and, with abundant booty, returned without resistance.

Encouraged by this success, they broke into Aquitania along the outer borders of Brittany, near Angers, and devastated the land with extensive destruction. They carried off men, women, and children. They cut down the older people of both sexes; they enslaved the children; and they prostituted the women who seemed beautiful.

## 7. (892.) King Odo prepares an army against the pirates

[Note: [Col. 0023] The fragments *x*, *pyra*, and *rcitum* are cut off.]

Some, however, escaped through varying circumstances and were saved by flight. As these survivors recounted their sufferings, the news was soon reported to King Odo. Moved by the magnitude of the disaster, he ordered by royal edict that as many soldiers and infantrymen as he could gather from Aquitania should assemble.

From Provence also—which is enclosed on every side by the Rhône, the Alps, the sea, and the borders of the Goths—he obtained men from Arles and Orange.

[Note: [Col. 0023D] Inhabitants of the district whose chief city is Orange.]

From Gothia, too, he obtained men from Toulouse and Nîmes. Once these forces had been assembled, the royal army consisted of ten thousand cavalry and six thousand infantry.

He proceeded beside the Brivadois,

[Note: [Col. 0023D] Brioude, which the Allier flows past.]

making his way toward the fortress of Saint Julian the martyr. After honoring the saint with royal gifts, he entered the district of Auvergne.

The enemy had already arrived there and were violently pressing the fortress called Montpensier.

[Note: [Col. 0024D] Montpensier, on the left bank of the Allier near Aigueperse, below Clermont.]

The king, surrounded by the leading men of the Franks and Aquitanians, discussed the conduct of the war with them, although after uncertain deliberation. He urged them to fight and greatly exalted their courage as something arising from their nature. He reminded them that they were superior to other peoples in strength, boldness, and arms; that their ancestors had conquered nearly the whole world and had savagely crushed Rome itself, the head of the world. Therefore, he asserted, it was necessary to renew their ancestral courage in their sons, so that the magnanimity of their fathers might be commended by the virtue of their children.

[Note: [Col. 0023] The first copy reads “he reminded them.”]

## 8. King Odo’s attack on the pirates and the character of the battle

When he had persuaded them by these words, being himself a bold and forceful man, he attacked the barbarians with sixteen thousand men under arms. He sent the infantry ahead and made the first attack with them. He himself followed with the cavalry, waiting to see what fortune would attend the infantry.

The barbarians likewise had drawn up their battle line and intended to receive their adversaries as a united force. The royal infantry advanced directly against the enemy and at the first engagement shot arrows. Closing ranks, they moved against them with leveled spears.

Received by the barbarians, many fell away, though not without causing the enemy’s destruction. Some of the barbarians were thrown down, and many others were wounded.

After the infantry, the royal cavalry followed and, with great effort, broke into the enemy’s battle line, which had been divided by the infantry forces. It is said to have cut down thirteen thousand, with only a few escaping by flight.

When victory had already been secured and the army was intent on plundering the spoils, four thousand barbarians who had been lying in ambush in hidden places attacked from the side of the roads. As they approached with a marching advance, observers recognized them by the gleam of their weapons.

At the signal, the army regrouped. The king, thinking that a much larger number was arriving, urged his attendants to recover their former courage and, indeed, not to lose it. In many speeches he declared that it was honorable to die for one’s country and glorious to give one’s body to death in defense of Christians.

The army therefore closed ranks. Although weakened by wounds from the earlier battle, it did not delay in confronting the enemy.

## 9. Ingo, a man of humble station, enters the battle with the king’s standard

[Note: [Col. 0023] The fragments *ibus cum*, *no*, and *gre* are cut off.]

When it was being debated who should carry the royal standard—for in so great a gathering of nobles no one seemed to be without a wound, and everyone avoided the task—Ingo sprang forth from among them all and, offering himself for military service, said fearlessly:

> “I am one of the king’s humble attendants,

[Note: [Col. 0024D] *Marescalcus*, a marshal.]

> “and, if this does not detract from the honor of my superiors, I shall carry the royal standard through the enemy lines. Nor am I afraid of the uncertain fortune of war, since I know that I must die once.”

King Odo replied:

> “By our gift and with the consent of the princes, be the standard-bearer.”

Taking up the standard, Ingo advanced surrounded by the densely packed ranks. Becoming the point of the military wedge, he entered the enemy ranks, brandishing his weapon. The barbarians were thrown into confusion and lost their strength.

The royal army, returning, attacked again and cut them down. Attacking a third time, it overwhelmed almost all of them. As the air grew dense with their tumult and became heavy with dust, Catillus,

[Note: [Col. 0023] “King of the barbarians” corrected to “Catillus.”]

with a few companions, slipped away in flight through the darkness and hid himself in the thickets. While he was hiding, the victorious men, ranging everywhere, found and captured him. After those who had hidden with him had been pierced with the sword,

[Note: [Col. 0023] The fragments *m*, *la*, and *t* are cut off.]

he was brought before King Odo after the spoils had been taken.

## 10. The tyrant’s baptism and death

[Note: [Col. 0023] The fragments *i*, *et*, and *o* are cut off.]

After this useful victory had been achieved, the king took the captured tyrant with him to Limoges. There he gave him the choice between life and death, promising life if he were baptized, but death if he refused.

The tyrant immediately asked to be baptized without objection. It is doubtful, however, whether he possessed any faith.

Since the feast of Pentecost was approaching, on June 11, and a gathering of bishops was present with the king, the bishops imposed upon him a three-day fast.

On the appointed day, in the basilica of Saint Martial the martyr, after the bishops had completed their offices, he descended into the sacred font to be received by the king. Once he had been baptized by triple immersion in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Ingo, who had previously been the standard-bearer, drew his sword and ran him through mortally, horribly staining the sacred font with the outpouring of blood.

The king, indignant at so great a crime, ordered the murderer to be seized and killed, while the princes roared in anger. Ingo threw down his sword and fled, embracing the altar of Saint Martial. He begged pardon from the king and the leading men, and with many cries demanded an opportunity to speak.

By royal command he was brought forward to answer for the crime he had committed. He began as follows.

## 11. Ingo’s persuasive speech on his own behalf before the king and the princes

“I call God, who knows my will, as witness that nothing was dearer to me than your safety. Your love drove me to this act. For your safety I cast myself into these miseries. For the life of all I did not fear to undergo such danger.

“The deed is indeed great, but greater is the benefit of the deed. I do not deny that I injured the royal majesty, but I assert that many advantages were secured by the act. Let the mind of the doer be considered, and let the future usefulness of the deed also be weighed.

“I perceived that the captured tyrant had sought baptism out of fear, and that, once released, he would repay us with many injuries and avenge the slaughter of his people with the utmost severity. Because he appeared to be the cause of future disaster, I turned the sword against him. This is the cause of my deed. This drove me to the crime. I did it for the safety of the king and his people.

“And would that through my death the freedom of my country and peace in public affairs might follow! But if I am killed, I shall seem to have been killed for the safety of the king and the leading men. Let each person now consider whether one ought to serve for such a reward, and whether, for keeping faith, one should receive such a return.

“Look at the recent wounds on my head, chest, and side! The scars of earlier times are visible, and bruises are scattered across the remaining members of my body. Exhausted by their constant pain, after so many sufferings I expect no end to my troubles except death.”

By this lament he moved some to goodwill and drove others to tears. Accordingly, the soldiers pleaded for him, softened the king, and urged him toward merciful clemency. They asserted that nothing benefited the king if one of his men should perish; rather, one should rejoice at the tyrant’s killing, either because life had been granted him if he died faithful, or because his plot had completely failed if he had received baptism deceitfully.

The king restrained his anger. After the barbarian had been buried, he restored Ingo to favor. He also generously granted him the fortress called Blois,

[Note: [Col. 0025D] Blois.]

because the man who had held the fortress had been killed in the pirate war. Ingo also took the abandoned wife of that man in marriage as a royal gift.

From then on, enjoying the great favor of the king and the princes, he conducted everything prosperously and happily. But this lasted only briefly. The pus from his wounds, badly removed by surgeons, produced an internal swelling beneath the newly healed surface. Afflicted for more than two years by an excessive flow of humors, he took to his bed. When the rheum became obstructed, he swelled up completely. Thus, with his entire body covered by erysipelas, he died, leaving behind a young son, Gerlon.

[Col. 0026A]

The king entrusted the boy to a guardian, and he possessed his patrimony with his mother.

## 12. Charles’s elevation to the kingship

[Note: [Col. 0025] The ending of *promotio* is cut off.]

[Note: [Col. 0025] The ending of *regem* is cut off.]

Meanwhile, after leaving the city of Limoges, the king went to Angoulême and there arranged whatever matters required attention.

[Note: [Col. 0025D] Angoulême.]

Not long afterward, going to Périgueux, he settled there, with the greatest fairness, the cases of the nobles that were being disputed in litigation, and dealt extensively with common matters before the leading men.

[Note: [Col. 0025] The deleted text read: “He dealt extensively with private matters and much with communal affairs”; a line beneath these words has also been deleted.]

While he was deeply occupied with these affairs and intended to remain there for some time, Fulk, archbishop of Reims, was discussing Charles’s elevation to the kingship among the Belgians (893).

For it seemed that the present opportunity offered some advantage for this undertaking. This was encouraged especially by the absence of the Neustrians,

[Note: [Col. 0025] The words “who live between the rivers Seine and Loire” have been deleted.]

for they were then detained with the king in the regions of Aquitania. The young man’s repeated complaints also encouraged it. Already fifteen years old, he was complaining bitterly to his friends and household about the loss of his kingship and was striving with great effort to recover his father’s kingdom.

All the princes of Belgica and several of those of Celtica therefore strongly favored him. Their agreement was confirmed under the metropolitan of Reims by an oath.

At the appointed time they assembled: from Belgica, the metropolitans of Cologne, Trier, and Mainz, with their diocesan bishops or their credible representatives; from Celtica, the aforementioned metropolitan of Reims, with several of his diocesan bishops, namely those of Laon, Châlons, and Thérouanne.

[Note: [Col. 0025D] It is established that Lothair’s kingdom at that time obeyed Arnulf; therefore these three archbishops did not choose Charles as their king.]

[Col. 0026C]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 893, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, a Sunday, January 28,

[Note: [Col. 0025] The year and the words “of the Lord” are cut off.]

[Note: [Col. 0025] The date “the fifth day before the Kalends” is already cut off.]

they gathered at Reims in the basilica of Saint Remigius and created fifteen-year-old Charles king. They established that, having been clothed in purple in the city, he should issue edicts in royal fashion.

Very few from Celtica followed his cause. From Belgica, however, all were devoted to him. They received him with the greatest devotion and conducted him most graciously through all their cities and towns.

[Note: [Col. 0025] The words “through all” are cut off.]

[Note: [Col. 0025] The words “and towns” are cut off.]

## 13. Odo’s return from Aquitania and his death

[Note: [Col. 0025] The ending of *Odonis* is cut off.]

[Note: [Col. 0025] The phrase “from Aquitania” is cut off.]

When King Odo learned what had happened, he returned from Aquitania. Going to the city of Tours, he honored Saint Martin with royal gifts. Then, received at Paris, he lavishly endowed the holy martyrs Denis, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.

At last, having crossed the River Marne, he entered Belgica. After being received at a town called Fara, he began to suffer sleeplessness because of excessive anxiety. As this increased greatly, it produced mental derangement. When the humors overwhelmed him, in the tenth year of his reign he met the end of his life—some say from mania, others from delirium—in 898, on January 1.

[Col. 0027A]

He was buried amid the great lamentation of his people in the basilica of Saint Denis the martyr.

[Note: [Col. 0027] The words surrounding *tumulatur* are cut off.]

## 14. The character of Charles

Once Charles had been created king, he aimed at winning much goodwill. He had an impressive body, a good and straightforward intelligence.

[Note: [Col. 0027] The deleted text adds: “In the earliest years of his adolescence, peace and tranquillity in the commonwealth, the concord of his people, and the prosperity of private persons were pleasing to him. But this was soon deleted.”]

He was not especially accustomed to military exercises, but he was highly educated in the liberal arts. He was generous in giving and not at all avaricious. He was marked by two vices: he was intemperate in lust and somewhat negligent in carrying out judgments.

The princes of Gaul were attached to him by loyalty and oath. Robert also, the brother of the deceased King Odo, an energetic man of great boldness, offered himself for military service to the king.

[Note: [Col. 0027] The deleted passage reads: “Thus the king, surrounded by the princes and distinguished by the great service of his people, made laws and issued decrees in royal fashion. He also appointed Robert . . .”]

The king appointed him duke of Celtica and entrusted him with the ordering of all affairs there. For nearly four years he used his counsel and became greatly accustomed to him.

[Note: [Col. 0027] “His” and *plurimum* have been deleted.]

Robert led him through Neustria,

[Note: [Col. 0027] The deleted words read: “which is part of Celtica.”]

and the king was received by him in cities and towns. Going to Tours, he generously bestowed many talents of gold and silver upon Saint Martin. He asked the saint’s servants to offer prayers on his behalf and obtained their daily prayers continually.

After returning from there, having secured everything he sought, he went back to Belgica and honored Saint Remigius with splendid gifts.

Then, having entrusted Celtic Gaul to Robert,

[Note: [Col. 0027] Up to the words “he appointed” was copied by Ekkehard in the *History of Henry*, but not accurately.]

he withdrew into Saxony.

[Note: [Col. 0027] Corrected from “Belgica” to “Saxony.”]

[Note: [Col. 0027C] Here and in what follows, comparison of the earlier reading with the present one shows that the author, led astray by an insane enthusiasm for his people, substituted Saxons for Belgians and Henry for Giselbert. No reliance at all should be placed on such passages copied by Ekkehard of Aura; historians should return to the older reading noted below.]

Inspecting its cities, royal residences, and towns, he took possession of them without resistance. There he appointed Henry, distinguished by royal birth and descended from that region, duke over all.

The Sarmatians submitted to him without a battle.

[Note: [Col. 0027] The letter *S* and the following text are deleted.]

He also won over the English and the other peoples overseas through remarkable goodwill.

[Note: [Col. 0027] The word “military” is deleted.]

Yet this lasted scarcely a decade.

[Note: [Col. 0027] The surrounding letters are cut off.]

And perhaps he would have been fortunate in every respect if he had not made one excessive mistake.

## 15. Charles’s excessive affection for Haganon

[Note: [Col. 0027] The ending of *dilectio* and the name *Haganon* are cut off.]

For although he treated the princes with great kindness, he held Haganon in exceptional favor. He had raised him from humble station to power, to such an extent that, while all the leading men remained at a distance, Haganon alone clung to the king’s side and frequently took the cap from the king’s head and openly placed it upon his own.

This brought great disgrace upon the king.

[Note: [Col. 0027] Corrected from “calamity” to “disgrace.”]

The leading men regarded this as intolerable, approached the king, and complained to him at length that a man born of obscure parents greatly diminished the royal dignity by standing beside the king as though, in the absence of nobles, he alone were advising him. They declared that unless Haganon ceased this close association, they would completely withdraw from the king’s council.

The king, not at all persuaded by these warnings, did not abandon his beloved companion.

## 16. (920.) Robert’s indignation against Haganon

[Note: [Col. 0027] The endings of *indignatio*, *Robert*, and *Haganon* are cut off.]

Meanwhile, after firmly securing the cities and towns of Belgica,

[Note: [Col. 0027] In a scraped place, but in the same ink and hand: “of Gaul.” Ekkehard, who copied these passages, has this reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0027] Corrected from “borders” to “cities.”]

[Note: [Col. 0027] With the feast of Easter approaching, he withdrew to the palace at Aachen. Here Ekkehard.]

The king returned to Celtica and took up residence in the city of Soissons. Princes from all Gaul flocked there. Lesser men also gathered there in great numbers and with much enthusiasm.

[Note: [Col. 0027] The first copy reads “commoners.”]

[Col. 0028B]

[Note: [Col. 0027] They assemble; the dukes are also present: Henry from Saxony and Robert from Gaul. Every day they remain near the doors of the royal chamber; every day they await the king’s departure from the inner rooms of the palace. When the king gave them no answer for four days, Henry, taking this very badly, is said to have remarked either that Haganon would someday reign with Charles, or that Charles would sink to humble circumstances with Haganon. Indignant, he departed without consulting the king. Ekkehard of Aura, who subsequently recounts in three lines Henry’s reconciliation through Heriveus, narrated below in chapters 23 and 24. Of the preceding tale, although it suits Richer’s disposition very well, there is no trace in the manuscript; nor did it originate with Richer, as the account below in chapter 20 of the cause of Henry’s enmity shows. Compare above, p. 566.]

Among these men, Robert believed that he was held in greater favor by the king, since the king had appointed him duke over all Celtica. When the king was seated in the palace, at his command the duke sat on his right, while Haganon likewise sat on his left.

Robert silently regarded it as disgraceful that a man of humble station should be made equal to him and placed before the leading men. Yet restraining his anger, he concealed his feelings and spoke only a few words to the king.

He therefore rose quickly and conferred with his men. After taking counsel, he sent envoys to the king to report that he could not endure Haganon’s being made equal to him and preferred to the leading men. It also seemed disgraceful that such a man should cling to the king while the noblest of the Gauls were kept far away. Unless the king reduced him to humble circumstances, Robert would strangle him by a cruel hanging.

The king, unwilling to tolerate the humiliation of his beloved companion, replied that he could more easily do without the conversation of everyone else than without Haganon’s intimacy.

Robert was excessively angered by this. Together with most of the leading men, and without the king’s order, he went to Neustria and took refuge at Tours. There he was greatly indignant at the king’s fickleness.

[Note: [Col. 0027] Corrected from “complaint” to “indignation.”]

He also carefully discussed among his own people how supreme power might be transferred to himself. Although he favored the king, he nevertheless begrudged him the kingdom to no small degree, since he believed that after his brother he himself ought to inherit it.

[Note: [Col. 0027] The fragments *Q*, *r*, and *non* are cut off.]

He also plotted several things against Fulk, the metropolitan of Reims, who had raised the king from infancy and promoted him to the kingship.

[Note: [Col. 0029D] The sequence of events already sufficiently demonstrates that Fulk’s murder must not be wrongly connected with Haganon’s affairs.]

For he thought that if Fulk alone were removed, the kingdom could more easily be transferred to himself. He was also pressing this matter strongly upon Baldwin, prince of the Morini. Persuaded by Robert, Baldwin had already abandoned the king and was following Robert’s cause.

[Note: [Col. 0029] The words “by Robert” are deleted.]

## 17. The Murder of Archbishop Fulco (899)

When the king learned of this, he marched against Baldwin and, after a vigorous siege, took the fortress of Arras from him; he then granted it, together with the entire abbey of Saint Vaast, to the aforesaid metropolitan Fulco. But after some time the metropolitan, because of the journey’s distance and the inconvenience of the brothers [Note: [Col. 0029] “fra, mo” cut off.], summoned Count Altmar [Note: [Col. 0029] “a. rationibus habitis” deleted.], and received from him the Abbey of Saint Medard, which the count himself held. In exchange for it, after the accounts had been mutually settled, he gave him the Abbey of Saint Vaast together with the fortress of Arras.

(900.) As a result Baldwin was driven to extraordinary cruelty. Afflicted by great anxiety, he turned wholly to revenge. He therefore pretended friendship toward the metropolitan. Through envoys he also sent assurances of great goodwill [Note: [Col. 0029] “spondet,” “he promises,” instead of “mandat,” “he sends word.”], and pledged his loyalty. Yet with great diligence he observed whether Fulco was accustomed to go to the royal palace alone or with the king’s troops, for he was eager to attack him when alone.

While matters stood thus, it happened, on royal business, that the bishops of Belgica were assembled before the king. Accordingly, when the metropolitan was summoned and was preparing to hasten his journey, he proceeded incautiously with only a few companions. At once a certain Winemar arrived against him, sent by Baldwin with a troop [Note: [Col. 0029] “the most wicked of all whom the earth supports” deleted.]. Since the metropolitan was traveling with only a few men, he and his companions were intercepted by the troop. No opportunity for escape appeared. They were surrounded on every side and attacked. They fought fiercely on both sides; men fell wounded on both sides.

(900, June 16.) Winemar attacked the metropolitan and pierced the unarmed man with a spear [Note: [Col. 0029] The manuscript reads “tranfigit.”], then threw him down, wounded among his men by seven blows. When he continued to direct blows against him, several of Fulco’s men, moved by their great love for the bishop, threw themselves upon him. They too were immediately pierced and killed with him. Only four escaped by flight [Note: [Col. 0029] “having been rescued,” in witness 1.], and they reported the affair at Reims.

Then a great band of soldiers was quickly led out from the city with weapons and attempted to pursue the adversaries. But when those men had escaped, they gathered up their slain lord and his companions and carried them to Reims amid much lamentation and grievous cries of sorrow. There, together with the priests, they buried the priest with the utmost honors due to his dignity.

## 18. The Death of Winemar [Note: [Col. 0029] “e.” is cut off.]

Meanwhile, when the bishops had been assembled before the king, these events were soon reported. This caused excessive grief in everyone’s hearts. The king himself dissolved in tears and lamented the bishop’s death [Note: [Col. 0029] “of his friend” instead of “of the bishop.”] with profound sorrow. The bishops likewise mourned with great compassion the death of their brother and fellow bishop.

After taking counsel, they condemned Winemar and his accomplices with a dreadful anathema. Before long he wasted away, struck by God with an incurable disease of dropsy. His belly swollen, he was burned externally by a slow fire and internally by a monstrous conflagration. A huge swelling of the feet was also present. His private parts teemed with worms. His swollen legs were shiny. His breath was foul. His entrails gradually seeped out through his anus. In addition to all this, he endured an intolerable thirst. At times he had an appetite for eating, but the food brought to him caused disgust. He suffered continual sleeplessness. Having become intolerable to everyone, he was regarded by all with horror [Note: [Col. 0029] The word is cut off.].

Thus, abandoned by his friends and household servants, who were exhausted by the great stench of his body—in fact, no physician could approach him, even for the purpose of treating him—and dissolved by all these afflictions, deprived of every communion of Christianity, already partly consumed by worms, he was driven from this life as a criminal and sacrilegious man.

## 19. Heriveus’s Promotion to the Episcopate [Note: [Col. 0029] “tio, in, tum” is cut off.]

After Lord Fulco the metropolitan had been buried, Heriveus, an eminent man and member of the palace, succeeded him in the pontificate by the king’s appointment, with the consent of the bishops and the agreement of the people of Reims. If anyone wishes to know fully with what usefulness and devotion each of them flourished in the Church of Reims [Col. 0030C], let him read the book of the priest Flodoard, in which he has written a very full account of the bishops of that city from its foundation [Note: [Col. 0029] That is, from the foundation of the city of Reims.] [Note: [Col. 0029] “enum, e cupit” is cut off.].

Once Heriveus had obtained the episcopate, he followed the king with great loyalty and was exceedingly hostile to deserters. He first admonished, in ecclesiastical fashion, Count Erlebald of Castricum [Note: [Col. 0030D] “Erlebadum”—through “concesserat” is taken from Flodoard’s *Annals* for 920; compare this source in what follows as far as book III, chapter 21.], who had seized the property of his bishopric and held the town called Macerias, urging him to come to his senses. Later he condemned him by anathema (920). Since Erlebald was not satisfied even after his condemnation, Heriveus marched against him with a large force of soldiers and vigorously pressed the siege of the town for four weeks.

Unable to endure the continual assault, Erlebald secretly slipped away from the town with some of his men. Those who had remained, now defeated, opened the gates and submitted to the metropolitan. After expelling them, he stationed his own men there and drove the fugitive Erlebald from the entire district.

## 20. Mutual Appeal to the Rhine and the Killing of Count Erlebald [Note: [Col. 0031] “ad R, p, tis E” is cut off.]

The king had gone to the district of Worms to speak with Henry of Transrhenania. Count Erlebald also arrived there, intending to complain before the king that the metropolitan of Reims had treated him savagely. Henry was earnestly occupied with arranging affairs faithfully before the king [Note: [Col. 0031] “about maintaining friendship between them” is added, then deleted.].

While he was devoting himself intensely to this matter [Note: [Col. 0031] “both of them” deleted.], young men from the Germans and the Gauls, offended by differences of language [Note: [Col. 0031] “ling, ma” cut off.], began, as is their custom, to provoke one another with insults and great agitation [Note: [Col. 0031] “to attack” instead of “to provoke.”]. They drew their swords, engaged one another, and inflicted mortal wounds.

In this tumult, when Count Erlebald approached to settle the quarrel, he was killed by the enraged men. Thinking that this was treachery, the king quickly rose and surrounded himself with his men. Henry, however, believing it a deception [Col. 0031B] [Note: [Col. 0031] “being unaware of the circumstances” deleted.], returned to his fleet and was forced by the king’s guards to cross the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0031] “On that day there was no harmony, no friendship between them” deleted.]. For those who stood with the king thought that Henry had come with deceit.

From that time onward Henry was also said to have been hostile to Charles [Note: [Col. 0031] “Henry” deleted.].

## 21. The Deserters’ Deceitful Persuasion of King Charles to Reject Haganon (920) [Note: [Col. 0031] “Dese, regi, de Haganonis” is cut off.]

On one side Henry, and on the other Duke Robert, pressed Charles. Placed between them, he was harassed from both directions. After this, returning to the interior of Belgica, he withdrew to Soissons and complained bitterly among his followers about this misfortune.

To this place also, from Belgica where it borders Celtic Gaul, and from Celtic Gaul, several princes flocked. Duke Robert too, having drawn nearer, withdrew to Étampes and sent envoys to the palace, intending to discover what royal business was being conducted there.

Those who had gathered supported Robert’s cause. At his urging, they discussed before the king the rejection of Haganon—not because they actually wished it to occur, but so that an opportunity to reign might be prepared for Robert.
