They therefore lightly recommended Haganon’s expulsion. They also declared, with only moderate insistence, that the duke would withdraw from the king if Haganon were not expelled, so that the king, admonished by this slight rebuke, would not fear persisting in what he had begun. They believed that afterward they would have a most just cause for indignation against him.

Everything turned out according to their wishes. For the king, moved by no persuasion [Note: [Col. 0031] “the slightest” instead of “no.”], replied that he would never separate himself from the beloved man, and he maintained this in many speeches full of arguments.

When Duke Robert perceived that this was firmly fixed in the king’s mind [Note: [Col. 0031] “When the princes perceived this in his mind” is an alternative reading; after four lines, the entire account of the plot had been completed. When these lines had been erased, a second hand wrote everything beginning with “For the king, being anxious...”], he sent envoys to Henry of Transrhenania and urged him to expel the king [Note: [Col. 0031] The words “rans, legat, ejec, et, Com, im, stipa, fugam, un, idem, acit” are cut off.]. For he had learned that Henry had been forced to flee by the king’s guards; hence Robert immediately gave Henry an assurance of his loyalty [Note: [Col. 0031] The same fragmentary sequence is cut off.].

With Henry’s consent, the tyrant soon rejoiced [Note: [Col. 0031] The manuscript has “mo . . . tus” or “me . . . tus”; the middle is cut away.] and worked most diligently to transfer the kingdom to himself [Note: [Col. 0031] “reg, erre, issime, abat, itaque, atque” is cut off.]. He therefore distributed many gifts and promised unheard-of things [Note: [Col. 0031] The middle is cut off; the surviving text is plain, so greater promises should not be supplied.].

At last he openly addressed the princes who had already been induced to defect. He said that they had the king of Soissons in their hands as a private man [Note: [Col. 0031] “um” is cut off.], and that, apart from a very few, the Belgians had gone over to his side. He declared that the opportunity was therefore at hand [Note: [Col. 0031] The initial “a” is cut off.], asserting that the king could be captured very easily and without difficulty if they all went to the palace as though to consult with him, and, while consulting in the very bedchamber of the palace, seized and held the king.

Almost everyone from Celtic Gaul supported this proposal, and they conspired with the tyrant to carry out the crime. They therefore went to the palace and surrounded the king as though they intended to consult him. Once he had been brought into the bedchamber, they spoke with him briefly, then seized and held him.

## 22. Heriveus the Metropolitan Frees Charles, Captured by the Deserters, and Leads Him to Reims [Note: [Col. 0031] “us, litanus, rto, m liberat, ucit” is cut off.]

They were already trying to lead him away when the metropolitan Heriveus suddenly entered the city of Soissons with troops. Concerned for the king, he had foreseen the deserters’ treachery. At first he himself was admitted with a few men; afterward his followers were admitted as well, with the support of Riculfus, the bishop of that city.

Surrounded by armed men, he entered the council of the deserters, to everyone’s astonishment. Becoming terrifying, he cried: “Where, I ask, is my lord the king?” Of so many men, very few had the strength to answer, believing themselves utterly deceived. Yet when they recovered their courage, they said: “He has gone inside with a few men to consult.”

The metropolitan forced the barred door. After breaking the bolts, he found the king sitting there with only a few men [Note: [Col. 0031] “with only two,” in witness 1.]. They had captured him, appointed guards, and assigned him to a prison.

The metropolitan seized him by the hand and said: “Come, king; use your own men instead.” Thus the metropolitan led him out from the midst of the deserters. Then, mounting a horse, he left the city with 1,500 armed men and reached Reims.

After his departure, the deserters, confused with shame, were indignant that they had been mocked. Ashamed and angry [Note: [Col. 0031] “and enraged,” in witness 1.], they returned to Robert and reported to the deserter and traitor that the affair had not gone well.

King Charles, accompanied by the metropolitan and by a few others who had indeed defected from him but had returned to him through the counsel of wise men, returned to the interior of Belgica and proceeded to Tongeren. There, after the bishop had died, with the clergy electing Hilduin and the people supporting the election, he ordained Hilduin bishop through Archbishop Herimannus—a generous and vigorous man, but factious.

For as soon as he had been ordained bishop, he immediately attached himself to and supported those princes of Belgica who had favored Duke Robert in rejecting the king [Note: [Col. 0031] “who had rejected the king together with Duke Robert,” in witness 1.], plotting a great deal against the king with them.

But the king, following the good counsel of his men, summoned through the metropolitan Heriveus Duke Henry, who held supreme authority throughout Saxony [Note: [Col. 0033] “Belgica,” in witness 1.]. For, persuaded by Robert [Note: [Col. 0033] “Henry,” in witness 1.], he had withdrawn from the king together with others. [Note: [Col. 0033] The first author initially wrote: “But the king, using the counsel of Heriveus, metropolitan of Reims, summons by envoys Gislebert, who was more powerful than all others in Belgica. For, persuaded by Henry, he had departed from the king with several others. When summoned, he is admitted before the king with great honor.” After changing these matters, the first hand wrote a much fuller history.]

## 23. The Complaint of Heriveus, Metropolitan of Reims, before Henry on Behalf of King Charles [Note: [Col. 0033] “tio, ensium, ani, um” is cut off.]

Before him the metropolitan, speaking in the king’s place, began as follows:

“Until now, most noble man, peace among the princes and harmony among all have flourished usefully through your prudence and generosity. But after you relaxed your vigilance toward the envy of wicked men, the force of discord emerged from its hiding places all around us. This circumstance has persuaded our lord the king to come before you in supplication.

“Previously you were dearly loved by him, and not moderately so, because of your merits. Your outstanding loyalty, recognized by him, has given him great confidence in times of grave danger. He does not fail to recognize that, when he possessed the kingdom with all its dignity, he strayed from you somewhat [Note: [Col. 0033] “often” is deleted.]. Yet he is eager to correct this with complete loyalty. Nor is this unusual or exceptional [Note: [Col. 0033] “but frequent and common” deleted.]. Everyone sometimes acts foolishly; it is characteristic of good men to return to sound judgment.

“It must therefore be endured and forgiven with the greatest kindness. You too, best of the Germans [Note: [Col. 0033] “of the Belgians,” in witness 1.], seem to have departed too far from what is right. Nor is this surprising. For Duke Robert, thirsting for everything and savagely coveting the kingdom from the king [Note: [Col. 0033] “I do not know whether he enticed you because you were incautious or because you desired evil,” in witness 1.], lured you, while you were off your guard, by his persuasions. What can a persuasive speech, carefully arranged, fail to accomplish?

“I say that both sides have strayed too far. But now at last let your former virtue return to you. Let each strive with all his strength, so that you may have a king especially advantageous to you, and the king may have in you a man entirely worthy of himself. For he wishes you to excel over all those known to inhabit Germany [Note: [Col. 0033] “Belgica,” in witness 1.].

“Therefore recall your mind to better things. Receive your rejected lord, so that you may in turn be received by him and raised up.”

## 24. Henry’s Reply to the Metropolitan Heriveus concerning Charles [Note: [Col. 0033] “R, ad, He” is cut off.]

Henry replied [Note: [Col. 0033] “of Gislebertus,” in witness 1; “Gislebertus” is also given in witness 1.]:

“Many things dissuade me from this, unless your outstanding virtue, Father, somehow draws me toward the same course. For I know how difficult and arduous it is to give him counsel, both because of his own fickleness and because of the envy of his followers.

“It is not unknown to me how long ago I contended for him both at home and in the field. It is also perfectly well known how greatly he has abused the loyalty he owed me. Perhaps, Father, you are persuading me to do something of which I shall repent once it has been done.

“But because no one can be sufficiently skillful concerning the future, and no one sufficiently prudent, and because evil counsels more often succeed than good ones, I shall go wherever you command. Having experienced your virtue, I shall lower my modesty beneath your dignity.

“For my part, I had resolved to withdraw from him by intelligence, counsel, and arms.”

Thus, persuaded by the metropolitan, Henry was brought before the king. He was received with much ceremonial honor, and the two were bound together in friendship.

## 25.

When these events had taken place, Hilduin, bishop of Tongeren, was accused of having conspired against the king with those who had defected from him [Note: [Col. 0033] “before” instead of “against.”]. Since he was hostile to the king, the king persecuted him [Note: [Col. 0033] Corrected from “was attacked” to “was persecuted.”].

The force of this hatred went so far that the king promoted Richerus, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, and deposed Hilduin (921). But when Richerus, having received a royal gift, was pressed by Archbishop Herimannus because he had unlawfully accepted the episcopate from the king over the head of the man who held it, a man who had been overcome by no confession of guilt and condemned by no judgment, he hastened to Rome at the king’s command. There he explained to Pope John both the king’s decision and the circumstances of his own case.

The pope, indignant at Hilduin as a deserter, suspended him from office and condemned him by anathema. He ordained Richerus bishop and granted him the blessing of his authority.

While these things were taking place, Hilduin pursued his case, pouring out a lengthy complaint before the pope to no avail and laboring earnestly with him for absolution. While he was making his complaint, Richerus returned and, ordered by the king, entered the vacant see.

## 26.

While matters stood thus, the king turned his journey toward the inner regions of Belgica. Because of the many circumstances that had arisen, a synod was convened by royal decree and at the metropolitan’s command at Trosleium [Note: [Col. 0033D] Compare Flodoard, for the following, under the year 921.].

Lord Heriveus presided over this synod, with the king also presiding there. After many matters judged most useful had been determined, Lord Heriveus the metropolitan, with the king’s intervention and the consent of all the bishops who attended the synod, absolved the aforesaid Erlebald, count of Castricum, from the bond of excommunication [Note: [Col. 0033] “ex” is cut off.].

There too, after Rodulf, bishop of Laon, had died, he solemnly ordained Adelelmus, treasurer of that same city, as bishop, the king having granted him the office with the broad consent of the bishops.

## 27.

After these matters had been successfully and usefully settled, the king returned to upper Belgica to arrange certain affairs of his followers there. He marched against Count Richuinus because he too was a deserter and supported Robert’s party. He therefore laid siege to his towns and harassed him with a vigorous assault.

But when Richuinus perceived that the cavalry force was unbearable, he was overcome by the law of hostages [Col. 0034D] and returned to the king. The king received the defeated man, softened his anger [Note: [Col. 0033] The manuscript reads “animum ab ira mitig...”], and restored him to favor.

## 28.

While these things were taking place, Robert, duke of Celtic Gaul, was fiercely attacking pirates. For they had suddenly invaded Neustria under their leader Rollo, the son of Catillus. They had already crossed the Loire with their fleet and occupied its territories unharmed. They roamed about everywhere and returned to their fleet with rich plunder.

The duke had gathered forces from all Neustria and had also summoned many men from Aquitaine. Four cohorts from Belgica, sent by the king, were also present; the aforesaid Richuinus commanded them. Dalmatius commanded the Aquitanian legions. The duke Robert himself arranged the Neustrian forces.

Thus the duke’s entire army amounted to forty thousand horsemen. He placed Dalmatius with the Aquitanians in the front line; then he arranged the Belgians [Note: [Col. 0035] “He arranged them under Duke Gislebertus; then the Neustrians,” in witness 1.]; the Neustrians he stationed in reserve.

The duke himself went around the legions, calling the leading men by name and exhorting them to remember their courage and nobility above all. He declared that they must fight for their homeland, their lives, and their freedom. They should not be anxious about death, since it is uncertain for everyone. But if they fled, he said, they would leave nothing behind for the enemy.

With these and many other words he inflamed the soldiers’ spirits. After speaking, the duke led the ordered ranks to the place where the battle was to be fought.

## 29.

The enemy army likewise arranged its military forces against them with great boldness. Their army, consisting of fifty thousand armed men, advanced in orderly ranks. Observing that the greatest force of the battle was about to bear down upon them, Duke Robert joined Dalmatius in the front line with one thousand sturdy men from Neustria.

He therefore advanced with Dalmatius and the Aquitanians [Col. 0035C] [Note: [Col. 0035] “With the fronts marked by a maforto” is unclear; “at” is found in witness 1.].

The pirates’ legions had extended themselves in a long line [Note: [Col. 0035] The manuscript reads “profenderant,” apparently for “protenderant,” “had extended.”], and they had curved their formation to receive the enemy in the shape of the waxing moon [Note: [Col. 0035] “which is fifth,” in witness 1.]. Thus, when the enemy rushed upon them with great fury, they would be received by the army’s encircling movement. In this way, those who remained on either wing could attack the enemy from behind and throw them down like cattle.

## 30.

When these preparations had been made on both sides, the two armies engaged with standards joined [Note: [Col. 0035] “with the greatest shouting and hostile standards,” in witness 1.]. Robert with the Neustrians and Dalmatius with the Aquitanians penetrated the pirates’ legions, and were immediately attacked from behind by those who were on the wings.

Soon the Belgians too pursued unexpectedly [Note: [Col. 0035] “Gislebertus with the Belgians unexpectedly pursues,” in witness 1.], and slaughtered with monstrous carnage the pirates who were pressing their own men from behind [Note: [Col. 0035] “he strikes them down,” in witness 1.]. The Neustrians also pressed forward with extreme ferocity.

In this confusion, the Aquitanians, surrounded by the pirates, forced those whom they were attacking to flee with great exertion. But the men who had held the wings were pressed on one side by the Belgians and, on the other, were mortally assaulted by the Aquitanians after they had wheeled around.

Overcome, they laid down their arms and begged loudly for their lives. Robert therefore asked that such slaughter be spared and urged that they be rescued. The army scarcely ceased from the killing, incited by the success of its much more prosperous fortune.

When the tumult had been calmed, the duke captured those who seemed to be the leading men among them; the rest, under the law of hostages, were permitted to return to the fleet.

## 31.

After the victory had been won and the army disbanded, Robert placed the captives in Paris. He questioned them as to whether they were Christians [Note: [Col. 0035] The note, marked “ex conjectura,” proposes the readings “t, n, e, l, h, g, a, d, presbite, M, Christ, Q, sem, a, i, ni”; the forms are conjectural and fragmentary.], and discovered that none of them had any knowledge whatsoever of this religion [Note: [Col. 0035] Same conjectural, fragmentary note.].

He therefore sent the venerable priest and monk Martin to instruct them [Note: [Col. 0035] Same conjectural, fragmentary note.], and they were converted to the faith of Christ [Note: [Col. 0035] Same conjectural, fragmentary note.].

Among those who had returned to the fleet, some were found to be Christians and others pagans, mixed together [Note: [Col. 0035] Same conjectural, fragmentary note.]. These too, after being instructed by the aforesaid man [Col. 0036B] [Note: [Col. 0035] “guests,” in witness 1.], were led to the saving sacraments after the duke returned the hostages they had given [Note: [Col. 0035] Same conjectural, fragmentary note.].

## 32.

When the matter of baptism was being discussed, the duke entrusted their preaching to Witto, metropolitan of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0035] The reading is obscure.]. But Witto, not content to act alone, sent a letter to Heriveus of Reims, asking him by what order and in what manner a formerly faithless people ought to be joined to the Church.

The metropolitan Heriveus, wishing to arrange these matters with great care, ordered a gathering of bishops to be held, so that the matter might be suitably determined according to the reasoning of many.

## 33.

On the appointed day a synod was held. First, the synod dealt soundly and appropriately with the peace and religion of the holy Church of God and with the condition of the kingdom of the Franks. Afterward it discussed at length the appeasement and conversion of the pirates.

It was also decreed that an account of this matter should be sought from Divinity itself and that everyone should fast for three days. The matter was to be brought to the attention of the lord pope, so that, after God had been invoked through fasting and the lord pope had been humbly consulted, the affair might be arranged more effectively.

Having reviewed the decrees of the Fathers, the venerable metropolitan Heriveus arranged twenty-four chapters in a volume. They were rationally and usefully composed and set out how those who were inexperienced in the faith ought to be treated. He entrusted all of this to the venerable Witto of Rouen.

Witto received the assignment and completed the undertaking usefully [Note: [Col. 0035] “most effectively and usefully,” in witness 1.].

## 34.

At this same time, Ragenerus—an illustrious and noble man of consular rank, surnamed Long-neck, whose death also brought great damage to the commonwealth in Belgica—was struck and overcome by an ordinary bodily illness and ended his life at the palace of Marsna [Note: [Col. 0035] The manuscript has “u. c.”].

King Charles is said to have attended his funeral and, with his eyes filled with tears, to have said:

“From lofty, lowly; from broad, exceedingly narrow!”

By the first phrase he indicated the man himself, and by the second his tomb.

After the funeral rites had been completed, he most generously conferred his father’s honor upon Gislebertus, his son, who had now become a young man, before the princes who had gathered.

[Note: [Col. 0035] Ekkehard of Aura excerpted chapters 34–40 in his *History of Henry*.]

## 35.

Although he was renowned for the most illustrious ancestry and was exceedingly fortunate in his marriage to Gerberga, daughter of Henry, duke of Saxony [Note: [Col. 0037] “marriage,” in witness 1.], he was carried headlong, through insolence, into excessive recklessness.

In military discipline he was too bold, to such a degree that he did not fear attempting whatever seemed unconquerable. He was of medium height and thickset, with hard bodily strength, an inflexible neck, and hostile, restless eyes—so mobile that no one fully knew their color. His feet were altogether impatient; his mind was fickle.

His speech consisted of ambiguous reasoning; his questions were deceptive; his answers uncertain. The parts of his discourse rarely cohered with one another clearly. He was exceedingly generous to his own people, but greedily coveted what belonged to others. In public he favored his superiors and equals, but secretly envied them. He took great pleasure in confusion in affairs and in setting disputing parties against one another.

## 36.

Such was the man who, with excessive fervor, turned against the king. He also gave much thought to rejecting the king and discussed the matter extensively with those who seemed most powerful in Belgica. He sought the kingdom not for Robert but for himself, distributing almost everything among the princes.

He generously endowed the great with estates and splendid houses, while effectively enticing men of moderate rank with talents of gold and silver. Thus many in Belgica reached an agreement with him.

But this was done very imprudently and inconsiderately. For although he attracted those whom he had won over through great benefits, he did not bind them to himself by an oath for the perpetration of the crime. Accordingly, those who had been lightly attracted were afterward just as lightly separated from him.

## 37.

When Charles heard this and returned from Celtic Gaul with an army, preparing to wage war against the Belgians, the Belgians did not venture to resist openly alongside Gislebertus. Instead, they shut themselves up in towns and fortified settlements [Note: [Col. 0037] “fortifications,” in witness 1.].

The king sent envoys to each of those who had defected from him. Through them he announced that he would bestow upon them by a royal and solemn grant whatever estates and houses Gislebertus had given them. He also declared that he would fight against Gislebertus on their behalf if Gislebertus wished to reclaim anything from the benefits he had conferred.

Captured by this offer, they soon returned to the king under oath. After the accounts had been settled, whatever benefits Gislebertus had granted them were most firmly confirmed and granted to each one by royal generosity. Thus, withdrawing from Gislebertus, they were steadfastly reunited with the king and marched with him against Gislebertus.

## 38.

Gislebertus was enclosed with a few men in the town of Harbure [Note: [Col. 0037D] This is today the village of Geul at the place indicated, on the right bank of the Meuse, where the Geul—called Gulia in the *Acta Sanctorum*, I, 603—flows into it, below Utrecht.].

The town was protected on one side by the Meuse and on the other by the river Geul; at the front it was defended by a monstrous ravine and by a great mass of terrifying thorn bushes.

The king hurried there with his army and established a siege, with ships on both sides and cavalry in front. While he persisted in the assault, Gislebertus escaped by ship [Note: [Col. 0037] Gislebertus slipped secretly over the wall, swam across the river, and, crossing the Rhine with two retainers to live in exile, remained for several years in exile with his father-in-law Henry, deprived of his patrimony. The townsmen, left without their leader, submitted to the king.].

The townsmen, having been captured, fell under the king’s command. Gislebertus, however, deprived of his paternal inheritance, crossed the Rhine with two little retainers to live in exile. There, deceived by Henry his father-in-law, he remained in exile for several years.

After several years had passed, Henry earnestly persuaded the king that Gislebertus should be recalled and restored to the king’s favor. This was done on the following condition: the king’s judgment concerning the benefits that had been granted would remain inviolable, while Gislebertus would receive through royal clemency only those benefits whose possessors had already died during the many years of his exile.

## 39.

Thus recalled from exile, he obtained the king’s favor through Henry, but—as stated—on the condition that he remain without the benefits he had insolently distributed for as long as their possessors lived. Those whose possessors had died during the intervening years he might reclaim through the king’s mercy.

He therefore received those properties that had been left vacant by their deceased holders, including the greater part of his possessions: Utrecht, Juppila, Herstal, Marsna, Litta [Note: [Col. 0038D] Compare the donation of Queen Gerberga for Saint Remigius of Reims, 12 February 968, in Bouquet IX, 666.], and Mont Caprémont.

Once he had recovered these, King Charles returned to Celtic Gaul, preparing to lead forces against the Northmen who were harassing the outermost regions of Gaul along the maritime districts.

When Henry had crossed the Rhine to campaign against the Sarmatians, Gislebertus, through his men, savagely harassed and crushed those who held the property granted to them by the king [Col. 0038C]. Killing some by clandestine attacks and continually pressing others to abandon what was theirs, he finally overcame them and took possession of all his former property. From then on he plotted against the king with still greater ferocity.

He therefore approached his father-in-law and tried to dissuade him from supporting the king, asserting that Celtic Gaul alone could suffice for the king, while Belgica and Germany greatly needed another king. By many arguments he urged Henry not to refuse to have himself crowned king.

But when Henry perceived that Gislebertus was proposing something wicked, he strongly resisted the persuader’s words and, with many emphatic arguments, pressed him to desist from his unlawful designs.

40. And when Gislebertus achieved nothing with his father-in-law, so that [Note: [Col. 0037] *u, sib, p*, conjecturally supplied] he might prepare a kingdom for himself [Note: [Col. 0037] *u, sib, p*, conjecturally supplied] [Note: [Col. 0037] *u, sib, p*, conjecturally supplied], he withdrew into Celtic Gaul and crossed into Neustria. There he consulted Duke Robert about the same enterprise, urging him to accept the kingdom and reject Charles. The tyrant rejoiced and immediately favored the tyrant’s cause. Thus they both deliberated and, after the deed was to be carried out, confirmed their fidelity by oath [Note: [Col. 0037] *ex*, reading 1] [Note: [Col. 0037] “by oaths,” reading 1].

[Col. 0038D] [Note: [Col. 0037] c. “And after [Col. 0039] this Gislebertus returned to Belgica, filling the strongholds with troops sufficient for military purposes and arranging everything against the king. Wherever ruins provided access, he rebuilt them with stronger defenses. Thinking that the soldiers might defect from him unless he bound them to himself by oath, he obtained from all of them an oath of loyalty and also hostages, whom he wished to take; he shut them up in the stronghold of Harburg, which seemed almost impregnable, openly arranging everything against the king. The king, moved by these actions, destroyed [the passage].” [Deleted by the author.] “Nor did he obtain [deleted: ‘from his father-in-law’] less than this: whatever he himself plotted against the king would not be counted as an injury to his father-in-law, especially because, being severely pressed by the attacks of the Sarmatians, he could not usefully attend to other affairs. Thus moved by these events, the king in Celtic Gaul attacked Belgica. But Gislebertus, since he had broken faith, not only disdained to come to the king, but by promises of money and possessions drew away from the king as many men as he could. The king, knowing that these matters had to be endured patiently for a time, remained quietly at Tongeren with those who had come with him from Celtic Gaul, asserting that whatever is endured through patience becomes less severe. He also recognized that he was exposed to the hatred of his enemies, since Robert pressed him on one side in Celtic Gaul and Gislebertus on the other in Belgica. Robert, for his part, labored so earnestly for the king’s rejection and his own advancement, and prevailed so far with the leading men, that almost all of them conspired with him most cruelly against the king. [The passage concerning the date has been deleted.]]

[Col. 0039A] 41. At the appointed time, when the king had returned to Tongeren and was living there as a private person, Robert entered the city of Soissons. The leading men from all Celtic Gaul gathered around him and held a most determined council concerning how they might reject the king. Gislebertus too was present from Belgica, and immediately, without deliberation, began loudly insisting that Robert should be made king.

Accordingly, by the common decision of all who were present, Robert was elected (29 June); and, raised up by great ambition, he was led to Reims and made king in the basilica of Saint Remigius. Three days after his coronation, Heriveus, metropolitan of Reims, worn down by a prolonged illness, died (2 June). If he had been well at that time, an opportunity for so great a crime would not have arisen. He was immediately succeeded by Seulfus, bestowed by Robert [Note: [Col. 0039] “by the king,” reading 1], who at that time held the office of archdeacon of that city [Note: [Col. 0039B] “was holding,” conjecturally supplied]; a vigorous man [Note: [Col. 0039] “liberal and vigorous,” reading 1], distinguished by extensive knowledge of affairs.

42. (923.) In the meantime, Charles discovered that he had been deserted by the Gauls, apart from a very few Belgians [Note: [Col. 0039] “When the power to rule and the freedom to possess had been entirely seized by the tyrant, scarcely any hope had even been left to him,” reading 1]. Among the chief men who had not defected from him, he complained at length of his misfortune. He said that, if he were oppressed by this calamity, he would be more wretched than if he closed his eyes in final death, since in the former case the pains would increase, whereas in the latter they would be removed [Note: [Col. 0039] “they would be removed. The leading men of Belgica,” reading 1]. He said that it would be preferable for him to be killed by the sword than to be deprived of the kingdom by an usurper. For after the loss of the kingdom, all that would remain would be deportation into exile. Even there, he remembered, he ought to receive support from those whom he had always held in the greatest affection, among whom he had lived for so long, and against whom he had never devised any harm.

43. His men replied: “It is disastrous, they say, for those who have sworn allegiance to the lord to defect from him, but it is most criminal to stand against the lord. If we are speaking of deserters and fugitives, and if the meaning of these names is considered, whatever they have attempted is contrary to right and justice. Therefore, without doubt, if the necessity of battle drives them to it, they will not escape divine vengeance.

“But know this with complete certainty: the kingdom cannot be recovered by you unless you attack the tyrant in war. You will not break into the kingdom that has been snatched away unless you violently open a path with the sword. And since circumstances now advise battle, an oath must be given, so that, once we have sworn to you, the matter may not remain uncertain. Then at least fifty men must be chosen who will attack the tyrant with certainty and inflict force upon him, so that, when the violence of war has driven some against others, these men may devote themselves solely to the tyrant and strike down the one they find. For what good will it do if everyone is killed and the cause of the evils is left alive?”

By common decree they therefore conspired against Robert.

44. Soon, by royal command, all those in Belgica who appeared not to have defected from the king were summoned. The number of those gathered, as is reported, was scarcely reckoned at ten thousand [Note: [Col. 0039] “five,” corrected to “six,” then corrected to “ten” in the codex]. Nevertheless, insofar as could be observed, no one unfit for military service [Note: [Col. 0039] “for battle,” reading 1] was admitted. All were strong in body and not sluggish in combat. All were also united against the tyrant.

With these men surrounding him, the king advanced against the enemy through Condroz and Hasbaye. Breaking into the kingdom that had been taken from him, he entered Attigny, formerly his royal seat. There, after restoring his army for a while, he advanced against his opponent [Note: [Col. 0039] “Crossing the river Aisne, he proceeded toward Soissons. For the tyrant had gathered his army there,” passage later deleted].

45. When he had drawn nearer to the tyrant, he arranged his army for battle and sent six thousand strong men ahead. He appointed as their commander a man of consular rank named Fulbert (15 June) [Note: [Col. 0039] “u. c.,” as in the codex] [Note: [Col. 0039D] “That is, a count; see below, chapter 46.”]. He himself, surrounded by four thousand men [Note: [Col. 0039] “two thousand,” reading 1], assigned himself to support the first troops if they began to give way. After moving through the individual legions, exhorting the leading men at length and with great force to undertake the violence of war [Note: [Col. 0039] “those distinguished in military service and glory of reputation, and by the nobility and usefulness of their fathers’ sons, he exhorted them greatly and for a long time,” reading 1], and encouraging the ordered ranks with many appeals, he led them to the place where the battle was to take place.

Crossing the river Aisne, he proceeded toward the city of Soissons. The tyrant had gathered his forces there. His army numbered twenty thousand men. Since King Charles was conducting the war with prudence, however, the bishops and other religious men who attended him persuaded matters so that the king himself would not enter the battle, lest, in the confusion of events, the royal line should be destroyed if he fell. The commanders and soldiers also compelled him to do this.

Thus, compelled by everyone, he placed in command of the four thousand men who surrounded him [Note: [Col. 0039] “two thousand,” reading 1] and whom he had inflamed [Col. 0041A] a man of consular rank named Hagrald [Note: [Col. 0041] “u. c.,” as in the codex]. He strongly urged them to implore only God’s help, reminding them that they had nothing to fear and nothing by which to lose confidence in victory. He asserted that the usurper of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0041] “the tyrant,” reading 1] would scarcely last a single moment:

“Since God abhors such a man, and there is no place with him for anyone who is proud, how will one stand whom God does not protect? How will one rise whom God casts down [Note: [Col. 0041] “whom he does not raise up,” reading 1]?”

After this, he climbed with the bishops and religious men who were present to a mountain situated opposite the place, where a basilica dedicated to the blessed virgin Genevieve also stood, intending to observe the outcome of the battle from there.

Meanwhile, the army advanced together, and the high-spirited army hastened toward the enemy. The tyrant also advanced, not inferior in courage [Col. 0041B], but superior in numbers of legions.

46. The battle between Charles and Robert, and the latter’s flight.—When both sides had seen each other at close quarters, the two armies rushed together amid the greatest shouting, their standards hostile. In the engagement countless men fell on both sides.

King Robert, since he was unknown in the fighting and was raging across the entire field, striking in every direction, was seen by the conspirators, who asked whether he was Robert himself. Fearlessly, he immediately uncovered his veiled beard [Note: [Col. 0041] “he drew it out from his cuirass,” reading 1] and showed that he was indeed Robert [Note: [Col. 0041] “he showed,” reading 1], brandishing his sword with great force against Count Fulbert.

Fulbert received a mortal blow [Note: [Col. 0041] “intercepting the blow with his shield,” reading 1] and swerved aside to his right. Through the sleeve of Robert’s cuirass, he then wounded him in the side with a most grievous thrust of his lance, driving the weapon through his liver, lung, and the hypochondrium of his left side, all the way into his shield [Col. 0041C]. Robert was surrounded by the others and, pierced by seven lances [Note: [Col. 0041] “The conspirators rushed in from all sides, and Robert was surrounded by them,” reading 1], fell headlong and stiffened. Fulbert, meanwhile, soon exhausted from loss of blood and still fighting, fell dead.

After Robert had been killed, both armies raged with such violence of slaughter that, according to Flodoard the priest, eleven thousand men on Robert’s side and seven thousand one hundred and eighteen on Charles’s side are said to have died by the sword [Note: [Col. 0041] “This did not happen either in the Annals or in the History of Reims.”].

Victory now seemed to belong to Charles, since those who had belonged to the tyrant were fleeing after his death. But then Hugh, Robert’s son, scarcely yet of age to grow a beard, was led into the battle by Heribert and came to the aid of the falling troops. Although he arrived with forces, because he regarded everyone with suspicion after losing his father [Note: [Col. 0041] “king,” reading 1] and trusted no commander, he refrained from the violence of battle [Col. 0041D].

The only memorable thing reported of him is that, without resistance, he occupied the site of the battle and stood there for some time, as though he intended to plunder the enemy’s spoils. Hence he seemed to himself to be victorious [Note: [Col. 0041] “they seemed to themselves to be victorious,” as in the codex]. Charles, however, thought that he had gained the victory because the tyrant had been killed.

Therefore the victory was uncertain: the Gauls [Note: [Col. 0041] “the Gauls,” reading 1]—the deserters—had lost the king who had been killed, while Charles had obtained none of the spoils. Neither of them succeeded in plundering the other’s spoils [Note: [Col. 0041] The repeated sequence “m, uis, it, o, arolo, sset, men, idi” is supplied conjecturally throughout this sentence]. Although the opportunity for this had not been lacking for Charles, he nevertheless, led by no desire for gain, completely avoided the matter [Note: [Col. 0041] “m, uis, it, o, arolo, sset, men, idi,” conjecturally supplied]. For, placing little trust in the deserters [Note: [Col. 0041] “the Gauls,” reading 1], since he had lost the greater part of his army, he immediately turned back toward Belgica without spoils [Note: [Col. 0041] “Germany,” reading 1], intending to return later to Gaul more fiercely [Note: [Col. 0041] “return to Gaul later,” reading 1] (922).

At this time an earthquake occurred in the district of Cambrai, by which several houses were overturned. From this the calamity of affairs could also be perceived: the prince of the kingdom had been seized contrary to right and thrust into prison until the final day of his life. For while he was arranging military affairs and preparing to bring a larger army into Gaul [Col. 0042B], and the Gauls were being greatly frightened by it, they were carried along in a milder mood. Understanding this, King Charles tried through envoys to recall them and sought to persuade them by many arguments. He also persuaded the Northmen so effectively that they were willing to pledge their loyalty to the king and serve him wherever he commanded. But when they were preparing to come to the king to serve him, they were prevented by Gauls who intervened. Thus the king was deprived of their assistance.

47. The advancement of King Rudolf and the capture of Charles.— [Note: [Col. 0041] *i, otio, i*, conjecturally supplied] The Gauls, not ceasing in their obstinacy, summoned Rudolf, son of Richard of Burgundy, and made him their king at Soissons, although he protested vigorously (13 July). He was an energetic man and not moderately accomplished in the liberal arts.

Heribert, the instigator of such great evils, pretended that he wished to conceal his intentions; he summoned King Charles through envoys, sending word that he had wished to resist such great crimes but had been completely suppressed by the multitude of the conspirators. At that time, he said, there had been no opportunity for counsel, but now he had found the best part of a remedy. Charles should therefore come more quickly, so that Heribert might meet him; he should come with only a few men, however, lest, if they arrived with many, the hostility of the opposing parties should compel them to battle. For the security of the journey, if Charles wished, he could receive from the envoys themselves an oath of good faith.

The king, believing these promises, received an oath from the envoys as a guarantee of fidelity and did not delay in going to meet the traitor, without consulting his own men. The traitor too, concealing his deceit, came to meet him with an equally small company.

After they had been received with kisses, they engaged in friendly conversation. While they were speaking, Heribert brought out a band of armed men from hiding and led them against the unsuspecting king. Since Charles could not resist the multitude, he was captured by the band; some of his companions were captured with him, others were killed, and the rest were put to flight.

He was taken to Péronne and assigned to prison custody. The Germans [Note: [Col. 0043D] That is, the Belgians], deprived of their king, were driven in different directions. Some of them labored for the return of their lord; others, cast down from hope, favored King Rudolf, though they did not wholly submit to his allegiance.

The former group, waiting for their lord’s freedom with prolonged expectation, frequently confronted the traitor Heribert concerning his violation of faith and complained bitterly about it to those who were ill-disposed toward him. Unable to persuade them, they inflicted no shame on them concerning the charge of perjury, even though God’s wrath threatened them.

48. (934.) The levy of public money to be given to the pirates.— [Note: [Col. 0043] *E, c. c*, conjecturally supplied] While these things were taking place, pirates [Note: [Col. 0043] “Northmen,” reading 1] invaded Gaul, devastating the land by driving away flocks and herds, exhausting many resources, and taking very many captives. The king, grieving over their attack, followed the advice of his men and ordered the collectors to levy a contribution of money, to be handed over to the enemies as part of a peace agreement. After the money had been collected, they made a treaty according to the common wish and withdrew to their own territory. The king, though distressed, turned his attention to other matters.

He therefore prepared an army against William, ruler of Aquitaine, because William disdained to submit to him. At the appropriate time he appeared with his army on the Loire. William, unable to endure the multitude of soldiers, went to meet the advancing force through envoys [Note: [Col. 0043] “but deceitfully,” reading 1]. Since the river flowed between them, the entire day was spent in the envoys’ negotiations. At last, on the following day, they mutually pledged their faith and departed from one another.

[Col. 0043C] 49. (925.) King Rudolf’s engagement with the pirates and their defeat.— [Note: [Col. 0043] *Co, R, r, f*, conjecturally supplied] The king returned from there but was seized by an acute fever at the city of Sens. When he had recovered on the critical day, he was again overcome by a relapse of the illness. Losing hope of recovery, he had himself carried to Reims, to Saint Remigius. After bestowing many gifts upon the saint, he recovered satisfactorily after a month and went to Soissons to attend to other matters.

While he was consulting with the leading men there about public affairs, envoys arrived and asserted that the pirates [Note: [Col. 0043] “Northmen,” reading 1], having broken faith, had invaded the interior regions of Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0043] “Gaul,” reading 1]. They said that, after engaging Count Manasses and Count Warner, together with the bishops Jozselm and Ansegisus, the pirates had been so thoroughly defeated that 960 of them had been cut down near Mount Calaus, while some had been captured and held; the remaining smaller force had escaped by flight. Warner, however, had been killed after the horse on which he was riding was slain, having been pierced by ten wounds.

Moved by this report, the king spent the entire next day deliberating about the matter. On the third day, by royal edict, he gathered recruits from central Gaul within fifteen days. Having collected them, he led them, together with several magnates, against the enemy across the river Seine.

The pirates [Note: [Col. 0043] “Northmen,” reading 1], advancing in order to resist, were forced by the Gauls to return to their camp. The Gauls pursued them as they fled and set fire to the camp. Engaging with great force, they struck down the defeated enemy. Some escaped by flight on foot, others by sea in ships; some were burned with the camp, and some three thousand were killed by the sword.

Those whom flight had driven away later gathered in one of their own towns situated beside the sea. Its name was Angae.

[Note: [Col. 0043D–0044D] “The reader will observe that the foregoing differs greatly from Flodoard’s account, and that what is narrated here does not correspond to it.”]

50. The death of the pirate Rollo and the destruction of his men.—Their leader Rollo filled the town with sufficient forces and openly prepared for war. The king departed from there and led his army against the challenger, without delaying to engage him. He attacked the town. After arranging the siege, he broke through the rampart that surrounded it [Note: [Col. 0044D] Flodoard shows that this means the wall]. Thus the recruits, climbing the perimeter wall [Note: [Col. 0044D] “the wall,” as Flodoard demonstrates], overran the enemy. After gaining possession of the town [Note: [Col. 0043] “They gouge out Rollo’s eyes”; these words have now been crossed out and deleted], they slaughtered all the males. They spared the women unharmed.

They demolished and burned the town. As the air grew dense and black from the fires, some of those escaping in the dreadful darkness seized a neighboring island [Note: [Col. 0043] The word is repeated on folio 13]. The army attacked them without delay and, after defeating them in a naval battle, crushed them. The pirates, losing hope of life, threw themselves into the waves and were drowned; others, swimming away, were slaughtered by the lookouts; others, overcome by excessive fear, attacked themselves with their own swords.

Thus, after all had been destroyed and considerable booty seized, the king returned to Beauvais and remained there.

51. (926.) Another defeat of the pirates.— [Note: [Col. 0043] *ira, inte*, conjecturally supplied] After hearing that another group of pirates was ravaging the region of Arras, the king took an army from among the inhabitants of the coastal areas and suddenly advanced against them. The pirates, unable to engage at close quarters, were forced to retreat before the army. Hemmed in, they attempted to preserve their lives in a certain woodland. But the army surrounded them on every side and pressed them hard.

They made a sortie by night and rushed into the king’s camp. The army surrounded them completely, and they succumbed to a miserable fate. Eight thousand of them are reported to have been killed there [Note: [Col. 0044D] Flodoard gives “one thousand one hundred”]. In the tumult the king was wounded between the shoulders [Note: [Col. 0043] “The king was wounded from behind,” reading 1], while Hildegaud, a count of very distinguished birth, was killed; several others also died, though they were not distinguished by any name. The king, having won the victory, returned to Laon.

52. (927.) An eclipse of the moon.— [Note: [Col. 0043] *de, io*, conjecturally supplied] At that time, too, the moon, on the fourteenth day, was darkened by the interposition of the earth and disappeared from the sight of those observing it. Fiery battle-lines were also seen in the sky at Reims. These signs, portending the future, were followed immediately by an illness of fevers and coughs. Some, grievously afflicted, died.

Along with these events, considerable agitation and conflict in lawsuits followed and was stirred up between the king and Heribert, who was holding Charles in custody [Note: [Col. 0045] “A considerable dispute arose,” reading 1], because Heribert demanded too much from the king, while the king granted nothing to him as one insatiable.

53. Charles freed by Heribert.— [Note: [Col. 0045] *rolus, eratur ab, berto*, conjecturally supplied] Heribert, therefore, making threats against the king, led King Charles out of prison and brought him into the district of Vermandois—not to restore him faithfully to the kingdom, but to inspire some fear in those who were under suspicion by displaying his release.

After summoning the Northmen and gathering them at the town of Eu, he brought Charles with him [Note: [Col. 0045] “Charles,” reading 1]. There the son of the pirate Rollo, whose death has already been reported, committed himself to the king’s service, pledged his loyalty, and confirmed it by oath.

[Col. 0045B] 54. (928.) The pope’s judgment against Rudolf, requested by Heribert and rejected.— [Note: [Col. 0045] *nten, papae in, dulfum, Heriberto reje*, conjecturally supplied] After this Heribert, jealous of King Rudolf, plotted against him intensely. Thus, coming to Reims with Charles, he sent envoys to Rome on Charles’s behalf and sent a letter to Pope John. In it he stated that he had neither conspired against Charles nor been aware of the conspiracy, but had yielded unwillingly to the conspirators. He therefore claimed that he very much desired Charles to be restored to the kingdom, since he had been rejected innocently and without cause.

Nor, he said, was he alone of this opinion, but many of the best men as well [Note: [Col. 0045] “some,” reading 1], except those who had been corrupted by numerous gifts [Note: [Col. 0045] “st,” as in the codex]. Therefore the pope himself should, by apostolic authority, order the rejected king to be restored to the kingdom; whoever attempted to resist his command should be condemned by anathema to everlasting curse. For this purpose he should also send a letter to the bishops and princes of Gaul and Germany containing the blessing of the good and the curse of those who opposed him.

The envoys hurried to Rome to carry out the mission [Note: [Col. 0045] “mission,” deleted]. But after exhausting themselves in the journey, they accomplished none of their instructions. For the pope had been captured by the prefect, because he was strongly opposed to him, and was being held by him in prison custody. Thus the envoys departed without achieving the purpose of their embassy and returned to Gaul.

Heribert, meanwhile, turning to other matters, was deeply concerned to establish mutual loyalty with Hugh [Note: [Col. 0045] “Hugh,” as in the codex], Robert’s son. He attracted him effectively by his persuasions and bound him to himself by a sworn agreement. Persuaded by Hugh’s influence, he returned to Rudolf and, reconciled with him, remained for some time. Received into Rudolf’s great favor, Heribert, in order to demonstrate that he was carrying out his obligations of loyalty, immediately thrust Charles back into prison at Péronne.

55. Heribert received the bishopric of Reims from the king.— [Note: [Col. 0045] *Her, a r, mense acc*, conjecturally supplied] Accordingly, requesting a gift from the king, Heribert received the bishopric of Reims from him under the pretext of his son, who was still a child. For at that time Seulfus, the metropolitan of blessed memory, had also departed this life [Note: [Col. 0045] “pious,” reading 1; “divine,” reading 2]. But because the boy’s tender age prevented him from performing sacred duties, Heribert permitted a certain Odelricus, expelled from the bishopric of Aachen by the persecution of the pirates, to minister in his place [Col. 0046A]. He also assigned him the abbey of Saint Timothy the Martyr for his own use and, in addition, supplied him with the provision of the canons.

Meanwhile King Rudolf, wishing to demonstrate how great was the justice of his conduct, went to Charles where he was being held. He complained at length before him about his misfortunes and humbly asked forgiveness in an extended speech if he had offended him. Since he could not entirely surrender the height of the rule he had undertaken, he restored to Charles what reason allowed him to restore—namely, the royal seats of Attigny and Ponthion—and then returned to Soissons.

56. The death of Charles.—After these events, Charles, overcome by weariness and anguish, fell into a prolonged illness [*macronosiam*]. Afflicted by harmful humors, he died after a prolonged illness (7 October 929).

King Rudolf, meanwhile, learning through envoys that pirates had invaded Aquitanian Gaul and were ravaging it with hostile violence, considered bringing force against them.

57. The battle between the king and the pirates, and their defeat.— [Note: [Col. 0045] *R, pyra, flic, que f*, conjecturally supplied] By royal edict, therefore, all those capable of military service were summoned from Celtic Gaul. Together with many Belgians, the king organized twelve cohorts. Setting out with them, he advanced as far as Limoges.

There, after arranging his legions, the pirates, unable to withstand the royal cavalry and attempting to escape by flight, were driven back by the Aquitanian legion. The king pursued them with his cohorts and inflicted a grave slaughter, routing almost all of them; only a few escaped by flight. Some of his own men were wounded but recovered from their injuries [Col. 0046C]; some were also killed.

As a result, the Aquitanians gave thanks to the king, wished to submit to him with great goodwill, and entered into the firmest allegiance by oath. After these matters had been successfully accomplished, the king led his army home and dismissed it from active service.

58. The disagreement between Heribert and Hugh.— [Note: [Col. 0045] “Heribert and,” conjecturally supplied] While these events were taking place, disputes arose between Hugh [Note: [Col. 0045] “Hugh,” as in the codex] and Heribert concerning the dignity of precedence. Enraged, they inflicted serious harm upon one another through plunder and fires.

The king, indignant at Heribert because he recognized him as ready for treachery, supported Hugh’s party [Note: [Col. 0045] The sequence “Hugonis, pa, stab, un, He” is conjecturally supplied]. Accordingly, after summoning Hugh, he attacked and stormed Heribert’s town called Donincum [Note: [Col. 0045] “fort,” reading 1], captured it, and destroyed it. He also captured Arras after laying siege to it [Col. 0046D], and, having defeated the citizens, bound them to himself by oath.

The king then departed (931), thinking that he was at peace. Heribert, however, led out the Germans who inhabit the banks of the Rhine and advanced against the king, carrying out fires and plundering with execrable fury. In addition, he occupied, captured, and destroyed Hugh’s town situated beside the stream called the Vitula, known as Braina.

59. Heribert’s preparation against the king.— [Note: [Col. 0045] *Heriberti praepa, contra*, conjecturally supplied] Understanding that he had made himself the cause of this affront, the king sought to reduce Heribert’s power. He therefore sent envoys to the citizens of Reims and ordered them to choose a bishop. If they failed to do so, he declared that he would impose someone upon them against their will.

The citizens received the royal envoys’ command and replied through their own envoys with what they wished and believed: namely, that by royal order they had accepted Heribert’s son, although he was still a child, and had elected him bishop; they had also already pledged their loyalty to him. It was therefore impossible for them, without violating their faith, to defect from him in this way.

When the king understood that the citizens favored Heribert’s party, he gathered an army and suddenly attacked the city. Prevented from entering, he began a siege and fiercely pressed the townspeople who resisted. Worn down by repeated assaults, they finally, in the third week, opened the gates, defeated and supplicating.

60. The persuasive speech of King Rudolf to the citizens of Reims on his own behalf.— [Note: [Col. 0047] *d, ses, ria*, conjecturally supplied] The king entered the city and, after making certain arrangements, consulted with his men and summoned the citizens [Note: [Col. 0047] “called them forth,” reading 1]. He addressed them publicly as follows:

“Surely, as I think, you know very well how much slaughter and how much plunder the commonwealth has recently suffered from the faction of evil men [Note: [Col. 0047] “the commonwealth,” as in the codex]. It could not happen that, while so many evils raged everywhere, you would be left entirely untouched and unharmed. For, since your necessities have often been plundered and often burned, you have endured their calamity.

“And not only public goods outside, but also private goods here within, are being diminished every day by the most savage exactor, Heribert. Therefore I think you must take counsel for yourselves and, by common agreement, choose a suitable shepherd, since the tyrant’s son, still a mere infant, is not fit for you, and canonical authority does not permit a church to remain without a shepherd for so long.

“Nothing dishonorable will accrue to you from this, since, having been defeated and captured by military force, another necessity drives you to follow this course. I confess that you have not gone astray in this affair as much as I have. Therefore I regret what I have done. Let it also grieve you that you have brought loss upon your own affairs. Recall to mind how great a calamity has afflicted you. Consider also how greatly you might advance through the success of prosperous circumstances if you were governed by a good shepherd.”

61. The election of Artoldus.— [Note: [Col. 0047] *i*, abbreviated] Persuaded by the king, the citizens yielded to the royal commands. Accordingly, at the king’s order, the monk Artoldus was immediately taken from the monastery of Saint Remigius with the consent of all [Col. 0047D]. At the appointed time, by the laying on of the bishops’ hands and through royal gift, he was consecrated bishop. Acting prudently and energetically in all things, he benefited his people greatly and, because of his good deeds, enjoyed the goodwill of everyone, especially his own people.

62. The capture of Bovo, bishop of Châlons, and of the fortress of Laon.— [Note: [Col. 0047] *Bo, uni, Lau, castri*, conjecturally supplied] While these events were taking place, Bovo, bishop of Châlons, was accidentally captured while traveling by royal attendants and, because he too had defected from the king as a deserter, was brought before the king. Convicted before him when those aware of his deed gave evidence against him [Note: [Col. 0047] “reasonably convicted,” reading 1], he was committed to prison.

After this had been done, and without ceasing to work for Heribert’s destruction, the king, having summoned Hugh, approached Laon with eight thousand men. While Heribert was being hard pressed there by a lengthy siege, he asked the king for permission to leave, because he did not have sufficient troops or provisions. Having obtained this permission from the king, he left the city with his men, leaving his wife in the fortress he had built and believing that he would soon return with forces to support her.

The king entered the empty city and, recognizing the deceit completely, subjected the fortress to a prolonged assault. He surrounded it on every side and blocked every avenue of exit, engaging the defenders in continuous battle. But after such a struggle, the strength of those resisting proved unequal to the task. They laid down their arms, surrendered, and begged for their lives.

The tyrant’s wife, likewise defeated, came with her attendants to the king to plead for herself. She surrendered the fortress and asked only for permission to depart. The king, disdaining to retain a woman, permitted her to leave with her attendants. He then gained possession of the fortress and the city.

63. (932.) The killing of Count Adelelm, deceived by a certain cleric seeking the bishopric of Noyon.— [Note: Col. 0047: conjectural restoration from the fragments “ctio, comi, cleri, vio, peten, to.”]

After he had organized what was necessary for defending the city [Note: “When the king was arranging what was necessary for defending the city, and was making other arrangements with Hugh concerning the disgrace of the aforesaid tyrant, and was deliberating about the bishopric,” etc.], he was also deliberating to whom the bishopric of Noyon should be given, since Bishop Ayrard had by then died. For Walbert, abbot of Corbie, was being sought as his successor—a vigorous and generous man, who greatly delighted in every form of honorable conduct.

Nor was a certain cleric of the aforesaid city any less eager to be made his successor by the king. He was a barbarous man, excessive in hand and boldness, and accustomed to take pleasure in stealing what belonged to others. Rejected by the king and the citizens, he turned his heart to schemes. He therefore sought to deceive Adelelm, count of Arras, whose misfortune has implanted remembrance in many, humbly begging his assistance and promising his own [Note: “and also promising him his own support” 1.], while completely concealing from him that he had been despised by the king:

“If,” he said, “through your agency I obtain the dignity of the bishopric, through me you will effectively obtain the honor of the countship. This too will be possible if you climb the city walls at night and, while I arrange matters within, bring in your men. I shall also be present with many others. Once gathered into a column, we shall overrun the city. Thus it will come about that we either capture the citizens or drive them out.”

Believing these words, Adelelm favored the adviser’s proposal. Preparing, therefore, to attempt the crime, he approached the city by night with immense forces. The cleric, suspecting no evil from anyone in the city, was awaiting the place where the deed was to be carried out. When Adelelm approached, he and his men were received by the cleric. Packed together, they threw the city into tumult in the darkness of night with trumpets, shouting, and the clamor of weapons. The citizens, awakened by this, realized that they had been overcome by treachery and escaped from the enemy by flight. No one was captured, because the enemies, having joined together in one body, were afraid to scatter through the city. Thus an avenue of escape lay open to everyone.

The citizens who had fled obtained weapons and other assistance from neighboring places, and on the fifth day they boldly advanced upon the city. The suburban inhabitants also came successfully to their aid. They therefore engaged in battle with the greatest readiness. Adelelm and the cleric, together with their men, resisted with the utmost ferocity. But the common people who had remained in the city, and who had sworn fidelity to them, broke their oath and violently struck them from behind. Caught in the midst of the enemy, they were forced to flee into a church. The townsmen, admitted from within, did not cease pursuing Adelelm and the cleric. Having cut through the church doors, they attacked the enemy and cruelly slaughtered both men, together with many others, beside the altar. Taking possession of the city, they recovered what was theirs.

When this had been done, and the church had been cleansed by the lawful purification, Walbert of Corbie, monk and abbot, appointed by the king, was consecrated bishop of Noyon by Artold, metropolitan of the Noyonese.

64. The princes of Aquitaine and Gascony meet King Robert in order to serve in his army.— [Note: Col. 0049: conjectural restoration from the fragments “Aquitaniae, co, pe, m, oc.”]

Meanwhile the Gothic princes Ragenmund and Ermingaud came to meet the king, who was approaching beyond the Loire, in order to serve him in war, and placed their hands in his. They promised military service and thereafter granted their allegiance as the king commanded. The king then departed and made his way into the outer regions of Aquitaine. There too Lupus Acinarius, a Gascon who was said to possess a horse more than one hundred years old and still exceptionally strong in every part of its body, came to meet the king in order to serve him. After he had surrendered the administration of the province, the king generously restored it to him and granted him the right to rule under his authority.

65. (934.) A series of evil portents.— [Note: Col. 0049: “lo” cut off.]

At this time fiery battle-lines were seen in the sky at Reims, and blood-red flames, like javelins or serpents, ran about. Soon a plague also followed [Note: “It followed afterward” 1.], killing countless people with erysipelatous pustules. Not long afterward the king’s decline also followed. For when, in the autumn season, melancholy abounded among sufferers, he was afflicted throughout the autumn by cachexia—that is, what the Latins call “a bad condition of the body.” Overcome by an excess of humor, he declined and departed from human life (936, January 14 [Note: Compare the Annals of Saint Columba, SS. I, 105.]). He was buried in the basilica of Saint Columba the virgin at Sens, amid the extensive mourning of his friends and the attendance of his household. He made no arrangements concerning the administration of the kingdom; rather, he left it to the leading men, since he had no sons who might possess the affairs of the kingdoms.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0049]

## 1. The Gauls deliberate about creating a king.— [Note: Col. 0049: conjectural restoration from the fragments “orum, rat, ge, do.”]

After his funeral, the princes were being drawn in different directions and were seeking divergent outcomes. The Gauls—for the Celts together with the Aquitanians—were following Hugh, son of King Robert, while the Belgians were following Louis, son of Charles. Neither of them had the advantage needed for ruling: Hugh remembered that his father had perished because of his arrogance and therefore feared to reign; Louis was living in the regions of England, since, as a child, he had been taken there to his uncle, King Athelstan, because of the persecution by Hugh and Heribert, who had themselves seized his father and thrust him into prison. The Gauls, striving to appear freer in advancing a king, assembled under Hugh as their leader to deliberate about creating one.

## 2. Duke Hugh’s speech to the Gauls on behalf of Louis.— [Note: Col. 0049: conjectural restoration from the fragments “Hu, cis, os, ovico.”]

Their leader, standing among them, after extensive consultation turned his mind toward great goodwill and began to speak as follows:

“Since King Charles has died by a pitiable fortune—whether he deserved this, or whether the Divinity, angered by our crimes, inflicted it for anything committed by our fathers or by ourselves by which the majesty of the Divinity was offended—we must first of all, with great exertion, abolish and remove from sight whatever this may have been. Let the attempts at discord therefore be absent, and let us deliberate with the common agreement of all concerning the prince to be preferred.

“My father, once created king by the will of all of you, did not reign without a great crime, since the man to whom alone the rights of ruling were owed was alive, yet was confined alive in prison. Believe that this was not acceptable to God. Therefore let it be far from me that I should be restored in my father’s place.

“Nor do I think that anyone of another lineage should be advanced after the divinely remembered Rodulf [Note: “The codex has ‘of divine memory’; chapter 3 shows that ‘my lord’ should not be read.], since in his time it became apparent what might now arise: contempt for the king, and consequently dissension among the princes.

“Let the line of royal succession, interrupted for a short time, therefore be resumed; and let us recall Louis, son of Charles, from across the sea and properly create him king for you. Thus the ancient nobility of the royal stock will be preserved, and the supporters [Note: “many” 1.] will cease their complaints. Since this is the preferable course, let us follow it and recall the young man from the maritime shores [Note: That is, from the coasts].”

At these words the princes of Gaul yielded with remarkable goodwill [Note: “And they loudly proclaimed that Louis should be summoned” deleted.]. The duke therefore sent envoys and spokesmen across the sea to summon Louis. They were to urge him, on behalf of the duke of Gaul and the other princes, to return; to guarantee the safety of the journey by the force of an oath; and to announce the arrival of the princes as far as the very sands of the shore. They soon departed and reached Morini [Note: Boulogne 1.] [Note: Boulogne.]. Entering ships in its harbor, they were swiftly carried to land by favorable winds filling their sails.

King Athelstan was in the city called York [Note: “Everwich, Eboracum, York; the archbishop of Canterbury was made [archbishop]”], arranging the affairs of the kingdoms among his people with his nephew Louis. When the envoys arrived there, they approached the king and were courteously greeted by the duke and the magnates of Gaul.

## 3. The embassy of the Gauls to King Athelstan on behalf of Louis.— [Note: Col. 0051: conjectural restoration from the fragments “io, rum, anum, douico.”]

They also announced their embassy:

“By the goodwill of the duke and of all who are most eminent in Gaul,” they said, “we have come here across the waves of an unknown sea; such is the will and agreement of everyone. When the divinely remembered Rodulf had been taken from the world [Note: “D. M.” in the codex.], the duke arranged for Louis to succeed, although many granted this unwillingly because they regarded the son as so suspect on account of the capture of his father. Nevertheless, through the duke’s efforts, this was granted by everyone with the greatest pleasure.

“Accordingly, everyone wishes Louis every good in every respect. Nothing is greater or dearer to them than his safety. They all therefore ask that he be restored—the man whom they wish to reign usefully in Gaul. They wish a date to be fixed on which the duke, together with the princes, may meet the future king at the very shores of the sea.”

King Athelstan, as though he did not sufficiently trust foreigners [Note: That is, strangers or outsiders.], sought from them an oath concerning this matter and received it according to their wish. A time for holding the conference was also fixed.

The envoys, rewarded by the king, departed and returned to Gaul across the sea. They conveyed the king’s thanks to the duke and promised him his great friendship in return for his advocacy of creating a king.

The duke therefore came with the princes of Gaul to receive their lord king at Boulogne. Gathered beside the very sands of the shore, they displayed their presence to those who were on the opposite shore by the burning of huts [Note: “Also to those same men” 1.]. For King Athelstan was there with the royal cavalry, intending to send his nephew to the Gauls who were awaiting him. At his command several houses were set on fire to show those across the water that he had arrived [Note: “Some houses were also set alight” 1.].

## 4. Hugh and the other princes of Gaul recall Louis from exile, become his men, and create him king.— [Note: Col. 0051: conjectural restoration from the fragments “Hu, Gal, L, ab e, ca, eumque.”]

The king therefore sent Bishop Odo [Note: “The envoy Odo, abbot” 1.], later metropolitan of Canterbury [Note: Anno 933.], to the Gauls stationed opposite. He was a man of great fairness and eloquence. The king instructed him to announce that he would gladly send Louis if they advanced him in Gaul to as great an honor as he had been advanced to by his own people, since they too were no less able to do this; and that they should confirm by oath that they would do so.

“If they do not wish this,” he said, “I shall give him one of my kingdoms, so that, content with it, he may rejoice in what is his and not covet what belongs to others.”

The duke, together with the other magnates of Gaul, asserted that he would do this, provided that, once created king, Louis did not withdraw from their counsels. He did not refuse to complete the sworn obligation.

The envoy returned and reported all this to the king, who was awaiting him. The king, now secure, sent his nephew with those who were most eminent among his people, with great display, aboard ships. Entering the open sea with their sails swelling in a favorable breeze, they were carried to land over calm waters, their oars foaming.

After the ships had been secured on the shore, Louis disembarked. He received the duke and the others who had come to meet him and bound them to himself by the law of the oath.

The duke then hastened forward and brought out a horse adorned with royal insignia. When he tried to make it suitable for mounting, and the horse, impatient, reared in different directions, Louis sprang lightly forward and suddenly mounted the snorting horse without using the stirrup. This pleased everyone and provoked many congratulations.

The duke took up his arms and went before him as his arm-bearer until, being ordered to do so [Note: “He gave them to Count Heribert; he too served as arm-bearer until he himself was ordered to return them to Count Arnulf. Thus also to the magnates” 1.], he handed them over to the magnates of Gaul.

With these men serving him, Louis was escorted to Laon with great ceremony and devotion. There, receiving the rights of kingship at the age of fifteen, he was created king with everyone’s approval by the lord metropolitan Artold, together with twenty bishops (June 19). From there he was escorted onward and was received with joy in the neighboring cities. Everyone applauded him; everyone rejoiced. There was one and the same mind among them all.

## 5. The king goes with the duke to Burgundy and recaptures and takes the city of Langres by war.— [Note: Col. 0051: conjectural restoration from the fragments “Re, B, pe, Li, repet, ca.”]

The duke also urged the king to visit Burgundy and inspect its cities and royal seats. The king agreed to his advice and entered Burgundy accompanied by the duke. The princes of the cities came together to meet him in a friendly manner and received him magnificently. When asked, they gave their allegiance by oath.

Only Hugh, brother of King Rodulf, who possessed the city of Langres, delayed meeting the king, being exceedingly angry with those who did come to meet him [Note: That is, Hugh was angry with those who came to meet the king.]. While the king inspected his possessions for several weeks, he perceived the hostility of his enemy.

Planning, therefore, not to pass by any city before his departure, he sent envoys to Hugh to recall him from his obstinacy and persuade him to preserve faith with him. The envoys pleaded with him but obtained nothing of peace and nothing of royal honor. They therefore departed and reported what they had heard to the king [Col. 0052D].

Hugh, recognizing that he had acted against justice, assigned troops to the city and withdrew himself into the outer regions of the kingdom for a time. The king, angered by his obstinacy, brought his army against the city and launched a fierce attack from the side where it presented a plain. On the other side, where the flank of the mountain rose, it was almost inaccessible.

The king therefore, together with the duke, brought soldiers against the city at the point most suitable for a siege. While they attacked, the enemy resisted most fiercely, filling the air with missiles and stones and wearing down the attackers. They could not, however, persist to the point of driving them back. Unable to endure the assault of the royal cavalry, they left by night through the precipitous side, which was not pressed by the siege, and fled.

The citizens who remained soon opened the gates to the king, joyfully receiving him and his men into the city without opposition. Having gained possession of it, the king received hostages from its bishop and the other nobles of the kingdom, and thus turned back with the duke toward Paris.

## 6. (937.) The king removes the administration from the duke.— [Note: Col. 0053: conjectural restoration from the fragments “is, ra, m, it.”]

The king, elated by the success of favorable events, considered that his affairs could be arranged without the duke’s administration. Accordingly, he was already arranging the conduct of military affairs without him. He proceeded to Laon and there appointed his mother, Queen Eadgifu, to guard the city. From then on he undertook whatever actions he wished without the duke. This also became the seed of no small disgrace [Note: “It became a great source of disgrace” 1.].

For when the duke perceived that the king had rejected the arrangement of his administration, he took Count Heribert as his ally and carried out many measures with him against the king’s dignity. They mutually confirmed their friendship by agreements on both sides.

## 7. Heribert takes the castle called Theoderic’s by treachery and throws the traitor into chains.—

Heribert therefore approached by deceit Walon, the king’s faithful man, who was in charge of the castle called Theoderic’s. He spoke to him about desertion. Without delaying long, he persuaded the deceived man [Note: “The faint-hearted man” 1.], making greater promises and offering more.

Walon immediately demanded an oath concerning the promises and pledged that he would do what was asked of him. The tyrant willingly agreed. The deserter, likewise sworn, indicated the time for carrying out the crime. Indeed, he then committed himself to serve under the tyrant’s authority and pledged his loyalty in exchange for military service. This completed, they departed to their own places.

The appointed time arrived. Walon, under pretense of business, sent the royal soldiers who were stationed with him off in different directions, as though they were going to act on the king’s behalf. After emptying the castle, he remained alone there with his servants.

Nor was the tyrant absent with his troop. Received by the deserter, he entered and occupied the castle. Looking at the deserter, he said: “Do you think that this stronghold should be entrusted to your care?” He immediately had him seized and thrown into chains, and entrusted the guarding of the castle to his own men.

On the night that followed the day, a part of the sky was seen to burn in the north, with flames breaking forth prodigiously.
