Soon afterward the sudden invasion of the Hungarians through Gaul followed this portent. Raging excessively [Note: “Also because of the disagreement of the princes” 1.], they devastated several towns, villages, and fields; they also burned many churches; and, because of the princes’ dissension, they were allowed to return unharmed with a great multitude of captives.

For the king, lacking troops, endured the disgrace and, abandoned by his own men, yielded to the ravagers.

## 8. (938.) The king captures the town of Montigny through a troop and seizes its ruler.— [Note: Col. 0053: “at, em” cut off.]

After they had departed, the king sent a troop to the town of Montigny to occupy it and, once captured, destroy it, because a certain Serlus, practicing brigandage, had established himself there as a refuge.

The troop therefore attacked the town and its brigands. Without delay, it took the place by force, burned it, and demolished it. After capturing the brigand leader, it brought him to the king, while releasing the lesser men. When, by royal command, he was handed over to the executioner to be beheaded, he obtained the king’s pardon through the intervention of Artold, metropolitan of Reims. After swearing that he would no longer practice brigandage, he was permitted to depart.

When these events had taken place, the king withdrew into the parts of Belgica adjoining the sea, attempting to build a town at the very harbor of the sea. The place was also given the name Guiso. Received by Arnulf, the prince of that region, he discussed with him the construction of the town.

While he was delaying in the negotiations, Heribert entered by treachery and captured the castle of the church of Reims called Causostem, situated beside the River Marne and built by Bishop Artold. Attacking the men of the castle, he led away their leading men. He devastated the surrounding countryside, filled the town with immense spoils, stationed soldiers there with their weapons, and withdrew elsewhere himself.

## 9. The king captures the fortress at Laon.—

Meanwhile these matters were reported to the king by the metropolitan through envoys. The king immediately interrupted the enterprise he had begun and returned to assist him. He gathered soldiers and prepared an army.

Coming with it to Laon, he besieged the fortress that Heribert had recently built there and that his men still held. Those inside the fortress, however, prepared themselves for rebellion. The king therefore stationed archers all around and pressed them with missiles in order to overcome them. In the ensuing tumult many on both sides were wounded, since those in the fortress also used arrows and other missiles.

Since the king had not yet brought the assault to an end by force, he began to consider how to capture them by ingenuity.

## 10. Construction of a siege machine.— [Note: Col. 0053: “co” cut off.]

He therefore built, from extremely strong timbers fastened together, a machine shaped like a long-sided house. It could hold twelve men and was as high as a man’s stature. Its walls were constructed from massive, sturdy timber, while its roof was made from hard interwoven hurdles.

Inside it he also fitted four wheels, so that the machine could be pushed by those hiding within it as far as the fortress. The roof, however, was not level, but sloped down from its peak to the right and left, so that stones thrown at it would slide off more easily.

Once constructed, it was immediately filled with recruits and pushed on its movable wheels toward the fortress. When the enemy tried to crush it from the heights above, they were shamefully driven back by the archers stationed all around.

After the machine had been brought up to the fortress, part of the wall was undermined and overturned. Fearing that a multitude of armed men might be brought in through this breach, the enemy laid down their arms and implored the king’s mercy. The king therefore forbade further tumult and captured them almost unharmed, except for those who had been wounded in the military fighting. He stationed his own men in the fortress to protect the city.

## 11. (939.) Arnulf’s deception and the capture of the town of Monstreuil.— [Note: Col. 0055: “a, M, i” cut off.]

While these things were being done, the aforementioned Arnulf, prince of the Morini, was planning to add to his own side the town of Erluin, situated beside the sea and called Monstreuil [Note: Montreuil.], because considerable profits arose there from the transport of ships. He therefore devised a stratagem for acquiring it.

He sent some clever men of his, dressed in shabby clothing and concealing their deceit, to a certain guardian of the same town, whom he did not doubt would be particularly easy to win over to treachery. They entered, greeted him on behalf of their lord, and asked for an opportunity to speak with him. They withdrew.

Pretending that the matter for which they had come was so important that they did not at all know how to begin, they hesitated for a while. At last, sighing, they said:

“Ah, Robert, Robert!”—for that was his name—“from how many evils you have escaped, from how many dangers you have been rescued, and how many successes in prosperous affairs are owed to you!”

Immediately they produced two rings, one gold and the other iron.

“And see,” they said, “what may be understood from these.”

Since he did not know what they meant, they continued:

“In the gold, imagine splendid gifts; in the iron, the chains of imprisonment. For the time is approaching when this town too will pass into another’s jurisdiction. We entrust these matters, which must be kept secret, to your loyalty. Arrangements have been made without your knowledge. We ourselves are completely ignorant of the details. Yet we do not deny that we know the substance of the matter. We speak of death or exile.

“Thus Count Arnulf, advising you, has signified through his messengers the calamity of the disaster that is to come. He urges you to cross over to him and receive from him insignia of gold and silver, an abundance of land, and a multitude of soldiers, together with the king’s gift.

“By some means unknown to us, you are soon to fall into the hands of the Northmen. Do not delay to answer through us, your friends, what you have decided concerning these things.”

Led by greed, he hesitated over the treachery [Note: “He promises and, having sworn, gives his pledge of loyalty” 1.]. He stood there stunned. At last he proposed to himself that the disgrace of treachery could be excused by necessity, since he had learned that all the townspeople would soon either go into exile or die.

He therefore promised the treachery and, having sworn, gave his pledge. They too swore concerning the promises they had made. A time for the crime was set and confirmed by oath. The envoys departed and reported that they had persuaded him.

## 12. Arnulf’s entry into Monstreuil.— [Note: Col. 0055: “sus, na” cut off.]

Arnulf therefore gathered a force of chosen soldiers in order to carry out the planned crime. Taking the road with two cohorts, he came almost as far as the town [Note: “As far as” 1.]. The sun had already set.

The traitor had sent some men out through the gate, as though they were going to attend to some useful task. He himself, standing on the wall, held out a blazing torch, as though he were going to provide light for the servants he had sent out. By this sign of the light he had also indicated the entrance to the envoys.

Arnulf rushed up with his cavalry and entered the town through the open gate. Having taken possession of it, he captured Erluin’s wife and children and plundered his treasures. Erluin, however, changing his clothing, slipped away through the midst of the enemy.

After Arnulf had overrun everything, he stationed his own men in the town. He transported Erluin’s wife and children across the sea to King Athelstan of the English for safekeeping. Thus, having fortified the town with his own men, he returned to his own territory.

## 13. Erluin’s complaint to Duke William about the loss of his castle, wife, and children.— [Note: Col. 0055: “st, ini, il, ux, na, ssi” cut off.]

Erluin, scarcely freed from the danger of death, withdrew to William, prince of the Northmen, and made the greatest complaint to him about his misfortunes. He said that he was the most unfortunate of men: deprived of his town and soldiers, bereft of his wife and children, he possessed nothing except his body.

He said that he was not so deeply distressed by the loss of the town, since there was some hope of recovering it, because land is immovable and the town could not be taken away. But the loss of his wife and children seemed to portend an unending calamity. If they had been killed, he would be tormented by continual grief; if they were not killed but held under another’s rule, he himself would be deceived by an empty hope.

For this reason, he said, he had come to seek consolation, and, groaning, he repeatedly begged for it.

## 14. Erluin assaults and captures the town.—

The prince, moved by these complaints, granted his assistance and entrusted him with a force of soldiers. Erluin therefore hurried to the town and attacked it at the opportune time with his forces, surrounding it on land and sea. He pressed forward and attacked it fiercely.

At last, after it had been worn down by many assaults, he entered and overran the whole place. He captured all Arnulf’s soldiers. Some of them he killed with the sword; others he preserved in order to recover his wife and children.

## 15. Erluin’s engagement with Arnulf’s soldiers.— [Note: Col. 0055: “sus, um” cut off.]

Arnulf, crushed by such a calamity among his men, gathered soldiers and sent them against Erluin to devastate his territory as far as the town. Once dispatched, they raged everywhere with fires and plundering. After carrying away a great quantity of booty, they were hurrying away when envoys from Erluin arrived and announced that, unless they immediately returned all the booty, they would immediately have to fight him.

The enemy rejected the embassy and hastened to carry away what they had captured. The envoys returned and reported that they had been dismissed with contempt.

Erluin soon advanced with four hundred armed men and overtook them as they hurried away. They abandoned the booty, turned, and faced the attackers. Once the standards had been joined, they fought fiercely.

Almost all the raiders fell by the sword, except those whom flight rescued from the violence of battle. Yet even these, as flight drove them on, were brutally cut down by Erluin, who pursued them from behind. Erluin recovered the booty and returned successfully to his own territory with immense spoils taken from the enemy.

## 16. The complaint of the Belgians to the king about his rashness.— [Note: Col. 0057: “B, que, le” cut off.]

At that time the princes of Belgica came to the king and complained most seriously to him at Laon because he undertook everything without consultation. They declared that, if he also accepted their counsels, his affairs would reach a good outcome. They said that they had come for this purpose as well: so that he might impose upon them whatever he wished and assign to them whatever he desired.

“If you wish,” they said, “we shall engage the enemy by counsel and arms, on land and sea.”

The king accepted their pledge of loyalty and, with great goodwill, permitted them to return, ordering them to come back whenever fortune should require it.

Not long afterward a fleet was also sent to the king with forces by Athelstan, king of the English. He had heard that the king was being harassed by those who inhabited the maritime regions. The fleet was to fight against them and bring assistance to the king, his nephew.

When it was discovered that none of them was standing against the king and that the king himself had withdrawn successfully into the regions of Germany, the fleet crossed the sea again and returned home.

## 17. The king allies the Belgians to himself and drives the supporters of Otto beyond the Rhine.— [Note: Col. 0057: conjectural restoration from the fragments “Re, ca, at, fau, Rhe.”]

The king, having spoken in the district of Elsass with Hugh, the Cisalpine prince, was bringing over to his side the outer Belgians who had not yet come to him. He forced those who favored Otto’s party to flee beyond the Rhine.

For he had foreseen that Otto wished to transfer Belgica into his own jurisdiction. He therefore did not regard him with equanimity. Acting more harshly against him, he expelled from the kingdom those who appeared to belong to him in outer Belgica [Note: “All those who appeared to belong to him from outer Belgica” 1.].

He accepted those who agreed with him—namely Gislebert, duke of the Belgians, and also the counts Theoderic and Isaac—and conferred with them. He obtained an oath from them in order to secure their loyalty, and afterward returned to Laon.

There he expelled from the city Rodulf, bishop of the same city, who had been most clearly accused of treachery. He also expelled his supporters at the same time and transferred their possessions to his own men.

[Note: “For the king, in the first place. What follows Ekkehard has freely adapted for his own use; in the codex it is written in a continuous hand, and was not disturbed by correction as was a large part of the first book.”]

## 18. Otto devastates Belgica.— [Note: Col. 0057: “cum” supplied conjecturally.]

Meanwhile Otto, learning that the Belgians were supporting the king’s party and had completely deserted him, crossed the Rhine and entered Belgica [Note: “He entered with an army” Ekkehard.]. He devastated many of its places with fires and immense plunder [Note: “For he was striving, as though by hereditary right, to become prince of Belgica. He alleged that this was contrary to justice, since his father had been appointed duke only of Saxony, which is part of Germany, because of the attacks of the Slavs” Ekkehard.].

He did this because, while the Belgians despised him, he claimed that he should become their prince by paternal grant [Note: “King” 1.], although his father had been created king of Saxony alone because of the violence of the Slavs, since Charles, to whom supreme authority was owed, was still rocking in his cradle [Note: “Then, as a child, he was crying in the cradle” Ekkehard.].

Taking away a great deal of booty, he crossed the Rhine.

## 19. Gislebert’s attack on Germany and the destruction of him and his men

[The heading’s readings “Im,” “be,” “m,” and “a” are supplied by conjecture.]

But Duke Gislebert, wishing to avenge the injury of his dishonor [Note: “hastening to go, he gathers an army and accelerates after the enemy, crossing the Rhine and laying that land waste as far as the sun reaches.” Ekk.], traversed all Belgium, gathered together the choicest recruits, and left only the experienced old men in their homeland. Having formed his army, he crossed the Rhine and laid waste his homeland as far as the sun reaches with immense fires. The army also gathered and carried away an enormous booty of cattle and livestock.

He was now preparing to enter the river, when Otto led in an army that was hastening [Note: “they were preparing, and behold, Otto, having gathered forces from all Saxony, arrived.” Ekk.]. The Belgians, resisting resolutely with their duke [Note: “Thus the Belgians, resisting without hesitation with their duke.” Ekk.], engaged the Germans beside the river [Note: “with hostile standards.” Ekk.], and there was a great slaughter on both sides [Note: “and many on both sides were cut down.” Ekk.]. On that day German victory was maintained only with difficulty, and although innumerable Germans lay slain [Note: “the words from ‘was maintained’ through ‘slain’ are absent in Ekk.”], it nevertheless prevailed.

For Duke Gislebert, realizing that his army had been weakened by the slaughter of his men [Note: “when two-thirds of them lay slaughtered, and Gislebert judged that his men had failed while the enemy remained unharmed, he fled amid such confusion of affairs.” Ekk.], tried to escape the danger by flight. He therefore leapt with his horse into the current. But when the horse could not swim across the deep river, overcome by the force of the waters it perished [Note: “died.” Variant 1], and plunged its rider beneath the water.

[Note: “But the Belgians, unaware of their duke’s death, fought with all their strength, and displayed such valor that, after the dreadful and innumerable death of their men, some of those who remained were captured and others drowned in the river. But King Louis …” Ekk.]

Of the Belgians, some were killed in the river, some cut down by the sword, some captured, and some escaped by flight [Note: “were rescued.” Variant 1]. King Louis, learning that Gislebert had perished, felt great compassion at his death. Then he went into Belgium, married Gislebert’s wife Gerberga, Otto’s sister, and had her crowned with him as queen in his kingdom.

## 20. (940.) Duke William of the pirates swears allegiance to the king against all men

[The readings “mus,” “ta,” “ntra,” and “jurat” are supplied by conjecture.]

While these events were taking place at Laon, William, duke of the pirates [Note: “that is, of the Rouen Normans”], sent envoys to the king, who declared that he was entirely faithful to him: wherever the king should order him, he would come to meet him and would promise fidelity against all men.

The king received their embassy with great goodwill and arranged that they should meet him in the county of Amiens, because certain matters of particular importance had to be settled there through them [Note: “which had to be settled.” Variant c]. After taking the envoys with him, the king arrived at the appointed place at the appointed time. The aforesaid duke also came to meet him. Received honorably by the king, he received from him the province that his father, King Charles, had formerly granted him. Thus, having become the king’s man, he was bound to him by such complete agreement that he was already proposing either to die for the king or to restore to him the whole power of the realm.

## 21. Archbishop Artoldus storms and captures Causost

When this business had been successfully completed, the king withdrew into Burgundy. During his absence, the metropolitan Artoldus, lest he should seem helpless in his own affairs, attacked the stronghold of Causost without royal forces and surrounded it on every side with a siege. Harassing it with continual assault [Note: “storming it.” Variant 1], he finally entered and captured it on the fifth day. He also seized those who had slipped away from him. But, being a good man and no enemy of anyone’s life, he allowed them to depart unharmed. He also demolished the town to its foundations and so returned to his own lands.

## 22. Heribert and Hugh besiege and capture Reims and expel the bishop

Heribert, finding an opportunity for wrongdoing [Note: “an opportunity for misfortune.” Variant 1], as though grieving that his own stronghold had been destroyed, pressed Hugh the duke most insistently concerning how he might attack Reims and expel the bishop. Hugh, himself a tyrant consenting to a tyrant, immediately promised to help him.

Thus, having gathered their forces, the two rushed against the city and surrounded it with a substantial siege. The townsmen, favoring Heribert because by royal command they had previously chosen his son in place of Artoldus, yielded to the attack, abandoned the bishop, and, to increase the measure of their punishment, crossed over as deserters to the tyrants.

When the gates were opened on the sixth day of the siege, they admitted the tyrants into the city. Expelled, Artoldus went to the monastery of Saint Remigius, where he poured out before God, who sees all things, his complaint about what had happened to him. There he was soon surrounded by some bishops and certain nobles, who urged him to be content with the abbey of Avenay and the possessions of Saint Basolus and to renounce the dignity of the episcopate. Subjected to many terrifying threats, he consented, though, as is reported, he repudiated the oath [Note: “he repudiated it.” Codex]. And at last, satisfying the hounds, he departed for Saint Basolus, where he was to remain.

## 23. In the king’s absence Hugh and Heribert attack Laon

After Hugh the deacon, son of the tyrant, had been left at Reims—he had also long before been summoned to the episcopate of that city—Heribert and Hugh themselves attacked Laon with their forces, laying siege to it on every side. They thought the city empty of soldiers because the king was attending to other matters in the outer regions of Burgundy. Attacking wherever they could, they tried to enter. But, unable to match the height of the hill above, they were forced to withdraw more than once. Nevertheless, they continued their efforts and tried to prevent the king from entering.

## 24. The king arrives and the siege is lifted

[The heading’s readings “R,” “ni,” and “s” are cut off.]

They had now been attacking for seven weeks when the king, summoned by news of this affair, arrived in good time in the district of Reims in Champagne. Although he had only a few men, he nevertheless crossed the river Aisne and advanced against the enemy. When the tyrants—Heribert and Hugh [Variant 1]—learned this, and considered both the king’s courage and his justice, they withdrew from the siege.

The king entered, provided his men with the necessary supplies, and arranged everything beneficially. Then, intending to settle other matters, he returned to Burgundy. During his departure, Guy, bishop of Soissons, persuaded by the deserters—for he too secretly supported their party—came to Reims and ordained Hugh, Heribert’s son, as a priest. His father, wishing to raise him to the priestly dignity and have Artoldus legally deprived of the episcopate, pursued the matter insistently. He discussed the case with Duke Hugh and strongly requested that it be carried into effect.

## 25. (941.) Artoldus is rejected by the bishops of his province and Hugh is elected in his place

[The readings “A,” “c,” “e,” and “et” are supplied by conjecture.]

When the substance of the case had been arranged, they summoned the bishops of the diocese of Reims to settle the dispute between Artoldus and Hugh and to bring the charges to an end.

They assembled near the city of Soissons, in the basilica of the holy martyrs Crispinus and Crispinianus. There they heard the complaint of the citizens of Reims, who said that they had long been deprived of a shepherd and humbly requested that someone be given to whom they might be subject and obedient. They said that they no longer wished to have Artoldus because he had rejected the episcopate by oath, but that they desired Hugh because he had been elected by the united consent of all and was acceptable to everyone.

The bishops agreed with their complaints and declared Hugh worthy of the priesthood, since not only the nobility of his flesh but also the highly chaste character of his mind commended him. They also judged that it would be fitting if the summit of so great an honor were adorned by the nobility of his person.

Thus, with the agreement of almost everyone, they raised Hugh up and brought him to Reims. In the monastery of the monks of Saint Remigius they solemnly consecrated him metropolitan; then, having received him honorably in the city, they honored him with great service and reverence.

While the king was in Burgundy, learning from travelers what had been done, he immediately returned to Laon. He also expelled Arnold and his brother Landricus, who had been accused of treason but not entirely convicted, because they appeared particularly eager in this matter.

## 26. The king gathers an army in Burgundy against the tyrants

Since the king, lacking military resources, could do nothing against the tyrants, he returned to Burgundy in order to obtain an army there and lead it into Reims. He was attempting this especially so that he might drive Heribert from the city he had occupied.

While he delayed in gathering soldiers, the tyrants—Hugh and Heribert [Variant 1]—approached and surrounded Laon with a large cavalry force, relying on the hope that certain people would betray it.

While this was happening, the news promptly reached the king. Taking with him as many men as he was able to gather from every quarter [Note: “he was able to gather.” Codex], he arrived in the county of Porcien. There, while he was organizing his forces and preparing to make war on the enemy, the tyrants abandoned their siege of Laon [Variant 1: “of Reims”] and marched against the king. Attacking his army unexpectedly, they struck down some and forced the rest to flee.

Led away by his men, the king barely escaped death with two companions, taking refuge in the stronghold called Altus Mons. The tyrants, disappointed in their hope of treachery, lifted the siege and withdrew to their own lands.

## 27. The tyrants are warned by the pope not to persecute their king

Meanwhile, the distinguished man named Damasus was sent into Gaul by Pope Lord Stephen [Note: “Stephen VIII”], carrying letters of the Apostolic See containing an apostolic command that the princes of the provinces [Note: “of the kingdoms.” Variant 1] should no longer delay receiving their king Louis and should not continue to pursue him with a hostile sword. If they did not cease, all of them were to be struck by the weapon of anathema.

When the bishops of the diocese of Reims learned this, they immediately assembled and earnestly discussed the anathema that would fall upon them unless they repented [Variant 1: “usefully”]. They decided to send someone to Heribert and humbly ask him to approach the duke and plead with him on behalf of receiving the king. They were to point out the danger of anathema and the great ruin awaiting those who did not fear to be despisers and persecutors of their lords [Variant 1: “who are afflicted with ruin”].

This persuasion produced no result [Variant 1: “since it had no result”].

The aforesaid pope soon sent another embassy through legates of the church of Reims. From that same pope they brought the metropolitan Hugh the priestly pallium, declaring that the sentence of the apostolic command was that the princes of Gaul should cease persecuting their king and, moreover, exalt him greatly. If they did not do so within the appointed day, the authors, accomplices, and supporters of this action were to be punished most severely by a horrible anathema. But if they willingly obeyed the apostolic command, they were to send legates to Rome to report their goodwill toward their king to the pope.

Even so, nothing was persuaded to the tyrants. Since they continually sought the king’s ruin, their whole enterprise turned out contrariwise.

## 28. Through Count Rotger, the king wins Duke William over to himself

Indeed, the king, following the advice of good men, sent the distinguished Rotger to speak on his behalf to William, prince of the pirates. Rotger performed his embassy for the king most successfully, but died there. Before his death, however, he persuaded the prince to the point of accomplishing the matter.

Not long afterward, William faithfully summoned the king through his own envoys. He received him at Rouen and loaded him most honorably with immense gifts [Variant 1: “most humanely”]. As a result, others, now fearful, came more promptly to the king.

Thus William, duke of Aquitaine, and Alan, duke of the Bretons, learning that the pirates were protecting the royal cause, hastened to come. They approached the king and, having agreed to the terms, swore military service to him.

After gathering these men, the king proceeded to the river Oise to confer with the aforesaid tyrants [Gloss: “Hugh and Heribert”]. The tyrants, fearing the royal cavalry, went ahead, destroyed the bridges, and carried the boats everywhere to the opposite bank. Thus they settled with their men on the far bank of the river.

With only two small boats moving back and forth, the dispute between them was conducted through intermediaries. At last, under a truce, they withdrew from one another under the security of hostages.

## 29. Kings Louis and Otto enter into friendship, and Hugh does so through Otto

After dismissing the princes in peace, the king turned back with a few men toward Belgium, going to speak with Otto, whose sister he had taken as his wife. After their agreement had been firmly established through much concord, they mutually arranged their friendship under specified conditions.

When the business was concluded, the king returned to Laon. Otto, however, was striving to restore Hugh to the king’s favor. Rebuking him familiarly and with mild anger, but with many verbal goads, because he opposed his king and did not fear to persecute his lord, Otto brought him back to the king. At the proper time, after sending forward embassies of prudent men, he restored the duke to the king and reconciled him to him.

## 30. The princes’ assembly before the king and William’s disturbance at their meeting

When the duke had been restored to his former favor, since he surpassed the others in power and resources, the remaining men were restored afterward. When all had returned to the king, the king announced that, after thirty days, the princes were to hold a conference with him at the royal estate of Attigny.

On the appointed day the king arrived there with the princes of the provinces: Hugh, surnamed the Great; Arnulf of the Morini; William, duke of the pirates; and the tyrant Heribert. King Otto of Saxony was also present.

When King Louis had withdrawn into a private chamber with King Otto [Variant 1: “with”] and the princes, whether by deliberation or by chance, Duke William alone was not admitted. Waiting outside for a long time, and not being summoned, he took the matter angrily.

At last, turning to anger, since he was excessive in strength and boldness, he forced the closed doors and pushed his way backward into the room [Variant 1: “fiery.”]. Once inside, he saw a bed with a seat [Variant 1: “spread with cushions and other necessities.”]. Otto was seated at the head, on the higher side, while the king sat at the lower and humbler end. In their presence Hugh and Arnulf were seated on two chairs, awaiting the order of the council.

William, unwilling to endure the king’s insult, said: “Was I not supposed to take part in these proceedings? Have I at some time been stained by the disgrace of a deserter?”

Then, approaching in anger, he said: “Rise for a little while, O king!” When the king immediately rose, William himself sat down. He said that it was unbecoming for the king to appear lower while someone else appeared higher. Therefore, Otto ought to be removed from that place and yield to the king.

Ashamed, Otto rose and yielded to the king. The king therefore sat higher, while William sat lower.

## 31. Otto conceals the insult under the pretext of maintaining loyalty, and his complaint

Otto entirely concealed the insult and, leaning on his staff, tried to bring the business that had begun to an end while standing. When the arguments had been settled, the king rose with his advisers and departed.

Otto, concealing William’s insult most vehemently [Variant 1: “goodwill”], discussed with him at length the constancy of the loyalty that they ought to maintain among themselves. Thus he covered the offense he had conceived beneath various verbal disguises.

When this had been done, the king returned to his own lands with William. Otto, however, consulting with Hugh and Arnulf, complained to them still more about the insult inflicted upon him. He recalled that he had been despised beyond what was fair and lawful and removed from his seat in the presence of his friends.

He said that friends ought to sympathize and that a friend ought to regard the injury done to him as his own. He maintained that such insolence ought to be repelled from them with the greatest force, since it could more easily reach them. For the man who had not spared his own king would spare them even less.

This speech produced great hatred and stirred his friends against William, since they themselves, although secretly, greatly envied him. King Otto returned to his own lands.

## 32. Hugh and Arnulf deliberate about William’s death

Hugh and Arnulf deliberated about what they should do with William. They said that, if they killed him with the sword, they would be freer to undertake everything. They would also more easily bend the king to whatever they wished if William alone perished, since, relying upon William, the king could not be bent to everything.

If, however, they did not kill him, disagreements and quarrels would undoubtedly arise, and, once an occasion had emerged from these, many would be slaughtered. Yet they judged both alternatives harmful, since murder would bring the guilt of homicide upon them, while sparing him would make future tyranny apparent.

At last, persuaded to kill him, they summoned the men who were to commit the crime, explained the character of the undertaking, and made them swear a conspiracy against William.

The plan for his murder was soon arranged among the conspirators as follows. Envoys were to be sent by Arnulf, who would perform a suitable embassy before William, requesting a conference to be held shortly on a matter of great necessity. They were to ask when he could meet them. They were to request a place beside the river Somme, so that he might deign to leave his own land and come to meet those who wished to confer with him.

When he arrived and had been received by his friends, they were to speak at length about friendship and also at length about loyalty. Since at that time he could not be attacked while surrounded by his men, the blows were to be postponed until he returned to his ship, if it happened that he had arrived by boat.

When he was already sailing across the open water, the conspirators were to call him back with a great shout, as though he were about to hear of some important matter that had been forgotten. Having come in a small boat with a few men, while the others waited out on the water, he was to be attacked unawares by the conspirators with drawn swords.

If he arrived on horseback, then, after the council had ended and Arnulf had departed, the conspirators were to call him back repeatedly, pretending that they had something important to report. They were to detain him by summoning him to various affairs until all the others had gone ahead and he was walking last at the rear. They were then to attack him and pierce him through with their swords.

They would escape the force of the pirates rising against them if, carried away on swift horses, they hastened promptly to flee to their lord, who would be waiting with his forces. At that point the pirates would do nothing except either hasten their flight or arrange their lord’s funeral. Thus it would appear that so great a crime had been committed without Arnulf’s knowledge, since he had been absent.

## 33. (943.) The murder of Duke William

The envoys were sent, requested the conference, and obtained it. The time was set for thirty days later. A place in the county of Amiens, beside the river Somme, where there is the island of Pinchinea, was granted.

When the business had been completed, the envoys returned. At the appointed time Arnulf came to the designated place by land and William by water. They spoke at length about friendship and still more about the loyalty that each ought to preserve toward the other. After some conversation, they separated.

Arnulf pretended to return and withdrew a short distance. William returned to his fleet. As he entered a small boat and sailed across the open water, the conspirators called to him with a great commotion [Variant 1: “shout”], and he turned the prow around. Rowing back to the shore to ask what they wanted, he returned.

They immediately declared that they were bringing him something extremely important which their lord had forgotten to mention. When the duke had brought his boat to shore, he received them; they immediately drew their swords [Variant 1: “drawn”] and killed him.

They also wounded the two young men who were with him unarmed and the sailor. The criminals leapt from the boat and hastened in flight to their complicit lord. Those who had already been sailing across the open water turned around, returned to the shore they had left, and found their lord dead, together with the two young men and the wounded sailor. They took up their lord’s body and carried it away for burial with lamentable service.

## 34. The king grants William’s land to his son Richard

Not long afterward they also brought to the king his son Richard, born of a Breton concubine, and disclosed the course of the deed that had been carried out.

When the king observed the young man’s attractive appearance, he received him generously and bestowed upon him the province that his father had formerly possessed. The leading men who had come with the young man also became the king’s men through the giving of their hands and oath.

Delighted by the king’s great generosity, they departed for Rouen [Codex: “Rouen”]. Some of the other Normans, indignant that Richard had gone over to the king, went to Duke Hugh.

## 35. The king is summoned by his men to Rouen and fights the pirates

Those who supported the king’s cause summoned him through envoys and received him honorably at Rouen.

There he was informed that Sétric, king of the pirates, had entered the river Seine with a large fleet, and that his duke Thurmod had subsequently arrived with naval forces, intending to overrun everything without royal permission and persuade the dead duke’s son to adopt idolatry and introduce the pagan rite.

The king gathered forces with which to engage them. Trusting that he would win God’s favor, he went out against the foreigners with eight hundred men. Since he had only a few soldiers, he could not arrange his battle line in separate divisions so as to enclose the enemy.

Surrounded by his men, he advanced with standards raised and his forces drawn up in close order. The pagans also proceeded in infantry formation. As they approached, they threw their swords according to their ancestral custom in the first clash. Thinking that the density of the swords had frightened and wounded the cavalry, they followed with shields and weapons.

But the royal cavalry, protected by the barrier of their shields after the cloud of swords had passed, charged the infantry. In close formation [Variant 1: “in a compact mass”], cutting down and killing as they went, they penetrated the enemy line and emerged from it. Then, turning back, they penetrated and broke through it again.

When the violence of the battle forced Sétric, too, to flee, he was soon found in a thicket and pierced by three spears thrown by the pursuing soldiers.

While the battle was still being fought with all its force, Thurmod was thrown down by the chest of Louis’s charging horse. As the king passed him in his advance without recognizing him, Thurmod, attacked by the enemy and standing his ground in the place, engaged him at close quarters. Surrounded by his men, he attacked the king from behind, came up on his right side, and wounded him with a spear through the sleeve of his cuirass almost to the hypochondrium of his left side.

The king, driven back for a short time by the force of the blow and the great slaughter around him, looked at the man who had wounded him. Then, angling his blow toward the right, he cut off the head of his challenger together with his left shoulder.

The pagans were slaughtered in such great numbers that nine thousand of them were reported to have been killed there [Note: the manuscript first has “IIII,” then “V,” and in the margin, in the same hand, “VIIII”]. The rest, very few in number, escaped by fleeing to their ships.

The king obtained victory from God, although a few of his own men were killed and some were wounded. Intending to return after caring for them, he entrusted Rouen to Erluin and himself returned to Compiègne.

## 36. Archbishop Artoldus abandons the tyrants and goes over to the king

When Artoldus, who had been expelled from the city and was staying in the monastery of Saint Basolus the confessor, learned that the king had arrived, he immediately abandoned whatever the tyrant had left to him and went to the king. He preferred to remain with the king, content with little, rather than be detained by the benefits of an unsociable tyrant.

The king, grieving that the metropolitan by whom he himself had been consecrated king had been unjustly deposed, urged him not to lose confidence and promised that he would restore the supreme priesthood to him.

## 37. The death of Heribert

While matters stood thus, Heribert was considering every harmful plan and arranging many things concerning the calamity of certain people. As he sat among his men [Variant 1: *apud*, “among/at”] in a costly garment and addressed them with outstretched hand, he was struck by a severe apoplexy because of an excess of humors.

At the very moment when he was arranging affairs, his hands became rigid and his nerves contracted; his mouth was twisted toward his ear. In great horror and trembling, he expired unexpectedly before his men.

His men took him up and buried him at Saint-Quentin. After he had been buried, his sons immediately approached the king and were received kindly; he recalled none of their father’s injuries against them.

Bishop Hugh was also received, but on the condition that, at a suitable time, he should not delay giving an account in his own defense concerning his acquisition of the episcopate. The king also departed with them for Amiens. There, wishing to arrange certain important matters not without the leading men among his own people, he summoned Erluin, who was staying at Rouen, through an envoy.

## 38. The engagement between Arnulf and Erluin

When Arnulf learned this through the report of evil-minded men, he laid an ambush and, without the king’s knowledge, led a troop against Erluin as he approached.

Erluin soon perceived this and engaged him after the standards had been brought together. The battle was not slight on either side. Arnulf, with his men defeated, fled and barely escaped the man who was pressing him.

Erluin, having won the victory, killed some, captured others, and forced others to flee. In that same battle he captured the killer of William, who, together with Arnulf, had attacked him with force [Variant 1: “forces”]. Cutting off the man’s hand, he sent it to Rouen in vengeance for his friend. After recovering the spoils from the slain, he went to the king.

## 39. Hugh receives great favor from the king and becomes duke of all Gaul

At this time Duke Hugh was held in great favor by the king and received the king’s daughter from the sacred font as her godfather. Therefore the king appointed him duke of all Gaul [Variant 1: “the king of France appointed him duke”].

With this duke, the king prepared his cavalry and went with Queen Gerberga into Aquitaine (944). Arriving at the city of Nevers, he received there Duke Raimund of the Goths and the leading men of Aquitaine, who had come to meet him.

There he discussed the administration of the provinces, so that all their affairs might appear to be under his jurisdiction. He received the provinces from them but did not delay entrusting their administration back to them. Thus he committed them to their charge and established them as rulers by his gift, allowing them to return rejoicing in the king’s royal happiness.

Then, returning with the duke on his journey into Gaul, he withdrew to Laon.

## 40. At the king’s urging Arnulf and Erluin return to friendship

[The heading’s readings “asi” and “de” are cut off.]

There, gathering the leading men of his own people apart from the duke, he urged them to bring about the reconciliation of the illustrious men Arnulf and Erluin, so that they might forget the injuries that had been done and be united in goodwill. He judged that prosperity ought to attend his affairs through the concord of his men.

After summoning them, he urged them to restore their friendship, promising that he himself would act as judge between them and would do complete justice to both parties. They consented and obeyed the royal commands. After hostages had been given, they carried out the laws of equity.

Since the king favored both men, he intended to grant generosity to each of them. When he observed that Arnulf was hesitant about compensation for the things that had been taken from him, while Erluin more insistently sought the return of what he had lost, he judged that Arnulf ought to restore more because he himself had inflicted the greater loss upon Erluin. He therefore granted Amiens to Erluin, on Arnulf’s account, in compensation for his losses.

Thus it happened that Erluin’s possessions were restored and Arnulf’s were not diminished. Restored to friendship by the king’s effort, they thereafter attended to the king’s affairs.

## 41. A miraculous sign of the disaster of the Bretons

[The heading’s readings “de,” “ti,” and “ta” are cut off.]

At that time it was reported that a whirlwind had suddenly arisen at Paris and rushed about with such force that walls founded upon a great mass of stones were utterly overthrown on Montmartre.

Demons, seen in the form of horsemen, were also said to have overturned a certain basilica situated not far away and to have struck its beams against the aforesaid walls with such force that they brought them down. They also tore out the vineyards of that same mountain and devastated the crops.

Soon after the prodigy was seen, the destruction of the Bretons followed. Divided by the dissension of their princes Berengar and Alan, they were attacked by the Normans with whom they had made a pact and were worn down by great slaughter.

The city of Nantes was also captured [Note: “Flodoard reports that its bishop had been from Dol”]. When its bishop, terrified by fear of the approaching enemies, was forced to flee into the church, he was crushed and suffocated by the press of his own people.

In the very first assault the Bretons recovered their strength and drove the enemy back from the city with a mighty effort. Then they attacked them and routed them with heavy slaughter.

But the Bretons, encouraged by this more favorable turn of fortune, attacked the fleet on the third day and engaged it. Innumerable men were slain on both sides. The Bretons, unable to withstand the enemy’s forces, were put to flight.

The victorious Normans killed some of the Bretons with the sword, forced others into the waves, and expelled others from the borders of Brittany, except those who did not refuse to submit to the yoke of slavery.

## 42. The king invades and captures the land of the Normans

[The heading’s readings “R,” “N,” “r,” and “c” are cut off.]

When this news reached the king, he summoned Counts Arnulf and Erluin, together with several bishops of Burgundy. He had perceived that some of them had abandoned their loyalty and gone over to Hugh.

He marched against them with an army. Arnulf, preceding the king with his own men, successfully engaged and routed the Normans who were keeping watch at Arques [Note: “archas” corrected to “arcas,” i.e. Arques], and cleared the king’s advance.

When the king came to Rouen, those who had remained loyal received him. The deserters, however, took to the sea and withdrew. They left the fortified towns protected by troops.

The king, judging that the forces of the evil men were too numerous, requested through envoys that Duke Hugh provide reinforcements for the engagement. He offered him the city of Bayeux, so that, if he should conquer it with the rest [Note: “si” corrected from “ut”], he might do so.

The duke accepted the royal gift, prepared reinforcements, and came to the king’s aid. Traveling with his men and certain powerful Cisalpine men beyond the river Seine, he reached Bayeux and attacked it, pressing it with a long siege.

Meanwhile, persuaded by the king’s attendants, the Normans returned to the king. The duke, however, continued to press the men of Bayeux.

Through envoys the king ordered the duke to lift the siege [Variant 1: “to withdraw from the siege”]. But the duke, regarding it as something granted by the king, attacked all the more. The king sent word again that, unless he withdrew quickly, he would march against him with his forces.

Unable to oppose the royal commands, the duke was forced to withdraw from the siege. The king then entered the city. After calling its citizens back to him, he went to Évreux and entered it without resistance. Having also received hostages from the people of Évreux, he obtained the rest without opposition (945).

## 43. The duke urges his men against the king’s injury

[The heading’s readings “D,” “i,” and “i” are cut off.]

The duke, frequently recalling this injury among his men, plotted the king’s destruction, urging his faithful followers and friends to hasten to avenge it. He magnified the matter with many complaints and incited his men against the king.

Bernard of Senlis [Note: “that is, of Silvanectum”] and Theobald of Tours, satisfying the complainant, attacked the king’s stronghold of Montigny during the very days of Easter and captured and destroyed it.

They also suddenly entered the hall of the royal residence at Compiègne, seized and carried away all the royal insignia, and not long afterward the same Bernard captured the king’s huntsmen and dogs and carried them off, together with the horses and hunting spears.

## 44. The king presses the city of Reims with a siege

[The heading’s readings “bem,” “obsi,” and “it” are cut off.]

When the king at Rouen learned of these events, he gathered a large Norman army. Having assembled it, he returned, entered the county of Vermandois, and utterly ravaged it.

He also summoned Counts Arnulf, Erluin, the other Bernard, and Theoderic, and marched against the city of Reims. He surrounded it with a siege arranged on every side because Hugh, the bishop of that city, favored the duke’s party and refused the king entry.

The first assault was fiercely contested. Archers were stationed on both sides, and those who resisted on the wall were wounded by missiles. When they had been removed, others who were unharmed took their places and carried on the fighting in turn.

Men outside were also struck by weapons and stones that were thrown, and some of them yielded. The disturbances were repeatedly renewed: sometimes at the gates, sometimes at the wall, they engaged at close quarters.

Fierce in spirit on both sides, they were unwilling to yield in any way. They would never have ceased until mutual destruction, unless the siege had been lifted and they had withdrawn in response to the entreaties of those who intervened.

45. The Duke urges the king through envoys [Note: [Col. 0067] “egi, su, ab, ne” is cut off.], that he withdraw from the siege [Note: [Col. 0067] “egi, su, ab, ne” is cut off.].—For during the siege itself the Duke requested through envoys that Count Ragenaldus, having taken hostages from him, come to meet him for a discussion. The king granted that this should be done. Accordingly, under the protection of the hostages, Ragenaldus came to the Duke. After lengthy deliberation with him, the Duke finally arranged that the king, having received hostages from the bishop and the townspeople, should withdraw from the assault on the city, so that the same bishop might come to give an account whenever and wherever the king wished.

Ragenaldus conveyed the Duke’s intention to the king and approved the plan, urging that it be carried out. After suitable hostages had been taken, the king lifted the siege on the fifteenth day and fixed a time for hearing the account forty days later, on the very day of the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 0069] “ati” has been erased.]. Meanwhile other matters were attended to, and the day appointed for the conference arrived. The Duke came to meet the king in order to discuss the affair mentioned above. When their respective cases had been presented, they scarcely reached agreement. Since their arguments were not proceeding usefully, nothing favorable to peace was achieved, except that under a truce they postponed the hearing of the case until the middle of August.

46. The death of Theotilo, bishop of Tours [Note: [Col. 0069] “he, si” is cut off.].—At that time, while Theotilo, of blessed memory, bishop of the city of Tours, was striving most earnestly to restore peace between the princes, and was departing from Laon deeply occupied with these efforts, he was seized by pneumonia on the journey itself. When it had brought swelling and fever to his lungs, he departed this life on the fourth day after the illness began.

Although he breathed his last during the deep darkness of night, a globe of light, as is reported, soon appeared flashing through the air and was seen by those keeping watch. Those carrying his lifeless body used its light sufficiently to dispel the darkness of the night, and by the comfort of this light they carried the most blessed body for 150 miles [Col. 0069C]. Flodoardus writes approximately two hundred miles [Note: [Col. 0069D].]. They brought it to the city of Tours and laid it with great reverence in the basilica of Saint Julian the Martyr, which that holy man himself had built with the utmost devotion.

47. The capture of the king by the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0069] “re, rt” is cut off.].—After he had been buried, while no peace had yet been established between the king and the Duke, and the king had not yet perceived that the Duke was planning treachery, he returned to Rouen with Erluin and some others. He had no fear of remaining there with only a few men, since he was accustomed to do so.

A plot had been prepared at the Duke’s side by deserters, and had previously remained concealed; when an opportunity arose because of the small number of soldiers, it broke into the open. For when the king arrived at a suitable time, he was summoned by an embassy from Hagrold, who governed Bayeux. He went without suspicion to Bayeux, with only a few men, to the man who had summoned him, regarding him as loyal and never having suspected him in anything [Note: [Col. 0069] “habebat” in one witness.]. But the barbarian, observing the scarcity of soldiers, attacked the unsuspecting king with a multitude of armed men. Wounding some of his attendants and killing others, he forced the king to flee. He would indeed have captured him, had he not been delayed for a while by the king’s arms-bearer, who resisted and was immediately killed there.

By this delay the king was carried away by the speed of his horse [Col. 0070A] through byways and reached Rouen alone. When he entered the city, the citizens captured and detained him, because they had conspired with the people of Bayeux (13 July).

48. The king is released by the Northmen through hostages and is again captured by the Duke through treachery [Note: [Col. 0069] “R, tm, ob, m, it, a d” is conjecturally supplied.].—When Duke Hugo learned that the king had been captured at Rouen, he went to Bayeux, intending to give thanks for the king’s capture and to argue that the captive should be entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 0069] So in the text.]. The Northmen, however, not sufficiently trusting the Duke [Note: [Col. 0069] “v. duci non satis creduli,” “not sufficiently trusting the Duke,” is already deleted.], replied that this should be done on just conditions: if the Duke received the king, they themselves were to receive all the king’s sons under the security of hostages, and they would release the king to him under no other arrangement.

The Duke concealed his intention concerning the capture and, as though he were arranging the matter for the king’s benefit, sent envoys to Queen Gerberga for the king’s sons. But the queen, recognizing the necessity of the matter, sent the younger son under oath, being unable to compel the elder to be sent. For there were only two sons. When the younger hostage had been offered [Note: [Col. 0069] “dato,” “given,” in one witness.], this was not enough for the Northmen, who demanded the elder in particular [Note: [Col. 0069] “quaerentes,” “seeking,” in one witness.].

But because those whose minds were more faithful thought that the nobility of the royal line might be utterly destroyed if all the sons were held together with their father by deserters, they replied that they would not do this. They would accept only the younger son and, in place of the elder, would release whichever person they might choose from among their own men. Thus they requested Wido, bishop of Soissons, whom they regarded as the foremost among all, and accepted him as a hostage in exchange for the king’s son.

The king was then released, and while it was thought that the Duke would escort him to his own territory, the Duke detained him and assigned him to be guarded by Teutbold of Tours. From this it became evident that the tyrant had wished to abolish the dignity of the royal line completely through the destruction of the father and the sons. But when the matter turned out otherwise, only one son of the king survived the captivity [Note: [Col. 0069] “ita,” “thus,” in the text.].

49. (946.) Otto and Edmund, kings of the Germans and the English [Note: [Col. 0069] “O, g, n, r, pr” is conjecturally supplied.], take action against the Duke on behalf of the king [Note: [Col. 0069] “O, g, n, r, pr” is conjecturally supplied.].—The queen immediately reported the whole course of this affair through envoys to Edmund, king of the English, and Otto, king of the Germans beyond the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0069] “O, g, n, r, pr” is conjecturally supplied.], and sent them a letter containing a most serious complaint.

Otto, grieving over the misfortune of the king and of his sister, promptly sent an embassy to Hugo for the king’s restoration, making many demands and also issuing certain threats. King Edmund likewise complained so bitterly about the sufferings of his cousin that, through his own embassy, he displayed to the same Duke the great indignation of his heart. He declared that, if the king were not returned, he would take vigorous action against him; moreover, he would bring enemies against him by land and sea and utterly ravage his territory.

If the Duke shut himself within any fortified town, Edmund would besiege it with the greatest determination; moreover, against the Duke he would obtain aid from the Gauls. Unless he returned the king immediately, Edmund would attack him at once by land and sea.

50. The Duke’s indignation against King Edmund [Note: [Col. 0071] “ti, E, r” is cut off.].—The Duke, exhausted by the grave embassy, partly disagreed with Otto and partly favored him. To King Edmund’s envoys he replied that the matter could be undertaken neither immediately nor without due consideration. He would do nothing because of the English threats. If they came, they would very quickly learn what the Gauls were capable of in arms. But if fear prevented them from coming, they would nevertheless one day learn the strength of the Gauls for their arrogance in making such demands, and would also pay the penalty.

He therefore expelled the envoys in anger. Then, withdrawing to deliberate, he consulted his own men and employed their counsel in the process of discussion. After the consultation, the Duke sought Otto. When he sought through envoys an opportunity for discussion, he failed to obtain an interview with Otto, toward whom he was hostile. Greatly angered, he withdrew to his own territory and, following the advice of his men, approached the king and addressed him as follows:

51. Hugo’s address to the king [Note: [Col. 0071] “utio, regem” is cut off.].—“The persecution of your adversaries, O king, once drove you, while still a little boy, into the lands across the sea. By my ability and counsel you were recalled from there and restored to your kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0071] One witness reads “regnis,” ‘to the kingdoms.’]. Afterwards, while you followed my advice, you flourished in the prosperity of favorable circumstances. Never did I abandon you except because of the obstinacy of your own fury.

Using the arrangements of base and imprudent men, you strayed far from the counsels of the wise. Hence the calamity of events rightly followed. For how can one whom folly throws headlong stand firm? [Note: [Col. 0071] The phrase “Quomodo enim stare potest, quem socordia praecipitat” has been erased; it is also absent from Trithemius.] How could you suppose that anything necessary and glorious for you could come about apart from me? I say that you have suffered great loss in this matter.

Now remember that you are a man. Consider also what is advantageous to your interests. Let courage return in such a way [Note: [Col. 0071] One witness, Trithemius: “quae,” ‘which.’] that it recalls us to goodwill: you governing and I serving as a soldier [Col. 0071C], and through me bringing back the rest to serve you in arms. And since you were made king by me and have granted me nothing, at least generously grant me Laon, where I shall serve as a soldier. This too will provide a reason for preserving our loyalty.”

The king, being in captivity, yielded to the speaker’s words. Accordingly, once released and Laon having been given to him [Note: [Col. 0071] “lauduno a duce regno,” ‘Laon, a kingdom from the Duke,’ has been erased.], he withdrew to Compiègne. Queen Gerberga, memorable for her great virtue, was present; several fellow bishops from Belgica were also present; and a number of distinguished men gathered there.

52. The king’s complaint before private persons concerning Hugo’s persecution [Note: [Col. 0071] “pri, ugonis, ne” is cut off.].—Before these people the king also complained in the following words:

“Ah, you Hugo! Ah, you Hugo! From how many good things have you deprived me, with how many evils have you afflicted me, and with how great a sorrow am I now held! You seized the city of Reims. You stole Laon. These two alone received me; these two alone enclosed me. My father, captured and thrown into prison, lost together with his life these hardships that now weigh upon me.

But I, cast headlong into the same condition, offer nothing from my father’s kingdom except a spectacle. Now I neither wish to live nor am I permitted to die. Where, then, shall I go?”

As he prepared to complain further, he was restrained by those who were indignant. Then, calming his spirit, he consulted with his own men.

53. After this consultation, he communicated his deliverance to King Otto through envoys, recalling that he had previously been captured and was now deprived of all his possessions. He therefore asked his friend to bring him assistance and to help him recover the cities he had lost. If Otto did so, he promised that he would repay him with great gratitude.

Otto received the embassy most graciously, promised that he would go with forces to aid the king, and appointed a time. The envoys returned and reported his instructions. He likewise requested troops from King Conrad of Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0071D] “Burgundiae,” ‘of Burgundy.’] and received them.

54. Meanwhile, as King Otto crossed the Rhine and led his army through Belgica, he met King Conrad [Col. 0072B], who had then come out from the Alps and was hastening with a large expedition to aid Louis. The two kings therefore joined together and proceeded with a large cavalry force.

When Louis recognized their approach, he went quickly to meet them. The three kings, assembled as one, decided that the first effort of battle should be directed against Laon. Without delay they led the army there. When they saw the height of the mountain opposite and examined the city’s position on every side, they realized that they would fight there to no purpose. They withdrew from that city and attacked Reims.

There, because the plain offered a suitable site for armies, they arranged the siege all around the city. They fought at close quarters in the first engagement. Missiles and stones were hurled so thickly that they fell like dense hail. The city was therefore attacked throughout an entire day by continuous assaults [Col. 0072C]. Afterwards they fought at close quarters seven times, and this continued for approximately six days.

55. Yet the citizens were not defeated by the continual attacks and did not yield in any way. Their bishop Hugo spoke outside the city with certain princes who were related to him in some degree, asking them what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided. He asked whether the matter might be remedied through the intervention of others, whether there was need for prayers, or whether the struggle should instead be pursued.

They immediately described the kings’ determination and declared that they were firmly resolved not to yield to anyone’s intervention, but to continue the siege until it achieved its purpose. If the city should happen to be captured by force, they themselves would have the bishop’s eyes put out; this had been settled and fixed. Therefore he should depart quickly and rescue his people from the kings’ indignation.

Terrified by these words, the bishop showed them to his own people. After taking counsel, on the sixth day of the siege he went out with his followers. The gates were opened to the kings [Note: [Col. 0071] “P. quoque” has been erased.].

56. The kings, however, restored Artoldus and then brought him into the city. Between the two metropolitans, Frederick of Mainz and Rotbert of Trier [Col. 0073A], he was restored by them, hand in hand, to his former see.

There they immediately appointed Queen Gerberga, together with several distinguished men, to guard duty. The three kings themselves then advanced with the army against Duke Hugo. They attempted to break into Silletum by force, but, after considering the strength of the fortified settlement, withdrew from it—not, however, without burning the suburb and killing some of its inhabitants. They then hastened toward the Seine River.

57. How a few young men, through cunning, recovered the ships withdrawn by the Duke and brought them to the army [Note: [Col. 0073] “juv, a d, per a, tas, ad” is cut off.].—The Duke, anticipating their attack, had ordered all the ships to be removed twenty miles from the shore facing the enemy, so that the adversaries would have no convenient means of crossing. But his plan was frustrated, and the outcome was known to have been quite different.

For ten young men, firmly resolved to undergo every danger, disguising their military appearance as that of pilgrims, had gone ahead of the kings, pretending to be engaged in devotional supplication [Note: [Col. 0073] It is also said that this had been arranged through the cunning of Count Bernard; the note has now been erased.]. With baskets hanging from their shoulders and iron-shod staffs, they proceeded. Disguised as pilgrims, they crossed the city of Paris and the bridges over the Seine. No one troubled them.

They then made for the outer banks where the ships were kept. Turning aside to the lodging of a certain miller [Note: [Col. 0073] Concerning the miller, the keeper of the Seine’s mills, see *Gesta consulum Andegavensium*, chapter [lacuna], in Dachery, *Spicilegium* X, 444.], they reported that they had come from the farther bank in order to visit holy places [Note: [Col. 0073] “itore ex conject.”, conjecturally supplied.]. The miller, observing that the young men were handsome despite their humble clothing, gladly offered them lodging and treated them especially kindly.

Planning their deception, they gave him money, bought wine, and made their host drunk. Thus they spent the entire day in the pleasures of a feast. When the young men noticed that their host had been made more compliant by the wine, they asked what his occupation was. He said that he was a miller.

They continued to question him, asking whether he could do anything more. He also claimed to be the Duke’s chief fisherman and said that he earned something from arranging the ships. They replied:

“Since we have found you to be exceptionally kind to us, we desire something further as well. Therefore, if you do something for us, we promise to give you ten solidi, namely, to carry us across the river, since, exhausted by the length of the journey, we cannot proceed any farther on foot to pray.”

When the host replied that, by the Duke’s order, the ships had been taken to the inner bank so that access would not be open to the Germans if they attacked, they insisted that this could be done at night without risk [Col. 0073D]. The man, greedy for money, accepted the fare and gave his word that he would undertake the task.

Night came. The young men demanded that he fulfill his promise. He immediately took along his stepson, and with the young men hurried to the ships in the darkness of night. The young men accompanied him. Seeing that the place was deserted, they seized the boy and submerged him in the current. When the host tried to shout, they attacked his throat. They threatened him with death unless he did what they wanted, namely, release the ships [Col. 0074A].

Overcome and terrified, he therefore released the ships. After making a plan, they threw him bound into one vessel, and each of them brought one ship separately to the bank. Then, having thrown the bound host out, they all boarded one ship, went back for the others, and brought nine more across. They crossed and recrossed the river eight times and carried away seventy-two ships.

58. While these events were taking place, the army of the kings reached the river at the very dawn of sunrise and found the ships ready with their oars. The recruits entered them with their weapons, sailed across, and leveled them out. Then, scattering in every direction, they seized other vessels from various ports without anyone preventing them and brought them to the armies. For all those who lived in the countryside had fled from fear of the invaders.

The Duke, however, had withdrawn to Orléans. Consequently, no one remained to resist [Col. 0074B]. Having joined the ships together and strengthened them by assembling them in great numbers, they made the boats secure. The army boarded them and crossed the river.

Afterward, once they had reached land, they ravaged the entire region as far as the Loire with fierce fires and plundering. After this they advanced into the land of the pirates and devastated it to the ground. Having thus taken cruel vengeance for the king’s injury, they turned their journey back toward their own territories. King Louis, meanwhile, returned to Reims.

59. How Deroldus was deceived by a certain physician and deceived him in turn [Note: [Col. 0073] “ceptus, ceperit” is cut off.].—At that time Deroldus, bishop of Amiens, departed this life. He was a distinguished courtier, once greatly beloved by the king, and highly skilled in the art of medicine.

It is also reported of him that, while he was still serving the king at court, he was deceived by a certain physician from Salerno and in turn deceived him [Col. 0074C]. For since both men were highly capable in the art of medicine, and Deroldus was regarded as superior for the king while the Salernitan was considered more skilled for the queen [Note: [Col. 0073] “Frederunae” has been deleted.], the king devised a test to discover which of them had the greater knowledge of the natures of things.

He ordered them to sit at table as his dinner companions, carefully concealing the reason for the test, and often proposing questions to them. Each solved the questions as best he could. Deroldus, being educated in the arts of letters, defined the matters presented to him plausibly. The Salernitan, although endowed with no literary learning, nevertheless possessed, through natural ingenuity, extensive practical experience in such matters.

By royal command they therefore sat together every day and continually shared the royal table. One day they discussed the differences among *dinamidia* [medicinal preparations], and considered at greater length what is produced by pharmacy, what by surgery, and what by botany. But the Salernitan, not understanding these foreign terms and ashamed to ask for their interpretation, remained silent [Col. 0074D].

He therefore became extremely envious and planned to prepare poison for Deroldus’s death, while deceitfully pretending great goodwill toward him. When the poison had been prepared, and they were sitting together at lunch, the Salernitan, having poisoned his indecent fingernail [that is, his unclean nail], fatally contaminated the pepper liquor in which they both dipped their food.

Deroldus, taking it unwittingly, soon began to fail as the poison spread through him. His attendants carried him out, and *teriaca* counteracted the force of the poison. After three days had passed, he returned in the presence of the king and resumed his customary relations with the Salernitan. When asked what had happened to him, he replied that he had been lightly affected by the coldness of phlegm, concealing the fact that he had perceived any deception. Thus he made his enemy careless.

When they had returned to table, Deroldus concealed the poison between the ring finger and the little finger and sprinkled it onto the Salernitan’s food. As it soon spread through his veins, it drove the warmth of life away. His attendants carried him out in distress. He devoted himself to expelling the poison but accomplished nothing by treatment.

Accordingly, he praised Deroldus and proclaimed him supreme in medicine, earnestly asking him to undertake his care. Deroldus, persuaded by the king’s command, administered antidotes and skillfully purged him of the poison—but not completely.

For after the *teriaca* had been taken, the force of the poison flowed entirely into his left foot, so much so that, while he was going about familiarly among his household, the poison, as is reported, rose through a vein from the foot in the shape of a chickpea and, meeting the opposing antidote, was driven back into the foot. Since these forces resisted one another for a very long time, the foot was pierced at the surface of the skin. When the disease had developed, it was later cut off miserably by surgeons.

60. (947.) Meanwhile, grieving that Neustria had been burned and plundered, the Duke prepared an army and, since he did not dare to attack the king, turned ferociously against Arnulf. He also attacked several of Arnulf’s fortified settlements. But when, after six days, he could capture none of them, frustrated in his purpose, he returned to his own territory.

While the Duke was conducting these operations, the king was pressing the siege of Mouzon, because the Duke’s nephew Hugo, having been expelled from the episcopate, was staying there [Col. 0075C]. He harassed him as an insult to the Duke. But when he learned that the Duke had withdrawn from the siege, he too returned to Reims.

At this same time Bovo, bishop of Châlons, departed this life. He was immediately succeeded [Note: [Col. 0075] “s. donatus vox,” ‘the word *donatus*,’ has now been erased.] by Gipuinus, an excellent young man chosen by the unanimous clergy, who was consecrated bishop by Lord Artoldus, metropolitan of Reims.

61. Afterwards [Note: [Col. 0075] Trithemius described the king’s journey to Aachen somewhat more fully under the years 948 and 949 . . . . [The king] returns to the city of Reims. By royal command nearly all the bishops, abbots, counts, and nobles from Celtica assembled there, except only those who followed the party of Duke Hugh. By the common decree of all, it was resolved that provision should be made for the royal dignity before King Otto the Great, since he was then staying in Belgica, and before others to whose prudence the commonwealth seemed fit to be entrusted. Envoys having been sent in both directions, King Otto appointed a general conference in the palace at Aachen, to be held at the approaching feast of the Lord’s Resurrection (949). In the aforesaid year King Otto and Louis of the Gauls assembled at Aachen, as agreed, for the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection; several princes, bishops, abbots, and counts from Germany and Gaul also gathered there, and all celebrated holy Easter in the said palace with the highest reverence and honour. It is clear that these statements, being a sixteenth-century commentary, have no authority.] the king proceeded into Belgica, and King Otto came to meet him there so that he might speak with him. Arranging whatever was necessary, both kings celebrated Easter at Aachen, honoring one another with great reverence—and Otto doing so to an even greater degree. Otto also honored Louis most generously with royal gifts [Col. 0075D].

62. The Duke attacks the city of Reims [Note: [Col. 0075] “urbem, ensem, im, nat” is cut off.].—While matters stood thus, the Duke discussed the king’s injury with his own men. He declared that the king’s absence provided an opportunity to capture the city of Reims, since at that time the city was empty both of its bishop and of soldiers, while the king himself was occupied elsewhere and had other matters to pursue.

He therefore asserted that the city could easily be captured and declared that he very much wished to attempt it. The soldiers advised that cohorts should be sent into the city. Once assembled, these troops marched with the Duke. They attacked the city and pressed it with a siege on every side. They spread out in various directions and brought grain from the neighboring places for use in the fighting. They fortified their camp with ditches and surrounded it with hurdles.

Each day they launched an attack, either once or twice. The citizens resisted no less vigorously. They had been carrying this on for nine days when observers announced that the king, extremely indignant, was returning [Col. 0076B]. They immediately lifted the siege and withdrew from the city on the twelfth day.

63. The king did not delay long before entering the city to bring it assistance. The princes soon gathered around him and deliberated concerning his safety and the common safety. Since the needs of the situation required Otto to participate in the counsels, envoys were sent to him. Through them the necessity of the matter was explained, and a conference to be held at the end of August beside the River Chara was announced to him [Note: [Col. 0075] “Ottoni” corrected to “ei”; “Talia omisi,” ‘I have omitted such matters.’].

64. While matters stood thus, the Duke grieved that his nephew had been expelled from the episcopate. He therefore urged him to continue in the clerical office and, lest he appear completely deprived of his dignity as a private person, promoted certain persons through the ecclesiastical ranks.

He summoned Tetbald, a deacon of the church of Soissons, ordained him priest, and afterward, with the Duke’s intervention, consecrated him bishop of the church of Amiens [Col. 0076C]. In this matter only Wido, bishop of Soissons, appeared to give support. The following events will show that he later regretted this.

The time for the kings’ conference arrived, and they met beside the River Chara. The Duke was also present. He had pitched his camp near the village of Douzy so that he might plead his nephew’s case before the bishops.

65.
