The Duke strives to have the case of his nephew heard before the bishops [Note: [Col. 0075] “Du, ut, c, nep, episcopo” is cut off.].—While the kings were conducting their affairs, the Duke presented his nephew’s case to the bishops, among whom there was also very great indignation, recalling that his nephew had been unjustly and without any evident fault cast down from office.

When this had been reported to the kings, at Otto’s initiative it was decreed that the case of Artoldus and Hugo should be examined there by the bishops, but on the condition that the Duke should also give satisfaction to the king at an appropriate time.

When the bishops received the case, they rejected most emphatically, among the many matters explained there, the claim that Hugo, after being deprived of the priesthood, had ordained the bishop of Amiens contrary to law. The kings’ judgment therefore determined that this matter should be transferred to another synod. It seemed that the dispute could not suitably be settled with equity, since no synod had been summoned for this purpose.

By royal decree, a synod was announced for the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December. In the meantime the see of Reims was granted to Artoldus, while Hugo was permitted to reside in the fortress of Mouzon. Through Otto’s intervention, a truce was also granted to the king and the Duke by each party to the other, and it was confirmed by oath until the time appointed for the synod.

66. The synod held at Verdun [Note: [Col. 0077] “nod, ni h” is cut off.].—The appointed time arrived, and a synod of bishops was assembled and held at Verdun, presided over by Rotbert, metropolitan of Trier, with Artoldus of Reims. Also seated were Adalbero of Metz, Gauslinus of Toul, Hildeboldus of Minden, and Israel the Briton; assisting them were the venerable Bruno, an abbot, together with other revered abbots and monks, Agenoldus and Odilo.

Hugo was summoned to this synod, and Bishops Adalbero and Gauslinus were sent to bring him. He refused to come. Therefore, by the judgment of the bishops [Note: [Col. 0077] “sensentia” corrected to “sententia.”], Artoldus was permitted to retain the episcopal see. Thus, since no substantive grounds of the case had been determined, the synod was dissolved.

67. (948.) The synod held at Mouzon [Note: [Col. 0077] “Mo” is cut off.].—A second synod was announced for the Ides of January. When the appointed time had passed, a second synod was held in the basilica of Saint Peter at the fortress of Mouzon, again presided over by the aforesaid Rotbert, metropolitan of Trier, together with almost all the bishops of his diocese and several from Reims. Artoldus, whose case was to be examined, was also seated there.

Hugo was not absent, but he refused to enter the synod. Through his own men he presented for reading at the synod a letter bearing the name of Pope Agapitus [Note: [Col. 0077] “per quendam clericum suum,” ‘through a certain cleric of his,’ in one witness.].

When it had been unsealed and read, it seemed to possess no canonical authority and to signify nothing in support of his case except that the episcopal see should be restored to him. After reading it, the bishops withdrew for deliberation and judged that it should be annulled, because it ordered that the matter under dispute be surrendered to the deposed man without justification.

And because a little earlier a letter had been delegated by Pope Agapitus himself through Frederick, bishop of Mainz, and delivered to Rotbert, metropolitan of Trier, in the presence of the kings and the bishops of Gaul and Germany, containing the authority of an apostolic command—and because they had already carried out part of his instructions—the bishops soon agreed unanimously that what had been begun regularly should be pursued reasonably and canonically.

At the same time, the metropolitan ordered that chapter 19 of the Council of Carthage be read, a chapter that concerns the accused and the accuser. After it had been read, they determined, according to the judgment of that chapter, that the diocese of Reims should be restored to Artoldus, and that Hugo—who refused to hear the proceedings of any synod and, having already been summoned to two synods, had scorned to come—should abstain from governing the episcopal see of Reims until he came to a third synod [Note: [Col. 0077] “which was announced as to be held on the Kalends of August” has been deleted.] to be cleared of the charges brought against him.

The aforesaid chapter was committed to writing on parchment, formally guaranteed by the bishops, and sent to Hugo. When Hugo saw the bishops’ guarantee bearing their subscriptions, he was moved to anger and returned it insultingly to Rotbert, who presided over the synod, asserting that he would do nothing in accordance with the bishops’ judgment. Thus, with the case entirely unexamined, the synod was dissolved. A third synod was announced for the Kalends of August [Col. 0078B].

68. After these events, Artoldus sent a letter to the Roman See, most fully setting out both the sequence of his injuries and the account of the king’s troubles. Lord Pope Agapitus, directing his attention toward extensive goodwill, immediately summoned the venerable Marinus, bishop of Ostia, a man of great equity and prudence. He explained to him the force of the letter and earnestly urged him to correct the situation.

The venerable Marinus, vicar of the lord pope, was therefore sent to King Otto to summon and assemble a universal synod. Several letters were also sent individually to certain bishops of both Germany and Gaul, urging them toward an equitable settlement.

69. The synod also held at Ingelheim [Note: [Col. 0077] “odus, gle, bita” is cut off.]. See *Leges* II. 24.—Meanwhile, at the appointed time, a universal synod was assembled by order of Pope Agapitus under his vicar Marinus, in the palace at Ingelheim—which is interpreted as “the house of angels”—beside the River Rhine, in the basilica of Saint Remigius, apostle of the Franks.

With Lord Marinus presiding, the bishops who had gathered from various places also took their seats according to ecclesiastical law: Rotbert, metropolitan of Trier; Artoldus, metropolitan of Reims; Frederick, metropolitan of Mainz; Wicfridus, metropolitan of Cologne; Adaldacchus, bishop of Hamburg; Hildeboldus, bishop of Minden; Gauslinus, bishop of Toul; Adalbero, bishop of Metz; Berengarius, bishop of Verdun; Fulbertus, bishop of Cambrai; Rodulfus, bishop of Laon; Richoo, bishop of Worms; Reimboldus, bishop of Speyer; Boppo, bishop of Würzburg; Chounradus, bishop of Constance; Odelricus, bishop of Augsburg; Thethardus, bishop of Hildesheim; Bernardus, bishop of Halberstadt [Note: [Col. 0077D] That is, bishop of Halberstadt.]; Dudo, bishop of Paderborn; Lioptacus, bishop of Ribe; Michahel [Col. 0079A], bishop of Regensburg; Farabertus, bishop of Tongeren; Doddo, bishop of Osnabrück; Evherus, bishop of Minden [Note: [Col. 0079] “Euherus” in the text.]; Baldricus, bishop of Utrecht; Heiroldus, bishop of Salzburg; Adalbertus, bishop of Passau; Starchandus, bishop of Eichstätt; Horath, bishop of Schleswig; Wichardus, bishop of Basel; and Liefdach, bishop of Ripa [Note: [Col. 0079D] The name has already occurred above, as also in Flodoardus.].

70. The arrangement of the matters to be conducted and the presiding authority of the judgment [Note: [Col. 0079] “tio, dor, da, tu” is cut off.].—Although each of all these men was permitted to produce from the canons or decrees whatever seemed useful to the case, the authority to organize the proceedings and interpret the arguments was nevertheless entrusted to Lord Rotbert of Trier, because he was regarded as exceptionally distinguished in knowledge of divine and human matters and in eloquence.

The authority to pass judgment, however, remained with Lord Marinus, the lord pope’s vicar [Note: [Col. 0079D] Compare below the council at Saint-Basle in 991 [Col. 0080D]: “Marinus therefore assumed the role of president, and Rotbert that of relator.”].

When everyone had taken his seat, after the prayers prescribed for the orderly celebration of a council had been offered and the sacred chapters of the decrees had been read, the most serene kings Louis and Otto were admitted into the holy synod. When they too had taken their seats, the lord and venerable Rotbert began as follows:

### 71. Prefatory Address of Rotbert of Trier, Metropolitan, at the Synod

[Editorial notes, Col. 0079: *Pr*, *R*, *ri*, and *li* are cut off; *cognoscimus* is written above *videntur*; *galliarum* is written above *regnorum*. A deleted passage reads: *c. multo intuitu multo caritatis affectu [considerandum corr.] insistendum arbitror ut sic res, etc.*—“with much consideration, with much affection of charity [corrected to *considerandum*], I think it must be insisted that thus matters, etc.”]

*See* **Legg.** II. 19–21.

“Many are the matters, reverend fathers, for which we have been compelled to sit assembled here in the presence of the most serene kings. There are also very many matters which appear to require ordering by your probity. It is evident that the commonwealth of nearly all Gaul has been thrown into confusion by the recklessness of wicked men and lies exposed to great dangers. Hence divine and human laws alike are indiscriminately despised by evildoers, while he to whom the rights of the kingdoms are owed, and to whom the power of ruling was entrusted by hereditary succession, has been seized through the persecution of his own people, brutally thrust into confinement, and is still being assailed by their swords [the correction *appetitur*—“is attacked”—appears in witness 1]. Moreover, thieves are pursuing the metropolitan church of Reims with the utmost ferocity, without a shepherd; divine worship is held cheap, and canonical religion is treated as nothing.

“Therefore, fathers, I believe that we must insist upon these matters with the greatest force, and strive with much diligence—those of us who have been brought together here by the grace of the Holy Spirit—so that matters previously dissolved may return to such an alliance that both the power of ruling may be restored freely to our lord, the most serene king, and through him the honor owed to the Church of Reims may be restored to its proper state.”

[Col. 0079D] **72. Response of Marinus, Legate of the Roman See**

[Editorial note, Col. 0079: *ponsio*, *ni*, *Ro*, *sedis*, and *ti* are cut off.]

At this, Lord Marinus, vicar of the Holy Roman See, said:

“Very well and usefully, brother and fellow bishop Rotbert, has set forth the sequence of events. For although he himself recognizes that divine laws must be preferred to human ones, nevertheless, having considered the circumstances, he first declared that the authority of royal rule must be restored, so that once its strength has been secured and its power usefully restored, the honor of the churches of God may thereafter increase through his generosity, and, through his protection, virtue may return to all good men. In order that this may be accomplished with God’s consent, it seems first of all necessary to hear and vigorously settle the case of our lord, the most serene king—if the judgment of your tribunal also allows this.”

The synod said: “Let him be heard.”

### 73. Complaint of King Ludovicus before King Otto and the Synod concerning his Kingdom

[Editorial note, Col. 0079: *estio*, *ci*, *regis*, *gem et*, *m*, and *i* are cut off.]

Then King Ludovicus rose from King Otto’s side and, standing, modestly requested permission to make his complaint. But when asked by the synod, he sat down and delivered his complaint as follows:

“How greatly, and how much at his instigation, I am compelled to complain because of Hugo, that man bears witness whose grace was given as the reason for your being assembled here. To begin at the beginning: his father, envying my father’s kingdom, although he owed him service at home and in war, brutally deprived him of his kingdom and had him kept confined in prison until the end of his life [the manuscript has a deletion concerning *ergastulo inclusum*—‘confined in prison’]. He compelled me, still a small child, concealed by my own people in a bundle of chaff, to flee overseas and almost as far as the Rifean regions.

“After my father had died [witness 1 reads ‘had been captured’] and I had been carried into exile, this man, remembering his own father, feared to take charge of the kingdom because of the insolence with which that father had been killed. Therefore, out of envy toward us, he advanced Rodulfus [witness 1 reads ‘another man’]. But the Divinity, determining his affairs as well as everything else, gave him an end to his reign when it willed. When the kingdom was again vacant, he recalled me, an exile in foreign lands, by the counsel of good men, and with the agreement of everyone advanced me to the kingdom, leaving me nothing except Laon.

“When, having been advanced, I strove to reclaim those things that appeared to belong to royal right, he bore this with the utmost envy. Becoming secretly my adversary, he overthrew with money whatever friends I had and incited my enemies to greater hatred. At last, driven by envy, he arranged with pirates that I should be captured by them through treachery, thinking that the kingdom could be transferred to himself if this happened. Nor was the plot without effect. I was captured and handed over to prison [the phrase ‘for a year’ has been deleted].

“But while pretending to rescue me, he demanded that my sons be handed over as hostages. When all those who were bound to me by loyalty protested that they should not be surrendered, he released one of them and recovered me from the pirates. Already hoping for freedom, I wished to go wherever my mind urged me. But it is clear that matters turned out otherwise. For he soon threw me, once captured, into chains and consigned me to a year’s imprisonment.

“When he perceived that my relatives and friends, indignant, were preparing to attack him, he promised me freedom if I surrendered Laon [witness 1 reads ‘return’]. I was confined only in this place; only on this condition was I received, together with my wife and children. What was I to do? I preferred life in the fortress; for the fortress I earned my freedom. And now, deprived of everything, I ask the help of everyone! If the duke dares to oppose this, let us meet him alone in single combat.”

### 74. Speech of Rotbert on Behalf of Ludovicus

[Editorial note, Col. 0081: *Or* and *berti* are cut off.]

After these matters had been made public, Rotbert, the metropolitan, added:

“Since we have heard, as I think, the complaint of our lord, the most serene king, set forth sufficiently briefly and clearly, it seems appropriate that we determine his case insofar as is lawful. Since the duke has transferred nearly all the rights of the kingdom to himself, and we are unable to resist him by force, I believe that this should be attempted more mildly, so that he who fears neither God nor respects man may, by many arguments and much consideration of the circumstances, be brought back to the proper standard with God’s help.

“Therefore, in accordance with the decrees of the fathers and the rule of the canons, he must first be fraternally admonished to make satisfaction and, with words of persuasion, be recalled to this course with the utmost moderation. But if, after the gentle admonition of recall, he refuses to repent [the words ‘on the third day of this synod’ have been deleted], let him be struck with the anathema of all. We have this protection: he has already been corrected by our lord the pope and ordered to cease persecuting his lord.”

### 75. Response of Marinus, the Legate, on Behalf of the Same Man

[Editorial note, Col. 0081: *Res*, *Ma*, *pro*, and *eo* are cut off.]

To this Lord Marinus added:

“I remember that before this past year the lord pope sent an anathema against those guilty men who were persecuting this lord and king of the Franks. He also sent a letter of exhortation, addressed to various good men, urging them not to abandon him, and a written complaint concerning the same matter was likewise entrusted to men of sounder judgment. Hence I believe that it was most justly said: since he was previously summoned and corrected by the pope, he must now also be recalled for the sake of charity and admonished with the most diligent persuasion to cease from evil; and afterward he must be condemned by the anathema of all.

“And not he alone, but all who favored and continue to favor him in his evils. Yet this is the only help he will receive from us. Will he receive no help from anyone else? In the closing words of his complaint he asks for everyone’s help. But if we come to his aid, what will he receive from King Otto? The holy decretal writings also proclaim that, after the bishops have imposed the anathema of condemnation upon a tyrant, force must likewise be applied by good and powerful men, so that, if they refuse to return to the proper order through ecclesiastical correction, they may at least be compelled by the vehement force of the powerful to return to what is good, so that good may be secured even against their will.”

[Col. 0082A] **76. Speech of King Otto on Behalf of the Same Man**

[Editorial note, Col. 0081: *Or* and *nis* are cut off.]

King Otto then said:

“Many are the benefits, fathers, which can usefully be supplied by you to our lord, the most serene King Ludovicus. For if you attack his persecutors with divine weapons, they will consequently either collapse, defeated by an easy disturbance, or, if anything remains to be attacked, will more easily be weakened by our weapons. Therefore, at the command of the pope’s legate, draw forth the instruments of your order and pierce the adversaries of so great a king with the sword of anathema.

“If afterward they dare to raise their necks against this and are not afraid to resist the prohibitions of the Lord, it will then be our task—we who have been entrusted with protecting the holy Church of God in this part of the world—to take up arms against such men and overcome them in this way. And if necessity presses, with drawn swords we shall rage even to the most savage slaughter of the utterly depraved, having the most just cause for indignation against them: they attack what is unlawful, and, when admonished concerning their unlawful conduct, they do not reform.

“Therefore, you attend only to what belongs to you; afterward our strength will follow your moderation.”

### 77. Letter Sent by the Synod to Hugo

[Editorial note, Col. 0081: *a si*, *ad Hugonem*, and *ata* are cut off.]

After these words, by decree of the synod a letter was immediately composed and publicly read, containing the following wording [the editorial note states that the letter was genuinely written at this synod, although Flodoard makes no mention of it; the acts of the synod testify to this, and therefore the editor does not believe that Richerus fabricated it while consulting Flodoard’s account of the acts of the Synod of Laon]:

“The holy synod, usefully held at the palace of Ingelheim under the lordly and orthodox kings Ludovicus and Otto, to Hugo the duke.

“How many evils, and with what persecution, you have inflicted upon that venerable metropolitan church of Reims, and with what cruelty you have raged against your lord the king, is proclaimed by the mouths of all and discussed among everyone. How criminal and how destructive this is, divine and human laws disclose most fully. Therefore, sympathizing with you, we admonish you to cease from such conduct. We exhort you to return as quickly as possible to your lord with great meekness and humility.

“But if you despise this, before we are carried away into opposing directions, we shall without doubt bind you with anathema, until either you make satisfaction or go to Rome to render an account before our lord the pope. You have already been admonished twice by his letters and forbidden to commit so great a crime. Therefore, following him, we now call you for the third time back to correction [witness 1 reads ‘we admonish’].”

This letter, strengthened by the authority of the entire synod, was immediately sent to the duke through legates.

### 78. The Case of Artoldus

After this, Archbishop Artoldus rose and most clearly explained the sequence of events, as well as the beginning of the very dispute that had arisen between himself and Hugo, the bishop who had been substituted for him. He also produced a letter recently sent to him by the lord pope, by which the pope indicated that he was to retain the episcopate.

After its interpretation, a certain Sigeboldus, a cleric of the aforesaid Hugo, immediately presented another letter to the synod, bearing the pope’s seal and brought by him from Rome. This letter was also read in the presence of the bishops and examined with the greatest care. Its text said only that Rodulfus, bishop of Laon, Wido, bishop of Soissons, Hildegarius, bishop of Beauvais, and the other bishops of the diocese of Reims had sent a letter to the apostolic see concerning Hugo’s restoration and Artoldus’s abdication. It therefore stated that the lord pope wished everything to be done according to their wishes and petition.

After it had been read, the bishops named above immediately rose and completely refuted the meaning of the letter, publicly denouncing its bearer as a most depraved man and a spreader of calumnies. Since he could not oppose them, he attacked them with certain insults and publicly accused them of treachery. [Editorial note, Col. 0083: up to this point the ink is dark brown; the remainder of the codex is written in blacker ink.]

[Col. 0083B] **79. Rejection of the Calumniator of the Bishops**

[Editorial note, Col. 0083: *Cal*, *tor*, and *repro* are cut off.]

Then Lord Maninus decreed that the chapters issued concerning calumniators should be read. When these had immediately been read, and the calumniator was unable to resist, he was deprived, by the judgment of the bishops, of the office of deacon that he held. Publicly rejected with contempt from the presence of the synod, he was compelled to leave.

As for Artoldus, the synod decreed and confirmed, in accordance with the institutions of the canons and the decrees of the fathers, that he should retain the dignity of the episcopate, since he had not refused to take part in the proceedings of any council. These decisions were made on the first day of the assembly.

### 80. Condemnation of Hugo

On the second day, after the readings from sacred authority and the address of Lord Rotbert, the venerable Marinus decreed that, since the episcopal dignity had been restored to Artoldus in accordance with the judgment of sacred law, a synodal sentence should be pronounced against the one who had usurped it.

The decrees of the canons and the institutions of the holy fathers were therefore read: those of Innocent, Alexander, Symmachus, Sixtus, Celestine, Zosimus, Leo, Boniface, and other distinguished teachers of the holy Church of God. In accordance with their decrees, they unanimously anathematized and excluded from the communion of the whole Church Hugo, usurper of the Church of Reims, until, having come to his senses, he should repent and make satisfaction to those offended for his crime.

### 81. Further Proceedings

*See* **Legg.** II. 24, line 55.

During the remaining days, decisions were also made concerning the incestuous and unlawful marriages of priests; concerning priests who handled the Eucharist unworthily; concerning churches improperly seized by laymen; and concerning several other matters brought forward there [the manuscript reads *prolatata*, apparently an error for *prolata*]. These matters were investigated with the greatest care and usefully defined. Thus the synod was dissolved.

It was decreed, however, that another synod should be held after thirty days at Laon, in the basilica of Saint Vincent the Martyr, so that the anathema might there be pronounced against Hugo the tyrant.

[Col. 0084A] **82. Anathema of the Bishops against the Duke and His Supporters**

[Editorial note, Col. 0083: *A*, *episco*, and *ej* are cut off.]

When these matters had been carefully and canonically completed, King Ludovicus received from King Otto a force of soldiers under the command of Duke Conradus, to campaign against Hugo the tyrant.

While these troops were being assembled over forty days, the bishops mentioned above gathered on the thirtieth day after the completion of the synod in the basilica of Saint Vincent the Martyr at Laon, under King Ludovicus [the editorial note observes that what follows was not dealt with at the Synod of Laon but at the Synod of Trier, as is clear above from Flodoardus; Richerus therefore omitted the acts of the Synod of Laon and the beginning of the Synod of Trier].

Again presided over by the aforesaid Marinus, and after passages of Holy Scripture had been read and discussed there with much consideration, they condemned Hugo the tyrant by anathema and expelled him from the holy Church, unless, coming to his senses, he made satisfaction to his lord or went to Rome to render an account before the lord pope for his absolution.

At this synod they also dealt with the bishops who had been summoned together with the duke but had delayed coming, and with those who had unlawfully taken part in the consecration of Hugo, a bishop already deposed, or who appeared to have been promoted contrary to law by him while he was in possession of office or after his deposition.

Thus two pseudo-bishops ordained by Hugo were condemned: namely Tetbaldus and Ivo [a deleted reading is *H. pulso vel abdicato*: “Hugo having been expelled or deposed”]. The former had been consecrated bishop of Amiens by the expelled man; the latter bishop of Silletum by the deposed man.

Adelelmus, a deacon of the Church of Laon, was also condemned. He had been accused by his own bishop, Rodulfus [the words “at the synod” have been deleted], because he had rashly brought the excommunicated Tetbaldus into the church. These men, having already been summoned with the duke at the earlier synod, had refused to make satisfaction.

Hildegarius, bishop of Beauvais, was summoned by a delegation from Lord Marinus and the bishops, either to come to them or to go to the apostolic see to render an account of his crime, because he had taken part in the ordination of the pseudo-bishops mentioned above.

Heribertus, son of Heribertus the tyrant, was also summoned because of the evils he had inflicted with great brutality upon churches and bishops.

Wido, bishop of Soissons, was attacked by many on the ground that he himself had consecrated Hugo as bishop. At the synod he confessed himself guilty and, lamenting his guilt with much penance, obtained absolution through the intercession of the archbishops Artoldus and Rotbertus before the synod.

Wicfridus, bishop of Thérouanne, who had been accused of taking part in the matter, was found free of the charge.

Silvester, a priest, appeared as the legate of Transmarius, bishop of Noyon, asserting that his bishop was so severely confined by fever that he had been unable to come to the synod. He confirmed this before the synod with witnesses.

After this, the bishops were sent back to their own dioceses.

Lord Marinus, at the request of King Otto conveyed through legates, withdrew into the German regions. There he dedicated the church of the monastery of Werden, and, after the winter had passed, returned to Rome.

When these matters had been completed, Rodulfus, bishop of Laon, worn out by the final illness of his body, departed this life. His successor was Rorico, the king’s brother by a concubine, distinguished in every branch of knowledge.

### 83. The King Sends Cohorts to and Captures Mouzon

Meanwhile, after an army had been assembled from all Belgium under Duke Conradus at the king’s command, three cohorts were sent to Mouzon. For the king had learned that Hugo, who had been deposed, was confined there and that he was held with very little military support.

At twilight the cohorts attacked the town and suddenly assailed it on every side. They pressed forward bravely to capture it. Since they knew that there were in fact very few soldiers there and scarcely any weapons, they exerted their strength without interruption and pressed on with their arms. When some became exhausted, others who were still fresh took their places. Thus, without interruption, the numerous soldiers wore down the very few defenders.

The townsmen, worn down by the continual assault, were compelled on the following day, when the sun was already setting, to surrender together with their lord. In the confusion, Hugo the deposed man escaped by some kind of flight unknown to us. The soldiers who appeared to be the more prominent were captured and, after others had been assigned to the town, were brought before the king.

### 84. The King Captures Montaigu

The king was besieging with his army the fortress called Montaigu, which is also adjacent to Laon. Since it was not yet sufficiently enclosed by the strength of its walls, and since a sufficient number of soldiers could not conveniently live there, the townsmen were unable to resist the pressing siege for long. Defeated, they yielded and ceased their resistance.

After the town had been captured, the king stationed his men there and thus brought his army to Laon. He arranged the siege at suitable places and concentrated his forces [the manuscript corrects *conferret* to *confert*].

Very often they fought at a distance. They also engaged in close combat nine times. Yet at that time the royal attack achieved no success of favorable fortune. For winter’s severity was approaching, and therefore the engines of war could not be built in the short time available; without them, the height of so great a mountain could not be stormed.

At the king’s command the army withdrew, intending to return after the winter had passed. The king himself withdrew to Reims as a private man.

### 85. Hugo Attacks Soissons and the Reims Region

Duke Hugo, disregarding the bishops’ anathema and refusing to submit to the king, attacked the royal city of Soissons with a large force of Northmen and pressed it with a heavy siege.

He attacked some men with the sword and killed them; others he wounded mortally with a cloud of arrows and crossbow bolts. He also set fire to the mother church by means of burning javelins. He burned the canons’ cloister and most of the city down to the ground.

When he was unable to capture the city, he turned his savage march toward the Reims district, where the king was then living as a private man. Hearing of his arrival, those who lived in the countryside fled with their possessions into the churches of the saints. But the tyrant, without mercy toward the crowds of poor people, is said to have burned more than 560 of them inside the churches. Then he returned to his own territory.

[Col. 0086A] **86. Ludovicus Sends Queen Gerberga to King Otto**

King Ludovicus sent Queen Gerberga to her brother Otto, asking him to hasten troops to his aid [a deleted note says: “to send troops, although he himself had dismissed the army he had assembled and had determined that it would not return until after winter and spring”].

She set out as Easter approached and celebrated Holy Easter with her brother Otto at the palace of Aachen. Several princes from Germany assembled there. All the leaders from Belgium were present. Nor were there lacking legates of the Greeks, Italians, English, and many other peoples.

After the queen had taken counsel with her brother and received from him a promise of assistance, she returned confidently to King Ludovicus.

### 87. Counsel for the Capture of Laon

Ludovicus, angered against the tyrant, was planning, with excessive ardor, to anticipate Otto’s assistance. He thought that, because of the army’s long delay, the injury might appear to have gone unavenged.

He therefore took counsel with my father [the note reads “already mentioned previously”], since my father was his soldier, useful in counsel, and very strong both in eloquence and in boldness. Hence the king was greatly accustomed to him and very often consulted him.

My father therefore explained to the king and the few who were present the following plan for capturing Laon. First, he said, he would observe the opportunity for carrying out the enterprise and would investigate most carefully whether the nature of the place permitted it, and whether the citizens were extremely vigilant in guarding the city. Then, he said, he would arrange everything so effectively and bring it so usefully to completion that no one after him would be left with any unfinished part of the undertaking to complete.

### 88. The Scouts Observe the Citizens’ Routine

While the king remained at Reims for several days, Rodulfus [the note reads “already mentioned previously”—thus was my father called] investigated through his men the opportunity for carrying out the enterprise.

Having sent scouts, he learned that every day, in the evening, the citizens’ muleteers went out of the city in groups of fifty or sixty and brought bundles of fodder into the city on horses, with their heads wrapped against the heat of the sun. This happened every day and at the same time.

When this had been reported by the observers to my father [“already mentioned previously”], he realized that they could be deceived by a similar maneuver. He therefore returned to the king and, in the presence of only a very few men, delivered the following proposal:

### 89. The Plan to Enter Laon Disguised as Muleteers

“It would indeed seem a great undertaking, O king, if this matter were to be attempted solely by arms and force. But since prudence advises that its beginning be approached by cunning, it seems to me that several cohorts should be placed in hiding beside the mountain. We must also wait for the time when the muleteers lead out the horses to graze and drink.

“When they have gone out at their usual time, and their departure and number have been reported to us by the observers, let a number of selected young men equal to their number, wearing caps in the same fashion and in the same number as they do, carry fodder on horses to the gate from which the muleteers had recently gone out, as though the muleteers themselves were returning. Since the height of the bundles will conceal their appearance, they will easily enter the city.

“And lest you think that I have proposed anything impossible, I offer myself as their leader in this contest. Let them only be steadfast in spirit. With God’s will, the outcome will be favorable.

“If, however, the citizens discover the ambush too soon and bring battle upon us while we are fewer in number, let us have firmly resolved either to defend only the entrance of the gate until the cohorts, aroused by the sound of the trumpets, come to our aid, or, with great steadfastness, to die bravely where each man is stationed.”

### 90. Capture of the City

This arrangement appeared suitable to everyone. Scouts were therefore sent out, and they promptly reported the muleteers’ customary behavior, their appearance, the time, and their number.

Once this had been reported, cohorts were stationed in hiding beside the mountain. Soldiers equal in number to the muleteers, sworn together with my father to carry out the enterprise, were also sent.

The muleteers, numbering sixty, took up their arms and, as usual, wearing caps on their heads, descended along the slopes of the mountain to gather fodder. While they were occupied gathering sedges [the margin supplies “whence also” in place of the words concerning the gathering of sedges], they delayed their return for a little while.

But my father and those who were sworn with him followed with resolute spirit. Forming a column, wearing caps on their heads like the muleteers and carrying bundles of fodder, they hastened their return, concealing their faces completely beneath the large bundles.

When they arrived, the gate was opened. They entered the city without breaking ranks. They threw down the bundles and drew their swords. Trumpets sounded, and with great shouts they threw the city into confusion.

When the townsmen discovered the ambush, they rushed upon the enemy with their weapons. Everyone pressed forward, and very many of them vigorously attacked the few. But the royal soldiers were protected on the left by a tower, on the right by houses, and behind by the city wall; they had the whole force of the battle in front of them and therefore fought more safely.

They did not dare advance farther against the enemy, lest their opponents return behind them to the gate they had seized and, thus placed amid the enemy, perish. Each man therefore held his position.

By now all were excessively wounded and almost collapsing, when the royal cohorts, roused by the trumpets, burst forth from their hiding places. With a powerful attack they came to the aid of those who were already almost defeated, entered through the defended gate, and attacked the townsmen with terrible slaughter. The latter were soon defeated and captured by the cohorts, except for a few who withdrew into the defense of the towers.

### 91. The King Is Unable to Capture the Tower

King Ludovicus, having gained possession of the city, was unable to overcome the tower by any assault. He therefore isolated it from the city by constructing a wall inside it.

When the duke learned of this, he hastened there with his army. But unable to exert any effective force, he returned to his own territory in sorrow. The only thing he is said to have accomplished was to send troops down to the citadel.

### 92. The King’s Campaign in Belgium

The time had come when the king was awaiting troops from King Otto. Duke Conradus therefore arrived with an army from all Belgium, sent by King Otto.

King Ludovicus then entered the duke’s territory with an army from Belgica. First he went to the city of Silletum. Wishing to fight the first engagement there, he removed all supplies and baggage from the city.

He therefore burned the suburb on every side and reduced to level ground whatever appeared to stand outside the city. He established the siege and surrounded the city.

A fierce battle was fought on both sides. Very many were wounded on each side. But the Belgians, because they were attacked too heavily by the townsmen with crossbows, ceased resisting. They used nothing against them except a tortoise formation of shields. Therefore, by royal command, they withdrew from that city, not only because of the attack of the crossbowmen but also because of the strength of its many towers.

### 93. The Army Reaches the Seine

They therefore turned their march elsewhere and, for forty miles as far as the river Seine, pursued with terrible violence everything belonging to the duke that came into view.

But when the river prevented the royal cavalry from advancing farther, the king gave thanks to the army and led it back with him until they separated. The duke, however, immediately led the assembled army into the Soissons district.

### 94. A Truce until Easter

When the duke was preparing to attack the king there, the bishops Wido of Auxerre and Ansegisus of Troyes intervened. After oaths had been exchanged on both sides, their dispute was deferred under a truce until Easter.

All these events took place in the month of July [witness 1 reads “in August”].

### 95. The Roman Synod under Pope Agapitus

At the same time a synod was held at Rome in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, presided over by Lord Agapitus the pope.

There the lord pope himself confirmed before the Italian bishops the council held the previous year at Ingelheim and decreed that it should also be confirmed by them. He also condemned Hugo, duke of Gaul, who had been condemned at the aforesaid synod, until he made satisfaction to his king or came to Rome to render an account there.

An anathema was immediately written out, confirmed by the synod, and sent to the bishops of Gaul.

### 96. The Bishops Admonish the Duke

**(950.)** The bishops of Gaul, moved by the anathema, gathered before the duke and made the most serious complaint against him. From the decrees of the fathers and the sacred canons they demonstrated to the duke that no one ought stubbornly to stand against his lord or rashly plot anything against him.

They also clearly showed, according to the Apostle, that the king must be honored, and asserted that not only the king but every higher authority ought to rule over those subject to it.

Furthermore, they declared that it was most destructive stubbornly to disregard the apostolic anathema, since it is a sword that penetrates the body as far as the soul and thus drives those put to death away from the kingdom of the blessed spirits. They also stated that they themselves would be in danger if, through negligence, they failed to make known that which brings danger to souls.

### 97. Reconciliation between the King and the Duke

Persuaded by such arguments, the duke humbly requested reconciliation with the king and promised that he would make satisfaction to him.

The organizers of this agreement and peace were Duke Conradus and Hugo, surnamed the Black, together with the bishops Adalbero and Fulbertus.

On the appointed day the king and the duke met. Having conferred beside the river Marne, with the aforementioned princes acting as intermediaries, they returned most graciously to complete harmony.

And the more fiercely they had previously attacked one another, the more greatly thereafter they honored one another in friendship. Duke Hugo therefore became the king’s man by the laying on of hands and an oath, and returned to the king the tower of Laon after evacuating his own men from it, promising that from then on he would preserve great loyalty.

### 98. Ludovicus in Burgundy

**(951.)** Ordered by the king, he prepared an army for the king in Aquitaine. When it had been assembled within a short time, the king, as circumstances required, led the army with him into the interior regions of Burgundy.

When he was pitching camp in the territory of Mâcon, Karolus Constantinus, ruler of the city of Vienne, met him and became his man, pledging loyalty by oath.

He had indeed been born of royal stock, but was disgraced by a concubine’s lineage as far back as his great-great-grandfather. He was an old man, very often worn down by many reversals of war, yet one who had repeatedly distinguished himself by successful combat in the earlier disturbances involving the pirates.

Stephen, bishop of Auvergne, was also present and entrusted himself to the king. Likewise, capable legates from William, prince of the Aquitanians, were present to swear on behalf of their prince the oaths of loyalty that were required.

After royal orders had been given to them, the king led the army with the duke to the city of Besançon, the capital of the Genaunenses, past which flows the Dubis (Doubs), described in the source as *Aldis* and as situated in the Alps [reading uncertain]. There Letoldus, ruler of that city, transferred himself by oath into the king’s service.

### 99. The King Falls Ill and Recovers

After these matters had been successfully and usefully completed, as autumn advanced and the elements changed, the king, suffering from a bilious disorder, fell into an acute fever.

Since, oppressed by illness, he was unable to attend to military affairs, he ordered the duke to lead the army back. Letoldus, however, the ruler, served the king with the greatest loyalty and humanity throughout the king’s illness.

On the critical day after the beginning of the fever, however, though it came unfavorably (*impariter*), he recovered firmly and without relapse. After thirty days had passed since his bodily recovery [the manuscript corrects twenty to thirty], he returned to Francia with Prince Letoldus.

### 100. The Capture of Briona

When he was already reaching the borders of Burgundy, he learned from travelers that certain men who were ravaging the province by banditry and raids—namely Angelbertus and Gozbertus—had built a fortification called Briona, to which they also withdrew after their shameful activities.

The king therefore attacked it, surrounded it with a siege, and wore it down by continuous fighting and hunger. At last he captured it and destroyed it to the ground. At Letoldus’s request, he allowed the little brigands to depart under oath.

### 101. Queen Aethgiva Marries Heribertus

Meanwhile, while the king was still detained in the regions of Burgundy, his mother, Queen Aethgiva, without his knowledge, married Count Heribertus and was led away by him after leaving the city of Laon.

The king, greatly angered by this [the words “together with Gerberga” have been deleted], hastened to return and entered Laon with Gerberga, his queen. Taking estates and royal houses away from his mother, he assigned them to his wife [the note indicates that the word *omnia*—“all”—has been deleted].

### 102. Queen Gerberga Gives Birth to Twins

Meanwhile Queen Gerberga gave birth to twin sons at Laon. One was called Karolus and the other Heinricus. But Heinricus died soon after receiving holy baptism, while still in his white baptismal garment. Karolus, however, was raised with the natural strength of his body.

103. King Louis, returning to Rheims, when he was approaching the river Aisne, saw a wolf running ahead across the open country. Releasing his horse, he pursued it and drove it through trackless places. At every turn the beast made, he impatiently wheeled his horse after it. Nor would he allow himself to rest until he had overcome the fleeing animal in an equestrian contest. Thus forced through impassable ground, the horse struck against a turf-covered obstacle and fell. The king, severely bruised by the fall and caught by his attendants, was carried to Rheims amid the great grief of everyone [Note: “grief” corrected from “sorrow.”]. He was afflicted throughout his body by grievous pains. After a prolonged illness, his internal organs became diseased through an excess of humors, and he was miserably covered throughout his body by the plague of elephantiasis. Worn down by this for a long time, in the eighteenth year of his reign and the thirty-sixth of his age he ended his life. He was buried in the monastery of the monks of Saint Remigius, situated about a mile from the city, amid the many lamentations of all.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0089]

[Col. 0089D] 1. When the funeral rites had been completed, Queen Gerberga sent envoys to her brothers, King Otto and Bruno, formerly a bishop and now a duke, and also to Hugh, duke of the Gauls, asking through them that her son Lothair succeed his deceased father in the kingdom. Accordingly, all the leading men from Belgium came from King Otto, together with Duke Bruno, and some also from Germany. Hugh, duke of the Gauls, was present as well. The leading men of Burgundy and Aquitaine, and likewise those of Gothia, also assembled. Bishops too came from various cities of the regions. All these men, united in the city of Rheims before Queen Gerberga, were of one accord [Col. 0090D]. There was universal agreement: all desired that Lothair succeed his deceased father.

2. By the unanimous consent of all, Lothair, twelve years old, was made king in the basilica of Saint Remigius, where his father lay buried with the other kings. He was made king by Lord Artold, metropolitan of Rheims, with the support of his maternal uncle Bruno and the acclamation of the princes of the various peoples. Then, together with his mother Gerberga and the leading men, he was conducted with great display to Laon [Note: “Laon” corrected from “Laudum”], which was known to have been the royal seat from ancient times and was celebrated for its wealth. The duke remained constantly at his side; and, intent on winning the king’s great favor, after the princes had departed to their own territories, he maintained private conversations with the king. To demonstrate fully the strength of his loyalty, he asked—and obtained permission—to have the king and his mother visit his cities and strongholds throughout Neustria.

3. The duke therefore led the king and his royal mother through Neustria, and received them with the utmost distinction at Paris, Orléans, Chartres, Tours, Blois, and many other cities and strongholds of Neustria. From there they proceeded with an army into Aquitaine. After envoys had been sent ahead, when Prince William refused to come out to meet them, they attacked Poitiers, believing that the prince was there. Since the army was battering the city with the utmost violence and had long been engaging its inhabitants in battle, some royal troops secretly entered and captured the castle of Saint Radegund, adjacent to the city, and set it on fire [Col. 0091B]. When it became clear that the prince was not present, after two months had passed, the army exhausted by want, they withdrew from the siege.

4. William, meanwhile, was traversing the borders of Auvergne, which is part of Aquitaine, drawing soldiers out of the strongholds and gathering an army for battle. Once it had been assembled, he advanced against the king. When the king learned this, with the duke’s support he led his army against the enemy. They engaged with hostile standards displayed. The battle was fought with great ferocity, and some on both sides were slain. But when the royal cavalry prevailed, it drove the Aquitanians into flight [Note: “cavalry” corrected from “army.”]. The royal troops pursued them with the greatest eagerness. During the flight some Aquitanians were killed, while many were captured. William, however, following byways, escaped with difficulty over precipitous ground with two companions.

5. The king, distinguished by this favorable outcome of the war, ordered the army to be brought against Poitiers once more [Note: “army” corrected from “troops.”] [Note: “to be brought against it” corrected from “brings it against it.”]. He thought that the city could then be captured very easily, while the army was still inflamed by the excitement of its recent victory and the townspeople were held by great fear because of their prince’s flight and the disastrous outcome suffered by his soldiers. The duke therefore, receiving the king’s boldness with great approval, led the army back to the city, although it was weary, yet won over by his kindness. The townspeople, exhausted by the fortunes of war, begged for their lives and pleaded for the city’s preservation [Note: “preservation” corrected from “safety”] [Col. 0091D]. When the army wished to break into the city by force and carry away the spoils, the duke dissuaded them, and at the king’s command left the city untouched. The king nevertheless took as many hostages from the townspeople as he wished. Thus, through the duke’s intervention, the city was freed from the army [Note: “from the army” corrected from “from the plunderers”], and under a provisional peace the siege was lifted. With fortune favoring his affairs, the king returned to Laon with the duke and the army [Col. 0092A]. The duke, however, after being received at Paris, fell ill and, afflicted too severely, died (956). He was buried in the basilica of Saint Dionysius the martyr.

6. Meanwhile, while King Otto was waging war against Bulizlao, king of the Sarmatians, a certain Ragener, whom King Otto had left in Belgium to maintain order, was presuming to do many unlawful things. Among these, with tyrannical recklessness, he seized the royal houses and royal estates belonging to Queen Gerberga that were in Belgium [Note: “recklessness” corrected from “cruelty.”]. The queen did not delay in privately consulting her people about recovering the estates and royal houses.

7. Since my father appeared suitable among them for arranging this matter, they urgently asked him to organize it. He undertook the arrangement and said: “Allow me to investigate this for several days. If indeed it is within our power, we shall certainly examine the matter during this interval. Meanwhile, turn your attention to other things. Let this one matter only be settled among you: if God grants us an opportunity to undertake it, there must be no delay among you in making the attempt” [Note: “among you” corrected from “with you”]. Thus they were released from the matter.

8. My father therefore sent some of his men, whom he himself had trained in military matters, to the aforementioned stronghold of Ragener called Mons Castriloci [Note: “Mons Castriloci” corrected from “mons,” an error by the author, who had initially omitted “castrati.”] [Note: “Mons Castriloci,” Bergen or Mons, the capital of Hainaut], where Ragener’s wife also lived with their two young sons. He instructed them to examine with the utmost care the character of the place, the number of soldiers, the circumstances of the enterprise, the outcome for the servants, and the diligence of the guards.

Only two of them proceeded, dressed as poor men, and came as far as the gate of the stronghold. At that time walls were being built in places with more substantial structures. Consequently, carriers of stone and mortar frequently went out through the gate and returned, in the presence of the man supervising the work [Note: “the man supervising the work” corrected from “the guard”]. The scouts arrived and offered themselves to carry stones. They were assigned to the work and given a basket with a carrying frame. They carried mortar and stones and received one coin each per day [Note: The letter “d” had first been written, that is, “denarii.”]. Twice they also ate before the lady, together with the masons and mortar-workers, while carefully observing everything. They carefully noted the lady’s chamber, the quarters of her children, the coming and going of the servants, and the timing of their activities, including where the stronghold was most exposed to ambush [Col. 0092D]. After four days had been spent, Sunday was approaching. Having received their payment for the work [Note: “payment for the work” corrected from “the price of the labor”], they were released from it. They therefore returned after investigating everything and reported these matters to my father.

9. Placing all his hopes in this undertaking, and with the queen’s knowledge, he approached the stronghold with two cohorts. Guided by those whom he had sent ahead, he entered by night through a suitable place [Col. 0093A]. He overran all the gates and exits and stationed guards so that no one could escape. He himself hastened toward the lady’s chamber with the utmost intensity. Entering it, he seized the mother with her two children. Others occupied themselves with carrying away the ornaments. He also captured the soldiers and set the stronghold on fire. After it had been burned, he returned to Queen Gerberga with the lady, her children, and the captured soldiers.

10. When Ragener learned this, driven by such necessity, he appealed to Bruno, the queen’s brother, asking that a meeting be arranged promptly, at the queen’s command, in which he himself would receive back his wife and children and the queen would recover the houses [Col. 0093B] and estates. This was done at the appointed time. For after the claims of both sides had been heard, the queen recovered the estates from the tyrant, while he restored his wife and children and the soldiers [Note: “Here, as the sign indicates, something appears to be missing.”].

11. (959.) After these events, Robert, prince of Troyes, son of the tyrant Heribert and brother of the deposed Hugh, plotted an injury against King Lothair in the following manner. He ardently desired the royal stronghold called Dijon, built beside the stream of the Ouche, because he thought that, if he could obtain it, the best part of Burgundy could pass under his authority through it. Through envoys he therefore approached the man who appeared to command the stronghold, speaking to him about defecting to his side, promising him many things and, under oath, pledging still greater rewards. He asserted that the king was in great want, while he himself possessed abundant resources, several strongholds, and other highly desirable distinctions [Col. 0093C]. Then the young man, captivated by desire for such things, asked what reward he would receive for defecting. They told him the amount of the reward. He demanded and received an oath concerning the promises. At the appropriate time, he welcomed the tyrant with a large force of soldiers inside the stronghold and, committing himself to him, offered his loyalty in exchange for military service. Once the stronghold had been overrun, the royal soldiers were driven out with insults. The tyrant’s soldiers were stationed there.

12. (960.) These events were reported to the king. The king sent envoys to his uncle Bruno, asking him for troops. Bruno did not delay: with two thousand armed men from Belgium, he occupied the tyrant’s territory and surrounded the city of Troyes with a siege [Col. 0093D]. The king, together with his mother, having recovered the stronghold, led an army into the region. When the tyrant was pressed by the two armies, he was defeated and asked the king for mercy. Forced to do so, he gave hostages and oaths; moreover, once defeated, he handed over the betrayer of the stronghold. By the king’s sentence, the man was soon beheaded before the gate of the stronghold, in the presence of his father.

13. (961.) Having taken possession of the stronghold, the king returned to Laon with his mother [Col. 0094A]. Here princes from various regions gathered around the king. The two sons of the deceased duke, Hugh and Otto, were also present, and they solemnly promised the king loyal military service by oath before everyone. The king, showing generosity equal to their kindness, made Hugh duke in place of his father and moreover added the territory of Poitiers to his principality; he granted Burgundy to Otto.

14. During this distribution of territories, Lord Artold, the highly revered metropolitan, had worked intensely throughout the day and had sweated over his entire body under the heat of the sun [Note: “sun” corrected from “summer”]. When he cast off his clothing, autumnal cold entered through the pores opened by the heat [Note: “autumnal cold” corrected from “cold”]. An internal chill produced a disease of the liver, and, worn down by severe pains, on the day before the Kalends of October he ended his life, after twenty years in his episcopate [Col. 0094B] [Note: “years” abbreviated as “ann.”].

15. (962.) After his funeral rites had been completed, Hugh, most recently made duke of the Franks by the king, humbly approached the king and asked that the episcopal dignity be restored to him [Note: Editorial error by the author: Hugh, son of Heribert, had seized the archbishopric of Rheims; and below, in chapter 17, his brother is correctly called Robert]. He stated that he himself had obtained it before Artold and that Artold had been imposed upon him not through his own wrongdoing but through the hostility of King Rudolph. He therefore persisted in asking that it be returned to him. Immediately, by royal decree [Note: “decree” corrected from “command”], a synod of bishops was announced for forty days later.

16. When the appointed days had elapsed, a synod of thirteen bishops was assembled in the district of Meaux, beside the river Marne, in a village called . . . , from the provinces of Rheims and Sens, under the presidency of the bishop of Sens. Some of them appeared to favor Hugh’s cause, especially those accustomed to attend upon the duke, namely the bishops of Orléans, Paris, and also Sillé [Col. 0094C]. They were conducting public deliberations. But when Rorico, bishop of Laon, and Gibuin, bishop of Châlons [Note: “Gibuin” as written], resisted and insisted most forcefully that one who had been excommunicated by a multitude of bishops could not be absolved by a smaller number, the matter was left to be deferred until the pope of Rome had been consulted.

17. Not long afterward, an embassy was sent into Gaul by Lord Pope John, who had now succeeded Octavian [Note: As written], successor of Lord Agapitus. It asserted that the aforementioned Hugh, who had been deposed, had been anathematized by the bishops of Italy both at a Roman synod and at the one recently held at Pavia, unless he ceased pursuing the things he was unlawfully demanding. Once this embassy’s message had been made known to everyone, the basis of the complaint collapsed [Col. 0094D]. Hugh was received by his brother Robert and died at Meaux within a few days, overcome by excessive anxiety.

18. The metropolitan and duke Bruno was seeking the episcopate before the king for a certain man from the college of canons of Metz named Odelric. When he had obtained it, he had the man brought before him. This notable man, distinguished by wealth, noble birth, and learning, was asked whether he dared to accept the bishopric if the king granted it. For at that time it was being sought by a certain illustrious man whom the duke was supporting. But he, as a magnanimous man, replied that if the king granted it, he would both accept it and defend it against everyone. This also earned him much of the duke’s hostility.

19. He was therefore ordained in the basilica of Saint Remigius by the bishops belonging to the dioceses of the metropolitan church of Rheims: Wido of Soissons, Rorico of Laon, Gibuin of Châlons, Hadulf of Noyon [Note: “N.” and several others deleted], and Wicfrid of Verdun (963). Having become bishop, he immediately summoned before the ecclesiastical court the tyrants who had seized the property of his church, so that they might return to make restitution. He then granted them three periods of forty days for deliberation.

[Col. 0095B] 20. (964.) When the appointed time had passed, he condemned Tetbald of Tours, together with other usurpers of ecclesiastical property, under anathema. After not many days, they returned, moved by penitence, to make satisfaction to the bishop, and legally restored the property they had seized (965). Thus Lord Bishop Adalbero received from Heribert the populous and wealthy village of Épernay, and from Tetbald the stronghold of Château-Thierry; he absolved them from the bond of anathema. To Tetbald’s son, who had committed himself to him for military service, he granted the stronghold on condition that he preserve his fidelity.

21. At this same time Arnulf, prince of the Morini, died. King Lothair entered his territory, generously returned it to the deceased man’s son, and bound him to himself with the soldiers by the authority of oaths [Col. 0095C] [Note: These words, beginning at the start of the page with “namely: And to Tetbald’s son,” were written by the author in a place that had been scraped, while four other lines had already been erased and left blank. He then continues.] [Note: Since Flodoard’s Annals fail here, the author composed what follows on his own initiative.]

22. (969.) Adalbero, a man of royal nobility [Note: Son of Godfrey, count of the Ardennes], likewise from the college of Metz, succeeded him energetically and successfully. How greatly he benefited his own people, and how much more than was just he suffered from his rivals, will be made clear in the work that follows. At the beginning of his promotion, he devoted great attention to the structures of his church. He completely demolished the vaults that extended in lofty construction from the entrance of the church through nearly a quarter of the entire basilica [Note: “basilica” corrected from “oratory”] [Note: “extended” corrected from “extended,” singular in the source]. Thus the entire church was adorned with a more spacious enclosure and a more worthy appearance. He also placed the body of Saint Calixtus, pope and martyr, with due honor at the very entrance of the church, in a more elevated location [Note: “elevated location” corrected from “more prominent location”]. There, dedicating an altar, he fitted out a most suitable oratory for offering prayers to God. He adorned the principal altar with golden crosses and covered it with shining screens on either side.

23. In addition, he fashioned a portable altar with work no less splendid [Note: “splendid” corrected from “lesser”]. While the priest was celebrating before God upon it, there stood four images of the evangelists, embossed in gold and silver, one at each corner [Col. 0096A]. The outstretched wings of each covered the two sides of the altar as far as the middle. Their faces were turned toward the spotless Lamb. In this he also seemed to imitate Solomon’s litter. He likewise made a seven-branched candlestick; since seven branches rose from one, it appeared to signify that the seven gifts of grace are divided from one Spirit. He decorated an ark no less elegantly [Note: “made of silver and gold” deleted]; in it he covered the rod and manna—that is, the relics of the saints. He also hung crowns, fashioned at no small expense, as ornaments of the church. He made the church bright with windows containing various scenes, and gave it bells that roared as though it were thundering.

24. He also instructed the canons, who had been living in their own lodgings and caring only for their private affairs [Col. 0096B], to live according to the law of shared community. For this reason he added a cloister to the monastery, where they would remain during the day and live together, as well as a dormitory, where they would rest in silence at night, and a refectory, where they would sit together and be nourished from a common table. He also prescribed rules: during the time of prayer they were to ask for nothing in the church except by a sign, unless necessity compelled them to speak. They were to take their food together in silence; after the meal, in thanksgiving, they were to sing praises to God. Once Compline had been completed, they were not to break silence in any way until the morning praises. When the horologe sounded, they were to rise and strive to anticipate one another in performing the praises. Before the first hour of the day, no one was permitted to leave the cloister except those who were occupied with their duties [Col. 0096C]. And so that no one might leave anything undone through ignorance, he ordered that the institutions of Saint Augustine and the decrees of the Fathers be read to them daily.

25. It would be impossible to say adequately with what affection and diligence he corrected the monks’ way of life and distinguished it from worldly custom. For he strove not only to make them conspicuous in the dignity of religion, but, wisely, also compelled them not to be diminished in external goods, but rather increased. Although he cherished them with great love, he especially exalted the monks of blessed Remigius, patron of the Franks, in his affection. Therefore, desiring to secure their property for the future, he went to Rome (971?) [Col. 0096D]. As a noble and energetic man, and one whose reputation for a celibate life was known to all, he was received with great reverence by Pope John of blessed memory. At the pope’s command, after mutual conversations, he celebrated the solemn Mass on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, with twelve bishops preceding him. He was held in such favor by the pope that the pope asked him to request whatever he might desire.

26. Metropolitan Adalbero asked Pope John to issue a privilege concerning the property of Saint Remigius [Note: The fragment “metropolitan, concerning the property, pa…, egium” is cut away] [Col. 0097A]. He began as follows [Note: The ending “...tiit” is cut away]:

“Since, most holy father, you have embraced your son with great affection and drawn him more closely to yourself, I do not think that I should ask you for anything burdensome. For I know that a loving father sometimes rejoices to be burdened by his son. But I have resolved to ask for something that will not burden so great a father and that will provide considerable benefit to the petitioner.

“I have in Gaul a monastery of monks, situated not far from the city of Rheims. There the most holy body of blessed Remigius, patron of the Franks, rests most fittingly, and due honor is shown to him [Note: “is shown” corrected from “is preserved”]. Desiring firmly to secure its property for the future, I now ask that it be confirmed by a privilege of your authority: namely, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods and pastures, vineyards and orchards [Note: As written], streams and ponds; likewise the fortification of their stronghold and the generous authority over their villages, within and outside; finally, may the dignity of your apostolate establish and confirm all their movable and immovable property [Col. 0097B]. I also grant them, in the presence of your authority and with these bishops as witnesses, the abbey of Saint Timothy the martyr, which appears to belong to our jurisdiction, so that its resources may be distributed to the poor and our memory may be maintained among the servants of God in the monastery. Let these things, therefore, added to what was mentioned above, pass into the right of the aforesaid saint and, by your similar authority, be confirmed as his property.”

27. To this the lord pope replied: “I willingly grant that the property of our lord and patron Remigius be established by the judgment of our apostolate and made safe forever; indeed, I also grant that whatever you wish may be added from your own property [Note: As written]. I decree that this be strengthened in writing not only by my authority but also by the authority of the bishops who are present” [Col. 0097C]. He immediately ordered the document to be written and commanded that the written text be read aloud in his presence.

28. Its text was as follows: “John, servant of the servants of God [Note: The parchment on which the charter was written has now disappeared. Guillaume Marlot states that a copy survives in *Historia metropolitanae Remensis*, II, 2, but it is suspect because of the year of the pontificate, which is given as the eighth]. [lacuna]

29. After it had been read aloud in the hearing of all who were present, he marked it with the sign of his seal and handed it to the bishops for confirmation. When these things had been done, the metropolitan, with the permission of the lord pope and the bishops, departed and returned to Gaul. Taking the direct route, he devoutly sought the tomb of the aforementioned saint and presented the written privilege to him among the college of monks. The monks accepted the gift, ordered it to be preserved in the archive, and suitably offered thanks for such generosity.

[Col. 0097D] 30. Adalbero had the privilege confirmed by the bishops in a synod [Note: The fragment “...ivi, sino, scopis, confir, cit” is cut away].—After these matters had been settled, six months later the same metropolitan held a synod of bishops at the mountain of Saint Mary [Note: Mont Notre-Dame, in the district of Tardenois, east and south of Soissons, near the village of Bazoches], a place belonging to the diocese of Rheims. When they were seated, after certain matters useful to the synod and beneficial to the holy church had been arranged, the metropolitan addressed them as follows [Col. 0098A]:

“Since, reverend fathers, by the grace of the Holy Spirit we have been gathered here and have arranged what seemed useful concerning the condition of the holy church, one matter still remains, which is exceedingly pleasing to me and will benefit some of the sons of our church now and in the future. I believe it should be brought before your dignity and confirmed.

“As you also know very well, seven months ago I went to Italy and arrived at Rome. I enjoyed very familiar conversation and goodwill with the lord apostolic man John, and he urged me to ask for whatever I might desire. I judged that I should ask him to establish the property of our lord and patron Remigius by the privilege of his authority against all tyrants, and to unite to it the abbey of Saint Timothy the martyr, which I had granted to them. I obtained this without opposition. He wrote the document, ordered it to be read aloud before twelve bishops, and handed it to them for confirmation. Marked with the sign of the lord pope’s seal, I have brought it to you also for confirmation, so that, supported by the authority of many, it may never be undone by anyone’s machinations. Therefore I wish it to be confirmed by you as well.”

The synod said: “Let it be confirmed.”

The metropolitan then produced it, read it aloud in the council, and handed it to them; each of them confirmed it by laying on his hand. The monks who were present also received it and returned it to the monastery archive.

31. The metropolitan’s complaint concerning the monks’ religious observance and the correction of their customs [Note: The fragments “...estio, polita, ona, eligi, ritu, ctione” are cut away].—Among these and other useful matters established there, the metropolitan made a very serious complaint concerning the monks’ religious observance, because the customs established by their predecessors appeared to have been corrupted and altered by some. Therefore, in the presence of the bishops, he decreed that the abbots of various places should assemble and deliberate usefully on the matter. The time and place for this deliberation were immediately fixed, and thus the synod was dissolved.

32. How Abbot Rodulfus became first among the abbots.—Meanwhile the appointed time arrived. Abbots from various places were gathered together in one body. Their chief and first-ranking member was appointed to be the man of blessed memory, Rodulfus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Remigius. With him presiding and holding the dignity of first place, the others were arranged around him [Col. 0098D]. The metropolitan sat opposite them on a *cliothedrum* [Note: A woven chair, a *faldistorium* or armchair]. At the urging of the first-ranking abbot and the other fathers, he delivered an address, beginning as follows:

33. The metropolitan’s opening address in the synod of abbots [Note: The fragments “cutio, opolitani, odo, um” are cut away].—“It is a great thing, most holy fathers, for good men to assemble, if they strive to seek the fruit of virtue. From this come both the benefits of good men and the honor of their affairs. Conversely, it is harmful if wicked men gather together in order to seek and carry out unlawful things. Therefore I urge you, whom I believe to have been gathered here in God’s name, to seek what is best, and I warn you to undertake nothing out of ill will.

“Let worldly love and hatred have no place among you; through them justice is weakened and equity suffocated. The ancient religious observance of your order has, as rumor reports, strayed exceedingly far from the honor of antiquity. For you disagree among yourselves even in the customary practices of the regular order, since one person wants and thinks one way and another another way. Consequently, much has hitherto been taken away from your holiness. Therefore I have judged it useful, since you have been gathered here in one body by God’s grace, to urge you to want the same thing, think the same thing, and cooperate in the same thing, so that through one will, one judgment, and one cooperation, neglected virtue may be recovered and the disgrace of depravity may be driven away with the utmost force.”

34. The first-ranking abbot’s reply and his indignation against the wicked [Note: The fragments “pons, atis, vos, atio” are cut away].—To this the first among the abbots replied: “What you have proclaimed here, most holy father, must be committed to deep memory, since you are concerned both for the dignity of bodies and for the salvation of souls. It is clear that no one has attained the way of virtue unless he was fortified by such a disposition that he sought what ought to be desired and rejected what ought to be avoided. Hence it is evident that we have incurred some disgrace, since we have strayed somewhat from what ought to be desired. This must also be condemned with much reproach, since neither laziness has thrown us into it nor poverty compelled us to it” [Col. 0099C].

35. Again, the first-ranking abbot’s indignation against the monks [Note: The fragments “I, ind, prima, monach” are cut away].—“What force compelled a monk, who ought to be devoted to the divine services within the monastery cloister, to have and be called a *compater*, a godfather? And consider how greatly this conflicts with our order. If, I say, he is a *compater*, then, to draw a plausible conclusion from what is likely, he is a father together with the one who is a father. If he is a father, there is no doubt that he has a son or daughter. Therefore he should be called a fornicator rather than a monk.

“But what of a *commater*, a godmother? What is discerned in this name by secular people except something corresponding to disgrace? Although I say this as a probable conclusion, I do not condemn secular people; I condemn what is unlawful in our order. Since this appears absurd, it must be prohibited by your solemn warning” [Col. 0099D].

The venerable metropolitan added: “If it pleases the synod, let it be forbidden.”

The synod said: “Let it be forbidden.”

By the metropolitan’s authority, therefore, it was prohibited with everyone’s consent.

36. The first-ranking abbot’s second objection [Note: The fragments “secunda, obj” are cut away].—The first-ranking abbot began again: “I shall bring forward another matter hostile to our order. Some men are known among us who have acquired the custom of leaving the monasteries alone, remaining alone outside with no witness to their work, and, worst of all, both leaving without the brothers’ blessing and returning without it. It is therefore beyond doubt that those whom the blessing of praying brothers does not protect can be led astray more easily. Hence the disgrace of their life, the depravity of their conduct, and their private possessions are brought against us by our accusers. It is therefore necessary that we be exposed to these accusations, since we cannot have witnesses to repel them. Let your judgment prohibit this as well.”

The synod said: “Let it be prohibited.”

The memorable metropolitan added: “We also prohibit this by our authority.”

37. The first-ranking abbot’s third indignation [Note: The final “te” is cut away].—The first-ranking abbot added another matter: “Since I have begun to speak of the vices of our order, I have decided to leave nothing untouched, so that once these things have been removed, our religious observance may shine forth as though the clouds had been cleared away. There are, I say, certain men of our order who take care to place visibly on their heads caps with ears and to prefer foreign furs to the regular cap, and who, instead of the habit of rejected clothing, put on exceedingly elegant garments [Note: After “put on,” the following words had originally been written: “since all good men are content with whatever covering of the head. Are these men, then, who differ from the religious, not so? For since they delight in the dignity of clothing rather than in what is lowly, they undoubtedly utterly reject the humility by which religion is recognized in part.”].
