For they greatly desire tunics purchased at a high price, which they tighten so closely on both sides and spread out with their flowing sleeves and folds that, with their buttocks constricted and their backsides thrust out, from behind they resemble little prostitutes rather than monks.”

38. On excessive color in clothing [Note: The fragments “De s, vest” are cut away].—“What, then, shall I say about the color of their clothing? How have they been deceived to such an extent that they compare the merits of dignity with colors? Unless a tunic is becoming in black, they are in no way willing to wear it. But if white wool has also been mixed into the black by the work of the cloth-maker [Col. 0100C], this too makes the garment unacceptable. Tawny is also rejected. Nor is natural black sufficient unless it is additionally dyed with the juices of bark. So much for clothing.”

39. On the excesses of footwear [Note: The fragments “De, ea torum, tate” are cut away].—“What shall I say about the excesses of their footwear? They are so insane about it that they deprive themselves of a great deal of comfort through it. They put on shoes so tight that, as though fettered, they can scarcely move. They also shape projections on them, raise up ears on either side, and work very carefully so that they will not gape. They even instruct their servants, who know the secret, to make them shine.”

40. **On linen garments and excessive coverings.** — “Should I remain silent about elaborate linen cloths and fur coverings? Although, I say, our forebears permitted the wearing of modest skins for the sake of indulgence, the vice of excess crept in. Hence now they surround foreign coverings with borders two palms wide and double them on top with Noric cloths. The use of linen instead of blankets was by no means permitted; but by certain less religious men this was added to the other excesses. Since their number was very great and they came from different places, the multitude of evils persuaded the few good men to accept this.”

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0099], “De l, bu” is cut away; the same note is printed twice.

41. **On improper breeches.** — “But why should I mention the improper breeches? Their leg-pieces extend six feet in width, and, because of the fineness of the thread, they do not protect even the private parts from the eyes of those looking at them; and in their construction one [layer] is not enough, whereas two would have been fully sufficient. You who are present here, indicate whether you wish these things to be prohibited. The remaining matters must be corrected privately in our councils.” The synod said: “Let them also be prohibited.”

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0101], “De, f, in” is cut away; the note is printed three times.

42. **The metropolitan’s response to the primate.** — At this the metropolitan added: “It was indeed characteristic of your gravity to spare many by saying little; but since the matters we have criticized fall under your order, and you judge some to be corrected by us and others by private councils, I hold and commend the same judgment. Therefore, whatever your gravity requests to be prohibited here, our authority forbids. What you have reserved by remaining silent, we leave to be altered according to your judgments.”

After these words the synod was dissolved. At that time monastic religion flourished greatly, since the metropolitan, thoroughly versed in their religious life, was its encourager and promoter. And, in order to answer in every respect to his nobility, he diligently sought to educate the sons of his church in the liberal studies.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0101], “rim” is cut away. “Studuis” is corrected to “studiis.”

43. **Gerbert’s arrival in Gaul.** — While he was deliberating with himself on this matter, Gerbert was sent by Divine Providence: a man of great intellect and extraordinary eloquence, through whom later all Gaul shone and flashed forth like a burning lamp. By birth an Aquitanian, he had been raised from childhood in the monastery of Saint Gerald the Confessor and had been taught grammar.

While he remained there as a young man, still devoted to his studies, it happened that Borrell, duke of nearer Spain, came to the same monastery to pray. Received with the greatest courtesy by the abbot, and after as many mutual conversations as they wished, he asked whether men were considered fully accomplished in the arts in Spain. When he affirmed this most readily, the abbot immediately persuaded him to take one of his own men and carry him away with him to be instructed in the arts.

The duke, therefore, not refusing, generously granted the petitioner’s request; and, with the consent of the brothers, he took Gerbert and brought him to Bishop Hatto to be instructed. Under him Gerbert studied mathematics—*mathesis*—with great dedication and effectiveness. But when Divinity wished to make already-darkening Gaul shine with a great light, it inspired the duke and the bishop mentioned above to go to Rome to pray. After making the necessary preparations, they set out and took the young man entrusted to them with them.

When they had entered the City, and after prayers had been poured out before the holy apostles, they approached the pope of blessed memory [lacuna]. They revealed themselves to him and most pleasantly imparted to him whatever seemed appropriate from their own affairs.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0101], “Galliam” is cut away; the manuscript reads “...gus.” “Quotlibet” corrects “qtlibet.” The note “Aurillac, in the prefecture of Cantal” identifies Gerbert’s monastery. Hatto was bishop of Auch. The pope was John XIII, who occupied the see from October 965 to 5 September 972.

44. **How Atto, after remaining in Rome, departed.** — The pope did not fail to notice the young man’s diligence and his desire to learn. Since music and astronomy were then entirely unknown in Italy, the pope soon informed King Otto of Germany and Italy through a legate that a young man had arrived there who knew mathematics very well and could teach his subjects vigorously.

The king soon suggested to the pope that he should retain the young man and in no way provide him with an opportunity to return. The pope also most tactfully informed the duke and the bishop who had come from Spain that the king wished to retain the young man for a time and would shortly send him back with honor; he would moreover repay them with thanks for this favor.

Thus the duke and the bishop were persuaded that, after leaving the young man under these conditions, they themselves should turn back and return to Spain. The young man, therefore, left with the pope, was presented by him to the king. When questioned about his discipline, he replied that he was sufficiently capable in mathematics but wished to acquire knowledge of logic. Since he was striving to attain this, he did not remain there very long as a teacher.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0101], “tto, mora, s” is cut away; the note is printed three times. One further word is cut away.

45. **How he was entrusted by King Otto to a teacher of logic.** — At that time G., archdeacon of Reims, was regarded as highly distinguished in logic. During that same period he was also sent as an envoy from Lothair, king of the Franks, to Otto, king of Italy. Delighted by his arrival, the young man approached the king and obtained permission to be entrusted to G[lacuna]o. He remained with G[lacuna]o for some time and was brought by him to Reims.

Receiving from him instruction in logic, he made very rapid progress. G[lacuna]s, however, when he devoted himself to mathematics, was overcome by the difficulty of the discipline and was rejected by music. Meanwhile Gerbert, commended to the metropolitan by the distinction of his studies, won his favor above all others. Consequently, when the metropolitan asked him, he brought him groups of students to be instructed in the arts.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0101], “ab, mis” is cut away; the note is printed twice.

46. **The order of books he followed in teaching.** — Proceeding through dialectic in the order of the books, he explained it by means of lucid expressions of its propositions. First he expounded Porphyry’s *Isagoge*, that is, *Introduction*, according to the translation of Victorinus the rhetorician; then he explained the same work according to Manlius.

Next he carefully elucidated Aristotle’s book of the *Categories*, that is, the *Predicaments*. He showed with great precision the nature of the labor required by the *Peri Hermeneias*, that is, the book *On Interpretation*. After this he presented to his pupils the *Topics*, that is, the seats of arguments, translated by Tullius from Greek into Latin and clarified by the consul Manlius in six books of commentary.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0101], “or, libr, do, ser” is cut away; the note is printed four times. The manuscript reads “aristelis” for *Aristotelis*.

47. **What provision he made for advancing his students in rhetoric.** — He also usefully read and explained the four books on the differentiae of the *Topics*, two books on categorical syllogisms, three on hypothetical syllogisms, one book of definitions, and likewise one of divisions.

After completing this work, when he wished to advance his students to rhetoric, he was concerned that one could not reach the art of oratory without the modes of expression that must be learned from poets. He therefore introduced poets, with whom he thought they should become familiar.

He accordingly read and taught Virgil, Statius, and Terence among the poets; Juvenal, Persius, and Horace among the satirists; and Lucan, the historian. After making them familiar with these authors and forming them in their modes of expression, he led them on to rhetoric.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0101], “ve, icis” is cut away; the note is printed twice. At [Col. 0103], “it” is cut away.

48. **Why he introduced a sophist to them.** — Once they had been equipped in this way, he introduced a sophist, under whom they could exercise themselves in controversies and argue according to the art in such a way that they appeared to act beyond the art—something regarded as the chief achievement of an orator.

But enough about logic. It does not seem inappropriate to say how much toil was expended in mathematics. For arithmetic, which is the first discipline of mathematics, he adapted by arranging it appropriately.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0103], “is, am, erit” is cut away; the note is printed three times.

49. **What labor was expended in the mathematical disciplines.** — From there he also made music, long unknown in Gaul, widely known. Arranging its kinds on the monochord, distinguishing their consonances, or symphonies, by tones and semitones, as well as by ditones and dieses, and distributing the tones rationally among the sounds, he reduced it to the fullest possible understanding.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0103], “bor, emati, it” is cut away; the note is printed three times.

50. **The construction of the solid sphere.** — It is not useless to describe with how much toil he gathered the principles of astronomy, so that both the sagacity of so great a man may be recognized and the effectiveness of the discipline may be most conveniently grasped by the reader.

Although the subject is almost beyond comprehension, he nevertheless brought it to knowledge with the aid of certain instruments, not without provoking admiration. First, reasoning from the fact that the sphere of the world is solid and round, he represented the greater sphere by means of a smaller likeness made of solid, rounded wood.

When he inclined it upon the horizon by means of its two poles, he assigned the northern constellations to the more elevated pole and the southern ones to the lower. He regulated its position by the circle called by the Greeks *horizon* and by the Latins *limiting* or *determining*, because on it he distinguishes and limits the signs that are visible from those that are not visible.

Having set it on the horizon so that it might usefully and plausibly demonstrate both the rising and setting of the constellations, he set forth the natures of things and instructed his pupils in the apprehension of the constellations. At night he devoted himself to the burning stars and arranged that they should observe how these were inclined in the various regions of the world, both at their rising and at their setting.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0103], “s, so, comp.” is cut away; the note is printed three times.

51. **The comprehension of the intelligible circles.** — The circles called by the Greeks *parallels* and by the Latins *equidistant*, which are unquestionably incorporeal, are also known to have been comprehended by him through this art.

He made a semicircle divided by a straight diameter. He made this diameter into a tube, at whose extremities he established that the two poles, the northern and the southern, should be marked. He divided the semicircle from pole to pole into thirty parts.

After marking off six of these from the pole, he attached a tube by which the circular line of the Arctic circle could be indicated. After these he separated five more and added another tube to indicate the summer circulation. From that point he divided four more and again added a tube, so that the equinoctial circle could be represented. He divided the remaining space up to the southern pole by the same measurements.

The efficacy of this instrument was such that, when its diameter was directed toward the pole and the extension of the semicircle turned upward, it afforded scientific knowledge of circles not previously apprehended by sight and stored them deep in memory.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0103], “In, li, compre” is cut away; the note is printed twice. A surviving editorial note reads: “But this concerns the intelligible circles. Nor would it be tiresome to say with what zeal he also disclosed the circles of the wandering stars. What follows is erased.”

52. **The construction of a sphere especially suited to learning about the planets.** — Since the circles of the wandering stars move within the world and strive in opposite directions, he did not lack the skill by which they could be seen by an investigator.

First he made a circular sphere, that is, one composed entirely of circles. In it he interwove two circles called by the Greeks *coluri* and by the Latins *intersecting*, because they intersect one another; at their extremities he fixed the poles.

He placed across the colures five other circles called *parallels*, so that thirty parts from pole to pole divided the hemisphere—and this neither casually nor confusedly. For, of the thirty parts of the hemisphere from pole to pole, he established six from the pole to the first circle; five from the first to the second; four from the second to the third; likewise four from the third to the fourth; five from the fourth to the fifth; and six from the fifth to the pole.

Across these circles he inclined the circle called by the Greeks *loxos*, or *zōē*, and by the Latins *oblique* or *vital*, because it contains the figures of living creatures among the stars. Within this oblique circle he suspended the circles of the wandering stars by a marvelous device. He demonstrated most effectively their apsides, their heights, and even their distances from one another.

It is not convenient to set out here how this was done, because of the length of the explanation, lest we seem to depart too far from our subject.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0103], “no, tis” is cut away; the note is printed twice. The phrase “which are called by the Greeks parallels and by the Latins equidistant” is deleted.

53. **Another construction of a sphere suitable for learning the constellations.** — In addition to these he made another circular sphere. Within it he did not place circles; rather, above it he fashioned the figures of the constellations with iron and bronze wires. In place of an axis he passed through a tube by which the celestial pole could be marked, so that, once it had been observed, the apparatus could be aligned with the heavens.

The result was that the stars of each constellation were enclosed within the corresponding constellation of this sphere. There was also something divine about it: if someone ignorant of the art were shown one constellation, he could recognize the others throughout the sphere without a teacher.

From this he also instructed his students generously. Thus far concerning astronomy.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0103], “Alia, comp, cogn, ido” is cut away; the note is printed three times.

54. **The construction of the abacus.** — In geometry, too, no less labor was expended in teaching. For the introduction to this discipline he constructed an abacus, that is, a table suited to measurement, by the work of a shield-maker.

Dividing its length into twenty-seven parts, he arranged in them nine signs representing every number. In imitation of these he made a thousand horn characters, which, by being moved through the twenty-seven parts of the abacus, indicated the multiplication or division of each number. By this device numbers were divided or multiplied with such economy that, because of the immense quantity involved, they could be understood more readily than demonstrated in words.

Whoever desires to know this science fully should read the book he wrote to C., the grammarian; there he will find these matters treated sufficiently and abundantly.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0105], “confe, ci” is cut away; the note is printed twice. The deleted wording reads: “in which previously Gaul had possessed no writings, how much labour was expended cannot be adequately told.” At [Col. 0105D]: “To Constantine, *On the Division of Numbers*.”

55. **(969.) Gerbert’s fame spread through Gaul and Italy.** — He was fervent in his studies, and the number of his students increased day by day. The name of so great a teacher was spread not only throughout Gaul but also among the peoples of Germany. It crossed the Alps and spread into Italy, as far as the Tyrrhenian and Adriatic seas.

At that time Otricus was considered distinguished in Saxony. When he had heard the philosopher’s fame and observed that in every disputation he used a systematic division of things, he arranged among his people that some diagrams of divided subjects should be brought to him from the philosopher’s school—especially a diagram of philosophy—so that, by examining its orderly division, he might more easily determine whether the man who appeared to be philosophizing truly understood, since he professed knowledge of divine and human matters.

A certain Saxon was therefore sent to Reims, as one who seemed suitable for this task. While attending the school and carefully collecting the divisions of genera arranged by Gerbert, he nevertheless made considerable disorder in the particular division that fully divides philosophy.

56. **Gerbert’s philosophical diagram corrupted by malicious men and criticized by Otricus.** — For although Gerbert had placed mathematics and physics as equal and coeval disciplines, this man subordinated mathematics to physics as a species to a genus; it is uncertain whether he did this deliberately or by mistake.

Thus, together with a multiplicity of divisions of different things, the diagram was brought to Otricus. He examined it with the greatest care and accused Gerbert before his own people of having divided the subjects badly, because the diagram falsely represented one of two equal species as substituted for the other as a species under a genus. On this account he boldly declared that Gerbert had understood nothing of philosophy.

He also said that Gerbert was completely ignorant of the subject in which divine and human matters consist, without which no one should philosophize. He therefore brought the same diagram to the palace and explained it before the emperor Otto and those who appeared to be wiser. Since the emperor himself was regarded as extremely devoted to such studies, he wondered whether Gerbert had erred. He had seen him and had heard him disputing more than once. Hence he very much desired Gerbert himself to resolve the aforementioned diagram. The opportunity was not lacking.

57. **(970.)** The venerable Adalbero, metropolitan of Reims, was going to Rome with Gerbert in that same year and found the emperor at Pavia with Otricus. He was received by him magnificently and was taken by ship down the Po to Ravenna.

At the appropriate time, by order of the emperor, all the wise men who had gathered were assembled within the palace. The venerable metropolitan mentioned above was present, as was Abbot Adso of Dervy, who had come with the metropolitan. Otricus too was present, the man who in the preceding year had shown himself Gerbert’s critic.

A considerable number of scholars had also gathered, eagerly awaiting the impending dispute. They were wondering whether anyone would dare resist Otricus, the most learned of them. The emperor too was shrewdly arranging for such a contest to take place.

He was trying to set the unwary Gerbert against Otricus, so that, if Gerbert were attacked while off guard, he might be driven to greater eagerness for argument in opposition. He encouraged Otricus to propose many points but resolve none. When all these men had taken their places in order, the emperor, seated among them, began from his elevated position as follows:

*Editorial apparatus:* Otto stayed at Pavia from January 970, moved to Ravenna in March, and issued diplomas at Ferrara on the 22nd and at Ravenna on the 30th of that month. The words “who had considered the matter, and on that account” are deleted. “Otrico” corrects “eorum doctissimo.” “Ex ordine” corrects “jussi.”

58. **Emperor Otto’s address to the assembly of wise men concerning the correction of the diagram.** — “Human knowledge, as I suppose, is improved by frequent meditation or practice whenever the subject matter of things is competently arranged and expressed by carefully chosen words through the agency of learned men.

For when we often grow sluggish through leisure, if we are challenged by the questions of others, we are immediately stirred to the most useful meditation. From this the knowledge of things has been drawn forth by the most learned. From this it is that what they have brought forth has been handed down in books and left to us for the glory of beneficial exercise.

Let us therefore also be affected by certain questions, through which the mind may be led to more excellent and more certain understanding. Come, then, I say: let us now reconsider that diagram of the parts of philosophy which was shown to us last year.

Let everyone examine it most carefully, and let each say what he thinks either in its favor or against it. If it needs no external support, let it be strengthened by the approval of all of you. But if it appears to require correction, let it either be rejected by the judgments of the wise or brought back to proper form. Let it now be brought forward for inspection.”

Then Otricus produced it openly and replied that it had been arranged in this manner by Gerbert and accepted and written down by his students; he handed it to the august lord to read. After it had been read, it was brought to Gerbert. He carefully went through it, approving one part and criticizing another, and at the same time asserted that he had not arranged it in that manner.

59. **The theoretical division of philosophy into species.** — When the emperor asked him to correct it, he said:

“Since, great Caesar Augustus, I see that you are superior to all these men, I shall obey your commands, as is fitting. Nor will I be moved by the envy of malicious men, at whose instigation this was done: a perfectly correct and lucid division of philosophy, recently arranged by me, was corrupted by the substitution of a single species.

I therefore say that mathematics, physics, and theology belong equally beneath the same genus and that they participate equally in their genus. It is impossible for one and the same species, in one and the same respect, both to be equal to another species and to be subordinated to it as a species to a genus.

That is my opinion on these matters. But if anyone contends against it, let him seek a reason for doing so and make us understand what perhaps the very nature of things has not yet seemed to grant to anyone.”

*Editorial apparatus:* The deleted words read: “For I do not fail to know that malicious men continually assail every good thing with calumnies.”

60. **The division of philosophy.** — At this, with the emperor’s indication, Otricus said:

“Since you have touched briefly upon several parts of philosophy, you ought to divide it fully and explain the division. In this way it may be possible, from a plausible division, to remove from you the suspicion of having produced a faulty diagram.”

Then Gerbert said:

“Although it is well established that philosophy is the comprehension of the truth of divine and human things, nevertheless, so that we may not be accused of laziness and so that some of the hearers may make progress, I shall not hesitate to speak according to the division of Vitruvius and Boethius.

Philosophy is a genus; its species are practical and theoretical. The species of practical philosophy, I say, are administrative, distributive, and civil. Under theoretical philosophy are understood, not improperly, natural physics, intelligible mathematics, and intellectual theology. Again, we place mathematics under physics, not without reason.”

61. **Otricus’s futile criticism of the division and Gerbert’s reply.** — Attempting to pursue what remained, Otricus added:

“I am exceedingly surprised that you have subordinated mathematics so closely to physics, since a subordinate genus, physiology, may be understood between them. For it seems very faulty if a part sought from too great a distance is brought into the division of a genus.”

Gerbert replied:

“For that very reason it seems more surprising that I should have subordinated mathematics to physics, its coeval, as a species. Since coeval disciplines are held under the same genus, it seems deserving of still greater astonishment if one is subordinated to the other.

But I say that physiology is not the genus of physics, as you propose, and I assert that there is no other difference between them than the one I recognize between philosophy and philology. Otherwise, philology would be admitted to be the genus of philosophy.”

At this the multitude of scholars became angry that the division of philosophy had been interrupted and requested that it be resumed before the emperor. Otricus, however, said shortly afterward that it should be resumed only after the nature of philosophy itself had first been considered. Turning his attention to Gerbert, he asked what the cause of philosophy was.

62. **What is the cause of the created world?** — When Gerbert asked him to state more clearly what he meant—namely, whether he meant the cause by which philosophy was discovered or the cause to which its discovery was owed—Otricus immediately replied:

“I mean the very cause for which it appears to have been discovered.”

Then Gerbert said:

“Since it is now clear what you propose, I say that it was discovered for this reason: so that through it we may know divine and human things.”

Otricus replied:

“Why have you named the cause of one thing in so many expressions, when perhaps it could have been named in one, and it is characteristic of philosophers to strive for brevity?”

63. **That not all names of causes are expressed in single words.** — Gerbert replied:

“Not all causes can be expressed in a single word. For when Plato declared the cause of the created world to be God’s good will, he made it clear in not one but three words; it is evident that the cause of the created world could not otherwise have been expressed.

For if he had said that will is the cause, the consequence would not have followed; any will whatever would appear to be meant, which is not the case.”

Otricus then said:

“If he had said that God’s will is the cause of the created world, it would have been expressed more briefly and sufficiently, since God’s will has never been anything except good. No one denies that God’s will is good.”

Gerbert replied:

“On this point I do not at all contradict you. But consider: it is established that God alone is good in substance, whereas every creature is good by participation. To express the quality of his nature, the word ‘good’ was added, since this is proper to him and not to every creature.

In any event, whatever the matter may be, it is undoubtedly established that not all names of causes can be expressed in one word. What, then, do you say is the cause of a shadow? Can this be indicated in a single word?”

64. **What is the cause of a shadow?** — “I say that the cause of a shadow is a body placed in the way of light. This cannot possibly be said more briefly. For if you say that a body is the cause of a shadow, you have stated something too general. If you wish to say ‘a body placed in the way,’ that too does not go far enough, insofar as something is still left out.

There are some bodies, and even some bodies placed in different positions, that cannot be the cause of a shadow. I do not deny that the causes of many things are expressed in single words, such as genera, which no one is unaware are the causes of species—for example, substance, quantity, and quality.

Other things, however, are not expressed simply, such as ‘rational’ in relation to ‘mortal.’”

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0107], “uae, sit, a, umbr” is cut away; the note is printed four times.

65. **Which is more comprehensive, “rational” or “mortal”?** — Otricus, greatly surprised, then said:

“Do you subordinate mortal to rational? Who does not know that ‘rational’ includes God, an angel, and a human being, whereas ‘mortal,’ being greater and more comprehensive, gathers together all mortal things and, through them, infinite things?”

Gerbert replied:

“If, following Porphyry and Boethius, you considered the division of substance by a suitable partition down to individuals, you would undoubtedly regard ‘rational’ as more comprehensive than ‘mortal’; and it is readily possible to explain this with appropriate arguments.

Since it is established that substance is the most general genus and can be divided through subordinate genera down to individuals, it must be considered whether all subordinate genera are expressed in single words.

It is plainly evident, however, that some terms are expressed in a single word and others in several: in a single word, as ‘body’; in several, as ‘animate and sensible.’

By the same reasoning, the subordinate term ‘rational animal’ is predicated of the subject ‘rational mortal animal.’ I do not say that the simple term ‘rational’ is predicated of the simple term ‘mortal’; that does not follow. Rather, I say that ‘rational,’ joined to ‘animal,’ is predicated of ‘mortal,’ joined to ‘rational animal.’”

As he flowed on at great length in words and propositions and was preparing to say still more, the emperor’s nod brought the disputation to an end, since they had nearly consumed the entire day with these matters and the listeners were already wearied by the long and continuous argument.

Gerbert was therefore magnificently rewarded by the emperor and returned illustriously to Gaul with his metropolitan.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0109], “conti, tius, atio an, tale” is cut away; the note is printed three times. “Alia” corrects “nova.” “Dicere pararet” corrects “omnes exspectarent.”

66. **A synod held at Saint Magram.** — At the same time Queen Emma and Adalbero, bishop of Laon, were accused of the disgraceful crime of sexual misconduct. The accusation was nevertheless pursued secretly, without any manifest witness to the intention. But since the matter, though spoken privately, had reached everyone’s ears, the bishops thought it should be investigated, lest their brother and fellow bishop be subjected to so great an infamy.

The metropolitan mentioned above therefore convened a synod of bishops at Saint Magram, a place belonging to the diocese of Reims. After they had taken their seats and discussed each useful matter, when the metropolitan [lacuna: nearly one line, and perhaps several further lines, have been cut away].

*Editorial apparatus:* One manuscript reads “E. R. et Ad. L.”

67. **Otto’s elevation to kingship by the Germans and Belgians.** — After the death of Lord Otto, king of the Germans, his son Otto was made king by the Germans and Belgians. He administered the state vigorously and beneficially: a man of great intellect and complete virtue, distinguished by his knowledge of the liberal arts, so that in debate he both proposed arguments according to the art and drew plausible conclusions.

The kingdom of Germany, together with part of Gaul, remained in his possession until the final day of his life, though sometimes in an uncertain condition. For between him and Lothair, king of the Gauls, there were at times immense hatred and an evenly balanced outcome.

When Belgium was held by Otto and attacked by Lothair, they contrived deceptions or mustered forces against one another, since each maintained that his own father had held it and neither distrusted his ability to defend it with a multitude of troops. For it had belonged to Lothair’s father Louis, and after Louis had given it away, Otto, the father of this Otto, obtained it. Thus Belgium was the original cause and stimulus of their discord.

*Editorial apparatus:* “Creatus” corrects “elevatus.” “Quandoque” corrects “plerumque.” The marginal note reads: “Richer is talking nonsense.”

68. **Lothair’s indignation against Otto.** — While Otto was staying at the palace of Aachen with his pregnant wife Theophanu, Lothair was fiercely angered that he had come so near. He therefore gathered Hugh, duke of the Franks, and the other leading men of the kingdom at Laon to seek their counsel.

The duke came forward. The others, too, whose advice was required, were admitted successively before the king. When they had taken their seats, the king declared that a twofold injury had been inflicted upon him: part of his kingdom had been usurped by an enemy, and the enemy himself had rashly approached his borders.

He said that it was no greater injury that the enemy held the territory than that, while holding it, he had not feared to approach his borders. He also declared that he wished to avenge this with great eagerness if they were willing to follow his counsel, and that he could not restrain himself from this intention if he did not lack a sufficient number of soldiers. He added that he would one day repay them with thanks if they undertook with equanimity the action he desired.

*Editorial apparatus:* At [Col. 0109], “io, n” is cut away.

69. **The spontaneous attack of the Gauls against Otto.** — Immediately the duke and the other leading men, without deliberation or consultation, endorsed the king’s proposal. They promised that they would go voluntarily with the king and either capture Otto, kill him, or drive him into flight.

The plan of this enterprise, kept concealed, could at that time come to the knowledge of only a few, so that those who were marching did not know where they were going. At length the assembled army advanced so densely that the upright spear shafts suggested a grove rather than weapons. It proceeded in wedges distinguished by a standard.

When they had crossed the fords of the Meuse, the centurions, appointed and arranged by companies of a hundred, carefully observed that Otto did not possess a sufficient army. They therefore drew near and proclaimed the enemy’s great lack of military resources.

*Editorial apparatus:* The deleted words read: “The Gauls deliberate and arrange the affair.” *Simbolo* means “by a banner.” The words “Centuriati i.” are deleted.

70. **Otto’s withdrawal before Lothair.** — When these reports were brought to Otto’s ears, he, being a man of bold spirit, replied that Lothair had never undertaken such an action. Nor, he said, could Lothair have approached his territories, since he had neither enough soldiers nor sufficient confidence in his own men.

But when one person after another said that Lothair was already there and persisted in saying so, Otto is said to have declared that nothing could persuade him to believe them unless he himself learned it by seeing it with his own eyes.

He therefore called for and brought out horses and rode forward to see. He perceived Lothair advancing with twenty thousand men. He considered at one moment resisting, at another withdrawing for a time and returning later with a large army.

At last, because Lothair was pressing him, he could not remain. He withdrew, not without tears, with his wife Theophanu and the leading men of the kingdom, abandoning the palace and the royal furnishings.

*Editorial apparatus:* The phrase “with the princes” is deleted. One manuscript reads “XX.”

71. **Lothair arrives with his army and plunders the palace.** — Lothair arrived with his army, believing that he would capture Otto. And indeed he would have done so if his army had not been delayed on the road by transport duties. For if he had arrived one day earlier, before Otto’s departure, he could have captured him or put him to death.

The palace was therefore occupied by the enemies. The royal tables were overturned. The arrangements of food were plundered by the camp servants. The royal insignia were also snatched from the inner chambers and carried away.

They turned the bronze eagle, which Charles the Great had fixed atop the palace as though flying, toward the south-east wind (*Vulturnus*). For the Germans had turned it toward the west, subtly signifying that the Gauls could at some time be defeated by their cavalry.

After making an unsuccessful attack, Lothair led his army back without taking hostages or securing a peace agreement, confident that he would return later.

*Editorial apparatus:* The words “against the Gauls” are deleted.

### 72. Otto Wins Back His Followers

Otto, upon whom the whole burden of disaster had fallen, won his men over to himself by numerous gifts and many acts of favor. Eager as he was to conquer, he recalled those whom he had injured, either by returning what he had taken from them or by granting what he had promised. When all had been pacified and recalled—if any had perhaps departed [Note: the words “in mind” are deleted]—and the leading men of the realms had been gathered together, he addressed them as follows:

### 73. Otto’s Speech to His Followers

“I did not wish you, illustrious men, to assemble here without good reason. Your excellence prompted me to seek counsel from you, men whom both intelligence adorns and strength of character shapes. Nor did I hesitate to seek from you the judgment of the best counsel, since I have not forgotten with what spirit and what courage you have until now remained faithful. In former days, most illustrious men, you strove with immense courage for the honor and glory of distinguished praise; you shone both in counsel and as unconquered in war. Now too we must strive with the same courage, lest disgraceful infamy follow upon distinguished praise.

“Therefore strive with all your strength, and if you have incurred any dishonor, remove it from such great renown. You are not unaware that recently we suffered the disgrace of flight at Lotharius’s hands. It is fitting for your renown, and the present hour requires it, while opportunity also urges it, that this disgrace be repelled not only by war but even by death. If, then, you are more ready to command than to serve, while your age is vigorous and your spirit strong, do not regard this deed as insignificant. By your immense courage make yourselves objects of fear to those before whom you were ignoble and common.”

After this speech, everyone was persuaded that it should be done.

### 74. The Cavalry into Gaul

Meanwhile Otto was preparing to go into Gaul with thirty thousand cavalry [Note: “XXX”]. Without delay, he set out after sending forward centurions. He filled Celtic Gaul with his army, burning part of it and laying waste to another part. Thus, in turn, pressing Lotharius hard because he did not have a sufficient number of soldiers, he compelled him to cross the Seine and forced him, groaning, to go to the duke.

Disturbed, therefore, by the enemy’s sudden arrival, the king went to Étampes [Note: Étampes], while the duke remained at Paris to gather an army. While these things were happening, Otto hurried forward and plundered and burned the royal estate at Attigny. Passing through the territory of the city of Reims, he showed great honor to Saint Remigius. He also passed by the city of Soissons and, venerating Saint Medardus, nearly plundered the palace at Compiègne.

The advance centurions, moreover, without his knowledge, utterly demolished and burned the monastery of Saint Balthild at Chelles. Deeply grieved by this, he assigned many resources for its restoration. At last he reached the Seine, pitched his army’s tents there, with Paris in view, and ravaged nearly the entire region for three days.

### 75. The Two Armies Separated by the Seine

The cavalry therefore went about with the camp-followers, carrying provisions from a distance of 160 stadia in every direction. Since the Seine flowed between them, neither army approached the other. The duke was gathering soldiers on the opposite bank of the river, but those three days were insufficient to assemble an adequate number of troops, and it was not possible to obtain a force with which to engage.

[Note: The encounter of the two men, one a German and the other a Gaul, does not seem to be something that should be passed over; the following words, beginning “When each of the two …,” are deleted.]

### 76. Single Combat between Two Men

While both armies were thus in an uncertain position and each side was wholly intent upon seeking victory, a certain German, confident both in spirit and in strength, came forward armed for single combat. He offered to meet one opponent alone at the bridge, where the gates were secured with bars and iron bolts.

He repeatedly shouted for an enemy to come and fight him alone. When he began to pour out certain insults against the Gauls, and no one answered him, the guards reported to the duke and to the other leaders—who had by then arrived in small numbers—that at the bridge gate there was a man who was offering to fight one opponent alone, and who was provoking the leaders with insults and verbal abuse. He declared that he would not withdraw unless either someone met him in single combat or the gates were cut down and the whole army was admitted.

Unable to bear this insult, the duke urged the recruits [Note: “soldiers,” and above “or recruits,” in the manuscript] to drive back the madman [Note: corrected from “the barking dog” to “the madman”], and, once purged of so great a disgrace, to seek for themselves the glory of a renowned name [Note: “not merely themselves but also the whole nation,” deleted, along with a continuation extending indefinitely].

Immediately, many men burning with courage offered themselves for resistance. One of the many, Ivo [Note: the name is written with a capital letter and underlined; it seems that it ought to be deleted], was chosen and came forward to fight. A reward was promised to the brave man, and when the bars had been removed, the gates were opened.

Each opponent advanced to meet the other. Raising their shields and resisting with their weapons, they exchanged a few insults in a fury of spirit. At last the German hurled his weapon and pierced the Gaul’s shield with a heavy blow. When he drew his sword and was pressing his attack, the Gaul immediately struck him with a deflected weapon and deprived him of life [Note: corrected from “arms” to “life”].

The Gaul, victorious, carried away the weapons he had seized from his enemy and presented them to the duke. The brave man asked for and received his reward.

### 77. Otto’s Departure from Gaul and the Flight of His Men

Otto, aware that the army of the Gauls was gradually gathering, and knowing that his own forces could be diminished both by so long a march and by the enemy’s attacks, decided to return. At the given signal, they moved the camp. They also hastened to accelerate the transport of baggage; after everything had been moved, they proceeded briskly, though not without fear.

Some had already crossed the fords of the Aisne, while others were entering them, when an army sent by the king arrived behind those who were hurrying onward. Those who were found were immediately cut down by the enemy’s swords—many of them, certainly, but none distinguished by name.

[Editorial note: Here it seems appropriate to record an ancient inscription preserved in the royal codex at Paris, no. 3839 A, on parchment, twelfth century, pages 143–144:

“Fulco, count of Jerusalem, caused this inscription to be written in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Loches, where he was buried with great honor, because of the gifts made to his predecessors by the king of France.

“When God wished to raise Robert, the duke’s son, to be king, Geoffrey Grisagonella served his lord, King Robert, with three thousand armed men. Otto, king of the Germans, had besieged Montmartre [the manuscript has: ‘the Mount of Mortiaci’] with all his Saxon and Danish forces and was making many disgraceful assaults upon the city of Paris.

“In this crisis of battle, King Robert and his father entrusted the command of the first division to Count Geoffrey Grisagonella and appointed him duke and counselor for pursuing the German army. King Robert therefore pursued the German king, with Geoffrey Grisagonella leading the way, as far as the River Aisne [the manuscript has: ‘Esne’]. Count Geoffrey, skilled and experienced in warfare, had inflicted such slaughter upon the enemy beside the river before King Robert’s arrival that you might have thought it was tin rather than a river.

“After the Germans had been put to flight, King Robert, having convened a general council and acting on the counsel of his father and of the bishops, counts, and barons, gave Count Geoffrey whatever King Lotharius had possessed in his bishoprics, namely those of Anjou and Le Mans.”]

Meanwhile Otto departed with his army, made for Belgica, and there dismissed the campaign. He enjoyed such favor and goodwill among his men that they promised to expose themselves for him both to imminent danger and to every other peril.

### 78. Lotharius Considers Reconciliation

(980.) Lotharius, considering that Otto could be defeated neither by deception nor by force, often and at length debated with himself whether it would be preferable to stand against the enemy or to be reconciled with him.

If he stood against him, he thought it possible to corrupt the duke with wealth and cause him to fall back into friendship with Otto. If he were reconciled with the enemy, he thought this had to be done quickly, lest the duke perceive it and himself also wish to be reconciled. He was troubled by such thoughts day after day. From then on he regarded the duke with suspicion for both these reasons.

Nevertheless, those who were consulting together decided that Otto should be restored to the king’s friendship, because he was a man of courage and through him not only might the duke be subdued, but the tyrants of other peoples also might usefully be brought under control.

Ambassadors sent by Lotharius were received with the greatest generosity by Otto, and they worked to secure friendship between the two men without the duke’s knowledge.

### 79. Speech of the Gauls to Otto

“Until now,” they said, “those who loved discord, envy, and slaughter have flourished, since they held so much influence between the most noble kings. Discord was a delight to them, because they thought they could acquire much for themselves from kings who were at odds. Indeed, they were considering the common corruption of affairs so that, amid the disturbance, they might seize a position of greater glory and honor.

“But it will greatly benefit the commonwealth if the wickedness of the depraved, long since, is now restrained, and the virtue of good men shines forth with purer light. Let virtue therefore return and flourish between the most glorious kings, so that by your virtue the authors of such great evils may henceforth cease, and the commonwealth may be governed by your virtue rather than collapse through the envy of grasping men.

“You will both reign more securely when, joined in friendship, you possess two armies as one. If either of you decides to go to the farthest peoples of his realms, he will have the other as a brother and faithful guardian of his affairs. Let peace and friendship therefore please the most serene kings, whom kinship of blood has also joined. Let those whose discord brings corruption to the commonwealth be bound together by friendship; their concord will provide benefit and supply strength.”

### 80. Otto’s Reply to the Gauls

To this Otto replied:

“I know how great a corruption discord has often brought upon the commonwealth, when the leaders of realms have at times plotted against one another. Nor am I unaware how much safety friendship’s virtue has secured for the commonwealth.

“I confess that until now I have held peace and concord in the highest esteem and have always hated the envy and discord of malicious men. Therefore, reconcile the minds of those who are at odds through your efforts. I see that you are especially suited to this task, since previously, through mutual injury, we did great harm to the commonwealth. I approve the substance of your counsel. Let actions at last agree with words.”

Having won his agreement, the ambassadors returned. Reporting to each king the goodwill of the other, they brought the two kings into friendship. A time for conference was fixed, and a place convenient to both was appointed. Since the realms of both bordered one another around the River Meuse, they agreed to meet at a place called Margut.

### 81. Reconciliation of Kings Lotharius and Otto

They therefore met. Having given each other their right hands, they most graciously exchanged a kiss without any dispute. They confirmed their mutual friendship by oath.

The part of Belgica that had been in dispute passed into Otto’s jurisdiction. After establishing peace in his kingdom, Otto went to Italy and reached Rome, intending to visit his own people and inquire into the condition of the kingdom, to suppress any disturbances that might perhaps exist, and to restore to peace any leaders who might be at odds.

Lotharius, meanwhile, came to Laon and attended among his own people to whatever matters concerned him. He no longer had any hope in the duke, since he regarded him with considerable suspicion because he had sought peace by deception.

(981.) When all this was being publicly reported and some people, angered by it, were also grumbling on the duke’s behalf, the duke, concealing his sorrow with steadfast spirit, endured everything. As was his custom, he deliberately considered every matter, summoned the leading men, and sat down to deliver a speech.

### 82. The Duke’s Speech to His Followers

In their presence he began as follows:

“Counsel for a useful and honorable end is not sought from learned men without profit. To them alone one properly has recourse, and from them a plan of counsel is disclosed for a troubled situation. I judge you fit to give counsel [Note: Deleted in the manuscript: “men whom both the ability to think and the skill to speak have made more distinguished; men whom I do not doubt grieve over the ruin of the good, since they have resolved with immense courage to displease the wicked”], since I have not forgotten how often you have surpassed your adversaries in courage and intelligence.

“Since I do not doubt that, bound to me by hand and oath, you will preserve inviolable loyalty, I confidently seek counsel from faithful men. If it is granted to me, you too will share in it. If it is not offered, there may perhaps be no lack of loss, into which you may fall dishonorably.

“Since the matter concerns our lives, freely disclose useful counsel. You are not unaware with what subtlety King Lotharius deceived me through his tricks, when he wished to be reconciled with Otto without me and carried it out. He has entirely forgotten with what generosity of spirit I undertook so great a danger, since through me he recently put his enemy to flight and also secured Belgica for himself after its distinctive enemy standards had been taken away. What hope, then, should I expect any longer, when he has treacherously broken faith?”

### 83. The Counsel Given by the Duke’s Followers

The leading men replied:

“We know not only how often you have exposed your life with us on behalf of King Lotharius, but also how great a danger your renown still faces, if, as rumor has it, the two kings have conspired against you.

“For if you undertake a defense against one army, you will soon find both standing against you. If you strive against both, you must encounter countless disadvantages: an intolerable cavalry force, numerous ambushes, fires, and plunder—and, worst of all, the wicked rumors of a faithless populace. They will not say that we are defending ourselves against adversaries; they will accuse us of standing in rebellion against the king, reckless and perjured.

“They will also lie that one may approach any people whatsoever, so that men may withdraw from their lords without guilt or the sacrilege of perjury and arrogantly raise their necks against them.

“The final and useful counsel in this danger seems to us to be that, since two men have joined together against us, we should deprive one of the other. If one cannot be taken away from the other, at least we should bind one of them to us in friendship, so that, while one is devoted to us, he will not provide the other with strength or encouragement.

“This too is possible if, with caution and prudence, you approach Otto, who is now at Rome, after sending ambassadors ahead. Otto is not so lacking in intelligence that he does not know that you are superior to Lotharius in arms and resources, since he has often heard it and has experienced it himself. You will therefore obtain his friendship more easily. The closeness of your blood will also help, since in this matter you are related to him just as Lotharius is.”

### 84. The Duke Sends Ambassadors to Otto

This counsel, having been offered, was favorably received by the duke [Note: thus in the codex]. He therefore sent ambassadors and informed Otto at Rome of his intention. Otto received the ambassadors with remarkable goodwill and did not deny that he was entirely prepared for friendship between them. If the duke himself would come to him, so that each might experience more fully the strength of their friendship, he would receive him and his men fittingly and honorably.

The ambassadors returned and reported Otto’s message to the duke. The duke therefore took with him certain men of great prudence and shrewdness—namely Arnulf, bishop of Orléans, and Burchard, as well as [Note: the place is blank in the codex] [lacuna] other men who were especially necessary—and proceeded to Rome. He honored the holy apostles and then went to the king.

### 85. Otto’s Meeting with Hugh

Otto, wishing to win glory for himself, deliberately arranged that, after everyone had been sent out from the royal chamber, his sword should be placed upon a folding chair and that the duke should be introduced alone with only one bishop. Thus, while the king spoke [the transmitted word *latiariter* is uncertain], the bishop, as interpreter of Latin, would explain to the duke whatever was said to him.

They entered and were received by the king with great favor. The king laid aside his complaint over the injuries he had suffered and, giving the duke a kiss, graciously bestowed his favor upon him as a friend.

After many conversations concerning friendship, when the king was leaving and looked back toward the sword, the duke stepped slightly away from him and bent down to lift it and carry it behind the king. For this reason it had been left upon the chair: so that, when the duke carried the sword before everyone’s eyes, he might indicate that he would carry it in the future as well [Note: the wording is conjectural; the manuscript has fragmentary forms such as “all,” “with,” “sword,” “behind,” “he might indicate,” and “would carry”].

The bishop, however, advising the duke, snatched the sword from his hand and himself carried it as he walked behind the king. The king admired both his prudence and his shrewdness and afterward frequently mentioned him among his own men with praise. He also received the duke into very close friendship and had him escorted with honor and peace almost as far as the Alps.

### 86. Lotharius’s Letter to Conrad

King Lotharius, together with Queen Emma, was everywhere preparing ambushes and setting traps so that they might capture the duke on his return. He therefore sent a letter to Conrad, king of the Alemanni, in the following terms:

“Lotharius, king by the grace of God of the Franks, to Conrad, king of the Alemanni, whatever is due to him.

“It has always been agreeable to me to preserve inviolate the friendship established between us long ago. Since many benefits can proceed from it for me, I have thought it useful to disclose something to you and to ask that it be done according to my wishes.

“Know that until now I have regarded Duke Hugh as a friend. But when I discovered that he was secretly my enemy, I withdrew from his intimacy. Now, as he goes to Rome, he has approached Otto, intending to persuade him greatly to my disgrace and to the ruin of my kingdom. Therefore strive with all your strength and all your ingenuity to prevent him from escaping.

“Farewell.” [Note: “Farewell.”]

Scouts were therefore stationed all around, among the steep mountain slopes and crags and at the exits of the roads, waiting for his arrival.

### 87. Queen Emma’s Letter to Her Mother

Queen Emma likewise sent her mother a letter in the following terms:

“To Adelaide, my mother, ever august empress, Emma, queen of the Franks, sends greetings.

“Although I am separated from you by a great distance of land, I, your daughter, nevertheless ask aid from my mother. Duke Hugh, by his schemes, has not only drawn the leading men of our kingdom away from their loyalty to us, but is also attempting to turn my brother Otto away from us. For this reason he has approached him at Rome.

“Therefore, lest he boast that he has achieved his desire completely, I, your suppliant daughter, ask you, my mother, to impede so great an enemy on his return. If it can be done, either hold him captive or do not allow him to return unpunished.

“But lest he escape you through his evasive tricks, I have taken care to have communicated to you the distinctive features of his entire appearance.”

She then went on to describe the distinguishing features of his eyes, ears, lips, teeth, and nose, as well as those of the remaining parts of his body. She also explained the tenor of his speech, making him recognizable through these signs and identifying him to those who did not know him.

### 88. Hugh Escapes the Ambush in Disguise

The duke, who was not unaware of these plans, hastened his return. Fearing the plots, he changed his clothing and pretended to be one of the attendants. He himself drove and urged on the horses carrying loads. He loaded and unloaded the baggage and made himself ready to serve everyone.

With such skill did he disguise himself as duke in a lowly garment and unkempt appearance that he both passed through places where ambushes had been laid, which he could not avoid, and effectively deceived those lying in wait.

At one lodging he was nearly discovered. When it was time to go to bed, a bed was prepared for him with careful arrangements, and everyone gathered around him and offered their services. Some, kneeling, pulled off his leggings, while others received them after they had been removed. Others, sitting below him, rubbed the seated man’s bare feet and cleaned them with the folds of their garments.

The host watched this through the cracks of the door. When they discovered that he had been spying, they immediately summoned him, lest he reveal the matter, and let him in. After threatening him with death with drawn swords if he uttered a sound, they seized him, bound his hands and feet, and threw him into a prison.

With his voice suppressed, he lay there, bent together, until twilight [Note: the codex reads “conquexus”]. After the night had passed, they rose at the first light. They took the host, placed him on a horse, and carried him away until they had passed beyond the suspicious places. Once these had been crossed, they set him down and released him, then completed the rest of their journey rapidly.

He likewise often escaped the schemes of King Conrad by pretending and concealing his identity, since the plotters also worked diligently to devise their deceptions. At last, secure from such great dangers, he reached Gaul.

### 89. The Damage Caused by the Rivalries

When each side had learned of the other’s plots, they raged against one another with such cruelty—not by open arms but through hidden ambushes—that for several years the commonwealth suffered greatly while its leaders were at odds.

At that time, certain wicked men also committed many usurpations, oppressed the miserable, and inflicted criminal calamities upon those who were less powerful. When the wiser men of both sides assembled to deliberate together, they complained with great compassion that the leaders were at odds.

### 90. Reconciliation of Lotharius and Hugh

They therefore decided that supporters of one side should cross over to the other to urge reconciliation, so that, once either man had been won over by the goodwill of the other, he might yield more easily and repent more usefully of the friendship that had been injured.

This counsel was put into effect not long afterward. They were persuaded most effectively and became joined to one another by the greatest affection. Thus the power of friendship between both sides also appeared to have been firmly established.

### 91. Louis’s Advancement to the Kingdom of the Franks

When the king wished his son Louis to succeed him in the kingdom and also sought to have him ordained by the duke, the duke replied that he would undertake this ordination with a generous spirit.

After sending ambassadors, he gathered the leaders of the realms at Compiègne. There, on the holy day of Pentecost, Louis was acclaimed king by the duke and the other leaders and was advanced to the kingdom of the Franks by Adalberon, metropolitan bishop of Reims, a man worthy of remembrance.

[Note: Since these events had already occurred in the year 979, the order of events seems to have been reversed by our author, unless Louis was perhaps confirmed as king in 981 with Hugh’s approval. In two charters of Lotharius, dated July 9 of the year 981—and only in those—I read the formula: “Given … while his son, the lord Louis, an outstanding youth, is reigning in his third year.”]

With two men therefore reigning, the duke commended himself for many days through great affability and various services, exalting the royal dignity in every respect and showing himself their suppliant [Note: “in every respect” is deleted] while promising that he would ensure that both would rule powerfully over peoples already subdued and would effectively tame those still unsubdued [Note: “efficately” in the codex].

He was also planning that, although they were situated in different kingdoms, they should exercise royal authority, lest the narrowness of a single kingdom diminish too greatly the majesty of two kings.

### 92. Louis’s Advancement to the Kingdom of Aquitaine and His Marriage

While he was arranging these matters with great effort, certain other men, excessively shrewd, learned of it and wished to transfer such glory to themselves. They approached Queen Emma and said that they wished to consult her about a matter of the greatest importance.

Received by the queen, they said that it seemed best to them that King Louis should take as his wife Adelaide, formerly the wife of Raimund, the recently deceased duke of the Goths. From this, they said, not only could the power of his reign be increased, but some advantages could also be acquired for themselves.

Indeed, it might become possible to bind all Aquitaine and Gothia under his authority, once, by right of the wife he had taken, he had brought the most strongly fortified towns back under his jurisdiction. Something great and useful could also be achieved in this matter if, with the father stationed on one side and the son on the other, the duke and the remaining enemies were enclosed in the middle and continually harassed.

### 93. Preparations for the Expedition to Aquitaine

After this plan had been proposed to the king, it prevailed with Count Gozfred, who was present, and was put into effect. These preparations were made without the duke’s knowledge. When he later noticed what had happened, he concealed the insult, lest he appear to wrong the kings, and offered no resistance at all.

Meanwhile, after the leaders of the kingdom had been gathered, the royal cavalry was organized, the royal insignia were brought forward, and various foods were prepared and loaded onto wagons. When these things had been done, both kings set out for Aquitaine with a large cavalry force and reached the fortress called Old Briddam.

### 94. Adelaide’s Advancement as Queen in Aquitaine and Their Divorce

They were received there by the aforementioned Adelaide with elaborate preparations. On the appointed day, after the arrangements had been most suitably made and the dowry had been granted according to law, King Louis took her as his wife and, after she had been crowned, advanced her with him into the kingdom through the bishops.

Yet the royal title had no such force among them that they could in any way exercise ruling authority over the leaders. Nor was there almost any conjugal love between them. Since he was still reaching maturity while she was already an old woman, they disagreed in their contrary ways.

They did not permit themselves a common bedchamber. When they wished to rest, they stayed in separate lodgings. Whenever they had to converse, they met in an open-air place. To prolong their conversations, it was enough for them to say very few words. This was almost always their practice for two years.

Their dispositions were so utterly discordant that divorce followed not long afterward.

### 95. Louis’s Decline and Adelaide’s Second Marriage

Louis, because he had no instructor in proper conduct, being a young man, devoted himself to the frivolities of trivial matters. He had completely abandoned the customary clothing of his native people in favor of foreign dress [Note: “garments” corrected to “dress”; “dress” appears in the codex].

Thus everything collapsed into a pitiable condition: he became degenerate in character, inglorious through his inability to rule, and the man who shortly before had been a powerful king by birth, reputation, and resources was now wretched and destitute, filthy with the misery of both his household and military affairs.

When King Lotharius learned of these things from many reports, he considered recalling his son, knowing that he would fall into still worse circumstances since he received no honor there appropriate to royal dignity. He therefore prepared cavalry to recover his son. Entering Aquitaine, he went to Briddam. He reclaimed his son and brought him back.

The queen, grieving that she had been widowed and fearing injury from a greater misfortune, approached William of Arles and married him. Thus, as a result of the divorce, public adultery was committed.

### 96. Otto’s Death

At this time Otto, having engaged the barbarians, succumbed to a miserable fortune. He lost his army after it had been routed and was himself captured by the enemy, but by divine grace he returned.

Later, when he was suffering at Rome from indigestion and from intestinal scybala (*squibala*, hardened fecal masses) caused by a melancholic humor, he eagerly took aloe in a dose weighing four drachms, seeking restoration of health. His internal organs were disturbed, and continual diarrhea followed. Its uninterrupted flow produced swollen hemorrhoids. These, pouring out an excessive quantity of blood, caused his death after no more than a few days (983, December 7).

### 97. The Succession of the Child Otto

After his death, his surviving son Otto was five years old. Although certain leading men wished him to succeed his father in the kingdom, this was opposed by some others (983, December 25).

Nevertheless, with immense courage and through varying fortune, they later secured the kingdom for him (984). For Hezilo, a cousin of the king who had recently died, had until then been held bound in prison by him because he had sought the kingdom against him. Hezilo escaped through the schemes of wicked men to the ruin of the commonwealth and was received into the fortifications of certain people.

He was a man as noble as Otto, with an elegant and vigorous body, desirous of honor and factious, great in spirit but deceitful. Eager for kingship, he made all sacrilegious men, those convicted in trials, those who feared trial for their deeds, and finally all the dissolute whom guilty consciences tormented, his closest companions and intimates (Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 14).

Through the schemes of such men, he seized the surviving young son of the dead king, little Otto, believing that he himself would reign in his place. Thinking that the kingdom had thus been transferred into his own jurisdiction, he prepared a scepter and crown for himself.

While he was considering seeking this from Lotharius and attempting to make him a companion and friend by granting him Belgica, he sent ambassadors ahead, among whom the common enterprise was to be confirmed by oath. By this oath, moreover, both kings were to promise one another that they would meet at an agreed place on the Rhine.

### 98. Lotharius’s Failed Expedition against Hezilo

After these matters had been sworn through the ambassadors, Lotharius, at the appointed time, passed through Belgica with an army and reached the agreed place on the Rhine, so that he would not remain bound by the obligation of the oath.

Hezilo, fearing that he would fall under suspicion among the leaders if he met Lotharius, as though he wished to receive him into the kingdom and would thereby be guilty of perjury, delayed going to meet him.

Lotharius realized that he had been deceived and turned back, though not without the hardship of difficult labor. The Belgians, through whose territory he had passed with his cavalry, were angered by his passage. They obstructed the roads by placing trees across them or prevented the returning men by digging ditches—not so that they might fight at close quarters in an open field, but so that they could harass those delayed by these obstacles from behind, or, safe on the mountain ridges, strike with missiles those passing below.

Since they did not have the courage to stand in the open, archers with bows and crossbows were stationed among the mountains. As the army advanced, some were struck by arrows from above and others wounded by various missiles. Whenever the recruits saw a place accessible for climbing, they turned against the enemy there; inflamed by their arms, they wounded some and killed others.

They raged among them three times with such violence that the mass of corpses, piled up, resembled hills. Others, descending, either cut through the dense opposing foliage with drawn swords or, by driving in poles, removed the mass of trees that had been laid across the road and opened a path for themselves and the approaching army [Note: corrected from “for himself and the army that was coming” to “for himself and the approaching army”].

At last, after great effort, they were drawn out from the midst of the enemy.

### 99. The Disorder in Germany

At this time Germany was held without the authority of a king [Note: “Belgica and Germany” has been deleted], since the weakness of his age prevented the child Otto from ruling, while the more powerful men opposed Hezilo’s desire to reign.

Taking advantage of this, Lotharius again considered invading Belgica, intending to restore it to the jurisdiction of his rule, since Otto was no more [Note: “the enemy” has been deleted], the leaders were at odds, and the dignity of the kingdom was being administered by no royal authority.

### 100. Lotharius Prepares to Invade Belgica

He therefore summoned the illustrious and powerful men Odo and Herbert and disclosed to them the secret of his desire. Since shortly before he had generously given them the excellent lands, with their strongly fortified towns, of their paternal uncles who had died childless, they immediately replied that they were entirely ready to serve both at home and in war.

When the king, with their support, declared that he intended to recover Belgica and conquer it with military forces, they said that the beginning of this undertaking should be made at Verdun. The city was closer, they said, and they would attack it with a prolonged siege and never withdraw from it until it had been captured. Once it had been captured and attached to the king by oath and hostage, they would proceed farther.

They also said that they would remain in Belgica for as long as necessary, until either it was conquered by arms or the defeated Belgians all submitted.

Having accepted their offer, the king immediately moved the army with them toward Verdun.

[Column 0122B] **101. The Capture of Verdun** [Note: [Column 0121] “V,” beginning on a cut-off leaf.] —This city is situated in such a position that, on its front side, an accessible plain provides approach to those advancing; at the rear [Note: [Column 0121] “and on either side” deleted.] it is inaccessible. For there, from the summit toward the rear, a deep chasm extends all around. From below, however, the steep cliffs narrow the approach to the summit. The place is not only supplied with springs and wells, and thus suitable for its inhabitants, but is also wooded, with the river Meuse washing it on its precipitous side.

Since, then, on its front it presents a plain, those preparing to fight set up siege engines of various kinds. The men in the city were no less preparing themselves for resistance. At last they fought for nearly eight continuous days. But when the citizens saw that no assistance was being sent from outside by their own people, and that they could not endure the burden of the battle for long [Note: [Column 0121] “and that the few were yielding to the multitude” deleted.], they took counsel and surrendered to the enemy unharmed and uninjured. They opened the city and, defeated, presented themselves to Lothair.

**102.** When this had been accomplished, the king left Queen Emma in the city to defend it. He himself returned with the army to Laon and also allowed his men to return to their homes. He enjoyed such great favor from their goodwill that, if he ordered them to march farther when the campaign was resumed, they promised to do so, and to fight the enemy at close quarters, neglecting for the time being their homes and children.

Meanwhile Lothair was deliberating among his own men whether it would be preferable for him to continue farther and subjugate all Belgium to himself by arms and force, or to remain at Verdun and, through envoys and persuasion, shape the enemy’s character according to his own will. For if he conquered them by the sword—and he was considering that this could not be done without much bloodshed—he thought that afterward they would have to be trusted less, since he would have inflicted a stain upon their friendship. If, however, he waited for them to return through goodwill, he thought he had to beware lest, in such prolonged leisure, the enemy become more insolent.

**103. The Belgian Attack on Verdun** [Note: [Column 0121] “V,” beginning on a cut-off leaf.] —While he was weighing these matters in prolonged deliberation, Theoderic, duke of Belgium, together with the noble and vigorous Godefrid, the distinguished Sigefrid, and also Bardo and Gozilo, brothers of great renown and reputation, along with several other princes, secretly attempted to break into Verdun and drive out the Gauls [Note: [Column 0123] “the enemy” corrected to “the Gauls”].

Having laid an ambush, they entered the merchants’ enclosure, which had been built like a fortified town. It was separated from the city by the intervening Meuse, but connected to it by two bridges laid across the river, and they entered with select troops. They had soldiers scattered throughout the surrounding area bring in all the grain. They also took the merchants’ provisions for military use.

They ordered beams from the Argonne Forest [Note: [Column 0123] A forest west of Verdun.] to be gathered, so that, if engines were brought up against the walls from outside by the enemy, they too might attempt to resist from within with engines occupying the walls. They also wove strong screens of wicker and branches of trees, to be spread over the raised engines if circumstances required [Note: [Column 0123] “to be spread over them,” feminine, corrected to “to be spread over them,” neuter.] They prepared many stakes, sharpened with iron and scorched by fire, to be driven through the enemy. [Column 0123B] Craftsmen prepared missiles of various kinds. They brought together a thousand coils of rope for different uses. They also had shields arranged for forming a tortoise formation. Moreover, they did not lack a hundred instruments of death.

**104. Lothair Recaptures Verdun** [Note: [Column 0123] “Com,” with “m,” beginning on a cut-off leaf.] —These events were reported to Lothair. He was fiercely indignant that so great an undertaking had occurred, recalled the army he had dismissed, and proceeded to Verdun with ten thousand fighters. He suddenly attacked the adversaries.

At the first assault, archers [Note: [Column 0123] “sagittarii” corrected to “sagitarii.”] were drawn up against the enemy. Arrows, crossbow bolts, and other missiles were sent so densely through the air that they seemed to pour down from the clouds and rise up from the earth. To withstand their attack, the enemy constructed a tortoise formation before themselves and above their heads, against which the missiles, striking and having their force thwarted, fell away.

After this assault, the Gauls arranged the siege all around and secured their camp with steep ditches, lest the adversaries, if they sallied forth against the unsuspecting men, find an easy approach.

**105. Construction of a Certain Siege Engine** [Note: [Column 0123] “Com,” with “m,” beginning on a cut-off leaf.] —They brought tall oaks, cut down by the roots, to construct a siege engine. From these they laid four beams, each thirty feet long, on the ground, so that two, projected lengthwise and separated by an interval of ten feet, were joined to two others laid across them at the same interval.
