The space of length and width enclosed within their joints was ten feet. Whatever projected beyond the joints was likewise extended for ten feet.

At the joints of these beams they raised, with the aid of pulleys, four uprights, each forty feet long, arranged in a square but elongated configuration and standing at equal distances from one another. Twice across the four sides they placed ten-foot crossbars, one set in the middle and another at the top; these, passing across, firmly connected the uprights to one another.

From the ends of the beams on which the uprights rested, they extended four beams, slanting almost up to the upper crossbars, and joined them to the uprights, so that the engine, thus braced externally, would not sway. They also laid timbers over the crossbars in the middle and at the top that connected the engine. These they covered with wicker screens, upon which the fighters would stand; raised higher, they would overwhelm their adversaries below with spears and stones.

They intended to bring this completed structure up to the enemy’s position. But because they regarded the archers with suspicion, they sought a means by which it could approach the enemy without injury to their own men. At last, after more careful investigation, a method was found by which it could be pushed against the enemy with excellent skill.

**106. Bringing the Earlier Engine against the Enemy** [Note: [Column 0123] “ad,” “ioris,” “ae,” beginning on a cut-off leaf.] —They devised the following plan. Four very thick posts were to be fixed in solid ground, buried ten feet in the earth and projecting eight feet above it. They were also to be strengthened by extremely strong bars laid across the four sides. Ropes were to be passed through the bars. The ends of the ropes running away from the enemy were to be attached: the upper ones to the engine, and the inner ones to oxen. The inner ends, however, were to extend farther than the upper ones. The upper ends were to hold the enclosed engine by a shorter pull, so that the engine would stand between the enemy and the oxen.

Thus, the farther the oxen withdrew by pulling away from the enemy, the nearer the engine, drawn toward the enemy, would approach. By this device, with rollers placed beneath it so that it could move more easily, the engine was brought up to the enemy without injuring anyone. [Column 0124C]

**107. Lothair’s Victory** [Note: [Column 0123] “ria,” “rii,” beginning on a cut-off leaf.] —The adversaries also constructed a similar engine, though inferior in height and strength. When both had been constructed [Note: [Column 0123] “raised” written above “constructed.”], men climbed up on both sides. Both sides fought with the greatest eagerness, yet neither yielded in any way.

When the king was near the walls, he was wounded on the upper lip by a sling-stone. Enraged by this injury, his men threw themselves into the battle with greater force. Since the enemy, strong in both their engine and their weapons, would not yield at all, the king ordered iron hooks to be used. Once these had been fastened to ropes and thrown onto the enemy’s engine, and had caught on its crosswise timbers, some men lowered ropes while others caught those that had been lowered. By these means the adversaries’ engine was tilted and almost submerged.

As a result, some of the enemy slid down through the joints of the timbers; others leaped down to the ground; and some, seized by shameful fear, defended their lives in hiding places. Seeing that the danger of death was pressing upon them, the enemy yielded to their adversaries and begged for their lives. Ordered to do so, they laid down and surrendered their weapons.

Immediately the king issued an order that the enemy should be seized without any injury inflicted in revenge and brought unharmed before him. [Column 0125A] Thus captured, unarmed and uninjured except for the blows they had received amid the tumult of battle, they were admitted before the king. Falling at the king’s feet, they begged for their lives. For, as offenders against royal majesty and convicted of the charge, they had no confidence in their survival.

**108.** Having won the victory, the king ordered that the captured princes of Belgium be guarded by his men and returned at a suitable time. He allowed the rest of the force to return. He himself returned with the army to Laon and there dismissed the army.

He held the city of Verdun without any resistance until the final day of his life. He was also making plans for extending his kingdom by proceeding farther, since his affairs were meeting with the greatest success and the fortune of the kingdom, through the capture of the leading men, encouraged this course. But the Divinity, who determines worldly affairs, granted the Belgians respite and brought this king’s reign to an end. [Column 0125B]

**109. (986) The Death of Lothair** —When the mildness of spring returned in that same year after winter had afflicted the world, the air changed as nature requires, and Lothair began to fall ill at Laon. Afflicted by the condition that physicians call colic, he fell into bed.

He suffered intolerable pain on the right side above the genitals. From the navel to the spleen, and from there to the left groin, and thence to the anus, he was struck by severe pains. There was also considerable distress in the ileum and kidneys; continual tenesmus; bloody evacuation; and his voice was repeatedly cut off. At times he stiffened with the chills of fever. There was rumbling of the intestines [Note: [Column 0125] “of the intestines,” with “c.”]. Constant nausea. [Column 0126A] Belching and futile straining, distension of the abdomen, and burning of the stomach were also present.

Thus, amid immense mourning, the entire household resounded [Note: [Column 0125] “resounded” written above “rang out.”]. There was every kind of sound and varied crying. None of those present could remain without tears at such a calamity. Having outlived Otto by ten years [Note: [Column 0125] “13.”], in the thirty-seventh year [Note: [Column 0125] “33rd.”] from the time when, after his father’s death, he obtained the kingdom, but in the forty-eighth year from the time when, while his father was reigning, he received the crown and scepter in order to reign, and in the sixty-eighth year of his age [Note: [Column 0126] He was born in the year 941; Richer is mistaken in counting his age from Louis IV; cf. II.4 and III.2], he failed and yielded to nature (March 2).

**110.** Meanwhile the royal funeral was magnificently prepared with a great display of royal wealth. A bier adorned with royal insignia was made for him. His body was clothed in a linen garment [Note: [Column 0125] “purple” corrected to “linen.”], and above it he was covered with a purple pall ornamented with gems and woven with gold. The leading men of the kingdoms carried the bier.

Bishops and clergy went before it with Gospels and crosses. Among them walked the man who carried his crown, shining with much gold and precious stones, together with many other insignia; he proceeded wailing. The funeral chant could scarcely be uttered, obstructed by tears. The soldiers too followed in their proper order with mournful faces. The remaining force came after them with lamentations.

He was buried at Rheims in the monastery of the monks of Saint Remigius, with his father and mother, as he had previously ordered his men. The monastery was 240 stadia from the place where he had ended his life, and he was carried that entire distance amid the devoted service and equal affection of all.

# BOOK FOUR

[Column 0125]

**1.** After Lothair was buried, his son Louis was installed as king by the duke and the other princes. He was therefore surrounded by the favor of everyone. They promised goodwill and pledged loyalty. They also proposed that his attendants should be appointed in various forms of dress [Note: [Column 0125] “cul,” said to be from a conjecture.].

Some thought that he should reside in the palaces [Note: [Column 0125] “of his own cities” deleted.] so that princes might come to him and serve under his authority, lest royal dignity be diminished if, as though impoverished, he had to seek the resources of others elsewhere. In every position of dignity it was also necessary to beware lest, at the beginning of an assumed honor, sluggishness and cowardice overcome the virtue that ought to be present. For if that happened [Note: [Column 0125] “thus” corrected.], the whole enterprise would most disastrously fall into contempt and degradation.

Others maintained that he should remain with the duke, since the young man needed to be formed both by the prudence and by the virtue of so great a prince. It would also be highly useful for him to yield for a time to the disposition of a powerful man, since without him he could not fully possess the power of kingship, and through him everything could be administered vigorously and advantageously.

After hearing both sides, the king deferred his decision. But after taking counsel with the duke, he favored him from that point onward, devoting himself to him wholeheartedly.

**2. Louis’s Speech before the Duke and the Other Princes, against Adalbero the Metropolitan** [Note: [Column 0125] “Or,” “vi,” “cet,” “in,” and “m,” from a conjecture.] —Before him and a few others, remembering the past, he complained as follows:

“My father, when he fell into the illness from which he died, instructed me to govern the kingdom according to your counsel and your arrangements, and to regard you in the place of relatives and friends [Note: [Column 0125] “kinsmen” corrected to “friends.”], undertaking nothing of importance without your knowledge. He declared that, if I possessed your loyalty, I would undoubtedly have wealth, armies, and the fortifications of the kingdom. This conviction has the greatest force in me [Note: [Column 0127] ‘and will always remain strongest in me as long as I live’ deleted.].

Therefore, be pleased to give useful advice, since I have resolved not to depart from you. In you I have wished to place my counsel, my mind, and my fortunes.

Adalbero, metropolitan bishop of Rheims, the most criminal of all the men whom the earth supports, despising my father’s authority, favored Otto, the enemy of the Franks, in everything. With his cooperation Otto brought an army against us. Through his cunning he devastated the lands of Gaul. With him providing guides for the journey, he returned unharmed with his army.

It seems just and useful that he should pay the penalty for so great a crime [Note: [Column 0127] ‘For it is just that the wicked be condemned by a just punishment, and useful that…’ deleted.], so that, once this pestilent man has been restrained, fear of undertaking such acts may be instilled in every wicked person.”

**3.** His speech had no persuasive force, because, enraged by the accusations of evil men against the supreme pontiff, he seemed to have said certain unworthy things beyond what was just. He was supported in part, but in part restrained; in such a way, however, that no injury was done to the king and the duke, while not consenting to the wicked undertaking, nevertheless obeyed.

The king, impetuous in his resolve, advanced with the duke and an army against the metropolitan. He made for the city itself and attempted to break in. Yet, following the counsel of the princes, he sent envoys ahead to ask whether the bishop would resist the king or whether he would be prepared at an appointed time to clear himself of the charges brought against him.

They were to say that, if he resisted, the king would immediately lay siege to the city and, once it had been captured, crush both the city and the enemy within it. But if he did not hesitate to answer the charges, the king would accept hostages from him and take them away.

[Column 0127C]

**4.** To this the metropolitan replied:

“Since it is well known that all good men are continually torn apart by the accusations of the wicked, I am not surprised that this injury has occurred in my case. But I am much more surprised that eminent princes can so easily be enticed into believing with certainty what has not been examined before a judge and, if it is brought forward for examination, cannot be proved credible by any argument.

If it has pleased you to examine what has been alleged, why is it being demanded with arms and an army? Do not such circumstances therefore make us suspect one thing in place of another?

If the matter concerns the past, I have until now desired the safety of the kings. I have honored their dynasty. I have also loved the interests of the princes in proportion to reason. If it concerns the present, I do not delay in carrying out the king’s commands. I surrender whatever hostages he wants, and I do not postpone presenting my defense against the charges.”

After both sides had presented their arguments, he gave hostages: Ragener, a military man distinguished by nobility and wealth, and several others, as many as sufficed for the king.

**5. The Death of Louis** —The king then withdrew his army and reached Senlis. While he was engaged there in summer hunting, he fell while on foot and was afflicted with severe pain in the liver. Since physicians assert that the liver is the seat of blood, when that seat was shaken the blood overflowed into a hemorrhage (987, May 22).

Blood flowed copiously from his nostrils and throat. His breasts were afflicted by continual pains. An intolerable heat throughout his body was also present. Thus, having survived his father by only one year, he died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June and paid nature’s debt.

His death occurred at the very time when the metropolitan’s purification from the charges was to take place. He was therefore present, ready to be cleared and to satisfy the royal majesty. But because of the calamity of the royal funeral, the case was suppressed: neither party pursued the controversy, nor was any judgment issued from it.

The bishop himself, however, lamented the king’s death with the greatest compassion. After they had arranged the royal funeral, he was buried at Compiègne by decree of the princes, although while alive he had asked to be buried beside his father. This was deliberately done so that, while many of them avoided the length of the journey and departed separated from one another, the most useful deliberation for the commonwealth would not be postponed. They therefore decided to meet before departing and to deliberate concerning the interests of the kingdom.

**6. Adalbero’s Purification from the Charges Brought by Louis** —After these arrangements had been made, the duke began as follows:

“You have been summoned here from different places by royal command, as I believe, and have gathered in good faith to examine the charges brought against the supreme pontiff Adalbero. But the king of blessed memory [Note: [Column 0127] “D.M.,” manuscript.] who brought the charge has been deprived of this life, and has left us to examine the state of the controversy.

Therefore, if there is anyone besides him who dares to bring the charge and possesses the courage to take up a part in pursuing the case, let him appear publicly and declare what he thinks. Let him bring a charge against the accused without fear. If he speaks the truth, he will undoubtedly have us as approvers of his words. But if the accuser has fabricated falsehoods, let him silence his voice, lest, convicted of so great a crime, he pay the penalty.”

The call for the accuser to come forward was proclaimed three times [Column 0128C]; three times all denied that there was one.

**7.** The duke therefore spoke again:

“If the case has now ended because there is no one to bring the charge, the metropolitan, being a noble man distinguished by great wisdom, must be yielded to. Abandon this suspicion completely, therefore, and honor the supreme prelate with the greatest respect. Revere such a man, and proclaim how great are his virtue, wisdom, and nobility. For what benefit is there in holding a suspicion against one who had no power to say anything in court?”

Therefore [Note: [Column 0127] “after he had been cleared” deleted.], with the consent of the other leading men, the duke assigned the supreme pontiff the honor of conducting the deliberation, for the benefit of the kingdom, since he excelled in knowledge of divine and human matters and possessed great power through the effectiveness of his eloquence.

[Column 0128D]

**8.** Having thus become the mediator of all matters together with the duke, he said:

“Since our most pious king has been transferred among the intelligible things, and since, by the goodwill of the great duke and the other princes, I have been cleared of the charges, I have taken my seat to deliberate for the commonwealth. It is not in my mind to declare anything except what will advance the commonwealth. I seek common counsel because I wish to benefit everyone.

Since I see that not all the princes are present, although the affairs of the kingdom could be administered by their prudence and diligence, the search for a king ought, as it seems to me, to be postponed for a time, so that at the appointed time they may all gather together, and the carefully weighed judgment of each may be brought into the midst and directed toward the common good.

Therefore, let it please you who are present here to deliberate, to bind yourselves with me by oath to the great duke and to promise publicly that, concerning the appointment of a prince, you will seek nothing and undertake nothing until we return and meet together, and then deliberate about the prince to be chosen.

For it is of the greatest value to give time for deliberation, during which each person may examine whatever matter is at issue and, once examined, refine it with great care.”

This decision was accepted and praised by everyone. They were therefore bound by oath to the duke. A time for returning and assembling was fixed. In this way they were released from one another.

**9. Charles’s Complaint to the Metropolitan concerning the Kingdom** —Meanwhile Charles, who had been Lothair’s brother and Louis’s uncle, went to the metropolitan at Rheims and addressed him concerning the kingdom as follows:

“It is known to all, venerable father, that by hereditary right I ought to succeed my brother and nephew. Although I was driven from the kingdom by my brother, nature nevertheless deprived me of none of the human qualities proper to me: I was born with all the limbs without which no one could be promoted to any dignity.

Nor do I lack those qualities that are usually sought most of all in anyone who is to reign: noble birth, and—so that I may dare to say it—virtue. Why, then, have I been expelled from the territories that no one doubts were possessed by my ancestors, when my brother is dead, my nephew has died, and they have left no offspring?

My father left us two brothers as survivors. My brother possessed the entire dominion of the kingdoms and granted me nothing. Subject to my brother, I served him no less faithfully than did others. From that time, I confess, nothing was dearer to me than my brother’s safety.

Cast down and wretched, where shall I turn, when all the protections of my family have also been extinguished? Whom should I call upon, if not you, when I lack every honorable resource? Through whom, if not through you, shall I be restored to my father’s honors?

Would that an honorable end had come to me and my fortunes! For what can I be, cast down before those who look on, except a spectacle? Let some compassion proper to humanity touch you. Take pity on one exhausted by such injuries.”

**10.** After Charles had finished his complaint, the metropolitan remained unmoved [Note: [Column 0129] The manuscript has “stubborn” above “unmoved.”] and replied to him only briefly:

“Since you have always been devoted to perjurers, sacrilegious men, and other wicked people, and you do not yet wish to abandon them, how do you intend to attain the principate through such men and with such men?”

When Charles replied to this that he ought not to desert his own men, but rather acquire others, the bishop reflected within himself:

“Since he is now deprived of every dignity and attached to all manner of wicked people, whose companionship he absolutely refuses to relinquish, what destruction would he bring upon the good if he came forward as a torch [i.e. as an incendiary]?”

At last, after replying that he would do nothing in this matter without the consent of the princes, the metropolitan dismissed him.

[Column 0130A]

**11. The Metropolitan’s Speech on Behalf of the Duke** [Note: [Column 0129] “Or,” with “po,” beginning on a cut-off leaf.] —Losing hope of the kingdom, Charles, disturbed in mind, set out for Belgium. Meanwhile, at the appointed time, the princes of Gaul, bound by oath, assembled at Senlis.

While they were seated in council, with the duke’s approval the metropolitan spoke as follows:

“When Louis of blessed memory, bereft of children [Note: [Column 0129] “bereft of this life” corrected to “bereft of children.”], was taken from us, it was necessary to deliberate at length about who would supply his place in the kingdom, lest the commonwealth, neglected without a governor, should collapse.

For this reason we recently thought it useful to postpone this matter, so that each person might first pour out here, in consultation with those present, whatever individual gift had been granted him by God; and so that, when the opinions of all had been collected, the sum of the entire counsel might be shaped from the mass of the multitude.

Now that we have been brought together, we must consider the matter with great prudence and great good faith, lest hatred scatter reason or affection weaken truth.

We do not fail to recognize that Charles has supporters who maintain that he is worthy of the kingdom on the basis of his parentage. But if the matter is to be judged on this basis, neither is the kingdom acquired by hereditary right, nor should anyone be promoted to the kingdom unless he is distinguished not only by nobility of body, but also illuminated by wisdom of mind, protected by faith, and strengthened by magnanimity.

We read in the annals of emperors of the most illustrious lineage who were cast down from their dignity because of cowardice, and of others succeeding them who were sometimes their equals and sometimes their inferiors.

But what worthy quality can be attributed to Charles? Faith does not govern him; sluggishness weakens him; and finally, he has been so diminished in his head [i.e. in his judgment] that he was not ashamed to serve a foreign king and took as his wife a woman unequal to him in military rank.

How, then, will the great duke endure that a woman taken from his own soldiers should become queen and rule over him? How will he place above his own head one before whom his equals and even his superiors bend their knees and place their hands beneath her feet?

Consider the matter carefully, and see that Charles has been cast down more by his own fault than by another’s. Desire the prosperity of the commonwealth rather than its calamity. If you wish it to become unhappy, promote Charles. If you wish it to be fortunate, crown the distinguished duke Hugh as king.

Therefore let no one be enticed by affection for Charles, nor let hatred of the duke remove anyone from the common good. For if you condemn what is good, how will you praise what is evil? If you praise what is evil, how will you despise what is good?

But what does Divinity itself threaten against such men? ‘Woe,’ it says, ‘to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness’ (Isaiah 5:20).

Promote, therefore, your duke, a man most distinguished in conduct, nobility, and resources, whom you will find to be the protector not only of the commonwealth but also of private affairs. With his own goodwill favoring you, you will have him in the place of a father. For who has fled to him and failed to find protection? Who, deprived of the assistance of his own people, has not been restored by him to his own?”

**12. (987, June 1) Hugh’s Promotion to the Kingdom** —After this judgment had been proclaimed and praised by everyone, the duke was promoted to the kingdom by universal consent. He was crowned at Noyon by the metropolitan and the other bishops and, on the Kalends of June, was proclaimed king over the Franks, Britons, Danes [Note: [Column 0131] “Danes?” that is, Northmen.], Aquitanians, Goths, Spaniards, and Basques [Note: [Column 0131] “king” deleted by all witnesses.].

Surrounded by the leading men of the kingdoms, he issued decrees and established laws according to royal custom, arranging and distributing everything with fortunate success. To match his blessed position, he was uplifted by the great success of prosperity and devoted himself to great piety.

In order to leave a certain heir in the kingdom after his departure from life, he took counsel with the princes. After deliberating with them, he approached the metropolitan of Rheims, first through envoys and then in person, at Orléans, concerning the promotion of his son Robert to the kingdom.

When the metropolitan replied that it was not right to create [Note: [Column 0131] “to ordain” corrected to “to create.”] two kings in the same year, Hugh immediately produced a letter sent by Borrell, duke of Further Spain, [Column 0131B] which indicated that the duke was requesting assistance against the barbarians.

He further asserted that part of Spain had already been almost conquered by the enemy, and that, unless he received forces from the Gauls within ten months, all of it would pass into the barbarians’ submission. He therefore requested that another king be created, so that, if one of the two should fall amid the tumult of war, the army would not lose confidence in its prince.

He also maintained that it could happen that, if the king were killed and the country left desolate, discord among the leading men and the tyranny of the wicked against the good would follow, and from this the captivity of the entire nation.

**13. (988) Robert’s Promotion to the Kingdom** —Understanding that this could indeed happen, the metropolitan yielded to the king’s arguments. Since the princes of the kingdoms had then gathered at Christmas to celebrate the honor of the royal coronation, he solemnly crowned his son Robert in the basilica of the Holy Cross, after the Franks had acclaimed him and he had received the purple, and appointed and established him as king from the river Meuse to the western Ocean.

He was so distinguished by industry and skill that he excelled in military affairs, was regarded as highly distinguished in divine and canonical institutions, devoted himself to liberal studies [Note: [Column 0131] “thus” in the manuscript.], attended synods of bishops, and discussed and settled ecclesiastical cases with them.

**14. Charles’s Complaint to His Friends concerning the Kingdom** —Meanwhile Charles made a grievous complaint among his friends and relatives and stirred them to support him through his lamentations.

Suffused with tears, he said:

“I see my life advancing and myself being stripped day by day of the resources of my patrimony. Therefore I cannot look upon my little children without tears, the offspring of an unhappy father. To them I am the author of future sorrow rather than honor.

I have been an unhappy father indeed, since I have scarcely ever been able to be present for my children. But at least, my friends, take counsel for a grieving father; assist a parent who has been abandoned. Stand by my children, who at their tender age already know hardship. Protect those cast down into circumstances from which I do not know whether they will emerge irrevocably.

Let the bond of our common blood persuade you at least to show some compassion [Note: [Column 0131] “to show some compassion” deleted.]. Let the nobility that must not be neglected persuade you. Let recompense also persuade you—recompense that will return with no small multiplication of benefit.”

**15.** Immediately all were moved [Note: [Column 0131] “by this complaint” deleted.], promised assistance, and prepared themselves most eagerly to help him.

Using their counsel, Charles began sending scouts to investigate carefully whether any opportunity might present itself by which he could enter Laon. Those sent out investigated and discovered that no entrance was open. Nevertheless, they held a secret conference with certain citizens who sought to bring the undertaking to completion [Note: [Column 0131] “who could both conceal it and…” deleted.].

At that time Adalbero, bishop of the same city, was inflicting excessive legal injuries upon his citizens concerning the agrarian law. As a result, some who had secretly withdrawn their loyalty from him and were pretending goodwill promised the scouts that they would receive Charles into the city.

**16. How Charles Entered Laon** —They soon promised Charles the betrayal of the city if he came, provided that he left them their property [Note: [Column 0131] “their good things” deleted.] and increased it besides.

After the scouts had confirmed the agreement by oaths, they reported these matters to Charles. He immediately disclosed the plan to his own men, whom he had stirred up by his earlier complaint. They gathered unanimously at the appropriate time and presented themselves to him.

Taking the troops, he arrived at Laon at sunset, at the proper time, and sent scouts to the turncoats to report what had to be done. They hid among the vineyards and hedges, ready to enter the city if fortune allowed it and to resist with weapons if the outcome required it.

Those who had been sent to the ambush met the traitors at the appointed and familiar places and announced that Charles had arrived with a large cavalry force. The traitors rejoiced, sent the scouts back, and instructed them to tell Charles to come quickly.

When he learned this, Charles and his men attacked the city gate along the slopes of the mountain. But when the guards sensed from the neighing of horses and some clashing of weapons that people were approaching, they shouted from the wall asking who they were and pressed them with thrown stones. The traitors immediately replied that some of the citizens were there.

By this device the guards were bribed; they opened the gate inward and received the army at twilight. Soon the army filled the city. Guards were also posted at the gates so that no one could escape.

Some sounded trumpets; others roared with their voices; others created a tumult with the noise of weapons. The citizens, terrified because they did not know what was happening, poured out of their houses and tried to escape by flight.

Some hid themselves in the secluded parts of the churches; others shut themselves in various hiding places; still others threw themselves headlong from the walls. One of them was the bishop. He had already slipped down the mountain slopes and was found by the watchers among the vineyards. He was brought to Charles, who thrust him into prison.

Charles also seized Queen Emma, whom he believed had caused him to be rejected by his brother, and placed guards over her. He overran almost the whole remaining nobility of the city as well.

**17.** After the disturbances had been calmed and the city restored to tranquility, Charles began to deliberate and make arrangements concerning the city’s fortifications and the provisioning of the soldiers.

He therefore appointed five hundred guards, who each night, armed, would keep watch throughout the city and along the walls. He also ordered grain to be brought in from the entire district of Vermandois. In this way he fortified the city for resistance.

He built up the tower that still stood with low walls, giving it projecting battlements, and surrounded it on every side with open ditches. He also constructed engines against the enemy. [Column 0133B] Timbers suitable for raising engines were likewise brought in [Note: [Column 0133] “a thousand beams” corrected to “timbers.”].

The stakes were sharpened and the screens woven. Craftsmen were summoned no less, to manufacture missiles and to restore with iron whatever necessities arose. Nor were there lacking men who could shoot crossbows with such extraordinary skill that they could pierce with a sure shot a storehouse open through two apertures on a straight diameter, and could also strike birds flying in the air with an unerring blow and hurl them, transfixed, down from the heights.

18. Hugh’s attack on Karolus.—While these events were taking place, they were reported to the ears of the kings. Although deeply stirred, they did not act with sudden haste; rather, as they were accustomed to do in all matters, they deliberated most carefully about this, concealing their anguish of heart as best they could. They dispatched envoys in every direction. They invited the Gauls whom the Matrona washes on one side and the Garunna on the other to take arms against the tyrant. When these men had been assembled and they had gathered an army, they deliberated whether they should attack and capture the city before it could be fortified with larger forces by the enemy and, after its capture, stab the tyrant to death—since, if he alone were captured or killed, they would soon possess the kingdom in peace—or whether they should receive him graciously as a suppliant, if he should perhaps present himself as such, and should ask the kings, as a gift, to allow them to retain the territories they had seized.

Those, however, who were more ardent and resolute in spirit judged that they should press the siege; that the enemy should be harried; and that the region they had overrun should be utterly consumed by fire. Accordingly, after assembling six thousand horsemen, they marched against the enemy. At the appointed time they approached the city and arranged the siege; having measured out positions for their camps, they surrounded them with ditches and ramparts.

19. When they had remained there for many days, they were able to exert neither force nor any effective pressure against the enemy: the city was impregnable because of its great height and the defensive projection of its sides. The autumn days, too, following a shorter circuit, did not suffice for these operations. The long nights also wearied the watchmen through the great amount of time they had to spend on duty. Therefore, after holding a council with the leading men, they withdrew, intending to return after the spring season.

When they had departed, Karolus walked all around the city. Wherever an accessible place lay open to the enemy, he inspected it. He therefore blocked the gates that were easy for the enemy to enter. He closed the rear entrances hidden behind the houses. He restored walls that had fallen through age. He also enlarged and strengthened the tower, both within and without, with stronger structures.

20. The Bishop’s Escape.—When the bishop had been confined in a chamber, he was lowered by ropes through a window and, riding away at night, escaped. To show that he had not favored Karolus, he went to the kings and cleared himself of so grave a suspicion. For he thought that his accusers might fabricate certain conjectures, as though he himself had prepared the opportunity for his capture. Received by the king as an executor of fidelity, he was held in no less favor.

21. (989.) Meanwhile, when the severity of winter had passed, spring smiled upon the world in milder air and caused the meadows and fields to turn green, the kings, having gathered an army, attacked the aforementioned city with eight thousand men. First, they fortified their camp with a rampart and ditch. Then a battering ram was constructed, intended to break through the walls.

22. Construction of the Battering Ram.—They erected its machine from four beams of extraordinary thickness and length, arranged in an elongated rectangular framework, with transverse braces attached along its four sides at the top and bottom. In the middle, however, they had inserted timbers only on the left and right sides. Across the upper joints of the erected beams they laid two longitudinal beams and made them immovable, occupying in the middle a third of the upper space between the beams. From these longitudinal beams they lowered ropes wound around them. With the ropes they suspended a beam of great thickness, furnished with an iron head.

They also attached ropes to this beam in the middle and at its end; when these were pulled and released by a multitude of men, they gave motion to the iron mass. Hence this kind of machine is called a battering ram, because, after being drawn backward like a ram, it rushes forward with force; it is especially suitable for breaking walls of any solidity. They fitted the machine upon three wheels arranged in a triangular formation, so that, being turned obliquely, it could more easily be directed wherever necessary. But because the position of the city prevented approach—the city itself stood high upon the summit of a mountain—the constructed battering ram was abandoned.

23. Hugh’s Withdrawal with the Army from Laon.—After they had labored for many days in the siege of the city with watches, anxieties, and frequent battles, one day, when the guards of the camp had been weighed down by wine and sleep, the townsmen, exhilarated by wine, came on foot with weapons to the camp (August). Armed horsemen followed afterward, awaiting the outcome, so that, if an opportunity for battle arose and favorable fortune promised a successful result, they might engage the enemy at close quarters.

When the infantry had already approached the camp and realized that the guards were asleep, they threw torches into it. The smoke of the fire thickened the air and not only obstructed the sight of those looking on with a dreadful blackness, but also blocked the passages of their noses and throats with a heavy vapor. Soon the infantry began shouting, and the soldiers began sounding their trumpets. The king and those who were with him, disturbed by the confusion of the elements and the great shouting of the men and blaring of the trumpets, moved their position away from the city. For he saw that the camp, together with its food and all its possessions, had been consumed. He therefore resolved to withdraw the army for a time, so that he might afterward prepare a return with larger forces. All these events took place in August.

24. Death of Adalbero, the Metropolitan.—After these events, not long afterward, the metropolitan fell ill with the disease which the Greeks call *causon* (καῦσον) and the Latins *incendium* (“burning” or “fever”). Through envoys he informed the king, who was then staying at Paris, that he had fallen into serious illness; hence the king needed to hasten, lest Karolus should overrun the rest of Reims as well.

The king summoned those who were present and immediately resolved to go. Since he was delayed somewhat on the journey, while the metropolitan was greatly afflicted both by sleeplessness and by derangement of mind, and while all the critical days suitable for this illness passed without any crisis, his bodily elements being dissolved, he paid the debt of humanity on the tenth day before the Kalends of February (990, January 23). On that day the king, arriving at the proper time, was received into the city.

At the bishop’s funeral he grieved with the deepest compassion. Indeed, he uttered several complaints about him, not without tears, and buried his body with great honor. He consoled the citizens, who had been deprived of their lord, with remarkable goodwill. When asked about preserving their loyalty to the king and defending the city, they swore their faith and promised the city’s protection. After binding them by oath, and after the king had granted them the freedom to choose whatever lord they wished, the king departed from them and arrived at Paris.

25. How Arnulfus Sought the Archbishopric.—While the king remained joyfully among the citizens of Reims because of their generosity and loyalty, Arnulfus, the son of Lotharius, sought a bishopric from the king through certain of the king’s attendants. He sent word that he would abandon his uncle Karolus, pledged his loyalty, promised to avenge the king’s injury, and declared that he would do everything possible against the king’s enemies. He also promised that he would soon restore the city of Laon, which had been seized by the enemy.

The king’s attendants rejoiced and urged that the bishopric be granted as quickly as possible to the petitioner, asserting that the king would lose nothing if he bestowed what Arnulfus requested upon one who would serve him and keep faith. It would also greatly benefit the king if he did so, since, once the grant had been made, Arnulfus would seek the safety of all. The king, yielding to their persuasion, came to Reims to present this request to the citizens, so that he would not become bound by a pledge made in bad faith.

26. The King’s Address to the Citizens of Reims.—After summoning everyone, he spoke as follows:

“Since I have found you to be executors of loyalty, you will not find me alien to loyalty. For loyalty exists when what is said is done: because I perceive that you have done this, I also confess that I have observed the same principle completely.

“Arnulfus, son of Lotharius of blessed memory, born of a concubine, has sought the dignity of this see through certain men who attend me. He has promised to restore whatever has recently been taken from us and also to undertake many things against our enemies. I have submitted his promises and his loyalty to your judgment, so that they may either be approved or rejected by your examination.

“He persists in his request. It is within your power whether he should receive what he seeks. Nor have I favored him in any way. Nothing has yet been decided. Whatever the matter may be, I have thought it should be referred to your judgment, so that, if it proves honorable, it may bring advantage to you and glory to me. But if it proves harmful, I shall certainly not be accused of any treachery, deceit, or fraud. You, however, will either incur, together with the deceitful man, the false reputation of complicity in deceit, or else, if you do not, you will continually raise your hands against the deserter.”

27. The Citizens’ Reply to the King.—The citizens replied:

“Since, by the gift of your majesty, the choice of selecting a lord has been granted to us, we must strive with great loyalty and intelligence both to ensure that no diminution of the royal dignity occurs and to avoid the stigma of a false accusation and the blame for future misfortune.

“Arnulfus, whom we have just heard mentioned, recently asked the same thing of us, promising with the greatest confidence that, if this were done, he would advance the king’s interests in every respect and would show considerable goodwill toward the citizens. But because, as is natural in the case of a young man, we regard his character and inclinations as uncertain, we do not think that our own considerations alone suffice for this matter.

“Let those who advise you be present, then. Let us compare our arguments on both sides. Let each person say what he thinks preferable and conceal nothing of what he considers most important, so that honorable success may bring us common glory and we may likewise suffer together the misfortune of a harmful decision.”

28. The Promotion of Arnulfus.—The king approved the citizens’ judgment and ordered that the matter be deliberated in their presence. The arguments were set out openly. They therefore declared that Arnulfus, if he did what he promised, was worthy of the highest priesthood.

He was summoned and admitted before the king. When questioned about the loyalty he would owe the king, he replied most modestly, to the approval of all. The king and the leading men then led him to the monastery of the monks of Saint Remigius, situated one mile from the city, where, according to ancient custom, the ordination of bishops was to take place.

There, while the king sat among his men, after holding private consultations with his own advisers, he addressed Arnulfus in generous eloquence:

“After Louis, son of Lotharius of blessed memory, was taken from the world without offspring, it would have been fitting for his descendants to succeed him, had any survived. But since there is no successor of the royal stock, and since it is plain to all that this is so, I stand foremost, chosen by the choice of you and the other princes, including those who were preeminent in the military order.

“Now, since this man alone has survived from the royal lineage of which we are speaking, you have asked that this survivor be endowed with some dignity, lest the name of so great a father should still be darkened by oblivion. Therefore, if he promises the right of preserving his loyalty, pledges to defend the city, and promises that he will have no association with the enemy but will instead attack them, it will not displease the judgment of your council to grant him the bishopric—provided, however, that according to the arrangement of prudent men he is bound to me by the authority of an oath.”

29. The Written Chirograph.—“And, to disclose fully what I have conceived in my mind, I think that after the oath has been sworn he should write a chirograph. It should contain an anathema of cursing of this kind: that he should invoke upon himself insults in place of prosperity, ruin in place of safety, shameful things in place of honorable ones, an end in place of long duration, contempt in place of honor, and, to sum it all up, every evil in place of every good.

“I also think it should be made in two parts: one should be granted to me and the other retained by him. At some point this document will also expose him to accusations if he disgracefully turns away from his loyalty.”

When this judgment had been announced, everyone approved that it should be done in this way. Arnulfus therefore came forward. He was asked whether he approved the proposal and whether he would receive what he sought on those terms. Desiring the honor, he approved the proposal and declared that he could accept it in that form. Ordered to do so, he wrote the chirograph in two parts, retaining one for himself and preserving the other for the king.

30. The Eucharist Given as a Cause of Perdition.—Although this was entirely sufficient for the king, it was nevertheless considered insufficient by the bishops, as is reported, unless this additional condition were imposed: that during the celebration of Mass he should receive the Eucharist from the priest and publicly invoke it upon himself as a cause of perdition if he should ever become a deserter by violating his loyalty.

This was also done. For, during the celebration, the priest offered the Eucharist, and Arnulfus then received it and prayed that it might become his judgment if he should in any way prove a violator of his loyalty. This finally convinced the king and the leading men of his good faith.

31. Reproach Concerning the Same Matter.—Nevertheless, some whose minds were purer regarded this as wicked and contrary to the law of faith. They said that he was the sort of man whose character could easily be corrupted from within by himself, and even more readily driven from outside influences toward criminality.

They also asserted from the decrees of the Fathers and the writings of the canons that no unwilling person should be compelled to receive the Eucharist, nor should the Eucharist be offered to anyone as a cause of perdition. Rather, it should be understood that, as a grace of redemption, it is to be offered to those who ask for it and withheld from those who do not wish it.

It also seemed unworthy that the bread of angels and human beings should be rashly given to the unworthy, since the Divinity itself abhors the unclean; the text then repeats, in a corrupt or repetitive form, that the wondrous Divinity abhors the unclean and cherishes the pure with wondrous sparingness, according to what is written: “The holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding, and will be reproved by the iniquity that comes upon it” (Wisdom 1:5).

Arnulfus was therefore ordained by the bishops of the diocese of Reims and suitably adorned with the priestly insignia. Not long afterward he received from the Roman pope the pallium sent with apostolic authority.

32. How Arnulfus Loved Karolus More Than Was Just.—Although he emerged distinguished by so great a dignity, he nevertheless considered it a misfortune that, as the sole survivor of his father’s family, he had no one besides Karolus. It also seemed most wretched to him if Karolus were deprived of honor, since the only hope of restoring his paternal line rested in him.

He therefore pitied his uncle; he thought of him, honored him, and held him dearer than his parents. After conferring with him, he sought a way to raise him to the summit of honor while ensuring that he himself would not appear to be a deserter from the king.

33. The Capture of Reims.—He thought the matter could be arranged as follows: a time should be fixed at which Arnulfus himself would gather in the city as many leading men as he could, as though he were about to organize some great undertaking. Then Karolus would arrive with an army at the city gates during the silence of the night. There would be someone who would open the gates to the invading army, having sworn to keep the secret.

Once admitted, the army would invade the city, seize Arnulfus together with the assembled leading men, use force against them, and thrust them into prison. In this way royal power would be weakened, his uncle’s ability to rule would be increased, and Arnulfus himself would not appear to be a deserter. The plan was carried out.

34. He invited Counts G. and V., together with other men of consular rank. He sent word that he was about to arrange something important, and that they therefore needed to hasten greatly. They came without delay, showing themselves fully prepared to serve their lord.

Arnulfus concealed what he was truly planning by substituting one pretext for another. No one knew what he was really aiming at. He entrusted the entire matter, in confidence, to one man whose silence and loyalty he did not doubt. He disclosed that Karolus’s army was to be admitted that night and ordered him to take the keys of the gates from his own pillow and open the city to the armed men.

Not long afterward, the night destined for this crime arrived. At the appointed time Karolus appeared by night at the city gates with his army. A priest named Algerus—for that was his name—was inside with the keys. He immediately opened the gates, and the army was admitted. The city was then plundered and stripped by marauders.

35. The Capture of Arnulfus and His Men.—When shouting arose throughout the city and the uproar of people running about awakened the unsuspecting citizens, Arnulfus pretended that he too was thrown into confusion by the shouting. Feigning fear, he sought the tower and climbed it. His companions followed him and bolted the doors behind them.

Karolus searched for Arnulfus and, not finding him, investigated where he might be hiding. When it was disclosed to him that Arnulfus was concealed at the top of the tower, he immediately placed guards at the door. Since they had stored neither food nor weapons there beforehand, they yielded to Karolus and came out of the tower.

36. They were captured and taken to Laon, where they were assigned to the custody of guards. When Karolus returned and asked them for their loyalty, they unanimously resisted. Thus they pretended mutual hatred and revealed their affectionate relationship in no way. Each simulated some complaint against the other, since each accused the other of being, respectively, a deserter and an invader.

At last Arnulfus, establishing his loyalty by an oath, obtained his freedom and returned to his own possessions. From then on he favored Karolus in everything and completely broke the obligation of loyalty owed to the king.

G. and V., after being confined in prison for several days, were not long afterward bound by an oath and permitted to return. Karolus, therefore, distinguished by this successful outcome, obtained the metropolitan city of Reims together with Laon and Soissons and their towns.

37. Hugh’s Attack.—There was no lack of someone to report this to the ears of the king. Struck by this insult, the king asked what ought to be done about it. He learned that the matter could be shaken loose not by prayers or gifts but by force and arms, with the Divinity invoked.

He therefore gathered six thousand soldiers, intending to march against the tyrant. He wished to besiege him if his forces proved sufficient and, if fortune favored him, to continue the undertaking until he brought down the enemy either by arms or by starvation.

He set out with great courage. He led his army through the land from which the enemy transported their grain. He utterly ravaged and burned it, becoming so fierce that he would not leave even a hut for a senile old woman.

Then, turning his army against the enemy with impetuous resolve, he attempted to impose a siege. Since Karolus had already prepared forces for himself, he tried bravely to resist the advancing king. He had gathered four thousand fighting men at Laon and strengthened their resolve, so that they would remain at rest if they were not attacked and resist if they were pressed.

38. The Army Is Arranged in Three Divisions.—Meanwhile, as the king led in his army, he saw Karolus’s legion arranged for battle. He therefore divided his army into three parts, lest a large army, burdened by its own mass, should be deprived of the use of its strength.

He established three battle lines: the first to begin the initial assaults of the war; the second to come to the aid of the faltering line and restore its strength; and the third to be assigned to carrying off the spoils. After they had been divided and arranged in this way, the first line advanced with its standards raised to engage the king, while the other two stood ready in their appointed positions and awaited the opportunity to give support.

39. Karolus advanced to meet them with four thousand men, invoking the supreme Divinity to protect the few from the countless and to demonstrate that one must not trust in numbers or despair because of fewness. Arnulfus accompanied him as he advanced, exhorting his men to stand with courageous hearts and to proceed in ordered, undivided formation. They should in no way doubt victory from God. If they stood bravely after invoking God, they would soon gain victory with great glory and renown.

The two armies advanced until each could see the other; then both stood fixed in place. There was considerable hesitation on both sides. Karolus lacked military experience, while the king’s conscience, aware of his own crime, accused him of acting against justice: he had deprived Karolus of his paternal honor and transferred the rights of the kingdom to himself.

Each remained fixed upon these considerations. At last the leading men appropriately advised the king that he should stand with his army for a while. If the enemy advanced, he should engage them at close quarters; if no one provoked an attack, he should return with his army. Karolus made the same decision.

Therefore, because both remained in position, each yielded to the other. The king withdrew his army; Karolus, for his part, retreated to Laon.

40. (991.) Meanwhile O., desirous of Dreux, pretended to complain to the king that he had become deeply distrustful of capturing Laon, since the battering ram had failed, the soldiers lacked confidence in their strength, and even the city itself, relying on its inaccessible position, scornfully resisted them.

The king, overcome with grief, asked O. for assistance, promising to repay the favor if he supplied troops and completely captured the city. If O. should presently ask for something that ought to be granted, the king declared that he would undoubtedly show himself generous.

O. promised that he would soon attack and capture Laon, provided that he received Dreux from the king. Desiring the glory of victory, the king granted the petitioner the castle. He openly yielded it to him, trusting in his promises concerning Laon. O. likewise publicly pledged to everyone that he would soon restore the lost city.

He therefore took possession of the castle granted by the king without delay, binding the castle’s men to himself by right of an oath and associating with them several others whose loyalty he knew to be strong. From then on he diligently managed the king’s affairs.

The outcome of his intention, however, was nothing, because a timely betrayal of the city prevented it and sudden circumstances showed that the matter had to unfold otherwise.

41. A Subtle Plot against Karolus and Arnulfus.—From this time Adalbero, bishop of Laon, who had earlier escaped after being captured by Karolus, sought by every means an opportunity by which, in turn, he might capture Laon and seize Karolus.

He therefore sent Arnulfus envoys exceptionally skilled in such business, conveying assurances of friendship, loyalty, and assistance. He also declared that he wished to be reconciled with Arnulfus as his metropolitan. He said that he considered it an injury to be called a fugitive and deserter, since he had not obeyed Karolus after pledging his loyalty. If the opportunity arose, he wished to cast off this disgrace.

He wished to return to Arnulfus’s high authority and desired the friendship of Karolus, his lord. Accordingly, he instructed Arnulfus to meet him wherever he wished.

Arnulfus, unaware that the loyalty was feigned, received the deceptive envoys and honored them most courteously, as though they were bringing news of some good fortune. Through them, rejoicing, he designated the place where they would meet and confer. They rejoiced that they had deceived him and reported this to their lord.

Recognizing that the seed of the deception had been planted effectively, Adalbero perceived that the fraud might give rise to a more elaborate plot. After this, they met at the appointed place, congratulating one another with many embraces and kisses and displaying such great affection that no pretense or deceit seemed possible.

42. Adalbero’s Deceptive Plot.—After there had been enough embracing and enough kissing, Adalbero, who bore the appearance of pretense and the burden of deceit, addressed the unsuspecting Arnulfus first:

“The same misfortune and the same fate weigh grievously upon us both. Therefore, we seem to need to adopt the same counsel and the same plan. Recently, both of us fell: you from the king’s favor, I from Karolus’s friendship. Hence now you favor Karolus, while I favor the king. He readily trusts you, and this man readily trusts me.

“If, therefore, through you Karolus’s affection is restored to me, the king’s favor will not be absent from you. This will not be difficult to accomplish. Go, then, to Karolus and, if he is willing, plead with him on my behalf. It will not be useless to say much about the loyalty that should be shown to him. If anything in these matters seems doubtful to him, then say that it should be confirmed by oaths.

“If he restores the bishopric to its see, let the relics of the saints be present; I am prepared to establish my loyalty. If this suffices and he restores it, you may place great confidence in the king’s favor.

“In this speech and in this hand, peace and discord lie. I will approach the king. I will promise him an advantage that will benefit not only him but also his descendants. I will expose Karolus’s deceits. I will assert that an injury was done to the unsuspecting metropolitan, and I will affirm, with several embellishments, that this metropolitan deeply regrets what happened.

“The king, naturally credulous toward me, will receive this with great pleasure. Since this plan will be pursued on both sides, two advantages will arise. From these two, a third will emerge. For when the king’s favor is restored to you and Karolus’s favor to me, the interests of others will consequently be advanced through us.

“But now enough of words; let what has been said be tested by deeds.”

After exchanging brief kisses and promising what they had pledged, they departed from one another.

43. Arnulfus Deceives His Uncle Karolus through Ignorance.—Arnulfus went to Karolus and, unaware that Adalbero was a deceiver, praised him highly, declaring that he would be of great benefit and testifying that he would preserve his loyalty. At last, deceived, he persuaded Karolus that there was nothing to doubt in him. Favoring his nephew, Karolus promised that he would do this and did not refuse to restore the bishopric on those terms.

While these matters were being faithfully arranged with Karolus, Adalbero was negotiating with the king concerning Karolus, Arnulfus, and the capture of the city. When he unfolded the earlier *technai* (τέχναι, “contrivances” or “arts”), there was considerable rejoicing and hope of recovering the city.

Not long afterward Arnulfus sent envoys to Adalbero, generously announcing that Karolus’s favor had been granted him and that he should be received into the city with great ceremony. He would also recover his honor without delay. Therefore, he should not delay but come as quickly as possible to experience the promised generosity.

44. Adalbero Deceives Karolus and Arnulfus by an Oath.—Without delay, Adalbero came at the appointed place when summoned by Karolus and Arnulfus. They received him graciously, and he found no small joy there. If any disagreement had preceded them, they passed over it after touching upon it lightly and briefly. They extolled in various ways the right of friendship, which henceforth ought to be cultivated more fully between them.

They often recounted how much advantage would result if they made good use of their friendship, and how much glory, honor, and protection would follow. They also touched upon the possibility that, in a short time, both the advancement of their own side and the downfall of their enemies could be achieved. Nothing, they said, could obstruct this unless the Divinity alone intervened.

If their wishes achieved their intended result, the state would one day be heaped with great honor and glory and would flourish through them. After these words, they bound themselves to one another by an oath and departed.

Adalbero went to the king and explained what he had done. When the king heard it, he approved the undertaking and promised that he would receive Arnulfus if he came. He also said that he would willingly hear Arnulfus’s defense against the charges brought against him and, if he cleared himself properly, would treat him with no less favor than before.

Adalbero reported these things to Arnulfus. He declared that the king was benevolent and merciful and that he wished willingly to hear Arnulfus’s defense and restore his favor without delay. Arnulfus therefore needed to hasten and make his request as quickly as possible. He should approach the king at once, lest the deceit of certain men break off the plan.

Thus both men set out for the king.

45. Arnulfus Went to the King to Receive His Favor.—When Arnulfus was admitted to the king, the king kissed him. When Arnulfus wished to undertake some defense against the charges brought against him, the king said that it was enough for him to abandon the past and thereafter preserve his loyalty to the king inviolate.

He said that he fully understood that Karolus had used force against Arnulfus and that this had been done under the greatest necessity, so that Arnulfus might for a time withdraw from the king and favor Karolus even against his will. But since this had happened and could not be undone, Arnulfus needed to consider carefully how he might somehow compensate for the loss of the city.

If he could not possess the city as before, he should at least induce Karolus to transfer his allegiance to the king, so that, with the king’s consent, Karolus might retain what he had seized. Arnulfus promised to do this and more, provided only that the king’s favor was restored to him and that the king honored him as metropolitan.

The king granted him his favor and allowed him to receive the greatest honor in his presence. Thus, on that very day at the meal, Arnulfus sat at the king’s right hand and Adalbero at the queen’s left.

When matters had been arranged in this way, Arnulfus was dismissed by the king. He reported to Karolus the king’s remarkable goodwill and, explaining the honor he had received in the king’s presence, greatly boasted of the king’s favor. From that time onward he sought a reconciliation and friendship between the king and Karolus.

46. Adalbero’s Reception by Karolus.—While these matters stood thus, Adalbero departed from the king and, going to Karolus, was received at Laon with great ceremony. His followers returned to him, those who had earlier been exiled from the city. They arranged his household affairs as before, without any hesitation and in hope of peace thereafter.

He revisited the clergy whom he had lost, sympathized with them, promised them his goodwill, and urged them not to abandon him. After he had conversed sufficiently with his followers, Karolus questioned him about the security of his loyalty and of the city. He began as follows:

“Since the Divinity, merciful in all things even when punishing, acts mercifully, I recognize that by his just judgment I was both cast out and received. By his equity I think that I have been received into this city; by his kindness I await what remains. I also believe that he himself has restored you and this city to me.

“Therefore, I seek to have one restored by God joined to me. The holy things are present; place your right hand upon them and promise loyalty against everyone. There will be no refusal if you wish to become my companion.”

Eager for the fulfillment of his wishes, Adalbero promised everything that was requested. He extended his right hand over the holy relics and did not hesitate to swear to whatever had been proposed. Consequently, everyone trusted him, and no one suspected him. No one avoided him in any matter. He himself asked and deliberated about fortifying the city. He inquired into everyone’s affairs and consulted on behalf of all. Thus, unknown to everyone, he remained hidden from them all.

- 18, heading: [Col. 0133], `I, in abscisa`—“I, cut off in the abbreviated text” (the precise referent of the isolated `I` is uncertain).
- 23: [Col. 0133], `sponderet supra posito annueret cod.`—the manuscript reads *annueret* (“should grant/assent”); *sponderet* (“should promise”) is written above it.
- 24, heading: [Col. 0135], `albe, opo abscisa`—“albe-, opo- cut off”; damaged heading text. The illness is called by the Greeks *causon* (καῦσον), and by the Latins *incendium* (“burning fever”).
- 25, heading: [Col. 0135], `Arnulfus, archi, m abscisa`—“Arnulfus, archi-, m cut off”; damaged heading text. In the body, [Col. 0135], `per burch deletum`—*per burch* has been deleted.
- 26, heading: [Col. 0135], `regis abscisum`—“of the king, cut off.” [Col. 0135], `D. M.`—*divae memoriae*, “of blessed memory.”
- 27, heading: [Col. 0135], `io, em abscisa`—damaged heading text. [Col. 0135], `videtur supra pos. est`—*videtur* (“it seems”) is written above *est* (“is”).
- 28, heading: [Col. 0135], `Ar abscis.`—“Ar- cut off.” [Col. 0135], `D. M.`—“of blessed memory.”
- 29, heading: [Col. 0137], `Cir abscis.`—“Cir- cut off.”
- 30, heading: [Col. 0137], `E abscis.`—“E- cut off.”
- 31, heading: [Col. 0137], `R abscis.`—“R- cut off.” [Col. 0137], `et et cod.`—the manuscript has the repeated *et et* (“and and”).
- 33: [Col. 0137], `statuertur codex`—the manuscript reads *statuertur* for *statueretur* (“should be appointed”). [Col. 0137], `secretum hoc nunquam proditurum deleta`—“never to betray this secret” has been deleted. [Col. 0137], `custodie supra posito ergastulo codex`—*custodiae* (“to custody”) is written above the manuscript’s *ergastulo* (“to prison”).
- 34: [Col. 0137], `. uc.`—an unclear or damaged note. [Col. 0137], `exercitus supra posito K. codex`—*exercitus* (“army”) is written above the manuscript’s `K.` (Karolus). [Col. 0137], `ita cod.`—“thus in the manuscript,” concerning *intromitendus* (“was to be admitted”).
- 35, heading: [Col. 0137], `i, p abscisa`—damaged heading text. [Col. 0137], `commites cod.`—the manuscript reads *comites* (“companions/counts”).
- 36: [Col. 0139], `praedicaretur supra posito, enuntiaretur cod.`—*praedicaretur* (“was proclaimed”) is written above the manuscript reading *enuntiaretur* (“was declared”). [Col. 0139], `episcopus supra posito Ar. cod.`—*episcopus* (“bishop”) is written above the manuscript’s `Ar.` (Arnulfus).
- 37, heading: [Col. 0139], `tus, nis abscisa`—damaged heading text. [Col. 0139], `regum supra posito is codex`—*regum* (“of the kings”) is written above the manuscript reading *is* (“of the king”).
- 38, heading: [Col. 0139], `tus, o, tur abscisa`—damaged heading text. [Col. 0139], `tumultus corr. impetus`—*tumultus* (“confusions/onsets”) has been corrected to *impetus* (“assaults”).
- 39: [Col. 0139], `fecisse supra posito agere codex`—*fecisse* (“to have done”) is written above the manuscript reading *agere* (“to do/act”).
- 40: [Col. 0139D], `Dreux` identifies *Drocarum* as Dreux. [Col. 0139], `intempestiva corr. tempestiva`—*intempestiva* (“untimely”) has been corrected to *tempestiva* (“timely”).
- 41, heading: [Col. 0139], `Sub, ma abscisa`—damaged heading text.
- 42, heading: [Col. 0141], `Adelberonis, machin abscisa`—damaged heading text. [Col. 0141], `abscesserunt supra posito ab se digressi sunt codex`—*abscesserunt* (“they departed”) is written above the manuscript’s *ab se digressi sunt* (“they departed from one another”).
- 43, heading: [Col. 0141], `Arnulfus, ran, pa abscisa`—damaged heading text. [Col. 0141D], `Τεχνάς, artes`—Greek *technas*, “arts/contrivances.” [Col. 0141], `aperiret supra posito effunderet codex`—*aperiret* (“should disclose”) is written above the manuscript’s *effunderet* (“should pour forth”).
- 44, heading: [Col. 0141], `A, sa, d, abscisa`—damaged heading text. [Col. 0141], `eis supra posito his codex`—*eis* (“them”) is written above the manuscript’s *his* (“these”).
- 45, heading: [Col. 0141], `regem, it, b eo, turus abscisa`—damaged heading text.
- 46, heading: [Col. 0143], `ptio, Karolo abscisa`—damaged heading text. [Col. 0143D], `Scil. Karolus`—“namely, Karolus,” identifying the speaker.

### 47. The Capture of Charles by Adalbero  
*[Note: “[Col. 0143] hensio” is cut off.]*

Meanwhile, after he had thoroughly discerned the disposition of Charles and his men, and saw that he himself was suspected by no one, Adalbero pretended various kinds of treachery, so that he might both restore the city to himself and hand Charles over as a captive to the king. He therefore engaged Charles in conversation very frequently and displayed ever greater goodwill. He even offered, if necessary, to bind himself more tightly by oaths, employing such crafty caution that he completely concealed his deceit beneath the coloring of pretense.

Thus, one night, while he was sitting cheerfully at dinner (March 29), Charles was holding a golden cup in which he had broken bread and mixed it with wine. After much reflection, he offered it to Adalbero, saying:

“Since, according to the decrees of the Fathers, you have today sanctified palms and branches, and have consecrated the people with sacred blessings, and have offered us the Eucharist [Note: [Col. 0143]: the manuscript has *populum*, with *plebem* written above it.], disregarding the slanders of certain whisperers who deny that you should be trusted, as the day of the Passion of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ is approaching, I offer you this vessel, appropriate to your dignity, together with wine and broken bread. Drink this cup as a sign that faith is to be held and preserved. But if you do not intend in your heart to preserve faith, spare the cup, lest you reproduce the dreadful likeness of Judas the betrayer.”

When Adalbero replied, “I will accept the cup and freely drink the potion,” Charles immediately continued and said that he must add, “and I will keep faith.” Having drunk, Adalbero continued: “And I will keep faith; otherwise, may I perish with Judas!” He uttered many similar words of anathema to those dining with him.

The night that would witness grief and betrayal was approaching. They decided to retire quietly and sleep until morning. Adalbero, conscious of his treachery, removed the swords and weapons from the heads of the sleeping Charles and Arnulf and had them hidden (March 30). Calling for the doorkeeper, who knew nothing of this plot, he ordered him to hasten on his way and summon one of his men, promising in the meantime that he himself would guard the door. When the man had departed, Adalbero planted himself across the doorway, holding a sword beneath his clothing. His own men, who were privy to the crime, immediately joined him, and he admitted them all.

Charles and Arnulf were resting, overcome by their morning sleep. When the enemies appeared before them in battle formation, and the two men awoke and perceived their adversaries, they sprang from their beds and tried to seize their weapons, but could not find them. They asked what this morning’s event signified.

Adalbero replied:

“Since you recently stole this fortress from me, forced me to leave it in exile, you too are now being driven from here, though under a different fortune. I have remained in possession of my own right; you will enter upon what belongs to another.”

Charles answered:

“Do you mean, bishop, that you have forgotten yesterday’s dinner? I am greatly astonished. Will the very reverence owed to God not restrain you? Is an oath worth nothing? Is yesterday’s invocation worth nothing?”

With these words, he rushed headlong at the enemy. The armed men surrounded him as he raged, drove him back onto the bed, and restrained him. They attacked Arnulf no less fiercely. After capturing them, they confined them in the same tower. They fortified the tower with keys, locks, and bars, placing guards over it.

Then, as the shouting of women and children, together with the howling of the servants, rose toward heaven, the citizens throughout the city were thrown into confusion and awakened. All who favored Charles’s party immediately freed themselves by flight—and only with difficulty, for while they were still almost in the act of fleeing, Adalbero ordered the entire city to be sealed at once, so that he could seize everyone whom he considered his enemy. They were sought but not found.

Charles’s two-year-old son was also secretly removed; he bore his father’s name and was freed from captivity. Adalbero immediately sent envoys to the king at Senlis, reporting that the city formerly lost had now been recovered, that Charles had been captured with his wife and children, and that Arnulf had been found and seized among the enemy. He therefore urged the king to come without delay with as many men as he could. He was not to delay in gathering an army. He was to send envoys to all the neighboring men in whom he trusted, asking them to follow him. And he was to come at once, even if with only a few men.

### 48. The King Enters Laon with Charles and Arnulf as Captives  
*[Note: “[Col. 0145] Re, Karolo et, num i” is cut off.]*

The king took as many men as he could and proceeded without delay to Laon. Having obtained the city and been received with royal dignity, he inquired and learned about the safety of the faithful, the recovery of the city, and the capture of the enemies. On the following day, after summoning the citizens, he discussed the faith they were to show him. Both those who had been captives and those who had already passed under another’s authority swore faith and bound themselves to the king by oath. After securing the city, the king returned to Senlis with the captured enemies. He then questioned his own men and sought their advice about what course of deliberation should be followed.

### 49. The Deliberation of Certain Men before the King concerning Charles  
*[Note: “[Col. 0145] Deli, quo, apu, super” is cut off; the manuscript reads *cloro* for *claro*, and has the fragment “st.” after *indignaturi sint*.]*

Some advised that, from Charles—a distinguished man of illustrious royal descent—all his sons together with his daughters should be taken as hostages. An oath should also be demanded from him, by which he would pledge to the king that he would never seek to recover the kingdom of France and would make a testament to that effect even against his children. Once this had been done, they thought Charles should be released.

Others held a different opinion. They said that so distinguished a man of ancient lineage should not immediately be returned, but should be held with the king until those who would resent his capture became visible. If such men, under such a number, name, and leader, should prove so formidable that they would not undeservedly be called enemies of the king of the Franks, then the matter should be considered; if they were inferior, another course should be followed. Thus, if only a few and inferior men resented the capture, they thought Charles should be retained; but if the resenting party proved more powerful and more numerous, they advised that he should be returned on the grounds stated above.

The king therefore committed Charles, together with his wife Adelaide, his son Louis, and his two daughters—one called Gerberga and the other Adelaidis—as well as his nephew Arnulf, to prison.

### 50. The Difficulty of the Journey from the City of Reims to Chartres

*[Note: [Col. 0145]: “ultate, is ab ur, notum” is cut off. The manuscript reads *yppacratis* for *Yppocratis*; “rebat, datoque, motim, us” is cut off; *a. m.* is the manuscript reading, and the abbot is identified as Arbodo; *ceteriisque* is the manuscript reading; “tertio” is corrected to “VI.to”; *cap.* is an abbreviation; the manuscript has *uexatus*, with *tortus* written above it; on Abbot Augustine, see the note below; “mis, dui” is cut off; and *ita c.* means “so in the manuscript.”]*

About fourteen days before the capture of these men, while I was living in the city of Reims and was often and at length reflecting eagerly on learning the logic of Hippocrates of Cos, as well as the liberal studies, I happened one day to encounter a horseman from Chartres. When I asked him who he was and whose man he was, and why and from where he had come, he replied that he was the envoy of Heribrand, a cleric of Chartres, and that he wished to speak with Richer, a monk of Saint Remigius.

Immediately recognizing the name of my friend and the purpose of the embassy, I identified myself as the man he was seeking. After exchanging a kiss, we withdrew privately. He then produced a letter of encouragement to read the aphorisms. I was therefore exceedingly pleased, and, taking along a certain boy with the horseman from Chartres, decided to set out for Chartres.

When I departed, I received from my abbot only the assistance of a single small riding horse. Also lacking money for changing mounts and every other necessity, I reached Orbais, a place renowned for great charity.
