*[Note: Orbais, near the great road leading from Châlons to Meaux. It therefore seems that he crossed the Marne at Épernay on the first day and reached the Castle of Theodoric on the second.]*

There I was refreshed by a conversation with the lord abbot D. and sustained at the same time by his generosity. On the following day I set out to travel as far as Meaux.

After entering the winding paths of the woods with two companions, we did not escape misfortune. For, when the diverging roads deceived us, we went astray by the excess of six leagues. After we had passed the Castle of Theodoric, the little riding horse, which had earlier appeared like a Bucephalus, began to become rather sluggish, like a small donkey.

The sun had already moved past midday and, as the entire sky dissolved into rain, was turning toward sunset, when that sturdy Bucephalus, overcome by its final exertion, collapsed between the legs of the boy who was riding it and, as if struck by lightning, died six miles from the city.

How great was our confusion then, how great our anxiety, can be judged by those who have at some time endured similar misfortunes and can infer similar consequences from similar circumstances. The boy, inexperienced in the difficulty of so long a journey, lay exhausted in every limb after losing the horse. The baggage was present without a bearer. Rain poured down in excessive torrents. The sky threatened clouds. The sun, already near setting, threatened darkness.

Amid all these circumstances, God did not fail to provide counsel for one who doubted. I left the boy there with the baggage, instructing him what to answer if travelers questioned him and how to resist the sleep that was overcoming him. Accompanied only by the horseman from Chartres, I reached Meaux.

Seeing the bridge only barely in the fading daylight, I entered upon it. As I examined it more carefully, I was again tormented by fresh misfortunes. It was so open with so many gaps that scarcely any of the citizens who needed to cross it that day had managed to pass over it.

The energetic horseman from Chartres, sufficiently prudent in carrying out the journey, searched everywhere for a little boat but found none. He therefore returned to the dangers of the bridge and implored heaven that the horses might be brought across safely. At the open gaps he sometimes placed a shield beneath the horses’ feet, sometimes fitted discarded boards into place; now stooping, now standing upright, now advancing, now retreating, he successfully crossed with the horses, while I accompanied him.

Night had grown terrible and covered the world with a dreadful darkness when I entered the basilica of Saint Faro, while the brothers were still preparing the drink of charity. That day they had dined solemnly, after the chapter concerning the monastery’s cellarer had been read—a matter that had caused the drinking to be so late.

*[Note: “cap.” is an abbreviation for “chapter.”]*

They received me as a brother, refreshed me with kind conversation and sufficient food, and I sent the horseman from Chartres back with the horses, leaving the boy behind, so that he could attempt the dangers of the bridge again.

He crossed it by the method described above and, wandering about during the second watch of the night, reached the boy. Only after calling out to him repeatedly did he scarcely manage to find him. When he had taken him up and reached the city, fearing the dangers of the bridge, which he had learned through perilous experience, he withdrew with the boy and the horses into someone’s hut. There they remained without food throughout the day and were gathered there that night for rest, not for dinner.

Those who have at some time been compelled to keep watch because of concern for dear ones can judge how sleeplessly I passed that night and by what anguish I was tortured during it. When the desired daylight had returned, they arrived, exhausted by excessive hunger. Food was brought to them, and grain mixed with chaff was placed before the horses.

I dismissed the boy on foot to Abbot Augustine—*[Note: “Aug. c.”; he seems also to occur in the necrology of Saint Faro of Meaux; see Gallia Christiana.]*—and, accompanied only by the horseman from Chartres, hurried on to Chartres. From there, after sending the horses back, I recalled the boy from the city of Meaux.

Once he had been brought back and every anxiety removed, I devoted myself diligently to the aphorisms of Hippocrates under the guidance of Lord Heribrand, a man of great generosity and learning. Since from them I had acquired only the prognostics of diseases, and the simple knowledge of illnesses did not satisfy my desire, I also asked him to let me read his book entitled *On the Concord of Hippocrates, Galen,* *[Note: “ita c.”]* *and Soranus.* This request too I obtained, for he was so skilled in the art that the *dynamidia pharmaceutica*, the botanical sciences, and surgery were not unknown to him.

### 51. How, as a Result of the Complaint of Those Rebuking Arnulf’s Capture, a Synod Was Held by Royal Command  
*[Note: [Col. 0147]: “uere, endentionem, gio jus, us ha, t ex conj.” is cut off; *ex conj.* means “by conjecture.” The reading *scolasticorum* is corrected to *amicorum*, and *decreto* to *edicto*.]*

But, to return now to the sequence of the earlier affair: when some of the friends were indignant at the bishop’s capture, and certain scholars wrote various things in his defense and brought forward other written materials concerning the canons, and when this had been reported to the ears of the kings, a royal edict decreed that all the bishops of Gaul who were able to come, and especially those of the same province, should assemble in one place. Those who could not be present were to clear themselves of suspicion concerning their absence through suitable envoys.

There they were either to condemn the accused on the basis of definite and firm reasons derived from the decrees, or, once he had been cleared, to restore him to the dignity of his former see.

They therefore assembled in the monastery of the monks of Saint Basolus the Confessor (June 17): the diocesan bishops of Reims, namely the comprovincials of the metropolitan of Reims—Guido, bishop of Soissons; Adalbero, bishop of Laon; Herivevus, bishop of Beauvais; Godesmannus, bishop of Amiens; Rathbodus, bishop of Noyon; Odo, bishop of Senlis; and Daibertus, metropolitan of Bourges.

Also present were the comprovincials of the metropolitan of Lyon: Gualterus, bishop of Autun; Bruno, bishop of Langres; Milo, bishop of Mâcon; Siguinus, metropolitan of Sens, together with his bishops Arnulfus of Orléans and Herbertus of Auxerre.

When they had taken their seats together, they ordered the abbots from various places who were present to sit with them after conducting their own private discussion.

### 52. Deliberation concerning the Dignity of Holding the Judgment and Presiding

*[Note: [Col. 0147]: “ra, digni, udi, praela” is cut off.]*

After consideration had been given to holding the synod, they thought it necessary to determine to whom authority over the judgment of each matter should be entrusted and whom they should appoint as guardian and interpreter of the proceedings.

The dignity of judging was entrusted to Siguinus, metropolitan of Sens, because he was highly commended by the respect due to his age and by the merit of his life. The authority to arrange the proceedings and the office of interpreting the arguments were entrusted to Arnulfus, bishop of Orléans, because among the bishops of Gaul he flourished through the power of his eloquence and effectiveness in speaking.

After these arrangements had been made, and after the clergy had entered and statements relevant to the case had been read, Arnulfus began as follows:

### 53. Arnulfus’s Address in the Synod

*[Note: [Col. 0147]: “El, Arnulfi in” is cut off; the manuscript reads *sinoni* for *sinodi*.]*

“Since, reverend fathers, we have assembled here at the command of our most serene kings and also for the sake of sacred religion, it seems that we must take great care, with great faith and great diligence, lest we who have been gathered here by the grace of the Holy Spirit be led astray from the standard of righteousness by hatred of anyone or love for anyone.

Since we have been gathered here in the name of the Lord, we must conduct everything before the sight of the supreme Divinity with truthful judgments; we must not deprive anyone of the opportunity to speak; we must devote ourselves to truth; we must stand vigorously on behalf of truth; and, in response to the charges, we must both make arguments and give answers in simple and pure judgments.

Let the honor due to each person be preserved; let everyone have the power to speak. Let the freedom both to present arguments and to refute them be granted to all.

Now, since you have wished me to speak before everyone else, I think that the case of this synod should be stated openly, so that, once it has been properly arranged, it may appear to all as it truly is.

That most illustrious metropolitan city of Reims was recently overrun by enemies through treachery. The Holy of Holies was defiled by the attack of the enemies; the sanctuary of God was violated by every kind of wickedness; the citizens were also carried off by the plunderers.

The man accused of being the author of these evils is the one who ought to have protected the city from the enemies: Arnulfus, bishop of that same city. This is the charge brought against him. To investigate it, the royal dignity has assembled us here.

Work, therefore, reverend fathers, lest the treachery of one man bring the dignity of the priesthood into contempt.”

### 54. Daibertus’s Speech in Favor of Judgment

*[Note: [Col. 0147]: “Sermo, berti pro” is cut off.]*

When some of those seated there replied that such a man should be convicted as quickly as possible and then punished by a just judgment, Bishop Siguinus answered that he would not permit the man accused of treason against the majesty of the king to be subjected to judicial examination unless he first received from the kings and bishops a sworn promise of pardon.

He asserted that this had to be done on the basis of chapter 31 of the Council of Toledo. Since we are hastening toward brevity, we have omitted its text.

#### 54*. Daibertus, Archbishop of Bourges, said:

“Since the deed is established and there is no doubt about the identity of the deed, and since the magnitude of the crime is also being weighed, I entirely fail to see how, by necessity, pardon must be granted to the accused.

For necessity seems to arise here because the judgment cannot be pronounced unless pardon for the punishment has first been granted to the man who is to be convicted. But if one looks to secular laws, whatever crime someone may have committed, he will be subjected to the severity of penance according to the measure of his crime.”

### 55. Herivevus, Bishop of Beauvais, said:

“We must take the greatest care lest we compare divine laws with forensic laws. They differ greatly from one another, since divine laws are concerned with ecclesiastical matters, while secular laws are applied to secular matters. The former surpass the latter as greatly as the latter are inferior to the former.

Therefore, in every respect, the honor due to divine laws must be preserved. If, then, our brother and fellow bishop Arnulfus is convicted of treason against the majesty of the king, I do not refuse to acknowledge that, out of priestly reverence and kinship of blood, some pardon should be granted to him by the most serene kings.

Nevertheless, he will not altogether escape the sentence of judgment if, by his own confession, he is shown to be unworthy of priestly dignity.”

### 56. Bruno’s Indignation against Arnulfus

*[Note: [Col. 0149]: “Ind, Bru, Arnulfum” is cut off; the manuscript reads *Manas* for *Manasse*.]*

Bruno, bishop of Langres, said:

“I seem to have plunged the man about whom this discussion is being held into these miseries, when, against the wishes of many good men, I raised him to the summit of honor. I did this not only because of our kinship of flesh, but also to draw him toward a better way of life.

I was not unaware that he was the usurper of the city of Laon and the rash leader of a wicked faction. Under the authority of a *chirograph*—a written bond—he had sworn faith to the kings, promising that for no oath, past or future, would he ever violate the faith he had pledged; that he would attack the enemies of the kings according to his ability and strength; and that he would share nothing with them.

But since Charles, my uncle, is plainly an adversary of the kings, when the man of whom we are speaking joined Charles and gave him faith under oath, he completely severed the bond of the faith he had promised.

Are Manasse and Rotgerus not to be called adversaries of the kings? They were, together with Charles, the usurpers of the city of Reims, and they entered the basilica of Holy Mary, Mother of God, with an armed band, violating the sanctuary by their wicked entrance. This man even kept them as guardians of his counsel and as his chief friends.

Since this is most evident, let him now say at whose instigation or persuasion he undertook this act. Otherwise, he will turn his accusation against others, or, overcome by testimony, he will collapse. No love of kinship and no favor arising from former association will in any way lead me astray from the form of a righteous judgment.”

### 57. Godesmannus’s Praise of Bruno’s Magnanimity and Request that He Establish the Judgment

*[Note: [Col. 0149]: “Laus, man, nani, et ut a, constitu” is cut off.]*

Godesmannus, bishop of Amiens, said:

“We know the magnanimity of the venerable Bruno, whom no love of kinship and no familiarity separates from the truth. Rather, the rigor of his mind and the uprightness of his character most readily show him to be truthful and worthy of belief.

Since, therefore, mention has already been made of examining the guilt of our brother and fellow bishop Arnulfus, it seems that he should be asked what judgment ought to be rendered in this matter, since he ought to temper the severity of the judgment, being placed between the two in such a way that he owes faith to the king and affection to Arnulfus on account of their blood relationship.

He will therefore not be held under any suspicion of deceit: loyalty to his lord will incite him to judgment, while love of his neighbor will keep him from ill will.”

### 58. Bruno’s Reply

To this Bishop Bruno replied:

“I understand your mind quite clearly. The man accused of treason against the majesty of the king is related to me by blood, since he is the son of my uncle, King Lothair. Therefore, your kindness fears that I would be wronged if you pronounced a judgment concerning him that was deserved.

But far be it from me to regard love of kinship as more precious than the love of Christ. Let your holiness examine with me, by careful investigation, the matter under discussion. Let us fear nothing concerning the condemnation to be imposed upon the convicted man, since it is equally just both that the man guilty of treason should be condemned and that the innocent should be released.”

### 59. Rathbodus’s Demonstration that They Wrongly Slander the Fidelity Document of the Bishops of Lotharingia

*[Note: [Col. 0149]: “Ratbo, bellum, episcopi L, perperam” is cut off.]*

Rathbodus, bishop of Noyon, said:

“If it pleases you, reverend fathers, I think that the document of fidelity once presented by Arnulfus to the kings concerning the faith he was to maintain should now be examined by you. It seems sufficient by itself for his condemnation, since he has wholly violated by the sacrilege of perjury the faith promised under oath and confirmed by his written signature.

But there is something that troubles me: namely, that, as is said, the bishops of Lotharingia are arguing against him. For they slander the document as having been written, read, and stored away contrary to the divine laws. Therefore, if it pleases you, let it now be brought forward for examination in your presence.”

The synod said: “Let it be brought forward.”

### 60. The Text of Arnulfus’s Fidelity Document

*[Note: [Col. 0149]: “elli fide” is cut off.]*

It was therefore produced, containing the following text:

“I, Arnulfus, by the prevenient grace of God archbishop of Reims, promise that I will preserve the purest faith toward the kings of the Franks, Hugh and Robert, and that I will provide them with counsel and assistance according to my knowledge and ability in all matters. I will knowingly aid none of their enemies, either by counsel or by assistance, to their disloyalty.

Standing before the divine majesty, the blessed spirits, and the whole Church, I make this promise, and for having kept it well I shall receive the rewards of eternal blessedness.

But if—which I do not wish and which may it never be—if I should deviate from this, may all my blessing be turned into a curse; may my days become few; and may another receive my bishopric. May my friends depart from me and become perpetual enemies.

To this *chirograph* issued by me, as testimony to my blessing or curse, I subscribe, and I ask my brothers and sons to subscribe as well.

I, Arnulfus, archbishop, have subscribed.”

### 61. Arnulfus Approves and Criticizes the Document in Part

*[Note: [Col. 0151]: “bellum, probat, vitu” is cut off.]*

After it had been read, the synod investigated whether it seemed to possess force either for criticism or for defense. Then the venerable Bishop Arnulfus, because the office of interpreting had been entrusted to him, said:

“It contains, in part, a defense of him, and in part gives strength to his accusers. For Arnulfus himself was the author of the reason for which it was written. Since he was suffering excessively from the disease of detestable greed, he did what can be criticized when, having sworn, he did not preserve faith. In this respect he succumbs to criticism.

But the fact that wise and good men did what opposed the deceit and cunning of a most depraved man provides firmness and strength for the defense against those who complain. Whatever the matter may be, however, it must nevertheless be confirmed by testimony.

Let the presbyter Adalgerus come forward. He is present and knows the entire sequence of the betrayal exceptionally well. Let him, I say, appear and declare this unheard-of crime to your eminence, so that you may recognize where blame is to be assigned and where praise is to be granted.”

### 62. Adalgerus Is Brought Forward for the Prosecution. Here Is a Lacunary Accusation

*[Note: [Col. 0151]: “ovetur, rus, ac, ni, io” is cut off; the printed heading itself has the defective words “Hic rar . . accusatio.”]*

Adalgerus was therefore summoned and appeared. Questioned about this matter, he answered without delay:

“If only, holy fathers, some indulgence of remission may be granted me in this summons. But since I have reached the point where, if anything can be found that might support me, it seems likely to stand against me, I will state in a few words what you ask.

Dudo, a soldier of Charles, urged me to undertake this betrayal about which you are inquiring here, swearing that this would please my lord. Since I did not believe him, I myself questioned my lord. He replied that he wished it to be done.

But, so that this disgrace might be concealed beneath the appearance of honor, I gave my hand to Charles, became his man, and promised the betrayal under oath. And I did it—but not without orders.

If this seems false to you, I am prepared to undergo every kind of judicial test.”

### 63. Guido the Bishop’s Brief and Clear Demonstration of the Crime

*[Note: [Col. 0151]: “et di, mon, minis, piscopo” is cut off.]*

Guido, bishop of Soissons, said:

“As can reasonably be understood from this account, perhaps both men are guilty of one and the same offense. For since this man asserts that he carried it out, his lord is not free of guilt, because he urged the crime to be committed, having himself supplied the cause of the crime.

Since, therefore, the matter concerning both men is established by clear indications—one having urged the crime and the other having carried it out—the severity of judgment is not unknown to your fatherly wisdom.

There is also something that lends force to the judgment to be held. Since the bishop himself was the author of the betrayal, in order to cover his own disgrace with the zeal of a better cause he separated from the body and blood of the Lord, by the anathema of a heavy excommunication and curse, and suspended from the Church of the faithful the authors, perpetrators, accomplices, and supporters of the Reims plundering, as well as those who alienated property from its rightful owners under the name of purchase.

But since the bishop himself is the author of so great an evil, it is manifest that he is entangled in the anathema. This too contributes substantially to his condemnation.”

### 64. Gualterus’s Indignation against Arnulfus

Gualterus, bishop of Autun, said:

“Can this bishop be of sound mind when he attempts to offer defenses on his own behalf, although his wickedness is plainly evident to the kings and to so many fathers, and, moreover, he is convicted by the testimony of a presbyter who knew of his crimes?

Could the inventor of the evil himself have escaped the danger of anathema, when he, the inventor and supporter of the evil, pierced the inventors, perpetrators, and supporters with the weapon of his curse?

Did he fail to consider the Divinity itself in this matter, when it is written that the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the wicked in every place (Proverbs 15:3)? Indeed, I think he said in his heart, ‘There is no God’ (Psalm 52:1).

Consider, therefore, fathers, how corrupt and abominable the perpetrator and supporter have become in their pursuits.”

### 65. Odo’s Admonition to Hasten the Judgment

*[Note: [Col. 0151]: “admo, juditio, ndo” is cut off.]*

Odo, bishop of Senlis, said:

“Since we have assembled here for the sake of religion and at the command of our most serene kings, the examination leading to judgment must not be delayed. The kings are awaiting it. The clergy and the people are likewise expecting it.

Nor should we linger any longer over the very different arguments of the various opinions, since the matter is evident and the course of judgment is readily apparent. You read not only the decrees of the fathers concerning these matters, but you also know how to deliver a judgment of equity through the consequences of the facts.”

### 66. Arnulfus’s Appeal to the Defenders to Argue Freely

Arnulfus, bishop of Orléans, said:

“Although, venerable fathers, these matters are certainly as they are being reported concerning Arnulfus, so that he could be condemned by a just judgment on the basis of numerous decisions of the fathers, nevertheless, lest we appear to rejoice in the ruin of a brother and burn without justice for his condemnation, I think that we should establish by common decree that anyone who attempts to say anything in his defense should have an opportunity to defend him.

Let him consult the books, bring forward as many judgments as he wishes, and fearlessly pour out here before us everything he has prepared for the defense. I think, however, that we must establish that no further opportunity for defense will be open to them. Let them now state only what they have considered.”

Then Bishop Siguinus approved Arnulfus’s statute and prohibited its violation by decretal interdicts. *[Note: The manuscript reads “inter interdictis” on two lines.]* He therefore urged anyone who had something to say to declare it.

### 67. The Scholars’ Defense of Arnulfus

*[Note: [Col. 0153]: “defensi, ticorum” is cut off.]*

Although several people who were attempting to defend him were present there, the chief defenders were the abbots Abbo of Fleury and Ramnulfus of Sens, together with John, the scholar of Auxerre. They were regarded as distinguished among their peers both for learning and for eloquence.

When silence had been proclaimed, many volumes of books were opened; many passages from the decrees of the fathers were brought forward; and several arguments were offered in defense.

Among these, they principally advanced four points. First, they said that Arnulfus should be restored to his own see. Second, that he should be given a legitimate summons. Third, that the matter should be made known to the Roman pontiff. Finally, that, by the authority of the Roman pontiff, the entire crime should be examined in a general synod. They asserted that this too was required by both divine and human laws.

### 68. Refutation of the Defense

*[Note: [Col. 0153]: “nfir, defensio” is cut off.]*

The opposing side replied that he should not be restored to his former see, since he had been convicted by the clearest charges brought by a credible accuser and appeared more inclined toward crimes than suited to the honor of religion and fidelity to his lords.

Nor, they said, should he now be summoned again, since after the crime of betrayal he had been summoned for six continuous months and had refused to come to account.

The matter could not be notified to the Roman pontiff, because the difficulty of the journey and the threats of the enemies greatly prevented this.

Nor, they said, did the crime now need further examination, since everything was established: the accuser had brought the charge and supplied numerous proofs, while the convicted defendant had no effective reply.

After the bishops’ opinions had been presented with many arguments, the defenders withdrew.

### 69. Arnulfus’s Examination

When the defenders had ceased their defense, the bishops thought that nothing remained except to bring Arnulfus forward, so that he might answer for himself whatever he wished.

He was therefore summoned and took his place among the bishops. After the bishops had brought forward many charges against him, by which he was cornered and fell silent, he put forward some arguments and rejected others as best he could. Nevertheless, overcome, he yielded to the force of their reasoning and confessed publicly that he was guilty and unworthy of the priesthood.

### 70. The entrance of the kings into the synod

When this was reported to the kings, they entered the sacred assembly of the bishops with the leading men, thanking the bishops because they had deliberated for a long time on their behalf and for the safety of the princes. They also asked that the sequence of the proceedings and the conclusion at which the arguments had arrived be unfolded for them. Then the entire course of the proceedings was explained to the kings.

After hearing the order of the narrative, they declared that the time for judgment had now arrived. The bishops then advised Arnulf to prostrate himself at the knees of the kings, confess his guilt, and beg for his life and the integrity of his limbs. Immediately he fell at the feet of his lords, confessed the crime, and, declaring himself unworthy of the priesthood, begged amid tears for his life and limbs. As a result, he compelled the entire synod to weep.

The kings, moved by great compassion, granted him his life and the integrity of his limbs. They decreed that he should be kept under guard, but without iron or chains.

### 71. The decree

After he had been raised from the ground, he was asked whether he wished his abdication to be solemnly carried out by the authority of the canons. Since he entrusted the whole matter to the bishops’ decision, it was immediately decreed that, because he confessed himself unworthy of the priesthood and did not conceal his crime, he should be deposed through the ranks by which he had been advanced.

Accordingly, after being persuaded, he returned to the kings what he had received from them, while without delay he surrendered the priestly insignia to the bishops. He was also asked whether he would compose a document of abdication and renunciation; he replied that he would do everything according to the bishops’ wishes. The document was immediately written and presented. He read it before the kings in the council and signed it.

### 72. Text of Arnulf’s document of renunciation

The text of the document was as follows:

> “I, Arnulf, by the grace of God formerly bishop of Reims, recognizing my frailty and the weight of my sins, have appointed as witnesses and confessors of my offenses Siguin, archbishop; Daibert, archbishop; Arnulf, bishop; Godesmann, bishop; Heriveus, bishop; Ratbod, bishop; Walter, bishop; Bruno, bishop; Milo, bishop; Adalbero, bishop; Odo, bishop; Wido, bishop; and Heribert, bishop. I have constituted them judges of my offenses and have made to them a pure confession, seeking a remedy through repentance and the salvation of my soul, so that I might withdraw from the office and ministry of the episcopate, in which I acknowledge myself to be unworthy. making myself an alien on account of my offenses—in which I confessed to them privately that I had sinned and concerning which I was publicly accused— in such a way that they may be witnesses and may have the authority to appoint and consecrate another in my place, one who can worthily preside over and benefit the church over which until now I have presided unworthily.
>
> “And so that thereafter I may have no authority, under canon law, to make any further claim or appeal, I have confirmed this with my own hand by signing. Having read it thus, I have signed it thus. I, Arnulf, formerly archbishop of Reims, have signed.”

The bishops who were present were also asked by him to sign, and they signed. In this manner they responded to him:

> “According to your profession and signature, withdraw from your office.”

After this, by the authority of his oath, he released those who had been his men from their oath and granted them freedom to enter another’s service.

### 73. The deposition of the priest Adalger from the clerical ranks

While these matters were being conducted with much deliberation, the priest Adalger, because he had been deprived of communion, prostrated himself at the feet of the kings and complained bitterly, asking to be restored to communion. He thought that the censure inflicted upon him should be lighter, since he had obeyed his lord’s command.

Arnulf, bishop of Orléans, confronted him:

> “Will your fabricated excuses today make you exempt from judgment? Are you not the man who opened the gates to Charles and entered the holy of holies with him as an enemy? Are you not the man who brought ruin upon the young man together with your associates? Confess, most infamous man!”

When he replied, “I cannot deny it,” Arnulf immediately continued:

> “Is that why you should be restored to communion, so that, while your lord mourns, you, most wicked man, may laugh?”

At last it was decreed that he must choose one of two punishments: either be deposed from the clerical ranks or remain under perpetual anathema. After considering the matter at length within himself, he finally preferred to be deprived of his rank rather than remain under perpetual anathema.

Immediately, at the bishops’ command, he was clothed in priestly garments. As each of them stripped away the individual garments without any compassion, each said to him:

> “Withdraw from your office.”

They restored to him only the communion of the laity, subjected him to penance, and in this manner were released from the synod.

If anyone wishes to know more fully what each of them brought forward in the council from the canons and the decrees of the Fathers, what was enacted there by them, what was sent by the kings and bishops to the Roman pontiff, and by what arguments Arnulf’s abdication was confirmed, let him read the book of the lord and incomparable man Gerbert, Arnulf’s successor in the episcopate. Since it contains all these matters arranged in order, it is comparable to Cicero’s language in the remarkable elegance of its eloquence. Filled with objections and responses, complaints and speeches, invectives, conjectures, and definitions, it presents, assumes, and concludes its case with exceptional clarity and reason. It is considered highly useful not only to those acquainted with synodal cases but also to those who understand the principles of rhetoric.

### 74. Odo’s complaint before his followers about the seizure of Melun

Meanwhile Odo was seeking to increase his possessions. Therefore, among those whose unquestionable loyalty he knew, he was preparing to transfer the fortress of Melun into his own jurisdiction. He told them that it would be a most wretched situation for him if he had no crossing on the Seine by which armies could be transported. Hence the thought had occurred to him that he should turn Melun—which, being surrounded by the Seine, was exceptionally secure and accessible through two harbors—to his own side, especially since several harbors were open to him on the Loire.

There was no need to fear the crime of perjury, since Melun had already been possessed by his grandfather and was now held not by the king but by another. He therefore urged all who were pledging their loyalty to hasten, so that by whatever means they could, they might transfer it into his dominion.

### 75. Odo’s emissary induces the governor of Melun

Then one of his men, approaching the governor of the fortress, pretended the firmest friendship and promised great loyalty. The agreement was soon confirmed by an oath on both sides.

Addressing the governor, he asked who had formerly owned the fortress. The governor did not deny who it had been. The emissary continued:

> “By what process did it come into the royal jurisdiction?”

The governor likewise explained this. Then the emissary said:

> “Why is Odo being wronged, when he has often asked that it be returned to him, and when someone inferior to him now possesses it?”

The governor replied:

> “Because that is what seemed right to the king.”

The emissary said:

> “Do you think that the Divinity Himself is not offended when, after his father’s death, a ward is deprived of his paternal inheritance without compensation?”

The governor answered:

> “Yes.”

The emissary continued:

> “And not only that, but he is also deprived of hope of his possessions. For who among the leading men is more powerful than Odo? Who is more worthy of every honor?”

To this the emissary added:

> “If you wished to transfer yourself to Odo, do you not think that you would be raised to greater power? If you belonged to him, you would undoubtedly have his favor, counsel, and assistance. Instead of one fortress, you would possess many things. Thus the glory of your name would advance still further, in proportion as you attained a higher summit of honor.”

The governor replied:

> “How can you be confident that this could happen without sin and disgrace?”

The emissary answered:

> “If you transfer yourself and the fortress to Odo, whatever crime you think might arise, let it be mine and be called mine. I will suffer the penalties and render an account to the Supreme Divinity. Consult your nobility. Increase your possessions. The time is pressing. Opportunity recommends it, since the king is inglorious through his inability to rule, while success always follows Odo more favorably.”

Greedy for the possessions that had been promised, the governor asked for an oath. The emissary gave it and demanded hostages for the execution of the agreement. Believing that he would receive great honor, the governor did not delay in giving hostages. The emissary took them, led them home, and reported all this to Odo.

### 76. Odo’s seizure of Melun

*He therefore advised Odo to persist in what he had begun. Meanwhile Odo secretly prepared troops so that he might enter and seize the fortress. When all was ready, he attacked at the appointed time and entered. Pretending to be enraged, he attacked the traitor and committed him to prison.

Not long afterward, the man was released from prison. In Odo’s presence he gave an oath of loyalty and henceforth prepared himself to resist together with Odo. All these events were soon reported, it is said, to the ears of the kings.

Moved by the loss of the fortress, the kings prepared soldiers against the enemy, declaring that they would not withdraw from the siege until they either recovered it by force or, if circumstances required, met the enemy face-to-face with strength and arms.

### 77. The kings’ approach to Melun

Having prepared their forces, they approached to take the fortress. Since the fortress was surrounded by the Seine, they first established their camp on the bank; on the opposite side they arranged the lines of pirates whom they had summoned. To prevent the siege from being broken anywhere, they deployed armed fleets throughout the river.

Thus, carried across the surface of the river, they pressed the fortress fiercely in a naval battle. The men in the fortress were not unequal to them and resisted the attackers. They fought with all their strength and yielded to their adversaries in no way.

When they had resisted for a long time and were fighting at close quarters without giving way, the rear passage, which had been concealed below, was broken open by the strength of those striking it, and the pirates were admitted. Coming upon those fighting on the wall from the rear, they raged among them with great slaughter.

It also happened that the rest of the army, which was still standing on the bank, was brought in on foot through the fleets, and suddenly overran the fortress.

### 78. The men of the fortress are granted their freedom

The men of the fortress were captured and defeated, and were immediately brought before the king. Their friends addressed a speech to the king on their behalf. After giving their pledge to the king, they were released, since, they maintained, they ought to be called faithful not so much to the majesty of the king as to their own lord; moreover, they had been led to this not by the fault of treachery but by great courage.

After the hostages had thus been released and the fortress restored to its former lord, the traitor whose deceit had brought about this misfortune was immediately seized and died by hanging beside the fortress gate. His wife likewise was hanged by the feet in an unusual form of mockery, stripped naked as her clothing fell away all around her, and perished a cruel death beside her husband.

While these events were taking place, Odo was waiting not far away with his army for the outcome, thinking that his men could defend the fortress against the enemy and being somewhat suspicious of the pirates’ ambushes. While he hesitated, wavering over the outcome, messengers arrived and reported that the fortress had been captured and that his men had been seized and disarmed.

When he heard this, he withdrew his army toward his own territory in no cheerful mood. When certain mourners charged him with having caused that consular man to die by hanging, Odo is said to have replied that he had been more seriously harmed by the capture of his men than by the hanging of the traitor.

### 79. The quarrel between Odo and Fulk concerning Brittany

Not long afterward the civil wars were renewed. For Fulk, who favored the side of the kings, prepared an army against Odo, intending to demand from him the part of Brittany that he had taken from him not long before.

He gathered four thousand men, who were not to engage in close combat, since their strength was insufficient for Odo’s power, but were to afflict his territory with fires and plunder. He thought this should be done until Odo either, overcome by weariness, restored the territory or exchanged for it another possession of equal value.

He therefore rushed forward and afflicted the land with booty-taking, plunder, and burnings. When he was burning the suburban areas at Blois, the fires, spreading everywhere as the wind blew, sent a great blaze into the monastery of the monks of Saint Laumer the Confessor. It was soon burned and destroyed, and the food supplies were consumed as well. Thus the monks were also forced to migrate.

After these events, Fulk turned his army toward other places and devastated them. After his departure, Odo in turn led an army into his territory and raged through it so fiercely that he left neither hut nor cock, challenging the enemy and inviting him to come and fight.

But Fulk, recognizing that his forces were insufficient, yielded to the challenger and returned to his own lands. Such was the situation for approximately two years.

### 80. Odo’s ambassadors’ speech before the king concerning the seizure of Melun

Meanwhile Odo, frustrated by the loss of the fortress, was especially cautious in this matter. He believed that he could be tormented by a double calamity, since he was deeply grieved by the loss of the fortress and was also being pressed considerably by the angry king.

He therefore sent ambassadors to the king, through whom he suggested that he could make an excellent defense against every accusation. He would show that he had injured the royal majesty in no respect. If the matter concerned Melun, he had plotted no evil against the king, since he had taken it not from the king but from his fellow soldier. Nothing had been taken from the king, since the person from whom Odo had taken it belonged to the king just as Odo did. Nor did it matter, as far as royal dignity was concerned, who held it.

He had also accomplished this for just reasons, since it could be demonstrated that Melun had long ago been possessed by his predecessors. It might therefore even appear that it ought to be held more worthily by him than by anyone else.

Finally, if anything sacrilegious had been done, the punishment for the disgrace had fallen upon Odo himself, and so great a crime had been wiped away by an equal dishonor. He therefore deserved to be forgiven more readily and to be spared all the more in so great an injury.

The king, recognizing the force of the speech, satisfied the ambassadors and sent word to Odo seeking his goodwill. The ambassadors reported this to Odo. Odo then approached the king. In the king’s presence he made effective use of his speech and obtained his favor. He was so distinguished by affability that they renewed their former friendship, and the king regarded him as suspect in nothing.

### 81. War between Odo and Fulk concerning Brittany

At this time the civil wars were likewise renewed. For Fulk, deprived of a part of Brittany, continued to prepare ambushes. Having gathered an army, he rushed into Brittany and attacked Nantes.

He corrupted some of the guards with gold and enticed others with various promises. He persuaded them to satisfy him fully by opening the entrance to the city. Once persuaded, they fixed a time by oath. Not long afterward they admitted him into the city.

After entering, he overran it and received hostages from the citizens according to the terms of their oath. He was unable to take the citadel, however, because it had brave soldiers. Therefore he withdrew, intending to return with larger forces, engage the enemy, and take the citadel.

### 82. Conan deliberates with his men on military affairs in the outer parts of Brittany, at the place called Bruerech

Conan was conducting deliberations among his men about military affairs in the outer parts of Brittany, in a place called Bruerech, when these events were reported to him. He then devoted himself even more firmly to the undertaking, gathered an army, and prepared for war.

Since the time recommended that he press the siege, he led the assembled army against the city and arranged a land siege along one side of it. On the other side, he deployed pirate fleets on the Loire.

Thus, with the siege arranged on every side, the townspeople were fiercely pressed by the pirates on the river and by the Bretons on land. Those who had remained in the citadel were no less harassed, hurling various kinds of missiles down from above. Those in the middle were attacked by the forces above and below with equal violence.

For those fighting in the citadel and those conducting the siege supported Conan’s side, while the townspeople labored for Fulk’s victory.

Fulk also prepared forces and gathered an army both from his own men and from hired troops. When he heard that Conan had laid siege to the city, he immediately brought the army of Brittany against it.

### 83. The stratagem prepared for Fulk

There was a broad field not far away, extensive in both length and width, containing a very large bed of fern. Conan chose this place for conducting the battle and buried there the devices of an ambush.

He dug a great many trenches and covered their openings from above with rods, twigs, and stalks, fastening branches inside so that they would support the upper layer and imitate the solidity of the surface. To conceal the false surface completely, he scattered collected fern over it and disguised the ambush.

### 84. Conan’s stratagem against the enemy

After setting his own lines in place, Conan employed such a deception that he declared he would remain there and would not seek the enemy any farther. If the enemy pressed him, he would defend his life only there.

He claimed that he would act in this way not out of fear but so that, if the enemy sought and attacked him, they would act against justice. Their downfall could thus occur more easily, since through their own rashness they would attack men who were quiet and harmless.

He therefore drew up his lines there, keeping the ambush in view. He remained in place and waited to receive the enemy.

When Fulk saw Conan remaining there and noticed that he would not leave the spot, but did not know about the ambush, he urged his men with much insistence to make a vigorous attack and not hesitate to assault the enemy. They should not distrust victory, since the hope of strength was excellent, provided that the Divinity had not turned away.

At the signal, they rushed forward. Thinking the route solid, they approached the trenches without hesitation.

### 85. The enemy’s plunge into the traps laid by Conan

Thinking that the Bretons remained fixed in fear, Fulk’s men resisted their missiles and rushed upon the trenches. They plunged in with their horses and, confused in a blind collapse, as many as twenty thousand were submerged and crushed.

The rear part of the army, when the front had plunged into the trenches, turned its back and fled. Fulk therefore, concerned only for his life, attempted to escape by flight.

### 86. The killing of Conan

While flight was driving him onward, Conan meanwhile withdrew into a thicket with three companions. Having laid down his arms, he was cooling the heat of his body in the breeze.

One of his opponents caught sight of him, rushed upon him, and pierced him with a sword, thereby bringing victory to Fulk.

Fulk, recovering his courage, returned to Nantes and entered it, fiercely harassing those who were in the citadel. Deprived of their prince and almost lifeless, they yielded to the attacker and, when asked, gave their pledge of loyalty.

### 87. The repudiation of Queen Susanna by King Robert

With matters standing thus, King Robert, while flourishing in the bloom of youth at the age of nineteen, repudiated Susanna, his Italian-born wife, by divorce because she was an old woman.

After she had been repudiated, she wished to recover what she had received as her dowry. Since the king would not agree to this, she turned her mind elsewhere. From that day onward, while seeking what belonged to her, she plotted against the king.

For she wished to restore to her own jurisdiction the fortress of Montreuil, which she had received as her dowry. Since she could not accomplish this, she built another beside it, called [lacuna], while the king was occupied with the affairs of Odo and Fulk. From this fortification she thought that she could prevent all transport by ship, since those coming to her would first present themselves to her, and she would therefore be able to prevent them from proceeding farther.

### 88. Criticism of the repudiation

The crime of this repudiation was sufficiently torn apart at that time by certain men who possessed a more refined understanding, although it was condemned secretly and without open opposition.

### 89. The synod held at Chelles

During these days, when the abdication of Arnulf and the promotion of Gerbert were repeatedly denounced in many letters sent by the German bishops to Pope John XVI, and when the bishops who had been responsible for this matter, together with their other collaborators, were also reproved with various criticisms, the bishops of Gaul decided to assemble and deliberate concerning this accusation.

After they had gathered at Chelles, a synod was held. King Robert presided, while the metropolitans sat with him: Gerbert of Reims, to whom the entire examination of the synodal cases had been entrusted; Siguin of Sens; Erchembald of Tours; Daibert of Bourges; and several others from their respective provinces.

After they had promulgated, from the decrees of the Fathers, their arguments concerning the condition of the holy Church, they decided, among other useful matters, to establish and confirm that from that day onward they should think alike, will alike, and cooperate alike, according to what is written:

> “They were of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

They also wished it to be decreed that, if any tyranny arose in any church which appeared to be worthy of being struck down by the weapon of anathema, this should first be considered by everyone and then handled by common decree. Those who were to be released from anathema were likewise to be released by common decree, according to what is written:

> “Seek counsel from the wise” (Tobit 4:19).

They also decided to enact that, if anything were proposed by the Roman pope contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, it should be made null and void, according to what the Apostle says:

> “Avoid entirely a heretical person who dissents from the Church” (Titus 3:10).

No less did they decide that Arnulf’s abdication and Gerbert’s promotion, in the form in which they had been ordered and carried out by them, should be confirmed forever, according to what is written in the canons:

> “What has been established by a provincial synod must not be rashly weakened by anyone.”

### 90. Odo’s and Fulk’s attack upon each other

At this time the civil wars were renewed. When, through the intrigues of the tyrants Odo and Fulk, the quarrel concerning the principality of Brittany arose again, the other princes of the kingdoms were also stirred up by their dissension and took opposing sides.

The king supported Fulk’s party. Odo advanced relying on his own men, on pirates who had abandoned the king and crossed over to him, and on forces from Aquitaine.

Fulk therefore rushed against Odo, devastated his territory, and afterward built and fortified a stronghold in it, not far from the city of Tours. He stationed forces there and filled it with soldiers. Since he hoped that Odo would come to destroy it, he approached the king to request assistance.

When the king promised him help, Fulk proceeded with an even more obstinate spirit. He prepared forces to engage the enemy, gathered an army, and declared war against Odo.

Odo, touched by shame, requested assistance from the Gauls and Belgians. He promised that, if they came, he would repay their favor. They generously agreed and gave their pledge.

He also summoned the Flemings and asked their protection, promising to repay them if they did not refuse his request. They too, with generous spirit, supplied what he sought.

He sent ambassadors even to the pirates, demanding that they not deny him their forces. A time and place were appointed for everyone to assemble and come together.

Meanwhile Odo appeased, gathered, and encouraged his own men. Thinking that the Belgians and pirates would arrive at the right time, he rushed against Fulk with only a few of his own men, so rapidly that he had no more than four thousand fighters in the engagement. Nevertheless, he laid siege to the fortress and deployed armed men. He pressed the men of the fortress with great exertion.

### 91. Fulk’s petition to Odo through ambassadors

Fulk, thinking that the king was delaying and would not come to his aid, and that Odo’s army was unbearable, soon became more yielding in spirit.

Accordingly, through ambassadors he sought Odo’s friendship. He sent word that he would pay one hundred pounds of silver for Conan’s death; in place of the slain soldier, he offered his own son to serve in his stead; he promised to demolish the fortress that had been built in Odo’s honor and evacuate it with his own men; and he offered to serve Odo voluntarily, provided that doing so would not injure the king.

Since this could not be done without injury to the king, he would give his hand by oath to Odo’s son. Thus he himself would serve with his son: he would give his son to Odo in place of Conan and commit himself to serve Odo’s son.

He also promised to give an oath of loyalty against everyone’s cause except that of the king and of those to whom he was bound by special kinship and affection, namely his son, brother, and nephews.

After Odo had learned these terms, he used the counsel of his men and sent word that he would accept them gladly if Fulk returned Nantes, the city of Brittany, which had been captured by deceit, and evacuated it with his men. For it seemed unjust to make peace with the enemy without first demanding the return of what had been taken and without having what was withheld restored.

### 92. Fulk’s withdrawal of his petition

While these matters were being discussed, and while Odo thought that his army was gradually increasing, the king arrived with twelve thousand men before Odo had forces sufficient for battle, while six thousand of Fulk’s own men surrounded him.

When these forces joined, the armed army became densely concentrated. Fulk therefore grew more insolent and rejected the offers he had previously made as a suppliant. He eagerly pressed for war to begin and urged them to cross the fords of the Loire, which flowed between them, and attack the enemy.

Odo, realizing that those whom he had expected according to their promise had not come because the shortness of the time had not allowed them to gather their armies, was greatly disturbed in spirit. Nevertheless, with four thousand men he opposed them and blocked the fords of the Loire.

### 93. The king, prevented from crossing the ford, turns toward Amboise

Prevented from crossing the ford, the king turned his army toward the fortress of Amboise, which rose not far away on the same bank of the river among the cliffs. His intention was to cross there and then move obliquely, so that he might unexpectedly confront the enemy from the rear and press them.

Odo, unable to withstand the king’s army, sent ambassadors to him, declaring that he had attacked his enemy, not the king, and that he intended no plot against the king but only against his enemy. If the king ordered it, he would immediately go farther and satisfy him in every respect.

The king perceived the reasonableness of the argument and considered that so great a man had been injured by him without cause. Therefore, so that Odo would not wholly defect from him, he took hostages from him under a guarantee of peace, intending afterward to hear from him an account of everything with which he had charged him.

He then withdrew his army and came to Paris. Odo likewise, having lost nothing, came with his men safely to Melun. Not many days later, he proceeded to the fortress called Dunum, intending to arrange his affairs there.

### 94. Odo’s death

While he was deliberating at length about those of his men whom he had delivered to the king as hostages under a guarantee of peace, he was afflicted by an excess of bodily fluids due to the change of season and fell into an illness which physicians call *synantica*.

Although this illness is located within the interior of the throat and arises from a rheumatic flow of phlegm, at times it sends swelling accompanied by severe pain into the jaws and cheeks, and at other times into the chest and lungs. After these parts have swollen and become inflamed, it kills the patient after the third day, except for the initial day.

Odo therefore fell into this illness and was attacked on every side by fierce pains in the throat. The heat of the arteries also caused interruptions in his speech. The pain did not pass upward into the higher parts of the head; instead, attacking the vital organs, it afflicted the lung and liver with very sharp pain.

There was therefore mourning among the soldiers, shouting among the servants, and frequent cries among the women, because they were losing their lord without counsel and no hope of rule was being left to his sons. The kings still remained hostile in spirit toward their father, while Fulk, with a spirit of insolence, was disturbing the peace in many ways.

Nevertheless, expecting that he would live only a short time, Odo sent swift ambassadors to the kings. They were to plead for him in a persuasive manner and promise the most just compensation for the injuries inflicted.

The old king wished to receive from the ambassadors a correction of the wrongs, but he was restrained by his indignant son. He therefore utterly rejected the ambassadors’ arguments and forced them to return unharmed.

While they were delayed on the journey, and before they had returned, on the fourth day after the onset of the *synantica*, Odo became a monk and died. Thus he brought his life to an end. He was carried to Saint Martin’s and buried with much service from his men in the place called the Greater Monastery [Marmoutier-les-Tours].

### 95. Pope John sends Abbot Leo to Gaul to dissolve Arnulf’s abdication

At the same time, when the German bishops repeatedly urged the lord Pope John in letters to revoke the promotion of Gerbert, metropolitan of Reims, and expressed indignation that Arnulf’s abdication had been carried out contrary to law, Pope John sent Leo, a monk and abbot, to Germany.

Acting in the pope’s place, Leo was to investigate this matter with the bishops of Germany and Gaul and carefully deliver a judgment concerning it. He was received with great courtesy by the bishops and discussed with them the holding of a synod concerning this matter.

The bishops sent ambassadors to the kings of Gaul—namely Hugh and his son Robert—to explain to them the pope’s mandate as well as the will of the bishops, and to persuade them reasonably to assemble with their own bishops. They were also to learn from the kings the place and time at which the assembly should be held and report their disposition concerning the matter.

[Source columns: the passage runs from Col. 0153D through Col. 0164A; the intervening column references mark the corresponding successive portions of the narrative.]

### Editorial and textual notes

- §70, heading: the running-title fragments “Regum ing[ressus]” and “Decret[ale]” are cut off ([Col. 0153]).
- §72, heading: *repu[dii]* is cut off ([Col. 0153]); in the text, the manuscript reads *ipsi* ([Col. 0153]).
- §73, heading: “Dep[ositio], a gra[dibus]” is cut off ([Col. 0153]).
- §74, heading: “Con[questio] Odonis a[pud] … de … ere[ptione]” is cut off ([Col. 0155]).
- §75, heading: “In[ductio] ab [legato] … in … [praesidem] Mili[duni]” is cut off ([Col. 0155]).
- §76, heading: “per[vasio] Mili[duni] ab Odone” is cut off ([Col. 0155]).
- §77, heading: “Acce[ssus] regum ad Mili[dunum]” is cut off ([Col. 0155]). In the text, *accitae* corrects the manuscript’s *accita*, which required correction ([Col. 0155]).
- §78, heading: “Castr[enses] capti libertati da[ntur]” is cut off ([Col. 0157]). The word *in primo* (“at first”) was deleted ([Col. 0157]); *VC* (“a man of consular rank”) is the manuscript reading ([Col. 0157]).
- §79, heading: “Ri[xa] Odonis et Fulconis de Britannia” is cut off ([Col. 0157]). The reading *redderet* (“should restore”) is corrected to *conferret* (“should offer/exchange”); *percutit* is corrected to *affecit*; and *castrum* (“fortress”) was deleted after Blois ([Col. 0157]). The manuscript has “O. c.” ([Col. 0157]).
- §80, heading: “Ora[tio] legatorum Odonis apud regem de Miliduni pervasi[one]” is cut off ([Col. 0157]). The manuscript has *id e[tiam]* where the text reads *etiam id justis c[ausis]* ([Col. 0157]).
- §81, heading: “Bellum inter Odonem et Fulconem” is cut off ([Col. 0157]); *Nantes* is supplied for *Namtas* ([Col. 0157D]).
- §82: *parat* is corrected to *congregat*; the manuscript’s *per* is corrected by a supralinear *ad*; and *adhibuit* is corrected to *adhibet* ([Col. 0159]).
- §83, heading: “Dol[us] Fulconi paratus” is cut off ([Col. 0159]).
- §84, heading: “Dol[us] Conani contra ho[stes]” is cut off ([Col. 0159]); after *exiturum*, *advertens* (“noticing”) was deleted ([Col. 0159]).
- §85, heading: “Praecipita[tio] hostium a Con[ano]” is cut off ([Col. 0159]); the manuscript has *XX* (“twenty”) ([Col. 0159]).
- §86, heading: “Interfectio Conani” is cut off ([Col. 0159]).
- §87, heading: “Re[pudium] re[ginae] Susannae a rege Rot[berto]” is cut off ([Col. 0159]); the name of the fortress built beside Montreuil is wholly absent, represented above as [lacuna] ([Col. 0159]).
- §88, heading: “Re[prehensio] repudii” is cut off; the manuscript reads *a* ([Col. 0159]).
- §89: the pope is John XVI; Benedict VII had died in 985 ([Col. 0159D]).
- §90, heading: “Im[petus] Odonis et Fulconis inter se” is cut off ([Col. 0161]). The manuscript has *castrum* written above *oppidum* (“stronghold”), and *frandrenses* is corrected to *flandrenses* (“Flemings”) ([Col. 0161]).
- §91, heading: “Fulconis suppli[catio] Odoni per legatos” is cut off ([Col. 0161]); the manuscript has *c p* (“one hundred pounds”) ([Col. 0161]).
- §92, heading: “Abj[ectio] supp[licationis] ab Fulcone” is cut off ([Col. 0161]).
- §93: *Ambatiam* is Amboise ([Col. 0161D]); *Dunum* is queried in the source ([Col. 0162D]).
- §94, heading: “Obitus Odonis” is cut off ([Col. 0163]); the manuscript has *homorum* for *humorum* (“bodily fluids”), and has *aequissimam* (“most equitable”) written above *justissimam* (“most just”) ([Col. 0163]). “The Greater Monastery” is Marmoutier-les-Tours ([Col. 0163D]).
- §95, heading: “Johannes [papa] Leonem [abbatem] in Gallias mittit ut Arnulfi abdicationem dissolvat” is cut off ([Col. 0163]); “of Germany” was deleted after “bishops” ([Col. 0163]).

## 96. That it was announced to the kings that the bishops of Germany were convening in synod

[Note: the manuscript heading is cut off at the words “that,” “announces,” “German,” and “synod.”]

Envoys were therefore dispatched. The embassy too was presented. The kings, receiving it with the utmost composure, at that time opposed none of the pope’s or the bishops’ commands, replying that they would seek counsel on the matter and do justice in everything.

After the envoys had departed, certain persons informed the kings that Adalbero, bishop of Laon, had contrived all this by deceit, and that he had previously discussed the matter at length with Odo. Both of them, they said, had desired to bring King Otto into Gaul and to drive the kings out by cunning and force. The bishops of Germany were also assembling for the purpose of completing the deceit they had devised.

[Col. 0164B] When the kings perceived the fraud, they informed the bishops—who had already assembled at the place appointed by the kings, through their envoys—that they would not go there, because they did not have with them the leading men of their realm, without whose counsel nothing seemed either to be done or omitted. It also seemed unworthy to them to submit their own men to the correction of the German bishops, since these men were no less noble, no less powerful, and equally or even more wise. Let the bishops themselves, then, if they needed anything, hasten into Gaul and announce there what they wished. Otherwise, let them return and attend to their own affairs as they pleased.

Thus their business fell into the opposite outcome. For Adalbero, who had offered himself as their agent, unaware of the disclosure [variant: “treachery”], was urging the kings to meet those who were coming. But the veteran king, not ignorant of frauds, demanded back from him Louis, son of Charles, whom, after capturing him at Laon, he had entrusted to Adalbero’s custody. He also demanded back the citadel of that same city, which he had likewise entrusted to him.

## 97. Adalbero is reproached as the cause of the entire fraud

[Note: the manuscript heading is cut off at “Adalbero,” “fraud,” and “reproached.”]

When he resisted returning what had been entrusted to him, the king’s attendants, indignant, added:

“Since you, bishop, have sought many schemes for the destruction of kings and princes, both with King Otto and with the tyrant Odo, how are you not ashamed to fabricate such grand stories here before your lords, the kings? Why are you afraid to return Louis and the citadel, if you do not doubt that you have kept faith with the kings? What, then, is refusing to return what was entrusted to you, except plotting misfortune against the kings? You most plainly broke faith when you discussed the destruction of the kings with Otto and attempted to undermine their honor. Hence you are held guilty of perjury.

“You also delivered to King Otto an embassy as though it had been sent by them, and deceitfully arranged with him that he should come with a few men and have a large number of soldiers equipped not far away [the words specifying the place, ‘which is called Mouzon,’ are deleted]. You persuaded our kings to meet their adversary with only a few men, and promised that no harm would come of it. You even said that this meeting would be useful to both sides, when you pretended that these men and that one would converse familiarly about public and private matters.

“But you had conceived something else, when you put this forward in order to have your lords, the kings, seized by King Otto and to transfer the kingdom of the Franks into his jurisdiction, so that you, naturally, might be regarded as metropolitan of Reims, and Odo as duke of the Franks. This then became entirely clear to us, but for a time it was suppressed.

“And, O immeasurable mercy of the supreme Divinity! From how many wretched circumstances have we been rescued, and from how great a mockery withdrawn! The time is at hand when the ambushes prepared will produce their result. For the bishops, under the appearance of religion, as though they were about to inquire into the promotion and abdication of the bishops Gerbert and Arnulf, have arrived after sending envoys ahead. King Otto too is present at Metz; an army is said to have been gathered not far away. If we go, then, we shall either fight or be captured. If we do not go, we shall be accused of perjury. Yet it is not expedient for the kings to go, since they do not have a sufficient number of soldiers. The guilt of perjury, however, will rebound upon you, since you alone have sworn an oath to the kings, who know nothing of the matter.”

## 98.

At this the bishop, ashamed, fell silent. When one of his own men saw that he had been terrified by these accusations, he rose to answer them and attacked the speaker in these words:

“Let the one who accuses me of all these things speak to me. I am here to give an account on behalf of the accused. Let one man alone make these charges. Let him set his own head against mine. Let him match weapons with weapons, and strength with strength.”

While this man raged and burned with zeal for his lord, Count Landricus addressed him as follows:

[Col. 0165C] “O excellent soldier, as I see, you are entirely unaware of these frauds. Although they were pursued without your knowledge, they were nevertheless pursued, as is being reported. Therefore control your spirit and moderate your fervor. Do not impose upon yourself the necessity of battle. Do not drive yourself into a situation from which, once entered, you will be unable to return. But now follow my advice: withdraw a little from here and ask your lord whether these things are true. If he urges you to fight, engage. If he says that you must desist, restrain your fury.”

He therefore withdrew, summoned his lord, and asked him whether the matter stood as alleged. Since the bishop had been convicted by one who knew the facts, he confessed to the questioner that it was so. Consequently he forbade the fighting. Once the soldier’s great fury had subsided, the whole matter became known. He was therefore detained by order of the kings and handed over to guards as a deserter. His soldiers were soon bound by oath to the kings.

## 99. The synod held at Mouzon for Arnulf

While these events were taking place [Note: the word *age* is cut off], the bishops of Gaul had been forbidden by the kings to come to the appointed synod. The bishops of Germany, however, lest they be accused of deceit if they did not attend, assembled at Mouzon at the appointed time, bringing with them the lord pope’s legate.

They gathered in the basilica of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, and sat in orderly ecclesiastical fashion: namely Suger of Mimagavard, Leodulf of Trier, Nocher of Liège, and Haimo of Verdun. In their midst sat Abbot Leo, who exercised the authority of the lord pope. Opposite them sat Gerbert, metropolitan of Reims, who alone among the bishops of Gaul had come despite the kings’ prohibition, intending to answer for himself. Abbots from various places also sat there, together with a number of clerics. Among the laymen were Count Godefrid with his two sons, and Ragener, vicedominus of the people of Reims.

## 100. Introductory speech of Haimo, bishop of Verdun, concerning the cause of the synod

When everyone around them had fallen silent, the bishop of Verdun, because he knew the French language, rose to set forth the cause of the synod:

[Col. 0166B] “Since it has very often been brought to the ears of the lord pope that the metropolitan church of Reims had been usurped and deprived, contrary to right and equity, of its proper shepherd, he has more than once and twice urged us by letter, so that, gathered together as one, we might weigh so great a crime fairly on both sides and restore by our authority what had been corrected by us to the proper rule.

“But because the diversity of circumstances led us to defer doing this, after so many admonitions he has now wished to send this lord, Abbot Leo and monk, to exercise his authority and investigate the matter mentioned among us who are obedient.” Through him he has also sent a written statement of his will, so that, if anything should escape our memory, it might be preserved in writing. It is useful that this too should be heard at once.”

Immediately he produced the document and read it aloud to those seated there. Since we are concerned with brevity, and since it was less convenient for us, we have avoided inserting it in our own writings.

## 101. Gerbert’s speech for himself, read before the council

After it had been read, Gerbert rose and immediately recited before the council the speech he had written on his own behalf. He spoke before them with sufficient brilliance and force. But it seemed worthwhile to include it here, since, being full of arguments, it provides the reader with very great benefit. Its text is as follows:

[Note: the inserted leaf on which the speech was written was lost; I have inserted it from the Lyon manuscript among the Vossian codices, no. 54, where it survives in a much more corrected form than that in which it was read by the Centuriators.]

## 102. Exordium

“Always, most reverend fathers, I have kept this day before my eyes, and ever since I was admonished by my brothers I have directed my hope and desire toward it, when I undertook this burden of the priesthood—not without danger to my life. The salvation of the perishing people mattered greatly to me, and so did your authority, by which I believed I should be kept safe.

“I remembered your past kindnesses, your sweet and accessible goodwill, which I had often enjoyed, to the great praise of distinguished men. But suddenly a rumor insinuated that you were offended and labored to assign as a fault what had clearly been prepared with great courage among others. I confess that I was horrified; and, because of your indignation, I set aside the swords that I had previously feared.

“Now, since a propitious Divinity has brought before me those to whom I have always entrusted my salvation, I shall say a few words concerning my innocence and explain by what counsel I was placed over the city of Reims.

“After the death of the blessed Emperor Otto, I had determined not to leave the service of my father, the blessed Adalbero. Without my knowledge, I was chosen by him for the priesthood; and, at his departure to the Lord, I was designated in the presence of illustrious men as the future shepherd of the Church.

“But the Simoniacal heresy, finding me standing upon the solidity of Peter, rejected me and preferred Arnulf. Nevertheless I offered Arnulf faithful service beyond what was proper, until I openly understood, through many witnesses and through myself, that he had apostatized. Then, after delivering him a written renunciation, I abandoned him and all his apostates—not, as my rivals say, in the hope or expectation of obtaining his honor, but terrified by monstrous works [Note: the edition adds ‘of the devil’s power,’ hidden in human form].

“I did not, I say, abandon him for that reason, but lest I incur the prophetic saying: ‘You give help to the wicked and join friendship with those who hate me, and therefore you deserved the Lord’s wrath’ (2 Chronicles 19:2).

“After ecclesiastical sanctions had been carried out over long periods of time and the peremptory law had been completed, when nothing else remained except that he should be restrained by the judicial authority of the prince and removed from the principal see as a seditious and rebellious man, I was again summoned and admonished by my brothers and by the leading men of the kingdom, in accordance with the law of the African council, to take charge of the people who had been divided and torn apart after the apostate had been excluded.

“I delayed doing this for a long time, and afterward consented only with great reluctance, because I fully understood what kinds of tortures would accompany me.

“This is the simplicity of my course, this the purity of my innocence, and before the Lord and you priests, in all these matters, this is the cleanliness of my conscience.”

## 103. Division

“But behold, an accuser confronts me from the opposite side. Delighting in novel accusations so as to increase hatred, he cries out:

‘You betrayed your lord, handed him over to prison, seized his bride, and usurped his see!’”

## 104. Confirmation and refutation arranged alternately

“Was it so? Did I betray a lord whose servant I had never been and to whom I had never rendered any kind of oath? Even if I served him for a time, this was done at the command of my father, Adalbero, who ordered me to remain in the church of Reims until I had learned the character and conduct of the bishop consecrated there.

“While I was waiting to do this, I became the prey of enemies. The violent hand of brigands carried away what your generosity and the liberality of great leaders had bestowed in a conspicuous and distinguished manner, and it grieved them that I had been almost naked and barely rescued from their swords.

“Finally, after I abandoned that apostate, I did not follow his roads or journeys, nor did I communicate with him in any way. How, then, did I betray a man when I did not know where he was at that time?

“Nor did I hand him over to prison. Only recently, in the presence of faithful witnesses, I approached my elder, so that on my account no custody whatsoever might be imposed upon him even for a moment [Note: the edition reads ‘at the warning’]. If your authority stood on my side, Arnulf would become so insignificant that he would scarcely wish to harm me. And if, which God forbid, your contrary judgment were pronounced against me, what would it matter to me whether Arnulf or another were appointed bishop of Reims?

“As for what is said about the seized bride and the usurped see, it is ridiculous. First, I say that she was never his bride, since, under the pretext of a legitimate gift of spiritual dowry, he stripped, ravaged, and tore apart what had been conferred upon him beforehand. He had not yet been marked with the priestly ring, and already the satellites of Simon had devastated everything that seemed to belong to the so-called bride.

“I also say that, even if she had in some way been his bride, she certainly ceased to be so after he delivered her—polluted, violated, and, so to speak, made adulterous—over to his brigands. Did I therefore seize as his bride one whom he had never possessed, or one whom he had lost through his own crime?

“And how could I, an outsider and stranger, relying on no resources, usurp a see filled with a multitude of people?

“But perhaps the Apostolic See is being brought against us, as though this supreme matter had been investigated either without consulting it, through ignorance, or in defiance, through obstinacy. Certainly nothing was done or was to be done that had not been reported to the Apostolic See, whose judgment was awaited for eighteen months.

“Since no counsel could be obtained from human beings, however, we turned to the surpassing word of the Son of God: ‘If your eye causes you to stumble’—and the rest [Note: the edition reads ‘tear it out and cast it away from you’] (Matthew 5:29).

And he decrees that a sinful brother who has been admonished before witnesses and before the Church but does not obey is to be regarded as a pagan and a tax collector [Note: the edition reads “heathen,” consistently].

“Arnulf was therefore summoned and admonished by letters and envoys of the bishops of Gaul to desist from the madness he had begun and, if he could, to cleanse himself by some means from the crime of destruction. Since he despised salutary warnings, he was treated as a pagan and a tax collector.

“Nevertheless, he was not judged as a pagan on account of reverence for the Apostolic See and the privileges of the sacred priesthood. Rather, the sentence of condemnation had been pronounced by himself against himself; and it was judged that this alone had been done excellently by him throughout his life: namely, that if the bishops absolved him after he himself had condemned himself, they would incur the punishment of his crime.

“‘If,’ says Pope Leo the Great, ‘all priests and the whole world agree that the condemned man should be condemned, condemnation involves those who consent; their agreement does not absolve them from transgression. For God, who destroyed the sinful world by the universal flood, has revealed this to all.’

“And Pope Gelasius says: ‘An error that has once been condemned together with its author carries its own execration and punishment into any participant who becomes involved in wicked communion.’

“After he had therefore been excluded from the church of Reims, my brothers, the bishops of Gaul, imposed this burden of the priesthood upon me, despite my resistance and my great fear of what I had suffered and still suffer, calling upon the divine name as witness.
