“If anything perhaps has deviated from the sacred laws, it was not malice but the necessity of the time that caused it. Otherwise, in a time of war, to guard against every right and everything permitted—what is that other than to destroy one’s country and bring death upon it?

“Indeed, the laws are silent amid arms. That savage beast O—[Note: the edition reads “Otto”; another note reads “Odo, count of Meaux and Troyes”]—abused them so greatly that he seized God’s most reverend priests as though they were worthless slaves, did not even refrain from the sacred altars themselves, and cut off public supplies.”

## 105. Epilogue

“I return to myself, most reverend fathers. Because of the salvation of the perishing people and of the whole state, raging death with all its forces has especially attacked me. On one side, armed scarcity claims the granaries and storehouses for itself; on the other, the sword outside and fear within have made days and nights sleepless [Note: the words ‘on the other … sleepless’ are absent from manuscript C.].

“Only your authority has been awaited as a relief from such great evils. It is believed to possess such power that it can aid not only the church of Reims but also the entire church of the Gauls, desolated and reduced almost to nothing. With a favorable Divinity, we await this, and we all pray together that it may come to pass.”

## 106.

When he had finished reading this, he immediately handed it to the pope’s legate to read. Then all the bishops rose together with Count Godefrid, who was present with them, withdrew apart, and deliberated about what should be done next.

After a short time they invited Gerbert himself. After several speeches, they wished to prohibit him, in the presence of the legate, from receiving the body and blood of the Lord from the lord pope and from exercising the priestly office. But he immediately demonstrated confidently from the canons and decrees that this could be imposed upon no one unless he had either been convicted of a crime or, after being summoned, had refused to come to the council or give an account.

He maintained that he was not liable to this penalty, since he had come even though forbidden and had not yet been convicted of any crime. He asserted the same from the councils of Africa and Toledo.

Yet, so that he would not appear to resist the lord pope altogether, he promised that he would abstain from celebrating Mass until the next synod [Note: the edition reads “the other synod”]. After saying this, they immediately returned to their seats.

## 107.

While they were seated, the bishop of Verdun rose again, since he was regarded as the interpreter of the synod, and addressed the others who had not taken part in the bishops’ council:

“Since,” he said, “the matter being dealt with here cannot now be settled, because one side of the controversy is absent, it seems good to these lords, the bishops, that it should be demonstrated to you that the case now under consideration must be transferred to another time, so that there the one who brings the charge and the one who refutes it may stand before the judge, and, after the claims of each side have been examined, the judgment of a right decision may be pronounced.”

Everyone agreed and approved. A place was therefore appointed at Reims, at the monastery of the monks of Saint Remigius; the time was likewise fixed for the eighth day after the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. Once these decisions had been established and announced, the synod was dissolved.

[Col. 0169] After the end of the History, several notes written in Richer’s hand are found in the manuscript. They seem to have been intended as material for the continuation of the work. They are as follows:

## (995)

At the appointed time a synod of bishops was assembled at Senlis, where the case between Gerbert and Arnulf was also discussed in person, in the presence of Leo, abbot and legate, and many others.

Berta, the wife of Odo [Note: manuscript O reads “O”], accepted King Robert as defender and advocate of her affairs.

Richard, duke of the pirates, died of a minor apoplexy. Hilduin likewise died from drunkenness.

A synod of five bishops was held on Mount Saint Mary. Duke Henry of Bavaria also died [Note: “Duke Henry of Bavaria died on 27 August 995”; the remainder of the note was deleted again].

Another synod was likewise summoned at Ingelheim, to be held on the feast of Saint Agatha; it was indeed held at the appointed time (996, 5 February) [Note: the word is obscured].

Berta, wishing to marry Robert, consulted Gerbert and was refuted by him.

[Col. 0169D] Gerbert went to Rome to argue his case. After the matter had been presented there before the pope, and since no one was bringing an accusation, another synod was summoned.

[Note: up to this point the manuscript is written in dark brown ink, as are folios 1–28; the remainder, folios 28–55, uses black ink.]

King Hugh, afflicted with pustules over his entire body, died in the town of Hugh’s Jews [Note: that is, at the hands of Jews, perhaps physicians, as Hincmar writes concerning Charles the Bald].

King Robert, succeeding his father, took Berta as his wife on the advice of his men (23 October), using the reasoning that it is better to undertake a small evil in order to avoid a great one.

## (997)

King Robert, having taken Berta as his wife, is said to have gone against Fulk, who had been Odo’s adversary, and to have recovered from him by force the city of Tours and other places that Fulk had usurped.

King Robert pressed Hildebert by siege in Aquitaine on behalf of his nephew William.

Gerbert went to Rome again, and while he remained there, Arnulf was released by King Robert.

When Gerbert recognized King Robert’s treachery, he frequented King Otto. After revealing his intellectual ability, he received from Otto the bishopric of Ravenna (998).

Pope Gregory permitted Arnulf to exercise the priestly office for so long, until in due course he should either acquire it lawfully or lose it lawfully.

[Note: Pope Gregory died in the year 999, on 18 February; on 2 April Gerbert obtained the Roman pontificate.]

[Note: this is the end of the notes. The remaining page was left blank, except for a pen trial and the following sentence added below in Richer’s hand: “Send me the little book on medicine and on the kinds of metals that you gave this year, when we were together in the library.”]

# APPENDIX TO THE TENTH CENTURY

## AUTHORS OF THE TENTH CENTURY OF UNCERTAIN DATE

### GERARD, DEAN OF SAINT MEDARD OF SOISSONS

[Col. 0171]

## GERARD’S PROLOGUE TO THE LIFE OF SAINT ROMANUS, BISHOP, ADDRESSED TO HUGH, BISHOP OF ROUEN

*(In Mabillon, New Analecta, new edition, p. 429.)*

[Col. 0171A]

Gerard, by the grace of God venerable Father of the monks, to Lord Hugh, archbishop of the city of Rouen, and to the entire community serving God there: prosperity in the present life and the prize of unfailing blessedness hereafter.

Let the discernment of your goodwill know that, concerning the Life of your patron Saint Romanus, for which you petitioned me with the most humble prayer, I have been unable in any way to fulfill the agreement I made with you, because of the difficulties of the adversities that we have suffered on every side in our region during the present year.

Now, however, I am sending you the ancient Life composed in heroic verse, so that it may be entirely clear to everyone that I am sending you no falsehoods of invention. But since I am retaining with us, on account of its extreme antiquity, the one depicted in historical style, I am sending you this one, arranged in imitation of its style.

I shall also explain briefly to you the sequence of events and how I deserved to obtain it. At Braina, a place under your authority, this Life was lost through negligence, together with many other books. But a certain cleric of the city of Soissons purchased it from the finder and gave it to our niece to possess in the monastery dedicated to God and to the Mother of God, Mary. After a short interval had passed, she presented that same Life to me as a gift, many years having already elapsed.

Moreover, bending the knee of my heart, I ask the modesty of your generosity to repay us with a return of affection—namely, by sending us through our messenger relic-gifts of that most blessed patron of yours, Romanus, and of the sacred pledges, as you promised—so that we too may be able worthily to celebrate his memory.

For the rest, I humbly beg you to order the entire community of brothers at that place to pour out prayers to the Lord for me, and likewise to have this done in the monastery of Saint Ouen; and command it to be done in all places under your authority. For I am weighed down by such a great burden of weakness that the final hour of my departure always seems to be present.

May the Lord’s grace preserve you without limit,

and, bearing his gentle yoke upon a meek neck,

may you joyfully be able to approach the angelic hosts.

## ANOTHER PROLOGUE

“Dearest brothers, we ought to celebrate the lives of the holy Fathers, revolving through the periods of the whole year, with the devotion of a single love, etc.”

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

“Therefore, throughout the ages of the worldly kingdom and of perishable life, etc.”

## NOTES

This Gerard presided over the monastery of Saint Medard of Soissons, where the memory of Saint Romanus, bishop of Rouen, has been celebrated since the ninth century. But it is difficult to determine when he lived. We read of many Gerards in the catalogue of the abbots of that monastery, and likewise of many Hughs who were archbishops of the church of Rouen; yet none of these Gerards agrees in date with any of the Hughs.

For this reason I think that Gerard, the author of the Life mentioned above, was not an abbot but the dean of that monastery under a secular abbot; and that the Hugh to whom Gerard dedicated his work was Hugh II, who, formerly a monk of Saint-Denis, governed the church of Rouen for twenty-eight years from 942 onward.

Certainly, at that time the castle of Braina was under the authority of the church of Rouen. Count Heribert was harassing the territory of Soissons, and Braina as well, with many attacks, as I shall say later. Therefore this Gerard, the dean, succeeded Ingrannus, who was appointed to the bishopric of Laon in 932, as Frodoard testifies in his Chronicle.

### “Gerard, venerable Father of the monks, to Hugh”

This might seem presumptuous: both that Gerard calls himself “Venerable Father” and that he places his own name before that of the archbishop Hugh. But it was customary among the people of that age to call themselves illustrious men. Thus Count Warin, in the Brive charter collection, subscribes a letter of the noble man Hildegarius in the third year of Louis, king of Aquitaine, in these words:

“Sign of Warin, by the grace of God count of good character, rector”—that is to be read “of the count, rector”—“of that church, who consented to this.”

Other examples of the same kind occur in that collection. In the Life of Saint Boniface the martyr, archbishop of Mainz, Willibald likewise calls himself, as he does Lull, “a man of good industry.”

As for the second point, in the golden age of Latin literature, a person writing a letter to another always placed his own name before that of the recipient, however much inferior he might be in dignity. Indeed, as that happy condition of letters began to decline, Ausonius of Bordeaux, when writing to Paulinus and compelled by metrical necessity to place his own name second, excuses the arrangement in these verses:

> Ausonius to Paulinus. The meter has so decreed that you should be first  
> and that you should precede my name.

Although the same author, writing to the Emperor Theodosius, places his own name second. In this way most of us act today as well; and some even consider it a religious scruple to say “you” and “your” when addressing the highest persons.

### “Father”

The deans of monks were also addressed by this name. They were sometimes called “pro-abbots” by Ekkehard in the *History of Saint Gall*—that is, those who were subordinate to secular abbots.

### “During the present year”

I think this occurred in the year 950, when the men of Count Ragenold secretly captured a certain fortification of the church of Rouen, situated on the river Vidula and called Braina. Hugh the prince, angered by this, sent to the king, and the king, having gone there, expelled those same invaders, as Frodoard writes in his *Chronicle*. These and other military disturbances that occurred in that year brought many difficulties upon the territory of Soissons.

### “The ancient Life”

This Life, composed in heroic meter, is thought to have been lost [Note: we place it here from Martène, *Editors of the Patrologia*]. The other, written in historical or rhetorical style, appears to be the very one that Nicolas Rigaltius brought to light, reworked by Gerard in different words.

### “Under your authority”

Therefore this Life was written at a time when the castle of Braina was subject to the rule of the church of Rouen. But under Hugh III it had already been transferred to the counts of Braina. It must consequently be referred to an earlier Hugh, during whose time Count Heribert of Vermandois took this castle from the church of Rouen, as Frodoard testifies in his *Chronicle* under the year 931 in these words:

“Meanwhile certain of Heribert’s faithful men, departing from the city of Reims, captured and destroyed a certain castle of Hugh’s on the Vidula, called Braina, which Hugh himself had taken from the bishop of Rouen.”

Gerard appears to have had this destruction before his eyes in the present passage.

[Col. 0173]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LIFE OF SAINT ROMANUS

*(Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III.)*

Gerard, dean of the monastery of Saint Medard of Soissons after the middle of the tenth century, mentions in the preface to the Life of Saint Romanus, archbishop of Rouen, which he himself wrote and dedicated to Hugh II, archbishop of Rouen, two Lives of Saint Romanus. One was written in heroic verse, the other in historical style—that is, in prose.

He says:

“We are now sending you the ancient Life composed in heroic verse, so that it may be entirely clear to everyone that I am sending you no falsehoods of invention. But, retaining with us on account of its extreme antiquity the one depicted in historical style, I am sending you this one arranged in imitation of its style.”

Mabillon thinks that the Life which Gerard retained with him because of its great antiquity is the very one that Nicolas Rigaltius brought to light, reworked by Gerard in other words. But the Life published by Rigaltius recognizes a much later parent, Fulbert, archdeacon of the church of Rouen, who afterward, around the year 1130, embraced the monastic life in the celebrated monastery of Saint Ouen.

We learned this from his own prologue, omitted by Rigaltius, which we found in a manuscript of the church of Évreux, written during his lifetime.

The ancient Life composed in heroic verse, which learned men regretted having been lost, has been copied from a very old manuscript of the Rouen abbey of Saint Ouen. We present it here, deservedly venerable for its antiquity, since it is already a tenth-century work, and, as we hope, not unwelcome to more impartial readers.

[Col. 0173]

## LIFE OF SAINT ROMANUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

[Col. 0173C]

In the time of Lothair, first king of the Franks,

among magnificent nobles and serene fathers,

there was one nobleman, a hero of distinguished life,

called Benedict by name through divine will,

worthy, for the merits of his faith, of a blessed pledge.

For although exalted by the august dignity of his possessions,

and enjoying the highest favor of king or dukes,

nevertheless, preserving in an obedient mind

the pious commands of the Thunderer,

he despised the allurements of the world,

which wickedly deceives.

[Col. 0174C]

Moreover, a wife worthy of such a husband,

named Felicitas, strove to live for Christ.

They were moved to pour out their wealth for the wretched,

so that after death they might attain the eternal kingdom,

not to place their hope in riches soon to perish.

But because they had no fruit of posterity,

both asked for a gift from the supreme Divinity.

Christ looked down from heaven upon their persistent prayers

and gave his devoted servants the pledge they desired.

[Col. 0175A]

For while the senator slept in gentle repose,

an angel appeared with a shining face and said:

“Peace from heaven be with you, faithful Benedict.

The Ruler of Olympus promises you great joys

and, through me as his messenger, grants you the gift of blessedness.

A happy pledge, a noble child, will Felicitas bear you,

Romanus by name, great in the height of virtue.

He will become a bishop of the people, a shepherd of the flock,

the standard-bearer of the Church, a brilliant lamp of wisdom,

a pillar in the temple of the supreme Divinity because of his merits.

He will also be for many an image of eternal salvation

and a skillful teacher of the souls entrusted to him.”

After speaking these words, the angel returned to the stars.

Awakened from sleep, the illustrious hero

reported to his wife what he had seen;

she rejoiced at Christ’s gift.

[Col. 0175B]

Nor was there delay: she conceived, and the child was born happily,

Romanus by name, whom the water brought forth reborn.

He would thunder with the divine stream of the eternal Word;

as a heavenly trumpet, driving away the harms of pestilence,

he would cleanse sins and abound in streams of compassion.

Both parents rejoiced and applauded the divine gift.

The fortunate birth of the child offered them a happy omen:

that a sweet and tranquil harbor might lie open to him

across peaceful waters,

and a paradisiacal field through many sowings;

that he might receive a fiery diadem gleaming with red beryls

after the course of his struggle and the passage of his swift life.

Now let the pen, touched by the divine breath,

run through the child’s youthful excellence

and the later deeds of the bishop.

Externally flourishing, but also inwardly such,

the boy was first nourished in the noble house of his parents,

like Jacob, simple and blossoming in the character of his conduct.

[Col. 0175C]

Then he was handed over to schools and to wise teachers,

so that he might receive instruction in the threefold philosophy.

The Holy Spirit endowed him with such a gift

that, while still young, he understood the great mysteries of Christ

contained in the unformed and ancient page of the Law.

From there he was summoned, according to custom, to the palace court.

He was clothed in the toga and, burning with a celibate life,

was devoted to being regarded as a soldier within God’s camp.

All the leading men of the court greatly admired

his talent, character, judgment, and the brightness of his speech,

through which he obtained the greater favor of the king.

Meanwhile the bishop of Rouen departed this life,

and the flock remained widowed by the death of its shepherd.

Therefore, seeking someone who could preside over so great a flock,

who could worthily govern the Church as Christ’s follower,

the people heard, as rumor proclaimed, of the blessed Romanus,

holy above all others and endowed with the highest virtues.

[Col. 0175D]

They desired and requested to be raised up under so great a shepherd,

to be ruled by such a leader and adorned by such a jewel.

When the king of the Franks perceived the people’s welcome desire,

he approved it with the counsel of all the nobles

of the western nation and of his own court.

He heard what the people demanded

concerning the magnificent friend of the supreme ruler.

Thus, although Romanus resisted and feared the burden,

he appointed God’s chosen one to the city.

O compassion of Christ, who holds the reins of the world,

who orders and preserves what he has created and governs!

For when the man of God was already entering the gates,

as once happened to the Savior when he came to Jerusalem,

the devout people all came out to meet him with praises.

[The supplied source ends here.]

And so that you may marvel still more and render praise to the Lord,

the boys, who could scarcely speak, divinely moved,

sing out together in a clear voice: “Hosanna,”

you who come blessed in the name of Christ.”

They sing the sweet song which the same company had sung

when the humble and gentle king proceeds to you, daughter Zion,

not riding on Pharaoh’s horses or lofty chariots,

but coming upon an ass, served by the heavenly order,

a small, wayward, ignoble beast,

which carried the noble burden by whom the world breathes.

Such a procession befitted the king of peace,

so that the people might go forth rejoicing with palms,

not with cruel weapons,

carrying branches and flowers,

[Col. 0176B] which signify the royal trophy, the crown of life,

by which, dying, he cast down death and defeated the enemy.

Thus Romanus, innocent from his earliest character,

is chosen from heaven and receives divine praise;

God, taking him up as a light beneath a covering,

compels him to shine through him as an example to all ages,

so that the true lamp may burn with Christ’s radiance,

and neither be consumed nor suffer decline,

but illumine the household through him without being extinguished.

Therefore, as the sacred order requires,

the pontifical mitre is given to God’s servant, though unwilling;

he is worthily consecrated and placed in the pastor’s seat.

All rejoice, especially the people of Rouen;

Christ’s flock of sheep applauds under such a bishop,

who subjected himself wholly in mind to the Lord of heaven,

[Col. 0176C] despising earthly things and seeking nothing but necessities;

distributing the rest, frugal for himself and generous to the needy;

an enemy of avarice, which reigns everywhere as the worst evil,

which weighs down this world so that it cannot reach heaven.

That inextinguishable burning pyre, those mournful torches—

this vice hurls its deadly poison against everyone:

it goads prelates and finally strikes their subjects;

it devastates the Church and everywhere slaughters the common people;

it changes morals and bestows honors on the unworthy.

Suddenly a noble and renowned man is called avaricious,

a former tribune whom a single [act of] dizziness had made a knight,

but whom the power of mad lords did not drive away;

subject to vices and oppressed by the chains of injustice,

and although suddenly a gloomy judge or a groom may be,

although powerful in possessions, he nevertheless leaves as a slave to crime.

[Col. 0176D] Money, the queen, governs human laws,

and—what is more grievous to lament and deeply deplore—

by corrupting spiritual authorities themselves,

it frequently brings the ministers of holy things into mortal danger.

Above all, it completely attacks many whom they call simoniacs,

with the flame of desire blazing within them.

Money appoints these men, not a noble life of action;

a wolf guards the sheepfold, and the evil man seeks divine things,

whom black greed brought forth from the nest of the demons.

He flies out and seeks the heights. The absence of Peter causes this.

For I believe he would fall if Cephas were nearby.

But Romanus ascends the citadel of the pontificate,

whom the devout whole people, holding fast to the decrees of piety,

obtained from heaven by fasting, keeping vigil, and earnestly pressing their prayers,

[Col. 0177A] just as his angel had once foretold,

proclaiming his birth with honeyed speech.

Let us revisit his history, omitting satire.

Let not an enemy assign to spite what love writes,

since it is a sin, without the deceits of hypocrites,

to strike even the gift of the tongue with a sword,

and to condemn as utterly foul the chair of Caiaphas.

When this man, divinely elected and consecrated,

a holy pontiff worthy of reverent worship,

had been chosen, the citizens of Rouen approached him seeking counsel,

and humbly begged him, relating their troubles in these words:

“Holy Father, a most savage enemy presses upon us,

bringing countless losses, dwelling beside the city walls.

For there is a fortress there, strengthened by masonry,

in which the black house of harlots lies concealed,

[Col. 0177B] shut away in various vaulted and blind recesses.

There are obscene lovers or parasites there,

or men whom the gluttony of the impure Epicure delights.

They always thirst to stain themselves with brothel-filth.

In the middle of the fortress an enclosure lies open, like a theater,

where a shrine of Venus, bearing the title of an unclean woman,

is falsely frequented, and the form of a prostitute is worshiped.

Beneath it yawns a cavern extending deep into the abyss,

narrow at its mouth, like the depths of Styx;

it cannot be reached or penetrated by any sight.

No one has been able to break its barriers or entrances;

so great is the power of the demons of wickedness there.

There is another assault of death, Holy Father, equal to these.

For we suffer the vast danger of the waters of the Seine,

[Col. 0177C] while, contrary to custom, exceeding its former limit,

the river overflows its bed, ravages the surrounding lands far and wide,

overturns houses, and destroys little ones at the breast;

it brings ruin to many and loss of well-being.

Hence pain, lamentation, and bitter sorrow do not cease,

because of the calamities which the river’s force inflicts;

we are afflicted by such hardships and dangers.

Unless a fountain of mercy drips down for us from heaven,

which may relieve the wretched, filthy lust will drag our city

to punishments like those of Sodom and Gomorrah.

But your hand, Holy Father, strengthens weakened limbs,

drives away bloody monsters, and shines with divine power.

May it expel this pollution and overthrow Babylon’s fortress.”

When he heard these things, the Roman pontiff, the lordly bishop,

prayed to Christ, the refuge of all who are in need,

[Col. 0177D] asking him to spare the afflicted, as once he spared the Ninevites,

to avert death and crush the enemy of goodness.

Then the leader of faith went to the places of destruction,

and against the strongholds marshaled his own forces for battle,

the choirs of psalm-singers according to custom and the remaining faithful,

with sacred crosses and precious relics.

Thus entering the fortress and planting the divine darts,

he destroyed the shrine and tore apart the barriers of the labyrinth;

he shattered the idols and removed the deadly chapels,

cleansing the place of the demons’ filth.

Terrified and bloodless, the serpent’s power immediately perished,

when he laid down its dominion beneath Christ’s standard.

As once Joshua, the warrior, in the city of Jericho,

with the great blare of trumpets and the offices of praise,

overthrew the walls and subdued every stronghold,

[Col. 0178A] so our faithful leader of Israel,

surrounded by both choirs singing divine praise,

cast the shrines to the ground, whose purpose had been destruction.

Then the bishop, powerful in merits, approached the river,

accompanied by the remaining people and shining ministers,

and armed with the faith of Peter walking upon the sea.

By the name of the Triad, by the power of the Trinity,

and by the sign of the cross, which removes every harmful thing,

he commanded it to stand still and not proceed farther,

but to resume the course it had held from its beginning.

The flowing nature of the element obeyed this faith,

and returned to its channel without overflowing the riverbanks.

When this had been done, the most holy leader shone forth,

not unequal to Joshua, whom we mentioned earlier,

[Col. 0178B] who, devoted to the Lord of heaven with faithful mind,

while fighting the enemy, commanded the sun to stand still

until the battle had consumed its inexhaustible weapons.

An equal power shines forth, although the elements differ.

For if reason or circumstance had required him to command it,

then, just like the flowing water, the sun itself running along the heights

would have rendered obedience, and the glorious sign would not have been absent.

Thus the city is saved and stripped of such great evils;

fertile abundance smiles upon itself with its full horn;

death flees, the enemy is absent, the water stands still, devotion rejoices;

the bishop in the Church applauds worthy praises.

Christ is worshiped, by whom the hostile power is driven away;

the Virgin is praised, through whom the Cytheraean woman is consumed;

this lovely honor has abolished the filth of the brothel.

O most blessed woman, who deserved to bear Christ,

pure, bearing the world, yet purified by him;

the rod bearing a flower, yet drawing greenness from the flower!

Hail, Virgin Mother, fragrant with such great piety.

With what praise you shine, and how you surpass the saints,

renowned above all who possess a bodily lineage.

Through you, protect from heaven the devout city that rejoices.

Do not let the Judge strike; suspend the threatening sword.

Do not let him condemn the wretched; restrain the anger of the Thunderer.

Be the first mediator of your people in God’s presence,

bringing hope of pardon, lest they fall through the stain of sins.

Star of the sea, harbor, garden planted with spices,

draw us from the world’s waves to the shores of peace.

With these matters thus arranged, let us proceed to the rest,

so that in holiness we may deserve to praise God through him,

[Col. 0178D] because the apostolic man, the friend of the heavenly King,

made the city immune from pagan rites,

and caused its citizens safely to hope for salvation.

Then moving his steps onward, he went through the places of his bishopric,

scattering among the peoples the seeds of the eternal word.

He set before everyone together the spices of salvation,

concerning heavenly hope, and also the bitter wormwood of the Law,

which threatens sinners with the bitterness of eternal Gehenna.

Learned and skilled at stripping away pallid morals,

as reason required, he carried a staff and a club,

offering the former to citizens and using the latter against robbers.

Therefore, hastening through the diocese and exploring its hidden places,

he found the wicked memorials of former error,

and certain images of rotten gods,

which the still foolish populace regarded with empty honor—

those of incestuous Jupiter, Apollo, and Diana—

[Col. 0179A] duly worshiping orgies and paying impious vows.

Then the holy man thundered, broke up the sacred groves and shrines.

He burned the idols, cast away, scattered, crushed, and expelled

the traces of the ancient deceit in their entirety.

When the filth had been scraped away, he established new temples of Christ

in the places where the altar of superstition had formerly stood.

He preached that God must be worshiped with a sincere mind,

the God who made all things, not the idols fashioned by human hands;

the One who formed us, not what the craftsman shaped

in marble or plaster, gleaming bronze or gold.

He explained the mysteries of Christ to the rustic people:

how the Almighty, powerful by divine authority,

compassionate toward servants, though they were rebellious against his rights,

came into the world, deep in darkness and death,

[Col. 0179B] and became flesh without stain from the Virgin’s womb;

how he endured death in patience in order to conquer the enemy,

broke open hell, and made heaven accessible,

if all earthly people kept the teachings of the light

and held fast to faith without turning their necks back toward idols.

Teaching these and many other things, and proclaiming whatever was salutary,

he removed error and increased the honor of the Godhead.

Meanwhile, the distinguished teacher and chief citizen,

so that pontifical honor might be adorned by holy morals,

was arrayed for the rites of Aaron in symbolic vesture,

so that he might worthily offer libations to the supreme Father.

For a linen garment, the *poderis* (long robe), covered the man,

who continually governed the limbs of his own body.

[Col. 0179C] Under Sarah’s rod, lest Hagar grow proud,

he chastises her well, harshly disciplines and oppresses her;

he breaks her with hunger and torments her with many sweats,

so that she may know her mistress and fear the strict woman,

obey the one who commands and submit her neck to the ruler.

By this good virtue, strong in the contest, he rejoices in his crown as victor;

the executioner mourns through Tartarus,

and the powerless desire lies prostrate, unable to rebel,

driven entirely from the solid ground of the heart.

Hence he is adorned with the rational breastplate,

the sacred pontiff’s bands fastened across his chest,

on which are written the names of the twelve patriarchs.

This ornament signifies the mind’s radiance and modesty.

By it, joined to the Lord of heaven through devoted zeal,

he recalls all things before the presence of Him who sees all things,

[Col. 0179D] whose face leaves nothing unavenged.

With reason he restrains the volumes of his heart in every way,

weighing them in the balance, should anything creep in below.

He diligently examines the deeds of the holy forefathers,

whose beautiful character shines as a model of conduct.

As Israel once wept beside the waters of Babylon,

remembering Zion and recalling how joyful she was,

he draws streams of tears, the finest of gems,

turning the vision of his eyes toward the goods of heaven;

night and day he draws forth these rains from his heart.

Often he remembers the Redeemer and his many sufferings:

how he groans and weeps, thirsts, hungers, and labors.

For servants, the Lord, patient and kind, endured indignities:

he was betrayed, confined, struck on the cheek, and scourged;

[Col. 0180A] enduring death, he tasted gall and vinegar beforehand.

Life was given to death, by which death was conquered and driven away.

Holding these things in his mind and clinging to these torments,

he finds it pleasing to tear open the depths of his heart,

so that he may bring forth from his eyes floods, sighs, and mourning.

By these clean waters he washes the stain from his steps.

Still beautiful in appearance, he covers this with the shoulder-cloak,

displaying outwardly the appearance of the revered bishop’s actions.

Here gold is beaten, so that the pontifical mind may be wise in all things,

distinctive in counsel,

cautious, chaste, grave, skillful, moderate, and gentle,

so that he may truly be the Lord’s fellow-priest,

often touching heaven with his inward light,

the light, treasure, and ark of eminent wisdom,

by which he may handle the mysteries of the ancient Law.

[Col. 0180B] Royal purple increases the dignity of such great honor;

he receives from Christ the diadem of honor,

whose scepter is the staff, the watchful ruler of souls,

who leads them to the kingdom after stripping the satraps of darkness.

The bishop of Christ grants them the liberty of faith,

and the yoke of Satan decays at the touch of the olive.

Hence the hyacinthine form of an airy color signifies

the bishop’s longing for Christ, toward whom he directs his bow,

by which he flees from the mind that wholly desires heavenly things;

by which, day after day, he brings to the pontiff,

who alone removes sins, the sacred offerings of his devout prayers.

Upon these the ancient Law adds scarlet dyed twice,

which clearly signifies a pledge of twofold love,

because the gracious Spirit is fittingly given twice to his children.

But let there be pious love on earth for one’s brother,

[Col. 0180C] chaste, serene, seemly, and burning with divine nectar,

comforting the wretched, visiting those held in prison,

compassionating the sick, and granting solace to the needy.

Then, by teaching the faith, the same [color] is sent from heaven,

so that the devout mind may love the supreme Father above all things,

burning with the love of the Godhead after the manner of the seraphim,

and, like a thirsty stag panting intensely for a spring,

may long, desire, yearn, burn, and pray.

Like the woman who found the stream of faith,

having willingly cast away from herself the vessel of vices,

the highest byssus shines, twisted and adorned,

signifying the pontiff’s mind free from stain.

Adorning it, a white robe of virginity surrounds it,

as solar light pours over the fields at dawn.

The golden royal virtue of integrity shines,

and, like a rose blazing, like incense and melting perfume,

it buds and gives off fragrance, strong with fruitful growth.

God, having become our flesh, came forth from the Virgin’s womb,

so that this discipline of modesty might please us.

Whoever is clothed in it merits imperial honor,

tramples the enemy’s neck, and seizes the diadem of glory.

A plate gleaming on the forehead flashes with the brilliance of gems,

and the cap binds the shining hair according to custom.

For the devout mind, supreme in the citadel of the soul,

constant and stable, not fluid, wandering, or empty,

shone like a work of gold with the gems of virtues.

Having been adorned with these vestments, polished according to their symbolic meaning,

Romanus stood at the sacred altar,

sacrificing the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world.

[Col. 0181A] Before the sacred day on which the new people of Christ-worshipers

celebrate sweet Easter, by which they pass joyfully to the stars,

this athlete of God, though habitually sparing of himself,

then pressed the limbs of his exhausted body still harder,

persisting in vigils, prayers, and streams of tears,

and applying care to souls against the enemy’s ambushes.

Now the day of peace and of reconciling the people had come,

and had filled the sacred hall with crowds.

Then the devout bishop shed more abundant tears,

among those who mourned and wept over their sins,

and by holy prayers asking pardon for their guilt,

absolved the peoples and consecrated the oil with chrism.

But the clergy, less prudently than they should have done,

divided all of it among the churches;

scarcely one flask of liquid remained for them,

preserving it for the rite of washing.

[Col. 0181B] When the third venerable day had dawned,

bringing great joys and joining heavenly things to the depths,

and Phoebus, hastening onward, was already closing the ninth hour,

[Note: [Col. 0181D] On Holy Saturday, before the ninth hour—which corresponded to our third hour in the afternoon—they did not assemble for the office, nor did they begin Mass before the star appeared in the sky.]

the holy bishop came forward to perform the office.

Then, during the solemnities of the sacred Mass,

while he stood beside the font where he was to sanctify it,

he ordered the sacred vessel bearing the chrism to be brought.

But by chance, while the crowd pressed around and the minister hurried on foot

so that he would not delay the pontiff,

the vessel slipped from his hands, broke, and was emptied.

The greedy sand almost drank up all the liquid.

When the father standing beside the font learned what had happened,

he was not at all frightened by it, but firm in the strength of faith.

[Col. 0181C] Gathering up the small fragments, he stretched his arms toward Christ,

laid his limbs upon the ground, and poured forth devoted prayers,

beseeching him who wondrously repairs the world,

broken at its hinges, by pouring out his own blood,

to restore to the sorrowful what the hostile plague had destroyed.

Why delay in words? At the command of the Almighty,

behold, it is remade; what had come apart is consolidated,

and the glass vessel is restored, filled with liquid as before.

Holy Father, consolidate and restore your servants,

freed from the stain of sin, so that they may bravely ascend to the stars.

May he who established you as great and lordly pontiff,

adorned and strengthened you with virtues from heaven,

guide this trembling ship, which now holds the heights,

so that we may sail well and not strike upon these reefs.

[Col. 0181D] This father, thoroughly inflamed with love for Christ,

often desired to lead a contemplative life.

When he felt the heavy burden, cares, and weight of affairs,

hastening toward the repose of peace at the end of his days,

remembering Zion and turning over in his mind beautiful Jerusalem,

he wept over exile and sought the joys of his homeland.

For one day this most holy bishop,

while celebrating the annual solemnities of the sacred Mass,

the living victim of God, the venerable temple of peace,

while he gazed toward the heavens, as though suspended on high,

rose above the depths and was burned by seraphic fire.

As he was intent upon these things and carrying the sacred offerings,

the right hand of the Lord Christ appeared above the altar,

[Col. 0182A] the right hand of power, true peace, and salvation,

shining with the beauty of light like the sun,

which gently called him to the heavenly hall of paradise.

For the right hand signifies a devout life above the ether,

peaceful, beautiful, and flashing with brilliant radiance.

Those embrace it who do not walk on the left,

who subdue this fragile and fleeting life.

After the man of God had completed the sacred mysteries,

he ordered the company of just men to be summoned,

reported the heavenly vision, and gently added:

“Learn, little sons, your father’s final words; now farewell,

and protect my departure with sacred prayer.

Heavenly grace now calls me to itself,

so that at last it may enrich me with the reward of my labor.

Yet I warn you now, brothers: keep these things silent,

[Col. 0182B] and, I ask you, keep the secrets of this vision concealed,

until nature compels this clay vessel, this covering of the body,

to be returned to the womb of earth.”

At once a cold terror seized all their limbs,

when the final destiny of so great a father sounded in their ears.

He restrained their mourning and grief—

salt, honeycomb, prudent in speech, and gentle in all things.

Called by the Lord’s mercy to his homeland,

he kept constant vigil and wearied his body with toil.

He awaited his master as one awaiting his return from the bridal chamber,

so that he might quickly open his doors to his father when he knocked.

More removed from the world’s noise and tumult,

he was enriched by a celibate life more strictly within his cell.

The livid enemy, seeing these things, grieves at every hour.

This basilisk, crushed beneath venerable heels,

[Col. 0182C] groans in anger and, irritated by new furies,

hisses bloodlessly, deprived of its shrine and altars.

It devises ambushes, deceptions, and other arts;

it displays its ingenuity and stretches the bow of lust,

with which it had already struck Samson and Solomon,

weakening their hearts and shooting them with the arrow of a woman’s love.

Therefore, roaring with grief because the holy man had overthrown its fortress,

it gathered itself by cunning art in the guise of Venus,

pretending to be a beggar and roaming through the bishop’s halls.

After wandering, late in the day it sought the hidden places of the closed cell;

it stood at the threshold weeping and thus addressed him tearfully:

“O father, O father, lover of holy piety,

protective wall of the city, refuge of all in need,

who offer shelter to the wretched, have mercy on the destitute.

[Col. 0182D] Open the doors of your house; rescue one near death,

a woman who, wandering, naked, and languishing, is about to perish.

Unhappy, I am driven here by terrible cold and storms;

winter wears away my limbs, harsh ice cuts my feet,

the power of the North Wind torments me, and I am oppressed by a dreadful anxious night.

If only you would cover this naked body, already loosened by the cold dew,

with a worn garment or a cloak with a hood,

warm me a little by the fire, and feed me within your doors.

You will not lack the reward that will be given to the just.”

But the father received these many whispers with a deaf ear

and shunned the companionship of such a bedfellow.

At this the plague, bursting into dreadful lament from its breast,

groaned more deeply and poured forth lamentations and howls.

[Col. 0183A] “O father, O guardian, where now is your concern,

which you owe to the sheep whom Christ entrusted to you?

Behold, one of the flock you guard is perishing in suffering.

Unless you now come to my aid, I, your little sheep, am dying, shepherd.

If I die, what account will you render for me

before God’s face, when he will leave nothing unavenged?”

Moved by the inward compassion of pity at these cries,

the father at last received the savage enemy, unaware of its identity.

When the plague entered, warmed by embers, it sat down,

spreading its crime and falsifying its yellow complexion.

It bared its breast, if it could bend his senses.

It shone whiter still, mingled gestures with playful movements,

and hurled seductive words as weapons at the priest.

It tried everything, but the royal heart was not pierced.

He stood firm, an adamant impenetrable by any art,

[Col. 0183B] nor did the rock soften that had wholly cleaved to Christ.

For, fortified by angelic weapons from heaven,

he brandished the signs of the cross.

Struck forcefully by that spear, the wandering shadow vanished,

fleeing through the empty air,

leaving foul traces throughout the cell.

He, born of God and brought forth from the Virgin’s womb,

always made Romanus illustrious by such character,

so that he could neither fall nor be violated in any way.

As Phoebus completed the course of his hours,

the age of the holy bishop had now come to its limits,

which Christ’s shining right hand had known and marked,

so that he might rejoice at evening’s hour in a good reward.

The mystical vineyard had him as a strong cultivator,

not sluggish through torpor nor idle because of heat,

whom angelic modesty raised in integrity,

[Col. 0183C] so that he might become a vessel of purity, a temple of the Godhead.

For he shone forth in this virtue from his earliest character,

by which he subdued the flesh that inclines toward degradation through luxury,

so that with pure hands and a clean heart

he might always offer the blessed Lamb sweetly in worship.

Therefore, rejoicing in heaven and exulting in such a robe (*cyclas*),

the sweet-voiced singer sings a melody for his virginity.

The stream of piety was free from the plague of avarice;

the feet of the weak, the golden hand, the patron of the needy—

whatever wealth there was, he scattered for the use of the poor,

so that he might depart freely and blessedly die without stain.

And when the final day was already drawing near,

and a long fever held his fragile limbs,

he summoned the peoples and duly gathered them together.

[Col. 0183D] To the servants of the Church he delivered these words of peace:

“Behold, from Christ, whom I have humbly served with a kindly heart

and to whom I have rendered service to the best of my ability,

I am summoned, and by the common lot I am released.

Therefore I admonish those whom I now leave behind in part:

let peace and harmony of conduct remain with you,

which is the sign of faith, the fountain and origin of good things.

Let twofold love keep hearts joined to one another,

by which, as if with twin wings, one rises toward heaven.

With these equal beams the golden garment is woven,

whole and lasting, unable to be undone by any art.

[Col. 0184A] Opposite one another, the beams are placed on the right and left,

so that what you desire to be done to you, and what you rightly wish returned,

you may do to others; but what you do not want and refuse,

do not do to another. Thus grace joins minds;

thus you will worthily come to the Lord’s sacred altar,

receiving the sweet food of angelic life.”

Having admonished them in these and many other ways,

bringing forth the nectar of his words,

he entreated and urged them to walk royally

according to the rule of faith and not depart from the level path

that leads the just to the halls of life they have deserved.

After offering these first words, and giving everyone the kiss of peace,

he entrusted the flock to the supreme Shepherd to govern,

the flock he had gathered and redeemed with his own blood,

so that he might preserve and govern those he had created,

and fortify them beforehand against the enemy’s ambushes and arrows.

[Col. 0184B] Then, when he had worthily received the life-giving body

and the holy blood, as he had received them from the fountain,

amid prayers and the long sighs of his dependents,

he gave his soul in peace to the heavenly ranks.

The beautiful phalanx of heaven’s inhabitants received it

and carried it to the heavens amid the praises of harmonies.

Golden Jerusalem opened its gates and citadel to him,

who had utterly despised Babylon’s burden from his earliest character.

The blessed companion entered the apostolic senate,

with which he ascends the blessed judgment seat.

Strong in adversity, he deserved to be crowned and adorned

with the palm in the company of martyrs.

He shines in the camps like the sun of virginity,

because he brought forth a hundredfold fruit of integrity.

All grieved together at the father’s death,

[Col. 0184C] performed the funeral rites, and laid his holy limbs in the tomb.

On account of the bishop’s merits, Rouen rejoices forever,

and continually honors his precious remains.

Audoenus succeeded him in the pontificate:

no less distinguished—a blazing sun, lightning, and rainbow,

fragrant frankincense, cedar, nut tree, myrtle, olive, and cypress,

a counselor of peace, a refuge for the whole homeland;

through him France flourished and all Neustria shone,

among the camps of the saints, like shining stars.

His fame even traverses the farthest Britons;

the Greek echoes it, and golden Rome proclaims it.

There, while the leader of faith, wholly intent upon the heights of heaven,

sang psalms with a ten-stringed plectrum,

he drank in from heaven the response of an angelic voice.

But since the life of this magnificent patron is plainly open

[Col. 0184D] through the polished prose and verse of another’s work,

here I shall briefly bring this little book to its covered conclusion.

Yet I do not write this poem for the holy man without hope of gain;

I beg, beseech, and pray with all my strength

that holy Romanus may be my guide to heaven.

Although we plow the great seas in a small boat,

rowing under the guidance of the saint and suffering no danger,

and pass unharmed by the dogs of Scylla,

we have reached the harbor.

Praise be to the Lord of lords;

honor without end be to him who reigns, three and one.

## ALBUINUS THE HERMIT

[Note: [Col. 0185] Sander (*Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, part I, p. 113) mentions a certain Albuinus, a recluse, who had dedicated a book to Heribert, appointed archbishop of Cologne around the year 999. Only the prefatory letter addressed to him has been published; the book itself has not yet seen the light. A manuscript exists in the library of the Regular Canons of Tongeren.]

[Col. 0185]

## LETTER OF ALBUINUS TO HERIBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE

(According to Martene, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, from a manuscript of the Regular Canons of Tongeren.)

[Col. 0185A] Albuinus, an unworthy hermit, sends everlasting glory and peace in Christ to the lord Heribert, bishop of Cologne.

Ever since I obtained the favor of your mercy, my father, I have entreated the goodness of our Lord day and night that he may allow you to reign with him forever after this life, and that, inflamed by the divine commandments, you may be able to accomplish the good things you desire.

Therefore, since you desire to hear the Sacred Scriptures through pious study, as you commanded me, unworthy as I am, I wished to write to your piety certain examples which I find written in their entirety in the divine books as I read them.

If, however, with the help of almighty God, this could achieve some benefit, everything I have written in this little book I retain gathered from the holy Fathers. I do not invent what I say from my own understanding, nor devise it myself.

Without doubt, whoever does these things will see the eternal light. Let no one despise me for such an admonition; for although I am unworthy to provide such things, what I say is nevertheless true. Since no one ought to remain idle, through these teachings one ascends from virtue to virtue toward him who lives forever and ever. Amen.

If it nevertheless pleases you, holy Father, and if it seems good to you, have it copied more often, [so that] I may not regret having labored so much, and do not despise me, a sinner, in your prayers, so that he who reigns in himself with the Father and the Holy Spirit may not despise you. Amen.

Know with certainty, all of you, that no little book will lead you more quickly to the heavenly treasures than this one, if you take care to recite it frequently.

I know that the one who saves only himself, with the Lord’s help, is not greatly blessed; but happier is the one who desires to draw others with him to the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore, O man, I admonish your charity—whoever you may be who read this writing—to fulfill it with a perfect mouth and show others a good example, so that through your own labor and that of others you may deserve to receive a reward from God.

With a curious mind, always consider that you must not do these things in such a way as to displease the Creator; for if you persevere in goodness, he will grant you what eye has not seen and ear has not heard, where many of the saints rest.

[Col. 0186B] Since, then, I desire to admonish you concerning many virtues, I wish first of all that you strive above all to possess the virtue of charity, etc.

## TERALDUS

[Col. 0185]

## LETTER OF TERALDUS TO GUIDO: WHY VERSES ARE JOINED TO THE ANTIPHONS ON THE FEASTS OF SAINTS PAUL AND LAWRENCE

(According to Martene, cited above, from a manuscript of Fleury.)

[Col. 0185B] [Note: [Col. 0185B] Who Teraldus was who wrote the following letter, and who, moreover, was the Guido to whom it was addressed, is uncertain. Both may perhaps have been monks of the monastery of Fleury, from whose library, through the efforts of D. Martene, the following letter or short treatise was published.]

Teraldus sends greetings in the Lord to his brother Guido.

The question which you put to me a year ago concerning the office of the solemnity of the apostle Paul and the martyr Lawrence—namely, why verses were joined to the antiphons—I shall now answer and return to your charity as far as the Lord, the author of understanding, grants me insight.

It should therefore be known that all the saints who were devoted to almighty God worshiped him either by faith alone or certainly by faith together with works.

Yet many pleased him by faith alone, having neither opportunity nor time to act, and suffered for their profession of his name.

But no one ever could or can please him by works without faith. To state more aptly what I mean, this is the distinction of the twofold way of life which they call the contemplative and active life.

To this distinction also belong the two things frequently mentioned in the Psalter, namely the canticle and the psalm.

For the canticle, which is produced by the emission of the human voice through understanding alone, pertains to knowledge of the inner man and to the truth of faith.

The psalm, however, which is performed harmoniously with the aid of a material instrument, refers to outward and bodily works.

Among these works of justice, the greatest work of justice—the one they call *eleemosyna* in Greek, “almsgiving”—stands out.

The apostle Paul, the chosen vessel and teacher of the nations, was most firm in faith, filled with teaching, and burning with divine love in his whole soul, as is common to all the saints.

He also labored incomparably diligently in works of mercy, as the text of his Epistles teaches, where he frequently exhorts his disciples or hearers to almsgiving and commands that a collection of money be made to carry to Jerusalem, asserting that he had undertaken the ministry of serving the poor and needy who lived there.

[Col. 0188A] Likewise Lawrence, archdeacon of the Roman Church, although he too was steadfast in faith, prudent in knowledge, and cheerfully devoted to the generosity of alms, confidently distributed to the poor the treasures of that Church entrusted to him, as the account of his passion relates.

Therefore, on his solemnity an apostolic reading is recited which is entirely composed as an exhortation or praise of one who gives alms, and several other passages pertaining to the same matter are inserted into this office.

Thus the holy Fathers, the organizers of the divine offices, wishing to signify together these two things that I have mentioned—namely, the canticle and the psalm, and likewise their figures, which we have described—ordained that on the feast of each of these two saints a verse should be recited along with the antiphons that were to be sung.

In this way, their sincerity of faith in God and their works of mercy toward their neighbors might be displayed: the antiphon would resound in the place of the canticle, through which, as has been said, devotion of mind is expressed; while the verses would be recited as a psalm, by which outward action and the works of mercy that these two saints had practiced more diligently than others would likewise be indicated.

Farewell in the Lord, dearest one.

## AMBLARDUS, ABBOT OF SOLIGNAC

[Col. 0187]

## LETTER OF AMBLARDUS TO HERVEUS, A CANON OF TOURS

He sends him a book on the Life of Saint Eligius, bishop.

(According to Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. IV, p. 155.)

[Col. 0187C] To my most excellent and God-beloved lord ARVEUS, distinguished by good works, the most humble of all, AMBLARDUS, abbot, and the entire congregation subject to me in the monastery of Solignac, send perpetual salvation in Christ.

The sacred remembrance of you clings so closely to our hearts that it can in no way escape because of any disturbance of the world.

Although we are placed amid the storms of the world, nevertheless, by God’s generosity, we remember you in our prayers as far as we can.

For we know that from almost your very cradle you have loved nothing except to live for God.

Placed under your authority, I have recognized that you increase daily in wondrous virtues; therefore we ask that you remember us in your prayers.

We have written, as best we could, the life of the most blessed confessor and bishop Eligius, which you requested from us some time ago, and, God willing, have sent it to your presence.

We therefore beg you, most reverend Father, that when you have eagerly received it and committed it well to memory, you also show it to King Robert, so that from it he may learn with how much familiarity and kindness he ought to concern himself with our house.

For when I was living with you and had often spoken with him, he himself asked me to arrange that he might have it.

## WORKS WITHOUT AN AUTHOR OF THE TENTH CENTURY

[Col. 0189]

## ON THE FOUNDATION OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT ARNULF OF METZ

(According to D. Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, Proofs, p. 545.)

[Col. 0189A] Since we wish briefly to touch upon the memory of those whose patrimony has caused the church of Saint Arnulf—called in ancient times the church of the holy apostles—to flourish again down to the present day, it seems fitting to relate in a few words through whose zeal an altar of holiness was first erected here.

The tradition of the ancients, handed down successively to posterity, relates that blessed Patiens, the fourth bishop of Metz, was a disciple of blessed John the Apostle and Evangelist. This blessed apostle, having attained a longer span of life while his fellow disciples were already reigning in heaven, sent many of his disciples, workers in the Lord’s harvest, throughout numerous regions. Among them, when a similar task was assigned by divine revelation to blessed Patiens, radiant with the light of his merits, he—eager for the presence of his teacher—declared that he would not undertake it unless he could somehow obtain a pledge of his teacher’s bodily relics.

Blessed John the Apostle, embracing the faith of his devotion, asked the Lord that this might be done, since by his will all nature turns aside from the force of its own law. After praying, he summoned his faithful disciple and, pulling a tooth from his mouth without pain, said: “Take this as a pledge of my love for you. The author of piety also grants you this: when you are near the city of Metz, to which you have been appointed as teacher, you shall speak fully in the language of its inhabitants.” For, it is said, he was Greek by tongue.

Just as blessed Nicholas was raised to the highest rank of the priesthood by divine revelation, so this holy Patiens, by the same grace, was sent through the Apostle John to govern the city of Metz, while his predecessor, blessed Felix, bishop of Metz, was still living in the body.

### On the First Consecration of the Church

[Col. 0189C] Thus blessed Patiens, endowed with consecration, blessing, and the distinguished gift of the relic of his beloved John, undertook the journey. By the ordering of heavenly mercy, he became the shepherd of the people of Metz. Directing his mind toward divine contemplation and prayer, he built and consecrated a basilica to God and to his teacher, the Apostle John, south of the city, outside its walls. He honored it with the apostle’s tooth, twelve portions of the apostles’ garments, and other sacred relics; he appointed those who were to serve God there; and, when the course of his labors was finished, he rested there in peace, in the time of the emperors Antoninus Pius and Hadrian, during the days of Pope Hyginus.

[Col. 0190A]

### From the Time of Saint Patiens to the Time of Saint Arnulf

From the time of this saint until blessed Arnulf, more than five hundred years passed, with twenty-four bishops succeeding one another in the interval, although the church remained vacant for many years. From blessed Arnulf until Deoderic, bishop of Metz, who founded the church of Saint Vincent, more than three hundred years passed, with seventeen bishops succeeding one another; the last of them was the aforementioned Deoderic.

He took away from the aforesaid church—that is, from the churches of the holy apostles and of blessed Arnulf, from Gorze (the abbey of Gorze), from Saint Glodesind, and from blessed Stephen—the possessions with which he restored the church of Saint Vincent. He also removed certain monks from the monasteries of Gorze and Saint Arnulf, so that they might lead a monastic life there and devote themselves continually to divine service.

[Col. 0190B] (Here follows a catalogue of the bishops of Metz, from Saint Clement, the first bishop, to Adalbero, who was the forty-fifth bishop of that see. Under his governance the monastic order was introduced into the church of blessed Arnulf. The author continues:)

“To this day, every year, when the conventual churches, the canons, the clergy, and the people assemble there, the bishop of the see performs the consecration of the palms. All the priests of the entire city are required to come to that church for the consecration of the palms before the canons arrive, and they must send their palms there to be consecrated.”

### Blessed Patiens Adhered to the Apostle John in All Things

Thus, as we have learned through the successive testimony of our predecessors, Saint Patiens, founder of the church of the holy apostles, sprang from a renowned Greek lineage. As distinguished by worldly nobility, so he shone forth in the glory of wealth in the region of Asia Minor.

The beloved evangelist of the Lord, John, received this region of Asia as his allotted field of preaching by divine dispensation and subjected it to the yoke of faith. For, while he confirmed the splendor of his words by the radiance of his virtues, very many people destined for life—powerful, wealthy, and of humble station—were moved by the grace of his teaching to obey.

Accordingly, among other distinguished men, blessed Patiens submitted himself in the faith of obedience, abandoned the pomp of the world, and adhered intimately to the holy apostle. When Christ changed water into wine at the wedding feast, John followed him and abandoned carnal marriage; Patiens, hearing the word of God from John himself, renounced the pleasures of the world.

John remained in fellowship with Christ when he raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in her chamber; Patiens was present with John when he raised the son of the faithful widow. John was present with Christ at the Transfiguration on the mountain; Patiens stood beside John when, after the conversion of two nobles who repented of their riches, he brought them back from eternal damnation through the wondrous turning of gold into leaves.

John stood beside Christ’s cross; Patiens stood beside that same John when he was cast into boiling oil. After conquering death, Christ commended to his disciples, in the honeycomb of true divinity and the union of his humanity, the mystery of that reality; John, after his release from exile, set forth in writing for Patiens and his fellow disciples the inseparable substance of the Father and the Word.

### On the Life of Saint Amalarius, His Glorious Tomb, and His Holy Miracles

We also append to this page the memory of the most devout priest Amalarius, archbishop of Trier, who, it is said, had been chancellor of Charlemagne. His monument, worthy of veneration, can be seen in the middle of the crypt beneath the monastery.

When, in order to found a more splendid oratory, the tombs of others were broken open and their bones exposed, his burial place could in no way be disturbed by divine intervention. At last, with God favoring the work, its completion was achieved. Then a certain brother, the church’s custodian, named Gregory, was perhaps touched by doubt. Taking some small bones from Amalarius’s tomb, he began to investigate the man’s merit.

When he brought them to glowing coals, you would have seen them—wondrous to behold—spring back and, as if by their movements, protest. They did not dare touch the bones of the man of God, because, while he lived, he had prudently extinguished within himself the flame of vices with heavenly dew. Terrified by this sign, Gregory hastily replaced the bones in the tomb.

That night, while he was enjoying the gift of sleep, the man of God appeared with a certain sound of footsteps at the left entrance of the crypt. There was the bed of the aforementioned brother. Amalarius rebuked him harshly, striking him with trembling, because he had dared to disturb him. The monk was therefore overcome by bodily affliction, but it was eased when he had made a fitting satisfaction.

Not long afterward, Adalbero, bishop of Metz and a faithful friend of our community, desired to have a mausoleum placed for him in the same crypt. This would have been carried out there when the bishop’s end of life was approaching.

The same man of God, Amalarius, appearing to the brother mentioned above, asked him: “For whom is the burial place being prepared beside me?” He replied: “For Adalbero, bishop of Metz, of pious memory.”

At this the man of God Amalarius said: “Make this known publicly among the people: by God’s favorable will, so long as I am buried here, no one shall share a tomb with me.”

Although the bishop had disclosed little about this, the outcome of the matter nevertheless confirmed it. For, while the bishop was still alive and had ordered himself to be carried there, the plan was prevented by the advice of certain persons, and he received his tomb in the basilica of the Holy Savior, which he himself had magnificently built.

How highly this Amalarius is regarded in the sight of God is proved by the deliverance of many who suffer from fever; we omit speaking of it at present, because, if faith is present, it happens every day. Women also, when they come to him to pray, ought to be reconciled with their husbands; men likewise often believe that they receive help through prayers and Masses.

When the order was changed—that is, when the regular canons were transformed into a monastic order—Arbert became the first abbot in the church of Saint Arnulf.

I, Arbert, a monk of Gorze, make known to you that Otto, emperor by divine providence, and Adalbero, bishop of Metz, having expelled the regular canons, appointed me abbot of Saint Arnulf.

Therefore, inflamed by the goad of anger, as though they had been driven from their paternal revenues, certain of them went to our elder king, namely Otto, chattering out an empty protest on this matter: that I had unjustly taken away what was their own, as though it were an hereditary place.

When I had reported everything I had done to the aforesaid elder, he, as a wise and just king, disregarded their argument, so that thereafter those serving God there would not be troubled by the complaints of the envious. He then confirmed what I had done by a document of royal authority, ordering that our church should repeatedly express its agreement in order to strengthen the authority of the confirmation.

Carrying this out according to the ardor of my desire, so that henceforth the arrangement we had established might remain with the consent of our duke, namely Otto, and of our entire church, we strengthened this writ of confirmation with our own hands. We also gave it to the aforesaid duke, to our fellow bishops, and to our faithful, so that it might be strengthened by their authority.

In the Lord and for the Lord, I humbly ask all our successors that, just as we have determined, those who wish their own determinations to remain valid should also consent to ours.

Therefore I, Arbert, undertake this care for the Lord and for those who have asked me—that is, pastoral care—so that it may profit me and the monks forever.

He held the pastoral office of the church for only two years.

After him, the lord Ansteus assumed the office.

It is not fitting to pass over in silence the lord Ansteus, monk and most glorious abbot of the monastery of Saint Arnulf. While still in secular dress, he had been the companion and blood relative of the aforesaid father. Having first abandoned his possessions and followed his footsteps, he was truly changed from an archdeacon into a poor man of Christ and became a monk.

He flourished so greatly in wisdom and eloquence that, whenever necessary, the honey of his sermons flowed continuously from him, as from an excellent rhetorician. He was also highly skilled in architecture.

First made dean in the monastery of Gorze, he demonstrated by his work and example how greatly he flourished in holiness and in the administration of affairs. Thus, as his merits required, he became abbot of the monastery of Saint Arnulf after the distinguished man Arbert, who had first been placed over that community by the lord Bishop Adalbero, after the clergy had been removed and the regular order of monks introduced.

Ansteus greatly increased the resources of the monastery, which was suffering from severe poverty. Within four years he completed all the dwellings of the brothers. With the lord Bishop Adalbero providing the labor for the abbey, he accomplished the work in four months—a marvelous thing to say—had not the conflict within the kingdom hindered it, the conflict between Otto, then king and later Caesar, and his son Luitulf and his son-in-law Conrad.

Nevertheless, in the following summer, with Christ’s help, he completed the work he had begun. Nor did external concerns diminish his pastoral diligence. On every Sunday and principal feast he sang Mass publicly; every Wednesday he celebrated privately with the greatest devotion and many tears. In fasting, vigils, prayers, humility, care for the sick brothers, hospitality, and the other works of mercy, he was outstanding.

Having completed his course, after sixteen years spent in the labors of holy perseverance, he was laid in a tomb on the northern side of the basilica on the day before the Nativity of the Mother of God, while a multitude of devout men attended and the lord and venerable Bishop Adalbero performed the funeral rites, in the year of the Lord 960.

After Ansteus, the second abbot, the monks of Saint Arnulf elected John as their third abbot.

### John

After Ansteus, John assumed the pastoral office of Saint Arnulf. In the time of this John, there lived the palatine count Teubertus, during the reign of the first magnificent and most renowned Emperor Otto, father of the second of that name, who for the defense of the holy Church of God fought a battle in Apulia memorable for all ages against the Saracens.

Teubertus was rich in possessions, a most energetic man in divine and human affairs, and distinguished by every virtue. By his wife Ermentrude he had offspring of the female sex; but since he lacked a male child, he persevered constantly in prayer, asking God to grant him a son.

While intent upon this, it happened that one day he went to the monastery of Saint Arnulf for that very reason and prolonged his prayer for a long time, prostrate on the ground before the most holy altar.

John, the abbot of that place, stood motionless before the doors of the basilica until the Palatine Count came out. As the count was leaving the church, John greeted him and, offering him a kiss, said: “Rejoice, most noble of men, and know that your prayers have been heard by the Lord.”

When the count, struck with astonishment at the novelty of the matter, stood reverently before him and asked how he knew this, John said: “I have learned, through him to whom the secrets of minds are open, that you have obtained from God the male child for whom you have long been praying. For soon a male offspring shall be born to you from a chaste marriage, named Benedict, to be blessed in every way by him who calls things that are not as though they were. Take care not to change the name which he who created all things from nothing has given him. When he is born, deliver him to the Lord and to holy Arnulf to be reared under a regular superior, and in time he shall shine forth as his propagator far and wide.”

Trusting the words of the man of God, the count returned home joyfully, accepting the response he had received. Meanwhile, after not many days had passed, the mother safely gave birth to the son whom she had conceived with Christ as her protector.

The father secretly took the child from his mother and, together with the nurse, brought him to the monastery mentioned above, to the abbot John, asking that John make him a catechumen. The holy man did not refuse; he fulfilled the count’s request at once and gave the child his name.

After this, the count brought the child, wrapped in a purple cloak, into the church. He placed him upon the altar and offered him to the Lord and to Saint Arnulf, while the abbot and the brothers stood by. The abbot then lifted him up and returned him to the nurse to be cared for, and so the child was taken home.

At length, when the mother had recovered from her illness, she said to her husband when she thought the time appropriate: “The time has come, if it pleases your highness, for you to order that our child be initiated into the sacraments of Christ and receive a name from the line of his great-grandfathers.”

“This has already been done,” replied the count.

When she asked where and by whom, he said: “At the monastery of blessed Arnulf, by John, the abbot of that place, who also ordered that he be called Benedict.”

The matron was distressed. “That name,” she said, “is appropriate only for monks who have renounced the world; it has been handed down to them from Saint Benedict.”

“He too,” said the count, “will become such in the course of time.”

Hearing this, she said: “May the Lord not allow such disgrace to be brought upon our family, that I should ever see a child born from me wearing the habit of that profession.”

The count gently corrected her and at the same time announced the prophecy of the man of God. He not only turned her away from her intention but also made her rejoice in the gift granted to her by God.

This John, who is pastor of this church of Saint Arnulf, shone with many miracles. When he was at Gorze, he obeyed his abbot’s command with submission and obedience, without delay. The abbot, however, was subject to spiritual matters.

When John was abbot of Saint Arnulf and was still a cloistered monk, he prudently managed all external affairs by the counsel of the abbot of Gorze. The abbot often said:

“Brother John shows us by manifest works how greatly he flourishes in the pursuit of religion. To test his patience, I, his prior, assigned him various duties—now this, now that. He never contradicted me but completed each task with complete zeal. He endured with the greatest patience many insults and reproaches unjustly inflicted by certain of our brothers. Truly he is a friend of Christ and a disciple of our father Benedict . . .”

Thus his abbot frequently praised John in his absence.

Blessed John, fervent in his zeal for religion, often cleaned the brothers’ lamps—an extraordinary example of humility. When he was kitchen server, he himself carried water on his shoulders, poured it into the cauldrons, and cooked the food. Often, while a young boy poured water for him, he alone mixed and leavened three modii of flour and made bread from it.

In food, clothing, bed, baths, and medicines, all of which he despised; in the care of the brothers; and in his devotion to reading, he was found to be truly holy. As far as he could, he imitated the most holy Ambrose in steadfastness, blessed Martin in humility, and John of Alexandria in generosity of almsgiving.

In the exercise of justice, when the monastery’s cause was at issue, he was especially energetic. He was careful and highly capable in acquiring mills, rivers, vineyards, herds of cattle, flocks, birds, and other things for the use of the brothers.

Having hired masters of various arts, he surrounded the monastery with a very strong wall. He repaired the workshops that threatened to collapse because of excessive age. As for the cloaks and white curtains, mitres, golden panels, chalices at each altar, crosses, cruets, crowns, the lectern where the Gospel is read, the other golden objects, the various lamps arranged in their ranks, and the other benefactions, I cannot adequately express them in words.

It happened at that time that Bishop Adelbero withdrew the customary benefice from the brothers of Gorze. But, inspired by divine grace and at John’s urging, he came to Gorze and restored to them the estate that had once belonged by right to the monastery, called Warigis estate (Varengeville).

John also went to the tyrant Boson, son of Richard, prince of the Burgundians, asking him to restore to the brothers of Gorze the estates that he had unjustly taken from them. At first Boson answered him quite arrogantly and threatened him with death.

But John did not fear him. Courageously contradicting him, he returned to the cloister, although he encountered many dangers from robbers, none of whom could do him any harm. Immediately the tyrant was struck by a severe illness. He sent messengers to Gorze and restored everything he had taken away.

Blessed John also made many requests of Bishop Adalbero. Although the bishop had initially refused to comply, afterward, terrified by visions of Saint Peter, he fulfilled everything.
