After this it should be known that the Saracen king of Spain sent his envoys to Otto, the most serene emperor, seeking friendship but describing many things contrary to the faith. Blessed John, our abbot, was sent to preach baptism and correct error. He was prudent in his actions, reproved his subjects appropriately, and admonished them always to observe the Rule throughout their lives.

### John the Younger, Fourth in Governance, Succeeded John

John was asked by the brothers of Saint Arnulf to become their pastor, and he consented most graciously. He immediately ennobled the already famous reputation of their place throughout the world by his devotion to letters, so that very many people came to his instruction not only from the neighboring cities but from every direction, even from the regions of Saxony and Bavaria.

We know that some of these men were later chosen, both for the merit of their lives and for their excellence in wisdom, for the episcopate or to govern monasteries. Among his contemporaries he stood out for the elegance of his character and the capacity of his intellect.

This John, of pious memory, among the many exercises he undertook within the school of Wisdom, composed responsories for the blessed virgin and martyr Lucia in an authentic melody, as well as the life of blessed Glodesind with its nocturnal office.

He also began to write the life of his predecessor, the lord abbot John, but, overtaken by an untimely death, left it unfinished.

### Epitaph of King and Emperor Louis, Son of Charlemagne, Who Lies in This Place

The thunderbolt of empire, the noble summit of the Franks,

Removed from the world, is laid in this tomb,

King Louis, so great a friend of piety,

Whom the people call “the Pious,” and so does the title.

Hildegard, offspring, pious child of Charlemagne,

By piety gathers him into the bounds of peace.

The estate of Rumilly, and whatever is connected with it,

He bestowed upon Saint Arnulf and upon this place.

From him sprang the line of nobles, kings, and emperors,

By whose gifts this place is sustained.

### Epitaph of Drogo, Archbishop of Metz, Son of Charlemagne, Who Lies in This Place

[Col. 0196C]

In this marble-carved tomb lies Bishop Drogo;

His spirit, rejoicing in rest, exults with Abraham.

He was the son of the great Emperor Charlemagne,

A pious and prudent man, renowned for integrity.

Ruler of the royal court, shepherd of the flock,

Truly father of his country to Metz and to the Church.

Here the bishop, ruler, and lord, first among those beyond the Alps,

By his judgment brought peace to the region.

This man solemnly raised the bones of Glodesind

And honorably buried them in a distinguished place.

[Col. 0195]

### SERMON ON SAINT CLODOALD THE CONFESSOR

(From Mabillon, *Acta*, Century I, p. 134.)

[Col. 0195D] A day of gladness and joy is at hand, to be celebrated with the utmost devotion especially by your city: the day on which the venerable confessor of Christ Clodoald [Saint Cloud], released from the bonds of bodily frailty, deserved to enter the joy of eternal blessedness and was joined to the angelic spirits, so that he might enjoy without end in heaven the fellowship of those whose purity he strove to possess on earth during his mortal life. By the Savior’s granting grace, this day became for him a birthday out of death; the end of life gave him the beginning of life; for him, as for Paul, “to live was Christ” (Phil. I.21); without Christ, he had no life.

[Col. 0196D] Rightly, therefore, his desire is satisfied with good things, because while he lived in this flesh his heart was cleansed from every wickedness and malice. His marvelous life is now worthily held in remembrance among men, since by the merit of his holiness he passed into the joy of the angels. Rightly, too, divinely inspired Scripture commands us to praise holy men, saying: “Let us praise glorious men, who conquered the kingdoms of the world”—who conquered, not who were conquered. For Scripture is not inconsistent with itself when it says elsewhere: “Do not praise a man during his lifetime” (Ecclus. XI.30). What it forbids before death because of the uncertain changes of this perishable life, it commands us to praise after death.

[Col. 0197A] Let us now, in safety, extol with praises the excellence of his holiness, when neither flattery stains the one who praises nor pride tempts the one praised. Let us praise him now safe after the danger has been passed; let us praise the victor, but only after he has attained his triumph. Let us confidently magnify the merits of his deeds, now placed beyond danger: he advanced tirelessly, armed with the helmet of hope, the shield of faith, and the sword of God’s word against the ancient enemy, until, having conquered and cast him beneath his feet, he deserved to receive the palm of eternal reward.

2. Therefore, with all the diligence we can, let us follow his footsteps. Hastening by the narrow way toward the breadth of heaven, he showed us the way by which we might follow him. Today he deserved to hear, from the Savior’s own mouth, the desired word which he had gained by praiseworthy deeds: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV.23). For he returned the talent entrusted to him doubled. Already by faith he is saved through grace; he beholds the glory of the Lord, transformed into that same image.

[Col. 0197B] For the winter of afflictions has now passed and the rain of tribulations has withdrawn; now, inseparably cleaving to the eternal fountain, he is made drunk with the abundance of God’s house, and the Lord gives him to drink from the torrent of His delight, and he drinks everlasting joy according to his capacity. Nor does he forget our miseries, since he always beholds with clear light Him who sees all things and disposes and governs them with equitable justice. From the highest to the lowest state of creatures, and looking down upon the low places of earth from the lofty citadel, he sees kings, dreaded by countless peoples, as tyrants in exile. Moved with pity for human errors, he cries with the compassionate affection of one who has mercy: “O unhappy and wretched citizens, where are you going? This is not the way that leads to the fatherland, but the way that leads to impious Tartarus. Return to your heart, you transgressors; abandon the paths of error, and you shall live. Why do you, dulled by the blindness of your mind, seek outside yourselves the eternity of blessedness that is set within you?

[Col. 0197C] If you wish to seek well, seek within yourselves; there you will find it, where he found it who said: ‘I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me, because I shall pass over to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and thanksgiving’ (Ps. XLI.5), where there is the true light of light, which the darkness of error cannot obscure. Whoever deserves to see this light will reject the bright rays of the sun. There you will find and hear Christ saying: ‘I am the light; I am the way.’ But if you listen with the ear of your heart, you will also hear the prophet, long before the times of new grace, proclaiming and warning behind you: ‘This is the way; walk in it, and do not turn aside to the left’ (Isa. XXX.11). This is the way from which you wandered far away and became for yourself a land of want,

[Col. 0197D] when you squandered the inheritance that the sweet Father had given you; you fed swine, and, descending from Jerusalem, fell among robbers, who also stripped you, inflicted wounds upon you, and departed, leaving you half dead. But the mercy of that Samaritan did not abandon your misery: he became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and redemption; he bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, dead to sins, we might live to righteousness. He says to us: ‘Run, and I will lead you through.’ Living in that righteousness, we have been set upon the way, returning to the fatherland and making our way back to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is built as a city whose participation is in unity. The Apostle declares her to be free and the mother of us all, a city whose founder and maker is God.

[Col. 0198A] As is read in the Apocalypse, she has no need of the light of the sun, for the Lord God illumines her and her lamp is the Lamb (Apoc. XXI.23). For her we sigh, not wishing to be unclothed, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

3. But on this way of righteousness by which we travel, very many snares and traps are set for us by the angels of Satan, deserters from that same sacred warfare. As Peter says, God did not spare them when they sinned, but, having cast them down to Tartarus, bound with the chains of hell, he reserved them to be punished at the judgment of the great God. Therefore they go about like a roaring lion, seeking whom they may devour, in order to draw us away from the way of truth. Against them we must wage unrelenting war, because our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual powers of wickedness in the heavenly places.

[Col. 0198B] Therefore, lest we fail in their conflict and be caught in their snares, a table is prepared for us on the way of our pilgrimage, filled with the delights of various riches and possessing every pleasure and sweetness of every flavor. But a law has been appointed and prescribed for all who sit at it. “When you sit at a great table,” it says, “consider what is set before you, knowing that you must prepare such things yourself” (Ecclus. XXXI.12). Yet behold: openly on either side, and secretly on either side, rise up many vanities and deadly sweetnesses and pleasures. But what does the Psalm say? “The wicked have told me fables, but not such as the law of God” (Ps. CXVIII.25), which says: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world, because everything that is in the world is the lust of the eyes

[Col. 0198C] and the pride of life” (I John II.15–16). Therefore restrain yourselves from the monstrous savagery of pride, from the idle pleasure of luxury, and from the curiosity of knowledge falsely so called. See that you are neither deceived nor led astray. For it is best that the heart be established by grace, not by foods which did not profit those who walked in them. Do not vainly promise yourselves a long life. For what is your glory? It is a vapor appearing for a little while, and afterward it will vanish.

4. Walking on this way, hold fast to righteousness. When the Savior set it before us to be observed, he treated only three matters in carrying it out: prayer, almsgiving, and fasting. In prayer he showed all the rules of holy desire. For the whole life of the true Christian is holy desire. In almsgiving he displayed every kindness and beneficence: in conferring benefits and in forgiving wrongs committed against oneself by others, which everyone must first receive from himself. For it is written: “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX.24).

[Col. 0199A] In fasting, moreover, he indicated every discipline of the body, which is chiefly exercised by restraining all the passions of the soul. Attend as though your patron were present, warning you and exhorting you to receive everlasting rewards: “Be as I am. Do not make excuses concerning strength: what I was able to do, you too, if you wish, can do. For I was able to do nothing from myself; my ability came from him who said: ‘Without me you can do nothing’” (John XV.5). Therefore, if any of you are striving toward perfection, ask daily in prayer from the Father of lights for perseverance in good works; and, in doing this, be confident that you are not strangers to the election of the elect, whom he chose before the foundation of the world, that they might be holy and without blemish in his sight.

[Col. 0199B] But far be it from you to despair of yourselves because you are commanded to place your hope in him and not in yourselves. For cursed is everyone who trusts in man and whose heart departs from the Lord. But blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence, because it is good to trust in the Lord. Why, then, do you still linger in the condemnable delight of sins? Lay hold of the most health-giving salvation and discipline; serve the Lord with fear and rejoice in him with trembling. Do not presume upon yourselves, nor wish to glory as though in your own works; rather, whoever glories should glory not in himself but in the Lord, who gave you both the will and the power.

[Col. 0199C] To him we say with the prophet: “He has wrought all our works in us” (Isa. XXVI.12). Therefore there is nothing in which to glory, when nothing is ours; for our heart and that of our community are not in our own power, but our steps are directed by the Lord, so that we may will his way. This is what all who have pleased God from the beginning believed; this is what they did.

5. This our holy Father also believed with an undoubting mind, taught in words, and preserved to the end in his actions. For otherwise he could not have been holy: although the lineage of his family is well known to all, I have judged it fitting to insert it in this page for you and to relate the conspicuous piety and uprightness of his character from his very childhood.

He descended from the high blood of kings. His grandfather Clovis, who nobly ruled the kingdom of the Franks, arranging and ordering it well, completed the course of his life and died at Paris. He left in the kingdom his wife, named Clotilde, with three sons—namely Clothar, Childebert, and Clodomer—and, assigning portions to them, divided among them the monarchy of his realm.

But Clodomer, the father of this holy confessor Clodoald, to whom Burgundy had fallen by lot, died not long afterward and himself left three sons. One was called Theobald, another Gontarius, and the third was Clodoald. Their grandmother, the aforesaid queen, nourished and educated them with royal customs and ceremony, wishing to raise them, in place of her son, to the summit of the kingdom. But she was disappointed in her hope by the treachery of her sons, who were plotting the slaughter of the innocent.

At length, while Childebert was residing at Paris, instigated by the ancient serpent to invade and unjustly possess the kingdom of his deceased brother, he secretly sent for his brother Clothar, the accomplice of his faction and crime, who at that time was staying in the city of Soissons. He urged him not to delay coming quickly to Paris, so that, once they were together, they might pursue the advantages and interests suitable to themselves and divide between them the kingdom of their brother, who had then departed this life; while his sons, like a helpless handful of infant children, would either be killed by the sword or remain concealed and overshadowed beneath a commoner’s covering.

When Clothar heard this, he hastened there with the greatest speed, breaking through the intervals of the hours. The aforementioned Childebert, however, had craftily spread false rumors among the people, claiming that the two brothers wished to have a mutual conference for the sole purpose of making their brother’s sons—his nephews—reign in their father’s place. Accordingly, they sent a swift messenger to their mother, who was then at Paris, asking her to send the boys without delay, so that they might be sent forward or raised to their father’s kingdom.

The queen, filled with joy and unaware of the deceit and pretense, immediately sent the boys, surrounded by numerous attendants and a crowd of children serving them. She exclaimed: “I do not consider that I have lost a son if I see these little ones established in his kingdom.”

As soon as they came to their uncles, however, they were separated from their attendants and nurses. A most savage messenger named Archadius was deliberately summoned and sent to their mother carrying an unsheathed sword and a pair of shears. As soon as he arrived, in accordance with his masters’ command, he displayed the instruments of terror to the queen and struck her with the terror of his dreadful message, saying:

“O glorious queen, your sons, our lords, earnestly wish to know what you think should be done with the boys, and they wish to be informed immediately whether you want them to live with their heads shorn or to end their present life by the sword.”

When she heard this, wounded by unbearable anguish of spirit and as if carried away in an ecstasy, she did not know, in her overwhelming grief, what to say. She replied: “I consider it preferable, and it seems better to me, that they should end this life by death than that I should see them living—degenerated and without honor—with their hair cut off.”

But that man of perverse spirit, who had brought such an execrable and harsh command, did not wait until the queen had regained composure of mind and given the petitioner an appropriate answer. He returned quickly, reporting that the mother had decided that what they themselves had planned should be done with the boys.

6. Then Clothar seized one of the boys, threw him to the ground, and, driving a knife into his side, cruelly killed him. As the boy cried out, his brother fell at Childebert’s feet, clasped his knees, and said with tears:

“Come to my aid, most merciful father, lest I perish as my brother has perished.”

Moved to pity, Childebert, his face covered with tears, said: “I ask you, dearest brother, to grant me this boy’s life through your kindness, so that I may not delay giving whatever you command in exchange for his life.”

But Clothar attacked him with insults and, stirred by the gall of bitterness, said: “Unless you quickly drive this boy away from you, you will die in his place.”

He immediately pushed the boy, drenched in tears, away from him, unable to endure his brother’s fury. But Clothar, more savage than the most savage man, without repenting of the crime he had already committed, deprived this boy also of life, like the first, forgetful of the future judgment and eternal fire.

The third, Clodoald, was then sought for a similar death, but he could not be found. Protected by the will of almighty God and freed from the hands of the cruel by the assistance of brave men, he was preserved. With their help he was also established by his uncle as the sole heir of his father, his two brothers having been killed. He strove rather to avoid the empty happiness of the world’s deceitful flatteries, like a monstrous shipwreck, and to reach the mercy of the eternal King through works of mercy, than, under a royal name, to turn away from the homeland of the eternal Father through earthly prosperity.

Therefore he suddenly despised royal splendor. The flashing metals of gold and silver became worthless to him; the beauty of gems was scorned; garments woven with gold and silk were rejected. Meanwhile his heart was instructed and formed by divine teachings, so that everything that appears temporal became contemptible to him. Whatever many people regard as enormous profit had already become filth to the holy man and was judged by him a very great loss.

[Col. 0201C] 7. He frequently delighted in reading the sacred books. With the sharpness and eagerness of his mind he observed and discerned their mystical meanings; he was nourished by the food of the sacred word and licked its sweet honey. “How sweet,” he says, “are your utterances to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb!” (Psalm 118:3.)

In the divine praise of choirs singing psalms, he preferred to take part rather than to hear and absorb the seductive words of men spoken unlawfully. His patrimony, which had come to him by hereditary right from his very wealthy father, he took care to distribute with praiseworthy generosity to the needy, neither a deaf hearer nor a sluggish executor of the Lord’s commandments.

When a certain rich man had sought counsel from the Lord about receiving eternal life, and the Lord had instructed him to observe the commandments of the ancient law, the man replied that he had kept all those commandments. He then said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21).

But this man did not withdraw sadly as that one did. For it is now written: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Therefore he subdued the little body that had been nurtured in royal luxury, in linen and purple, with the roughness of a poor garment. He who earlier, because of excessive delicacy, had been unable to sleep on feathers now, covered with a hair shirt upon the bare ground, enjoyed sweet sleep, chastising himself according to the Apostle and subjecting himself to servitude (1 Corinthians 9:27), in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness.

Cutting away from body and soul every delight in earthly things, through the grace of God that went before him and followed him, he strove, according to the same Apostle, to become rich in good works, to lay up for himself a good foundation for the future, and to live justly and devoutly in this age, so that he might take hold of the true faith (1 Timothy 6:18).

Forgetting what lay behind and stretching himself toward what lay ahead, he ran toward the prize of heavenly reward, desiring to grasp Christ, by whose mercy he had already been grasped. He also despised the delicacies of various foods; in this theatrical contest he was sustained rather than refreshed by eating cheaper and coarser food.

8. Like a skilled and learned merchant striving to increase his merchandise, he considered it a small thing to give away what was cheap and to buy what was precious. When he found the good pearl and the hidden treasure in the field of the divine Scriptures, he gave everything he could possess, reserving nothing for himself, and bought it.

Because of his love for that sweetness and clarity, the things that had previously seemed sweet and pleasant suddenly became worthless and were judged to be dung. The world, full of deceit and deception, was scorned. Possessions already held were left behind; accumulated goods were scattered among the needy in their necessities, so that his righteousness might endure forever and his horn might be exalted in glory.

Then, striving wholeheartedly to strip off the old man with his deeds and put on the new man, who is renewed inwardly according to the image of the one who created him, he went to the blessed Severinus [Note: [Col. 0201D] He must not be confused with Severinus, abbot of Agaunum, who appears to have died before Clovis.], who, shut up in a cell and devoted to divine contemplation, earnestly admonished many with exhortations, asking him to place upon him the habit of sacred religion and also to change his appearance by cutting his hair with his own hand [Note: [Col. 0201D] Gregory of Tours speaks of him thus in Book III, chapter 18: “They could not capture Clodoald because he was freed by the help of brave men. Abandoning the earthly kingdom, he went to the Lord; cutting his own hair with his hand, he became a cleric, and persevering in good works, he departed from this world as a priest.”].

The aforesaid man eagerly undertook to fulfill his devout request, seeing that he burned intensely with divine love. Having assumed the belt of holiness and the sacred garment of military service, like a strong champion within the camp of the eternal King, he did not hesitate, with divine power aiding him, to enter into single combat with the crafty enemy.

He therefore shattered that enemy’s strong forces with vigor because he renounced his works and splendors completely. He chose to be afflicted for a moment by squalor and hunger in order to attain the joys of heavenly happiness, rather than to be burned forever in the fires of torment for the sake of fleeting and seductive pleasures.

9. Therefore, after following the Savior’s command in an invisible manner and depositing his abundance of treasures in the heavenly treasury, and after confirming by testament that his estates and vineyards would perpetually benefit their cultivators, monasteries, and the churches of Christ, he counted himself as earth and ashes and regarded himself as worthless in his own eyes so that he might be precious in the eyes of God.

He resolved to avoid and shun the applause of people who favored him and exalted with vain human praises a splendid work undertaken solely out of divine love. He decided to go to a distant region called Provence (la Provence), so that there, as an unknown man, he might serve God in the purpose he had begun.

But because a lamp cannot remain hidden, nor can darkness obscure it when it knows that the lamp drives and disperses darkness with its flashing light, he shone brightly in that region with the great radiance of his virtues.

Then through prayer he drove demons from possessed bodies, opened the mouths of the mute, restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and walking to the lame; and for all who asked in faith, he obtained from God’s mercy the aid of healing.

[Col. 0203B] 10. Nor do I consider it right to conceal in silence the deed by which his gift became renowned. While he was building a house of prayer in a part of the aforesaid region, a poor man came and asked him to give him alms.

The man of God, who at that moment had nothing to give the needy man, gave him the hooded garment he was wearing. The poor man accepted it and departed, then came to the house of a certain faithful man in order to find lodging.

After food and drink, the host had given himself over to sleep. When a large part of the night had passed, the head of the household rose during the night and saw his house shining with a bright light. He immediately took care to tell his wife, awakened from sleep.

Observing this unusual event, she said: “This pilgrim, whom we have received, has brought with him some divine gift.”

Questioned by them in the morning, the poor man reported how he had received the hooded garment as a gift from the holy man. This event was spread throughout that place by the voice of the people in praise of almighty God and was proclaimed everywhere in celebrated speech.

11. Honored by such gifts of charisms from the Holy Spirit, he returned to Paris. At once that city became filled with the joy of those giving thanks to God for his return, whose hearts had formerly been deeply saddened by his departure.

He was therefore received with extraordinary rejoicing by the people and acclaimed by the unanimous voice of all as worthy of the priesthood. Eusebius, bishop of that city, ordained him priest [Note: [Col. 0203C] Eusebius succeeded Saffaracus around the year 551 and preceded Saint Germanus, as Charles le Cointe learnedly proves under that year, no. 1; this is also clear from the Life of Saint Droctoveus the Abbot, section VI.], consenting to the voice of the clergy and to the petitions of those residing at Paris.

He judged that the man who had already offered himself as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God through contrition and devotion of mind, should be established as a minister of the saving and life-giving sacrament, so that those whom he tried to draw from the jaws of Satan by word and deed, once rescued from that savage enemy, might be refreshed by divine food.

He also founded a monastery in a place that was formerly called Novigentum [Note: [Col. 0203C] Novigentum, Nogent, is seen two miles below Paris on the River Seine; it is now called the town of Saint Clodoald, commonly Saint-Cloud. In its collegiate church, after the monastery had long since been destroyed, the body of the saint is preserved.]. Because of his distinguished holiness it is now called the monastery of Saint Clodoald. It possesses both his name and his merit. He enriched it with sufficient earthly resources, built suitable dwellings for himself and for the servants of God living with him, and, for the rest of time, for those who would serve God there through succeeding generations for the salvation of their souls. He also assigned it by testament to be held perpetually by the mother church of that city, namely Saint Mary’s.

There he himself decided to await the end of his life, together with many whom fear of hell had terrified and love of the heavenly homeland had inspired. Setting the ascents in his heart in this valley of tears, he desired to climb from virtue to virtue, persevering in prayers, fasts, almsgiving, vigils, and divine readings, so that he might deserve to see the God of gods in Zion.

Endowed with divine grace through these exercises, he learned by divine revelation the time of his departure from this life. He awaited his final hour joyfully, desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ.

Thus he departed from the body on the seventh day before the Ides of September, receiving the crown of his merits, which the Lord, the just judge, gave him in return for his labors. His body was buried with the greatest honor in that same cell, where, through the assistance of his merits, the request of the faithful petitioner is fulfilled, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are power, honor, and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0203]

## Booklet on the Successors of Saint Hidulf in the Vosges

(From D. Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, Proofs, p. XLIX.)

### Chapter One

[Col. 0203C]

Meanwhile, in the penultimate year of the aforementioned lord abbot Leutbald—specifically, in the year 703 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ—the venerable body of Saint Boniface the martyr, removed from the people of Trier, was brought by divine assistance to the monastery of Medianum.

For just as Victor and Ursus, with several others, reached the fortress of Solodorum [Note: [Col. 0203] Otherwise Salodorum, a town of Switzerland, in French Soleure.], the blessed Gereon with his three hundred and eighteen companions, and likewise five hundred Mauri, reached the colony of Agrippina, so this precious martyr of Christ also reached Trier with three hundred of his companions.

In body, though not in heart, he withdrew from the same Theban Legion as the aforementioned martyrs when, at Agaunum, the victims were being offered under the emperor Herculius Maximian. Yet it must be believed that those most steadfast witnesses of Christ, who afterward became so, did not wish so much to avoid the sentence of a swift death—since, in obedience to the command of truth, they wished to flee from persecution in that city to another—as they were scattered throughout the barbarous regions of Gaul by the marvelous arrangement of divine providence, lest the narrowness of one place confine so many and such distinguished thousands of holy martyrs.

At length, when he had happily completed the course of his struggle at Trier, he and his companions were condemned to death. Beside the bridge of the river adjacent to the town, he obtained, through the desirable exchange of temporal loss, the shortcut to eternity. After being placed in the poor graves prepared by Christian people who feared the fury of the pagans, and after the passage of many years, they were honorably reburied in a small crypt of the basilica of Saint Maximin.

This was accomplished through the vigilance of our blessed patron Hildulf. The relics of the aforementioned martyr were preserved for many generations by an old little oratory of Saint Martin situated to the right of the church of Medianum, until their memory had been entirely withdrawn from mortals. Since their discovery must not be passed over in silence, it will be explained more fully in its proper place.

### Chapter Two

[Col. 0205C]

Lord Regimbert, therefore, having become the successor of the saint in accordance with the wish of the brethren, honorably administered both forms of livelihood in the monastic life for no fewer than fifty years, as is confirmed by reliable charters from the times of the kings.

In his days the illustrious matron Theudelinda, moved by consideration of the dreadful judgment, with the consent of her husband dissolved the bonds of her marriage and, having become the wife of a better husband, was consecrated to Christ under the veil of sanctity. With the immediate goodwill of her former husband Rupert [otherwise Ricpert], she granted to our place an honorable estate called Hahenaim.

At that time also a certain distinguished man named Gumbert, son of Trupper, contributed a portion of his property in another estate called Hundinisheim.

In these places the aforesaid abbot built two basilicas: the first in honor of Saint Maximin, bishop of Trier; the other in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. Having completed the course of his life, he died on the fifth day before the Kalends of February.

### Chapter Three

A man equal to him in zeal and character, Sundrabert, succeeded him. After he had vigorously governed for twenty years and more and then died, his brother Maldawin succeeded him. Freed long before from worldly entanglements, Maldawin had sought the shore of monastic tranquility, and through praiseworthy zeal he surpassed the two men mentioned above.

He commissioned the construction of a shrine over the blessed remains of our patron Hildulf and also adorned it honorably with metals of gold and silver. In the same way he embellished the reliquary of the holy relics, together with small shrines, censers, and candlesticks. He also made a large chalice bearing his name, which is still preserved for our poverty.

For the adornment of the altars of the blessed Mother of God and Saint Peter, he fitted and decorated two panels with precious metals, leaving many memorials of this kind to the place entrusted to his diligence.

He himself also donated to the jurisdiction of our monastery an estate called Peter’s Bench, enlarging it by this gift. He died on the third day before the Ides of March, when, on carefully investigating the years of his administration, scarcely twelve can be found.

### Chapter Four

[Col. 0206B]

Immediately, at the election of a successor, the bile of discord crept into the multitude of the brothers. But because the merits of this blessed man prevailed, the unexpected radiance of divine mercy rose for them.

For when they had been divided into two factions, driven by the obstinacy of mutual disagreement, the leaders of both parties came together before Prince Charles. When the peaceful prince perceived that the monks’ quarrel would be difficult to settle, he was eager above all to provide for concord.

By a marvelous arrangement of divine providence, the venerable patriarch Fortunatus was found there. He had left Jerusalem and traveled abroad to greet the famous prince and to visit the places of the saints whom he had learned about through widespread report.

Some years earlier, he had observed that among Aaron, king of the Persians, the love of Charles was valued more highly than that of any other prince. Aaron had shown this also by sending him, through a deacon, the only elephant he possessed, along with relics of the wood of the Passion and with a man of no small reputation for his way of life among the followers of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The patriarch had repeatedly pleaded and insisted that Charles send the following embassy to the aforesaid Aaron through his own men:

“I earnestly beseech your clemency on behalf of holy Zion, the place of the Resurrection of the Lord my God: do not, through your permission, allow it to be trampled indiscriminately by the nations, nor allow the Christian pontiff who carries out there the worship owed to religion to be opposed.”

At that time not only the blessed city but almost all Asia, except India, obeyed Aaron’s authority. The king was so captivated by the friendly suggestion of the beloved prince that he ordered the revered place to be assigned to Charles’s care and confirmed that grant by sending couriers from his own power with a display of Oriental gifts.

For this reason the patriarch sent his deacon to Charles once again, with small gifts. On the third occasion he himself came, wishing to satisfy the mutual affection of the two religious men through a personal meeting. He found Charles confronted with the aforementioned storm of monastic dissension.

The king, eager to settle it and believing that counsel should be sought, suddenly turned the entire discussion of the royal council toward Fortunatus, as though he had been divinely sent for this very purpose [Note: [Col. 0207D] The manuscript copies read *Retractio*. In its place Martenius printed *Oratio* in *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, p. 1115. John of Bayon has *Retractatio*.], provided that the great bishop could be persuaded to undertake it.

After being tested by the king’s importunate prayers and those of his nobles, he could scarcely be persuaded to accept the care of this monastery, yielding to the authority of the holy priests who happened to be present at that time.

The excellence of his holiness and the reverence due to his former dignity completely extinguished the cloister’s discord at its roots. Under him the monks, as was customary, became one heart and one soul.

This servant of the Lord, Recalvaster, is said to have been physically thin and small, angelic in face and conduct, adorned with a somewhat long beard sprinkled with gray. During his days numerous estates were contributed for the enlargement of the place, and they remain well known to this day through the record of their charters.

Through his donation, this place also deserved to receive from nearly all the instruments fashioned for human life and the Passion of the Lord certain embraceable pledges, together with relics of the precious martyrs Stephen, Lazarus who was buried after four days, George, and Pancratius, along with many others. It would be lengthy to pursue all of this now.

### Chapter Five

During these times, by divine direction, two most distinguished lights were sent to this monastery from the regions of the East: a certain king among his own people named Lazarus, with his daughter Aza, who had also been queen in those lands.

Out of devout zeal they left behind their own possessions and sought foreign places, so that in the city of Romulus they might deserve to reach the thresholds of the apostles and also visit the memorials of the saints whom threefold Gaul venerated.

After traveling through many places of the saints and satisfying their religious curiosity, they finally entered the residence of the monastery of Medianum, which had long been known to them through rumor.

There they found the venerable patriarch Fortunatus presiding over the heavenly-sighing choir of the monks, whom they had known before. Moved by the holiness of his way of life and by his admonition, they brought their pilgrimage to an end there.

At length, after pressing their request with exceedingly earnest prayers that they be permitted to be enclosed, they could scarcely obtain permission. The king was therefore enclosed in a cell prepared for him beside the oratory of the blessed apostle Peter; the queen was enclosed beyond the bed of the Rabodon, beside the basilica of the blessed confessor Aper. The small windows through which they received what was necessary for human weakness can still be seen in those places.

After they had lived there for several years, devoting themselves solely to heavenly matters, they were stripped of their corruptible members and departed to the palaces of the unbounded Spirit. For this reason they are more truly to be called kings: sin had not ruled in their mortal bodies.

They were buried in their own cells. Later, however, the sacred remains of the venerable queen were transferred from the place of the earlier tomb and joined to the remains of the venerable king, so that those who had been joined in blood, mind, and body might share one tomb.

The blessed patriarch Fortunatus, finally perfected in merits and age, was removed from this temporal life on the fourth day before the Kalends of March and led to the endless infinity of the days that stand forever. His venerable body was entrusted to a fitting burial behind the bases of the altar of Blessed Pope Gregory.

The years of his governance of the monastery of Medianum are found to have been twenty.

### Chapter Six

It is pleasing to touch briefly upon the names of the successors of so capable a Father, both because of the desire for brevity and because Scripture or a reliable account has scarcely been able to transmit anything substantial to us from their deeds; it is wearisome to linger over them.

The first to govern the same monastery after him was Waldo, descended through a sister from Maldawin [Note: [Col. 0207D] Waldo was abbot in 825. He was followed by Isimundus, Theodoricus, Reginardus, Humbertus, and Pippinus, down to the year 896.].

The second was Isimundus, formerly a bishop, in whose time an estate at the house of Lord Juvinus passed to our place. The third was Theoderic, the fourth Reginard, and the fifth Humbert [Note: [Col. 0208D] The Epternac manuscript reads *Humbertus*.].

The sixth, Pippin, governed only a few monks for several years, being severely pressed by the princes [Note: [Col. 0208D] Thus John of Bayon.].

The age of these six Fathers had as rulers of the state the aforementioned Louis, Lothar, another Lothar, Louis, and Arnulf. In their times the abbey itself was greatly weakened. Because of the wickedness of the age, it was almost desolated by Lothar, who became anathema maranatha, although until that time it had flourished in religion and abundance of possessions.

This deceitful, disgracefully fickle, and slippery man continually provoked the patience of his uncles by his schemes [Note: [Col. 0208D] In both manuscripts this word is absent; it has been supplied from John of Bayon.]. He repeatedly drew up a battle line against them, but his engagements did not have happy outcomes. The aforesaid abbot, compelled by the continuous exaction of troops for the royal expedition [Note: [Col. 0208D] John of Bayon read *exactione* rather than *ex acie*.], and especially hating the parricidal conflict, refused to send into the army the wing of armored soldiers that he used to send—namely, thirty soldiers together with the customary number of shield-bearing men.

He said that he was asking the king not to impose such a burden upon monks who were serving God, but rather to provide for his own interests from the resources of the abbey.

For this reason, the tyrant, provoked, handed the aforementioned monastery over by right to the duke of the province, on the condition that he might dispose of the property of the place according to his pleasure and provide a troop of soldiers for the royal army.

Then the house of God was almost destroyed. Food supplies were taken away from the monks, and consequently they were gradually scattered in different directions and, compelled by poverty, abandoned the cells all around.

Only a few were permitted to remain at the principal site itself; for their necessary expenses, a nearby village with its small fields and a few farmsteads was assigned to them.

But the duke’s ambition seized for itself one thousand five hundred and eleven manses, together with the dependent churches, from the abbey itself [Note: [Col. 0209D] Thus the Epternac manuscript, Richerius, and John of Bayon.]. [Note: [Col. 0209D] In the Epternac manuscript, the division of this chapter occurs here, and it is split into two.]

When the year 896 from the incarnation of the Lord was approaching, Arnulf was made emperor at Rome. Immediately an unheard-of plague of mortality followed, together with a famine that forced people to eat human flesh.

Zuendebold, the tyrant and son of Arnulf, having been permitted to govern the province of Lotharingia, disgraced the beginning of his rule with the indelible mark of an unspeakable crime. In that same year mentioned above, he granted as a benefice to Count Hillin the very small provision that was still supplied there for the monks keeping watch under Abbot Pippin [Note: [Col. 0209D] Richerius calls him Hasuma, Book II, chapter 7.].

Under Hillin’s patronage, scarcely a few canons were permitted to remain. The monastic order was uprooted completely, since the clerics had a different manner of living and relied more upon private than common resources.

Riquinus the second succeeded him, and Otto the third. During Otto’s lifetime the city of Basel was conquered by the Huns and leveled to the ground.

In the monastery of Medianum and the three monasteries adjoining it [Note: [Col. 0209D] Senoniensis, Styvagiensis, and Sandeodatonsis.], scarcely a single cleric in each is said to have remained for several months, keeping watch there for the ordinary parish.

At last, when Henry—called the Fowler—had established the summit of his kingdom, the barbarian invasion was forbidden, and the homeland gradually recovered strength. The diminished number and order of the canons were restored there.

Count Otto was succeeded in the administration of the affairs of that monastery by Boso, the fourth, and Boso in turn by Amard, the fifth and last administrator of its external possessions. But Gislibert became the first restorer of monastic religion in that place [Note: [Col. 0209D] Gislibert, the abbot-count, favored monastic religion [Col. 0210D].], for the time had already come for mercy to be shown to it.

Nevertheless, after sixty-six years had passed—almost until the reign of the unconquered prince Conrad—the practice of religion there recovered somewhat through God’s mercy, though not as before, through the efforts of Lord Bruno, the reverend bishop of Toul.

### Chapter Seven

The monastery of Gorze, under the direction of Amald [more correctly Ainald], an abbot of exceedingly venerable life, was sending the rays of monastic religion far and wide.

At that time a certain Adalbert, exalted by the blood of the kingdom’s leading families, was living there in the monastic habit. Relying upon the assistance of his own people and especially of the aforementioned Count Gislibert, he was brought before Duke Frederick, who at that time had the administration of the monastery of Medianum.

After being granted the governance of the place, he was ordered to restore the monastic order there. At that time also the devout duke, under the confirmation of a charter, restored to this place the churches that it was known to have possessed formerly, together with whatever the canons were proved to have held.

Adalbert, therefore, supported by the aid of his aforesaid abbot, gathered men of the monastic profession in the aforementioned monastery. Among them were Blidulf, formerly first officer of the church of Metz, and Gundeloh, a most noble servant of God.

These two men, worthy of God, monks in life and appearance and obedient in everything to the paternal will, had been commended by Abbot Amald to this abbot [Note: [Col. 0210D] This is how it is read in the Epternac manuscript.].

### Chapter Eight
After this, the oratory of the glorious virgin and Mother of the Lord, Mary, repeatedly threatened to collapse with a loud crashing, and the same abbot wished to demolish it and restore another, grander one in its place. But because his efforts were greatly hindered by the fact that the venerable body of Saint Bishop Hildulf was still preserved there in a stone coffin, he summoned a council of abbots and neighboring clerics and religious men, and resolved to raise it from the tomb and place it in a prepared shrine.

When this had pleased everyone and they were pressing on with the completion of so great a task, the plan was that, if they wished and were able to rebury the sacred limbs, they should carry them around the monastery as an act of devotion. But because a threatening cloud hung overhead, denying the earth the sight of sun and stars, and the violence of the monthly rain [the manuscript reads *mensurni*, “measured”] had made the roads impassable, they could not proceed with the ecclesiastical ornaments beneath cover. The abbot therefore agreed that they should be carried around the cloisters in the sun.

When, however, they had reached the saint’s tomb with candles and incense burners [perhaps: “thuribles”], and its cover had been removed, at that very moment the pregnant, rain-sodden mantle of the air was torn apart [Col. 0210C]; the clear sky smiled, and the long-sighed-for light was immediately restored to the inhabitants of the earth. Thus it became clear to all with what brightness of merit the soul of one who had already died shone in the realm of the living, since the skies smiled upon his remains on earth. For it was wrong that the element should not spare mortals whose devotion was opposing its terrors to the dwelling place of the Trinity.

Struck by the evidence of this event, the spirit of those present grew warm with desire for the invisible kingdom. In that kingdom, the man whose body they now saw was showing by evident signs that he had already received one robe and would receive another on the final day. No tongue of flesh can adequately describe how many tears and sighs poured forth there sweetly from the innermost marrow of the heart.

At last, wrapping the sacred relics in a shining pall, they placed them in a wooden shrine. Taking it upon their shoulders, they carried it into the oratory of blessed Aper, confessor of Christ. From there they soon brought it out and, returning by another route, carried it into the monastery cloisters on the seventh day before the Ides of November [Note: [Col. 0210D] It should read “the sixth,” not “the seventh,” since the feast of this translation is celebrated annually on that day at the monastery of Medianum and is recorded in the manuscript of its ancient Martyrology.], with the sky unexpectedly providing an escort for so great a funeral and preserving the same condition for several days after its placement.

Because of this, by the common vote of all, it was decided that this day should be kept solemnly with an annual recurrence [Col. 0211A]. It is still customarily celebrated with greater solemnity than the deposition itself, which is commemorated in the month of July—either because that is an especially busy season or because provisions are then less abundant.

At that time they also placed together in one shrine the blessed bodies of the holy brothers John and Benignus, just as they had been taken from one mausoleum. Their translation from the place of their former burial took place on the sixth day before the Ides of May, and it remained a solemn observance, because the devotion of earlier generations wished to offer this holy bishop a distinctive annual feast.

## CHAPTER IX

The order of events requires that, mindful of my promise, I now recount the discovery of Saint Boniface the martyr.

When the church of the blessed Mother of God and perpetual virgin Mary had been demolished, together with the small chapel of blessed Martin attached to it—in which, as has already been stated, the martyr had been buried—the places formerly occupied by prayer had necessarily become ruins, open to human beings and animals alike.

The martyr’s spirit, which was wondrously honored in heaven, could not endure such neglect of his relics. One night he appeared in a vision to a young monk named Tietfrid, in military dress and with the dignity of countenance that makes him venerable. The young man was born of moderately distinguished local stock but was thought likely to become a man of good works. The martyr addressed him in these words:

“I am exceedingly distressed that I am pressed beneath ruins, trampled beneath the feet and filth of men and animals, crushed underfoot, and defiled. Therefore rise as quickly as possible, hasten to tell the abbot that, if he wishes to care for his own salvation, he should provide rest for my body.”

The brother then questioned him as follows:

“My lord, whom am I to say that you are, and where do you wish to have your burial?”

The martyr replied:

“Know that I am called Boniface, associated by number and merit with the glorious legion of the Theban martyrs. Indeed, by the grace of God, I am preserved in heaven with a glory equal to that of my companion Maurice. Labor and military service made us equal in all things, as did the exhortation we gave to our faltering comrades and our perseverance in the faith unto death.

“After some years I was secretly separated from the bodies of my fellow soldiers and brought to this place by certain men devoted to God. Here I was entrusted to the earth in the oratory [Note: [Col. 0211D] The Epternac manuscript has *oratoriolo*, ‘little oratory’] of blessed Martin. Until the present, all my limbs have lain hidden there, except for my head, which the former site retained among the bodies of my companions.

“There, I have explained to you the whole matter concerning my relics. Now go without delay and explain this very thing to the abbot.”

Immediately, the martyr’s appearance vanished from the monk’s sight. When he awoke, he preferred to attribute the revelation to a phantom rather than place any faith in it, and he prayed for divine mercy concerning the matter. He postponed carrying out the command, either because he feared being branded a hypocrite and a liar or because he feared bringing envy upon his own insignificance.

For this reason, the martyr appeared again and struck him with a most severe rebuke [Col. 0212A]:

“Why,” he said, “do you not fear the severity of my anger? What compels you to make me come to you again? Know, then, that you will pay the penalty for contempt and disobedience before you are deprived of this corruptible light.”

After terrifying the brother with such threats, he recounted the entire sequence of the earlier vision and ordered him to inform the abbot. But when he initially either concealed or disregarded the matter, the glorious martyr condescended to visit him a third time. He rebuked his foolishness with excessive harshness of speech and, after summarizing the message of the first and second revelations, immediately added:

“I perceive that the hardness of your unbelief cannot be bent toward obedience unless it is softened by the remedy of some sign. Therefore, when you rise for the nocturnal hymns, go to the altar situated at the head of Saint [Col. 0212B] Hildulf. Above it you will soon find a small cross together with the blessed bishop’s crozier. Remove from the recesses of your soul the callus of every doubt.

“Nevertheless, since it will be more tolerable for you to undergo temporal punishment than to be irrevocably consigned to everlasting Gehenna, know that you will suffer vengeance for this neglect in this life. Enough—more than enough—punishment remains for your excessively carnal life; how much more if so great a crime of disobedience is added to it?”

Terrified by this threat, the young man awoke. To test the truth of the command, he entered the church when the sign of the nocturnal vigils had been given. There, when his bodily eyes had taken in the clear evidence of the sign, he put aside every doubt and summoned the abbot and brothers to the place while the morning twilight still lingered [Col. 0212C]. After showing them the sign before their eyes, he also disclosed the full account of the other revelation.

Then he hurried with them to the martyr’s tomb and pointed out the place to them just as he had learned it through the revelation [Note: [Col. 0212D] The Epternac manuscript reads “vision”]. When they dug, they found a well-formed mausoleum. As they opened it, those present perceived through their nostrils the fragrance of an exceedingly sweet odor.

At last, finding the martyr’s remains in accordance with the vision, they wrapped them in a clean shroud and, placing them in a shrine, carried them quickly to the cell of Bego, since no suitable place for their reburial was available to them in the ruined monastery.

(But through the negligence of his successors, the aforementioned cell was permitted to retain the sacred limbs until the time of Abbot Lambert, who in the year 1043 from the Lord’s Incarnation, on the Friday that fell on the second day before the Nones of November, carried them back.) [Col. 0212D]

But the brother who had so often been warned and had delayed giving assent to so clear a vision, after some years, while standing before the house of the sick, was suddenly struck by paralysis. He wasted away so completely that, against his will, he traveled backward until he fell inside the doorway of that very house and died with his neck broken.

## CHAPTER X

Meanwhile Duke Frideric, laboring over affairs that served his own interests, built a fortress called Bar on an estate belonging to the Church of Toul.

For this reason Gerard, a man to be extolled for every mark of holiness, approached the elder Emperor Otto and informed him of the injury inflicted upon his city [Col. 0213A]. The duke was ordered by the emperor to make satisfaction for his seizure of the estate. Under an arrangement of mutual exchange, he granted him two abbeys—Medianum monastery and Galilea—together with several villages belonging to his patrimony, so that he himself might peacefully possess what he had presumed to take.

When the places named had thus passed into the diocese of Toul, and the bishop mentioned above had bound their officials to himself by oath, he took away with him, as a memorial of this cession, the croziers—that is, pastoral staffs—of the blessed bishops Hildulf and Deodatus. They were indeed extremely plain in appearance, neither elaborately vaulted nor polished, as is commonly seen in our age; yet they were highly effective for displaying the holy mortification and merit of the men, since artistic workmanship had added no pomp to them [Col. 0213B], nature being sufficient for everything.

After that devout bishop had adorned them alike with precious metals and with the relics of saints, he ordered them to be kept in the treasury of the sanctuary, as is still done.

He also took the larger and better bell of our monastery. Many were equal to it in the quantity of their metal, but none surpassed it in the quality of its sound. Abbot Adalbert had acquired it. Yet barely twelve yoke of oxen could haul it to the town, whereas after the bishop’s death only four could easily bring it back.

Indeed, for as long as it remained at Leucha, it lacked the sweetness of its accustomed sound. But once, by God’s will, it regained its own place, it regained its accustomed tone as well.

## CHAPTER XI

Adalbert, who at that time held the office of abbot, had for several years devoted himself energetically—as far as human judgment can determine—to the care of the abbey entrusted to him. He then began to suffer from a slight illness. Struck severely by paralysis, and after spending several painful months in bed, he was taken from this world amid great mourning.

His successor in governing the place was Almannus, born of the distinguished family of Saint Peter the martyr [In the Epternac manuscript, the word “martyr” appears], most elegant in body, tall in stature, modest in conduct and action, less accomplished in literary learning, exceedingly vigilant in rebuilding the abbey, and, within the limits of his ability, fervent in recalling his subjects to the institutions of the Rule.

Finally, believing that the learning of his people was his own, he hired them a teacher of grammar and even took pains to acquire many volumes of that art for the monastery. He brought to completion the construction of the monastery, with all its workshops, which his predecessor had begun but left largely unfinished.

While this construction was being repaired, however, he kept the bodies and relics of the saints in the bishop’s hall, which was then joined to the cloister buildings. In that hall innumerable benefits were divinely granted to the sick, which I have judged it best to omit for the sake of brevity.

One event among the others that occurred there should nevertheless not be omitted. A certain possessed man, doing wicked things at the prompting of his master and saying even more wicked things, was brought there by the service of his relatives. While he was being held unwillingly for some time before the altar [Col. 0214A] of the saints, he suddenly fell and was driven across the pavement in a dreadful whirling motion.

This spinning and the captive’s torment clearly revealed to those standing by the scourges and torture of the evil robber by which he was being compelled to depart. Finally, after excessive whirling, he was forced to leave by the same entrance through which he had been brought in. With the indecency of vomit, something resembling a two-legged worm was expelled from the wretched man’s innermost organs.

As soon as he had taken a little of the sleep long denied him, he gave thanks to the Creator of all things and to His faithful servants, and returned home unharmed.

## CHAPTER XII

Meanwhile, when Bishop Gerard had been removed from the troubles of this life, Stephen, from the clergy of the city of Mediomatricum, was appointed to the bishopric of the diocese of Toul. He consecrated the oratory of Saint Mary through his own [Col. 0214B] efforts . . . . . . . . . . On that same day he restored the bell once removed from the place by his predecessor.

He governed the church for scarcely two years. Although he died at the monastery of Bodo, he nevertheless wished to be buried here, and this was done. He lies buried to the right of the altar of the ever-virgin and Mother of the Lord, Mary, in the mausoleum from which the relics of the holy brothers John and Benignus had previously been raised. A small cross was placed upon his breast, and he had the following couplet of Abbot Sicco inscribed:

> Here once was Stephen, bishop of the Leuci.
>
> On the Ides of March he departed from the fields.” [The added *terna* is metrically or textually uncertain.]

Later, while two brothers were standing upon his tomb and singing the Mass chants, a tremendous crash suddenly resounded beneath their feet and forced them to collapse from their standing position onto the pavement [Col. 0214C]. But whether this happened because of the mausoleum of the saints or out of reverence for the buried bishop, I have not learned with certainty.

His successor in the bishopric was Bertoldus, a Suevian by birth. He was especially devoted to worldly respectability, second to none in constructing new and lofty buildings, and a cunning oppressor of the common people and monasteries through unprecedented laws. He is known to have inflicted irreparable disaster upon Medianum monastery.

For when the aforementioned abbot, in the time of Prince Henry, thought that God had divinely offered him an opportunity to reclaim the estate of Bercheim, long held by unjust possessors, he rendered the emperor an enormous service at the urging of the aforementioned Bertoldus. For the cost of that service he was compelled to remove almost all the furniture and livestock of the abbey [Col. 0214D], and even to strip away every ornament—from crosses and candlesticks, as well as from the bed of Saint Hildulf and the bier of the holy relics.

For that good and simple man thought little of dispersing the church’s wealth with a lavish hand in such an undertaking, since he hoped it would be restored to him many times over from the revenues of that estate.

After he had therefore weighed two pounds of gold for the emperor’s treasury, in addition to the expenses of the aforementioned service, he formally received from him the estate with its appurtenances.

After he had possessed it peacefully for one year, Bishop Bertoldus—who ought by his authority to have rescued the monastery’s property from the snares of evil men—did not fear to vindicate it through the deceit of his wickedness, by means of a substituted document [Col. 0215A] and a conspiracy of crafty machination. He had forgotten divine judgment and disregarded the unspeakable loss by which the house of God had nearly been destroyed because of the acquisition of that estate.

Pierced by the point of such monstrous cruelty, the abbot’s heart passed few, if any, days in this life thereafter without grief. After countless exercises of his diligence, through which he had taken care to benefit the place entrusted to him, he was worn out by age and illness, yielded to nature, and deserved burial in the basilica of blessed Mary.

## CHAPTER XIII

His successor was Nardulfus [Note: [Col. 0215D] The Epternac manuscript reads “Hardulfus.” The same form appears in John of Bayon; hence we believe that an error entered here], whom the aforementioned abbot had received from the font of holy baptism and whom he had sent to various places to learn monastic life.

When the abbot himself was dying, he commended Nardulfus to Bishop Bertoldus in whatever speech he could command and obtained his succession to the office [Col. 0215B].

During his administration, many miracles were divinely displayed in that place, by which the insolence of the wicked was blunted and the goodwill of the upright strengthened. I shall append some of those that presently come to mind.

The feast of the deposition of our holy father Hildulf was approaching, and the masons were working on rebuilding the dormitory wall. When they wished to interrupt the work out of reverence for the solemnity, the provost Encibolus opposed them, repeatedly impressing these words upon them:

“It is the service of the saint. It must not be interrupted because of his feast; rather, it must be carried out with greater diligence.”

Inflamed by these admonitions, the masons [*macones caementarii*, “masons, bricklayers”] pressed on with the work they had begun, more vigorously than usual [Col. 0215C]. But when the hour of refreshment arrived and they went together to the table to take food, everything they had accomplished during the entire week suddenly collapsed to the ground. Thus it became clear that the saint preferred obedience to sacrifice.

Consequently, no one dared undertake that construction on that day. In its destruction they understood what misfortune might have overtaken them if the Lord’s mercy had not spared them.

The account of the next miracle will show with what kindly ear this saint attends those who truly invoke him. The solemn feast of his translation, which is celebrated there with a large attendance, was at hand, and there was absolutely no supply of fish for the needs of the brothers and the visitors.

The monastery’s provost, Marbodus, was grieving that he had been deceived by vain hope while waiting for fish to be supplied from various places. As the monks and canons were celebrating the solemnities of the Mass with the greatest devotion, and public necessity compelled it, he openly approached the saint’s bed in the crypt, bathed in tears, and, prostrating himself for some time before the venerable body, poured out a silent prayer with profound contrition.

When he rose from prayer, some men immediately came and said that several “Allabroces” [Note: [Col. 0215D] We think “Allobroges” should be read here. By this name the author intended to indicate fish called *Umbrae*, very similar to certain fish native to the lakes of the Allobroges. See Aldrovandi, *On Fish*, book V, chapter 51. Perhaps they were also pike, commonly called *brochets*.] were present in the neighboring river [Col. 0216A]. The fishermen hurried there with every possible speed and immediately surrounded so many and such large fish with their nets that the catch could fully suffice not only for the feast day but also for the brothers throughout the entire week.

## CHAPTER XIV

When his most sacred deposition was being renewed for mortals by its annual recurrence, and the brothers were still held by sleep before the morning office, a sudden fire seized the kitchen building. Advancing rapidly toward the roofs of the buildings and drawing excessive strength from the dry shingles, it spread unchecked through the surrounding structures.

As no one confronted so great a terror and everyone was sunk in deep sleep, the saint appeared in a vision to Hermann, the church custodian, as Hermann himself was accustomed to admit. With fierce severity [Col. 0216B]—for such was the wickedness of Hermann’s conduct deserving of it—he shook Hermann’s hair and said to him:

“Rise quickly, for the entire structure of this place is being consumed by an excessive fire.”

Awakened by fear, Hermann rose. He saw the fire just as he had learned of it in his sleep, roused the others with tremendous cries, and urged them to attempt to resist the fire that had seized the buildings.

As they immediately tried to do so, the noise awakened the country people, who came running with buckets. While some fought to overcome the barely defeated flame by continually pouring water upon it and by various devices [that is, techniques], it burst so violently from the roofs of the buildings that it seemed more likely to be nourished than extinguished by the opposing element.

At last, utterly broken by the greatest despair concerning the suppression of the flames, they fled together to the saint’s tomb amid loud and confused [Col. 0216C] wailing. Among other things, they repeatedly cried to him through their tears:

“Because of our crimes this place has been handed over to the just flames; yet may you deign to spare it for the joy of your solemnity and the holiness of your name.”

It was as though the Almighty Father were answering them through the merits of His beloved Hildulf, in accordance with the words of the prophet Ezekiel:

> “It is not for your sake that I act, house of Israel, but for the sake of my holy name, which you profaned among the nations, so that they may know that I am the Lord” (Ezekiel 36:22).

Without delay, all the force of the fire collapsed in upon itself. Growing weak with swift exhaustion, it abandoned everything it had been ravaging. The danger of the badly victorious [Note: [Col. 0216D] The Epternac manuscript reads “burning”] fire, which the opposing element of water had been unable to restrain, was restrained by the merits of the saint through a rain of tears.

## CHAPTER XV

When the inhabitants had accepted, by priestly authority, the celebration of his feast of deposition, the religious and honorable agreed solemnly to conduct it as prescribed, as is customary in such observances. But the brutish and foolish crowd of peasants, in their customary stubbornness, decided to neglect it.

Among them was a certain Uvalpertus at Cicomacum [Col. 0217A] [Note: [Col. 0217D] Today at Saint Prejectus, commonly Saint Preyè. See John of Bayon, book XI, chapter 5], a man poor both in understanding and in possessions. He despised the priestly command and on that very day was busily mending his shoes.

But if no scourges of heavenly judgment restrained the wicked, the Almighty might be thought not to attend to human affairs. Therefore, by a sudden contraction, the man’s hands were drawn up, his fingers fixed inextricably within the palms and grotesquely twisted outward, so that he paid the penalty for contempt and disobedience.

As long as he lived, the example of his punishment terrified others and kept them from presuming to undertake the forbidden work.

## CHAPTER XVI

On that same day a certain Belzo lived scarcely two stades from the monastery, in a house that had come to him by hereditary right. As commonly happens in the exchange between old and new crops [Col. 0217B], compelled by a shortage of bread, he cut several sheaves from the new harvest.

But because he could not find in the huts of his little village a fire that could be placed beneath them, he went without delay to another village nearby to seek a firebrand [Note: [Col. 0217D] The Epternac manuscript reads “little village”]. Taking a log from there, he returned, but found that the entire building of his house, together with the drying shed, had been handed over to avenging flames.

As everything was rapidly reduced to ash, the wretched and foolish man, compelled by his loss, said—though late—that ecclesiastical commands must be obeyed.

## CHAPTER XVII

Meanwhile, at Oblisiacum, which lies within the boundaries of the parish of Acervallensis [Note: [Col. 0217D] The Epternac manuscript reads “Acera vallensis” [Col. 0218D], commonly Azeraille], a basilica was built with the consent of Bishop Bertoldus, because it was intolerable for the country people to visit the mother church for every service required by the Christian congregation [Col. 0217C].

Since this church had been consecrated to Christ under the name or through the relics of blessed Bishop Hildulf, a certain woman arrived there, exhausted by the late hour and the long journey, but strong in the faith of her heart and devout according to her modest means.

Some people were attending to their own affairs and others were refreshing their bodies. She found no one there after the solemn services, and the church doors were locked. Intending therefore to summon the caretaker, she placed a candle before the door; but when she quickly returned with him, she saw that it had been lit by divine power.

After they had marveled at this for some time, they carried it together into the little oratory and reverently placed it before the altar.

The woman, however, touched inwardly by joy, proclaimed praises and thanks to God as best she could for His faithful servant Hildulf. Her cheeks were bathed in the abundant dew of tears that sweetly burst forth. Through the visible light, not only she but the whole neighborhood experienced that the confessor of Christ was a son of the invisible light and that, through his merits, they possessed the greatest confidence in entreating the Lord in their necessities.

Their hope was not conceived in vain. For afterward that little place became so widely renowned for its numerous miracles and continues to heal the causes of various illnesses to such an extent that, if they could be recorded individually in writing, they would substantially enlarge the size of a volume.

Therefore, omitting these matters, let us turn to others [Note: [Col. 0218D] In the Epternac manuscript, the present chapter is divided here].

In the year 1014 from the Lord’s Incarnation, a manifold and entirely reliable revelation showed how brightly the souls of the saints Lazarus and Aza shone in heavenly merit, although their lifeless limbs were shown to lie neglected in the womb of the earth.

For as the passage of time had entirely removed both their names and their tombs from the memory of survivors, they were divinely restored to knowledge through harmonious visions granted to monks, clerics, and faithful people of both sexes—not only those nearby but also those from the most distant places.

Moreover, as evening twilight descended, something resembling the singing of two people was frequently heard at the place where Aza had previously been buried, namely in the basilica of blessed Aper [Col. 0218B]. Outside it, in a fig tree opposite one of its windows, a light shone at night so brightly that people said several lamps had been lit there.

In the basilica of all the apostles, an arch had also been founded in a corner adjoining the screens toward the north. It had been deliberately prepared solely as a place of refuge for the venerable bodies. Because its interior, on account of the Pannonian people hostilely pressing upon Gaul, had been blocked over the sarcophagi like a solid wall, the place of so great a treasure gradually slipped from everyone’s memory over ninety-five years, so that nothing was thought less likely than that any body lay hidden there.

The material placed above it, however, was observed to be extremely cracked and almost collapsed, shaken as it was by the continual pressure of the rising monument. When at last they brought it down [Col. 0218C], they found the bodies of the saints deposited, in accordance with the revelation, in two closely joined coffins that had once been prepared for this purpose with the greatest care.

When they had sung the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* in their honor, they left them there just as they had found them. Through the novelty of the discovery, they repeatedly brought relief to fevers, migraine, and various attacks of illness, until they spread knowledge of their merit abundantly throughout the surrounding region.

Thus the saints, whose memory was still recent, implanted reverence for themselves in the minds of men.

## CHAPTER XVIII

It was customary in certain provinces for parricides to have their arms or necks bound with penitential iron and to be forbidden to enter the boundaries of their own people. Instead, they were to seek the aid of the saints wherever they could, until the visible iron was divinely loosened and gave proof that the invisible bond of parricide had been released.

One of these men therefore came to this monastery. He had long been bound by iron rings around both arms. One of them had fallen away in Palona [undoubtedly Polonia], at the venerable tomb of the blessed martyr Adalbert; the other was released here through the merits of the saints whom we venerate.

He had arrived there on the evening of a Saturday and devoutly attended the office. On Sunday he wished to go to Sens [Col. 0219A], but suddenly changing his mind, he hurried back from the middle of his journey.

He found the brothers already beginning the solemn Mass and chose to stand at the entrance of the choir. With a humble expression and unwavering gaze, he contemplated the image of the crucified Savior set before him. A learned sculptor’s hand had fashioned it in such a way that even now it can pierce the hardest human hearts with a kind of blade of compassion, as though they had before their eyes the exceedingly merciful death of the Redeemer still hanging upon the cross.

As the pilgrim stood before it groaning, after the holy Gospel had been recited, the iron ring suddenly cracked; tearing the flesh that had grown over it from the continual pressure of the iron, it sprang from his arm with such force that it struck the opposite wall at a distance and disturbed those standing nearby with a loud clang [Col. 0219B].

Whether from the new pain of the old scar or from sudden astonishment at so great an event, the man became almost lifeless and fell. Stretched upon the ground, over the edge of the cloak placed beneath his wounded arm, he shed a great quantity of blood [Col. 0220A].

The monks raised a cry to help the fallen man. Astonished by his condition, they watched to see how the matter would end. And behold, after a little while, as the blood returned from his vital organs, the upper parts of his cheeks became marked with red spots.

Then, gradually raising his collapsed limbs, he was completely restored to his former condition. He gave thanks to God for the merits of the saints—not only for the loosening of the visible bond and his long exile, but also, and especially, for the forgiveness of the accursed parricide, which he rejoiced to know with certainty that he had obtained through the testimony of the present event.

After he had sufficiently exhorted the inhabitants, by word and evident sign, to honor and embrace the holiness of their patron saints, he happily departed from their territory [Col. 0220B]. The aforementioned ring was hung beneath the feet of the crucified figure as testimony to the event.

Thanks be to God.

---

[Col. 0219]

## THE DEEDS OF THE BISHOPS OF AUXERRE (C, G)
