### PART ONE

*(In Labbe’s Library of Manuscripts.)*

### CHAPTER I — Saint Peregrinus

The account of his passion faithfully teaches those who wish to know that Saint Peregrinus was consecrated bishop through the intercessions and merits of blessed Sixtus, primate of the apostolic see [Col. 0219C].

The religion of Christianity, which from the time of Pope Clement had spread through the most faithful ministers of the word of God—namely Savinianus, bishop of Sens; Dionysius of Paris; Ursicinus of Bourges; Martial of Limoges; Saturninus of Toulouse; Memmius of Châlons; and others throughout the provinces of Gaul—had gradually begun to decline from the rectitude of its original condition. It was being assailed by attacks both powerful and tyrannical.

For the Emperor Aurelian, profane toward the Lord of heaven and wishing to please his own gods [Col. 0219D], had burned with such madness of persecution against Christians that, after the sufferings of many martyrs whom he had condemned to a cruel death at Rome, he himself also came into Gaul to eradicate the Christian name.

When he arrived at the city of Sens, he ordered all the Christians whom he found there, together with the blessed virgin Columba, to be punished by the sword. Then he sent companions of his ferocity throughout Gaul to search for Christians.

The ominous satellites therefore departed from the emperor’s presence and went around the cities, fortresses, and even the hidden places of the forests. So that each might obtain the result of his crime, they divided the various districts among themselves for investigation.

At last the district of Auxerre fell by lot to the impious Alexander, the protector of the emperor’s sacred flank [Col. 0220C]. At that time “protector of the sacred flank” was the title of the man whose duty was to guard the emperor so that he could not suddenly be wounded in any way by anyone.

Many Christians from different cities, following the Lord’s command—“When they persecute you in one city, flee to another”—had abandoned their own homes and withdrawn to the district of Auxerre, because at that time most of it was deeply covered by the density of its forests.

This did not escape Alexander, the protector of the sacred flank. When he reached the place called Totiacum, he found Priscus, a most Christian man of great nobility and outstanding among many companies gathered there. Priscus had arrived with many others from the city of Besançon.

Alexander burst into their ranks at a furious pace and said:

“What sedition has compelled you to gather here in a crowd, or what religion do you follow?”

The most holy crowd replied:

“It was not sedition but the most reverend religion that brought us together in this place. We have assembled to offer Christ the libations of our prayers, for by pouring out His blood He redeemed and reunited us in our dispersion.”

Seeing that they were unconquerable athletes in the faith of Christ, Alexander ordered them all to be killed by the sword.

In the same way, the most cruel emperor sent to the heavenly kingdom the holy martyrs of God Benignus the priest, Andochius, and Thyrsus, whom Saint Polycarp, disciple of the blessed apostle and evangelist John, had sent from the city of Ephesus into Gaul, after subjecting them to numerous tortures [Col. 0221A].

He likewise ordered Saint Symphorianus, together with many others whom they had already won for Christ, to be killed after they had endured various torments.

With this persecution raging everywhere, very few men could be found who admitted that they were Christians.

After some time had passed, it was secretly reported by the most faithful Christians to the ears of Sixtus, pope of the city of Rome. They asked him to send such a man as could illuminate by his words the lamp of faith, which had already been extinguished, and, with divine assistance, restrain the unbelief of the barbarians.

Then the aforesaid pope assigned the aforementioned man of God, Peregrinus the presbyter, and Corcodomus the archdeacon to the Levitical order; he appointed Jovianus as subdeacon, and Jovinianus as lector. Since Jovinianus was eloquent in every respect and exceptionally learned in the divine Scriptures, he placed him among them as their companion. For the most blessed Sixtus, pope of the city of Rome, led these worshipers of the Most High God with complete confidence as far as the Port of Marinus, and earnestly instructed them to preach the word of the Lord confidently until death.

The athletes of the Lord, making for Massilia by sea, were brought as far as Lugdunum; they were entirely unable to remain concealed. From there, reaching Autricum, they began publicly to preach the glory of Christ. At that time a great crowd of nobles had gathered to observe the vain cults of the gods. When the pagans questioned them, they declared that they were Christians and that they had come there for the preaching of the word of the Lord.

Then, when the most blessed priests were shining through their preaching and because of the continual miracles that divine power performed through them, all the leading men of that place who were there flocked to the grace of Christianity. Soon the holy bishop Peregrinus, imparting a new doctrine to the people, built a church on a small site and consecrated it to the name of Christ.

When all worship of the gods had been extinguished there, he left behind the brothers whom he had brought with him from the city, so that he might complete the ministry of preaching that he had begun. He then went to Interranum, where at that time a great multitude of pagans was gathering with the utmost zeal to celebrate the festivals of Jupiter.

[Col. 0221D] What he did there, and what contests he endured for the name of Christ, is made entirely clear by the account of his passion. At that place, while persecution was already raging with excessive violence, this most blessed bishop left the city, but completed his martyrdom by the cutting off of his head, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, during the consulships of the emperors Gallienus and Valerian, and of Aemilianus and Bassus.

## CHAPTER II — On Saint Marcellianus

Marcellianus, a Gaul by nationality, occupied the see for 33 years. Faithfully laboring in the ministry of preaching, he happily departed to Christ on the third day before the Ides of May, and was buried on Mount Autricum. He lived during the reigns of the emperors Alexander and Maximus, in the consulship of Aurelianus and Marcellinus, while Felix and Eutychianus were presiding over the Roman Church.

## CHAPTER III — On Saint Valerius

Valerius occupied the see for 17 years. He lived during the reigns of Diocletian and Maximian, in the consulship of Carus and Carinus, while Gaius, Marcellinus, and Marcellus were administering the dignity of the priesthood in the city of Rome; they too were martyred by those same tyrants. This blessed man, faithfully completing the course of his life, departed to Christ on the second day before the Nones of May, and was buried near Mount Autricum beside his predecessor, Saint Marcellianus the bishop. [lacuna]

## CHAPTER IV — On Saint Valerianus

Valerianus, a Gaul by nationality, occupied the see for 30 years. He was a man of the greatest holiness and simplicity. When this blessed man was summoned by the parents of Saint Amator to attend Amator’s wedding—namely, so that he might sanctify both parties with his blessing—he took up, by God’s will, the little book of the sacraments and, instead of a nuptial blessing, imposed upon them the Levitical office.

Together with the other co-bishops—Severinus of Sens, Solemnis of Chartres, Camillianus of Troyes, Pronicius of Meaux, and Marcellus of Paris—he also ordained Saint Evurtius bishop of Orléans. He lived during the time of Pope Melchiades and Saint Silvester, under the emperor Constantine, in the consulship of Constantius and Volusianus. Full of holiness, he died on the day before the Nones of May and was buried beside his predecessors on Mount Autricum.

## CHAPTER V — On Eladius

[Col. 0222C]

Eladius occupied the see for 23 years. He lived during the reigns of Constantius and Constantine, the sons of Constantine, under the Roman pontiffs Marcus, Julius, and Liberius.

When this most blessed bishop was converting many to Christ by word and example, Saint Amator and Martha, who had by then become his spiritual bride, came to him together and set forth before him the desire of their vows. He asked that he be made a cleric.

Then the bishop, considering and observing that they enjoyed the love of God and wished, for love of him, to exchange their secular clothing, readily complied with both requests: he relieved the man of his hair, and most devoutly joined and united the woman to the company of women living under religious discipline. This man, full of holiness and virtues, as we read in the deeds of that same Saint Amator, sent his body to the earth and his soul to heaven on the eighth day before the Ides of May, and was buried beside his predecessors on Mount Autricum.

## CHAPTER VI — On Saint Amator

Amator, a native of Auxerre, son of Proclidius and Isiciala, occupied the see for 30 years, one month, and five days. He lived during the reigns of the emperors Constantius, Julian the Apostate, and Jovinianus, under the Roman pontiffs Felix, Damasus, Siricius, and Anastasius.

When this most blessed bishop was still a young man and, being of very noble birth, had been compelled by his parents to become betrothed to a girl of equally noble lineage named Martha, the time of their union was already approaching—as we mentioned above—and the blessed Valerianus had been invited to their wedding. By divine prompting, instead of a blessing, he had assigned them to the Levitical office.

Amator then addressed the virgin who had been joined to him in marriage with these words:

“Tell me, I beg you, virgin devoted to an immortal bridegroom: do you think you have understood the blessing of the bishop poured out upon us?”

The virgin replied:

“I have understood it, dearest young man, and I have been cast down by an exceedingly great terror of fear.”

The young man answered her again:

“Do not, I beg you, be afraid, nor attribute this to ignorance; rather, ascribe it to the power of God.”

While they thus alternately encouraged one another with the Lord’s commandments, blessed Amator saw an angel of God holding two crowns in his hands. The angel said to them:

“Receive, young people, the gift granted to you by the Lord’s mercy, and preserve in every respect the purpose of your undefiled minds.”

Hearing these words spoken from the angel’s mouth, the vigilant young people, having obtained the fulfillment of their vows, remained in their virginity. Likewise, the girls who were present in service to their lords, seeing these things, themselves professed the title of virginity.

Later, after he had been tonsured by Bishop Eladius and, following Eladius’s death, had been elected bishop by the entire people, he showed himself so great and excellent in divine matters that he gave sight to the blind, cured the paralyzed, drove demons from possessed bodies, and raised the dead, as the book composed about his life plainly declares.

This most holy prelate also devoted himself to preaching and converted many from the worship of idols to the truth of the faith. Since at that time the number of Christians converting from idols to the Lord was still small, there was as yet only a modest basilica there, at the gate called Balnearis—now called “of the temple”—by ancient authors. Through the preaching of the most blessed Amator, it began to flourish and to propagate Christian branches so greatly that, because of the multitude, the church could in no way contain them within its narrow confines.

At that time a certain very noble citizen of Auxerre, Ruptilius, possessed within the circuit of the city a large and lofty residence, left to him by his father’s testament. When blessed Amator saw that it would be suitable for the church of God, he addressed Ruptilius as follows:

“We know that, by God’s agency, you have been reborn through the waters of the sacred bath, and you must obey in every respect the one who rescued you from the errors of idols and brought you into his truth. You know, most illustrious man, that the house of God is small and insufficient for the Christian people. Since I consider it unjust that you, a servant, should possess a dwelling better than your Lord, consent to us, so that this house of yours may be consecrated as a church to Christ the Lord.”

He received the holy man’s admonition harshly and at first declared that he would in no way consent to him. Later, however, when he was struck by a very severe illness, he surrendered to the holy man what he desired.

Then the servant of God, having obtained the fulfillment of his wish, consecrated that same house to Christ the Lord on the fifth day before the Nones of October and handed it over to the people for worship. This is the basilica frequented by the Christian people in honor of the protomartyr Stephen.

[Col. 0224A] In this same basilica, Germanus, a very noble man endowed with every excellence, who at that time had obtained from the Roman emperors the highest rank of military command in Gaul, was seized—after an angel had shown Amator where to find him—and his hair was cut. Finally, when the Lord had revealed it to him, Amator chose Germanus as his successor.

At last, overcome by fever, Amator ascended the pontifical throne on the day of the Kalends of May and, amid the hands of the attending clerics and the crowds of weeping people, breathed out his spirit at the third hour of the day. Immediately, a choir of saints arrived—wonderful to relate—and carried his spirit to heaven with hymns and praises in the form of a dove. He was buried amid miracles, by the hands of the most blessed Germanus, who was then still a presbyter, beside his predecessors on Mount Autricum. The episcopate remained vacant for 30 days.

## CHAPTER VII — On Saint Germanus

Germanus, a native of Auxerre, son of Rusticus and Germanilla, occupied the see for 25 years and 30 days. He served in the army under Valentinian the Elder and Gratian. He held the dignity of the priesthood under Theodosius, Arcadius, and Honorius, continuing until Valentinian the Younger, son of Constantius and Placidia. During this period Innocent and Zosimus, and then Boniface and Celestine, presided over the Roman Church.

For, as we read in the pontifical records, Eulalius was ordained together with Boniface amid a dispute, on the same day, as bishop of the apostolic see in the city of Rome. When the Augusta Placidia heard this, while she and her son Valentinian Augustus were seated at Ravenna, she reported it to Honorius Augustus, who was seated at Milan. At that time both Augusti issued an order directing that both men should leave the city until they had been examined.

We have prefaced this account in order to establish more precisely the period in which blessed Germanus flourished. He was of the noblest birth and, from the earliest beginnings of childhood, was trained in the liberal studies. So that the fullness of literary accomplishment might flow together in him, after attending the schools of Gaul he added, within the city of Rome, the knowledge of law to the completeness of his education. Among the Romans he attained such distinction, authority, and glory that he even deserved to wear the toga.

While he was shining with a manifold brilliance of praise in that office, he took as his wife Eustachia, noble by birth, wealth, and character. Thus the state sent him to Gaul, where he was to hold the highest rank of military command and the dignity of complete authority.

While he was performing this office, Saint Amator, who at that time governed the Church of Auxerre, went to Autun, moved by a divine revelation, where Julius was prefect and governor of the state. Saint Amator approached him and addressed him as follows:

“I have learned, by the Lord’s making it known to me, the time of my end. Since there is no other person to assume the governance of the holy Church except the illustrious Germanus—as my Lord God has deigned to reveal to me—I ask your Excellency to grant permission for me to tonsure this same Germanus, as I request.”

The prefect replied:

“Although he is necessary and extremely useful to our state, nevertheless, since God has chosen him—as your blessedness testifies—I cannot act against God’s command.”

Having received this permission, the most blessed man returned to his own place.

One day Germanus, surrounded by a throng of his men, wished to enter the church of Saint Stephen. When blessed Amator learned of this, he went out to meet him and addressed them, saying:

“Lay down, dearest sons, the weapons in your hands; cast the arms from your shoulders, and then enter the house of God, for this is a house of prayer, not a station of impudent Mars.”

Hearing this, they promptly obeyed the man of God.

Then Saint Amator, seeing that the illustrious Germanus was carrying no burdensome weapon, ordered the doorkeepers to secure the church doors with their bars. He himself, together with the gathered crowd of clerics and noblemen, laid hands on Germanus and seized him. Calling upon the name of the Lord, he cut off the hair of his head, exhorting and strengthening him with these words:

“You must strive, venerable brother, to preserve undefiled and unstained the honor entrusted to you by the Lord. For know that, when I depart, Almighty God has entrusted you with the pastoral office.”

And so it happened. After only a few days had passed, Saint Amator, called by Christ, breathed out his final breath. Suddenly all the people proclaimed Germanus bishop with one voice.

Unable to resist their desire, he accepted the priesthood on the thirtieth day after Saint Amator’s death—unwillingly, under compulsion, and constrained. But suddenly he was changed in every respect: the service of the world was abandoned, that of heaven was assumed; worldly pomp was trampled underfoot; humility of conduct was raised up; his wife was changed from a spouse into a sister; his property was distributed among the poor; poverty was sought.

O man to whom the highest honors are always owed! Out of love for eternal life, he embraced voluntary poverty, gave everything to Christ, and kept nothing for himself.

It cannot now be recounted with what hostility he inflicted violence upon himself, or what crosses and punishments he imposed upon his own body. For whatever and however much he displayed, mortal speech is insufficient to express it, because everything he did was beyond the human scale.

We shall pass over the miracles by which he became famous, since books composed for the benefit of many are extant concerning them.

He increased the Church over which he presided not only in spiritual but also in temporal resources, and it can easily be understood how meager its possessions had been before him if one examines with what resources he left it enriched and by what means. For in birth he was the noblest of the noble; in fortune, among the wealthy in possessions and estates, he was the wealthiest of the wealthy. He made the Church heir during his lifetime to everything that had come to him by paternal right; and today we know that it consists in very large part of those inheritances.

These estates were very numerous, immense in extent, spacious in boundaries, adjoining one another, most pleasant in their situation, and distinguished by the abundance of their revenues. In one of them—called Epponiacus from ancient times—his venerable father Rusticus, mentioned above, and his mother Germanilla lie decently buried in a church dedicated in the name of blessed John.

This most blessed bishop gave to the basilica of Saint Stephen the protomartyr the noble estate called Varciacus, together with all its equipment and appurtenances. Likewise he gave Vercisum, containing within it a remarkable palace with its appurtenances; Poliacum, or Marciniacum; and also Tociacum, likewise with its appurtenances; as well as the estates Patriniacum and Cutiacum, equally with their appurtenances; and finally many other properties unknown to us today but all known to God.

He also founded a monastery in honor of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, where he established monks, and assigned these estates for their support: the estate called Monticellus, for gathering wine; Fontanetum, for sowing grain; and the estate called Miciglis, for maintaining the nourishment of calves and other livestock. Later Saint Marianus was sent by the brothers of that monastery to tend those animals.

Even today, in that monastery, an oratory consecrated in the name of Saint Germanus is shown. We know without hesitation that it was the cell which bore witness to his afflictions and tortures. I do not know whether to call its opening a little door or a window; it was so exceedingly small in its humility that no one, however small his body, could have crawled through it except while lying prone.

He also built a basilica in honor of the holy martyrs of Agaunum—Mauricius and his companions—and offered these gifts there: Vuarchiacum in the territory of Sens with all its appurtenances; in the territory of Auxerre, Corvallis with its appurtenances; and also mills, likewise with their appurtenances.

In that same oratory he ordained Saint Saturninus, a man of thoroughly tested life and his own disciple, as presbyter, so that under the profession of the priestly title he might serve the memorials of the martyrs there.

He also built a basilica within the walls of the city itself in honor of Saint Alban the martyr, dedicated it in honor of that martyr, and honorably placed there the relics of Alban that he had brought with him from Britain.

How many tombs of venerable martyrs, discovered by that most blessed bishop during his pontificate, shone forth! Who could rightly judge that any should be excluded?

The sacred bodies of that holy multitude whom the savagery of the persecution at Orléans slaughtered together with blessed Priscus at the place called Quotiacum were secretly removed by Christians—who at that time were exceedingly few—and indiscriminately piled into a certain very ancient cistern because of the raging violence.

Their memory, obscured and washed away by the long passage of time, remained hidden from everyone until the time of the most holy Germanus. While he was bishop, God—in whose sight the death of his saints is always precious—determined to assist the people through their intercession and revealed their venerable bodies. Germanus built a church there and established a monastery of monks.

This monastery continued until the time when the Huns devastated almost all of Gaul. Destroyed by their persecution, the same monastery was again reduced to solitude.

Almighty God also revealed, in wondrous ways, the head of the aforementioned most blessed martyr Priscus to that holy bishop. Germanus built a basilica four miles from the city for its burial, consecrated it, and handed it over to the people for worship.

At the same time, an embassy sent from Britain announced to the bishops of Gaul that the Pelagian perversity had widely seized the peoples of that region and that the Catholic faith ought to be aided as quickly as possible. For this reason a numerous synod was assembled, and by the judgment of all, two illustrious lights of religion were sought through the prayers of everyone.

Germanus and Lupus of Troyes, apostolic priests who possessed the earth in their bodies and heaven in their merits, accepted the task with all the more eagerness as its necessity appeared more arduous. These most devoted heroes hastened the undertaking, impelled by the demands of faith.

Thus, under Christ’s guidance, they boarded the Ocean Sea and reached Britain. The blessed bishops filled that island with their preaching and virtues. At last, after the conflict with the Pelagians had been completed, the bishops confirmed the faith both by the word of truth and by signs of miracles.

They also, by divine power, repelled the war that the Saxons and Picts had undertaken against the Britons with united forces. Germanus himself became the leader of the battle and, not by the sound of a trumpet but by the cry of “Alleluia,” raised by the voice of the entire army to the heavens, put the monstrous enemies to flight.

Thus the damnable perversity was suppressed, its authors refuted, and everyone’s minds set in order through the purity of faith. The most blessed priests returned with the same prosperity with which they had come.

Not long afterward, it was again announced in Britain that the Pelagian perversity was spreading once more through a few leaders. Germanus therefore took with him Severus, archbishop of Trier, a man of complete holiness, and again went to Britain to destroy the aforementioned Pelagian heresy.

Thereafter the preaching was turned toward the people for the correction of their deviation. By the judgment of all, the authors of the depravity were seized and handed over to the priests to be taken to the Mediterranean regions. This was done with such salutary effect that the undefiled faith continues to endure in those places to the present day.

When everything had thus been properly settled, the most blessed priests returned home in triumph. Even today very many testify that they learned that those heretics had been sent by the most holy Germanus to Pope Celestine.

Thus this most divine bishop, the Lord Bishop Germanus, was given as an unquenchable light to the world lying in darkness. After his wondrous life in this world, after he had sprinkled Gaul, Britain, and finally Italy itself with doctrine and miracles, he was called by Christ. Strengthened by the saving viaticum, he died at Ravenna, a city of Italy, full of the Holy Spirit.

At that time Valentinian the Younger, son of Constantius, together with his mother Placidia, held the monarchy of the world. Because of their admiration for his holiness and the frequency of his miracles, they received his body there with honor, as the fuller book of his Deeds explains. When the Lord Christ appeared to him, he learned beforehand the day of his death and, although with great difficulty, secured the return of the earthly remains of his body to his own city.

Then everyone vied with one another in contributing his efforts to the preparation of the deceased. Acolius, the royal master of the bedchamber—whose young son Germanus had once cured of the affliction of a most savage demon—prepared the venerable body with a compound of various aromatics.

The Augusta, who had served him while he was alive and now desired from her heart to serve him also in death, arrayed the sacred body in elaborate and highly refined garments, placing it for transport and preservation in a carefully fitted coffin of the purest cypress.

When these preparations had been made, the emperor anxiously saw to it that nothing was lacking for the sacred rites: he arranged the journey, provided the necessary means of transport, and assigned servants and companions to escort the funeral. He lavishly supported it with expenditures and every form of kindness.

The bishops took the greatest care that the offices of religion should not be absent for even an hour from the sacred obsequies. They provided for these offices in the present and, by arrangements sent ahead, ensured that they would not fail as the journey progressed.

Thus the funeral, splendidly equipped, advanced toward Gaul with a great crowd of escorts.

Saturninus was the presbyter and disciple of the most blessed Germanus, whom we mentioned above, distinguished by the holiness of his life. When Germanus had gone to Italy, Saturninus had remained in the city by his command and as his representative.

On the night when the glorious confessor of the Lord happily departed at Ravenna, Saturninus, who was at Auxerre, learned of his sacred passing when an angel announced it. Instructed by a divine revelation, he proclaimed it to the people. Gathering a great multitude with him, he hastened to the Alpine passes, where the people of Gaul received their own patron, prepared to serve his great funeral all the more eagerly as an affection mingled with love compelled them to offer him the greater reverence.

From the day before the Kalends of August, on which the extraordinary confessor was relieved of the burden of the flesh and admitted into the heavenly sanctuaries, the fifty-third day was passing when the sacred treasure of his body was brought back to his own city and received with the solemn service of the people. It was placed within the precinct of the principal church over which he had presided.

There it was honored for ten continuous days with the lavish performance of rites, until everything pertaining to the right of burial had been prepared with the utmost devotion, as befitted an apostolic man, and he was handed over to burial.

When everything had been properly prepared, and when there was no respite from the crowds pouring in, while those who had gathered could scarcely be contained even by the extent of the region, the heavenly treasure was placed in the hidden chamber of the tomb on the day of the Kalends of October. Such was the service of the whole world and such the devotion of the human race that it was clearer than daylight to everyone that he possessed the highest merit in heaven, for whom such honor was provided on earth.

The city remained without a bishop for four years.

## CHAPTER VIII — On Alodius

Alodius occupied the see for 30 years, one month, and 22 days. The merit and dignity of this Alodius can be inferred from the fact that, while blessed Germanus was still alive, he presided as archimandrite over his monastery.

After Germanus himself had been raised to the heavenly kingdoms, Alodius deserved to succeed him in the episcopal office. As imitator and heir of his teacher, he benefited many by word and example.

During his episcopate, Saint Marianus came from the region of Bourges and asked to be associated with the monastery of Saint Germanus, because that monastery, retaining the condition of its ancient blessedness, exuded a most pleasing fragrance. The little book published about the holy man’s life more fully reveals how distinguished he was in memory and how great in holiness.

Saint Alodius, therefore, rich in the support of excellent merits, departed in peace on the fourth day before the Kalends of October and was decently buried in the basilica of blessed Germanus.

After his death the city remained without a bishop for ten years, because of the savagery of the barbarians who were devastating Gaul. He lived during the time of Leo the Great and Hilary, Roman pontiffs, while Leo and Zeno were emperors.

## CHAPTER IX — On Fraternus

Fraternus occupied the see for one day. On the very day that he was ordained bishop by the faithful, he was crowned with martyrdom by the barbarians, on the third day before the Kalends of October. He was buried in the church of the most blessed Germanus. The city remained without a bishop for six days.

## CHAPTER X — On Censurius

Censurius occupied the see for 38 years, 3 months, and 6 days.

It was during his time that Constantius the orator, at the request of Saint Patienus, bishop of Lyon, composed the life of blessed Germanus in a remarkable style and with every diligence, and afterward sent it to that same Bishop Censurius to possess.

The blessed bishop himself, faithfully imitating his predecessors, completed the course of his life and died in the twenty-eighth year of his age, on the fourth day before the Ides of June, full of holiness and rich in every good thing. He was buried in the church of Saint Germanus the bishop.

He lived during the time of the Roman pontiffs Felix, Gelasius, Anastasius, Symmachus, and Hormisdas, while Anastasius and Justin the Elder were emperors. The city remained without a bishop for one year and two months.

## CHAPTER XI — On Ursus

Ursus occupied the see for 6 years and 4 months.

A trustworthy account commonly reports of this most holy man that he lived as a recluse and anchorite near the basilica of Saint Amator, where an oratory dedicated to the memory of his name remains to the present day.

At that time the city happened to be consumed by a sudden fire. When the cry of the people, raised high, reached the man of God, he judged that the danger must be answered and sent there his familiar staff. He himself applied himself intensely and persistently to prayer. When the staff had been placed among the threatening flames and the remains of what had not yet burned, the entire fire was extinguished sooner than words can say.

On this occasion the merit of the holy man was made manifest. After the city’s bishop had died, six days were sufficient for him to be elevated to the episcopate; his cell became a church. He completed the period of his life in 81 years and, precious in character and merits, passed beyond the burden of frailty on the third day before the Kalends of August. He deserved an honorable burial in the basilica of Saint Germanus, beside his predecessors.

He lived during the time of Pope John and Felix. This was the John whom the heretical king Theoderic killed at Ravenna by afflicting him in custody, while Justin was emperor and Lampadius and Orestes were consuls. The city remained without a bishop for one year and six months.

## CHAPTER XII — On Theodosius

Theodosius occupied the see for 8 years and 23 days. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August he reached the final day of his life, having completed 75 years. Because of the merit of his holiness, he received an honorable burial in the church of blessed Germanus.

He lived during the time of Boniface and Mercury, who was also called John, continuing until Agapitus, while Justinian Augustus was emperor and Lampadius was consul.

We also find that this holy man took part in the council of bishops held by order of the most glorious Clovis, great king of the Franks, at the Gallic city of Orléans.

The city remained without a bishop for one year.

## CHAPTER XIII — On Gregory

Gregory occupied the see for 12 years and 6 months. Having completed his term of office, he laid down his human life on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June and received his final reward in the church of blessed Germanus. He completed the whole period of his life in 84 years.

He lived during the time of the Roman pontiffs Silverius and Vigilius, while the aforementioned Justinian Augustus was still emperor. The city remained without a bishop for seven months, while the most glorious king Clovis was still reigning.

## CHAPTER XIV — On Optatus

Optatus occupied the see for 1 year, 8 months, and 5 days.

He built a basilica in honor of Saint Christopher the martyr beside the basilica of Saint Germanus, on its eastern side, with the assistance of his two presbyters, Sanctinus and Memorius.

This most holy bishop, having completed the course of his life, ended his temporal life on the day before the Kalends of September and attained eternal life together with those same holy presbyters. He was buried with them in the same basilica that he had built.

Later, after the passing of many years, by the counsel of noble and wise men, their sacred bodies were transferred to the church of blessed Germanus with such devotion and solemnity that the day of their translation is recorded in all the Martyrologies, especially the oldest: the sixth day before the Nones of May. Their passing or burial, as we stated above, is recorded as having occurred on the day before the Kalends of September. All of them rest together in one and the same sarcophagus.

The city remained without a bishop for one year. He lived during the time of the aforementioned Pope Vigilius, while Justinian Augustus was still emperor and Clovis the Frankish king was reigning.

## CHAPTER XV — On Droctaldus

Bishop Droctaldus died on the sixth day before the Ides of November. We have been unable to find anything else memorable about him that we could insert into the present work.

## CHAPTER XVI — On Eleutherius

Eleutherius occupied the see for 28 years, 8 months, and 9 days.

He lived during the time from Pelagius I to John, while Justin the Younger was emperor. [The author is mistaken here, as in certain other places.]

During his episcopate, King Clovis died, and his sons Childebert and Chlothar succeeded to the kingdom. This holy man, together with his blessed archbishop—namely, Leo, bishop of Sens—attended the Second Council of Orléans at the summons of Lord King Childebert, in order to deliberate concerning the welfare of the Churches of God established in his kingdom and concerning various matters.

He died full of days, remaining in holiness, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, and was joined in burial to his holy predecessors in the basilica of Saint Germanus the bishop. The city remained without a bishop for one year, two months, and ten days.

## CHAPTER XVII — On Romanus

Romanus occupied the see for 3 years and 4 days. Glorious in good works, he is said to have completed his martyrdom by decapitation on the day before the Nones of October. He was buried beside his predecessors in the basilica of Saint Germanus the bishop.

He lived during the time of the aforementioned Pope John, continuing until Benedict, while Justin the Younger was emperor. The city remained without a bishop for six months and six days.

## CHAPTER XVIII — On Aetherius

Aetherius occupied the see for nine years and 6 months. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of August and was buried in the basilica of blessed Germanus.

He lived during the time of Pope Benedict, while Tiberius Constantine was emperor. The city remained without a bishop for four days.

## CHAPTER XIX — On Aunarius
Aunarius, by birth an Orléanais, son of Pastor and Ragnoara, held office for 43 years, 10 months, and 20 days. During the reign of Maurice, while this most blessed bishop was still a young man residing in the palace of King Gontran [Col. 0231C]—for he was of very noble birth—he was moved by the grace of the Holy Spirit to abandon the earthly kingdom, so that he might remain in the heavenly kingdom with the eternal King. Then, without his parents’ knowledge, he went to the city of Tours, accompanied by two boys, and there, led to the tomb of Saint Martin by the love of God, he cut off his hair. From there he sought Saint Syagrius, bishop of Autun, who was then regarded as pre-eminent in the affairs of God. Syagrius received him with the greatest affection and instructed him in such learning and discipline as befitted an apostolic man.

Thus, with divine grace favouring him and his merits increasing, he was filled with the Holy Spirit and appointed bishop of the Church of Auxerre. On that very day, the feast of the most blessed Germanus, on the day before the Kalends of August [Col. 0231D], he received the office of the episcopate in the same basilica, and deservedly flourished in holiness. He had a full brother named Austrenus, bishop of Orléans, and also a nephew through his sister Agia, Lupus, a most holy man, archbishop of Sens, resplendent with miracles.

This holy man Aunarius, once he had become bishop, began to flourish in virtues and shine with miracles. What mortal tongue could recount his teaching, his love for the citizens, his diligence toward the clergy, how faithful a steward he was to the poor, or how great was his care for holy things? His face displayed an angelic vision; in his speech there was learned exposition; in his administration, the most abundant grace of humanity. He refreshed everyone with honey-sweet words, while seasoning the hearts of the faithful with the salt of divine preaching [Col. 0232A]. The people burned with remarkable eagerness for the worship of God, who worked miracles through him and had enriched and glorified him with such great and extraordinary virtues.

A booklet composed about his life makes known more fully to those who wish to learn by what miracles he became renowned and what glory he possessed in Christ. For we read in the ancient canons that this most blessed bishop attended the synod of Mâcon, held in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of our lord, the most glorious King Gontran. Present at that council were the venerable archbishops Priscus of Lyon, Evantius of Vienne, Praetextatus of Rouen, Bertechrannus of Bordeaux, Artemius of Sens, Sulpitius of Bourges, and Syagrius of Autun, together with many others. At this synod they treated, as befitted such great and distinguished men, many matters appropriate to the welfare of holy Mother Church, touching upon the principal points in twenty chapters [Col. 0232B].

Likewise, we find that the same holy man attended another synod held in the same city at the summons of the same prince and by the same venerable bishops. There too they treated all that was honourable and most useful to the holy Church of God, dividing the principal matters into eighteen chapters.

There also survive letters of Pope Pelagius to this same most blessed bishop. One, darkened by excessive antiquity, we were unable fully to extract from the authoritative books; the other we have judged worthy of inserting into this work.

### Copy of the Letter of Pope Pelagius of the City of Rome to Aunarius, Bishop of Auxerre

[Col. 0232C]

“To his most beloved brother Aunarius, Pelagius.

The more you make yourselves pleasing to God through your reverence for the Apostolic See, the more readily your confidence in charity is received by Him whose see it is. Nor do we confess one single Church of God in any other way than by being built together upon the rock on which the Catholic faith has been founded. Therefore the desire of your affection has obtained its fulfilment—promptly and easily—for the shrines of those are being sought from whom the proclamation of truth first took its beginning.

As for your indication that new churches abound in your regions, we receive this gladly. Yet if you diligently seek to embrace the teaching of the prophetic voice, seek his face always [Col. 0232D]. For the more fully the truth of the Incarnation of our Lord is disclosed to human understanding, the more it is honoured and worshipped.

Just as you desire to be commended to God by our prayers, so also, amid the needs and anxieties with which we are incessantly burdened, offer us the continual comfort of your intercession by praying and acting with whatever strength you possess. Thus, just as you are in harmony with the preaching of the Apostolic See, may your intercession rejoice in its peace and tranquillity.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

Given on the day before the Kalends of November, in the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, Emperor Augustus, in the third year, in the fifth indiction.”

Moreover, this same most blessed bishop established many regulations in the Church of Auxerre, as is found in the ancient canons. To ensure that they were observed with particular vigour, he strengthened them greatly by the counsel and authority of the most Christian King Gontran. For the protection of the flock entrusted to him by the Lord, he ordered that the following institution be observed both in the city of Auxerre and throughout the parishes of its district.

On the first day of the Kalends of January, the city, together with the clergy and people, shall hold litanies.

On the second day, at Epponiacus and Vendosa.

On the third day, at Gaugiacus and Nautriacus.

On the fourth day, at Corevicus, with the clergy and people.

On the fifth day, at Bacerna and Accolacus.

On the sixth day, at Matriacus, with its dependencies.

On the seventh day, at Curcedomus, with its dependencies.

On the eighth day, at Drogia, with its dependencies [Col. 0233B].

On the ninth day, at Varciacus, with its dependencies.

On the tenth day, at Columbariacus, with its dependencies.

On the eleventh day, at Campus Lametii, with its dependencies.

On the twelfth day, at Bargiacus, with its dependencies.

On the thirteenth day, at Domiciacus, with its dependencies.

On the fourteenth day, at Soliacus, with its dependencies.

On the fifteenth day, at Massua, with its dependencies.

On the sixteenth day, at Condida with Draptiacum.

On the seventeenth day, at Eliniacus, with its dependencies.

On the eighteenth day, at Novus Vicus, with its dependencies.

On the nineteenth day, at Brioderus, with its dependencies.

On the twentieth day, at Giemus, with its dependencies.

On the twenty-first day, at Blanoilus, with its dependencies.

On the twenty-second day, at Cassiniacus and Nantiniacus, with the cella of Salvius and Maurus [Col. 0233C].

On the twenty-third day, at Laoderus, with its dependencies.

On the twenty-fourth day, at Vitriacus and Arcucius.

On the twenty-fifth day, at Balgiacus, with its dependencies.

On the twenty-sixth day, at Interranis, with its dependencies.

On the twenty-seventh day, at Tauriacus, with its dependencies.

On the twenty-eighth day, at Liccadiacus, with its dependencies.

On the twenty-ninth day, at Pulverenus, with its dependencies.

On the thirtieth day, at Odona, with its dependencies.

He also established that the same litanies should be celebrated at the beginnings of the twelve months as follows:

On the Kalends of January, at the basilica of our lord Germanus; on the Kalends of February, at the basilica of our lord Amator; on the Kalends of March, at the monastery of our lord Marianus; on the Kalends of April, at the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle [Col. 0233D]; on the Kalends of May, at the basilica of our lord Valerianus and the monastery of Vulfinus; on the Kalends of June, at the basilica of our lord Martin; on the Kalends of July, at the basilica of our lord Julian; on the Kalends of August, at the monastery of Decimiacum, at Saint Cyricus; on the Kalends of September, at the monastery of Fontanetum; on the Kalends of October, at the monastery of Coacum, at the Saints; on the Kalends of November, at the monastery of Saffiacum; on the Kalends of December, at the monastery of Manuacum.

On the remaining days of the months, as above. He likewise established that on every Sunday vigils should be held in this manner by all the archpriests or abbots in their own places.

[Col. 0234A]

From Holy Easter until the Kalends of October, from the first evening until daybreak; from the Kalends of October until the Nativity of the Lord, from the cockcrow; and from the Nativity of the Lord until Easter, from midnight. He also established by whom vigils should be celebrated in the basilica of Saint Stephen in the city, together with the abbots.

On Sunday night: the basilica of our lord Germanus and the monastery of Decimiacum.

On Monday: the basilica of our lord Amator and the monastery of Fontanetum.

On Tuesday: the monastery which our lord Germanus built, where Saint Marianus rests, together with Sessiacus.

On Wednesday: the basilica of Saint Peter and the monastery of [Col. 0234B] Manuacum.

On Thursday: the basilica of our lord Martin and the monastery of Vulfinus.

On Friday: the basilica of our lord Valerianus and the monastery called Varrenas.

Finally, he convened a venerable synod in the city of Auxerre. There, treating many matters concerning the salvation of the people entrusted to him, he touched upon whatever was necessary and very useful in forty-four chapters. These are the names of those who confirmed and subscribed to the same chapters, since we did not think it necessary to insert the chapters themselves:

Aunarius, bishop in the name of God, confirmed and subscribed this constitution. Winebaudus, abbot, subscribed. Desideratus, abbot. Frannulfus, abbot. Gregorius [Col. 0234C], abbot. Amandus, abbot. Caesarius, abbot. Baudoueus, abbot. Tegridus, abbot. Audoueus, priest. Ananias, priest. Many others who were present also subscribed.

That this holy bishop was diligent in every useful matter is also demonstrated by a copy of a letter he sent to Stephen, an African priest, asking him to describe the life of Saint Germanus in verse and that of Saint Amator in noble prose. It ran as follows:

“To my dearest and most beloved brother Stephen, priest, joined to me by the inward bond of charity: Aunarius, bishop by the grace of God, eternal salvation in the Lord.

The prudence of your teaching, already proved to us by many experiences, has compelled us to place upon your shoulders a certain burdensome little pack, but one that will be not a burden to you but an honour, and that will not press downward with an unjust weight but rather lift you upward to heaven [Col. 0234D].

You know, dearest brother, both the diversity of human minds and the way in which not only the empty multitude but also the whole nobility is divided among opposing pursuits. Some take pleasure in a prose style, while others confess that they delight in metre, rhythm, and the songs of verse. Therefore, so that I might meet everyone’s wishes and no one be deprived of his desire, it pleased me to describe some lives of the most blessed confessors in free verse, while arranging others under the constraint of metrical law.

For this reason I beseech the friendship of your affection, united with mine, that you not cease to transform the life of the most blessed Bishop Germanus into the form of verse, but describe that of Saint Amator in prose. Thus, becoming followers of apostolic preaching, we may become all things to all people and owe nothing to anyone except that we love one another.

May divine mercy preserve your undivided charity toward me, venerable brother.”

### Reply of the Aforementioned Priest

“To the most blessed lord, adorned with apostolic insignia, the spiritual father AUNARIUS, bishop: Stephen, servant of all Christ’s servants.

Having read the letter of your apostleship, I have recognised with perfect clarity how the ardour of your holy desire displays itself with the greatest eagerness. Your intention, therefore, is to describe the deeds of the renowned men Germanus and Amator, noble in their flourishing lives; but direct your intention along the path of your most graceful skill toward those who can behold the lights of their virtues with equal inspiration [Col. 0235B].

But I, whose sluggish talent grows numb under a double rigidity, and whose stammering tongue, amid the rancid passages of my throat, obstructed by the squalid harshness of thirst, does not speak but rather hisses—how shall I be able to set forth in polished speech the divinely inspired gifts of these most holy men, when I cannot even explain the private affairs heaped up by human circumstance? Whoever assumes a burden beyond the capacity of his strength, if I am not mistaken, exposes himself to ridiculous, inexplicable disgrace and mockery.

Will not the followers of wild beasts, if less deceptive skill has not shaped them, be ruined by bold recklessness [Col. 0235C]? Never has a recruit carried the trophies of victory on a painted shield, unless the trained hand of a veteran model had equipped him. Nor has a bird safely cut through the open path granted to the air if a winged mother had not gone before it as guide. Surely anyone who, trusting in his own presumption, places an untrained hand upon the rudder of a ship will lie broken by the striking of the waves. So each person is cut apart on the hook of inexperience in a different way if he is not assisted by the favour of teachers.

Therefore, most blessed man, I beg you to place upon me that summit of your high office which does not doubt that I can complete it with ease—provided that, in this work too, you bear patiently whatever rustic chatter may arrange inelegantly or awkwardly. Shall I begin, and do what paternal authority commands and requires?

Farewell for a long time, lord pope.”

This angelic and blessed man Aunarius, although of the noblest birth, offered great gifts from his estates to Almighty God, thereby making the holy Church his heir.

Accordingly, he gave to the basilica of Saint Stephen fields and estates that had come to him by hereditary right from his father: Brioderus with Venolius and its other dependencies; also Noluetum and Gaionnum; likewise Oscellum with their dependencies; and finally, in the district of Orléans or Blois, Meldunum and Brigium with their dependencies, as well as Rocca, Manuisum, and Villare with their dependencies, and the estate of Bove with its dependencies.

Similarly, he gave to the basilica of our lord Germanus—where he had decided that his body should be buried—a certain most noble estate in the district of Wastanum, called Corbilias, with all its dependencies; in the district of Avala, Decimiacum with Vidiliacum and Calminiacum and their other dependencies; and in the district of Sens, Baldiliacum with its dependencies.

Thus, after arranging everything properly, the holy man, full of days and renowned for holiness and the glory of miracles, departed to Christ on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, while heaven rejoiced and earth mourned. He was buried beside his predecessors in the basilica of Saint Germanus, and the episcopate remained vacant for seven days.

### CHAPTER XX — Concerning Desiderius

Desiderius, an Aquitanian by birth, from his mother Necteria, held office for 18 years and 25 days. He was a man of the noblest birth and the gentlest character, a lover of the clergy and of all holy religion [Col. 0236B].

He lived during the time of the glorious King Chlothar, under the Roman pontiffs Gregory, Sabinianus, Boniface, and again Boniface, while Phocas and Heraclius were emperors. His secular dignity was so great that no one of his time, however powerful, could be regarded as his equal. He was related to Queen Brunhild and to her sons, the kings of the Franks and Burgundians. Through their princely generosity he acquired an immense extent of estates.

His mother, the aforementioned Necteria, lies buried in the monastery of Saint Amantius, situated in the district of Cahors. Later, in memory of his mother and in honour of the relics of his holy predecessors Germanus and Amator, which he had brought there, he adorned that monastery with worthy gifts and a very great endowment of lands, as the following account will make clear.

He also requested the episcopal pallium from blessed Gregory, who sent him the following letter in response:

“Gregory to Desiderius, bishop of Auxerre.

We have learned through John, the regional official, of the desire of your fraternity. We are indeed ready to fulfil it willingly, provided that we are carefully informed about the matters he reported. He says that he learned from your affection that certain privileges were once granted to your church by the Apostolic See and that its priests formerly possessed the use of the pallium. Since you earnestly request that this be restored, we have had the matter sought in the archive of our church, but have found nothing [Col. 0236D].

Nevertheless, the more earnestly you desire to obtain this, the more we suppose that you are diligent in searching for the documents of your church. We admonish you to devote vigilant care to the search, and if any writings can be found there that might inform us, see to it that they are sent here. For although we do not grant new privileges, we most willingly restore ancient ones.”

Thus this holy bishop became so rich in estates that no principal church in either central Burgundy or Aquitaine can be found that he did not increase with the finest possessions.

He greatly enlarged the basilica of blessed Stephen, in which he presided, with wonderful splendour. He attached to it a great vaulted structure on the eastern side and decorated it most magnificently with gold and mosaic, in the likeness of the one which Bishop Syagrius of Autun is known to have built [Col. 0237A]. He also moved the ancient altar there and solemnly dedicated it on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May.

There he offered the following gifts:

A gilded anactean serving dish, weighing 50 pounds, bearing seven human figures with a bull and Greek letters.

He also gave another serving dish, likewise an engraved anactean vessel, weighing 40½ pounds. In its centre it has a wheel with a *stephadion*, and around it people and wild animals.

A third anactean serving dish, weighing 35 pounds; on its upper surface it bears a scene of salt with a tree and serpents.

A fourth anactean serving dish, weighing 30 pounds; it bears an Ethiopian and other human figures.

A gilded bacconica vessel, weighing 12 pounds and 2 ounces; it bears a fisherman with a trident and a centaur with a maritime design.

Another anactean bacconica vessel, ringed and blackened, weighing 14 pounds and 9 ounces.

Another bacconica vessel, likewise anactean, weighing 13 pounds; it bears figures of players.

Another anactean bacconica vessel, weighing 10 pounds; it bears a horned man and a tree, together with two little human figures holding infants in their hands.

Four anactean cups, weighing 11 pounds and 2 ounces; they bear little human figures and wild animals, one of them gilded.

He gave anactean dishes, one of them blackened, weighing 4 pounds; it bears a bear holding a horse.

Another anactean dish, weighing 3 pounds; it bears a lion holding a bull.

Another, weighing 2 pounds and 9 ounces; it bears a lion holding a goat.

Another anactean dish, likewise, weighing 2 pounds; it bears a horned he-goat.

Another, weighing 1 pound and 7 ounces; it bears a grazing deer.

Another, weighing 1 pound and 9 ounces; it bears a leopard holding a goat.

He also gave four anactean salt-cellars, weighing 4 pounds.

He gave six bowls, weighing 16 pounds.

One medium anactean bowl, weighing 3 pounds; on its base it has four small seals, and around them engraved ornamental motifs with decorated grilles and capitals, weighing 6½ pounds.

He also gave two anactean vessels, weighing 4 pounds and 3 ounces.

Three anactean vessels, weighing 5 pounds.

He also gave nine spoons, weighing 2½ pounds.

One spoon, weighing 1 pound and 10 ounces; in the middle it has a blackened little wheel and around it a band.

He also gave one *anafus*, weighing 2 pounds; it has gilded lion and bull figures.

One aforesaid trident; it has a lion’s head and weighs 3 pounds.

He also gave an anactean pitcher weighing 4½ pounds, and an *agemanile* weighing 3½ pounds.

Two matching gilded vessels, weighing 5 pounds; around them he placed figures and little animals.

A plain serving dish, weighing 8½ pounds; it has a wheel in the centre, and within the wheel a monogram.

Another serving dish, weighing 8 pounds; it has a cross in the centre with two human figures.

An anactean bacconica vessel weighing 10 pounds; it bears little human figures with two winged little animals.

Another anactean bacconica vessel, weighing 8½ pounds; in the centre it has a mounted man, and at his feet a viper.

Another ringed anactean bacconica vessel, weighing 7½ pounds; it bears three large human figures, with little human figures and wild animals around them.

He also gave gilded anactean bowls weighing 18 pounds; they bear little human figures with small fish.

A medium gilded anactean bowl weighing 8 pounds; it bears human figures and sea creatures in the centre.

Five matching lily-decorated bowls, weighing 9½ pounds.

A medium anactean bowl weighing 3 pounds; it bears a bearded human head in the centre.

A plain medium bowl weighing 12 pounds and 3 ounces; it bears a cock in the centre.

An anactean, column-decorated bowl weighing 3 pounds; it bears human figures and wild animals around it.

An anactean dish weighing 2 pounds; it bears a little human figure and a small field with a tree in the centre.

An anactean dish weighing 2 pounds; it bears two little human figures with spears in the centre.

A small dish weighing 1 pound; it has a little wheel in the centre, blackened around the edge.

An anactean salt-cellar weighing 1 pound; it bears a human figure with a dog in the centre.

An anactean basin weighing 9 pounds; it bears a man and a woman in the centre, with a crocodile at their feet.

A small salt-cellar with a little cross, weighing 9 ounces.

An anactean footed vessel weighing 1½ pounds.

Twelve spoons weighing 3 pounds and 2 ounces.

Twelve spoons weighing 2 pounds and 9 ounces.

Twelve spoons weighing 3 pounds; they have inscribed handles.

Three column-decorated anactean vessels; each weighs 1 pound.

One vessel weighing 1 pound and 1 ounce.

A grille weighing 1 pound and 1 ounce.

An anactean pitcher weighing 3 pounds; it has a blackened handle and a human head in the centre.

Two *agmanilia* weighing 2 pounds and 10 ounces; in the centre they have a lily-shaped wheel and, at the end, a human head.

A gilded *recentarium* weighing 2½ pounds; on the outside it has incised designs.

Another *recentarium*, weighing 1 pound and 9 ounces; it has a little band and wild animals in the centre.

A *schinon*, weighing 1 pound; it has a blackened handle.

A strainer weighing 2 ounces.

The total is 420 pounds and 7 ounces.

The following document likewise reveals how this holy bishop established Christ and the Church entrusted to him by God as heirs of his possessions [Col. 0238D].

He gave to the basilica of Saint Stephen the estate of Magniacum, situated in the district of Auxerre, which he exchanged with Queen Brunhild, together with its houses, outbuildings, and everything belonging to it.

He also gave the estate of Matriacum, where he built a church in honour of Saint Memmius, with its small estate and other dependencies, together with slaves, vineyards, woods, pastures, and all its rights and boundaries. He solemnly assigned to the same basilica herds of oxen, horses, sheep, cattle, and pigs.

Likewise, the estate of Ganniacum, situated in the district of Tonnerre, with its buildings, slaves, and all its dependencies.

He also gave houses and plots situated within the walls of the city of Chalon, which he had exchanged with Bishop Wadelinus, likewise together with the vineyards situated in the hills of the same district, in the estate of Miliacum, with the vine-dressers and remaining slaves, woods, lands, and all their dependencies [Col. 0239A].

He gave the estate of Puniacum, situated in the district of Avala, near the fortress of Censurium, which he had exchanged with the illustrious man Maccus, together with all its buildings, slaves, vineyards, woods, and other dependencies.

He also gave the estate of Genusiacum or Talnisiacum, together with the *nucleatorium*, situated in the territory of Sens, with their buildings, slaves, lands, woods, and all their dependencies.

He gave houses and plots situated within the walls of the city of Sens, together with olive trees planted in the suburb.

Likewise, in the district of Saintes, he gave the estate of Siviriacum, which he had exchanged with Queen Brunhild, together with its buildings, slaves, and all its dependencies.

He also gave the estate of Flacciana [Col. 0239B], situated in the district of Fréjus, which Lord King Theoderic had granted to him and confirmed by his decree, together with its buildings, slaves, olive groves, and all property belonging to it by right.

Likewise, in the territory of Saintes, he gave the most noble estates which he had exchanged with the apostolic man Mummo, bishop of the Church of Cahors, and with its clergy: namely, Melredantum and Lopiacum, Noiogalum and Vriliacum, with all their equipment and dependencies.

In the district of Avala, he gave the small estate called Piciacus, with everything belonging to it by right.

Likewise, in the district of Autun, he gave the estate of Dementiriacum, with its colonica, *tilio*, and other dependencies.

He also gave to the aforementioned mother church the estate of Palliacum, situated in the district of Avala, with all its equipment and dependencies [Col. 0239C].

In the district of Sens, he gave Patriciacum, which he had exchanged with Bishop Aetius, likewise together with its buildings, slaves, and other dependencies.

He also gave the estate situated on the river Chora, called Campania, and its dependent farms, Riviacum and Crarium, together with Novavilla, situated partly in the district of Avala and partly in that of Auxerre, with their buildings, slaves, lands, and all their dependencies.

During this bishop’s tenure, the aforementioned Queen Brunhild, through the hands of this bishop, offered to God and Saint Stephen a chalice of wonderful beauty made of onyx stone and decorated with the purest gold.

Moreover, to the basilica of our lord Germanus, where he had decided that his body should be buried [Col. 0239D], he offered the following gifts:

A silver serving dish bearing the written name *Thorsomodus*. It weighs 37 pounds and bears a scene of Aeneas with Greek books.

Another plain serving dish weighing 30 pounds.

An anactean bacconica vessel weighing 15 pounds. It has a lion and a bear in the centre, and little human figures and wild animals around it.

Another bacconica vessel weighing 9½ pounds; it bears a man and a woman, with little animals at their feet.

An anactean dish weighing 5 pounds and 6 ounces; it bears a mounted man holding a serpent in his hand.

An anactean dish weighing 3 pounds; it has a blackened little wheel with a wild animal in the centre.

Two matching bowls, lily-decorated on the inside, weighing 8 pounds and 2 ounces.

An anactean pitcher weighing 4 pounds; it has a blackened handle and a lion’s head in the centre.

Two *agmanilia* weighing 3 pounds and 9 ounces; in the centre they bear Neptune with his trident.

On the day of his burial, this distinguished bishop ordered that 100 solidi of the purest gold be carried with his body to the basilica of our lord Germanus, to adorn his burial. The total is 119 pounds and 5 ounces.

Moreover, this holy man transferred to the same basilica of our lord Germanus estates belonging to him by right: namely, Bringa in the district of Sens, with its buildings, slaves, vineyards, lands, and all its dependencies.

Also Roboretum in the same district, with its dependencies.

The estate of Sessiacum, situated in the territory of Auxerre, which, at his suggestion, Queen Ingundis assigned to the basilica of our lord Germanus and confirmed by her decree for it to possess [Col. 0240B]. The holy bishop himself held it in usufruct during his lifetime at the queen’s command, and after his death ordered that the aforementioned basilica of our lord Germanus should receive it without any further conveyance or judicial process.

He also assigned to the same basilica, for the hospice of the poor, the small estate of Feriolae, situated in the district of Auxerre on the little river Lupa, with buildings, meadows, woods, a herd of cattle, and a herd of pigs.

In the district of Saintes, he gave the estates of Saturiacum and Ursio, with their buildings, slaves, woods, and all their equipment, as well as plots with houses built upon them, both at Metulla and in the city of Sens, which he had purchased from the matron Vigiligunda for a price paid.

He also gave, through the hands of Palladius, then a priest and abbot of the basilica of our lord [Col. 0240C] Germanus, later his successor in the episcopate, to the same basilica Orgiacum and Marciacum, with everything belonging to them in full, together with Nantilla and Pociacum, with all their buildings, slaves, vineyards, newly planted trees, and every dependency.

For Lord King Chlothar and his most noble wife, Queen Ingundis, also adorned the same basilica with great and excellent gifts through the hands of the same Lord Bishop Desiderius. The *freda* placed over the most sacred body, moreover, the king magnificently decorated with gold and silver, while the queen devoutly honoured it with a chalice and paten adorned with the purest gold and most precious gems.

[Col. 0240D]

To the basilica of our lord Amator he gave the estate called Talonensis, situated in the district of Auxerre, with its buildings, slaves, lands, livestock, herds of mares and pigs, and all its dependencies.

To the basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, situated in the suburb of the city of Auxerre, he gave the small estate called Brittoilus, situated in the district of Auxerre, with its buildings, slaves, woods, lands, herds of pigs and mares, and all its dependencies.

To the monastery which Bishop Germanus built on the bank of the river Yonne, where the lord Marianus, of blessed memory, rests bodily as a confessor, he gave Villare, called Capelinarius, situated in the district of Auxerre, in full, with its livestock and herds of pigs [Col. 0241A].

To the basilica of our lord Julian the martyr, where Niginaldus Alba presided, he gave the estate in the district of Watinum called Mansiones Teudbaldi, belonging to his estate of Auroli, with buildings, slaves, meadows, livestock, herds of pigs, and its other dependencies.

To the Monastery of the Girls, built in honour of our lord Martin beyond the river Yonne, he gave the small estate called Necariola, which he had purchased from Eperia, a religious woman, for a price paid, with its buildings, slaves, lands, meadows, woods, and other dependencies.

Regarding the basilica of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, he placed the following in his testament:

“To the basilica of the holy lords and martyrs Nazarius, Gervasius, Protasius, and the boy Celsus, which our deacon Marinus appears to be building for our consolation, and where we have also deposited the relics of those same martyrs, we give the small estate called Briennicum, beside the estate of Nanturiacum, which we exchanged with the lord Evodius, formerly bishop, of blessed memory.

Likewise, we give Accolatum, situated above the river Chora, as they are possessed by us at the present time. We decree that they are donated to the aforementioned basilica for the remedy of our soul, to be possessed perpetually by that basilica and by those serving there.”

To each of the monasteries and to the basilicas of Saint Columba and Saint Leo, which are built near the city of Sens, he gave the small estate called Viscla, situated in the same district, with its buildings, lands, woods, and all its dependencies, on the condition that the administrators of these basilicas [Col. 0241C] divide the same estate equally among themselves.

To the basilica of our lord Ursicinus of Bicicrinsensis, once a disciple of blessed Germanus, he gave the small estate from the estate of Maternus Bonus, situated in the territory of Auxerre, with its buildings, slaves, and lands in full.

He also gave to the basilica of Saint Amantius, built in the district of Cahors for the support of the monks serving God there, where his mother, as we have already mentioned, rests bodily, the estates whose names are as follows: Marciriacum and another Marciriacum with their dependencies, Lintiniacum, Conclusa, Ultrarida, Siniriacum, Augiriacum, Teponniacum, Vetraria, Quintiacum, and Cremona. These are situated in the district of Cahors, with their buildings, slaves, and all their dependencies [Col. 0241D].

He also distributed the estate of Crispiniacum, situated in the same district, on the condition that two parts should go to the basilica of Saint Amantius, while the third should belong to the basilica called “at the Saints of Brittones,” where the bishops rest bodily.

He also gave the estate called Cassinatus, situated in the same territory of Cahors, with all its dependencies.

Likewise, a portion of Atro Macrinio and Reclinis, situated in the territory of Albi, with its buildings, vineyards, slaves, and other dependencies.

In the district of Rodez, he gave the valley of Catemaria, Versella, Grossumniacum, Siacum, and Atratum, with their buildings, slaves, and all their dependencies.

He also gave Vitaliacum, situated in the district of Cahors, in full.

[Col. 0242A]

Moreover, he gave to the basilica of Saint Saturninus the martyr, situated in the suburb of the city of Toulouse, the estate called Silviniacus, situated in the same district, in full and with all its dependencies.

Likewise, he gave the estate of Melgiacum, situated in the same territory, with its buildings, slaves, lands, and other dependencies.

He also gave to the senior church of Cahors the estate held by Betto, which he himself had received through royal generosity, situated in the territory of Bordeaux, with its buildings, slaves, and all its dependencies.

He possessed many other things as well, as the page of his testament makes clear, and he bestowed them upon his nephews and other relatives. He also permitted no fewer than two thousand slaves to become free, allowing them to retain as their own the possessions they appeared to hold at that time [Col. 0242B].

Truly fortunate, having happily completed the allotted time of his life, he departed to Christ, full of virtues, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, and was buried beside Saint Aunarius in the basilica of blessed Germanus.

### CHAPTER XXI — Concerning Palladius
Palladius held the see for 26 years and 3 months. He lived during the reign of King Dagobert, while Deusdedit, Boniface, Honorius, Severinus, John, and Theodore were presiding over the Church at Rome. He was a vigorous man and, during the time of his predecessor Desiderius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus. After Desiderius’s death, because he was a wise, generous, and compassionate man, he was chosen by the entire people for the episcopate. Once he had received the priesthood, he devoted himself wholly to ecclesiastical disciplines. For he enriched the basilica of Saint Stephen with many and very costly gifts: he made two crosses of the purest gold and presented them, and also many silver anactea vessels, which remained preserved in the treasuries of that same church down to our own time. We ourselves saw these marked with his name.

He also built the monastery of the martyr Saint Julian, where he constructed another basilica and dedicated it in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God. He established this monastery as one for virgins; before his time it had been built within the city walls on a small site and had certainly belonged to men. He greatly enlarged that monastery with substantial buildings and surrounded it on every side with a wall. Since all the churches of Auxerre were subject to his authority, he richly endowed it from the estates of both Saint Stephen and Saint Germanus.

He also built a basilica near the city walls in honor of Saint Eusebius, bishop and martyr of Vercelli. He adorned and dedicated its eastern apse with mosaic and gold, and enlarged it with various gifts. He likewise established it as a monastery for monks and surrounded it on every side with a wall. He also built a basilica of Saint Germanus in the district of Auxerre, at a place called Vercisus, and adorned it with a noble apse of mosaic and gold.

He further decreed that every year, on the feast of Saint Germanus, celebrated on the Kalends of October, after the solemn celebration of the Masses had been completed, the canons of the basilica of Saint Stephen should receive one hundred solidi from the hand of the bishop, out of love and reverence for so great a prelate, so that during the succeeding years they might take greater pleasure in celebrating the joys of that same feast with eager hearts.

He died on the fourth day before the Ides of April and was buried in the basilica of Saint Eusebius, which, as we have said, he himself had built. The episcopal see remained vacant for ten days.

## CHAPTER XXII—On Vigilius

Vigilius held the see for 25 years and five months. He lived during the pontificates of Popes Martin, Eugenius, and Vitalian, while Chlothar the Younger was reigning among the Franks and Burgundians. He was noble by birth and distinguished in holiness.

Among his other marks of virtue, he built a monastery in the suburb of the city of Auxerre. He endowed it with many gifts, as the wording of his testament demonstrates, and dedicated it in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God. Surrounding it with a wall, he established it as a monastery for monks and also ordered that a hospice for the poor be established there.

A truthful account reports that this holy man suffered martyrdom in the Cotia Forest at the command of Waraton, master of the palace, who had succeeded Ebroin in that office. In this respect he imitated that same predecessor, Ebroin, who had formerly ordered Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, to be put to death by the sword.

Saint Vigilius was martyred on the fifth day before the Ides of March. When his sacred body was being carried back to his own city, it happened that the procession passed through the city of Sens. As it passed a certain house in which criminals were held bound in chains, all the bonds suddenly burst apart. Thus the crowd of wretched prisoners escaped the penalties of that prison and began to serve at the funeral rites of the sacred body. Those same chains, still attached to his holy tomb, remain today as a testimony to so great a miracle.

He was buried in the basilica of holy Mary, Mother of God, which he himself had built. The city remained without a bishop for five days.

## CHAPTER XXIII—On Scopilio

Scopilio held the see for eight years. He lived during the pontificates of Adeodatus, Donus, and Agatho, the Roman bishops, under King Theodoric. We find nothing else about him worthy of record, except that we saw certain small silver vessels in the treasury of the church over which he presided, marked with his name.

He was buried in the basilica of the martyr Saint Eusebius.

## CHAPTER XXIV—On Tetricus

[Col. 0243D]

Treticus, or Tetricus, held the see for 15 years and three months. He lived during the time of the Roman bishops Leo, Benedict, John, Conon, and Sergius, under Childebert the Younger, king of the Franks, who was called “the Just,” a most gentle man adorned with every virtue.

Before becoming bishop he had been abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus. In that office he conducted himself in such a way, and showed himself such a man, that he was rightly sought out by all with the greatest eagerness. For he was generous, devout, chaste, and compassionate.

With God’s favor, the entire people, from the least to the greatest, moved by divine inspiration, chose him for the episcopal order. Thus he was taken from the basilica of Saint Germanus, elected as a bishop worthy of God, and ordained a priest.

Once he had received the priesthood, he immediately devoted himself to preaching and spiritually instructed the Church entrusted to him by God. In the first year of his ordination, he held a council and established how the abbots and archpriests were to perform the divine office in the church of Saint Stephen. He arranged it as follows:

- Kalends of January: first week, the basilica of Saint Germanus; second week, the basilica of Saint Amator; third week, the basilica of Saint Peter; fourth week, the basilica of the monastery of Saint Julian.
- Kalends of February: first week, the basilica of Saint Marianus; second week, the basilica of Saint Eusebius; third week, the basilica of Saint Martin; fourth week, the basilica of Saint Mary.
- Kalends of March: first week, the basilica of Saint Nazarius; second week, the monastery of Longoretum; third week, the monastery of Sessiacum; fourth week, Scolius Village.
- Kalends of April: first week, Bacernae Village; second week, Vendosa and Gaugiacus; third week, Nauteriacus and Licaiacus; fourth week, Tauriacus.
