- Kalends of May: first week, Chorae Village; second week, Corcedomus and the oratory of Saint Memmius; third week, Troia, Cornacus, and Auciacus; fourth week, Varciacus.
- Kalends of June: first week, Bargiacus and Nantoniacus; second week, Massua; third week, Condida; fourth week, Dactriacus and Soliacus.
- Kalends of July: first week, New Village; second week, Brioderus; third week, Giemus and Laoderus; fourth week, Blanoilus.
- Kalends of August: first week, the clergy of Dominicus; second week, Eliniacus; third week, Baugiacus; fourth week, Tauriacus.
- Kalends of October: first week, the clergy of Dominicus; second week, the basilica of Saint Germanus; third week, the basilica of Saint Amator; fourth week, the basilica of Saint Peter.
- Kalends of November: first week, Domiciacus; second week, the monastery of Saint Julian; third week, the basilica of Saint Mavianus; fourth week, the basilica of Saint Eusebius.
- Kalends of December: first week, the basilica of Saint Mary; second week, the basilica of Saint Martin; third week, the basilica of Saints Gervasius and Protasius; fourth week, the monasteries of Longoretum and Sesciacum.

[Col. 0245A]

Having strengthened this arrangement, he decreed that the abbots and priests, together with the clergy, when they assembled to perform the office described above, should receive an adequate allowance from the lord’s storehouse through the church steward. If they arrived late or appeared negligent, they were to abstain from wine for forty days.

If the vicedominus or the steward withheld anything that they were legally required to provide, they were to be confined in a monastery for half a year, content with bread and water, and perform the required penance.

This blessed bishop transferred to the basilica of Saint Stephen, over which by God’s authority he presided, a villa called Maximiacum, situated in the district of Sens, which had come to him by inheritance from his parents, with its buildings, serfs, vineyards, woods, and all its appurtenances.

After successfully completing the course of his life, he was killed by the sword, it is said, by one of his archdeacons, named Regenfredus, who was instigated by the devil. While the bishop was resting, overcome by sleep, on a bench, the archdeacon struck him with a sword. He ended his life in martyrdom on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April and was buried with the greatest devotion of the faithful in the basilica of the martyr Saint Eusebius.

An ancient account reports concerning that same Ragenfredus that, as soon as he left the house in which he had murdered his bishop, he was suddenly carried away by a whirlwind and disappeared without trace.

The city remained without a bishop for three years. Many people suffering from toothache obtained relief from the bench on which he had been killed, through the merits of the holy man. At the same place, moreover, in memory and reverence for the martyr, his successors built an oratory in his name, which to this day is venerated and honored by the devotion of the faithful. The boards of that same bench, bearing the marks of his martyrdom, still exist.

## CHAPTER XXV—On Flocoaldus

Flocoaldus held the see for five years, four months, and ten days. He died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of April and was buried in the basilica of Saint Eusebius. The city remained without a bishop for seven days.

## CHAPTER XXVI—On Savaricus

Savaricus held the see for five years and four months. As report confirms, because he was of the noblest birth, he began to decline somewhat from the dignity of his station and to devote himself to secular concerns more eagerly than was fitting for a bishop. To such an extent did this proceed that he invaded by military force the districts of Orléans, Nevers, Tonnerre, and Avallon, as well as that of Troyes, and subjected them to his own authority.

At that time the Franks, divided among themselves and stirring up many civil wars, fell upon one another in the Cotia Forest and slaughtered one another in a great massacre. Then that same bishop, setting aside his episcopal dignity, gathered a very large multitude from every direction and marched toward Lyon in order to subjugate it by force of arms. Struck by a divine thunderbolt, he died a swift death. His body was brought back to his own city and buried in the basilica of Saint Germanus beside his predecessors.

[Col. 0246A]

He lived during the reign of the younger King Dagobert and of Daniel—who, after changing his name, was called Chilperic and became king from being a cleric—while Pepin, with Plectrude, was governing as master of the palace.

## CHAPTER XXVII—On Hainmarus

Hainmarus, called to the episcopate, held the office for 15 years. He was a vigorous man, adorned to no ordinary degree by the nobility of his birth and also exceedingly wealthy in the dignity of his estates. His secular power grew so greatly that it extended almost to the dukedom of all Burgundy.

At that time Pepin, son of the earlier Charles, had gone into Aquitaine at the invitation of Eudo, duke of the Aquitanians, against Aimon, king of Zaragoza. Aimon had taken Lampagia, Eudo’s daughter, in marriage and had broken the marriage alliance.

When they came together at a place called Iberra and began to fight one another, Hainmarus fell upon the multitude of the Saracens with his men and struck them down in a great slaughter. He defeated them and, with his king, emerged victorious by Christ’s favor.

Thus Pepin returned triumphantly to the regions of France. Not long afterward, however, the aforementioned Eudo treacherously abandoned the agreement he had made with Pepin. Consequently, at the command of that same Pepin, Hainmarus once again marched toward Aquitaine with a multitude of his own men and challenged Eudo to battle. When the two forces met, the Aquitanians fell in so great a slaughter that their duke Eudo himself barely escaped by flight.

But through the envy of certain people—an evil that is always present in prosperous affairs—it was suggested to the king that Eudo had escaped only with Hainmarus’s consent. Because of this, Hainmarus was summoned by that king to Bastonea, a villa situated in the Ardennes Forest, and handed over to prison custody.

After a few days, he was released through the ingenuity of one of his nephews. Seizing a horse, he began his flight. His adversaries pursued him with the greatest speed and caught up with him at a place called Lufaus in the district of Toul.

Seeing that he could not escape their ambush, he turned entirely to divine aid. With his arms extended in the form of a cross and his eyes raised toward heaven, he prayed for heavenly grace. He was pierced by the lances of his pursuers and fell together with the nephew mentioned above. He is said to have been buried there.

To this day, a golden cross of the Lord’s wood is preserved at Auxerre on the altar of the mother church, displaying upon itself the signs of his martyrdom.

He also faithfully distributed some of his property among the churches of God, having obtained the advice and direction of the lord Theodrannus, who had by then, at Hainmarus’s wish, been ordained bishop.

He gave to the basilica of Saint Stephen, for the support of the clerics serving God there, a villa called Matriacus, situated in the district of Sens, with its buildings, serfs, vineyards, woods, and all its appurtenances.

Likewise, in the district of Auxerre, he gave to the hospice of the aforementioned mother church a villa called Miliacus and another called Viriliacus, with all their appurtenances.

To the basilica of Saint Germanus, for the support of the monks, he gave a villa called Abundiacum, situated in the district of Auxerre, with its buildings, serfs, woods, and all its appurtenances.

He also gave, in the district of Gâtinais, a villa called the Bridge of Maxentius, likewise with its appurtenances.

To the hospice of that same basilica of Saint Germanus he gave villas situated in the district of Auxerre, namely Nigrontum with its appurtenances, and Linerolas likewise with its appurtenances, together with Lagunas.

Boniacus and Vitriacus, however, passed into the lord’s fisc at the time of his killing.

## CHAPTER XXVIII—On Theodrannus

Theodrannus was ordained bishop with the consent of Hainmarus, while Hainmarus was still alive. He died on the third day before the Nones of December and was buried in the basilica of Saint Eusebius.

## CHAPTER XXIX—On Quintilianus

Bishop Quintilianus was noble by birth. His father, Quintilianus, built the monastery of Miteretum, endowed it with his own property, and established there a hospice for Britons traveling to Rome.

Before becoming bishop, this blessed bishop had been abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus. Because of the merit of his life and the nobility of his birth, he was summoned from the monastery by popular election and appointed pastor of the Church. He was therefore buried beside his predecessors in the basilica of Saint Germanus.

## CHAPTER XXX—On Cillianus

Bishop Cillianus held the see for six years and two months. He died on the day before the Nones of August and was buried in the basilica of Saint Germanus.

## CHAPTER XXXI—On Clemens

Bishop Clemens held the see for five years, one month, and ten days. Having suffered bodily blindness, he maintained a lodging near the basilica of the apostles Peter and Paul. He died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April and was buried in the basilica of Saint Amator.

## CHAPTER XXXII—On Aidulfus

Aidulfus, formerly a cantor, held the see for 15 years. He lived during the time of Charles the Great and continued until Pepin. He was vigorous in the divine offices and renowned for episcopal generosity.

In his time, ecclesiastical property was withdrawn from the authority of the bishops by that same ruler and passed into the control of secular men. Only one hundred mansi were left to the bishop; everything that remained of the villas was distributed among six Bavarian princes. The abbeys, however, were distributed to individual abbots. The same devout bishop grieved almost to death over this humiliation of the Church, so much so that, after being struck by paralysis, he was deprived of the use of all his bodily faculties.

Thus, while the aforementioned Clemens was still alive, Aidulfus was confined in the same lodging and supported from the church’s provision until the day of his death, while Maurinus, at the will of that bishop, administered the public functions.

Aidulfus gave to the basilica of Saint Stephen his own property in the district of Tonnerre, in a villa called Montiniacus, on the condition that it should serve perpetually for the support of the poor. He died on the Ides of November and was buried in the basilica of Saint Germanus.

## CHAPTER XXXIII—On Maurinus

[Col. 0248A]

Bishop Maurinus held the see for 28 years. He lived around the beginning of the reign of Charles the Great. He was a vigorous man, extraordinarily eloquent in graceful speech, and richly adorned with the marks of holiness.

He is said to have foretold several things in a prophetic spirit, which events soon proved true. Although unequal to many in secular power, he nevertheless showed himself the equal in dignity even of many very powerful men.

It is certain that, through exceptional ingenuity and prudence, he recovered, with the approval of Charles the Great—then king and later emperor—the property of his church that had been taken away, as we related earlier.

He received gold which, as is said, had been found in that city in Brunhild’s tower. This gold, as is said, having been distributed by the pound, he tied here and there into the knots of the scarf that he wore. He hung this around his neck and carried it before the aforementioned king in an unconventional manner. At the same time, he made known to the king the poverty of the church entrusted to him and the substance of his petition. He claimed that he had initially planned to win over each of the palace officials to his aid with a pound of gold apiece, but had afterward changed his mind and judged it better that he alone should receive everything.

The ruler’s generosity consented, and by royal decree he ordered that, as each of those who then held ecclesiastical property died, Maurinus should gradually recover everything. With God’s approval, matters proceeded favorably, so that within scarcely two years almost none of those who held church estates contrary to what was lawful remained.

At that time the abbeys of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, of Saint Martin, and of Saint Eusebius returned to the use of Saint Stephen. Most of the villas that had hitherto been alienated likewise returned.

During the episcopate of this bishop, the first count of the district of Auxerre, named Ermenoldus, built on his own estate a monastery in honor of the Savior. The same bishop solemnly dedicated it and gave it, from the property of Saint Stephen, a villa called Cocciacus as an augmentation. Later, moreover, through the bishop’s intervention, the aforementioned count transferred that monastery to Saint Stephen.

This bishop also offered upon the altar of the mother church a pallium, most precious and handsomely ornamented with gold and pearls. He also made a cross of the purest gold and precious gems, inscribing his name upon it.

As an imitator of his predecessor of blessed memory, he likewise gave his own property to Saint Stephen, so that it might be distributed for the needs of the poor. It is situated in the district of Tonnerre, in a villa called Fontanetus.

He also gave, for the support of the canons, a small estate of his own property called Villare, not far from Varciacus, which he had obtained from a certain noblewoman named Rocla.

He died on the eighth day before the Ides of August and was buried in the church of Saint Gervasius, which he himself had also renovated.

## CHAPTER XXXIV—On Aaron

Bishop Aaron held the see for 13 years. It is known of him that, when Charles the Great set out for Rome to strengthen the dignity of the empire under Pope Leo, Aaron departed together with him and, during that expedition, obtained from the aforementioned emperor the abbey of Saint Marianus.

This same bishop magnificently made a ciborium of gold and silver over the altar of Saint Stephen. He died on the Ides of February and was buried in the basilica of Saint Gervasius.

## CHAPTER XXXV—On Angelelmus

Bishop Angelelmus, a Bavarian by birth, son of Obtelmus and Hogarde, held the see for 17 years.

He was a man of the greatest simplicity and charity. After being ordained a priest, he was appointed abbot of the basilica of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.

When Bishop Aaron died, Jeremiah, archbishop of Sens, came to Auxerre at the command of Emperor Charles and assembled the clergy and people in the church of Saint Germanus. With the general consent of the assembly, Angelelmus was unanimously elected and ordained bishop.

Having received the episcopal ministry, he devoted himself entirely to divine service: constant in prayer, frequent in tears, outstanding in almsgiving, and almost unique in his age. He is said sometimes to have pretended to be ill out of love of generosity, so that he could distribute to the poor, without anyone’s opposition, whatever he was able to possess.

He enriched the church of Saint Stephen with no ordinary generosity. He fitted the altar of the older church everywhere with silver panels, and likewise adorned the altar of Saint Mary with a silver panel. He decorated the altar of Saint John the Baptist with a similar ornament.

Before the altar of Saint Stephen he prepared three silver crowns of exceptional weight. Around the altar he set up ten very large silver candelabra. He gave a fine silver chalice with a paten and marked it with his name.

He also placed there a very large cross, which he adorned most beautifully with gold and silver and with the image of the Savior. Before it he set up an altar decorated with a silver panel.

He adorned the same church with four very large and sonorous bells. He also made a chest of exceptional workmanship, elegantly decorated with gold and silver, in which he placed the reliquary of the blessed Amator together with many relics of the saints. He contributed many excellent tapestries for adorning the seats of the basilica.

During his episcopate, Emperor Louis held a general assembly, imposed a regular life upon the canons, established the enclosure of the cloister for the protection of religious observance, and arranged various suitable workshops for their use. Pleased with this authority, the same bishop assigned a villa called Pulverenus for the support of the canon brothers.

Since certain benefices had been granted and could not immediately be taken away, it was decreed that, when their holders died, the canons should at once turn them to their own use. He also assigned to their use property that had come to him by his own legal right, both at Biliacum and at Amau.

He placed many excellent silver vessels of exceptional quality in the treasuries of the same church. To Saint Germanus he gave a silver chalice with a paten of the same design as the one he had made earlier, identifying this generosity by an inscription of his name.

To Saint Amator he gave a silver chalice with a paten of the same workmanship, though of lesser weight; and likewise to Saint Peter.

He adorned the altar of Saint Eusebius with a silver panel. He gave a silver chalice with a paten and also prepared a silver Gospel book with silver candelabra and a silver censer. He donated altar curtains and several vestments as well.

At the monastery of Saint Savior he gave a silver panel with a very sonorous bell.

Finally, throughout the diocese under his authority, he distributed three pounds of silver to the village churches for the preparation of a chalice and paten. To the smaller chapels he assigned only 15 solidi for similar work, and in the aforementioned villages he also distributed an appropriate quantity of silver for decorating crosses in the churches.

Full of these and similar fruits of good works, he died on the day before the Nones of July and was honorably buried in the basilica of Saint Germanus.

## CHAPTER XXXVI—On Heribaldus

Bishop Heribaldus, son of Antelmus, a Bavarian, and Frotilde, from the district of Gâtinais, held the see for 33 years.

He had been raised at court from early childhood. After the death of his uncle Angelelmus, the clergy and people, having held a solemn election, chose him for the episcopate. Aldric, archbishop of Sens, managed the matter with his fellow bishops by command of Emperor Louis.

It is established that he was designated by election and advanced through ordination in the church of the blessed Germanus.

He was a man of very noble birth, elegant in appearance, polished in speech, and distinguished by exceptional prudence. For this reason he wielded great influence with kings. He became chief chaplain at the palace and was also extremely powerful in secular dignity at that time.

As human affairs are, however, for as long as he flourished at the summit of this power, he devoted himself moderately to secular business. At last, inspired by divine concern and weighed down by bodily illness—which often restrains the appetite for worldly things—he changed his conduct and pursuits in another direction. He devoted himself wholeheartedly to divine service and ecclesiastical interests: constant in prayer, abundant in tears, generous in supporting the servants of God, most zealous in restoring churches, and singularly remarkable—remarkably singular—in relieving the poor.

He renovated the church of Saint Stephen in its walls and ceilings and adorned it with excellent glasswork and paintings. He established four silver crowns. Around the altar of Saint Stephen he renewed the silver panels, both in their sculpture and in the elegance of their workmanship. He also magnificently decorated with gold and silver a reliquary in which he placed the vestments of the most holy Germanus.

After the old basilica of Saint John the Baptist had fallen into disrepair, he rebuilt it from its lowest foundations, raised it to a lofty summit, and solemnly dedicated it on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

Later, he decently placed in the same church the relics of the holy martyrs Alexander and Chrysanthus, which he had brought from the city of Rome. He also adorned the chancel and its screens with gracious care.

For the perpetual maintenance of the lights to be kept burning in honor of the patronage of those same saints, he generously gave, with apostolic authorization, a small estate of five mansi called Bunuorum, from the estate of Matriacus.

He renovated the basilica of Saint Mary with ceilings, paintings, and glasswork.

He ennobled the community of canons both through literary learning and through dedication to ecclesiastical discipline. He brought in teachers from every direction to advance the divine service through study and enlarge it through diligence.

No one can doubt how generous he was in their stipends. Whenever those who held anything from the possessions mentioned above departed, he reserved it for the canons’ use without any relaxation or concession.

He restored to their wardrobe a villa called Condida, and assigned to the same use the cell of Saint Remigius with its appurtenances and two vineyards, Corticanum and Plautas.

Since he was dear and close to King Charles after the death of his father Louis, he obtained from the king’s generosity certain villas that had formerly been alienated from ecclesiastical right. Their names are Gajacus with its appurtenances, Garsiliacus likewise, Camplemesium likewise, and Maximiacus likewise.

Dividing them equally, he distributed one half for the lights of the church and ordered the other half to serve for the support of the canons, with the royal command confirming this arrangement. He also irrevocably decreed that, in memory of the aforementioned king, a meal should be prepared from that villa twice each year—once by the provost and once by the archiclave of that church.

In the second year of the civil war, which was the year 841 from the Incarnation of God the man, this same bishop, by command of Kings Charles and Louis, solemnly transferred the body of the most blessed Germanus on the Kalends of September from the place where it had first been buried.

He found it so intact in its solidity and so uncorrupted in its garments that it was as it had once been most beautifully prepared by the venerable Empress Placidia.

Thus, fruitful in the harvest of excellent virtues and full of age and goodness, he was gathered to his fathers on the seventh day before the Kalends of May. As he himself had requested, he received a noble burial in the crypt of Saint Stephen in the basilica of Saint Germanus. While still alive, he had adorned its altar with a silver panel and had also given a silver chalice with a paten.

## CHAPTER XXXVII—On Abbo

Abbo, made bishop from being a monk and the brother of the aforementioned Bishop Heribaldus, held the see for two years and ten months. He was a vigorous man, distinguished by eloquence of every kind and exceptionally learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular studies.

He had been abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus. After his brother’s death, he was elected and appointed to the episcopate by command of King Charles.

What sort of man he was, and how richly endowed with the best intentions, the brevity of his tenure and his untimely death did not allow him to demonstrate.

He gave Saint Stephen a golden cross with precious gems and a very fine pallium. He began the western stairway from its foundations and had resolved to adorn the altar of Saint Stephen with pure gold and gems; but, prevented by death, he left a considerable sum of gold to carry out the work.

Full of such good intentions, he was overtaken by death on the third day before the Nones of December and was honorably buried in the church of Saint Germanus.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII—On Christianus

Bishop Christianus, an Alemannian by birth, son of Arcambertus and Emelinde, held the see for 13 years.

He was a simple man, as though suffused by a natural cheerfulness of spirit and countenance, outstanding in humility, and a most ardent lover of the ecclesiastical household.

He brought to completion the western stairway begun by his predecessor. This same bishop, together with Frotarius, archbishop of Bordeaux, ceremonially transferred the remains of the body of the most blessed Amator from the place of its first burial into the crypt of his own church.

He also took care that whatever the canons lacked from the revenues due for their support should be restored through swift and generous kindness. He gave the same canons a villa called Albaris, so that every year a commemoration of him might be made from its revenues.

He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of December and was buried beside his predecessors in the church of Saint Germanus.

## CHAPTER XXXIX—On Wala

Bishop Wala, a Frank by birth, son of Ardradus and Witelai, and brother of Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens, of blessed memory, held the see for seven years and 28 days.

At the beginning of his episcopate he devoted himself to reading the wise men of the world. Later, because they burdened the Church, he decently and prudently removed from himself the burden of the vassals whom he had brought with him from the county of Carloman.

The concern of this father of whom we speak was to embrace teachers of literature with affection, to make use of their conversation and advice, and to share his table with them. For this reason, the two lights of our college, Rainogala and Alagus, with Herricus the theosopher and monk laboring alongside them, composed the Acts of the Bishops of this see in concise and carefully divided pages.

This man had a sincere and intimate affection for the servants of God. He had made them so united with him through his benefactions that even at his final hour they gratefully performed the day’s office for him.

In his time, two eminent Fathers, namely the lord Trutbertus and the elder Hictarius, died.

The first of these, full of a prophetic spirit, remained so during the time of his illness. From the holy Nativity of the Lord, when he began to fall ill, he recognized as though present certain members of the college of brothers who were absent.

The second revealed what merit he possessed on the day of his burial. When a great number of clergy and people were present and were rendering the service of burial, the little body—which could scarcely have been prepared by the labor of a full day—was cut through by a single blow of a hammer.

Let no one think that I have said such things frivolously; let him recognize the friendships with which he was blessed. He was never absent from the night office; indeed, he expressly asked after the absent, both brothers and boys. Whenever he knew of a supply of books anywhere, he eagerly desired to bring it here. He avoided touching the treasure of the church as though it were sacrilege. He gave Saint Stephen silver gifts, golden gifts, and very fine pallia.

He carried out the restoration of the churches with the greatest diligence and, in his time, brought almost all of it to a happy completion. While some despoil their dioceses and enrich their relatives, he distributed among the sons of his Church the greatest benefits he received from his own kinsmen. He did not transact with alien gifts but with his own.

In every gathering and private conversation he made use of the presence of his clergy, not allowing anything unfavorable about them to be heard or spoken. He used the common proverb: “Let laymen not know what clerics do, and let equals associate with equals.”

An untimely death carried him away, but Christ lifted him above the stars. An urn covers the remains of his body in the monastery of Saxiacum. He ended his final day on the seventh day before the Ides of March, leaving behind a brother who lived happily after him and who also gave generously for his memory: with royal and episcopal consent, he gave the canons of Saint Stephen two mansi at Rivo, and, for the maintenance of the divine altar-light of Saint Stephen, one mansus in the villa of Piscaliolum.

## CHAPTER XL—On Uribaldus
Uribaldus, by nationality a Frank, a native of the city of Cambrai, was sent by the most glorious and ever-August Louis to become bishop of this city. Born of very noble parents—[Col. 0253C] his father Leutfridus and his mother Doda, who faithfully and chastely maintained a lawful marriage with one another—he was imbued with spiritual disciplines from the earliest training of his life and thoroughly instructed in the studies of the liberal arts. He became a follower of John Scotus, who at that time was spreading the rays of wisdom throughout Gaul. Remaining for a long time under his instruction, he learned to discern both divine and human matters and to weigh prosperous and adverse circumstances alike in an even balance.

Afterward, having attained the full strength of youth, he was introduced at the royal court. There, serving in the royal service with Christ’s favor, when Wala, bishop of this see, had died, he deserved to receive the episcopal throne. The aforesaid King Louis worthily rewarded his service, while the clergy and people of this Church, united in agreement, applauded his ordination as bishop. Thus, with God’s aid [Col. 0253D], he was ordained bishop by the venerable archbishop Ansegisus on the Nones of April, amid the greatest rejoicing of the whole people.

Many still survive who testify that they saw with their own eyes how splendidly he lived, how earnestly he desired to exalt the house entrusted to him, how gentle he was toward the Lord’s flock, and how generous a steward he proved to be. He feared neither the heat of the sun nor the bitter cold of winter if he could labor without ceasing for the honor of the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen. From the gifts of royal munificence he therefore offered many presents in order to attach the abbey of Saint Julian to the service of Saint Stephen. He accomplished this only with great difficulty, but an untimely death prevented him from possessing the royal charter which he had obtained for that purpose—the death, I say, which rarely enters among the sorrowful, but very often among the joyful. [Col. 0254A]

On the western side of the church of Saint Stephen he built two altars: the upper one he dedicated in honor of the holy Cross, through which salvation shone upon the whole world; the lower one he dedicated most honorably in honor of the blessed Gregory, intercessor for our calamities, and of the outstanding apostle Paul, as well as Amator, Germanus, Martin, and Benedict. He did not forget his own salvation: through the blessed Gregory, he knew that a soul bound in the deepest jaws of the underworld, not yet reborn through the bath of baptism, could nevertheless be saved, since he had learned that the saving and universal command of baptism had been conveyed to the heavenly realms. He therefore trusted without doubt that through Gregory’s prayers he too could be saved even in death.

Finally, to the community entrusted to him he granted half of the estate of Chichirei, confirming it by royal charter, so that on the day of his ordination, the day of his death, the day of the death of his lord King Louis, and the day of the dedication of the sacred altars—that is, the crypts—a fitting meal might be prepared, so that at least through the bestowal of this gift, and every year thereafter, the memory of his honor might be revived among posterity. He also granted eight manses to the canons of Saint Eusebius at the estate of Molendini, assigning them perpetually to their use by royal charter, so that through their intercession affection might be shown toward his frailty.

Finally, while such things were being carried out, the sudden decline of life crept upon him. Forgetful of all things that appear and pass away, he began to be pressed only by fear of death. He loudly proclaimed himself guilty, confessed himself a most wicked sinner, and tearfully begged forgiveness from everyone, as was necessary. His hope was raised toward heaven, and his mind and resolve were turned without delay toward Christ. After the intercession of the blessed Stephen, whose see he had governed, he entrusted himself to the suffrages of Saint Clement and earnestly requested that his bodily remains be buried at the threshold of the house, outside the church. Thus, wholly turned toward better things, he passed to Christ in a blessed departure.

The affection of the clergy buried him not outside but inside the church of the blessed Clement, through whose aid he believed that, while still living, he would be earnestly assisted before the mercy of the supreme Judge. He governed the Church for 7 years, 1 month, and 8 days, and died on the Fourth Ides of May. The Church remained without a bishop for 3 months and 17 days.

## CHAPTER XLI — Concerning Herifridus

[Col. 0254D] Herifridus, by nationality a man of Chartres, lived gloriously in the episcopate for 22 years, 1 month, and 16 days. It would be most improper not to commit to writing how this most noble man acquired this dignity, what he was as bishop, and what he had been before. At that time Charles, second to no one in virtue, governed the empire of the whole world. The affairs of the world were fortunate under this ruler, because the king philosophized and the philosopher held the reins of the kingdom. Although his mind extended itself in many directions, as befitted the most powerful of all kings, he never allowed the disciplines of the liberal arts to be absent from the palace; rather, you would have marveled that the court of royal dignity had become a gymnasium of every kind of wisdom.

From every region noblemen and the offspring of the kingdom’s leading families, both secular and ecclesiastical, were sent to this place for the sake of learning, certain that the teaching of both disciplines shone there with great brilliance. Among other youths of proud blood who flocked there with eager minds was the aforesaid man, Herifridus by name, descended from a most noble lineage of the Armorican region. He was highly distinguished for the holiness of his conduct, angelic in appearance and manner of life, and a burning ray of divine contemplation amid human darkness. His father was named Herifridus, and his mother Hisemberga. Noble by birth, they were nobler in holiness. Although they were married in the world, their conduct was nevertheless heavenly; cherishing the child mentioned above, they entrusted him to the service of the Almighty and of blessed Mary.

In the city of Chartres, from which they themselves originated, they had him tonsured with great rejoicing. There he was instructed for a time in the liberal studies, so that literary knowledge might converge in him. Through the efforts of Lord Gauterius, bishop of the holy Church of Orléans, from whose lineage he had sprung, he was sent to serve the aforesaid emperor. There he thoroughly searched the pages of Scripture and attached himself to the service of his lord, wishing never to depart from his presence or to be separated from ecclesiastical affairs.

Meanwhile, when the clergy and people of the city of Auxerre had assembled together, counsel was sought concerning the election of a pastor, and a messenger was sent swiftly to the ears of royal magnificence. No sooner had the king heard of the bishop’s death than, laying aside every impulse of personal desire, and with divine clemency ordering the decision of the nobles of the royal court, while all acclaimed him, he conferred the pastoral staff with the greatest reverence upon Lord Herifridus and sent him to the city of Sens for ordination.

The most divine archbishop Gauterius received him with the greatest honor. With the consent of the clergy and people who had gathered there for this purpose, he ordained him at the monastery of Nigellum on the feast of Saint John, the day on which, after his head had been severed, he was admitted into the heavenly sanctuaries. With the greatest rejoicing he enthroned him in this see.

How he lived there, and how nobly he presented himself to all as a standard of virtue, is known more clearly than daylight to many who still survive. But since the enemy of the human race keeps ever more watchfully spreading the snares of his deceit against the righteous, he inflicted various trials upon this apostolic man, attempting through evil persuasion to turn him aside from the path of truth toward his own counsels. For the city was unexpectedly consumed by flames and utterly reduced to ashes, except for ruins and rubble.

When these things had taken place, the dear Lord Herifridus resolved in his mind that he would build no dwelling for himself in the city until the houses of God—the churches, namely, of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, of Saint John, and likewise of the first martyr Stephen—had been restored to their former condition. Content with a small hut, he immediately began to rebuild them, and adorned them from the foundations with marvelous workmanship. He remained devoted to this undertaking until the end of his life. Thus, while the churches were nobly rebuilt, unfortunate death prevented him from building the houses of his predecessors.

Many benefices had been taken away from the aforesaid see. By careful diligence and the utmost vigilance, he restored them to their proper place, sanctioned by royal charters and apostolic privileges. Among these, he granted half of Malliacum with its dependencies to the altar for the preparation of lights, and assigned the other half to the canons for the meal to be prepared on the day of his death. After long and strenuous effort, he also obtained the estate of Crevennum, together with Narciacum and Novicum and their dependencies, for perpetual service to himself and his successors.

He also granted Artadum, one mansus at Capilliacum, another at Lindriacum, and the flour-mill beside the city wall, so that food might be prepared for the brethren on the day of his ordination. He restored the oratory of the most blessed Clement, which was in the same city and had been burned by fire. At the request of Herimbertus, who held these possessions by beneficiary right, he assigned to it the estate of Chimiliacum, together with the church of Saint Andrew at Gurgiacum, confirming the grant by royal charter.

He established by the same authority that Herimbertus, that most faithful son of the Church entrusted to him, who had labored after the aforesaid bishop for the restoration of all the churches, should continue to enjoy these possessions while he lived, and that after him one relative whom he chose should do likewise. Thus they would provide what was necessary for the aforementioned oratory and furnish the canons with a fitting meal on the feast of the martyr Saint Clement. In this way, through Clement’s intercession before Almighty God—he for whom a house has also been prepared in the sea by angelic hands—may that intercession introduce him, freed from the waves of his sins, into the harbor of eternal rest by the anchor of his virtue, and continually cherish him in the bosom of Clement’s mercy. Lord Gauterius, the archimandrite, and the bishops of his diocese confirmed this arrangement by their authority so that it should endure forever.

At Arbricum he also donated four manses to the altar of the church of Saint Stephen, in the domain of the archiclave (archiclavus). In the district and county of Sens, at the estate of Noerolium above the river Yonne, he granted thirty-six manses and one-third of a mansus. Together with the allod at the estate of Pomerium above the river Oreuse—formerly the benefice of Agano—which Wulfagius had given to Saint Stephen for the restoration of the fabric of that martyr’s church, he assigned these possessions to the service of the archiclave, on the condition that the aforementioned Wulfagius and his son Anseisus should hold both the estate and the allod and pay fifteen solidi in rent to the archiclave. After their deaths, the same possessions were to return to the service of the archiclave.

Indeed, the marks of his holiness are innumerable, and mortal speech is wholly insufficient to recount them. Now, while the blessed man was continually meditating upon Christ, an illness of gout suddenly attacked him, followed by a severe affliction of chiragra and a great weakness in all the joints of his body; for a long time he was burdened and tormented by this suffering. Yet his spirit never ceased from divine meditation. He continually begged to be relieved through the suffrages of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, of Saint John, the precursor of the Lord’s Incarnation, and of Lord Stephen.

One day a most powerful swelling seized his feet, so that it completely prevented him from being able to taste or chew. Then suddenly a raven, a bird friendly to corpses but forgetful of its own nature, seized in its open beak a piece of tin with which a spoon had been covered and threw it down beside the bishop’s window, near which he was lying. The piece of tin was brought before the bishop. Taking it up, invoking the name of the Lord, and trusting that he could be healed through the merits of Saint Stephen, the bishop placed the tin upon his feet, and immediately the pain departed. Nor is it surprising that this bird, by the Lord’s command, brought a remedy to the feet of the holy man, since it also once refreshed Elijah’s hunger with food.

For some time afterward, desiring to enjoy conversation with Lord Rithuerus, bishop of the city of Augusta Treverorum, he went to Villare above the river Yonne, where the aforesaid bishop came eagerly to meet him. There they refreshed one another with mutual embraces and held a lengthy discussion concerning religion.

There was a spring there bubbling with delightful waters. When the distinguished bishop Herifridus saw it, he ordered an earthenware flask filled with the same water to be brought. Sitting on his horse, he received the vessel after making the sign of the cross over it. But the very fierce horse, feeling the unfamiliar flask upon itself, leaped up and threw the vessel to the ground, just as it was, full. A marvelous thing: the vessel, still full, settled upon the earth as though it had been gently placed there by hand, retaining the water within it so that it did not spill. All who were present marveled.

He then ordered the water to be brought back to him and, blessing the name of the Lord, drank deeply enough. He gave it to his fellow bishop and the others, who were all astonished, to drink. No sane person would doubt that this miracle was the merit of Bishop Herifridus and of Lord Rithuerus. After long conversation and sweet embraces among the holy men, each returned to his own place.

When Lord Herifridus was preparing to return to the walls of the city, Hermembertus, his most faithful servant, begged his magnificence to withdraw for that night to the church of Saint Andrew at Gurgiacum. He granted the request. He remained there that day, and while the aforesaid Hermembertus was preparing what was fitting for the bishop, he was suddenly so inflamed by the heat of fever that he felt nothing but burning. When Herifridus the glorious man saw this, he invoked the name of the Lord and, by that same Lord, commanded the affliction not to trouble him any longer. Immediately all pain subsided in him.

Afterward, having eaten, night fell, and the aforesaid bishop went to bed. Almighty God, who is the boundless searcher of hidden things, also tested his servants secretly in various ways. For human weakness being what it is, lest the bishop become exalted because of the great gift bestowed upon him, the heat which he had removed from another’s body by his command and merit was, by God’s just judgment, turned back upon his own strength. Although he had happily and healthily laid his limbs upon his bed in the silence of the deep night, he was awakened from sleep and felt an intense fever throughout his body.

Struck by this illness, he hurried to the church of Saint Andrew and spent the remainder of the night there supplicating the Lord. At daybreak he prepared to celebrate the sacred solemnities of Mass. Having received counsel from the divine fountain, he took the offering of the body and blood of the Lord, so that by its power every assault of illness might subside. Divine power did not deny his request: as soon as he received in his mouth the immeasurable gift of our redemption, the heat of the fever was extinguished as though it had never been in him.

We also know that the following was widely reported both in the episcopal see and in the surrounding places. Those who at that time devoted themselves to school studies assert that if they were fortunate enough to enjoy his blessing in the morning, or at least his presence, all fear that they would be beaten with rods or a staff that day was removed. He became all things to all people: by his example he invited the elderly to better things; with gentle speech he corrected the young so that they would not act foolishly; he sustained adolescents in the bosom of supreme piety; with constant diligence he instructed the rich to give their possessions to the Lord and to remember that they had been appointed stewards, not masters, of their wealth. To the poor also he denied nothing, as a cheerful giver. Clerics in need of support and clothing, for as long as he was present, he sustained as sons and supplied with everything necessary. Whenever he departed for some place, he ordered his ministers to feed individually, from the daily provision for the canons, those whom necessity pressed, until his return.

It was his concern and his anxiety that no sheep from the Lord’s fold should be torn by the bite of the ever-ambushing wolf. Like a good shepherd, he continually defended the flock entrusted to him by fasting, keeping vigil through the night, and praying.

While such things were taking place, the all-powerful disposing and most just governing power and wisdom of God did not delay testing the merit of his servant. A prolonged illness began gravely to dissolve the structure of his body, so that no limb was able to perform its proper function. Yet even then he did not cease serving his God. His tongue alone remained sound and resounded with the praises of the Lord, while meditation upon the divine Scriptures comforted his mind. And so that he might not lack in the future the saving sacrifice, which is Christ, he himself became in the present a living sacrifice, following the example of the outstanding preacher Paul, who said: “I am already being sacrificed, and the time of my dissolution is at hand.”

It may confidently be said that Almighty God was inviting him into his own company, whose example he had followed while placed on earth. The clergy, covered in the mournful garment of grief and needing their pastor’s blessing, were saddened and lamented, sighing because prolonged illness wearied him.

When the bishop perceived that his departure was drawing near, and realized that what he had planned could not be completed, he distributed the sum of money he had collected for this purpose: thirty pounds for making a panel before the altar of Saint Stephen, and twenty for adorning the altars of blessed Mary and blessed John. Remembering that the church of Saint Eusebius had been utterly destroyed, he gave it two and a half manses at the estate of Loconuacum, and likewise two and a half at Ceriacum; in the waterway of Niolum, he gave one-third of a mansus, granting half to the altar and the other half to the canons of that place. He confirmed this arrangement, through the hands of his fellow bishops, as something that would endure perpetually, long before his death. He distributed all the rest to his canons and his faithful.

“Naked,” he said, “I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there,” after the manner of holy Job. For all his limbs had died, while only his tongue trembled in his mouth, confessing the Lord.

What more is there to say? At last the illness spread through his limbs and reached his vital organs. A great multitude of the city gathered there. Everyone came seeking the gift of his blessing; the clergy were present, wailing and singing psalms for the departure of his soul. Then, after ashes had been prepared and a hair shirt spread over them, he ordered himself to be laid upon it, as befit a Christian man. Thus, giving thanks to the Lord with the others and shielding himself and all who were present with the sign of the holy Cross, he passed to the Lord in a blessed departure. He was buried honorably within the city walls before the altar of the ever-virgin Mary, to whose service he had devoted himself perpetually while alive.

## CHAPTER XLII — Concerning Gerannus

Gerannus, bishop, a Frank by nationality and a native of the town of Soissons, was born of his father Otardus and his mother Wia. He governed the episcopal chair for 4 years, 6 months, and 11 days.

Thus, from the beginning of his birth, he was raised on the nurturing milk of infancy. When he began to enter the threshold of his earliest childhood, his parents’ prudent example and solicitous care committed him to the elementary studies of the school, by which the still tender and dull understanding of babbling infancy is customarily educated—now by soothing it, now by frightening it with gentle severity. Finally, after he had been instructed in the melodies of David, by the favoring providence of the supreme Author he attained the discipline of the clerical life and was attracted to the assembly of the glorious martyr Gervasius. There, regularly instructed and made obedient to the venerable Fathers of that place, he learned to traverse the fields of historical books with the graceful plectrum of his speech and to resound, with the sweetness of his voice, the melodious modes of the musical art in the court of Christ.

Each day there grew in him distinctive wisdom, a chaste life, upright conduct, and, together with all these things, abundant material resources. His granaries and storerooms overflowed with grain and wine, but avaricious love of money did not possess him. Rather, generous charity dwelt within him and made these things common to all. The door of his house stood open to travelers, and he offered the benefits of consolation. He rejoiced with those who rejoiced and wept with those who wept. He covered the exposed backs of the poor with clothing and caused the purulent heads of wards or orphans to be cleansed with water and a cleansing preparation (lomentum).

Adorned with these and similar displays of good works, he began to please all the Fathers and brothers of that church so greatly that he was no longer received by everyone as a son but as a father. What more shall I say? Gradually ascending from the lowest degrees of service, he was promoted to the office of provost and at the same time attained the dignity of archdeacon.

Raised to this rank of honors, he carefully strove to conduct himself with such moderation that neither arrogance, swelling with pride, should lift itself above him, nor the favor of flatterers move him from the state of the religious life he had undertaken. With the vigilant care of a shepherd, he most diligently kept watch over Christ’s flock, driving away from himself and others the monsters of vice, and faithfully supplying the appropriate food and clothing required by bodily need.

Raised by such praises, as has been said, and by many others of various kinds to the stars of heaven, he shone so brightly in the world’s esteem that he was most pleasing to the royal majesty, dear to bishops, acceptable to nobles, revered by all clerics, loved by soldiers, and most beloved by persons of high and low rank, of either sex.

After the death of Lord Herifridus, the pious pastor of Auxerre, the Church was harassed by many and excessive troubles, especially concerning the pastoral election, for which certain men were panting, not out of spiritual zeal but from anxious ambition for honor. At that time there was a certain powerful man named Ragenardus, viscount of the same city. He was exceedingly wealthy in estates and buildings, immensely rich in treasures of gold and silver, and most abundantly supplied with every kind of possession. He was highly distinguished by the nobility of his ancestors, surrounded by bands of soldiers, and, so to speak, second to no one at the court of Richard, that great and flourishing prince, except Manasses, his brother.

Since he was such a great man, burning with the fever of avarice, he placed himself above everyone, desiring to appear uniquely outstanding. So that, as a powerful man, he might become more powerful, and as a rich man, richer, he plotted with poisonous intent to place over the Church such a bishop as he could subject to his authority, compel to submit to the counsels of his own will, and who would be wholly silenced by the threatening force of his tyranny if Ragenardus attempted to seize for himself the benefices of God’s house which he desired.

Having therefore taken up this wicked scheme, he approached Duke Richard and, offering gifts, requested that the election to that Church be granted to him. At last, having achieved the fulfillment of his desire, he summoned the venerable choir of the canons together with the military order and asked them whom they wished to have elected and ordained as bishop.

When they all remained silent and answered nothing except, “Whomever God chooses,” he said:

“I burn with the flame of affection for all of you, and, desiring to favor the will and petition of everyone, I wish to venerate you all above others as fathers and honor you as faithful friends, wholly obedient to God, if only I may deserve so much from you—something which I long to suggest to you for the general honor.”

When they replied with various things pleasing to him, he added:

“There is a certain Frank who is most familiar to me, acceptable to God and to men, named Gerannus, distinguished for the uprightness of his conduct, outstanding in faith, and vigorous in steadfastness of mind. If, by God’s favor, he is good to his fellow citizens, he may be better for you if he becomes your pastor through your affection.”

But they perceived his power and, wishing to avoid the injuries which his cunning might inflict, promised to obey his counsel. He immediately hastened the business, obtained the permission of the aforesaid prince, and, supported by the assistance of relatives and friends and finally by the election of the clergy and people, approached the most serene and most pious king Charles, relying upon the authority of Lord Gauterius, the archbishop. Through divine assistance he succeeded in having that vigorous man elected and ordained bishop.

After receiving the most holy and laborious office of blessing, he was welcomed joyfully by all. With the greatest devotion of the clergy and an innumerable multitude of the people, while choirs of singers went before and followed behind, the religious carried him on their shoulders to the court of the first among Christ’s martyrs, Saint Stephen. There he was clothed with the episcopal stole and honorably seated upon the priestly throne.

After a short time had passed, it will be possible to explain, at least briefly, how piously he lived and how many persecutions he suffered from the aforesaid Ragenardus and from the barbarous people of the Normans for the protection of himself and his people. Immediately after he had obtained the episcopal see, that same Ragenardus did not blush to spew forth before everyone the poison of malice which had been concealed in his swift-moving heart. Taking what he regarded as an opportunity arising from the terms of his promise, he seized from the bishop’s authority the estate of Gaiacum, three miles distant from the city, with all its dependencies, and shamelessly attached it to his own possession.

Moreover, so that he might become even more reckless in diminishing the resources of that Church, through his instigation and plotting his brother Manasses—then more powerful and wealthier than all the rich men of Gaul, and the most secret investigator of every kind of worldly counsel, from which he became famous among kings and nobles to the furthest corners of the earth—did not shrink from bringing the estate of Nareiacum into his own use.

That most hostile enemy of the bishop, Ragenardus, as has been said, also tried to enclose him so completely within his commands that he would attempt nothing outside Ragenardus’s advice and will. None of the bishop’s clerics, and none of his soldiers, dared resist him; rather, he commanded all of them as though they were his own.

Meanwhile, while his mind was troubled by such misfortunes, other calamities of misery broke in upon him, by which he was especially disturbed and compelled to turn himself entirely toward divine assistance. The savagery of the Normans was raging everywhere, openly and secretly ravaging the whole region day and night with unceasing blows, destroying the entire land through slaughter, the seizure of estates, and the conflagration of fires.

When the heroic man and outstanding pastor saw this, he was shaken by intolerable grief of heart, ready to come to the aid of the flock entrusted to him, mindful of the saying of the Lord: “For the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10:11). He summoned his people, encouraged them with words, strengthened them with his blessing, and begged them to go forth with him armed for battle. He sent Ragenardus a pleading message asking him to go with him to the fight, but he did not obtain his request.

He nevertheless went out of the city with his own men, sent scouts ahead, found the enemy, and joined battle. He gained the victory, and, with divine grace assisting him, after the adversaries had been routed, three of their banners were brought back. Two noble enemies were captured there: one of them was thrown from the city wall and perished; the other was handed over to Ragenardus.

Afterward, strengthened by the power of the supreme God, whenever hostile forces broke out to carry on plundering, he willingly threw himself into their encounters, attacking them sometimes when they were unaware, sometimes when he had observed them, and prospering in no small slaughter.

His victorious right hand, together with Richard and Robert, two very great nobles, took part in the battle fought near the city of Chartres. There, through the intervention of Mary, the Mother of God, a very great slaughter of the pagans took place, so that, when an innumerable multitude had scattered, more than 6,500 corpses of the slain were found, apart from those swallowed by the abyss of the river Eure, and those whom the long course of the flight and the vastness of the forests held wounded and lifeless.

At another time, when the fury of Norman power was plundering the district of Nevers and carrying away an immense amount of booty even with loaded wagons, Richard, most invincible in battle, met them. The same Bishop Gerannus, placed in the front line with a few men, attacked them without fear. Soon they were put to flight, and the hostile force was so overcome and defeated that, if any remained, having lost the confidence of their noble warriors, they dared neither to offer battle again nor to ravage any lands thereafter. Instead, they voluntarily surrendered themselves to Frankish rule, submitted their necks to the yoke of Christ, rejected demonic deceptions, and eagerly sought the bath of baptism. Finally, by the gift of the king and the nobles, they occupied a portion of the kingdom assigned to them for habitation, a region previously laid waste by the madness of their own plundering.

But Ragenardus, his persistent slanderer, seeing with envious eyes that he possessed such successes, wasted away from the sickness of envy. He observed that everything he undertook prospered under favorable auspices, while the efforts he himself had planned failed daily.

Thus this glorious pastor, who did not hesitate to persist as an invincible athlete in the military contest for the peace of the holy Church of God and the protection of Christ’s flock, watched over the safety of his sheep with the prudent eye of solicitude, like the most discerning shepherd. Through himself and through his people he continually strove to rescue them from the viperous cunning of the invisible enemy.

No mortal tongue could adequately express the greatness of his love for them—in his conversation, at table, and in his reception of them. Yet the abundance of his gifts clearly demonstrates how great it was. To celebrate the solemn memorial of his election, he generously gave the estate of Logniacum and Solium for the use of the canons, so that from them one modius of oil might be paid for the lights of the churches of Saint Mary, Saint John, and Saint Stephen, while Nancradus and Lupinus were to provide the stipends of the brothers.

On the day of his ordination he also assigned to the same brothers, in the county, Gagiacum with all its dependencies, and the vineyard located in the suburb of the city called Circeredus. Whoever held it by charter for the love of God was to pay to those same canonical brothers one modius of wine according to the smaller measure.

In the county of Auxerre he also granted Tauriacum with its dependencies, the estate of Quodpertorium, and one mansus in the estate of Prisciacum. In the county of Sens, above the river Ormentio, he granted one mansus at Germaniacum, and on the stream called Belca, Cervernum, which he himself had bought from Bocardus, the brother of Archbishop Gauterius, together with its servants and all its dependencies.

On the day of his death he was also striving to add something to their stipends, but, while traveling, he was overtaken and cut off by death and breathed his last. He was traveling to Francia in order to appeal to the ears of the royal majesty concerning the estates mentioned above, which had been taken from him as described, hoping that by the king’s authoritative command, at the request of the nobles and in the absence of Richard, the most merciful duke, he might perhaps recover them.

When he reached the city of Soissons—indeed, before he arrived there—he had already begun to feel somewhat ill and had begun to be burdened by the inconvenience of sickness. He was received honorably. When he saw that he was approaching death, a mournful groan burst from his heart, and he poured out abundant showers of tears, crying that although he was in his homeland he would die like an exile and foreigner, without the presence of his beloved flock, and would be committed to the bosom of the earth without the funeral rites of those to whom he had most ardently desired to entrust himself.

Then, as the moment of death approached, and after receiving the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, he commended himself and the people entrusted to him to God, the Savior of all, and gave up his spirit. He departed to the Lord on the Fifth Kalends of August.

There, beside the tomb of his uncle Rodohinus, formerly bishop of that place, Abbo, the revered bishop of the same city, came to perform his burial together with two other bishops. With the communities of various churches assembled and hymns of praise sung, he was fittingly buried and received his resting place in his homeland.

The Church was without a bishop from the Twelfth Kalends of January until the Sixth Kalends of March.

## CHAPTER XLIII — Concerning Betto
Betto, bishop, a native of this our Burgundy—[Col. 0263D] a Burgundian and citizen of the city of Sens—was born under a fortunate auspice to his father Alberic, likewise a Burgundian, and to his mother Angela, a Frankish woman. A monk from childhood, instructed in monastic disciplines and not inadequately imbued with the liberal arts, he became abbot, in the time of Ewrard, whose kinsman he was, of the monastery of Saint Heraclius, the distinguished confessor of Christ. Afterwards, in his own place—that is, the monastery of Saint Columba, to whose service he had been bound—he was appointed superior at the will of the brothers.

Holding this office for a long time with the greatest distinction, he devoted himself especially to cultivating that monastery with laborious buildings and adorning the structure of God’s church with ornaments of gold and silver. [Col. 0264A] In the middle of the church stood a lofty tower which, because of its size at the time when he assumed the office, lacked a roof and appeared to observers to suffer from a certain shortness. He raised it higher, constructed it with beautiful workmanship according to an ingenious design, and covered it with a vaulted roof. For greater strength he ordered other arches to be built beneath the earlier ones, supported on marble columns. He also surrounded the apses of the blessed Lupus, confessor of Christ, and of Saint Columba, virgin and martyr, with gold and silver sheets engraved by skilled craftsmanship. He supplied the monks with various foreign ornaments for their vestments to be worn on solemn days.

At last, observing the unstable and fearful course of our perilous age, and discerning with the provident eye of concern that, amid the hostile [Col. 0264B] ranks of the pagans, the monastery’s structure could not remain inviolable in its existing condition, relying on the most abundant mercy of the Almighty and with the permission of Richard, the great prince and abbot of that place, he undertook a costly work and brought it almost to completion through intense labor. For he laid the foundations of walls with towers around the monastery and raised them as far as the battlements. He would have completed that fortress with tireless zeal had God’s favor not decided to summon him to become a future bishop.

When Geranno, bishop of the see of Auxerre, had been removed from this fellowship of corruptible life by the debt of death, this man, commendable in morals and life, was acclaimed with great insistence by all the clergy and people as they sought him for the episcopate of the Church of Auxerre, because he shone among his associates with these and many other marks of good repute. [Col. 0264C] But he protested that he was unworthy of this and pleaded with all his strength; finally, through the assistance of the aforementioned prince, he obtained the episcopal chair. There, according to the rule of wisdom that he had learned from heaven, he strove to live so perfectly that no teacher’s vast reputation or eloquence of speech could adequately proclaim his greatness, nor any skilled hand record it with a pen.

We, however, touching briefly upon the character of his life, assert this most truthfully: he was outstanding in teachings of wisdom, illustrious in the brightness of holiness, clear-sighted in prudence, flourishing in the graciousness of gravity, clothed in the vigor of frugality, and richly adorned with the kindness of generosity.

It was his custom at mealtime, after the company had taken their places at table, to direct the first serving of food almost entirely to twelve needy people seated in his presence [Col. 0264D] and to others placed elsewhere; immediately another, no smaller serving followed. During that meal, after the conclusion of the divine reading, no one dared to say anything indecent or clownish. Whoever attempted to utter something from his own mouth took care that his words should sound either religious or suitably human.

Shining, therefore, with such lamps of virtue in his life, he pleased both God and all people. From the time of Bishop Geranno, Ragenard, the viscount, had held the villages of Caiacum and Juliacum, situated not very far from the city, under his own authority. This excellent man, however, since he could not wrest them from Ragenard’s jurisdiction either by personal admonition or by persistent entreaty, found a salutary expedient: by presenting gifts of money, he restored them to his own control. Then, perhaps in imitation of his predecessors, so that on the day of his death the rejoicing canons might recall his memory, he granted them the church of Vendosa, the village of Rontonicum, and one mansus at Carboiacum.

While he was planning to rebuild the episcopal residence, which no one had even moderately repaired after the city’s burning, and to undertake diligently whatever might contribute to the honor of Christ’s household, he was severely seized by pleurisy. After being held by it for a long time, while he was guarded by crowds of the faithful and divine praises and readings were celebrated around him, he returned his spirit to God with a confession of the Catholic faith on the very day VI Kalends of March. He was buried in the crypt of the church of Saint Germanus. [Col. 0265A] He sat for 10 years, 11 months, and 14 days. The Church was without a bishop from VI Kalends of March until V Kalends of April, that is, for 33 days.

## CHAPTER XLIV—Concerning Gualdricus

Gualdricus, bishop of the Auxerrois, a native of the region, descended from a noble lineage. His father was Gualdricus and his mother Hemmena. At the very beginning of his life, both parents devoted him to God and Saint Germanus with fervent intention as a future monk, and, after raising him in his father’s household, at the appropriate time they handed him over to the monastic fathers for education.

Among them, within their community, he was sufficiently instructed in literary knowledge. With divine providence protecting and gradually advancing him, he later became an energetic abbot of that place. At the summit of his governance, he strove to balance himself on the scales of equity toward everyone, so that in matters he ought to undertake he would show himself neither too easy nor too difficult. He was keen in intellect, prudent in speech, cautious in administration, perceptive in counsel, and capable both within and without.

Finally, after the death of Bishop Betto, because he shone among his associates with these and many other marks of good repute, by the will and permission of the most excellent lord Richard, the prince, he was sought and acclaimed by the whole clergy and people as their future bishop. He came forth from the monastery, was clothed with sacred anointing, and was consecrated and ordained bishop.

How commendably he presided over the Church of God in the chair of that dignity, and what he accomplished there, must not be concealed in silence; rather, the pen must be instructed to select a few matters from the many. At his departure, he found no episcopal residence in which he might stay. Instead, he withdrew to a dwelling of monks situated within the city, and lived there temporarily until, at his command, the larger dining hall—begun by his predecessor Bishop Herifrid but left unfinished, and later partially supplemented by Bishop Betto—could be completed.

Afterwards he added another wooden dining hall, prepared for summer, beneath the sun’s heat, to cool the bodies of those dining and feasting. Above, beside the stairway of that house of God, he also constructed two stone chambers, one to the south and the other to the north. One was most suitable for eating and sleeping, the other for storing household goods. A chapel was placed between them and dedicated in honor of the Holy Cross.

He also opened the middle crypt of that stairway as an entrance for those passing through from the western side, and in front of it erected a portico built entirely by himself. Between the crypt and the portico he placed elaborate doors of wrought iron, decorated with certain images made from the iron itself and covered everywhere with hides joined by glue and colored with reddish dye, for the protection of the church; opposite them, facing the city street, he placed other unadorned doors.

Finally, inside the church he raised a small platform at a height, with wooden steps, so that by these there might be ascent above and descent below. Often, if he wished to leave the upper house and was reluctant to descend to the lower level, he could from there look more clearly over the flock.

Within the church precinct he also had a single silver crown made for solemn adornment. In honor of Saint Stephen he placed one golden hand polished with gems, and another in honor of Saint Germanus without jeweled ornament; in both he placed relics of those saints, together with an increase of other relics. He also gave to God and Saint Stephen two small crosses of the finest gold. One, made with electrum, shines brightly; inside it he placed relics from the bone of Saint Lawrence. On the outside, in the noble sculpting of the electrum, the passion of that blessed martyr Lawrence is depicted above his gridiron.

Since in that same house of God there was a most precious pallium bearing images of lions, on which was written between the lions in Greek letters, ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ ΔΕΣΠΟΤΗΣ—“Christ the Lord”—he did not rest until he found another pallium of the same likeness. Having bought it, he presented it there, so that the one pallium might seem to answer the other. The second pallium was of a dioprasus color and bore swallows; on it, Phrygian work previously made by Herifrid in gold above the altar shines on feast days.

He also gave one banner adorned with gold, to be carried with the others during public processions. Finally, when he went to Rome with the purpose of making a most salutary prayer, he succeeded, through the greatest entreaties, in obtaining from the apostolic lord John relics of the aforementioned martyr Lawrence and of Saint Eugenia. After bringing them back with him and placing them in the church of the First Martyr, amid considerable crowds of clergy and people accompanying him, with great joy and honor, he rendered immense thanks and praises to Almighty God, by whose generous munificence he, unworthy as he was, had been able to obtain such great relics of the saints in a distant region and bring them here.

Of these relics he gave one portion to the monks of Saint Germanus, who had gone out to meet him. The other portion, which he kept for himself, he divided so that the smaller part retained there might be preserved, while the larger part was carried with him to Varciacum, where he later deposited it in the church of that blessed virgin and martyr. For in the time of his predecessors, a noble basilica shone there in honor of the apostolic man, the blessed Germanus, and was frequented by the most fervent devotion of great crowds of people.

But this same most zealous man, having become a lover of divine worship, acted as a father to all and as the propagator of that church, cultivating it energetically within and without. He arranged it everywhere from its very foundations, adorned and embellished it with roofing, glass windows, and painted ceilings, and rendered it most sacred by dedicating several altars, with the relics of the saints, under their proper titles.

Afterwards he accumulated there whatever was appropriate for divine service: books, vestments, altar cloths, standards, and vessels necessary for the sacrifice of God. Beside the church he built dwellings for himself, his successors, and his household, constructed with beautiful workmanship and suitable both for religious life and for bodily needs.

Likewise, in the same village of Varciacum, he took pains to restore completely two churches ruined by age, one in memory of Saint Peter and the other of Saint Saturninus. At the monastery of Sanxiacum, the church of Saint Baudius, burned by the furious violence of the Normans and later collapsed, he restored at his own expense to the integrity of its former condition, burning with the sacred fire of divine love, and ennobled it with no small offering of gifts. There he gave a reliquary covered with silver plates and gilded, and a large silver cross, similarly fashioned and sculpted in the likeness of the cross of the church of Saint Stephen.

He also offered two excellent pallia upon God’s altar, three cloths or towels, a chalice and paten made of silver, one richly ornamented alb, and a green chasuble with a humeral veil and belt, both adorned with gold. To the monks of that place, who were accustomed to suffer the distress of poverty, he frequently gave much of his own food; and, so that they would not fail in the service of God, he encouraged them through pious words to undertake the labors of body and soul.

Meanwhile, for the restoration of the church of Saint Eusebius, situated in the city’s suburb, he assigned one hundred solidi. He did the same for the church of Saint Gervasius, which lies across the river Yonne, and this already near the end of his life. If God’s will had prolonged his life for some time, he would have restored both churches at his own expense.

In the church of Saint Germanus he frequently distributed many gifts, among which shines a silver panel placed at the entrance of the church before the altar and tomb of Saint John, as well as a silver crown customarily hung before the view of the altar of the holy and glorious confessor of Christ, Germanus. When he was carried lifeless to the tomb, that same place received from his chapter one precious pallium.

Moreover, he established in his church the following most salutary custom: on the feast days of Pentecost, all the diocesan priests of his bishopric, together with their parishioners, were to come with crosses and banners to the principal church of Saint Stephen. After making a circuit around all the abbeys, they were there to be refreshed by the archdeacon with the feasts of spiritual teaching. Then, if the bishop were present, having received the gift of his blessing, they were to return cheerfully to their own places with thanksgiving.

Having thus disclosed these distinguished works by which he shone, the following matters reveal the virtues with which he excelled in spirit. [Col. 0268A] He was an active lover of the divine offices and, at the solemn celebrations of God or the saints, a most exact singer of musical rejoicing. He was joyful in spirit, cheerful in face, pleasant in manner, generous at table, gentle in drinking, mild in patience, restrained in conversation, and composed in every form of decency. He was a lover of clerics, but especially of monks, by whose studies and way of life he had been instructed from the beginning. He valued the fellowship of soldiers, but he had an even greater affection and more lavish generosity toward his relatives. At suitable times he devoted himself to prayers, and at other times he applied himself to conversations with his faithful, in matters appropriate to himself and to them.

Every day, after the completion of Mass, when many poor people had been gathered, he himself attended as distributor of bread and wine amid the chanting of psalms. He gave each person, according to that person’s condition or stature, either a whole loaf or half a loaf, together with an excellent cup of wine. Although he did this at all times, during Lent he distributed more to more people, giving denarii to some, apart from the provision made on the day of the Lord’s Supper, when clothing was given and brighter food and drink were served.

We have said little of the many things by which he flourished in life, most renowned before the world.
