But the Lord God granted that these and other, greater deeds should be written for his successors. Thus, honored by the pious labors of a blessed life, he was seized by illness and returned his soul to the Creator. He received a noble burial for his body in the church of Saint Germanus. He sat in the episcopal chair for 15 years and 24 days, and passed to Christ on XI Kalends [Col. 0268C] of May. The Church was without a bishop from the day of his death until XIV Kalends of June, that is, for twenty-seven days.

From the blessed Palladius until the twelfth year and two months of the episcopate of Lord Guido III—that is, until the Kalends of August—on which day that same bishop raised from their own tombs, with hymns and praises, the bodies of the holy bishops Palladius and Treticus, long buried in the church of Saint Eusebius, so that they might be venerated by the people and assist them more readily, and placed them upon the altar: there are 325 years, 3 months, and 6 days, apart from the years of the two bishops Theoderannus and Quintilianus, who are included in this catalogue and counted in its heading.

## CHAPTER XLV—Concerning Guido

[Col. 0268D] Guido, by the operation of God’s mercy alone, became bishop of Auxerre. He was born in the region of Sens, of his father Boso and his mother Abigail. In the toys of his earliest age he was handed over and tonsured for the church of Saint Stephen of Auxerre, under the governance of Lord Bishop Herifrid. There he was instructed, as far as possible, in both divine and human letters, and remained there until he reached full maturity.

Afterwards, setting aside all other matters, with God protecting him, he devoted himself to the service of King Rodulf and his wife Emma. While he was staying there, upon the death of Bishop Waldrichus he was immediately invited to episcopal honor. Through the election of the clergy and people, the king, at the queen’s request, granted him the chair.

Thus, on XIV Kalends of January, he was ordained at Sens; finally, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, he was enthroned, as is customary, in the church of Saint Stephen of Auxerre, coming from the monastery of Saint Germanus. Although the property he received was meager, he worked as diligently as he could to increase and adorn the church over which he presided. But so that what he accomplished there might not be consigned to oblivion, nor be removed from the church’s possession through the greed of successors and ministers, we have judged it right to insert it into this little work, knowing that the one who acts will not lack his reward.

First, through a royal decree and with the king’s agreement, he restored to its former place the village of Crevennum, which had been taken from Saint Stephen, together with its dependencies. He gave half of that village to the canons, for the absolution of the soul of that bishop; the other half he gave to the aforementioned canons on the day of the death of the aforesaid queen, for the commemoration of the soul of the aforementioned bishop. The fishermen, however, were to remain in the bishop’s service by order of the canons’ provost.

Observing there a cheap ambo, he placed above it one honorably arranged with crypts, constructed with distinction. Beside it he established an altar in honor of Saint John the Evangelist, Saint Lawrence the Martyr, and all the Saints, so that Mass might be celebrated there by the bishop, if he were present, and by the clergy of the church. Through their intercession, he most devoutly consecrated it so that the needs of the living and the dead might be aided.

He ordained that on these three days the canons should annually be refreshed for the remedy of his soul. He obtained from the archbishop and the bishops subject to him the tithes of three churches: one at Aggliviacum, consecrated in honor of Saint Stephen; another at Matriacum, in honor of Saint Felix; and another built in honor of Saint Martin. He established that from these three churches three meals should be provided for the brothers: one on the feast of Saint John the Evangelist, II Nones of May, when he was cast into a cauldron of boiling oil; another on the Octave of Saint Lawrence; and the third on the feast of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist. Whatever remained from the tithes of the churches was to serve as the canons’ stipend, for the acquisition of absolution for his soul.

Finally, the provost of the canons of Saint Stephen of Auxerre was to choose priests for those churches with the agreement of the brothers. They were to receive the tithes of the churches faithfully for their own use and that of the canons, and render synodal service to the archbishop of Sens, as did the surrounding churches; nothing else was to be demanded by the archbishop or his ministers.

To make this firm and lasting forever, Archbishop Archembaud of Sens confirmed the written document with his own hand and asked that it be strengthened by the hands of his fellow bishops. He ordered it also to be confirmed by the names of his archdeacons Prodagius, Bernardus, and Theodericus, and of the other canons.

He splendidly adorned the silver panels by leaving their bases uncovered. He also made seven excellent lamps there from silver, each containing, including its shaft, fifteen pounds; two candelabra adorned with silver; two silver-plated shafts on which golden crosses were carried; two silver crowns weighing ten pounds; and an excellent *cliotedrum* [a term for a liturgical stand or furnishing, the precise object is uncertain] constructed of gold and silver.

He raised high the entrance which Waldrichus had begun to build, adorning it with a vaulted ceiling and painting on the walls the hosts of paradise and the torments of the infernal world. Thus he made the entrance pleasing to those who looked upon it. There he buried his own body, but later ordered the burial moved before the face of the Savior and the altar of Saint Lawrence, which, after the burning of the city and church, he had honorably adorned and dedicated through his own labor.

Above that chapel he built another in honor of the saints whose memory was scarcely or rarely celebrated within or outside the city. Their names are: Matthew, Thomas, Philip, Matthias, Dionysius, Maurice, Ignatius, Demetrius, Desiderius, Jerome, Sylvester, Augustine, Vigilius, Eugenia, Anastasia, Margaret, Lucy, Agatha, Genovefa, and Columba. Through their intercession, the city might be protected both outside and within.

He gave it an estate at Cavanni, a village acquired by Hildebert, servant of Saint Stephen, to provide lamps there night and day for the remedy of his soul. That estate was to remain in the hands of the priest who celebrated the solemn Mass above or below. He also ordained that the person who held the vineyard he had planted in the place called Plantas should, on the feast of each of the saints named above, when the canons celebrated a vigil and Mass, pay six sextarii of wine to provide charity on his behalf.

After the two parents or his faithful persons to whom he had left the aforesaid vineyard, the canons were to receive it into their possession and themselves fulfill what he had instituted on his behalf. If they failed to do so, his reward was not to be taken from him, and God would demand an account from them.

Finally, through the intervention of Lord Hugh, duke of France, and by a royal decree confirmed by the hand of King Louis, he restored to the church, with great zeal and labor, the abbeys of Saint Julian—namely, Saint Amator and Saint Mary—which had long been withdrawn from the authority of the bishops, together with the churches it had lost.

He most honorably surrounded the central altar of Saint Stephen with purple completely covered with golden images. Seeing also that the church precinct was not sufficiently large, he built a new arch near the altar between the two doors. By opening the walls, he constructed two oratories there in the form of a cross, so that more people might serve God there.

While he was doing this, through what I suppose was the envy of the devil, the old wall, together with the new one, collapsed from arch to arch down to its foundations. He did not delay in having it rebuilt. For just as the aforementioned church of Saint Stephen had been completely destroyed after the fire, so afterwards he raised it again from its foundations, with greater beauty than before, adorned with large glass windows and a vaulted ceiling.

He also rebuilt the two oratories on the right and left according to the earlier design, adding crypts to the oratories themselves, in which he also established altars, so that arriving people might find places where they could linger in tearful sighs, praying for and obtaining the mercy of God and of the saints in whose honor those altars had been established.

Thus enlarged and adorned with the greatest elegance, this same basilica displayed the form of a holy cross in its upper parts. In the middle of the church he established galleries and placed there the face of the Savior affixed to the cross. He also adorned the altar with a raised silver panel bearing images and other paintings, consecrating it on V Ides of August in honor of the Holy Cross, Saint Matthew the apostle and evangelist, and Saint Romanus, soldier and martyr.

The aforementioned Bishop Guido was a man relying upon simplicity and possessing moderate prudence. As far as he was able, he wished not so much to rule over all as to benefit them. Among his other works of decency, he composed with his own hand responsories with antiphons to be sung on the solemnity of Saint Julian the Martyr. They had a melody modeled on the harmony of the glorious Germanus, especially because, as is found in that bishop’s deeds, the most holy pontiff, when the Lord revealed it to him, showed that the previously unknown solemn birthday of that martyr was to be celebrated by all.

Thus, as long as he lived, he was a lover of the religious and good, and a stern reprover of the wicked. He sat in the episcopate for 29 years and died in peace on VIII Ides of January. He was buried in the larger church of Saint Stephen, which he himself had rebuilt. The city was without a bishop for 3 months and 8 days.

## CHAPTER XLVI—Concerning Richard

Richard, a native of Auxerre, was born of his father John and his mother Mary. From childhood he was a monk of Saint Germanus. As happened with several of the men mentioned above, he was requested from that bishop’s monastery by both clergy and people and appointed bishop.

He was a man of excessive simplicity and limited ability, and for that reason far inferior to the achievements of his predecessor in the advancement of the Church entrusted to him. [Col. 0271C] He lived during the reigns of King Lothair the Younger and his son Louis, who brought the reign of his line to an end.

He sat in the episcopate for 9 years, 1 month, and 2 days, and died on XVII Kalends of June. He was buried in the church of the blessed Germanus. The city was without a bishop for 7 months and 24 days.

## CHAPTER XLVII—Concerning Heribertus

Heribertus, a Frank, was the son of Hugh, duke—surnamed the Great—by a concubine named Raingarda. He obscured his paternal nobility by the disparity of his maternal origin. For through the aforementioned Hugh he was born the brother of Hugh, later king, and of the two dukes of Burgundy, namely Otto and Henry. The more elegant he appeared in bodily form, the more inclined he proved to be toward worldly desires and pleasures.

Nevertheless, he showed the religious, especially clerics and monks, the reverence of the highest honor. During his pontificate, therefore, his brother, Duke Henry, who was a lover of all religious observance, entrusted the monastery of the blessed Germanus to Lord Maiolus as abbot, so that he might establish there the path of the regular rule, just as he was known to have done in many places, both in Italy and in Gaul, for the monks.

For a long time the place had been governed without an abbot by provosts. Maiolus gladly received it and corrected to the letter, with regular discipline, every deviation he found there. Afterwards the holy and venerable man Maiolus placed there a worthy man, Heldricus, as abbot. He too instructed the aforesaid place in the path of the regular way of the blessed Benedict.

The aforementioned bishop and his brother, Duke Henry, loved him greatly, together with their own people. But, as we have said, relying excessively upon worldly pomp, Heribertus gave soldiers more generous gifts than was just, so much so that Odo, count of Chartres, and Heribertus, count of Troyes, submitted to his authority out of gratitude for his benefactions.

Finally, in his own diocese, without any compelling need arising from fear, but rather through the wantonness of hunting, he established and fortified two permanent castles: one at Rivo Lanuto, near the village of Ferredi; the other ten miles from the city, called Tuciacum. He claimed that these castles would be of great and lasting benefit not only to the church entrusted to him but also to the defense of the entire region.

But all in vain. From the beginning, he reaped the corruption of human flesh’s ambition, because “God knows the lofty from afar” (Psalm 137:6). What happened afterwards was very different from what any mortal could have expected.

Eventually, through tyrannical rapacity, the castles became instruments for the destruction of that province, and their inhabitants became rebels against the bishops and usurpers of ecclesiastical property. As for the ornaments of the church, which were then very numerous—both in books by many authors and in other furnishings—he extended his hand less aggressively, so that he did not root them out and scatter them. This was in part commendable: although he did not increase them through his own efforts, he nevertheless did not diminish them excessively.

According to ancient custom, he consented that the ecclesiastical and monastic institutions of his predecessors should be maintained by the clerics with willing spirit.

He lived during the reigns of his brother Hugh and Hugh’s son Robert; during the pontificates of the Roman bishops Marinus, surnamed Peter, Sergius, and Bruno, surnamed Boniface; during the reigns of the emperors Otto II and Otto III; and during the archiepiscopates of Sens of the excellent man Anastasius and Sewinus.

He sat in the episcopate for 25 years, 7 months, and 16 days. He died at the castle of Tuciacum, which, as we said above, he himself had built, on X Kalends of September. This greatly displeased certain religious people, because, when he began to fall ill, he had not immediately ordered himself to be brought to his proper see.

He was buried in the church of Saint Mary within the city walls. The city was without a bishop for 7 months and 15 days.

## CHAPTER XLVIII—Concerning John
[Col. 0272D] John, by nationality Auxerrois, was born of his father Ansaldus and his mother Raingarda, parents indeed of modest station; but, in accordance with the prophetic significance of his own name, by the grace of God bestowed upon him he flourished exceedingly in nobility of mind, which is more precious than the flesh. From the natural disposition of his earliest age he devoted himself to literary studies, in which he was most brilliantly trained and distinguished himself. Later he was among the pupils of Gerbert—a man, however learned, who was then archbishop of Reims, afterward of Ravenna, and finally attained the chair of the Roman See and the papal tiara.

John strengthened the summit of his knowledge of the liberal arts by public speaking. Thereafter he first shone forth as a most effective teacher of boys; then, as a distinguished tutor, and he was advanced to the dignity of the archdeaconate. For when the aforesaid bishop Heribert had departed this life, certain clerics—whom the loftiness of the world had enticed and driven to this—sought to force their way into the episcopal chair by the arrogance of family connections and the public offering of money. When Henry the duke had urged King Robert to consecrate as bishop a certain man, especially one Guido who was excessively worldly, and the king, as he was being urged, had given his assent, while Sewinus, the metropolitan bishop of Sens, had already been summoned to carry out the customary rite, the matter happened to be suspended.

The entire assembly of the canons and brothers therefore unanimously complained about this, and the rest of the common people who possessed sound judgment testified that the proceeding was wrongful, chiefly because, according to ancient custom, the pastor of the Church ought to be appointed by the election of the clergy. When the archbishop learned this, he returned to his own place, saying that he did not wish to set a lion or a wolf in the sheepfold of Christ in place of a shepherd.

Meanwhile a messenger was sent to the king, and the complaint was laid before him, together with the common decree of both classes of people, of either sex and every rank: namely, that John, by the choice of them all, was fit to be bishop. When the king heard this, he most willingly consented, for he loved John generously on account of his learning and piety; nor, in truth, did he wish to appoint a bishop contrary to law and justice, without the election of the clergy and people. As soon as the king’s will became known, the citizens once again recalled the archbishop, and thus John was consecrated according to custom and established in the pontifical office, to the joy of all.

[Col. 0273A] Once he had become bishop, the elevation of the episcopal dignity did not change in him the conduct of his former humility. Rather, he strove with every diligence to appear humbler than before: in teaching, in conversation, in his clothing, in the frugality of his food, and in his participation with the brethren in the common hours. He so fashioned himself as the humblest of men that scarcely anyone could recognize—unless he was performing the principal office—that the man whom he saw had been a bishop.

He was not so much frequent as assiduous in psalmody, and watchful and energetic in the vigils of prayer. For he spent most nights alone in the church, performing prostrations (*metanoeae*) beside the altar of blessed Stephen, until the brothers’ common morning office was announced.

He therefore gave to the sustenance of the canonical brothers five altars with their revenues: Pulverenus, Partiaci, Gargiaci, Monasteriolus, and Campiniacus. Under threat of anathema he forbade anyone—whether any of his successors in the episcopate or any other person—to presume to invalidate any gift of his generosity, lest, through want and poverty, the clergy of the church should be unable to perform offices worthy of God, although it was known that in this very see the official ministry of the clergy had formerly flourished most fully and more splendidly than elsewhere. But Scripture bears witness: “From the source where the good man prospers, there the wicked man wastes away.”

Alas! Wicked citizens mocked him because their bishop lacked the arrogance of worldly pride and was not related to them by blood; and, laughing and jeering, they derided both his lineage and other matters concerning him.

[Col. 0273B] Nevertheless, God, who chooses the mind rather than the race, foresaw that vengeance for such things would eventually be exacted upon them. For afterward secular pride and pomp destroyed those same men who had disparaged the humblest of men, together with their lineage, down to the ground.

He confirmed by his authority the privileges which both Heribert and the other predecessors of his had granted perpetually to blessed Germanus concerning the altars established in his diocese; he also gave him vineyards and excellent volumes of books. From him, too, he humbly obtained permission to deserve burial there.

In January he began to fall ill, having been seized by bodily pain. When he had been brought almost to the final breath of life, he was carried away in ecstasy and saw a very beautiful vision. Immediately he summoned the illustrious man and his dearest friend Achardus, then provost of the monastery of blessed Germanus and afterward its abbot, and related the vision to him in these words:

“Just now,” he said, “my Lord Jesus Christ appeared to me, and with him the most blessed Germanus and many other most radiant men. Their presence brought me the greatest relief from my pain and peace of soul. They also promised me that, as soon as I am summoned from the body, by the mercy of the Lord I shall immediately be joined to their company.”

After saying this, he uttered the names of the saints in prayer with scarcely moving lips; then, with frequent sighs and tearful eyes, gazing toward heaven, he departed from the body on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February [21 January]. He was buried at Saint Germanus, not within the church but outside, beside the wall, as he himself had requested, in order to display humility.

[Col. 0274A] Later, when the monks enlarged the church, he was suitably relocated within its enclosure, before the altar, namely that of blessed Peter. He had sat in the episcopate for one year, seven months, and ten days; and the city remained without a bishop for one year, one month, and sixteen days.

## CHAPTER XLIX — Concerning Hugh

Hugh of Chalon was born of his father Lambert, a most venerable count, and his mother Adelaide, a woman of the noblest birth. The aforementioned Count Lambert had built the most splendid monastery of Paredus, endowed it with very generous resources, and rests there honorably.

After his father’s death, Hugh was traveling to the royal court and had to pass through the city of Auxerre. Turning aside there for the sake of prayer, he entered the church of blessed Stephen the protomartyr. It was then the first hour of the day. While he was devoting himself to prayer, he heard the choir sweetly resounding with the hymn of that hour. Since he was a man of devout heart and readily moved to tears, he later reported that he had said:

“O Lord, king of heaven and earth, creator of all good things and distributor of honors, if your foreknowledge has wished me for this purpose to receive episcopal dignity from you at some time, I beg that your will be done in me here.”

And afterward it happened just as he had asked. From boyhood many had hoped that, because of his nobility, he would attain one of the episcopal sees of the cities.

[Col. 0274B] When Bishop John departed this life and a dispute arose concerning the restoration of a bishop, with Duke Henry favoring him and King Robert consenting, the aforesaid Hugh was elected according to custom and consecrated in the church of blessed Germanus; from there he was given as bishop to the principal see of Auxerre.

He had a brother who was not his equal in lineage, but who, by hereditary right, could have governed their paternal possessions. Consequently, being entangled in many disturbances and occupied by the concerns of both dignities, he was less able to benefit either one individually.

It happened also at that time—after the death of Duke Henry, who had married Hugh’s full sister—that the very powerful Burgundians became rebels against King Robert. They refused in every way to remain subject to his authority or obey his commands. Moreover, they seized and usurped for themselves the sees and castles of the aforementioned duke, their king’s maternal uncle.

At last Hugh, preserving unshakable fidelity to his king together with all his people, endured the hostility of the others for a long time and with great courage. Often prevented from entering his own see, he remained content with his paternal possessions, supported by the assistance of those who loved him greatly.

Whenever it happened that he had to fight those aforementioned foolish enemies, he always emerged victorious in every respect, and not without reason, following the apostle’s command: “Fear the Lord, honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17); and again: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities” (Romans 13:1).

And although Scripture always says, “Peace with the good, and war with vices,” and although it is more useful to allow scandal to arise than to abandon the truth, if it cannot be otherwise, nevertheless, because of fear of this matter, he went to the Roman pope and loudly proclaimed that he bitterly repented. He cried out that he was unworthy and guilty of exercising pastoral care and pontifical dignity.

[Col. 0274C] The pope then gave him the following written response:

“John, by the grace of God bishop of the Roman See, to all the sons of the Church throughout the world.

“No greater offense can exist in the Catholic Church than to suppose that any stain of sin, especially in one who repents, cannot be removed by the key granted by the Lord to Peter. We ought to bring before the eyes of our mind the fall of that first shepherd himself: when he denied his Master, as soon as he repented, he not only did not lose the rank or dignity of the apostolic summit, but rather Christ afterward entrusted him more clearly with the guardianship of his own fold. This, we believe, was nothing other than a remedy for those who had fallen.

“Therefore, for our brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, who confesses his sins to God and to us and declares himself guilty, we promise—God being the guarantor—that he shall obtain complete pardon of indulgence, in accordance with the promise of the same Lord, who said: ‘I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance’ (Matthew 9:13). For this reason he ought to become especially dear to us, because, corrected by the fear of God, he appears most humble, and because God rests in such people.”

Moreover, King Robert, having gathered together a strong army from both the Frankish and Norman peoples, and having with him Richard, their most powerful duke, occupied and devastated a very large part of Burgundy.

When he first arrived at the city of Auxerre and wished to capture it—a thing which, it is said, had never before happened to that city—the citizens of the city resisted him bravely. Then, when the entire royal phalanx, and the king himself in armor, advanced to storm the castle of blessed Germanus, he was terrified by divine command. Returning from there after much slaughter of his men, he penetrated as far as the upper reaches of the Saône in Burgundy, with the aforementioned Hugh accompanying him.

[Col. 0275A] When the king returned to France, he accomplished nothing beyond the devastation of the region. After some years, however, the leading men of Burgundy came peacefully into the king’s favor. Nevertheless, through Hugh’s counsel, he arranged whatever the king had decided to do, and he most willingly granted him whatever it pleased him to receive.

To restore or strengthen peace, he therefore convened a council of bishops and an innumerable multitude of nobles and commoners in the county which he governed, Chalon, at a place called Viridunum. There, too, relics of the saints, brought from various regions, bestowed various healings upon the sick.

He likewise convened another council for the same purpose in the district of Auxerre, at Airiacum, a village of blessed Germanus. King Robert was present there with bishops and abbots, together with innumerable sacred relics from nearly the whole province. When certain people asked that the body of the glorious Germanus be brought there, Bishop Hugh replied:

“Far be it that the bones of a man without equal should ever be moved for any reason.”

The others who heard this gladly agreed.

In the same way he frequently caused councils to be held throughout all the surrounding places, for example in the districts of Dijon, Beaune, and Lyon.

In his time the city of Auxerre was disastrously consumed by fire, and human possessions were reduced to ashes, except for the church of the martyr Saint Alban, built by blessed Germanus. Then the principal church of the protomartyr Stephen collapsed completely. The same bishop immediately began to rebuild it on a larger scale, with curved crypts and hewn stones fitted together with care; for previously it had been made of more delicate material and the smallest stones.

When the church building had already been raised higher, the city was again set on fire, but the new work on the church remained unharmed.

[Col. 0275B] In approximately the nine hundred and sixth year from the Passion of the Lord, the monastery of Melerus, at the command of Heldricus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus, was honorably enlarged and elevated through the agency of the monk Lord Tealdus, who succeeded him as third in governance. It was greatly adorned both with buildings and possessions and with furnishings of gold and silver; and it is established that it was solemnly consecrated by the same bishop, as was fitting.

At that consecration he imposed an anathema forbidding anyone thereafter to presume to inflict violence, injury, or any wrong upon the property of that church for any reason or occasion.

Afterward it happened that the faithful, and especially the aforementioned brother Tealdus, who had exalted that place, requested that the body of the outstanding bishop Desiderius of Auxerre—believed to have been buried in the church of Saint Germanus—be brought there.

As usually happens in such matters, some time passed amid the conflicting wishes of the parties. At last, through the bishop’s efforts, the monks, the rest of the clergy, and the people of the entire district granted the requested transfer.

The venerable body of the aforesaid bishop was placed in a silver chest weighing one hundred pounds, and thus, with the rejoicing of the whole people, it was carried honorably to the monastery of Melerus, also called the Valley of Pentane. There it is known to have been placed in the church of Mary, Mother of God. At that place, through his intercession, many benefits are granted to those who ask.

[Col. 0275C] This, too, must be committed to memory: originally, two churches had been built there by Quintilianus, a most noble man. One was in honor of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of the Lord; the other was in veneration of the outstanding bishop Germanus. These churches are now joined within a single, more spacious enclosure and precisely divided among thirteen altars, each with its own apse.

That place has been renowned from the beginning for miracles of power and for the healings of the sick. It often happened—as we ourselves saw—that when devoted faithful came to that place from far away, carrying unlit candles in their hands, more or less a stadium before reaching the monastery, flame-devouring fire would burst forth from those same candles.

If anyone, however, committed fraud by force or theft against any of the goods belonging to that place, the ruler and avenger of the just immediately and most clearly manifested himself; and whatever was faithfully requested there was obtained in abundance.

Furthermore, in the thirty-seventh year of his ordination, the aforementioned Hugh went to Jerusalem to pray with considerable honor at the Lord’s sepulchre. Returning from there cheerfully, and relying upon his own see, he lived more gently.

He afterward took greater care to adorn the seat of the mother church, which he had previously elevated with buildings, and he worked more diligently to distinguish it with gifts suitable for God’s service. Thus, by the cooperation of God’s grace, he deserved to provide it with two vestments suitable to episcopal dignity, of marvelous craftsmanship, workmanship, and value.

One of these, which appeared as if of lesser value, was throughout most becomingly adorned with marvelous Phrygian gold: its amice about the neck, and its stole and maniples in their proper places, covered the neck down to the lowest part. The purple chasuble displayed great eagles woven all around in scarlet, and its surface glittered with star-like tracery of Phrygian gold.

The other—its character is attested by the munificence of Emperor Otto, from whose hand it was given to him—was such that, as is said of the head of holy Aaron, a golden plate interwoven with pearls and precious stones in the amice illuminated the high priest’s head like a royal diadem. A linen palla, gleaming about the breast with a golden rational, and extending from the knees to the ankles in all-silk fabric with a gilded border, wonderfully enclosed the pontiff’s feet.

[Col. 0275D] To say something adequate about the stole and the maniple would sound like a fable, since both of them, made entirely of the purest gold and adorned with pomegranates, displayed a work of the most elegant craftsmanship beyond explanation.

The chasuble, however, of an ethereal color and bearing a palm in Phrygian work, honorably displayed the image of the superhumeral and rational in the manner of an archiepiscopal pallium.

Moreover, the bishop wore within the Holy of Holies all the vestments that were present among them and were excellent in their proper and fitting manner.

He again honored the church of Saint Stephen with other necessary furnishings for the church. Among these he gave a missal inscribed in golden letters, sufficiently suitable for the service and office of bishops. He also gave one excellent chalice with a paten, an imposing work of gilded silver, remarkable for its size and weight.

He further had two bells of great size made in the same church; in proportion to their size they were worthy of God, harmoniously attuned and fitted with a sweet modulation.

Among the other matters, we judged that the following must not be consigned to oblivion: at the castle of Varzy, which was under his own authority and that of his predecessors, the church of Saint Eugenia had been founded by Bishop Gualdricus, of blessed memory. He had also brought there relics of that holy virgin, obtained from John the Apostolic.

Because, over the passage of many years, the negligence of certain fathers had gradually crept in, the church was scarcely visited with any regularity of divine service. Hugh, by God’s gift, restored it to such glory that work upon it, both inside and outside, is visible down to the present day.

[Col. 0276A] He had the walls whitewashed and adorned the church with glass windows and ceilings; he also donated there hangings, books, and ornaments of various kinds. At the same time, from the revenues of his own property, he selected approved persons of the canonical order and permanently appointed ten prebendaries for divine service.

Likewise, at the castle of Conada, belonging to his mother church, he built a church of the holy martyr Lawrence. Giving from his own resources, he ordered that the worship of the Divinity be increased and that the care and services of God’s faithful be honorably maintained by the hands of priests.

He gave to the sustenance of the canonical brothers the *paredae* (dues) of all their churches in the bishopric of Auxerre; likewise, he allowed them to retain the dues of the granaries—that is, the *grangaticum*—which belonged to him. He also ordered that, in the woods of Saint Stephen, the pasturage tax for their pigs should never be collected.

At that time he also established that every year the same canons should celebrate the feast of the holy martyr Vincent with solemn ceremony until the eighth day.

He also gave for the sustenance of the canonical brothers a part of the village of Cravant, which he had purchased from Archdeacon Arduino.

When he began to fall ill and realized that he would not live much longer, he ordered the church of blessed Mary—said to hold the first rank within the city walls—to be honorably rebuilt from its foundations with his own resources. He nevertheless left this work unfinished.

[Col. 0276B] Seeing that his death was approaching, he devotedly withdrew to the monastery of blessed Germanus. There he put on the monastic habit, and on the fourth day thereafter, namely on the day before the Nones of November [4 November], he reached the end of his present life.

He had ruled the bishopric for forty years, eight months, and four days; and the city remained without a bishop for thirty-six days.

## CHAPTER L — Concerning Heribert II

The second Heribert, who is number fifty in the catalogue of bishops, was an Auxerrois by nationality, the son of Vauterius and Hemma. His predecessor Hugh chose him for the episcopate; afterward King Henry, coming into Burgundy with a very large army, customarily granted him the bishopric.

On the day of his ordination, when, according to ecclesiastical custom, he was leaning upon the episcopal chair and being carried on the shoulders of nobles to the mother church of the holy protodeacon, he gave the Church a large and excellent pallium, commonly called a dorsale. It is visibly preserved to the present day among the other ornaments of that Church.

In the time of this bishop, Lord Pope Leo came to Gaul and held a council in the metropolitan city of Reims. There he notably reproved certain bishops face to face before the Church for the heresy of simony. Among them were Gelduinus, archbishop of Sens, and Hugh of Langres, infamous for the vices of many iniquities. Though they had often been reverently admonished and corrected by their own fathers, as was fitting, they clung wickedly to the mire of their depravity and were almost apostates.

The pope removed them from authority over their sees and left them to prolonged penitence for the examination of their reprobate lives, committing them to divine judgment.

[Col. 0276C] This bishop followed the pope on his return as far as the city of Toul, in which that blessed man had formerly sat as bishop before becoming pope. Refreshed by his conversation, instructed by his sacred exhortations, and gladdened by his blessings, Heribert returned peacefully to his own see, quite cheerful and joyful.

Not long afterward, however, he was harassed for some time by Robert, duke of Burgundy, who at that time still ruled the city of Auxerre. Inflated by his own authority and by the fraternal power he shared with King Henry, the duke caused him many troubles, especially on account of his clergy.

Then, renouncing worldly affairs through a certain impatience and anguish of spirit and longing for eternal things, after he had presided over the episcopate for thirteen years, Heribert became a monk at Saint Savior in the district of Sens.

There he lived many subsequent years according to the rule in God’s service. After Goffridus had been appointed his successor and was successfully occupying his chair, Heribert departed to Christ on the seventh day before the Kalends of February [26 January] and was buried in the same monastery.

## CHAPTER LI — Concerning Goffridus

Goffridus, a bishop worthy of blessed memory, was the son of Hugh, viscount of Nevers, from the castle called Campus Alemannus (“the Alemannic Field”). His mother, Ermengardis by name, was descended from consular men.

King Henry, who had this man as an honorable cleric in his palace, granted us—through the working of divine mercy and with our whole Church praising him—a bishop who was truly necessary and useful in every respect.

For, to use the entire clergy as witnesses of how great he will be on that day, when he entered the Church he found the presbytery so bare of vestments, the body of the church so stripped of ornaments, and the choir so deprived of copes that the choir could sing triumphantly with only five threadbare garments and a sixth which was good. No hangings except one dorsale covered the walls, apart from certain woolen pieces and a few small cloths which remained for the Church’s use. Finally, there were no pontifical vestments in which he could celebrate Mass becomingly.

He received the church in an unadorned state, but he labored so that his successor would receive it in a different condition. He gladdened the choir with thirteen respectable copes and decorated the walls with five royal dorsalia. He also adorned the order of those entering the altar on feast days and ordinary days with suitable vestments.

[Col. 0277A] He gave four purple chasubles, a splendid dalmatic, very fine tunics, white stoles, and numerous costly manuterga. He gave a silver altar, and likewise all the following objects in silver: a chalice, a censer with its incense box, two candlesticks, two flasks, a pitcher for holy water, and a pitcher for washing the priests’ hands. He also gave a towel and a basin for receiving the water from those washing their hands. Moreover, he renewed this volume, *The Deeds of the Bishops*.

If all his other benefactions, which ought worthily to be added to these, were still to be written out in full, a large skin would be needed to contain them all in number and extent.

For since love is more widely diffused among all the Lord’s commandments, and since his love for his clergy was shown to be no small thing—not only in the most agreeable affability but also in the very sharing of the table—even the unwary could easily recognize that same love in him.

Beyond the pleasures of regular meals, he daily refreshed not a few assembled clerics with the noble joy of his company. What love could be broader than this?

We must nevertheless continue writing about him, so that some unjust judges do not say that I am flattering the truth. In this matter he was accused almost as though guilty. Yet, as we very often heard him lay open his conscience under solemn protestation, we believe—and assert that it ought to be believed—not so much for the sake of excusing him as because of the evident truth of the matter:

[Col. 0277B] namely, that he was an enemy to none of them in his heart and was infected with hatred toward none. Rather, those who were conscious that they had deserved his anger laid this charge upon him, although he himself neither consented to their evil deeds nor did they submit to his correction.

For, to speak in the faith of God and the saints, with all those as witnesses who knew his will truthfully, his mind and spirit were always such that no good man was not perfectly dear to him, and no bad man, if he could neither correct nor oppose him, failed at least to displease him.

Indeed, unless he loved his clergy, how did he give them those excellent lands near Saint Priscus? How did he give them the pleasant and fertile estate of Arlacum, which the most illustrious Hugh the knight left to him at his death because he held it from the bishop as part of his fief? Unless he loved his clergy greatly, how could he have given these things to them all together?

It is written: “You will know them by their fruits.” Let his successors in the episcopate now take heed, mindful of him, of how highly they too ought to honor his memory. For he acquired through labor things which they may enjoy in peace.

The customary rights of the castle of Conada and the episcopal revenues—which, whether through negligence or carelessness, the wealthy power of earlier bishops had disdained to visit and had ceased to reclaim, almost to the point of oblivion—had meanwhile been violently seized by the greed of certain plunderers, who had diverted those revenues to themselves as though they were owed to them. Goffridus restored them courageously, with great cunning, exertion, and sweat, after they had already passed into another’s jurisdiction.

[Col. 0277C] In the same way he recovered two abbeys situated in the suburb of the city, namely those of blessed Mary, the Mother of our Lord, and of Saint Amator, which had been anciently handed over and assigned to the authority of the bishops. A certain tyrant had received them from a bishop as a benefice, possessed them for a long time, and afterward granted them by hereditary right to one of his sons, namely the bishop of Autun.

The upright man repeatedly summoned approved persons, as we ourselves saw, both clerics and laymen; he examined and compared the judgments of the sacred canons; and by a settled and firm decision he restored the abbeys from unlawful domination to their just and rightful authority.

It is also appropriate to add that he displayed such skill in secular affairs and always used such freedom and courage of speech that even princes did not dare to lie in his hearing.

The third abbey, that of Saint Eusebius, had been established in the canonical order from its beginning but had declined up to his time and had by then been destroyed. He restored it, reinstating the canons and the abbot, as is recorded in the privilege of that restoration.

He also cleansed Varzy—because it is a refuge of bishops and a pleasant place—of its enemies at the outset; then he successfully rebuilt it and finally fortified it inside and outside with the protection of walls. For as long as these things benefit future bishops, so long do we wish him to be surrounded by the blessings of all.

Finally, if they wish to imitate his good works, we beg them never to consign to oblivion his devout humility, by which every day throughout Lent he was accustomed to wash the feet of thirteen poor people with his own hands and minister to them while fasting, and also to clothe those same people at Easter.

[Col. 0277D] For the flourishing and perpetual use of these poor people, he valiantly recovered through victorious struggle the chapel of Saint Peregrinus, situated on the riverbank near the city, together with its dependencies, which had been seized by the prolonged injustice of the aforementioned invaders.

But while these matters delight only bishops in whom concern for their own interests remains, we must again take care lest, by delaying too long, we incur more enemies over matters which concern almost everyone.

Therefore, to bring forward still more of his many benefactions, how great was this achievement: when this church had been consumed by fire almost two years before the death of that most beloved father, he himself, with constant care and diligence, restored it within the short space of a single year. He supplied the carpenters, servants, and other workers, and personally supervised their labor.

He distributed the five windows in the vault of the highest chancel among five of his retainers, so that each might glaze one. He also designed the sixth, larger and most important of all, which illumined the altar of Saint Alexander, so that his chaplain might execute it.

[Col. 0278A] Nor is it right to remain silent about the crown of the wall enclosing the altar and bearing the images of the holy bishops. He placed it before the eyes of the singing priests not only to exclude empty and unlawful sights from them, but also so that, if anyone weighed down by vanity or weariness should be carried outside himself—as often happens through the weakness of our nature—that present vision and the open remembrance of so many good things in the paintings might restore his mind to the strength of devotion, as though recalled by the living counsel of all those figures.

Thinking up these and other such things, this prudent and kindly man chose whatever temporal and eternal benefits he could for his church. With the praise and thanksgiving of his chapter, he also appointed certain men as gratuitous canons for a fixed obedience: namely, a worthy and suitable priest who would offer daily on behalf of our deceased canons; a remarkable goldsmith; a skilled painter; an ingenious glazier; and others who, each according to his ability, would serve in his own office.

Full of complete goodwill toward his church and content with this sole concern, he gradually began to fall ill as his distaste for food increased. He therefore summoned his dean and certain other brothers. In their presence he prudently arranged his almsgiving and distributed many gifts according to the urgent demands of necessity.

Then, departing with the kiss of peace and the sign of blessing—for he was a most devoted father among us—he had himself carried to Varzy amid abundant tears, so that from there he might more easily be taken to the monastery of Charity on the Loire, where he was to be buried.

That holy place, together with certain other religious sites in the district of Auxerre, had been begun in his time and had scarcely ever lacked his counsel, indeed his assistance. Therefore, if he wished to be buried there, let no one think it unjust, as though it were evident that he preferred that place to this one or loved it more.

Rather, let him reflect that the truth is the opposite: because he loved this place with all his heart, he therefore loved greatly the other place, which was built for the perpetual honor and assistance of this one, quickly and magnificently, through the mercy of Jesus Christ visiting it.

He hoped for one thing with complete certainty: that however many servants of Christ there might be, the Church of Auxerre would have that many faithful helpers with the Lord in everlasting prayers.

Accordingly, strengthened by the remedy of so great a hope, when he already sensed that the fall toward the end of life was near, he summoned Hugh, bishop of Nevers, whom he himself had promoted to the priesthood and who was his nephew and at that time provost of our Church. Hugh was a man of holy conduct and, following Christ, bore his own cross.

He also summoned Girardus, prior of the aforementioned place, its builder, and its first inhabitant in the religious habit, so that, after confessing his sins among their holy hands, he might give up his spirit to Christ the Redeemer.

When these things had been carried out, he was taken there and buried in peace on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October [15 September]. He was enthroned on the fifth day before the Kalends of January [28 December]. He ruled the bishopric for twenty-four years, seven months, and twenty-one days.

## NOTICE

It is an honorable custom of the Church of Auxerre that, as soon as its bishop departs from the world, the length of his life, the beginning of his tenure, and especially his good works are immediately written down.

It happened, however, not without great loss to the homeland, that Robert, the illustrious patron of that Church, died, and none of the matters we have mentioned was written down for the space of three full years. Such grief arose from his death, and such disagreement intervened concerning the appointment of a future bishop.

At last, after three years, when the grief had been moderated and the Church had been calmed by the consolation of a shepherd, a certain brother, slightly educated and almost unlettered, was asked by the chapter’s assembly and admonished by the bishop. Since he did not dare avoid obedience, he set down whatever seemed to him not at all to be left unsaid concerning Robert. Although he did so as inadequately as he was unworthy of the subject, and with as little ornament and eloquence as he possessed, he nevertheless pursued the matter in writing as best he could.

## CHAPTER LII — Concerning Robert
[Col. 0283C] Robert was born of William, count of Nevers, nephew of King Henry, father of Philip, and of his mother Hermengarde, called countess of Tonnerre. From this noble lineage, whatever men were skilled, handsome, and good, he surpassed them all here in learning, antiquity, and character, just as the flower surpasses the tree from which it grows, and the fruit the flower. Therefore, even before his age made him appear suitable for honor, he was so in the dignity of his virtues. Accordingly, after the death of Goffrid, of blessed memory, in September, he was immediately elected bishop; but his consecration was deferred until August, when he was happily elevated near the altar of the blessed protomartyr. Thereafter he was a strong protector of the Church and a moderate ruler. For of everything he found in the church, both outside and within, no mortal while he lived dared remove or steal anything [Col. 0283D]; moreover, by giving certain things and laboring over others, he added to its possessions. How much this was done with discretion, anyone who reads his deeds may now learn.

Thus, against the plots of the people of Sens, the perpetual enemies of this Church and city, he firmly fortified Apogniacum, raising it into a fortified town as soon as he became bishop. Previously they used to rush through this village as far as the city walls, frequently and with impunity plundering us by stealthy attacks; they had also afflicted Apogniacum itself with every kind of suffering, so that at that time the few who could not flee, filled with beggary and misery, were so enslaved to their service, to whatever extent they commanded [Col. 0284A], that they could scarcely preserve their very lives. But once that castle had been established, those townsmen, as though raised from death, came back to life, and our citizens, freed from fear, now wander wherever they wish.

Likewise, when certain tyrants, by violently seizing every year the unjust custom of a double salvamentum, had made Pulverenum—the better land of this Church—almost deserted of farmers and deprived of its other benefits, the strength of this prelate came to its aid. By the mere fear of a threatened war he so terrified those sycophants that they who at first disdained even to receive the canons’ prayers—or rather their money—for the redemption of their unjust share, eventually proclaimed that the whole land was entirely free from that invasion, as though voluntarily and willingly, though in fact unwillingly rather than voluntarily [Col. 0284B]. Such strength, joined with justice, is powerful: by crushing the guilty, it preserved the innocent.

He also engaged in a conflict over the Church’s possessions against the rebellion of the people of Tociacum, which had to be broken. Although he quickly subdued them, he harmed our land considerably by building the castle of Partiaci at his father’s command. For this reason he prostrated himself in the chapter and wept over his fault, and he repaired the damage. He had promised us that, if wise men whom he ought to consult advised it, he would give us the restitution we desired—namely, the provostship, a dignity increasingly desired by the community of the Church for many days already. But because the incumbent still survived at that time, he gave us, as the investiture of the prefecture, the abbey of Blessed Mary, unwilling that an unproductive delay should meanwhile make us murmur against him [Col. 0284C]. He also gave two prebends, to be assigned to whomever they wished.

How purely he loved us with charity throughout his life is testified by that distinguished and, above all, memorable gift in which he showed himself so merciful toward us that, if we love our own souls, we must in no way forget him. His holy predecessors, the bishops, had established that, when any brother died, his memory should be celebrated from the income of his own prebend only on the days of Lent. He, however, became so much more compassionate than they in this kindness, although in other respects he seemed their inferior, that he added and decreed that no canon should be deprived of the full income of his prebend for an entire year after his death. Instead, a priest—not, however, one of our canons—should receive all its revenues for the deceased [Col. 0284D], celebrating Mass daily, offering the sacrifices of the Hours, and praying continually. We trust in God’s mercy that whoever was so generous in obtaining remission for his subjects will never lack the forgiveness of his own sins.

There is still another matter. During his episcopate, a certain knight named Atto, holding by episcopal charter from the bishops a share of the mills beneath the wall—so they are called—while the canons held the other share, brought the matter to court. The bishop approved the settlement, except that we promised to celebrate his anniversary each year.

There are other indications of his pious solicitude for this church. Since they either adorn the body of the Church or establish its institutions, we have preferred to record them briefly in plain truth [Col. 0285A] rather than color them with brilliant flowers of speech, to the reader’s weariness. At his entrance he offered a dorsal of blood-red color. At another time, from his own resources, he had a pulpit made at a cost of four hundred solidi. Later, except for the head of the church, he glazed the walls of the choir. Then he illuminated the previously excessively dark crypts with twin entrances. Finally, building the towers of the bells upward from the lowest foundations of the church, he completed them.

Here we cease to mention the rest of his good works—not because there were none, but because he possessed one particular virtue, namely, balance of spirit; and if we delay speaking of it further, that is a most impious offense, let alone if we should wish to pass over it entirely. For although he was a man of the highest nobility and immense power, followed by worldly glory [Col. 0285B] and adored by every temporal prosperity, he always guarded his mind with such vigilance that neither an act of shameful pleasure ever stained him nor a word from his mouth, even when angry, gained him an enemy. Indeed, we saw—and no enemy of his, if he has one, can deny it—that whenever some unworthy person, seeing or hearing him, slandered him or directed some insulting word against him, he restrained himself from responding with such gentleness and meekness that often the very person who provoked him with curses, seeing his patience and becoming frightened within himself because of it, immediately afflicted himself with such pain of repentance, beating his breast and lips with his fists, that anyone who saw it would judge that the bishop showed him great mercy if, instead of this, he had imposed upon him the deserved torments of punishment.

I shall speak more briefly [Col. 0285C]: there was never any harshness of malice that the beauty of his gracious speech could not soften. But what shall we say of the temptations of pleasure—that is, of the wanton movements of his flesh? He was so diligent in restraining and suppressing them that he scarcely ever drank wine. Although physicians repeatedly warned him not to avoid wine completely unless he wished to die quickly—for he did not wish to die, but, being fervent by nature and age, feared that wine would become both the cause of death and fuel for lust—he would not yield to any warnings or exhortations until that abstinence so weakened him, as we ourselves saw, that, in accordance with the physicians’ judgment, although still a young man, he was carried off before his time by the last and greatest of all necessities, namely death [Col. 0285D]. Even if medical treatment could delay it for a little while, it could not hold it back forever.

Thus, having been seized by illness at Nevers, he put on, as they say, the habit of Saint Benedict, lamented with bitter tears the wrongs he had committed, and died in the Catholic faith and confession. He was happily buried there in the basilica of the blessed protomartyr on the second day before the Ides of February [February 12]. There his remains receive magnificent honor; here, day after day, the benefits he bestowed bear fruit for us. Therefore, while his memory lives in this writing, he will neither depart from our hearts nor lack our prayers.

The deeds of two others among the deeds of the pontiffs.

A cleric described the lives of both of them.

[Col. 0286A] Frodo faithfully composed them, adding first that of Goffrid and then that of Robert,

for he said nothing except what he knew.

A poor man could not give the Lord a greater gift

than to preserve for Him something certain that would never die.

Therefore, though sorrowful, give praises to God from your heart;

he asks that God pardon both him and them in these words.

## Epitaph of Bishop Robert and Lament

Count and bishop, worthy of doubled honor,

you depart, O dying Robert, like the least of men.

However great their goods may be, what use are they to those who die?

They would be better if they fell to the living, since they are lesser things.

Would that it might happen thus, with few possessions and prosperity,

so that the losses of a long life might overflow.

With a short life rather than many joys,

[Col. 0286B] but God bestows such an outcome through posterity,

so that the best of things comes about obliquely,

and life is prepared for the one to whom death is promised,

while the one who thinks he has life as his support is made secure against it.

Look now and see what has happened to our bishop:

noble and wise, young, handsome, and lovable,

he has passed away as though he had never been born.

## CHAPTER LIII — On Humbaud

Humbaud, of blessed memory, became bishop from the position of dean. A native of Auxerre, he was born of a noble lineage, his father being Humbauld and his mother Adela. He occupied the see for 22 years, 4 months, and 17 days. He was bishop during the times of the Roman pontiffs, Pope Urban II and Paschal II, while the most illustrious men, Philip, glorious king of the Franks [Col. 0286C], and his son Louis, happily ruled among the Franks.

From infancy he was devoted to the study of letters. His predecessor Heribert made him a cleric and canon. Distinguished by simplicity and prudence, chastity and temperance, and the other flowers of virtue, he served in every office within the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, striving to serve God there honorably, suitably, and religiously.

When the outstanding bishop of bishops, Robert, departed from this world—most noble in character and birth, and most excellent in prudence and bodily appearance—Humbaud was elected bishop by the clergy and people of the city. Having been elected, he was presented at Milan, a city of Italy, for consecration to the aforesaid Pope Urban, who had descended into Lombardy because of certain people deviating from sound doctrine [Col. 0286D]. Consecrated there by that same pope, he was brought back to his own city and received with glory and hymns, according to the custom of the Church, by the clergy and people, who met him devoutly at the episcopal throne.

Meanwhile, certain *casati* of the Church rose against it, seized episcopal property, and wished to retain it as their own. But Humbaud, a simple and prudent bishop, relying on useful counsel and trusting in God’s power, sagaciously removed Gaufrid of Dunziacum, who had occupied the castle of Varziacum and was devastating the land and its people beyond measure, by ecclesiastical justice; he judged that the castle should be retained for himself and his successors.

He also freed Cona from the tyrannical invasion of Hugh, who had usurped the episcopal revenues of that place with perverse audacity and desired to retain them for himself thereafter. Similarly, he restrained the people of Tociacum by ecclesiastical discipline and compelled them to return what they had stolen from episcopal jurisdiction.

His distinguished deeds demonstrate how piously he conducted himself toward the Church entrusted to him and how kindly and prudently toward his subjects. For he adorned the church within and without with many gifts, increased it with buildings, and ennobled it with honors. He would have conferred still more goods upon the Church had not the devil, who always envies good things, through the aforementioned and certain other tyrants inflicted losses upon him in his possessions and honor.

The roofs of the church, consumed and collapsed through age, he renewed with new shingles [Col. 0287B]. He raised the tower of the church above the altar of Saint Alexander with a remarkable and lofty wooden covering. He also had another tower, situated above the choir, covered with squared stones, lest its bells be destroyed by a sudden conflagration, should such a thing occur, or break after being worn away by icy rains.

He had four windows, which supplied light to the older altar, glazed with remarkable workmanship; in the front part of the church he glazed twenty-two, and near the choir two more. He placed five exceptionally tall candelabra before the altar, so that candles set upon them would brighten the church during the night hours and provide still clearer light to clergy and laity entering it.

He also gave a linen curtain, decorating one wall of the church on feast days, painted with images of kings and emperors [Col. 0287C]. Above it he placed three most precious hangings, worth one thousand solidi. One of them shines with multicolored lions arranged in circles; the second is adorned with images of kings, likewise arranged in circles, riding in royal fashion; the third, with golden-colored lions arranged in circles, delights those who look upon it.

Again, for the adornment of the church, remembering the Psalmist’s words, “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Psalm 25:8), he gave two large woolen dorsals, elaborately decorated with multicolored lions, and placed two excellent carpets above the choir seats.

For the ornament of the church, and also to suggest to us that, having put aside vices, we ought to be clothed inwardly and outwardly with virtues [Col. 0287D], he gave four good capes of silk, three dalmatics, seven albs, excellent chasubles, stoles, and many manuterga, as well as numerous books suitable for episcopal office.

He decorated the head of the church above the altar of Saint Stephen with a remarkable and precious painting. In the crypt of the Holy Trinity he adorned both the upper and lower parts with paintings. In another crypt he honored the altar of Saint Nicholas with an image of the Savior, and with painted images of Saint Mary and Saint John the Evangelist.

He renewed the church of Saint Mary, the Holy Mother of the Lord, situated within the walls, which was falling and almost collapsed, and he himself dedicated it after its renewal. He had the gable of the church of Saint Mary outside the walls covered with new shingles.

Finally, for the support of the canons, he gave the church of Accolacum [Col. 0288A], together with the tithes he had acquired from Guibert, knight of the castle of Censurium, and he donated a *pareda* to the same canons. He likewise gave the church of Crevennum to the brothers, together with its tithes, and donated a *pareda*; nevertheless, at the request of the chapter, he assigned two prebends to two clerics under that arrangement.

He also gave the church of Collumnum, together with the aforesaid tithes, to the canons. He had acquired it from Morundus, a knight, on the condition that the canons restore the ruined church, and he donated a *pareda*.

He had also promised to give the church of Ausiacum, possessed by Hugh Mansellus almost as hereditary right, together with its presbytery and tithes, for the support of those same brothers. If the canons could meanwhile wrest it from him by any means, he granted it by episcopal donation, intending that we should possess it perpetually [Col. 0288B], had he not been overtaken by death before the appointed time.

Nor did we consider it worthy to pass over in silence the fact that he acquired half of a certain estate called Laurea, situated between Carcedonum and Andraia and highly suitable for bishops, together with woods and cultivated and uncultivated lands, from Gaufrid Bolsarius and his heirs, paying them thirty pounds and more. He judged that it should be held perpetually by himself and his successors.

At Auxerre he restored the episcopal vineyards, enclosed by walls, which had been worn out by age and almost dead, to their former greenness and good fertility. He also obtained from the younger William, count, for himself and his successors in perpetuity, the abolition of a wicked custom: namely, that all the household goods of the episcopal residence, which counts had been accustomed to seize and appropriate for their own use when a bishop died [Col. 0288C]. To preserve this in memory, he ordered that it be confirmed in writing:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let it be known to all, both present and future, who love truth and seek the salvation of their souls, that I, William, count of Nevers, for the remission of my sins, and of those of my father, my mother, and their ancestors, with the approval of my wife Adelaya, countess, relinquish to the church of Blessed Mary, Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, and to Humbaud, bishop of Auxerre, and to the canons of that church and their successors, a certain wicked custom which my predecessors were accustomed to exact [Col. 0288D]—namely, from the episcopal residence and from the bishop’s property, which after the death of bishops they possessed, devastated, and plundered as though it were their own.
>
> “I make this renunciation of such a custom so that henceforth none of my heirs may presume to take anything from it; and if anyone should presume to take anything from it, let him lose all my honor. This renunciation was first made above the altar of Saint Stephen; afterward, in the same church, publicly on the Lord’s Day, the day before the Kalends of September.”

He also restored the episcopal enclosure at Apogniacum, which had been destroyed and badly dissipated, to fertility; restored a furnace that had been taken from episcopal jurisdiction to the mill situated on the River Yonne; and restored the fields which are commonly called [Col. 0289A] Catalaunicae.

[The supplied text is materially incomplete or corrupt at this point; the surviving passage resumes with a request concerning the transfer of a sacred body.]

He earnestly begged that, because the place where this sacred body lay in the open air had been completely destroyed, he be given permission to transfer it to a place where it could be preserved more devoutly and reverently.

After he had persisted for a long time in his prayers and finally obtained the fulfillment of his request, he summoned a boatman and is said to have paid him the fare, on the condition that he should await his arrival at the riverbank during the night, before the cockcrow.

When, at the appointed hour of the night, three men accompanied by a certain priest were present at the riverbank, sent by this count, the boatman was absent, and the boat was fastened to the farther bank of the river. While these men waited a long time for the boatman’s arrival and called out in turn, with no one answering them, they were overcome with grief and fell prostrate upon the ground, devoutly praying that, if it was pleasing to God for the body of that saint [Col. 0289B] to be transferred from that place, He might deign to show them this by certain signs.

At once, by divine power, the boat was released from the bond by which it had been fastened and miraculously approached the bank where they were waiting. Seeing this with amazement and giving the greatest thanks to God, they boarded the boat, now made more confident by God’s will.

They approached the place of the tomb, opened the stone sarcophagus in which the sacred remains lay, and reverently lifted them, transferring them into a small reliquary newly prepared for this purpose. Then, returning to the boat with immense joy, they quickly crossed the river, carrying this pledge with hymns of praise to the village of Balbiacum (Balby), where it is established that it was reverently preserved for three years.

After this it was honorably brought to the church of Saint Remigius and devoutly entrusted to the church’s custodian [Col. 0289C]. It was honorably placed beside the tomb of this most holy father.

After two years, the aforesaid count, together with his wife Herisinde, humbly approached Lord Fulco, the bishop, asking him to grant him a place of burial on the right side of this church, beside the entrance to the crypt. When this was obtained, an altar was established and covered with silver ornamentation, and these venerable remains were decently deposited there.

Finally, after they had been removed from the aforesaid place of burial, a certain blind woman named Erentrudis came there carrying a candle, seeking healing. When she learned that the sacred body had been completely removed from that place, she began to complain with intense anguish and weeping: Why had this saint of the Lord allowed himself to be taken away from there? Why had he abandoned his neighbors, to whom he had been accustomed to grant divine benefits [Col. 0289D]?

Asking amid her groans that she be helped, she believed that she ought to go to the village of Matusgum (Maroug), where his brother Saint Vetanus rested. Placing her candle at his tomb and prostrating herself in prayer, she began, weeping, to invoke both brothers.

While she repeatedly called upon the name of the saint, Gibrianus, the cloudy whiteness began to break away from her eyes. Thus, through God’s merciful favor, she was restored to her former light.

Finally, the aforementioned venerable bishop Fulco, solicitous for the worship of God and ecclesiastical order, and ardent in his love of wisdom, restored two schools at Reims that had almost collapsed: one for the canons of the place and the other for rural clerics. He summoned Remigius, a teacher from Auxerre [Col. 0290A], and had the young clerics trained in the studies of the liberal arts. He himself devoted time with them to reading and the contemplation of wisdom.

He also summoned Hucbald, a monk of Saint-Amand, a man nobly learned in the sophistic disciplines, and enlightened the Church of Reims with distinguished teachings.

## CHAPTER X — On the Killing of Archbishop Fulco

It happened that King Charles took from Count Baldwin the abbey of Saint Vedast, which Baldwin held together with the castle of Arras, because of Baldwin’s infidelity, and granted it to this bishop. At that time a certain count named Altmar held the abbey of Saint Medard. The bishop thought it advantageous to exchange it with that count, and he did so.

Thus he received from Altmar the abbey of Saint Medard and gave him the abbey of Saint Vedast, having recovered by force of siege the castle of Arras from Baldwin [Col. 0290B]. Inflamed by the distress caused by this, Baldwin and all his retinue sought how they might avenge themselves. They pretended to restore friendship with the bishop, seeking an opportunity for revenge and investigating how he was accustomed to travel from his encampment to an audience with the king, surrounded by guards.

One day, when he was traveling with only a very small escort to seek an audience with the king, they attacked and intercepted him on the road, led by a certain Winemar. At first they spoke as though about friendship and Baldwin’s restoration; then suddenly they attacked him with lances, struck him down, and killed him.

Some of his men, because of their excessive love for him [Col. 0290C], threw themselves upon him and were pierced and killed together with him. The survivors carried news of this greatest grief to those who had remained at the hospitals. Struck by the novelty of the event and armed, they attempted to attack the bishop’s slayers in revenge.

When they could not find them, they lifted the lifeless body, lamenting with immeasurable cries of grief, and carried it to the city of Reims amid the immense mourning of all his people. There it was washed, honored with fitting obsequies, and committed to a suitable burial.

His epitaph is as follows:

Here the remains of the great Fulco are covered,

the distinguished bishop of the see of Reims.

France produced him, born from a noble stock,

and the court took him from the schools and cultivated him.

God took him from there and established him, tested by virtue,

a mirror of the Church and a pious bishop,

over which he presided for seventeen years,

three months, and ten additional days.

He increased the episcopal residence, adding many possessions,

and restored the walls of this city.

Honor of the world, guardian of his homeland, lover of piety,

he was pierced by arrows for his devotion to peace.

June had already reached its seventeenth day

when he departed, slain by a dreadful death. [Baronius: “died.”]

May the piety of the Mother of the Lord,

and likewise of the blessed bishop Remigius,

obtain rest for him. Amen.

Finally, Winemar, his slayer, was excommunicated and anathematized by the bishops of the kingdom of the Franks together with his accomplices. Moreover, God struck him with an incurable wound [Baronius: “ulcer”], so that, as his flesh rotted and pus poured forth, he was devoured alive by worms.

…had ordained that a *prodam* [uncertain reading] be given for one year to the priest celebrating Mass for a dead canon. He also gave many churches to the regular canons of the abbey which his glorious predecessor, the ornament of bishops Robert, had raised to abbey status: the churches of Warchi, Tratiacum, Saint Martin of Truncetum, and Saint Quentin. He removed them from lay hands and granted them to the canons in perpetuity by apostolic and episcopal authority.

He likewise granted many churches to the monastery of Charité, which he had acquired from the laymen who possessed them. As a lover of divine offices and ecclesiastical order, he also removed from lay possession the baptisteries, burials, and other offerings of churches, which laymen had usurped for many years and already possessed by long usage as though by custom [Col. 0291B]. He also removed wicked customs—namely, the banquets which parish priests paid each year to lay lords—from lay possession, firmly and reasonably.

To prevent priests of God from thereafter obeying laymen in such matters, he prohibited it by episcopal authority at a synod, proclaiming the decree of Pope and martyr Stephen: although laymen may be religious, no power to possess anything from ecclesiastical resources has ever, it is said, been granted to any of them.

This bishop, therefore, a friend of peace and kindness, adorned with these and similar displays of good works, showed himself so lovable and dear to all good men that he deserved to become worthy of everyone’s praise. He was sharp-minded, prudent in speech, farsighted in counsel, gentle in patience [Col. 0291C], cheerful in appearance, pleasant in bearing and dress, kindly approachable toward everyone, and capable in all things, inwardly and outwardly.

At suitable times he devoted himself to prayer, and sometimes enjoyed conversations with his intimates. In arranging the interests of himself and his people, he valued the company of soldiers and nobles, but his affection for clerics was greater; at table and in the provision of clothing, his generosity toward them appeared more abundant.

Nor should we be silent about unlawful movements of the flesh. He diligently suppressed them by moderation in food and drink. From the time he became bishop, he abstained from meat; the eating of legumes was sufficient for him, and he drank only a little wine.

At banquets he was generous, practicing hospitality toward one another and toward all. At table he was never without Christ’s poor, avoiding what is written: “Unless he has received everyone, a bishop is inhuman.” During Lent he refreshed twelve poor people every day; on Holy Thursday he gave them denarii, and at Easter he clothed many of them.

When, as often happens, the fury of anger and discord entered the hearts even of his subordinate barons through the devil’s prompting, by his remarkable patience and the grace of his humility he reconciled their discordant minds. To make peace and quiet more secure, he very often gave of his own to the one causing unrest.
