If at any time a layperson had a complaint against a cleric, or alleged that an injury had been inflicted upon him by a cleric, and brought the matter forward in protest, the bishop, equipped with the simplicity of a dove and the prudence of a serpent [Col. 0292A], would have the fault kept secret so that the Church would not be disgraced; and, if it could not otherwise be done, he sometimes bought off the complainants by paying a price.

Thus, through the merciful action of Jesus Christ, who both anticipates the actions of His faithful by inspiring them and accompanies them by assisting them, after peace had first been restored among the brothers, in the twenty-second year of his episcopate he undertook the journey to Jerusalem for love of the Savior and for the remission of his sins.

After visiting the holy places according to custom and praying everywhere for his sins with a rain of tears, he was returning and carrying many ornaments for his church. Amid the raging waves of the sea, he implored the mercy of our Savior Jesus Christ, crying out that he was guilty, and loudly singing psalms [Col. 0292B] and hymns to God. When the ship broke apart, he surrendered his spirit to his Creator.

## CHAPTER LIV — On Hugh, Bishop and Abbot of Saint-Germain

Hugh occupied the see for 21 years. He was born in the territory of Cluny, at the castle of Monteacutum, and came from noble parents. His father was called Dalmaticus; his mother’s name was . . . . .

His parents loved him greatly, not only in the flesh but also spiritually. By the will of God, who orders all things, he was destined for the Church and given over to letters. While still in the innocence of childhood, he received the monastic habit in the monastery of Cluny, where he lived for many years under Saint Hugh, his maternal uncle, then abbot of that monastery. In the cloister of the same monastery he wisely learned the Rule of blessed Benedict.

For, as is reported of him, he always remained without complaint, humble and obedient to his superiors, as befits a monk. But the almighty Lord, who regards the humble in heaven and on earth (Psalm 113:6), seeing that this man’s humility would benefit many, did not permit him to remain long in the cloister.

After the death of Lord Guibert, abbot of Saint-Germain at Auxerre, he was elected and blessed abbot in that same church. He did not become more exalted because of the title of abbot; rather, he was a humble monk like one of the others. As befits a good teacher, he began to do and to teach (Acts 1:1), demonstrating by example what he taught in words.

When it became known that Lord Humbaud, the venerable bishop of Auxerre [Col. 0292D], had departed this life on the road to Jerusalem, most of the clergy of that Church, after a very short interval, elected this abbot as bishop.

But the provost of the same Church, named Hulgerius, and certain canons with him—those who had nominated that provost in the election—resisted the election of the holy man. They also secured the assistance of King Louis, son of King Philip, who was then reigning, to support their opposition, so that he entirely refused to grant Hugh any of the royal rights belonging to the bishopric.

Then Hugh, compelled and drawn along by his electors, and his opponents, went to the threshold of the apostles, so that the supreme pontiff might judge the election there. But the most merciful Lord, distributor of all good things, against whom neither wisdom nor counsel can prevail, granted the venerable abbot such favor in the eyes of the supreme pontiff, who at that time was Pope Paschal, that he deserved to receive from him the grace of episcopal consecration. He returned in peace to his own see, while the clergy and even the people came out to meet him with great rejoicing.

He also found the count of the region, who at that time was being held captive by Mansellus—who later took the religious habit in the Carthusian order—rejoicing over the confirmation of his election. He visited the king of the Franks, who had previously opposed him, as soon as he arrived, and found him reconciled.

Finally, how pure his spirit was and how humbly he lived in his episcopate [Col. 0293B], although not in every respect, the following letter will make clear. It was almost a prophetic sign, a foretelling divinely assigned to him, and ran as follows: “Hail, Mary, full of grace,” etc.

It is no wonder that the Son of the Virgin, without whose will not even a leaf falls to the ground, wished that this singular and admirable greeting of grace should be found in the prognostic of the servant of His Mother, whom He knew would remain a virgin, so that it might indicate what kind of life he would lead.

He frequently visited the Cistercian Order, which at that time was still new and surrounded by joyful and voluntary poverty, with the sweetest attentiveness, and according to his means supplied it with many necessities. During his time the abbeys of Regniacum, Rupes, and Bonusradius also had the beginnings of their foundations [Col. 0293C], and through his hands they received considerable growth, both through his supplying their needs and through his acquiring possessions for them.

The monastery of Pontigny had been founded before his consecration. He did not forget the sick of that Order, but comforted them with gentle conversation and often provided them with nourishment at his own expense.

He willingly avoided the city and the crowds of people whenever the proper time came, frequently visiting the monks’ cloister with joyful simplicity of spirit. Among them he did not wish to be called or regarded as a bishop, but as a monk, remembering that evangelical command: “Let the greater among you become as the lesser, and the leader as one who serves” (Luke 22:26).

He also continually turned over in his mind the saying of blessed Jerome, who was both a monk and a teacher of monks:

> “To me, the town is a prison; solitude is paradise. If you desire to be what you are called—a monk, that is, one who is alone—what are you doing in the cities?”

In the cloister of the monks of La Charité, who lived according to the Cluniac order, he frequently stayed; and from his castles at Varzy and Cona he often ordered grain and wine to be transported for his own use and for the refreshment of the sick there, so as not to burden the Church.

It is also believed of him that he possessed the spirit of prophecy, in which he left a certain sign of truth for the clerics of his church. There was at that time a certain cleric named Stephen, extremely cautious in acquiring and providing, [Col. 0294A] who had been greatly loved by and familiar with the abbey over which he had presided, and especially by Abbot Gervase, his successor, since he belonged to the household of that church. On his behalf, therefore, when the monks of that church and especially the abbot frequently petitioned the bishop to make him a canon in the church of Saint Stephen, but the bishop was unwilling to listen to them in this matter, and when they did not cease to assail him daily with continual prayers, he is said to have given them this answer:

“You pour out prayers for him in vain, for in my time he will never be a canon. I believe this about him: as soon as he is made a canon in the church of Saint Stephen, he will be an excessive exactor of his own advantage from the church’s property.”

And what more need be said? The holy man’s word was followed by the truth. After his death, his successor made the aforesaid cleric [Col. 0294B] a canon in the church of blessed Stephen and held him in the greatest familiarity; and what the holy man had foretold concerning him was proved by the result in that same cleric.

He retained in his own hands throughout the days of his episcopate the archdeaconry that had come into his possession during his tenure—not from avarice, but so that the priests would not be burdened. He knew that the revenues of the archdeaconry were very small and could not suffice for the expenses required by the title of that office.

Once it happened that he wished to visit the Roman pontiff for a certain necessity. Accordingly, compelled by the advice of those attending him to provide the expenses of so great a journey, he was obliged to request assistance from the priests of his diocese. The priests gave, each according to his own judgment, [Col. 0294C] and no more was asked of anyone than he freely chose to give. When everything necessary had been prepared, he undertook the journey he had planned. Crossing Mount Cenis, he came to the Cluses, where he learned that the road was unsafe. After taking counsel, he returned to his own see; and, not forgetting that he had taken money from his priests for the journey he had begun, he consulted the written record of how much each priest had given and returned to each the same amount.

There was also one of his familiars to whom he had conferred an ecclesiastical benefice. Not forgetting the benefice he had received, after some time had passed he came with a certain sum of money to a monk who carried the bishop’s money-chests [Col. 0294D] and was steward of his entire household. He offered him the money, saying:

“Lord Bishop spends much and needs much. Accept this gift and set it aside for the expenses necessary to him.”

The monk gratefully accepted the gift and put it away. Before much time had passed, however, recalling the money he had received and uncertain whether some scruple might lie hidden in the gift that could offend the bishop’s conscience—whose purity he knew well—he acted as a prudent and wise steward: he disclosed to the bishop what sort of gift had been given to him and by what sort of man.

When the bishop heard this, and was considering from where such a gift, and one so large, had proceeded, it immediately came to his mind [Col. 0295A] that he had done the man a favor by granting him an ecclesiastical benefice. In anger he is said to have addressed his steward as follows:

“Brother, it is not our purpose to retain what was said by a pagan: ‘Do not concern yourself with where you have it; what matters is to have it.’ Return it in full to the giver, just as he gave the gift to you, lest my conscience be polluted in the granting of an ecclesiastical benefice.”

The monk immediately obeyed and, as he had been ordered, returned the gift to its giver.

It also happened that, because of a shortage of vineyards, wine was sold in one year at a somewhat higher price than usual. Considering that the houses of those living according to a rule within his episcopate—especially amid their other needs—had either no wine at all or far too little for drinking, he arranged for wine to be supplied to the monks of Les Roches, to those of Bonneray, [Col. 0295B] and to those of La Charité from Varzy and Cona, according to the quantity of wine he had there and as was appropriate for each church.

To the communities of Pontigny and Régny, and to the virgins of Christ at Crisenon, he distributed it in the following manner. One day, having summoned the cellarer of Auxerre, he entered his own cellar. Learning that the casks were full of wine, he is said to have spoken as follows to his cellarer:

“Let this cask be for the community of Pontigny; that one for the community of Régny; that one for the poor virgins of Christ.”

He marked each one with a little rod that he held in his hand.

Now the cellarer, knowing that the wine intended for the virgins of Christ was wine from Megrana, and that the cask of forty modii was of great value, tried, as though on the advice of his own prudence, to turn the bishop’s mind away from so great a gift, saying:

[Col. 0295C] “My lord, this wine is from Megrana, and the cask of forty modii is of great value and has been reserved for pruning the vineyards and for other necessities. May it please you to give wine of lesser value, since you have some other wine at hand, which they will receive with great charity of heart.”

The bishop replied:

“You do not understand the things that are God’s. What I have said, I have said. You do not know that the word of God must never be idle.”

And what more need be said? He spoke, and it was done.

But let us still hear what the Lord added to this man for the increase of his charity. The steward of the nuns was summoned and ordered to take away the wine given for the virgins’ use. But when he realized that the wine was so good and so valuable, he offered it for sale, intending to buy cheaper wine with its price and reserve the remainder for other necessities.

When the bishop heard this, [Col. 0295D] he ordered the monk-steward to be summoned and asked why he wished to sell the wine. The monk explained the reason. When the bishop understood, he said:

“I want the wine that I gave, at the same price at which it would have been given to someone else, to return to my control.”

The monk complied with the bishop’s wish. The price was paid to the monk, no less than he could have obtained from another purchaser. When this had been done, the bishop said to the monk:

“Now you have the price of the wine. Behold, I again give this wine to the brides of Christ as before, and I order that they have it and drink it.”

It is also believed of him that, once, a second time, and a third time, when he felt bodily illness, he distributed everything he possessed for the love of God in such a way that he retained nothing movable except clothing [Col. 0296A] scarcely sufficient for himself.

During one illness, when he had ordered everything to be given away, a small box was brought to him containing an electuary and a little silver spoon. He immediately ordered the spoon to be given away, so that he would retain nothing that could offend the purity of his conscience.

It also happened that, at a certain time, he was at Clairvaux, where he often stayed with great willingness of spirit for the counsel of his soul. At that time the venerable lord Bernard, an abbot of great renown and merit, whose life and teaching were celebrated throughout the universal Church and had drawn many with him to Christ, was there.

One day, when the abbot and the community of monks—whose custom it is to reap with their own hands what will sustain them and provide for those in need—were going into a field [Col. 0296B] to reap, the bishop joined the community with a sickle, greatly anticipating the fruit he would gain whenever it happened that he shared their labor.

They came to the field where the crop stood. All cut; the grain was gathered into sheaves. Then suddenly a dark cloud, filled with abundant rain, obscured the sky and enveloped the field where they were.

When the venerable abbot Bernard, undaunted and always carrying Christ’s faith in his heart—of which it is written, “All things are possible to the one who believes” (Matthew 9:22)—saw this, he turned to the bishop and said:

“Father, say that the threatening flood of rain should pass.”

He, always mindful of humility, replied:

“I am not worthy of this. You pray, and I trust that the Lord will grant it to you.”

The abbot answered:

[Col. 0296C] “And you, Father, pray, and I will pray with you.”

After these words, each prayed. Immediately the Lord’s ears attended to their prayers, and the darkness of the clouds withdrew. Clear weather followed, and the holy reapers gathered their harvest in dryness.

At another time, because of an unusual violence of the winds, a wooden tower of the church of Saint Stephen collapsed completely. It fell silently during the night upon the episcopal residence while the bishop was sleeping. The beams and timbers, piercing the roof of the house, fell on either side around the bishop’s bed, even across it, yet every injury was kept away from the holy man.

What shall we say of this? It is clear that the one and only guardian of the sleeping bishop was he who neither slumbers nor sleeps and who guards Israel (Psalm 120:4). [Col. 0296D] For he has always guarded all who love him, of whom alone it is truly written: “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Psalm 126:1).

When a dispute concerning the customs of his church had long continued between the provost and the canons, he established peace between the provost and the brothers under oath, with the customs written down and sworn to for the most part by witnesses, both canons and laymen. He confirmed the written document with his seal and had it secured by the authority of the supreme pontiff for the peace of his church. He had regard for the fruit he had read about in the work of blessed Martin: before his impending death, Martin had taken care to restore peace in the church of Condat. The Author of peace, through the Psalmist, promised this fruit of peace, saying: “There is a remnant for the peaceful person” (Psalm 37:37). [Col. 0297A]

Although among all the prelates of the Church, whatever their order, scarcely one can be found who does not exalt his relatives—even when they are unworthy—with honors and benefices of the churches, this man, singular among countless others, never wished during his lifetime to give a prebend to one of his nephews.

Although, for the sake of the peace of spirit that he found among the cloistered monks, he was not very assiduous in his own church, he nevertheless displayed great concern for it. Thus, in order to increase the service of his church, he considered that nothing in the church would be so useful to the common good of the brothers as for the provostship of the church to be ceded to them for their common use. One day, after taking counsel not from a human being but from [Col. 0297B] God, he offered the provostship upon the altar of Saint Stephen through the hand of Saint Stephen himself, and granted and donated it to the community of the brothers to possess forever, especially for their sustenance. To ensure that this gift could not be violated by anyone, he had it confirmed by the authority of Pope Innocent.

Nevertheless, what was done concerning this donation was not observed during the time of his successor.

He also gave the church of Deoysi to the church of blessed Stephen, and the church of Saint Ferreolus to the church of Saint Germanus.

He rebuilt the episcopal residence entirely in stone, made it spacious, and covered it with tiles. In that part of the same house which faces east, he constructed a certain gallery, called *logis* in the vernacular, exceedingly pleasant to behold and [Col. 0297C] adorned with very beautiful columns upon the city wall. From there the river below could be seen, as well as the vineyards and fields.

As the appointed term of his life approached, from him who then gives sleep to his beloved and wishes to give them their inheritance (Psalm 126:2), an unnatural heat seized all his limbs. While his flesh suffered, he compelled his spirit to serve its Creator through psalms and prayers.

When the final day arrived, he admonished the brothers standing around him, with all the diligence he could muster, around the ninth hour of the day, in these words:

“Let us pay to the Lord the remaining hours of the day that we owe him, for when the hours are finished I shall immediately rest.”

They therefore sang to the Lord. When the hour of Compline had been completed, the term of his life was completed; thus the effect of truth followed the word [Col. 0297D] he had foretold. When those hours were finished, he rested in the Lord, though the bystanders did not understand this at the time. They had thought that his words concerned bodily rest.

His death occurred on the fourth day before the Ides of August. From the episcopal see, where he surrendered his spirit to the Lord, his body was carried with due reverence to the church of Saint Germanus, as he had requested while still alive. There, in the chapter-house of that church, where the brothers are disciplined, Providence granted him burial. The episcopal see was not vacant for a full week before his successor was elected.

## Chapter LV. Concerning Hugh

Hugh was born in the territory of Cluny, like his predecessor, [Col. 0298A] whose name he also bore. He was the first abbot of the church of Pontigny from the Cistercian order. After a fast had been proclaimed for both the clergy and the people of the town of Auxerre, and after an invocation of the Holy Spirit, he was elected bishop.

The father of this man . . .; his mother, however, . . .

Since he had no place for consecration in the Sens Church because of the suspension of Lord Henry, the metropolitan, he was consecrated at Ferrières by Lord Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, around the feast of Blessed Vincent. On the Sunday when “They surrounded me” is sung, he made an honorable entrance into his episcopal see and solemnly celebrated the divine office in the church entrusted to him.

Although he had come from the lineage of great men, he himself [Col. 0298B] contributed more to his family through the greatness of his spirit than his family contributed to him. In speaking he was extremely sparing; in action, effective and most prompt. Although, in keeping with the purpose of his order, he possessed marvelous patience, he mingled firmness with patience in restraining the hands of those raging against the Church and the property of the Church. Those whom he could not overcome through patience and humility, he subdued by the severity of justice, which, in the judgment of the wise, is always greatly necessary in the Church of God.

For evil increases daily and evils multiply against the Church, and few prelates in the Church of God are found who will put their lives at stake for the flock entrusted to them against its maligners, who will uphold the severity of justice in honoring the good and exercise vengeance against the wicked.

This man, however, understanding that the humble and the powerful alike [Col. 0298C] have one Lord, although he sometimes spared the humble in the administration of justice, always came against the more powerful to punish them with the rod. He kept Augustine’s saying at hand:

“A bishop serves in one way, and one subject to him in another: the subject by living faithfully; the bishop by issuing just commands and correcting sinners with appropriate severity.”

He also took as his example the deed of blessed Ambrose, who stood in the face of the emperor Theodosius when he came to the city of Milan and, because of the many murders committed at his command, did not hesitate to announce his crime to him and forbid his entrance into the church until he had made satisfaction to God.

Nor is it surprising that his spirit was so ready for justice, since he had learned that, on account of the vengeance carried out, the Lord was appeased and the Jewish people delivered from the plague of death [Col. 0298D] through the hand of Phinehas alone, who “stood and made atonement, and the plague ceased” (Psalm 106:30).

Instructed by such examples, just as he thought that, as part of his office of piety, forgiveness should be granted to the humble, so he judged it cruel and impious to forgive easily the proud who habitually raged against the Church’s property. He did not forget the saying of the wise: to forgive readily those who sin out of habit is nothing other than to provide them with an opportunity for sinning.

He also remembered what blessed Jerome wrote to instruct those who govern the Church of God, in his letter to the priest Paulinus on the study of divine teaching:

“For holy rusticity benefits only itself; and to the extent that it builds up the Church of Christ through the merit of its life, to that extent [Col. 0299A] it harms it if it does not resist those who destroy.”

By bringing Count William, who later assumed the religious habit in the Carthusian order, into a lawsuit, he compelled him through canonical judgment to restore many things to his church that belonged by right to the canons of his church, as well as many things belonging to episcopal right that the same count, because of the failure of justice on the part of his predecessor, had brought under his own control.

At that time the right of using the woodland called Monsbarri was restored to the canons of blessed Stephen. For that use, a certain part of the woodland was assigned to the canons by the count’s son, when a new village was being built in the same woodland.

He also recovered the hunting rights that the count denied belonged to episcopal jurisdiction throughout his woodlands. To ensure that the church remained invested with this right, [Col. 0299B] during his own tenure he kept both hunters and hounds, frequently ordering hunts to be held; and, in the count’s presence, game was carried through the middle of the city to the episcopal see with dogs and the proper hunting-clamor.

What more need be said? Through his prudence and the severity of his justice, he had compelled all the powerful men of his episcopate to honor his presence and fear his absence. Seeing his severity before their eyes, they did not dare presume to lay hands upon the property of the Church.

When castellans and other powerful men repeatedly came into his presence to seek pardon for some offense and poured out their prayers on bended knees, he did not answer them immediately. Sometimes he even appeared to turn his eyes away from them—not out of pride or indignation, but lest excessive humility, which cannot please such men, [Col. 0299C] diminish the reverence due to Peter’s sword.

Since he understood that hospitality, among the other virtues conferred upon him by grace, was first highly commended by the Lord in the Gospel and afterward by the Apostle, he did not forget the words he had promised at his consecration—“I wish to be hospitable”—and he wished his house to be hospitable.

Accordingly, he appointed a lay brother from Pontigny to preside over his household, so that, whether the bishop was present or absent, he would always be ready to receive guests, especially all members of his order who came to his house for lodging.

He also made it his concern always to protect and maintain religious houses, and, wherever the opportunity arose, to reform those who displayed religion only through their habit [Col. 0299D] into the truth of religious life.

Thus, in a certain church of Auxerre founded outside the city walls by his predecessor, Saint Vigilius, in honor of the Mother of God, he established a religious community from Prémontré through his own authority and with the assistance of the count, in pious devotion. He removed from the church those canons whose conduct was less honorable.

Finally, although in the considered judgment of the wise he was held pre-eminent among all the other bishops of the Gallican Church for his uprightness and great counsel, and although he had shown great concern for the common good of his church, he nevertheless gave the provostship of that same church to one of his nephews. The venerable Hugh, his predecessor of blessed memory, [Col. 0300A] had given it with the most kindly affection of charity, for the common good of the brothers, to the table of Saint Stephen through the hand of that protomartyr; and this gift had been confirmed both by the authority of the supreme pontiff and by his own authority.

He increased the episcopal revenues in many ways by purchasing and recovering pledges. He also acquired from lay hands and transferred to episcopal jurisdiction the house of a certain knight, which lay beneath the wall and was too close to the episcopal residence; from the middle of the night it had often disturbed the residence’s peace excessively with the games of the young men and maidservants of that household.

He also purchased the house before his own doorway, since it was very necessary for the episcopal residence. He gave the church of Saint Stephen the pledge of a certain woodland for twenty-two pounds, and the church of Landriacum as a memorial of his death.

His day of death was the fifth day before the Ides of October [Col. 0300B]. He departed from this world at the house of Pontigny, which was the first foundation of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Auxerre and where he himself had first been abbot, and he found a place of burial in the church of Pontigny.

He occupied the see for about fourteen years. The episcopal see was vacant for a year, from the feast of Blessed Denis until the coming of the Lord.

## Chapter LVI—Concerning Alan

Alan, abbot of Reigny, a religious man of Flemish birth, governed the episcopal see for fourteen years and greatly increased the episcopal revenues.

At Varzy he received many pledges, both in the tower and in other places. In the valley of the chapel of Saint Andrew he built a stone house. At Gagiacum he had a stone grange built [Col. 0300C] and roofed with tiles, together with dwellings for residence and a chapel; he also had vineyards planted.

He gave the chapter thirty solidi in annual rent from the church of Escolives. He also gave the church of Lindry with the right of presentation of the chaplain.

For the adornment of the church of blessed Stephen he gave two excellent cloth hangings, and for its service a book of forty homilies of blessed Gregory, written and ornamented with considerable elegance.

To the other churches of Auxerre he also gave many things mercifully, both in revenues and in other benefices. He accomplished many other deeds worthy of remembrance and record in the episcopate, which were not written down—not through any fault, but through the ignorance of the writer.

After living commendably for fourteen years in the episcopal see, pleasing God and men, he wished to strip himself entirely of the worldly anxieties and cares [Col. 0300D] which he had previously renounced. He therefore resigned the episcopate and, abandoning the active life, gave himself completely to the contemplative life. He went to Clairvaux and there, among the athletes of Christ, undertook the martyrdom of his own time. Devoting himself solely to fasts, prayers, readings, and other works of charity, he rested in the Lord, as we believe, with a blessed end.

He died on the fifth day before the Ides of October and was buried at Clairvaux. To celebrate his anniversary solemnly, his cleric, Master Abbo, purchased forty solidi of revenue in the mills of Cravant and, moreover, gave [a further sum] from revenue to the canons of blessed Stephen, to be distributed annually on that anniversary, so that no one would in any way be permitted to transfer the aforesaid revenues to other uses.

He was bishop [Col. 0301A] during the time of the most pious King Louis, with William, count of Nevers, who was buried at Saint Germanus and who had opposed him considerably during his lifetime; and his episcopate continued until the time of William’s son, who died in Jerusalem. In Rome, the popes were Adrian and Alexander III.

## Chapter LVII—Concerning William

William of Toucy was not merely illustrious but was also born of honorable parentage. His father was Gerard of Narbonne, a noble man; his mother was Agnes, in no way inferior to her husband in lineage. Although they were distinguished by wealth and nobility of blood, they were still nobler in character and more fortunate in the offspring they produced.

For by God’s will they begot not only this prelate but also the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Sens, [Col. 0301B] who was their firstborn: a modest and generous man, endowed with every moral excellence.

In his youth the aforesaid William first administered the archdeaconry and afterward the provostship of the Church of Sens. In that administration he flourished so greatly that among the clerics of Gaul he had no equal in generosity, hospitality, expenditure, or the size of his household.

When nearly the whole Church was wavering and schism was raging, through the counsel and prudence of this man his aforesaid brother, the archbishop—or rather William himself—received at Sens the blessed Pope Alexander III, not yet fully confirmed, and bound him to Sens. Even kings and princes feared to do this. It is not easy to say how honorably he conducted himself [Col. 0301C] in this reception and during the time that the curia remained with them.

Called to the episcopate by divine goodness, he entirely set aside worldly fame and the allurements of human praise. Nevertheless, he did not at all forget his customary hospitality; rather, for as long as he lived, he practiced it piously and generously.

With incomparable simplicity he showed himself approachable to all, merciful toward the oppressed, and kind toward the needy. Devoting himself to vigils and prayers, he scarcely ever fell asleep or awoke without psalmody resounding from his mouth.

He celebrated Mass every day, unless some grave necessity intervened. When riding, he rarely spoke with his household except about his affairs. Otherwise he either sang psalms quietly by himself or called one of his companions and sang psalms and litanies, or the whole Psalter or part of it, [Col. 0301D] according to the length of the road.

By divine goodness he obtained the favor and love of princes, of the prelates of the Church, and of the entire people. During his time there were frequent changes among the counts of Nevers. From this arose many tribulations and difficulties for his own principal church and for many others. With God’s help, this pious and humble man worked to calm them so effectively that neither his own church nor any other church subject to him suffered any loss whatsoever of the integrity of its rights.

He showed himself not only the spiritual and temporal patron and protector of the churches, but also of the people and the city in which he sat.

When Guy had obtained the county, he was led astray by perverse counsel and attempted to oppose not only the ancient customs of the churches but also [Col. 0302A] those of the entire city. First, he tried to bring the winepresses under his own jurisdiction, so that no one in the whole city would be permitted to own a winepress except under an annual tribute paid to the count.

The aforesaid prelate resisted this presumption so manfully that neither the clergy nor the people lost their ancient liberty or were burdened in any respect.

The same count also violently seized other tithes of the vineyards, with the consent even of the churches to which they belonged, so that guards were stationed at each gate and forcibly took from every passerby a tenth part—or even more—of the grape harvest.

When the prelate heard this, he summoned the count. When the count refused to cease his violence in response to the bishop’s admonition, the bishop generally pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication [Col. 0302B] and an interdict upon his land.

Not content with this, he consulted the lord pope through his messengers and obtained from him privileges and confirmation concerning both the tithes and the other property of the Church.

But the mercy of the Lord preceded his messengers and granted him both the count’s friendship and the restoration of the tithes with humble satisfaction, so that whatever had been taken from the clerics or the people of the churches was restored to each person according to his proof or at his request.

The same count, with royal consent, also wished to establish a commune at Auxerre. The distinguished prelate confidently opposed this presumption as well and undertook to have the matter debated in the royal court. This was not without danger or enormous expense, for he almost incurred the hostility of the most pious [Col. 0302C] King Louis, who reproached him for trying to take the city of Auxerre away from the king and his heirs, considering all cities in which communes existed to belong to them.

At length, after the matter had long been disputed, the privileges and charters of the Church of Auxerre were carefully examined and understood, and after both the king and his men had been appeased with a considerable sum of money, he won the case. He obtained royal privileges declaring that the count and others at Auxerre could in no way establish a commune there without the consent and permission of the bishop of Auxerre.

The divine clemency pacified these many persecutions and extremely grave attacks by the aforesaid count and his men when and how it wished.

For when the count was afflicted by almost continuous bodily illness, [Col. 0302D] he began to be detained by an even more serious condition at Clamecy and to suffer as though at the point of death. Not only nobles but also neighboring bishops gathered to visit him. At that time he was excommunicated.

When they feared for his life, all the bishops who were present began to plead for his absolution. The bishops of Autun and Nevers, however, were in no way willing or daring to yield to their prayers.

The prelate William, moved by the piety and confidence that characterized him, said to the barons:

“Far be from us, who are present here, this disgrace and everlasting reproach: that so great a man and our count should die excommunicated [Col. 0303A] in our hands. I will first place myself as surety for the Church of Vézelay (*Virziliaca*) and for the others on whose account the sentence was pronounced against him.”

When the barons heard this, they rejoiced—or rather, they marveled at and praised the prelate’s counsel and generosity. They all likewise constituted themselves sureties, and so he absolved the count.

For this kindness in absolving him, he obtained not only the gratitude of the nobles and the people but also so great a measure of the count’s friendship that, whenever William was mentioned before him, he was accustomed to call him not merely “lord” or “bishop,” but more often “my patron.”

Accordingly, the count afterward gave to him and to his church, to possess forever, all the men whom he held in the valley of the chapel of Saint Andrew.

He also granted, at the end of his life, a gift at Tonnerre which his mother made to the same bishop for the sake of his soul [Col. 0303B] and those of his family: the men whom she held at Varzy, of whom there were thirty or more households. After the count’s death, the same bishop obtained them through the hand and privilege of the pious King Louis, though not without great labor and the greatest expense.

At Varzy he acquired whatever Matthew “Loose Shoe” held in the same castle and castellany—possessions of great value and revenue. The episcopal residence and Fosseta now stand in part upon them.

He acquired many other things there, in vineyards, meadows, houses, and various properties, which we have not wished to enumerate because of their length.

At Corbuel he acquired several men. At Giac he built houses and a bakery, surrounded a large part of the place with a wall, and had vineyards planted. He acquired men and many other things [Col. 0303C] there, together with the dean’s meadow.

At Charbuy he purchased for one thousand solidi whatever the knight Gerard Poteret possessed there. He also acquired meadows and many other things in the same place, and established forest preserves.

At Appoigny he purchased meadows, vineyards, and arable lands. He also acquired there the fief of Iterius Raaudi, the fief of William the knight, and the lands and meadows that the knight Hugh of Burgi, his mother, and his brothers possessed between the river Yonne and Chaumeis.

He also purchased that part which they claimed in the same woodland, and everything else that they possessed around the same castle, both in fiefs and in allodial property—all of which he purchased for a large sum.

Before his time, too, Stephen of Petra Pertusa, a noble and powerful man, had seized arable lands that ought to have belonged to episcopal right, taking them for possession by himself and his men, and had unjustly retained them for a long time. When he learned of this, although Stephen was related to him in the first degree of blood relationship, the man of God, placing justice before kinship, did not desist until he had restored all the aforesaid lands to episcopal ownership through ecclesiastical justice and by judgment of the court of Sens. And so that no dispute might arise thereafter concerning this matter, he had a large cross fixed as a boundary between Stephen’s lands and the episcopal lands; afterward, for as long as he lived, he had those lands cultivated with his own plough teams.

Likewise, when the mill at Verno had been completely destroyed by a great inundation of water that occurred in his time, he bought the share that Josselin and his heirs possessed in it, and rebuilt the mill much better than it had been before. At Tociacum he built an episcopal residence and a cellar, and there he bought lands, meadows, and many other properties. He also gave twenty pounds toward the construction of the tower, on the condition that Lord Hargodus swore to him that whenever he or his successors wished to have that tower, both he and his heirs would hand it over, together with the guards of the aforesaid tower whenever it happened that they were replaced.

At Conada he bought from Mochis of Chaleneium the grange of Brueria, situated beside the village of Chael, together with oxen and a plough team, meadows, and all the lands belonging to that grange, for which he paid eighty Provins pounds. He also acquired many other properties in the same castellany. Although Hervé of Donzy, a man of such nobility and power, never ceased opposing him, nevertheless, with God’s help, he lost nothing of the rights of his Church during his time. Rather, when he himself was already lying on his deathbed, he compelled Hervé to come to his bedside and perform liege homage to him for the fief of Giem.

At Auxerre, near Saint Julian, he bought twenty solidi in censual rent. He also bought the houses of Lambert Hosmund, which stood adjoining and far too inconveniently close to the gate and episcopal residence; after demolishing them, he joined their sites to the square of his court and enclosed it with a wall. He likewise bought the houses that stood beside the postern and the squares of Remald, knight of Lindriacum, and the squares of Stephen of Sarmasia. He bought and acquired many other properties in the same city, which it would take too long to enumerate.

I shall truthfully touch briefly upon a few matters concerning his admirable simplicity and miraculous humility. One day, as he was passing through a poor and modest village, a little woman came out of her hut, like that Canaanite woman who, pleading with the Lord for her daughter, said, “Have mercy on me, Son of David.” With tears and lamentation, she cried out piteously as she ran after the bishop: “Have mercy on me, man of God, for my husband is being afflicted by a harsh and unusual death.”

Moved by her cry, he turned and, seeing her tears and recognizing the cause, left the road, dismounted from his horse, and entered the hut bent low. He found the woman’s husband so swollen throughout his face, tongue, neck, and throat that the tongue scarcely protruded from his mouth and left a life-giving passage for the breath; the sick man could utter no words at all. Immediately, overcome with tears, he took refuge in the aid of prayer. He touched the sick man’s throat, face, and neck, making the sign of the cross upon them and repeatedly marking them with his ring. Then, after giving his blessing, he departed; at once the swelling and illness began to subside.

After a short interval, when he was returning through the same village, the aforesaid woman met him joyfully and began to give thanks, declaring and publicly proclaiming that through him the Lord had freed her husband from such a grave danger of death and restored him to health.

Likewise, on another occasion, when he was hurrying to bless an altar in the ruined chapel of Grandmont at Fontanetum, he found a woman before the house of a certain farmer, mourning bitterly. She was inconsolably distressed over the illness of her son, whom she had brought from far away on account of the hospital to the aforesaid blessing. For the young man, confined within that house, was in his final agony.

When the bishop heard this, he entered the house, visited the sick man, sat beside his poor bed, touched the young man’s face and forehead with his hand, comforted him with tearful words, and admonished and urged him to confess. After hearing his confession, while he remained there, his companions began telling him that he ought to leave a chaplain there to give the sick man Communion of the Lord’s Body. For a crowd of people was waiting for him at the aforesaid chapel, and it was already nearly the third hour of the day.

He replied to them: “Nothing is more important to me than to complete the work of the Lord. I shall not leave this place in any way until this man has received Communion.” He therefore ordered me, who am writing these things, to mount his palfrey so that I might bring the Viaticum more quickly from the aforesaid chapel, which was almost a mile away. I did so.

When I had returned, he did not recoil from the uncleanness of the place, the sick man’s odor, or the poverty of the bed. Not recoiling from the uncleanness of the place, the sick man's odor, or the poverty of the bed, he personally gave the Viaticum to the kneeling sick man; after giving his blessing and offering much consolation both to the mother and to the sick man, he departed.

The blessing of the altar had been completed, and he had scarcely begun Mass, when he was informed that the young man had died. When he heard this, while preaching to the people, he said so much about him that he seemed confidently to assert that the young man was already enjoying blessed rest.

We saw many other things worthy of being committed to writing and memory, but knowingly omit them, lest we should appear tedious.

Now let us add a few words concerning what he piously and mercifully bestowed upon his own Church and upon other Churches. He surrounded the Church of Saint Stephen on every side with an elaborate stone structure; he built a front gable and a rear one, together with their associated glazed windows; he adorned the southern tower with new fortification and a handsome covering of brickwork. He covered the entire church with new timbers, beams, tiles, and bricks, partly covered with lead, and, insofar as it depended upon him, vaulted it.

In his time new altars were founded by him and by others in the same church and were consecrated. One stood before the cross; he himself consecrated it in honor of the Holy Cross, Saint John the Evangelist, Saint Lawrence the Martyr, Saints Quiricus and Julitta—whose relics he placed there—and Saint Giles the Confessor. There he also established two chaplains, who were to celebrate Mass every day in perpetuity for the soul of Count Guy and his predecessors; he assigned sufficient revenues to those chaplains.

He erected another altar at his own expense in the crypt, on the side of the episcopal court, and consecrated it in honor of the blessed Apostle Paul, Saints Quiricus and Julitta, whose relics are kept there, the blessed Bishop and Confessor Germanus, and blessed Mary Magdalene. The canons of Saint Mary are bound to serve this altar and to celebrate a daily Mass for his soul and for the soul of his cleric Fromundus, who first assigned revenues to it.

For the altar of the blessed Apostle Andrew, situated in the same crypt, he assigned stipends for those who served it. To the altar of Saint Nicholas and Saint Martin he granted forty solidi in censual rent, together with ten pounds of wax, from the Church of D. de Bruenium.

To the Church of Saint John the Baptist, which in his time was built by Stephen Ollandus and dedicated by him, he contributed much toward its construction, and from its revenues he gave it sixty solidi. In the Church of Saint Prisca, he also assigned two priests who were to remain there permanently.

To the Church of the Blessed Mary he gave the Church of Monasteriacum Siccum; and he granted to the canons of that church the rent which they possess in the Church of Blavellum.

To the Church of Blessed Peter he gave the Church of Venosa, and at that time the canons first began to reside there. To the abbey of Saint Lawrence he gave the Church of Cept. To the nuns of Crisannova he gave twenty solidi in censual rent from the Church of Monesterellum, and half the small tithe of Lugniacum.

But how long it would be to enumerate everything he bestowed upon the Churches! We say briefly that there is no conventual church in the whole diocese of Auxerre that is not bound, because of the benefactions granted to it by him, to celebrate his anniversary solemnly.

Nor have we thought this should be left unmentioned: for the adornment of the Church of Blessed Stephen he gave one excellent pallium. Likewise, when, during the schism, he was the first of all the Gallican bishops to travel to the papal court, at the beginning of his episcopate he gave his chapter the entire benefice of the Church of Bacerna, establishing that they should celebrate the feast of Saint Martin in winter solemnly, with the great bells rung, and should annually observe the anniversary of his brother Hugh, archbishop of Sens, with due and fitting honor.

Later, when he had returned from the Lateran Council, he gave an eight-mark silver ewer for the adornment of the church and for storing holy water.

He flourished, then, in the time of Pope Alexander III of blessed memory, while the pious King Louis reigned in Gaul. When the king spoke of him, he was accustomed very often to say that, in his judgment and estimation, William, bishop of Auxerre, was one of the better priests of his entire kingdom.

He lived until the time of the king’s son Philip and attended his coronation, which was celebrated at Reims in the year 1179 from the Incarnation of the Word, during the octave of All Saints. In that same year, around the feast of Saint Remigius, he began to fall ill. When he felt himself oppressed by a quartan illness, he went to the abbey of Blessed Marianus in order to rest, and there he remained bedridden until his death.

When winter came on and his illness pressed him with more severe affliction, he summoned Theobald, the venerable bishop of Nevers and his very dear friend, Gerard, abbot of Vézelay and his kinsman, together with certain dignitaries and canons of the Church of Auxerre. He made his testament and ordered everything he possessed, both provisions and cattle and sheep, to be sold and the proceeds paid toward his debts.

He also gave to the Church of Blessed Stephen there a silver cup weighing four marks, very finely gilded inside and out, for placing the Lord’s Body in it. He gave silver little vessels and basins for the daily service of the altar of Blessed Stephen.

He also gave priestly vestments: two albs decorated with marvelous workmanship, together with precious stoles and amices; a tunic with a dalmatic; and a mitre adorned with wondrous gold embroidery. He gave books and the other things that he had in his chapel, together with the chest in which they had been stored. He also gave the gold embroidery with which, after his death, two mitres were decently ornamented.

To the abbey in which he lay he gave forty solidi in censual rent from the churches of Lugniacum and Molins. Earlier, he had given the same church many other things, namely half the rent of Vincella, the lands that he himself had bought at Tangiacum, and certain other properties inside and outside the city walls.

He lived—or, more truly, suffered in illness and performed penance—until the end of February. Although he had become so weakened and debilitated that he could neither stand on his feet nor rise from his bed, he nevertheless observed his customary abstinence in every respect. For throughout Lent—from the feast of Saint Martin, that is, until the Nativity of the Lord—he fasted daily and took no food whatsoever except Lenten food.

Meanwhile, the number and frequency of visitors was so great that even a healthy and vigorous man could scarcely have endured them. Yet he, although now almost deprived of all bodily strength, ordered that everyone be received with honor. Giving thanks to all, he tearfully begged them to intercede for him with the Lord, so that he might be brought to a good end.

This saying was frequently on his lips both during his illness and when he was well: one ought to ask the Lord only for a good end. Thus we often heard him say, when the poor or others prayed that he might have many days of life, prosperity, or continual bodily health: “You ought not to ask this of the Lord, but only that my end may be good.”

Thus, with only his spirit surviving and his earthly body already dead, yet never ceasing from prayer, he suffered in this way until the end of February. Then, recognizing that his end was approaching, he summoned his household before him and absolved them from everything they had committed against him; he humbly and tearfully asked them to absolve him in turn.

He also distributed the few things that remained to him, namely his rings. Then, having summoned the dean and his chapter to his bedside, he entrusted his end to them, complaining bitterly and saying that he had been occupied with so many matters that he had not bestowed many benefits upon them. Nevertheless, he had conducted himself toward them in such a way that he had caused them little or no harm, and had loved them all with sincere charity.

So that his memory might remain among them forever, he gave them there the Church of Saint Prisca, on the condition that one hundred solidi from the rent of that church should be distributed each year on his anniversary equally among the canons and the priests of the choir of Saint Stephen who attended the service; to the other clerics, as might seem appropriate; and that the remainder should be distributed to the poor.

There he began to admonish and exhort them tearfully not to allow the destructive crime of discord, envy, or schism to creep in among them. Instead, as soon as he had been buried, they were to approach the king, announce his death, and ask him for the due permission to elect; then, without delay, after summoning the brethren, they were to elect an honest, learned, and well-mannered man. For a long delay could be harmful and dangerous to them.

He also asked to be buried in the humbler priestly vestments that were in the Church of Blessed Stephen.

Then, with great lamentation, he burst out in these words:

“May he mercifully grant you true peace who, about to depart from his disciples, said: ‘I leave you peace; I give you my peace.’”

And so, after making a general confession, obtaining their intercessions, and receiving absolution, he gave them his blessing and dismissed them.

Wishing to omit nothing concerning what was necessary, he sent messengers to summon the venerable Bishop Guy of Sens, humbly asking that he deign to be present at his end. Out of the piety for which he was known, Guy put his affairs second and hastened to him; he found him still breathing.

Although on many other occasions he had spoken about confession and absolution, at that time he spoke about them especially and more attentively, as the circumstances required. He also commended his nephews and household to him as to their lord and kinsman. Guy kindly received them into his protection and willingly promised that he would never fail them.

On the following night, when his illness oppressed him more severely than usual, his attendants asked him whether he wished to die in ashes and haircloth, as befits a Christian. He assented with his voice and gesture as best he could and requested it. Fortifying himself as he could with the impression of the cross, he marked his final bed with the sign of that cross, raising his right hand.

Placed there, while the religious and clerics who were present sang the litanies and psalms, he sang with them for as long as he was able. Around midnight, after the community had sung Matins, it came to visit him, and in their presence he gave up his spirit.

When his body was washed, those of us who were present began to marvel beyond what can be expressed, lamenting anew over his astonishing and unheard-of emaciation. We anointed his entire face and countenance with balsam, and after he had been clothed in priestly and pontifical insignia, they carried him to the church.

The next day, the extent of the mourning throughout the city, and the groans and lamentations of nearly all who came, cannot easily be described. His appearance already seemed to be that of blessed rest. For his face, as is usual with the dead, was not darkened by any pallor; rather, it was so serene and almost ruddy that to those who came he seemed to be sleeping rather than dead.

After the sung Masses and the completion of the funeral rites, the aforesaid archbishop humbly bent his knees before the bier and kissed the gloves in which the bishop’s hands were wrapped, and the sandals on his feet. Many of us did the same. Thus he became the first of the bishops of Auxerre to be buried in that same church, before the high altar, on the left side beside the wall.

Afterward Hugh, archdeacon of Sens and his nephew, had a sufficiently honorable tomb built over him.

The bishopric remained vacant for one full year, ten months, and nine days.

## CHAPTER LVIII — On Hugh of Noeriis

Hugh of Noeriis occupied the bishopric for approximately twenty-four years. He was taken from the office of treasurer and made bishop around the year of the Lord 1183, near the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary. He was indeed a man distinguished by the nobility of his blood, but even more distinguished by the magnificence of his spirit.

### From whom he was born and descended

His father, Milo, lord of Noeriis, and his mother, the lady of Gessia, were of no lesser nobility.

### How magnificently he conducted himself

Born, therefore, of such ancestors, he was not degenerate from his innate nobility. For, in the manner of nobles, he lived with great worldly magnificence and was unaccustomed to a private life. With numerous conveyances, a large retinue of clerics and knights, many household attendants, and magnificent equipment, he equaled the titles of his ancestors.

### With what natural gifts, learning, or eloquence he was endowed

He was of medium stature and handsome appearance, endowed with wisdom and energetic in action; among the prudent he was the more prudent. Whenever he was present at any deliberation, his opinion was awaited and more often prevailed. He possessed immeasurable eloquence and was effective in persuasion. In demonstrative speech—that is, the form containing praise and blame—he expressed the powers of an orator with the greatest eloquence.

He was so learned and possessed such a lively intelligence that in any liberal or mechanical discipline he could readily produce words suited to the subject, as though he had acquired a complete knowledge of it. Often, too, he composed songs and melodies at great speed and with intense effort in the Latin tongue.

His lively intelligence certainly deserves praise: in a short time he forged his compositions and brought them to the file before bringing them to his tongue. Yet such eagerness to publish what he had made burned within him that he brought unpolished works into public view, works that would have been better kept hidden until, refined on the anvil of careful correction, they shone with more brilliant ornament.

For this reason, his little works, which during his lifetime were frequently used more because of the favor he enjoyed than because of their own form, were buried along with him after his burial.

He delighted in being surrounded by large numbers of knights and was more willing to discuss military studies with them. For this reason he frequently reread Vegetius Renatus, who writes about such disciplines, and offered the knights much instruction on military matters.

He had remarkable affection for his own people. He was courteous toward those with whom he lived, so much so that at home among them he became all things to all people and was almost one of them; outside, however, his dignity was maintained by the proper moderation of his prerogative.

### In what respects his character could be criticized

He was favorable toward everyone, except insofar as the desire for possessions—which drives almost all powerful men toward exactions and oppression of their subjects and toward usurping rights that are not theirs—perhaps provoked him beyond what was proper; and except insofar as, once anger had been conceived against anyone, he too often gave the reins without restraint to the ruin of that person and to his own desire to do harm.

### With what fervor he zealously defended the Catholic faith out of charity against heretics

Nevertheless, he was a magnificent defender of the Catholic faith, and he burned with such fervor concerning it that he labored with complete vigilance to capture the little foxes that destroy the vineyard of the Lord of hosts and cause it to degenerate into wild vines through heretical doctrines.

Against them he armed himself all the more fervently at the distinguished village of Charité in his diocese because he knew that the error of the heretics raged there more intensely. He persecuted the heretics there with such firmness of spirit that some of them, publicly performing penance throughout various dioceses, safely returned to the bosom of Mother Church after renouncing their heresy. Others, more obstinate and to the detriment of their salvation, fled to Italy or to the Albigensians, to their companions in error, exiles from the land of their birth and their own kinship.

Thus he brought that undertaking to completion, so that he was rightly called the hammer of heretics.

### How he repaired or enlarged the episcopal residences of Auxerre

Although he made such progress in spiritual matters, in temporal affairs he advanced much further, for he devoted himself to them with greater attention. By repairing what had fallen into ruin and constructing new buildings, he improved the episcopal residences of Auxerre. He added, at great expense, a wine cellar with a stone vault adjoining the greater palace, and a kitchen beside the gate, of extraordinary construction.

### What he did concerning the royal river there

At his castle of Eponiacum stood an episcopal residence called the Royal River, situated in a most pleasant and convenient place. The river Yonne flowed around it on every side, spreading out through its depth broader and more fish-filled bays, except that the continuous land at the front, although leaving only a small interval, contained a considerable intervening space and did not allow an island to exist there.

That residence, humble in form and materials, provided the bishop with an undistinguished dwelling. He enlarged it at considerable expense with numerous buildings of magnificent nobility and beauty. Desiring to make the place a safer refuge for his people against hostile disturbances, he built, on the front side where the land was continuous, from one side of the river to the other, a fence of immense oak timbers and a wall, and placed numerous battlements above it.

He dug deeply into the earth and extended enormous ditches, so that through them he might divert the course of the river and bring about there, by the supplement of human art, what nature had denied: namely, an island. He had already brought the work partly to completion and would have carried his undertaking further toward perfection, had not Theobald, count of Champagne, with a strong force resisted his efforts and thrown the work, almost at the point of completion, completely to the ground. The episcopal residences, however, were left intact.

### How he built Belle-Retour

At Charbuia, an episcopal village, there was a place covered with thickets between the woods. Because of the continual and varied courses of water, it was entirely useless and suited to no purpose. It is now called Belle-Retour.

After completely uprooting the thickets and collecting the running waters into a single mass, he made two ponds filled with many fish: one upper pond and another lower pond supplied by the outflow of the first. He added a third pond, very large and full of fish, formed from the outflow of the earlier ponds, from the waves, and from the torrents flowing together into it from every direction.

He also built there houses of various construction, of the greatest nobility and immense beauty. He wonderfully fortified them with ditches containing water flowing in from the upper pond, with battlements, and with a very strong fence on the front side opposite the first pond, placing a brick wall above the pond itself.

On the side where the wooded thicket lacked the protection of the ponds, he submerged and lowered into the ground woods all around, providing a strong defense that was difficult to capture. There was an open but narrow road through the middle of the woods, by which access to the inner house was difficult because of the many intervening obstacles—gates, ditches, and bridges—and which in suspicious times could be guarded by a few men.

The same bishop advanced this place, as far as human ingenuity could manage, toward every kind of beauty and convenience. He completely uprooted the woods that were covered with thickets or low and sparse trees, and therefore offered less usefulness, and converted them to agriculture. He made gardens there and planted trees of various kinds, so that, besides the beauty that arose from them, he might obtain abundant fruit.

He also enclosed a considerable part of the woods with a continuous fence, extending from the gate on the front side of the woods all the way to the embankment of the third pond. Within it he enclosed pleasant woodland clearings filled with wild animals in abundance. These delighted the eyes of those who looked upon them from the palace, and often provided agreeable and noble gifts, either at the greater feasts or when guests were received, gifts pleasing to the Lord.

Within or outside those enclosures, the abundant retreats of rabbits likewise provided material for a pleasant and useful occupation.

Thus the place, endowed with manifold convenience and beauty, continues to provide the bishops with a most agreeable residence, except that the destruction of the fence—which could not be preserved intact without excessive destruction of the woods and expenditure—has restored the wild animals to their freedom.

### On the houses at Tociacum and Conada

At Tociacum and Conada, episcopal castles, he built episcopal residences of immense nobility on sites prepared by his predecessors.

### On what he did at Varziacum

His noble castle of Varziacum, which, because the place had previously been weakened, was exposed to frequent incursions by marauders, he fortified by repairing the ancient walls and surrounding them with enormous towers and ditches.

Beside the Church of Blessed Eugenia, he built the episcopal residences from their foundations, enclosing them with a solid wall and magnificent buildings, towers, and battlements. He also extended the episcopal stronghold into a secure and difficult-to-capture fortification by means of a stronger wall, more secure towers, and outworks. He surrounded it with ditches of remarkable breadth, filling them with an agreeable abundance of water from springs flowing around them.

This contributed greatly to the strengthening of the fortification. Moreover, both from the abundance of excellent fish raised there and from the mills that he built there, as well as from his other resources, many advantages arose for the bishop and the entire community.

### On what he did at Noeriis

We have thought it worthwhile to insert into the present account what and how much he accomplished in that noble castle of his patrimony. Noeriis shines with such nobility and immunity inherited from his great-grandfathers that it remains in the ownership of its lord and, by right, recognizes no superior lordship. Rather, as it is commonly said, it is regarded as allodial and as existing under its own separate dominion.

For this reason it was all the more enviable not only to its neighbors but also to the more powerful princes around it, since, in relation to the lands adjoining it, it could extend its strength more freely and with greater impunity, both because of the power of its lord and of its householders or vassals and because of the impregnable situation of the place; it itself posed the greater threat.

After Clarembald, the brother of the lord of that castle, died, the same bishop undertook the guardianship of his son Milo, who was still in childhood. He administered this guardianship with great anxiety, and perhaps beyond what was just. For because of it he was more negligent in the affairs of his Church. He devoted the full liveliness of his attention to advancing the fortification of the same community and spent money with all his strength.

For, above the walls of the lower borough, situated at the foot of the mountain and surrounded on every side by the river called the Seneen, he placed very strong battlements made either of masonry or of extremely solid timber. On the ascent from the borough toward the mountain, although the castle was impregnable by its situation on that side, he built enormous ditches cut into the rock of the mountain and stronger gates.

In the upper part, where the mountain spreads out more widely at its summit and where the stronghold was situated, the ground extended in a way suitable for raising engines. Besides the ancient walls of the fortification, one of which was stronger and outermost and had been built by his brother Clarembald shortly before his death, he raised an inner wall beyond it, of greater height, thickness, and solidity. At its head he constructed a stronger tower.

Along the outer wall he also made ditches cut into the bare rock, and sent other cuttings ahead into the mountain, so that they could hold back enemies from the stronghold through multiplied obstacles and impediments.

He also built outworks connected with the outer wall and above them interwoven with beams of immense strength, so that those beneath would fear neither volleys of arrows, nor throwing engines, nor any other efforts of the enemy. Secure, they could prevent the approach of those coming from the opposite side by means of the rear ditches and the wall to which the outworks were joined.

Beside that wall he found a bubbling spring. Although it was small, it nevertheless poured forth a continual stream of clear water.

Outside the enclosure of the principal stronghold he built a palace of great nobility. It provided the stronghold with no small degree of additional fortification and offered its lord an agreeable residence, which he adorned with lavish and delightful ornament.

He also made underground passages from the wine cellar beneath the principal tower to the lower palace mentioned above, so that it would not be necessary to enter or leave the principal stronghold for wine or any other provisions. Instead, provisions could be lowered through the lower wall of the stronghold, while wine or water was secretly conveyed through pipes by a marvelous artifice.

This was certainly a remarkable precaution: provisions brought or transported into the castle were preserved more faithfully under stronger guard, and, once the barriers had been closed so as to exclude every suspicion, they could be supplied by this device for whatever uses were required.

Nevertheless, he fortified the stronghold beyond measure with weapons, crossbows, and everything else necessary for its defense. He bought, at great expense, the lodgings of knights and of any others contained within the enclosure of the upper fortification, and transferred them into the ownership of his nephew.

Both in this work and in the construction of the aforesaid palace, he employed prudent care so that access by those wishing to approach their lord’s presence would be regarded as less suspicious at his palace outside the enclosure of the principal stronghold. With every outsider excluded, the lord of the castle would not be forced, in suspicious times, to admit anyone at all within the upper enclosure unless he had complete confidence in that person’s loyalty.

For this reason he also placed the community’s baptismal church outside the enclosure, allowing only the lord’s chapel to remain in the upper part.

These were magnificent works, worthy of much admiration and praise—except that in doing so he converted into timber and stone the possessions of the people entrusted to his custody, and consumed a large part of the episcopal resources, which would have been better applied either to the needs of the Church or to those of the poor.

He governed that castle with great magnificence and strength until his nephew grew to the age of puberty and became subject to his guardianship. He resisted with a powerful hand the ambushes of those around him and repelled with counterstrokes no weaker than theirs the incursions of those who frequently carried off plunder from the land under his protection, so that he appeared formidable to everyone in the surrounding region.

He repeatedly shattered with such prudence the designs formed against him and against the castle by the duke of Burgundy and by the other princes and powerful men that he always carried away an honorable reputation.

He also acquired for his nephew the village of Vallanto, beside the episcopal village of Giacum, buying it at great expense.

But enough of these matters. Let us now turn to others and discuss, as memory brings them to mind, how much he advanced the revenues of his Church or improved its conditions. We retain only a few of the many things concerning him and omit some in order to avoid wearying the reader.

### On the king’s procurations: how they were remitted
[Col. 0314A]

It was a royal right that whenever the lord king, or any of his household, was led by the occasion of travel or by a movement of his own will to turn aside to some episcopal residence, he was to be received honorably and provided for suitably. By divine mercy arranging the matter and bringing about an appropriate opportunity, the bishop abolished this burdensome and onerous obligation forever in the following manner.

When the most noble castle of Gien, belonging to Hervé de Donzy, count of Nevers, which was held in fief from the church of Auxerre, had come into royal ownership, and in accordance with the terms of the agreement which Lord King Philip had approved and concluded—namely, that he should marry the daughter of Peter, count of Nevers, to whom the county belonged by hereditary right—the lordship of the castle having thus been transferred to the king, the bishop repeatedly petitioned the royal majesty with great insistence, since he could not retain the church’s fief without prejudice to himself.

[Col. 0314B]

At last, in compensation for the fief, after a royal charter had been drawn up, he obtained that the king should forever remit such provisioning obligations from the bishops. He also granted that the bishop of Auxerre should not in any of his residences be required to receive the king, or anyone acting in his name, as a guest or to provide him with necessities. Nevertheless, the hundred-pound candle of wax was to remain: according to ancient custom, on the feast of the Finding of Saint Stephen, namely in August, the lord of the aforesaid castle was accustomed to pay it to the church of Auxerre.

[Col. 0314C]

To this day the lord king has had it paid by his provosts of Gien, imposing the penalty that whenever the provosts failed to deliver that candle at the appointed time, they were to pay the king irrevocably five Parisian solidi for each day by which payment was delayed. This was certainly a useful compensation and one that would benefit the church, since much of the bishops’ burden was remitted by it, while from the fief of Gien nothing accrued to them except honor, without revenue.

### How he acquired the tithes and the episcopal residence at Coulanges

Peter de Courson had purchased Coulanges, on the River Yonne, together with everything that the monks of La Charité possessed there, at a very high price. The bishop wished to reimburse him and offered to purchase it himself as ecclesiastical property within his diocese, asserting that he had the stronger claim. He would undoubtedly have succeeded had not royal favor, which Peter had secured for himself, stood in the bishop’s way.

[Col. 0314D]

Nevertheless, after much effort, the bishop eventually extorted from him by agreement the tithes and offerings and whatever belonged to spiritual matters; in addition, he obtained the residence which still exists there as an episcopal house.

### How he acquired the tithe of Varzy, and under what terms

At Varzy little or nothing was being paid from the wine tithe. He acquired it by an agreement with the inhabitants in the following manner: he remitted the mortmain and the March tallage, from which five solidi were paid each year in March by each principal household. He also remitted the gallows, the rake, and similar customary obligations, which were a great burden to them but offered little profit to the bishops.

[Col. 0315A]

In return for this remission, however, they were bound to pay the tithes to the bishops under these terms: namely, one load out of every ten, to be selected by one or more of the bishop’s servants appointed for that purpose. This was plainly a great benefit to the Church. For the remission granted on this account could scarcely amount to one hundred pounds annually, whereas the value of the tithes frequently exceeded five or six hundred pounds, and even more, in Provins currency.

He carried out many other useful and prudent undertakings in the bishopric, which either do not come to mind when recalled or had not previously come to our knowledge.

### How courageously he resisted the persecutors of the Church

[Col. 0315B]

He resisted the persecutors with great courage, restraining their rebellion by the severity of ecclesiastical discipline and by force. He endured with fearless and steadfast mind the many adversities which he suffered in the bishopric, whether on this account or for other reasons. He was a man magnificent in spirit and endowed with unconquerable patience. Of these matters, we have thought it proper to insert in these pages a few that are known to us.

### The form of interdict established in the time of Count Peter, and why it was established in that form

[Col. 0315C]

Count Peter—namely, Peter of Courtenay, cousin of Lord King Philip—ruled in the counties of Auxerre, Nevers, and Tonnerre. Through the king’s favor, Peter had married Agnes, daughter of Guy, formerly count of Nevers, to whom the aforesaid counties belonged by hereditary succession. For this purpose he gave the lord king the noble patrimonial castle called Montargis, so that he might obtain that marriage.

He was indeed a man of royal blood and immense power, but reckless in spirit, terrifying in his anger, and incapable of restraining the impulse of his mind from inflicting troubles or injuries. Consequently, under his rule, not only the bishop but also the churches subject to him and ecclesiastical men frequently suffered many grave afflictions, both from him and from others who either took from him a familiar example of harming others or, because he did not resist them, found greater freedom to rage against the Church of God.

[Col. 0315D]
