From the beginning of his rule the Church suffered so much under him that the city of Auxerre remained nearly fifteen years under interdict because of his excesses. Its churches were closed and divine offices were silent, except that at rare and clearer intervals, when the count returned to the Church’s embrace through satisfaction, his church occasionally resumed its services. Yet within a short time the count would repeat his injuries and would not allow its tranquility to last, but caused it to relapse into silence.

Finally, after the bishop and the chapter of the church of Auxerre had adopted a more salutary course, since frequent interdicts caused vices to increase without measure and heresies were feared to be taking root, and since people’s minds were being hardened against their salvation by measures imposed for that very purpose, they agreed after prudent deliberation that, while the count lived, they would temper this kind of punishment in the following manner.

[Col. 0316A]

The count’s person, struck by the sword of excommunication in accordance with the demands of his excesses, was to remain under interdict in the city of Auxerre in such a way that, whenever he arrived, a single bell in the major church would be rung with the great bells. Once his arrival had thus become known, the churches would be closed for as long as he remained present, and divine offices would be conducted in the silence of interdict. Upon his departure, the same ringing of the bell, publicly announcing it like a herald’s proclamation, would restore to the churches the pleasing brightness of their solemn services, as though the clouds had dispersed. The count’s men, however, were excluded from entering the churches, since they alone were subject to the interdict.

This was surely a sound and salutary statute. For the count could neither enter nor leave his own city without great shame, nor, because of the people’s outcry, remain there for long; and the Church was not forced by its silence to neglect edification and the progress of souls.

### How he conducted himself manfully in adversity

[Col. 0316B]

The bishop endured the almost unbearable and terrifying storms of this tempest with great courage and without fear, devoting his entire self to defending the rights of the Church. For her sake he set himself as an unconquerable wall against those who came against her. He resisted manfully not only the attacks of the count but also those of others, and did not cease until, after they had been humbled beneath the powerful hand of God (1 Peter 5:7), he reached a praiseworthy conclusion to the honor of Him and of His bride, the Church. Of this, we have thought it appropriate to sketch a few matters from among many.

### How Count Peter of Auxerre removed from the ground a child whom he had ordered to be buried in the bishop’s chamber

[Col. 0316C]

Although it was familiar and frequent for him to be separated from the unity of the Church by excommunication, the count had at one time been excommunicated by the bishop of Auxerre, and the city had been placed under interdict because of his grave excesses.

Inflamed by the fire of violent indignation, he expelled from the city by herald’s proclamation not only the bishop, who, as his vassal, ought to have been his loyal man, but also the canons and clerics. A small dead child could not receive ecclesiastical burial because of the city’s interdict. Stirred by the untimely cries and tears of the child’s mother, the count had the body buried in the bishop’s own chamber, before his lord bishop’s bed, as an insult to him and a contempt of God.

[Col. 0316D]

The bishop pursued this utterly sacrilegious crime with the strictness of ecclesiastical discipline and complete steadfastness, and finally compelled him to offer satisfaction in the following manner.

On Palm Sunday, during a solemn procession, in the presence of Blessed William, the count’s uncle and archbishop of Bourges, who came to strengthen him in humbling himself, and Peter, archbishop of Sens, together with many others whom either the bishop’s concern had summoned or the novelty of the event had attracted to witness it, the count opened the grave with his own hands and removed the dead body. It was exceedingly foul and rotten, and a great offense to the nostrils, since it had lain there buried for several months.

[Col. 0317A]

From that chamber to the cemetery of Mont-Autric he carried it on his own shoulders barefoot, dressed only in linen, like any common man going to bury it there. In this way he humiliated himself salutarily before God, who bends the necks of kings and inclines their heads.

### What became of this count

We think it worthwhile to indicate to posterity what became of this count, so that people may fear provoking the Lord’s anger against themselves all the more securely by learning from another’s example how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God (Hebrews 10:31). He abundantly repays those who act proudly (Psalm 30:24), giving grace to the humble and resisting the proud (1 Peter 5:5).

[Col. 0317B]

After Count Peter’s wife Agnes had died, he married Yolanda, sister of Henry, emperor of Constantinople, in a second marriage. When Henry had been removed from this life, Peter was raised to the empire by right of kinship, through his wife’s claim. At her urging he undertook the journey there. Pope Honorius confirmed him as emperor of Constantinople and anointed him together with his wife.

Afterward, he reached as far as Dyrrachium with a large army of Latins and besieged the city, while his wife proceeded by a prosperous route through the safer regions of Romania, which had long been subject to Latin rule. The emperor made no progress in the siege, and the siege was lifted. He then took the more common route through hostile lands toward Constantinople, proceeding incautiously and intending to recover the empire, presumptuously relying on his own strength.

[Col. 0317C]

But the Most High Lord, who regards the lowly and knows the lofty from afar (Psalm 137:6), enclosed him and his entire army in the hands of the enemy and delivered their strength into captivity.

Let human pride hear and take heed: behold this man, of such nobility and power, who had so often raised his heel against God and the Church; now he is an inglorious captive, delivered into prison custody. May the Lord in His mercy grant that, if only at the last, he may be pierced with remorse for his sins by the hand of the Lord chastening him—or, if he is not crushed, that the punishment for them may at least begin in the present life.

But now let us return to the subject before us and proceed to explain how he sought vengeance upon the persecutors of the Church, to the praise of God and the honor of the Church.

### How he took vengeance on Peter de Courson

[Col. 0317D]

Peter de Courson, whom we mentioned above, was second to the count in all his undertakings. At his nod and on his advice, Count Peter, of whom we have spoken, was governed in everything. As we said, Peter de Courson greatly incited the count, who was disorderly in spirit, to oppress the churches, as far as he could; he was likewise hostile to their tranquility and peace.

To tame the savagery of this beast, the bishop armed himself with every argument demanded by the circumstances. As long as the favor of the count supported him and the summit of his power shone forth, Peter de Courson did not cease persecuting the Church of God and the bishop himself.

[Col. 0318A]

The bishop, who possessed considerable worldly resourcefulness, waited for an opportune time for vengeance. At last he subdued Peter’s insolence in the following way, setting before the Church and the nobles a useful yet terrifying example, although in this the bishop may perhaps appear to have departed from the gentleness of evangelical religion.

When the count’s favor had been withdrawn from Peter and the cloudy times of his glory and power had obscured their former brightness, the bishop, finding an opportunity suited to his wishes, seized him and took him up in a chariot. He bound him in fetters, placed him with his head uncovered—his head having long since been disfigured by the baldness he had acquired—and had him dragged quite shamefully through the streets and squares of the city of Auxerre, publicly displaying him as an object of ridicule to the people.

[Col. 0318B]

Thus, where he had once exercised the honor of supreme power, he suffered the mockery of his affection more disgracefully; and all who stand in high office might learn not to act perversely or be elated by success, but to humble themselves beneath Him who has cast down the mighty from their seats and exalted the humble (Luke 1:52).

### How he convicted Euraudus of heresy

Euraudus of Castronovo succeeded him in office and power. He was a knight no less malicious, neither inferior in intelligence nor less eager to do harm, and a most savage persecutor of the Church. Infected as he was with heretical depravity, he had resolved to oppose, as far as he dared and was able, those who professed ecclesiastical doctrines.

Of his monstrous acts, we have thought it appropriate to transmit the following to the knowledge of posterity.

[Col. 0318C]

A certain man who had incurred his displeasure was being pursued by his enemies to the point of death. To escape the danger of imminent death, he fled into the church of Blessed Mary within the walls, taking refuge there because of the place’s immunity. With no reverence shown to God and the church’s immunity violated, Euraudus had the man killed in the church itself by the sword of his pursuer, and atrociously profaned God’s sanctuary with innocent blood.

But the Lord, the righteous judge, as will be explained below, repaid him with a fitting return according to his merits.

Eventually, after offending Count Peter, Euraudus left him and went to Count Hervé of Nevers, to whom the county of Nevers had passed through his marriage to Mathilda, Count Peter’s daughter. As stated above, she had married Hervé through royal favor, since the county belonged to her by hereditary right.

[Col. 0318D]

Euraudus was received so favorably by Hervé that he held under the count of Nevers the same position he had held under Count Peter. Under Hervé’s authority, the Church again suffered many oppressions, as it had previously in the county of Auxerre.

At last, when the infamy of the heresy with which Euraudus was branded became more widespread, the bishop—being, as he was, a foremost champion of Catholic doctrine and a fervent exterminator of heretical perversity—publicly accused him of heresy at the council convened in Paris by Octavian, cardinal priest of the Roman Church, who was then carrying out a legation in France. Many archbishops, bishops, and other persons holding ecclesiastical dignities or lower offices were present.

[Col. 0319A]

The bishop convicted the accused by irrefutable testimony. Once convicted, Euraudus received a sentence of condemnation with the council’s approval. Having been condemned, he breathed out his profane soul in the burning of the fire, receiving the deserved wages of his merits and imprinting upon his family a shameful mark of his perversity and an everlasting disgrace.

Learn, all you who work iniquity and who seek the support of the powerful in order to do harm; learn that the hand of the Lord is extended over all the sinners of the earth. Behold this man, great and powerful, feared even by the powerful themselves, dragged to the punishment of a disgraceful death and receiving in temporal terms the fitting payment for his iniquity.

Would that, even at the hour of death, he had been crushed in remorse, like the thief who was crucified with the Lord and who, though late, repented with a fruitful confession (Luke 23:39–43), so that he might not receive the return for his crimes in punishments to come!

[Col. 0319B]

### Concerning the Caputiati: how he exterminated them

In those days, near the beginning of his promotion, an exceedingly dreadful and dangerous presumption arose in Gaul. It had begun to draw all the common people into rebellion against and destruction of their superior authorities. Although it seemed to have its origin in good, it suggested deadly things while pretending to be an angel of light, as Satan transforms himself into an angel of light.

Under the pretext of mutual charity, they bound themselves together by oaths, agreeing that they would provide one another mutual counsel and assistance in their needs against everyone. The members of this confederation had taken as their emblem and sign woven hoods bearing leaden badges, said to belong to Blessed Mary of Le Puy; these distinguished them from others. It was plainly a diabolical and pernicious invention.

[Col. 0319C]

For it followed from this that no fear or reverence was shown to superior authorities. Instead, all strove to assert for themselves the liberty which, they claimed, they had inherited from their first parents at the beginning of creation, not understanding that slavery was the punishment deserved for sin.

It also followed that there would be no distinction between lesser and greater, but rather confusion—a confusion that would soon drag into ruin the whole order of affairs which is now governed, by the Lord’s authority, through the direction and service of superiors.

Consequently, every discipline, whether political or Catholic, would be destroyed, to the detriment of human peace and the salvation of souls; and heresies that asserted only carnal things would multiply as ecclesiastical authority weakened.

[Col. 0319D]

Although this movement later began to spread through many regions of Gaul, it especially invaded the territory of Auxerre and Bourges and the regions of Burgundy. It had already burst into such madness that its supporters were ready, with their forces combined, to claim their degenerate liberty by the sword.

Against this dreadful pestilence, which could be restrained not by gentle exhortations but only by immense efforts, the bishop girded himself all the more boldly because it had extended its branches more abundantly throughout his diocese and especially through his own villages.

[Col. 0320A]

Coming with a multitude of armed men to Giac, his own village, which that contagion had almost entirely seized, he arrested all the Caputiati he found there. He fined them, cut off their hoods, and, so that the vengeance for such presumption might be public and so that servants might learn not to grow insolent against their masters, ordered them to spend an entire year without hoods, their heads completely bare and exposed to the air, enduring the heat, cold, and various conditions of the weather.

One could see the wretched men in summer wandering through the fields with their heads exposed and without any covering, sweltering beneath the sun’s heat; in winter they stiffened from the excessive cold.

[Col. 0320B]

They would have spent the entire year under this punishment had not the archbishop of Sens, Guy, the bishop’s uncle, happened to pass that way. Moved by compassion for them, he reproved the bishop for such severity and shortened the period by the time remaining before the year was completed.

Thus, within a short time, he exterminated the madness of such presumption both in his own villages and throughout his territories. Following his example, within a short time, by the Lord’s favor, this kind of rashness was uprooted throughout other towns, dioceses, and provinces as well.

### How, while the see was vacant, he governed the church of Langres and safeguarded the royal rights

[Col. 0320C]

The reputation for his great skill and prudence, in which he excelled, especially in secular affairs, spread widely throughout the surrounding regions. When the church of Langres was also vacant and had long been troubled by a division over the election, he was specially summoned because the royal rights, which in part marked the boundaries between the empire and the kingdom, required careful guardianship. The episcopal possessions had to be governed and administered not with relaxed simplicity but with great strength.

Throughout the entire period of his summons, he governed the church magnificently and powerfully.

### How, while the see was vacant, he was postulated as archbishop of Sens, but without success

After the death of Michael, archbishop of Sens, of blessed memory, he was chosen to govern the church of Sens by the unanimous consent and votes of all, on account of the outstanding marks of his integrity. Everyone petitioned the Apostolic See that he be transferred to it from Auxerre.

[Col. 0320D]

But Innocent III, who was then pope, a man who perhaps too often followed the impulse of his own will beyond what was proper, prevented his transfer at his own discretion. He wished his own master and, as it were, foster-father in the schools while he was in France—namely, Master Peter of Corbeil—to advance in that Church, or rather to intrude into it, even against the opposition of the chapter.

This he did, and he did not admit the postulation made concerning the bishop, not so much by law as by his own will, if one may say so. Thus, by divine providence, it came about that the church of Auxerre, with which he had contracted a bond of spiritual marriage, did not remain widowed by the separation of so great a father.

### Concerning the ornaments he gave to the church

For the adornment of his church of Auxerre he gave two precious silk cloths of immense size, called *Miradola*.

[Col. 0321A]

We believe that he would have covered the image of the Crucified with silver and, from his own resources, supplied both the two marks lacking beyond the valuation of the golden cross and the more than thirty marks assigned for this purpose which he had at some time taken for his own needs, promising their future restoration with an excess.

But death prevented both this work and the promised repayment. Thus he transmitted the burden of this debt to his successors.

### How he improved the form and arrangement of the church

He enlarged the windows in the façade of the church’s older structure and the glazed windows, so that the church, which until then had been rather dark in the old manner, might shine with greater light.

[Col. 0321B]

He removed two altars which had stood on either side of the church toward the front, where the lateral doors now exist, and which considerably narrowed the church’s spaciousness. He drew out the doors that remain there to this day.

He filled with earth the church, which had been situated much too low, and had it paved for the sake of beauty. He greatly ennobled the roof and the sides of the building. We will refrain for the present from explaining many other things of this kind, or even greater works, which he carried out usefully or prudently in the bishopric, lest, since we have either heard them insufficiently clearly or, having heard them, have not retained them as they were because memory has faded, we depart from the path of truth by asserting uncertain things as fact.

### Concerning what he gave to the chapter for the church’s daily bread, and other matters

[Col. 0321C]

To the chapter, for its daily bread, he generously granted Oisy and one hundred solidi from the church of Saint Priscus, which are distributed each year on the anniversary of his death.

### How he went to Rome, and concerning his death

At last, out of devotion to pilgrimage and perhaps also to advance certain matters he had undertaken, he went to Rome, where he was honorably received by the aforesaid Pope Innocent III.

But he was immediately seized by a severe illness and, within ten days after entering the city, paid there the debt owed by human nature. He died at Saint Clement’s, and in the Lateran church of Blessed John, called the Constantinian Church, in the presence of the lord pope and the cardinals, he earned an honorable burial.

[Col. 0321D]

He was placed among the papal pyramids, in a mausoleum somewhat humbler but nevertheless honorable and made of marble, in the year of the Lord 1206, on the feast of Saint Nicholas. The bishopric remained vacant for two months and somewhat more, namely until the Friday after the Purification of Blessed Mary.

He governed his church for nearly twenty-four years, during the reign in France of the illustrious King Philip III, and during the pontificates of Urban, Lucius, Clement, Celestine, and Innocent III.

He left the bishopric completely free and exempt from every burden of debt, except for the two marks of gold for the cross and the thirty marks of silver, which we mentioned above and which had been assigned to cover the image of the Crucified.

### Concerning the signs of his death

We have thought it worthwhile to add to the present work the signs and indications of his death, which, by the Lord’s will, became known not only at Rome, where he lay ill, but also among us through several people.

[Col. 0322A]

Three days before he died, at the beginning of the night—when beds prepared for sleep were calling weary limbs, exhausted by the day’s labor, to rest—a tremendous crash was heard, as if some ancient building near the church of Saint Clement, where he was staying as a guest, had collapsed completely.

The bishop and his attendants were awakened by the crash. On the following day, through their servants and also by their own efforts, they began to investigate where the ruins of so great a collapse might be, since it had seemed to fall so close by. But throughout the whole city, neither near nor far, they could hear or discover that any ruin had occurred or that any crash had been heard.

[Col. 0322B]

From that time the bishop began to suspect his own approaching end. On the very night, or near the time, when he departed from the body in the city of Rome, the wall at the episcopal residence by the royal river, near the lower hall, which separated the adjoining meadow from the Yonne, and at Varzy the walls of the town which he had built, partially collapsed, as though they wished to die with their dying lord.

In those same days Stephen of Saint-Sauveur of Auxerre, canon and sacristan, and the bishop’s table-companion at Auxerre, lay suffering from a grave illness. On the very day of the bishop’s death, as was discovered afterward, the bishop appeared to him in a vision—not in sleep, but while he was awake, and during the day. Among other things he said to him:

“Come, follow me, for I have already gone ahead.”

[Col. 0322C]

Stunned by the dreadful vision, Stephen called his attendants, who had just left the room where the sick men lay. He asked whether they had seen the bishop return from his Roman journey. Wondering why he said such things, they replied that the bishop could not yet have returned.

He answered: “He certainly departed from here just now, and I am greatly surprised that you did not see him.”

He then related the entire vision to them in order. Within three days after the bishop’s death, Stephen himself departed this life, following the bishop who had called him to the passage to which he had gone ahead.

Eustace, likewise a canon and table-companion of the bishop, who later also became sacristan, was resting in his bed during those same days when he dreamed that one of the bishop’s companions, whom the bishop had taken with him to Rome, came to him with his face somewhat downcast and sorrowful.

[Col. 0322D]

When Eustace asked why he did not look at him with an uplifted and cheerful face, the man briefly replied in a verse:

“Death is near, pestilence ready, salvation far away.”

Although Eustace turned this vision over in his mind, he was not yet thinking of the bishop’s death. He shared it with one of the bishop’s companions who had remained behind when the bishop of Auxerre departed. When messengers announced the bishop’s death and the day of his death, Eustace discovered that it had been not so much a simple vision as a forewarning of the bishop’s death.

Indeed, a revelation of this kind had been made to him concerning the bishop’s death.

O magnificent man, whose departure was perceived by insensible things, and whose death was foretold by many signs of revelation to those living in distant regions!

Let us therefore pray, dearest friends, to the Lord for him, that with His saints and elect he may deserve to receive a share in everlasting glory.

## CHAPTER LIX — Concerning William

[Col. 0323A]

William, from the territory of Auxerre and the castle of Chilly, was the son of Bouchard, brother of Deimbert, lord of that same castle—a man of immense severity but exceptional loyalty. His mother was Aanor, daughter of the noble Andrew, lord of Montbar. He derived a distinguished origin from both parents: from his father, unconquerable steadfastness; from his mother, a holier way of life.

[Col. 0323B]

For he belonged to the family of that most holy Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who first founded that monastery. Having become its abbot, and having been distinguished by many miracles, both during his life and after his death, as evidence of his merit, he was received, with the approval of the Roman Church, into the catalogue of the saints as a most brilliant jewel throughout the universal Church of God. There his memory is celebrated annually with particular distinction.

### Concerning the holiness of his mother

The aforesaid mother of William, Aanor, imitated the holiness of this man. As though she had inherited goodness and showed herself co-heir to it in her conduct, although she shone through the lineage of her husband and ancestors, she nevertheless laid aside every proud brow and displayed herself as a servant in the manner of a handmaid of Christ.

From her resources she personally ministered to the poor like a poor woman of Christ. She was constant in prayer, frequent in church, vigilant in the divine offices, and outstanding in the immense goodness of her conduct.

### Concerning the miracle that occurred at his mother’s death

At last, looking upon the humility of His handmaid, the Lord provided this sign of her holiness at the end of her life.

[Col. 0323C]

When she had died at her town of Esnon, she ordered herself to be carried to the Cistercian monastery called Pontigny, so that she might be placed beside her husband, who had previously been buried there. This monastery is known to lie two leagues or more from the aforesaid town.

As she was being carried out, there was that day such abundant and continuous rain, while a violent wind was also blowing, that those who had gathered for the funeral procession could not keep the rain from penetrating their cloaks, and the silk cloth spread over the bier, although fastened firmly to it with bast or hempen cords, scarcely withstood the wind’s fury without being carried away through the air.

[Col. 0323D]

Four candles, as was customary at such funerals, were carried with the bier. Although they had been taken out burning from the church of Esnon, adjoining the house of mourning, everyone thought that they could not continue to burn on the road, both because of the abundance of rain and because of the violence of the wind.

They came to the monastery where the body was to be buried and entered the church. To everyone’s astonishment and wonder, and amid outbursts of praise to God, all the candles were found burning, as though the most tranquil calm had accompanied them, untouched by any storm of wind.

[Col. 0324A]

We have briefly digressed to touch upon this matter so that, through this present miracle, the power and mercy of our Lord in His saints might be made evident, to God’s honor and for our instruction. The Lord set this woman, whom we have mentioned, before us as an example of humility and goodness.

Now let us return to our subject.

### Concerning his character

William, born of such parentage, began from his earliest age to be a boy of good character, possessing a certain innate simplicity and natural maturity. He did not, like his other contemporaries, incline his mind at that age toward childish songs and frivolities.

Even then, in his face, walk, and gestures, one could discern from his prematurely developed maturity the appearance of the gravity he would later possess; and his childhood itself foretold the goodness that would follow.

### How he became a cleric

[Col. 0324B]

His father loved him most tenderly because he had been born later, as is often found in paternal affections. He took him with him as a knight so that he might train his still tender age in military disciplines, intending to devote him to military studies.

But the providential arrangement of divine dispensation, which had destined him to become a future bishop, changed his father’s plan for the better. For his brother Guy, archbishop of Sens, obtained him from their father through much and earnest pleading, so that he might be handed over to clerical service.

### At what age he became a cleric, and how he advanced in the clerical state

[Col. 0324C]

When he had reached his eleventh year, he sat down to the first elements of literary learning. Continuing his studies in this field, he progressed in time so far that, climbing the ladder of that discipline with a keen intelligence, he passed beyond childish beginnings and advanced from one degree to another.

First he was competently instructed in the liberal arts. Then he advanced so far in the knowledge of legal and canon law that he was rightly regarded as a jurist.

Finally, abandoning secular sciences, he labored so diligently in sacred Scripture that afterward he could offer others more abundantly from a full heart the streams of divine eloquence, although he never ascended a master’s teaching chair in the schools.

### What teachers he had, and concerning the formation of his character

[Col. 0324D]

His uncle, the archbishop whom we mentioned above, always provided him with teachers approved in knowledge, life, and conduct. They watched over him no less carefully to preserve his innocence and form his character than to advance his learning.

Thus it came about that, just as heated wax placed before a fire receives any image the craftsman wishes to impress upon it, so his tender age, cultivated by the life, teaching, and example of good men, received the form of holiness. He is therefore believed to have remained a virgin and undefiled in the flesh.

### What dignities he attained, and how energetically he conducted himself in them
Thus, as he advanced in wisdom and grew in years, he went from virtue to virtue. From his earliest youth his progress was accompanied by the attainment of so many and such varied ecclesiastical dignities that he could say with Solomon: “I loved wisdom above health and every beauty, and I resolved to have her as my guide; all good things came to me together with her” [Col. 0325A]. For in the cathedral church of Sens he obtained the treasurership and the archdeaconry of Provins, while in Auxerre he obtained the deanery. Though absent and living in distant regions for the sake of study, he was unanimously elected to it by the canons of the church; they waited for him for more than a year, until his return from the schools. In the administration of these dignities he was exceedingly energetic and effective. For he labored with great effort and diligence, as best he could, whether by peaceful means or through litigation, to dispense spiritual things faithfully while preserving temporal possessions, to gather what had been scattered, and to bring into the light rights that had lain hidden under the cloud of anyone’s oppression or exaction.

### How he prosecuted the rights of the deanery of Auxerre against the bishop

[Col. 0325B]

He watched over the rights of the deanery all the more vigilantly because the bishop’s encroachment upon his jurisdiction made resistance especially necessary. He resisted him so successfully that no one except himself or his official would hear the city’s cases—apart from the parish of Saint Lupus, which was not within the dean’s jurisdiction—unless they had been brought by appeal before a higher court.

### The disobedience of the priests, whom Bishop Hugh defended against him while he was dean, and the satisfaction imposed

Certain priests who governed parishes in the city did not observe a sentence of interdict pronounced in the city of Auxerre, which the dean himself had ordered to be observed, because the bishop had commanded the contrary. The dean therefore suspended them; but the bishop absolved them, and, since the bishop had thus relaxed the dean’s sentence, they did not cease exercising their offices, supported by episcopal authority.

At length, while the bishop defended their disobedience, the dean pursued the matter with such victorious constancy before the metropolitan see of Sens that, justice having spoken and the bishop having been defeated in law, they were compelled to satisfy the dean for their disobedience. Visiting their iniquities with the rod and their sins with scourges, he made them undergo publicly and solemnly the discipline of the rods in the chapter of Auxerre.

[Col. 0325D]

Among them was a man of great gravity and reputation, namely Master Robert, prior of Blessed Mary outside the walls. Although he was esteemed highly by everyone, and for that very reason was more ashamed to suffer defeat, he had been more obstinate and rebellious. Shut up in the cloister at Saint Marien and temporarily removed from the administration of his priory at the dean’s discretion, he performed penance for several days on bread and water. His abbot also imposed upon him the penalty customarily inflicted on rebels and disobedient men.

He likewise imposed a penalty, as he himself had prescribed, upon certain canons of Blessed Mary within the walls whom the bishop had ordained without the dean’s presentation, after those ordained had made satisfaction to him for that offense.

### How he compelled Bishop Hugh to restore to the Church the trees that he had taken from the Church’s forests against his will

[Col. 0326A]

The bishop, despite the opposition of the dean and of certain canons who supported him, and with other canons favoring the bishop, had some trees felled in the Church’s forest of La Buscha and transported by force from the royal river to the episcopal residence. The dean did not cease prosecuting this injury until, by a sentence of the metropolitan see, he compelled the bishop to restore the trees to the chapter and to have them carried back before the church doors in the bishop’s own carts.

### How, while he was dean, he compelled Count Peter to come to the chapter to make satisfaction for injuries inflicted upon the Church

[Col. 0326B]

He governed the commonwealth of the chapter energetically and faithfully against the injuries of anyone, setting himself up as an insuperable wall. He spared neither his own labors nor those of his associates in embracing the Church’s affairs with such virtue that, because of the injuries he had inflicted upon the Church, he placed the count himself under excommunication and his city under interdict. Thus at length he compelled him to come to the chapter and make satisfaction to it for the injuries.

### Under how strict a prohibition it was forbidden to sell or alienate the Church’s lands without the consent of the chapter

A grave and exceedingly costly presumption had arisen from the greed of certain leading men. Eagerly pursuing their own advantages by right and wrong, they alienated the Church’s estates in the villages where they received prebends, and, without the chapter’s consent, sold them to purchasers for an agreed price subject to a censual charge. With the same presumption they also sold the Church’s forests or gave them away at their own pleasure.

He decided to remedy this deadly disease as follows. After summoning the chapter, he and all the priests together, with candles lit, excommunicated everyone who in future should attempt such alienations, sales, or gifts without the chapter’s consent; and this was commanded to be observed permanently as law.

### How he established the celebration of the Office of Blessed Mary on weekdays in the Church

While he was still dean of Blessed Mary, he added Offices to be recited at the canonical hours on weekdays, and antiphons over the psalms at those hours [Col. 0326D]. Previously, except at Matins and Vespers, nothing but a simple Alleluia was said over them as an antiphon, as is customary during Easter week. With the chapter’s consent he also added many other things conducive to the dignity of divine worship, completely abolished others, and altered still others.

### Concerning his brother Manasses and the unity of the two men

He had only one brother surviving from among the many who had died in the first flower of their youth: Manasses by name, archdeacon of Sens and Auxerre, who was later appointed bishop of Orléans. Through the distinguished marks of his courtesy and generosity he had spread the rays of his renown far and wide.

Because Manasses was the elder, William—the subject of this account—revered him with such affection [Col. 0327A] that he depended entirely upon his will. In them one could see the same love in two persons. As they had come forth from one womb, so they were governed by one spirit. They had one dwelling at both Auxerre and Sens, one table, and the same vessels for food in which they ate together; one bed; equality in household matters, equality in clothing, and equality in love. Neither possessed anything as his own apart from the other; everything was common to them. Nor could anyone say, in their household, which of the brothers served the other more.

That singular bond of fraternal love which united them was spoken of everywhere, so that they were rarely designated by their proper names. Instead, by a distinctive appellation, they were antonomastically called “the brothers of Sens.”

### With what fervor they loved one another

[Col. 0327B]

The fervor of the love between them scarcely allowed them to remain apart for long. Indeed, we often saw that when a visitation of their archdeaconries or some other necessity forced them to be physically separated, their affection could not endure the delays of a prolonged absence and caused them to abandon their plans.

On one occasion it was learned by experience—certainly not without wonder—that during their periods of absence they were occupied by the same meditations and studies. At a certain time, when William had remained in the house at Sens to have blood removed, his brother was traveling through his archdeaconry of Sens in order to visit the deanery of Saint Florentin. For the sake of providing recreation during the journey, a topic for verse-making happened to be proposed to those who were riding with the archdeacon.

[Col. 0327C]

It was an agreeable occupation, each man competing to compose the better verses on the subject. While these things were taking place with the archdeacon and his companions, his brother—unaware of it, having remained at Sens—was engaged at the same days and hours in Sens, with his own companions, in studies on the same subject and of no different kind.

When this was discovered, everyone was astonished, and in the thoughts of some there arose omens of fraternal harmony.

### How they refused to consent to the election of either of them as archbishop of Sens while the see was vacant

All ambition was far from them. After the death of Michael, archbishop of Sens, of blessed memory, the Church was vacant, and on the day appointed for the election of a pastor the chapter was deliberating about his replacement. Certain persons of the Church, whose designs appeared hostile to the brothers, were supported by the favor of many canons who adhered unanimously to their will. Together with their followers, they wished to consent to the appointment to the Church of Sens of whichever one of the brothers they chose.

But the brothers judged that they ought not to be preferred to the venerable Hugh, bishop of Auxerre. Both the bishop and those who unanimously supported him were striving, with the brothers’ favor, for Hugh’s promotion to that Church. The brothers therefore refused to allow discussion of their own election, and instead worked together so that everyone would agree to request that bishop.

Innocent III, who presided over the Roman Church, refused to assent to this request [Col. 0328A], wishing to place in the chair of Sens his own master in the schools when he was in France—namely, Master Peter of Corbeil—and he did so, although the canons resisted and were unwilling.

### How William refused to consent to his election to the Church of Nevers

Again, after Walter, bishop of Nevers, had departed this life, the canons of that Church unanimously elected William. When his consent was sought through solemn envoys sent by the Church of Nevers, he deliberated with his brother Manasses. They agreed that they should immediately lead their lives together in a humbler state rather than that either of them should ascend the higher summit of rank and thereby separate them from one another.

Thus he refused the prelacy of the Church of Nevers [Col. 0328B], which was calling him to govern it. Later, when he had become bishop of Auxerre, he was accustomed to remember this with the greatest penitence and bitterness of heart, his conscience pricking him because he had preferred Auxerre, as though it were richer, to Nevers, as though it were a poor Church.

### How he was elected bishop of Auxerre, and how he did not wish to be preferred to his brother in the election

At length, after the aforesaid Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, of magnificent memory, had been taken from human affairs, the day appointed for the election arrived. The votes of all—clergy and people alike—converged upon one of the two brothers, namely Manasses. As the elder, and as one considered more approachable, more courteous, and therefore more popular [Col. 0328C], he was unanimously urged to accept the governance of the Church.

But he refused to undertake the burden, fearing the dangers of governance and considering it unworthy that he should be preferred in the prelacy to his brother, the dean of the Church. Although William was the younger, Manasses maintained that by the prerogative of his dignity and by the merit of his life he was the superior.

Thus the electors, to whom the chapter had entrusted the election by compromise, chose the dean. He, too, burst into tears and refused the honor with no less affection, considering it unworthy that he should be preferred to his elder brother, whose life was no less worthy than his own.

So a marvelous contest arose between the brothers. Though they had one heart and one soul, their hearts were divided and their souls torn apart in this matter, because neither wished to be preferred. Everyone, with tearful eyes, watched the astonishing and unexpected contest.

[Col. 0328D]

At last Peter, archbishop of Sens, who was present there, was summoned to the chapter and brought the contest to an end. Moved both by the needs of the Church and by a particular concern—namely, that the treasurership of Sens and the archdeaconry of Provins, which William held in the Church of Sens, should come under his right of collation—he urged William by persuasive arguments to accept the governance of the Church that was calling him. With his brother’s insistence intervening, he compelled and bound him to do so.

### How he obtained from the king a privilege concerning the royal rights of the Church of Auxerre

After his election had been held on the Friday after the Purification of Blessed Mary in the year of the Lord 1206, approved by the archbishop’s confirmation, and finally completed by his consecration, he went on the very day of his consecration to the lord king.

From the time of the election, the king had been asked through solemn envoys of the Church to restore to him the royal rights that he had occupied after Hugh’s death, but he refused to restore them. Indeed, the king’s servants appointed by him to guard the royal rights were behaving very improperly with regard to the episcopal possessions.

During all that time and until then, they had miserably dissipated the episcopal goods, violently extorted money from the people, and sold off the forests—which had remained untouched for a long time—with great loss. Everything was handed over to plunder and prey in hostile fashion, so that in a short time it would have been utterly destroyed had divine providence not provided the Church with a pastor sooner.

The king received him with considerable royal graciousness, and William received the royal rights from him without difficulty. He also appealed to the royal majesty concerning the seizures made during the vacancy. At length, through the intervention of certain leading men of the royal palace, the dispute was settled by a friendly agreement. After the bishop had paid a considerable sum of money, a privilege was obtained from the king concerning the grant to the Church of the royal rights during a vacancy. We have decided to insert its tenor here for present reading.

### Text of the privilege concerning the royal rights

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. Philip, by the grace of God king of the Franks. Let all present and future persons know that, out of regard for divine mercy and for the remedy of our soul and those of our parents, we give and perpetually grant to the Church of Auxerre whatever right we held in the royal rights during a vacancy of the see.
>
> Accordingly, the dean and chapter of the same Church shall guard the royal rights during a vacancy, together with all revenues arising from them and any prebends that may happen to become vacant in the meantime, for the use of the bishop, saving our service, our riding-service, our army, and our summons, as the bishops of Auxerre have rendered them to us.
>
> That this may possess perpetual force, we confirm this present document by the authority of our seal and by the character of the royal name written below.
>
> Done at Paris in the year of the Lord 1206, in the twenty-sixth year of our reign, in the presence of those whose names and marks are set below. [Col. 0329D]
>
> No seneschal present. Sign of Guy the butler. Sign of Matthew the chamberlain. Sign of Drogo the constable. Given, the chancery being vacant, by the hand of Guarinus.”

### How he conducted himself in the episcopate, and how fearful of God he was

Thus, placed in the pontifical chair in the year of the Lord 1206, he was exceedingly energetic and prudent in the administration he had undertaken. He did nothing rashly, nor did he allow anything suggested by his concerns to proceed to action unless it had first been thoroughly refined in the furnace of much deliberation.

From the beginning of his life he had acquired the habit of deliberating at length about what needed to be done, to such an extent that many attributed this to slowness. Sometimes, though rarely, they felt the cost of a longer delay caused by excessive deliberation, when matters might have been brought to maturity more advantageously through the economy of some prompt action.

He was therefore circumspect in counsel, gentle in speech, outstanding in hospitality, a diligent distributor to the poor, moderate in prosperity, long-suffering in adversity, and singular in patience. He was an indefatigable pursuer of his rights, according to the Apostle’s rule. He presided well over his household, so that to his household he was an example and model of sober, just, and godly living.

He was so fearful of God that, as those who judged his conscience in the forum of penance knew more fully, he mourned light offenses as though he had committed grave ones. He displayed a pastoral affection toward everyone. When he traveled through his diocese, men and women from every direction came to him with their needs—not only spiritual but also temporal—and he would stop and graciously allow them an opportunity to speak with him. Sometimes he became burdensome to his own attendants because he prolonged his conversations with such people.

### His affection for the citizens

He showed extraordinary affection toward the citizens, for whose protection he frequently endured serious conflicts with Hervé, count of Nevers. He resisted him so that, while Count Peter, the father of his wife Matilda, was alive, Hervé would not usurp dominion over the city.

He had sought this dominion all the more eagerly because, if the aforesaid count had obtained it, the city of Auxerre ought to have come into his own possession in the name of his wife, since he had gone to Constantinople to receive the empire so called. But the count could not achieve his wish until, under pressure from the authority of the Roman see, the bishop himself was transferred to the bishopric of Paris.

### He diminished the dean’s jurisdiction

In judgments he always walked the royal road, as the Lord revealed it to him, knowingly deviating in no way to the right or the left. Yet he was easily persuaded by arguments, if any could be made to cast a shadow over what the favor of his own advantage dictated. Thus he greatly oppressed the deanery.

There was a public assertion that the city’s cases belonged ordinarily and in the first instance to the dean’s jurisdiction. Accordingly, if anyone subject to the dean’s jurisdiction was summoned in court or in the bishop’s presence, and had not first been summoned before the dean’s court, the dean often recalled the case, claiming the right to hear it by reason of jurisdiction. Frequently, when an exception of forum was raised, such persons were not compelled to proceed further before the bishop or his official.

While he was dean, he himself exercised this right. After becoming bishop, he allowed his successors, the deans, to exercise it for some time. Eventually, however, in these and other matters belonging to the jurisdiction claimed by the dean, the bishop began to attack the deanery. He began to hear the city’s cases not only personally but also immediately and without appeal through his official.

Although the archpriests, who had anciently held the place of officials, were not yet able to hear cases involving those subject to the dean’s jurisdiction, he nonetheless weakened the deanery’s jurisdiction considerably more than any bishops before him.

In him we find this chief imperfection of human frailty: he tried as far as he could to extend his own jurisdiction and right of domination, and he wanted to preside greatly, not so much with gentleness as with the rod.

### The mutual affection between him and his brother Manasses

His brother Manasses, archdeacon of Sens and Auxerre, adhered to him as his inseparable companion. Everything was done according to his will and direction; nothing great or small was undertaken without his counsel.

The bishop had placed him over himself in such a way that he was greater only in name. Both considered themselves fortunate if they were allowed to retain their inseparable companionship in this manner.

But the provident dispensation of God, who was pleased with both of them, just as it had placed the younger over the Church of Auxerre, so within a short time raised the elder, Manasses, to the height of the see of Auxerre. Thus the territory of Orléans could no longer boast of its ancient prerogative: that it had once brought forth from its womb two brothers, born of the same mother and the same loins, one Austrenus, bishop of the Church of Orléans, and the other Aunarius, bishop of Auxerre.

The territory of Auxerre likewise tasted, in equal measure, the privilege of producing two brothers, although unequal in merit: one, Manasses, presiding over Orléans, and the other, William, over the Church of Auxerre. Both were natives of the territory of Auxerre.

### How his brother Manasses was elected bishop of Orléans

When Manasses was requested as bishop by solemn envoys of the Church of Orléans at the general synod of Sens, a unanimous election having been made, he himself refused to consent. But Archbishop Peter, who presided at the synod, pressed him with the same determination and for the same reason that we have remembered him applying to his brother, the bishop of Auxerre.

Thus compelled and taken away, he accepted the burden of pontifical governance in that Church, abandoning the plan he had long conceived: namely, to resign the archdeaconry of the Church of Auxerre, remain content with what he held in the Church of Sens, and lead a quiet, almost private life there, unless the necessity or desire of his brother, the bishop of Auxerre, should at some time draw him away.

### What Manasses did in the episcopate of Orléans, and how he conducted himself there

For the sake of fraternal fellowship and out of regard for that extraordinary affection which lasted between them until the end of their lives, it is pleasant to touch briefly and summarily upon a few of Manasses’ many deeds, so that anyone who reads about one brother may not remain wholly ignorant of the other.

After passing beyond the levity of youth, during which, because he was excessively open-handed for the sake of human favor, he had gained a great reputation as a squanderer of his substance [Col. 0332A], he at length, through the companionship and example of his brother—who had always been modest and mature—laid aside every kind of frivolity.

Even before becoming bishop he had so thoroughly cast off the old man with his deeds that, being of an exceedingly fervent spirit, he seemed to surpass his brother in the newness of the spirit and to walk more ardently in the exercise of virtue.

In the episcopate, so great a lamp of virtues shone forth in him that, remaining in the fear of the Lord and, according to the Apostle’s word to Timothy, exercising himself especially in godliness, he was most sparing—indeed, rather severe—with himself, generous toward his own people, and a distributor to the poor with all his heart and strength.

He burned with such eagerness and desire on behalf of his subjects that he might usefully discharge a pastor’s care. When he died, they learned and lamented what affection, what counsel, and what consolation they had lost in him.

### How he defended the rights of the Church of Orléans against the king and his ministers

With great steadfastness he overcame many adversities in the episcopate through great patience. He frequently and vigorously contended against the king and the royal ministers on behalf of the rights of his Church, recovering, with much labor and as far as he could, episcopal rights that they had usurped over a long period.

This concerned both the forests of the Holy Cross, in which he vindicated the Church’s rights over the charcoal burners as firmly as courageously, and other matters through which he greatly improved the condition of the Church.

### Concerning the gemstones of his predecessor’s rings, which he recovered from the king

With great steadfastness against the same king, he obtained the return of the gemstones from the rings of his predecessor Hugh, while the king retained the gold. He did this for the preservation of the Church’s privileges [Col. 0332C]. The king had claimed by royal right whatever gold and silver he had found among the goods of that bishop Hugh at his death.

### How he partly freed the vassals of the Church of Orléans from service in the royal armies

The king had long compelled the vassals of the Church of Orléans to serve in his expeditions at their own expense, as though this had already become an established custom. Manasses did not hesitate to dispute with the lord king over their injury, and he brought them to such freedom that, in expeditions of this kind, the bishop could have as many of them as he wished at his own expense.

Their burden was thus lightened immeasurably, and the condition of the bishops became far better than before. For when the bishop was summoned by the lord king to an expedition, his own vassals did not fail to offer themselves eagerly and competitively to serve with him, so that they would not be compelled to serve by the king. Previously he had been accustomed to hire outsiders at great expense and only with difficulty.

### How he recovered the Church’s privilege concerning royal agents in episcopal territory

After many labors and the long distress of exile—which he and his brother William steadfastly endured because of the royal expeditions in which they had wished to follow no one but the reigning king, thereby courageously placing their shoulders beneath the ruin of the Church—he recovered and had re-established a privilege that had been lost through the renunciation of his predecessor Hugh and of the chapter of Orléans.

Under the pretext of some peace, it was restored in exchange for an annual payment of sixty pounds for the king’s procurations in episcopal territory.

### At what danger he acquired the tithes of wool in the archdeaconry of Sologne for the parish priests

In the archdeaconry of Sologne he labored steadfastly and unconquerably against a conspiracy of the inhabitants formed against him. These inhabitants had been stirred up against him because of the tithes of wool. He was compelling them, contrary to the custom of that land, to pay those tithes to their priests.

They gathered almost as one man under arms and besieged the bishop for one night in a certain castle into which he had withdrawn because of them, thirsting for nothing but his blood. After their rebellion had been successfully overcome, he finally obtained from them, with satisfaction acceptable to himself, full compensation for the injury and the tithes he wanted for the priests.

### Concerning the demolition of the fortress of Égry, the ambushes of John of Orléans, and how he recovered Pithiviers through the king

John of Orléans, a knight, was erecting a fortress at his estate of Égry, beside the episcopal village of Estrepéau. The bishop girded himself against him all the more vigorously because, after the bishop had notified him of the new construction, John insolently attempted to complete what he had begun, contrary to the bishop’s prohibition.

At length, after enduring many injuries from John and his men, the bishop compelled him, against his will, to demolish the battlements and everything he had constructed for the fortress.

On one occasion, when the bishop was traveling to Pithiviers, he also miraculously escaped an ambush laid for him by John. The Lord arranged that he should turn aside from the road to visit a sick man. Had he then fallen into John’s ambush, as was believed, he would undoubtedly not have escaped the danger of death.

Pithiviers, too, a noble castle of the Church of Orléans, which John himself had treacherously entered and seized by armed force during the same period, he recovered through much labor and persistence from the king, who had appeared inclined to overlook the matter. From the beginning, the king had taken it badly that whenever he had anything against John, the bishop did not hesitate to resist him boldly to his face.

At length he recovered the castle, and John was expelled, not without disgrace.

### How he compelled John and his men to perform public penance

At last he subdued the pride of John and his men, compelling them to undergo public penance with a monetary satisfaction. He added that they also went to the Apostolic See to obtain absolution.

By this the others could rightly be frightened lest they attempt similar things against him.

In that episcopate he steadfastly overcame so many struggles, so many hardships, and so many perilous dangers. He afflicted his body with such great suffering for God that what was said of the blessed Germanus could appropriately be applied to him as well: amid so many crosses he endured a prolonged martyrdom.

In short, one may say of him that during the twelve years or more in which he occupied that episcopal see, he labored and accomplished more than the others of his own time.

### Concerning the palace that he built at Meung

At Meung, an episcopal fortress where the bishop previously had no suitable dwelling, he constructed a residence of great nobility: a palace with towers and battlements, an impregnable and noble stronghold for the bishop, when he had assigned a residence to that castle.

### Concerning the bridges of Jargeau and Meung

There and at Jargeau over the Loire he built stone bridges.

Since the death of his holy ones is precious in the sight of the Lord, let us briefly touch upon his blessed departure [Col. 0334B]. When he was already unmistakably and irrevocably approaching death, his companions urged him to send for his brother William.

“Let me be,” he said, “let me be. I desire to look upon nothing more than my Lord Jesus Christ alone.”

And so he ended his life without summoning his brother. Nevertheless, although his companions summoned William unexpectedly, he arrived quickly for the funeral.

Those present dissolved in abundant tears, especially the poor, who wept and proclaimed with deep sighs and lamentations that they had lost the support of their life, showing the tunics and garments he had made for them.

He alone, with unmoved face and dry eyes, displaying no outward sign of a troubled spirit, gazed upon his brother’s face as though it were already the face of a glorified man.

### Those who had come to Orléans by chance on the day before his death, not to visit him but because they had been summoned by their own affairs

[Col. 0334C]

The archbishops of Sens and Tours were present, together with the bishop of Le Mans, as well as an immense multitude of religious men, canons, other clergy, and laypeople of the city who had gathered there.

As though it had been divinely revealed to them that he had already flown away to the region of the citizens above, they covered with devout kisses his feet, hands, and whatever part of him they could touch. Whoever had touched something belonging to him considered himself blessed.

Thus, at last, he was buried by the hands of archbishops and bishops and rested in the Lord after a blessed death. A great crowd of the weak and sick came to his tomb, and even to this day some continue to come, awaiting through his merits the healing of their ailments from the Lord.

But let what has been said about him suffice for the present. Let us now return to William, whose history we began to weave.

### Concerning the establishment of the lectorship and succentorship in the Church of Auxerre, and of the schoolmastership

William, therefore, diligently undertaking the care of the governance he had received, earnestly labored to improve the condition of the Churches.

In the principal cathedral church, besides the other things he prudently provided or generously bestowed, he enlarged the lectorship and succentorship—through which the entire service of reading and singing is administered—and likewise the schoolmastership. These offices had previously been so scanty in revenues and so poor that no one could be found willing to undertake their burdens without profit.

With the chapter’s consent, while retaining for himself and his episcopal successors the right of conferring them, he increased their revenues without charge. To the schoolmastership he assigned approximately ten pounds; to the lectorship and succentorship, in addition to their ancient stipends, he assigned the revenues of one prebend together with the minor portions, which he set aside for all these offices with the chapter’s consent.

### Concerning the matricularies

The sacristan was required to provide and maintain one clerical matriculary, together with others capable of ringing the bells and performing the duties belonging to his office.

The bishop established three matricularies for these purposes: one cleric, whom he assigned to the altar of the Holy Cross in the same church so that he might serve there in the priestly office, permanently attaching to that matriculary half the benefice of the same altar, together with one hundred deniers in Pentecostal solidi to be received annually from Varzy; and two laymen, to each of whom he assigned ten pounds in revenues.

For the payment of these stipends, the Church of Vermenton was required to pay twelve pounds annually, and the Church of Berriaco eight pounds.

### Concerning the division of the feasts of Saint Alexander and Saint Bricius, and the feasts of the Apostles

He ordered the feasts of Saints Alexander and Bricius, which had customarily been celebrated together in a certain confusion, to be celebrated separately. He also ordered the feasts of the Apostles, which had previously been observed with less solemnity, to be celebrated more solemnly than usual, with the ringing of the larger bells.

For the sacristan, he assigned suitable and agreeable revenues for the lights and other things required by the greater solemnity of such a rite beyond that of a simple feast.

He also established a solemn procession on the winter vigil of Blessed Stephen after the Vespers of the Nativity, with each person carrying lighted candles in silk copes.

### How he adorned the church with a cross and a golden chalice

For the adornment of the church he gave one very fine and large silk cloth, together with two smaller but nevertheless precious ones, for the decoration of the altar. He also had an excellent antiphonary made in two volumes.

The chapter likewise made another one equal to it in every respect. In addition, he gave nine marks of gold for the making of a cross and a golden chalice, as well as his very precious gold rings and thirteen Parisian pounds.

But, when dying, he contributed these gifts toward the expenses that were to be incurred.

### Concerning the improvement of the episcopal palace
At the beginning of his advancement, when part of the roof of the episcopal palace collapsed on Good Friday, he adorned the palace itself with a much finer roof structure than before and greatly widened the windows of the upper chamber, leaving a considerable interval between their pinnacles, while shutting out the unwelcome blasts of wind by means of transparent glass. We have judged it worthy to transmit to posterity what miracle occurred in the aforementioned collapse, so that God may be praised in all things for his benefits.

### On the collapse of the palace and the miracle that occurred there

On Good Friday, then, he was alone in his upper chamber, intent upon psalmody and prayer. Below, in the larger palace adjoining that chamber, a certain man from the castle of Druya and his wife were waiting to confess their sins and receive penance from the bishop. As the third hour was already approaching, the archdeacon, passing that way, went to the bishop. He found them rising to meet him and, having learned why they were waiting, informed the bishop, who immediately ordered them to be summoned to him. They had scarcely left the palace when, behold, in the very place where their feet had stood, the roof of the palace collapsed, dragging with it enormous fragments of timber and tiles into the ruin. These would have crushed the penitents completely had divine power not come to their aid: it held back the collapse until they had departed, although the ruin hung so near and seemed on the point of falling.

O marvelous power of penance, which so restrained divine justice that those already about to die were rescued from the peril of imminent death solely by God’s mercy! The bishop dissolved in tears and astonishment, and, beholding the image of death, burst forth from the depths of his heart into the praises of God. A crowd rushed together at the sound of the collapse, and all rejoiced at the sight of the manifest miracle, proclaiming the greatness of God.

### On the establishment of prebends at Apponiacum, Tociacum, and Conada

For the enlargement of divine worship in the episcopal castles—namely, Apponiacum, Tociacum, and Conada—he established canons and prebends. In addition to other things that he contributed for this purpose, he assigned and allotted to them parish churches with their revenues [Col. 0336C] and … to the church of Saint Amator and to the canons of his chapel of the Trinity … To the chapter of Antissiodorum … to the church of Saint Amator and to the canons living there under the regular discipline of Saint Satyrus, the place of Boticem toward Saint Savior, the churches of Alenset and Petrosium, and the chapel of Mota in the parish of Chevannis; but to the four canons of his chapel at Antissiodorum, namely, that of the Trinity, he granted, with pious generosity, a certain tithe at Tociacum, which he had purchased for them with his own money. He further gave the chapter of Antissiodorum whatever they lacked for the full receipt of the grain tithes in the territory of Crevenno. This was for the daily distribution of bread made in the church to those who had attended Matins or Mass, with the share which the priest of the church had customarily received when it was vacant separated from the church of Crevenno [Col. 0336D] and assigned to the canons, though they made a certain recompense to that church.

### How he secured the compensation made to the chapter at Osiacum for what it possessed at Billiacum

It was also through his insistence and power that, when Count Hervé of Nevers was erecting a fort on the hill of Mures near Billiacum—which belonged to the estate of the church of Antissiodorum—and the canons of Antissiodorum, fearing the count’s violence, were disputing their right with him only half-heartedly, the count, through his own intervention and that of his brother Manasse, bishop of Orléans, whom we mentioned above, exchanged with the canons everything he possessed at Osiacum for what they possessed at Billiacum. The tithes which the canons held there were excepted: they could not be included in the exchange but remained with them. Thus no small advantage accrued to the church of Antissiodorum.

### On the abbey of Cellis and what he bestowed upon that abbey

Among other things, he bestowed upon the new foundation at Cellis a house in the market of Antissiodorum which had belonged to the knight Iterius Bornus. He had purchased it with his own money. He also bestowed annually one measure of wheat and two of rye from the grange and revenues of Brenchis, which he had obtained from the monks of La Charité at great expense and restored to his own property.

### How he bestowed Brenchis and its dependencies upon the hospital of Appogniacum

[Col. 0337B]

He further assigned the same village, with its woods and other dependencies, as well as part of the woods of Courum—which he had purchased from the knight William Grossus—to the hospital of Appogniacum as a perpetual alms, except for what, as we have said, the nuns of Cellis received there. Nevertheless, he arranged that Andrew, archdeacon of Antissiodorum, whom he had raised from childhood, should hold all these possessions for life under an annual rent, paying it each year to two canons of the aforesaid hospital, who would serve continually in the parish church of Brenchis. In addition to that rent, the archdeacon assigned them the small tithes, offerings, and all the revenues of the church after his death [Col. 0337C], so that they would possess everything in full and thereby enlarge the benefits available for receiving the poor in the aforementioned hospital of Appogniacum.

### What he acquired for the episcopate of Antissiodorum

For the episcopate he acquired in the city of Antissiodorum the liege homage of Campo de Moreto and of everything which the knight Milo son of Filo held freely at Antissiodorum as allodial property. At Varziacum he likewise acquired the liege homage of everything which the knight William of Chanlemis possessed there, a considerable sum of money having been given to him for it. The church was thereby provided for all the more advantageously because it had rightly been feared that these possessions might otherwise pass into the hands of a stronger lord—namely, the count of Nevers or some other powerful man—from whom considerable trouble might arise for the aforesaid town or for the bishop himself. He therefore gave the count one hundred pounds to be applied toward the increase of his fief.

At Appogniacum, among other things, he purchased for one hundred Pruvinsian pounds a share of the tithe in which the nobleman William, count of the Holy Caesar, participated, together with the others who held a share therein. At Charbuia, likewise, among other acquisitions which we do not remember in detail, he acquired the entire jurisdiction of the village, of which the bishop had customarily held about one quarter. There were many other acquisitions of his in the episcopate which do not come to mind.

### On the fief of Malliacum and Betriacum, and on the towers of Saint Savior and the New Castle being handed over to him

Regarding Malliacum and Bitriacum, castles belonging to the fief of the church of Antissiodorum, which Count Peter of Antissiodorum was attempting to transfer into the right and fief of the countess of Champagne, to the prejudice of the church, he acknowledged in letters which he issued concerning the matter that he had rendered homage for them to that countess. After pursuing the church’s case against that count, through many labors and expenses before judges delegated by the Apostolic See, he prosecuted it with such constancy that at last he brought the matter to the point where the count, recognizing the church’s right in both places, rendered manual homage to the bishop specifically for each of them. In accordance with the tenor of the episcopal charters drawn up on the matter, he ordered that the castle of Malliacum be handed over at the bishop’s pleasure to his representative, namely Hugh, then archdeacon, who received the castle in the bishop’s name.

He also prudently brought Count Hervé of Nevers—though not without difficulty—to the point of confessing the church’s right and drawing up a public document to that effect. By it he was bound to return to the bishop of Antissiodorum, whenever he wished and according to the tenor of the aforesaid charters, the towers of Saint Savior, the New Castle, and Conada, which the charters expressly identified. He also caused the towers of Saint Savior and the New Castle to be handed over to him at his pleasure, for the declaration of episcopal right; and he brought him the keys of the gates, thereby introducing him into the incomparable possession of his right, which the count did not wish to do for their possessor. “And he who saw it has borne witness, and we know that his testimony is true.”

### What religious houses were established under him in the diocese of Antissiodorum

In his time religious houses were established in his diocese and received growth from their very beginnings: Spallo, under the regular observance of the brothers of Val-des-Roses, although that place is in no respect subject to them; and Bello Loco, also called Beaularriz, as it is more commonly named among us, where brothers of the Carthusian order serve the Lord. These two religious houses were founded and endowed by Count Hervé of Nevers. A third place was the new foundation of the abbey of Cellis near Antissiodorum, assigned to nuns of the order of Saint Anthony of Paris.

### How he caused the old structure of the church of Antissiodorum to be demolished in order to construct a new one

At that time the devotion of the people was flourishing everywhere with regard to new church buildings [Col. 0338D]. The bishop therefore saw that his church at Antissiodorum was suffering from the squalor and decay of an old and poorly arranged structure, while other churches all around were raising their heads with remarkable beauty. He resolved to adorn it with a new structure and with the painstaking craftsmanship of experts in masonry, so that it would not be utterly inferior to the others in appearance or workmanship. He caused it to be completely demolished from the rear, so that its aged antiquity might be renewed into a more elegant appearance of novelty.

The first year’s construction accounts declared how lavishly he poured out money on its costly works: the building, advancing beyond expectation, raised its head to an immense height. Indeed, in the first year he spent about seven hundred pounds of his own money [Col. 0339A], in addition to the offerings of the faithful and the revenues of his jurisdiction, which from the beginning he had assigned to this purpose. In later years he sometimes spent ten pounds a week, and sometimes at least one hundred solidi, in addition to the sums already mentioned and to the collections of his own diocese and of neighboring dioceses.

### On the collapse of the towers and the miracle

In passing, we must here insert for the contemplation of divine mercy the miracle which is known to have occurred during the demolition of the old structure, and transmit it to posterity. In the year of the Lord 1207, on the Sunday before Advent, we were celebrating a solemn day in honor of the most holy Trinity. In the old church there were two towers, one on either side, of considerable height [Col. 0339B] and immense solidity: one to the south and the other to the north. Beneath them lay the entire breadth of the choir and the seats of the canons.

When the support of the old structure, by which they had previously stood firmly, was removed for the new construction, they began to collapse. The continuity of each had first been loosened by a small fissure, though no one foresaw that they threatened such an imminent fall. During the solemnity just mentioned, as is customary on such occasions, not only the smaller but also the larger bells were rung. Their shaking naturally caused fear that the towers ought to collapse and crush everyone together—those who had gathered at the church in unusually large numbers that day on account of the feast—if they were thought to be on the point of falling.

The southern tower, however, opened with a larger fissure than usual [Col. 0339C]. Some people, observing this, began to discuss the matter, and the report reached the canons. The master of the works was summoned as the third hour was approaching and was asked whether the collapse of the towers was presently to be feared and whether the community could safely celebrate the divine offices beneath them. He firmly asserted that there was nothing to fear. One of his disciples, who was present, said that it would not be safe to remain beneath them even for an hour.

The master began to rebuke him as though he were needlessly alarming the canons, pointing out certain beams extending from one tower to the other which held the entire structure together and prevented it from falling. When he was pressed more insistently about the safety to be expected and was asked to give a definite answer, as though overcome by the persistence of his questioners, he said: “I can affirm nothing at all with certainty, since I do not know what the future hours may bring.”

At these words, as though by a certain foreboding of mind, everyone agreed that, once the procession then imminent had been completed—it was the third hour in the church of Saint Mary, which had been one of the dependencies of the greater church—the solemn Mass should be celebrated. This was nevertheless done in the customary manner, as though nothing were feared; all the bells were rung.
