Given their ringing, no structure could have withstood the force of the shaking except a very strong one. Yet the collapse was delayed, so that in its sudden falling the divine power which had been able to restrain it and the benevolence which wished to reveal itself might appear more clearly, once all the shaking had ceased.

Since the place where the divine offices were celebrated had thus been transferred [Col. 0340A], the books used in daily service were also transferred, together with all those kept in the cupboard beneath the southern tower, as though it were believed that the towers would immediately collapse. When the solemn Mass had ended, the canons had already gathered for dinner when, behold, with a sudden crash, the southern tower, shaken, fell against the tower opposite it, its foundations being completely shattered on the inner side.

### On the two young men and how they escaped miraculously

In this collapse there occurred one especially remarkable miracle worthy of narration. Two young men, attracted by the excellence of the new construction, were standing near the collapsing tower, supporting the new structure. When it began to split open and fall, while trying to avoid the danger they placed themselves in greater danger, hastening along the passage which lay open beneath the falling tower.

But divine providence miraculously held back the collapse until they could secure their lives by fleeing. They had scarcely reached a place where they stood safely, though still under suspicion of danger, when the aforementioned tower fell. The people, aroused by the crash, came running together. The northern tower, standing opposite, still appeared to remain solid and secure, when, behold, scarcely half an hour later it toppled to the ground and cast the whole mass of its structure upon the tower which had fallen first.

### How the Lord mercifully and miraculously delayed the collapse until the proper hour

Here it is clear that there was a divine miracle. Human reason offered an incontrovertible argument that, if the collapse of the towers had been so imminent that the ringing and clamor of the bells—by which they had been shaken and battered more than usual, day and night, in accordance with the solemnity—could affect them, they ought rather to have fallen sooner. Such a fall could not have occurred without an immense slaughter. Divine power therefore miraculously delayed the collapse until the proper time, providing an opportune hour in which, with everyone absent, it could occur with less injury and danger to human beings.

### What should be considered in this divine mercy

Here we should also consider with what great mercy the Lord was calling us to penance, not desiring the death of the sinner but rather that he should be converted and live. Although unworthy, we were mercifully delivered from such imminent death, yet we had been bound to his service. In the same mercy he preserved unharmed the bells, concerning which no one doubted that under the collapse of so great a mass they ought to have been utterly shattered and broken. Here it was equally evident how greatly he embraces rational creatures in the bowels of his compassion: even toward insensible objects devoted to divine uses, he did not withhold the entrails of his kindness.

### On the crucifix and the altar of the confraternity

Let us continue with the great deeds of divine power. In the nave of the church, adjoining the choir, stood two altars. The one on the right belonged to Saint Thomas the Martyr and was also called the altar of the Confraternity, because Mass was celebrated there daily for the members of the church’s confraternity. The one on the left belonged to the Holy Cross. Although the towers at the rear were almost adjoining it, they projected farther toward the front part of the church. Above them were two pulpits: on one, lessons were read on feast days, and on the other, the Gospel.

In the pulpit above the altar of the Holy Cross there was a cross of considerable size bearing an old image of the Crucified One, representing the Lord’s death. On its rear side it had a silk cloth attached to it and adhering closely, so that the cloth touched the cross on every side. The collapse of the tower crushed this cloth into tiny fragments, while leaving the cross and image completely untouched, so that scarcely any trace of it remained. The altar beneath it, which, as has been said, projected toward the front part of the church, was likewise so thoroughly shattered that none of its parts remained joined to another, while the pulpit above remained intact [Col. 0341B].

Opposite the altar of the confraternity, which we mentioned above and which adjoined the southern tower—and whose destruction seemed no less to be feared—the altar remained unharmed and intact, while the pulpit above it was partly demolished.

### What should be considered in this miracle

In this event we should consider that the Lord miraculously preserved, to arouse the devotion of the faithful, both the image of his Passion and the place where the divine mysteries were celebrated daily especially for the members of the confraternity, while everything else was destroyed. Although the collapse reached the high altar and filled its front and sides with a great heap of debris, it did it no harm. It completely scattered and tore apart only the costly silk cloth which, because of the solemnity of the day [Col. 0341C], had been placed before its front. The cases beneath the altar, containing relics of the saints, remained entirely untouched.

### On the miracle of the book in which the office of Prime was read

The book in which the rule of the holy Fathers and the catalogue of the saints were read at Prime, together with certain other books necessary for Mass, was crushed beneath the same collapse along with the chest in which they were kept, in the middle of the choir. The chest was completely shattered. The books lay beneath the ruin for about a month or longer, exposed to the rains, which were heavier at that time because it was winter. At last, when the heap of debris had been removed, the chest was found broken into fragments, while the books, their boards intact, had suffered no damage at all from the collapse or the rains [Col. 0341D], except that they were somewhat darkened by a sprinkling of dust, which nevertheless came away with a light shaking.

Who would not have been astonished at such a spectacle of miracles? Who, considering himself shut in by so great a chasm of death, would not have been terrified? Who would not have extolled the greatness of divine power with whatever praises he could? Who would not have burst into thanksgiving with tears for such manifest mercy on the part of the Creator?

The devotion of the priests and of the aforesaid people was fervently aroused to remove the heap of debris. Of both towers an outer wall remained from the collapse. The portion that remained from the southern tower had developed a fissure and a gap, and constantly threatened imminent collapse. Nevertheless, the devout people and others hired for wages labored diligently to remove the heap [Col. 0342A], and the danger of the impending collapse did not obstruct their efforts.

### On the miracle of the man who retrieved his tunic beneath the collapse

One day, after they had labored more urgently until evening to remove the mass of debris in the place where the fissured wall was more inclined to fall, and while the work was proceeding vigorously, that portion of the wall which threatened to collapse suddenly began to dissolve. When those standing nearby saw this, a cry arose that those working below should hasten to save themselves by flight. As they fled, one man left his tunic behind. Although everyone was shouting to him to flee, he turned back to retrieve it.

By divine power the collapse was suspended until he had picked up his tunic. Then, falling with a tremendous crash and merely touching the edge of his garment, it fell harmlessly upon another heap of debris, dragging nothing at all with it into the ruin.

O ineffable goodness of divine mercy, which thus preserved those who were about to perish for penance and formed the minds of all toward devotion! We have digressed a little, but not inappropriately, since, in the words of the Wise Man, it is excellent to recount the works of God. Now let us return to our course and turn our pen back to what remains.

### How he was transferred to the church of Paris

William, then, of whom we are speaking, had already completed his fourteenth year in the episcopate of Antissiodorum, which he had governed vigorously. After many struggles, both against Hervé of Nevers and against Peter of Antissiodorum, as well as against the lord king, had been successfully brought to an end and he had set everything in tranquility, it pleased the Lord that he should not grow sluggish through repose in idle leisure. He therefore placed him over the vacant church of Paris.

That church had been without its shepherd, Peter, who had died at Damietta, and had for some time been troubled by a disputed election. William was appointed despite his resistance and unwillingness. He petitioned Pope Honorius, whom he had personally approached for this purpose, at no small risk to his body, so that he might not be compelled to go. The summer heat was already approaching around the feast of Saint John, and this was especially contrary to him, since he was weak and choleric and suffered very easily from heat. Nevertheless, he gained nothing by his petition and was compelled to travel to Paris [Col. 0342D], so that he might preside there with the diligence and vigilance which he was known to have displayed in the episcopate of Antissiodorum.

### In what condition he left the episcopate of Antissiodorum at his departure

As he was about to depart for Paris, he left the episcopate of Antissiodorum enlarged in its temporal possessions, abundant and well supplied, and free from the burden of debts. He had improved its condition both with regard to the royal rights, as we have stated, and in very many other respects. All the episcopal residences were abundantly furnished with mattresses, hay, various utensils and household goods, presses, and a considerable number of wine vessels wherever necessary—namely, vats and casks of immense capacity [Col. 0343A]. He also left each chapel fully supplied with books, chalices, and vestments.

### What he left to the church at his departure

He left to the church from which he was being transferred the episcopal vestments which he had reserved especially for the use of the principal solemnities, including a most precious mitre adorned with gold and many gems—margaritae, or, in ordinary speech, perlae (pearls); two silver basins, additionally gilded, weighing about eight marks and decorated with marvelous workmanship; baskets of wondrous beauty and ornament; and other things of this sort necessary for sacred uses.

He also left, together with certain other relics of the saints, a visible finger of the blessed Protomartyr, with a silver vessel of marvelous workmanship which had been brought from Constantinople [Col. 0343B], and a small golden cross made precious by gold and topaz, because it visibly enclosed within the gold some particle, beyond doubt, of the wood of the Lord’s Cross.

### On his houses, the Hanging Gate, the cross, and the golden chalice

To the chapter he granted the noble houses which he possessed adjoining the Hanging Gate, together with their dependencies, and the vineyard which he had entirely replanted anew in the territory of Saint Gervais and which was attached to the same house. He granted them with the provision that whoever held these possessions should be bound to pay each year, on his anniversary, one hundred solidi to the canons and the clerics of the choir. He further gave the nine marks of gold for making the cross and chalice [Col. 0343C], which we mentioned above.

### What he left to his successor, the bishop of Antissiodorum

To his successor he left, in all the episcopal residences, an abundance of hay, houses furnished with utensils and household goods, as we have already described, and the wine of that year in its entirety, together with a considerable portion of the tallages.

### What he contributed to the construction of the church of Antissiodorum at his departure, throughout the whole year

For the construction of the church he assigned a portion of the tallages and, for its expenses, gave at least one hundred solidi each week for an entire year after his departure [Col. 0343D]. But why dwell at such length on these matters and extend our writing, while we try to touch upon each detail, even briefly? In sum, we can say this: he left the church almost bereft of its shepherd, being himself almost bereft of possessions.

### How he refused to prejudice the chapter, so that the election of his successor at Antissiodorum might be made with its counsel

We also do not think that the following should be passed over in silence. He had personally approached the Apostolic See to obtain permission to remain in the church of Antissiodorum and not be transferred elsewhere. When his petition failed, he rejected what the Roman authority was willing to grant him—namely, that the election of his successor in the church of Antissiodorum should be made with his counsel [Col. 0344A]. He did not wish the chapter to be deprived in any respect of its absolute freedom to elect.

### How great a loss his departure was to the church and city of Antissiodorum, and what evils befell the church after his departure

How much not only the church but the entire city lost when he departed became clear at his departure. Many evils came upon both the city and the church, as though they had lost their liberator, Othniel. Count Hervé, a man who oppressed others and was feared for his cruelty, had often aspired to such things while the bishop presided over the episcopate of Antissiodorum and resisted him openly, but had achieved nothing. While William was still laboring on his journey to Rome, as soon as Hervé learned with certainty through messengers of his translation [Col. 0344B], he occupied the city of Antissiodorum by armed force, since the citizens did not dare resist, and brought it under his control. At that time nothing was yet certainly known of the death of Count Peter, who, as we said above, was being held captive by Comnenus in the regions of Greece. When Peter had been preparing to depart for Constantinople, he had commended the city to the bishop; hence Hervé’s entry was all the more suspect to everyone, since he was regarded as especially savage.

After the departure of the aforesaid William, Hervé exercised the first acts of his tyranny against one of the bishop’s men who had moved from Antissiodorum to the episcopal village of Giacum to live, together with many others who had migrated there in William’s time. Hervé secretly captured and carried him away, but eventually restored him. Yet on the very night on which he was returned, the man did not dare remain at Giacum; he returned to Antissiodorum under the count’s jurisdiction. Following his example, the others who had moved to Giacum under the bishop returned to Antissiodorum, although the citizens, fearing the count, were fleeing from that same city.

He likewise secretly abducted and extorted a certain man of the chapter. After the man was restored, he never dared openly, even under oath, to acknowledge that he had been extorted by him. Taking advantage of the opportunity, Hervé did many other things of this sort against the church, which did not remain firm in the strength of its virtue when William departed for Paris. At that same time the church suffered much not only from Hervé, since he soon departed this life, but also from those living around it, as though the bishop mentioned above had been taken away as a pillar which supported the whole building.

For Regnaud Rungefer, a knight of no great power, while the princes who were responsible for defending the church looked on, attacked his successor Henry, a man of great kindness and simplicity, with extreme violence. He captured and dishonorably treated Henry’s own cleric, the custodian of the episcopal houses at Varziacum, and kept him in captivity for a long time. He also carried away men and the spoils of the episcopal land, violently broke into the castle of Varziacum, and inflicted a loss of five hundred pounds and more upon the episcopate, becoming bolder against the defenseless because no one opposed him.

At the same time a certain knight named Gregory, whose father, Peter of Brullato, had been the first in his family of humble origin to receive the military belt, captured the dean of the church and held him for a long time in prison beyond the Saône, at Bufresia, outside the borders of the kingdom, as far as … [Col. 0345A].

Certain armed evildoers also broke into the cloister at night, violating the church’s immunity. They drove out through the church, with drawn swords, the canons and clerics who had gathered for Matins. They wounded one of them and trampled another beneath the feet of horses, profaning the church itself with blood and defiling it no less with horse dung. Nor was there any respite for the wretched men, since attacks were made upon the church’s people by noblemen such as Drogo of Meloto, Stephen of Basso, the lord of Arseium, and other knights or men-at-arms throughout the surrounding region, whom private malice, presumptuous rashness, or greedy poverty stirred up not only to plunder but often even to slaughter and oppression; or villages were attacked, and there was no one to help [Col. 0345B].

### What the aforesaid William accomplished in the episcopate of Paris

Let us now briefly touch upon the few matters among the many that come to mind concerning what the aforesaid William accomplished at Paris. With the same patience and constancy with which his brother Manasse, bishop of Orléans, of whom we have spoken above, pursued the rights of the church against the king and royal officers, he brought to an amicable settlement by agreement controversies which, until then, had remained undecided through the bishops’ dissimulation out of fear of royal power: concerning a certain right which the church ought to have in the king’s castellany, namely at the Petit-Pont; concerning the halls built by the lord king at Les Champeaux; and concerning justice and measures in a certain territory near Saint-Victor, called the enclosed fief of Brunel. On this account King Philip, who then held the sceptre, assigned in perpetuity annual revenues of twenty pounds of Parisian money to the bishop and his successors, and one hundred solidi to the chapter. Thus he secured, by an agreement embodied in royal and episcopal instruments, and also in an instrument of the chapter, that the rights of kingdom and priesthood should remain distinct, so that no dispute might again arise concerning matters before that day.

He so expelled from the town certain student-assassins, who went about armed at night, committing abductions, adulteries, thefts, murders, and often other crimes, and disturbing not only the peace and security of the scholars but also that of the citizens themselves, that he shut some of the chief offenders in a principal prison, banished others, and restored peace and security to the whole city against such persons. To them not only the nights but even the days themselves were greatly suspect. He accomplished many illustrious deeds in the episcopate, worthy of perpetual remembrance, which we either leave unknown to you or pass over to avoid weariness in reading. Let us now speak of his blessed end, insofar as it has come to our knowledge.

### On his blessed end

[Col. 0346A]

After he had presided well and commendably over the see of Paris for three years and almost a half, and had made nearly everything tranquil, except the affair of the scholars, who wished in certain respects to emancipate themselves from the jurisdiction of his church and of its chancellor, making certain statutes for themselves on their own authority and striving, as the bishop believed, to arrogate to themselves the right of making such statutes to the prejudice of the bishop and chancellor, he was at length broken by the chronic illness of a quartan fever. After his often-mentioned brother Manasse had departed this life, he finally seemed to have recovered from the quartan fever, but was seized by a continuous, though slow, fever. As though that illness were to bring about his end, he made arrangements for his household; and, on the day before he died, summoned the chief members of his chapter to Saint-Cloud, the episcopal manor where he lay sick, together with religious men—the abbot of Saint-Victor, Lord Ralph of the Hospital, and companions who stood by. He foretold the day of his death; he ordered that he be buried at Pontigny, a house of the Cistercian order, among his elders, who sleep there as founders of the place; and, instructing all present on the following day with divine sayings and commending himself to their prayers, he earnestly exhorted the canons of the church of Paris who were present to a harmonious election. While speaking, he gave up his last breath into the hands of the religious, so that the truth of his prediction of the day of his death might be proved. Thus he was carried to Pontigny and, as he had commanded, buried in the chapel of Blessed Thomas the Martyr before the principal altar; he rested in a blessed end in the Lord [Col. 0346C].

He died on the feast of Blessed Clement at Saint-Cloud, of which we have already spoken, in the year of the Lord 1223, when Louis was reigning near the beginning of his reign. He sat in the episcopate of Antissiodorum for about thirteen and a half years, and at Paris for about three and a half years, under the Roman pontiffs Innocent III and Honorius III, while Philip and Louis, of whom we have spoken above, reigned in France. Here ends the account of William.

## CHAPTER LX. On Henry, who was native to the district called Villanova, in the diocese of Paris.

He was succeeded by Henry, a native of the district called Villanova [Col. 0346D], in the diocese of Paris, formerly cantor of the church of Auxerre. Later, through that form of election which in law is called compromise, he attained the episcopal see. Though of moderate birth, he was neither puffed up by nobility nor cast down by lowliness. Although many said that the virtue of his gentleness exceeded proper measure, he nevertheless preserved the rights of the episcopate so unimpaired by the rigor of justice that the tyrants who had been accustomed to usurp them were compelled to restore them and to cease from the violence of their tyranny.

He was the man who caused the fortress of the castle called Varzy, built at a place called Becherellum [Col. 0347A] by Galcher of Puisaye—a powerful and noble man, hostile to the church of Auxerre and its most bitter persecutor—to be demolished, and had it utterly overthrown, not without great danger to himself and his men. In his time a single loaf was distributed to the servants of the blessed Protomartyr; but he himself added a second from his own resources. Moreover, in his final will he bestowed one thousand Parisian pounds upon the church.

He enlarged the church of the blessed Protomartyr with gifts, won the hearts of the canons to his favor by gentleness, and brought the Church’s enemies back to peace. After completing the course of this present life, he slept and rested together in peace (Psalm 4:9). At the place called Pulcher Redditus, he completed the labors of his present service through an illness of quinsy, and slept with his fathers, old and full of days. Buried in the church of the blessed Protomartyr, he awaits the blessed resurrection of the saints, destined to receive the prize for which he had run so as to obtain it. He sat for thirteen years and four months.

## Chapter LXI. Bernard of Soiliacum

Bernard of Soiliacum, a man of extraordinary holiness, succeeded the Fathers mentioned above; by holy simplicity and simple holiness he surpassed many of his predecessors. Although he possessed the distinction of noble birth, the greater nobility of his character so concealed it beneath the cloak of humility that, according to the Apostle, he did not set his mind on high things but consented to humble things (Romans 12:16).

His venerable gray hair, serene face, modest appearance, orderly gait, restrained speech, chaste conduct, frugal table, and the other signs of virtue provided the most effective evidence of the virtue overflowing within him. And because a lamp should not be hidden under a bushel but placed upon a lampstand, so that it might pour light upon those entering the house (Matthew 5:13), he first obtained from the aforementioned venerable Father Hugh of Noyers, bishop of Auxerre, a prebendal benefice in the church of Auxerre. Once he had become a priest, he devoted himself so completely to the divine offices that, as we ourselves saw with our own eyes, scarcely a single hour passed by day or night that did not devoutly pass through his lips—except that on feast days, when the people flocked to his sermons, the streams of sacred teaching flowed from him with the utmost devotion and abundance. Thus he continually bore the marks of the Lord in his body (Galatians 6:17). He persevered in fasts and prayers, with a hair shirt always clinging to him beneath his clothing.

Furthermore, to show that he had no abiding city here but sought the one to come, and to experience with the Apostle dangers from rivers and robbers and the other twelve hardships which the Apostle recalls having endured when speaking to the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 11:26–27), he journeyed to Jerusalem. There that great lamp could not remain hidden; indeed, the rays of his holiness shone so brightly in those regions that he was elected archbishop of Nazareth and preferred to all the others, even those distinguished for holiness. But humility, turning in upon itself and disregarding exalted rank, chose rather to preserve modesty than to be exposed to the dangers of eminence.

Therefore, having returned to his own country and continually becoming better than himself, he was promoted to the archdeaconate of Auxerre. There he undertook the care of souls with such solicitude that, mindful of the command concerning the feeding of lambs and sheep, repeated three times to Peter (John 21:16–17), he fed them with teaching, example, and temporal assistance. Constantly devoted to this work by day and night, he was scorched by heat and chilled by frost, and sleep fled from his eyes.

When Henry, then bishop of the church of Auxerre, had entered upon the way of all flesh, and the grace of the Holy Spirit had been invoked upon the electors assembled to provide the church with a pastor, an extraordinary event occurred, unheard of in the churches of Gaul in our time. The multitude of electors was so completely of one heart and one soul that, with one voice and one spirit, they all cried out that the archdeacon ought to be appointed, since the Lord had endowed him with the prerogative of holiness. Thus, when the votes of all converged upon him, he was seized against his will, dragged while resisting, and compelled to consent though unwilling.

From the time he was consecrated bishop, he mortified his flesh with such severity that on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays his fasts were broken only with Lenten foods, unless labor or illness happened to permit something more nourishing. His affection for Christ’s poor was so great that, following Tobias’s teaching, he was always merciful as far as he could be (Tobit 4:8). When he had much, he gave abundantly; when he had little, he nevertheless took care to distribute even that mercifully. We ourselves often learned by experience that he frequently deprived himself and his table companions so that the hunger of the poor might be relieved.

In his hearing, and while he patiently endured it, the servants murmured; his companions also murmured at the lack of delicacies and the frugality of the rich man’s table. Yet, while maintaining this frugality toward the wealthy with a clear conscience, he considered it less burdensome to be accused by them of avarice than to endure the complaints of the poor at the judgment, unless he had given to them in alms what remained, according to the Gospel’s teaching (Luke 11:41). The empty glory of the world was also so hateful to him that, as we fully learned from trustworthy poor people, he forbade those to whom he gave alms to tell anyone.

He pursued the church of the blessed Protomartyr with such favor that he enlarged it with lamps and every kind of ornament. He also increased the revenues to be distributed among the canons and clergy at the morning hours. Moreover, his ways were so pleasing to God that he brought his enemies back to such peace that the tyrants who had invaded the lands of the episcopate in the time of his predecessors frequently confessed that they ceased their invasions for fear that, if they offended him, God would immediately take visible vengeance upon them.

His fame, like the fragrance of a full field blessed by the Lord, had reached the ears of the most illustrious king of France, Louis, so strongly that the king kept him as a familiar companion above the other prelates, smiled graciously upon his simplicity, and ordered his affairs to be expedited with particular care.

But when the troubles of old age began to afflict him more severely than usual, and an illness of the joints of the legs—which physicians call “the dead disease”—tormented him, he feared that, under these burdens, he could not adequately bear the burdens of the episcopate. Although, as we often heard from the king’s own mouth, the king promised him that he would defend the rights of the episcopate as his own, Bernard nevertheless persistently petitioned Innocent, bishop of the Roman see, and with great difficulty obtained release from the bond by which he had been attached to the church of Auxerre.

After this, all concern for temporal matters was cast aside, and, turning his whole spirit inward upon himself, he cared only for his conscience. His sole repose was contemplation; his conversation was continual prayer; and with men renowned for religion he constantly discussed holy conduct. What more is there to say? Fever was added to the aforementioned infirmity and the troubles of old age. His body was laid upon a bed. The physicians offered nature remedies against disease, but he used them rarely and sparingly, and only those which the Preaching Brothers and the Friars Minor attending him compelled him, with great force, to use.

At last, after resting briefly following a lengthy discussion of holy religion with the aforementioned Brothers, so that those standing by thought he was asleep, he was released into a precious death. He returned his spirit to God with such serenity that all his limbs were at rest, his face serene, and no sign whatsoever of pain appeared at the final moment of death. The man who had refused to be stripped during his illness was stripped after death: the hair shirt clinging to his flesh was removed. It was so infested with lice and worms that it produced immense horror to the sight and stench to the smell; his flesh, eaten away by worms, exposed the bones in places [Col. 0349C].

The sacred body was therefore clothed in pontifical vestments, he was placed upon a bier, and he was carried from the place called Pulcher Redditus—where he had lost death and found life—to the church of Auxerre, where he had chosen to be buried. The devout clergy of the city came out to meet him with the people. A disorderly crowd of every age and sex rushed to meet him, and they eagerly sought to touch the bier. Those who had touched it with their hands or kissed the silks with which it was covered considered themselves distinguished by a certain privilege above the others.

When the divine funeral rites had been celebrated, the canons and clergy came forward, and all who managed to enter first kissed the feet, hands, or face of the sacred body. Nor, as is customary at other funerals, did they commend his soul to God and the holy angels [Col. 0349D]; instead, they earnestly begged in devout prayers that his merits might assist them before the divine mercy, which he had devoutly served.

The aforementioned Father slept with his fathers in the year of the Lord 1244, in January, on the sixth day of the month. He sat for nine years.

> Bishop Bernard, ever slow to every evil,  
> Thus living, subdued the world, together with flesh and demon,  
> So that, dying, he deserved to return pure to Christ.  
> In the year one thousand two hundred and forty-four,  
> He departed in the light of the Magi.

## Chapter LXII. Reginald of Siligniacum

Reginald of Siligniacum succeeded him. He had first been dean of the church of Auxerre and was later promoted to the episcopate through that form of election which in law is called scrutiny. He was a man tall in stature, fair and ruddy, and in bodily beauty chosen from among thousands. To him, in keeping with the high nobility of his lineage, had been given a lofty and noble heart.

He loved the company of noble clerics and also of knights, and with a generous hand, as befitted his nobility, he distributed gifts among them. He promised that he would accomplish great things for the church of Auxerre; but while the Fates begrudged his happiness, his beauty withered like the flower of grass, and the Lord cut down his glory while it was still budding (Isaiah 38:12). From the very day of his promotion, an illness afflicted him so severely [Col. 0350B] that he was unable to devote himself to the interests of his church; on the physicians’ advice, he could attend only to those matters by which his illness might be relieved.

He slept and was gathered to his fathers, honorably buried in the monastery of Les Roches in the diocese of Auxerre, where he had chosen his burial place. He sat for one year, eleven months, and sixteen days.

## Chapter LXIII. The Deeds of Lord Guido, Bishop of Auxerre

A bishop of memorable reputation, Guido of Melloto, succeeded him. His deeds demand an even more attentive hearer because they are known to have been loftier and nobler in action. He was born in the diocese of Auxerre of noble blood on both sides.

His father was William of Melloto, a knight and lord of the castle of Saint-Prix in this diocese [Col. 0350C], a man who loved every form of courtesy and generosity, a cheerful sharer of his own table, and a supporter of poor nobles. It is also said that, having acquired a surname corresponding to the matter and to a certain quality of his goodness, he was commonly called “Peace-Bearer.” For whenever he learned that discord had arisen among any of his neighbors, he devoted himself with all his strength to restoring peace and did not cease to undertake the labor until, if possible, he had recalled the disputants to harmony.

His mother traced her origin to the lineage of the lords of Mont-Saint-Jean and was in no way inferior to her husband in the distinction of her ancient nobility.

The bishop of whom we speak, born of these parents, was sent to the study of letters from childhood and progressed so far that, first grounded in grammar, he became a profitable student of the liberal arts. Then, having acquired knowledge of both laws—canon and civil—he later became a diligent reader of Sacred Scripture whenever opportunity allowed.

His purpose in this regard was more often impeded by the business of ecclesiastical affairs. In adolescence, while adorning himself with good morals and teachings and rejecting frivolities, he did not concern himself with bodily adornment, unkempt limbs, or carefully arranged hair, as is customary among noble youths. For this reason he was held less dear by his father than the other children. But the disposition of the Most High, who was reserving him to become a future bishop, so adorned his neglected appearance in the course of time that the wise son became his father’s glory. The name of son having been changed by the father, he was regarded as father and lord, and the sons of his mother bowed down before him.

He was tall in stature, well proportioned in body, magnanimous in heart, an industrious promoter of ecclesiastical affairs, a provident dispenser of the public good, and an indefatigable protector of the people. He was restrained in speech, devout in prayer, and angelic at the altar. His singing, melodiously resounding like a sonorous trumpet, filled the house of God and delighted the minds of his hearers with sweet-sounding harmonies.

He was no less distinguished for counsel in the councils and gatherings of prelates. Surpassing the others in bodily beauty, he seemed, by his venerable bearing and almost commanding gaze, to preside over them. If anything had to be debated before him in a judicial examination, or something else had to be arranged [Col. 0351B], he offered a ready and attentive hearing to arguments and reasons. Turning over what he had heard in his discerning mind and weighing everything, he did nothing rashly.

From the very beginnings of his discretion he had therefore acquired this habit: to refine his affairs in the furnace of such deliberation. Many attributed this to leniency, since sometimes—though rarely—matters that could have been settled by a quicker and shorter process were completed only after a costly outcome. Although he was careful in conducting business and affairs successfully, the frequency of secular occupations was scarcely ever so great that he did not prefer divine service at its appointed hour.

It was almost an inborn habit of his to exercise the rigor of justice: to reward the deserving, punish the wicked [Col. 0351C], pity the oppressed, spare those who pleaded, exalt the humble, humble the proud, and defeat the rebellious. At times, not from the arrogance of malice but from zeal for justice, he exceeded the gentleness of the rod to some small degree. The Lord also granted him this good fortune: in everything he undertook for the honor of God and the rights of his churches, the Lord always gave him victory and directed his works with grace and favor.

### How he conquered the citizens of Verdun

When he was about thirty-two years old, he was called by canonical election to govern the church of Verdun, although he was not from that church’s own body. After being consecrated bishop, while nevertheless retaining by dispensation the deanery of the church of Auxerre, which he had previously held, he learned that all jurisdiction—spiritual and temporal—over the city and citizens of Verdun belonged to the bishop. The bishops of Verdun in the distant past had possessed it peacefully and by full right. But through the negligence or weakness of certain bishops who had immediately preceded him, the crafty citizens had usurped the city’s temporal jurisdiction and many episcopal rights. They had also created mayors and aldermen, through whom the city was governed at that time.

They had imposed public exactions and tolls, from which they claimed to govern the commonwealth and fortify the city’s walls and defenses. Having summoned them into his presence [Col. 0352A], he, being prudent in mind and following evangelical teaching, first admonished and entreated them personally in gentle speeches and kindly appeals. Afterwards he had other great and wise men address them carefully, urging them to restore to the church the jurisdiction they had thus usurped and the episcopal rights they had taken away, and to abstain from presuming upon similar acts.

They refused to do so, turning a deaf ear, and, under the feigned sweetness of their words—as is customary in that country—offered multiple excuses for their sins. Then, compelled to proceed by the royal road, he canonically warned them and struck with the sword of excommunication those who, with proud eyes, refused to obey his warnings. As justice required, he aggravated the excommunication so severely that the force of ecclesiastical censure could proceed no further against their persons. They endured it with hardened minds and became even more stubborn through correction, advancing all the more lightly beyond the obstacle.

Seeing their wickedness—among whom usury and deceit had flourished and continued to flourish from their ancient ancestors—he first deliberated carefully. Then, leaving the town with a solemn procession of all the city’s clergy and having the body of Christ carried outside, he placed the city and its inhabitants under a general interdict. He left there only a few priests to hear the penances of the dying and to baptize infants. Suspecting that they would willingly plot some evil against him if they could, he withdrew into the castles and fortifications of the episcopate.

Provoked most bitterly by these measures, they took up the spirit of rebellion and began to devise how they might unjustly oppress the just man. Thus it happened that one day, after reaching a common decision among themselves and issuing a public proclamation, they came out of the city armed, amid great clamor and pompous tumult. All who were capable of bearing arms and fighting, from young to old, went out with hired soldiers estimated at nearly twelve thousand, to ravage the lands of the episcopate. Among them, it is said, one of their leaders and chief men carried an episcopal mitre placed upon a helmet, to the disgrace of pontifical honor.

On that same day the bishop had gone out with some of his armed men to the castle of Charniacum, apparently to raid the animals that the citizens had released outside the city for grazing. But when the company of his own men, which was not far away and for which he had sent, saw the enemy at a distance and came to him, they assembled in small numbers—about three hundred men, and no more, as is believed—though experienced in warfare and skilled with weapons.

The prudent bishop held a brief council with them. Occupying a height, he surrounded the adversaries, who were untrained in war and had been placed with the sun against them. Then, attacking them with his men as prudently as forcefully, while almighty God, who teaches his servants’ hands to fight, defended his cause, he defeated them—not merely victoriously but miraculously. With his onset he trampled down the maliciously raised heads of the rebels in their offenses [Col. 0353A]. Some were put to flight, others fell by the sword, and the rest were captured and led away.

The number of the captured was far greater than that of the captors. In this conflict, mindful of his priestly ministry and pontifical modesty, he mortally wounded no one; by encouraging and exhorting his men to battle, he contributed more to the fight through the office of his tongue than through his own hands. Having won the victory, he returned joyfully to the castle from which he had set out.

After a few days had passed, the citizens, taught by the rod of correction—those whom the warnings of gentleness had been unable to bend shortly before—began to seek peace. Through the mediation of good men, they reached this agreement: after restoring all temporal jurisdiction and the rights of the Church, they would pay the bishop ten thousand pounds for damages and expenses [Col. 0353B]. From then on the bishop sat governing the city in tranquility; he presided over it for one year.

### How, after being transferred to the church of Auxerre, he conquered the house of the knight Reginald Rongefer of Mont

After some interval of time had passed, Reginald of Siligniacum, bishop of Auxerre and of blessed memory, was taken from human affairs. As stated above, Guido was transferred with great rejoicing of the people and clergy to the church of Auxerre, in which he had retained the deanery, through both election and canonical postulation, with apostolic authority intervening.

How he governed there and what he accomplished is sufficiently demonstrated by the evident record of his works. We shall touch upon some of them briefly in this short account.

At the beginning of his tenure, a certain knight named Reginald, called Rongefer, secretly altered the old and depressed condition of his house of Mont near the castle of Varzy, situated in the castellany of the episcopate. Attempting to raise the house into a fortress, he quietly began to surround it with new and strong walls, among other wooden and old structures belonging to the house.

If he had completed the work according to his desire, it could in time have brought grave loss to the episcopate and perpetual harm to the village and inhabitants of Varzy. For that place of Mont is naturally difficult and strong for the most part, while the knight was injurious to his neighbors and accustomed to oppress them; he had already repeatedly harassed the village and inhabitants of Varzy.

When the aforementioned bishop learned of this, giving notice of the new construction, he ordered the knight to desist from the work begun and to have demolished whatever new structure he had built. According to general custom, no one was permitted to construct another castle within any recognized castellany against the will of the superior. But the knight, stubborn and contemptuous of everything, did not cease any more than before from the work he had undertaken.

The bishop, strengthened by firmness of spirit and calling upon the arm of secular power, besieged the house. After conquering it in a few days, he had every new and old fortification he found utterly demolished and overthrown, as the ruins of the structure still testify to those who see them. For this reason, it is said that the wicked knight repeatedly laid secret plots against the bishop’s life. Yet, fearless and much more powerful than his enemy, he always escaped them safely with God’s help, if he chose to use the protection of arms [Col. 0354A].

### The affair of Robin, the cleric of Caprarius

It happened that a certain cleric named Robin of Caprarius, having been temporarily banished from Auxerre under penalty of death by secular authority—perhaps without the knowledge of the prelate then in office, while the family of the Suavis were prosecuting the matter—and having returned to Auxerre before the term of his banishment had, as they say, ended, was again arrested by secular justice at the insistence of those same Suavis and publicly handed over to hanging on the gallows.

This occurred although the same venerable Guido, then presiding over the church of Auxerre, had repeatedly and urgently demanded that he first be restored to him as a cleric [Col. 0354B]. The injury done to the Church was brought by appeal before Pope Innocent III of happy memory, then residing at Lyons. At last, and not without many expenses imposed upon the adversaries, Guido avenged it for the honor of God in the following manner.

He went out in procession from the city and suburb with all the clergy and people. Lebin, then provost of Auxerre, Peter and Drogo Suavis, the brothers, and their accomplices were compelled by ecclesiastical censure to walk in breeches and shirts, with rods in their hands and completely barefoot, leading the way. They publicly carried a certain bier bearing a clerical image from the place of the gallows themselves all the way to the cathedral church in the aforesaid condition.

There the same bishop celebrated a mass for the dead and, according to due custom, buried the corpse of the deceased man—already long kept in a certain chest—beside the church of blessed Mary in the city [Col. 0354C]. The aforesaid wrongdoers were nevertheless fined an immense sum of money for the excess of such great presumption and for the expenses; from this, in due course, he paid three hundred pounds to the same church of blessed Mary for the soul of the deceased.

### How he caused the castles listed below to be handed over to him

For understanding this passage, it should be assumed that, as is clearly shown by the tenor of a charter of the blessed Bernard, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, the house of the count of Nevers and Auxerre and the castle fortifications which he is known to hold from the bishop of Auxerre—namely, Château-Neuf, Saint-Sauveur, Conada, Mailly, and Betry—were to be handed over to the bishop at his pleasure. The condition was that, upon his death, they should be restored intact to the count or his officials.

But because, in the distant past, the bishop’s predecessors were not found to have exercised this right, Guido compelled Matilda, then countess and of illustrious memory, by ecclesiastical censure to hand over the aforesaid fortifications and castles to him, to be held at his pleasure. He held them for some time, spent the night in each of them, left his own guards there when he departed, and finally restored them to the aforesaid countess.

### The coinage of Auxerre

[Col. 0355A]

For understanding what follows, it should likewise be known that among the bishops of Auxerre there is a letter of Philip, king of France and of illustrious memory. From its wording it is clearly established, among other things, that if the count of Nevers wished to have new money struck, he was to have it struck with the proper legality and weight specified in the said letter; and the ecclesiastical persons of the county of Nevers were to have it examined whenever they wished.

It happened that the noble Odo, son of the duke of Burgundy, who had succeeded to the county through his wife, began to have new coin struck at Auxerre. While he was away, his officials publicly put it into circulation before it had been examined by the ecclesiastical authorities [Col. 0355B], as should have happened—in fact, without their knowledge. They ordered it to be proclaimed generally, under a very severe penalty, that no one should issue or accept any other coin except that one, although the scarcity of that same coin was still so great that one tenth of the amount would not suffice for the needs of the commonwealth and for the people’s food.

The bishop, having summoned the chapter and the ecclesiastical authorities of his city, admonished the count’s officials at their insistence to restore what they had attempted concerning these matters to its former condition and to present the coin for examination. They refused to do so.

The bishop, having taken counsel with those same ecclesiastical persons, personally sought the presence of Louis, king of the Franks at that time, a most Christian man, carrying trustworthy letters attesting to the facts [Col. 0355C]. Explaining to him the harm, the sequence of events, and the public complaint, he obtained from the king an order that the makers of the coin be expelled and that the coin be publicly denounced throughout the city of Auxerre by royal authority.

### How he compelled the Templars to remove the bell they had hung in their house of Monastello

This too deserves to be written on a memorial parchment. The Templars were accustomed to exceed the limits of their liberty and frequently to turn to harm what had been granted to them by apostolic favor. They had hung a bell high in their house of Monastello and publicly rang it to summon the people to hear the divine offices in their oratory. They had also rashly solemnized the blessing of certain newly married couples there, although the generosity of their privileges in no way permitted them to do so.

He canonically admonished them to remove the bell and to make satisfaction for what they had presumed to do concerning the nuptial blessing. When they refused, the complaint was brought before the reverend Father Simon, by the grace of God cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, who was then serving as legate in the regions of Gaul [Col. 0355D]. Before him Guido pursued the matter with such vigor that, prevailing in law, he obtained through the legate’s sentence that the Templars, condemned to him, remove the bell and make satisfaction for what had been attempted regarding the blessing of the newly married.

When Louis, of illustrious memory, was reigning by the grace of God as king of France [Col. 0356A], a royal order was issued at the urgent request of sailors that everything which could impede the passage of ships along the river Yonne be removed. The executors appointed for this task, boasting—as is often the way with many bad men—of doing more and greater things than their office required, drove two beams into the riverbed at Bochello beneath the bridge of Auxerre, which belonged by its own right and property to the episcopate. They placed iron fleurs-de-lis upon their tops, here and there, as a sign of royal dominion.

As soon as he heard of this, the courageous man had them forcefully dug up and carried into the episcopal residence. But, because of this, his rivals arranged for him to be summoned into the king’s presence. Before the king he argued that, since the king’s officials, without sufficiently consulting him, had extended the edges of their mandate by driving beams into Bochello—which belonged to the episcopate’s own dominion and right, and in which there was absolutely nothing obstructing the free passage of ships—he had rightly dug them up.

Thus it happened that, after these and other arguments had confounded and stunned his adversaries, he departed free and victorious.

### The buildings he constructed
With how many additions to buildings he adorned the sites of the episcopal residences ought not to be passed over in silence. At Auxerre, indeed, beside the old episcopal hall, he erected another, double hall of remarkable beauty, above a stone-vaulted cellar in which wine had customarily been stored, raised upon a mighty cement foundation, constructed with window openings, adorned with conspicuous sculpture and illuminated by transparent glass. For the honor of divine worship, he joined to it, in an orderly arrangement and in a pleasing position, a double chapel of no inferior workmanship and a double chamber, one below and one above, thereby making the hall itself into a delightful sight with a suitable little tower. Moreover, he almost completely repaired the episcopal chamber above Pratellum, which was old and already collapsing through age, and restored it to a more elegant appearance of newness. Again, since from that same Pratellum as far as the prison, beneath and on the side of the Yonne, there was an open and easy ascent to the episcopal residence, with no obstruction, or one entirely useless, blocking the way, he surrounded that whole circuit with new and strong walls, a gate, and fortifications of costly workmanship and beautiful appearance.

At Ragenna, near Appoigniacum, he constructed a noble episcopal residence, whose circuit the river Yonne surrounds at the rear and along its sides. First, he built a wall enclosing, from one side of the river to the other, a continuous and level strip of land lying in front between the fortification and the ditches, and there he established the principal entrance. Along the inner side of this wall he attached stables for horses, constructed for the entire length of the wall. Then he restored the brick enclosure of the fortification, which was ruinous and partly collapsed and which enclosed scarcely half of the circuit: wherever the ruined masonry could provide material, he rebuilt it with excellent brick walls; throughout the remainder, he rebuilt it with stone walls, battlements, and towers, enclosing the whole on every side. Near its entrance he erected a very strong and extremely large square tower, called the Portellum, containing several divisions of dwellings, constructed with thick and broad masonry walls. Within the enclosure of the aforesaid fortification, he restored the old episcopal hall, adding certain features and transforming others for the better, and brought it into a condition more beautiful than usual. He also constructed two chambers, each double, extremely large, corresponding and adjoining the hall: one, of more noble workmanship, joined transversely to the rear gable and shining with small yellowish windows, he built of commendable stone paneling. The old loggias above the Yonne, worn out by age and already near collapse, he completely repaired and restored to a form of graceful and most beautiful elegance. On the other side, he constructed and arranged in proper order the necessary annexes attached to those fortification walls.

At Bel-Retour, a place rich in fish because of the confluence of ponds and suitable, because of the neighboring woods, for relieving the winter cold, he transformed a certain low-lying house—an unglorious lodging for bishops—into a double hall of tranquil beauty and a gracious residence, with an adjoining chamber of similar construction for the bishops’ private repose. He also pushed back an inlet of one of the ponds, which extended as far as the walls of the hall, by casting up an enormous mass of earth like an embankment, thereby adding greater depth to the inner waters. In the mass of earth that he had deposited and leveled, he planted trees of various kinds and made a pleasant grove suited to the capacity of the place. Moreover, he constructed there the annexes necessary for guests and household servants between the hall and the chapel, as well as loggias of great convenience leading from the hall to the chapel and back again, together with other building retreats. He might perhaps have enlarged the residence with still greater additions, but because the site was not favored by much natural beauty and abounded in various revenues, he perhaps pursued it with a rarer—and not surprising—degree of affection.

At Varzy, he rebuilt at great expense a very large double episcopal hall, containing several chambers, which had been consumed by fire, and restored it in a more splendid form. He skillfully repaired the walls and battlements of the castle’s fortification, which had for the most part been broken or collapsed at their summits, and constructed annexes for tranquil habitation and open convenience, attached to the walls of the fortification.

At the village of Catulus, near Conada, a place elevated on the Church’s own land, past which the Loire flows, conspicuous for the beauty of its situation and offering a far-reaching prospect, he chose a site. Attracted by its delights, he began there, as is sometimes expedient, a certain retreat for the refreshment of nature and the relief of wearied unrest. But he was prevented from continuing the work by a secular prince, namely the aforesaid Odo, son of the duke of Burgundy and then count of Nevers. He pursued this prohibition at the king’s court with such victorious firmness that at last, when the count had been defeated in law and the royal judgment had declared that he could not lawfully prevent the undertaking once begun, he was provoked by the resistance of the one who had prohibited it and advanced the work already begun into a fortification, a double hall, and a chapel of exquisite nobility, suitable for a royal residence. The natural rock was cut away all around; these works, by their praiseworthy beauty, hold the eyes of those who see them, delight their minds as they gaze, and refresh the inhabitants with a pleasant dwelling.

Again, by cutting deeply into the dry rock beneath the hall, he made hollow chambers for storing wine, which during the seasons of boiling summer and scorching Leo provided a chilled drink of pure wine. Outside the *poprisia* [reading uncertain], but still within the bounds of the site, enclosed by low walls, he built stables for horses and a granary of immense capacity. Not far from these, outside the fortification, he planted vineyards from selected cuttings of various vine-stock, which each year produce abundant harvests for drunkenness.

### How he went to the aid of Charles, King of Sicily

At the time when Manfred, a prince of accursed memory and the most wicked imitator of his father’s crime, son of the former Emperor Frederick, had seized the kingdom of Sicily, the patrimony of Saint Peter, and the duchy of Capua, he was disgracefully treating ecclesiastical affairs, overthrowing churches, and driving away prelates. The supreme pontiff summoned the magnificent Charles, son of the king of France, to accept this kingdom and free it from the hands of the aforesaid impious man, and the apostolic see granted a general indulgence for their sins to all who set out to aid him. Inflamed by zeal for this devout pilgrimage, he went to Rome to assist Charles, though he was to depart only with apostolic permission. There he was honorably and joyfully received by the most holy Father Clement IV, then presiding over the Roman Church, and by the cardinals. The office of legate was entrusted to him for that expedition, and by command of the same supreme pontiff he set out with Charles, who had been consecrated king, and with his army, to aid that same Charles.

When they had already drawn near the city of Benevento, where the adversary stood with a warlike multitude of Germans, and the battle lines on both sides were already prepared to engage, he himself—armed inwardly with divine weapons and outwardly clad in military armor—stood above the king’s army. After first delivering an exhortation of salvation to encourage them, he raised his armored hand for battle and, relying on apostolic authority, absolved them all from all their sins, promising them an unhindered flight home if any of them should die after fighting valiantly.

Then, to prove himself a teacher of his exemplary preaching—not one who followed, but one who went before—he was seen to lead the battle. He kindled the hearts of those who saw him with such ardor that, rushing everywhere through the enemy and their swords, they seemed not to attack but to rage. Yet, not forgetful of pontifical moderation, he discharged by gesture and speech the office which he perhaps feared, because of the danger of irregularity, to exercise against the persons of the enemy: now breaking through the battle line, now striking down the enemies’ horses with his sword, now shouting and encouraging. If it is permissible to believe that a man courageous in a just war and deadly conflict might not resist those striking him hand to hand.

At last, when Manfred had fallen in battle and his men had either been captured, fled, or been killed by the sword, the victorious struggle was completed, and the king had obtained peaceful rule and dominion over all Apulia. After remaining with him for some time, he took his leave and departed, returning to the apostolic threshold. There he was received with joy and veneration by the pope and the brethren. After staying several days, he departed with the apostolic blessing and, with the Lord granting him a prosperous journey, returned to his own country.

At his arrival, a joyful crowd of the rich and poor of both sexes rushed out from his city to meet him. The humble people, rejoicing that their father had been restored to them, considered themselves to have found the lost drachma. The clergy of the church rejoiced, and, receiving their shepherd with a solemn procession and the singing of divine praises, gave thanks to God in loud voices.

### On his death

Afterward, when the course of three years and two months, or thereabouts, had passed, he was seized by a severe illness—namely, dysentery and the discomfort of fever—and lay down as one grievously afflicted. With prudent forethought he arranged his final testament. In it, after forgiving his servants according to the measure of their merits, he ordered that the treasure gathered from the goods of the Church be distributed for common uses, after a public summons of the poor had first been made, not once but repeatedly, and through other pious forms of distribution. He left considerable sums of money to poor religious persons and to the monasteries of his diocese, to increase the number of those serving God in their places.

To the Church of Auxerre, his bride, he bequeathed two pairs of extremely costly pontifical vestments, one white and the other purple, and a crozier. He also bequeathed six deniers of annual income, under a specified condition, to each canon who attended continuously in the church for the day at the canonical hours. To fulfill this provision, he had made over to the aforesaid Church the village of Lecheries, near Clamecy, with its appurtenances, and all the acquisitions he had made concerning the house of Brechia, near Auxerre, as well as the village of Fleury in the diocese of Sens with all its appurtenances. He had acquired these together with all the revenues and profits of the aforesaid properties, and he ordered his executors to have the properties amortized at his expense, if any of them were feudal.

Again, he permanently established there the double feast of Saint Augustine and the solemn feast of the Nativity of the glorious Virgin, and ordered sufficient revenues to be assigned for them. Likewise, since he bore a devoted concern for the increase of divine worship, he established and endowed six perpetual priestly chaplaincies in the chapel of Saint John the Round, beside the cathedral church, for the honor of God and of the most blessed Forerunner, and an equal number in the chapel of Saint Michael on the other side, near the cathedral church, for the remedy of his soul. He founded them from revenue that he had acquired from the toll at Troyes through a donation made to him, in recognition of his preceding merits, by his kinsman of illustrious memory, Theobald, king of Navarre and count of Champagne. He likewise established and endowed an altar in the house of God situated in the cloister of Auxerre, and issued many other pious dispositions, which are more fully expressed in the text of his final testament.

It is also clear and true that from the time he took to his sickbed he devoutly recited the canonical hours every day, for as long as he retained the ability to speak, or at least listened to them. Always thinking more about the salvation of his soul than the health of his body, he permitted few people to approach him except those who could assist him either spiritually or bodily.

When, weakened by the worsening flux and with his limbs seemingly consumed, he sensed the imminence of his approaching dissolution and realized that there was no further hope of recovery, he ordered his sister, nephews, nieces, and all his other relatives who were present to be excluded, lest their presence provide an occasion for some earthly or carnal affection that might interrupt the thought he had cast upon the Lord. He kept with him only the venerable Erard, then dean of Auxerre, his beloved nephew and successor, to whom he confidently entrusted whatever occurred to him concerning the salvation of his soul.

Those who were present heard with what detestation he accused himself of having loved worldly pomp, with what supplication he despised himself, and with what abundance of contrite tears he testified to his repentance. At last, clothed in the final anointing, he had the sign of the Lord’s cross and an image of the blessed Virgin placed before him. Fixing his eyes on them in turn, while certain friars of the Order of Friars Minor stood around him and prayed for him, he did not cease, as long as he could utter any word either clearly or half-clearly, to repeat in alternating turns:

> In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be put to shame.  
> Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit.  
> Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you.  
> Mary, mother of grace, mother of mercy, protect us from the enemy and receive us at the hour of death.

While saying these words, he fell asleep and departed from the world in the year of grace 1270, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, on the feast of Saints Sequana and Ferreolus, as dawn was rising. He breathed out his spirit and was buried among his predecessor Fathers in the cathedral church. His fame lives publicly in the world, and may his soul live forever with God. Amen.

He sat as bishop of Auxerre for twenty-three years and six months.

### Chapter LXIV — Deeds of Lord Erard of Lisigniis, Bishop of Auxerre and Cardinal

Erard, his nephew, Lord of the castle of Lisigniis in the diocese of Langres, succeeded that bishop of such great renown, the most famous man Lord Guido of Melloto, bishop of Auxerre. His memory deserves solemn recitation.

This Erard was born of a magnificent stock of nobility on both sides. His father was William Marshal of Champagne, who stood in a close degree of kinship to the prince of Achaia; his mother was Margaret, sister of the aforesaid Guido of Melloto, his predecessor. The nobility of his lineage becomes evident to anyone who examines the chronicle of the said Bishop Guido.

Erard was of medium bodily stature and displayed an angelic face, suffused with such grace that he showed himself pleasing and lovable to those who looked upon him. In speech he was most eloquent, so that he could rightly be called another Ulysses. In the melody of his voice he surpassed his contemporaries, so that when his resonant voice was emitted, its sweetness could rightly be compared with the melodies of the nightingale.

Although the nobility of his lineage might have raised him to worldly arrogance, his outstanding refinement of manners preserved him in such humility that, acquiring a mature and religious bearing, he was always free from every kind of wantonness. Though he possessed dove-like simplicity, he was nevertheless considered exceedingly magnanimous in defending the rights of his church. He loved generosity to such an extent that he often seemed to exceed its bounds. He possessed such an innate sweetness of liberality and kindness that he was affected by the blush of shame whenever he was unable to bring the requests of those who justly sought something from him to the fulfillment of their desired petition.

Although in his childhood, because of his parents’ special affection, he had been raised in luxury above their other children, through the austerity of abstinence he so subdued his flesh that in the fervor of his youth he laudably acquired chastity. At a tender age he was very extensively trained in the art of singing. Later, given over to the liberal studies, he flourished with a powerful intellect, so that in his youth he commendably taught in the arts. Then he applied his intellect so diligently to legal science that he acquired the pearl of that discipline. Subsequently turning to the faculty of canon law, he was laudably licensed in decretals at Paris.

Around that time, when Geoffrey, dean of the Church of Auxerre, had been taken from this life by the common fate of humanity, the canons of that church unanimously elected Erard dean of the same church. While he was personally resident in the Church of Auxerre and vigorously defended the rights of his deanery against everyone, and especially against his aforesaid uncle, after about two years had passed the Church of Auxerre was deprived of the consolation of its shepherd by the death of the said Bishop Guido, his uncle. The canons of that church proceeded to the election of a future bishop and, with the Lord directing them, unanimously elected Erard bishop by way of compromise. Having become bishop, he treated his subjects with his customary gentleness, instructing them alike by the word of preaching and by example.

Although, after he had been licensed in decretals, he had little time for study in the theological faculty because of the duties of his prelacy, though we believe that he ardently desired it, nevertheless, through the clarity of his intellect and the laborious investigation of intense study, he acquired the name and favor of an excellent preacher. He kept the austerity of abstinence as far as he could in secret, and for the sake of the good of chastity he wore a hair shirt beneath his clothing. He also possessed three silver chains, full of knots and attached to a certain handle, with which at night he often disciplined his flesh. We learned these things from the truthful report of trustworthy persons who knew his secret penance.

This most fervent lover of his church obtained the grace and favor of his chapter. After he had attained the height of episcopal dignity, it rarely happened that he entered that chapter without the church and chapter receiving in some respect an overflowing grace from his lavish goodness.

Accordingly, during his lifetime, he bestowed upon the aforesaid church and chapter two silver angels of remarkable beauty and immense value, with relics of Blessed Mary Magdalene reverently inserted in them. He also gave a silver cross adorned with precious gems, worth five hundred Tours pounds; this magnanimous and munificent bishop likewise gave the chapter one thousand Tours pounds for increasing the canons’ bread allowance; a mitre with a pontifical ring, worth four hundred Tours pounds; a purely golden chalice; and four pairs of priestly vestments in different colors, some of *examito* and some of *diaspro*, namely, in each case, a tunic, dalmatic, and chasuble. He also gave two further pairs of vestments, each consisting of a tunic, dalmatic, chasuble, and cope.

He did many other good things for the aforesaid episcopate, church, and chapter. Indeed, as the most sonorous celebrant of divine service, and its outstanding lover and devoted enlarger, he arranged that in the Church of Auxerre, on Sundays, [certain provisions were] distributed among the canons and clerics of that church.

At Bel-Retour he also built a new hall and a new house above the gate, with houses adjoining the gate. At the castle of Appoigniacum, subject to his authority and that of his predecessors, although the inhabitants of that place were subject to the servitude of mortmain, taille, high and low jurisdiction, at the lord’s will, and to several other forms of servitude, they had nevertheless always refused until that time to pay the rightful tithe of grain, wine, and other fruits produced by agriculture, contrary to the salutary observance of divine law.

Moved by an instinct of his innate generosity and urged by pastoral concern, he desired both to restore them to freedom and to remedy the dangers to their souls. By the vigilance of his judgment and the diligent effectiveness of his exhortation, he induced the inhabitants of that place to bind themselves, under an authentic written charter, to him and his successors in perpetuity for payment of the rightful tithe of all the aforesaid fruits. In return for this concession, with the consent of his chapter, he completely abolished from that place the servitude of mortmain—the inhuman line imposed upon the human race—and restricted the aforesaid voluntary taille to an annual revenue of one hundred and sixty Tours pounds. Nevertheless, through the grant of that tithe, he increased the episcopal revenues to three hundred Tours pounds of annual income and more.

He also purchased from the noble knights Milo of Auxerre and John, his brother, the furnace, jurisdiction, and several other properties that they possessed at the aforesaid Appoigniacum. By this purchase he increased the episcopal revenues by eighty Tours pounds of annual income. In his final will, from the aforesaid acquisitions that he had made at Appoigniacum beyond those eighty pounds of annual revenue, he granted the Church of Saint Stephen twenty Tours pounds of annual income, to be distributed on the day of his anniversary.

He increased the scholasteria of the Church of Auxerre from the properties of the episcopate by ten Tours pounds of annual income. He hoped, with ardent desire, to make still greater gifts to that church, had he not paid the inevitable debt of all flesh after so short a time.

For after an interval of about two years, while he was at La Charité on the Loire, during the priorship of the former Milo, he wished to examine a certain burgess woman of that prior, suspected of heresy. Since the prior, although warned several times, refused to hand the woman over to him, the bishop placed the said town under a general interdict.

The prior and his monks, not fearing to violate that interdict to the prejudice of episcopal jurisdiction, caused the bodies of the dead to be buried in the cemeteries of that town. Because of this, through the agency of the enemy of the human race, grave dissensions arose between the bishop and the aforesaid prior.

Finally, through the bishop’s efforts, and with the mediation of the archbishop of Sens and the abbot of Cluny, the matter was brought to this conclusion: the woman was delivered to the bishop, and one of the monks of the aforesaid monastery, on behalf of all those who had been culpable in causing the interdict to be imposed upon the town and in violating it, humbly and devoutly knelt before the bishop and begged him to relax the interdict imposed upon the town. He made satisfaction to the bishop both for the interdict and for its violation.

Twenty bodies had been taken from the earth. They had been buried in the cemeteries mentioned during the interdict, and after absolution had been obtained from the bishop, they remained unburied above ground until a general sermon had been preached to the people in the Church of Saint Peter of the aforesaid La Charité and a Mass for the dead had been celebrated. When these things had been done, the bodies were given over to ecclesiastical burial.

After four years and more had passed, a great dispute arose between the bishop and John of Chalon, count of Auxerre. As the count’s arrogance increased and he attempted to violate and invade the rights of the Church of Auxerre, the bishop did not hesitate to strike the count and his wife with the sword of anathema.

While the count and his wife persisted in their wickedness, so that ecclesiastical severity might restrain them more effectively, he placed the city of Auxerre, its suburbs, and the whole territory that the count held in the county of Auxerre under a general interdict.

When the count attempted to cloak the wickedness of his deed through the remedy of an appeal, the bishop—tireless in acquiring rights for his church and unafraid to expose his life to danger for those rights—resolved, out of pious deliberation, to go to the Roman Curia to defend them. Although he conducted himself manfully in the matter, prevented by death, he was unable to bring it to a final conclusion.

The lord Pope John XXI and all the cardinals received with honor this man, whose fragrant reputation had already spread not only attractively throughout the region of France but also throughout Italy. After he had resided in that region for about two years, he, who had been nourished in the temperate climate of Gaul, was unable to endure the boiling heat of that country. Suffering from fevers and dysentery, he contracted the ailments of a chronic illness.

Nevertheless, he conducted himself so commendably in that region that his merits shone so clearly before Lord Pope Nicholas III, successor of the aforesaid Lord John, and before the cardinals, that he was raised to the dignity of the cardinalate and made cardinal-bishop of Palestrina.

Although he was the sixty-fourth in the number of the bishops of Auxerre, he was the first among them to be advanced to so great a dignity. Not long afterward, as the dysentery worsened, he composed a final testament with great deliberation and prudence.
