When he perceived that a failure of strength was dragging him toward death, he reverently received the sacrament of extreme unction. These rites completed, in the year of the Lord 1277, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, at the first silence of night, he happily escaped the wickedness of this world.

Because he had chosen to be buried with his aforesaid uncle in the basilica of Auxerre, his bones were carried from the city of Rome to that basilica and honorably placed with those of his uncle in a single mausoleum. He sat in the episcopate of Auxerre for seven years, two months, and approximately three weeks, while the illustrious King Philip was governing the kingdom of France. May the Lord, by his grace and mercy, grant him everlasting rest. Amen.

## Notice by an Unknown Author

[Col. 0365]

Here ends the first volume of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Auxerre*. The second volume is for the most part missing, as it was formerly copied. It is said to exist in Paris in the library of a certain counsellor, whence the following were excerpted by a trustworthy man. Receive these things, reader; bring a receptive mind, and you will perceive the truth of the matter.

## Part Two

### Chapter LXV — On William de Gressibus

[Col. 0365A]

A most ancient and praiseworthy custom of the Church of Auxerre has hitherto prevailed from its first bishop, namely Saint Peregrinus: that, after the death of each bishop, the notable deeds of the individual bishops of that see should thereafter be written and entered in a book wisely and clearly arranged for this purpose, so that by their frequent recitation praise for their deeds might be rendered to God and their successors might be further stirred to vigorous acts by imitating the examples of their predecessors. Yet through negligence or a lack of historians this custom was eclipsed from, but not including, the time of the death of the lord Erard of Lisigniis, of happy memory; the day of whose death was in the year of the Lord 1277. Thus, for a hundred years, nothing concerning the foregoing is found written in the aforesaid book, until the arrival of the reverend father in Christ, Lord Nicholas des Arcies, now the eighty-first bishop of that Church, promoted by the holy apostolic see in the year of the Lord 1373. He was so promoted by the most holy father in Christ, Lord Pope Gregory XI, in Advent of the aforesaid year. It seemed expedient to this lord, the present bishop of the oft-mentioned Church, to return to the practice of that custom; and he caused the truth concerning the deeds of the bishops who had presided over that Church in the intervening period to be diligently investigated. Whatever was discovered was entered in sequence and clearly, with all possible diligence, according to the purpose stated; and by the most exact diligence exercised in these matters, the following have been found.

[Col. 0365C]

But since certainty concerning every individual matter could not be discovered in full, let the reader of this work spare its historian. He did not see all the following bishops concerning whom he wrote below, namely the first four; he wove their deeds into writing from fitting testimony. But he saw the rest and knows that what he wrote of them is true, having been the continual servant of many of them and a diligent investigator of the deeds of the others. For they performed many other holy works for their own salvation and that of their subjects; although these are not written in the present book, one must firmly believe that they are not lacking in the books of life. Nevertheless, trusting in the example of Saint Gregory in the beginning of his *Dialogues*, book III, chapter 3, at the words, “The things which are mine,” etc., where he says that “the evangelists Mark and Luke learned what they described not by sight but by hearing, I shall remove from readers any occasion for doubt by making known, point by point, how the things I shall write came to my knowledge from those who heard them.” But I wish all who read this work to understand that in some matters the sense alone, and in others the words together with the sense, must be retained; for if he had wished to preserve the very words particularly in every individual case, the writer’s style would not suitably admit expressions uttered in rustic usage. I learned the things I relate from the testimony of very venerable elders, while nevertheless submitting this little work to the due correction and testimony of the elders.

[Col. 0366A]

William de Gressio, the sixty-fifth bishop, a Frenchman by nationality, native of the Vexin, noble in lineage and character, immediately succeeded Erard of Lisigniis. He was a learned and vigorous man, so much so that before this promotion he was among the ecclesiastics most closely attendant upon and most influential with the king. For this reason, and more pleasingly because of his other virtues, he obtained the said promotion. He was very liberal and generous. Throughout his province he brought many disputes, which had long existed between the bishops of Auxerre and other nobles, to an end, partly by litigation and partly by settlements; and thus at the end of his administration he left no apparent controversy to the bishopric. He made many acquisitions, especially in the territory of Appoigny, upon which he founded his anniversary, of twenty pounds annually to be paid to the Church of Auxerre and distributed on the day of that anniversary. He sat long and peacefully, namely for about sixteen years, reckoning from the death of his predecessor Erard, which was in the year of the Lord 1277; his own death was in 1293, on the Friday before the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary. He was buried in the choir of the church, on the left side of the choir, adjoining the steps and near the noble tomb of the lord Guido of Melloto, of happy memory. There is a gilded image on black marble [the wording is corrupt] of that Guido, who was the sixty-third bishop.

### Chapter LXVI — On Peter de Mornay

Peter de Mornay, the sixty-sixth bishop, a Frenchman of Bourges and a noble man, succeeded William de Gressio in the bishopric. He was indeed most skilled in both laws, of great counsel, and highly influential with the king. Thereupon, having become the king’s chancellor, he was created bishop of Auxerre and held the aforesaid office of chancellor until the end of his life. He made many acquisitions for the episcopal see.

[Col. 0366D]

First, he acquired the land of Oudan from the lord of Tholet, to whom that land belonged, though it was held of the episcopal see. But because the lords of Tholet inflicted many injuries upon the inhabitants of Varzy—for at that time that whole land was of servile condition for the uses of the bishopric of Nevers—he made this acquisition principally in order to procure peace and quiet for his town of Varzy. Likewise, near the town and castle of Moret, he acquired a handsome house with its appurtenances, namely lands and vineyards, in the village of Broce in the parish of Héry, near the Cistercian monastery of Barcelle, on the opposite side of the town and bridge of La Mothe, on the river Seine. He also acquired a great part of the episcopal residences in Paris adjoining the gate called Inferni, though in ancient times it used to be called de Ferto; and he obtained from the king a large open space adjoining the walls, outside which he caused most pleasant courts and gardens to be made and enclosed with walls. But because of wars, ditches were later dug there. He also gave his Church of Auxerre a most beautiful Lenten veil, which still endures.

[Col. 0367B]

He also made many acquisitions at Appoigny, upon which he founded his anniversary of twenty pounds of annual income, to be paid to the Church of Auxerre by his successors. At the end of his days he retired to Ragenna and ended his life there; his body was brought back and honorably buried in the choir of his church, on the right side, beside the noble tomb of the above-mentioned lord Guido of Melloto, in the year of the Lord 1306, on the day written on that tomb. Thus he sat for about thirteen years.

## Chapter LXVII — On Peter of Bellapertica

Peter of Bellapertica, the sixty-seventh bishop, a Frenchman by nationality, from the Bourbonnais region, from the castle of Bellapertica on the River Allier [Col. 0367C], was born of parents of moderate rank and status. He succeeded the aforementioned Peter of Mornay both in the episcopate, by apostolic provision, and in the office of chancellor, by royal promotion.

This man was extremely learned in civil law, in which north of the Alps he was regarded as one of the experts. His work and expertise consisted in elucidating the obscure difficulties and uncertainties of civil law, as is evident in this book of his on appeals—namely, the Glossary on the Code—and in many of his other writings. According to these works, those wishing to become fully learned are chiefly instructed in the kingdom’s universities, especially at Orléans. For he had as his master the very famous Lord James of Ravigneio, who likewise wrote on the Old Digest; Peter diligently followed this master and became his equal in teaching [Col. 0367D].

That Peter resided only briefly in the diocese, being continually occupied with the aforementioned chancellorship and in communication with the king. Nevertheless, he made his ceremonial entrance into the city, at which the king was present and introduced him into the city by royal authority, without the ancient solemnity according to which the Count of Auxerre, the Baron of Donzy, the Lord of Toucy, and the Lord of Saint-Verain in Puisaye, by the nature and obligation of their fiefs, ought and are bound to carry the new bishop from the church of Saint-Germain to the Church of Auxerre. The right of the said bishops and lords to this solemnity in the future was reserved on the royal side.

He died in Paris, but the day is uncertain. Nevertheless, considering the date of his predecessor’s death and the date of the promotion of his immediate successor, which occurred in the year of Our Lord 1308, it follows that Peter occupied the see for approximately two years.

He founded four prebends in the church of Villeneuve near Bellapertica, for the benefit of his soul.

### Epitaph

Here lies in the cell Peter, surnamed Bella—

Pertica, clear in speech and faithful also in deeds,

Gentle, truthful, prudent, humble, and chaste;

Learned in law, straightforward, like another Justinian,

The highest of teachers, the surest rule of morals,

Dean of the canons of Paris,

Worthily taking for himself the see of Auxerre,

After the middle years, succeeding as its beloved bishop,

In the year one thousand three hundred and seven,

On the feast of Sulpicius he departed from the troubled world.

May the gracious spirit grant him consolation. Amen.

[Col. 0368B] He has such an epitaph because of the eagle in the choir of the cathedral church, in which he had been dean.

## Chapter LXVIII — On Peter of Gressy

Peter of Gressy, the sixty-eighth bishop, a Frenchman by nationality and from the Gâtinais region, was noble by birth, as was his aforementioned uncle William. He was learned in both laws, chancellor of France, and was promoted to the episcopal see through his merits, with appropriate royal favor and apostolic provision. He surpassed his contemporary prelates in the distinction of generosity and hospitality. After relinquishing the aforementioned chancellorship, he governed his see vigorously and was loved by all.

His exceptional hospitality excluded no one who sought him. At length, burdened by the weight of the flesh [Col. 0368C] and consequently so hindered in the exercise of government, he had coadjutors. Finally, when he came to his last day, he gave his soul back to God on the twenty-first day of September, namely on the feast of Saint Matthew the Apostle, in the year of Our Lord 1325. His body was honorably buried in the choir of the Church of Auxerre, beside the tomb of his aforementioned uncle, on the left side of the choir, adjoining the tomb of Lord Guy of Melloto mentioned above.

## Chapter LXIX — On Peter of Mortemer

Peter of Mortemer, the sixty-ninth bishop, an Aquitanian by nationality and of moderate birth, was a man of exceptionally keen intelligence and a solemn professor of both laws. Among the king’s councillors he was the most energetic. He was promoted by the Holy Apostolic See through the intervention of royal prayers and because his merits demanded it [Col. 0368D].

He succeeded the immediately preceding Peter of Gressy and entered the city and the Church of Auxerre with due solemnity, accompanied by the princes and other temporal lords who were required to carry him and did so. Among them was the Count of Flanders, by reason of the barony of Donzy. After rendering homage to the bishop, the count wished and attempted to seize the bishop’s ring, but was unable to do so. Nevertheless, the bishop promised that he would investigate whether this belonged to the count’s right and would render him an account of the matter.

He governed the see energetically, but for only a short time, because he became a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. In that state he lived while vigorously bearing part of the Church’s burden of responsibility and enjoying a reputation for holiness. In his native place he founded four religious houses: one of monks, namely Carthusians, and two others belonging to the Mendicant Orders [Col. 0369A].

At length his soul departed from human life, and his body was carried to the aforementioned place and buried among those religious. He was promoted to this see in the year of Our Lord 1325, on the feast of All Saints, and to the cardinalate on the twenty-eighth, on the feast of the Nativity of the Lord. Thus he occupied the episcopal see for three years. He died around the year 1336, at the beginning of the pontificate of Pope Benedict XII.

He had been the former special companion of that great man whom Pope John XXII had flayed alive, namely the Bishop of Cahors. But, wisely withdrawing from the curia, he came for refuge [Col. 0369B] to the King of France, who honorably received him as a principal councillor and afterward as chancellor; finally, he became the king’s godfather. From these circumstances proceeded his worthy promotion mentioned above.

## Chapter LXX — On Talerand

Talerand, son of the Count of Périgord, an Aquitanian by nationality, was a most noble man and learned in civil law. Promoted by apostolic provision, he succeeded the aforementioned Peter of Mortemer.

He did not enter the city, but remained almost continually studying at the house of Odant near Verziac, which had been acquired by the aforementioned Lord Peter of Mornay. There Talerand had a splendid hall and chamber constructed, as well as a cloister behind them, in the manner of religious houses, for the work of study; and there he made great progress in his studies [Col. 0369C].

He was eventually made a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. In that state he conducted himself with great energy, and he was promoted to the see of Auxerre in the year of Our Lord 1328. He was transferred to the cardinalate in the following year, 1330. The see remained vacant for almost a year because of opposition to the promise made in the Sacred College to promote Lord Stephen of Mornay, Chancellor of France; but he had many adversaries. Therefore the man who follows was promoted in the year 1331, on the feast of the Nativity of the Lord. Thus Talerand occupied the see for only about three years.

He died as a cardinal in the year 1364. He was buried at Avignon, and afterward, it is said, his body was transferred to his homeland. For the foundation of his anniversary he bequeathed one hundred florins to the Church of Auxerre [Col. 0369D], and they were paid.

## Chapter LXXI — On Aymericus

Aymericus Guenaudi, a Frenchman by nationality and a native of Poitou, was the seventy-first bishop. He was noble by birth, learning, and character; a professor of law; a royal councillor residing in the royal household; and he held the office of Master of Requests for many years.

At length, through the intercession of the king and queen and because of his merits, he was promoted to the see of Auxerre after the aforementioned Talerand, in the year of Our Lord 1331, on the Ember Saturday before the feast of the Nativity, during the time of Pope John XXII.

This man was held in great honor, was pleasing to everyone, full of courtesy, and highly agreeable to the nobility [Col. 0370A]. He governed his see peacefully during his time, except for a major dispute that he had with the religious of La Charité, namely the prior of Bonny, over two English clerics whom the provost of Bonny had caused to be hanged. He pursued the matter vigorously and therefore sent two prudent men to England, one of whom was called Boutevilain of Auxerre, to investigate and report on the clerical title. The matter was so fully brought to judgment through the court of Parliament that the honor of spiritual jurisdiction was preserved.

He consecrated the high altar of Saint Stephen in the year 1334. He also founded a chaplaincy at the altar of Saint Martin in the Church of Auxerre, endowed with twenty pounds [Col. 0370B] of annual and perpetual income from several acquisitions that he had made at Appoigny. He likewise founded his anniversary there, endowed with twenty Tours pounds of annual and perpetual income.

He was the first to construct a rabbit enclosure at Regennes in Garenne. He was transferred to the see of Rouen in the year 1338. Thus he governed for eight years.

## Chapter LXXII — On John of Blangy

John of Blangy, the seventy-second bishop, a Frenchman by nationality and a native of Normandy, was a famous master of theology, studying and teaching at Paris. By the spontaneous decision of Pope Benedict XII, on the translation of Lord Aymericus, he was promoted to the episcopal see of Auxerre in the year of Our Lord 1338.

It was remembered that the two men had been contemporaries in their studies at Paris, in that discipline, competing with one another in teaching it; they had also together attained the honor and summit of the licentiate and doctorate. Therefore, on his own initiative, the pope provided the Church of Auxerre with him. Yet he governed it only briefly, always longing to return to Paris.

For this reason, during the time of Pope Clement VI, successor to the aforementioned Pope Benedict, he resigned his bishopric. A fixed lifelong pension was arranged for him by the said see, and he returned to Paris to lead a contemplative life. While traveling by ship, he suffered from cold and rheum and contracted a continuous fever. He entered Paris with it and died within a few days. His body was buried in the church of the Carthusian brothers during the Easter season [Col. 0370D], in the year 1345, in the month of April. He occupied the see for approximately six years.

## Chapter LXXIII — On Peter of Villaines

Peter of Villaines, the seventy-third bishop, a Frenchman by nationality and a native of Normandy, was promoted to the episcopal see through the favor of the Apostolic See after the resignation of the aforementioned Lord John of Blangy. He was a noble, eloquent, and energetic man.

He repaired the strongholds of Regennes and Ville-Catuli, restored them to proper fortification, and defended them with war engines and ditches. He was eventually transferred to the see of Bayeux, from which he originated. Nevertheless, at the house of Odant he had built a chapel and chamber of exceedingly noble, kingly workmanship.

He granted freedom to the people and land of Odant [Col. 0371A], in return for an annual payment of grain and other goods from each family and household. His successor, mentioned below, strongly opposed this grant, and for good reason.

When he had been transferred to the see of Bayeux, the severity of the wars made him regret that he had abandoned his first see. He was transferred from the Church of Auxerre to the Church of Bayeux around the year of Our Lord 1347. He occupied the see for approximately three and a half years.

He entered the city alone with the Count of Auxerre, in the evening hour of a Saturday. On the following day, however, he held a banquet without summoning or informing the other nobles.

He was therefore promoted to this see of Auxerre through the resignation of John of Blangy recorded immediately above [Col. 0371B], in the year of Our Lord 1344, according to French reckoning in wintertime, namely after the feast of the Nativity of the Lord. Thus he occupied the see for three and a half years. He was buried at Bayeux; the exact day is unknown to us.

## Chapter LXXIV — On Bernard Bruni

Bernard Bruni, the seventy-fourth bishop, a Frenchman by nationality and a native of Limousin, was transferred from the bishopric of Thérouanne to the see of Auxerre immediately after the transfer of the aforementioned Peter from the see of Auxerre to Bayeux, in the year of Our Lord 1347, at Pentecost.

This man was extremely old, wise, and wealthy, beyond all his contemporary prelates. He was a most vigorous guardian and prosecutor of the rights of the Church [Col. 0371C]. He did not enter his city.

He began to challenge the freedom that his predecessor had granted to the people of the land of Odant. Because he was burdened by the illness from which he died and was unable during his lifetime to bring the said lawsuit to its desired conclusion, he left in his will a bequest of one thousand gold florins to his successor, mentioned below, to be used solely in pursuing the lawsuit against those people and against his predecessor.

His way of life was as follows: he ate his midday meal at sunrise and had supper before the ninth hour. He was said to have adopted this regimen from an uncle of his, a cardinal, who lived in the same manner; he had learned it from his uncle’s care during his early youth.

He died in the castle of Ville-Catuli in the year of Our Lord 1349, around the feast of All Saints [Col. 0371D]. His body was carried to Limoges and buried there. He occupied the see for two years and four months.

He greatly loved the residence at Odant. He surrounded the place and house with palisades and large towers and had three square towers constructed there. Only one was lacking for a square fortification to have stood there, with walls connecting tower to tower. But all this was afterward destroyed during the wars, when Lord Iterius de Jarossa was bishop, as is related below.

## Chapter LXXV — On Peter of Cros

Peter of Cros, the seventy-fifth bishop, a Frenchman by nationality and a native of Limousin, was an outstanding master of theology [Col. 0372A]. First he was dean of Paris, then Bishop of Senlis, and finally he was transferred to the see of Auxerre by Pope Clement VI, after the death of the aforementioned Bernard.

For the said pope and Peter had been contemporaries in their studies, teaching and presiding there, and they were countrymen. This man, in addition to his excellence in learning, possessed extraordinary charm in speech and in every gesture; he was greatly loved by everyone, and prudent and shrewd in his undertakings.

After receiving the aforementioned one thousand florins for litigating against the people of Odant, he began to persevere in the lawsuit. At length, an amicable settlement and agreement was reached: the annual payments in place of servitude were increased for each person according to his portion. Thus the lawsuit was brought to an end.

He was immediately made a cardinal. He did not enter the city, but on his departure approached it in the meadows near the fountain of Saint Amator. There he preached splendidly and received an honorable farewell from clergy and people.

He occupied the see for one year and six months and was made a cardinal at the beginning of the year 1351, around the feast of the Nativity of the Lord. He died as a cardinal in the Roman Curia, namely at Avignon, in September of the year 1361. He bequeathed a large sum of florins to the Church of Auxerre for his anniversary, but the will was concealed and its truth has not yet been discovered. His body was buried in the church of the Preaching Brothers.

## Chapter LXXVI — On Audoin

[Col. 0372C] Audoin, the seventy-sixth bishop, a Frenchman by nationality and a native of Limousin, had previously been Bishop of Noyon and afterward Bishop of Paris. He was finally transferred to the see of Auxerre when his predecessor Peter was transferred to the cardinalate, namely at the beginning of the year 1351, on the Nativity of the Lord.

This man was learned and extremely well versed in both laws. With the consent of the dean and chapter of Auxerre, he judged that the house of Belle-Retour was useless and burdensome because of the great expense of repairs, considering the number of episcopal houses existing elsewhere and nearby. Nevertheless, it was ordered that the long double stables be retained in their present condition.

Within the grounds of the said house were also retained the great, high gateway at the entrance to the house [Col. 0372D], and the small house adjoining that gateway, to receive the bishop’s people when they came there for hunting or other purposes; likewise, an oven on the other side of the gateway. These facilities were deemed sufficient for the farmer and his family, who were to be placed there in the future to care for the feeding of the livestock.

He was transferred to the cardinalate in the following manner. At that time there were two cardinals bearing the title of Auxerre, namely Talerand of Périgord and Peter of Cros. He was transferred to the see of Maguelonne in the year 1353 according to Roman-curial reckoning, on the Nativity of the Lord, but in French reckoning in the year 1352, on the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary. In the following year he was made a cardinal and was therefore called Cardinal of Maguelonne [Col. 0373A].

This occurred during the time of his uncle, Lord Innocent V, at the beginning of his pontificate, namely after the first year had elapsed. He occupied the see of Auxerre for two years less two months. He died in the year 1364, on the eleventh day of May, at Avignon, and was buried there in the monastery of the Carthusian brothers, which is in the kingdom near Villeneuve and which his aforementioned uncle, Lord Innocent, founded.

For the foundation of his anniversary he gave three hundred gold florins to the Church of Auxerre, and they were paid.

## Chapter LXXVII — On John of Auxerre

John of Auxerre, the seventy-seventh bishop, a Frenchman by nationality and a Burgundian by origin, was a noble man of the house of Tournelles in the county of Nevers and learned in both laws. He had previously been Bishop of Troyes.

He was elected through the way of the Holy Spirit, a method that had not produced a result in any cathedral church in the kingdom of France for a long time. By the pope’s own initiative he succeeded the aforementioned Audoin in the bishopric of Auxerre.

He was a gentle, pious, merciful man, wholly devoted to hospitality. He occupied the sees of Troyes and Auxerre for sixteen years: ten years at Troyes and six years at Auxerre less three weeks. He had been promoted at Auxerre in the year 1353, on the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary according to the custom of the Roman Curia, and he died on the eighth day of January in the year 1359, calculated according to that same custom.

Each year, while he presided over the see of Troyes, he perfectly carried out the duty of visitation [Col. 0373C] and personally performed the episcopal office without interruption, both in the conferral of orders and in other matters. There, at great expense, he transferred the body of Saint Syria and honorably placed it on high in a suitable reliquary.

At the see of Auxerre he regularly celebrated ordinations in person, except for the last ones, namely those before the feast of the Nativity of the Lord preceding his death, since he was held by a grave illness, as his death made clear.

At that time, on the feast of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the English enemies, in the name of the King of Navarre, violently seized the stronghold of Regennes. This greatly distressed him.

When they proceeded day after day to attack the city of Auxerre, finally, on the Thursday after the Epiphany of the Lord, at the ninth hour, the cry to arms suddenly arose because the enemies were attacking the city. At that same hour, as his illness worsened, he received the sacrament of extreme unction. Ecclesiastical persons who had been armed and had returned from guarding the walls for this purpose attended him in great perplexity.

After this, following the example of Saint Augustine, who ended his life in a similar manner, and using tears as bread, he commended his soul to God with full possession of his senses and complete command of speech. With tears he gave his soul back to God, and his body was reverently buried in the choir of the Church of Auxerre, on the left side, between the tomb of the noble Lord Guy of Melloto and the choir staircase [Col. 0374A].

He made his first entrance into the city of Auxerre with all due solemnity. A dispute nevertheless arose over the silk pallium placed on the chair and over him. Those carrying this pallium seized it and carried it away when it slipped from his shoulders, asserting universally that it belonged to them. Since they were warned under penalty of excommunication to return it, a scandal arose. As a result, they afterward denied him entry to the tower of Toucy and the tower of Saint-Sauveur.

They later established their repeated possession of the pallium on three occasions. He therefore ordered them to return the pallium, which by common agreement had been placed in sequestration. The person who wrote this knows that these things are true, because he was present at everything.

Moreover, because the people of the Archdeacon of Sens had not been present at the proper hour during his first entrance, they nevertheless came while he was before the altar and enthroned him in the chair. Being displeased with him because he had entered the church doors without their authority, they afterward demanded a gold mark on account of the enthronement. The bishop replied that he would deliberate about it. Later, after reaching an agreement with them, he sent them approximately half the value of the mark, and those people were satisfied.

Furthermore, this John was at Sens, where he made the customary profession before the altar and paid a certain sum of money, about six pounds. Soon afterward he sent them a silk cope, according to the ancient custom which he said he knew, since he had previously paid for a cope there on such an occasion [Col. 0374C].

He established a double office in the Church of Auxerre on the feast of the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist, the day on which he made his first entrance into Auxerre. In his will he bequeathed one hundred pounds per year to the Church of Auxerre for the foundation of his anniversary, as is clear from the wording of the will.

During his lifetime he also gave the Church of Auxerre a book called the Rationale of the Divine Offices. Because of the destruction of the city, it could not be found for a long time. Later, however, it was found by Lord Peter of Auxerre, his nephew and heir, who presently retains it.

## Chapter LXXVIII — On Iterius de Jarossa

Iterius de Jarossa, the seventy-eighth bishop, a Frenchman by nationality and a native of Limousin [Col. 0374D], noble by birth, learned in both laws, vigorous in action and in law, in spiritual and temporal matters, and a magnanimous man, remained in the Roman Curia after the death of the aforementioned John of Auxerre. Being very close to the pope, he was promoted by the Apostolic See to the see of Auxerre and was received through a procurator on the eighth day of March, namely the Thursday after Ash Wednesday, in the aforementioned year 1358 according to French reckoning, but in 1359 according to Roman reckoning.

On the following Sunday at dawn, the city was captured by the enemies, namely the English, in the name of the King of Navarre, with scaling ladders, through the negligence of the guards in the section entrusted to the townsmen. These enemies committed so many and such great evils against persons and property [Col. 0375A] that they cannot be recounted—not merely in destroying the city, but subsequently the whole surrounding country and the entire kingdom. They held the city from the last day of March in that year until the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary immediately following.

At midnight on that feast, the Constable of France arrived with fifty thousand armed men. Among them was the energetic and experienced soldier Lord Henry of Poitiers, Bishop of Troyes. They entered the city, closed the gates, and with indescribable diligence placed empty barrels on the stripped walls, filled them with stones, and arranged them in the form of bulwarks and ramparts. In a day and a half they surrounded and fortified all the walls.

Finally, at suitable locations [Col. 0375B], they stationed and fortified the city with four hundred men-at-arms and a large number of brigands to guard it. These remained for a long time. But the King of England occupied and devastated Champagne, Burgundy, and the regions of Auxerre with his army.

When truces had been agreed between that king and the Duke of Burgundy, he withdrew from the duchy of Burgundy and returned through the regions of Orléans. After the truce between the lord king and him had been concluded and agreed, and after the King of England’s departure, the aforementioned men-at-arms and brigands—who, while guarding the city and country, had already stripped them of all their possessions—left the city. Divided here and there into bands among themselves, they secretly entered fortified places and oppressed the countryside no less than enemies [Col. 0375C] for a year and more.

As for the castle or stronghold of Regennes, which the king had recovered from the hands of the English and kept fortified with men-at-arms, the Bailiffs of Troyes and of Chaumont personally resided there. In his own time the king returned this castle to the said Bishop Iterius at the request of Pope Innocent V, but on the condition that it be so guarded that it could not thereafter bring harm or danger to the kingdom. During Iterius’s time the castle was guarded at great expense, both for repairs and fortifications and for the maintenance of armed men. A large sum of money was likewise paid to the said bailiffs for the expenses of the guard during his tenure.

During this bishop’s time, the inhabitants of Varzy [Col. 0375D], considering that the enemies lay in wait for them day and night and intended to fortify the place of Odant to the detriment and danger of the town of Varzy, caused the said place of Odant to be destroyed.

When he was planning to come to his diocese, Iterius was swiftly overcome by the plague of the groin then raging in the Roman Curia. He ended his days on the eighth day of June, in the year of Our Lord 1361, and on the following day his body was honorably consigned to burial in the church of the Preaching Brothers.

It is said that the Apostolic See had arranged to transfer him to the see of Arles and afterward promote him to the cardinalate. For he was very well known and esteemed by the supreme pontiff and beloved by the cardinals, who regarded him as a true and most wise man; and such he was.

He occupied the see for two and a half years. For the foundation of his anniversary he bequeathed one hundred gold francs at the écu standard to the Church of Auxerre, and they were paid.

## Chapter LXXIX — On John Germani

John Germani, the seventy-ninth bishop, a Frenchman by nationality and a Burgundian from the region of Sens, was born at Dimont. He was first dean of the Church of Auxerre. He was afterward made Bishop of Chalon at the request of the Queen of France, whose special councillor he was.

Finally, by the spontaneous decision of Pope Innocent V, without his knowledge, he was transferred to the see of Auxerre upon the death of his predecessor, the aforementioned Iterius. He held a licentiate in both laws, was prudent in counsel, and had lived in the household of the aforementioned queen, where he was the senior and principal of her councillors.

Later, as a member of the secret council of King John, when that king returned from captivity in England and came into Burgundy to take possession of the duchy by succession from the last descendant in the direct line, namely Philip, son-in-law of the Count of Flanders, he brought this bishop with him as his principal councillor and, by royal authority, introduced him into the city of Auxerre.

This occurred despite the omission of the ancient solemnity that was supposed to be observed at his first entrance: namely, spending the vigil lying in the monastery of Saint-Germain; on the following day being carried in a chair by the Count of Nevers for the barony of Donzy, by the Count of Auxerre for the county, and by the Count of Bar for the land of Puisaye; being carried likewise by the Lord of Saint-Verain on his own shoulders to the doors of the aforementioned Church of Auxerre [Col. 0376C]; and afterward swearing fealty there concerning the lands mentioned above.

The aforesaid king wished and granted that no future prejudice should be inflicted upon anyone because of the omission of this solemnity, while reserving by the authority of royal majesty everyone’s future right.

It seems useful to set down in writing the manner of the aforementioned entrance. After dining at Regennes, the king came to Auxerre in the evening. At the entrance to the city gate, the bishop was beside him; shortly afterward he rode ahead of the king and came before the church doors in his customary vestments. Dismounting, he approached to pray before the image of the Blessed Virgin Mary at the portal. Immediately after completing his prayer, he returned in ecclesiastical attire to the church doors. A book containing the form of the new bishop’s oath was presented to him; at the dean’s request he read the form and devoutly took the oath [Col. 0376D].

The dean then delivered possession of the Church to him by his taking hold of a cord thrown through the upper window before the doors. At that moment the doors were opened. Immediately the aforesaid king arrived, dismounted, and came to pray before the aforementioned image. Having done this, he returned to the said doors, and together they entered the church, the bishop on the right and the king on the left, while the choir sang the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*.

In the prescribed order they came before the altar. After each of them had completed his prayer and the antiphon with its verse had been said [Col. 0377A], the bishop recited the prayer aloud. Having thus obtained possession through the dean, they both departed. After accompanying the king to the place where he was to lodge, the bishop went to the episcopal house, intending to celebrate ordinations on the following day.

These events had taken place on the Friday after the feast of Saint Lucy. But on the following day, as the king hastened his departure, and since the country and especially the city had many difficult matters to conduct with the king, the bishop was occupied with this and therefore did not celebrate the ordinations. He accompanied the king as far as Saint-Prisque, returned late for dinner, and afterward sent to Saint-Germain for the customary provisions. At the request of the religious, however, he put the matter on hold, and eventually an agreement was reached between them.

On the following day [Col. 0377B] after the aforementioned entrance, the official of the archdeacon arrived with a canon of Sens and complained about the enthronement of the bishop, which he asserted belonged solely to his lord the archdeacon. After hearing this and consulting about the matter, the bishop went to the church on the morning of the third day. In order to preserve the archdeacon’s right, the official and vicar of the archdeacon placed the bishop in the stone chair on the right side of the altar. The official then demanded one gold mark for the said archdeacon on account of the enthronement. He also demanded one silver mark for the office itself, and the canon demanded the same by ancient custom. The demand was submitted for deliberation, and the bishop promised to do what was reasonable.

On the following Sunday he held a banquet for his chapter. On Monday he followed the king into Burgundy and there, with other magistrates, governed the duchy on the king’s behalf until the feast of the Resurrection of the Lord immediately following, at the beginning of the year of Our Lord 1362.

After returning from Burgundy, the bishop remained in the diocese, celebrating ordinations and carrying out other episcopal duties, restoring cultivation on the lands and vineyards, and diligently repairing and fortifying strongholds and other buildings. Among other things, he redeemed his castle of Ville-Catuli from the hands of those who had held it since the time of his predecessors and refused to return it. He paid them eight hundred gold écus. For his land of Toucy he likewise paid those holding the tower of that place a large sum of florins.

[Col. 0377D] After these events, while he was staying in his aforementioned castle of Ville-Catuli, and while an epidemic was raging in the regions of Auxerre, a swelling under his armpits seized him and soon forced his soul from his body. He received the sacraments of the Church with great devotion—namely the Eucharist and extreme unction—and completed his will, with everything properly arranged.

During the time of his governance, indeed within the space of a single year, he conferred ten canonries and prebends of Auxerre. This has not been heard of in the case of any of his predecessors. Nevertheless, he assigned good men to them, all natives of the regions of Auxerre or Sens.

He died on the vigil of the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in the year of Our Lord 1362 [Col. 0378A], in his castle of Ville-Catuli. His body was brought to Auxerre and honorably buried in the choir on the right side, near the choir seats. His is the first burial on the upper side.

Since he had been promoted to the said see in the preceding year, around the feast of Saint John the Baptist, it follows that he occupied it for only one year and approximately two months.

He left ten pounds of annual income to the Church of Auxerre for his anniversary.

## Chapter LXXX — On Peter Aymon
[Col. 0378B] Petrus Aymonis, the eightieth bishop, a Frenchman by nation and born in the region of Auvergne, a doctor of civil law and holder of the office of subdeacon to Pope Urban V, was promoted to this bishopric by the aforesaid most holy Father, Pope Urban V, in his new creation, in the year of the Lord 1362, around the feast of All Saints. This Petrus was the first person whom that pope himself promoted to the episcopate. He was distinguished and ceremonious in all his acts, both ecclesiastical and secular, upright in character, generous, and affable. Indeed, he had been brought up in the Roman Curia, both among cardinals and supreme pontiffs. Because of these virtues, he was repeatedly chosen for the most important affairs of the kingdom as ambassador, or solemn envoy, and often went alone, without a companion, to the pope, the emperor, the king of England, and the king of Hungary. Having been repeatedly and variously engaged in such missions, [Col. 0378C] he was honorably placed in the secret council of our lord the king.

During his time there were always wars, and he had his fortresses guarded with courage and at great expense, especially those of Regennes and Villa Catuli. He also had the episcopal residence at Auxerre repaired, and likewise his episcopal house in Paris, which was very pleasant and agreeable to those who visited him, although they had no business concerning him to conduct with him. It was widely expected that he would be made a cardinal, on account of his merits, the intercession of the emperor and the kings mentioned above, and the favor of many cardinals with whom he had been a fellow student. [Col. 0378D] But in the year of the Lord 1373, in September, on the second day, the fellowship of body and soul was separated in him by a wasting illness, in the episcopal house at Auxerre. His body was given a fitting burial in the choir, before the stairs on the left-hand side, beside the tomb of the late Lord Jean of Auxerre. That tomb is joined to the tomb of the late Lord Guy of Mellot, formerly bishop of Auxerre, and of his nephew Lord Erald of Lisignies, likewise a bishop; both rest in the same sarcophagus and tomb. Erald was the first bishop of Auxerre to be made a cardinal. A fuller account of his death at Rome, and of how his bones were brought back to this church of his, is given above in his deeds, namely in Book I of the Deeds of the Bishops of the Church of Auxerre.

[Col. 0379A] Petrus entered the city, making his first entry without the ancient and customary solemnity, and without being carried to the church by the noble feudal vassals of the church. Of these, only the count accompanied him in that new entry. Since, according to the report of the ancients and a very ancient tradition, no lawsuit in formal legal form between any bishop of Auxerre and the deans and chapter of the Church of Auxerre appeared in any books, letters, other documents, or reports, this man was the first to engage in litigation with them over several sums of money and other things owed annually by the bishops, which he had ceased to pay. Through the mediation of wise men, however, he withdrew from the litigation, and he came to love the said dean, chapter, and individual persons. As he often expressed it, he had great devotion to the church, especially to helping with the construction of the church, had not the lot of human existence brought a swifter impediment.

[Col. 0379B] For the founding of his anniversary, he gave this church three hundred French gold deniers. He made the customary profession at Sens and, instead of a silk cope, gave there a silk or gold-embroidered cloth, which the dean and chapter of Sens at first refused to accept but finally did accept. Nothing, however, was done concerning his enthronement on the part of the archdeacon of Sens; and if anything was paid to that archdeacon, it is unknown. He sat for ten years, less approximately two months. During his lifetime he had given this church a gilded silk cloth, which on the great solemnities is placed at the top of the high altar, namely before the candles.

[Col. 0379C] **CHAPTER LXXXI — On Nicolas of Arcy.** — **LXXXII — On Guillaume of Totavilla.** — **LXXXIII — On Ferric Cassineti.** — **LXXXIV — On Michel of Creney.** — **LXXXV — On Jean of Thoisy.** — **LXXXVI — On Philippe of Essart.** — **LXXXVII — On Jean of Corbey.** — **LXXXVIII — On Laurent Pynon.** — **LXXXIX — On Pierre of Longueil.** — **XC — On Enguerrand of Synart.** — **XCI — On Jean Baillet.**

## CHAPTER XCII — On François of Dinteville

[Col. 0379D] François of Dinteville was born of the most noble father, Claude of Dinteville, chamberlain in Burgundy and lord of Échenet, Polisy, and many other places, and of his mother Jeanne of La Baulme, from the counts of Montrevel. Claude of Dinteville, just as he had been raised and educated in the household and family of the dukes of Burgundy—for he was one of their treasurers and councillors—so followed their fortunes in every affair, and finally fell bravely with Duke Charles in the battle at Nancy.

While the affairs of those dukes were still prosperous and successful, he married Jeanne, a woman of distinguished standing and of a wealthy and powerful family. By her he had fourteen children, namely ten sons and four daughters. The youngest of these was François, first bishop of Cistarcium (*Cistarciensis*); then, in the year of the Lord 1504, when the see of Auxerre had become vacant through the death of the late Reverend Jean Baillet, he was requested as bishop by the common vote of all the canons and was transferred by Pope Leo X from the Church of Cistarcium to that of Auxerre, [Col. 0380A] in the forty-ninth year of his age, on 5 March.

As a boy he first devoted himself to humane letters at Dijon and afterward at Autun, where, in the judgment of everyone, he was considered the most learned among his peers and gave no ordinary promise of himself. Finally, after applying himself seriously for five years at Pavia to the civil laws and the decrees of the pontiffs, when the wars had been quieted and affairs settled between the Most Christian King of France, Louis XI, and the Burgundians, he returned home and to his parents as a doctor of both laws.

A few months later he was received into the household of the most reverend Lord Georges of Amboise, archbishop of Rouen and afterward cardinal and legate, because of his outstanding and excellent qualities of mind and body. Aided by the favor of his brothers and parents, he formed important friendships at the court of King Louis XII. [Col. 0380B] At that time Guillaume Pot, bishop of Tournai, was his uncle; Jacques, the chamberlain, a knight; Jacques, the grand huntsman of France; and Gauthier, the royal steward, or master of the royal household, lord of Polisy, were his brothers. They were very dear to the same Most Christian King Louis XII and were his councillors. Through their efforts and assistance he obtained many priestly offices and benefices, and very excellent ones: the abbey of Castillon-sur-Seine, the monastery of Dervent, and the aforesaid bishopric of Cistarcium.

[Col. 0380C] When, in the year of the Lord 1510, the see of the Church of Autun had become vacant, and he had been requested as bishop by the greater and sounder part of the chapter—for he had long been a canon there—at the request and wish of the aforesaid King Louis, he yielded his right in favor of Lord Jacques Hurault. As a young man he had obtained the parish of Ricey, prebends in the Churches of Autun, Beaune, and Dijon, and the priory of Choisy in the diocese of Meaux. On assuming the bishopric of Auxerre, he relinquished all these, reserving only the monastery of Dervent for himself.

[Col. 0380D] Once he had obtained possession of the bishopric, this splendid man, whose character was noble, liberal, and magnificent, repaired the episcopal houses at Varzy and Regennes. At Regennes he restored an excellent tower and built from the foundations a most magnificent palace and ambulatory. The buildings now visible in the monasteries of Dervent and Castillon—which he had found so ruined by wars that neither a house for the abbot nor regular quarters for the monks remained, namely cloisters, dormitories, and refectories—sufficiently show how industrious, diligent, and magnificent the man was.

In the monastery of Dervent, the choir of the church, the bell tower, the pinnacle, the nave doors, the cloister, and the abbot’s house had been weakened by wars, fires, and the long-standing poverty and negligence of abbots and monks. He repaired them so thoroughly that within a few years everything could appear new and far more costly than the earlier buildings.

He also splendidly adorned the castle of Sommeura—the stronghold, protection, and defense of the whole region—with four extremely well-fortified towers, a double moat, bridges, conduits, gardens, stables, and everything else useful and ornamental for such a castle, as well as the things necessary for its needs. [Col. 0381A] In that castle, after he had been placed over the monastery, he built within a few years, after removing and clearing away the rubble and ruins produced there, as in other places, by the fires of war and the negligence of former abbots, a magnificent palace with a most beautifully decorated chapel attached to it, enormous double granaries, a pantry, and a very large cellar, all at incredible expense and with even greater diligence.

In the monastery of Castillon, he erected from the foundations a cloister, chapter house, and dormitory. He repaired the church, refectory, and abbot’s house, of which the fury of Mars had left no recognizable appearance of a monastery, so that everything now looks new and the guest houses welcoming. He enlarged and increased the produce, revenues, and income of those monasteries with such careful foresight that he ought rightly to be called and regarded as their founder rather than their administrator.

[Col. 0381B] As for the Church of Auxerre, he magnificently adorned the church itself, the temple consecrated in that city to Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. At his own expense he gave a pulpit for reading the Epistles and Gospels, the most beautiful in all Gaul, with an extraordinary and elegant arrangement of stones and workmanship, as can be seen. He had organs installed, sparing no expense, which at that time were both exceptionally beautiful and exceptionally refined. He gave two extremely precious gold cloths suitable for the high altar, numerous chasubles, copes, and other priestly vestments woven with gold, pearls, and precious stones—so splendid that no other church in Gaul possessed anything more magnificent.

Through his great assistance and frequent advocacy, that part of the province of Auxerre which lies beyond the Yonne—namely Donzy, Clamecy, and the surrounding places—which had formerly been assigned to the jurisdiction of Sens during the war that raged everywhere between the king of France and the Burgundians, was restored to the jurisdiction of the magistrate of Auxerre by a decree of the supreme court of Parliament, or Senate, of Paris.

[Col. 0381C] At that time, alas, the new insolence of the Lutheran heresy crept in. To eradicate it from the roots and expel it completely from the theater of the faithful, provincial councils were repeatedly assembled by the archbishops of Sens, Poncher and de Prato. [Col. 0381D] Many suffragan bishops and orthodox Fathers gathered at these councils. This man above all, burning with great zeal for the faith, was always present. As that pernicious disease gradually and secretly began to sprout and spread through the neighboring places, he protected his diocese with such diligent care and prudent vigilance that no one was found among the flock entrusted to him who had imbibed that deadly poison.

He was especially dear to Kings Louis XII and Francis I, and was their councillor and ordinary almoner. Every year he frequented the court for three or four continuous months, with a great retinue, elegant equipment, and enormous expense. Hence, as human custom dictates, he was exceedingly welcome to all the princes, nobles, and courtiers.

[Col. 0382A] Finally, he possessed such refinement of character, such ease of spirit, and such caution and foresight in conducting affairs that he never had any disagreement or controversy, and scarcely any hatred or envy, with the chapter or any canon. So far was it from being the case that anything was lost from the church’s rights or revenues on this account that he even increased them considerably, as was said above also concerning the monasteries of Dervent and Castillon.

At length, after he had occupied the bishopric of Auxerre for seventeen years, one month, and twenty-six days, in the sixty-sixth year of his age, on the Friday that was the penultimate day of April 1530, he entered the way of all flesh after a prolonged flux of the bowels.

[Col. 0382B] Sensing that the end of his life and the limit of his days appointed for him by the Lord had arrived, on the Sunday preceding his death, after hearing Mass and making beforehand a careful and general confession of his sins, he received the saving Eucharistic viaticum, as is proper for a Christian, worthily and reverently. On the following Tuesday, after again hearing Mass and making a full confession, he communicated once more, devoutly and with great contrition of heart.

Then, having summoned notaries, he made his will and named as executor François of Dinteville, his nephew through his brother, recently bishop of Riez and dean and canon of the Church of Auxerre. In his favor he had earlier resigned his bishopric of Auxerre. In his will he piously founded what are called twelve annual and perpetual obits, to be celebrated on the last Friday of each month in the Church of Auxerre, and ordered twelve Tours pounds to be distributed to the canons for each celebration. His heirs immediately and faithfully fulfilled this.

[Col. 0382C] When the following Thursday began to dawn, he asked to be anointed with holy oil. This final anointing was not performed that day but on Friday morning, when the choir of canons had assembled. It was administered by the venerable cantor. Sound in mind, steadfast in spirit, vigorous in understanding, and even responding properly and distinctly to all the psalms and verses, he received it with all the humility and reverence of which he was capable.

[Col. 0382D] After the anointing, and after the cantor and all the canons, who stood there sorrowful and in tears, had asked his pardon for their offenses, he commended himself to their prayers and, as they departed, said his final farewell. His nephew François was present. Although, by reason of his dignity—for he was dean—he owed his most beloved uncle this service and duty of the final anointing, he was utterly unable to perform it because of the tears and inexhaustible grief that overwhelmed him.

From the hour at which he was anointed until three o’clock that afternoon, he thought of nothing worldly or earthly, but always spoke of the kingdom of God. With the greatest hope, still greater faith, and a constant and unbroken spirit, he awaited God, who was calling him. Remaining in this state, shortly before four o’clock he left his body to the earth and returned his blessed soul to heaven.

[Col. 0383A] He took care to have the funeral conducted with funeral candles, with processions appropriate to rank, status, and dignity, and also with public and private prayers and almsgiving, all with the greatest diligence possible, so as to fulfill the will whose executor his nephew François had been appointed by his uncle. In the course of time he ordered a noble mausoleum for his uncle, decorated with his marble likeness, to be sculpted, fashioned, and painted, to the great admiration of everyone:

> Nobility, virtue, and magnificence lie here with you,  
> François; these gifts are worthy of heaven . . . 1548

## CHAPTER XCIII — On François of Dinteville the Second

François, the nephew, was appointed in place of his deceased uncle. He was the son of Gauthier of Dinteville, governor of Troyes, and Anne called of the Peaceful Seat.

[Col. 0383B] While still a tender child, he learned the first rudiments of grammar at Troyes. He was then sent by his parents to Paris, where, at the famous royal school of Navarre, he was trained in the gentler Muses and the liberal disciplines. He next attended the schools at Poitiers and Padua devoted to jurisprudence, and learned the secrets of both civil and pontifical law. His moral character and life were so upright that, after returning from there, he was summoned to the court of King Francis I and endowed with the treasurership of Poitiers, the priory of Choisy in the region of Meaux, and the priesthood of Ricey in the territory of Langres. This was arranged by the royal mother, Louise, to whom this nephew François was then chaplain and almoner.

While he diligently performed this office without any blemish to his reputation or name, the Church of Riez became vacant, and the king nominated him as its pastor. After governing that church commendably for several years, while his uncle was already advancing toward old age, and while his uncle willingly and spontaneously renounced the bishopric of Auxerre and the monastery of Dervent, which he governed, François resigned the episcopate of Riez and, by the common vote of all, was placed in charge of the Church of Auxerre and the monastery of Dervent.

[Col. 0383C] Before he could be publicly and solemnly received by the people according to custom and joyfully admitted to his own church, the king, knowing the man’s mind to be adorned with varied and manifold forms of learning and virtue, sent him as envoy to Pope Clement VII. How prudently, holily, and successfully he conducted that business is certainly known to anyone who understood public affairs even moderately. Apart from the sacred and fortunate marriage agreement then negotiated between Henry II, son of King Francis, and Catherine, Clement’s niece, countless other difficult affairs entrusted to him also succeeded according to their intention.

[Col. 0383D] Nor should this be passed over in silence. During that embassy, while he was speaking to the pope on behalf of certain men seeking the rank of cardinal, the pontiff, astonished at such eloquence, modesty, and sincerity in the envoy, said:

> “Why do you press and charm our ears on behalf of men who are absent and entirely unknown to us? Why do you not rather look after yourself? You have come anxiously to pray for others, but show no concern for yourself.”

[Col. 0384A] He, being as he was entirely free from ambition, replied boldly:

> “Most blessed Father, I have come here not on my own account but on that of my prince. I have come to conduct his business, not mine; and just as I am bound and ought to do so, so I wish and desire to do so. Whoever performs this office must and ought to act as a public, not a private, person. As for honors themselves—or rather, these burdens—I neither care for them nor seek or pursue them.”

After faithfully completing his embassy, he returned to Gaul and began, as a most watchful shepherd, to govern and direct the flock entrusted to him with diligence. For this purpose he issued constitutions suited to good morals and Christian devotion.

[Col. 0384B] Meanwhile, plots were devised against a man who suspected nothing of the kind. Certain courtiers and magnates, whose malicious minds had been deeply infected by the stain of envy because of the man’s more successful achievements, gradually brought him into the king’s hatred. Consequently, having been promptly persuaded by friends, lest he be attacked more savagely by his maddened rivals, he left his native land and spent nearly three full years exercising a primacy among foreigners.

During this exile he came to Rome, where Pope Paul III received him and consoled him graciously. He also enjoyed the favor of several cardinals and even of the Venetian nobles. While he remained among them during that period, he won considerable goodwill for himself.

At last, when the fraud of the impostors had been discovered, the king ordered the innocent and blameless man to be recalled. He granted him the lawful right to proceed against those who had occupied the absent man’s see and possessions. François afterward pursued them legally and severely vindicated himself against the slander brought against him.

[Col. 0384C] After returning by restoration, he traveled through and visited his diocese with pastoral concern. Among the sheep entrusted to him he found not a few that had been weakened by the secret disseminators of Lutheran heresy and had rushed headlong into the byways of error, with hirelings conniving at them. He diligently strove, as befits a good shepherd, to lead them back to the folds of the faith, to the sheepfold of Christ, and to the bosom of the Church. He spared neither time, health, nor expense.

As he strove by every means to cleanse the Lord’s field of harmful thorns, several of their number were discovered who had been granted permission to preach because of heresies that had long since been buried and condemned but which they had asserted during their preaching. After first rashly and impiously retracting what they had said, they were deprived of ecclesiastical rank and honor and compelled to go into exile.

[Col. 0384D] A priest from the town of Genabum, or Giemo, was also discovered unexpectedly. Making little or nothing of the sacred orders he had received, he was lured by the appearance of a young widow, carried her away to Conada—as though she were of the same sort as he—and by a pretended marriage fathered adulterous offspring with her. Once discovered, convicted, condemned, and degraded, he was removed from the world by victorious flames.

In short, the pious bishop did everything possible to keep the wolves concealed beneath a sheep’s fleece away from the flock and drive them off. Had those to whom the king had then delegated jurisdiction over the criminal heretics not ceased, perhaps everything in this diocese would have remained safe and peaceful from heresies.

[Col. 0385A] When he undertook the governance of the monastery of Dervent, he found many of the monks advancing through the precipices of vice. Having summoned good religious from elsewhere, he compelled them to turn themselves toward a better way of life. Because of the wickedness of certain men who strongly coveted that rich and excellent benefice, he was eventually compelled to exchange it for the monasteries of Aremar and La Celle in the region of Troyes, after having governed it for ten years and more. He later resigned both the monasteries of Aremar and La Celle for the benefit of his dear ones before he departed this life.

[Col. 0385B] The buildings that he restored and constructed at Auxerre, Regennes, Varzy, and the monastery of Aremar bear witness to the man’s care and diligence and to his marvelous, almost astonishing genius. The enormous gifts he bestowed upon churches proclaim the generosity of a pious and good shepherd. The alms distributed day after day to hospices, religious houses, colleges, and hospitals show that he possessed a truly Christian heart. His sparse food, rare drinking, moderate sleep, continual labor, and persistent, tireless study declared a life worthy of a philosopher.

For, besides the disciplines of the liberal arts, he also knew remarkably well the mechanical arts, as they are called. He took the greatest delight in painting and always kept experts in that art in his household. Being extremely sparing of time, he repeatedly quoted the old saying of Apelles, so that no day should pass without a line being drawn.

Just as he welcomed, revered, and supported the learned, educated, studious, knowledgeable, skillful, ingenious, and vigilant, so he was intensely hostile to the idle, dull, cowardly, drowsy, and inactive.

[Col. 0385C] Yet since nothing is blessed in every respect, so great and distinguished a man suffered for the most part from fever, stone, dysentery, gout, and various kinds of illness. Even when afflicted in this way, he never forgot himself. Carrying his cross after Christ, glorifying God with the Apostle in his infirmities, he hoped joyfully and gladly that by this road he would enter the kingdom of heaven.

After spending twenty-four years in the episcopate, once he had prudently arranged his affairs, he paid the debt of nature at the command of death—which must be obeyed—being not yet sixty years old, in the year 1554 of the incarnate Word, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October.

[Col. 0385D]

## CHAPTER XCIV — On Robert of Lenoncourt. — XCV — On Philippe of Lenoncourt. — XCVI — On Philibert de la Bourdaisière. — XCVII — On Jacques Amyot

Jacques Amyot was born at Melun, a town situated twenty miles above Paris on the Seine, on 3 November 1513, to respectable rather than wealthy parents, Nicolas Amyot and Marguerite des Amours.

Supported from childhood by their limited means, he first made progress at Melun and then at Paris in the study of good letters and the rudiments of philosophy, so that around his nineteenth year he was honored with the master’s degree of the Faculty of Arts, as it is called, and easily shone more brightly than his peers.

[Col. 0386A] In Latin he had ordinary teachers, such as those who generally wear out their lives in the public schools of Paris. In Greek, however, when he was beginning with the first elements of that language—which at that time were familiar to very few—his first teacher was Jean Evagrius of Reims. Evagrius directed a class in the new College of Cardinals, separated from the others according to an unusual practice; it was called the Greek class because nothing but Greek was read and taught in it.

When the royal lecturers were established by King Francis I, of august memory, Amyot became for several years a constant auditor of Jacques Toussain in poetry and of Pierre Danès in oratory and philosophy. Under Danès’s instruction he learned several of Cicero’s Latin speeches, to the great admiration of all learned men. He also applied himself diligently to mathematics under Oronce Fine, the royal professor.

[Col. 0386B] Thus equipped with knowledge of languages and the liberal arts, he afterward went to Bourges with the distinguished lawyer Canaye, who was a celebrated advocate in the Parliament of Paris, in order to study civil law.

There the Reverend D. Colin, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Ambrose at Bourges, who at that time was ordinary lecturer, reader, and chamberlain to the great King Francis, entrusted his nephews to Amyot’s instruction. Through the same man’s good offices and at the urging of the august Marguerite, the king’s only sister, queen of Navarre and duchess and governor of Bourges, the maternal grandmother of Henry IV, of blessed memory, Amyot was appointed professor of Greek and Latin letters at the royal school of Bourges, with respectable annual remuneration assigned for the purpose.

He carried out this office and professorship for nearly twelve years with such care, diligence, and learning that he acquired great fame for scholarship and integrity. [Col. 0386C] As this reputation spread, the distinguished Lord Morvilliers, then deputy governor of the city of Bourges, moved by Amyot’s learning and integrity, entrusted to his instruction and direction his nephews on his sister’s side, as well as the sons of the most distinguished Bucetelli, lord of Sacy, councillor, secretary, and correspondent of the king.

During this period of instruction, in the hours left free, Amyot worked on rendering certain Greek tragedies into French verse and translating other Greek works into French: Heliodorus’s story of Theagenes and Chariclea, and likewise the Greek bucolic prose drama by Longus concerning Daphnis and Chloe. He committed his translations to print.

[Col. 0386D] At that time, however, the Greek manuscript of Theagenes that he had used bore nowhere the author’s name, so that the translator did not know the parentage of the work until, after traveling to Rome, he found in the Vatican Library a handwritten copy of the story in which the name of Heliodorus was written. He declared this in the third French edition.

[Col. 0387A] A little later he undertook a French translation of some of the Lives of Illustrious Men by Plutarch of Chaeronea. He offered and dedicated it to Francis I, the great king. The king approved this splendid translation so highly that he ordered Amyot to continue the translation he had begun and bring it to completion. In return for so great a labor and undertaking, the king’s generosity granted him the abbey of Bellozane, which had perhaps become vacant at that time. This was the last benefice that king conferred, because not long afterward he exchanged life for death.

Amyot therefore judged that greater fortune would scarcely correspond to his labor among the French, and that he was unlikely to advance to other degrees of honor. He planned to go to Italy, where he could spend his life on his modest income, intending to consult the Italian libraries, compare the badly printed text of Plutarch with manuscripts, and converse freely on the subject with the learned men whom he might meet there.

While he was considering these things, a very suitable opportunity of that kind presented itself to him in 1546. Morvilliers, sent by King Henry II as ambassador to Venice, took Amyot with him as a traveling companion. Amyot had then reached his thirty-second year, while Morvilliers was somewhat older.

[Col. 0387B] During the embassy, the royal ambassador became bound to him by so strong a bond of friendship and familiarity that he could not bear to let him leave him, even though he knew that Amyot was burning with an extraordinary desire to see the libraries of the other cities of Italy.

After diligently searching every corner of the extremely rich Venetian library in order to compare, correct, and translate Plutarch’s writings into more elegant French, Amyot went from Venice to Rome. There he was received with great kindness by the bishop of Mirepoix, who kept him in his own house and had him as a companion at table for nearly two years. The two exchanged conversation freely and discussed letters and disciplines.

[Col. 0387C] At approximately the same time Amyot entered into the friendship of the illustrious Cardinal Tournon. When the cardinal was recalled by the king to court, he took Amyot as a traveling companion, together with Dionysius Lambinus, a most distinguished man and extremely skilled in both languages, who afterward became royal professor of Greek letters at Paris.

[Col. 0387D] When that cardinal had gone to court and heard that the king had entrusted certain bishops and nobles especially dear to him with the task of diligently investigating and asking, as though the matter were of the greatest importance, for a worthy, learned, and sensible man who could carefully educate and teach the royal children, the dukes of Orléans and Anjou, already destined to rule, he presented Amyot to the king. He knew and had tested Amyot’s character, intelligence, learning, and other qualities of mind.

[Col. 0388A] Accordingly, Amyot, one among the many great men with whom that learned age flourished, was immediately appointed to this distinguished and weighty office. He discharged it so energetically and faithfully, to the benefit and honor of the kingdom of France, that he was pleasing and acceptable to the king and queen. He remained so over a long succession of years, until the death of Francis II.

When Charles IX gained possession of the kingdom of France, he did not forget the services and merits of his teacher, whom he therefore always called his master. He appointed Amyot grand almoner of France and wished him to belong to his more sacred and august council. Shortly afterward he honored him with the abbey of Rupes, and soon afterward, of his own accord and without Amyot seeking it, with another vacant abbey, namely that of Saint-Corneille at Compiègne.

When the Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, de la Bourdaisière, died at Rome, Pope Pius V, moved by the reputation of Amyot’s virtue, learning, piety, and fervent devotion toward the Catholic, Apostolic, and Roman Church, placed him over the bishopric of Auxerre. This was willingly granted by the king, who desired nothing more than to advance him to the highest honors and dignities, as he had shown in fact and made clear to the leading courtiers and princes.

[Col. 0388B] Amyot always proved himself grateful and mindful of this royal goodwill, kindness, and beneficence, not only while the prince was alive but also after his death. He continually exalted him to heaven with praises of which he was truly worthy, cherished his blessed memory, and always invoked blessings upon his pious remains.

Moreover, when King Henry III, returning from Poland, passed through Savoy, in the land of the Allobroges, the king’s aunt, the duchess, commended Amyot to him so warmly that the king promised her that Amyot would remain with him in his rank and office as grand almoner of France, since he had been his first tutor; for that reason, the king said that throughout his life he would always call him his master. The king himself, on his return, brought news of this promise to Amyot [Col. 0388C] and in turn asked him to continue displaying in his royal office the goodwill toward him and the faithful service of which he had hitherto made use.

This benefaction bestowed upon Amyot by so excellent a king may certainly be regarded as a singular and unprecedented example: one and the same man became the grand almoner of two successive kings, although it was customary for princes succeeding to the kingdom by hereditary right to confer the highest offices and foremost dignities upon those companions and servants whom they had held especially dear before coming to power.

Now, shortly after his return from Poland, the same Most Christian King established the order of the Knights of the Collar and Governors, or Commanders, of the Holy Spirit. He did not forget his Amyot; indeed, he appointed him [Col. 0388D] the first Governor of that knightly order. What is more, in Amyot’s favor and for his benefit, he wished the following article to be inserted into the constitutions and statutes of the order:

> Whoever shall be grand almoner shall also be governor or commander of the said order, and on that condition shall not be required to produce the proofs and testimonies of the nobility of his lineage, as all the others are required to do.

But the piety with which he began his episcopate is evident from this: as soon as he had received the papal bulls, he took possession through a procurator, while at Paris he was receiving the sacrament of consecration, so that later, after obtaining the king’s permission, he himself might actually go to take possession and exercise the episcopal office; for he regarded it as a matter of conscience to enjoy the ample revenues of a benefice in which he had as yet performed no duty.

[Col. 0389A] Moreover, because he clearly understood that the first and principal duty of a bishop consists in the preaching of the word of God, which could not be rightly and worthily carried out without knowledge of theology—and in this he had been only moderately versed, since he had devoted less study and labor to sacred letters than to other disciplines and sciences—he then began to apply himself seriously and with the utmost intensity to theology. At once, besides his daily reading of the Holy Scriptures, he undertook, day and night, to turn over the volumes of the Greek and Latin Fathers and Doctors of the Church.

Meanwhile, he summoned Master Peter Viel, a doctor of theology, and asked him to assist him when he went to take actual possession and [Col. 0389B] undertook the beginning of his episcopal entrance. The pious and learned doctor readily granted this request to the bishop. In his presence he delivered many sacred sermons in the cathedral church, and frequent conversations were held between them about divine matters and the exposition of notable passages of Sacred Scripture, about theological controversies, and about scholastic questions.

The bishop held the writings of St Thomas Aquinas in such high esteem that he followed them almost word for word, admiring the profundity and subtlety of so great a mind. Therefore, at length, urged on by that man’s encouragement and arguments, he resolved to preach. On the solemn day when he had determined to celebrate the sacred rites, he approached—not unprepared, certainly, but distrustful of his own strength—with timidity.
