Although he spoke in a very thin and subdued voice, he nevertheless expressed the thoughts of his mind so openly, purely, and clearly, [Col. 0389C] and spoke with such choice and abundance of words, such weight of thought, and finally such admirable order, that the learned departed more learned, while the uneducated and common people departed better and more eager for the duties of piety.

When these preliminary exercises in preaching had met with such happy success, he continued to perform this ecclesiastical duty much more eagerly and with the greatest assiduity. Thereafter he never failed to conduct the sacred rites and preach on any solemn day or annual feast, whenever he was permitted to remain among his flock. Of his sermons, however, he left the principal points and authorities of the preliminary studies (*protheoriae*), woven into the form of homilies, written in Latin and transcribed by his own hand.

From that time he began to devote himself entirely to sacred discourses and to the writings of the Greek and Latin Fathers. [Col. 0389D] To satisfy this vehement thirst for reading their books, after pouring out prayers to God he would withdraw to his study before five o’clock in the morning, remaining there until certain canons came with members of his household to accompany him to the sacred building and the solemn liturgy of the Mass. He always attended its celebration in the choir, wearing the proper and decorous dress of the canons. There, after the formula of confession had been recited according to the custom of the Church at the beginning of Mass, he gave his blessing at the end.

From there he went to dinner with his guests. Among them there was always someone adorned with a dignity, or one of the canons, in addition to the hebdomadary by whom the sacred rite had been celebrated. Even over the cups there were conversations about literature and honorable matters, so that his table could rightly be called [Col. 0390A] a school of every virtue, learning, and piety. Hence any very learned person would honestly admit that he had departed from it more learned and better.

After dinner he conversed for an hour with the same company. Then, when his friends had departed and said farewell, he returned to the library and to the studies he had begun. He often indicated to his secretary Martin—whom he treated familiarly and whom, on account of his piety and merits, he soon arranged to honor in his church with a canonry and prebend, and not long afterward with an archdeaconry—that it was his wish to withdraw from court for a large part of the year, so that he might devote himself more frequently and freely to his episcopal office.

For this reason, immediately after the judicial sessions held at Blois, he returned to Auxerre. But he was received there, during those most difficult times, so badly by certain men whom factions, suspicions, and calumnies were [Col. 0390B] driving astray that, frustrated in his pious purpose and plan, he was compelled to yield to circumstances and superior force. This occurred to the evil example of others: without cause he was kept not merely from the sanctuary but even from the entrance to the church, and he was confined within the precincts of the episcopal residence, so that he could perform none of the duties of a bishop.

At last, so as to omit nothing that he thought might satisfy simpler and more scrupulous minds, although, so far as he himself was concerned, he had no need of it at all, he humbled and abased himself to the point of first requesting what they call absolution “by way of precaution.” Finally, through the most illustrious legate, he obtained full and absolute absolution from the Supreme Pontiff. That legate had received particular instructions to comply in every respect with the said bishop’s wishes, since the integrity of the bishop’s life, his most honorable and devout conduct, and [Col. 0390C] his other merits were sufficiently evident both to the legate himself and to the Supreme Pontiff.

This was therefore an incredible consolation to the bishop, since he had obtained what he desired most: he was now free to perform the ecclesiastical duties and offices. He resumed them completely at the earliest opportunity, beginning with sacred preaching, his first and principal duty, on Ash Wednesday, the first day of Lent. He did so with the same feeling, equal modesty, and almost the same gestures as he had been accustomed to use, entirely unmoved by any disturbance. He was free from every desire for revenge and used no complaints or invectives against the injuries and affronts inflicted upon him, or against the insolence of his own people.

This seemed extraordinary to many who did not know the prelate inwardly and well. [Col. 0390D] Yet he was by no means eager for revenge and was most ready to erase the memory of injuries through forgetfulness. He was somewhat prone to anger, but he easily and quickly restrained it, and he never reproached anyone shamefully with past offenses.

He was commonly regarded as grim, severe, harsh, difficult and morose in approach. Yet those who had for some time enjoyed his companionship did not consider him such. Rather, he was recognized as sensible, steadfast, and candid. For, speaking freely in the Roman manner, he did not pretend; he did not know how to dissemble, not even before nobles and princes. He paid no heed to pleasing their ears and did not know how to flatter them. So far was he from doing anything for their favor that he judged inconsistent with honesty and equity that he openly declared he would never commit such an act.

[Col. 0391A]

For this reason his wiser familiars and household members took particular care never to propose to him or request from him anything doubtful, ambiguous, controversial, or even slightly suspect. Otherwise they sometimes endured a refusal accompanied by the gravest reprimand.

For the rest, being a great lover of peace, he shunned quarrels and disagreements more than a dog or a snake, especially with his canons and chapter. He took pleasure in musical harmony and, within private walls, performed his own part among the singers. For this reason the canons were especially dear and welcome to him when he observed them willingly ascending the pulpit with the intention of singing. The same was true of the other choristers, precentors, succentors, assistants, and instrumental musicians, especially when, together with skill in singing and the sweetness of their voices, they displayed upright and ecclesiastical morals.

[Col. 0391B] He also enjoyed musical instruments and often liked to strike the keys with his fingers before dinner, so that after his most serious studies his mind might sit down to the meal in a more cheerful mood.

But let us proceed to matters more serious and more fitting for a bishop. When Amyot resided in the episcopate, he himself performed the sacred rites on solemn and annual feast days. He also preached at midday. For that reason, only on Mondays did he receive those who had ministered to him at the altar and in the choir during the sacred sacrifice of the Mass.

On Sundays and feast days he attended the privileged First Vespers; on the feast itself he attended the morning psalmody and prayers. After leaving them, he went to the chapel and devoutly celebrated Mass, as he was accustomed to do on each day of Advent and Lent. He then attended the celebration of High Mass, as it is called, and the evening prayers.

[Col. 0391C] On other days and ordinary weekdays he attended the principal liturgy. After it had been celebrated, the hebdomadary came to the prelate’s dinner. Moreover, even when he himself was performing the duty of preaching, he nevertheless took care to seek out and summon learned and approved men to preach in his church and throughout the diocese, especially in towns where he had heard that certain adherents of the new religion and heretics were living—for example, Gien.

For this purpose he appointed a pious, learned, and prudent man to the dignity of cantor in the chapter of the church of Saint Stephen. He did the same in other cities, whose parochial benefices he had duly provided for.

Moreover, when he first came to the church of Auxerre, he found it internally and in its innermost parts like a building about to collapse. He therefore began to repair and restore it, [Col. 0391D] starting with the choir and the more august altar, which he entirely rebuilt and strengthened with six cast copper columns. He adorned it with a crozier or staff projecting above the altar at the rear.

Then he had high and low stalls constructed on both sides of the choir, for the seats of the dignitaries and canons. At the farthest and highest part of the right-hand side he had an episcopal throne made, on which it is customary for the bishop to sit while performing his office. At the extreme end of the choir, on the upper panel, he wished the following words to be inscribed:

> James Amyot, bishop of Auxerre, having found this temple foully torn apart, plundered, and stripped of all its ornaments by rebellious heretics, took care to restore from the ground up this platform, fitted for the singing of divine praises, [Col. 0392A] to the glory of God Almighty and the adornment of his house, 1573.

He had a new organ built and installed from the ground up in the corner of the choir. He also supplied the ornaments of two chapels, one made of cloth woven with gold and the other of patterned velvet. Likewise, he donated two silver candlesticks, a large vessel with a sprinkler for carrying holy water, and two silver censers or thuribles.

Finally, he adorned his church with every ornament that his means allowed. He would have added others as well, had the disturbances of war not stood in the way. Indeed, during the civil war he was reduced almost to the point at which his resources scarcely sufficed to support himself and his household, since his fields and revenues had been seized and plundered by the opposing party because of the factions and evil rumors fabricated by malicious, greedy, and ambitious slanderers.

[Col. 0392B] The castle of Régennes—formerly exceedingly beautiful, magnificently built and adorned, but burned by the heretics—he repaired in such a way that he could live there comfortably with his entire household and with friends who came to visit.

He had also built a spacious and splendid school at Auxerre, in a very suitable part of the city and in a healthy climate, between the cathedral church of Saint Stephen and the abbey of Saint Germanus. He had intended to establish there the Fathers of the Society of Jesus, to educate the city’s youth and inhabitants, to imbue them with upright morals, Catholic piety, and good letters, even through theological studies.

[Col. 0392C] This is clear from the agreement and compact made with Father Pigenat, who carried out the matter too slowly and coldly, until the bishop was compelled to leave to meet the king at Blois, where the judicial sessions were being held. The undertaking was therefore postponed until the prelate’s return, and that pious work was interrupted—not because he had changed his purpose, for he was steadfast in such matters.

He had decided to endow the same Fathers with an income of one thousand gold coins, together with twelve hundred Tours pounds, so that before they departed from Paris they might purchase suitable furnishings according to their desire. But the disputes of the civil wars that arose toward the end of the sessions, and the expulsion of the Jesuits from France, prevented this institution, which can never be praised enough, though they did not render it entirely fruitless.

[Col. 0392D] For the prelate persisted in his intention that the school he had built should be devoted to the education of youth. It now serves that purpose, as the following inscription, carved on a tablet above the lintel of the door, testifies:

> SACRED TO CHRIST THE SAVIOR, BEST AND GREATEST.

> The truth of religion, probity of morals, and cultivation of the liberal arts are acquired here—not with money, but through study, piety, and labor. Therefore, you who are base, impious, and degenerate through sluggish idleness, keep far away from these doors.

To this inscription, so that the mind and purpose of its author might be understood, the same secretary added the following appended statement:

[Col. 0393A]

> James Amyot, bishop of Auxerre, wished this inscription to be placed upon the school whose construction he had undertaken.

At last, after this bishop had endured in body and suffered in spirit, during the disastrous period of factions and civil wars, many things difficult to relate and harsh to behold, as the tragic poet says—enduring as much as human nature can steadily bear—he finally succumbed, overcome by so many hardships. The vigor of that excellently constituted body, so enduring of cold and heat, was extinguished. Then, seized by a slow fever, which pressed heavily upon him, it consumed the breath of his lungs and gradually drove him toward death.

At the age of eighty-nine, he fell asleep in the Lord, as befitted a bishop worthy of so great a name, on the Nones of February in the year of salvation 1593, fortified, as was fitting, with the sacraments of penance, [Col. 0394A] the Eucharist, and extreme unction. His household, dependents, and men of the highest standing were present and assisted him: Dionysius Peronnet, a most eloquent doctor of theology and penitentiary ecclesiastic of the cathedral church; Gilbert Le Comte; Reginald Martin; and Victor Camus, his servants and canons. They admonished, consoled, and steadfastly rendered every pious, salutary, and final service.

*(This was written in Latin in a sudden composition in the year 1612 by Federicus Morellus, dean of the royal professors. It was excerpted from the material that Master Reginald Martin, secretary to that same Amyot, bishop of Auxerre, had written in French concerning the life of his excellent patron.)*

[Col. 0393]

# POEM ON THE MONASTERY OF JUMIÈGES

*(*Neustria pia* [Pious Neustria], pp. 263, 264, etc.)*

## Argument

[Col. 0393B]

Pause, prudent traveler, and plant your firm step;

Look upon what is depicted in these painted tablets.

Here before you clearly appear, just as the image of one who looks into water,

or as a figure is accustomed to appear in a smooth mirror,

the beginnings of this radiant jewel.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] *Gemmeticum*: Jumièges.]

*(For the earlier writers called it Jumièges [*Gemmeticum*] from a jewel [*gemma*], because it surpassed the other places like an Eastern jewel.)*

From this you will learn which kings and dukes gave

so many goods, so many lands, so much wealth, so many estates and revenues,

from which nine hundred solitary men, moved by heaven,

could lead a life shut away more strictly here.

You will also learn what disasters the bands of the Leleges and the Dacian phalanxes brought,

and who at last restored these places,

torn down by ancient ruin, from their deepest foundations.

I shall set forth the deeds in brief,

embracing them in a short song.

## The First Foundation of the Said Monastery

[Col. 0393C]

When Phoebus had revolved six centuries and eight five-year periods

since the Virgin gave birth,

the holy man Philibert—whom Celtic Burgundy brought forth

in a glorious birth—

came to these regions, accompanied by as great a multitude

as Jacob’s when he was to cultivate the wilderness of Goshen itself.

Although this land had once been dreadful with thorny forests,

surrounded on every side by marshes stagnant in different places,

and although no people had previously cultivated it,

nor any settlers,

and it was wholly unknown either to Ceres or to sweet Lyaeus,

nevertheless no land in the whole world proved more fertile.

After that father, by the gift of King Dagobert,

laid the first foundations of this sacred temple,

[Col. 0393D]

everything soon changed its ancient appearance.

Where the caves of goat-footed gods had once lain hidden,

inhabited by beasts wandering alone,

now, accessible to holy men,

golden temples shine, like dripping Olympus.

By night and by day prayers pour forth;

[Col. 0394B] now the famous songs of the saints resound,

now the companies of monks perform sacred duties of praise to the Thunderer,

imitating angelic choirs,

where once monstrous beasts filled the empty air

with terrifying cries.

The melancholy earth, previously nourishing

fruitless growths of the forest,

covered with dense thickets,

began to produce fertile and ambrosial fruits.

The fragrant yew, the supple linden trees, aconites, and hemlocks

give way to the groves of Alcinous.

the black berry gives way to clusters of grapes;

purple grapes swell on their heavy vines,

and the renewed field produces sweet ears of grain.

Where reeds and marsh rushes once grew,

meadows glitter with gems of varied color.

From the marsh-growing canes there now rise rich pastures,

and enormous fish glide from the open water,

[Col. 0394C] driven by the waves,

whenever the Titanian daughter of Latona joins her rosy chariot to either horizon

and the swift river turns back, its waters swelling.

Thus streams flow back through the fields and green meadows,

to water the fertile fields and their crops,

as the Nile waters Egypt with its sevenfold stream.

All this was given by that Sower of creation

who sets boundaries to the world,

who established the solid earth above the waters,

and restrains the immense rivers within prescribed limits,

lest Cybele be overwhelmed by the swollen waves of Tethys.

With rain he moistens the mountains and barren sands,

so that the all-bearing earth may bestow her gifts upon all,

from which all creatures that require food may draw life,

whether animals wander through untilled fields,

whether they cut the clear air with shrill wings,

[Col. 0394D]

or whether sea-monsters swim, distinguished by varied forms.

Whatever feeds by breathing the air of heaven,

he cherishes and supplies each creature with its proper nourishment.

Finally, he who once drew waters from dry rocks

and sent down flesh from the heights,

[Col. 0395A]

and manna, as rain pours from the cloudy heavens,

to nourish the Hebrew people, while heaven marveled,

as they wandered through barren fields and deserted lands—

in the same way bestowed his gifts upon the settlers of Jumièges.

He made the wilderness that had once been harsh

become most cultivated, contrary to the laws of nature.

The Seine encircles it in a winding course,

just as the tail of a twisting dragon encircles the Bear.

## The Destruction of the Same Monastery

Eight five-year periods and as many passing centuries

had entered the stars after the beginnings of Christ.

Then the barbarian Hasting, coming forth from the Dacian shores

like a lion thirsting for prey emerging from its den,

assailed the Belgian coasts of the Franks in Gothic warfare,

[Col. 0395B]

where France faces the cold Bear,

and subdued neighboring cities and many fortresses.

Alas for the crime! He destroyed the most renowned temples

of the Thunderer enthroned on high,

overturning everything with hostile Mars.

At last, with his fleets equipped and the North Wind favorable,

he entered the ports of the Seine.

Swiftly the report of so great a disaster flew through the terrified cities.

Then Neustria was mingled everywhere with wretched mourning:

everywhere wars pressed upon it, enemies ravaged,

and the horror of arms descended;

the standards of Cradivus flashed.

From here the monks fled far away.

The monks sought the remote wilderness of Hanspreadum,

where the cloisters and houses belonging to us stood,

lest they should be forced to break their sacred vow,

breathe out their lives,

and send their bodies, overwhelmed by terrible torments,

to Stygian death.

[Col. 0395C] Some, however, remained here with weapons

and filled these places with soldiers,

so that they might repel the threatening enemies.

They judged it better to succumb to a brave death

than to leave the sacred things to be defiled by a barbarous people.

Meanwhile the naval army, with its wings spread,

ploughing through the wave-tossed waters of the refluent river,

O fateful day!—

came gliding to these very shores.

As soon as the armed enemies poured forth from their ships,

they pressed a siege around the lofty walls

of this monastery, in companies massed in ordered ranks.

At the first assault they attempted, through missiles and fire,

to force open the gates

and climb the walls by ladders.

The guards, on the other hand, thrust them back with stiff pikes

and hurled frequent missiles through the open windows.

But when the Dacians undermined the walls under the cover of a tortoise formation,

and the twisted ballista hurled its missile with powerful arms,

[Col. 0395D]

then neither the rampart, nor the swelling earth,

nor the cloisters, nor the guards themselves were sufficient.

The walls were of no avail.

The stones gave way, and, as the gates collapsed,

they invaded the innermost strongholds.

Some slew every body that they encountered

in indiscriminate, ill-fated slaughter;

others mingled fires with the half-ruined buildings.

The renowned church of the Virgin Mother of Christ,

rising toward the heavenly air beneath its vaulted roof,

stood conspicuous.

They battered it, hacked into it with iron,

and undermined its foundations with repeated blows.

But, overcome by its final wound,

it groaned and, shaken from its ridge,

dragged its ruin down with it.

A cloud of thick dust was lifted toward heaven,

[Col. 0396A]

and the earth trembled, shaken by so vast a weight.

Then they entered, their limbs drenched in blood,

and girded for plunder, carrying off the sacred vessels

and all the treasures, whatever there were.

Nor did they cease from any form of devastation

until they saw the cloisters, houses, and sacred buildings

overturned from their foundations

and collapsing amid the flames.

## Its Restoration

Meanwhile the sun had touched the circle of the Ram and Libra

a hundred times.

At last, as the weapons gave way,

Ceres, nurtured by peace, restrained the anger of Mars.

Immediately two Fathers left the cloisters of their refuge

among the Haspreadi and returned to their own holy sanctuary.

[Note: The construction of *refugis ... claustra ... Haspreadum* is awkward; the sense is their departure from the place of refuge and return to the ruined monastery.]

When they saw it covered with dreadful thickets,

reduced to brambles and the hidden lairs of wild beasts—

the place that had once been consecrated

[Col. 0396B] to the All-Seeing Thunderer—

they dissolved entirely into groans and bitter tears,

and with heavy sobs turned their faces toward the stars.

> “O Father, O Goodness,” they said, “sole hope of all things,

> you who never leave those who trust in you empty-handed,

> behold how many destructions and disasters,

> how many deaths and misfortunes,

> how many evils we endure;

> heal our ruins.

> Remember now the covenant you made with our forefathers,

> that, just as you once restored the venerable temple of Jerusalem,

> so you might restore these buildings,

> destroyed by a sacrilegious people,

> which were constructed for you with such renowned devotion.

> May the throng of monks offer you vows

> and perform the duties of praise in sacred perpetuity,

> enlarged by solemn triumphs,

> and may the ancient piety and reverence of worship

> flourish once more.”

Such were the vows and prayers they persisted in pouring forth,

[Col. 0396C]

sustained by the waters of Tethys and by vegetables alone.

There was no delay. He who watches from highest Olympus sent help:

the leader William, descended from the blood of Rollo,

whom heaven inspired to turn his course here while hunting.

When he encountered the monks, he began to question them:

“What has brought you, so decrepit, to these shores?

What religion do you follow, or what confidence have you in your vow?

What structures were built here in this immense wilderness,

from which such extensive traces of ancient ruin are visible?”

When they had narrated the sequence of events,

beginning with the earliest annals and proceeding in order,

they offered him food according to their custom.

One of them held out bread;

the other offered water to the thirsty,

for they led their lives on such provisions.

But the leader, recoiling from such poor fare,

immediately left the place,

wholly given over to anger.

[Col. 0396D]

Hardly had he entered the depths of the dense forest

when, driven by divine power, he encountered a Stygian boar.

Raging with rapid movement and hoarse gaping jaws,

heedless of the spear that wounded it,

it passed through the hunting spears and nets

and struck the leader down half-dead with its sharp tusks.

[Note: The printed *culmis*, “stalks,” is difficult in context; “tusks” follows the apparent sense of the boar’s attack.]

But, remembering the offense, soon recovering his strength,

he returned to the Fathers to atone for his crime.

He took the food he had despised and reclined with them,

promising to repair the ruins of this monastery.

Then he ordered sanctuaries, cells, and houses to be built,

and restored many estates and riches,

overturned by ancient ruins,

from which those solitary men could live

without resorting to commercial gains

and lead their secluded life.

At once the craftsmen, attracted by the promised wage,

[Col. 0397A] prepared to renew the structures,

reducing them to a smaller design

reducing the original in its scale and boundaries

and in the extent of the houses and the site.

At last, when the temple had been skillfully rebuilt,

the dedication of the church of the Virgin Mother of Christ,

which had once been consecrated to her,

[Col. 0398A] was celebrated anew.

You shall be the perpetual guardian and salvation of this flock.

# ANCIENT COLLECTION OF CANONS

[Col. 0397]

## Mai’s Notice on the Following Canonical Collection

*(*Spicilegium Romanum* [Roman Gleanings], vol. VI, p. 397.)*

. . . Now, if I wished to disclose elsewhere the riches of the pontifical library in canonical matters, I would be making the beginning of a far too lengthy discourse. Certainly, I shall speak elsewhere and at another time about several of the noblest Greek manuscripts; for I have long been fired by no vain desire to enrich the canonical law of the Greeks with some notable work.

For the present, one Latin codex above all others has moved me: Vatican Codex 1349. I believe no one except the Ballerini brothers, *Dissertation on the Collection of Canons*, part IV, chapter 18, § 6, has mentioned it. They, pressed—as they say—by lack of time and intimidated by the difficulty of the writing, left this collection, older than the others, to be examined by others.

After carefully examining this codex, I therefore thought I would accomplish something more useful by reciting its chapters or titles individually, as I did with Anselm, than by listing numerous codices of the aforesaid library merely by name. Such a bare notice would increase the bibliographical catalogue but would not assist knowledge of canon law.

This is a parchment codex of 225 large leaves, written in very intricate Lombard script, with rubricated titles. It belongs to the early tenth century and is therefore older than Anselm of Lucca.

[Col. 0397]

# ANCIENT COLLECTION OF CANONS

[Note: [Col. 0397D] This title of the work and its prologue are written at the beginning of Book Six in the codex; nevertheless, they seemed to me to belong to the work as a whole.]

[Col. 0397B]

Here begins the most welcome collection of canons, strengthened by testimonies of Scripture and sayings of the saints, which edifies those who read it. Wherever anything seems to disagree, the reading is to be chosen that is judged to possess the greater authority.

## Preface

Considering the multitude of synodical exemplars [codex: *innumerositatem*, “countlessness”], and foreseeing that the obscurity of many of them would be useless to the unlearned, while also recognizing that the diversity of the others was discordant and destructive, tending more to tear down than to build up, I arranged an exposition from the immense forest of writings into the text of a single volume, brief and harmonious.

I added several things so that more might be copied out, and I set the names of the individual authorities before their individual testimonies, so that no one might offer one thing in place of another [Col. 0397C] as though it were uncertain. Thus, when he returns to the general titles that we necessarily set forth, let him observe the numbers carefully; once these have been observed, he will find without any hesitation whatever question he wishes.

## The Preface Ends

The authors and books generally cited in this canonical collection are as follows.

[Col. 0441C] Acumianus Longius. (Thus in manuscript folio 193, but he seems to be the same person who is called Commeianus below.) Alcuin. Ambrose. Athanasius. The Hebrew Annals. Antherus, pope. Augustine. Basil. Bede. [Col. 0441D] The Holy Bible. The edition of Bishop Boniface, *On Distinguishing Penance*. Celestine, pope. Callistus, pope. The Canons of the Apostles. The Canons of the Romans. King Charles. Cassian. Greek Chronicles. Clement of Rome, pope. *Conferences of the Fathers*. Commeianus. Responses of synods. Cyprian. Damasus, pope. Decrees of the pontiffs. The decretals before Siricius are used very sparingly. [Col. 0442C] Deusdedit, pope.—This is the single letter of Pope Deusdedit to Bishop Gordianus that exists in the collections of the Councils. In the manuscript, however, Gordianus is said to be not the bishop of Hispalis—which is impossible—but the bishop of Hispania, consistently with the Pistoia manuscript, where he is called “the bishop of the Spains.” Evaristus, pope. Eucherius. Eugenius, pope. Faustinus.—We published two sermons of Bishop Faustinus in the fifth volume of the *Spicilegium*. The fragment in the canonical collection, folio 91, is as follows. FAUSTINUS: “I do not deceive you, because what does not benefit you after death is not from God. For I say that you should amend your life and redeem your merit either by prayers or by alms. For what benefit does a living voice provide to the dead, which they do not hear, and which does not give alms?” Felix, pope. Gelasius, pope. Bishop Gordianus.—In the text there is produced a fragment of a letter to Pope Deusdedit, which editors Labbe and Mansi do not mention in their editions of the acts of Deusdedit in the collections of the Councils. Letter of Gordianus, bishop, to the holy Deusdedit, bishop of the city of Rome: “You know that, just as there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so there are seven gifts of baptism: from the first nourishment of consecrated salt and entrance into [Col. 0443A] the holy church, up to the confirmation of the Holy Spirit through chrism. From this first gift of the Holy Spirit until the seventh, no Christian ought to take his godmother in marriage; and whoever presumes to do so shall be bound forever by the bonds of anathema, unless he performs worthy penance. Likewise, whoever gives his daughter, who is within these seven gifts mentioned above, either to himself or to his son in marriage.” Since, then, we see Gordianus writing to Deusdedit, it follows that the doubts of Labbe and Mansi concerning the authenticity of the pontifical letter to Gordianus are now almost dispelled. Gratian’s collection of canons. Gregory Nazianzen. Gregory of Rome, pope. Jerome. Hilary, pope. Hormisdas, pope. Innocent, pope. [Col. 0443B] Isidore of Hispalis. John Chrysostom. Pope John (VIII). Josephus of Caesarea in his *Ecclesiastical History*. Canonical judgment. Synodal judgment. The laws of Justinian. Leo, pope. *Book of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. [Col. 0444A] *Book of Soliloquies*. Bishop Martin. Origen. A certain penitential. The canons of Paterius. Prosper. *Rule of Clerics*. Serapion the abbot. Sylvester, pope. Siricius, pope. Smaragdus. Symmachus, pope. Various African synods: Agathensis, Alexandrian, Ancyrean, Antiochene, Apostolic, Arausican, Arbenensis (unless this is a corruption of Narbonensis), Aurelian, Braga, Carthaginian, Constantinopolitan, Chalcedonian, Gangrian, Irish, Hispalensian, Ilerdan, Iliberitan, Laurasian (unless this is a corruption of Arausican), Laodicean, Mâcon, Narbonensian, Neocaesarean, Nicene, Roman, Sardican, [Col. 0444B] Terracinian, Toletan, Valensian, Valentinian, Vasian, Vercellian, and Urban. Bishop Theodore. Vigilius, pope. *Lives of Monks*. *Lives of the Egyptian Fathers*. *Lives of the Saints*. Zacharias, pope. Zosimus, pope.

[Col. 0443]

# Canonical Letter

Which priests, deacons, and subdeacons ought to fulfill. [Note: [Col. 0443D] From a most distinguished tenth-century Vatican manuscript written in Lombard letters.]

(*In Mai, New Collection of Ancient Writers*, VI, 101.)

[Col. 0443C] I. First of all, let all priests, deacons, and subdeacons commit the Catholic faith to memory, so that if anyone neglects to do this, he shall abstain from wine for forty days; and if, after the abstinence, he neglects it, the sentence shall be repeated against him until he amends.

II. Let no priest [Note: [Col. 0443D] The word *presbyter* is absent in the Vatican manuscript but is present in the Barberini manuscript.] or deacon or subdeacon presume to live or associate with women. If he is found doing this, let him be deposed from his rank; moreover, let him be sent into exile and complete his days in penance.

III. Let no one presume to remove from churches or titles those things that have been brought or may be brought by the love of God for the preservation of Christian rulers, lest sacred possessions be devastated. If anyone presumes to do so, let the things defrauded be restored fourfold; [Col. 0443D] or, if he has nothing with which to make restitution, let him lose those very places. Let the defrauded goods themselves be gathered up by his bishop and restored in the very place from which they were taken.

IV. Concerning priests who receive into communion those who contract incestuous marriages—that is, who take as wives their godmother, a kinswoman, a mother-in-law, a stepdaughter, or a woman related to them by the nearest degree of kinship—and who come before them: let them be admonished to separate. If they delay, let them be deprived of communion, and let their offerings not be received at the sacred altar. If a priest knowingly neglects this and, under pressure or out of regard for temporal friendship, receives such a person into communion without amendment or penance, let him be subject to canonical judgment.

V. Concerning priests who, after a first or second correction or admonition, receive idol-worshippers or foolish people who commit sacrilege at springs and trees, and who also observe Thursday and Friday according to pagan custom [or fashion little stags or little old-woman figures—that is, make fumigations and enchant horns [Note: [Col. 0444D] These words occur in the Barberini manuscript but are absent from the Vatican manuscript]], and who, after a first or second admonition, give them communion or accept their offerings: let them be content with bread and water for forty days.

VI. Let no priest be permitted to accept secular administrative duties without the command of his bishop, except at the command of his pontiff in religious matters—namely, matters concerning churches, clerics, the poor, or widows—as the sacred canons prescribe. If anyone is found to have involved himself in such matters in contempt of this observance, let him be subject to canonical judgment for his presumptuous undertaking.

VII. If any priest is accused concerning any woman in such a way that an evil suspicion may arise, let him have no association with her, neither in private nor in public. If afterward, following a second and third warning, he is found to have persisted as a contemptuous person, let him bear the danger of losing his rank.

VIII. In no church of any diocese where baptism is administered should a priest be found without a deacon. [Col. 0445B] Therefore every priest who does not have a deacon should choose a person for himself and make him known to his people; then he should present him to his bishop, attesting that he has a tested life, and let him be ordained deacon. If the priest delays, saying that he does not have such a cleric, his bishop should provide a suitable person from his own church or wherever he wishes; the essential point is that he should not be without a deacon.

For we establish that the deacon should remain in one room with his priest, showing him the honor that is fitting. In front of their beds, let the clerics likewise be seen to remain, so that they may always be without suspicion and God may show mercy. When the priest is not in the house, wherever he has gone, the deacon, after his departure, should occupy his place in receiving or arranging whatever the needs of the household require; but only in such a way that he does not become proud against his priest. If he attempts this, let him be judged by his bishop for contempt arising from pride. The church’s income, whatever is placed upon the altar or may come from any source, must be under the seal of both of them; and neither should presume to spend it where necessary without the other’s knowledge.

[Col. 0446A] IX. Let no priest, deacon, or cleric established in a diocese have the power to sell church estates—that is, lands—or to give them to any of his relatives. Those who have done this must, with all speed, return them, once the price has been repaid, to the sacred places to which they belong. If anyone, in contempt of this observance, presumes to do so, let him leave his own property in that church and be cast out himself, since it accords with divine reason that those who receive churches receive them for governing, not for scattering.

Likewise, let them have no power in any way to alienate, pledge, or sell church property, nor, without the consent of their bishop, to appoint substitutes or set free dependents. Whoever presumes to do this, as we have decreed above, if he has property of his own, shall restore an equal amount; if he has none, let him be stripped of everything and cast out. The goods themselves, however, must return to the church whose goods they are.

X. It has been reported to us that certain married men who hold titles in which they serve make women’s or their daughters’ ornaments from sacred vestments and claim them for themselves by right of ownership. Such conduct is unfit even to be mentioned among Christian people: sacred objects, or things offered in a sacred place, must not be appropriated for their women, children, or relatives. If this is proved, let them be struck by the sentence prescribed above.

XI. All priests, deacons, subdeacons, and the entire clergy known to be under a bishop, if they have disputes and are unable to deliberate among themselves, should then come to their bishop to state their case. They must not presume to approach secular courts for any reason. Those who disregard this command shall be subject to the foregoing penalties, so that they remain in penance, abstaining from wine and from eating meat, until they approach their metropolitan.

# Diplomatic Monuments

## Ecclesiastical Laws of the Anglo-Saxon Kings Who Flourished in the Tenth Century

(*In Mansi, Collection of the Councils*, volume XVIII.)

### [Ecclesiastical Laws]

[Col. 0447]

# Preface, or Introduction, of King Alfred, Surnamed the Great, to His Laws

*(Years 872–900.) Translation by William Lombard from the Saxon. Manuscript of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge.*

[Col. 0447B] I. The Lord spoke a word to Moses and said: “I am the Lord your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt and out of its slavery. You shall not love other, foreign gods besides me” (Exodus XX).

II. You shall not use my name for vanity, for you are not innocent before me if you use my name for vanity.

III. Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. Work for six days and rest on the seventh, you and your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, your livestock, and the person who enters within your gates. For in six days Christ created the heavens, the earth, the seas, and all the creatures that are in them, and he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord sanctified it.

[Col. 0447C] IV. Honor your father and your mother, whom the Lord has given you, so that you may live long upon the earth.

V. You shall not kill.

VI. You shall not steal.

VII. You shall not commit adultery.

VIII. You shall not give false testimony against your neighbors.

[Col. 0448B] IX. You shall not unjustly desire your neighbor’s inheritance.

X. You shall not make for yourself gods of gold or silver.

XI. These are the laws that you must set before them. If anyone buys a Christian slave, let him serve for six years; in the seventh let him be free without payment. In whatever clothing he entered, in such clothing he shall leave. If he has a wife, let her leave with him. But if the lord gives him a wife, let she and her children belong to the lord.

If the slave says, “I do not wish to leave my master, or my wife, or my children, or my inheritance,” then let his master bring him to the temple service and pierce his ear with an awl, as a sign that he will always remain thereafter a slave.

XII. Although someone sells his daughter into service, [Col. 0448C] she shall not be a slave in every respect like other female servants. He shall not have the power to sell her to a foreigner of my people; but if she does not please the man who bought her, let him release her free to a foreign nation. If he permits his son to have intercourse with her, let him give her a gift; let him see to it that she has clothing and the price of her chastity—that is, let him grant her dowry. If [Col. 0449A] he provides none of these things for her, then she shall be free.

XIII. If anyone voluntarily kills a person, let him die by death. But if he kills him under compulsion, unwillingly, or unintentionally—as though God had delivered him into his hand—and if he had never lain in wait for him, let him be worthy of his privilege and, if he seeks asylum, of the lawful compensation of the nations. But if anyone deliberately and willingly kills his neighbor by ambush, drag him away from my altar to die.

XIV. Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall die by death.

XV. Whoever steals a free person and sells him, and is caught so that he cannot recover him, shall die by death. Whoever curses his father or his mother shall die by death.

[Col. 0449B] XVI. If anyone strikes his neighbor with a stone or a fist, and the injured man can nevertheless go out leaning on a staff, let him provide him with a physician and perform his work for him for as long as he is unable to do so.

XVII. If anyone strikes his own male or female slave, and the slave does not die on that same day but lives for two or three days, the master shall not be held equally guilty in every respect, because the slave was his property. But if the slave dies on that same day, then guilt shall rest upon him.

XVIII. If anyone, while fighting, harms a pregnant wife, let him compensate for the injury according to the judgment of the laws. If she dies, let him give life for life.

XIX. If anyone gouges out another person’s eye, let him compensate with his own: tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound [Col. 0449C] for wound, and stripe for stripe.

XX. If anyone knocks out the eye of his male or female slave, and the slave becomes one-eyed after the act, let him immediately set the slave free. If he knocks out the slave’s tooth, let him do the same.

XXI. If an ox gores a man or woman so that they die, let it be stoned, and let its flesh not be eaten. Let its owner be innocent if the ox had previously been unruly for two or three days and the owner did not know this. But if he knew it and was unwilling to keep it confined, and it then killed a man or woman, let the ox be stoned, and let the owner be killed or redeem his life by a payment, as the wise determine to be just.

If it gores a son or daughter, let the same law apply to him. But if it gores a male or female slave, let him pay the owner thirty silver shillings, and let the ox be stoned.

XXII. If anyone digs a well or opens an enclosure and afterward does not close it, let him compensate for every animal that falls into it, and let him keep the dead animal.

XXIII. If one person’s ox wounds another person’s ox and the latter afterward dies, let that ox be sold [alive] and let the price be divided, as well as its flesh, just as with the dead ox. But if the owner knew that the ox was unruly and was unwilling to confine it, let him give the other owner another ox in its place, while retaining all the flesh [of the dead ox] himself.

XXIV. If anyone steals another person’s ox and kills or sells it, let him compensate for it twofold, and one sheep for four. If he has nothing with which to compensate, let him himself be sold for that amount of money.

XXV. If a thief breaks into someone’s house at night and is killed there, the person who killed him shall not be guilty of homicide. But if he does this after sunrise, he shall be guilty of homicide and shall then die, unless he was driven to it by necessity. If anything alive that he had previously stolen is found with him, let him compensate for it twofold.

XXVI. If anyone causes damage to another person’s vineyard, field, or any of his land, let him compensate according to whatever valuation is made of it.

XXVII. If fire is set to burn a crop, let the person who set the fire compensate for the damage.

[Col. 0450B] XXVIII. If anyone deposits money with a friend and the friend steals it, let him compensate twofold. But if he does not know who secretly took it, let him clear himself by asserting that he committed no fraud in the matter. If it was a living animal and he says that an army took it, or that it died of itself, and he has witnesses, he need not compensate for it. But if he has no witnesses and the other person does not believe him, then let him provide an oath.

XXIX. If anyone deceives an unmarried woman and has intercourse with her, let him compensate her and afterward take her as his wife. If the woman’s father is unwilling to give her to him, let him pay that money as her dowry.

XXX. Do not allow a woman who is accustomed to receive enchanters, magicians, and witches to live.

[Col. 0450C] XXXI. If anyone has intercourse with a beast, let him die by death.

XXXII. If anyone offers a sacrifice to any being except God alone, let him die by death.

XXXIII. Do not afflict the stranger or foreigner, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.

XXXIV. Do not harm or afflict widows and orphans. If you do any of these things, they will cry out to me, and I will hear them; I will kill you with my sword, and I will make your wives widows and your children orphans.

XXXV. If you lend money to your neighbor who wishes to dwell with you, do not act as his exactor, nor humiliate him with your interest.

XXXVI. If anyone has only a single garment [Col. 0450D] with which to cover and protect himself, and gives it as a pledge, return it to him before sunset. If you do not do so, he will cry out to me, and I will hear him, because I am very merciful.

XXXVII. Do not slander your lord; do not curse the ruler of your people.

XXXVIII. Give to God your tithes and firstfruits, of creatures that walk and things that grow.

XXXIX. Do not eat any flesh that wild beasts leave behind; instead, give it to the dogs.

XL. Do not heed the word of a false man, nor listen to him; do not favor his lawsuit, nor give any testimony after him.

[Col. 0451A] XLI. Do not follow the people’s wicked counsel, nor its course that loves injustice, nor its outcry against your right; and do not favor it even in the most foolish doctrine.

XLII. If you come upon anyone’s straying livestock, even if it belongs to your adversary, return it to him.

XLIII. Always judge with a just judgment; do not establish one law for the rich and another for the poor, nor one law for a friend and another for an enemy.

XLIV. Always avoid falsehood.

XLV. Never oppress a guiltless and innocent man.

XLVI. Never accept gifts, since they very often blind the counsel of wise men and pervert their words.

XLVII. Do not allow an unaware traveler or stranger to be subjected to any injury.

[Col. 0451B] XLVIII. Never swear by the gods of the gentiles, nor invoke them for any reason.

XLIX. These are the laws which God Almighty Himself spoke to Moses and commanded him to observe. After the only-begotten Son of God, our God—that is, Christ the Savior—had come into the world, He said that He had not come to violate or abolish those commandments, but to fulfill them with all goodness. He also taught mercy and humility.

Then, after His Passion, before His apostles had gone out to teach in all the lands, while they were still gathered together, they converted many gentiles to God. When all these had assembled, they sent messengers to Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia to teach the laws of Christ. When they learned what had happened to them, they sent them a letter. This is the letter which the apostles sent to all in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia who had then been converted from the pagan nations to Christ:

“From the apostles and the elder brothers, greetings to you. We inform you that we have heard that some of our companions came to you with our words and, in grievous fashion, ordered you to observe things which we had not commanded them, misleading you with various precepts and weakening your souls rather than instructing them.

“Therefore we assembled on this matter, and it pleased us all to send Paul and Barnabas, men who are prepared to give up their lives [Col. 0451D] for the name of the Lord. With them we send Judas and Silas, so that they may tell you the same things.

“It seemed good to the Holy Spirit [Col. 0452A] and to us to impose no burden upon you beyond what was necessary for you to observe: namely, that you beware of worshiping what has been sacrificed to the devil; that you do not eat blood or what has been strangled; [that you abstain] from hidden sexual intercourse; and that whatever you wish other people not to do to you, you do not do to others.

“A person can remember this one law: that he should judge everyone justly and have no need of another book of statutes. Let him beware of judging any man, since he does not wish that man to judge him if he should seek some right against him.

“After this had happened, and many nations had embraced the faith of Christ, many synods were convened throughout the world, and likewise among the English people after they had received the faith of Christ, consisting of holy bishops and other distinguished wise men. Out of the mercy which Christ taught, they established for the person who sinned most gravely that the rulers of the world should, with their permission and without incurring guilt, make monetary compensation for the most serious offense, according to what those rulers determined.

“They excepted treason against the Lord, for which they did not dare to assign any mercy, since Almighty God never established any for one who had despised Him, nor would Christ, the Son of God, ever show mercy to the one who handed Him over to death. He also commanded that the Lord be loved as oneself.

“Thus, in many synods they established penalties for many human crimes and commanded them to be written in many synodal books, so that one law might prevail in one place and another elsewhere.”

[Col. 0452C] I, King Alfred, ordered many of the things which our ancestors observed and which pleased me to be collected and committed to writing. Many things which did not please me I rejected with the counsel of my wise men, and I ordered them to be observed in another manner, because I did not dare to commit any of my statutes to writing. Moreover, I did not know what would please those who would succeed us.

But when I discovered certain provisions from the days of my kinsman Ine, or of Offa, king of the Mercians, or of Æthelberht, who was the first in the English nation to receive baptism, I collected what seemed to me most just from them and neglected the rest.

I, Alfred, king of the West Saxons, consulted all my wise men here; and they said [Col. 0452D] that they all greatly approved of these provisions being observed.

[Col. 0451]

# ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS OF ALFRED THE GREAT, KING OF THE ENGLISH, EXCERPTED FROM HIS OTHER CIVIL LAWS

## I. On oaths and pledges

[Col. 0451D]

First of all, we teach what is most necessary: that every man carefully observe his oath and his agreement. If anyone has been compelled, contrary to this, through error, or into treason against the Lord, or into some unjust assistance, then it is better for him to disavow this than to fulfill it.

But if he makes an agreement to perform what is just for him to perform and violates it, let him humbly lay down his weapons and entrust his property to his friends to hold, and remain forty days in prison in the king’s town, suffering what the bishop imposes upon him. His relatives shall feed him if he has no food; if he has no relatives, or then has no food, the king’s reeve shall feed him.

If he must be compelled to do this and is unwilling to do otherwise, let him be bound, and let him lose his weapons and inheritance. If he is killed, let him lie without vengeance. If he flees before the appointed term and is caught, let him remain forty days in prison, as he should have done before. But if he escapes, let him be an exile and excommunicated from all Christ’s churches.

If he is then another man’s surety, let him make amends for the broken faith as seems just to him, and for the breach of the agreement as his confessor directs him.

## II. On those who seek refuge in churches (LL. Sax. c. 2)

If anyone takes refuge in a church dwelling for any offense, where it does not belong to the king’s firm or to another free and honorable household, let him have three days in which to hide there, unless he wishes to be reconciled.

If anyone weakens him during this period by blows, bonds, or wounds, let him compensate for each according to the law of the country, both by the assessed value of the person and by the penalty. Let him also pay [Col. 0453B] 120 shillings to the ministers of the church for violation of ecclesiastical peace, and let his property be seized.

## III. On violation of a surety-pledge (LL. Sax. c. 3)

If anyone violates a suretyship given to the king, let him compensate for this injury as seems right to him [that is, to the king], and pay five pounds of good currency for violation of the suretyship.

For violation of faith given to the archbishop, or for violation of peace, let him make amends with three pounds. For violation of the faith or peace of another bishop or ealdorman, let him make amends with two pounds.

## IV. On ecclesiastical peace (LL. Sax. c. 5)

We also establish this peace for every church consecrated by a bishop: if any criminal runs or flees to it, no one may remove him from there for seven days.

If anyone does so, let him be liable for violation of the king’s peace and the Church’s peace—and for the greater offense if he carries off several persons—provided that the fugitive can live without starvation, unless he himself has forced a way out.

If the churchwardens have greater need of their church, let them guard him in another house which has no more doors than the church. Let the elder of that church take care that he is given no food during this period.

If anyone wishes to surrender his weapons to those who have captured him, let them guard him for thirty days and then deliver him to his relatives.

Church peace also applies if anyone flees to a church for an offense which had not previously been disclosed and confesses it there in God’s name: half of his penalty shall be remitted.

## V. On sacrilege (LL. Sax. c. 6)

If anyone steals something in a temple, let him pay its value and whatever fine may be attached to that value, and let the hand with which he committed the offense be cut off.

If he wishes to redeem his hand, and this is permitted him, let him pay the amount corresponding to his assessed value.

If anyone steals on Sunday, or on the feast of Christ’s Nativity, or Easter, or the feast of the Lord’s Ascension, or on the days of lustration, we decree that he pay double in the same manner as on the fast-days of Lent.

## VI. On one who removes a nun from a church (LL. Sax. c. 8)

If anyone removes a nun from a church without the permission of the king or bishop, let him pay 120 shillings: half to the king, half to the bishop and the reeve of the [Col. 0454A] church who has charge of the nun.

If she outlives the man who removed her, let her receive nothing from his inheritance. If she bears a child, let the child receive no more of his inheritance than its mother. If her child is killed, the king shall receive the portion of the penalty owed by the mother’s kin, and the other portion shall be given to the father’s relatives.

## VII. On fornicators (LL. Sax. c. 10)

If anyone has intercourse with the wife of a man assessed at 1,200 shillings, let him pay 120 shillings as the assessed value of the person. Let him compensate with 100 shillings for the wife of a man assessed at 600 shillings, and with forty shillings for a ceorl’s wife. Let this be settled in money while the husband is alive, and let no man be sold on that account.

## VIII

[Col. 0454B]

If anyone touches the breasts of a ceorl’s wife, let him compensate her with five shillings. If he throws her down but has no intercourse with her, let him compensate with ten shillings. If he has intercourse with her, let him pay sixty shillings.

If another man had previously had intercourse with her, the compensation shall be half this amount. If anyone accuses him, let him clear himself with sixty hides, or lose half the compensation.

If this happens to a husband of noble family, the compensation shall increase according to the assessed value of the person.

## IX. On fighting (LL. Sax. c. 15)

If anyone fights or draws weapons before an archbishop, let him compensate with 150 shillings. If this occurs before another bishop or an ealdorman, let him compensate with 100 shillings.

## X. On touching a nun (LL. Sax. c. 18)

[Col. 0454C]

If anyone touches a nun, or her clothing, or her breasts, for the purpose of fornication and without her permission, let him pay double, as we previously imposed for laywomen.

## XI. On one who entrusts money to monks (LL. Sax. c. 20)

If anyone entrusts money belonging to another to a monk without the permission of the monastery’s reeve, and the monk loses it, the person who previously possessed the money shall receive nothing from it.

## XII. On a priest’s fighting (LL. Sax. c. 21)

If a priest kills someone, let everything with which he purchased his dwelling be seized, and let the bishop strip him of his sacred orders. Then let him be handed over by the church, unless the lord of the slain man wishes to obtain his pardon by paying the assessed value of the person.

## XIII. On violation of a woman (LL. Sax. c. 25)

If anyone threatens a ceorl’s servant-woman with sexual violation, let him compensate the ceorl with five shillings and pay sixty shillings as a fine.

If a male slave compels a female slave to sexual intercourse, let him compensate for this with his virile organ.

If anyone threatens a young girl with illicit intercourse, let him be punished in the same manner as one who does this to an adult slave woman.

## XIV. On one who gives a pledge to God on behalf of another (LL. Sax. c. 29)

If anyone is accused of having stood surety before God on behalf of another and wishes to assert that he did not provide some of what was owed to him, let him then make a preliminary oath in four churches. If the other person wishes to clear him of the charge, let him do so in twelve churches.

## XV. On fighting before an ealdorman (LL. Sax. c. 34)

If anyone fights before the king’s ealdorman amid a gathering of the people, let him pay the assessed value of the person and the penalty, as is just, and first pay the ealdorman 120 shillings as a penalty.

If anyone incites a gathering of the people by drawing weapons, let him pay the ealdorman 120 shillings as a penalty. If this occurs before the king’s ealdorman’s deputy or the king’s priest, the penalty shall be thirty shillings.

## XVI. On violation of peace in a town (LL. Sax. c. 36)

The compensation for violation of peace in the king’s town shall be 120 shillings; in an archbishop’s town, ninety shillings; for violation of the peace of another bishop or an ealdorman, sixty shillings; of a man assessed at 1,200 shillings, thirty shillings; of a man assessed at 600 shillings, fifteen shillings; and violation of a ceorl’s enclosure, five shillings.

If any of these things occurs while the army is traveling, or during the Lenten fast, the compensation shall be double.

If anyone removes a sacred veil [Col. 0456A] before the people during Lent without permission, let him compensate with 120 shillings.

## XVII. On hereditary land (LL. Sax. c. 37)

If anyone possesses hereditary land which his parents left to him, we establish that he may not sell it away from his kinsmen who are heirs, if there is a document or witness showing that the man who acquired it at the beginning was forbidden to do so, and that the man who sold it was likewise forbidden, so that he could not make such a sale.

This shall then be recited in the king’s or bishop’s testimony before his kinsmen.

## XVIII. On the observance of feast days (LL. Sax. c. 39)

These days shall be days of rest for all free men, except slaves and laborers: twelve days at Christmastide; the day on which Christ overcame the devil; the memorial day of Saint Gregory; the seven days before Easter and the seven after; one day on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul; in autumn, the full week before the feast of Blessed Mary; one day before the celebration of All Saints; and the four Wednesdays in the four weeks of fasting.

All these are days of rest for everyone, according to each person’s good pleasure—for the one who does something good in God’s name, or for the one who can earn something through some work of his own.

[Col. 0455]

# ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS ENACTED BY ALFRED THE GREAT, KING OF THE ENGLISH, AND GUTHRUM, KING OF THE ANGLO-DANES, IN THE COUNCIL WHERE THEY ENTERED INTO A TREATY

*(Absent from Lombard’s Archaionomia [‘Ancient Laws’; Ἀρχαιονομία]; but here added from the manuscript History of York, or Jervaulx.)*

## TITLES OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS

[Col. 0455C]

I. On love of God and the peace of the Church (LL. Sax. ch. 1).  
II. On those who neglect Christ’s law and worship paganism (LL. Sax. ch. 2).  
III. On ordained persons living wickedly (LL. Sax. ch. 3).  
IV. On priests falsely declaring a feast or fast (LL. Sax. ch. 3).  
V. On priests who do not obtain chrism at the proper times, or who deny baptism (LL. Sax. ch. 3).  
VI. On brothers or kinsmen committing fornication with one woman (LL. Sax. ch. 4).  
VII. On an ordained man who commits an offense (absent in the Saxon text).  
[Col. 0455D] VIII. On a person condemned to death who wishes to confess to a priest (LL. Sax. ch. 5).  
IX. On tithes owed to God and other ecclesiastical rights being withheld (LL. Sax. ch. 6).  
X. On those who conduct business on Sundays (LL. Sax. ch. 7).  
[Col. 0456C] XI. On those who work on Sundays (LL. Sax. ch. 7).  
XII. On violated fasts (LL. Sax. ch. 8).  
XIII. On the days on which trial by ordeal and oaths are prohibited (LL. Sax. ch. 9).  
XIV. That an offender not be killed on Sunday (LL. Sax. ch. 10).  
XV. … … … … LL. Sax. ch. 10.  
XVI. On diviners, enchanters, poisoners, perjurers, and their like (LL. Sax. ch. 11).  
XVII. On ordained persons or foreigners seduced in some matter concerning money or life (LL. Sax. ch. 12).

# PREFACE

[Col. 0456D] I. This is the council [Note: [Col. 0455D] King Alfred of England, after capturing London in the year of Christ 866, held a synod there, which is mentioned in the Winchester Annals: “The most devout King Alfred,” says the annalist, “so that the holiness and wisdom of the man of God Grimbald might be made known to all, assembled in London, the metropolis [Col. 0456D] of the whole island, a council from all England, of bishops, abbots, and noblemen.” Harpesfeld also mentions this synod, *Saec.* IX, ch. 7. Pagi, under the year of Christ 886, no. 11.] which King Alfred and King Godrun selected and agreed upon when the English and Danes had fully come to peace and concord; and the wise men and those who succeeded them later, renewing this more and more frequently and continually, brought it always to greater good.

[Note: [Col. 0456D] The same man who is also called Guthrum, Gutrum, and so forth. He was king of the Danes; after his conversion to the faith of Christ, Alfred, who received him from the sacred font and granted him part of the kingdom, gave him the name Æthelstan.]

# ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS OF KINGS ALFRED AND GUTHRUM

[Col. 0457A]

## I

First, they are to desire to love one God and diligently renounce all paganism. They established secular justice because they knew that many could not otherwise be disciplined, while many others were unwilling to be bent toward the worship of God as they ought to be.

They also established a secular compensation common to Christ and the king wherever anyone refused to observe God’s law justly according to the bishop’s declaration.

This is the Church’s first decree: that peace within its walls and the king’s Hangrid [the printed reading is uncertain] remain always unshaken.

## II

If anyone wickedly changes his Christianity in order to worship paganism in word or deed, let him repay the *wergild*, the *wite*, and the *lahslite* according to what was done.

## III

If any ordained person steals, fights, commits perjury, or fornicates, let him compensate according to what was done—*wergild*, *wite*, and *lahslite*—and at least make amends before God according to the teaching of the holy canons. Let him provide surety for this, or be sent to prison.

## IV

If a priest misinstructs his people concerning a feast or fast, let him pay thirty shillings among the English and three half-marks among the Danes.

## V

If a priest does not obtain holy chrism at the proper time, or refuses baptism to one who needs it, let him pay the *wite* among the English and the *lahslite* among the Danes—that is, twelve oras.

Concerning sub-reeves, the wise men established that the king should have authority over the superior and the bishop over the inferior, unless a more worthy compensation is made before God and the world according to the nature of the act, as the bishop shall teach.

## VI

If two brothers or two kinsmen commit fornication with one woman, let them make amends with all gentleness as shall be permitted them—whether *wite* or *lahslite*, according to the nature of the act.

## VII

[Note: [Col. 0457D] This is not found in the Saxon text or in Edward’s treaty in Lombard.]

If an ordained man commits an offense, let him, if he is to be punished by death, be proceeded against according to the acts [reading uncertain], and be reserved to the bishop’s judgment.

## VIII

If anyone condemned to death wishes to confess to a priest, this must never be denied him. Let all God’s requirements be diligently reconciled through God’s mercy and through the *wite* which the wise men shall prescribe.

[Col. 0457D] IX. If anyone withholds a tithe, let him pay the *lahslite* among the Danes and the *wite* among the English.

If anyone withholds the *Rofeil* [Col. 0458A] [Note: [Col. 0458D] That is, a Roman coin, or Saint Peter’s penny], let him pay the *lahslite* among the Danes and the *wite* among the English.

If anyone fails to give the candle-penny, let him pay the *lahslite* among the Danes and the *wite* among the English.

If anyone suppresses any of God’s rights, let him pay the *lahslite* among the Danes and the *wite* among the English.

If he resists and wounds a man, let him forfeit his *wite*. If he casts anyone into death, let him be an *utlah*, an outlaw, and everyone who loves justice shall pursue him with a public outcry.

If he causes someone to kill him because he stood against justice and the king’s command, and this is proved, let him lie without *wergild*.

## X

If anyone dares to conduct business on Sunday, let him lose the capital involved, and pay twelve oras among the Danes and thirty shillings among the English.

## XI

If a free man works on feast days, let him lose his freedom, or pay the *wite* or *lahslite*. Let a slave lose his hide or *hýdgild*.

If a master compels his slave to work on feast days, let that master pay the *lahslite* among the Danes and the *wite* among the English.

## XII

If a free man breaks the proper fast, let him pay the *wite* or *lahslite*. If a slave does this, let him lose his hide or *hýdgild*.

## XIII

Trial by ordeal and oaths are forbidden by law on feast days and on the appointed days of fasting. Whoever violates this shall pay the *lahslite* among the Danes and the *wite* among the English.

## XIV

If it can be done, no one shall ever be killed on a Sunday feast day, whatever he has done; instead, he shall be captured and kept until the feast day has passed.

## XV

If an offender, having been disabled in his limbs, is released, and lives for four nights after the punishment, assistance may thereafter be given him with the bishop’s permission, if anyone wishes to alleviate his bodily pains and save his soul.

## XVI

If female sorcerers or enchanters, perjurers and poisoners, foul and filthy women, or prostitutes appear anywhere, let them be banished from the country and let them despair of everything, unless they cease and make deeper amends.

## XVII

If an ordained person or a foreigner is led astray in some matter concerning money or *wite*, then the king, or the earl of that region, and the bishop of his people must stand by him in place of relatives and an advocate, unless he has someone else altogether.

Let him diligently make amends according to what was done, to Christ and to the king, as is appropriate; or let the king who rules that people avenge the deed most severely.

# ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS OF EDWARD THE ELDER, KING OF THE ENGLISH, AND GUTHRUM, KING OF THE DANES, IN EAST ANGLIA

First established by the kings Alfred the Great and Guthrum, and now renewed and confirmed at Intingford, as it seems, by Edward, son of the same Alfred, and Guthrum when they entered into a treaty [Note: [Col. 0459C] These should be placed under Pope Sergius III]. (A.D. 905–906.)

[Col. 0459]

## ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS

### TITLES OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS

[Col. 0459A]

I. On the peace of the Church.  
II. On apostates.  
III. On the correction of ordained persons, that is, those initiated into sacred orders.  
IV. On incest.  
V. On a person condemned to death who desires a confessor.  
VI. On tithes and ecclesiastical dues being withheld.  
VII. On those who conduct their business on Sunday.  
VIII. On fasts.  
IX. On oaths and trial by ordeal.  
X. On assistance being given after the third day to one whose limb has been cut off.  
XI. On diviners, enchanters, perjurers, and so forth.  
XII. On those initiated into sacred orders and on foreigners.

## PROEM

[Col. 0459B] This is the decree which King Alfred and King Guthrum, and afterward King Edward and King Guthrum, selected and established when the English and Danes entered into peace and friendship; and the wise men who came later frequently and continually renewed and improved the same provisions.

First, they established that they should desire to love one God and diligently reject all heathenism. They also established secular discipline, because they knew that they could not govern many in any other way, and that many would not otherwise be bent toward ecclesiastical correction as they ought to be.

They established secular compensation common to Christ and the king wherever a man was unwilling to submit to ecclesiastical compensation by virtue of the bishops’ authority.

## I. On the peace of the Church

[Col. 0459C]

This, therefore, is the first provision they declared: that the peace of the Church within its walls, and the peace granted by the king’s hand, should remain equally undisturbed and unimpaired.

## II. On apostates

If anyone despises Christianity or worships paganism in word or deed, let him pay both the assessed value of the person and the fine, as well as the penalty for violation of the law, according to what was done.

## III. On the correction of ordained persons

If anyone initiated into sacred orders steals, fights, commits perjury, or fornicates, let him compensate according to what [Col. 0460A] was done, both by the assessed value of the person and by the fine and penalty for violating the law. Let him at least make amends before God as the canons prescribe, and let him find a surety or be thrust into prison.

If a priest misinstructs his people concerning a feast or fast, let him pay thirty shillings among the English and three half-marks among the Danes.

If a priest does not prepare chrism at the proper time, or denies baptism to one who needs his ministry, let him pay a fine among the English and, among the Danes, the penalty for violating the law—that is, twelve oras.

If a person initiated into sacred orders commits anything deserving death, let him be seized and brought before the bishop’s judgment.

## IV. On incest

Regarding incest, the wise men established that the king should have the men of higher rank and the bishop those of lower rank [Col. 0460B], unless a man makes compensation before God and the world according to what was done, as the bishop prescribes.

If two brothers or two blood-relatives have intercourse with one wife, let them make amends with all gentleness, as shall be permitted them—whether by a fine, by the assessed value of the person, or by the penalty for violating the peace, according to what was done.

## V. On a person condemned to death who desires a confessor

If a person condemned to death wishes to confess, this must never be denied him. Let all God’s laws be diligently advanced through God’s mercy and through the penalties which the wise men shall impose.

## VI. On tithes and ecclesiastical dues being withheld

If anyone withholds tithes, let him pay the penalty for violating the law among the Danes and a fine among the English.

If anyone withholds Saint [Col. 0460C] Peter’s penny, let him pay the penalty for violating the law among the Danes and a fine among the English.

If anyone withholds one candle-penny, let him pay the penalty for violating the law among the Danes and a fine among the English.

If anyone does not give the plough-alms, let him pay the penalty for violating the law among the Danes and a fine among the English.

If anyone suppresses any ecclesiastical right, let him pay the penalty for violating the law among the Danes and a fine among the English.

If he fights and wounds a man, let him lose his life. If he inflicts death on anyone, let him then be an outlaw, and let everyone who loves justice pursue him with a public outcry.

If he causes someone to kill him because he opposed the right of God [Col. 0461A] or of the king, and this is confirmed, let him lie without compensation.

## VII. On work on feast days

If anyone dares to trade on Sunday, let him lose the goods involved in the trade, and pay twelve oras among the Danes and thirty shillings among the English.

If a free man works on a feast day, let him lose his freedom, or pay a fine and the penalty for violating the law. Let a slave be flogged, or redeem the flogging by payment.

If a master compels his slaves to work on a feast day, let the master pay the penalty for violating the law according to Danish law, and a fine among the English.

## VIII. On fasts

If a free man breaks the proper fast, let him pay a fine or the penalty for violating the law. If a slave does this, [Col. 0461B] let him be flogged, or redeem the flogging by payment.

## IX. On ordeal and oaths

Trial by ordeal and oaths are prohibited on feast days and on the appointed days of fasting. If anyone violates this, let him pay the penalty for violating the law among the Danes and a fine among the English.

If it can be done, no one who has committed an offense shall ever be killed on the feast of Sunday [Col. 0462A]; instead, he shall be captured and held until the feast day has passed.

## X. On assistance after the third day to one whose limb has been cut off

If a piece of the limb of a condemned, crippled person is cut off, and he lives for three days afterward, assistance may thereafter be given him with the bishop’s permission, if anyone wishes to heal his pains and save his soul.

## XI. On diviners, enchanters, perjurers, and so forth

If female diviners or enchanters, perjurers or poisoners, or foul, polluted public prostitutes appear in any region, let them be banished from the land and let the people be cleansed; or let everything be taken from them there, unless they cease and make more substantial compensation.

## XII. On those initiated into sacred orders and on foreigners

If a person initiated into sacred orders or a foreigner is led astray in some matter [Col. 0462B] concerning money or life, then the king, or the earl who is in that region, and the bishop of his people must stand by him in place of relatives and patrons, unless he has others elsewhere.

Let him diligently make compensation according to what was done, to Christ and to the king, as is proper; or let the king who rules that people avenge this deed as harshly as possible.

# ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS OF ÆTHELSTAN, KING OF THE ENGLISH

[Col. 0461]

## THE COUNCIL OF GREATLEY

Held by Æthelstan, king of the English, around A.D. 928, at which many laws, both civil and ecclesiastical, were established; omitting these, however, the compiler has arranged the following.

### TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS

[Col. 0461C]

I. On rendering tithes, feeding a poor person, and distributing alms annually from the royal estates (LL. Sax. in the proem; Jorn. ch. 1).  
II. On breaking into a church (LL. Sax. ch. 5; Jorn. ch. 10).  
III. On diviners (LL. Sax. ch. 6; Jorn. ch. 11).  
IV. On moneyers (LL. Sax. ch. 14; Jorn. ch. 20).  
V. On those who pledge themselves to submit to ordeal (LL. Sax. ch. 23; Jorn. ch. 30).  
VI. On the purchase of goods on Sunday (LL. Sax. ch. 24; Jorn. ch. 32).  
VII. On perjurers (LL. Sax. ch. 25; Jorn. ch. 34).  
VIII. On those who do not enforce these laws (LL. Sax. ch. 26; Jorn. ch. 34).  
[Col. 0461D] IX. On legislators and the place [of legislation] (LL. Sax. final chapter; Jorn. ch. 35).

# CONSTITUTION OF KING ÆTHELSTAN

I, King Æthelstan, on the advice of my archbishop Wulfhelm and my other bishops, command all my reeves throughout my kingdom, in the name of the Lord and all the saints and by my love, first to pay tithes from my own property, both of living animals and of the annual produce; and I command that my bishops, ealdormen, and reeves do the same from their own property.
