I wish my bishops and reeves to enforce this upon all who owe them obedience, and that each person complete by the same appointed term what we establish here. This shall be done by the day of the beheading of Saint John the Baptist.

Let us remember what the patriarch Jacob said to the Lord: “I will give You my tithes and my peace-offering.” The Lord Himself also said in the Gospel: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound.”

We must also consider what is written so terribly in these books: if we are unwilling to render our tithes, let nine parts be taken from us, so that one tenth remains to us.

Evangelical teaching admonishes us to earn heavenly things by earthly things and eternal things by temporal ones. Now you have heard what the Lord commands us and what we ought to accomplish [Col. 0463A]. See to it that you willingly grant what you can lawfully bestow upon me. I do not wish you to give me anything in error.

If I grant all your possessions to you, I do so with the intention that you will willingly grant me mine. Beware, for your own sake and for the sake of those connected with you, of God’s anger and mine.

I, King Æthelstan, make known to all the reeves in my kingdom, on the advice of my archbishop Wulfhelm, all my other bishops, and the ministers of God, for the remission of my sins, that I wish you in every way to support one poor Englishman, if you have one or find one anywhere.

From two of my estates, one measure of flour shall be given him every month, and one side of pork, or one ram worth four pennies, together with clothing for twelve months, each year.

You shall also redeem one slave who has been fined by restoring his freedom. Let all this be done out of God’s mercy and for love of me, under the testimony of the bishop in whose jurisdiction it lies.

If a reeve neglects this, let him compensate with thirty shillings, and let the money be divided among the poor in the town where the omission occurs, under the testimony of the bishop.

## II. On breaking into a temple

We also decreed concerning breaking into a temple: if the accused is convicted by the triple ordeal, let him compensate according to what the law-book prescribes.

## III. On sorceries

We also decreed concerning enchantments, barbarous sacrifices, and killings: if anyone kills another and cannot deny that he did so, let him lose his life.

If he wishes to deny it and is convicted by the triple ordeal, let him remain 120 days in prison. Then let his relatives take him out, pay the king 120 shillings, compensate the slain man’s relatives for the assessed value of the person, and become his sureties that he will always abstain from a similar act.

Concerning incendiaries: incendiaries and those who avenge a thief are liable under the same law. If anyone wishes to avenge a thief and has wounded no one, let him pay the king 120 shillings as a fine for the offense.

## IV. On moneyers

We establish that there shall be one coinage throughout the king’s dominion, and that no one shall mint money outside the gate.

If a moneyer is convicted, let the hand with which he committed the offense be cut off and fastened to the mint.

But if he is accused and wishes to clear himself, let him go to the red-hot iron and purge the hand of the offense of which he is accused—namely, that he committed this fraud. If he is then convicted by the ordeal, let whatever was previously stated be done to him.

In Canterbury there shall be seven moneyers: four belonging to the king, two to the bishop, and one to the abbot. In Rochester, three: two belonging to the king and one to the bishop. In London, eight. In Winchester, six. In Lewes, two. In Hastings, one. Another in Chichester. [Col. 0464A] In Southampton, two. In Wareham, two. Two in Exeter. Two in Shaftesbury. In the other boroughs, one in each.

## V. On one who pledges himself to undergo ordeal

If anyone pledges himself to undergo ordeal, let him come to the priest three days beforehand, and let the priest sanctify it.

Before he undergoes it, let him nourish himself with bread, salt, water, and herbs; let him attend Mass on each of those three days and make an offering; and on the day when he is to undergo ordeal, let him receive Holy Communion.

Before he approaches the ordeal, let him swear that, according to the law of the people, he is innocent of the accusations.

If it is the ordeal by water, let him be immersed to the depth of an ell and a half on a rope.

If it is the ordeal by iron, let three days pass before the hand is opened. Each person shall pursue his accusation under oath, as we said earlier. All those present on both sides by command of God and the archbishop shall fast, and no more than twelve persons shall be present on either side.

If the accused man is accompanied by more than twelve supporters, the ordeal shall be void, unless they are willing to depart.

## VI. On one who purchases goods

[The supplied source ends here.]

Whoever buys property in the presence of witnesses, and afterward someone claims that it is his, then let the seller who first purchased it recover it, whether he is a slave, a free man, or anyone else.

[Col. 0464C] And [we order] that no purchase be made on Sundays. If anyone does so, let him forfeit the purchase price and pay thirty shillings as a fine.

### VII. Concerning Perjurers

Whoever gives a false oath and is thereafter convicted shall never again be trusted, nor shall he be buried in any consecrated cemetery when he dies, unless he has a certificate from the bishop in whose diocese he is, stating that he has made appropriate compensation according to what his confessor prescribed for him. His confessor shall inform the bishop within thirty days whether he wishes to return to the matter of his compensation. If he does not do this, let him make compensation according to what the bishop imposes upon him.

### VIII. Concerning Those Who Do Not Execute These Laws

[Col. 0464D] If any of my prefects does not wish to do this, or is negligent in carrying out what we have said, let him pay for his contempt toward me, and I shall find another who is willing [to execute this]. And let the bishop punish that contempt in the reeve who is in his division. Whoever departs from this ordinance shall pay five pounds the first time, the valuation of his life the second time, and the third time shall lose everything he possesses, together with the friendship of all of us.

### IX. Concerning the Lawmakers and the Place of the Council

All this was established at the great synod of Gratanleage, at which Archbishop Wulfhelm was present with all the nobles and wise men whom King Æthelstan assembled.

[Col. 0465]

## THE ANCIENT VERSION OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS OF KING ÆTHELSTAN

According to the royal and Jornhal manuscript codices, presenting much that is lacking in the Saxon exemplar and, separately, other divergent material.

## TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS

[Col. 0465A]

I. Concerning the careful payment of tithes, etc. (Saxon Laws in the preface; Jornhal, chapter 1).  
II. Concerning the payment of the church census, called *cyricsceat* (Saxon Laws and Jornhal, chapter 2 in the preface).  
III. That each of the king’s reeves should feed one poor person, etc. (Saxon Laws, chapter 3; Jornhal, chapter 3).  
IV. Concerning the violation of churches (Saxon Laws, chapter 5; Jornhal, chapter 10).  
V. Concerning sorcerers and poisoners (Saxon Laws, chapter 6; Jornhal, chapter 11).  
VI. Concerning moneyers and minters (Saxon Laws, chapter 14; Jornhal, chapter 20).  
VII. Concerning the preparation of one who approaches the ordeal (Saxon Laws, o.; Jornhal, chapter 31).  
[Col. 0465B] VIII. Concerning the procedure for celebrating the ordeal (lacking in the Saxon and Jornhal texts; taken from the royal manuscript).  
IX. That trading should not take place on Sunday (Saxon Laws, chapter 24; Jornhal, chapter 32).  
X. Concerning those who commit perjury (Saxon Laws, chapter 25; Jornhal, chapter 34).  
XI. Concerning the office of the bishop and what belongs to his office (Saxon Laws, o.; the following chapter in Jornhal).  
XII. That fifty psalms are to be sung every Friday for the king and the people (Council of Exeter in the Saxon Laws, chapter 3; Jornhal, chapter 6).  
XIII. Concerning *wer* and *wergild*, that is, valuations of lives (Saxon Laws, final chapter; the following chapter in Jornhal).

## CHAPTERS

[Col. 0465C]

### I

I, King Æthelstan, with the counsel of my archbishop Wulfhelm and my other bishops, command all my reeves throughout my entire kingdom, and order them in the name of the Lord and of all the saints, and upon my friendship, first to pay tithes from my own property to God, both from living livestock and from the fruits of the earth after they have been harvested. My bishops likewise shall do so from their own property, as shall my aldermen and my reeves. And I wish my bishops and reeves to announce this to all who ought to obey them, and to complete it by the date we set for them, namely the beheading of Saint John the Baptist.

Let us consider what Jacob the father said to God: “I shall offer you tithes and peace offerings” (Genesis XVIII). And the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “To everyone who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound” (Matthew XXV). We must also remember how terrifyingly it is written in the books: if we do not wish to give the tenth, so that nine parts may be offered to us and only the tenth remain.

[Col. 0466A]

### II

And I wish the *cyricsceat* to be rendered to the place to which it rightly belongs, and there to benefit those in those places who are more worthy to serve God and us in this matter. Divine speech urges us to earn the eternal together with earthly things, and heavenly things together with perishable ones. Now you have heard what I command in God’s name and what you ought to fulfill. Also act so that you desire what is properly mine, which you will be able rightly to acquire for me. I do not want you to acquire anything for me unjustly, but I grant you all your own property on the condition that you likewise desire what is mine for me. Beware both for yourselves and for those whom you ought to admonish, lest you incur God’s anger and transgress against me.

### III

I, King Æthelstan, make known to all my reeves throughout my kingdom that, with the counsel of my archbishop Wulfhelm, all my bishops, [Col. 0466B] and the ministers of God, for the remission of my sins and the acquisition of eternal life, I wish you in every way to feed one needy English poor person, if one is there, or to find another. From two *nith-firms*, let a full measure of flour, one ham, or one ram worth four pence, and four cheeses be given to each of them every month; and on the third day of Easter, thirty pence for clothing for twelve months, each year. And free one *wire-theowne*, that is, a forfeited slave. Let all this be carried out in the mercy of God and in my friendship, under the testimony of the bishop in whose episcopate the person is located. If a reeve withholds this, let him pay thirty shillings, and let this money be distributed, on the testimony of the bishop, among the poorer people in the village where this was not [Col. 0466C] carried out.

### IV

Concerning the violations of churches: if anyone appears guilty in the triple ordeal, let him make compensation as the judicial book prescribes.

### V

We have also decreed concerning sorcerers, *liblacs* [term uncertain], and those who give lots: if they kill a person and cannot deny it, let them be judged guilty of their lives. If they wish to deny it and are found guilty in the triple ordeal, let them be imprisoned for 120 nights; let their kin feed them; let them compensate the king with 120 shillings; let them restore the slain person to his relatives; and let them give security to those relatives that they will refrain from such acts forever.

### VI

It has pleased us that there be one coinage throughout the entire kingdom and that no one mint outside the city gate. If a moneyer is found guilty, let his hand be cut off and placed beneath the minting apparatus. If there is an accusation and he wishes to clear himself, let him go to the hot iron and place his hand upon the *canifera*, swearing that he did not make a false coin. If he is found guilty in the ordeal, let what was stated above be done to him.

In Canterbury there are eight royal moneyers, four belonging to the bishop, and three belonging to the abbot; in Rochester, three royal and two episcopal. In London, eight; in Winchester, six; in Lewes, two; in Hastings, one; in Shaftesbury, two; in Oxford, two; and in the other boroughs.

### VII

If anyone has given security for the ordeal of iron or water, let him go three nights beforehand to the priest who is to consecrate him. Let him feed himself on bread, salt, water, and herbs; let him hear Masses on each of those three days and make an offering; and let him receive the most holy communion on the day on which the ordeal is to be examined. Before he comes to the ordeal, let him swear that, according to the common law, he is innocent of that accusation.

If it is the ordeal of cold water, let him be immersed to a depth of one and a half ells by a rope. If it is hot iron, let three nights pass before it is examined. Let his hand be inspected, and let every person pursue his claim under oath, as stated above. Let both parties fast by the command of God and the archbishop, and let there not be more on one side than on the other: there are to be twelve men on each side. But if the accused has a greater defense than twelve men, let the ordeal itself be invalidated for him, unless they wish to withdraw from it.

### VIII

Concerning the ordeal, we command in the name of God and by the command of the archbishop and all my bishops that no one enter the church after the fire has been brought in, from which the implement for the judgment is to be heated, except the priest and the person who is to undergo the judgment.

Let nine feet be measured from the stake to the mark, according to the foot-measure of the person who is to undergo the judgment. If it is the judgment of water, let it be heated until it is brought to boiling. Let the vessel be of iron, bronze, lead, or clay. If it is an *anfealt tybla*, let the hand be immersed beyond the stone or the test until the wrist; if it is a triple accusation, up to the elbow.

When the judgment is ready, let two men enter from each side. Let them be certain that it is as hot as we have stated. Let an equal number enter from both sides and stand on each side of the judgment along the length of the church. Let them all fast and abstain from their wives that night. Let the priest sprinkle blessed water over them all. Let each humble himself before the blessed water, and let the priest give all of them the text of the Holy Gospel to kiss, together with the sign of the holy cross.

Let no one tend the fire longer than until the blessing begins. Let the iron lie upon the coals until the final collect; afterward let it be placed upon the *staples*. Let there be no other speech there except earnest prayer to God the almighty Father, that he may deign to reveal his truth in this matter. Let the accused drink blessed water, and let the hand with which he must carry the judgment be sprinkled with it; then let him approach.

Let the nine measured feet be divided into three sections. At the first mark beside the stake, let him place his right foot. At the second, let him transfer the right foot to the third mark, [Col. 0468A] when he throws down the iron, and let him hasten to the holy altar. Let his hand be sealed, and on the third day let it be examined to see whether it is clean or unclean within the seal. Whoever breaks these laws shall have the ordeal—that is, the judgment or examination—invalidated against him, and shall pay the king 120 shillings as a *wite*.

### IX

Whoever buys anything shall buy it with witnesses. If a claim is made concerning it, let his seller, from whom he bought it, recover it, whether he is free, a slave, or whatever he may be. Let no trading or legal proceeding take place on Sunday. If anyone dares to do this, let him forfeit the principal itself and make amends for his disobedience to me (*overhirness*).

### X

Whoever swears a false oath and is convicted of it shall never afterward be worthy of belief on oath, nor, if he dies, shall he lie in any consecrated churchyard, unless he has a certificate from the bishop in whose diocese he is stating that he has undertaken penance. Let the priest report this to the bishop within thirty nights, [and report] whether he has come to make compensation and satisfaction. If he does not do this, let him make compensation as the bishop grants him.

All this was instituted and confirmed at the great synod at Greatley, which Archbishop Wulfhelm attended, together with all the nobles and wise men whom King Æthelstan was able to assemble.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] This is from the Jornhal manuscript.]

### XI

By right, it belongs to the bishop to promote every kind of justice, both God’s and the world’s. Above all, he must instruct every person ordained by God concerning what he ought rightly to do and what secular matters they ought to judge. He must also diligently work for peace and concord with the secular judges who love what is right, and teach them in the allegation of claims, so that no one acts improperly against another in an oath or ordeal.

Nor must he tolerate any deception through an unjust measure or unjust weight. Rather, through his counsel and testimony, all measures prescribed by law, the borough measure, and every weight should be established according to his direction and made entirely correct.

Let no one deceive his neighbor, thereby falling into sin. Every Christian ought always to take precautions against all the things mentioned above. For this reason he ought to concern himself with many matters, so that he may know how the flock acts which he has undertaken to guard in God’s hands, lest the devil tear it apart or sow anything evil over it.

[Col. 0468D]

For the people will never be well advised, nor will they be worthily preserved for God, where impious and especially false profit is loved. Therefore all God’s friends ought to weaken what is unjust and raise up what is just. They must not allow people, because of falsehood and the pursuit of money, to forfeit themselves before the truly wise God, who detests all injustice.

It is necessary for all Christians to love what is right and condemn what is unjust, and at least those who have been raised to holy orders must always uphold justice and put down what is crooked. Hence bishops ought to be present at judgments together with secular judges, so that, if they can, they do not permit [Col. 0469A] the shoots of any such wickedness to spring up. [Note: [Col. 0469] This note appears at the foot of column 469, but its callout number, (9), is not printed in the text: “Who is now called a count.”]

It belongs to priests in their own dioceses diligently to help anyone toward what is right, and, if they can, not to permit any Christian to harm another: neither the powerful one the powerless, nor the highest the lowest, nor the prelate his subjects, nor the lord to be troublesome to his men, whether slaves or free. According to the bishop’s direction and by his measure, it is fitting that testamentary slaves should work throughout the entire *scir* over which he presides.

It is right that no measurable rod should be longer than another, but that all should be established according to the bishop’s measure and equalized throughout his diocese. Every weight should conform to his direction; and if any dispute arises, the bishop should decide it.

It is the particular duty of every lord to sympathize with and show consideration toward his slaves as indulgently as he can, because they have been bought by the Lord God. Slave and free are equally dear, and he redeemed them all at the same price. We are all necessarily servants of God, and he will judge us as we previously judged those over whom we held authority on earth.

### XII

Every Friday, let all God’s ministers in all monasteries and greater churches sing fifty psalms for the king himself and for all who obey him, as well as for any others who deserve such prayers.

Let anyone who wishes also be permitted to make compensation for any crime that is charged against him, unless it was committed on the days of lustration, which they call *Gang-days*. Thereafter let the matter stand as it did before.

### XIII

The king’s *wergild* among the English, according to the common law, is thirty thousand *thrimsas*, that is, “of three” (*trium*). Fifteen thousand *thrimsas* belong to the *wer*, and fifteen thousand to the *cynedom*, that is, the royal authority. His birth-price belongs to his kin, and his *cynebot* to the people of the land.

The *wergild* of an archbishop and a count is fifteen thousand *thrimsas*.

[Note: [Col. 0469D] [ [Col. 0469D] This note does not appear in Migne’s printed edition.]

The *wergild* of a bishop and an alderman [Note: [Col. 0469D] Whom they now call a duke.] is eight thousand *thrimsas*.

The *wergild* of *messetheins* and *woruldtheins*, that is, priests and secular thanes, is two thousand *thrimsas*.

[Col. 0469D] These immediately follow the preceding chapter on *wergilds* in the royal codex, folio 143, column 4.

At one time it was in the law of the English—that is, in their law—that the people and the laws were governed by counsel. At that time there were wise men of the people, men of very great name and worth: the count, the *villanus*, the thane, and others, each according to his rank.

If a *villanus* had increased in status so that he fully possessed five hides of his own land, a church and a kitchen, a bell-tower, a gate, a seat, and a bell or horn-call in the king’s hall, he was thereafter worthy of the rank of a thane.

If a thane rose so as to serve the king, and performed the duty of cavalry service in his household, and if he then had a thane who possessed five hides [at the corrupt reading *ad ut Waram regis*] and served his lord in the king’s hall, and who had come three times as his messenger to the king, that man could thereafter swear on behalf of his lord in a great necessity and rightly summon his accuser before the court wherever necessary. Whoever does not have a man promoted in this way must either swear his own case over again or lose it.

If a thane is advanced to the office of *consul*, he shall thereafter be worthy of the justice and honor of a count. If a *massere*, that is, a merchant, rose so as to cross the great sea three times, he became thereafter worthy of the justice due to a thane through his own business.

If a scholar advanced in learning, passed into holy orders, [Col. 0470B] and ministered to Christ the Lord, he was finally worthy of as much dignity and peace as belonged to that rank, unless he committed a forfeiture by failing to use the office of that order.

If it happened that an ordained man or a foreigner was disturbed somewhere by words or deeds, it belonged to the king and the bishop to compensate him as quickly as they could.

The *wergild* of a *ceorl*, that is, the valuation of a peasant, is 200 shillings according to the law of the Mercians.

A thane’s *wergild* is six times as much, that is, 1,200 shillings.

The king’s single *wergild* is six thanes’ *wergilds* according to Mercian law: this is thirty thousand *sceattas*, that is, altogether 120 pounds. That is the amount of the *wer*, but because of the dignity of the kingdom an equal amount must be added as *cyningild*. His *wer* belongs to his relatives, and the compensation for him belongs to the people of the land.

The oath of a *twelfhynd* man [Note: [Col. 0470D] Valued at 1,290 shillings.] counts, in opposition, as the oath of six *villani*, because if a *twelfhynd* man must be avenged, full vengeance would be exacted through six *ceorls*, and his *wergild* is the *wergild* of six *ceorls*.

The oath of a priest and of a secular thane is considered equally valuable in the king of the English, and, on account of the seven orders of the Church through which a priest rises by God’s gift to possess them, he is worthy of a thane’s justice.

1. There are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and seven grades of the Church and of the holy orders, and seven times a day praises are to be sung to God by the whole Church. It rightly belongs to all God’s friends to love and honor the holy Church and gladly to protect God’s ministers in peace. Whoever harms them by word or deed shall make compensation sevenfold, according to what has been done and according to the rank involved, if he wishes to have God’s mercy, because holy things and orders, and houses dedicated to God, must always be diligently revered out of fear of God.

2. For compensation according to rank, if an ordained man is killed, beyond the proper *wer* let one pound be paid for the first grade, [Col. 0471A] and let worthy penance be diligently sought.

3. For compensation according to rank, if life is lost, beyond the proper *wer* let two pounds be paid for the second grade, together with penance worthy before God. [lacuna]

4. [lacuna]

5. For compensation according to rank, if a complete violation occurs, beyond the proper *wer* let four pounds be paid for the fourth grade, together with penance.

6. For compensation according to rank, beyond the proper *wer* let five pounds be paid for the fifth grade, together with suitable penance.

7. For the sixth grade, let six pounds be paid together with penance.

8. For compensation according to rank, if the seventh grade is violated, let compensation be made by seven pounds beyond the proper *wer*, together with the penance imposed.

[Col. 0472A]

9. For compensation according to rank [supplement: “compensation”], let a violation of peace be suitably settled according to what was done. Judgment must always be rendered, and moderation according to measure must be exercised for God and the world. Of the compensation according to rank, one part belongs to the bishop, the second to the altar, and the third to the fellowship. See above under the title “Concerning compensation for holy orders.”

And in the council of the bishops of London, chapter 12, this is found concerning members of a *congild*:

“And we have also said to all those who have given security in our *gildscir* [fellowship]: if it happens that one of them dies, every member of the *congild* shall give one loaf and an accompaniment of food for his soul, and shall sing one fifty-psalm service, or arrange for it to be sung within thirty nights.” Jornhal, folio 44.

# THE ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS OF HOEL DHA, KING OR PRINCE OF ALL WALES

(circa 940)

[Col. 0471]

## ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS

[Col. 0471C]

By God’s providence, Howel Dha [Note: [Col. 0471D] That is, “the Good,”] son of Cadell and king of all Cambria, seeing his Welsh subjects abuse the laws insolently, summoned from every *kemut*—that is, hundred—of his entire kingdom six laymen distinguished by authority and knowledge, together with all the ecclesiastics of rank in his kingdom: those bearing pastoral staffs, archbishops, bishops, abbots, and priors. He summoned them to a place called Guin on the Taff in Deheubarth, where he had ordered a house to be built of white rods as a lodging for himself when he came into the regions of Dyfed; for this reason it is called *Ty Guyn*.

The king and those assembled remained there throughout Lent, praying to the Most High through a complete fast and asking for grace to do good according to the king’s purpose. From those assembled the king selected twelve of the most learned laymen and one very learned cleric, called Blangoridus, to instruct him concerning laws and customs, so that he might aim more closely at truth and justice. He ordered them to be written in three parts: the first, the daily law of his court; the second, the law of the country; and the third, the customs of both. He ordered three identical lawbooks to be made: one always to accompany his daily court, another for the court at Dinewr, and a third for the court at Aberfrau, or for whichever of the three regions of Wales it might be—namely Gwynedd, Powys, and Deheubarth—so that it would possess the authority of the law ready for use.

[Col. 0472C]

### I

When the *distein*, that is, the prefect or steward, has stood in the hall after dinner on the three principal feasts, establishing peace there—the peace of the king, the queen, and the nobles of the court—whoever violates that peace shall have no refuge anywhere, and [the text is corrupt: “*navt. tc' n' omnium refugium*”]. If anyone therefore violates the refuge of the king and of all, he can be defended nowhere, neither by the refuge of one person nor by that of the remaining saints, except by the Church.

### II

Whoever commits *sarhaed*, that is, an injury, against a priest, or kills him, shall be punished by the judgment of the synod, apart from *gueli tanavd*.

### III

The lodging of the priest and clerics shall be the house of the village chaplain. The priest of the queen shall lodge there as well.

### IV

The *offeirad euleu*, that is, the king’s priest, shall have garments for the king’s Easter such as he used during Lent.

### V

Likewise, the queen’s priest shall have the garments in which the queen performs penance. The queen’s priest must receive a horse from the queen. Horses for the priest, the falconer, the *penkynyl*, the court judge, and the *guvastraud afvyn* are restored by the king whenever necessary. He shall hold his land free.

### VI

The court priest’s office in legal proceedings is threefold: to remove from the written record disputes that have been properly settled; to preserve unresolved disputes in writing for judgment; and, for the king’s business, to be ready regarding letters sent and to be sent, and never to be drunk.

[Col. 0473A]

### VII

Three matters belong to the judge: to resolve questions, to distinguish disputes, and to confirm by security what he has determined by judgment, if the litigant then contradicts him by another [claim]. This is his activity throughout the year.

When the year has elapsed, the chaplain shall go to the church, accompanied by the twelve more distinguished officials of the court. After Mass has been celebrated and everyone has made an offering at Mass, the chaplain shall make him swear by the sacred rite that has been celebrated, by the altar, and by the relics placed upon it, that throughout his life he will knowingly make no false judgment, neither through entreaty, nor payment, nor love, nor hatred.

After this has been done, they shall come to the king and report to him what has taken place concerning the judge. If the king approves his office, he shall confirm him in it, and he shall be placed in the seat due to him. Then he shall receive *ouer elysseu*; from the king, a *taulbord*; and from the queen, a gold ring. He shall neither sell nor ever give away these gifts. No one ought to be a judge unless he has been approved in such a solemnity.

### VIII

If any ecclesiastic belonging to the kin of a murderer or of a slain person is bound by holy orders or religious profession, or is a leper, mute, or foolish, he shall neither pay nor receive anything for *galanas*, that is, the price of a homicide. No vengeance on account of the slain person is to be exercised against them or by them, lest such persons be compelled by this law in any way to pay or receive anything.

### IX

If a thief, before a priest, makes known the names of his accomplices and confirms it by oath at the door of the cemetery and at the door of the choir, whatever afterward happens concerning him, the priest’s word concerning that statement is to be believed without dispute.

The same procedure applies when someone, for a reward, names the thief who stole an object and does this before a priest in the manner described above. If someone is accused of plundering another and denies it, he has to deny it by the oath of fifty men.

Among these there is one man whose word alone is believed, namely *Managur*, the declarant, together with the testimony of a priest, provided that he comes with the person who suffered the loss before the priest at the church. The priest shall admonish him in the same way, forbidding him, for God’s sake, to lead the matter into falsehood. He shall do this at the church door, if the man swears there that he is speaking the truth and not falsehood. He shall do likewise at the entrance to the chancel, and afterward the same thing upon the altar.

If the person accused still denies it, the priest shall affirm three times by his word what he saw and heard, and shall confirm it once by oath. After this, the person who had previously denied it shall be regarded as confessing and will not be able to contradict it. The one who made the accusation shall immediately receive his reward, and the testimony of the priest who confirms the declarant’s oath shall not be contradicted. The person is regarded as confessing, and this is called *dogynuariac*.

### X

There are three kinds of *dirwy*, that is, fines: one for fighting, another for *treis*, that is, abduction, and the third for theft. The *dirvy* and the *camlurv* are each doubled, in the court and in the church.

If the church fine is the higher one, for fighting that takes place in the cemetery fourteen pounds are to be paid. If it occurs outside, that is, in the *nodva* or asylum, seven pounds are to be paid. Half of these pounds belongs to the abbot, if he is legally qualified—that is, instructed and literate in ecclesiastical doctrine—and the other half belongs to the priest and canons serving God there.

Such a division shall apply between the abbot and the priests concerning fighting by those, namely, *navtur*, that is, refuge, who have received refuge from the abbot and priest. Everything given solely to the saint, and not to another person or to another abbot, is divided in this way. In a fight in the *nodva*, blood and *cleis* shall stand as witnesses for the abbot and priests according to the ecclesiastical dignity of the abbey.

### XI

The tongue is worth as much as all the limbs. The total value of all the limbs is eighty-eight pounds. The blood of any human being is priced at twenty-four pence. The price of Christ’s blood is thirty pence; that is, it seems unworthy that God’s blood should be of less value than a human being’s.

### XII

For three reasons a wife may separate from her husband and retain her *egveti*, that is, her dowry: if her husband is infected with leprosy, if he has foul breath, or if he is unable to have intercourse with her.

If the husband has known another woman, the wife shall receive *vynebwerth*, that is, compensation, three times: the first time, half a pound; the second, one pound; the third time, with all her rights, she may openly or freely depart from him. But if she patiently endures it beyond the third time, she shall no longer have *vynebwerth*.

*Redwit* says that the third time she receives thirty shillings; the fourth time she departs free, with all her rights. If she patiently endures it thereafter, she shall no longer have *vynebwerth*.

### XIII

When the proper time comes for a girl’s *cowll*, a type of garment, to be purchased, unless she declares her will about it in the morning, before she rises from bed with the man, it shall be held in common between the man and the woman.

If a girl of marriageable age is given to a man and the man says that he received her after another man had deflowered her, the girl, if she can, shall establish by the oath of five people—namely, her father, mother, brother, sister, and her own oath—that this is false and that she came to him undefiled. This means that she is mature in pubic hair and breasts, and that her menstruation, that is, her *teithi*, has come, indicating the age of *gveric*, or puberty.

If he is silent at first, then knows her on the second occasion, and sleeps with her until morning, even if he first finds her defiled, he can take nothing from the girl’s legal rights. But if he learns this immediately, rises and goes before the wedding men, and testifies to them, with no one contradicting it, he shall not owe her anything by law.

### XIV

If someone’s wife is accused of infidelity with another man, but the matter remains uncertain, let her clear herself by the oath of seven women. If she is accused a second time, let her do so with fourteen. If it is said a third time with some certainty, she shall clear herself by the oath of fifty women.

### XV

If a woman has *datores* [reading or meaning uncertain], the husband shall remain under her dowry for seven years. If he has completed three nights of the seventh year, the woman shall have half of all his property upon their divorce.

The property shall be divided in this way: the man shall have the cattle, and the woman the sheep. Afterward the woman shall divide, and the man shall choose.

First, let the household goods be divided as follows. All milk vessels except one *sinus*, that is, a woman’s *bacol*, shall belong to the woman, and she shall have all the dishes except one; [lacuna] those two shall belong to the man. The cart with one yoke, all drinking vessels, and the casks shall belong to the man; whatever is above them shall belong to the woman.

If the man immediately takes another wife, he must send away the clothing of the first bed, that is, of the woman repudiated. The man shall have the cauldron and the carpet, that is, the *brycan* and cushion, and the knife, the wood axe, the auger, etc.

### XVI

If a man repudiates his wife without legal cause and brings another woman over her, the repudiated wife shall by right return to the house and remain there for nine days. On the ninth day, if she is entirely dismissed by the man, all that belongs to her shall first leave the house, and she herself shall leave the house last with her possessions.

Afterward the man shall proclaim *dilys*, that is, a repudiation, against the repudiated woman, having brought in another, because by right no one ought to have two wives at the same time.

If anyone dismisses his wife and afterward regrets what he has done, but she has been given to another man, then, if the first husband can touch one of her feet while she lies in bed with the other man and the other foot is outside, the first husband ought by right to recover her.

### XVII

If a woman denies adultery, let her give the oath of fifty women. Likewise, if the adulterer denies it, let him give the oath of fifty men.

Such an oath is given for three reasons: if the woman is seen coming from one side of a grove and the man coming from the other side of the same grove at the same hour; if they are seen lying together under one cloak; or if the man is seen between the woman’s thighs.

### XVIII

If any woman has done something shameful with another man, whether by a kiss, by the hand, or by intercourse, she may legally be repudiated by her husband and must lose all her rights—even for a single kiss, not to mention the other acts.

For intercourse, the adulterer shall pay the injury with one *elevation* to the man whose wife he has violated, because this belongs to the category of hostility. For manual touching of the vulva, which is called *govys*, he shall pay the injury without an elevation. For a kiss alone, the adulterer shall pay the injury, but one-third of the injury shall be deducted, because he did not have complete relations with her and did it for the purpose of deceiving her. So some say; others, however, say that, unless they follow it, the matter is determined according to however the act was performed [reading uncertain].

### XIX

Whoever kisses another man’s wife shall pay him one quarter of the injury. The same applies to *govys*, except in a game called *guare raffau*, at a feast, or when someone has come from far away.

### XX

Goronwy ap Morydyc said that a man who abuses another man’s wife with her consent owes nothing, so long as the woman praises the author of her deed. But if the act becomes known, the woman must render *saraed* to her husband, or the husband may freely repudiate her and separate from her.

### XXI

No one shall give a woman to a man before obtaining from him a guarantor for the payment due to the lord. A girl is said to be the king’s property, and therefore the king is entitled to receive from her *amaabyr*, that is, the price of virginity.

If anyone takes a woman in *lathrud*, that is, the abduction of women, and goes with her to the house of a nobleman, the nobleman must obtain from the man, before they sleep together, a guarantor for the abducted woman’s entire legal right.

### XXII

There are three men whom no one may take as surety through the king against any judgment.

The first is the king, when he cannot stand in a dispute before his judge according to the law, whether bringing or answering a case, by his natural dignity or by the dignity of the land, as a nobleman or anyone else.

The second is an ecclesiastic bound by holy orders.

The third is an ecclesiastic bound by religious profession.

For according to the law no one may give security against a judgment except under the risk of the price of his tongue. But no price is established in Howel’s law for a limb and blood, or for the *saraed* of an ecclesiastic such as those mentioned above. Therefore none of them may legally give security against a judgment or together with a judgment. All sacrilegious injuries inflicted upon ecclesiastics must be compensated in a synod according to ecclesiastical law.

### XXIII

There are three men, none of whom can by law be a worthy judge.

The first is a defective person, that is, an *anavus*, or a blind, deaf, leprous, or foolish person; one who has once been bound because of his foolishness, that is, a *goyffvyllauc*; one who does not know how to speak correctly; or a *cryc anennual* [terms unclear in the supplied text].

The second is an ecclesiastic bound by holy orders or religious profession.

The third [Col. 0476C] is a layman without the power to judge by reason of the dignity of the land or of service.

### XXIV

There are three kinds of claimants in a case who are to be punished by the king on account of their complaints. The first is one who gives a pledge against a judgment that can be confirmed against him by another [kind of] evidence, namely *ghurgvystyl*, and by written authority from the laws; he is to be punished by the price of his tongue. The second is one who gives a pledge against a judgment that is given concerning someone other than himself; he is to be punished by his *camlvrv* (that is, a fine). The third is one who lacks the dignity to give a pledge, namely a priest or another such person: he is permitted to contradict a judgment by authority from the laws; but if he so contradicts it and the authority fails him, he shall lose his *camlvrv*. No one, however, shall lose more than a *camlvrv* through contentious litigation, unless it is a genuine pledging, pledge against pledge.

[Col. 0476D]

### XXV

It is found in Roman law: “Where the number of witnesses is not defined, two are sufficient.” The law also says: “The testimony of one person is not to be admitted.” This, however, is said because there are nine men whose testimony, each individually and only each individually, is to be believed, though under oath.

The first is a lord between two men, provided that he is not a party to the litigation or to the property to be obtained from the litigation, and that they acknowledge that their dispute previously took place before their lord, and that there was no *undull* (that is, uniformity or agreement). But if one of them denies it, he shall deny it under oath. In another case, nine days are granted to the lord [Col. 0477A] to reckon how he gave the oath; to a priest, however, an interval is granted for the same purpose until the time when he can celebrate Mass.

The second is a patron priest between two of his parishioners, or between two of his monks.

The third is a father between two of his sons, placing his hand upon the head of the one against whom he testifies and saying: “By the Lord who created me from my father, and you from me, I speak the truth between you.”

The fourth is a judge concerning his own judgment, namely when those who doubt the judgment he gave between them contend with one another.

The fifth is a surety concerning his suretyship, if he partly denies and partly acknowledges it.

The sixth is a priest concerning testimony given about him between two of his parishioners.

The seventh is a girl concerning her virginity, if the man to whom she was given says [Col. 0477B] that he found her corrupted, in order to deprive her of her right; nevertheless, the right belongs to her, and she is to be believed before she has reached maturity. Likewise concerning a girl, if she has been overcome by force and the violator says that he found her deflowered, her testimony is to be believed against him.

The eighth is the common shepherd of a village concerning an animal killed by another among the animals entrusted to his keeping.

The ninth is a thief led to the gallows and certain of his death: his words, without an oath—that is, *creir*—concerning his companion or companions, or concerning the property he himself stole, are to be believed. That companion, however, is not to be condemned to loss of life or limb on account of the other’s statement. From the words of the man who is hanged, nevertheless, it is made clear that he is a thief, and he is to be believed, as this law provides. He is therefore to be condemned, not to lose [Col. 0477C] life or limb, but to make a redemption for himself. Concerning that thief who, after an oath has been established in the country, cannot purge himself of theft: “He shall be *dirvyus* and *n'lleidyr guverth*.” [Welsh terms; the precise sense is uncertain.]

### XXVI

A surety who denies his suretyship shall deny it by the redemption of the seventh of his nearest kin, or shall swear alone upon seven consecrated altars, *of bri duva divuad* [source wording retained; the sense is uncertain]. If he partly denies and partly confesses, he shall swear alone once, and thus *kynnogyn*, if he has denied the suretyship, namely concerning the seven.

### XXVII

If someone receives a thing from another in the name of a purchase, and then, taken from this life, leaves his property with his friends, while he himself had stood surety for returning the price of the thing received—that is, *yn uach kynnogyn*—the seller may recover the price of his property from the aforesaid friends, even though they were ignorant of the transaction and asleep. He must, however, [Col. 0477D] swear concerning seven of his nearest kin in the matter of redemption over the debtor’s grave, if he can find it; otherwise, over the consecrated altar of the man who sold him his property, and for whom he himself was surety.

### XXVIII

A surety ought not to be given who is an exile, nor one who is more powerful; nor a monk, unless his abbot consents; nor a scholar, unless his teacher consents; nor a woman, unless she is the principal debtor’s mistress; nor a son, unless his father consents, when the father is to stand surety for his son. Although any of them may give surety, the suretyship of none of them is to be compelled.

[Col. 0478A]

### XXIX

There are three things without which the king can exist: namely, a priest to celebrate Mass and to bless the king’s food and drink; a court judge to discern cases and give counsel; and a household prepared for royal business.

### XXX

A wound of the tongue is restored to three men: always to the king; to the judge when someone attempts to go against a judgment; and to the priest when he is in church, or on the three principal feasts.

### XXXI

Wherever the priest, the *distein* (that is, the prefect of the court or steward), and the court judge are together, there shall be the dignity of the court, namely *breint llys* (that is, the royal hall), even if the king is absent.

### XXXII

No king has power to establish a price upon any ecclesiastic bound by sacred orders, or upon his limbs, blood, or *saraed*, or upon any of his people, because every ecclesiastic, as aforesaid, has power under ecclesiastical law to prove in a synod any injury or damage that a layman, the king, or anyone else inflicts upon him. Likewise, such an ecclesiastic can in no way be compelled to answer anyone outside the synod concerning offenses alleged against him.

### XXXIII

But if such an ecclesiastic holds land under the king by tenure, from which service is owed to the king, he must answer in the king’s court concerning the land and its appurtenances, because the whole land of his kingdom belongs to the king; and unless he answers humbly concerning it, that land shall belong entirely to the king. Although such an ecclesiastic may, by the dignity of the land, be present in judgment with laymen until the time comes to recount the matter, he ought not to give any judgment between litigants, because no price has been established by law upon his tongue; by that price every judge is punished if he judges unjustly, when he confirms an unjust judgment by a pledge.

### XXXIV

When a dispute concerns the boundaries of villages or fields that pertain to the court, the court shall settle it; if it concerns the church and not the court, the church shall settle it. Afterwards, *Bremt*, and finally *hyguvarchadu*, that is, *ar deffeith, ty ac odyn ac ysgubaur*. But when it settles *maer* and *kygbellaur*, boundaries are to be assigned on its behalf; for the church, a staff and the Gospel are to serve this purpose. Otherwise, the disputed land is to be divided between the litigants into two parts.

### XXXV

If, with the king’s permission, a church is built in a rural village, Masses are celebrated there, and bodies are buried in its churchyard, then that village shall be free.

### XXXVI

If someone, in the name of the mother church, claims in judgment land belonging to it, the ninth day of the month need not be awaited.

### XXXVII

If a king’s villager, with the king’s approval, undertakes to raise an optimates’ son, then, when the villager dies, the foster-child shall succeed equally with the villager’s sons.

### XXXVIII

If, on the king’s land, the men of a bishop or abbot engage in conflict with the king’s men, their *diruy* (that is, fine or imposition of a fine) shall belong to the king.

### XXXIX

There are seven episcopal houses in Dyfed: Menevia, which is the principal see in Wales; the church of Ishmael; the church of Degeniam; the church of Yssyl; the church of Teilaw; the church of Teulidauc; and the church of Keneu. The abbots of Teilaw, Teulidauc, Ishmael, and Degenian are required to be clerics and ordained. The *ebodiu* of each of these shall belong to the lord of Dyfed, namely twelve pounds, or those who succeed them shall pay it. Menevia remains free and released from every debt. The church of Keneu [Col. 0480A] and the church of Yssyl shall be free from that debt, since they lack lands.

### XL

No dispute is to be brought concerning the redemption of theft in any matter unless there has first been a *manac* under oath in three places: at the cemetery gate, at the church gate, and at the choir door, before the priest of that church; and that priest must have testified to this in the lord’s court, whose word is then to be believed. Concerning theft—that is, *communicatio*—there shall be no dispute about an oath, that is, *reith*, concerning anything, unless there has first been a *manac* in the court.

## THE ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS OF EDMUND, KING OF THE ENGLISH

*(Circa 944.)*

[Col. 0479]

### [ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS]

### TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS OF PART I

[Col. 0479B]

I. On the chastity of those who enter sacred orders.  
II. On tithes and ecclesiastical dues, or the first fruits of seed.  
III. On homicide.  
IV. On the man who violates a nun, and on adultery.  
V. On the restoration of a sanctuary.  
VI. On perjurers and those who perform barbarous sacrifices.

*(Part II contributes nothing here.)*

### TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS OF PART III

I. On homicide.  
II. On one who attacks another in a sacred building or royal town.  
III. On the fines for fighting and homicide.  
IV. On bloodshed.  
V. He gives thanks because they helped him suppress thieves.

## PART ONE

### PREFACE

King Edmund celebrated a well-attended assembly at London on the solemn feast of Easter, composed of both ecclesiastics and laymen. Oda and Wulstan, archbishops, and many other bishops were present, so that provision might be made for the salvation of their souls and of all those entrusted to their care.

### CHAPTERS

I. First of all, those who have entered sacred orders, and from whom the people of God ought to seek an example of virtue for imitation, whether they are men or women, shall lead chaste lives, as the rule of their order requires. If they do not do so, they shall be punished according to the standards governing them: while alive, they shall be deprived of all their earthly property, and, unless they amend their conduct for the better, when dead they shall be denied sacred burial.

[Col. 0480B]

II. Every Christian shall religiously pay tithes of his seed, the first fruits, and the alms-penny; whoever does not pay shall be anathema.

III. If anyone sheds the blood of a Christian man, he shall not be admitted to the king’s presence, even if he serves him, until he has compensated for that crime in accordance with what the bishop commands him.

IV. If anyone violates a nun, let him either make compensation as a homicide or be denied sacred burial. The same law shall apply if anyone violates a marriage by committing adultery.

V. Every bishop shall restore the house of God at his own expense, and shall admonish the king to have the remaining sacred buildings suitably adorned, since this is very necessary.

[Col. 0480C]

VI. Those who commit perjury or perform barbarous sacrifices shall be excluded forever from all divine things, unless they quickly repent and amend their minds for the better.

*(Part II is omitted because it does not concern ecclesiastical matters.)*

## PART THREE

### PREFACE

I, Edmund, king, clearly declare to all who are under my authority and power, old and young alike, that I diligently asked the most learned men of my kingdom, in a distinguished gathering of both ecclesiastics and laymen, by what means the Christian faith might at last be advanced. It seemed most beneficial to all of us that we should foster love and mutual goodwill among everyone throughout our entire dominion. For we are all weary of these daily conflicts, and therefore have established the following arrangement.

### CHAPTERS

I. If anyone henceforth kills another, he alone shall undertake the deadly feud with the dead man’s relatives, unless, relying on the help of his friends, he pays within twelve months the full valuation of his life, whatever his status may have been. But if his relatives abandon him and are unwilling to pay anything, he alone shall immediately undertake the feud, and they shall not be regarded as enemies. Meanwhile, however, his relatives shall neither provide him with food nor make peace with him; and if any one of them does so, he shall be fined all his property to the king. The man who previously abandoned his kinsman shall then be regarded as an enemy by the relatives of the slain man. But if any of the kinsmen takes revenge upon and pursues anyone other than the killer himself, he shall be fined all his property and regarded as an enemy by the king and by everyone who loves him.

II. If anyone takes refuge in a temple or royal town, and another attacks or harms him there, the offender shall be liable according to what we stated above.

III. No fine imposed for fighting or homicide shall be remitted.

IV. I clearly declare that my house shall not be a refuge for anyone who has shed human blood until he has made full satisfaction to God and to the relatives of the slain person, and has moreover fulfilled whatever the bishop in whose diocese it occurred has ordered him to do.

V. I give the greatest thanks to God and to all of you who have assisted me with your help in this law of peace, which we have now enacted for the suppression of thieves; and I strongly trust that you will assist us in the future with even greater eagerness, as the necessity of observing this decree becomes more apparent.

## How a Virgin Is to Be Betrothed, and What Rites Are to Be Observed

[Note: [Col. 0481C] These have been added from another manuscript.]

I. If anyone wishes to take a virgin or a woman in marriage, with her consent and that of her friends, it is required both by divine law and by human institution that the bridegroom first not only give assurance that he will fulfill what has been discussed, but also give a pledge that he desires her in such a way that, according to God’s law, he will have her as his wife; and her friends shall likewise stand surety for this.

II. Then provision must be made for their maintenance, and it must be determined who will support them. The bridegroom himself shall stipulate this, and his friends likewise.

III. At that time the bridegroom shall declare what portion of his property he gives his wife, apart from that portion which she has previously chosen with his consent.

IV. If she outlives him—which, indeed, may happen—then it is just that she should have half of all the property; and if they have had children together, she shall have the whole of it until she enters a second marriage.

[Col. 0482B]

V. The husband shall always preserve intact the promises he has already made, after giving security for them, and his friends shall stand surety for them.

VI. If they have now agreed on everything between them, the kinsmen shall promise their kinswoman as wife to the man who has sought her, and shall receive security that the marriage will be celebrated.

VII. If the husband later takes her from the territory of the thane [or baron] in which she was raised into the territory of another thane, his friends shall receive a guarantee that no one will inflict injury upon her thereafter. If she herself commits some wrongdoing, her friends shall be ready to make compensation to her husband, if she does not have the means by which to compensate him.

[Col. 0482C]

VIII. A priest shall attend this marriage-giving with a missal; by law, he shall advance their union through God’s blessing into the fullness of all happiness.

IX. Care must also be taken to establish that there is no bond of kinship between them, lest those who were first joined unlawfully later be separated justly.

## THE ANCIENT VERSION OF EDMUND’S ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS

### TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS OF PART I

[Col. 0481D]

I. On the chastity of the ordained.  
II. On tithes and other dues owed to the church.  
III. On homicide.  
IV. On fornication with a nun or holy woman, and on adultery.  
V. On the appearance of churches [the source reading is uncertain].  
VI. On perjury and *liblaco*.

### PREFACE

King Edmund gathered a great synod of the order of God and of the secular world at the city of London on the holy solemnity of Easter. Odo and Wulstan, archbishops, and many other bishops were present, seeking counsel for our souls and for those subject to them.

[Col. 0482D]

### CHAPTERS

I. First, those raised to holy orders, who ought to teach the people of God the light of life, shall maintain chastity according to their order—whether they are *werhades* or *wifhades*, whether one or the other [the terms appear to distinguish male and female orders; wording uncertain]. They shall be worthy of what is stated in the canon: namely, they shall lose their secular money and the consecrated *legerstowa* (that is, the burial place), the place of interment, if they do not repent and amend.

II. We command every Christian to give a tithe concerning his Christianity, and to pay the *cyricsceat*, that is, the church tax, and *elmesfeoh*, that is, alms-money. If anyone refuses to give this, let him be excommunicated.

III. If anyone with criminal hands sheds Christian blood, let him not appear in the king’s presence until he undertakes compensation, as the bishop shall teach, and observes the prescribed penance.

IV. Whoever fornicates with a nun or holy woman shall be unworthy of the consecrated churchyard unless he makes compensation, as a homicide does. We have said the same concerning *ewice* (read *cuvbrice*), that is, adultery or a broken marriage.

V. I further decree that every bishop shall repair the houses of God at his own expense and shall admonish the king that all the churches of God be properly prepared, as this is a great necessity for us.

VI. Those who swear falsely and perform *liblacum* shall be separated forever from the fellowship of God unless they return in every respect to worthy satisfaction.

*(Part II contributes nothing here.)*

### TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS OF PART III

I. On homicide.  
II. On an assault on the road toward a church or the king’s borough.  
III. On *fihtewita* and *manbota*.  
IV. On those who shed human blood.

### PREFACE

I, Edmund, king, command and prescribe to all the people, old and young, who are in my territory, what I have investigated after inquiry with the wise clerics and laymen.

### CHAPTERS

[Col. 0483C]

I. First, concerning how I might raise Christianity more fully: it seemed greatly necessary to us that we maintain your friendship and goodwill among you throughout my entire kingdom. The numerous and unjust fights that occur among you are extremely displeasing both to me and to all of you. Therefore we have said: If anyone henceforth kills a man, he himself shall bear the making of the feud, unless, with the assistance of his friends, he pays the full *weregild* within one [term; the source is incomplete], whatever the man’s birth may have been. If his kin abandon him and are unwilling to pay the *gild* for him, then I wish the whole tribe or kindred, except the evildoer alone, to be outside the feud; but thereafter they shall give him neither food nor peace. If anyone of his kindred later supports him, he shall be liable to the king for everything he possesses and shall bear the *fudam* against his fellow tribesmen, because at first he had rejected him.

If anyone from the kindred of the dead man exacts vengeance upon anyone other than the evildoer himself, let him be the king’s enemy and let him lose everything he possesses.

II. If anyone seeks a church or my borough, and is attacked or harmed there, whoever does this shall be guilty according to what was stated above.

III. I do not wish any *fihtewita* or *manbota* to be forgiven.

IV. I further declare that I do not wish anyone who sheds human blood to have *socn*—protection or right of attendance—in my household until he has received divine compensation and submitted to every right, as the bishop shall teach in whose *scyra*—shire or diocese—he is.

[Col. 0484A]

## On Contracts of Betrothal in the Time of King Edmund

*(From the Jornalensis book.)*

If anyone wishes to take a virgin or widow in marriage, and this pleases her and her friends, then it is right that the *bridguinum*, by the justice of God and the applicable law of the secular world, should first promise and give security to those who are the bride’s representatives (*paranymphs*) that he seeks her in such a way that he wishes her to belong to him according to God’s law, as a bridegroom ought to have a legitimate bride; and his friends shall pledge this.

Afterward, it must be determined to whom the *fosterleanum* belongs. This the *bridguina*, that is, the bridegroom, shall guarantee: what he intends to give her, why he chooses her will, and what he assigns to her if she outlives him. If they agree on this as well, it is right that she should have half the property, and all of it if they have a child together, unless she thereafter takes another husband.

All this shall be confirmed by a pledge, and his friends shall stand surety. If they then agree on everything, the kindred shall approach and betroth her *to wyte and toryghtlyte*, that is, as a wife and for a right life, and shall receive a pledge from the person who has the right under the security.

But if he wishes to take her from this land into the land of another thane, it is advised that her friends make an agreement that no one will inflict injury upon her. If she commits an offense, they should be able to be closer to making compensation, if she has no means by which to pay.

A priest ought to attend this marriage-giving; with God’s blessing he ought to assist their union in all holiness. It is good to take care that they are not related by blood, lest those who consented to a wicked marriage later be separated justly.

## ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS CONCERNING MARRIAGE

[Col. 0484C]

*(Rochester text, from the new version.)*

### How a Virgin Is to Be Betrothed, and What Rites Are to Be Observed

I. If anyone wishes to take a virgin or a wife in marriage, and this pleases her and her friends, then it is right that the bridegroom, according to God’s law and the institutions of the world, should first give a promise and pledge to the man who is their spokesman (*paranymphus*) that he desires her in such a way that he intends to maintain her according to God’s law, as a man ought to maintain his wife; and his friends shall promise this.

II. Afterwards it must be determined to whom the provision of food belongs; the bridegroom shall then promise this, and his friends shall stand surety.

III. Subsequently the bridegroom shall declare what he is to give her because she has chosen his will, and what he will give her if she outlives him.

IV. If this has been agreed and contracted in this manner, then it is right that she should have half the property, and all of it if they have children together, unless she later chooses another husband.

V. Let him confirm by pledge everything he has promised, and let his friends stand surety.

VI. If they then agree on everything, let the kinsmen approach and promise their kinswoman as wife, and for a right life, to the man who desires her; and let them receive the surety who has the right under the pledge.

VII. If he wishes to take her from that land into the region of another thane, then his pledge shall be that which her friends agree upon: that her husband will inflict no injury upon her; and if she commits an offense, her relatives shall make compensation if she has no means by which to compensate.

VIII. A priest shall attend the marriage; by right, with God’s blessing, he shall join their union in the fullness of every happiness.

IX. It is also good to take care that it be known whether they are joined by blood relationship, lest those who were formerly joined unlawfully later be separated justly.

## [WORKS OF EDGAR, KING OF THE ENGLISH]

[Col. 0485]

### THE ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS OF EDGAR, KING OF THE ENGLISH

### THE COUNCIL OF BRADFORD, CONVENED BY KING EDGAR

In this council the decrees of King Edwin were rescinded, what had been taken from the Church was restored, and Dunstan was recalled from exile.

[Col. 0485B]

The formal records of the council’s acts are not available; they are briefly noted as follows in *Antiquities of the British Church*, chapter 13:

Meanwhile the Mercians and Northumbrians, and the people between the Humber and the Thames, took up arms against King Edwin. The monks carefully omit who had initiated this disturbance. In this upheaval Edgar, the king’s brother, obtained a portion of the kingdom. After many battles had been fought on both sides, they weakened the strength of the kingdom. But Edgar eventually prevailed and, having summoned a council of the kingdom at Bradford, rescinded the acts and decrees of his brother Edwin, restored the wealth taken from churches and monasteries, and recalled Dunstan from exile to his former honor. He then promoted him, they say, reluctantly and willingly, to the bishopric of Worcester, afterward to London, and finally, scarcely two years having passed, to the archbishopric of Canterbury.

## Privilege by Which King Edgar Confirms That the Church of Canterbury Is the Mother and Mistress of the Other Churches of His Kingdom

*(Given in the year 959, but placed here on account of the preceding council.)*

In the year of the incarnation of the Lord 958 [corrected to 950], I, Edgar, king of the English and, by divine clemency, monarch, renew with an eternal conclusion and strengthen in the Lord Most High the statutes of the ancient kings Æthelberht and his successors, and the privileges of the monasteries of Kent, with the advice and counsel of the venerable archbishop Dunstan, for the curse of impious plunderers—or rather, with God’s favor, for the goodwill and blessing of the just. We decree:

That the Church of Christ at Canterbury shall be the mother and mistress of the other churches [Col. 0486C] of our kingdom, and shall be perpetually free everywhere with all its possessions, except for military service, bridge-building, and fortress-building.

[Col. 0485]

## CHARTER OF KING EDGAR CONCERNING OSWALD’S LAW

That is, concerning the expulsion of married clerics and the introduction of monks.

*(Year 964.)*

[Col. 0485D]

By the bountiful clemency of the high-thundering God, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, I, Edgar, basileus of the English, and emperor and lord of all the kings of the islands of the Ocean that surround Britain, and of all the nations enclosed within it, give thanks to that almighty God, my king, who has so enlarged and exalted my empire over [Col. 0486D] the kingdom of my fathers. Although they attained the monarchy of all England, from the time of Æthelstan, the first of the kings of the English to subdue by arms all the nations inhabiting Britain, none of them nevertheless attempted to extend his rule beyond its borders.

But favorable divinity has granted me, together with the empire of the English, to subject to the kingdom of the English all the kingdoms of the islands of the Ocean with their fiercest kings, as far as Norway, and the greater part of Ireland with its most noble city, Dublin. With God’s favor, I have compelled all of them to submit their necks to my commands.

Therefore I devoutly resolved to exalt the glory and praise of Christ in my kingdom and to enlarge his service. Through my faithful supporters—namely, Dunstan the archbishop, and Æthelwold and Oswald the bishops, whom I chose as my spiritual fathers and counselors—I have for the most part accomplished what I resolved, and so forth.

Indeed, in the times of my predecessors, the kings of the English, monasteries both of monks and of virgins had been destroyed and utterly cast down throughout all [Col. 0487B] England. I vowed to restore them for the praise of God and the salvation of my soul, and to multiply the number of God’s male and female servants. With the vigorous efforts of my aforesaid cooperators, I have now established forty-seven monasteries with monks and holy women; and if Christ grants me life for so long, I have resolved to extend the offering of my devout generosity to the fiftieth number of remission—that is, the jubilee.

Accordingly, at the present time, the monastery which the aforesaid reverend bishop Oswald enlarged at the episcopal seat of Worcester in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, after removing the dirges and filthy wantonness of the clerics, and installed religious monks, God’s servants, with my consent and support [variant: “with my consent and assistance”], I confirm to those men of monastic religion by royal authority. With the counsel and assent of my princes and nobles, I strengthen and seal it, [Col. 0488A] so that from now on it shall be neither lawful nor right for the clerics to claim anything from it. They chose instead, at the risk of their order and to the detriment of their ecclesiastical benefice, to cling to their wives rather than serve God chastely and canonically.

Therefore everything that they possessed from the church, together with the church itself—whether ecclesiastical or secular, movable or immovable—I transfer and consign from this day forward to those monks, God’s servants, to be held perpetually by right of royal generosity. I establish this so firmly that no prince, nor even any succeeding bishop, shall have the right or permission to remove or seize anything from it, or to take it away from their authority and restore it to the possession of clerics, for as long as the Christian faith endures in England, and so forth.

[Col. 0488B]

These things were done in the year of the incarnation of the Lord 964, in the eighth indiction, in the sixth year of the reign of Edgar, king of the English, in the royal city which by its inhabitants is called . . . [lacuna], on the Nativity of the Lord, the feast of the Holy Innocents, on Wednesday.

### SUBSCRIPTIONS

I, Edgar, basileus of the English and emperor of the kings of nations, with the consent of my princes and archbishops, strengthen this gift with the sign of the cross.

I, Ælfrith, queen, consented and confirmed it with the sign of the cross.

I, Dunstan, archbishop of the Church of Christ at Canterbury, consented and subscribed.

I, Oscytel, archbishop of the Church of York, [Col. 0488C] consented and subscribed.

I, Ælfric, duke.

I, Bruthnod, duke.

I, Æthelgar, duke.

[Col. 0487]

## CHARTER OF KING EDGAR TO THE NEW MONASTERY OF WINCHESTER, CALLED HYDE

Granted to it, this charter recounts the creation and fall of the angels, and the making of man to take possession, with his offspring, of the place now left vacant in their order. The devil, it says, envies this and, after being deceived by fraud, makes man and his offspring like himself; Christ, taking pity on them, redeemed them. Among these is King Edgar, who, seized by such great kindness, pours himself out entirely in gratitude and good works. Therefore he establishes many monasteries for Christ and his household, including this one at Winchester, and imposes upon its monks rules of life and integrity, both ecclesiastical and secular.

*(Year 966.)*

[Col. 0487D]

[Note: [Col. 0487] From the chronicle of the monastery of Winchester, which was called Hyde.]

Here begins the charter of the privilege granted by Edgar, the most merciful prince, to the new monastery at Winchester, now called Hyde; its rubric is thus erased:

“King Edgar issued this privilege to the new monastery and granted to almighty God and his mother Mary the great works of his praise.”

### CHAPTER I

The Almighty, creator of the whole universe, in ineffable mercy wonderfully governs all that he has created. With the coeternal Word, he produced some things from nothing, while, as a subtle craftsman, he brought forth others from unformed matter.

The angelic creature, like unformed matter, when no other things yet existed, was formed by God and shone with a radiant face. But, alas, using its free will wickedly, arrogantly puffed up with stubborn pride, disdaining to serve the Creator of the universe, and making itself equal to the Creator, it was plunged with its companions into the fires of the eternal abyss and is justly tormented by perpetual misery. From this theme, then, the sin of all wickedness began.

### II. Why He Created Man and What He Entrusted to Him

When the heavenly seat had been emptied and the filth of swollen pride expelled, the supreme Arbiter of all goodness did not allow the radiant seats of heaven to grow idle without a worshipper. Having formed the various kinds of things from unformed matter, he finally formed man from clay and, by the breath of life, fashioned him in his own likeness. Having subjected to him the whole surface of the universe that he had created, he subjected man himself and his descendants to himself, so that his posterity, carrying out his purpose, might fill the number of the angels who had been thrust down from the seats of heaven because of their pride.

### III. How He Lived in Paradise Without Sin

Placed amid the pleasantness of paradise, he suffered no deprivation of anything; rather, the resources of the whole world supplied his wishes. For, enjoying the abundance of every good, he encountered no resistant obstacle. While he obediently loved the Most High, every creature served him in submission. He rejoiced in the Creator’s delight and gladly enjoyed the companionship of the angels. Bodily weakness did not enfeeble him, nor did anxiety afflict his mind. He was not carried away by the light-headed pride of vanity; rather, joining himself to his author, he flourished wondrously in humility. Empty glory did not trouble him with swelling pride; rather, remembrance of the Creator magnified his devotion. Envy did not torment him at another’s advancement; rather, charity continually rejoiced in embrace. He was not tortured by hostile anger; rather, he was relieved by the tranquility of charity and great patience. Sadness did not cast him down in grief; rather, he flourished through the strength of hope in spiritual joy. Avarice did not drive him into excessive desire; rather, he exercised himself most generously in the zeal of liberality. He did not delight in illicit, extravagant food, but, content with moderation, made use of lawful nourishment. Detestable lust did not spur him on; rather, suitable continence restrained him for rewards. As the *polycrates*—the master of all virtues—lacking every adversity and flourishing in every prosperity, he rightly prospered in freedom.

### IV. How He Confidently Expected to Ascend to Heaven Without Death, and How the Envious Devil Prevented Him from Ascending

After offspring had been produced in sufficient number, and with the entire race of the proud angels accompanying him, having tasted the forbidden fruit of the tree, he confidently expected, as a long-lived being, to ascend and reign with the Lord in the heavenly seats of eternal blessedness, threefold [*triniatim*; the precise sense is uncertain]. When the envious Devil observed this, struck by excessive envy, he began craftily and cunningly to search out how he might deceive him by treachery, so that he would not ascend to so great a glory of divinity. Perhaps counting the things granted as nothing, and praising what was forbidden by enticing it excessively, he seduced the very fragile woman. Not content with her own downfall, she charmed her husband, who had been womanishly overcome by flattering persuasion; having tasted the *exili heumalo* [source wording uncertain], she made him like herself and destroyed him.

### V. How, deprived of all virtues in this misery, they are cast down and finally by the cataclysm are . . . [read: “removed,” *dempti*].

At last, deprived of the aforesaid gifts [or: endowments; *odonariis*], both are expelled from the boundaries of paradise [Col. 0490B] and cast down into the utmost misery of the present life. Despising their Creator, they are pursued by all created things. Life came to an end; death took root. As the host of virtues withdrew, a heap of vices succeeded it. As the succession of descendants proceeded, a gathered collection of crimes followed. All, together with their sins, were swept away by the cataclysm; finally, with eight of both sexes preserved, they wasted away and perished. As vices arose in abundance, the Creator regretted having made man. At last, in his mercy toward mortals, he came to their aid, as he had promised.
