## VI. How Christ, when born, redeemed us through his Passion and enabled us to ascend to heaven

The morning star shone forth, driving away the darkness of the world with its ray. Blessed Mary shone resplendently; from her virginal womb Christ was ineffably born, and as the most merciful mediator he removed the darkness of sins. Christ flourished, full of virtues. Judaea, filled with immense rancor, burned fiercely. Taking flesh, he willed to suffer for us; and unhappy Judaea audaciously accomplished this with his permission. For, mounting the gallows of the wood, he redeemed the human race that had been lost through the wood. Indeed, insulting and mocking all the nations of mankind as the devil, he rightly held them as transgressors of the commandment and punished them with perpetual death. But the blood separated the avenger from the dead by the trophy of the cross. He snatched the prey from the mouth of the faithless lion and, carrying it with himself above the heavens, joined it to the assemblies of the angels on high, so that, enjoying common fellowship with him, resplendent in goodness, filled with the abundance of every virtue, free from sin, [Col. 0490D] and cleansed from every contagion, they might reign without end after the day of judgment, rejoicing in restored bodies.

Without doubt he promised this supreme glory to believers who, laboring in good works, follow the faith of the true Trinity and unity; and he most justly threatened unbelievers with eternal punishment, amid the everlasting fires of the abyss.

## VII. On the benevolent king’s meditation

From that point I, Edgar, by the favor of divine grace king of all Albion, began earnestly to consider what works I should undertake, so that, attaining such glory, I might enjoy fellowship with Christ and his saints placed in heaven, crowned among them, and might escape such misery of hell. For, prompted by the Lord’s clemency, it came to my mind that I should myself cease from all crimes and, devoting myself to good works, become an example to the flock, so that I might win those living under the governance of our rule.

Accordingly, inviting some by exhortations to rewards and compelling others by terrors toward glory, I built up what was good and, insofar as the Lord enabled me, scattered what was evil. For I remember that it is written through the prophet Jeremiah: “Behold, I have appointed you over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot, to destroy, to ruin, to overthrow, and to build and to plant” (Jeremiah 1).

Thus instructed by such teachers, through whom the Lord mercifully admonished us by the prophet, and doing on earth, with Christ’s favor, what he himself justly did in heaven, [Col. 0491B] namely, rooting out from the Lord’s cultivated field the filth of crimes, I, a diligent farmer, planted the seeds of virtues.

## VIII. How he expelled the clerics and installed monks

Fearing that I might incur eternal misery if, having obtained power, I failed to do what he made known by his own examples—he who works all that he wills in heaven and on earth, the just examiner—I, Christ’s vicar, expelled the bands of vicious canons from the various monasteries of our realm. They could benefit me through no intercessions; rather, as blessed Gregory says, they provoked the vengeance of the just Judge. Contaminated by the stains of vicarious vices, they did not do what God wished by his commands, but rebelliously did everything he did not wish.

But, observing that bands of monks pleasing to the Lord were eager to intercede unceasingly for us, I devotedly and gladly installed them in the monasteries under our jurisdiction.

## IX. How, moved by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he established an abbot and monks in the new monastery

For this reason, touched by the breath of the Holy Spirit and cleansing the Lord’s place, the Winchester church, I restored the *arcisterium* [perhaps *asceterium*, that is, “monastery”; HARD.] of the new monastery, dedicated to our Savior and his mother, the ever-virgin Mary, and to all the apostles together with the other saints.

Knowing what is written—“Those who consent and those who act are bound by the same penalty of rebellion,” opposing the will of the Almighty [Col. 0491D]—and refusing to tolerate the usurpation of the Lord’s possession, I drove away the wanton clerics. I chose true worshipers of God, serving in the monastic order, who would diligently intercede for the transgressions of us and of our people resting there, so that the condition of our rule might remain strengthened and protected by their intercessions. With Christ cooperating, I chose an abbot and, subject to the Most High, devoutly installed him there.

I earnestly beg and beseech this: that what I have done with regard to his possessions, he may do with regard to those bestowed on me by him—namely, that, casting down our adversaries, he may advance and exalt our friends, so that, crushing the enemies of God’s holy Church and blessing its friends, namely the monks, I may be justified.

## X. On the anathema against those who plot against the monks

[Col. 0492A]

If, however, on any occasion, at the devil’s instigation, it should happen that, through the pride of arrogant haughtiness, the expelled canons should plot to overthrow the flock of monks whom I, together with their shepherd, have established in God’s possession and whom I venerate—and all those who, blinded by any reward, have given them assistance—let what happened to the proud angels and to the first-formed man, seduced by the devil’s fraud, happen to them. Let them be expelled from the boundaries of paradise [perhaps *liminibus*, “thresholds”; HARD.] and from the lofty seats of heaven, thrust down into the fires of the abyss with those who, scorning the Lord’s service, have despised it, and let them be tortured by unending misery.

Nor should they boast that, once torn away from there, they have escaped their torments. Rather, joined in Acheron with Judas, the betrayer of Christ, and his accomplices, let them be punished with eternal lamentation: shivering with cold, scorched by heat, deprived of joy, anxious in sorrow, fettered with chains of fire, struck with terror at the executioners, confounded by the memory of their crimes, and cut off from the remembrance of every good thing.

## XI. Likewise, on the anathema against plotters

Whoever presumes or wishes to expel the aforesaid monks of the new monastery of the Winchester church, or any others of the same order living under our rule, from the monasteries which I acquired for Jesus Christ our Lord after purifying them from the filth of vices, having conquered the devil, let him be anathema.

Let him be held liable without end to the same curse by which Cain the fratricide, who, goaded by envy, murdered his brother Abel—[the text is corrupt: *mastigia, adductus*; perhaps “driven on by a scourge”]—was condemned. Persisting continually in persecution of God, let him acquire no honor of dignity in this life, nor remain in the future without misery; rather, let the Styx, together with Ananias and Sapphira, embrace him, torturing him as he wails in a single abyss [perhaps *voragine*].

## XII. On the blessing of those who honor the monks

Whoever wishes to enrich and endow the monks named above with any good things, may the Creator and Ruler of all mercifully enrich him and his offspring with every abundance of prosperity in this world and in the future age. May they have their names properly written in the book of life and receive a share with Christ in the dwellings of heaven—those who have honored, by word or deed and through devotion to holiness, his monks, whom he possesses gathered together in our times.

## XIII. What kind of monks, and in what manner, are to be maintained in this monastery

Therefore the regular monks, not secular ones, living in the aforesaid monastery with Christ as their companion, shall obey the customs of the Rule. Venerating their spiritual fathers, let them imitate the examples of the holy Fathers, doing nothing except what the common rule of the monastery or the standard of their elders has shown.

Removed from secular pomp, let them guard the chastity of body and soul with all their strength. Distinguished by devotion to humility, and reducing the body through the strength of frugality, let them bind themselves with a joyful spirit. Let them be ashamed to become perpetual guests of citizens within the city.

While living in the city, let them use in the refectory lawful foods of charity, avoiding the luxurious and wanton delicacies of secular people as though they were melancholy [the wording is uncertain]. Outside the refectory, let them eat nothing except in the house of the sick, when they are lying ill, and then only what they have been ordered to eat.

Guests of the sacred and highest order, if necessity requires it, and duly authorized pilgrims coming from distant lands, are to be invited with the greatest care to the abbot’s table in the refectory. Suitable hospitality is to be shown to laypeople in the guesthouse. No monk may, according to the decrees of the Fathers, have permission to eat or drink with them; nor are laypeople to be brought into the refectory for the purpose of eating or drinking. The poor, as Christ’s poor, are to be welcomed with immense rejoicing of heart.

## XIV. On the election of abbots

[Col. 0493B]

Most brilliantly instructed through devotion to the divine Scriptures, constantly occupied with frequent prayer, exceedingly joyful in the embrace of charity, most ready in the exercise of faith, most sincere through the advancement of hope, firmly established in concord through peace, and adorned with the flower of every virtue, let them carry through to the end, with Christ’s help, the beginning of such great goodness and enjoy the same glorious liberty which the blessed patron Benedict established by the precept of his Rule for all subject to it—namely, that after the death of the abbot then governing, they should appoint an abbot [lacuna], whom the entire harmonious congregation, or even the smallest part of the congregation, should choose by its more salutary counsel.

## XV. How the king, honoring the abbot and monks, is to protect them

[Col. 0493C]

Therefore, whatever kings may be our successors, let them not impose any outsider who exercises the right of tyranny over the monks, lest God, condemning them, remove them both from the kingdom and from life.

Let them graciously receive the one elected by the brothers as Christ’s vicar and, inflamed by the fire of charity, honor him by enriching him. Moved by love of Christ, let them gladly provide whatever assistance he requires. Strengthened by mutual help, agreeing in nothing contrary to the precepts of the Rule, let them, as faithful shepherds rather than hirelings, fearlessly defend the Lord’s flock by rescuing it from the jaws of wolves.

## XVI. How the abbot and monks are to rescue the king from the temptation of demons

[Col. 0493D]

The abbot, girded with spiritual arms, surrounded on every side by the band of monks, and drenched with the dew of heavenly gifts, is to fight against the aerial cunning of demons. With Christ’s help, by whose power they wage war, he is to defend the king and all the clergy under his rule from the rabid persecution of invisible enemies, skillfully protecting them with the subtle shield of faith. Fighting with a robust triumph, let the fearless soldier skillfully defend them with the sword of the Spirit and protect them with the shield of faith.

## XVII. How the king is to defend the abbot and monks from human persecution

Likewise, let the earthly king, strengthening the heavenly King’s camp with the strongest protection, fight visible adversaries with secular arms and, destroying the raging fury of enemies, guard the Creator’s pastures and flock with vigilant and impregnable protection. Thus, reaching the prize of life, may he rejoice in eternal goods—goods which no human eye has been able in any way to see, and which have not at all entered the human heart, but which God has prepared for those who love him.

## XVIII. On the liberty of the monastic possession

Let the lands of the aforesaid monastery and all the monks’ property—whether great or small, internal or external, urban or suburban—namely estates, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, mills, and the courses of streams, be endowed with perpetual liberty in the name of Christ and of his Mother.

## XIX. That no secular person may unlawfully usurp the monastery’s possession

[Col. 0494B]

Let no secular person presumptuously exercise the right of tyranny over the cultivation of Christ, with reckless audacity. Let no one, at the devil’s instigation, diminish what has been granted with such abundant generosity, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, both by me and by my predecessors, as well as by Catholic men and women.

## XX. On the blessing of those who increase the possessions

May the Maker of all things grant to the one who increases them a peaceful course through the present life, length of days in the time that remains, and a future recompense of eternal blessedness; sufficient abundance of provisions, an unending increase of prosperity, and plentiful assistance in every virtue.

## XXI. On the curse of those who diminish them

[Col. 0494C]

May perpetual misery possess the one who diminishes them. Persisting in persecution of the Lord, may he incur the offense of his Mother and of all the saints. May the adversity of the present life always befall him; may no prosperity of goodness come to him. May enemies standing by plunder all his possessions.

In the future, however, may eternal torments condemn him, most wretched, placed with the goats on the left, unless he corrects by suitable satisfaction what he has diminished by usurping the Lord’s authority.

## XXII. In what ways they are to obey secular authorities, and how no offense can diminish this privilege of the Lord

[Col. 0494D]

They are to obey secular commands only for three purposes: a duly authorized military expedition, the construction of a bridge, or the construction of a fortress. In all other matters, let them glory in being endowed with perpetual liberty.

If, through the devil’s incitement, anyone should be seduced—whether the abbot or one of the brothers—and, God forbid, should weakly incur some offense, let it be condemned as abolished after being purged by justice according to the precept of the Rule. Nevertheless, let the liberty of the aforesaid benefaction, offered to the Most High through our humility, remain inviolable for the use of the monks who freely serve him, joyful in perpetual liberty.

For God, who possesses this abundant grant of privilege, the place together with the entire community of monks, and all the rights subject to the sacred monastery, has never committed an offense and will never commit one at any time. Therefore let the aforesaid liberty be eternal, because God is the eternal possessor of liberty.

## XXIII. How often and why this privilege is to be read to the brothers during the year

[Col. 0495A]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 966, the charter of this privilege was written, with the following witnesses consenting, whose names are written below in due order.

## Subscriptions

I, Edgar, by the bounty of divine grace king of the English, granting this gift of privilege to our Redeemer and to his most holy place, the first of all kings to establish there a community of monks, have confirmed it with my own hand by impressing the sign of the holy cross.

I, Dunstan, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, venerating the benevolent king’s abundant donation, have strengthened it with the sign of the cross.

I, Eadmund, the legitimate and renowned son of the aforesaid king, flourishing in the age of childhood, have placed the sign of the cross with my own hand.

I, Edward, begotten by the same renowned king, have consolidated the aforesaid munificence of my father with the sign of the cross.

I, Aelfthryth, legitimate wife of the aforesaid king, establishing the monks in the same place by my embassy, with the king’s consent, have impressed the cross.

I, Eadgifa, grandmother of the aforesaid king, have strengthened this distinguished work by the miracle of the cross.

I, Oscytyl, archbishop of the Church of York, have confirmed it.

I, Athelwold, bishop of the Church of Winchester, [Col. 0495C] commending to him the benevolence of the most glorious king, the abbot by my high office [the wording is uncertain], and the pupils whom I educated, have blessed it with the sign of the cross.

I, Aelfstan, bishop of the Church of London, have consolidated it.

I, Osulf, bishop, have confirmed it.

I, Oswold, bishop, have signed it.

I, Bysentelm, bishop, have confirmed it.

Eaelfstan, bishop, has consolidated it.

I, Eadelm, bishop, have confirmed it.

I, Athulf, bishop, have signed it.

I, Urynryge, bishop, have confirmed it.

Aercwig, abbot, has consolidated it.

I, Osgar, abbot, have signed it.

I, Orobyrihe, abbot.

I, Aelfstan, abbot.

I, Adelgar, the first abbot appointed abbot of this place.

[Col. 0496A]

I, Osdgar, earl.

I, Aethelstan, earl.

I, Athelwine, earl.

I, Aethelweard, *minister*.

I, Elfweard, *minister*.

I, Wulrtan, *minister*.

All of us whose names appear to have been written into this royal privilege by the king’s command earnestly beseech our posterity not to violate and annul the pledge of our hands, sealed with Christ’s cross. If any of our successors should presume to violate it through an act of humility [perhaps “presumption”; the wording is uncertain], let him be deprived of participation in the body and blood of Jesus Christ and condemned to perpetual destruction; let him be anathema, unless, by God’s merciful regard, he should come to his senses, turn back, and make humble satisfaction.

## Another charter of King Edgar

In this charter he declares that there had never been monks in this monastery of Winchester before those whom he himself has now introduced from the monastery of Abingdon.

With the ruler of the Most High consenting, and having obtained the government of all Albion in a threefold manner [the wording is uncertain], not unmindful that what had been granted would be repaid, so that through these things I might diligently win eternal rewards, I, Edgar, king of all Britain, give and grant in pure and perpetual alms to the new Church of Winchester, dedicated to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and also to Saint Eadot, whose relics shine there through miracles, certain estates as they are named:

Dunkiton, where I possess five hides of land; the church of Sueyse, with twenty-eight hides of land; the church of Titlescumbe, with ten hides of land; and a certain portion of land, namely two cassates of land, in the place commonly called Wynterburna.

These are granted with all their implements—namely meadows, pastures, and streams—made conspicuous by an eternal inheritance, so that I might expel from the aforesaid church the canons who persisted in incorrigibility and substitute monks from Abingdon.

Let the aforesaid estates, land, dwellings, territories, and streams be forever free from every earthly service, except three: a duly authorized military expedition, the repair of a bridge, and the repair of a fortress.

If anyone should wish to transfer this donation of ours to anything other than what we have established, let him be deprived of fellowship with God’s holy Church and be punished continually, sorrowfully, with Judas the betrayer of Christ and his accomplices, in the eternal fires of the abyss, unless he corrects by suitable satisfaction what he has done against our decree.

[Col. 0495]

# The Ecclesiastical Laws of King Edgar

As they are preserved separately from secular laws in the Saxon book and translated by Lombard.

## Titles of the Chapters

[Col. 0495D]

I. On the immunity of the Church and the dues to be rendered to it.  
II. On the ecclesiastical payment, or firstfruits of seed.  
III. On tithes. [Col. 0496D]  
IV. On the penny imposed on each household.  
V. On feast days and fasting.

## The Laws of King Edgar

The laws which King Edgar enacted in frequent council for the glory of God, the adornment of royal majesty, and the benefit of the commonwealth:

### I

First, let the Church of God possess all its rights and immunities. Let everyone give tithes to the principal church to which he is subject, wherever the plow itself passes, whether this be on the thanes’ own estates or on the lands of the village stewards.

### II

If a thane has a church on land possessed by written title, and a burial place has been assigned around it, let him be fully entitled to contribute one third of his tithes to it. If no burial place has been designated around the church, let the owner of the estate give the priest whatever amount he thinks appropriate from the remaining nine parts. Moreover, from all the land of free men, the very firstfruits of seed are to be paid to the principal church.

### III

Let everyone pay all tithes of livestock before Pentecost; let him pay tithes of the fruits of the earth before the equinox; and let him render the firstfruits of seed on the feast of Saint Martin. If anyone fails to pay, let him pay the penalties prescribed in the judicial book.

If anyone refuses to give tithes in the manner stated, let the royal reeve, the bishop of that place, and the priest come together and, even against his will, render the tithe to the church to which it is owed, leaving him the remaining nine parts. As for the eight parts that remain, let the lord have four and the bishop four, whether the person in question is the king’s servant or the servant of any other thane.

### IV

Let the penny imposed on each household be rendered before the feast of Saint Peter. Whoever does not pay it then shall carry that penny and thirty more to Rome and, on returning home, confirm by a sure written testimony that he has taken it there; finally, he shall pay the king 120 shillings.

If anyone fails to pay a second time, let him carry that penny and three times ten more to Rome and, after his return, pay the king 200 shillings. If he commits the offense a third time, let him be stripped of all his possessions.

### V

Let Saturday be observed as a feast from the third afternoon hour of Saturn’s day until the dawn of the lunar day. Whoever does not celebrate it shall pay the penalties described in the judicial book. Let the other days likewise be celebrated as the priest has announced. Let the appointed fasts also be observed with the utmost religious devotion.

# An Ancient Version of King Edgar’s Ecclesiastical Laws

I. On rendering the Church’s dues.  
[Col. 0498A] II. On churches where there is a cemetery.  
III. On the terms for paying tithes.  
IV. On one who refuses to give tithes.  
V. On those who do not pay Saint Peter’s penny.  
VI. On observing solemnities and appointed times.

This is the ordinance which King Edgar established, for the glory of God, for his own royal dignity, and for the benefit of his people, with the counsel of his wise men.

### I

First, the rights of God’s churches are to be honored, and every tithe is to be rendered to the mother church to which the parish belongs, from the land of thanes and villagers, wherever the plow passes.

### II

If there is a thane who has a church on his estate where there is a cemetery, let him give it one third of his tithe. If there is no churchyard there, let him give the priest from his nine parts whatever he wishes, and let every free household also give the entire church-scot to the mother church.

### III

Let every tithe of young animals be rendered at Pentecost, the tithe of the earth’s crops at the equinox, and the entire church-scot at the feast of Saint Martin, under the full forfeiture prescribed by the judicial book.

### IV

If anyone refuses to give his tithe as we have said, the king’s reeve and the bishop and priest [the text notes: “and bishop, and priest, etc.”] of that church shall be present. Let him render his tithe to the church to which it belongs, leaving the ninth part to the one who withheld his tithe; and let the eight parts be divided into two, half to the lord and half to the bishop, whether the man is the king’s man or the thane’s man.

### V

Let every *heordpen* [a household payment or “herd-penny”] be rendered at the feast of Saint Peter. Whoever does not pay by that appointed time shall take it to Rome, together with thirty pence, and bring back from there a written indication that he paid that amount there. When he returns home, let him pay 120 shillings as compensation.

If he is unwilling to render it again, let him take it to Rome and pay the same additional amount. When he returns, let him pay 120 shillings to the king. At the third time, if he still has not rendered it, let him lose everything he possesses.

### VI

Let the solemnity of Sunday be observed from the ninth hour of Saturday until Monday’s dawn, under the additional forfeiture prescribed and taught by the book of judgments. Let every other festival likewise be observed as the priest announces it. Let every appointed fast be kept with complete devotion.

[Col. 0499]

# Canons Issued under King Edgar and Pertaining to His Laws

As they are found in this preface in the oldest Saxon manuscript of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge. This now pertains to Edgar’s ordinance concerning the manner of life of those initiated into sacred orders. (G)

[Col. 0499A]

### I

We teach that God’s ministers are to serve and minister devotedly to God, interceding for all the Christian people; that all of them are to be faithful and obedient to their elders; that all those promoted to office are to assist in common necessity; that each is to be a help and assistance to the others both before God and before human beings; and that they are also to be faithful and truthful toward their secular lords.

### II

We also teach that each person is to honor the other; that the younger are carefully to listen to and love their elders; and that the elders are diligently to teach their juniors.

### III

We also teach that those who go to any synod are to bring each year books and vestments for ecclesiastical service, ink and parchment for their ordinances, and provisions for three days.

[Col. 0499B]

### IV

We also teach that every priest going to a synod is to have his cleric and a suitable man as assistant, not some stranger who delights in foolishness. Let them all travel in due order and in fear of almighty God.

### V

We also teach that every priest is to announce at the synod whether anything is harming him, or whether anyone has inflicted a great injury upon him. Then let all the others take it as though it had been done to all of them and help toward compensation, as the bishop has determined.

### VI

We also teach that every priest is to announce at the synod if he knows of anyone in his parish who is rebellious toward God or who has fallen grievously into mortal sin and whom he cannot or dares not incline toward correction because of secular persons.

[Col. 0499C]

### VII

We also teach that no dispute among priests is to be brought before a secular court. Rather, their own associates are to settle and reconcile it, or, if necessary, transfer it to the bishop.

### VIII

We also teach that no priest is voluntarily to abandon the church to which he was consecrated, but is to have it as his legitimate wife.

### IX

We also teach that no priest is to do anything belonging to another—not in his church, nor in his parish, nor in his fellowship, nor in any of the matters belonging to him.

### X

We also teach that no priest is to accept another’s student without the permission of the one whom the student previously followed.

[Col. 0499D]

### XI

We also teach that every priest is diligently to learn a craft for the sake of increasing his knowledge.

### XII

We also teach that a learned priest is not to insult a half-learned one, but is to correct him if he knows better.

[Col. 0500A]

### XIII

We also teach that no priest born in an illustrious station is to despise a priest of lower condition. If anyone considers this rightly, he will find that all human beings are of the same birth.

### XIV

We also teach that every priest is to conduct himself properly and is not to be an unjust buyer or a greedy merchant.

### XV

We also teach that every priest is to perform baptism as soon as it is requested. Then, in his parish, he is to order that every infant be baptized within thirty-seven days and that no one delay too long in receiving confirmation from the bishop.

### XVI

We also teach that every priest is diligently to promote Christianity, utterly extinguish every form of heathenism, and prohibit the worship of springs, necromancy, augury, incantations, the worship of a human being as a god, and *offacias* [an uncertain term], which are practiced through various magical tricks, torches, divinations, arms, various trees, stones, and many other phantoms by which many people who ought not to be deceived are deceived.

[Col. 0500B]

### XVII

We also teach that every Christian is diligently to accustom his child to Christianity and teach him the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed.

### XVIII

We also teach that on feast days profane songs and devilish games are to cease.

### XIX

We also teach that on Sundays markets and public assemblies are to cease.

[Col. 0500C]

### XX

We also teach that false and foolish conversations and disgraceful haircuts are to cease.

### XXI

We also teach that concubinage is to cease and lawful marriages are to be loved.

### XXII

We also teach that anyone who wishes to lie in a consecrated cemetery or receive the holy Eucharist must learn the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed. For one who refuses to learn these is not a good Christian, nor may he lawfully lift others from the baptismal font or receive the bishop’s hand in confirmation unless he has first learned them.

### XXIII

We also teach that on feast days and appointed fasts there is to be absolutely no contention among any people.

[Col. 0500D]

### XXIV

We also teach that on feast days and fasts oaths and ordeals are to be omitted.

### XXV

We also teach that every man is to abstain from his wife on feast days and appointed fasts.

[Col. 0501A]

### XXVI

We also teach that priests are to guard the churches with every form of reverence, for ecclesiastical ministry and pure service, and for no other matters. Nothing useless is to be there, nor anything in the *vicima* [uncertain reading]. Vain conversations, vain actions, and unbecoming drinking are not to be permitted, nor any other vanity. No dog is ever to enter within the church enclosure, nor more pigs than one can control.

### XXVII

We also teach that nothing indecent is to be stored in the church.

### XXVIII

We also teach that everyone is to be very sober at the church’s dedication festivals, and is to pray diligently; let no drinking vessels or any useless activity be used there.

[Col. 0501B]

### XXIX

We also teach that no one is to be buried in the church unless it is known that he pleased God well in life, so that it may be judged that he is worthy of burial there.

### XXX

We also teach that a priest is to celebrate Mass in no house except consecrated churches, unless because of someone’s extreme illness.

### XXXI

We also teach that a priest is never, at least, to celebrate Mass except upon a consecrated altar.

### XXXII

We also teach that a priest is never to celebrate Mass without a book, and that the canon is to be placed before his eyes, if he wishes, lest he stumble.

### XXXIII

We also teach that every priest is to have a corporal when he celebrates Mass, an undergarment beneath his alb, and all the Mass vestments properly woven.

[Col. 0501C]

### XXXIV

We also teach that every priest is diligently to take care to have a good, or at least adequate, book.

### XXXV

We also teach that no priest is to celebrate Mass alone unless he has someone to answer him.

### XXXVI

We also teach that every priest is to receive the Eucharist fasting, except on account of extreme illness.

### XXXVII

We also teach that no priest is to celebrate Mass more than three times in one day at the most.

### XXXVIII

We also teach that a priest is always to have the Eucharist prepared as needed and is diligently to keep it in purity. He is to take care that it does not grow old. If it should grow old so that it cannot be received, it is to be burned in a pure fire and the ashes placed beneath the altar. The one who neglected this is to make diligent amends before God.

[Col. 0501D]

### XXXIX

We also teach that a priest is never to presume to celebrate Mass unless he has everything pertaining to the holy Eucharist, namely a pure offering, pure wine, and pure water. Woe to the one who begins Mass before having all these things! And woe to the one who adds anything impure to them! This would be like what the Jews did when they mixed vinegar and gall together and afterward offered it to Christ in mockery.

[Col. 0502A]

### XL

We also teach that a priest is never worthy to celebrate Mass if he himself does not receive the holy Eucharist; and that what has once been consecrated is never to be consecrated again.

### XLI

We also teach that the chalice in which the holy Eucharist is consecrated is to be cast, and that it is never to be consecrated in a wooden vessel.

### XLII

We also teach that everything approaching the altar and belonging to the church is to be very pure and properly arranged; nothing impure is to approach it. The sanctuary is to be kept with the greatest honor, and a light is always to burn in the church when Mass is sung.

### XLIII

We also teach that nothing consecrated is to be neglected—not consecrated water, nor salt, nor incense, nor bread, nor anything holy.

[Col. 0502B]

### XLIV

We also teach that no wife is to approach the altar while Mass is being celebrated.

### XLV

We also teach that the bell is to be rung at the proper appointed time, and that every priest is to sing his appointed daily office in the church, pray there diligently in fear of God, and intercede for all the people.

### XLVI

We also teach that no secular priest or member of a religious community is to enter the church door or the sanctuary without his surplice, nor, at least, come to the altar to minister there without that vestment.

### XLVII

We also teach that no person initiated into sacred orders is to consecrate his tonsure, nor permit it to be badly cut, nor grow his beard for any period of time, if he wishes to have the blessing of God, Saint Peter, and ourselves.

[Col. 0502C]

### XLVIII

We also teach that all priests are to be of one mind on feast days and fasts, and that all are to pray in one manner, lest they lead the people into error.

### XLIX

We also teach that every fast is to be honored with almsgiving. That is, whenever anyone wishes diligently to give alms out of devotion toward God, his fast is then more pleasing to God.

### L

We also teach that all priests are to labor together in the church’s ministries, and that there is to be equal remuneration throughout the year in all the church’s ministries.

[Col. 0502D]

### LI

We also teach that priests are diligently to teach the young and draw them toward crafts, so that they may thereby have assistance for the Church.

### LII

We also teach that every Sunday priests are to preach to the people and always provide them with a good example.

### LIII

We also teach that no Christian is to eat blood of any kind.

### LIV

We also teach that priests are to admonish the people concerning what they ought diligently to do for God: that they should be just in rendering tithes and other dues—first-plow alms fifteen days after Easter, tithes of livestock at Pentecost, the fruits of the earth at All Saints’ [feast], Saint Peter’s penny [Col. 0503A] at Peter’s feast, and the church payment at Martin’s feast.

### LV

We also teach that priests are to distribute the people’s alms in such a way that they both render God propitious toward them and accustom the people to almsgiving.

LVI. We also teach that priests should sing psalms when they distribute alms, and that the poor should pray diligently, so that they may earnestly intercede for the people.

LVII. We also teach that priests should carefully guard themselves against drunkenness and, by reproving it diligently, forbid it to other people.

LVIII. We also teach that no priest should be an ale-seller, nor in any way play the buffoon, whether by himself or with others; rather, he should be prudent and venerable, as befits his order. [Col. 0503B]

LIX. We also teach that priests should diligently guard themselves against taking oaths and should strongly prohibit it as well.

LX. We also teach that no priest should love the company of women excessively, but should love his lawful wife—that is, his Church.

LXI. We also teach that no priest should stand as a false witness, nor take part in the counsels of thieves.

LXII. We also teach that a priest should never attend ordeals or oaths.

LXIII. We also teach that a priest should not swear against a thegn in a compurgation unless the thegn has first sworn falsely.

[Col. 0503C] LXIV. We also teach that a priest should not be a hunter, nor a falconer, nor a drinker, but should devote himself to his books, as befits his order.

LXV. We also teach that every priest should teach confession and penance to the person who confesses to him, and should also help him to amend; that he should give the Holy Eucharist to the sick person when he needs it, and anoint him as well if he desires this; and that after death he should carefully wrap the body. Nothing vain should be permitted around the body; rather, it should be decently buried in the fear of God.

LXVI. We also teach that every priest should have oil both for baptism and for anointing the sick. He should also be ready diligently to advance the law of the people and Christianity [Col. 0503D] in every way, both by preaching well and by providing a good example. Then Almighty God will grant him what will be most acceptable to him.

LXVII. We also teach that every priest should know how to answer, when he receives the chrism, what he has done in the prayers for the king and the bishop.

## CONCERNING CONFESSION

I. When anyone wishes to confess his sins, let him act manfully and not be ashamed to confess his crimes and misdeeds by accusing himself, because indulgence comes from this, and because without confession there is no forgiveness. For confession heals; confession justifies.

[Col. 0504A] A large lacuna, or space in the manuscript, into which the scribe apparently intended to insert the remaining material elsewhere.

May your mercy, O Lord, I pray, go before this servant of yours, so that all his iniquities may be erased by swift forgiveness through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Hear, I pray, O Lord, the prayers of suppliants crying out to you; I pray, O Lord.

II. Whoever is a physician of human souls and knows their actions should carefully distinguish and discern how he is to impose penance for people’s actions; nevertheless, he should not condemn them or cause them to despair. When a person wishes to confess his offenses to him, let him first hear him patiently, discerning what his intention is. If he wishes and is able humbly to confess his actions, and you perceive that he repents of his sins, teach him lovingly and mercifully. If he cannot confess his actions or examine his guilt, [Col. 0504B]

III. question him about his conduct, draw out his guilt, and explain his actions. Consider that you must never judge rich and poor, free and enslaved, old and young, healthy and sick, humble and proud, strong and weak, the ordained and the laity in the same way.

A prudent judge must carefully discern every deed: when it was done, and where and at what time. At no time is injustice permitted; nevertheless, he should guard himself most diligently from it on feast days and fast days and in sacred places. And the more powerful and higher-ranking a person is, the more seriously he must make amends for injustice before God and before the world, because the powerful and the powerless cannot bear equal burdens, nor can the weak be like the strong. These persons, therefore, must be distinguished and discerningly judged.

IV. After this, let him rise humbly before his confessor and say first: “I believe in the Lord, the supreme Father, governor of all things, and in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit; and I believe that I shall live after death; and I believe that I shall rise on the day of judgment; and I believe that I shall merit all this through God’s power and mercy.”

V. Then, with a penitent and humble spirit, let him confess his confession to his confessor, bowing humbly, [Col. 0504D] and let him say:

“I confess to almighty God and to my confessor, my spiritual physician, all my sins by which I have ever been polluted through the malignity of the spirit, whether in deeds or in thoughts, whether with males or with females or with any creature, natural sins or unnatural sins.

VI. “I confess gluttony in food, both morning and evening. I confess all greed, envy, detraction, the vice of a double tongue, lying, unjust glory, idle talk, unjust magnificence, and all pride that has arisen from the evil counsel of my body. I confess that I have very often been the author of sin, a supporter of sin, conscious of sin, and teacher of sin.

[Col. 0505A] VII. “I confess the murder of my spirit, perjuries, sedition, pride, and neglect of God’s commandment. I confess everything that I have ever seen with my eyes for the sake of greed or detraction, everything useless that I have heard with my ears, and everything vain that I have spoken with my mouth.

VIII. “I confess all the sins of my body: of skin, flesh, bone, sinews, kidneys, cartilage, tongue, lips, throat, teeth, hair, marrow, and every soft or hard, moist or dry thing. I confess that I have kept my baptism worse than I promised my Lord, and that I have not kept in the proper manner my order, which I ought to have preserved out of love for God and his saints and for my own eternal salvation. I confess that I have often neglected my canonical hours [Col. 0505B] and have sworn falsely by the life of my lords, and have taken the name of my Lord in vain.

IX. “For all my sins I ask forgiveness from my Lord, so that the devil may never lie in wait for me, and so that I may not die without confessing and amending my sins. Thus today I confess all my guilt before the Lord and Savior Christ, who governs heaven and earth, and before this holy altar and these relics, and before my confessor and the Lord’s priest. I am in a pure and true confession and in a good will to amend all my sins and thereafter to abstain from them in whatever way I am ever able.

X. “And you, Christ the Savior, be merciful to my soul, and forgive and erase my sins and my guilt, which I formerly or at any time committed, and lead me to your exalted kingdom, where I may dwell with your saints and elect without end forever. Now I humbly ask you, priest of the Lord, to be my witness on the day of judgment, so that the devil may not have power over me, and so that you may be my advocate before the Lord: that I may amend my sins and my guilt and abstain from other things of this kind. May the Lord, who lives and reigns forever, help me in this. Amen.”

## THE MANNER OF IMPOSING PENANCE

I. An old person and a young person, a rich person and a poor person, a healthy person and a sick person, and a person of whatever order, and anyone who has sinned unwillingly, should not be treated as one who has sinned voluntarily, willingly, and deliberately. If anyone has offended under compulsion of necessity, he should always be worthy of the protection and correction of the law, because he was compelled by necessity to do what he perpetrated.

II. Every deed must be carefully distinguished before God and before the world.

These rites are observed overseas—that is:

III. Every bishop is to be in his episcopal see on Wednesday, which we call the beginning of the fast. Then everyone in that province who is polluted by mortal sins is to come to him on that day and confess his sins to him; and he is then to teach him penance according to the nature of his guilt. If the guilt is of great enormity, the person is to be removed from ecclesiastical communion; nevertheless, he is to be encouraged and admonished concerning his own needs, and then, with the bishop’s permission, he is to return home.

[Col. 0506A] IV. From there, on the Thursday before Easter, each person is to assemble at his own place, and the bishop is to sing over him and grant absolution. He is then to return home with the bishop’s blessing. This is to be observed by all Christian people.

V. Nevertheless, the priest must carefully consider with what contrition and with what degree of completion the person has made satisfaction for the penance imposed on him, and how he ought to grant him remission.

VI. If a layman kills another without cause, let him fast for seven years: three on bread and water, and four as his confessor instructs him; and after seven years let him make compensation. Thereafter let him diligently mourn his offense by whatever means he can, since it is unknown how his penance will be received by God.

VII. If anyone wishes to kill another but cannot fulfill his intention, let him fast for three years: one on bread and water, and two as his confessor instructs him. [Col. 0506B]

VIII. If a layman unwillingly kills someone, let him fast for three years: one on bread and water, and two as his confessor instructs him; and let him mourn his offense always.

IX. If he is a subdeacon, let him fast for six years. If he is a deacon, let him fast for seven years. If he is a priest, let him fast for ten years, and a bishop for twelve, and let him mourn always.

X. If anyone unwillingly kills his own child, let him fast for five years, three on bread and water, as above.

XI. If a bishop or priest kills someone, [Col. 0506C] let him lose his order and thereafter make careful satisfaction.

XII. If a wife kills her child within her, or after it has been born, by drink or other means, let her fast for ten years: three on bread and water, and seven as her confessor, out of mercy, prescribes for her; and thereafter let her mourn this.

XIII. If anyone kills his own slave in a fit of rage, without the slave’s having committed a fault, let him fast for three years.

XIV. If a woman strikes her husband out of jealousy, and he dies as a result, and he was innocent, let her fast for seven years; if he was guilty, let her fast for three years; and let her mourn her beloved always.

[Col. 0506D] XV. If anyone voluntarily kills himself with weapons or through some prompting of the devil, it is not permitted that Masses be sung for such a person, nor that his body be carried to the earth with the singing of psalms, nor that he lie buried in a proper burial. The same judgment is to be applied to one who ends his life by torments on account of his guilt, such as a thief, murderer, or traitor to his lord.

XVI. If anyone pollutes himself with a beast, or a male with another male, and is twenty years old, let him fast for fifteen years. If he has a wife and is forty years old when he commits such a deed, let him abstain and fast as long as he lives, and let him not presume to receive the Lord’s body before death takes him away. A young and foolish person who commits such a deed is to be severely beaten.

XVII. If anyone commits adultery, let him fast for seven years on bread and water three days each week, whether the offender is a wife or a husband.

XVIII. If anyone abandons his spouse and takes another wife, he commits adultery. He is to be granted none of the rights that pertain to Christians, whether dead or alive, and this person is not to be buried with Christians. The same is also to be done to a wife. Each of the relatives who have done the same is to lose his rights, unless they wish to return quickly and correct the matter diligently.

XIX. If anyone has both a wife and a concubine, no priest is to perform any office for him among Christians unless he returns to amendment and keeps only one of them, whether wife or concubine.

XX. If a man lies with another man’s lawful wife, or a wife with another woman’s lawful husband, let the offender fast for seven years: three on bread and water, and four as his confessor instructs him; and let him mourn his offense always.

XXI. If a wife takes two brothers in marriage, one after the other, they are subject to judgment, and are to remain diligent in penance as long as they live, according to what their confessor instructs them. At their death the priest is to perform the office for them as it is performed for Christians, if they have promised that they would have wished to amend more fully had they lived longer.

[Col. 0507C] XXII. If anyone remains in some shameful partnership of sin until he ends his life without any repentance, we know no counsel to offer him except that this pertains to God’s judgment, nor can he be absolved.

XXIII. If a woman is betrothed, no other man is permitted to take her away from the man to whom she is betrothed. If anyone does this, let him be excommunicated.

XXIV. If anyone deceitfully abducts a wife or virgin against her will for unlawful intercourse, let him be excommunicated.

XXV. If anyone, for the purpose of fornication, seduces another man’s maidservant away from him by his enticements and lies with her against her will, then, if he is an ordained person, let him lose his order; if he is a layman, let him be excommunicated from [Col. 0507D] all Christian offices.

XXVI. If a virgin is betrothed, and in the intervening period is led away or removed under some pretext from the man to whom she was betrothed, and afterward it happens that she comes into his presence, they may lie together with permission, since she had been absent from him against her will.

XXVII. If a consecrated woman afterward returns to worldly vanity, supports a household, and thinks that she can make amends from her property for having turned away from God, this is nothing. Rather, let her abandon the partnership of sin, return to Christ, and live her life as her confessor instructs her; thereafter let her correct her offense with the utmost diligence.

[Col. 0508A] XXVIII. If a presbyter or monk kills a person, let him lose his order and fast for ten years: five on bread and water, and five on three days each week; on the remaining days let him enjoy his food, and let him mourn his offense always.

A deacon: eight years on bread and water, and the remaining years as above.

A cleric: four years; six on bread and water.

A layman: five years; three on bread and water, as above.

XXIX. If anyone kills an ordained person or his own near kinsman, let him abandon his land and possessions, do as the pope instructs him, and mourn always.

XXX. If a presbyter or monk practices lustful intercourse or violates a marriage, let him fast for ten years and mourn always. A deacon: seven; a cleric: six; [Col. 0508B] a layman: five years, as for homicide.

XXXI. If a presbyter, monk, or deacon has a lawful wife before he is consecrated, let him leave her and receive orders, and afterward, if he repeatedly takes her back for intercourse, let each of them fast as for homicide, and let them mourn deeply.

XXXII. If a priest, monk, deacon, layman, or cleric lies with a nun, let each fast according to what is appropriate to his order, as for homicide, and abstain from meat always. Let the nun fast for ten years, as also the priest, and let them mourn always.

XXXIII. If anyone wishes to lie with a nun and she does not wish it, let him fast for one year for that unjust intention, on bread and water. If anyone wishes to lie with another man’s lawful wife and she does not wish it, let him fast for one year for that unjust intention, on bread and water.

XXXIV. If anyone wishes to lie with another man’s lawful spouse and she does not wish it, let him fast for three Lents on bread and water: one in summer, another in autumn, and the third in winter.

XXXV. If anyone wishes to have unlawful intercourse with his wife, let him fast for forty days on bread and water.

XXXVI. If anyone catches another man with his daughter, let him make compensation to the girl’s friends, and let both of them fast for one year on Wednesdays and Fridays as long as they live, and let them mourn their offense always.

XXXVII. If anyone lies with a beast, let him fast for fifteen [Col. 0508D] years: eight on bread and water, and the other seven every year on three days during Lent and on Wednesdays and Fridays as long as he lives; and let him mourn his offense always.

XXXVIII. If anyone voluntarily pollutes himself, let him fast for three years, during each of the three Lents on bread and water, and abstain from meat every day except Sunday.

XXXIX. If anyone kills another by poison, let him fast for seven years: three on bread and water, and the other four years on bread and water for three days each week; and let him mourn always.

XL. If anyone sticks a stake into a person, let him fast for three years: one on bread and water, and two on bread and water for three days each [Col. 0509A] week. If the person dies because of that stake, let him then fast for seven years, as written here, and let him mourn his offense always.

XLI. If anyone uses poison or sorcery to obtain another person’s love and gives it to that person in food or drink, or uses the art of incantation, then, if he is a layman, let him fast for half a year on Wednesdays and Fridays on bread and water, and on the other days eat his usual food except meat. A cleric: one year in the same manner, three days each week on bread and water. A deacon: three years in the same manner. A presbyter: five years—one of them on bread and water, and for four years every Friday on bread and water, while on the other days he abstains from meat.

XLII. If anyone shamefully pollutes himself in unnatural acts against God’s creature by any means, let him mourn always as long as he lives, according to the deed that was done.

XLIII. If anyone presses his child in sleep so that it dies, let him fast for three years: one on bread and water, and for two years on three days each week. If it happened through drunkenness, let him make more serious satisfaction, as his confessor instructs him, and let him mourn it always.

XLIV. If a sick child who is a pagan—that is, without baptism—dies, and this happens through the priest’s delay, let him lose his order and diligently correct the matter. If it happens through the negligence of the child’s friends, let them fast for three years: one on bread and water, and two years on three days each week; and let them mourn this always.

[Col. 0509C] XLV. If anyone sells a Christian into paganism, he is not worthy of any rest among Christians unless he afterward redeems from abroad the person whom he previously sold. If he cannot do this, let the entire price be divided, by God’s grace, and let him redeem another person at another price, then release him; in addition, let him make satisfaction for three full years, as his confessor instructs him. If he has no money with which he can redeem the person, let him make more serious satisfaction—that is, seven full years—and mourn always.

XLVI. If anyone greatly ruins himself through many sins and afterward wishes to abstain from them and correct them diligently, let him withdraw to a monastery and serve God and human beings there always, as he is instructed; or let him travel in pilgrimage far from his homeland and perform penance always as long as he lives, seeking the salvation of his soul at least on earth through the most severe satisfaction that he can ever undergo, as he is instructed.

## CONCERNING PENANCE

I. In this confession the necessary assistance of a theologian is of great benefit, just as a good physician is altogether the remedy of a sick person.

II. Through desire a person often sins, and not rarely through the devil’s prompting. It is a terrible thing that the ordained should sin so gravely before God that they lose their order.

III. To correct this, strict penance is necessary, always according to the person’s order and according to the measure of the sin, in accordance with the canonical laws. One must also inquire into the person’s strength, the manner of his satisfaction, and the contrition of his own heart. Some should do penance for a year, some for more than a year; then, according to the measure of the offense, some should do penance for a month, some for more than a month; some for a week, some for more than a week; some for a day, some for more than a day; and some for all the days of their lives.

IV. If a physician is to treat serious wounds properly, he must apply good medicines. No wounds are as bad as the wounds of sin, because through them a person merits eternal death unless he is healed through confession, abstinence, and penance.

V. Then the physician who is to heal wounds must be wise and prudent. The person is first to be healed through good instruction, and once this has been done, the poison that is in him is to be purged—that is, he must first cleanse himself through confession.

VI. Every person must vomit out his sins through good instruction together with confession, just as a deadly disease is treated by a good potion.

VII. No physician can treat a person properly before the poison has departed; likewise, no person can teach penance properly to one who refuses to confess, nor can anyone correct sins without confession. A person who has swallowed something deadly cannot be properly healed unless he vomits out all the poison.

[Col. 0510C] VIII. After confession, a person can quickly merit God’s mercy through penance if he weeps from his inmost heart and mourns that he was previously led astray into injustice by the devil’s prompting.

IX. Prudent penance is also especially fitting for a prudent confessor, just as it is entirely the task of a good physician to heal a sick person. Inquiry must be made, according to the canonical laws, concerning the necessary use of satisfaction and the person’s deeds; a measure must also be established according to his strength, his circumstances, and the person who acknowledges the grief and concern of his heart.

X. A severe penance is for a layman to lay aside his weapons, travel far barefoot, spend no night anywhere, fast, keep very strict vigils, pray diligently day and night, willingly weary himself, and remain so unkempt that he does not touch his hair or nails with iron.

[Col. 0510D] XI. He is not to enter baths, use a soft bed, or taste meat or anything by which he could become drunk. He is not to enter churches; nevertheless, he should diligently seek a holy place, confess his guilt, and ask for intercession. He should kiss no one, but mourn his sins deeply always.

XII. He acts cruelly who condemns himself in this way; nevertheless, he is blessed if he attends to nothing else except fully correcting his sins. For no person in the world has offended God so greatly through sins that he cannot make amends before God if he diligently undertakes this.

[Col. 0511A] XIII. Penance is performed in various ways, and many people can redeem it through alms.

XIV. If anyone has the means for this, let him build a church in praise of God. If he has further means, let him add land and admit ten young men who can serve there for him and minister to God there daily. Let him also restore God’s church everywhere according to his means; let him repair public roads by building bridges over deep waters and over muddy roads; let him diligently distribute, for God’s sake, what he has according to the measure of his resources; and let him diligently help the poor, widows, orphans, and pilgrims. Let him free his own slaves and redeem the freedom of his slaves from other people; and at least let him care for the poor devastated by war, feed the needy, clothe them, and provide them with lodging, fire, baths, and beds. Let him diligently offer intercession everywhere for his own needs in the singing of Masses and psalms, and out of devotion toward his Lord chastise himself most severely through abstinence from food and drink and from every bodily desire.

XV. If anyone has fewer resources, let him diligently do what he can according to his strength. Let him tithe, in the fear of God, everything he has; examine himself whenever he can appropriately; frequently visit churches with his alms; sanctify the place with the greeting of the candlestick; grant lodging, food, and protection to those who need them, as well as fire, sustenance, a bed, and a bath; and have the poor clothed and helped as much as he can.

XVI. Out of love for God, let him visit the sick in spirit and the physically sick, and bury the dead out of devotion to God. Let him often and repeatedly fall on his knees in hidden places, and often and repeatedly prostrate himself upon the whole earth; let him fast and keep vigil, and pray diligently day and night, often and repeatedly. If anyone has still fewer resources, let him diligently do whatever he can according to his strength; at least let him wear down his body through labor against lust. If he previously pleased the devil through soft indulgence, let him now fast in opposition to what he formerly perpetrated through unjust gluttony. Let him keep vigil and work in opposition to the sleepiness and laziness he previously displayed too often when he ought not to have done so, or to the excessive wakefulness he maintained uselessly. Let him endure cold and cold bathing in opposition to the heat that he everywhere aroused through his desire. If he has deliberately and unjustly angered anyone anywhere, let him make careful satisfaction; if anyone offends him, let him willingly forgive out of fear of God. Let him always consider as diligently as he can what he might do as satisfaction for each of the sins that had previously grown through the devil’s seed. If he has led someone off the road to gain something, let him afterward carefully lead that person onto the right road. This is what I wish: if he has incited anyone to sin, let him do what is necessary for that person, lead him away from it, and lead him onto the right road; and let him diligently dissuade everyone from sins. Then his own sins will immediately become lighter.

[Col. 0512A] XVII. With the advice of his confessor, a person who wishes steadfastly to abstain from his sins and correct them may judge himself by the same judgment. Let him distribute, out of devotion toward God, everything he has; let him abandon with them his entire land and homeland and every love of the world; let him serve his Lord day and night; and let him labor as much as he can, all the days of his life, against his own desire. What more can he do than urge every person, for the sake of his own good, toward justice as diligently as he can?

Here is prescribed how a sick person is to redeem his fast.

XVIII. A one-day fast can be redeemed with one denarius. Anyone can redeem a one-day fast with two hundred and twenty psalms. Anyone can redeem a twelve-month fast with thirty solidi, or by freeing someone who is valued at that amount. For a one-day fast, one may sing six times, “Blessed are the undefiled” (*Beati immaculati*), and six times the *Our Father*; and for a one-day fast, one may bend and bow the knees to the ground sixty times with the *Our Father*. A person can also redeem a one-day fast if he extends all his limbs toward God in his prayers, with true contrition and right faith, and sings fifteen times *Have mercy on me, O God* (*Miserere mei, Deus*) and fifteen times the *Our Father*. Then the alleviation of sins for that day should rather be granted to him.

XIX. A person can compensate for a seven-year fast in twelve months if he completes the psalms of the Psalter every day by singing them, and likewise at night, and once at Vespers. A twelve-day fast can also be redeemed by one Mass; a four-month fast can be alleviated by ten Masses; and a twelve-month fast by thirty Masses, if he wishes, out of true love of God, to intercede for himself, confess his sins to his confessor, correct them as he instructs him, and always diligently abstain from them.

## CONCERNING THE GREAT

I. Thus a powerful man rich in friends can greatly alleviate his penance with the help of his friends. First, in God’s name, let him demonstrate true faith through the testimony of his confessor; forgive all those who have sinned against him; make his confession without fear; promise abstinence; and accept penance with many groans.

II. Then let him lay aside his weapons and the vain adornment of clothing, take a staff in his hands, and go diligently barefoot. Let him clothe his body in wool or sackcloth, not enter a bed, but lie on the floor, and arrange for the number of seven years to be completed in three days as follows. First, let him take twelve men to help him, and let them fast for three days on bread, green vegetables, and water. To complete this, let him gather, in whatever way he can, seven times one hundred and twenty men, each of whom is to fast for him for three days. Thus as many fasts are performed as there are days in seven years.

III. When anyone fasts, let him distribute to all God’s poor the dishes of which he himself ought to partake. During the three days on which he fasts, let him neglect the affairs of the world, dwell in churches as frequently as he can day and night, keep diligent vigil there by the light of alms, cry out to God, and ask for forgiveness with a groaning spirit. Let him often bend his knees over the sign of the cross; at times rise, at times prostrate himself; and let the powerful man learn diligently to shed tears and mourn his sins. For three days let him feed as many poor people as he can. On the fourth day let him wash them all, receive them as guests, and give them money. Let him himself, while doing penance, be occupied with washing their feet. On that day let as many Masses as can ever be obtained be said for him. During the Masses let absolution be given to him, and then let him receive the Holy Eucharist—unless he is too great a sinner to be able to receive it yet. In that case, let him at least promise that from now on he will always wish to do God’s will; with God’s help abstain thereafter from every injustice; uphold Christianity as justly and vigorously as he can; utterly reject all paganism; diligently correct his mind and character, words and deeds; cultivate every justice; and avoid injustice, with God’s help, as diligently as he ever can. He who fulfills what he had promised to God will do so to his greatest advantage.

IV. This is the alleviation of the penance of a powerful man rich in friends. But a weak person cannot proceed in this way and must search within himself more diligently for the means. It is also most just that everyone should avenge his own offenses upon himself through careful correction. For it is written: “For each person shall bear his own burden.”

## ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS OF KING EDGAR

(From the manuscript collection, Corpus Christi, Cambridge, § 28 and k. 2.)

## THE LAWS OF EADGAR

This is the ordinance that Eadgar established with the counsel of his wise men, for the glory of God, for his own royal dignity, and for the benefit of all his people.

I. Concerning the immunity of the Church and the dues to be rendered to it.

Let this therefore be the first provision: that the churches of God should receive what is lawfully due to them, and that all primary tithes should be given to the chief church to which the parish belongs. This is to be rendered whether from a thegn’s land or from the land of villagers, according to the course of the plow.

II. Concerning the ecclesiastical census.

If there is a thegn who has a church in his estate with a cemetery, let him give one third of his own tithes to his church. If anyone has a church without a cemetery, let him give his priest whatever he wishes from the nine parts; and let every ecclesiastical due from every free piece of land pass to the chief church.

III. Concerning tithes.

Let each tithe of offspring be rendered at Pentecost, and the tithe of the earth’s crops at the equinox. Let every ecclesiastical due be rendered at the feast of Martin, under the full fine that the judicial book prescribes. If anyone refuses to render the tithe as we have said, let the king’s reeve, the bishops, and the priest of the church go to him; let them take from him, against his will, the tenth part belonging to the church and assign him the ninth part; let the eight parts be divided in two, and let the lord take one half and the bishop the other, whether the man is the king’s servant or a thegn’s.

IV. Concerning the penny imposed on each household.

Let every penny imposed on individual households be paid by the feast of Peter. Whoever has not paid it by that deadline is to carry it to Rome, together with thirty additional denarii, and bring back from there a certificate that he delivered that amount. Then, having returned home, let him pay the king one hundred and twenty solidi. If he again refuses to pay it, let him carry it to Rome again, make a similar payment, and then, having returned home, pay the king two hundred solidi. If he refuses to render it a third time, let him lose everything he has.

V. Concerning feast days and fasts.

Let every Sunday feast be celebrated from the afternoon of Saturday until dawn on Monday, under the fine prescribed by the judicial book; and let all other feast days be celebrated as is proper. Let the appointed fast be observed with complete devotion.

[Col. 0513]

## PRAYER OF KING EDGAR TO DUNSTAN, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, OSWALD, BISHOP OF WORCESTER, AND ETHELWALD, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER

(Year 967.) It enumerates the vices of married clerics, decrees that they are to be expelled, and that monks are to be introduced. He entrusts responsibility for the matter to the bishops, supported by royal authority.

[Col. 0513D] Since the Lord has magnified his mercy in dealing with us, it is fitting, most reverend Fathers, that we should respond to his countless benefits with worthy deeds. For we do not possess the land by our own sword, nor did our own arm save [Col. 0514D] us, but his right hand and his holy arm, because he was pleased with us. It is therefore just that we should subject both ourselves and our souls to him who has subjected all things beneath our feet, and that we should not slacken in ensuring that those whom he has subjected to us are subject to his laws.

It is indeed my responsibility to deal with laymen according to the right of equity, to administer just judgment between one man and his neighbour, to punish sacrilegious persons, restrain rebels, rescue the needy from the hand of his stronger oppressors, and deliver the destitute and poor from those who plunder them. But it is also my concern to provide for the ministers of the churches, the flocks of monks, the choirs of virgins, and their necessities, and to attend to their salvation, quiet, and peace. The examination of all their conduct belongs to us [read: to you]: whether they live continently; whether they conduct themselves honourably toward those who are outside; whether they are diligent in the divine offices; whether they are assiduous in teaching the people; whether they are temperate in food; whether they are moderate in dress; and whether they are discerning in judgments. I speak with your permission, reverend Fathers: if you had attended to these matters with careful scrutiny, such horrifying and abominable things concerning the clergy would not have reached our ears.

I say nothing of the fact that they have neither an open crown nor a suitable tonsure; but their lascivious clothing, insolence in bearing, and obscenity in speech reveal the madness of the inner man. Moreover, how great is their negligence in the divine offices, when they scarcely deign to attend the sacred vigils, and when they seem to gather for the solemn sacred Masses more for playing and smirking than for singing psalms. I shall say what the good mourn and the wicked laugh at; I shall say with grief—and even whether it can be said—how they run riot in feasts, drunkenness, bedrooms, and indecencies, so that the houses of the clergy are now thought to be brothels of prostitutes and meeting places of actors. There are dice there, dancing and singing; there are vigils prolonged amid shouting and uproar [Col. 0515C] until the middle of the night. Thus the patrimonies of kings, the alms of the poor, and—what is more—the price of that precious blood are squandered.

Did our fathers therefore empty their treasures for this? Did the royal treasury, after many revenues had been withdrawn, make gifts for this? Did royal munificence bestow fields and possessions upon the churches of Christ for this: that prostitutes should be adorned with the luxuries of the clergy, extravagant banquets prepared, and dogs, birds, and such other amusements purchased? The soldiers cry out about this, the common people murmur, actors sing and dance—and you neglect it, you spare them, you dissemble!

Where is the sword of Levi and the zeal of Simeon, who, when the Shechemites had violated Jacob’s daughter—representing those who defile Christ’s Church by polluted acts—even though they had been circumcised, cut them down [Col. 0515D]? Where is the spirit of Moses, who did not spare even those of his own blood who worshipped the calf’s head? Where is the dagger of Phinehas the priest, who, by stabbing the man fornicating with the Midianite woman, appeased God in his anger through this holy emulation? Where is the spirit of Peter, by whose power avarice is slain and the Simoniac heresy condemned?

Emulate, O priests, emulate the ways of the Lord and the justice of our God. The time has come to rise up against those who have scattered the law of God. I have Constantine’s sword, and you have Peter’s, in your hands. Let us join right hands and unite sword with sword, so that lepers may be expelled outside the camp, the sanctuary of the Lord cleansed, and the sons of Levi minister in the temple—the one who said to his father and mother, “I do not know you,” and to his brothers, “I do not recognize you.”

Act, I beg you, diligently, lest we regret having done what we have done and given what we have given, if we see it consumed with impunity not in God’s service but in the luxury of the worst men. Let the relics of the saints move you, relics among which they insult them; let the venerable altars move you, before which they behave madly. Let the extraordinary devotion of our predecessors move you, whose alms clerical madness abuses.

My great-grandfather Edward, as you know, tithed all his land to churches and monasteries. My ancestor Alfred of holy memory, in order to enrich the Church, thought that nothing should be spared—not patrimony, not expenses, not revenues. It is not unknown to your fatherhood how much my grandfather, the elder Edward, bestowed upon the churches. You ought to remember with what gifts my father and my brother filled the altars of Christ.

O Father of Fathers, Dunstan, contemplate, I beg you, my father’s eyes shining upon you from that radiant region of heaven. Hear, with some compassion, his plaintive voice resounding in your ears:

“You, Father Dunstan—you gave me sound counsel concerning the building of monasteries and the construction of churches; you stood by me as helper and fellow-worker in all things. I chose you as the shepherd, father, and bishop of my soul, and as guardian of my morals. When did I ever disobey you? What treasures did I ever prefer to your counsels? What possessions, at your command, did I not reject? If you thought anything should be distributed to the poor, I was ready. If you judged anything should be given to churches, I did not delay. If you complained that anything was lacking for monks or clerics, I supplied it. You said that almsgiving was eternal, and that there was no more fruitful almsgiving than what is bestowed upon monasteries and churches, so that God’s servants might be sustained and what remained distributed to the poor.”

O precious almsgiving, and worthy price of a soul! O salutary remedy for our sins! What reeks from Sibyl’s bosom in the little skin of a foreign mouse, what adorns her ears, arranges her little fingers, and binds her delicate body in linen and purple! Behold, Father, the fruit of my almsgiving and the result of your permission.

[Col. 0516D] What will you answer this complaint? I know, I know: “When you saw a thief, you did not run with him, nor did you share your portion with adulterers.” You rebuked, pleaded, and reproached them. Your words have been despised; we must come to blows, and royal power will not be lacking to you.

You have here with you the venerable Father Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester; you have the reverend bishop Oswald of Worcester. I entrust this matter to you, so that by episcopal censure and royal authority those who live shamefully may be expelled from the churches, and those who live orderly lives introduced in their place.

[Col. 0517]

## Charter of King Edgar Given at the Council of London in the Year 970 or 972

*(From an old manuscript codex of Glastonbury.)*

[Col. 0517A] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Although the decrees of pontiffs and the words of priests are fixed with unshaken bonds, like the foundations of mountains, nevertheless the religion of the holy Church is often scattered and broken by the storms and whirlwinds of secular affairs through the stains of reprobate men. Therefore we have determined that it will benefit succeeding generations if those things which are defined by salutary counsel and common agreement are strengthened and confirmed by our written documents.

Accordingly, it seems fitting that the church of the most blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary at Glastonbury, just as it has from ancient times held a principal dignity in my kingdom, should likewise be honoured by us with a certain special and singular freedom of privilege.

Therefore, at the urging of Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, and Oswald [Col. 0517B], archbishop of York, and with the consent and approval also of Brithelm, bishop of Wells, and of the other bishops, abbots, and leading men, I, Edgar, by divine ordinance king of the English and governor and ruler of the other peoples living round about, in the name of the gracious Trinity, for the soul of my father who rests there and for the souls of my predecessors, decree, establish, and confirm by this present privilege that the aforesaid monastery and all its possessions shall now and forever remain free and undisturbed from every tax arising from fiscal obligations, and shall possess soke and sake, and so forth, as freely and peacefully as I possess them throughout the whole kingdom.

The abbot and monks of the aforesaid monastery shall likewise possess in their own court the same freedom and authority that I possess in my court, both in releasing and in punishing, and in every kind of business whatsoever [Col. 0517C].
