If, moreover, the abbot or any monk of that place should encounter on the road a thief being led to hanging or to any other danger of death, he shall have the power to rescue him from the impending danger throughout my kingdom.

I also confirm and strengthen the following, which has hitherto been carefully observed by all our predecessors: that the bishop of Wells, or his ministers, shall have no authority whatsoever over this monastery or over its parish churches—namely, Streete, Mirielinge, Budeclea, Schapwicke, and Sowi—or over their chapels, nor over those situated on the islands, namely Bekeria, called Little Ireland, Godeneja, Marteneseja, [Col. 0517D] Ferramere, Padenebergia, and Adredeseja, except only when they have been summoned by the abbot for the purpose of dedicating or ordaining. Nor shall they summon their priests to their synod, chapter, or any court; nor suspend them from the divine office; nor presume to exercise any right over them whatsoever [Col. 0518A].

The abbot shall have his monks and the clerics of the aforesaid churches ordained, according to the custom of the ancient Church of Glastonbury and apostolic authority, by whichever neighbouring bishop he wishes, with the agreement of Archbishop Dunstan and all the bishops of my kingdom.

We permit the bishop of Wells to dedicate the churches if he has been requested to do so by the abbot. At Easter, moreover, the abbot shall receive from the bishop of Wells the consecrated chrism and oil according to custom, and distribute them among his aforesaid churches.

Above all this, by God’s prohibition and by our authority—while preserving the dignity of the holy Roman Church and of Canterbury—I forbid any person of whatever power, whether king, bishop, duke [Col. 0518B], or prince, or any of their ministers, to presume to enter the bounds of Glastonbury or of the aforesaid parishes for the purpose of investigating, seizing, holding court, or doing anything else that might be contrary to those serving there. Only the abbot and the community shall have authority, in known and unknown matters, small and great, and in every kind of business whatsoever, as we have stated above.

But whoever henceforth attempts, with sacrilegious presumption, on any pretext and by reason of any dignity, rank, or profession, to overturn the dignity of this privilege or render it void, let him know without doubt that before the strict Judge he will give an unsteady and trembling account, unless he first strives to correct the matter by worthy satisfaction.

[Col. 0518C] This charter of privilege was drawn up and confirmed at London by the common counsel of all my leading men, in the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 971, in the fourteenth indiction. The parties to this gift were the following, whose names appear written below.

### Subscriptions

I, Edgar, king of all Britain, have confirmed the aforesaid liberty with the seal of the holy cross.

I, Ealfgifu, mother of the same king, have gladly consented.

I, Edward, prince (*clyto*), have impressed my father’s gift with the triumph of the holy cross.

[Col. 0518D] I, Ciniod, king of Alba, have assented.

I, Mascusius, archpirate, have strengthened it.

I, Dunstan, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, together with the trophy of the holy cross and the assisting bishops, have confirmed the king’s gift.

[Col. 0519A] I, Oswald, primate of the Church of York, have subscribed in agreement.

I, Æthelwold, minister of the Church of Winchester and monk of Glastonbury, have impressed the sign of the holy cross.

I, Brithelm, bishop of Wells, have strengthened it in agreement.

I, Ælstan, bishop, have confirmed it.

I, Oswald, bishop, have assented.

I, Ælfwold, bishop, have granted it.

I, Winsige, bishop, have concluded it with the sign of the holy cross.

I, Segegar, abbot, have impressed the banner of the holy cross.

I, Escwi, abbot, have confirmed it.

[Col. 0519B] I, Ordgar, abbot, have strengthened it.

I, Æthelgar, abbot, have granted it.

I, Kinweard, abbot, have consented.

I, Fideman, abbot, have consolidated it.

I, Ælfheah, abbot, have subscribed.

I, Adulf, overseer (*catascopus*) of the Church of Hereford, have strengthened it.

[Col. 0520A] I, Ælfhere, duke, have confirmed with complete devotion, by the seal of the holy cross, the liberty of my lady Saint Mary’s Church of Glastonbury.

I, Oslac, duke, have consented.

I, Æthelwine, duke, have impressed this triumphant gift of the holy cross with the depiction made by my own hand.

I, Oswald, minister, have confirmed it.

I, Ælfric, minister, have strengthened it.

I, Æthelsige, minister, have consented.

I, Ælfkic, minister, have consented.

King Edgar confirmed this charter of privilege in the twelfth year of his reign, by a sacred written instrument at London, with the common counsel of his leading men. Pope John XIII likewise authorized this same charter at Rome in a general synod, and caused all the men of higher rank who presided over that council to confirm it, at the request of the aforesaid King Edgar, blessed Dunstan, and the other noblemen mentioned above. And, to provide firmer security, the same pope supported the said privilege with apostolic authority.

[Col. 0519]

## Charter of King Edgar Made for the Monastery of Malmesbury in the Year 974

It states that he expelled secular clerics and introduced monks living according to a rule.

[Col. 0519C] [Note: Ingulf, *History of Crowland*, p. 884; Malmesbury, *De gestis regum*, Book I, chapter 8.]

I, Edgar, basileus of all Albion and of the neighbouring maritime and island kings, exalted by the abundant grace of God so as to be subject to none of my ancestors, often and diligently considered, mindful of so great an honour, what gift of my empire I should offer above all to the King of kings.

Then heavenly piety suddenly suggested to my diligent devotion, as a pious and vigilant helper, that I should restore the holy monasteries in my kingdom. They had visibly been ruined down to the timber, like roofs torn apart by patchwork shingles and rotten boards, and—what was more important—had inwardly been neglected and almost emptied of the service of God.

For I expelled unlearned clerics, subject to no discipline of regular religion, and in many places appointed pastors of a holier order, namely of the monastic habit, providing them with ample expenditures from fiscal revenues to restore the ruined churches. One of them, named Eluric, a man ecclesiastical in every respect, I appointed guardian of the very famous monastery which the English call by the twofold name Maldemelsburh.

For the benefit of my soul, in honour of our Saviour, his ever-virgin Mother Mary, the God-bearer (*Theotokos*, Θεοτόκος), and the apostles Peter and Paul, as well as the blessed bishop Aldhelm, I restored to him, with munificent generosity, a portion of land—specifically land with meadows and woods.

This land, having been assigned to the aforesaid clerics, had been unjustly possessed by the contentious Edolnoth [variant: Edelnoth]. But when his superstitious and subtle argument had been heard by my wise men and his deceitful contention had been refuted by them in my presence, I returned it for monastic use, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 974, in the fourteenth year of my reign and the first year of my royal administration. This concerns Malmesbury.

### Subscriptions

I, Edgar, basileus of all Albion and of the neighbouring kings, have confirmed this charter with the sign of the holy cross.

I, Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, have strengthened this royal gift with the triumph of the holy cross.

[Col. 0520D] I, Oswald, archbishop of York, have subscribed.

I, Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester, have sealed it.

I, Lefwin, bishop of Dorchester, have consented.

I, Ælstan, bishop of London, have approved.

I, Turketul, abbot of Crowland, have undersigned.

I, Æthelgar, abbot of the New Minster at Winchester, have approved.

I, Adulf, abbot of Bury, have praised it together with the others.

[Col. 0521A] I, Ælfhere, duke, was present.

I, Æthelwine, duke, stood by.

[Col. 0522A] I, Brithold, duke, witnessed it.

And others.

# Laws of the Northumbrian Priests

## Laws of the Northumbrian Priests

Both for correcting their conduct and for advancing their ministries.

*(From manuscript collection Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, S. XVIII.)*

[Col. 0521A]

**I.** If anyone inflicts any injury upon a priest, all his fellow priests, with the assistance of the bishop, shall diligently see to the compensation, and shall be ready to do whatever is just, as it is written, being of one heart and one soul.

**II.** And, as though by God’s prohibition, we forbid anyone to buy or receive another’s church, unless that man has committed a capital crime by which he is no longer worthy to serve at the altar. If any priest does the contrary, let him lose his dignity and the friendship of his colleagues; let him celebrate Mass nowhere until the man who ought by right to possess the church has obtained it; and let the one who committed the wrong pay 20 oras to the bishop, 12 oras to the priest whom he expelled from his church, and 12 oras to all his colleagues. Let him also forfeit whatever money he unjustly gave for another priest’s church. Every priest shall also find twelve sureties that he will faithfully observe the laws of the priests.

**III.** If any priest commits an offence and celebrates Mass contrary to the bishop’s command, let him pay 20 oras for transgressing that command; and in addition let him compensate for the offence he previously committed.

**IV.** If a priest neglects the bishop’s own edict, let him pay 20 oras.

**V.** If a priest pays laymen a tribute that was owed to those ordained to sacred orders, let him pay 20 oras.

**VI.** If a priest neglects the archdeacon’s edict, let him pay 12 oras.

**VII.** If a priest is guilty of a crime and celebrates Mass without the archdeacon’s edict [Col. 0521C], let him pay 12 oras.

**VIII.** If a priest refuses baptism or confession, let him compensate this with 12 oras, and at least diligently intercede before God.

**IX.** If a priest does not seek chrism at the proper time, let him pay 12 oras.

**X.** Every infant shall be baptized promptly within nine days, under penalty of 6 oras. If an unbaptized infant dies through negligence within nine days, the parents shall make satisfaction before God without a worldly fine. If it is after nine days, they shall make satisfaction before God and pay 12 oras to the parish priest because the child remained a pagan for so long.

**XI.** If a priest wrongly announces a feast or fast to the people, let him make satisfaction before God and pay 12 oras.

**XII.** If a priest obtains ordination unjustly outside his diocese, let him pay 12 oras, and the deacon 6 oras; and let them lose their orders unless the diocesan bishop confirms their orders.

**XIII.** If a priest celebrates Mass in unconsecrated buildings, let him pay 12 oras.

**XIV.** If a priest celebrates Mass outside a consecrated altar, let him pay 12 oras.

**XV.** If a priest consecrates the Eucharist in a wooden chalice, let him pay 12 oras.

**XVI.** If a priest celebrates Mass without wine, let him pay 12 oras.

**XVII.** If a priest neglects the holy Eucharist, let him pay 12 oras.

**XVIII.** If a priest celebrates Mass more than three times in one day, let him pay 12 oras.

[Col. 0522B] **XIX.** If anyone violates ecclesiastical peace, let him make compensation according to the dignity of the church and its immunity.

**XX.** If anyone conducts trade with a church, let him pay the penalty for violating the law.

**XXI.** If anyone forces a church to serve his own needs, let him compensate this with the penalty for violating the law.

**XXII.** If anyone unjustly expels a priest from a church, let him compensate this with the penalty for violating the law.

**XXIII.** If anyone wounds a priest, let the treatment of the wound be compensated, and let 12 oras be given as compensation to the altar on account of his order. For a deacon, 6 oras shall be given as compensation to the altar.

**XXIV.** If anyone kills a priest, the full assessed value of his life shall be paid, and 24 oras to the bishop as compensation to the altar [Col. 0522C]. For a deacon, 12 oras shall be given as compensation to the altar.

**XXV.** If a priest disgraces the church, from which all his glory ought to arise, let him compensate this.

**XXVI.** If a priest places something indecent in the church, let him compensate this.

**XXVII.** If a priest removes a church’s property, let him compensate it.

**XXVIII.** If a priest voluntarily abandons the church in which he was ordained, let him compensate this.

**XXIX.** If a priest despises another, or mocks him by word or deed, let him compensate this.

**XXX.** If a priest fights with another, let him compensate both him and the bishop.

**XXXI.** If a priest assists others in an unjust matter, let him compensate this [Col. 0522D].

**XXXII.** If a priest denies others just assistance, let him compensate this.

[Col. 0523A] **XXXIII.** If a priest does not warn another of something he knows will be harmful to him, let him compensate this.

**XXXIV.** If a priest neglects to shave his beard or hair, let him compensate this.

**XXXV.** If a priest dismisses his concubine and takes another, let him be anathema.

**XXXVI.** If a priest does not ring the bells at the appointed times or sing the hours, let him compensate this.

**XXXVII.** If a priest enters a church with weapons, let him compensate this.

**XXXVIII.** If a priest improperly performs the church’s annual service by day or by night, let him compensate it.

**XXXIX.** If a priest improperly arranges an ordeal, let him compensate it [Col. 0523B].

**XL.** If a priest conceals his tonsure, let him make amends.

**XLI.** If a priest is a drunkard, a buffoon, or a *calscop* [uncertain term], let him compensate this.

**XLII.** If a priest conceals something among his parish neighbours in order to exercise unjust rule, let him make amends.

**XLIII.** If a priest omits the annual rites through forgetfulness, let him make amends.

**XLIV.** If a priest avoids the synod, let him compensate this.

**XLV.** If a priest does not submit himself to justice but resists the bishop’s decree, let him either correct this or be separated from the communion of the ordained and stripped both of his fellowship [Col. 0523C] and of every honour, unless he submits and gives clear satisfaction.

**XLVI.** If anyone slanders divine or human law, let him be severely corrected.

**XLVII.** We must all venerate and love the one God, hold firmly to the one Christian faith, and unanimously reject all paganism.

Therefore, if anyone hereafter discovers someone practising any pagan superstition—whether by divination, by a burning brand (*torrem*), or by delighting in magic—or worshipping idols:

If he is a royal thane, let him be punished with 10 half-marks: one half for Christ and the other for the king.

If he is another landholder who has done this, let him pay 6 half-marks, one half for Christ and the other for the lord of that land.

If he is an inferior person called a *faerbena*, let him pay 2 oras.

If the king’s thane denies this in a lawsuit, twelve compurgators shall be named for him, and he shall take twelve from among his kinsmen and twelve foreigners [lacuna]. If he fails, let him pay a *lahslite* of 10 half-marks.

If a landholder denies this, as many of his equals shall be taken as were assigned to the king’s thane; and if he fails, let him pay a *lahslite* of 6 half-marks.

If a *cyrlisc*—that is, a peasant or pagan—denies this in a lawsuit, as many of his equals shall be taken as were assigned to the others mentioned above; and if he fails, let him pay a *lahslite* of 12 oras.

**XLVIII.** If that superstitious gathering called *frithgear* is held on someone’s land around a stone, tree, spring, or other such foolish object, the person who does this shall pay the fine for violating the law, half to Christ and half to the lord of the land. If the lord of the land refuses to provide assistance for correcting this, Christ and the king shall receive the compensation.

**XLIX.** We forbid trading on Sunday, holding courts anywhere, every kind of work, and all forms of transport, whether in carts, on horses, or in carrying other loads. Whoever transgresses against this [Col. 0524B], if free, shall pay a fine of 12 oras; if a slave, he shall lose his hide—that is, be flogged—unless he is a traveller compelled by necessity, because of lack of food, or in order to avoid enemies. On the eves of feasts it is permitted, of necessity, to travel between York and a point six thousand measured paces from it.

**L.** Whoever violates feasts or the required fasts shall pay 12 oras.

**LI.** We also wish every Roman penny to be paid in full to the bishop’s see annually before the feast of Saint Peter. Moreover, we wish two faithful thanes and one mass-priest to be chosen in each wapentake to collect it; they shall immediately hand over what they receive, after taking an oath if necessary.

[Col. 0524C] If either the king’s thane or any other lord of the land detains this penny, let him pay a fine of 10 half-marks, half to Christ and half to the king.

If any villager conceals or detains this penny, his landed lord shall pay it, and shall take an ox from the villager in compensation. If the lord refuses, Christ and the king shall receive 12 oras as fuller compensation.

If a royal thane detains tithes, let him pay 10 half-marks; a landholder, 6; and a *cyrlisc*, or pagan, 12 oras.

**LII.** We also forbid, as God has forbidden, that anyone have more than one wife, and that she be properly married and previously given publicly. No one shall contract marriage within his kinship, namely below the fourth degree or knee [generation], nor with the person with whom he was co-sponsor at the sacred font. If anyone does the contrary, let him be deprived of God’s mercy unless he repents and makes compensation according to the bishop’s judgment. If he proceeds further in wickedness and dies, let him be deprived of an honourable burial and be alien from God’s mercy.

**LIII.** If anyone has intercourse with a nun, let both pay their *wergeld*, that is, the assessed value of their lives—both the man and the woman. If they die in this sin without repentance, let them be deprived of honourable burial and be alien from God’s mercy.

**LIV.** If anyone abandons his wife, who is living with him in a lawful marriage, and unlawfully takes another, let him be deprived of God’s mercy unless he makes amends. Each person shall rightly keep his marriage while his wife lives, unless it should happen that, on the bishop’s advice, they are separated so that they may thereafter live apart in chastity.

**LV.** If anyone henceforth violates just laws, let him continually pay compensation.

**LVI.** We must all venerate and love the one God, hold firmly to the one Christian faith, [Col. 0526A] and completely reject all paganism. And we wish land-purchase (*land ceap*) and law-purchase (*lah ceap*), the judgments of the wise, true testimony, just judgment, baptism (*fulloc*) and the first reckoning (*frum talu*) to remain firm; and likewise drink and food, and the rightful dues owed to the lord of the land, shall be paid. Let there always be one Christianity among the people and one kingdom.

Blessed be the name of the Lord, from this time forth and forever.

# Capitularies of the Frankish Kings and Emperors after the Division of the Empire, 840–921

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Laws, vol. I, p. 374.)*

[Col. 0525]

## Assembly of Lothar I at Ingelheim

*(Year 840, August 25.)*

[Note: Since his father had died and Lothar had returned to Germany, according to Flodoard in his *History of Reims*, Ebo, formerly archbishop of Reims, met him near Worms. After several days the emperor restored to him, by imperial decree, the see and diocese of Reims. The text of this decree preserved by Flodoard lists the names of the bishops who had initially gathered around Lothar during the disputes, in a formula of Ulrich of Bamberg abridged in Eckhart.]

[Col. 0525B] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God. Lothar [Note: “Lotharius,” Flodoard], by the ordering of divine providence august emperor.

Since confession of sins is no less necessary in adversity than in prosperity, and God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart, we do not doubt that there is joy among the angels in heaven over one sinner who repents. Nor do we mortals on earth despise those for whom, as we know by divine testimony, the angels in heaven rejoice.

Divine kindness has taught us that those who accuse and rebuke themselves for their excesses are not condemned but restored: the one who not only rescued the prostitute from legal condemnation but also did not condemn the humbled tax collector who accused himself, rather exalting him by justifying him; the one who said, “Everyone who humbles himself shall not be condemned, but shall be exalted.”

Therefore, because the sons of your Church have asked for it, we restore to you, Ebo, the authority which you lost when you were carried away on our account, and we restore to you the see and diocese of the city of Reims [Col. 0526B], so that, clothed again in the former pallium of holy apostolic liberality, after completing a humble satisfaction, you may exercise with us the harmony and grace of the divine office, receiving it through our solemn generosity.

Drogo [Note: of Metz], bishop, assented.

Otgarius [Note: of Mainz], archbishop.

Hecti [Note: of Trier], archbishop.

Amalwinus [Note: of Besançon], archbishop.

Audax [Note: of Tarentaise], archbishop.

Joseph [Note: of Ivrea], bishop.

Adalulfus [Note: of Grenoble], bishop.

David [Note: of Lausanne], bishop.

Rodingus [Note: mentioned in Lupus’s Letter 11], bishop.

Giselbertus [Note: compare Nithard, *History*, II.2], bishop.

Flotarius [Note: of Toul], bishop.

Badaradus [Note: of Paderborn], bishop.

Hagaeno [Note: of Bergamo], bishop.

Hartgarius [Note: perhaps of Liège], bishop.

Ado [Note: of Valence], bishop.

Samuel [Note: of Worms], bishop.

[Col. 0526C] Rambertus [Note: of Brescia], bishop.

Haiminus [Note: perhaps of Ceneda], bishop.

[Col. 0527A] Ratoldus [Note: designated for Strasbourg], called bishop, a priest.

Amalricus [Note: designated for Como], called bishop, with very many other priests and deacons publicly assisting.

It was enacted in the public palace at Engilenheim in the month of [Col. 0528A] June, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July [Note: from the judgment of Cointius and Pagi, it seems that it should be read “in the month of August, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September”], while the lord Emperor Lothar was reigning and ruling, in the first year of his return, having become his father’s successor in Francia, in the third indiction.

[Col. 0527]

## Pact of Louis II and Charles II at Strasbourg

*(Year 842, February 14.)*

[Note: We give it from Nithard’s *History*.]

### Announcement of Louis to the People in the Germanic Language

[Col. 0527A]

You know how often Lothar, after our father’s death, persecuted me and this brother of mine and attempted to destroy us utterly [Col. 0527B]. But when neither brotherhood, nor Christianity, nor any device could help us—while preserving justice—so that there might be peace between us, we were finally compelled to submit the matter to the judgment of almighty God, so that by his will we might be content with whatever was due to each.

In this, as you know, by the mercy of God we proved victorious; but he, having been defeated, withdrew with his men wherever he could. Then, moved by brotherly love and also taking pity on the Christian people, we did not wish to persecute and destroy them; rather, as before, we commanded that at least thereafter each person should receive his just due.

But after this he was not content with the divine judgment. With hostile force he has again not ceased to persecute both me and this brother of mine; moreover, he has devastated our people with fires, plunder, and killings [Col. 0527C]. Therefore, compelled by necessity, we have now gathered; and because we believe that you doubt our steadfast faith and firm brotherhood, we have decided to support this oath between us in your presence.

We do not do this because we have been lured by any unjust desire, but so that, if God grants us peace with your assistance, we may be more certain of our common advancement. But if—which God forbid—I should presume to violate the oath I have sworn to my brother, I release each one of you from my allegiance and also from the oath you have sworn to me.

### Announcement of Charles in the Roman Language

An announcement of the same subject and content as Louis’s.

### Oath of Louis in the Roman Language

[Col. 0528A]

For the love of God, for the Christian people, and for our common salvation, from this day forward, insofar as God gives me knowledge and power, I shall save this brother of mine Charles, and shall assist him in every matter, just as a man ought by right to save his brother, provided that he does the same for me; and I shall never enter into any agreement with Lothar that would be harmful to this brother of mine Charles.

### Oath of Charles in the Germanic Language

In God’s love and for the salvation of this Christian people and of us both, from this day forward, insofar as God grants me wisdom and power, I shall support this brother of mine as a man ought by right to support his brother, provided that he does the same for me; and I shall enter into no agreement with Lothar that, according to my will, would cause him harm.

### Oath of the Western Franks in the Roman Language

[Col. 0528C]

If Louis preserves the oath which he swears to his brother Charles, and Charles, my lord, on his part does not observe it, if I cannot turn him back, nor anyone whom I could turn back, I shall give him no assistance against Louis.

### Oath of the Eastern Franks in the Germanic Language
But if Charles fulfills the oath that he swore to his brother Louis, and Louis, my lord, breaks the oath that he swore to him, if I cannot turn him from it, neither I nor any of those whom I can turn from it will give Charles aid against him.

[Col. 0527]

KAROLUS II: ASSEMBLY AT THE ESTATE OF COLONIA. (A.D. 843, November.)  
[Note: [Col. 0527] Edited by Sirmond and Baluze from the following manuscripts: 1) the Tilianus; 2) Paris, Royal Library, no. 4638; and 3b) Saint Vincent of Metz. We have collated the edition with the aid of manuscript 2 and of 3), the Paris royal manuscript among the Latin Supplements, no. 75, of the tenth century. This last has the following as a preface: “The chapters issued and confirmed from the assembly held at the estate called Colonia, with the consent of their prince and of the other faithful, and to be observed as necessary by all the faithful.” We have collated the text. The estate of Colonia is Coulaines, near Le Mans.]

[Note.]

[Col. 0527D] Here begin the chapters enacted in the fourth year of the reign of the lord Charles, the glorious king [Note: [Col. 0527] absent in manuscript 2], son of the lord Louis the emperor, at the assembly held at the estate called Colonia. They were also confirmed by the subscription of that same prince, the bishops, and the other faithful [Col. 0528D] of God, with the consent of Warin and the other nobles, in the sixth indiction [Note: [Col. 0527D] Read “seventh,” which was current in November, when Charles, returning from his journey to Rennes—where on 13 November he granted a charter to his faithful Otto—held this assembly. See the preface to the synod held at Meaux in A.D. 845.].

The holy Church, like a ship—to say nothing of earlier ages—from the beginning of its institution has thus far crossed the sea [Col. 0529A] of this world, under the Lord’s direction, through conditions of varying character. At one time it has been burdened by calm; at another it has been shaken by the storm of some tempest, though never completely submerged; rather, when Christ its helmsman was aroused by the prayers of the faithful, it received the salutary security of freedom and was granted the serenity it desired.

Thus, in those regions of our world which in the time of our grandfather of blessed memory, and of the lord our father of holy memory, had for a while rejoiced in the sweetness of peace, the enemy, in accordance with the holy Gospel, having sown the weeds of discord in the Lord’s field among the wheat, the caritas beloved of God was so harassed by diverse and adverse troubles that, only with the greatest difficulty, through divine regard and the support of God’s faithful and our own [Note: [Col. 0529] “lovers,” in manuscript 2], reconciliation could be achieved between us and our brothers, division of our father’s kingdom by mutual agreement, and at least some breathing-space from the great labors of that holy Church and faithful people.

As time passed, however, just as traces of clouds commonly remain after the dense whirlwinds of the air have passed away, we confess that such materials and fuel for dissension remained among us and among ecclesiastical men, as well as among the administrators of our commonwealth, so that it became plainly evident that we needed divine grace in order to strip ourselves completely of the contagion of the former disease by which we had been overcome, so that we might recognize our common infirmity.

Therefore our faithful, assembling together—both those in the venerable clerical order and illustrious men established in noble lay rank [Col. 0529C]—and inflamed with zeal for God, remembering also the faith that they and their predecessors had shown to our predecessors, and placing before their eyes the love and fidelity that, after our father’s death, they had commendably and most steadfastly preserved toward us, exhorted one another, indeed all admonished one another [Note: [Col. 0529] absent in manuscript 2], as it is written in divinely inspired writings, so that all might drive from their hearts every resentment conceived over any matter, and might unite in concord and true friendship for the will of God, the fitting veneration of the holy Church, the preservation of their fidelity toward us, and the establishment and maintenance of due honor and royal power. Thus they might please divine mercy more earnestly, deliberate more loftily concerning the stability and welfare of the king and kingdom, and obtain more fully their own common advancement and that of the entire people, together with tranquility.

Accordingly, after this assembly, pleasing and praiseworthy to God, had been carried out unanimously and reasonably, they most faithfully presented their devotion and action to our gentleness. We, having carefully observed such great benevolence on the part of the faithful toward our rule, returned thanks worthy of them, as the matter deserved, and with complete devotion promised that we and our authority would, through goodwill, be partners and companions of their good agreement in this undertaking, which undoubtedly tends toward present and eternal salvation. We renounced everything which, so far as human frailty permits, our governing person had until then done, whether through ignorance, youth, or necessity, against what was beneficial and honorable for it, or had contracted through another’s cunning.

For this reason, after common deliberation, we proposed that this document be drawn up, and decreed that it should be strengthened by the subscriptions of all our hands. In it we have written what now seemed especially relevant to the common salvation, the stability of the kingdom, the advantage of all our people—in fact, to the fullest possible honor. We do not speak through the alteration of different persons, so that now royal exaltation, now episcopal authority, and now the advantage of the faithful might speak; but, according to the Apostle, under one head, Christ, so that, truly one person in the body of one Church, and each one members of the other, we may all speak with one voice, unanimously, for the benefit of all, through him and in him who said, and concerning whom it was said: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

1. Concerning, namely, the honor and worship of God and of the holy churches which, by God’s authorship, stand under the jurisdiction and protection of our rule, we jointly decree, with the Lord’s help, that just as they were cultivated, honored, and enlarged in their possessions in the time of the lord our father of blessed memory, [Col. 0530C] so they shall remain, preserving equity [Note: [Col. 0529] “preserving equity” is absent in manuscript 3]. Those that are honored and enriched by our generosity shall henceforth be preserved in the full integrity of their rights; and priests and servants of God shall obtain ecclesiastical authority and their due privileges, in accordance with revered authority. Royal power, the strength of illustrious men, and the administrators of the commonwealth shall, in every respect, reasonably and justly cooperate with them, so that they may properly carry out their ministry.

2. Royal honor also, the authority appropriate to royal dignity, and the sincerity and obedience owed to one’s lord shall be shown to us in every respect and by everyone, as had been customary in the time of our predecessors, with all negligence, cunning, and any improper association of anyone against our honor, authority, and welfare, or against the stability of our kingdom, removed. If anyone clearly learns that someone is plotting anything against us and against this pledged sincerity [Note: [Col. 0529] “learns” in manuscript 2], and cannot turn him back, let him openly expose and denounce him. Thus episcopal authority and the unanimity of the faithful shall strive and labor with all their strength to ensure, by counsel and aid, that our honor and royal authority remain unshaken [Note: [Col. 0529] absent in manuscript 3].

3. Since we recognize that it is right to honor those from whom we receive honor, according to the Lord’s saying, we wish all our faithful to hold it as certain that henceforth no one, of whatever order or dignity, is to be deprived of his deserved honor through our unsuitable whim, another’s cunning, or unjust desire, except by a judgment grounded in justice [Note: [Col. 0531] “to be deprived” is “to be deprived” in manuscript 3], and as justice [Note: [Col. 0531] manuscript 3 adds “or by what is just”] and reason and equity dictate. I promise to preserve for each person the law appropriate to him, in every dignity and order, just as his predecessors held it in the time of our predecessors, with God’s favor [Note: [Col. 0531] manuscript 3: “we promise that our magnificence will observe it, by the Lord’s favor”].

4. So that our authority may observe this more easily and earnestly [Note: [Col. 0531] “may be able” in manuscript 3], you shall strive to preserve everything, as you pledged in your well-remembered agreement [Note: [Col. 0531] “memorial agreement,” Bell]. Indeed, all shall henceforth carefully beware lest anyone, for any private advantage, rejected desire, or connection of kinship, familiarity, or friendship, make excessive suggestions to us, entice us by petitions or in any other way, so that we act against justice and reason [Note: [Col. 0531] Bal. reads “against justice and reason,”], the dignity of our name, or the equity of our rule.

5. And [Note: [Col. 0531] “But” in manuscript 3] if anything should happen to have been surreptitiously imposed upon us, as upon a human being, your faithful devotion shall take care that it be suitably corrected, as is fitting for royal majesty and beneficial to the needs of subjects.

6. Finally, it seemed right to us to add that if anyone violates with a rebellious and stubborn spirit this treaty of salutary concord, which we entered into and subscribed with the authority of a written indenture for the preservation of peace and charity, he should be admonished with Christian love and urged, in accordance with divine warnings, to return to the unshaken bond of charity. Anyone who tries to corrupt that bond can more easily tear himself apart than break it [Note: [Col. 0531] “her,” manuscript 3]. If he listens, let his restoration to the fellowship of the faithful be a joy to all. But if he refuses to obey, then pontifical authority, royal majesty, and the magnanimity of those who persist in the bond of charity shall, according as the matter and necessity require, reason demand, and the character of the person warrant, exercise the zeal of their devotion with the utmost fervor and carry out without resistance what, with God’s inspiration, they judge should be done for every purpose of salvation, usefulness, and honor [Note: [Col. 0531] “let him do” in manuscript 2].

[Col. 0531]

KAROLUS II: SYNOD AT TOULOUSE. (A.D. 844, June.)  
[Note: [Col. 0531] We have reviewed the edition of Sirmond and Baluze with the aid of manuscript 2, Paris, Royal Library, no. 4638.]

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0531C] The following chapters were enacted at the city of Toulouse in the fourth year of the reign of the lord Charles, in the sixth indiction [Note: [Col. 0531] read “seventh”], in June, before the measures that precede were enacted near the estate of Theodon, at the palace of Ver and in the city of Beauvais. They were placed before those measures [Note: [Col. 0531] namely, in manuscript 4638 and consequently in the editions of Sirmond and Baluze] because they take precedence both in the dignity of their general character and in synodal authority.

The chapters that follow, having regard to the needs of the bishops of Septimania and providing for the ability of the presbyters subject to them, and also considering the honor of a sacred, just, and blameless ministry, we, having been admonished by the presbyters’ complaint, decree with the moderation of our gentleness, pending more careful consideration by a general synod:

1. That the bishops inflict no disturbance or reproach upon the presbyters, either openly imposing it or contriving it on any other occasion, because they have come this time to complain to us; for prolonged oppression has compelled them to undertake the hardship of such a journey.

2. That the bishops receive from the presbyters one measure of grain, one measure of barley, and one measure of wine, using the measure that is public, approved, general, and lawful throughout the city, district, and surrounding area; and that they demand a *frischinga* worth six denarii, or six denarii in place of it, and no more [Col. 0532C]. If they do not receive these things, they may, if they wish, receive two solidi in denarii for all of them, as the bishops are said to have determined in the agreement [Note: [Col. 0531] perhaps “assembly” or “council”] at Toledo and Braga.

3. That presbyters who live within five miles of the city have the aforesaid provision delivered by their servants in the city designated by the city’s bishop. Those who live farther from the city shall have the bishops establish suitable places by deaneries, just as archpresbyters have been appointed, so that the remaining presbyters likewise bring their due provision by their servants to the archpresbyters or the bishops’ ministers. The bishops shall ensure that their ministers do not dishonor the presbyters, either by taking pledges shamefully or by demanding payment for receiving the provision; rather, they shall receive with thanks what the presbyters ought to contribute with cheerful hospitality, in accordance with the Apostle. If the bishops’ ministers dishonor the presbyters, the bishops shall thereafter impose suitable correction upon them; for if they do not, and the presbyters again complain to us on this account, the one found guilty will feel our displeasure.

4. That, during the visitation of the parish, the bishops henceforth do not plunder individual presbyters as they go from one little church to another and lie down at each one, as they have done until now [Col. 0533A], since it is written that they ought to evangelize, not for the sake of shameful gain [Note: [Col. 0533] “glucri” in manuscript 2], lest the holy ministry be disgraced. Instead, they shall inspect and announce places suitable for themselves and the people; and there the presbyters shall bring their congregations, as opportunity and moderation may provide. In those places the bishops shall preach, confirm, and inquire into and correct the people’s errors [Note: [Col. 0533] absent in manuscript 2].

Furthermore, since the Lord’s voice grants those who announce the Gospel permission to live from the Gospel, although the Apostle Paul made use of none of these things, the presbyters shall make such a contribution that the bishops receive assistance without the presbyters themselves being burdened. It seems to us that this can be done as follows: four presbyters shall strive to bring their congregations from the four directions to the place where the fifth presbyter lives and the bishop resides [Col. 0533B]. Each of them shall present to the bishop, as assistance for the sake of the blessing, ten loaves, half a measure of wine, a *frischinga* of four denarii, two chickens, ten eggs, and one measure of grain for the horses. Likewise the fifth presbyter, in whose house the bishop resides, shall do the same; nothing more shall be demanded from him, except perhaps that he lend wood and utensils for the needs of the ministry. Therefore the bishop shall ensure that his house or fences are not ravaged by the ministers.

5. That the bishops make this visitation once a year, at a suitable time. If they wish to carry out their ministry through the diocese more often, they shall nevertheless receive this provision from the presbyters no more than once each year.

[Col. 0533C] 6. If for any reason they omit the visitation for the salvation and needs of the people, they shall demand from the presbyters neither this provision nor its price, nor shall they allow others—their household members or friends—to demand it. When they make the visitation and stay in a presbyter’s house, they shall not, on the pretext of burdening the presbyters, bring an excessive and unnecessary number of servants, nor improperly summon the neighbors to provide food. If they wish to invite them out of charity, they may do so; but they shall demand from the presbyters no more than has been established, whether under the pretext of selling or in any other way, nor shall they take *paraveredi* or impose other exactions.

[Col. 0534A] 7. That the bishops do not divide the parishes of presbyters for the sake of shameful and dangerous profit. But if the needs of the people require that more churches be built or altars established, they shall do so with reason and authority—namely, if distance, the danger of water or woodland, or some other definite reason or necessity requires it, so that the people and the weaker sex, namely women and children, or the infirmity of the disabled, cannot reach the principal church, and the village is not so far away that the presbyter cannot come there at a suitable time without danger—then an altar may be established. If this is agreeable and useful to the people, the parish shall remain undivided, so that no one is scandalized without reason.

But if the aforesaid causes require it, and the people, neither induced nor stirred up by greed or envy, reasonably cry out that a church should be built for them and a presbyter appointed, the bishops shall deal with this episcopally, before God, with purity of conscience, reason, and authority, without any intention of shameful profit. After mature canonical deliberation, they shall carry out whatever must be done for the advantage and salvation of the people subject to them. In proportion to what they withdraw from any presbyter’s parish, they shall also receive less from him in the provision due; and they shall impose upon the other presbyter who receives the portion separated from the parish the same measure.

8. That the bishops do not, under the pretext that they possess the authority of the canons, in any way resist or neglect the provisions of our excellence; rather, they shall strive to understand the canons as they are to be understood and observe them in everything [Col. 0534C]. For if they act otherwise, they will be taught, by synodal judgment and our royal authority, both how the canons prescribe that the faithful are to be treated in regard to tithes and how they must be understood and observed together with the decree of our gentleness.

9. That the bishops demand synods from the presbyters only as the authority of the canons teaches—namely, two, and at the appointed times. At those synods, moreover, they shall not deal with, retain, and release the presbyters on the basis of pretext, but according to the truth of their ministry, before God, for which they were appointed.

[Col. 0533]

HLOTHAR I, HLUDOWIC II, AND KAROLUS II: ASSEMBLY NEAR THE ESTATE OF THEODON. (A.D. 844, October.)  
[Note: [Col. 0533] When Lothar, Louis, and Charles had assembled near the estate of Theodon in October of A.D. 844, as Prudentius of Troyes attests (*Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. I, p. 441 [*Patrologia*, vol. CXV]), these chapters were presented by the bishops and approved by the princes at the assembly of the faithful. We have reviewed the editions of Sirmond and Baluze with the aid of manuscript 2, Paris, Royal Library, no. 4638. The royal manuscript, among the Latin Supplements, no. 75, contains only excerpts, attached to the assembly at the estate of Colonia, as follows: “From the chapters held in the synod near the estate of Theodon we append certain matters requiring admonition; others, which at that time had to be stated for the occasion, we now cut short for the sake of brevity; and others, considering necessity and providing for order, we have inserted, following the custom of the fathers, so that they may be presented by the bishops for the salvation of the princes and the other faithful.”]

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0533D] The chapters enacted in the synod held near the estate of Theodon [Note: [Col. 0533] “held” is feminine in manuscript 2], at the place called Judicium [Note: [Col. 0533] “the estate of Juditz, not far from Diedenhofen,” Sirmond], follow. This was when the three glorious princely brothers—namely Hlothar, [Col. 0534D] Louis, and Charles—assembled together, in the fifth year of Charles’s reign. Drogo, bishop of Metz, presided over the synod with the consent of those same kings [Col. 0535A]. The princes themselves, after the chapters had been read again before them and their faithful, approved them and promised, with the Lord’s help, to observe them. This took place in October, in the seventh indiction [Note: [Col. 0535] read “sixth”].

The ship of the holy Church, often submerged by various disturbances from its beginning, has nevertheless never been completely submerged, because Christ its helmsman was roused by the prayers of the faithful. Although it once seemed, as it now appears, almost collapsed, through the zeal and devotion of your forebears it was, by God’s agency and in accordance with the measure divinely granted, recovered. Therefore we render immeasurable praises to the Lord our God, who aroused your hearts to a similar purpose and taught and inspired you to wish to follow in the footsteps of your fathers, so that through a temporal kingdom you may reach an eternal one.

We also repay your most noble lordship with manifold thanks [Col. 0535B], because, to avoid danger both for you and for us [Note: [Col. 0535] manuscript 2: “for us and you”], and to provide for the common salvation of the whole people, you deign to seek from us—although unworthy, yet vicars of Christ—and to await with kindly devotion, as truly from the mouth of God himself, the good and pleasing will of God and the divine counsel, according to the Lord’s command: “Ask the priests for my law,” and, “Ask your fathers, and they will tell you.”

The holy Church receives this heavenly gift of your humility with such joy that, in its consolation, it wishes to apply to you what the Lord said: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” [Note: [Col. 0535] manuscript 2: “therefore”]; that is, in place of those forebears [Note: [Col. 0535] Baluze: “the just”] who enriched, enlarged, and honored you with fatherly affection, these sons have been born to you, who may restore, recover, and preserve in you both you and the gifts of their fathers, and who, with faithful devotion, like young men of good character, while I watch over them and extend to them the hand of support, may protect and cultivate you.

1. With these matters prefaced, most noble lords, let us say with your permission that it is clear that this holy Church, redeemed by Christ’s blood and restored, reunited, and governed through the great labor of your predecessors [Note: [Col. 0535] manuscript 2: “our predecessors”], has been torn apart, disturbed, and afflicted by your discord. If you wish to reign happily in the present and be saved in the future, and if you wish to remove from this same Church, entrusted to you for governance, the many and destructive plagues of corruption—for which, in your royal ministry, you will render an account to the King of kings on the day of judgment—and if you desire to possess royal and lordly strength and authority over both your own people and those who oppose your authority, then strive to have among yourselves the charity taught by the Apostle, from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. Take care to manifest this with every virtue and purity to your faithful and unfaithful alike, as the Lord taught when he said: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

This love must be shown not merely in word and speech, but rather by removing every hidden scheme of harming anyone, and—God forbid—every open attack alien to charity. Whoever has need of anything should be helped by the other, according to his ability, with counsel and ready assistance [Note: [Col. 0535] absent in manuscript 2], for it is written: “A brother who is helped by his brother is like a fortified city.” Thus, among the people entrusted to you, in place of the discord that until now has been driven through its members by the activity of the devil, sow that peace which Christ, ascending into heaven, left as a great gift to his faithful when he said: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace”—without which no one will see God.

2. You know well that the Church was so ordered by him who alone could rightly become both king and priest [Note: [Col. 0535] absent in manuscript 2], that it is governed by pontifical authority and royal power. You clearly see that it is written: “Where there is no governor, the people fall.” And because the soul is much more precious than the body, the unanswerable authority of the canons, concerning the ordination of bishops, vigilance over the people received into their care [Note: [Col. 0535] “received” is feminine in manuscript 2], and steadfast stability in their sees, gives the clearest command.

Therefore, as those most fervently carrying out God’s embassy, we admonish you to ensure that the sees which, through your discord—an evil that should no longer even be named—remain deprived of sacred episcopal ministry and bishops, after the plague of simoniacal heresy has been utterly removed, receive without delay, according to canonical authority, either bishops given by God, regularly designated by you, and consecrated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, or, where they have been deprived of their bishops for any reason [Col. 0536C], receive those bishops canonically, without any excuse or delay.

3. We grieve that you have entrusted the sacred monastic order— inspired by God, founded by the Apostles themselves, cultivated by renowned and most holy fathers, and propagated throughout this empire by your predecessors of blessed memory—as well as certain especially venerable places, contrary to every authority and principle and to the custom of your fathers and preceding kings, to the care and power of laymen, at the greatest peril to yourselves, their destruction, and considerable provocation of God and the saints to anger.

Therefore, for Christ’s sake, we most devoutly implore you to drive from your souls and from the prosperity of your kingdom so great an offense, such just reproach, and such dangerous presumption, without precedent among earlier rulers [Col. 0536D]. Entrust the venerable places, their sacred habit and order, to those who have been called to this task: religious men from the clerical, ecclesiastical, or monastic order, and women of their sex dedicated and devoted to God, instructed in the school of Christ. Let them render to God what belongs to God and to Caesar what belongs to Caesar.

If they make insufficient progress in divine religion or in the usefulness of the commonwealth, let them either be corrected or replaced in their places by better and more useful persons [Col. 0537A]. The religious order and the most sacred places must not, because of the wickedness of the perverse, be entrusted to those for whom it is not lawful, since Scripture most clearly demonstrates that Uzzah was condemned to death because he tried to support the Lord’s ark as though it were falling, although it was unlawful for him even to touch it.

4. We also see that the occasion and fuel through which the ecclesiastical order, canonical discipline, and monastic religion often faltered from a much earlier time, when it had less religious princes, and almost collapsed and perished, but revived as though by a resurrection and regained strength when it deserved to receive devout princes fervent in God’s zeal, and then proceeded in its course—we say this not without great sorrow [Note: [Col. 0537] absent in manuscript 2] and divine retribution—has, in the time of your rule, resulted in destruction rather than edification, as Paul taught [Col. 0537B].

We truthfully attribute this also to our own sins, since we ought to have been administrators and shepherds of the churches. By divine authority we know with certainty that the preceding sins of those through whose faction this matter has so badly sprouted and grown deserved this result: so that “those who do harm may continue to do harm,” as it is written [Note: [Col. 0537] manuscript 2: “thus, that they might do harm”], and “those who are filthy may continue to be filthy” [Note: [Col. 0537] manuscript 2: “thus, that they might become filthy”].

Thus they would provoke God to anger more gravely; have as enemies the saints whom they ought to have as intercessors for their sins; provoke priests, religious men, and the poor of Christ—whom they ought to have won for themselves as intercessors and reconcilers through their own possessions—to become accusers against them; and add to the heap of their sins even those sins for which they would render an account before God on the terrible day of judgment [Col. 0537C], sins committed by persons who had erased those same sins through the intercession of most faithful offerings—offerings which the plunderers of ecclesiastical property recklessly and to their own ruin abuse without reverence.

The Lord testifies that this is true when he says: “They eat the sins of my people.” They eat the sins of the people who, against divine authority, improperly seize ecclesiastical property, and who neither labor for the sins of those who gave it, through the aid of intercession, the counsel of preaching, or any divine assistance, nor allow it to serve the pious work to which the faith of the faithful had entrusted it.

[Col. 0537D] Concerning this dangerous act, Christian princes, we reverently admonish you and most devoutly implore you: remember your salvation, both present and eternal; remember also the generosity of your forebears toward the holy churches, through which they reigned happily and overcame those opposed to them; remember, too, with what great religious reverence, even before Christ’s blood and during the time of famine in Egypt, the priestly land existed under the impious king Pharaoh through the discernment of holy Joseph. Recalling also the countless examples of Scripture, as those nourished by the Church’s milk [Col. 0538A] and adequately filled from the breasts of its knowledge, restore and repair as quickly as possible, in your time, the tunic of Christ who chose and exalted you—a tunic that even the soldiers did not dare to tear. Do not attempt to take away from the churches entrusted to you for protection, defense, and propagation either by violent seizure or by confirming unlawful commands.

Rather, restore them as your grandfather and father of holy memory left them to you to govern, with God’s favor; preserve and confirm the royal commands concerning those churches. Otherwise, just as the prophet Samuel threatened Rehoboam, son of Solomon, when he tore the robe, Christ himself may divide from you the present kingdom—God forbid—which was acquired for you through your fathers’ labor and left to you by inheritance, and may not grant you the eternal kingdom that he promised.

Do not regard the faces of people who are angered against God; for if you displease them for a time while you please God, he will fulfill in you what he promised: “When the ways of a man please the Lord, he turns all his enemies to peace.” So that you may fulfill this more effectively, every ecclesiastical man shall, according to the amount of the church’s property entrusted to him, readily and wholeheartedly prepare both the assistance of intercession and the support required by the commonwealth—while preserving the right that must thereby be devoted to divine administration—and shall diligently offer it, as had been customary in the time of your predecessors.

5. Since the holy Church, instructed in the Lord’s threshing floor, knows that some things must be rebuked, some passed over, and some endured with mourning until the proper time, we have perceived that, with the more fervent zeal by which greater matters must be corrected, your authority and the authority of priestly counsel are at present unable fully to correct certain things. Therefore, concerning the monasteries of canons and the communities of holy women, which are said to live according to the same rule, we have considered, as the Apostle Paul says, according to indulgence and not according to command: if, because of an impending need of the commonwealth, they are temporarily entrusted to laymen, the bishop in whose diocese they are situated, associating with himself some religious abbot, shall take care that restoration of the places, the diligence and custody of their office and religion, and assistance for their temporal need be provided and administered to those dwelling in those places, according to the character and extent of moderation [Col. 0538D].

Those who hold these places shall be obeyed in this, as in other matters of the Christian religion, out of reverence for Christ and for you. If anyone fails to do so, it shall be the responsibility of the appointed overseers to report this to your knowledge, and your lordship, according to the ministry entrusted to you by God and in proportion to the fault, shall correct what requires correction [Note: [Col. 0537] manuscript 2: “shall be corrected”].

It will also be necessary to appoint overseers throughout the monastic places of this same order, when your authority undertakes to appoint those who, according to the divinely prescribed rule, perform Christ’s offices [Note: [Col. 0539] absent in manuscript 2] in the monasteries.

6. Finally, we ask that whenever the ecclesiastical order needs to exercise the rigor of human salvation, it receive its strength through your authority and the ministry of your officials, according to ancient custom. Through your arrangement, may the whole people, together with ecclesiastical devotion, receive the judgment that honors the king and the justice by which his throne is established.

Through priestly admonition and counsel, may your majesty, and every person in whatever condition or order, repent of the robberies and other acts that occurred through the evil of discord and of past errors, and seek reconciliation with the Lord. Anyone who seeks it will easily find it if charity, which covers a multitude of sins, is planted in the place of discord, and if you attend to him rather than to us in the counsel—not ours, but God’s—who said: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.” For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.

[Col. 0539]

KAROLUS II: COUNCIL AT THE PALACE OF VER. (A.D. 844, December.)  
[Note: [Col. 0539] Edited by Sirmond and Baluze from the Tilianus and Pithoeanus manuscripts; we have reviewed it with the aid of manuscript 2, Paris, Royal Library, no. 4638. Baluze noted from Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, in his forty-second letter, that these chapters were written by him.]

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0539B] Canons of the council held at Verneuil, where Ebroin, bishop of Poitiers, presided [Note: [Col. 0539] The chief chaplain of King Charles, Laon Manuscript.], together with Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, as well as Hludowic, abbot of Saint-Denis, and Hincmar, subsequently bishop of Reims, in the fifth year of the reign of our lord Charles, son of the emperor Hludowic, in the month of December, in the seventh indiction [Note: [Col. 0539] Read: eighth.].

We, the bishops and the other faithful who have been summoned to Verneuil from various regions, give thanks to almighty God, illustrious King Charles, because, having laid aside the discord from which so many evils have proceeded—evils that it would take too long to enumerate and that it is still impossible to avoid—you have returned to peace with your brothers, a peace owed to you both by nature and by religion. We beseech you, through Christ, who is our peace, that you may always remain in it, so that, having seen your greatest affairs nearly collapse through discord, you may soon behold them restored through concord and faithful assistance.

For we must yield to God, concerning whom the Scriptures most truly declare: “The Most High has authority in the kingdom of men, and he gives it to whomever he wishes”; and he who, with wondrous graciousness, promises: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” Moreover, since, under the inspiration of that same God, you have deigned to order us to deliberate concerning the condition of the Church, which has been gravely disordered by the magnitude and multitude of our sins [Note: [Col. 0539] Omitted in Manuscript 2], we humbly disclose to your highness and to the devotion of the faithful people what we have discovered through common deliberation, in his name and with his help.

Nor do we claim to prove ourselves righteous. Considering our own conscience, let us humbly say with Jeremiah: “It is the Lord’s mercy that we are not consumed, for his mercies have not failed.” But as we meditate on returning to God and drawing you with us, we perform our duty, which, with everyone consenting, will benefit all. Indeed, we speak not by our own authority but by that of him who says: “He who is of God hears the words of God.” But far be it from you that what follows should be fulfilled: “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” [Note: [Col. 0539] “of these,” in Manuscript 2].

[Col. 0540B] 1. First, therefore, we address you so that, since your uprightness can benefit all your subjects, you may place the worship of God before all things. For he himself says: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be held of no account.” Furthermore, may you preserve mercy, judgment, and justice [Note: [Col. 0539] “and justice” are absent in Manuscript 2]; namely, so that mercy may temper the severity of power, judgment may restrain those who persist in sin, and justice may restore what is fitting to those who deserve it.

For: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” And: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times.” And: “The honor of a king loves judgment” [Note: [Col. 0539] “to be loved,” in Manuscript 2]. And the authority of the wisest Solomon—indeed, of God speaking through him—reveals that “justice establishes the king’s throne.” If you act in this way, divine grace will, as we believe, provide you either with a bloodless victory or with a just victory over your enemies.

David and Hezekiah may serve as examples to you: by reason of their holiness, they defeated the enemies of God’s people with wondrous speed, whether by fighting or by prayer. But there is also a light from within your own household: the emperor Charles, who adorned through his most illustrious deeds the name that gave rise to your family. Nor will God’s grace grant you only the greatness and stability of your kingdom; if you govern well, it will also bestow eternal glory upon you after the course of this life. To this glory the king and prophet sighed when he said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.”

We do not suggest these things rashly to your majesty, because care for you has also been entrusted to us. Through our ministry, you and the other faithful, cleansed through faith and baptism, await the day of the fearful judgment.

2. But, to return to us bishops: through this civil—indeed, more than civil—discord, we have sometimes neglected many matters in ourselves and in others entrusted to us, and sometimes have been compelled to neglect them. Thus religion has suffered great harm in every order; some, through ignorance, are heading toward destruction, while others, long accustomed to license [Note: [Col. 0539] Omitted in Manuscript 2], confidently believe that they can sin with impunity [Col. 0541A].

Therefore, turning at last to the correction of ourselves and of others, we ask that the perpetrators of crimes and despisers of apostolic discipline be restrained by legates of proven faith sent from your side, without regard to persons and without the blinding influence of gifts. Grant us as much leisure as possible, so that the word of God may bear fruit through preaching and the revered authority of the canons may everywhere possess its due force.

3. In holy places—that is, monasteries—we have discovered that some depart from their profession through deliberate intent, others through laziness, and many through the necessity of obtaining food and clothing. We ask that, in every parish, religious and suitable men sent by your gentleness, with the knowledge of the bishops, investigate and correct these matters, and report the condition of each place to your highness and to our lowliness at a time appointed by you [Note: [Col. 0541] “by us,” in Manuscript 2].

4. We order that monks who wander about because of greed and shamelessly disgrace the purpose of holy religion return to their own places [Note: [Col. 0541] “we have,” in Manuscript 2] and be received according to the rule through the diligence of their abbots.

For those who, after an evident monastic profession, have also abandoned the habit, or who are expelled through their own fault, we believe that this remedy [Note: [Col. 0541] “to know,” in Manuscript 2] may be applied: if they are confined in prisons, kept away from human society for as long as necessary, and, out of regard for piety, subjected to suitable works of discipline until they accept the health of correction. Those who were once monks but afterward, having abandoned the profession of solitude [Col. 0541C], fall into military service or marriage must, according to the decree of Pope Leo, be cleansed through satisfaction by public penance.

Concerning clerics who desert their own churches, the ancient rule of the Council of Chalcedon must be observed. It prescribes that if a bishop receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, both the cleric received and the bishop receiving him are to be deprived of communion until the cleric who migrated returns to his own church.

5. Those who illicitly associate with nuns and contract sacrilegious marriage-bonds with them are, by the judgment of Pope Innocent, to be suspended from communion. They are not to be received at all except through public and approved penance; or, if they have repented, the viaticum is certainly not to be denied them when they are departing from this world [Col. 0541D].

6. A girl betrothed by one man and abducted by another must, according to the statutes of the Council of Ancyra, be returned to the man to whom she had been betrothed, even if she suffered violence at the hands of her abductor. Concerning abductors, we think the best course is that, since they pay little attention to ecclesiastical excommunication, they should be terrified by the severity [Note: [Col. 0541] “authority,” in Manuscript 2] of secular laws.

7. If any nuns, for the sake of religion—as they falsely suppose—adopt men’s clothing or cut their hair [Col. 0542A], since we believe that they err through ignorance more than through deliberate intent, we decree that they be admonished and corrected, lest, as transgressors of the Old and New Testaments, they be cut off from the body of the Church by the severity of an anathema, in accordance with the Synod of Gangra.

8. Since bodily weakness prevents some bishops from undertaking military expeditions, while your indulgence grants others the rest desirable to all, care must be taken in both cases lest military affairs suffer loss through their absence. Therefore, if your highness consents, let them entrust their men who can benefit the public business to whichever of your faithful they judge useful, and let that person’s diligence be watched so that they cannot withdraw themselves from their duty.

9. We cannot acknowledge without immense sorrow that the Church of Reims, long deprived of a shepherd, has recently been stripped of its possessions and burdened with injuries. Since we desire to rescue both your highness and our lowliness from danger [Note: [Col. 0541] “to strip,” in Manuscript 2], we beseech you: let this Church, so shamefully [Note: [Col. 0541] “with such great disgrace,” in Manuscript 2] torn apart, be restored, and, in accordance with the constitution of the venerable canons, let a worthy bishop be sought and appointed to it without delay. Thus the clergy and people, worn down by such great spiritual and bodily afflictions, may receive consolation and, with their bishop, strive to offer prayers to the common Lord for your safety and prosperity.

10. The Church of Orléans is likewise known to be suffering from the greatest confusion. Nevertheless, since last year Archbishop Wenilo, with the support of his suffragans, ordained Aio, a palace priest [Col. 0542C], to the aforementioned church in that place [Note: [Col. 0541] “Aigum,” in Manuscript 2], having been furnished with the testimony of reputable canons and laymen and prompted by a petition, and since that church now lies exposed to danger for both us and you, we see no other outcome in this matter than that your piety should permit what was done by so many men to stand ratified.

11. We do not dare to decide anything concerning the prelatacy of the most reverend Drogo [Note: [Col. 0541] “anything else,” Bal.], except that one must await the greatest assembly of Gaul and Germany that can be convened, and that the consent of the remaining metropolitans and other bishops must be sought there. We neither wish nor are able to resist that consent. Yet, if such a matter may be entrusted to anyone and no other cause lies hidden beneath the one alleged, he seems especially suitable, since he is joined to us by the communion of the priesthood and to your excellence by the privilege of kinship [Col. 0542D].

12. We now come to the final part of our admonition. May God grant that you, the nobles, and all the other faithful receive it with the devotion with which we offer it. For we see the anger of God impending over us and over you, both because of plunder and other monstrous crimes, and especially because the resources of the Church—which kings and other Christians vowed to God for the sustenance of God’s servants and the poor, for receiving guests, redeeming captives [Col. 0543A], and restoring God’s temples—are now being held for the use of secular persons.

Hence many servants of God suffer lack of food, drink, and clothing; the poor do not receive their customary alms; guests are neglected; captives are defrauded; and the reputation of all is deservedly torn apart. If the Church suffered these things at the hands of pagans, she would demand patience. But now that we are oppressed by our sons—that is, by those whom we or our predecessors have begotten in Christ, making them Christians through our ministry—we receive no consolation of patience, because we fear for their destruction.

Certainly, no one, however shameless, will ever dare to deny what is beyond dispute: the possession of the Church is the vow of the faithful, the patrimony of the poor, and the redemption of souls. How, then, does anyone dare to take from God another person’s vow? With what recklessness does anyone presume to invade the inheritance of the poor? If some redeemed their souls from it, why do others lose their souls through it?

Accordingly, some venerable places are now, something never before heard of, possessed in their entirety by laymen; in some they claim a share for themselves; and the estates of others, divided in many ways, they have caused to be given to themselves as inheritances. When everyone else was selling everything because of famine, the Egyptian priests retained their own possessions, even false gods received reverence from their worshipers—reverence that, in this matter, the one true God alone does not obtain.

Uzzah was struck down because he presumed to support the tottering ark, which it was forbidden to touch. Let someone laugh at this, unless—as we say with the deepest sorrow—certain oppressors of the Church in our own time have found an end worthy of their conduct. The prophet cries out: “They said, ‘Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.’ My God, make them like a wheel and like stubble before the face of the wind.”

Finally, the Lord Jesus himself, its creator and redeemer, says: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but loses himself and suffers the loss of himself?” Is anyone so bold and desperate as to seize and invade God’s possessions to his own certain destruction [Col. 0544A]?

O faithful ones, faithful to God and to yourselves, do not, for the sake of temporal abundance in wealth, earn an eternal accumulation of miseries. Do not continue to defile the honor of your souls with so destructive, so unheard-of, and finally so certain a sacrilege! Return to God what belongs to him, so that you may possess what is yours in peace, escape eternal torments, and afterward, as faithful servants, be admitted to the joy of our Lord. Let secular persons possess secular honors; let ecclesiastical persons receive ecclesiastical honors.

Do not accuse us of insatiable greed, for, whatever we may be, you yourselves cannot fail to know that we speak the truth. And although few, there are nevertheless some among us who fear God, for whom the prophetic saying is fulfilled: “He will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer.” For the end of all things approaches daily; the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

If we wish to escape present calamities and avoid future miseries, let us all together turn from our wickedness to the Lord, and, turning away from evil, do good, so that we may deserve to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.

But you, most illustrious king—since it is most truly written, “Evil conversations corrupt good morals”—flee the companionship and counsels of the wicked, and let no one dare ask of you what it would not befit your majesty to grant. Do not fear angry human beings—that is, earth and ashes—more than God, who created you and who will judge you in truth. If you perfectly follow his will, we believe that he will free you from the insolence of any human beings, mercifully rescue you from every difficulty, and, after this temporal kingdom, lead you with accumulated happiness to the eternal one [Col. 0544C].

Finally, we address everyone: if you heed our salutary counsels, we shall greatly rejoice in your advancement. But if you despise us—or rather, God speaking through us—we shall be compelled by the necessity of fulfilling our ministry to do what we would not wish to do.

[Col. 0543]

[Col. 0539] The canons of the council held at Verneuil, where Ebroin [Note: [Col. 0539] chief chaplain of King Charles, Laon Manuscript] the bishop of Poitiers presided, together with Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, as well as Hludowic, abbot of Saint-Denis, and Hincmar, subsequently bishop of Reims, in the fifth year of the reign of our lord Charles, son of the emperor Hludowic, in December, in the seventh indiction [Note: [Col. 0539] Read: eighth].

[Col. 0540B] 1. We therefore first address you so that, since your uprightness can benefit all your subjects, you may place the worship of God before all things.

[Col. 0540C] 2. But, to return to us bishops, through this civil—indeed, more than civil—discord, we have sometimes neglected many matters in ourselves and in others entrusted to us, and sometimes have been compelled to neglect them.

[Col. 0541A] 3. In holy places, that is, monasteries, we have found some departing from their profession through ambition, others through laziness, and many through the necessity of food and clothing.

[Col. 0541B] 4. We order that monks who wander about because of greed return to their own places and be received according to the rule through the diligence of their abbots.

[Col. 0541C] 5. Those who illicitly associate with nuns and contract sacrilegious marriage-bonds with them are, by the judgment of Pope Innocent, to be suspended from communion.

[Col. 0541D] 6. A girl betrothed by one man and abducted by another must, according to the statutes of the Council of Ancyra, be returned to the man to whom she had been betrothed.

[Col. 0542A] 7. If any nuns, for the sake of religion—as they falsely suppose—adopt men’s clothing or cut their hair, they are to be admonished and corrected.

[Col. 0542B] 8. Since bodily weakness prevents some bishops from undertaking military expeditions, while your indulgence grants others rest, care must be taken lest military affairs suffer loss through their absence.

[Col. 0542C] 9. We cannot acknowledge without immense sorrow that the Church of Reims, long deprived of a shepherd, has recently been stripped of its possessions and burdened with injuries.

[Col. 0542D] 10. The Church of Orléans is likewise known to be suffering from the greatest confusion.

[Col. 0543A] 11. We do not dare to decide anything concerning the prelatacy of the most reverend Drogo.

[Col. 0543B] 12. We now come to the final part of our admonition. We see the anger of God impending over us and over you because of plunder and other monstrous crimes, and especially because the resources of the Church are being held for secular use.
