[Col. 0544A] Is anyone so bold and desperate as to seize and invade God’s possessions to his own certain destruction?

[Col. 0544C] Finally, we address everyone: if you heed our salutary counsels, we shall greatly rejoice in your advancement.

[Col. 0543]

## SYNOD OF CHARLES II AT BEAUVAIS. (845, April)

[Note: [Col. 0543] Edited by Sirmond and Baluze from the Tilian, Pithoean, and Metz manuscripts; we have revised it with the aid of 2) Royal Library of Paris manuscript no. 4638 and 3) Paris manuscript among the Latin Supplements no. 75. It also exists in the Vatican and Royal Paris manuscript no. 3878.]

[Note.]

[Col. 0543D] The following capitula were enacted in a synod held at the city of Beauvais [Note: [Col. 0543D] On 18 April the king granted possessions there to his faithful Nithard], in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 845, in April, in the sixth year [Note: [Col. 0543] Read: in the fifth year … in the eighth indiction] of the reign of lord Charles, in the seventh indiction. They were agreed upon between the same prince, lord Charles, and the bishops of his kingdom. The same glorious prince promised, with God as witness and under the pledge of his faith, that he would observe them toward all the churches and bishops of his kingdom. He accepted them from the hands of these bishops for preservation on behalf of all the bishops of his principate, both those who then existed and those who would exist in the future: Wenilo [Note: [Col. 0543D] of Sens], Erchanrad [Note: [Col. 0544D] of Paris], Ymmo [Note: [Col. 0544D] of Noyon], Rothad [Note: [Col. 0544D] of Soissons], Simeon [Note: [Col. 0545D] of Laon], Lupus [Note: [Col. 0545D] of Châlons], Ragenarius [Note: [Col. 0545D] of Amiens], Helias [Note: [Col. 0545D] of Chartres], Ebroin [Note: [Col. 0545D] of Senlis] [Note: [Col. 0545] “Erdoïn,” in Manuscript 2], Aio [Note: [Col. 0545D] of Orléans], and Hincmar, priest and designated archbishop [Note: [Col. 0545] These words are absent in Manuscript 3] [Note: [Col. 0545D] of Reims].

1. That you preserve ecclesiastical right and canonical law for us just as your predecessors, who observed them well and reasonably, did, insofar as this can be known and God grants you the ability, and as your predecessors preserved them [Note: [Col. 0545] “granted to our predecessors,” Manuscripts 2, 3, Sirmond, and Baluze].

2. That neither in my person nor in my order—unless, God forbid, I should henceforth manifestly act against God and against you in such a way that I ought canonically to be condemned—you act against me and my order in so condemnable a manner, for any past cause, that dishonor or condemnation should come upon me.

3. That you restore immediately, and preserve once restored, the possessions belonging to the church entrusted to me that were taken away during your principate, just as they existed in the time of your grandfather and father. Except for additions placed upon them, or what has been consumed from buildings, restore them as they then were, insofar as this is established concerning the properties that we ordinarily call possessions, when you took them away [Note: [Col. 0545] “on that day,” Manuscript 3].

[Col. 0546A] 4. That the illicit grants made by you concerning the possessions of the church entrusted to me be rescinded [Note: [Col. 0545] “rescidandur,” Manuscript 2; an OCR or manuscript form], and that you take care henceforth that such grants are not made.

5. That henceforth you exact no undue customary payments or unjust exactions [Note: [Col. 0545] “exactions,” Sirmond and Baluze] from the church entrusted to me, but preserve them as they were preserved in the time of your grandfather and father.

6. That you provide defense, according to your ministry and to the extent that God grants you ability, against the plunderers and oppressors of our churches and of the possessions belonging to them [Note: [Col. 0545] “to it,” Manuscript 3].

7. That you henceforth preserve as valid the grants that your grandfather and father made and confirmed for the churches entrusted to us, and preserved as stable [Note: [Col. 0545] “confirmed,” Baluze], which you too have confirmed [Note: [Col. 0545] Omitted in Manuscript 2].

[Col. 0546B] 8. If you act against these capitula, or if we—God forbid—act against you, not through malice or perverse zeal but through human frailty, ignorance, or deception, without being condemnable [Note: [Col. 0545] “against you,” omitted in Manuscripts 2 and Baluze], let us correct one another by mutual counsel, and let the agreement once confirmed remain thereafter firm.

[Col. 0545]

## CAPITULARY OF LOUIS II, KING OF ITALY. (844–850)

[Note: [Col. 0545] The beginning of a capitulary addressed to King Louis, son of Lothair, survives in a tenth-century Chisian manuscript; the remainder perished through the hostility of fate. It must therefore be assigned to some date between 15 June 844, when he was crowned king of the Lombards, and 6 April 850, when he received the imperial crown. The single capitulum that survives bears the name of Lothair in the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Verona, and Este manuscripts, and in Muratori, chapter 80; but the authority of the Chisian manuscript should prevail in this matter, and the other manuscripts could naturally call Lothair emperor.]

Also [Note: [Col. 0545] “And,” Chisian manuscript]: Capitula for lord King Louis.

[Col. 0545C]

Concerning [Note: [Col. 0545] “And,” Chisian manuscript.] those persons who [Note: [Col. 0545] “who” occurs in the Chisian manuscript and is absent in the others.] transfer their possessions to another person so that they will not be compelled to come to the hearing when summoned, in order not to correct the wrongs they have committed: if it should become clear that they transferred them for the reason that they would not do justice, we wish those possessions themselves to be placed under the ban [Note: [Col. 0545] The remainder has fallen out of the Chisian manuscript; I supplied it from the other manuscripts], until those who hold them bring their author to the hearing and that same wrongdoer does justice.

[Col. 0545]

## ASSEMBLY OF CHARLES II AT SPARNACUM. (846, June)

[Note: [Col. 0545] Peter Pithoeus first published the following after the books of the Capitularies, pp. 415–424; Lindenbrogius repeated his edition in his own manuscript, as did Goldastus. The edition of Sirmond and Baluze is based on the Tilian, Pithoean, Metz, and London manuscripts; we have revised it with the aid of 2) the Pithoean manuscript, now Royal Paris no. 4638, and 3) the Royal Paris manuscript among the Latin Supplements, no. 75, tenth century.]

[Note.]

[Col. 0545D] The following capitula were excerpted by lord King Charles and his princes from those capitula that the bishops issued in synods in the year 846 [Note: [Col. 0545D] At Meaux and Paris. The nineteen capitula that follow are all contained in the synod at Meaux under the numbers prefixed to the individual capitula; but those established at Meaux were finally completed and published at Paris, as the preface declares, in the year 846. Sirmond]—namely, Wenilo [Note: [Col. 0546D] of Sens] with his suffragans, Guntbold [Note: [Col. 0546D] of Rouen] with his suffragans, Ursmarus [Note: [Col. 0546D] of Tours] with his suffragans, Hincmar with his suffragans, and Amalo [Note: [Col. 0547D] of Lyons] with his suffragans. They were presented to the same prince, as he had ordered, having been collected for rereading at Sparnacum [Note: [Col. 0547D] Épernay], an estate of the Church of Reims.

And because the king’s mind had been stirred by the faction of certain persons against the bishops, while the leading men of his kingdom were at odds with the admonition of those bishops, and the bishops had been removed from the same council, they selected from all those capitula only the following to be observed and accepted by him, and delivered them in writing to the bishops, saying that they had accepted no more of their capitula than these and that they wished to observe these with the prince [Note: [Col. 0547] The rubric is absent in Manuscript 3] [Note: [Col. 0547D] Compare Prudentius, *Annales*, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores I, p. 442; *Patrologia Latina* CXV].

1. Concerning the honor and worship of churches.  
2. Concerning the honor of bishops and the veneration of God’s servants.  
3. Concerning judgments.  
4. That caution be exercised toward those who, through youth or foolishness, err in some matter or disregard the admonition of the bishops, lest they be suddenly or rashly condemned by anathema.  
5. Concerning those who attempt to become contumacious against royal power.  
6. Concerning precarial grants.  
7. Concerning hospices.  
8. Concerning the rapacious.  
9. That suitable time be allowed to bishops for carrying out their ministry.  
10. That clerics not take up military arms.  
11. That agents be sent to investigate whether grants concerning church possessions have been made to private persons by us.  
12. Concerning simoniacal heresy.  
13. That no one usurp an episcopal see while its own bishop is incapacitated [Col. 0547C].  
14. That canons sleep within the dormitory.  
15. That monks not come to the palace except for a matter of obedience, abbots being excepted.  
16. That laymen not touch the tithes of churches.  
17. Concerning nuns married contrary to authority.  
18. Concerning the betrothed of others.  
19. Concerning burials within a church [Note: [Col. 0547] Up to this point only in Manuscript 3].

The complete text of the capitula contained in the full record of the synodal proceedings, from which these summaries were excerpted, is arranged by sections as follows [Note: [Col. 0547] In Pithoeus, pp. 416ff., the complete capitula are included. Since they are already read above in the places indicated in Manuscript 2, I considered it superfluous, with Sirmond and Baluze, to repeat them, and followed the reading of Manuscript 2].

The first summary, concerning the honor and worship of churches, is contained above [Note: [Col. 0548D] Column 530, no. 1], in the estate of Cologne, confirmed by the subscription of the king and the princes [Col. 0547D].

The second summary, concerning the honor of bishops and the veneration of God’s servants, likewise.

[Col. 0548A] The third summary, concerning judgments, likewise.

The fifth summary, concerning those who attempt to become contumacious against royal power, likewise.

The sixth summary.

The remaining summaries that follow are contained in the aforesaid complete text together with their capitula.

20. Lest an unseemly and dishonorable necessity drive your magnificence to a place that your dignity does not draw you toward willingly—and since matters have been reported or requested to you partly from necessity, partly through deception, because the truth of the matter was otherwise than it was represented, especially in what concerned public affairs, or because of seizure of what is held under benefice law or taken as an allod [Note: [Col. 0547] “allod,” Manuscript 2]—it seems useful and necessary to us that you send faithful and energetic agents from both orders through each county of your kingdom.

Let them carefully record everything that, in the time of your grandfather and father, belonged either especially to royal service or to the benefices of royal vassals; what each person now retains from it, and in what manner and to what extent; and let the matter be reported to you according to the truth. Wherever you find that reason, utility, order, and truth are present in what has been consumed or granted, let those arrangements remain in force.

But wherever unreasonableness, or rather fraud, is found, correct it together with the counsel of your faithful in such a way [Note: [Col. 0547] “and,” Manuscript 2] that reason, utility, and justice are not abandoned, and that the dignity of your magnificence does not become so cheap through necessity as is recognized to be unbefitting to you. For your household cannot otherwise be filled with the services of your household members unless you have the means to reward their merits and provide assistance in their need. Thus, finally, your public affairs may be supported by their own resources, and the churches may remain exempt from burdens from which it is not expedient for them to be burdened [Note: [Col. 0547] The Pithoean edition, and those following it, insert here the chapter given below as no. 56: “That none of the bishops …”].

21. Let the precarial grants and exchanges made while the churches were widowed of their bishops, by those who had occupied the bishops’ places, be rescinded; and, if they are to be made again, let them be made anew with ecclesiastical or civil authority [Note: [Col. 0547] “to be made,” Manuscript 2].

22. Let no one presume to make precarial grants from ecclesiastical possessions, unless he receives from the Church’s possessions double the amount appropriately given from his own property, and in his own name only, if he wishes to hold his own [Note: [Col. 0547] “proprias” through “proprias” are absent in Manuscript 2.] and ecclesiastical possessions in usufruct. But if he has temporarily relinquished his own possessions, let him take in usufruct, in his own name only, triple the amount from ecclesiastical possessions. For everyone must manage them as a steward of another’s property, not as a donor of his own.

No authority should compel anyone to make a precarial grant from possessions specifically dedicated to God and his saints, since both reason and established practice hold that no one should be compelled, against utility and reason, to make a benefice from his own property for someone to whom he does not wish to grant it [Note: [Col. 0549] “to make a grant,” Manuscript 2].

Nor does reason allow royal grants concerning ecclesiastical precarial possessions to be made, nor does authority in any way permit it. For royal majesty must judge it unworthy to confirm grants in ecclesiastical law unless they are requested by an ecclesiastical ruler [Note: [Col. 0549] “unless they are rightly repeated,” Manuscript 2].

Let the same guardian of the Church carefully take care lest, forgetful of his order and of ecclesiastical communion, he request a royal grant to be made against authority for the sake of any flattery. If he does so, let him not be heard. But if he obtains it, let the grant be rescinded by royal coercion [Note: [Col. 0549] “in this way,” Manuscript 2; “discretion,” Sirmond] and episcopal judgment, and let the unjust petitioner be deservedly corrected for his unjust representation to the prince. Let precarial grants, according to ancient custom and authority, be renewed every five years.

24. Let you stand as defenders, according to your ministry and to the extent that God grants you ability, against the plunderers and oppressors of the churches and of the possessions belonging to them. Let the grants that your grandfather and father made and confirmed for the churches subject to your authority, and preserved as stable [Note: [Col. 0549] “confirmed,” Manuscript 2], as well as those that you have confirmed, be preserved in every respect as valid henceforth.

28. Let royal magnificence grant bishops greater freedom to carry out their ministry in their parishes than they have had until now because of various disturbances, especially during the most sacred seasons, namely Lent and Advent. Thus both the bishops and royal dignity may more safely escape the danger arising from the ministry entrusted to them and neglected, and may prevail to obtain divine mercy for carrying it out diligently.

Let the bishops turn the leisure granted to them not toward their own pleasures but toward divine and dutiful business, so that, applying themselves diligently to preaching and confirmation—which until now has been neglected throughout the parishes—they may henceforth correct and improve it with care and devotion.

Nor, for the sake of their own rest, are bishops to withdraw to more distant places, neglect their ministry, and abandon their own cities [Col. 0549D]; rather, let them either travel through their parishes with effective ministry or, with due religious observance, live canonically with their own people in their cities.

Adorned with hospitality—which has now almost been destroyed because of various acts of rapacity—let them become conspicuous not only in the eyes of the Lord through obedience to the divine command, but also acquire good testimony according to the holy Apostle. Let them likewise exhort and compel the priests entrusted to them to be adorned, according to their ministry, with doctrine, chastity, sobriety, and hospitality [Note: [Col. 0549] “to be adorned with ministry,” Baluze].

37. Let all who appear to belong to the clergy neither take up arms nor go about armed, but let them give the name of their profession a corresponding witness through religious conduct and religious dress. If they despise this, let them be punished by the loss of their own rank as despisers of the sacred canons and profaners of ecclesiastical holiness, since they cannot serve both God and the world.

40. The king’s greatness must be admonished concerning the hospices that were both established and cultivated in the time of his predecessors but have now been reduced to nothing. The hospices of the Scots also, which holy men of that people built in this kingdom [Note: [Col. 0549] Omitted in Manuscript 2] and enlarged with possessions acquired through their holiness, have been completely alienated from the same duty of hospitality [Note: [Col. 0549] Omitted in Manuscript 2].

Not only are newcomers not received into those hospices, but even those who have served the Lord in those places under religious observance from childhood are expelled from them and forced to beg from door to door. Hence the canonical sentence must be feared, especially the decree of Pope Symmachus: the person known to be the author and perpetrator of this crime must be struck, as a killer of the poor and a Judas who betrayed Christ [Note: [Col. 0549] That is, of Beauvais], with present and perpetual anathema [Note: [Col. 0549] Omitted in Manuscript 2].

Pope Symmachus says: “Those who ask kings for a little ecclesiastical possession—or whatever it may be belonging to the Church—and, moved by an impulse to corrupt piety, seize the substance of the needy: let what they obtain be held invalid [Note: [Col. 0549] “what they obtain,” Manuscript 2], and let them be excluded from communion with the Church, whose resources they desire to take away” [Col. 0550C].

Likewise, in the canon of Orléans: “If anyone at any time attempts to violate this constitution of ours, or takes away anything from the customary income or resources of that hospice [Note: [Col. 0549] The words ‘or anything from the resources of the hospice’ are absent in Manuscript 2], so that the hospice—God forbid—ceases to exist, let him, as a killer of the poor, be struck with irrevocable anathema.”

43. It must be guarded against, most diligently guarded against, and forbidden by the power of Christ’s blood to bishops and kings, to all the higher authorities, and to all supporters, electors, consenters, and appointors in ecclesiastical rank, that no one obtain a place of governance through the heresy of simony, by any faction, cunning, promise, advantage, or gift, whether directly or through an intermediary.

For the Holy Spirit, among other ecclesiastical testimonies, says through the mouth of Saint Gregory: “Why is it not considered that the blessing of the one who is promoted in order to become a heretic is turned into a curse?” [Note: [Col. 0549] Omitted in Manuscript 2]. And again: “For buyers and sellers alike are bound by equal punishment, since it is clear that this heresy was condemned at its very origin by apostolic detestation.”

The Apostle teaches: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to them, are worthy of death.” And again blessed Gregory says: “With grief I say, with groaning I declare: the priesthood, which has fallen inwardly among you, will not be able to stand long outwardly” [Col. 0551A].

The same man says [Note: [Col. 0551] “therefore,” Manuscript 2]: “The adversary of souls, under a crafty appearance, persuades us that we ought to receive from those who have possessions, so that there may be something to distribute to those who do not have them.” Yet it is written: “The sacrifices of the wicked are detestable, because they are offered from crime” [Note: [Col. 0551] “which are offered from crime,” Manuscript 2].

47. That no one, while a bishop is alive, presume to seize or dominate his church or the property belonging to it; nor, under the pretext of a voluntary election by clergy and people, may anyone endowed with any secular power appoint an administrator against the bishop’s will. But if the bishop is unable to perform ecclesiastical ministry because of bodily infirmity, this responsibility shall remain under the archbishop’s direction, with the consent of the bishop of that church, so that the required office may not be left unfulfilled. As for the service pertaining to the commonwealth, the bishop shall appoint and arrange for its execution, with the archbishop’s consent and for the preservation of peace and charity, through such men from among his subjects and ecclesiastical ministers as are not lifted up or troubled by an improper desire to succeed to the episcopate; provided he has proved himself such that, according to the instructions of blessed Gregory in the Book of Letters, he serves humbly in subjection and thereafter presides usefully, in conformity with the holy rules.

[Note: “subditione” (“subjection”) is printed as “subdito” (“a subject”) in witness 2; “prosit” (“may be of service”) as “proraesit” [uncertain/corrupt] in witness 2; and “utiliter” (“usefully”) as “humiliter” (“humbly”) in witness 2.] For we have seen great scandal arise on this account in many churches. If such a necessity should arise in an archbishop, he likewise shall make such an arrangement with the counsel of his fellow bishops.

[Col. 0551B]

53. That canons in cities or monasteries, as has been established, shall sleep in the dormitory, eat in the refectory, and receive the necessary care in the house of the sick; and that both the healthy and the sick shall be clothed canonically, reside in the cloisters at the proper hours, and, under canonical supervision, devote themselves to reading and to the other offices prescribed by divine institution. But if the bishop of the place lacks the means or resources to accomplish and arrange this, the prince shall consent according to the constitution of the lord Emperor Louis: that is, if land belonging to the same church is found near the bishop’s seat and is possessed by another, it shall be restored to the rector of the church for the construction of cloisters for the clergy or for making any other provision useful to the church. [Col. 0551D] But if it belongs to the fisc, the royal generosity should deign to grant that land for the construction of dwellings for the servants of God. If, however, it belongs to another house of God or to a private owner, permission to exchange it by mutual agreement shall be granted. And if the poverty of the place is insufficient for building the necessary houses, royal authority shall compel those who hold property belonging to that church as benefices to assist in their construction.

[Note: “lectioni” (“reading”) is printed as “lectionis” (“of reading”) in witness 2; “Qui” (“who”) as “quae” (“which”) in witness 2; and “domos necessarias” (“necessary houses”) as “domus necessarios” in witness 2.]

56. That no bishop deprive anyone of ecclesiastical communion without a certain and manifest cause of sin. Nor shall he impose an anathema without the consent of the archbishop or of his fellow bishops, and without the prior evangelical admonition, unless canonical authority so teaches; for anathema is a condemnation to eternal death, and ought to be imposed only for a mortal crime and upon one who cannot otherwise be corrected.

[Note: “praelata” (“having been set before,” i.e. “preceded by”) is printed as “prolata” (“uttered”) in witness 2.]

57. That monks who have not been entrusted with the care of monasteries shall not visit the palace indiscriminately and without authorization, nor remain there, nor presume, acephalous and without a head, to run about and wander everywhere. But if any of them are found to be useful and necessary to the church and to the prince, let them go with the bishop’s authority, canonically and religiously. Otherwise, let them reside religiously in their monasteries, as canonical and regular discipline teaches. Neither the bishop, nor the abbot, nor anyone else shall dispatch them insistently on missions in the manner of couriers; for through certain of them both ecclesiastical and civil affairs are disturbed, contrary to canonical authority. Nor, under the pretext of obedience, should they serve for a longer time in stewardships; rather, carrying out obedience in its regular turn, let them dwell in the monastery with one another, as is read concerning Saint Benedict, and recollect themselves.

Those who transgress these provisions—whether superiors by favoring such conduct or subjects by obtaining it—shall be excommunicated.

[Note: The words “et ubi” (“and wherever”) are absent from witness 2; “contra” (“contrary to”) is printed as “extra” (“outside”) in witness 2.]

63. Those who are required to pay ninths and tenths from ecclesiastical property and to restore the church’s roofs and structures according to ancient authority and custom, and who not only neglect this but also abandon it through contempt, permitting the clergy to be reduced by hunger and want and the ecclesiastical buildings to collapse through disrepair, shall be separated from ecclesiastical communion until they earnestly strive to repair through diligence what they neglected through negligence.

[Note: “diligentia” (“diligence”) is printed as “indulgentia” (“indulgence”) in witness 2.]

If they repeat the offense, then, after making satisfaction for the excommunication and compelled by royal power, let the ancient legal maxim be applied: “He who neglects the due shall lose the field.”

[Note: “iteraverint” (“they repeat”) is printed as “iteraverit” (“he repeats”) in witness 2; “perdat” (“let him lose”) is printed as “perdit” (“he loses”) in witness 2.]

The serfs of churches who are subject to any authorities shall be permitted to serve that same church, without harassment, for at least twenty days each year in repairing its ruins, unless a better custom or more devoted arrangement has been established over time by the command of the lord Louis, or certainly of the lord Charles, or even of Pippin. Wherever a more extensive arrangement and a better custom already exist, let them not be diminished because of our present concern.

[Note: One word is erased in witness 2.]

67. Those who abduct consecrated virgins or widows and, proceeding further in their crime, take them in marriage shall be subjected to public penance according to the measure determined by the bishop. The women themselves shall be confined in suitable places of penance and compelled to return to the religious habit. Both parties shall remain perpetually without any hope of marital union. If, however—God forbid—they presume to renew the marriages, they shall be subjected to a harsher punishment and expelled still more severely. If they should refuse to obey salutary admonitions, they shall be anathematized.

[Note: “quem” (“which,” referring to the measure) is printed as “quod” (“which,” neuter) in witness 2; “uterque” (“each of the two”) is printed as “utrique” (“to both”) in witness 2.]

68. Concerning those who abduct another man’s betrothed women, or take them with the consent of their parents, the ancient and synodal judgment shall be observed. If such an event is found to have occurred in the church, and the bishops, for the sake of salvation and religious propriety, are understood to be required to deal with it somewhat more humanely—as canonical authority teaches, to use its own words, “for the earlier definition dealt with the matter more harshly, whereas the later treated it somewhat more humanely”—nevertheless, even if we descend to the greatest indulgence, the taker of another man’s betrothed shall in no way pass without public penance, and shall pay a fine legally to the bridegroom.

[Note: “multam” (“a fine,” accusative feminine) is printed as “multa” (“many things” or “a fine,” nominative/ablative feminine) in witness 2.]

If he refuses to obey this, let him be anathematized without any opposition. His supporters, however, shall do penance by episcopal decree according to the measure of their guilt. But if—something we do not desire—someone from the ecclesiastical order has openly shown himself to be a consenting party or intermediary in such marriages, let him be removed from his own rank. If he has been driven out on the basis of plausible suspicions arising from this matter and cannot be cleared canonically, he shall be compelled to purge himself according to the statutes of the holy Fathers.

72. That no one presume to bury any dead person in a church as though by hereditary right, unless the bishop or priest has judged that person worthy on account of the character of his conduct and life. Nor may anyone cast the bones of any dead person out of his grave or violate anyone’s burial in any way through rash presumption.

[Note: “ejiciat” (“cast out”) is printed as “eicere” (“to cast out”) in witness 2. The following words, from “sepulturam cujusquam” (“anyone’s burial”) through “a Deo” (“by God”), are absent in witness 2.] Rather, let each person be allowed to await the coming of his judge in the tomb prepared and granted to him by God; especially since not only divine laws but also human laws within the human commonwealth judge violators of graves to be liable to death.

Nor should anyone, to use the words of Saint Gregory, attempt in any way to seek payment for the place of burial from earth that has been surrendered to corruption, or wish to make profit from another’s grief.

[Note: In the phrase “de alieno … luctu … compendium” (“profit from another’s grief”), witness 2 reads “nullo”; Bellovacensis, Baluzius, and Tilius read “ullo”; and “lucri” (“of gain”) appears in Tilius but is absent from witness 2.]

[Note: Witnesses differ over the wording of “nullo” (“in no way”): “nulla” in witness 2, “ull[o]” in Bellovacensis and Baluzius, and “ull[o]” in Trecensis. “lucr[i]” (“profit”) is absent from witness 2 and appears in Tilius.]

If at any time relatives or heirs willingly wish to offer something to the church as alms for the deceased, we do not forbid its acceptance.

[Note: “quando” (“at any time”) is absent from witness 2.] But we entirely forbid anything to be requested or demanded, lest—something wholly irreligious—the church be called venal, or lest we appear to rejoice in human deaths if we seek profit from them in any way.

[Col. 0553]

THE ASSEMBLY OF LOTHAR, LOUIS, AND CHARLES AT MERSEN. (A.D. 847, February)

[Note: We have revised the editions of Sirmond and Baluzius with the aid of Royal Parisian manuscript no. 4638.]

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0553C]

The following chapters were enacted when the three royal brothers—namely Lothar, Louis, and Charles—assembled together near the municipality of Utrecht, at a place called Mersen, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 847, in the month of February.

[Note: Compare the letters of Lupus of Ferrières, 50, 57, and 59. In the latter he says that the kings would hold a conference in the second week of Lent. According to Sirmond, the beginning of Lent in A.D. 847 was 16 February.]

The announcements of each of them follow these chapters.

CAP. 1. Concerning peace, concord, and unanimity among the three brothers and kings, and that they be united by a truly genuine and unfeigned bond of charity, so that thereafter no one may be able to sow occasions of discord among them.

2. That they mutually assist one another and, as circumstances require, help one another against the enemies of God, of his holy church, and of themselves.

3. That no one, through any greed, presume to tear down the laws of peace in the kingdom of any of them.

[Note: “convellere” (“to tear down”) is printed as “evellere” (“to pull out”) in witness 2.]

If anyone presumes to do this, he shall incur their common vengeance.

4. That the churches of Christ throughout their entire kingdom retain their former dignity and honor, and that whatever they lawfully possessed while the lord Emperor Louis was alive be restored to them without any diminution.

[Note: “Christi” (“of Christ”) is absent from witness 2.]

[Col. 0554C]

5. That such a law be preserved for each of their faithful as they are known to have had in the times of the earlier kings, and especially of their grandfather and father, provided that they too preserve their former loyalty toward them.

6. That the robberies and depredations which have hitherto been committed as though by lawful right be entirely prohibited, and that no one thereafter trust that he can presume to commit them with impunity.

7. That suitable royal agents be appointed in the several parts of the kingdom, able to examine the complaints of the poor, acts of oppression, and the cases of anyone whatsoever, and to decide them according to the equity of the law. If such presumptuous offenders flee from one kingdom into another, let them likewise be oppressed there.

[Col. 0554D]

8. That thereafter no one presume to commit abduction anywhere in their entire kingdom. If anyone does so, let him be legally punished.

9. That the sons of the kings retain the lawful inheritance of the kingdom after them according to the portions determined at the present time; and that whichever of these brothers survives the others consent to this on behalf of his brothers’ sons, provided that the nephews themselves agree to obey their uncles.

[Col. 0555A]

10. That envoys be sent to the duke of the Bretons to remind him of the common observance of peace toward them.

11. That envoys likewise be sent to the king of the Northmen, to warn him that he must either strive to preserve peace or have them all jointly hostile to him.

### Announcement of the lord Lothar

It seemed good to us and to our brothers that, in order to seek God’s will concerning how the holy church might be restored and how we, you, and this Christian people might possess peace, we should join together, as we have now done, and should be toward one another as brothers ought rightly to be.

[Note: “Nobis et” (“to us and”) is printed as “Nobis ex” (“to us from”) in witness 2.] Know this for certain: thanks be to God, this is how we are, and with God’s help we wish to remain so henceforth. In counsel and assistance, each of us is prepared to offer help to the other, as brothers ought to do according to God’s will and for the common advancement, in whatever we are able.

[Col. 0555B]

### Announcement of the lord Louis

1. Know that our brothers and we are sending our agents to our common nephew in Aquitaine, and are assigning him such counties as will meanwhile be sufficient for him and his people, so that the faithful of our beloved brother Charles may have peace in that kingdom until our same nephew comes to our common assembly.

[Note: Pippin is the “common nephew” named here. “idem” (“the same”) is printed as “inde” (“thereupon/from there”) in witness 2.]

We command him to come to that assembly with such security received from us that, insofar as God wills to preserve him, he may come safely, remain safely, and return safely. If he then wishes to listen to our counsel, with God’s help and your counsel we wish to consider how he may thereafter remain more advantageously according to the common advancement and welfare. If he does not wish to listen to our counsel, then we shall act as we are able to determine thereafter, with God’s help and your counsel, for the best.

[Note: “voluerit” (“he will have wished”) is printed as “noluerit” (“he will not have wished”) in witness 2.]

2. Know also that we are likewise sending our agents to the Bretons and exhorting them toward common advancement and peace. Whether they listen or do not listen, with God’s help and your counsel we shall also decide what to do thereafter.

3. Know that we are jointly sending our agents to the Northmen to obtain peace.

[Col. 0555D]

4. Know also that our beloved brother Lothar is sending his agents to his men who until now have been opposed to our beloved brother Charles, and he is ordering them that, if they wish henceforth to rejoice in God’s grace and his, they must by no device do anything against him or his faithful.

[Col. 0556A]

5. Know that we wish the property of the churches, in whichever kingdom its principal authority may be situated, both of bishoprics and of abbeys, to be possessed without opposition by the rectors of those churches, as they possessed it in the time of our lord and father.

6. Likewise, wherever the bishoprics and monasteries in our common kingdom are now otherwise situated than they ought to be, we wish, with God’s help, to correct this, so that the church of God may possess its due honor and the people may have their law and justice.

### Announcement of Charles

[Col. 0556B]

1. Know that our beloved brothers and we have jointly appointed an assembly at the mass of Saint John in Paris, where we shall consider these matters

[Note: “apud Parisius” (“at Paris”) is printed as “Parisium” in Sirmond and Baluzius.] that they have now mentioned and whatever else we may be able to discover concerning God’s will and our common advancement, yours and ours, and, with God’s help, bring them to effect.

[Note: “commune” (“common,” neuter) is printed as “communem” (“common,” accusative) in witness 2.]

We wish that from now on, wherever each of us may be, he remain in peace, and that each come peacefully to that assembly; for until now, amid these miseries and robberies, we have greatly offended God. Therefore we recognize that it is most necessary for us to implore God’s mercy.

2. We also wish every free man in our kingdom to accept from among us and our faithful whichever lord he wishes.

3. We also command that no one abandon his lord without just reason, and that no one receive him unless according to the custom that existed in the time of our predecessors.

4. We wish you to know that we desire to agree to what is right with our faithful and do not wish to act against reason toward them. Likewise, we admonish you and our other faithful to agree to what is right with your own men and not act against reason toward them.

[Note: “nostros” (“our”) is printed as “vestros” (“your”) in witness 2.]

5. We wish that a man belonging to any one of us, wherever he may be in the kingdom of any other, go with his lord to the army or to his other duties, unless an invasion of the kingdom of the kind they call *lantweri*—that is, the defense of the homeland—should occur, God forbid, such that all the people of that kingdom must go together to repel it.

[Note: A codex formerly belonging to Saint Remigius of Reims, now Royal Parisian Library no. 164 bis, contains among excerpts beginning at folio 283 a chapter under the heading “In the book of chapters of the lord Emperors Charles and Louis.” Baluzius has already printed it in volume II, p. 1264. It reads:

“And because one goes to the army either to defend land or to acquire land, concerning *lantweri*, that is, the defense of the homeland, we have no other provision except according to the manner written in this law or in the emperors’ capitularies, unless in the earlier chapters concerning poor Franks, who, if they do not have the means to pay the military due, are to surrender themselves into the king’s service and remain in that same service until the military due has been paid. If he should die in that service, his heirs shall receive his inheritance and shall become liable neither with respect to their freedom nor with respect to that due. Likewise, in the later chapters concerning poor Franks, we find written there that each count is to record how many there are in his county who cannot undertake military service on their own, so that they may furnish others with military support, as is written there.”]

[Col. 0557]

THE ASSEMBLY OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS II AT TICINUM. (A.D. 850)

[Note: Certain acts of the assembly at Ticinus, held by the Emperor Louis II in the autumn of A.D. 850, were first published by Henry Canisius, with the aid of a manuscript from Saint Gall, in *Lectures Antiquae*, vol. V, part II, pp. 674 ff. Here we present much more extensive material with the aid of the Gotha and Blankenburg manuscripts. First, concerning ecclesiastical laws, we publish the bishops’ reply to the emperor’s questions from the Gotha manuscript and Canisius, and the laws themselves promulgated by the emperor from the Blankenburg manuscript. Canisius had found only five secular laws, and those incomplete chapters; here, however, both the emperor’s chapters addressed to his counts and the laws themselves appear complete from the Gotha manuscript. Moreover, the laws enacted by Emperor Louis while his father Lothar was still alive were promulgated with the authority of both.]

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0557A]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 850, in the fourteenth indiction, and in the thirtieth and first year of the most pious Augusti Lothar and Louis, a synod was held in the royal city of Ticinus. It was presided over by Angilbert, archbishop of Milan; Theodemar, patriarch of Aquileia; and Joseph, venerable bishop and archchaplain of the whole church. At this synod the following provisions were established.

[Note: This heading appears in one Saint Gall manuscript.]

[Note: The name is corrected here to “Theodemar”; Canisius has “Theodemanus.”]

### Reply to the Consultation or Exhortation of the Bishops to the Lord Emperor Louis, Enacted at Pavia

[Note: This heading is present in one Gotha manuscript.]

May peace and life, salvation and victory, be bestowed by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ upon the glorious Emperor Louis.

[Note: One Gotha manuscript reads “Lord, even Jesus Christ,” extending the phrase.]

1. The holy synod decreed that the bishop’s domestic and inner conduct must be made inaccessible to every reproach and suspicion, so that, according to the Apostle, we may provide what is good not only before God but also before all human beings.

[Note: “praedicatores” (“proclaimers”) is printed as “praedicationis” (“of preaching”) in witness G.] Therefore sincere priests and clerics of good reputation ought to attend in the bishop’s chamber and in all his more private services; they should continually observe their bishop as he keeps watch, prays, and searches the sacred writings, and should be witnesses, imitators, and proclaimers of his holy conduct to the glory of God.

[Col. 0557B]

2. We establish that bishops should celebrate Masses not only on Sundays and principal feast days but, whenever possible, should also frequently offer the daily sacrifices. They should not disdain to pour out prayers privately, first for themselves, then for their fellow priests, for kings and all the rulers of God’s church, and for those who have specially entrusted themselves to their prayers, and above all for the poor,

[Note: “commiserint” (“have entrusted themselves”) is printed as “commiserunt” (“entrusted themselves”) in witness C.] and to offer sacrifices to almighty God, accompanied by devout contrition and religious feeling. This is especially fitting for those who sacrifice in secret, so that the priest himself may also become a living sacrifice and an offering to God with a contrite spirit.

[Note: “magis utique” (“especially indeed”) is absent from witness C.]

3. It is pleasing that a bishop be content with moderate meals and not urge his guests to eat and drink; rather, let him always provide an example of sobriety.

[Note: “urgere” (“to urge”) is printed as “urguere” in witness C.]

Let every form of disgrace be removed from his table: no theatrical entertainments, no empty chatter of performers, no foolish talk of fools, and no buffoonish tricks are to be admitted. Let pilgrims, the poor, and the weak be present, so that, blessing Christ from the priest’s table, they may receive a blessing. Let sacred reading be recited, followed by exhortation in the living voice, so that those dining may rejoice that they have been refreshed not only by bodily food but also by the nourishment of the spiritual word, and so that God may be honored in all things through Jesus Christ our Lord.

[Note: “convictibus” (“banquets,” “tables”) is printed as “convictu” (“banquet,” singular) in witness C. “se” (“himself”) is absent in one Gotha manuscript. “alimento” (“nourishment”) is printed as “alimenta” (“nourishments”) in witness G.]

4. That a bishop completely reject all pursuits that are alien to holy conduct and the priestly office. He shall not himself engage in hunting with dogs, hawks, or *capis*, which the common people call falcons.

[Note: *capis* is the printed term; its precise identification is uncertain.]

He shall despise excessive concern for horses and mules, avoid the cultivation of costly clothing, and avoid a loose and ostentatious gait, as though arranged for display.

[Note: The phrase “dissolutum … vitet incessum” (“let him avoid a loose gait”) is printed in witness C as “vitae incensum sit” (“let the incense of life be …”), an evidently corrupt reading.]

Let the priest’s speech be seasoned with spiritual salt, not swollen with insulting, insolent, and strutting words.

[Note: “injuriosis” (“insulting”) is printed as “curiosis” (“curious”) in witness C; “tumidum” (“swollen”) appears as “tumidus sit” (“let it be swollen”) in witness G.]

Let the bishop’s speech conform to the Gospel: “Yes, yes; no, no.” If something must be affirmed more forcefully because the hardness of the hearers perhaps demands it, let him rather insert into his speech, in the apostolic manner, “God knows!” or “before God!” than confirm his words by the emperor’s grace, as it is customary for men serving in the secular world to swear.

[Note: “per” (“by,” “through”) is absent from witness G.]

With the Lord’s help, let the episcopal dignity be cleansed of all levity and boastfulness, so that it may be able to become a mirror of good conduct for all Christians.

[Col. 0558C]

5. That bishops continually examine the canonical Scriptures and holy teachings in meditation, and that by treating and explaining them more subtly they open to their priests and clerics the hidden treasures of the sacred writings.

[Note: “sanctarum” (“holy”) is printed as “sacrarum” (“sacred”) in witness C.]

They should not neglect to offer the people the word of preaching on Sundays and feast days according to their capacity. If thereafter anyone withdraws from this observance or from the provisions established above, he shall be subjected to the divine laws as a deserter of his own office.

[Col. 0559A]

6. Let bishops carefully ensure what diligence each priest exercises toward the people entrusted to him. For it is necessary that the archpriests of the parishes visit each head of household in every village, so that both they and all who dwell in their houses and have publicly committed crimes may do public penance. Those who have sinned secretly, however, shall confess

[Note: “procurent” (“ensure”) is printed as “percurent” (“go through”) in witness G; “singulas” (“each,” feminine) as “singulos” (masculine) in one witness C; and “deliquerit” (“has sinned,” singular) as “delinquerunt” (“have sinned,” plural) in witness C.] to those whom the bishops and the archpriests of the parishes have chosen as suitable physicians for the more hidden wounds of the mind. If these should perhaps be uncertain about any matter, they should not hesitate to seek the judgment of their bishops.

If a bishop is uncertain, he should not disdain to consult neighboring bishops and to examine the doubtful matter with the agreement of another brother, or certainly of two or three.

[Note: “consensu” (“agreement”) is printed as “concessu” (“permission”) in witness C.]

If a matter is so entangled in obscurity or novelty that it cannot be resolved, and the crime of a particular person has been publicly reported, the public judgment of the metropolitan and provincial synod shall be sought, so that the Apostle’s command may be fulfilled: “Reprove those who sin publicly, so that the others may have fear.”

[Note: “ut” (“so that”) is printed as “ut et” (“so that also”) in witness C.]

But if the confession is secret and the person to whom it is made is not sufficient to explain the counsel of salvation, the nature and extent of the sin may be examined without disclosing the offender’s name, and an appropriate method of correction may be found. Likewise, in the individual districts and suburbs of the cities, the bishop shall make provision through the municipal archpriest and the other diligent ministers among the priests, observing completely in doubtful matters the procedure established above.

[Note: Witness G reads “et per” (“and through”) instead of “per” (“through”).]

[Col. 0559C]

7. It is also necessary that the priests in every town and village take care that penitents observe the form of abstinence imposed upon them, and whether they devote themselves to almsgiving or to other pious works that merit the remission of sins. They should also consider with what contrition of heart and lamentation the penitents afflict themselves, so that, after this consideration, the period of penance may receive a reasonable limit: it may be extended if the penitent has pursued the imposed obligations negligently, or shortened if he has earnestly striven to merit the reconciliation of pardon.

[Note: “praemissa” (“having been set forth beforehand”) is absent from witness C; “rationabilem” (“reasonable”) is printed as “rationalem” (“rational”) in witness C.]

The reconciliation of penitents, according to the ordinances of the ancient canons, must be carried out not by priests but by bishops, unless someone happens to be in danger and devoutly requests reconciliation. If the bishop is absent, the priest must of course consult the bishop and then reconcile the penitent at his command.

[Note: “episcopum” (“the bishop”) is absent from witness C; “reconciliare” (“to reconcile”) is printed as “reconciliari” (“to be reconciled”) in witness G.]

Otherwise, just as the preparation of chrism or the consecration of maidens may not be performed by priests, neither may the reconciliation of penitents in any way be performed by them.

[Note: “debebit” (“shall be required”) is printed as “debuit” (“was required”) in witness C.]

For by the laying on of hands this has been specially granted in the church to bishops alone, who hold the place of the apostles, just as it was granted then to the apostles when the Lord said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose you retain, they are retained.”

8. That salutary sacrament also which the Apostle James commends when he says, “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the priests, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him”—this must be made known to the people through diligent preaching.

[Note: “remittuntur” (“are forgiven”) is printed as “remittetur” (“will be forgiven”) in witness C.]

It is indeed a great and most desirable mystery, through which, if it is sought in faith, sins are forgiven and bodily health is consequently restored.

[Note: “et peccata” (“and sins”) is absent from witness C.]

But because it frequently happens that a sick person either does not know the power of the sacrament, or, judging the illness less dangerous, neglects to seek his salvation, or certainly forgets because of the violence of the disease, the priest of the place ought appropriately to admonish him, so that, according to the measure of his own ability, he may invite neighboring priests also to this spiritual care.

This must nevertheless be understood: if the sick person has been subjected to public penance, he cannot obtain the healing of this mystery unless he has first received reconciliation and thereby merited communion in the body and blood of Christ. For one to whom the other sacraments have been forbidden is in no way permitted to use this one alone.

But if the condition of the sick person is such that the bishop judges him worthy to be visited and anointed personally, the rite can most appropriately be performed by the bishop himself, since he is the one who prepares the chrism and to whom authority has been granted by the privilege of the office of remitting sins.

[Note: “quam” (“as much as” or “to the greatest extent”) is printed as “cum” (“when” or “with”) in witness G; “officii privilegio” (“by the privilege of office”) is printed as “officio privilegii” in witness C.]

[Col. 0560C]

9. It has come to the holy synod from various regions that some parents, when their daughters have reached marriageable age and are able to give them in marriage suitably according to their means, keep them at home longer than necessary. Hence it often happens that the girls are corrupted in their father’s house.

[Note: “tale nefas” (“such an abomination”) is printed as “n. est a.” [uncertain abbreviation] in witness C.]

[Note: “contingit” (“it happens”) is printed as “contigit” (“it happened”) in witness G.]

It is also reported of certain people—something shameful even to say—that the parents themselves provide opportunity to the corrupters of their daughters and become pimps for their own children.

The heads of households must therefore be admonished by the priests to arrange marriages for their daughters at the proper time and to forestall the heat of burning youth by the law of marriage. They should know first that even if such women, after their corruption, are joined to lawful husbands, they nevertheless cannot receive together with the bridegroom the solemn blessing from the priest.

Moreover, if such a disgrace occurs in their houses, then, if it happened without their knowledge, they must be subjected to penance for the sole fault of negligence.

[Note: “negligentiae” (“negligence”) is printed as “neglentiae” in witness C.]

But if they themselves consented to the disgrace of the corruption, a greater burden of penance must be imposed upon those who ought to have prevented it than upon those who committed it.

[Note: “sarcina” (“burden”) is printed as “sarcinam” (“burden,” accusative) in witness G.]

Finally, they should know that ecclesiastical sanctions have established this rule: no public penitent may contract marriage until the time of his penance has been completed. For this reason, the corrupted daughter cannot be joined in marriage until both she and her parents—if they are proved to have consented—have merited reconciliation and communion at the sacred altar through public penance.

[Note: “Ad ultimum” (“finally”) is printed in witness C as “ut vero hoc” (“but so that this”).]

10. [Note: In manuscripts Fl. fol. 129, V, Vn, and Est., and in Muratori among the laws of Louis II, this is chapter 3.] Concerning abductors, following the statutes of the ancient Fathers, we judge that the following rule must be observed: if they abduct women who have been initiated together with their bridegrooms through the priestly blessing, then, even if they have corrupted them, the women must nevertheless be taken away from the abductors and returned to their proper betrothed men.

Those who are widows or have not yet been betrothed, and are abducted without the consent of themselves and their parents, must likewise be restored to their parents or relatives and may marry others if they wish. For they can in no way become the lawful wives of those by whom they were abducted.

The abductors themselves and those who aided them—although the ancient canons command that they be anathematized—shall nevertheless not be denied, if they are at the point of death and devoutly request it, the viaticum of holy communion as an act of mercy.

[Note: Witnesses vary: “ipsos” (“the abductors themselves”) appears as “ipsi” (“they themselves”) in witness G; other witnesses read “transgressor vel cooperator” (“the transgressor or accomplice”) instead of “transgressoribus” (“the transgressors”).]

If anyone from the clerical order has been an accomplice of such transgressors, he shall lose the honor of his own rank.

11. Some people are found in various provinces and cities who possess property in several places. When they have publicly committed a crime and have been summoned by the bishop or priests of the place to do penance, they declare that they have already received, or wish to receive, penance from the bishop or priest of another city, and thus, mocking themselves, attempt to lie to God.

[Note: “penitentiam” (“penance”) is printed as “penitentiae” (“of penance”) in witness G; “fateantur” (“they declare”) is printed as “fatentur” (“they declare,” present tense) in witness G.]

Such persons shall therefore immediately be deprived of communion by the bishop of the city in whose parish the crime was committed and compelled to do penance.

The bishop who has deprived him of communion shall write to the other bishops in whose parish territories he possesses such estates, so that, knowing the matter, they too may remove him from their communion, lest they later complain that he was secretly admitted among them through ignorance.

For the ecclesiastical sanction is clear: it states that one who has been excommunicated by a single bishop ought not to be admitted to communion by other bishops.

[Note: Witness C reads “sanctio est” (“the sanction is”) as “et sanctio” (“and the sanction”); it has “continet” (“it contains”) instead of “continens” (“containing”), and omits “non” (“not”).]

### 12.

This, however, must be made known to all Christians: those who have been deprived of communion at the sacred altar, excluded from the venerable entrances on account of their crimes, and subjected to public penance may use no belt of secular military service [Col. 0561D] [Note: [Col. 0561] *concilio*, “council,” C., for *cingulo*, “belt.”], nor may they administer any office of public authority. For they ought neither to mix with popular assemblies [Note: [Col. 0561] *gentibus*, “peoples,” C., for *conventibus*, “assemblies.”], nor occupy themselves with greetings, nor judge anyone’s cases, since they themselves have been handed over to divine judgment. They are not, however, forbidden to attend to domestic necessities, unless perhaps—because of the enormity of their crimes, as often happens—they are tormented by the goads of conscience and stricken in mind [Note: [Col. 0561] *et in se*, “and in themselves,” C., for *et mente*, “and in mind.”] and therefore cannot carry out the administration of their private affairs [Col. 0562A] [Note: [Col. 0561] *regi*, “to the king,” G., for *rei*, “of the property.”].

Those who, when admonished by a bishop or priests [Note: [Col. 0561] *administrationem*, “administration,” C., for *admonitionem*, “admonition.”], refuse to accept the remedy of penance for a crime openly committed are to be rejected still more severely—namely, anathematized—and cut off from the body of the universal Church as putrid and hopeless members [Note: [Col. 0561] *desparata*, G., a spelling of *desperata*, “hopeless.”]. Such persons thereafter have no participation among Christians in law, morals, or fellowship [Note: [Col. 0561] *nullam*, accusative “none,” G., for nominative *nulla*. This reading concerns “no participation.”]; neither are they admitted to communion at the moment of death, nor is any commemoration made of them after death, at least among the faithful departed. But if contempt arising from a hardened heart drives someone to this irrevocable judgment, it must nevertheless not be undertaken without thorough examination. The priest must first try every measure, and we do not permit anyone to be anathematized without the metropolitan’s investigation and the common judgment of the provincial bishops [Col. 0562B].

### 13.

Because of our constant care for the people of God, we wish archpriests to preside over each parish. They are to care not only for the ignorant populace but also to keep watch with continual vigilance over the life of those priests who reside in the smaller titular churches; and they are to report to their bishop with what diligence each one carries out the divine work.

Let no bishop claim that the parish does not need an archpriest because he is able to govern it himself. For even if he is highly capable, it is nevertheless fitting that he share his burdens [the printed *parciatur* appears to stand for *partiatur*, as in the second recension below]; and just as he presides over the mother church, so archpriests should preside over the parish churches, so that ecclesiastical care may not falter in any respect. They must nevertheless refer everything to the bishop and presume to establish nothing contrary to his decree [Col. 0562C].

### 14.

Since monasteries of both men and women are found to have been destroyed not only by secular persons but also—something wholly unbecoming—by the bishops themselves, the holy synod has decided that the restoration of their condition must begin first with the bishops. All monasteries under episcopal authority are to be restored immediately; and any bishop who, by the time of the synod to be held in the coming year, God willing, is not found to have recovered at least some part of the monasteries neglected under his authority is to be excommunicated.

### 15.

Likewise, concerning the *synodochia*—hospice institutions—we decree that those under episcopal authority are to be governed according to the disposition of those who established them [Col. 0562D]. Those that are indeed under the protection of the Church but, according to the founders’ statutes, ought to be administered by heirs or relatives [Note: [Col. 0561] *pertinentes*, “persons connected with them,” C., for *parentes*, “relatives.”] who have undertaken a religious life: the bishop is to ensure that they are not neglected by those persons. If those persons are found guilty of mismanagement in any respect, they are to be subjected to ecclesiastical discipline.

But if the heirs, whether clerical or secular, attempt so obstinately to act against the decrees of their ancestors that they seek to suppress or obscure the founder’s institution and divide the property of the *synodochium* among themselves, the matter is to be reported to the most sacred emperor, and by his authority the wickedness of such transgressors is to be restrained [Col. 0563A].

### 16.

It must be brought to the attention of the most blessed emperors that those who placed monasteries and *synodochia* under the protection of the sacred palace are shown to have done so because they believed that they could be protected by no one better than the highest authorities. If the emperors give these institutions, contrary to the founders’ decrees, to persons to whom they may not be given, they themselves become their attackers, though they ought to have defended them.

The rulers must take the greatest care lest those who are now judged by no one because of this matter [Note: [Col. 0563] *quia minime*, “because not at all,” C., for *qui a nemine*, “who by no one.”] be judged more severely by almighty God at the future judgment [Col. 0563B]. For, according to the Apostle, it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God. We, however, because we are bound to proclaim these things faithfully, therefore humbly bring them forward, since we dare not remain silent.

### 17.

All Christians ought to know that they must faithfully render to God a tenth of all their possessions, and that these tithes are to be distributed, according to the bishops’ disposition, for the use of priests and the other clergy and for other ecclesiastical necessities. Whoever attempts to distribute them according to his own judgment and not according to the bishop’s disposition [Note: [Col. 0563] C. omits *episcopi*, “of the bishop.”] incurs a double offense: one, because he impiously withholds what belongs to the Lord; the other, because he presumptuously violates a sacred matter with sacrilegious boldness.

Therefore, whoever, after being admonished by the bishop and priests, either despises giving tithes [Note: [Col. 0563] C. omits *vel*, “either.”] or presumes to give them according to his own judgment to persons to whom they ought not to be given [Note: [Col. 0563] C. omits the second *vel*, “or”; G. omits *pro suo arbitrio*, “according to his own judgment.”], is to be punished with priestly severity as a despiser and violator of divine ordinances and removed from participation in sacred communion [Col. 0563C].

### 18.

Those who are governed under the discipline and oversight of no bishop are in no way to be regarded as clergy or priests. Ancient ecclesiastical custom has called such persons *acephali*, that is, “headless.”

Laymen must therefore be taught that, if they desire the divine mysteries to be continually celebrated in their homes—which is highly praiseworthy [Note: [Col. 0563] *debeant* (“ought”), C.]—they must nevertheless have them administered by persons who have been examined by bishops and who are shown to be accompanied by letters of recommendation from their ordainers when they happen to need to travel abroad [Note: [Col. 0563] C. omits *necesse*, “necessary.”] [Col. 0563D].

If any such persons are found to be contemptuous of the canons, ministering extraordinarily and unlawfully, and thereby violating the divine sacraments, both parties are first to be admonished by the bishop [Note: [Col. 0563] *amoveatur*, “is to be removed,” C., for *admoneatur*, “is to be admonished.”]: the wandering cleric or priest and the person who enjoys his usurped office [Note: [Col. 0563] *usurpative*, “by usurpation,” G., for adjectival *usurpativo*, “usurped.”]. If they refuse to restrain themselves from this presumption, they are to be excommunicated [Note: [Col. 0563] Here Canisius begins chapter XIX].

[Note: [Col. 0563] *Sed et* (“but also”) is absent in G.] That abuse must also be entirely prohibited in which certain laymen appoint priests or other clerics as tenants, agents, collectors, or exactors of fiscal goods, revenues, or taxes. Therefore, if anyone is thereafter found guilty of such an aberration [Note: [Col. 0563] *qui*, “who,” G., for *quis*, “anyone,” after “if.”], both are to be excommunicated: the one who appointed him and the one who unworthily obeyed [Note: [Col. 0563] In Canisius, the following is inserted here as chapter XXIV: “It is wholly unreasonable,” etc.].

### 19.

Because prophetic speech gives a terrifying warning that the person who lends at interest and takes more in return will not live forever, will not dwell in the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0563] *habitaculo*, “dwelling place,” G., for *tabernaculo*, “tabernacle.”] of the Most High, and will not rest on God’s holy mountain, we decree that anyone found to have committed this offense [Note: [Col. 0563] *homo*, “man,” G., for *hoc*, “this [offense].”], if those from whom he exacted interest are still alive, must restore to them what he is proved to have taken in excess [Col. 0564B]. If they have died [Note: [Col. 0563] *decesserit*, singular “he has died,” G., for plural *decesserint*, “they have died.”], he must refund at least half to their heirs, or redeem through almsgiving what he committed through greed.

Thereafter, whoever is found to pursue such practices, if he is a layman, is to be excommunicated. If he is a priest or cleric and, after the bishop’s admonition, does not restrain himself from this shameful and pestilential business, he will put his rank in jeopardy.

### 20.

We have learned that those who, according to worldly laws, claim guardianship over widows and orphans not only neglect them [Note: [Col. 0563] *nec regantur*, “nor are they governed,” C., for *neglegantur*, “are neglected.”] but sometimes even oppress them. We decree that these persons must be assisted through ecclesiastical care [Note: [Col. 0563] *qui sibi*, “who for themselves,” C., for *quibus*, “whom/to whom.”]. If such oppressors [Note: [Col. 0563] *suppressores*, “suppressors,” C., for *oppressores*, “oppressors.”] are willing to be corrected by the bishop’s admonition, this is to be welcomed. But if they persist in the impiety of their obstinacy, the matter is to be brought to the most merciful emperor, so that he may provide them with an effective protector, both that the protector may receive a reward from God and that the priestly order may not be condemned for useless silence [Col. 0564C].

### 21.

Certain clerics or monks travel about through various provinces and cities, spreading many errors and disseminating useless questions, deceiving the hearts of the simple. Concerning them the holy synod has decreed that they are to be detained by the local bishop and brought before the metropolitan for ecclesiastical examination. If they are found to be sowing these disturbances among the people for the sake of vanity and boasting, rather than for usefulness or instruction, they are to be disciplined with appropriate correction as disturbers of ecclesiastical peace [Col. 0564D].

### 22.

Many have been found, especially among the country people, who brought adult women into their homes in the name of their little sons; afterward those very fathers-in-law were convicted of having committed adultery with their daughters-in-law. We therefore decree that it is henceforth to be prohibited for an adult woman to be joined to a boy of immature age. When young men have reached a suitable age, they may then be joined in lawful marriage [Col. 0565A] [Note: [Col. 0565] *conjugio*, “marriage,” C., synonymous with *conubio*.].

### 23.

Since it has been reported to us that the poisonous shoots and remnants of the magical art still flourish to such an extent that certain sorceresses are said to instill illicit love in the minds of some people and hatred in those of others, while some are poisoners, widely accused by popular report of having killed certain persons, we decree that such ministers of the devil, once exposed by careful investigation, are to be subjected to the most severe penance. We permit them to be reconciled only at the very moment of death, and then only if they have first performed worthy works of penance.

### 24.

It is wholly unreasonable and is known to be harmful and contrary to the Christian religion that Jews should exact taxes from Christians or have any authority to judge civil or criminal cases among Christians [Col. 0565B]. Therefore, whoever permits a Jew to exercise any administration of judicial power over Christians is to be expelled from Christian communion [Note: [Col. 0565] *judicio*, “judgment,” C., for *Judeo*, “a Jew.”].

## Chapters Concerning the Ecclesiastical Orders

[Note: [Col. 0565] “Likewise, other chapters of Lord Lothar concerning the ecclesiastical orders,” Codex Blank.]

### 1.

The holy synod has decided that the bishop’s domestic and private conduct must be wholly irreproachable and beyond suspicion, so that, in accordance with the Apostle, we may provide what is good not only before God but also before all human beings. Therefore, priests and clerics of sound reputation ought to attend the bishop in his chamber and at his more private services [Note: [Col. 0565] *asistant*, C., a spelling of *assistant*, “attend.”]. They must continually attend upon their bishop as he keeps vigil, prays, and searches the sacred writings [Col. 0565C], and must be witnesses, imitators, and proclaimers of his holy conduct to the glory of God.

### 2.

We decree that bishops should celebrate Masses not only on Sundays and principal feasts, but, whenever it is possible, should also frequently offer daily sacrifices. They must not grow weary of pouring out prayers and offering sacrifices to almighty God: first for themselves, then for priests, kings, and all the rulers of God’s Church, and for those who have specially entrusted themselves to their prayers, and especially for the poor. This must be accompanied by devout contrition and the feeling of sacred devotion.

This is especially fitting for those who offer the sacrifice in secret, so that the priest himself may also become a living victim and a sacrifice to God with a contrite spirit [Col. 0565D].

### 3.

The bishop should be content with moderate meals and should not press his guests to eat and drink; rather, he should always present an example of sobriety. Every occasion of disgrace must be removed from his table: no theatrical entertainments, no empty chatter of performers, no foolish talk of fools, and no buffoonish tricks are to be admitted. Let strangers, the poor, and the weak be present, so that, blessing Christ, they may receive a blessing from the priestly table.

Let sacred reading be recited, followed by exhortation in the living voice, so that the guests may rejoice that they have been refreshed not only by bodily food but also by the nourishment of the spiritual word [Col. 0566A], and so that God may be honored in all things through Jesus Christ our Lord.

### 4.

The bishop must completely reject every affection that is alien to holy conduct and the priestly office [Note: [Col. 0565] *abhorent*, C., a spelling of *abhorrent*, “are alien to.”]. He must not personally engage in hunting with dogs, hawks, or *capis*, which the common people call falcons. He must also despise excessive concern for horses and mules, avoid the adornment of costly clothing, and shun a loose and ostentatious manner of walking.

The priest’s speech should be seasoned with spiritual salt, not swollen with insulting [Note: [Col. 0565] *juriosis*, C., an altered form of *injuriosis*, “insulting.”], insolent, or theatrical language. Let the bishop’s speech accord with the Gospel: “Yes, yes; no, no.” If the harsh minds of his hearers perhaps require something to be affirmed more forcefully [Col. 0566B], let him rather insert into his speech, in the apostolic manner [Note: [Col. 0565] *locutionis*, “of speech,” C., for *locutioni*, “to speech.”], “God knows,” or “before God,” rather than confirm his words by saying “by the emperor’s favor,” as it is customary for those serving in the secular world to swear.

With the Lord’s help, let the episcopal dignity be cleansed of all frivolity and boasting, so that it may be able to become in all things a mirror of good conduct for Christians.

### 5.

Bishops must examine the canonical Scriptures and sacred doctrines through constant meditation, and by treating and explaining them more subtly to their priests and clerics, open the hidden treasures of the sacred writings. They must not neglect to offer the people the word of preaching on Sundays and feast days according to their capacity.

If anyone thereafter withdraws from this observance or from the matters established above [Col. 0566C], he will be subject to the divine laws as a deserter of his own office.

### 6.

Bishops must carefully ensure what diligence each priest displays toward the people entrusted to him. For the archpriests of the parishes ought, in each village, to admonish every head of household that both they themselves and all those living in their homes who have publicly committed crimes should do public penance.

Those who have sinned secretly should confess to those whom the bishops and the archpriests of the parishes have selected as suitable physicians for the more hidden wounds of the mind [Note: [Col. 0565] The codex spells *idoneos*, “suitable,” as *ideneos*.]. If these confessors should be uncertain about anything, they must not hesitate to seek the judgment of their bishops.

If the bishop himself is uncertain, he should not disdain to consult neighboring bishops [Col. 0566D] and to examine the doubtful matter with the agreement of another, or certainly of two or three brothers, whenever the matter is entangled in some obscurity or novelty.

If the crime of a particular person has been publicly reported, the public judgment of the metropolitan and provincial synod must be sought, so that the Apostle’s injunction may be fulfilled: “Reprove those who sin publicly, so that the rest may have fear.”

If the confession is secret and the person to whom it is made is unable to explain a sufficient counsel of salvation, the nature and extent of the sin may be examined while suppressing the offender’s name [Note: [Col. 0565] *subpresse*, “secretly,” C., for *subpresso*, “suppressed,” agreeing with “name.”], and an appropriate method of correction may be found [Col. 0567A].

Likewise, in each of the cities’ districts and suburbs, the bishop must provide care through the municipal archpriest and the other diligent ministers among the priests, observing fully in doubtful matters the rule laid down above.

### 7.

In every town and village, the priests must also take care to determine how penitents observe the form of abstinence imposed upon them, whether they devote themselves to the distribution of alms or to other pious works that obtain remission of sins, and with what contrition of heart and lamentation they afflict themselves.

After this consideration has been made, the period of penance may receive a reasonable limit: it may be extended if the penitent has pursued the injunction negligently, or shortened if he has earnestly endeavored to obtain the reconciliation of pardon [Col. 0567B].

The reconciliation of penitents, according to the ordinances of the ancient canons, must be carried out not by priests but by bishops, unless someone happens to be in danger and devoutly requests reconciliation. If the bishop is absent, the priest must certainly consult the bishop and then reconcile the penitent by his command.

Otherwise, just as the preparation of chrism and the consecration of virgins may not be performed by priests, so neither may the reconciliation of penitents in any way be performed by them. For this has been specially granted in the Church to bishops, who hold the place of the apostles, by the laying on of hands, as the Lord himself granted it to the apostles when he said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” [Col. 0567C].

### 8.

That saving sacrament which the Apostle James commends when he says, “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the priests, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him,” must be made known to the people through careful preaching.

It is truly a great and much-desired mystery, through which sins are forgiven if it is sought in faith.
