But since it frequently happens that a sick person either does not know the power of the sacrament, or, considering his illness less dangerous, neglects to secure his salvation, or indeed forgets because of the violence of the disease, the priest of the place ought suitably to admonish him to invite the neighboring priests to this spiritual care according to the limits of his own ability [Col. 0567D].

It must nevertheless be understood that if the sick person has been assigned to public penance, he cannot obtain the healing of this mystery unless he has first received reconciliation and thereby merited communion in the body and blood of Christ. For one to whom the other sacraments have been forbidden may in no way be permitted to use this one alone.

If the condition of the sick person is such that the bishop judges him worthy to be visited and anointed personally, this may be carried out most appropriately by the bishop himself, by whom the chrism is made [Col. 0568A] and to whom authority has been granted, by the privilege of his office, to forgive sins.

### 9.

It has been reported to the holy synod from various regions that certain parents, when their daughters have reached marriageable age and are able to give them in marriage suitably according to their means, keep them at home longer than necessary. Hence it often happens that they are corrupted in their father’s house.

It is also reported of some—and it is an unspeakable thing even to say—that the parents themselves connive with those who corrupt their daughters and become procurers for their own daughters. Fathers of households must therefore be admonished by priests to arrange marriages for their daughters in due time and forestall the heat of their burning age by the law of marriage [Note: [Col. 0567] *proveniant*, “may come forth,” C., for *praeveniant*, “may forestall.”].

First, they must know that, even if such women are joined to lawful husbands after their corruption [Col. 0568B], they nevertheless cannot receive from the priest, together with the bridegroom, the solemn office of blessing. Second, if such an outrage occurs in their homes, then, if it happened without their knowledge, they are to be subjected to penance solely for the fault of negligence.

But if they themselves consented to the disgrace of the corruption, a heavier burden of penance must be imposed upon the parents who ought to have prevented it than upon those who committed it.

Finally, they must know that ecclesiastical ordinances have established that no person publicly performing penance may contract marriage until the period of penance has been completed. For this reason, the corrupted daughter cannot be joined in marriage until, through public penance, both she and her parents—if they are proved to have consented—have merited reconciliation and communion at the sacred altar [Col. 0568C].

### 10.

Concerning abductors, following the statutes of the ancient Fathers, we decree that if they abduct women who have been initiated together with their betrothed by priestly blessing, then, even if they have violated those women, the women must nevertheless be taken away from them and returned to their own betrothed husbands.

Those who are widows or have not yet been betrothed, and who are abducted without their own or their parents’ consent, must likewise be restored to their parents or relatives, and may marry others if they wish. They can in no way become the lawful wives of those by whom they were abducted.

Although the ancient canons prescribe that the abductors and those who assisted them are to be anathematized, nevertheless, if they are found at the point of death and devoutly request it, we do not refuse them the viaticum of sacred communion out of mercy [Col. 0568D].

If anyone from the clerical order has acted as an accomplice to such transgressors, he will lose the honor of his own rank.

### 11.

Some people are found who possess estates [Note: [Col. 0567] *passiones*, “passions/sufferings,” in the codex, for *possessiones*, “estates.”] in various provinces and cities. When they have publicly committed some crime and have been admonished by the bishop or priests of the place to do penance, they claim that they have already received penance, or wish to receive it, from the bishop or priest of another city. Thus they mock themselves and attempt to lie to God [Col. 0569A].

Such persons are immediately to be deprived of communion by the bishop of the city in whose parish the crime was committed and compelled to perform penance. The person who deprived him of communion must write to the other bishops [Note: [Col. 0569] *alii*, “others,” in the codex, for *aliis*, “to the other [bishops].”] in whose parish territories he possesses such estates, so that they too, knowing the matter, may remove him from their communion, lest they later complain that they had been deceived through ignorance.

For ecclesiastical ordinance plainly declares that one who has been excommunicated by one bishop ought not to be admitted to communion by other bishops.

### 12.

This must be made known to all Christians: those who have been deprived of communion at the sacred altar, excluded from the venerable entrances on account of their crimes, and subjected to public penance [Col. 0569B] may use no belt of secular military service and may administer no office of public authority. They ought neither to mix with popular assemblies, nor occupy themselves with greetings, nor judge anyone’s cases, since they themselves have been handed over to divine judgment.

They are not forbidden to attend to domestic necessities, unless perhaps, because of the enormity of their crimes—as often happens—they are tormented by the goads of conscience and stricken in mind and therefore cannot carry out the administration of their private affairs.

Those who, when admonished by the bishop or priests, refuse to accept the remedy of penance for a crime openly committed are to be rejected still more severely, namely anathematized, and cut off from the body of the universal Church as putrid and hopeless members. Such persons have no participation among Christians in law, morals, or fellowship [Col. 0569C]; neither are they admitted to communion at the moment of death, nor is any commemoration made of them after death, at least among the faithful departed.

But if contempt arising from a hardened heart drives someone to this irrevocable judgment, it must nevertheless not be undertaken without thorough examination. The priest must first try every measure, and we do not permit anyone to be anathematized without the metropolitan’s investigation and the common judgment of the provincial bishops.

### 13.

Because of our constant care for the people of God, we wish archpriests to preside over each parish. They are to care not only for the ignorant populace but also to keep watch with continual vigilance over the life of those priests who reside in the smaller titular churches [Col. 0569D], and they are to report to their bishop with what diligence each one carries out the divine work.

Let no bishop claim that the parish does not need an archpriest because he is able to govern it himself. For even if he is highly capable, it is nevertheless fitting that he share his burdens. Just as he presides over the mother church, so archpriests should preside over the parish churches, so that ecclesiastical care may not falter in any respect. They must nevertheless refer everything to the bishop and presume to establish nothing contrary to his decree [Note: [Col. 0569] The codex corrects *aliquod* to *aliquid*, both meaning “anything” here, with the latter the appropriate independent pronoun.].

### 14.

Since monasteries of both men and women are found to have been destroyed not only by secular persons but also—even though this was wholly unbecoming—by the bishops themselves [Col. 0570A], the holy synod has decided that the restoration of their condition must begin first with the bishops. All monasteries under episcopal authority are to be restored immediately.

Any bishop who, by the time of the synod to be held in the coming year, God willing, is not found to have recovered at least some part of the monasteries neglected under his authority is to be excommunicated.

### 15.

Likewise, concerning the *senodochia*, we decree that those under episcopal authority are to be governed according to the disposition of those who established them. Those that are indeed under the protection of the Church but, according to the founders’ statutes, ought to be administered by heirs or relatives [Col. 0570B] who have undertaken a religious life: the bishop is to ensure that they are not neglected by those persons [Note: [Col. 0569] The codex has *eglegantur*, an altered spelling of *neglegantur*, “are neglected.”].

If those persons are found guilty of mismanagement in any respect, they are to be subjected to ecclesiastical discipline. But if the heirs, whether clerical or secular, attempt so obstinately to act against the decrees of their ancestors that they seek to suppress or obscure the founder’s institution and divide the property of the *senodochium* among themselves, the matter is to be reported to the most sacred emperor, so that by his authority the wickedness of such transgressors may be restrained.

### 16.

It must be brought to the attention of the most blessed emperors that those who placed monasteries and *senodochia* under the protection of the sacred palace are shown to have done so because they believed that they could be protected by no one better than the highest authorities.

If the emperors give these institutions, contrary to the founders’ decrees [Col. 0570C], to persons to whom they may not be given, they themselves become their attackers, though they ought to have defended them. The rulers must take the greatest care lest those who are now judged by no one because of this matter [Note: [Col. 0569] *nun*, C., an incomplete spelling of *nunc*, “now.”] be judged more severely by almighty God at the future judgment.

For, according to the Apostle, it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God. We, however, because we are bound to proclaim these things faithfully, therefore humbly bring them forward, since we dare not remain silent.

### 17.

All Christians ought to know that they must faithfully render to God a tenth of all their possessions, and that these tithes are to be distributed, according to the bishops’ disposition, for the use of priests and the other clergy and for other ecclesiastical necessities.

Whoever attempts to distribute them according to his own judgment and not according to the bishop’s disposition [Col. 0570D] incurs a double offense: one, because he impiously withholds what belongs to the Lord; the other, because he presumptuously violates a sacred matter with sacrilegious boldness.

Therefore, whoever, after being admonished by the bishop and priests, either despises giving tithes [Note: [Col. 0569] The codex omits from the first *dare* through the second *dare*: “to give [tithes] has scorned, or according to his own judgment to those to whom they are not to be given to give.” The omitted span thus covers the refusal to give and the discretionary giving to unauthorized recipients.] or presumes to give them according to his own judgment to persons to whom they ought not to be given, is to be punished with priestly severity as a despiser [Note: [Col. 0569] *contempto*, witness 1, an uncertain altered form of *contemptor*, “despiser.”] and violator of divine ordinances and removed from participation in sacred communion.

### 18.

Those who are governed under the discipline and oversight of no bishop are in no way to be regarded as clergy or priests. Ancient ecclesiastical custom has called such persons *acephali*, that is, “headless.”

Laymen must therefore be taught that, if they desire the divine mysteries to be continually celebrated in their homes—which is highly praiseworthy—they must nevertheless have them administered by persons who have been examined by bishops and who are shown to be accompanied by letters of recommendation from their ordainers when they happen to need to travel abroad [Col. 0571A].

If any such persons are found to be contemptuous of the canons, ministering extraordinarily and unlawfully, and thereby violating the divine sacraments, both parties are first to be admonished by the bishop: the wandering cleric or priest and the person who enjoys his usurped office. If they refuse to restrain themselves from this presumption, they are to be excommunicated.

That abuse must also be entirely prohibited in which certain laymen appoint priests or other clerics as tenants, agents, collectors, or exactors of fiscal goods, revenues, or taxes. Therefore, if anyone is thereafter found guilty of such an aberration, both are to be excommunicated: the one who appointed him and the one who unworthily obeyed [Col. 0571B].

### 19.

Because prophetic speech gives a terrifying warning that the person who lends at interest and takes more in return will not live forever and will not dwell in the tabernacle of the Most High, nor rest on God’s holy mountain, we decree that anyone found to have committed this offense, if those from whom he exacted interest are still alive, must restore to them what he is proved to have taken in excess.

If they have died [Col. 0571C], he must refund at least half to their heirs, or redeem through almsgiving what he committed through greed. Thereafter, whoever is found to pursue such practices, if he is a layman, is to be excommunicated. If he is a priest or cleric and, after the bishop’s admonition, does not restrain himself from this shameful and pestilential business, he will put his rank in jeopardy.

### 20.

We have learned that those who, according to worldly laws [Note: [Col. 0571] C. omits *leges*, “laws.”], claim guardianship over widows and orphans not only neglect them but sometimes even oppress them. We decree that these persons must be assisted through ecclesiastical care.

If such oppressors are willing to be corrected by the bishop’s admonition, this is to be welcomed. But if they persist in the impiety of their obstinacy, the matter is to be brought to the most merciful emperor [Col. 0571D], so that he may provide them with an effective protector, both that the protector may receive a reward from God and that the priestly order may not be condemned for useless silence.

### 21.

Certain clerics or monks travel about through various provinces and cities, spreading many errors and disseminating useless questions, deceiving the hearts of the simple. Concerning them the holy synod has decreed that they are to be detained by the local bishop and brought before the metropolitan for ecclesiastical examination [Col. 0572A].

If they are found to be sowing these disturbances among the people for the sake of vanity and boasting, rather than for usefulness or instruction, they are to be disciplined with appropriate correction as disturbers of ecclesiastical peace.

### 22.

Many have been found, especially among the country people, who brought adult women into their homes in the name of their little sons; afterward those very fathers-in-law were convicted of having committed adultery with their daughters-in-law.

We therefore decree that it is henceforth to be prohibited for an adult woman to be joined to a boy of immature age. When young men have reached a suitable age, they may then be joined in lawful marriage.

### 23.

Since it has been reported to us that the poisonous shoots and remnants of the magical art still flourish to such an extent [Col. 0572B] that certain sorceresses are said to instill illicit love in the minds of some people and hatred in those of others, while some are poisoners, widely accused by popular report of having killed certain persons, we decree that such ministers of the devil, once exposed by careful investigation, are to be subjected to the most severe penance.

We permit them to be reconciled only at the very moment of death, and then only if they have first performed worthy works of penance.

### 24.

It is wholly unreasonable and is known to be harmful and contrary to the Christian religion that Jews should exact taxes from Christians or have any authority to judge civil or criminal cases among Christians. Therefore, whoever permits a Jew to exercise any administration of judicial power over Christians is to be expelled from Christian communion [Col. 0572C].

## Chapters Proposed to the Counts by the Emperor

### 1.

We seek the counsel of our counts concerning how the open depredations committed against those who travel to Rome for the sake of prayer, and against those who travel either to the market or for other personal necessities, may be restrained so that they do not occur any further.

### 2.

We also wish to learn from them how powerful men may be prevented from exercising around the houses in which they reside the oppressions by which the poor are afflicted [Note: [Col. 0571] *afligantur*, “may be afflicted,” in the codex, for *affliguntur*, “are afflicted”; the single *f* is a spelling variation.]. For they customarily, with their horses and other animals, crop the meadows of others amid their other acts of violence; moreover, in winter they distress the poor on the pretext of feeding their horses. We wish to know how this too may be corrected.

### 3.

When powerful men hurry to the palace or to other places and burden the poor by demanding lodging [Col. 0572D], we wish to inquire how this oppression may cease.

### 4.

We inquire also with what diligence the thefts that frequently occur far and wide throughout Italy may be suppressed.

### 5.

We also wish to know by what censure those men are to be rebuked who, despite being so often admonished by us, have neglected to build the bridge at Ticinum; and how not only that bridge but all the bridges of Italy that need repair [Note: [Col. 0571] The codex corrects *omnium*, “of all,” to *omnis*, “every/all”; the printed text reads *omnes*, “all [the bridges].”] may be restored to their ancient condition [Col. 0573A].

6. We prudently deliberate how the ships that were formerly stationed at sea to guard the coastline and forestall the ambushes of adversaries may be repaired according to that same arrangement, since through this negligence our people suffer the ambushes of enemies to a considerable extent.

7. We inquire, with the advice of our counts, how our palaces, which through long age or negligence have become obsolete, may be repaired and restored.

8. And so that the condition of our commonwealth may not appear weakened in this matter, let them tell us whether it is appropriate that each count should keep the houses entrusted to him by us properly inspected and maintained, or whether those requiring repair ought appropriately to be restored to their former sound condition.

9. It must also be stated how the envoys of our lord and father, of ourselves, and of the apostolic see are to be received with the honor due to them. We wish our counts to inform us from what resources or estates such expenses and provisions for the appointed embassy were formerly supplied, or from which persons the *paraveredi*—relay horses—were demanded, so that the same arrangement may be observed in our time and this practice not be diverted to other resources or persons.

10. We also desire to hear whether, in the counts’ courts, the cases of the wretched—namely, the complaints of widows, orphans, and the other poor—are to be settled first, and only afterward those of the more powerful. If any such poor of Christ have been despised by someone, let them inform us, when we inquire, how they intend to remedy this.

[Note: *insinuet*—the manuscript reads “let him inform.”]

## LAWS PROMULGATED BY THE EMPEROR

As for secular matters, the most pious emperor Louis established the following provisions, which were also confirmed by the authority of his glorious father, the most serene Augustus Lothar.

[Note: These provisions survive in one manuscript at Saint Gall, cited by Canisius.]

1. It has come to our attention that assembled bands of robbers plunder those who travel to Rome for prayer, as well as those who travel throughout our kingdom for the sake of commerce; sometimes they wound or kill them and seize their property. Therefore we wish our counts and their *sculdasii*, together with the bishops’ vassals if necessity requires it, to investigate such matters with the greatest diligence wherever they hear of them, and to capture and constrain the offenders. If they find them guilty of this crime, they are to execute against them, without any negligence, the penalties established by the laws, so that our kingdom may be cleansed of these evildoers and those who come here under our protection, whether for prayer or for commerce, may remain safe.

Let every one of our faithful know that any count or other public official who gives such evildoers his consent, or neglects to pursue them, will feel the force of our indignation and will be deprived of his own honor.

[Note: The manuscript reads “their *scudassii*.”]

[Note: The C version reads “or those who.”]

2. We have also learned that harmful men of this kind conspire among themselves in various places and, traveling through different counties, commit plunder and robbery in villages, on roads, and in forests; they prey upon and strip innocent people. We likewise wish these men to be sought out with diligent effort, captured, and constrained. If they are found guilty of this crime, they are to be subjected without delay to the legal penalties, so that such disturbance and unjust plunder may be removed from our people and all who live under our rule may be permitted to live in safety and peace, so that the order of the commonwealth, established according to just administration, may remain secure and tranquil.

[Note: The G version omits “We have also learned that.”]

[Note: The G version omits “among themselves.”]

[Note: The C version omits “and.”]

[Note: The C version reads “subjected.”]

[Note: The C version reads “and,” rather than “with.”]

[Note: The C version reads “properly,” whereas the manuscript reads “altogether.”]

3. We have also heard that certain men who possess houses and estates form alliances and associations with robbers arriving from elsewhere, secretly shelter them, and give them assistance in carrying out such crimes, so that they may share with them whatever the robbers acquire through their pernicious work. We judge this class of evildoers to be the worst, because they not only do evil themselves but also use the work and service of others for crimes.

Therefore, wherever anyone has fallen under such suspicion and a report has spread among the people that he practices these crimes, if the matter has not yet been made public, let him clear himself by oath together with twelve men.

[Note: The C version reads “clears himself.”]

[Note: The C version omits “not.”]

But if he has already been exposed or caught in some offense, let him immediately be captured and constrained and undergo the condemnation prescribed by the laws.

[Note: The C version reads “exposed.”]

Wherever the administrator of public office wishes to apprehend robbers, whether settled or wandering, and a robber attempts to defend himself, if it should happen in the course of this that the robber is killed, let no condemnation be imposed upon the person who killed him, nor let him suffer any hostility from his relatives or persecution from any friend or kinsman of the dead man.

[Note: The C version reads: “nor suffer any hostility from a relative or any persecution.”]

And if one of the dead man’s lords or relatives attempts to take revenge on this account, and the public judge is unable to restrain him, let such a person be brought before our presence by suitable sureties, so that the accomplices and supporters of criminals may be brought to submission by our punishment.

[Note: The C version reads “This.”]

Wherever there is a report that such men live, an inquiry under oath is to be conducted among all the surrounding inhabitants. Whatever their nation or status, those through whom this inquiry can best be carried out must not have the power to refuse to swear an oath when summoned by the count.

[Note: The C version reads “is,” rather than “are.”]

4. It has also come to our attention that when powerful and honored men, whether of ecclesiastical or secular rank, come to us, they forcibly take from the people in whose houses they receive lodging whatever is necessary for their own use and that of their horses, and on this account our people are afflicted. We therefore command that every one of our faithful who hastens to our presence take nothing forcibly from anyone either on the journey there or on the return; instead, unless he happens to receive provisions from friends, he is to purchase from his hosts, at a fair price, what is needed for his men and horses.

For whoever has acquired a reputation for this wrongdoing, when he comes to us, we wish him to produce a truthful man who will swear on behalf of all his men that they took nothing along the journey. If he acknowledges that he and his men have incurred guilt in some respect, let him provide a suitable man who will swear and restore everything that he appears to have taken from those concerned.

[Note: The C version omits “whether of ecclesiastical rank or secular.”]

[Note: The C version omits “that every.”]

[Note: The C version reads “or” instead of “and.”]

[Note: The C version reads “whatever he appears to have taken from those.”]

5. Many complaints have also been brought to us that powerful and honored men in the places where they reside despoil and oppress the lesser people and pasture their animals in the people’s meadows. They also establish lodging, against the will of private persons or poor people, in those people’s houses for their own men, and forcibly take whatever they please from them.

We therefore command that this shall not happen again. Each of our honored men is to feed himself and his men from his own resources. If he moves from one place to another, let him pass in complete peace and be neither burdensome nor damaging to others, whether while staying or while traveling.

Let everyone know that whoever thereafter dares to transgress this provision will suffer the force of our indignation and will lose his own honor.

[Note: The C version omits “in the places where they reside.”]

[Note: The C version omits “and.”]

[Note: The C version omits “in their houses.”]

[Note: This is the end of Canisius’s edition.]

6. Because through the laziness and negligence of those who ought to have restored our palaces according to ancient custom they are in a state of great squalor and neglect and have nearly reached ruin, we command that they be restored without delay. Whoever is negligent in this matter is to know that by our order he will remain there until what he neglected has been fully restored.

7. We have learned with certainty that the public buildings which were constructed long ago in each city for the adornment of our commonwealth have, through the negligence of those to whom they were entrusted, almost fallen into collapse and ruin. Therefore we command that they be restored at once and returned to their former condition, so that they may be sufficiently suitable and dignified for our use and for embassies of foreign peoples that come to us.

8. We have often commanded by our authority that the bridge at Pavia be restored according to its ancient plan, but this has hitherto been neglected by some. Therefore we command that whoever has not fully restored his allotted portion by the Kalends of March shall himself remain there until he has brought it to complete completion. We also urgently will that, in every province, bridges over any rivers where bridges were customarily made by ancient usage be restored; and if some circumstance anywhere requires a new bridge to be built, we will that a bridge be constructed there by the common labor of all the surrounding inhabitants.

[Note: The manuscript reads *soluti*, “loosed,” for *soliti*, “customarily accustomed.”]

9. Since we have reasonably ascertained, in each city, the sources from which travelling envoys used to receive either provisions or *paraveredi*—relay horses—and since this has now been violated through the recklessness of those to whom these places themselves were entrusted, so that resources assigned to this purpose are diverted from their proper arrangement to other uses, we command that they exact provisions and *paraveredi* from the sources from which they were customarily exacted under the earlier arrangements, and that resources assigned to this purpose be diverted in no way whatever to other uses.

[Note: The manuscript has *priorum*, “of the earlier [arrangements],” corrected from *priorem*, “the earlier.”]

10. We command that these measures which we have decreed above, by our authority, to be carried out and observed be observed in every respect by all our faithful with the greatest reverence. Nor do we permit our ordinance to waver in any respect or to be slighted by anyone. We announce to all that whoever presumes to oppose these provisions, or fails to maintain the order of our ordinance, or presumes rashly to violate or neglect what we have established, shall, if he is of ecclesiastical rank, be disciplined according to the discipline of his own grade; but if he is an administrator of secular office, let him know that he is to be punished by our judgment.

[Col. 0575]

## ASSEMBLY OF LOTHAIR, LOUIS, AND CHARLES AT MARSNA II  
### (A.D. 851)

[Note: We have collated the pact inserted in Prudentius’s *Annals* (*Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. I, p. 445; *Patrologia Latina* CXV, col. 1390), also edited by Sirmond and Baluze, with the aid of manuscript 2 of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 4638.]

[NOTE]

[Col. 0575D] The chapters that follow were enacted in the year 851 from the Lord’s incarnation, when the three royal brothers—namely Lothair, Louis, and Charles—assembled again near the township of Utrecht, at the place called Marsna. After consulting the bishops and the other faithful, they subscribed these chapters with their own hands and promised to preserve them perpetually among themselves and among their faithful. The public proclamation of each chapter to the people follows.

[Note: Sirmond observes, from Charles’s fourth chapter against Wenilo, Hincmar’s *De divortio Lotharii*, chapter 23, where chapters 4 and 5 are appended, that these chapters were therefore called *chirographa*, “handwritten instruments.” Prudentius, however, relates that the kings enacted them by common counsel and consent of the nobles and confirmed them with monograms of their own names.]

1. Let the abolition of all past evils and conflicts, acts of betrayal, evil schemes and machinations, and injuries committed against one another take place between us and among us, and let them be utterly torn from our hearts together with every malice and resentment, so that from now on nothing may arise from them even in memory for the purpose of repaying evil, conflict, reproach, or insult.

[Note: The Prudentius version omits “and reproach.”]

[Note: Manuscript 2 and Prudentius read *nocimentorum*, “injuries”; S and Baluze read *nocumentorum*, “harms.”]

2. With the Lord’s cooperation, let such great kindness of true charity remain among us from now on, from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith, without deceit or pretense, that none of us may covet or plot against his equal’s kingdom, his faithful, or anything pertaining to his salvation, prosperity, or royal honor; nor may anyone willingly accept carefully composed lies or slanders from secret whisperers.

[Note: Version 2 reads *Ut cum tanta…* (“That/so that with such great…”); the note supplies no word meaning “truth.”]

[Note: Version 2 reads “may they remain.”]

3. Let each of us faithfully assist his equal wherever necessity requires it and he is able, whether personally, through his son, or through his faithful, with counsel and aid, so that he may properly retain his kingdom, faithful, prosperity, and royal honor. Let each of us truly demonstrate toward the other, in mutual rivalry, that if adversity should befall his brother, he grieves for it in a brotherly manner, and that he rejoices in his prosperity. And just as we have now confirmed that we will preserve such faith among ourselves from this time forward, so each of us who survives will preserve it toward his brother’s children if his brother dies.

[Note: Version 2 reads “from now on.”]

4. Because the peace and tranquility of the kingdom are often disturbed by wandering men who, according to a tyrannical custom, show no respect, we decree that if such a man comes to any one of us so that he may evade giving an account and submitting to justice for what he has done, none of us shall receive or retain him for any other purpose than to bring him to a proper accounting and due correction. If he evades a proper accounting, let us all together pursue him in whatever kingdom he has entered, until he is either brought to account or expelled from the kingdom.

[Note: Version 2 reads “so that he may not be able to evade an accounting”; Prudentius reads “if he wishes to evade an accounting.”]

5. The same is to be done with a man who is rebuked or excommunicated by any bishop for a serious and public crime, or who, after committing a crime before excommunication, changes his kingdom and the rule of his king so that he may avoid undertaking the proper penance or completing it lawfully. Sometimes he even takes with him, while fleeing, an incestuous female relative, a nun, a woman whom he has abducted, or an adulteress whom he was not permitted to keep there.

When the bishop responsible for him has made this known to us, such a man is to be diligently sought, so that he may find no place in any of our kingdoms in which to stay or hide and infect God’s faithful and ours with his disease. Instead, he is to be restrained by us or by public officials, so that he returns to his bishop together with the devilish spoil he has taken with him and either undertakes due penance for whatever public crime he has committed or is compelled to complete the penance he has undertaken lawfully.

[Note: Version 2 omits “or.”]

[Note: Prudentius omits “or is excommunicated.”]

[Note: Version 2 reads “the name of the king’s rule.”]

6. Let our faithful, each in his own order and status, truly be secure concerning us, because from now on we will neither condemn nor dishonor anyone contrary to law, justice, authority, or a proper accounting, nor oppress anyone or afflict anyone by unlawful schemes. With the common counsel of those who are truly faithful to us, in accordance with God’s will and the common welfare, we will give our assent to whatever pertains to the restoration of God’s holy Church, the condition of the kingdom, royal honor, and the peace of the people entrusted to us.

In this matter, let those faithful not merely refrain from contradicting or resisting us in carrying these things out; let them also be faithful and obedient to us, and true helpers and fellow workers, with sound counsel and sincere aid, in accomplishing the things we have stated, just as each person, in his own order and status, ought rightly to be toward his prince and lord.

7. Let us therefore be joined together—both we brothers with one another, we with our faithful, our faithful with us, and all of us together with God—and, so that he may be favorable to us, let us offer him this as a devout gift. Let every one of us acknowledge, without personal excuse or self-justification, the matters in which, individually or collectively, we have acted or consented against his commands and decrees and those of his saints, whether in ecclesiastical order or in the condition of the kingdom. Let us bring each matter forward for discussion, and let none of us spare his own secular equal, or his relative, or his ally—indeed, not even himself—so that he may spare spiritually and beneficially.

Rather, just as we stated in the preceding chapter, let us strive with all our strength, through true counsel and sincere aid, to correct these matters together and in mutual rivalry, as quickly as we can reasonably do so.

[Note: Version 2 omits “his own.”]

8. If any of the subjects, in whatever order or status, departs from this agreement, withdraws from it, or contradicts this common decree, let the lords, together with their truly faithful men, carry out these provisions according to God’s will, the law, and a just accounting, whether the person who resists and contradicts divine counsel and decree and this agreement wishes it or not.

If any of the lords departs from this agreement, withdraws from it, or—God forbid—contradicts this common decree, when the greater number of our faithful lords and the leading men of our kingdoms have assembled together, we shall decide, with the counsel of those lords who have observed these provisions, and with the judgment of the bishops and the common consent, how to proceed against the person who, after having been duly admonished, persists in being incorrigible.

So that the chapters written above may be observed by us more firmly and inviolably, with the Lord’s help, and so that we may be more certainly believed to observe them, we have confirmed them below with our own hands.

## Proclamation of Lothar

We wish you to know what the purpose of our coming here has been. We came here so that, with God’s help, we might consider together with our faithful the will of God, the condition of the holy Church and the kingdom, and our common advancement and yours, just as we have done. Thanks be to God, we are thereby united both with one another and with our faithful, as we recognize that this is necessary for us both within the kingdom and beyond the kingdom, throughout our border regions.

[Note: Version 2 omits “so that you may know.”]

## Proclamation of Louis

As my brother has told you, it is a great necessity for us and for this Christian people entrusted to us by God that we be concordant and united with one another in the manner required by God’s will and true brotherhood. Until now, after God placed this kingdom in our hands following our father, we have not been so in every respect, as necessity required. Consequently, so many things contrary to God and harmful to us and to you have occurred.

Since now, with the Lord’s help, we are of one mind, as we rightly ought to be, know that each of us is ready to assist his brother wherever necessity requires it, both within and outside the homeland, either personally or through his child or his faithful, with counsel and aid, just as a brother ought rightly to act toward a brother.

## Proclamation of Charles

Know that both we and our faithful truly acknowledge that, partly through necessity and partly through an unlawful will, as my brother Louis has told you, many things have occurred in this kingdom that ought not to have happened to us. Know also that now, thanks be to God, we are united, both with one another and with our faithful. With God’s help, let us strive as well and as quickly as we reasonably can to see that what has been neglected is corrected, so that God may be favorable to us, the ecclesiastical order may receive its due honor, prosperity may come to the kingdom entrusted to us, this Christian people may have peace, the law and justice may be preserved for you, and you may show us the due honor and assistance that your predecessors showed our predecessors.

How this has been considered and truly confirmed by us with our own hands will now be read aloud to you.

And the chapters written above were read aloud in the presence of the whole people.

[Col. 0579]

## ASSEMBLY OF LOUIS, KING OF GERMANY, AT MAINZ  
### (A.D. 751, October 3)

[Note: We owe these proceedings to the scholarly work of Joachim Heinrich Jaeck, a man who rendered distinguished service to our project as public librarian of Bamberg. He had the document, found in a quarto manuscript of the ninth or tenth century belonging to his library, formerly from Saint Michael’s Mount near Bamberg, copied by Martin Joseph de Reider, a student of the history, antiquities, and architecture of his homeland, with a specimen of the handwriting appended. In 1821 he communicated the work to us, furnished with a learned preface and both critical and historical notes.

The distinguished scholar observed that this assembly had already been mentioned in the Fulda Annals under the year 852, and that all later writers on the subject had followed them. Rudolf of Fulda, indeed, inserting the very words of the following chapters into his narrative (*Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, I, 367), writes: “A synod was also held, at the will and command of that same most serene prince, in the city of Mainz, the metropolis of Germany, under the presidency of Rabanus, the venerable archbishop of that city, with all the bishops and abbots of eastern Francia, Bavaria, and Saxony.” He continues: “They were engaged in deliberating about the settlement of ecclesiastical questions, while the king, with the princes and the public governors of the provinces, devoted himself to settling public affairs and disputes; after he had approved their synodal decrees by his own judgment … he returned to Bavaria.”

That this cannot at all fit the year 852 is shown by the fact that, if the Mainz assembly had begun in October, it would have been impossible, after it ended, for King Louis to hold four further assemblies during the remaining part of the year—in Bavaria, Cologne, Minden, and Erfurt—to arrange the affairs of Bavaria, Saxony, and Thuringia and to hear the princes of Lothar, and then to return to Regensburg before Christmas.

Furthermore, the indiction and regnal year, which clearly deserve particular attention, do not fit the year 852. Indiction 15 points to October 851, while the eighteenth year of Louis’s reign points to October 850. The specimen of the handwriting shows that in the Bamberg manuscript “DCCCL” was written first, with “II” added to it. I have therefore judged that the matter should be resolved by following the indiction and assigning the assembly to the year 851. This also explains Rudolf’s entire narrative, which joins the proceedings of the last months of 851 to the proceedings of the following year.]

## Canon of King Louis

[Col. 0579B]

In the year 852 from the Lord’s incarnation, in the fifteenth indiction, in the eighteenth year of Louis, the orthodox and glorious king, distinguished by the true dignity of clemency, in the month of October, on the third day, a holy synod was held, at the will and command of that same most serene prince, in the city of Mainz, the metropolis of Germany, under the presidency of Rabanus, the venerable archbishop of that city, together with the other bishops of eastern Francia, Bavaria, and Saxony.

They were: Liutprand, archbishop of Salzburg; Zozbald, bishop; Solomon, bishop; Esso, bishop; Lanto, bishop; Otkar, bishop; Gebehard, bishop; Hemmo, bishop; Baturad, bishop; Gozpert, bishop; Erchanfrid, bishop; Hartwig, bishop; Lantfrid, bishop; Altfrid, bishop; Liutprand, bishop; the chorepiscopi Diatmar, Folchard, Alberic, and Reginhari; and the abbots Grimald, Rathleih, and Hanto, together with the remaining men of the ecclesiastical order, namely priests, monks, and deacons. They established the following synodal decrees, whose headings are appended below.

[Notes: Liutprand was archbishop of Salzburg; Zozbald, or Gotzbaldo, was bishop of Würzburg; Solomon was bishop of Constance; Esso was bishop of Chur; Lant was bishop of Augsburg; Otkar was bishop of Eichstätt; Gebehard was bishop of Speyer; Hemmo—also called Heinmo or Havmo—was bishop of Halberstadt; Baturad was bishop of Paderborn; Gozpert was bishop of the Suebi; Erchanfrid was bishop of Regensburg; Hartwig was bishop of Passau; Lantfrid was bishop of Säben; Altfrid was bishop of Hildesheim; Liutprand’s see is uncertain; Reginhari was chorepiscopus of Mainz. Grimald was abbot of Saint Gall; Rathleih, abbot of Seligenstadt; Hanto, abbot of Fulda.]

1. Concerning agreement between the bishops and the counts, who are faithful. It is certainly necessary that there be peace, concord, and unity among the Christian people, because we have one God the Father in heaven, one mother, the Church, one faith, and one baptism. Therefore we ought to live together in one peace and unity if we desire to reach the one true inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, because God is not a God of discord but of peace, as he himself says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.”

If peace and concord must therefore be maintained among all the faithful, as the Apostle says, “Pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God,” they must exist all the more between bishops and counts, who, after the dignity of the imperial office, govern God’s people. They must preserve such concord among themselves that, in carrying out God’s service and fulfilling their ministry, they not only do one another no harm but rather serve as mutual assistance.

[Note: Chapter 1 appears to have been taken word for word from chapter 1 of the provincial synod of Mainz of 847, recorded in Harzheim, *Collectio Conciliorum Germaniae*, vol. II, p. 155, except for the text “Blessed are the peacemakers … they shall be called.”]

2. Concerning the power of bishops. We wish bishops to have authority to inspect, govern, administer, and dispense ecclesiastical property according to the authority of the canons. Laymen are to obey the bishops in governing the churches and defending widows and orphans, and they are to obey them in preserving their Christianity. Counts and judges are likewise to cooperate with their prelates in administering justice according to the precepts of divine law. Under no lie, false testimony, perjury, or bribe is the just law to be distorted in any respect.

[Note: Chapter 2 agrees with chapter 7 of the provincial synod of Mainz, except for the words “in administering justice according to the precepts of divine law,” whose text is absent there.]

3. Concerning the collection of tithes. We wish the tithes given to each church to be distributed by the priests, after consultation with the bishops, with the greatest care for the uses of the church and of the poor. Four portions are appropriately to be made from both revenues and the offerings of the faithful, insofar as the resources of each church permit, as was reasonably decreed long ago. One portion is to belong to the bishop, another to the clergy, a third to the poor, and a fourth is to be applied to the building and repair of the church, according to the bishop’s constitution.

It must nevertheless be urged that the tithe owed entirely to God not be neglected, since God himself established that it be given to him. It is to be feared that if anyone withdraws from God what is owed to him, God may perhaps take away from that person the necessities of life on account of his sin.

For God says the following about tithes in Leviticus: “All the tithes of the land, whether from produce or from the fruit of trees, are the Lord’s; and the oxen, sheep, and goats which pass beneath the shepherd’s rod are sanctified to him; whatever comes as a tenth shall be sanctified to the Lord. If anyone is changed [probably read: ‘changes’], both what he changes and what is changed shall be sanctified to the Lord. Neither good nor bad shall be chosen, nor shall one be exchanged for another, and it shall not be redeemed.”

[Note: Leviticus 27:30.]

[Notes: The manuscript reads “from hereditary properties” instead of “from revenues.” It reads “under the shepherd’s rod” as “under the shepherd’s.” One manuscript reads “if anyone changes,” while another has “if anyone has changed.” The C version reads “it shall not be alienated.”]

But because many are now found unwilling to give tithes, we decree that they be admonished according to the Lord’s command once, twice, and three times. If they do not amend, let them be bound by the chain of anathema until they make suitable satisfaction and amendment.

We have judged this appropriate because the sacred canons command that the tithes of the faithful be divided into four portions, one of which belongs to the bishop’s reception. We decree that in the churches of monks or laymen, and in the lordly or beneficed chapels where tithes are given, bishops are to be received with due honor so that they may perform the ecclesiastical office there.

Churches established in ancient times are not to be deprived of tithes or other possessions on account of new chapels, nor are they to suffer any injury whatsoever.

[Note: Chapter 3 agrees with chapter 10 of the provincial synod of Mainz, except for “hereditary properties” instead of “revenues,” and “a fourth for the building of the church” instead of “a fourth for the church’s buildings.” The added text from Leviticus 27:30 concerning tithes is inserted here verbatim and only here.]

[Note: The last provision, which agrees with chapter 11 of the provincial synod of Mainz, appears to have introduced in later centuries the rule that, in the division of churches into dependent churches, the tithes usually remained with the mother church; this can still be seen in many churches after a thousand years.]

[Note: The C version reads “beneficed,” rather than “benefited.”]

4. That no one dare violate immunities. Whoever, lifted up by proud arrogance, treats the house of God with contempt, and dishonorably treats or dares to violate possessions consecrated to God and placed under royal protection by reason of God’s honor, is to be excommunicated as an invader and violator of God’s house.

For it is fitting that he should feel the indignation of the Lord and of the king himself, whose favor he has despised and whose constitution he has violated. Nevertheless, let the king command that the immunity granted by him be preserved unharmed by all subject to his authority. Let him not give his assent to those who rashly assert that the lordly possessions—that is, possessions handed over to the Lord of lords—ought not to be under the king’s protection in the same way as their own inheritances.

Let him pay ever greater attention to the fact that, just as God is higher than man, so the divine cause is more excellent than the possessions of mortals. Therefore whoever takes greater pride in his own possessions than in the lordly possessions is deceived. The defender and divinely appointed guardian of those divine possessions must preserve them with diligent care and also increase them; indeed, he ought to defend and augment what we have mentioned with greater excellence than his own.

If, therefore, some madman, through the importunity of his shamelessness, attempts to turn the king away from his right purpose and appears unable to be softened by any remedy, he must be cut off from the king and cast away, even if he is useful in certain temporary services, according to the Gospel saying: “If your foot, hand, or eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you.”

[Note: The marginal Germanic gloss is truncated at both the beginning and end: “… ut uuegisemi … hahtot.” Its wording and meaning therefore remain unresolved.]

[Note: A second marginal Germanic gloss is likewise truncated at the beginning: “… idiu … siuhan uuirdit.” Its wording and meaning remain unresolved.]

[Note: The C version reads “guardian.”]

[Note: Chapter 4 agrees for the most part with chapter 6 of the provincial synod of Mainz, differing only in several words: “for” instead of “on behalf of”; “royal” instead of “of the king”; “it is fitting” instead of “also”; “preserve unharmed the immunity from all subjects of his authority” instead of “command that the immunity be preserved unharmed by the subjects of his authority”; “handed over” instead of “owed”; “the defender of those divine things” instead of “the defender of those divine possessions”; “with greater excellence” instead of “the more excellent things”; “turn away” instead of “pervert”; “soften” instead of “be softened”; “cut off” instead of “cast away”; “Gospel” instead of “the Gospel”; and “tear it out” instead of “cast it away.”]

5. That churches belonging to heirs are not to be divided. It has been reported to us that churches established on private property are divided among the heirs, and that such hostility arises from this division that a single altar is divided into four parts, with each part having its own priest. Such a church cannot in any way be increased without discord and hostility.

Therefore it has seemed right to us that churches of this kind ought not to be divided among heirs. If the heirs come into conflict and hostility arises among them, so that a priest cannot canonically perform his office there, the bishop of the city is to order that the solemn celebration of Mass not be held there in any way until they return to agreement by common consent and counsel, and that church has a priest canonically appointed who can freely perform his ministry there.

[Note: The C version reads “the tithe” instead of “the church.”]

[Note: The C version reads “hostility.”]

[Note: The C version omits the word “which.”]

- **N2 · Col. 0573 · after `velint, inquirentibus nobis insinuent . LEGES AB IMPERATORE PROMULGATAE. De`:** source note: haec in uno Sangallensi apua Canisium extant. — These laws survive in a single Saint Gall manuscript printed by Canisius.

- **N69 · Col. 0581C · after `episcopo , Diatmaro chorepiscopo, Folchardo chorepiscopo, Albericho chorepiscopo, Reginhario chorepiscopo`:** source note: Moguntino P. — P identifies Reginhar as chorepiscopus of Mainz.

- **N74 · Col. 0581 · after `in coelis, et unam matrem aecclesiam, unam fidem, unum baptisma`:** source note: baptismam c. — C reads accusative *baptismam* for neuter *baptisma*, “baptism.”

- **N91 · Col. 0583 · after `quam in dominicis rebus gloriatur; quarum divinarum defensor, et custos`:** source note: custus c. — C reads *custus*, a corrupt spelling of *custos*, “guardian.”
- **N93 · Col. 0583 · after `et projice [Col. 0583C] abs te. 5. Ut heredes ecclesiam`:** source note: decimam e. — Edition E reads *decimam*, “tithe,” for *ecclesiam*, “church.”
- **N94 · Col. 0583 · after `rebus propriis constitute dividantur, et tanta per eandem divisionem simultas`:** source note: simultatas c. — C reads plural *simultatas*, “enmities,” for singular *simultas*, “enmity.”

6. That bishops are not to engage in hunting. Every controversy concerning ecclesiastical matters is to be settled according to divine law under two or three witnesses, as the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0584C] Deuteronomy, chapter 19, verse 15; Second Letter of Paul to the Corinthians, chapter 13, verse 1; Matthew, chapter 18; John, chapter 8]: “One [witness] shall not stand against another; but every charge against bishops who wish to keep dogs or other amusements shall be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

In Psalm 24 it is written: “Let all who act wickedly without cause be put to shame,” and in the thirtieth: “You hate those who observe empty things in vain,” or, as the Hebrew translation has it: “You hate those who guard vanities [Note: [Col. 0583] namely, vanities.] in vain.” Likewise in the prophet Jonah: “Those who guard vanities in vain abandon their own mercy” [Note: [Col. 0584C] Jonah, chapter 2, verse 9].

Therefore one must consider whether those who labor to acquire transitory things—which are sometimes thought necessary, although against such necessities he prays in the aforesaid psalms, “Deliver me from my necessities,” and “You have saved my soul from necessities”—are deserving of God’s shame or hatred, or whether they abandon their own mercy, namely God, to whom we say or sing: “My God, my mercy.” How much more, then, are those opposed to God who love things that are of no use whatsoever?

Likewise, in Psalm 39 it is written [Note: [Col. 0584C] Verse 37]: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not turned toward vanities and false insanities”; and according to the Hebrew: “Blessed is the man who has made God his confidence and has not turned aside toward the proud and the pomp of falsehood.”

In Psalm 118 [Note: [Col. 0583] CVIII in c.]: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity.”

In the Book of the Prophet Jeremiah, in the words of Baruch [Note: [Col. 0584C] Chapter 3, verse 16], it is written [Col. 0584C]: “Where are the princes of the nations and those who rule the beasts that are upon the earth? Those who play with birds, who hoard money and gold, in which human beings trusted, and there is no end to their possessions? Those who work in silver and are anxious, and there is no discovery of their works? They have been exterminated and have descended into hell, and others have risen in their place.”

All must consider the meaning of this statement: if it benefits neither princes nor laymen, even pagans, that they rule beasts and play with birds, how much more does it harm bishops and those who are not permitted to carry either a purse or a bag, or to wear two tunics, and who are not permitted to possess gold [Note: [Col. 0584C] “Do not possess gold or silver, or money in your belts; no bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff” (Matthew 10:9–10; Mark 7:8; Luke 9:3; 10:4).] or silver or bronze in their belts? How, then, will they be permitted to possess dogs? And those who ought not to carry a staff on the road—how will they be permitted to carry hawks?

Thus the canons properly prescribe that a bishop should possess simple table furnishings for the sustenance of the poor, and should seek the authority of his rank through faith and the merits of his life. For he is called a pastor from feeding sheep, not from dogs; as it is said through the prophet [Note: [Col. 0585D] Ezekiel 34:1]: “Are not sheep fed by shepherds?”

Therefore Boniface, in the synodal decrees held under Carloman, duke and prince of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0585D] See above, p. 17 (Patrologia, vol. 97, Carloman’s Capitularies for the year 742), and Benedict, book 1, chapter 2.], says that hunting and wandering through the woods with dogs are forbidden to all servants of God; likewise, that they are not to keep hawks or falcons.

In the Council of Agde [Note: [Col. 0586D] The Council of Agde in Narbonese Gaul was held in the year 506 (Hardouin, Acts, II, 995).] and in the other assemblies of the holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0585] “who assembled,” in c.], the matter was likewise defined as follows: Bishops, presbyters, and deacons may not keep dogs for hunting, or falcons [Col. 0585B], or other birds for amusement. If any person of these orders is found persisting in such a desire, then, if he is a bishop, he is to be suspended from communion for three months; a presbyter for two months; and a deacon for one month. Each is to be removed from every ecclesiastical office and from communion.

7. On the continence of presbyters. We also prescribe this by a special ordinance for the protection of life and reputation: no cleric is to associate with an unrelated woman through conversation or intimacy of any kind. Not only is an unrelated woman not to enter his house, but he himself is not to have permission to visit an unrelated woman. He may freely associate only with his mother, sister, daughter, or granddaughter, if he has one.

Likewise, in the following chapter [Note: [Col. 0586D] In the same place, II, 999.], it was decreed that female servants [Col. 0585C] or freedwomen be removed from the storeroom or private service, and from the same residence in which the cleric lives.

In the Council of Hilard [Note: [Col. 0586D] In the same place, II, 1066.], chapter 15, it is prescribed as follows: Although the holy Fathers, in ancient admonitions, have entirely commanded clerics to avoid intimacy with unrelated women, it has nevertheless now seemed good to us that anyone proved guilty of such conduct, if he neglects to amend after a first and second admonition, be deprived of the dignity of his office for as long as he persists in the offense. If, with God’s help, he corrects himself, he is to be restored to the holy ministry.

8. On the defense of presbyters and deacons. If a presbyter, careless of his way of life, has allowed evil to be suspected of him because of bad examples, and the people, bound by the bishop under oath or under the ban of Christianity [Note: [Col. 0585] “from a year,” in c.], have exposed his infamy, while no other accusers of his crime are present, he is first to be admonished privately by the bishop, and then in the presence of two or three witnesses. If he does not amend, the bishop is to admonish him publicly with a formal rebuke in the assembly of presbyters.

If he still does not correct himself, he is to be suspended from office until he makes fitting satisfaction, lest the faithful people suffer scandal because of him.

If, however, there are legitimate accusers who seek to prove his crimes by manifest evidence, and he denies them, then he is to clear himself of the charge, if he is able, together with six men of his own order. If a deacon is accused of the same crime, he is to examine himself with three others.

9. On infants accidentally suffocated. If anyone carelessly suffocates his own infant after baptism, or suffocates it beneath the weight of clothing, let him do penance for the next forty days on bread, water, herbs, and legumes, and abstain from marital relations. Afterward, let him complete three years in penance [Note: [Col. 0585] “Let him purge himself,” in the margin.] through the prescribed weekdays, and three Lents.

If he suffocates the infant before baptism, let him do penance for the next forty days as above. Afterward, let him complete five years.

10. On adultery [Note: [Col. 0585] It should read: “On incest.”]. If anyone secretly commits incest [Note: [Col. 0585] “Dishonestly,” in the margin.] and makes a secret confession to a priest, the priest is to indicate the canonical remedy that he would have had to undergo if his crime had been public. But because the offense remains hidden, the priest is to advise him to care for the salvation of his soul through hidden penance: namely, to repent sincerely and from the heart that he has grievously sinned, and to strive to purify himself through fasting, almsgiving, vigils, and sacred prayers with tears. In this way he may confidently hope to attain forgiveness through God’s mercy.

11. On homicide. If four or five, or even more, quarrel against one man, and he is wounded and killed by them, whoever inflicted the blow is to be judged a homicide according to the statutes of the canons and is to undergo seven years of penance. That is, for the next forty days he is to do penance on bread, water, legumes, and herbs; abstain from his wife and from entering a church; and then for three years abstain from meat, wine, mead, and honeyed beer, except on feast days and during serious illness.

For the remaining four years, he is to abstain only from meat on three prescribed weekdays in each week and during three Lents in each year.

Concerning Albgis, who publicly took away Patrick’s wife and led her to the farthest boundaries of the kingdom, into the still unformed [Note: [Col. 0585] “Into the new,” in the margin.] Christianity of the people of the Maraenses, and brought disgrace upon the Church of Christ by the crime of adultery, we decree by common counsel that, sent into exile at the king’s command, he is to perform penance fully according to the statutes of the sacred canons [Col. 0586D]: namely, three years on bread, water, legumes, and herbs, except on the principal festivals; afterward, four additional years, abstaining in the same way for three days each week and during three Lents, unless excessive illness prevents him from fulfilling this. Having laid aside his military belt [Col. 0587A], he is to remain without marriage for the whole of his life.

Concerning Batto [Note: [Col. 0587D] This chapter is to be compared with chapters 22 and 23 of the preceding synod of the year 847.], who is accused of having killed five men, we have judged that he is to abstain from marriage and persevere in penance until the end of his life.

12. On concubines. If anyone has a concubine who was not lawfully betrothed, and afterward takes a properly betrothed maiden as his wife after dismissing the concubine, he is to retain the woman whom he lawfully betrothed.

On this matter Pope Leo, in his decrees, defined as follows: “There is no doubt that a woman does not belong to a marriage when it is shown that there was no nuptial sacrament. Women joined to men by paternal decision are without guilt if the women whom the men kept were not in marriage, because a married woman is one thing and a concubine another” [Col. 0587B] [Note: [Col. 0587D] Through a scribal error, this chapter has been placed before the following chapter, “On homicides.”].

13. Likewise, on homicides. Whenever it can be established that anyone has committed homicide, a judgment of fitting penance is to be imposed upon him according to the canons.

If it cannot be proved by manifest evidence that he is a homicide, and he himself does not wish to confess, the matter is to be reserved for the judgment of almighty God, to whom all hidden things are manifest. Nevertheless, he is to be told that he is unworthy of ecclesiastical communion until he strives to free himself from the crime he committed through confession and fitting penance [Note: [Col. 0587] “Coercet,” in c.; which I corrected, P.].

If a husband kills his wife, or a wife her husband, equal judgment is to be applied to both, as the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0587D] Leviticus, chapter 19, verse 15]: “You shall not do what is unjust, nor judge unjustly; you shall not consider the person of the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful. You shall judge your neighbor justly, whether he is rich or a stranger. There shall be no distinction of persons: you shall hear the small as well as the great, and you shall not accept anyone’s person, because it is God’s judgment.”

Therefore, if either of them denies the charge in such an accusation, each is to be examined by equal judgment.

14. On servile works that are not to be performed on Sundays. We also establish, according to what the Lord commanded in the Law, that servile works are not to be performed on Sundays, just as my father of good memory commanded in his synodal edicts: men are not to perform rural labor, cultivate vineyards, plow fields, reap, cut hay, build fences, clear undergrowth in the woods, cut down trees, work in the quarries, build houses, or labor in gardens; nor are they to assemble at legal hearings or go hunting.

Three kinds of cart-work may be performed on Sunday: carts for the host, carts for provisions, and, if necessary, the transport of anyone’s body to the grave.

Likewise, women are not to perform textile work, cut garments [Note: [Col. 0588A] The reading is uncertain: “capulent vestitus.”], sew, or do needlework; they may not card wool, beat flax, wash clothing in public, or shear sheep. Thus rest from all work may in every way be observed on Sunday. But they are to assemble from every direction at the church for the solemn celebration of Mass, and praise God for all the good things he bestowed upon us on that day.

15. The man who has a wife and a concubine at the same time. A man who has a wife and also keeps a concubine is not to receive communion.

But a man who has no wife and keeps a concubine in place of a wife is not to be excluded from communion, provided that he is content to live in union with only one woman, either a wife or a concubine, as he chooses. If he lives otherwise, he is to be cast out until he ceases or returns to penance [Col. 0588B].

16. On baptizing sick infants. If a sick infant is brought from any parish to any presbyter for the sake of baptism, the sacrament of baptism is in no way to be denied to it.

If anyone delays granting this gift to one who requests it [Note: [Col. 0587] “To one doing penance,” in c.], and the infant dies without the grace of baptism, let him who did not baptize it know that he will have to render an account for its soul on the day of judgment.

17. That no presbyter presume to intrude into another’s parish. No presbyter is to persuade the faithful of God’s holy Church who belong to another presbyter’s parish to come to his own church, abandoning their own church, or to give their tithes to him.

Let each be content with his own church and people, and let him by no means do to another what he does not wish done to himself, according to the Gospel saying [Note: [Col. 0588D] Matthew 7:12]: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.”

Whoever acts against these decrees, or attempts to resist these admonitions of ours, is to know that he will either lose his rank or [Note: [Col. 0587] “That,” in c.] be held in prison for a long time.

18. That no one solicit another’s cleric. We prohibit this in every way also: none of you is to solicit or receive another’s cleric, because the sacred canons impose a severe judgment in this matter.

19. That no presbyter presume to give gifts in order to seize another church. If any presbyter is found to give or to have given gifts to a cleric or layman in order to seize another presbyter’s church [Col. 0588D], let him know that, for this robbery and savage greed, he will either lose his rank or be held for a long time in the misery of prison, doing penance.

20. On presbyters who have had marriages. Whoever separates himself from a presbyter who has had a wife, holding that one ought not to receive communion from the offering while he ministers, let him be anathema.

21. That presbyters are to be honored. A deacon ought not to sit in the presence of a presbyter, but should sit at the presbyter’s command.

Likewise, a deacon is to be honored by those serving under him, namely subdeacons and all clerics.

22. Festivals may not be celebrated during Lent. During Lent, the bread of blessing ought not to be offered except on Saturday and Sunday; that is, birthdays or feasts of the saints are not to be celebrated.

23. Clerics may not attend entertainments [Note: [Col. 0589] Gloss: *ein uuigi*—“a contest/fight,” uncertain.] or frivolous games [Note: [Col. 0589] Gloss: “shameful jokes.”] [Col. 0590A]. Priests or clerics ought not to attend any entertainments at banquets or weddings. Rather, before the theatrical performers [Note: [Col. 0589] In the margin: *fium. r sclm.*] enter, they ought to rise and depart from there [Note: [Col. 0589] “To leave” should be read.].

24. Mass may not be celebrated in a private house. Bishops or presbyters ought not to celebrate offerings in houses; that is, they ought not to sing Mass.

25. On the Council of Chalcedon. Bishops or any member of the clergy ought not to be ordained for money. Such persons are to be deposed—both the one who ordains and the one who is ordained, as well as the one who acts as mediator between them.

[Col. 0589]

SYNOD OF CHARLES II AT SOISSONS (Year 853, April 22) [Note: [Col. 0589] We reproduce these acts, first edited by Sirmond from the Tilian, Pithoean, Metz, and Beauvais manuscripts and then reissued by Baluzius, using the Dijon and Ripoll manuscripts, together with manuscripts 2) of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 4638; 3) Paris, Supplement Latin, no. 75; and 4) of the same library, no. 4761, namely the Dijon manuscript. We also found mention of this synod in manuscript no. 3878 of the Royal Library of Paris, although the year 804, the thirteenth year of the reign, indiction 1, and the sixth day before the Kalends of May are incorrectly written there.]

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0589B] These chapters were enacted by Lord Charles in a synod at the city of Soissons, in the monastery of Saint Medard, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 853, in the month of April [Note: [Col. 0589] Thus in manuscript 2. Sirmond says that this heading is absent from many manuscripts, and it is absent from manuscript 3.].

1. In the eternal reign of the Lord God of all things, in the year 853 of the incarnation of that same Lord our God Jesus Christ, and in the thirteenth year of the reign of the glorious Charles, son of the most devout emperor Louis, in the first indiction, when the bishops wished to celebrate a synod according to the institutions of the canons, the same King Charles consented and ordered them to assemble at the city of Soissons, in the monastery of Saint Medard and Saint Sebastian, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

There, setting aside secular concerns, the king himself also deigned to be present, so that he might show himself not only to be a son devoted to the Church, but also, wherever necessary, a protector displaying royal power [Col. 0589C].

When, therefore, the prelates of the various churches had discussed—rather than defined—certain matters, while the pious king proposed many things humbly and prudently, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May the synod was presided over by Hincmar, metropolitan bishop of Reims; Wenilo [Note: [Col. 0589] “Guenilo” in manuscript 2.] of Sens; and Amalric of Tours [Note: [Col. 0589] Thus in manuscripts 2 and 3.], metropolitan bishops.

The same venerable metropolitan bishop of Reims, Hincmar, demonstrated that not a few men had been irregularly ordained by his predecessor Ebo after Ebo had been canonically deposed, but had not been canonically restored. The king then entered the synod alone, without any ambition, and sat simply among the bishops.

After the account of the deposition of the aforesaid Ebo had been presented in full, and the many metropolitan bishops and numerous other bishops who had been responsible had been named, while his noncanonical, indeed scarcely credible, restoration was represented by naming only a very few prelates of other regions [Note: [Col. 0589] The sequence “n. c. i. n. v. s.” is absent from manuscript 3.], it became clear that the aforesaid Ebo had illicitly resumed the episcopal office and had promoted those whom he considered worthy to ecclesiastical ranks, thereby making them rather liable to condemnation.

Hincmar, however, his successor, had approached the see with careful and subtle observance of the canonical sanctions and had undertaken nothing whatsoever in this matter beyond the decrees of his predecessors, as is more fully shown in the synodal acts subsequently confirmed in canonical fashion by the bishops of that council [Note: [Col. 0589] The words “as far as this is taught” are absent from the Metz manuscript and manuscript 3.].

2. Subsequently, Herimannus, suffragan bishop of the church of Nevern [Col. 0590C] under the venerable Wenilo [Note: [Col. 0589] “Guenilo” in manuscript 2.], metropolitan bishop of the city of Sens, was moderately [Note: [Col. 0589] “Moderately and” is absent from manuscript 3.] and severely rebuked by the holy prelates for his excesses [Note: [Col. 0589] “Various [offenses] from the saints,” in manuscript 3.], which he was often said to commit because of bodily infirmity. Although he had frequently been corrected before, he continued to bring injury upon the most sacred order through his persistence in frivolity [Note: [Col. 0589] Baluzius remarks: “Herimannus seemed to be behaving foolishly.”].

In the presence of the prince, who by no means despised the infirmity of a shepherd, it was enjoined upon his metropolitan that, taking several bishops with him, he should go to the town of Nevern [Note: [Col. 0589] “Nivern” here in manuscript 2, but above as we have printed it.], and arrange all the ecclesiastical affairs there wisely. He was to keep his fellow bishop Herimannus with him at the city of Sens until the summer season, which was said to be very harmful to his illness, had passed [Note: [Col. 0589] The words “until the period of abstinence” are absent from manuscript 3; “until the summer season had been completed” is absent from manuscript 3b.].

Then, with God’s consent, once he had become accustomed to suitable abstinence, had been instructed in episcopal gravity, and formed according to apostolic conduct, the clergy and people would recall him usefully to his own see, with the favor of God’s grace [Note: [Col. 0591] “The Lord’s,” in manuscript 3.].

3. It was also decreed concerning Burchard, who held the church of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0591] “Chartres,” in manuscript 3.], that either, at the admonition of Wenilo, the metropolitan bishop, he should show himself suitable to receive the episcopal rank, or, recognizing the prince’s ready clemency toward him, he should withdraw [Note: [Col. 0591] “Withdraw from the episcopate,” in manuscript 3.], in either case destined to experience God’s judgment.

Accordingly, when his case was brought forward on the following day, the venerable bishops Hincmar, metropolitan of Reims; Pardulus of Lyon; and Agius of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0591] “His,” in manuscript 3.] were ordered to admonish him privately: if he were able to undertake the office without danger, he should acknowledge that he could do so; but if he could not, he should frankly confess his inability out of fear of God.

When the part of the clergy present, together with the laity, gave him a good testimony, and the aforesaid prelates urged him to do so, he was admitted to the council. He declared that to profess himself worthy of so great a rank would be arrogance, not truth. But if anyone wished to charge him with some crime, he affirmed that he was prepared to purge himself of it.

Since no one came forward to attempt this, the holy synod decreed that the see of Chartres should not remain vacant for long. Men were therefore to be sent there, according to the will of the venerable metropolitan bishop Wenilo, to investigate the election of the aforesaid Burchard [Note: [Col. 0591] “Burgchard” in manuscript 2.] and report back to the synod, so that, if they desired it, a bishop might be canonically ordained [Note: [Col. 0591] “They desired that he be canonically ordained,” in c. 2.].

4. Furthermore, Aldric, bishop of the city of Le Mans [Note: [Col. 0591] “Cenomannica,” in manuscript 2.], weakened by paralysis [Col. 0591C], sent a letter explaining the reason for his absence and asking that they assist him with sacred prayers, both while he was still alive [Note: [Col. 0591] The words “while still alive” are absent from manuscript 2.] and whenever he should die [Note: [Col. 0591] “At some time,” in manuscript 2.].

All promised, overflowing with charity, that they would do so. They also enjoined upon his metropolitan, Amalric, the venerable bishop of the city of Tours, that he go to the same city and diligently carry out whatever might benefit that church; and they unanimously ordered him to do so [Note: [Col. 0591] “He ordered,” in manuscript 2.].

5. Before this venerable council, while Pippin, son of King Pippin, son of the most pious emperor Louis, held Aquitaine—with the consent also of his uncle, the glorious King Charles, to whom the same province had fallen as his share—that region had been greatly devastated by its native inhabitants, ecclesiastical discipline and military order having been dissolved, and many people there had committed unlawful acts with impunity.
