At last, when God looked upon his people, Pippin was despised and abandoned by his own followers and reduced to the power of his uncle Charles. On the advice of the most reverend bishops and nobles, he was tonsured and taken to the monastery of Saint Medard, where he was to be kept and instructed in monastic dress.

There, two monks who had scarcely credibly transgressed the discipline of their habit and profession, burning with excessive greed, attempted to abduct Pippin and disrupt the peace of the Christian people [Col. 0592A].

In the presence of religious abbots from various monasteries, who carefully examined the matter according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the unanimous community of Saint Medard cut them off from its fellowship, declaring that it stood far from their crime—a crime that easily surpassed the customary faults of all monks from the beginning of this religious life, except only those of Eutyches and the other heretics.

By order of the venerable Rothad [Note: [Col. 0591] “Rothard” in manuscript 3.], bishop of Soissons, an archdeacon led the expelled men to the hearing of the synod. Partly by confession and partly by conviction, they were found to have perpetrated the crime of conspiracy. They were deposed with canonical severity—for they were presbyters—and were separately banished to monasteries of their order far away from one another, so that thereafter no one would dare to commit such an act except someone who did not fear suffering the same punishment.

[Col. 0592B] 6. After this, the most glorious lord King Charles brought before the sacred synod a certain deacon of the church of Reims named Ragamfrid, accusing him of having compiled false royal commands in the king’s name, as had been reported to him through the suggestions of certain persons and through plausible evidence.

Because some people thought that, by certain indications, the same deacon wished to evade clearing himself, while others gave a different account, all those present at the same sacred assembly judged that he should be prohibited from every council and should not presume in any way to leave the diocese of Reims [Note: [Col. 0591] “Presume,” in manuscript 2.] until he had shown himself free from the accusations brought against him or had arranged to make suitable satisfaction.

When all the bishops individually commanded this to him with episcopal authority, the prohibition was imposed by divine mandate.

7. In the seventh session, the same most Christian lord King Charles proposed the following chapters to the sacred synod and, with the advice of the same bishops, admonished, commanded, and confirmed that they be made known, carried out, and preserved throughout his kingdom.

[Col. 0592B] Codex Supplement Latin 75. [Note: [Col. 0592B] The following three paragraphs represent variant editions and should be read in parallel.]

6. That in cities and monasteries of both sexes and of every order, the worship of God should be restored as fully as possible, the holy synod decreed, with the pious prince’s support, that suitable legates be sent to investigate most diligently the condition of each place; and whatever they were unable to correct themselves, they were to reveal to the judgment of the next council and to the royal authority.

7. Moreover, the holy prelates decreed that churches which had formerly earned immunity through the indulgence of religious princes or through the devotion of other faithful persons should be allowed to enjoy it perpetually.

8. And that from possessions which are proven by certain evidence to be ecclesiastical, but which cannot be fully restored because of various necessities, at least the ninths and tenths should be paid.

9. And that in sacred places, on Sundays or other solemnities, public judgments should not be held; for it is not lawful for defendants to be punished there, where, out of reverence for God, they obtain mercy through the agreement of the faithful [Col. 0592D].

10. It was also confirmed with everyone's agreement that no one should dare to protect those, whether freeborn or slaves, who are punished by ecclesiastical discipline, or to turn vengeance on their account against any persons subject to the authority of the bishops. If anyone should thereafter presume to do so, he will suffer both ecclesiastical excommunication and the movement of royal indignation [Col. 0593A].

11. It was also obtained from the most devout prince that incestuous persons and any other lost souls who flee the examination of the bishops should be brought before them by the public judges, lest the impunity of vices nourish another person’s enticement to sin.

12. Finally, what had been preserved by some was established as a general rule to be observed by all: no ecclesiastical property is to be exchanged without the king’s consent.

CAPITULARY OF THE ROYAL ENVOYS. These chapters were enacted by Lord Charles in a synod at the city of Soissons, in the monastery of Saint Medard, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 853, in the month of April [Note: [Col. 0593] Thus in manuscript 2. “Chapters of King Charles the Younger enacted in the monastery of Saint Medard,” in manuscript 3. “Chapters of Charles, son of King Louis,” in manuscript 4. The Ripoll manuscript, from which Baluzius published them a second time under the year 867, gives this heading: “Chapters of King Charles enacted at Compiègne, in the twenty-seventh year of his reign, in the fifteenth indiction.”].

1. That our envoys are to visit the cities and each monastery—those of canons as well as those of monks and nuns—together with the bishop of each parish in which they are situated, and also with the advice and consent [Note: [Col. 0593] “And with,” in manuscript 3.] of the person who holds the monastery [Note: [Col. 0593] “Who holds the place,” in manuscript 3.], whom we expressly wish and command to be present [Note: [Col. 0593] The words “whom we wish ... to be present” are absent from the Metz manuscript.].

They are to investigate the life and conduct of those dwelling there; correct whatever requires correction; and, where suitable workshops or buildings are lacking, order appropriate ones to be constructed [Note: [Col. 0593] “Built,” in manuscript 2.]. Where such buildings have been constructed but have been destroyed through negligence [Note: [Col. 0593] “Are there,” absent from manuscript 2.], they are to order them restored.

They are to arrange food, drink, clothing, and all other necessities according to the quality and capacity of the place and the needs of its inhabitants. They are also to arrange and regulate hospitality for arriving guests and the reception of the poor.

They are to provide for the church’s lamps and proper adornment, and carefully inventory the treasury, vestments, and books, and bring the inventories back to us. They are also to inventory what each ecclesiastical prelate found there when he assumed the church’s leadership, what is now lacking from it, and what has been added, and in what quantity.

They are likewise to record what has been given to the Northmen through our recommendation or without our recommendation, what has been left behind, and what anyone has given there as alms [Note: [Col. 0593] The words beginning “What ... has been given” are absent from the Bellovacensis, Ripollensis, and Metz manuscripts.].

They are also to record and report to us the number of canons, monks, and nuns in each place, so that, according to the quality and size of the place, and with the advice of our bishops and faithful men, we may add to the number by our authority wherever it is too small; but wherever it has become excessive through the indiscretion of the prelates, we may reduce it to proper measure.

They are also to investigate how many persons were present in each place in the time of our grandfather Charles and of our lord father Louis, how many there are now, and where places have been destroyed and utterly wiped out by the Northmen or by anyone else. They are to determine how many persons can now be established or appointed there on account of the scarcity and devastation of the properties, so that, with the consent of our faithful men, we may determine what is to be done thereafter [Note: [Col. 0593] The passage beginning “They are also to investigate” through “what is to be done” is absent from the same manuscripts.].

They are to report to us most diligently and chapter by chapter how the prelates of the abbeys and those dwelling in sacred places have obeyed what our envoys commanded.

2. That our envoys diligently investigate throughout each parish, together with the bishop, the monasteries that God-fearing people built on their own property and, so that they would not be divided among their heirs [Note: [Col. 0593] Absent from manuscript 2.], entrusted to our parents and predecessors under the protection of immunity, and that were afterward given as allodial property [Note: [Col. 0593] “Allodium,” in manuscript 2.].

They are to record which properties these are, and by whom or to whom they were given as private property, and arrange to report this to us, so that, together with the bishops and our other faithful men, we may consider what we ought to do concerning them and how we ought to do it, according to God’s will and our salvation.

3. That our envoys throughout each parish, together with the bishop of that parish, investigate the chapels and small abbeys granted from the houses of God as benefices, and determine what revenue proceeds from them, so that the church from which they derive may be able to receive an endowment from them. They are to report this to us, so that it may be authorized and confirmed by our authority; and, according to the quality and size of the place, they are to arrange clerics and lamps there and have the buildings restored.

4. It is to be announced to all and arranged by our envoys that all churches and presbyters remain under the immunity, privilege, ordering, and disposition of the bishops of the individual parishes in which they are situated [Col. 0594C], according to canonical authority and the capitularies of our grandfather, the lord Emperor Charles, and of our lord and father, the pious Emperor Louis.

5. That our envoys diligently investigate, together with the bishop and the prelates of the monasteries, and through faithful and capable men, in each parish, the ecclesiastical properties given as allodial possessions.

As they discover through clear and reliable evidence [Note: [Col. 0593] Alternatively, “judgments,” according to Baluzius.] and authorities from whom and to whom these properties were given [Note: [Col. 0593] “Are given,” in manuscript 2.], and how much remains from them [Note: [Col. 0593] “Proceeds,” in manuscript 2.], they are to record it carefully and report it to us.

6. Let our envoys, explicitly and with all diligence, together with the bishop and the superiors of the monasteries in each parish, investigate the ecclesiastical properties from which the ninths and tenths ought to be paid [Note: [Col. 0593] “ought to be paid” (subjunctive) in 2.] but are not paid, and [Note: [Col. 0593] “so that” in 2.] compel those who retain the same properties to pay them in full [Note: [Col. 0593] “to them” in 2.]. If any objection arises that appears reasonable, let it be recorded, and let the superior of the house of God from which the properties are known to come, together with the person who holds them and refuses to pay the ninth and tenth [Note: [Col. 0593] “refuses” in 2.], be ordered to come with our envoys into our presence [Col. 0595A], so that, once the truth has been established and a decision determined, we may prescribe what we find reasonable. We also wish our envoys to investigate how those who possess these ecclesiastical properties, from which tenths are paid or are not paid, keep them secure—both in buildings [Note: [Col. 0595] that is, in edifices.] and in protected woods—and whether lands or bondservants belonging to them have been lost, or anything of this kind, or whether the household has been oppressed contrary to law; and let our envoys report all this to us in written briefs.

7. Let our envoys, throughout each parish, command the counts and the officials of the public authority in our name, that they presume not to hold courts or assemblies at the entrances and in the courtyards of churches, or at the residences of priests, nor on Sundays or feast days [Col. 0595B]. Rather, let the count identify and find a suitable place where he may establish a station for holding the court; for it is impious that those should be punished there who, out of respect for divine reverence, by the agreement of our faithful and by the decree of our predecessors, obtain mercy.

8. Let our envoys firmly announce and command, in our name, to the counts and to all officials of the public authority that, from the Wednesday before the beginning of Lent—not excluding that Wednesday—until after the octave of Easter, they presume not to hold a public court or assembly, except concerning the reconciliation and pacification of those in disagreement. Likewise, from the Wednesday before the Nativity of the Lord until after the consecrated days, and also during the Ember fasts, the Rogation days, and the days of Pentecost, let them strive in every way to honor those days of rest with the same observance [Col. 0595C].

9. Let our envoys announce to everyone throughout each parish that, if a bishop or the bishop’s officials have flogged peasants with rods for crimes, in order to frighten others and so correct the criminals [Col. 0596A], they are to do so with such discretion and without any improper provocation, as was agreed in the synod; and let the criminals, even unwillingly [Note: [Col. 0595] that is, let the criminals themselves be corrected.], perform temporal and bodily penance, lest they perish eternally. If the lords of those peasants [Note: [Col. 0595] “of the peasant” in 2.] take this indignantly and wish to inflict some retaliation on account of it, or presume to contend that those same peasants should not be disciplined, let them know that they will both pay our fine and, together with ecclesiastical excommunication, endure our very severe *harmiscara* [Note: [Col. 0595] absent in 2; *harmscara* in 2; *armiscara* in 3; *harmscara* in 4.].

10. Let our envoys announce to all officials of the public authority that the counts or public officials of each parish are to be present in their offices together with the bishop whenever that bishop tours his parish, once the bishop has informed them [Note: [Col. 0595] “with no one” in 2.]. Those whom the bishop cannot bring to penance by excommunication, let the officials themselves bring, by royal authority and power, to penance, judgment, and satisfaction.

11. Let our faithful also know that we granted in the synod to the venerable bishops that, concerning ecclesiastical benefices or leases, even if a bishop or any superior of a monastery should make an unreasonable request, we would in no way issue writs of confirmation. Therefore let each person restrain himself from making an unreasonable request.

12. Let our envoys announce throughout their circuit that no superior of those ecclesiastical properties may presume to exchange property or bondservants without our permission or consent [Col. 0596C], nor may anyone exchange an ecclesiastical bondservant except for freedom [Note: [Col. 0595] The words “anyone … will be given” are absent from the manuscript of Metz.]. That is, bondservants who are given in exchange for an ecclesiastical one shall remain in the church’s servitude; and an ecclesiastical person who has been exchanged shall enjoy perpetual freedom.

[Col. 0595]

## The Second Synod of Charles II at Verberie (853, August)

[Note: We have revised the editions of Sirmond and Baluze with the aid of manuscript 2, the royal manuscript Paris no. 4638.]

### Note

The following decisions were enacted at the synod held at the palace of Verberie in the year stated above, in the month of August, in the indiction previously mentioned.

1. To all brothers bound by holy love to whom this may come to the knowledge [Col. 0595D]: Wenilo of Sens, Hincmar of Reims, Paul of Rouen, Amalric of Tours, archbishops; Pardulus of Lyon [Note: That is, Lyon-la-Cluse. Manuscript 2 incorrectly calls him an archbishop.]; Teutbold of Langres; Hucbert of Meaux; Ansegaud of Avranches; Hrothad of Soissons; Immo of Noyon; Hilmerad of Amiens; Yrminfrid of Beauvais [Col. 0596C]; Erpeinus of Senlis; Baltfrid of Bayeux; Guntbert of Évreux; Eirard of Lisieux; Erloinus of Coutances; Hildebrannus of Sées; Godelsadus of Chalon [Col. 0596D]; Jonas of Autun; Braidingus of Mâcon; and Agius of Orléans, bishops, gathered synodally at the palace of Verberie [Note: *vermenam* in 2.] by order of the glorious prince Charles, in the year 853 from the Lord’s incarnation, in the first indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the name of that same Lord Jesus Christ—greetings.

We wish your brotherhood to know that recently, in the present year and first indiction, when we assembled for a synod at the city of Soissons on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, at which sacred assembly the same glorious king graciously deigned to be present, among other ecclesiastical matters a question was brought before us concerning our venerable brother Herimann, bishop of the city of Nevers. Namely, because he was overcome or hindered by bodily illness, he often seemed irrational and was accustomed to act indiscreetly in certain matters that could lead to the ruin of the church’s properties and resources and impede their preservation and proper or reasonable administration, unless swift assistance were provided.

When we sought more evidently for certain proofs of this allegation through the evidence of experience [Col. 0597B], we found some things that persuaded us to lend credence to other matters we had heard. Therefore, according to what we find exemplified in the decretal letters of blessed Gregory, we determined to persuade him to accept an administrator [Note: *economum* in 2.] who would provide him assistance and exercise the due and canonical guardianship of the church entrusted to him, until, with the Lord’s favor, the same venerable brother might desirably recover from his illness.

But because it was reported to us that no one could be found in his church who, meanwhile, whether from perhaps excessive affection or from the respect due to an elder, either wished or was able to guard the same venerable man according to the measure established by us, we urged him, after deliberation, to remain with the aforementioned lord Wenilo, namely our most reverend fellow bishop and his archbishop. We asked Wenilo to provide him suitable care and to supply and arrange through his visiting ministry whatever the church of Nevers required, until the summer season had passed—for that season is very harmful to the illness by which he was said to be hindered—and until our much-loved and venerable brother, as we have said, improved in health and was restored, as was proper, to his authority, to his own guardianship, and to the administration of his church.

Since these matters, thanks be to God, have been brought to their intended conclusion according to divine providence, just as they had been arranged, and since canonical authority commands that a bishop rejected by one bishop—not to mention one removed for a time and temporarily by so many—should not be received without the clearest evidence of testimony or letters, by this document of our goodwill we duly restore our venerable brother to his jurisdiction and authority, to episcopal guardianship, and to the governance of his church. We make it perfectly clear that we did not remove him from his church because of moral faults or public sins condemned by ecclesiastical censure—for this may not be done without open conviction or manifest confession—but because of his bodily illness, and out of concern for the needs of the church entrusted to him [Col. 0598A]. So that this may be more clearly known in the present and future, we have decided to confirm these proceedings below with our own hands.

2. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. We, the bishops who, by order of the glorious prince, our lord Charles, have assembled at the synod in the palace of Verberie—namely Wenilo, archbishop; Paul, archbishop; Amalric, archbishop; Hincmar, archbishop [Note: “Pardulus, archbishop” in 2.]; Teutbold, bishop; Ansegaud, bishop; Pardulus, bishop [Note: “Pardulus, bishop” is absent from 2.]; Hrothad, bishop; Immo, bishop; Yrminfrid, bishop; Erpoinus, bishop; Hilmeradus, bishop; Agius, bishop; Erloinus, bishop; Baltfridus, bishop [Col. 0598B]; Guntbertus, bishop; Eirardus, bishop; Hildebrannus, bishop; Jonas, bishop; Godelsadus, bishop; Braidingus, bishop—wish Chuonrad, illustrious and most noble man, present and eternal salvation in the Savior of all.

When, among other ecclesiastical matters, we were deliberating about the orderly administration of the monastery of Saint-Denis, the monks of that sacred monastery [Note: absent from 2.] came into the presence of the venerable synod [Note: “of the synod” in 2.], bringing documents: namely, the testament that Abbot Fulrad of blessed memory [Note: *Folradus* in 2., and likewise below.] had made concerning the monastery of Lebrah, where Saint Alexander the martyr lies buried, and concerning the cell called Saint Hippolytus, as well as concerning other properties that the same venerable abbot had transferred to Saint-Denis by that testament; and also the privilege that the holy apostolic see had issued through Pope Stephen for that same monastery concerning the aforesaid testament.

They said that their venerable abbot, their lord Hludowic, by order of the glorious king, our lord Charles, had consulted them and sought their consent, so that he might grant the aforesaid monastery to you as a precarious holding, after receiving in exchange properties to be transferred by your gift to that same house of God. They said that they did not dare consent to this without consulting their bishop and archbishop, indeed the sacred synod.

After carefully investigating the matter and learning the truth fully, we determined, in accordance with sacred and divine authority, and according to the testament of the aforesaid Fulrad of pious memory [Col. 0598D], as well as according to the decree of the apostolic see, that at no time should the aforesaid monastery of Saint Alexander, together with the properties belonging to it, be separated by any device from the greater monastery of Saint-Denis, nor be alienated under either benefice or precarious tenure.

The monks also added that, through your recommendation and command, indeed even through your action, you had reduced and taken into your authority the same monastery with the properties subject to it, and had even usurped it. You yourselves can see how absurd and contrary to law and justice this is, if the matter is indeed so [Col. 0599A].

Therefore, with paternal, charitable, and authoritative exhortation, invoking the divine name and episcopal authority, we urge and beseech your nobility not to attempt to do this any further; and if such an undertaking has been begun, restrain yourselves and your people from such an undertaking or action. For it is known to be against God, against every authority, and against your own salvation.

Know also that we have entreated our lord and elder, the most glorious king Charles, with humble supplication and by divine authority [Col. 0600A], and that we have commanded the aforesaid venerable abbot and his monks to give no one consent in this matter, since it is expedient neither for you nor for any of the faithful to make such requests. Farewell, most noble man, and most dear to us in Christ.

3. The capitula that lord King Charles had proposed to the sacred assembly by synodal deliberation at the aforesaid council in the city of Soissons, he also caused to be reread before his faithful at the same palace of Verberie; and they were unanimously received and accepted by all.

[Col. 0599]

## The Assembly of Lothar and Charles at Valenciennes (853, November)

[Note: We have rechecked the editions of Sirmond and Baluze against manuscript 2, the royal library of Paris, no. 4638. The capitula also exist in the Vatican and in the royal manuscripts of Paris: incomplete at the end in manuscript C, no. 1750, eleventh century; six chapters in manuscript C, no. 2859, tenth century; and in its paper copy, no. 2419.]

### Note

The lord kings Lothar and Charles announced the following capitula to the people when, in that same year of the Lord’s incarnation, they assembled at Valenciennes during the month of November.

### Announcement of Lord Lothar

1. Concerning envoys sent throughout the kingdom, so that the people may have peace and justice; concerning abductors, plunderers, robbers, and other evildoers; and concerning all forms of justice.

2. Wherever the circuits of the envoys adjoin, let the envoys come together. If men flee from one kingdom to another or from one circuit to another, let them jointly compel them.

3. Wherever they flee, let a written notice be sent there, so that the count may discipline them, either through their allod [Note: *alodo* in 2.] [Col. 0599C] or by whatever means he can, so that the offender returns there and makes amends where [Note: absent from 2.] he committed the wrong [Note: “the wrong that he did” in 2.].

4. Let it be entrusted to the envoys that they administer justice; and if they do not do so, you ought to go there yourselves.

5. If anyone is in need, let everyone be prepared to assist one another.

### The announcement of Charles, the glorious king, follows

1. Concerning episcopal announcements and the honor of priests.

2. Concerning the rebuilding of churches and the ninths and tenths.

3. Concerning observance of the capitula of lord Charles and lord Louis concerning churches.

4. Concerning observance of peace and avoidance of the seizure and oppression of ecclesiastical properties and of the poor.

5. Concerning what we wish to arrange with the counsel of our faithful: how we may live honorably and without want in our court, as our predecessors did. We also admonish the counts and our other faithful to arrange their affairs and their lives in such a way that their neighbors and the poor are not oppressed because of their needs.

6. Concerning concord and mutual assistance between bishop and count, for administering justice and carrying out divine service.

7. Concerning the administration of justice by the bishops, envoys, and counts in our kingdom [Note: “in” is absent in 2.].

8. Concerning abductions and unions with nuns, female relatives, or the betrothed women of others, so that what was done in the past may be corrected according to the counsel and judgment of the bishops, and so that such things may henceforth be avoided in every way.

9. If we have done anything out of necessity against the churches of God or against any of our faithful, we shall most willingly correct it as soon as we can. In the future, if anyone wishes to injure his equal before us, we wish to settle the matter according to the custom of our predecessors.

10. Concerning our assembly, common assistance against the Northmen, and our fraternal conference.

[Col. 0599]

## The Assembly of Charles at Silvacum

[Note: Sirmond published these capitula with the aid of the manuscripts of Tilianus, 2, the royal Paris manuscript 4638, 3b, Saint Vincent of Metz, and then Laon and Beauvais. Baluze additionally used 3c, the Palatine manuscript, and 4, the royal Paris manuscript 4626, tenth century. We have revised the text using manuscripts 2 and 3, the royal Paris manuscript, Supplement Latin 75, and 4, Paris no. 4626. Of those we have seen, manuscript 2 alone contains the formulas of the oaths and the entire list of the envoys at the end; 3—and certainly 3b and 3c—names only the envoys of the tenth circuit, namely that of Sens; manuscript 4 contains a fragment of the king’s letter addressed to the envoys.]

### Note

The following capitula were issued by lord Charles in that same year and month of November at Silvacum [Note: *Silvaco* in the Laon and Beauvais manuscripts; *Silvatico* in the others.] [Note: In the county of Laon.] after consultation with his faithful. He ordered them to be announced and observed throughout his kingdom by his envoys; and he also appointed his envoys throughout his kingdom, as follows [Note: “The capitula of the emperor Lothar and King Charles made at the palace of Valenciennes” in 3, 3b, and 3c.].

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles [Col. 0601A], by the grace of God king [Note: The words “in usque rex” are written above by another hand.], to our beloved and faithful envoys established throughout our kingdom, greetings.

As we believe is known to you, when we spoke with our beloved brother Lothar at Valenciennes, and by common counsel with our faithful considered matters of common concern [Note: absent in 2.], we decided that, among the necessary affairs of God’s holy church and of our principate and kingdom entrusted to us by God, we should especially admonish you concerning the matters that follow. Thus, as they are written here, with God’s help [Note: absent in 2.], you are to strive vigorously to carry them out as well as you can. You are to assemble without any delay or excuse for this immediately necessary work, just as you have been joined and assigned in the circuits, and begin as soon as possible to bring it to completion. Each of you, according to the circuit to which you have been assigned, is to report to us at the conference that we shall soon hold with our brothers what has been done and in what manner.

If it happens that one of you is detained by our service, illness, or any other circumstance, the others are not on that account to fail to undertake what has been entrusted to you. If one of you is free from the aforesaid circumstances [Note: “occupations” in 3b and 3c.], let him, insofar as God grants, strive to fulfill the orders [Note: “complete them” in 3, 3b, and 3c.] [Note: In place of this preface, manuscript 4 has: “These things are to be announced to the people by our envoys. The capitula that we ordered to be carried out when we spoke with our brother Lothar at Valenciennes. Our elders.” Manuscript 2.]

### These things are to be announced to the people by our envoys

1. Our lords, as you have heard, spoke together [Note: *Partaverunt*: “they spoke.”] and considered, with their common faithful [Col. 0601C], matters concerning God’s service, the condition of the holy church and the kingdom, and how you who dwell in the kingdom might have peace and justice. They appointed envoys throughout their kingdom to strive for this, insofar as God grants assistance.

2. Among all the forms of justice that they arranged for each person to receive, they first considered the honor of the churches of God, the cases of orphans and widows, and royal justice. Above all, they considered the abductors of girls, the cases of widows and nuns, those who presume to flog priests, and those who dare to expel or receive priests from churches without the consent of the bishops. They also considered those who are not afraid to exact a census from a mansus, or from the properties that our lord and father granted to churches in his capitula under immunity [Col. 0601D], and those who refuse to pay to churches the censuses [Note: “the census” in 2; “censuses” in 3.] owed from ecclesiastical properties. Such matters are to be firmly investigated, severely disciplined, and fully adjudicated, according to what is established in the capitula of our grandfather [Col. 0602A] and father.

The offenders themselves are to be brought by reliable sureties into the presence of the person in whose kingdom they are found, so that he may determine what is to be done with such a man—one who fears neither God, nor violating the holy canons, nor breaking the law and the royal command [Note: “of the kings” in 3.]—without prejudice to ecclesiastical censure and episcopal penance [Note: “judgment” in 4.].

3. Likewise, concerning the levies called *heriszuph* (“army-levy”) in the Germanic tongue, and concerning those who violate immunities, commit arson and deliberate homicide, and make attacks upon houses [Note: “upon a house” in 3 and 4.]. [Note: *theudisia* in 2; *theotisca* in 3.] [Note: *heris zuph* in 4; *herizup* in 3.]

4. Concerning robbers, they charged the envoys to announce to everyone, in the faithfulness that each person owes and has promised to God and the king [Note: absent in 2.], and [Note: absent in 3.] in that Christian duty by which [Note: *quam* in 3.] each person ought to preserve peace with his neighbor, that no one, without exception of person, whether out of friendship, kinship, affection, or fear, conceal any robber [Note: [Col. 0601] “of any person” in 3.]. Rather, let everyone reveal him to their envoys and provide whatever assistance he can for capturing him [Note: *capiendum* (“capturing”) in 2; consistently.]. Let the envoys require this by oath, as was customary in the time of their predecessors. If anyone does not obey their envoys, and is a royal man, let him be brought by sureties into the king’s presence. If he is another man’s dependent, let the lord whose man he is present him to the king.

5. They also charged that, if anyone is ordered to provide assistance for capturing a robber, or if anyone hears the signal by which people are summoned to capture a robber, and withdraws instead of providing assistance, then, if he is a free man, he shall pay the lord’s fine; if he is a peasant, he shall receive sixty blows. If the robber is killed there, the person who killed him shall pay no *leud* [Note: *liudem*, with no source indicated, in 3.], and no one shall presume to carry a feud against him on that account. If anyone presumes to do so, let him be brought by reliable sureties into the king’s presence.

6. Whoever indeed [Note: [Col. 0601] absent in 3 and 4.] hereafter receives a robber—especially one who has been outlawed, or one who receives those whom our envoys have outlawed after they have been outlawed by those same envoys—shall be judged according to what is established in the capitula of our grandfather and father, book III, chapter 23 [Col. 0602D]. If he is a Frank, let him swear with twelve comparable Franks that he did not know the man to be a robber, even if the man is his father, brother, or relative. If he cannot swear this, and another person convicts him of having received the robber as a guest [Col. 0603A], let him be judged as a robber and an unfaithful man, for he is a robber and an unfaithful man to us and to the Franks; and the person who received him is like him [Note: absent in 3.].

If he heard that the man was a robber but does not know it with certainty, let him either swear alone that he had never heard, whether truthfully or falsely, that the man was a robber, or be prepared, if the man is convicted of robbery, to be condemned in the same way [Note: “or” in 2.].

7. When our envoys outlaw a robber, let them make this known both to the other envoys and to the counts. If the robber flees from one circuit to another [Note: “from one transmitted circuit” in 2.] and comes into a neighboring area [Note: “they come” in 2.], the envoy who outlawed him is not for that reason to cease pursuing and capturing him. If he flees farther [Note: [Col. 0603] “has been” in 2.], the envoy into whose circuit he has fled, if he possesses an allod [Note: “allod” in 2, consistently.], shall take it from him and compel him [Note: [Col. 0603] “and that he” in 3.] to return there, willingly or unwillingly [Note: “return” in 2.], and make amends where he committed the wrong.

If he flees into someone’s estate and that estate defends him, let what is written in the capitula of our grandfather and father be carried out in this matter. If necessary, so that justice may not be delayed, let the advocate be notified to surrender the robber and present those who defended him, so that they may receive the discipline they deserve and make suitable amends. If he neglects to do this a second time, let him pay the lord’s fine; and let him then be brought by sureties into their presence, so that judgment may be rendered concerning him, those who opposed the capture, and the robber himself, according to the circumstances of the case [Note: absent in 2.], so that the others may have fear.

8. Our lords also charged that, if such evildoers, as we have said, flee from one kingdom to another, the envoys of the kingdom from which the offender fled are likewise to make this known to the other envoys in the kingdom to which he has fled. Those envoys are to compel the offenders to return to that kingdom and to those envoys, so that they may be disciplined there where they committed the wrong.

9. Concerning newcomers who have fled into parts of these kingdoms because of the oppression of the Northmen or Britons, our elders determined that they are to suffer no violence, oppression, or exaction from any official of the public authority. Rather, they are to be permitted to seek and possess their livelihood until either they themselves return to their own places or their lords [Note: *eorum* (“their”) in 2.] receive them [Col. 0603D]. No one is to presume to enslave them because they have remained with someone as hired workers, nor to exact a census or tribute from them [Note: Baluze added: “No one … to exact”; the words are absent from 2, 3, and 4.]. If any official of the public authority or anyone else [Note: “another” in 3.] is found to have done or to be doing anything contrary to this command of mercy, let him pay the lord’s fine.

10. Let it be announced to everyone how all are to be prepared for any impending necessity [Col. 0604A], so that, according to custom and as necessity arises, everyone may be prepared for God’s service, for their service, and for the defense of God’s holy [Note: the words “holy church” are absent from 2.] church and kingdom.

11. Those who do not possess the capitula of our grandfather and father that we have mentioned above, and who need them [Note: [Col. 0603] *eisdem* (“those same [capitula]”) in 3 and 4.] in order to correct matters entrusted to them, as those capitula command [Note: “as is contained in them” in 2.], are to receive them from our archive or from our chancellor, so that they may correct and arrange everything reasonably and lawfully.

12. Let each envoy have provision in his circuit, so that, if one of our faithful passes through his circuit [Note: absent in 2.], or remains or resides there [Col. 0604B] and commits robbery, plunder, or some other unlawful act by which God is usually offended and the people groan under oppression, he may investigate the matter carefully and truthfully and report to us, so that we may arrange it in such a way that neither he nor anyone else will wish to do such a thing.

13. Let the envoys take care in their circuits that our men, or anyone else, do not plunder or oppress their neighbors, whether greater or lesser, in summer, when they send their horses out to pasture, or in winter, when they send their marshals [Note: *marascalchos* in 2.] for fodder. If they do so, let our envoys, as we have said, investigate the matter truthfully and report to us [Col. 0604C], so that we may correct it in the case of the lord in such a way that he keeps his men under control, that they remain content with what is due to them, and that they do not unjustly seek what is not due [Note: All the remaining material, except the list of envoys in the tenth circuit, is absent from 3, 3b, 3c, and 4. Manuscript 4 appends to the preceding capitula a fragment of a royal letter to the envoys, which we report below.].

### This oath shall be sworn by Frankish men

I, so-and-so, shall not make an attack, that evil which they call *scach* [Note: *siach* in 2.] or *tesceia*, nor shall I consent that another make one. If I learn that anyone does this, I shall not conceal it; and the man whom I know now to be a robber or *scachcator* I shall not conceal from you, the royal envoys, so that I may not report him. So may God and these relics help me.

### This oath shall be sworn by the hundredmen

I, so-and-so, shall not make an attack [Note: *assaltura* in 2.], that evil which they call *scach* [Note: *scah* in 2.] or *tesceia*, nor shall I consent that another make one [Col. 0604D]. If I learn that anyone does this, I shall not conceal it; and the man whom I know now to be a robber or *scachcator* I shall not conceal from you, the royal envoys, so that I may not report him. Of the Frankish men residing in this county and in my jurisdiction, I shall conceal none, insofar as I am able to remember, so that I may not reveal him to you, the royal envoys, in a written brief. So may God and these relics help me.

### Envoys and counties assigned at that time by circuits

1. Hincmar, bishop; Ricuinus; Engilscalchus: envoys in the circuits of Reims, Voncq, Stenay, Perthes, Bar, Camizis, Châlons, Vitry, Bassigny, and Tardenois.

2. Pardulus, bishop; Altmarus; Theodacrus: envoys in Laon, Porcien, Soissons, Ouche, and Vexin.

3. Imino [Note: Thus corrected from 2; the editions have *Immo.], bishop; Adalardus, abbot; Waltcaudus; Odelricus: envoys in Noyon, Vermandois, Artois, Courtrai, Flanders, the counties of Engilramnus, and the counties of Waltcaudus [Note: *Uuatcaudus* in 2.].

4. Folcoinus [Note: Of Thérouanne.] bishop; Adalgarius; Engiscalchus; and Berengarius: envoys in the county of Berengarius [Col. 0605B], in those of Engiscalchus and Gerardus, and in the counties of Reginarius.

5. Hludowicus, abbot; Yrminfridus, bishop; Ingilwinus; Gozselmus: envoys in the Parisian, Melcian [Note: *Molcian* in 2.], Senlis, Vexin, Beauvais, and Vindoil circuits.

6. Paul, bishop; Hilmeradus, bishop; Herloinus; Hungarius: envoys in Rouen, Telleau, Vimeu, Ponthieu, and Amiens.

7. Eirardus, bishop; Teodericus, abbot; Herloinus; Hardoinus: envoys in Avranches, Coutances, Bessin, Corbonnais, the Saxon territory of Ot, and Hardouin’s territory, Ouche, and Lisieux.

8. Dodo [Note: Of Angers.] bishop; Hrotbertus; and Osbertus [Col. 0606A]: envoys in Maine, Anjou, and Touraine, Corbonnais, and Sées.

9. Burcardus [Note: *Berardus* in 2.] [Note: Of Chartres.] bishop; Hrodulfus; and Heinricus, abbot: envoys in Blois, Orléans, Vendôme, Chartres [Note: *Caretino* in 2.], Dourdan [Note: The words represented by “d d. e. st. c.” are absent from 2; they were therefore taken from Tilianus, Laon, or Beauvais.], Dunois, Évreux, Étampes, Château, Pincerais, and Méré.

10. Wenilo [Note: *Guenilo* in 3.] bishop; Odo; and Donatus: envoys in the county of Sens, Troyes [Note: *Tricassino*; *Uuastesino* in 3.], Gâtinais, Melun, Morvois, Provins [Note: *Proviso* in 2; *Pruviniso* in 3.], the three Archis districts [Note: *Archis* in 3; *Archisiis* in 3c.], and the two Brionnais districts.

11. Teutboldus, bishop; Jonas, bishop; Isembardus; Abbo, abbot; Daddo: envoys in the counties of Milo, and in the counties of Isembardus—namely Autun, Mâcon, Dijon, Chalon, the Hattuarian territory, and Tornedois, Belnois, and Duesmois [Col. 0606B]—in the county of Attela, and in the county of Romoldus.

12. Hugo; Gozso; Nivilungus: envoys in Nevers, Auxerrois, and Avalois.

### Fragment of the royal letter to the envoys, from manuscript 4

… We further command that, if you do not possess the written capitula of our lord grandfather and father, you send to our palace, according to the custom of your predecessors, one of your envoys and a scribe with parchment. There he shall receive those capitula from our archive and copy them. Then, according to those capitula, you are to take diligent care to correct lawfully the necessary complaints of God’s justice and of the people entrusted to us by God. Farewell.

[Col. 0605]

## The Assembly of Lothar and Charles at Liège (854, February)

[Note: We have revised the editions of Sirmond and Baluze with the aid of manuscript 2, the royal library of Paris, no. 4638.]

### Note

These are the announcements that Lothar and Charles made at Liège in the year 854.

## Lothar, Most Serene Emperor

[Note: *Serenus* in 2.]

1. We wish you all to know of our faithfulness, because frequently during the present year we invited our most beloved brother Louis to hold a common conference with our faithful, and with them to discuss and arrange, according to the Lord’s will, insofar as he might inspire it, matters concerning the welfare of God’s holy Church and our common advancement, and that of our people, their honor, and their necessities [Note: *profecto* (“advancement”) in witness 2]. But since our aforesaid brother has thus far postponed coming, as we had hoped, because of certain obstructing circumstances, we did not wish to omit joining together usefully.

[Col. 0605D] 2. We now wish to make you certain of our union: with Christ propitious, and according to God, for the salvation of God’s holy Church and for our common welfare and necessity, we wish to unite ourselves inseparably in heart and deed, so that we may be one in Christ and you may be one with us.

3. Know that the law which our predecessors—that is, our father and grandfather—granted and preserved for your predecessors, we likewise pardon to you, and we wish to observe it inviolably and incorruptibly in every respect, both now and in future times.

## KAROLUS GLORIOSISSIMUS REX

1. We postponed making this union until now for this reason: we wished our aforesaid brother, coming together with us, to associate himself with us in the same union [Note: *volumus* (“we wish”) in witness 2]. But since he, impeded by certain obstacles, omitted to come [Col. 0606D], and we have heard of the disturbance which his son is attempting to cause, we wished to unite ourselves. Know, therefore, that in prosperity and adversity alike we shall be together; nor, with God’s help, will any obstacle be able to separate us from that charity by which we are bound together as brothers. But wherever we need mutual consolation and assistance, insofar as the Lord permits, we wish to support and sustain one another, and to bring aid to one another against every earthly enemy.

2. But if that same brother of ours postpones doing this, as we desire and command him to do, we are so united that each of us may offer the other such consolation and assistance that, wherever necessary, each may henceforth and thereafter, as we have stated above, peacefully retain the kingdom divinely entrusted to him. And if one of the pair survives the other, he who remains shall keep his nephews, together with their father’s kingdom, under his protection and defense, so that, fortified in this way with God’s help against the machinations of adversaries, they may be able to retain their father’s kingdom in peaceful order.

3. We wish you, therefore, to know with complete certainty of our devotion that we truly recognize that we have offended God in many matters and have negligently troubled your hearts. We intend, with Christ’s favor, to correct all these things according to our ability, so that we may both appease God and satisfy your devotion. We shall take care to make you more fully informed about all these matters when more of our faithful have assembled, or when our aforesaid brother has come, as we have commanded him—if, indeed, he wishes to come—whichever way will be more pleasing to you [Col. 0608A]. Thus you may truly know that we wish in every respect to fulfill our promise and to observe it completely.

4. Moreover, let your prudence and that of everyone know in common that we wished to proclaim these things to you so carefully in this sacred place so that you may know that, with the Lord’s favor and with the support of his saints, in whose presence these things are proclaimed, we shall observe inviolably everything that we say.

This is the oath which they swore mutually [Note: “which the three Frankish kings swore to one another,” manuscript 2].

“From this day forward, if our brother Louis breaks or violates the oath which he has sworn against us, or if his sons act against that part of the kingdom which you hold against him [Note: *tua* (“your”) in witness 2], I shall, insofar as the Lord grants me power, provide you, if you request it, with the aid of defense against him, his sons, and all who may wish to take it from you without just and reasonable cause. But if I outlive you, I shall not take from your sons that part of the kingdom which you hold against me and my brother; rather, I shall consent to it. And if they or their faithful request assistance for their defense against that same brother of ours and his sons, and against all others, so that they may be able to hold it, I shall provide assistance insofar as I can [Note: *potuero* (“I shall be able”) in witness 2], provided that you or your sons provide that same assistance to me and do not separate yourselves from us.”

[Col. 0607]

## KAROLI II CONVENTUS ATTINIACENSIS  
*(The Assembly of Charles II at Attigny, A.D. 854, June)*

[Note: We have revised the editions of Sirmond and Baluze with the aid of manuscript 2, Royal Library of Paris, no. 4638; from this manuscript Peter Pithoeus was also the first to publish the oath of fidelity in the *Contemporary Writers* in 1588.]

[NOTA]

[Col. 0607C] The following memorial capitula were given by the lord Charles to his envoys in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 854, in the month of June, when he conferred with his brother Lothar at Attigny, so that each envoy might take care to carry them out in his own sphere of commission throughout that king’s realm.

1. Concerning envoys for robbers: namely, that envoys be added and supplied who may carry out what is contained in the capitula which we stated above that we had issued at Servais [Note: *quas* (“which,” feminine plural) in witness 2].

2. Concerning coastal defense: that it be arranged vigilantly according to custom.

3. Concerning routes across the waters: namely, that wherever they had recently been closed, they be opened, as they had been opened in ancient times.

4. Concerning bridges to be restored: namely, that, according to the capitula of his grandfather and father, they be repaired where they had formerly stood, by those who hold the honors through which the bridges had previously been built or restored [Note: *de quibus ante* (“through which previously”) is absent from witness 2].

5. Concerning ships that pass beneath bridges: namely, that no toll be demanded from them.

[Col. 0608C] 6. Concerning newcomers whom public officials afflict: namely, that those who have been afflicted by the Northmen or Bretons and have therefore come into this kingdom as beggars, or those who have come here because of the Aquitanian affliction, and from whom taxes or labor-services have been exacted, be compensated for this, together with their customary law. Whoever thereafter presumes to do this shall, in addition to the compensation, pay the king’s ban.

7. Concerning robbers who now do no wrong, who have made restitution for what they did long ago, and against whom no one now brings a complaint: namely, that they not be punished merely for this reason.

8. Concerning men who have been placed under the ban and in penance, and who continually act worse: namely, that they be seized and restrained by the envoys.

[Col. 0608D] 9. Concerning coins and counterfeiters, namely, that they be diligently investigated and corrected.

10. Concerning the property of churches given as allods: namely, that it be investigated and recorded by the envoys, and reported to the king [Note: “reported” in witness 2; “announced” in manuscripts S and B].

[Col. 0609A] 11. Concerning monasteries to be visited: namely, that the envoys take care to carry this out as it was ordained.

12. Concerning men who again commit abductions, as though beginning anew: that they be apprehended and restrained by the envoys and brought into the king’s presence [Note: “the kings’ presence” in witness 2].

13. Concerning the promise of fidelity to the king: namely, that all Franks throughout his kingdom promise him fidelity. Those who say that they have already promised it must either prove this through reliable witnesses, swear that they swore it previously, or make that same promise of fidelity.

The oath of fidelity is as follows:

“I, so-and-so, shall from this day forward be faithful to Charles, son of Louis and Judith, according to my *savirum* [Note: i.e. *savoir*, “knowledge,” from *sapere*], as a free Frank ought by right to be faithful to his king. So may God and these relics help me.”

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 854, on the fifth day before the Nones of July [Note: “of July” in witness 2], these men swore at the assembly of Reims that they had previously sworn fidelity.

[Col. 0609B]

These men had sworn previously:

[Col. 0610A] Teudacrus, Amalricus [Note: manuscript 2 appears to read *Ainalricus*], Rotboldus, Amalbertus, Dodo, Wigboldus [Note: corrected according to manuscript 2], Berulfus, Wala, Hecilo [Note: corrected according to manuscript 2], Heirbertus, Airardus, Gotlandus, Hilpricus, Gerlegius, Amalgisus, Heico, Amalricus, mayor of Buxido.

These men swore fidelity:

Goderamnus, Dodilo, Sigebertus, Fidentius, Ermenulfus, Teutgriminus, Wicboldus, Ermengaudus, Rotmundus, Gislulfus, Haimiricus, Teutbaldus, Drogo, Teodericus, Ebroinus, Rodoinus, Gislinus, Vulfridus, Haimuinus, Wandrebertus, Berecarius, Angelinus, Ado, Meinardus, Ottradus, dean; Guntbertus, dean; Heruwincus, dean; Ozias, Ailus, Teudaldus, Teodoldus, dean; Bertricus, Rothaus, Ingobertus, Amblinus, dean; Gozselmus, dean [Col. 0610B]; Vulfarius, Flodovius [Note: so in witness 2], Anglebertus, Emmenulfus, Sicbertus, dean; Hecto, Isaac, Gislardus, Alaricus, Gerardus, Madergaudus, dean.

[Col. 0609]

## HLUDOWICI II IMPERATORIS CONVENTUS TICINENSIS II  
*(The Second Assembly of the Emperor Louis II at Pavia, A.D. 855, February 4)*

[Note: The capitula proposed by the emperor to the bishops, the bishops’ response concerning them, and the laws subsequently promulgated were first published by Laurentius Surius in 1567, volume III of the *Councils*, pages 480–483. The capitula of the envoys, together with the laws, were published by Muratori from the Modena manuscript. Our edition is based on manuscripts 1, Blankenburg; 2, Gotha; 3, the Modena manuscript as printed by Muratori; and 4, the first edition.

The capitula placed at the end in the Blankenburg manuscript, and appearing here in print for the first time, occur after the bishops’ response and seem to refer to the statutes of the assembly held in 850.]

[NOTA]

[Col. 0609C] Capitula which the glorious emperor Louis commanded his bishops to consider concerning the condition of his kingdom [Note: From manuscripts 2 and 4]:

“Concerning the conduct of bishops, priests, and the other clergy; concerning teaching and preaching among the people; concerning the writing of books; concerning the restoration of churches; concerning the organization of parishes and hospices; concerning monasteries of men or women which ought to be arranged according to the rule of Saint Benedict or according to canonical authority: whatever in the aforesaid orders is out of order, whether through the negligence of superiors or through the sloth of subordinates, I greatly desire to know, and, according to God’s will and your holy counsel, I desire to correct it in such a way that, in God’s sight, neither I may be rejected nor you and the people entrusted to me incur the anger of his indignation. How this may reasonably be investigated and accomplished, we entrust to you for discussion and for reporting back to us. Concerning lesser matters as well, which affect everyone generally or particular persons specifically and require correction, we wish you henceforth [Note: *posthac* (“henceforth”) in witness 4] to investigate them and bring them to our attention [Col. 0610C], such as the conduct of counts and their officials: whether they neglect justice or sell it; whether they are rapacious or oppressors of churches, widows, orphans, or the poor; whether they attend preaching; whether they show due honor and obedience to their priests; whether they presume to undertake innovations or schemes that harm the people, such as acquiring properties or imposing unreasonable demands for assistance, or in other matters that may pertain to our sin and that of our people.”

## Response to the Inquiry or Exhortation of the Bishops to the Lord Emperor Louis

1. To the most glorious lord King Louis, may peace and life, salvation and victory, be bestowed by God the Father [Note: *pater* (“Father”) is absent from manuscript 1] and our Lord Jesus Christ.

We, in God’s name, Archbishop Angilbert and Patriarch Andrew, together with Joseph, archchaplain, when we came to this holy synod assembled in the royal city of Pavia, repeated to them your pious exhortation, which you delivered to us orally, aflame with the gift of the Holy Spirit and seasoned with such a flavor of moderation, gravity, and wisdom that the immaturity of this age seemed scarcely able to contain it. We also produced and caused to be read before them the memorandum handed over to us by your magnificence. When they had heard these things, all unanimously gave very lengthy thanks to almighty God for your character, because he had given his people so pious and so wise a prince [Note: “so holy” in witnesses 2 and 4], one who desires to arrange all things orderly and reasonably [Note: “and reasonably” is absent from manuscripts 1 and 2].

2. Since your religious concern first wished to inquire about the conduct of bishops, priests, and the other clergy, we too have maintained the same order, since no other course could be better [Note: witness 2 reads “because it could not be done otherwise in a kingly manner”; witness 4, “because it could not be done otherwise according to rule”]. We declare that a bishop ought to conduct himself so that his life may be a model of right living for everyone [Col. 0611B] [Note: this phrase is absent from witness 4]. Priests and clerics, however, ought to live in such a way that, by the example of their conduct, they may benefit the people subject to them.

But certain of our fellow bishops, who are conscious of good conduct, refused to admit it openly, lest they seem to praise themselves; while those who recognize their own negligence were afraid, in keeping with human nature, to accuse themselves. Nevertheless, examining matters more carefully in accordance with your admonition, we found some who are as you desire and as pastors and rulers of God’s people ought to be. In others, however, we found negligence either concerning the care and instruction of their clergy [Note: *suorumque* (“and of their own”) in manuscript 1] or concerning their concern for the parishes [Note: “care and instruction” are absent from witness 4]. We humbly ask that you grant them some time for correction. If they do not quickly correct their offenses, they shall be subject to a harsher judgment. Furthermore, if any layperson or cleric has a complaint against a bishop or against a cleric of any order, let him know that we are ready [Note: absent from witnesses 2 and 4] to provide a lawful hearing and to punish with due correction those who are proved to have acted wrongly [Note: “to be punished” in manuscripts 1 and 2].

3. Teaching and preaching among the people are not being carried out as necessary, partly through the negligence of the bishops and the other priests, and partly through the negligence of the people. The carelessness of the priests is in no way excusable. Certain laymen, however, especially the powerful and noble, whom it would have been especially proper to attend preaching, have basilicas near their homes; accustomed to hearing the divine office there, they come less frequently to the larger churches [Col. 0611D]. And when only the afflicted and the poor come, what else is there to preach to them except that they should endure their misfortunes patiently? If the rich, who are accustomed to wronging the poor, did not refuse to come, they ought certainly to be admonished [Note: in manuscripts 2 and 4, the clause “they ought certainly to be admonished” is absent; its place in manuscript 4 reads “they could certainly be admonished”] that they restrain themselves from plundering, that, while they can, they redeem their sins through almsgiving, and that they abstain from the overflow of temporal goods [Note: *ut quia* (“so that, because”) in manuscript 1; *quod* (“that”) is the corrected reading].

The powerful must therefore be admonished to assemble more frequently at the larger churches, where they can hear preaching [Note: absent from witnesses 2 and 4]. And in proportion as they surpass others in wealth and honors through the gift of almighty God, so much more eagerly should they hasten to hear the commandments of their Creator [Note: *audienda* (“to be heard”) in manuscript 1].

Certain counts and royal vassals [Note: *domici* in manuscript 2; *domestici* in witness 4] receive our priests and other clerics without our permission, although they are not even permitted to do this to bishops. Moreover, wherever they have been ordained, they make some celebrate Masses for them in our parishes without our examination—even some about whom it is uncertain whether they have been consecrated [Note: *sunt* (“are”) in witness 4]. This must be prohibited in every respect [Note: “for them” is absent from witnesses 2 and 4].

4. Therefore, the institutions of the sacred canons must be observed in the appointment of parishes [Note: witness 4 reads “the arrangements of the parishes and the citizens”], and the destructive vice of ambition must be uprooted from the roots [Note: manuscript 2 has the corrupt reading “rooted out, destroyed”]. No one unworthy may be ordained because of the relationship of certain persons, or out of favor toward someone’s friendship, or—what is most detestable—because of the acceptance of money [Note: this phrase is absent from witnesses 2 and 4].

First, the priests or other clerics of the place itself should choose a suitable rector for themselves; then the assent of the people who belong to that parish should follow. If no one can be found within that parish who is able to carry out the work competently, then the bishop shall appoint there one of his own whom he judges suitable.

The insolence of certain laymen must certainly be removed [Note: *procastitas* in manuscript 1]. On the sole pretext that they are admitted to participate in the election, they presume to dominate their archpriests and despise as subjects those whom they ought to venerate as fathers [Note: *debuerint* (“they ought to have”) in manuscript 2; *debuerunt* (“they ought to have”) in witness 4]. These men must therefore be confined within the limits of their own rights. If they presume to exercise extraordinary domination in churches, they must be restrained by royal discipline.

5. Those who have been lawfully advanced to govern parishes must not be expelled by their bishops unless they have incurred guilt for some crime or have badly treated those same parishes.

The wicked custom that has begun to arise in certain places must be entirely abolished. Some archpriests [Note: manuscript 1 reads “archbishops”], or custodians of other titles, carry grain [Note: *frues* in manuscript 2] or other church revenues away to their private homes [Col. 0612D]. Others rent the possessions of other people in order to store in them what they have wrongfully taken from their churches [Note: *subtraxerunt* (“have taken away”) in witnesses 2 and 4]. Some laymen make themselves accomplices in their wickedness to such an extent that they hide in their own homes what such transgressors have stolen from the church [Note: *subripuerunt* (“have stolen”) in witness 4].

Such men must first be rebuked by their bishops. If they do not quickly correct themselves, they must be struck by synodal judgment as men who have handled ecclesiastical property with sacrilegious recklessness. Laymen [Note: *laicos* (“laymen,” accusative) in witness 4] who, after this proclamation, offer themselves as partners in this spoliation shall be constrained by judicial authority as guilty of theft [Note: *coartabat* (“was constraining”) in manuscript 2].

6. Concerning the restoration of churches, the capitulum established by your glorious father [Note: “our father” in manuscript 1], at Olonna [Note: the word is missing from witness 4], is sufficient; but it requires your admonition in order to be observed [Note: “preserved” in witnesses 2 and 4].

7. Likewise, concerning hospices, what is contained in the same capitulary must be observed.

8. Concerning monasteries of men or women which ought to be arranged according to the rule of Saint Benedict or according to canonical authority [Col. 0613B]: since, as we believe, the inspiration of almighty God has stirred your governing heart to this inquiry [Note: this phrase is absent from witnesses 2 and 4], we ourselves give him thanks. For it is manifest to everyone that they have already lost their order for the most part [Note: “especially” in manuscript 2; “have lost” in manuscript 1]. Their restoration to their former condition depends upon the glorious disposition of your lord and father, and of yourself.

9. It is the duty of each bishop in whose parish monasteries are situated to take care that those monasteries which still retain their condition maintain their order [Note: *sint* (“may be”) in manuscript 2]. If he finds otherwise, he must correct the matter together with the monastery’s rector [Note: *quod* (“which”) in witness 4]. But if the rector of the monastery is principally at fault and neglects to correct himself and his subordinates at the admonition of his bishop [Col. 0613C] [Note: the phrase “and neglects to correct himself and his subordinates” is absent from manuscript 1], he must be struck by synodal authority.

10. Certain bishops and rectors of monasteries complain that the property of their churches has been taken away and granted to other persons as benefices [Note: “as a benefice” is absent from witness 4], and therefore say that they are entirely unable to fulfill ecclesiastical obligations. We appeal to your royal majesty for its restoration, humbly admonishing you [Note: this phrase is absent from witness 4] that, if those who have bestowed these things upon churches for the remedy of their souls deserve a reward, without doubt those who attempt to take them away deserve condemnation.

11. The sacred canons prescribe that tithes be distributed according to the bishop’s disposition. Certain laymen, however, who have basilicas either on their own property or on benefices, disregarding the bishop’s disposition, do not give their tithes to the churches where they receive baptism, preaching, the laying on of hands, and the other sacraments of Christ [Note: “the laying on of hands” is absent from manuscript 2]. Instead, they give them either to their own basilicas or to their own clerics according to their pleasure [Col. 0614A]. This is plainly contrary in every respect to divine law and the sacred canons. We therefore request your authority to correct them.

12. Sacred authority teaches that those who sin publicly should be subjected to public penance. Some are found who have contracted incestuous marriages and have been joined either to their close relatives or to women consecrated to God [Note: “sacred women” in manuscript 2]. Some have also publicly committed homicide or other crimes. We ask that, so that the bishops may be able to subject them to public penance [Note: the words “publicly—to public” are absent from witnesses 2 and 4], the bishops be supported by the assistance of your counts [Note: *axilio* in manuscript 2].

13. We have learned that certain officials of the counts afflict the poorer population excessively because of the frequent assemblies. We therefore beseech your majesty to command that your grandfather’s capitulary concerning this matter be observed [Note: “be caused to be observed” in witness 4].

[Col. 0614B] 14. Concerning the counts, about whose life and actions your sublimity wished to inquire of us: we know that some are such as God’s ministers and administrators of your commonwealth ought to be [Note: *debet* (“ought to be”) in witnesses 2 and 3]. Others need your admonition in order to correct themselves and their officials. Nevertheless, we ask that you grant them, just as to the bishops [Note: this phrase is absent from witnesses 2 and 4; “just as to the bishops” is absent from manuscripts 1 and 4], some time for correction. If they do not quickly correct themselves, they must be restrained by royal authority.

15. We also decree that, when bishops travel around the parishes to confirm the people [Note: “the people” in witnesses 2 and 4], they should not burden their archpriests, but be content with provisions of this kind: one hundred loaves, four *friskingae* [Note: *frischingae* in manuscript 1], fifty sextarii of wine [Note: “of wine” in witness 4], ten chickens [Note: seven in witness 4], fifty eggs, one lamb, one piglet, six modii of grain for the horses, three cartloads of hay, and as much honey, oil, and wax as is sufficient.

16. [Note: Manuscript 2 joins everything that follows to the preceding capitulum.] We also ask that you command the immunities of your forebears to be preserved [Note: “be caused to be preserved” in witness 4], as your glorious father established them at Olonna [Note: the place is missing in witness 4].

17. In each parish, let the people strive to observe those feast days which their own bishop has proclaimed worthy of veneration, so that they neither neglect those which the priests have instructed them to honor nor presume, through empty superstition, to celebrate those which ought in no way to be observed [Note: this clause is absent from manuscript 1]. If any are found unwilling to obey the priests, let them be compelled by the officials of the commonwealth to submit to the satisfaction of penance which the priests have imposed.

## LAWS PROMULGATED BY THE EMPEROR

[Note: From manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.]

In the name of almighty God, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 855, indiction 3 [Note: indiction 13 in manuscripts 2 and 4], in the month of February, on the fourth day of that month [Note: “the fourth” in manuscript 3].

When the lord and most magnificent Louis Augustus was sitting at Pavia in the imperial hall, intending to deliberate concerning the condition of holy mother Church, the peace of the empire entrusted to him by divine disposition [Note: “the divine disposition” in manuscript 2], and the general salvation of the entire people, he said in the presence of his nobles:

1. We have frequently admonished your faithfulness in times past, so that each of our faithful might strive to live according to the standard of the Christian religion and restrain his men from plunder. Yet because this has thus far been done less diligently [Note: “negligently” in witness 4; absent from manuscript 2], we now wish you all to strive with every effort so that plunder may be entirely eliminated from our kingdom, and so that the voices of the poor—until now striking the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth with their complaints—may begin to render praise to their Creator for the peace and quiet granted to us everywhere by the nations.

2. We decree that the churches of God founded throughout the boundaries of our entire kingdom remain secure, with their property and dependents, under the protection of our immunity, just as they are proved to have existed in the times of our predecessors, namely, the most pious emperors [Note: *prodecessorum* in the manuscript]. Their rectors shall use their own privileges [Note: *privilegibus* in manuscript 2]. And the monks shall maintain the regular order in their monasteries. Likewise, let the entire clergy perform its proper ministry, with no one troubling it through fear of our authority.

3. Nevertheless, we decree that each count and public official [Note: “and tax collector” in witnesses 2 and 4] shall ensure that justice is administered to the people lawfully in his sphere of office, shall protect orphans and widows, and shall restore the palaces at the customary places, so that when travel requires it they may receive us and our envoys, and the Church may not be burdened [Note: “so that the churches may not be burdened” in manuscript 3]. When a bishop, abbot, count, or any of our faithful happens to stay in his own estate, let him remain with his people in their own houses, so that under pretext of hospitality [Note: *bospitum* in manuscript 2] they do not oppress their neighbors or seize their property [Note: “their things” in manuscript 3].

4. Finally, since, under Christ’s merciful protection, we have deprived no one unjustly [Note: manuscript 3 reads “justly, having obtained it”], and we do not wish any of our faithful to be deprived of his benefice without legal sanction [Note: “we have not wished” in witness 4], we command that no one corrupt his own [Note: *ull[o]* (“any”) in manuscript 3] in any way, but restore it securely [Col. 0615D], lest those whom we send everywhere to administer justice, if they find it corrupted, compel them to correct it legally and thereafter prohibit them from enjoying it.

5. Moreover, whenever any of our faithful hastens to perform service for us, let him travel peacefully both on his way there and on his return [Note: manuscript 3 reads “both going and returning, let him travel peacefully”]. Unless general necessity demands that he come with *scarites* [Note: manuscript 3 reads *p. ut terrae g. exigit* (abbreviated; sense uncertain)], let him stay in the designated houses [Note: “in the houses designated by the lord” in manuscript 3] [Note: a word is missing in the manuscripts; witness 4 has a blank space].

The bishop and count through whose territory he passes must take careful measures that the inhabitants are not troubled, that he is not forced to invade their houses, or seize their property without an agreed price [Note: a passage is absent, with a blank space in witness 4]. Nor should the natives dare to deny guests, in the customary places, shelter, fire, water, and straw, or dare to sell their goods to them more dearly than to their neighbors [Note: manuscript 2 and witness 4 read “their good” in the singular].

6. Since it is beyond doubt that some in our kingdom have hitherto lived without restraint [Note: *qui* (“who”) in witnesses 2 and 4], we decree that each person take care concerning his own men, lest they presume to commit their customary plunder [Note: “perpetrate” in manuscript 3]. Therefore, if anyone, when pressed, abandons his lord [Col. 0616B], we absolutely forbid that he be received by another, so that, unless he wishes to be corrected, he may be entirely excluded from the borders of our kingdom.

7. These provisions, often inculcated in former times and promulgated by our imperial sanction, appear to have been neglected in part and in certain places; they therefore ought by now to have been punished by a harsher investigation. Nevertheless, out of our gentleness, so that they may be corrected, we grant a little time in which each may be able to amend what has been neglected [Note: manuscript 2 reads “be corrected”; manuscript 3 reads “may amend”]. After a short while we shall send energetic envoys to investigate what has been corrected [Note: manuscript 3 reads “afterward”]. Whoever is found negligent shall be deprived of his offices by our judgment.

## CAPITULA OF THE ENVOYS

### The Embassy

[Col. 0616C] 1. Let the justice of God’s churches be investigated and carried out with every effort; and, lest their treasure be plundered by sacrilegious persons, let it be faithfully recorded.

2. Let the cases of orphans and widows be investigated and examined mercifully with diligent care.

3. Let the complaint of the entire people be heard generally and decided lawfully.

4. The condition of the commonwealth must be investigated: when the lord emperor’s journey requires it, where the envoys sent by him in each sphere of administration ought to be received [Note: “where, in each sphere of administration, the services owed to him ought to be supplied” in manuscript 3]. From where are provisions to be supplied to them, and from where the *paraveredi* [Note: *paraveredae* in manuscript 3]? What annual gifts or public tributes are to be demanded, and from whom? Who ought to restore the palaces, and who the bridges? So that benefices are not destroyed and those destroyed are restored [Note: “recovered” in manuscript 2]. What benefice did the king’s *gasindus* [Note: *gisindus* in manuscript 2] possess [Col. 0616D]? Who possesses it now, or where does it lie?

5. The abbots who have been sent should visit the monasteries of monks and women and the hospices, and investigate whether they have the proper services from which they are administered [Note: “from which they may be administered” in manuscript 3] and whether they live in concord. Whatever they find disordered, let them correct according to rule [Col. 0617A]. Let them restore neglected hospices to their former condition; and let the hospitals for the poor, both in the mountains and wherever they are known to have existed, be completely and diligently restored [Note: “diligently” misspelled in manuscript 2].

## Likewise, an Ordinance of the Lord Emperor Louis

1. We wish each person to strive to administer justice in accordance with the circumstances of the time and the requirements of his office, and not merely admonish his subordinates but also compel them to do so. We establish and emphatically admonish that, in ecclesiastical offices, everyone strive to preserve what the holy Fathers determined at our assembly in the past [Col. 0617C] [Note: compare the Constitutions of the year 850], and promptly correct what was neglected in the past. The restoration of baptismal churches must be completed according to ancient custom [Note: “let him correct what was neglected and what is to be restored,” in the manuscript; corrected here].

2. Concerning tithes: whoever neglects what was determined at the assembly mentioned above [Note: compare the Constitutions of the year 850, chapter 17] must be corrected by canonical judgment. Whoever resists in any respect in this matter should know that he must be corrected by our imperial authority. Judges must be admonished to keep the fear of God before their eyes and not dare to alter justice for any person; rather, they must investigate what is true with the utmost justice and judge truthfully.

3. Bridges, wherever they customarily exist—especially those at Pavia—must be restored; and wherever bridges that do not customarily exist are necessary, they must be built. Boats prepared at the customary places must remain there; and they must be admonished not to burden those crossing.

[Col. 0617]

## HLUDOWICI II IMPERATORIS CONVENTUS TICINENSIS III  
*(The Third Assembly of the Emperor Louis II at Pavia, A.D. 855, July)*
