[Note: The capitula promulgated by the emperor at the people’s request, first published by Canisius at the cited place, page 685, from the Saint Gall manuscript, and then revised by Baluze with the aid of Royal Paris manuscript no. 4613, are presented here after that same manuscript has again been examined.]

The statutes placed into law are published, revised and enlarged with the aid of the Blankenburg manuscript and the royal Paris manuscript no. 4613, whereas previously only three of its chapters had been published by Baluzius, vol. II, pp. 349–350. I collated also the Florentine Fragment edited by Dato, and the Vienna, Verona, and Este manuscripts of the Lombard laws printed by Muratori among the laws of Lothar, chapters 65–67.

The chapters delivered to the royal envoys, found in a single Blankenburg manuscript, are here printed for the first time.]

[Col. 0617B] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. In the year [lacking in Canisius] of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ [Canisius: “in the years”], 854 [“CLIIII,” or Parisian], in the sixth year of our empire [Canisius: “in the sixth year of the empire of our lord Louis, august emperor”], in the fourth indiction. When we were summoning an assembly of our faithful at our palace in the city of Pavia [Parisian: “at the assembly”; Canisius: “when they were summoned”], and when, with the consultation of the bishops [C.: “of them”] and our nobles [N. C.: “our nobles”], we were striving to investigate not only the welfare of the Church and the peace or salvation of the people [“peace or salvation” is absent in C.], but also the condition of the entire kingdom, our people presented us with certain petitions, which we willingly accepted, moved by love of God and their fidelity. Therefore we caused the chapters written below to be set down for their benefit [C.: “to be subscribed”], and we confirm them for observance as law in the future [C.: “for the future”].

1. Concerning women whom the law of the Lombards prohibits, after their husbands’ death, from changing their clothing to religious dress or taking the veil before the lapse of a year [P.: “before a year”; C.: “the veil”], they asked that, with our permission, as soon as divine mercy should inspire them [P.: “had inspired them”], they might be permitted to take it without penalty. But we have considered that in the past, because of this delay [P.: “the past”; C.: “I suppose”], many women were also abducted and transferred to another party within that same period [P.: “during the same period”]. Therefore we accepted their petition, which we judged to be just [P.: “just”], and grant that it be done for them [P.: “that it be done”].

2. They complained to our majesty [P.: “to our majesty”; Baluzius inserted *tempore*, “at the time,” without manuscript authority] that excessive investigations had been made concerning them by our father or by us [C.: “by our fathers”; P.: “by our father or by us”]. Therefore we grant them that from now on no further investigations shall be made concerning them, except those that were made in the time of our great-grandfather and grandfather Charles [P. partly lacks “our great-grandfather”; P.: “grandfather”].

3. [This chapter is attributed in manuscripts V., Vn., and E., and in the printed editions, to the emperor Lothar; see Muratori, chapter 82.] Concerning free men who reside upon another person’s property [V., Vn., E.: “land”] and who until now have been unlawfully dragged by royal officials [C.: “administrators”; P.: “officials”] to assemblies, and for that reason have been distrained, we establish that their patrons shall bring them to the assembly according to law [C.: “it has been established”]. If anyone should presume to distrain or compel them contrary to this authority of ours and to their law [V., Vn.: “to distinguish”], he shall make amends to their patron for everything according to the law [C.: “shall make compensation”; P.: “shall compensate”]. Vn. adds in the margin: “that is, ninefold if he is a Lombard, fourfold if he is a Roman, or according to his law.” In addition, for this reckless presumption [C. and V., Vn., E. omit part of the phrase], he shall pay our ban [C.: “shall pay”; P.: “shall pay”].

4. [This chapter is counted among Lothar’s laws by Ambr., Fl., L., V., Vn., and E., in Muratori, chapter 89.] Concerning homicide, for which the law, because of the straightforwardness of the proof, requires three witnesses [P.: “proof”]: if someone cannot have witnesses, we grant that he may swear with twelve oath-helpers and, being acquitted from that straightforward proof [P.: “simplicity”; V., Vn.: “being acquitted from the simplicity”], shall not lose his property [C.: “shall not admit”; P.: “shall not lose”].

5. [This chapter is absent from the Paris manuscript.] Concerning documents which certain persons call false, we establish that, if the notary and witnesses survive, they shall establish it as genuine and valid; but if the witnesses have died and the notary survives, he shall establish it as genuine and valid with twelve oath-helpers.

Finally, after considering your petitions, we also considered matters that had reached us some time ago [C.: “already”; P.: “the day before,” or “previously], in order to add to these chapters measures for cutting off the plots of wicked men [C.: “to open up”; the final word is Canisius’s; P. explains it as “that is”].

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Louis, by the grace of God august emperor. When, by divine providence, we had held an assembly with our faithful in the royal city of Pavia, it came to our attention that, when certain men endeavor to seek justice for themselves within the kingdom, they are obstructed by the plots of wicked men. These men seek to compel either the claimants themselves or those whom they wish to produce as witnesses into service, whether personally or through others sent for that purpose, so that under such a pretext the claimants cannot obtain their justice. Therefore, in order to cut off such wickedness, we have deemed it appropriate to establish two chapters as law for the people dwelling within our Italian kingdom. In the thirty-sixth year of the empire of our lord and father, the pious emperor Lothar, and also in our sixth year, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, under the third indiction.

Likewise, statutes of lord Louis placed into law.

1. If anyone brings a claim against another person concerning some matter, and the person against whom the claim has been brought says that he does not wish to answer him because he is another man’s slave [Parisian: “was unwilling”; Florentine Fragment, Ambr., Fl., V., Vn., E.: “I do not wish”; P.: “is another’s”], or if he produces witnesses and likewise says that they ought not to be accepted [P.: “him”; P.: “ought not to be accepted”], because one of them is someone else’s slave [Florentine Fragment and the Lombard-law manuscripts: “is another’s slave”], let him name his master and give security concerning him, promising to bring him to the assembly [Florentine Fragment and the Lombard-law manuscripts: “to the assembly”]. Once the judges have allowed as much time as they say he can use to go to the place where he believes he can find him and return [Blankenburg: “return”], if, at the appointed assembly, he has not brought the master, let him offer an oath that he said this for no purpose of delaying his justice [Blankenburg: “justice”], unless he truly believed it to be so [P.: “believed it”].

But if he has not dared to swear [V., Vn., E.: “has been unwilling to swear”] because he said this as a pretext for prolonging justice [P. has a corrupt reading: “let him pay compensation because he blocked justice”; the Florentine and Lombard witnesses read: “because he said this in order to prolong justice”], let him pay him our ban and render full justice.

If, however, he brings someone who calls himself his master, and the man whom he accused of being in servitude refuses to answer the claim concerning his servitude [P.: “to return him to service”], then the one who called himself his master shall pay him our ban, because he dared to devise such a scheme for trampling upon justice [P. has a corruptly expanded reading: “because he did this to trample upon justice, in fasting, etc.”; the sentence concerning the imposition of charges is absent in Blankenburg].

If, however, he wishes to bring charges against him for delaying justice [P.: “justice”], he must prove them. If he cannot prove them, he must both render justice and, in addition, be compelled to pay our ban for so great a deception [P.: “cunning”; another P. reading: “calculation”].

[Col. 0620B] 2. If someone should bring a claim against another person, and the person against whom the claim has been brought says that he is his slave [P.: “a slave”], or if another person, entering the same dispute, claims him as a slave [P.: “someone else”], we order [the Florentine and Fragmentary witnesses: “we wish”] that they immediately give security to one another, so that they settle the matter at the first, second, or third assembly [the witnesses vary between “first or second or third,” “first and second or third,” and “settle” or “deliberate”].

There shall be fifteen days between one assembly and the next. For the third assembly, when the count holds the assembly, if the matter is within a single county, there shall likewise be fifteen days; but if it is in another county, there shall be twenty days [some witnesses omit the number], so that his justice is not prolonged on such a pretext. If, at these three assemblies, the claimant has neglected to come—except on the king’s service or because of unavoidable necessity—and the count has held the assembly, while the other party is ready to prove his freedom, then the count shall conclude the case as though the claimant himself had been present. Thereafter the claimant shall have no opportunity to speak concerning the other man’s servitude [the Fragmentary and Florentine witnesses omit this phrase], and, in addition, as stated above, he shall pay him our ban and render full justice.

3. There are some who, when they claim others into servitude and those others give security to prove their own freedom, so disrupt the proceedings by repeatedly changing the hearing-date that the others can scarcely escape because of their poverty [P. has a corrupt reading]. Therefore it seemed right to add a third chapter.

If someone claims another as a slave, and the person against whom the claim has been brought gives security that he will prove his freedom, we order, as above, that they settle the matter at the first, second, or third assembly [V., Vn., E.: “at the first or second or third assembly”]. There shall be fifteen days between one assembly and the next; for the third, when the count holds the assembly, if the matter is within one county, there shall be fifteen days [Blankenburg and P. omit this repetition]; but if it is in another county, there shall be twenty days [Blankenburg reads fifteen].

If, at these three assemblies, the claimant himself has refused to come, subject to the exceptions stated above [P.: “with the exception previously stated”; V., Vn., E. omit the exception], and the count has held the assembly while the other party is ready with his witnesses, then the count shall receive those witnesses and decide the case [P.: “let them receive them and let them decide the case”], as though the claimant himself had been present. Thereafter the claimant shall remain silent concerning the other man’s servitude [Blankenburg reads “shall have sought”; P. reads “had sought”; P. also has “silently”].

4. [This chapter is preserved in the Blankenburg manuscript.] We have determined concerning the Jews that no one shall remain within the Italian kingdom beyond the Kalends of October. They shall now be notified that all of them must leave by that date and go wherever they wish, without anyone’s opposition. If, after the Kalends of October, anyone is found, he may be apprehended by anyone and shall be brought, together with all his property [the manuscript lacks this word; either this or a similar word must be supplied], into our presence.

[Col. 0621]

CONSTITUTIONS OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS II. (A.D. 856, in March; perhaps at Mantua.) [These chapters are written in the Blankenburg and Paris manuscripts immediately after the constitutions of A.D. 855. Since they do not belong to that assembly, as is clear from the heading of the Paris manuscript and from the second chapter delivered to the royal envoys, I do not know to which assembly they should be assigned, unless perhaps to the first assembly held by Louis at Mantua, truly in the year 856 after Lothar’s death, as may be conjectured from a charter granted to the Venetians.]

At another time the aforesaid most serene Augustus deemed it appropriate to establish the following chapters [C.: “the edict”].

[Col. 0621B]

1. If any bishop, abbot, or count resides at his own seat, or in his houses or estate, and his men commit plundering, devastate crops or meadows during the period of protection, and, once this has become known, he does not make compensation without unjust delay [C.: “and”], nor impose suitable punishment on the perpetrator, he shall be compelled to make compensation for the wrong itself according to law, and in addition shall abstain from wine and meat for forty days and nights.

2. If, on the road while coming to or returning from the palace, his men commit robbery against anyone, and, once he knows of it, he does not immediately make compensation or impose suitable punishment on the perpetrator, he shall be compelled to make compensation according to law for everything that was taken, and in addition shall abstain from meat and wine for thirty days.

3. The rest has been lost.

Chapters delivered to the royal envoys [The Blankenburg manuscript: “Other chapters”; these chapters therefore appear here in print for the first time.]

1. They shall inquire concerning each monastery or hospice, how they were established by their founders, how they now continue, and by which persons they are held.

2. An inquiry shall be made concerning the mints: how they are guarded, by what fraud they are debased, and by which persons this has been perpetrated. They shall urgently order newly established coins to be struck [the manuscript: “they shall be struck urgently”]. Nevertheless, until the feast of Saint John, a silver denarius, unbroken, of whatever mint, shall be accepted. Punishment shall be inflicted upon those who reject it, according to the capitulary: either they shall pay sixty solidi or receive the same number of blows. Counterfeiters of coin, if discovered, shall be brought into our presence.

3. Our royal envoys shall inquire in each city about the ancient measure, and no one shall presume either to buy or to sell except according to that measure.

4. Our envoys shall inquire most diligently concerning usuries, which are practiced by many devices. When those who practice them have been found, they shall be handed over to their own bishops, so that they may be subjected to public penance.

5. [This chapter is found among Lothar’s laws in the manuscripts Ambr., Flor., Lond., Vind., Veron., and Est., and in Muratori, chapter 14.] An inquiry shall be made concerning the judges: whether they have been appointed as noble, wise, and God-fearing men. [In the Verona manuscript there is this gloss, inserted by a twelfth-century hand: “Nobles are those whose ancestors and parents have not been subjected to servitude.”] They shall swear that they will judge rightly according to their understanding, and that they will neither pervert nor delay justice for gifts or human favor; and they shall not shrink from confirming by their subscription what they have judged. Where such men are not present [the phrase is absent in the Blankenburg manuscript], our envoys shall appoint them and compel them to make the same oath. If inferior and less suitable persons have been appointed for this, they shall be rejected.

Likewise, notaries learned in the laws and of good reputation shall be appointed, and they shall give an oath that they will in no way write falsehood or collusion. Those who are found to have done this in the past shall be condemned immediately [Ambr.: “at once”].

6. Our envoys shall inquire most diligently throughout the individual counties who have not yet promised us the oath of fidelity, and shall compel them to promise it. They shall also inquire most diligently concerning estates and courts from which the king’s expenses are customarily supplied, by which persons they are now held, and also which estates ought to serve during the emperor’s passage or supply necessities to passing royal envoys.

7. Our envoys shall inquire in each city where palaces or public houses formerly stood [C., corrected: “had stood”], from what resources they were maintained, and on what occasion, by which persons, or under whose rule they were destroyed. By our authority they shall order that they be restored as quickly as possible. They shall also investigate each category of property belonging to our chamber, to the fisc, or to the various palaces.

8. Our envoys shall investigate in each city the benefices that clerics and vassals of our predecessors held in ancient times [the manuscript corrects “may have held” to “held”], and who now retains them, and shall report to us. Likewise, they shall investigate county property held by persons who do not possess counties, as well as property belonging to the churches of God that is held by persons other than their rectors, and shall report to us.

[Col. 0623B] 9. Baptismal churches which, through the negligence of those responsible for restoring them, have gradually fallen from their former condition shall, through the diligence of our envoys, be ordered to be restored by those who are baptized there or receive the sacred mysteries there. They shall be entrusted to the royal officials, so that the sons of the Church may be compelled by their diligence to restore them; and they shall likewise be compelled to give tithes to God there.

[Col. 0624A] 10. The same envoys shall investigate in each city how the life and conduct of the canons have been ordered, and concerning the church treasury, what has been lost from it [C.: “who”], by whom, or under whose authority; also whether the bishops keep their dioceses properly ordered, and whether anything has been distributed contrary to restoration, so that it may be corrected. If necessary, they shall report to us.

11. Concerning the plunderings committed in recent times by various men against the ecclesiastical property of deceased bishops, those who committed them shall make legal compensation with our immunity.

12. Concerning the offenses [the manuscript reads *caelestibus*, “heavenly”] and crimes that have increased in many ways, we wish them to investigate and correct them. Likewise, they shall correct harmful conspiracies according to the capitulary. Likewise, they shall investigate robberies, false witnesses, and perjurers [C.: “perjuries”], as well as monks who have abandoned their proper habit and those who, from among clerics or monks, have become secular or laymen.

13. They shall investigate roads, bridges, and other public watch-duties; they shall repair whatever they can, or report to us what they find [the manuscript: “The chapters written above in numbered order are complete”].

[Col. 0623]

ECCLESIASTICAL CHAPTERS OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS II. (A.D. 856) [They are found in the Blankenburg manuscript after the preceding chapters and appear to have been issued by an Italian synod.]

[Col. 0623C] 1. First, the faith of all priests must be examined: how they believe and teach others to believe. Examples should be proposed by which the Creator may, insofar as possible, be understood from a creature.

2. Second, it must be commanded that the Lord’s Prayer, in which all necessities of human life are contained, and the Apostles’ Creed, in which the Catholic faith is contained in its entirety, be learned by everyone, both in Latin and in the vernacular [that is, in German], so that what one professes with the mouth may be believed and understood in the heart.

3. Third, it must be made known that appropriate responses to the priests’ greetings are to be learned. Not only clerics and those dedicated to God should offer a response, but the whole devout people ought to respond with a united voice.

[Col. 0623D] 4. Fourth, priests are to learn the faith of Saint Athanasius and recite it from the heart every Sunday at the first hour.

5. Fifth, they are to know what the sacrament of baptism and confirmation are, and what the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood is; how a visible creature is seen in these same mysteries, while invisible salvation for the eternity of the soul is nevertheless supplied—something contained in faith alone.

6. Sixth, they must possess what is necessary for priests to say, namely: a sacramentary [the manuscript: “of the sacraments”], a lectionary, [Col. 0624C] an antiphonary, a baptismal book, a computus, a penitential canon, a psalter, and homilies appropriate to Sundays and to each feast throughout the year. If one of all these is lacking, the name of priest will scarcely remain valid in him. For the evangelical threats are exceedingly dangerous, in which it is said: “If the blind gives guidance to the blind, both fall into a pit.”

7. Seventh, they are to know the lawful times for baptizing during the year: namely, Holy Saturday of Easter, so that the three-day immersion in baptism may imitate the Lord’s three-day death, glorified by the resurrection. For this reason the sacred rebirth is celebrated by all Christian people until the eighth day. The other time for baptism is Holy Saturday of Pentecost. If necessity should arise, help must be given in danger at any time, because necessity scarcely has a law. They shall also have a vessel for the baptismal font, which must in no way be used for other purposes [the manuscript: “from”].

8. Eighth, it must be proclaimed that they are to know the times of abstaining from work throughout the year: namely, every Sunday from morning until evening, in honor of the Lord’s resurrection. Saturday, however, is to be spent working from morning until evening, lest they be caught up in Judaism.

The days of abstaining from work throughout the year are the following, as we began above: the Nativity of the Lord; Saint Stephen’s Day; Saint John the Evangelist’s Day; the Feast of the Innocents; the octave of the Lord’s Nativity; the Epiphany; the Purification of Saint Mary; and Holy Easter, as included in the preceding chapter. Also the three days of Rogations; the Ascension of the Lord; Holy Saturday of Pentecost; Saint John the Baptist’s Day; the feast of the twelve apostles, especially Saints Peter and Paul, who illuminated Europe by their preaching; the Assumption of Saint Mary; the dedication of Saint Michael the Archangel; and the dedication of any oratory or of any saint in whose honor that church has been founded. The last-mentioned feast is to be announced only to those living nearby, not generally to everyone.

But an announced fast, when proclaimed by the palace or by a royal household, is to be observed generally by all. The remaining feasts throughout the year, such as those of Saint Remedius, Saint Maurice, and Saint Martin, are not to be observed as days of abstinence from work. Nevertheless, they are not to be prohibited if the people wish to celebrate them chastely and out of zeal for God.

9. Ninth, the same priests must be commanded not to allow unrelated women to live with them, in accordance with the Council of Nicaea, except those concerning whom no suspicion of ill repute can arise.

10. Tenth, they are not to enter taverns, whether residing at home or traveling. If they need to buy something there, they shall send their agents, bring what is offered into another house, and receive it faithfully with thanksgiving.

11. Eleventh, they are not to attend secular assemblies, act as sureties, keep hunting dogs, goshawks, falcons, or sparrowhawks, or have permission for any game or spectacle. It is enough for them that it is said in the first psalm: “Their will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law they meditate day and night”; and that the Apostle commands: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has committed himself.”

12. Twelfth, they are to know that no one has been ordained for money, nor ought anyone to occupy a church through gifts. If this has happened, both the man ordained and the one who ordained him must be deposed. For it is manifest that those who do such things follow the heresy of Simon, and that such a man is not entering the sheepfold through the gate, in accordance with the words of the Gospel, but is a thief and robber climbing in by another way. Not only those who do this, but also those who consent to those doing it, are to be excommunicated.

13. Thirteenth, no one is to dare to receive a wanderer from another parish, allow him to live with him, or let him celebrate Mass, except through a genuine commission; nor is he to assume the governance of any church or people without our prior knowledge. If he does so, he shall be excommunicated.

14. Fourteenth, they are not to celebrate the mysteries of the Mass in huts, unconsecrated churches, or private houses, except perhaps for the sake of visiting those confined there by illness. If they do so, they are to know that they will be degraded for disobedience.

15. Fifteenth, the tithe given by the faithful is to be called God’s census, and therefore must be rendered in full. According to the canon of Toledo, one-third of it ought to belong to the bishops. We, however, do not wish to use this authority, but wish to have only a fourth part of it, according to the custom of the Roman pontiffs and the observance of the holy Roman Church. If anyone—whether cleric or layman—is found obstinately to press the contrary, he shall be deprived of communion and judged by synodal censure.

16. Sixteenth, everyone is to ensure that women do not approach the altar, nor are women dedicated to God to take part in any ministry of the altar. If altar cloths must be washed, clerics shall remove them, hand them over to women at the chancel rail, and retrieve them there. Likewise, when offerings are presented by the same women, the priests shall receive them there and carry them to the altar.

17. Seventeenth, the priests themselves are to preach by word and example to everyone that no one should accept usury, neither sixfold interest nor kind for kind [the manuscript reads “who”]. For the person who does this is exceedingly faithless and rebellious against God’s command, which is known to be equally forbidden to all Christians, but especially to priests, who ought to be a pattern and example to everyone.

18. Eighteenth, no ordained man or man awaiting ordination is to migrate from his own parish to another, or go to the thresholds of the apostles for the sake of prayer while abandoning the care of his church, or go to the palace to present a petition. Nor is anyone suspended from communion to be received into communion by another without the permission and presence of his own bishop. If he does so, such communion, ordination, or migration shall have no validity.

This must also be announced to all the faithful: those who wish to go to the thresholds of the blessed apostles for the sake of prayer should confess their sins at home and then set out. They are to be bound or released by their own bishop or priest, not by a stranger.

19. Nineteenth, nothing is to be read or sung in the church except what is of divine authority and what the authority of orthodox fathers has sanctioned. They must not venerate false names of angels, but only those taught by prophetic and evangelical Scripture: Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael.

Nor are they to make differing judgments in the case of penitents, wishing to please one by imposing less, another by imposing more, flattering one, and disparaging another. Rather, after considering the quality of the person [the manuscript: “considerately”], the severity of the penalty is to be applied according to the measure of the fault.

20. Twentieth, they are to be admonished to consider that whatever is given by the faithful is the redemption of sins. Therefore they should not glory in using such expenditures, but should rather fear what is said of priests in the Old Testament: that they must bear the iniquity of the people. Accordingly, they must be solicitous with great fear for those whose gifts they share. For it is a great danger to become judge of another’s life when one does not know how to govern one’s own life.

21. Twenty-first, they are to know and understand what the crime of incest is, and each person is to take care in his own parish that it does not occur. If it has occurred, it must be corrected as quickly as possible. That is, no one may take a spouse from among his relatives as far as the fifth degree.

If it has happened unknowingly, it is not to be readily believed, but examined by God’s judgment. They are not to be separated in the fourth degree, but are to persevere in penance throughout all the days of their union.

Likewise, two wives joined to one another in the same manner, or a wife and two husbands joined to one another in the same manner, or a godfather or godmother, a spiritual son or daughter from the font or from religious association, or a woman dedicated to God, or another man’s wife while her husband lives, or another woman’s husband while his wife lives—none of such persons may lawfully be joined in marriage for any reason.

If persons in the first or second degree are found to have committed the crime of fornication, they are to know that they have utterly lost the marital rights of the other party. If, however, persons in the third degree are found to have been polluted by such a crime [C.: “polluted”], suitable penance shall follow them; nevertheless, the rights of marriage are not denied to them—not reciprocally, but with others.

Where slaves belonging not to one but to different masters have been joined, such a union shall not be valid unless both masters agree. Whatever is consented to through negligence and not corrected with whatever strength one can exercise—the person who consents to it through negligence will be the author of that union [C.: “whatever is sensed”].

There are many more matters that could have been written concerning the crime of incest [C.: “incest”], such as cases involving mother, daughter, and stepmother, and almost innumerable cases that do not occur to the mind for writing. Nevertheless, marital union is permanently forbidden to such persons and to those similar to them.

22. Twenty-second, they are to be admonished to know how to announce to the people what the works of mercy are, together with their fruits, as contained in the Gospel and the apostolic writings, by which one reaches life; and what the works of iniquity are, together with their manifold fruits, by which one proceeds along the left-hand road toward eternal destruction.

They are also to avoid the crime of perjury in every way. For it is known that the crime of perjury is committed not only against the Gospel and the other saints, but against the truth itself, which is God, when someone lies.

23. Twenty-third, they are to be admonished to know that in the churches over which they preside they have become bridegrooms; therefore, with all vigilance, they must devote the care of their entire attention to adorning them and serving them without interruption.

24. Twenty-fourth, they are in no way to omit the canonical hours, whether by night or by day. For just as the Roman Church sings the offices, so must all who pursue the way of the same purpose do likewise. This formula is not established only by the teachings of the New Testament; its rationale is also evident in the Old Testament, because the prophet, moved by the Holy Spirit, declares: “Seven times a day I have praised you,” and “At midnight I rose to confess to you.”

25. Twenty-fifth, they are to announce to the congregations that they are to act as sureties for the spiritual sons and daughters whom they receive in baptism, to be sponsors in faith on their behalf, and to renounce on their behalf the devil, to whom those children had previously been enslaved. Therefore they are to keep them under their care until they become adults and have explained and rendered to them the pledge of faith and the renunciations. Whatever they had promised on the children’s behalf, they are to require from them in full.

[Col. 0627]

EXCERPTED CHAPTERS OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS II. (A.D. 856) [These follow the preceding material in the Blankenburg manuscript and, following the model of the Pavia constitutions of A.D. 832, have been drawn from earlier capitularies. At the end they present a few chapters also found in the Ticinian constitutions of A.D. 855. The text is very corrupt in several places.]

[Col. 0627D] Likewise, chapters of the Salic law.

1. [Ecclesiastical canon, 789, chapter 31.] Places that have once been dedicated as monasteries are to be monasteries and remain monasteries forever; they cannot thereafter become secular dwellings [the manuscript reads corruptly “they can”].

2. Virgins are not to be veiled before the age of twenty-five, unless they are compelled by reasonable necessity.

3. It must likewise be preached how the Son of God was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-virgin, for the salvation and restoration of the human race; how he ascended into heaven; and how he will come again in divine majesty to judge all human beings according to their own merits. It must also be preached how the wicked, because of their crimes, are sent with the devil into eternal fire, while the just enter eternal life with Christ and the holy angels.

4. The resurrection of the dead must likewise be considered and preached [the editor asks whether the reading should be *dicendum*, “it must be said,” or *diligenter est praedicandum*, “it must be preached diligently”], so that they may know and believe that in the same bodies they will receive the rewards of their merits.

5. Likewise, it must be preached to everyone with the greatest diligence for which crimes they are assigned to eternal punishment with the devil. For we read, as the Apostle makes clear [Note: [Col. 0627] *manifesta* in manuscript C]: “The works of the flesh are fornication, uncleanness, debauchery, idolatry, sorcery, contentions, rivalries, hostilities, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these, which I proclaim to you as I proclaimed before: those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.” The great preacher of the Church of God named these individually, and they must be prohibited with every effort. Thus, when reading these words, let them understand how dreadful is what he said: those who do such things will not attain the kingdom of God. But in every kind of righteousness [Note: *justia* in the manuscript] admonish them concerning the kingdom of God and love of God and neighbor; concerning faith and hope in God; concerning humility and patience; concerning chastity and self-restraint; concerning kindness and mercy; concerning almsgiving; and concerning confession of their sins. And let them forgive their debtors their debts according to the Lord’s Prayer [Note: *debito* in the manuscript; *suam* in manuscript C; *condonent* is absent in manuscript C], knowing with complete certainty that those who do such things attain the kingdom of God. We enjoin this upon your charity all the more diligently because we know that in the last times false teachers [Note: *per seupdodoctores* in manuscript C] will come, as the Lord himself foretold in the Gospel and the Apostle Paul testifies in his letter to Timothy. Therefore, beloved, let us prepare ourselves with all our heart in knowledge and truth, so that we may be able to resist those who oppose the truth; and, by the grace granted by God, may the word of God grow, advance [Note: read *excurrat*], and multiply for the progress of the holy Church and the salvation of our souls, and for praise in the glory of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Peace to those who preach; grace to those who obey; glory to the Lord our God.

6. Let no one presume to cast lots in the Psalter, or in the Gospel [Col. 0629C], or in any other matter, nor to observe any divinations [Note: *Ut* in manuscript C]. [Note: [Col. 0629D] 789, General Chapter 4.]

7. The evil of drunkenness must be altogether prohibited to everyone; and we prohibit and command those who perform these conjurations by Saint Stephen, or by us, or by our sons [Note: *percipimus* in manuscript C], so that bishops or abbots do not go from house to house [Note: *vadat* and *cassa* in manuscript C] mixing [or meddling].

8. Concerning the fact that our envoys must take care lest, perhaps, anyone’s complaint should arise against a bishop, abbot, abbess, count, or anyone of whatever rank, and that they must report it to us. [Note: [Col. 0629D] 789, General Chapter 11.]

9. Concerning monasteries and hospices which appear to exist under various counts: let them be regular institutions, and whoever wishes to hold them shall hold them by the benefice of the lord king. [Note: [Col. 0629D] 783, Chapter 6 of the *Leges*.]

10. Concerning the *aldiones*. *Aldiones* belonging to the public fisc, whether *aldiones* or *aldianae*, shall live in Italy in the service of their lords under the same law under which the royal fiscal dependants or *lidi* live in Francia [Note: manuscript C reads *quas fiscalines velidis*].

11. Likewise, concerning the Ripuarian law: if a free man strikes a free woman with a blow, he shall be judged liable to a payment of 15 solidi. [Note: [Col. 0629D] 803, Ripuarian Law, 6.1.]

12. If a royal man—that is, a fiscal dependant—an ecclesiastical man, or a *lidus* is killed, 100 solidi shall be paid in compensation. [Note: [Col. 0629D] Ripuarian Law, 2.] A free man who cannot pay any fine and has no sureties [Note: *fiiussores* in the manuscript] may place himself in *wadium* [*vatdium*] with the person to whom he is indebted [Note: *debito* in the manuscript], until he has paid the fine he owes. In the same chapter, concerning a *soniste* [Note: *clesoniste* in the manuscript], let him either pay 600 solidi, or swear with twelve men; or, if the person pursuing the case does not wish to accept the oath of twelve men, let him contend against him either at the cross or with shield and staff. [Note: [Col. 0629D] Ripuarian Law, 3.]

13. If anyone has been summoned to the court by legal ban, and the *sunnis* [Note: *sunis* in the manuscript] has not detained him, let him pay 15 solidi. Let the same apply to the second and third summons. But if he refuses to come a fourth time, let his property be placed under ban until he comes and renders justice concerning the matter over which he had been summoned. If he does not come within a year, let the king be consulted concerning his goods which have been placed under ban, and whatever he judges concerning them shall be done. The first warning shall allow seven nights, the second fourteen nights, the third twenty-one nights, and the fourth forty-two nights. Likewise, concerning a man’s benefice: if perhaps he has no property of his own, let him be placed under ban until the king is consulted. If the claimant comes and refuses to accept the disputed matter, let them contend in the field or at the cross. [Note: [Col. 0630D] Ripuarian Law, 7.]

14. Whoever has no sons and wishes to make someone else his heir shall do so by a formal act before the king, before the count, and before the *scabini* or royal envoys who have then been appointed to administer justice in that province. [Note: manuscript C reads *volueris*; [Col. 0630D] Ripuarian Law, 9.]

15. A *dinarialis* man may not come into his own recognition [or legal acknowledgment] before reaching the third generation. A *cartularius* man likewise. [Note: [Col. 0630D] Ripuarian Law, 10–11.]

16. Every oath shall be sworn in a church or over relics. Whatever must be sworn in a church, whether with six or with twelve men, shall be sworn by men of the sort whom he has been able to find according to the law; and let him swear that God and the saints whose relics these are may help him to speak the truth. [Note: [Col. 0630D] Ripuarian Law, 12. The manuscript has *mnis*, omitting the initial letter in red; therefore a new chapter begins.]

16. If property claimed in litigation (*res intertiata*) has been taken by theft, the person against whom the property has been claimed may clear himself by oath concerning the theft, declaring that what was taken was not done by his will or with his consent; or he shall restore it without further loss. [Note: [Col. 0630D] Ripuarian Law, 13.]

17. Concerning the man who apprehended a slave, and whose master ordered him to kill two children, one nine years old and the other eleven: finally, after his master had killed the boys, I threw that slave into a certain pit. It was judged that he should pay threefold *wergeld* (*udrichildus*) for the one who was nine years old, double compensation for the other who was eleven, and threefold compensation for the slave, together with our ban in every matter. [Note: [Col. 0631D] Ripuarian Law, p. 118, line 20.]

18. Laymen shall not be placed over monks within monasteries, nor shall archdeacons be laymen. [Note: [Col. 0631D] 805, p. 132, chapter 13.]

19. Concerning the following: if famine, devastation, an irregularity of the weather [Note: *erit* in the manuscript], or any other kind of tribulation should occur, our edict must not be awaited; rather, God’s mercy must immediately be entreated. In the present year, because of the scarcity caused by famine, let each person help his own people, as far as I shall be able, and let him not sell his grain at too high a price; nor let any food be sold outside our realm. [Note: [Col. 0631D] Ibid., chapter 4.]

20. Concerning arms in the army: let what we previously prescribed in another chapter be observed; moreover, every man who has twelve holdings shall have a coat of mail. Whoever has a coat of mail but does not bring it with him shall lose both his entire benefice and his coat of mail. [Note: [Col. 0631D] Ripuarian Law, 6.]

21. It has been decided by us that we should send our envoys—one monk and another a chaplain—throughout our kingdom to inspect and investigate the monasteries of men and women who ought to live under the holy Rule: how their lodging is arranged, what their life and conduct are always like, and how each monastery appears to possess sufficient resources from which it can live. [Note: [Col. 0632D] 790, Pippin, 11.]

22. Women whose husbands have died, whom the law of the Lombards prohibits from changing their clothing to the religious habit or receiving the veil before a year has passed [Note: manuscript Bl omits *ante*; manuscript Bl has *veste*; manuscript C reads *vellum*], requested our permission that, whenever divine mercy should soon inspire them, they might be permitted to receive it without harm. But, considering that in the past [Note: *p. tempore* in fragment Fl.] many women, because of this delay, had also been carried away by abduction [Note: omitted in manuscript Bl] to another party within that same period, we therefore received their petition [Note: *petitione* in fragment Bl], judging it just, and grant that it be done in this way. [Note: [Col. 0632D] See above, year 855, July, chapter 1.]

23. Concerning homicide, for which the law, because of the simplicity of proof, requires three witnesses: if a man cannot have witnesses, we grant that he may swear with twelve oath-helpers and, having been absolved by that same simplified procedure, shall not admit [the claimant] to his own property. [Note: [Col. 0632D] Ibid., chapter 4.]

24. Concerning documents which certain persons call false: we decree that, if the notary and the witnesses survive [Note: fragment Fl. reads *supervixerit*], they themselves shall make the document true and valid; and if ten witnesses have died while the notary survives, he shall make it true and valid with twelve oath-helpers [Note: fragment Fl. adds *ipsam chartam*, “the document itself”]. [Note: [Col. 0632D] Ibid., chapter 5.]

[Col. 0631]

### Capitula of Charles II Sent to the Franks and Aquitanians from Quierzy  
*(Year 856, July 7)*

[Note: [Col. 0631] We have revised the editions of Sirmond and Baluze with the aid of manuscript 2 of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 4638.]

[Note.]

[Col. 0631C] The following capitula were sent by the lord king Charles to the Franks and Aquitanians who had separated from him, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 856, on the Nones of July, from the palace of Quierzy, through his faithful envoys Adalard the abbot, Rodulf, Richuinus, Adalgarius, and Berengarius. [Note: *deest* in manuscript 2.]

1. Our lord sends you word that his uncle Rhuodulf informed him of your fidelity, and that you asked him to send to you, on his behalf, his named faithful men; and that through them you wished to communicate to him your needs and wishes. If you had done anything which needed correction, you would willingly correct it on their advice; and whatever advice they gave you for the fidelity of our lord and your salvation, you would willingly carry out.

2. Our lord sends you word that he is pleased by what his uncle reported to him concerning your fidelity and good will. In accordance with your petition, he is sending us to you, as you requested. He further sends you word that if any one of you complains that he has done something unjustly to someone among you, and has been unable to come to a proper hearing and just judgment; or if, through some plot, our lord himself or someone acting for him wished to apprehend one of you [Note: Sirmond also reads *comprehendere*; a later hand corrected it to *comperdere*. Baluze], and for this reason one of you temporarily withdrew from his presence and service [Note: *substraxit* in Sirmond and Baluze], he grants that anyone among you who wishes to come to him for a proper hearing and before his faithful men may do so. If it is justly and reasonably found that one of you has a rightful claim against him, he will willingly make amends for it with the counsel of his faithful men. But if it is found that he acted lawfully in the matter about which one of you wishes to complain, he wants the matter to remain, as it was done according to law, by the force of that same law.

3. He sends you word that if any one of you has sought a proper hearing from him and before his faithful men, and has come to such a hearing, and it is justly and reasonably found that he has no rightful claim against anyone among you, and that the proper hearing itself has convicted him, then, if he entrusts himself to him, humbles himself, wishes to make amends, and wishes to remain in that amendment, he is willingly prepared to show him reasonable mercy, just as he and his faithful men have reasonably determined.

4. He sends you word that if there is anyone among you who, because he does not trust his own conscience, cannot or dares not seek a proper hearing, but acknowledges and repents, and asks for his mercy and pardon, he willingly grants mercy and pardon to each person who acknowledges himself in this way, provided that thereafter he guards himself as he ought.

5. He sends you word that henceforth no one among you should doubt him, because he always wishes to preserve the proper hearing for the person who seeks it, and likewise always wishes to preserve the mercy which he now grants, provided that the person does not again commit another such offense [Note: omitted in manuscript 2] for which he ought to undergo a just judgment through a proper hearing.

6. He sends you word that if there is anyone among you who says that, because of poverty and necessity, he spent many days in his service and exhausted everything he had, and joined himself to some association in order to obtain something which he could not obtain through service; if he can demonstrate this to our lord before his faithful men, and if it is found to be true that it was our lord’s fault that one of you reasonably withdrew from his service in this way because of necessity, our lord willingly acknowledges this and, with the counsel of his faithful men, will correct it as quickly and reasonably as he can.

7. He sends you word that if anyone among you says that he did what he did neither because of disloyalty nor because of dishonor [Note: manuscript 2 has *deshonorantia*], and if anyone among you fears that our lord will henceforth regard this act as disloyalty or dishonor, and for this reason believes that he ought no longer to seek counsel from him, then whoever among you has become entangled in this matter in such a way—provided that henceforth he is faithful, obedient, and an aid to him in preserving his kingdom and rightful honor, as a man ought rightly to be to his king and lord—he will not hold this matter against anyone. Rather, he wishes from his heart to dismiss whatever he committed against his person in this affair, and he wishes duly and reasonably to reward the service which that person rendered to him before and, with God’s help, will render henceforth [Note: Sirmond and Baluze read *merere*; manuscript 2 has a variant reading, written in the margin by a second hand, from manuscript c, d, q, as indicated in the edition]. But if anyone has unjustly taken something from him or from someone else, the law shall settle this, as custom and right require.

8. And know that our lord has now, thanks be to God, brought to a good conclusion what he has repeatedly desired. He has asked his faithful men, without any evil suspicion of his anger or emotional disturbance, jointly to seek, discover, and set down what he ought to do according to his office, and what it would not be fitting for him to do. Wherever it is found that he has done what he ought not to have done, he is prepared, with God’s help and the counsel of his faithful men, to correct it and amend it as quickly as he can, consistently with reason and possibility, and thereafter to preserve what has been corrected. Whatever he ought to have done for his salvation and honor, but did less than he should have done, he will, with God’s help and the counsel and assistance of his faithful men, do as quickly as he can, consistently with reason and possibility.

9. Likewise, he wishes us to seek, discover, and set down what and how it is fitting for us, his faithful men, in each rank to do toward him, and what it is not fitting for us to do; so that we may do what is fitting and avoid what is not fitting. Wherever in the past anything has been done by us, his faithful men, in any rank, which was not fitting, we shall, with God’s help and his assistance and our common counsel, correct and amend it as quickly as we can, consistently with reason and possibility, and thereafter preserve what has been corrected. [Note: manuscript 2 reads *aliquid*, “something,” instead of *aliqua*.]

10. And know that he is so united with all his faithful men in every rank and condition, and that all of us, his faithful men of every rank and condition, are so united with him, that if, according to human frailty, he does anything contrary to such an agreement, we shall admonish him honorably and reverently, as befits a lord, so that he may correct and amend it and preserve for each person in his own rank the law that is due to him. If one of us in any rank acts against this agreement and against him, then, if the matter is such that he wishes to admonish that person so that he may amend it, let him do so. But if the matter is such that he ought not to admonish him privately, let him bring him before his peers for a proper hearing; and the man who does not wish to offer and observe the due agreement, the proper law, and the respect owed to his lord shall undergo the just judgment of justice. If he refuses to undergo it, becomes obstinate and rebellious, and cannot be converted, let him be expelled by all from our fellowship and kingdom.

And if our lord does not wish, through a proper hearing or suitable mercy, to preserve for each person in his own rank the law due to him—a law granted by himself and by his predecessors to us and to our predecessors—and if, when admonished by his faithful men, he does not wish to change his intention, know that he is so united with us and we with him, and that we are all so confirmed by his will and agreement—bishops and abbots with laymen, and laymen with ecclesiastical men—that no one should abandon his equal, so that, even if our king should wish it—which God forbid—he cannot act against anyone’s law, proper hearing, or just judgment.

11. And know that, for seeking, discovering, establishing, and confirming this, with the agreement of our lord and his other faithful men, our lord has appointed the place—the palace of Vermeria—and the time and day, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August. He has also named in writing his faithful men, through whose deliberation this matter may, with God’s help, reach completion. He has summoned all his faithful men generally to that palace of Vermeria on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, so that he may make known to all his will, his pardon, and the devotion of us who are his faithful men. Thus, may this agreement, which we shall confirm with God as witness, be preserved throughout the days of his life and ours; and may he leave it in God’s name to his successors to preserve with respect to our successors, and may we leave it to our successors to preserve with respect to his successors.

12. And know that our lord and we and his other faithful men wish that, if you, who ought to be his faithful men and counselors, wish—as we have told you—to come to his presence, fidelity, and service, and to join us in this fellowship, then both he and we willingly wish you to seek, discover, establish, confirm, and preserve these matters with us, and we likewise with you [Note: manuscript 2 reads *ita*, “thus”]. Henceforth he wishes to preserve for you, as for us, the due law and proper hearing, as is right, just as his predecessors, who acted more effectively and reasonably in this matter, preserved them in every rank for our predecessors and yours.

13. Our lord sends you word that if there is anyone among you who is dissatisfied with his lordship and pretends that he can obtain a better lord elsewhere than from him, let him come to him; and he, with a tranquil and peaceful mind, will grant him permission to depart, provided only that he does no harm or injury to him, his kingdom, or his faithful men. Whatever he can obtain from God and whatever he can secure from another lord, let him possess peacefully.

14. If there is anyone among you who wishes to say that he does not trust our lord’s faith and is suspicious of his destruction, and for this reason dares not go to him, we give you the faith of God and of our lord Charles, and the faith of his bishops and faithful clerics [Note: *damus* is attributed to Baluze]. As far as God preserves you and you preserve yourselves, you shall go there safely and remain safely with him; and, if matters do not proceed properly for you with him, you shall return safely. Only go peacefully and without rebellion, and do not incite his faithful men.

15. If you still have doubts and seek another guarantee—provided that you do not seek one contrary to reason—if you wish to go to him as we have said, we are also prepared to provide this, because we are certain that we can do everything securely. [Note: [Col. 0635] Here the manuscripts of Tilius and the Royal Manuscript of Paris no. 4638 end. With their assistance above all, the capitularies of Charles II for the years 843–856 were published. It should nevertheless be noted that the Council of the Nobles, which we publish on pages 447–448, precedes these capitula concerning Quierzy in the manuscripts.]

### Council of the Nobles of Charles II  
*(Year 856, August)*

[Note: [Col. 0635] We have revised the editions of Sirmond and Baluze with the aid of manuscript 2 of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 4638.]

[Note.]

[Col. 0635C] This is the counsel which the bishops and abbots [Note: [Col. 0635D] Baluze, volume II, p. 1267, publishes the following names of the bishops and abbots who attended the assembly: Amalricus, archbishop of Tours; Wenilo of Sens; Hincmar of Reims; Paulus of Rouen; Heribaldus, bishop of Auxerre; Erchenradus of Paris; Rothadus of Soissons; Teutboldus of Langres; Hirminfridus of Beauvais; Balfridus of Bayeux; Herluinus of Coutances; Herpuinus of Senlis; Guntbertus of Évreux; Jonas of Autun; Hariardus of Lisieux; Hildebrannus of Sées; Hildegarius of Meaux; Immo of Noyon; Agius of Orléans; Frotboldus of Chartres; Pardulus of Laon; Elmeradus of Amiens; Remedius of Avranches; Godelsadus of Chalon; Braindigus of Mâcon; Prudentius of Troyes; Dodo of Angers; Actardus of Nantes. Ludovicus, abbot of Saint-Denis; Adalardus, abbot; Lupus, abbot of Ferrières; Heinhardus, abbot; Frodinus, abbot; Odo, abbot of Corbie; Hunfredus, abbot of Dervy; Bernardus, abbot; Gautlenus, abbot; Abbo, abbot; Arcamboldus, abbot; Georgius, abbot; and likewise Abbo, abbot.] and the other faithful men of the lord Charles jointly delivered to him at Bonneuil, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 856, in the month of August.

The rebuke which we heard in the letter of the lord apostolic [Note: Sirmond likewise reads *vobiscum*, “with you.” The Pithaean manuscript has *nobiscum*, “with us,” which seems to be the correct reading. Baluze. A new collation of manuscript 2 does not indicate this.] together with you and your other faithful men would have touched us most severely, if we had acted otherwise than that same lord apostolic, with great authority, commanded us to act according to what he had heard. Since we did not consent to this matter for which he specifically reproved us, and since we have frequently and beneficially admonished you and your faithful men, whom it was appropriate to admonish concerning it, both by word and in writing—as you yourselves know and the surviving written documents attest—that what had been done contrary to salvation and authority should be corrected and that every precaution should be taken lest it be done again, we are not justly touched by this rebuke.

But now also, joining his admonitions to ours and adding ours to his [Note: *monita nostra* are absent in manuscript 2], we exhort you to strive, as quickly, effectively, feasibly, and reasonably as you can, to restore and correct the condition of the monasteries existing in your kingdom, which has been distorted and confused in a manner contrary to what is proper and fitting. We do not merely admonish you and those entrusted to you in your kingdom to do this; we also urge and entreat you carefully and frequently to recall and reread the capitula which you yourself confirmed with your faithful men at the royal estate of Cologne, as well as those which you accepted from the bishops at Beauvais under a clearly known condition; those which you approved with your brothers near the estate of Théodon, at the place called the Judgment; those which you accepted after they had been promulgated synodally at the palace of Ver; those which at Épernay you designated for observance concerning episcopal capitula together with illustrious men and your wise barons; those which you confirmed with your own hand together with your brothers at Meerssen; those which you accepted at the Synod of Soissons, at which you graciously presented your presence; those which you decreed at Silvacus; and those which you announced at Liège together with your brother Lothair.

You should ensure that whatever has been done in your kingdom against these measures, and against the divine and salutary authority which your progenitors and predecessors directly and consistently maintained and observed, is corrected as soon as reason and possibility permit. Henceforth, with the Lord’s cooperation, let us all jointly take care that nothing be done by anyone against these provisions. If anything is done against them, let it be corrected immediately, as soon as possible, as equity, reason, and possibility dictate, without deceit, with right intention, and with the law and authority appropriate to each rank.

And lest anyone consider it a small matter that has been confirmed with God as witness and mediator by one’s own hand, and has been expressed through an oath of such great truth, which is God, let each person learn from the safeguard of confirmation on earth, and from the confirmation of baptism and the other observances in heaven, by how many bonds he is held and bound. Let us all hear together what is said by the divine Spirit:

“Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword;  
he has bent his bow and prepared it,  
and in it he has prepared instruments of death.”

May Jesus Christ our Lord rescue us all from these things, turned toward him and the observance of his commandments, and remaining in their observance. To him belong honor, glory, power, and dominion throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

### Capitula of Charles II Sent to the Franks and Aquitanians  
*(Year 856, August–September)*

[Note: [Col. 0637] From the editions of Sirmond and Baluze. Here and there Sirmond published the capitularies of Charles the Bald chiefly with the aid of the manuscripts of Laon and Beauvais, which Baluze also used again.]

These capitula were sent by the king from Basiu through Hadabrannus and Betto.

[Col. 0637C]

1. Our lord sends you greetings. He also sends you word that he is greatly surprised that you did not observe such an assembly, as you promised him and as he himself commanded you.

2. Our lord sends you word that you abandoned this assembly because you wished to await the arrival of his brother, according to what you had communicated to him. He was unable to meet them without his other faithful men, whom he did not then have with him, so that it was necessary to defer the matter for a time.

3. Our lord has appointed another assembly for the Kalends of September at the estate of Nielfa [Note: Neaufle-en-Vexin. Sirmond], where his faithful men ought to meet him. Therefore he sends you word to come to a place suitable for you and near the aforesaid place, where he can send to you such of his faithful men as you request him to send.

4. Know that he wishes to observe this toward you according to what he granted you at Vermeria and as he had previously commanded you by word and in writing. Whatever else you wish to request justly and reasonably, he likewise does not refuse to grant. The same applies to the delay, according to what he and his faithful men determine is not unworthy of God’s will and of the honor of him and his faithful men. For the sake of God, and for the nourishment of the lord, his father and progenitor, and himself, and for the service you have rendered him, he does not refuse to assent to this.

5. He sends you word to remember God, your Christianity, the nourishment provided by his father and himself, your due fidelity, and the danger threatening the kingdom. Strive to become united, as faithful men, with the holy mother Church and with him, and faithfully to fulfill together with him the will of almighty God, his fidelity, and the common salvation, in resistance to enemies and persecutors of the Christian name.

This embassy was sent by the glorious lord king Charles through Adalard the abbot, Richuinus, Rodulfus, and Berengarius.

[Col. 0639A]

1. Our lord sends you greetings. He also sends you word that whatever he was able to find, according to the counsel of his faithful men, to be better and more honorable in your matter, he has already communicated to you twice through his faithful men and his capitula.

2. He sends you word that, as he made known to you through those faithful men and through the same capitula, so he wishes to attend to and observe it toward you. If you still wish to request from him some matter which concerns his honor and your advancement, he is also prepared to do this according to your petition and the counsel of his faithful men.

3. He also sends you word to remember God and your Christianity, and to grieve and sympathize with this holy Church, which has been miserably oppressed and despoiled both by you and by others, and which is being cruelly persecuted on the other side by pagans. Do not separate yourselves from the unity and unanimity of God’s faithful men; rather, hasten to unite and join yourselves personally to him and to the other faithful men of God and of himself, for the defense of holy Church and his fidelity.

4. But if you say that you cannot do this because of your peers who are not present, he commands you who are present to provide him with such security that you will not abandon what he commands you through us for any other reason except those of your peers who are not present. Give him the assurance that you will exhort and convert those peers of yours, as far as you can, to God’s service and to his fidelity. If you cannot convert them, do not withdraw yourselves from his service. For if you all wish to be converted to him, he is prepared, for the benefit of holy Church, his honor, and your common advancement, to receive and preserve all of you and always to hold you in honor; and, insofar as it concerns him, never to charge any of you with whatever you have negligently done in his service or have done against him in this matter.

5. He sends you word that, after he has learned of your fidelity, he will also assure you on his part that he will not hold against anyone what he has negligently done toward him in this matter—provided, however, that you preserve toward him the honor and fidelity owed to him, as faithful men of God and of himself.

6. If any part of you wishes to return to his lordship and fidelity, he is likewise prepared to receive them kindly and to fulfill toward them in every respect what is written above.

This embassy was sent by the king through the bishops Hincmarus and Yrminfridus, and through Adalard the abbot, Bodulfus, Richuinus, and Berengarius.

Our lord sends you greetings. He also sends you word that, for the love of God and because of the service once rendered to him by your fidelity, he wishes all of you to be safe, and desires to bring all of you, without any pretext, to God’s service and to his fidelity. [Col. 0640B] And so that it may be clear to everyone that he wishes to preserve all of you as his faithful men, and does not wish, under any pretext, to destroy any of you, and so that you may also remain safe from your peers without injury, as you ought and as Christians should, he most willingly grants you the matter which you requested from him, according to the counsel of his faithful men, until the agreed assembly, which is to be held at Chartres on the fifth day before the Ides of October.

This is provided, however, that you give him such assurance that you will remain at peace until that assembly, and that you will cause him or his faithful men no dishonor in any matter which you can reasonably and feasibly avoid and guard against. You must not hinder his faithful men, engage in plundering, or cause any disturbance [Note: Sirmond reads this way; a later hand wrote, “neither in plundering nor in any disturbance.” Baluze]. He grants you permission meanwhile to remain in your honors and allods, except for those whose honors our lord has already granted to others. If any among you have no honors, let them remain in their allods if they wish, or with other peers or friends of theirs. If they wish to remain with our lord, provided that they and their people live peacefully, he also grants this mercifully.

This is on the condition that you give him assurance concerning yourselves, and that you do not in any way withdraw any of his faithful men from his fidelity or incite them. If anyone among you refuses to keep this peace in this manner, expel him unanimously from your fellowship, if he refuses to amend what he is clearly shown to have done negligently.

[Col. 0639]

# CORONATION OF JUDITH, DAUGHTER OF CHARLES II  
*(A.D. 856, October 1)*

[Note: Judith was betrothed to the king of the English in 856 at the palace of Verberie. See Prudentius, *Annales*, MGH SS, vol. I, year 856 (Patrologia, vol. CXV). Sirmond published the coronations of Judith, Charles II, Ermentrude, and Louis, son of Charles, from a codex of Saint Lawrence of Liège; since that codex is no longer extant, we reproduce Sirmond’s edition.]

## Blessing over the queen whom King Æthelwulf took as his wife

[Col. 0639C]

Married in Christ, veiled with a heavenly cloud and refreshed by spiritual grace, protected from every unlawful desire, make a covenant with your eyes, so that you may not look upon another man in order to desire him, and do not commit adultery in body or in heart; turn your eyes away, lest they see vanity. Thus may you be brought to life in the way of the Lord, so that you may say with the prophet: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens.” And: “I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me.” Through our creator, redeemer, and Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever.

Bless, O Lord, these dowries [*detes*; possibly an OCR corruption of *dotes*], and graciously deign to endow those who receive them with your blessing, so that, preserving the fidelity of marriage and an undefiled marriage-bed, they may deserve to join the company of the holy patriarchs. Through the Lord.

Receive the ring, the sign of faith and love, and the bond of conjugal union, so that man may not separate those whom God joins together. He lives and reigns for ever and ever.

I betroth you, a chaste virgin who shall become the wife of one man, so that you may be like the holy women who were wives to their husbands: Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Esther, Judith, Anna, and Naomi, with Jesus Christ our Lord, the author and sanctifier of marriage, graciously assisting; he lives and reigns for ever and ever.

O God, who at the beginning of the growing world blessed the increase of offspring, be favorable to our supplications and pour out the help of your blessing upon this your servant and this your handmaid, so that in marital union, according to your good pleasure, they may be joined in equal affection, like-mindedness, and mutual holiness. Enrich them with holy fruits and blessed works. [Col. 0641C] Make them beget such offspring as may belong to the inheritance of your paradise. Open, O Lord, the gates of heaven and visit them in peace. Water their land, so that it may bring forth spiritual fruit. Sanctify them, you who were given to us from a virgin; and grant them the times of salvation that the holy prophet John foretold before your coming, so that, faithfully believing here and living blessedly, they may attain life and the eternal kingdom, by your grace, Christ our Savior, who with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God for ever.

## Blessing of the queen

We invoke you, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, that you may cause this your handmaid—whom, by the providence of your divine dispensation, you have allowed to grow joyful in youthful bloom until the present day—to advance, enriched by the gift of your mercy and full of truth, from day to day toward ever better things before you and before human beings. May she joyfully receive the abundance of heavenly grace in her rule, and, protected on every side by the wall of your mercy against adversity, deserve to live in the peace of your favor. Through the Lord.

[Col. 0642A]

## *Sursum corda*

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, strength of the elect and exaltation of the humble: at the beginning, through the outpouring of the flood, you willed that the sins of the world should be cleansed; through the dove carrying an olive branch, you showed that peace had been restored to the earth; again, through the anointing with oil, you anointed your servant Aaron as priest; and afterward, through the pouring of this ointment, you perfected priests, kings, and prophets for governing the people of Israel. Through the prophetic voice of your servant David, you foretold that the face of the Church would be gladdened by oil.

You also gladdened the face of your handmaid Judith with this ointment, for the liberation of your servants and the confusion of your enemies; and you made the face of your servant Esther so radiant through this spiritual anointing of your mercy that, at her prayers, you inclined the savage heart of the king toward mercy and the salvation of those who believe in you. We ask you, almighty God, that through the richness of this created substance you may adorn her with the peace, simplicity, and chastity of the dove. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who is to come to judge.

## Coronation

May the Lord crown you with glory and honor, and place upon your head a crown of spiritual precious stone, so that whatever is signified by the splendor of gold and the varied brilliance of gems may always shine forth in your character and in your deeds. May he himself deign to grant this, to whom belong honor and glory for ever and ever.

## Blessings

Bless, O Lord, this your handmaid, you who have governed the kingdoms of kings from eternity. Amen.

Receive the work of her hands, and by your blessing may her land be filled with the fruits of heaven, with dew, and with the waters beneath the earth. Amen.

May she rejoice in your blessing from the summit of the ancient mountains and the everlasting hills, from the produce of the earth and its fullness. Amen.

May the blessing of him who appeared in the bush come upon her head. Give her an abundance of the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth, of grain and wine, so that peoples may serve her and her offspring, and so that tribes may worship her and her seed in your honor. Amen.

Fill her with the blessings of breasts and womb. May the blessings of the ancient fathers be strengthened over her and over her offspring, as you promised your servant Abraham and his seed for ever. Amen.

Grant, we ask, almighty and merciful God, that these gifts of yours, which your faithful have received from your hand, may, through those who give, receive, and distribute them, serve the support of the present life, the redemption of souls, and the attainment of everlasting life. Through the Lord.

[Col. 0641]

# THE ASSEMBLY OF CHARLES II AT Quierzy  
*(A.D. 857, February 14)*

[Note: We have revised the editions of Sirmond and Baluze by consulting manuscript 3 of the Royal Library of Paris, among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75, which, like manuscripts 3b of Saint Vincent of Metz and 3c, Baluze’s Palatine manuscript, presents the text as it was directed in the fourth *missaticum* (reviewed above, col. 605), and manuscript 4, the Royal Parisian codex no. 4626, written for use in the eleventh *missaticum*.]

## Chapters [*quae*; manuscript 4: *quem*] which Charles issued at the palace of Quierzy

[Note: The entire heading is absent from manuscripts 3, 3b, and 3c.]

[Col. 0643A]

### 1

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, by the grace of God king, sends greetings in the Lord to that bishop [Note: Manuscript 3, 3b, and 3c: “to the venerable bishop Hunfrid, the counts and officials Ingiscalc and Berengar, and our faithful envoys”; manuscript 4: “to our beloved venerable bishop Jonas and the illustrious count Isimbard, our envoys”] and to those beloved and faithful envoys, counts, and others of ours.

Let your fidelity know that on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March [February 14], according to sacred authority, we caused a synod of venerable bishops and an assembly of our faithful to meet at Quierzy. With them we considered, among other matters concerning the utility of the Church and the needs of the kingdom, how the plunderings and devastations that are raging in our kingdom—partly because of the invasion of the pagans, partly because of the fickleness of certain of our faithful, and even through those who ought to defend and protect the Church of God and provide for the stability and peace of the kingdom—might, with the Lord’s approval, somehow be brought to an end and removed.

### 2

After consultation with them, we decreed that, because sins which at their beginning are judged to be of great weight gradually become lightened in depraved minds through their ruinous progress and even more destructive practice [Note: Manuscript 4: “pernicious”; manuscript S: “are made light”], making those minds almost insensible, and because, when they attempt to recover their senses, such sins often bind them so tightly that, even if they wish to rise, they cannot [Note: Manuscript 4: “cannot”], before ecclesiastical censure and legal judgments strike such plunderers with terror and condemnation [Note: Manuscript 3: “preachers” for “plunderers”; manuscript 4: “let the bishops also strike them”], each bishop in his own parish, the envoys in their districts, and the counts in their counties shall likewise hold assemblies. All servants of the state, royal vassals, and everyone, whoever they may be or whose people they may be, who live in those parishes or counties shall attend without any exception of persons, excuse, or delay.

### 3

The bishop of that parish shall read aloud to everyone the briefly noted judgments concerning this matter—namely, those of evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic authority, as well as the apostolic and canonical decrees—and shall take care to make known to all, in plain speech, what kind and how great a sin it is, what kind and how great a penance it demands, and what immense and most severe vengeance it calls forth, together with the other due, necessary, and useful admonitions.

### 4

The envoys shall also record the legal judgments as they know them, and make known to everyone the chapters of our predecessors, kings and emperors, together with our own chapters concerning this matter, collected into one body. The bishops shall forbid such depredations to everyone by the authority of God and of the episcopate. Our envoys and counts shall firmly strive to prohibit them by our royal ban, so that all may know that if, from now on, anyone in our kingdom presumes to do such things, he will, according to the divine judgments, incur episcopal sentence; according to the laws and royal chapters, he will be compelled to make restitution; and according to the judgment of our faithful, he will suffer a fitting punishment.

### 5

If the person in question is such that our bishops, envoys, or counts can correct the wrongful act in their jurisdictions, they shall strive to correct it according to the prescribed procedure, or shall cause him to come before our presence through sureties.

### 6

If anyone at all should prove disobedient, they shall make the matter known to us with the greatest haste, so that we may order him to come as quickly as possible before our presence and suffer fitting vengeance according to the judgment of our faithful.

### 7
