If, God forbid, someone should arise who sets aside the fear of God, despises ecclesiastical authority, and rejects royal power, whoever he may be shall know that, according to canonical authority, he will be made alien both in heaven and on earth from the assembly of all Christians and from the fellowship of the holy Church. By royal power and by the unanimity of all the faithful of the kingdom, he will be pursued as an enemy of God and the Church and as a devastator of the kingdom until he is expelled from the kingdom.

### 8

If there is a count who permits this in his county, or allows such things to increase there, so that he either does not correct them himself or does not inform us so that our authority may correct them, he shall know that he will suffer such a sentence for it as was customary in the time of our predecessors.

### 9

If any persons repeatedly commit depredations and plunderings throughout our kingdom, and the bishops, envoys, or counts cannot correct this, they shall take care to make it known to us as soon as possible. We shall then order those plunderers to return by the same route with our envoy and to make legal restitution for everything they have done wrong, and to suffer such an *harmiscar* [Note: Manuscript 4: *armiscar*], or such a judgment as seems appropriate to us, or as we have considered with our faithful [Note: Manuscripts 3 and 4: “so we have considered”; manuscript S and Baluze: “we have considered”].

### 10

If the offenders are the men of our beloved brother or nephews, and this is reported to us, we shall inform them, so that they may take care to punish their own men for such things in whatever way seems best to them—just as we wish to punish our own men if, God forbid, they presume to commit improprieties or any harmful acts in their kingdoms.

# Collection concerning plunderers

[Note: The heading is absent from manuscripts 3 and 4.]

[Col. 0645A]

Saint Gregory says in the *Pastoral Book*: “Those who strive to seize what belongs to others must be admonished to listen carefully to what the Lord will say when he comes in judgment: ‘For I was hungry, and you did not give me food.’” And so forth. To them he says: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

From this, therefore, it must be gathered how great a condemnation awaits those who seize what belongs to others, if those who indiscriminately kept what belonged to themselves are struck with so great a punishment. Let them consider what guilt the stolen thing imposes upon them, if a thing not given up exposes someone to such punishment. Let them consider what the injustice inflicted deserves, if unoffered mercy is worthy of such a blow.

Let plunderers hear: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own—how long?—and piles up thick mud against himself.” To pile up thick mud against oneself is to heap up earthly gains together with the weight of sin.

Let them hear what Christ says: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, but suffers the loss of his soul?” [Col. 0645B] That is: what does it profit a man if he gathers everything outside himself, but condemns the one thing that he himself is?

Let them hear that the things they seize will fail in this world, or that they will leave them behind in this world; but they will carry with them to judgment the causes of their plunder—that is, condemnation.

It is written elsewhere. Let them hear what the prophet Isaiah says: “The plunder of the poor is in your house, and the case of the widow does not enter before them.” And: “The widow’s tear descends to her cheek, and the Lord will not delight in them.”

Let them hear that in whatever house plunder exists—whether in the house of the body or in the house of one’s dwelling—the Holy Spirit does not dwell in that house, but an evil spirit does. And if such a person approaches communion of the body and blood of Christ before making worthy satisfaction, he is not cleansed from sin by that communion; rather, like Judas, when he dared to receive from Christ’s hand at the supper while full of plunder and iniquity, he is more fully possessed by the devil. Hence he also burst open when he was hanged.

And whoever does not allow the widow’s case to enter [Col. 0645C] will himself be unable to enter the heavenly Church unless he makes worthy satisfaction.

Let the rapacious and the plunderers hear what the prophet says again: “You who plunder—will you not yourself be plundered?” This is because the one who plunders the property of the poor, of churches, and of God’s servants is plundered by the devil and becomes his prey.

Let them hear what Saint Paul the Apostle says—through whom Christ spoke, who was caught up to the third heaven, who was caught up into paradise, and heard secret words such as it is not permitted for a human being to utter. For he says that neither the rapacious, nor murderers, nor adulterers will possess the kingdom of God.

Let them therefore understand what kind and how great a sin plunder is, since the holy Apostle compared it with adultery and murder. Let him say the same again: if anyone is a fornicator, adulterer, plunderer, or murderer, a disciple of Christ—that is, a Christian—may not even eat with such a person before satisfaction, that is, correction, restitution, and worthy penance.

Let them hear that Saint John the Apostle, chosen and beloved by Christ, who reclined upon his breast at the supper, forbids greeting such a person, saying: “Do not even say ‘Hail’ to him, nor receive him into your house.”

Let them hear what the holy bishops at the Council of Toledo decreed—bishops who reign with God in heaven and shine forth through miracles on earth, gathered from all parts of the world. “If,” they say, “anyone of the powerful has despoiled a cleric, or any poor person, or a religious person, and the bishop has sent to him ordering him to hear the case, and he has refused, let letters immediately pass in turn through all the bishops of the province, to whichever of them he can come, so that he may be held excommunicated until he hears the case and restores what belongs to another.” Behold the judgment concerning plunderers of the poor.

Let the plunderers and despoilers of ecclesiastical property hear what Saint Anacletus, pope—ordained presbyter by the blessed Apostle Peter himself—judged together with the priests of the whole world. He says: “Whoever takes anything from father or mother is a participant in murder.” Our father is undoubtedly God, who created us; our mother is the Church, which spiritually regenerated us in baptism. Therefore whoever plunders, takes away, or defrauds Christ’s money or the Church’s property is a murderer and will be reckoned a murderer before the sight of the just Judge.

Whoever plunders his neighbor’s money commits iniquity. But whoever takes away money or property belonging to the Church commits sacrilege, and as a sacrilegious person must be judged.

Likewise Saint Urban, pope and martyr: “The property and resources of the Church are called offerings because they are offered to the Lord; they are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor. Whoever plunders them is liable to the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira, and such a person must be handed over to Satan, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”

Likewise Saint Lucius, pope: “By apostolic authority we expel and condemn the plunderers of ecclesiastical property and resources from the thresholds of the holy Church as anathematized, and we judge them to be sacrilegious—not only them, but also all who consent to them, because not only those who do the acts are judged guilty, but also those who consent to the perpetrators. Equal punishment encompasses both the agents and those who consent.”

And Saint Augustine says in his sermon on the Gospel of Saint John: “The thief of the sacred and lordly money-boxes is Judas; and whoever steals and plunders anything from the Church is compared to the lost Judas.”

Likewise it is written in the sacred canons, dictated by the Holy Spirit and confirmed by Christ’s blood: “If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, or if he does not wish to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.”

The bishop must tell everyone what anathema is. And, so that they may not despair, he must show how long anathema lasts—that is, how long a person fails to correct his error and make satisfaction by worthy amendment—so that he may be able to deserve reconciliation and pardon.

But if anyone dies while persevering in his sins before satisfaction and the pardon of reconciliation, anathema will then be perpetual for him, and it will be the sin unto death concerning which the Apostle does not say that one should pray.

The bishop shall also take care to collect and state more matters if necessary.

## The chapters of the lords Charles and Louis, emperors, follow

*(Anseg., II, 6.)*

To you counts we speak, and we admonish you, because it especially belongs to your office to show reverence and honor to the holy Church of God, to live in harmony with your bishops, and to provide them assistance in carrying out their ministry. Thus you yourselves may establish peace and justice in your jurisdictions, and may strive diligently to ensure that whatever our authority publicly orders to be done is carried out in your jurisdictions.

[Col. 0646D] Therefore we admonish your fidelity to remember the faith promised to us and, in the portion of our office entrusted to you—namely, the making of peace and justice—to show yourselves before God and before human beings such that you may rightly be called our true assistants and the protectors of the people.

Let no matter whatsoever—whether the acceptance of gifts, anyone’s friendship, hatred, fear, or favor—compel you to deviate from the state of uprightness, so that you fail always to judge justly between one neighbor and another. Be helpers and defenders, according to your ability, of orphans, widows, and other poor people, and honorers of the holy Church and its servants.

Those also who, through rashness and violence in thefts, robberies, or plunderings, seek to disturb the common peace of the people, restrain through your diligence and correction, as is fitting. If any person causes you an impediment such that you cannot do what we say, make the matter known to us in due time, so that, aided by our authority, you may be able to fulfill your office worthily.

### (7)

We admonish all laypeople to preserve ecclesiastical honor, to show due reverence to bishops and priests of God, to attend devoutly with their households when those priests preach, and reverently to observe the fasts commonly proclaimed by them, teaching and compelling their own people to observe them.

Let everyone strive also to honor and observe Sunday as is fitting. And so that this may be done more freely, markets and assemblies are to be prohibited by the counts on that day, as has often been commanded.

### (II, 14)

Concerning the peace to be preserved on the army’s journey as far as the march, we wish this to be made known to all: whoever specifically knows the author of the harm inflicted upon him in the previous year may seek and receive justice from him.

### (II, 15)

Nevertheless, we wish henceforth to announce to everyone that each person must know all those who travel on such a journey in his service, whether they are his own men or others. He must know that he will be required to render an account of their actions, so that whatever offenses they commit in violating the peace will be charged to his own peril.

The condition is this: the violator of the peace must first pay a fitting penalty according to the nature of his crime, either before us or before our envoy. The lord who has brought with him such a person, whom he was unwilling or unable to compel to observe our command, and who moreover did not fear to commit plunder in our kingdom, shall, for his negligence—if he did not warn that person beforehand about these matters, and, after the negligence of the contemner came to his knowledge, neglected to correct him as was fitting—be deprived of his honor, so that neither of them may remain without just punishment.

### (II, 23)

The counts shall become assistants in every way to the ministers of the Church in their jurisdictions, so that those ministers may more fully obtain this both from our men and from themselves and their own men. Whoever, after being admonished by the count once and a second time concerning these matters, fails to correct himself, we wish his negligence to be reported through that same count to our knowledge, so that by our authority he may be compelled to undergo what is contained in our capitulary.

### (III, 1)

Concerning peace: we admonish that all who are rebellious on account of any crimes be restrained.

### (62)

Concerning peace and justice within the country: let it be fulfilled as we have often commanded through other chapters.

### (65)

If anyone breaks into another person’s house, whatever he takes away from it by force, plunders, or steals, let him compensate the person whose house was broken into and despoiled threefold according to the law, and in addition pay the royal ban.

If a slave does this, let him receive the foregoing sentence, and in addition make compensation according to his law. If any person causes another such harm that he is unable to make full compensation, let him strive to give himself as a pledge for a slave until he fulfills the full compensation.

### (III, 66)

If anyone, while on campaign, plunders crops or provisions in violation of the royal ban, pastures them, steals them, or devastates them with horses, let him compensate threefold according to the law after the damage has been assessed.

If a free man does this, he shall be compelled to pay the royal ban for the offense. A slave, however, shall restore the damage on the spot by threefold compensation according to the law and shall be subjected to bodily discipline for the damage.

### (Benedict. I, 341)

If anyone in the army, within the kingdom, wishes without royal command to plunder anything by hostile force, or to take hay, grain, large or small livestock, or to break into or burn houses, we absolutely prohibit such acts.

If some presumptuous person commits such an act, if he is free, he shall be liable to sixty solidi and shall restore everything of the same kind, or purge himself by twelve witnesses. If a slave does this, he shall be subject to capital punishment, and his master shall restore everything of the same kind, because he did not correct or guard his slave so that he would not commit such acts—for if we consume ourselves, we shall quickly perish.

Nevertheless, each person must guard his army so that no plundering may occur within the kingdom.

### (II, 97)

If anyone commits plunder within the kingdom, or takes anything by force from any of our faithful or from one of his men, he shall compensate threefold according to the law the person from whom he took it, and in addition pay our ban to us, namely sixty solidi.

Afterward he shall be brought before us by the count, so that, confined in the *bastonico*, he may suffer punishment until it pleases us. If the act was public, he shall perform public penance for it according to the sanction of the holy canons. If it was secret, he shall perform penance for it according to the counsel of the priests, [Col. 0648B] because, as the Apostle says, plunderers will not possess the kingdom of God unless they perform true penance.

Whoever takes anything from the property of churches shall be judged more severely, because the removal of sacred property is sacrilege, and the person who takes or plunders anything from it is called sacrilegious. Such persons are to be held as expelled from the thresholds of holy Mother Church until they make satisfaction to the Church whom they injured, and they are to be firmly marked as such.

[Col. 0648]

# CHAPTERS OF THE ENVOYS  
*(A.D. 857, February)*

The chapters were first published by Baluze from manuscript no. 4626 of the Royal Library of Paris. We have revised them against the evidence of that same manuscript.

Because of the needs known to you and the excessive disturbances that have occurred in this kingdom, as you know, our lord Charles, gathering at Quierzy in the middle of February many faithful men of his kingdom—bishops as well as abbots, counts, and the other faithful of his kingdom—sent us these chapters, confirmed by them, so that we might announce them to you. You too are to strive to observe them with all fear of God and lawful authority, with justice, together with all the Christians who belong to our district.

### 1

The first chapter contains our admonition concerning the honor of the holy Church of God, which must be observed in every respect by all faithful Christians: its immunities must in no way be infringed [Note: Manuscript B: “according to its law”]; sacred property and its produce must be plundered by no one, because those who plunder what belongs to others are excluded from the kingdom of God, as the Apostle says: “The rapacious will not possess the kingdom of God.”

The ninths and tenths must be faithfully paid. The priests of God and his ministers must not be dishonored or beaten, nor expelled from the Church or received into it without the consent of their bishop. Destroyed churches must be restored.

If anyone transgresses this, let him be struck by the punishment of anathema, restrained by the count’s coercive authority, and condemned through the exaction of the royal ban.

### 2

Nuns, widows, orphans, and the poor must not be oppressed in any way. Their property—whether crops, meadows, or even their hay—must be plundered by no one. Wherever they have been oppressed, they must be relieved by bishops, counts, and royal envoys, [Col. 0649A] and their oppressors must be restrained in every respect, as written above.

### 3

Concerning those who, while residing within the country, commit plunder, break into houses, kill people without cause, stir up feuds, condemn or oppress others, graze upon protected meadows, or devastate the crops of others, our lord commands that they first be judged by episcopal authority, then legally restrained by the counts, and in addition pay our ban, namely sixty solidi.

If they cannot restrain them [Note: Manuscript C: “break them”], they must be brought to the royal presence, so that they may receive fitting punishment.

### 4

Slaves belonging to others who flee into immunities, into our fisc, or into territory under another’s authority, and whom their masters pursue, must be returned or expelled without any payment or opposition, unless it is proved by law that they belong to those holding them. If anyone disputes the matter and refuses to return them, and they later flee, he shall make legal compensation for them.

### 5

No one shall presume to abduct virgins or widows or approach them in any way unless he has legally joined himself to them in marriage. No one shall abduct a woman consecrated to God, violate her, or take her as his wife.

If anyone transgresses this, let him be struck with ecclesiastical anathema and condemned by public judgment.

### 6

Let royal justice be carried out with every diligence.

### 7

Let no one, when moving from his own house to another or traveling on a journey, presume to commit plunder.

### 8

Let every priest record in his parish [Note: “Thus the codex”] all evildoers—namely, plunderers, the rapacious, adulterers, persons guilty of incest, murderers, and thieves—and exclude them from the Church unless they wish to do penance. If they refuse to amend their ways, let them be brought before the bishop.

[Col. 0649]

# THE ASSEMBLY OF CHARLES II AND LOTHAR II AT SAINT-QUENTIN  
*(A.D. 857, March 1)*

[Note: Sirmond says that, because these announcements were confused in the Beauvais manuscript, he followed manuscript 3b of Metz in arranging them, while retaining the heading found in the Beauvais manuscript. We have revised his edition by collating manuscript 3 of the Royal Library of Paris, marked among the *Supplementa Latina* as no. 75.]

## Announcement of Charles and his nephew Lothar at Saint-Quentin, on the Kalends of March in the year 857 from the Lord’s Incarnation

[Note: The Palatine and Metz manuscripts have: “Chapters of King Charles and King Lothar, his nephew, at Valenciennes.”]

[Col. 0649C]

## Announcement of Charles

### 1

We wish you to know that our assembly took place together. After God called our lord from this world, I have always found such counsel in my beloved brother Louis as I needed and as it was fitting for him to show; and I sought it in him. Through his encouragement and intervention, thanks be to God, such unanimity came to exist between me and my brother Lothar of blessed memory as ought to exist between brothers [Note: Manuscript 3: “as ought to exist”].

Because of such matters as had arisen between us, we found with our common faithful that it was necessary for a firm agreement to be made between us, according to God’s will, concerning our common advancement and mutual assistance, and concerning the safety of our sons, our kingdom, and our faithful, as we then made known to our common faithful who were present [Note: Manuscript 3: “then”].

He observed it toward us during his lifetime, and, thanks be to God, we observed it toward him and toward his sons, our nephews, with God’s help, as far as we know and are able. We wish to preserve it for them insofar as they seek it from us.

### 2

After his death, partly because of my illness, as you have heard [Note: Baluze: “and,” rather than “partly”], partly because of the invasion of the pagans, and because of the other circumstances [Note: Baluze corrected this to “occupations”; all manuscripts read “circumstances”] that occurred in our kingdom, until now there was no suitable opportunity for me and this beloved nephew of mine to speak together and to make known to one another our present intentions, which each of us held in his heart toward the other.

### 3

A suitable opportunity did arise, because this beloved nephew of mine spoke with my beloved brother Louis and found in him such a response and counsel as it was necessary for him to find and fitting for Louis to show. This pleased me greatly.

And now, when he spoke with me, he told me that in the firm agreement which I had made with his father, my brother of blessed memory, and in which I received him, he wished to persevere in that reception [Note: Manuscript 3: “in that very reception”; Sirmond and Baluze: “in that reception”]. He wished, with the Lord’s help, to observe in every respect the firm agreement which his father, my brother, had made with me.

### 4

We found with our common faithful that, in view of such necessities as you know and see arising in this kingdom, we should confirm one another, as we have done, so that, for the honor of the holy Church of God, the common advancement and safety of our faithful, and the preservation of our kingdom against anyone whom we may need to resist, we may save and help one another, as an uncle ought rightly to save and help his nephew, and a nephew his uncle.

### 5

Our faithful who were present and gave us this counsel told us that, with the Lord’s help, they were ready to assist us in everything so that we might observe this agreement with one another.

Therefore we wish to hear your consent and intention: whether this too seems good to you, and whether you wish to provide us assistance in it, so that with God’s help and yours we may observe it.

## Announcement of Lothar

As my uncle tells you, insofar as God has granted me knowledge and ability, I wish to persevere in that firm agreement made with my lord, in which he received me and which my lord made with him. With God’s help, I wish firmly to observe the agreement which I made with him.

Again, the proclamation of King Charles.—We wish you to know that, because of the robberies and plunderings which have increased in our kingdom—partly because the pagans have invaded us, and partly because of such occasions as have arisen in our kingdom—we have, according to the suitability of the time, summoned a synod of bishops and some of our faithful. We have considered with them that throughout our entire kingdom our bishops, envoys, and counts should hold assemblies in the individual parishes and counties, and that every man who is obliged to observe the assembly and resides in those counties should attend those assemblies without exception or excuse.

The bishops are to demonstrate to everyone how grave this sin is, what penance it requires, and what condemnation he will incur unless penance comes to his aid. Our envoys are to display to everyone the chapters of the law and of our predecessors concerning this matter, and forbid such great misery [Note: [Col. 0651] “such a great mystery” in 3.] And let everyone know that whoever thereafter presumes to commit such acts will receive both canonical and royal vengeance, as both our bishops and our envoys will then announce more fully to all.

Again, the proclamation of Lothair.—

1. Know also that we have determined that whenever any wrongdoer comes from one of our kingdoms into another, the bishop, envoy, or count from whose jurisdiction he has fled in order not to render justice or suffer a deserved punishment is to inform the envoys in whose jurisdiction he has taken refuge in the other kingdom. Those envoys are to constrain him in such a way that he returns either to make composition or to receive punishment in the place where he committed the offense.

[Col. 0652B] 2. And know that, just as through God’s mercy, through the kindness of my uncles [Note: [Col. 0651] Thus the older reading of the manuscript in 3; corrected to *mei avunculi* (“of my uncle”), which 3b also has.], and through the assistance of my senior and my faithful men [Note: [Col. 0651] *meorum fidelium* (“of my faithful men”), 3c. BAL.], I succeeded my senior in the kingdom, so I wish, with God’s help and with the counsel and assistance of my uncles [Note: [Col. 0651] *meorum avunculorum* (“of my uncles”), 3c.; *mei avunculi* (“of my uncle”), BAL.], and with your assistance, to persevere in every good work and in the observance of those chapters which my senior, together with his brothers, my uncles, considered and confirmed at Marsna by God’s will, for the honor of holy Church, the stability of the kingdom, and the salvation of the faithful of holy Church and of the kingdom.

The third proclamation of Charles.—May almighty God grant us that we may so merit your fidelity and your assistance—which you have always displayed toward us with your entire *barnatus* [Note: [Col. 0651D] That is, *baronatus*, “baronage.”]—as our predecessors merited them from your predecessors in what was good; and we wish to merit them from you in every good way.

[Col. 0651]

## The Assembly of Charles II at Quierzy

*(Year 858, March 21.)* [Note: [Col. 0651] Peter Pithou’s edition of 1588, in *Scriptores coaetanei*, was reproduced by Sirmond and Baluze; the former added from the Laon manuscript the names of the bishops and counts who subscribed to the oath.]

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0651C] The following acts were carried out at the palace of Quierzy in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 858, in the eighteenth year of Lord Charles’s reign, in the sixth indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, happily in the name of God.

### Oath of the Faithful

As much as I shall know and be able, with the Lord’s help, without any deceit or seduction, I shall be your faithful assistant, in counsel and assistance according to my office and according to my person, so that you may hold and govern, with due honor and vigor, the power which God has granted you in the royal name and in the kingdom, according to his will and for your salvation and that of your faithful men. For no man’s sake shall I withdraw myself from this, insofar as God grants me understanding and ability.

### The King’s Oath

And I, insofar as I shall know and be reasonably able, with the Lord’s help, shall honor and protect each one of you according to his rank and person, and shall preserve you, honored and protected, without any deceit, condemnation, or deception. I shall preserve for each one the law and justice appropriate to him. To whoever needs it and reasonably asks for it, I shall show reasonable mercy, just as a faithful king ought rightly to honor and protect his faithful men, preserve for each person the law and justice appropriate to each rank, and extend reasonable mercy to those in need who reasonably ask for it.

For no man’s sake shall I deviate from this, insofar as human frailty permits, through ambition, ill will, or anyone’s improper urging, insofar as God grants me understanding and ability. And if, through frailty, anything contrary to this should be secretly imposed upon me, when I recognize it I shall willingly take care to correct it.

Hincmar, archbishop; Immo, bishop; Yrminfrid, bishop; Hincmar, bishop; Hilduin, abbot.

Hungarius, Engilramn, Isembard, Odo, Osbert, Ratbod, Hunfrid, Odalric, Rhodulf, Engischalc, Herluin, Hitto.

[Col. 0653]

## The Synod of Charles II and Lothair II at Metz

*(Year 859, May 28 and June 4.)* [Note: [Col. 0653] Published by Baronius from the manuscript of Muretus and Antonius Augustinus, volume X of the *Annals*, and subsequently by Sirmond and Baluze.]

### The Bishops’ Embassy to King Louis

These chapters were discussed and confirmed by the bishops at the synod held at the city of Metz, concerning the indulgence of Louis, for the sedition and excesses perpetrated in the kingdom of his brother Charles.

[Col. 0653B]

To our beloved brothers in Christ and fellow priests, namely the envoys of divine peace and of our unity, Hincmar, Gunthar, and Wenilo, archbishops, and our venerable fellow bishops Herluin, Hildegarius, Adventius, Abbo, Hincmar, and Erchanrad, whose names are written below: with the favor of the Lord, and with the assent of our glorious princes Charles and Lothair, we bishops whose names are subscribed below assembled by synodal decree in the city of the Mediomatrici in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 859, in the seventh indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June.

[Col. 0653C] 1. The discord and destructive calamity which recently arose, through the faction of certain seditious men, between our brothers and kings, Louis and Charles, is known—alas, far too well known. Consequently, such grave and dreadful things have been perpetrated in the Church entrusted to us by divine favor for its governance, and in this kingdom, that they are recognized as horrifying even by the hearing of them. If this plague of discord should persist longer, through the activity of the ancient enemy of the human race, you yourselves know better how destructive and deadly it would be.

Therefore, remembering what the Truth commanded when preachers were sent—for the divine Paul says, “We are ambassadors for Christ; we beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God”—we, acting as ambassadors for Christ, send you, dearest brothers, as envoys of the peace beloved by God. Since we have already admonished our glorious princes Charles and Lothair by episcopal authority, we commission you, with the Lord’s help, to go to the glorious lord King Louis, just as the Savior says: “Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you.” For either someone will be predestined to life and will follow the heavenly word he hears, or, if no one wishes to hear, the preacher himself will not be without fruit, since the Lord will repay him with a reward for the labor of his work.

2. After peace has been preached and requested, the embassy of your brotherhood is to be on this condition: that the same king, beloved by us—and, would that he were always so, by God—may obtain the indulgence of the envoys.

3. Namely, if he truly recognizes all that was perpetrated through the persuasion and seduction of wicked men by him in our parishes and those of our brothers, as it is written: “The Lord is near to those who are contrite in heart.” And: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart.” Just as those who seek God deceitfully never deserve to find him, so the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth.

4. And if, after true recognition, he makes a pure confession—for Scripture says again: “Whoever conceals his crimes will not prosper, but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy.” And: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity.”

5. After a pure confession, if he promises that he will amend, according to his strength, what has been wrongly done through worthy fruits of penance, with divine grace going before, assisting, and following him—for it is written, “Produce fruits worthy of penance”—so that each person may seek greater gains from good works through penance in proportion to the greater losses he has inflicted upon himself through guilt; for blessed too are those whose sins are covered by good works. And, as it is written, since he sinned and caused the people to sin, his good works must be as great as the evils they cover.

6. Then, if he promises, in person and with his whole heart and mouth, peace and concord, and promises that, as soon as it can reasonably, feasibly, and suitably be done by common agreement, he will also return in bodily presence to peace and concord with his brother Charles, and remain in peace and charity pleasing to God with our aforementioned princes Charles and Lothair, provided they preserve that same peace and concord toward him; and if he has forgiven those who sin against him their due, just as he desires God to forgive him his own debts—for Scripture likewise says: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God”—then, since all evils are washed away by the good that follows, the evil of discord is so great that, unless it is utterly extinguished, it will in no way permit good to follow, as the Gospel bears witness. Charity is what covers a multitude of sins; without it, even if someone hands over his body to the flames, it will benefit him nothing except for the judgment of condemnation. And the Lord says: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins.”

7. After this, if he promises that he will never again renew such a schism, or one like it, in this holy Church of God and in this Christian people, concerning which it is written: “Whoever is baptized by a dead person and again touches him, what benefit does his washing provide?” He is baptized by a dead person who is cleansed from sin by tears; but after baptism he touches the dead person who returns to his faults after tears. And it is written again: “The dog returns to its vomit, and the washed sow to the muddy mire,” because whoever returns to sin after penance rolls himself about, as it were, in muddy water, removes the cleanliness of life, and makes even the tears themselves filthy before God’s eyes.

8. Then at last let him promise that he will separate himself from the protection and favor of those ruined men through whom he so gravely offended God. And let him cause those who came to him as if for his protection, but rather came to him faithlessly, to come to a proper reckoning at the next assembly before his brother Charles and his nephew Lothair, just as, God as witness, he had already confirmed at Marsna with his own hand, if he is able. Whoever among them is vindicated by a proper reckoning should enjoy his due honor. Whoever cannot be justified by a proper reckoning toward his senior, and asks reasonable mercy for that reason, should obtain such reasonable mercy.

But concerning the man whom a proper reckoning and just judgment condemn, let him, as a Christian king in concord with Christ the King of kings, refrain from involving himself in another’s destruction; for, as Paul says, not only those who do such things but also those who consent to those who do evil are worthy of death. Hence Saint Innocent says that there is little difference between the intention of the perpetrator and the favor of the one who consents. I add further that a person often learns to cease from error when no one consents to him. Again, Saint Paul does not permit Christians even to eat with such people.

And Saint David, when he bound himself entirely to the covenants of inward peace, testifies that he did not maintain concord with the wicked, saying: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become my enemies.” To hate the enemies of God with perfect hatred means to love them for what they were made to be, and to rebuke what they do; to suppress the ways of the wicked and benefit their lives.

Thus Phinehas struck down the sinful citizen who was joining himself to a Midianite, and in his anger appeased God’s anger. And Jehoshaphat, who is praised so highly for his former life, is rebuked when he was nearly destroyed through his friendship with King Ahab; the Lord says to him through the prophet: “Do you give aid to the wicked, and join yourself in friendship to those who hate the Lord? Therefore you deserved the Lord’s anger; but good works have been found in you.”

Thus the sacred canons, promulgated by the Holy Spirit, say that those who, after excommunication or an interdict, communicate with the excommunicated are to be condemned and held under anathema. And Saint Cyprian says that it is the duty of a king to destroy the wicked from the earth and not permit murderers, perjurers, adulterers, poisoners, and sacrilegious persons to live. And it is written in the Book of Kings, with the Lord speaking through the prophet: “Because you have spared a man worthy of death, your life shall stand for his life, and your people for his people.”

How harmful unjustified mercy toward the wicked is is shown in the deed of Saul and Samuel: for the man whom Saul spared, thereby offending the Lord, the prophet Samuel cut into pieces. For just as each person must, for God’s sake, forgive those who sin against him, so the king, as the Lord’s minister, must, for God’s sake, exercise due vengeance against those who sin against God, trample upon the Church, usurp the kingdom, ravage the Christian people, disturb the peace, and betray the fatherland.

Therefore let the king beloved by us know that just as a sick man cannot be healed while a burning iron is held in his body and cooks him from within, so no one can be healed from sin as long as he remains in sin, or as long as he knowingly and willingly associates with someone who remains in sin.

9. Finally, if he promises that henceforth he will, to the best of his ability and reasonably, become God’s helper and co-worker, so that the Church of God—which is one in his kingdom and in the kingdoms of our princes, just as there is one priesthood—may, according to the character of this dangerous time, be restored in every rank; so that God’s priests may obtain their due privileges and ecclesiastical authority, and the people may have justice and peace; then, once you have assembled, and with our—and rather, the divine—Spirit, who is the forgiveness of all sins, through the ecclesiastical power of apostolic authority, forgive him with ecclesiastical mercy and according to canonical custom the sins committed by him and through him in our parishes, grant indulgence to him as he asks for it, and restore him to sacred communion, from which he had deprived himself by communicating with excommunicated persons.

10. Although these crimes, according to the degrees of penance prescribed by the sacred canons, would require penance lasting many years, nevertheless, trusting in God’s mercy, with whom the measure of time is not valued in the same way as the measure of grief, nor abstinence from food in the same way as the mortification of vices, we write this without prejudging the judgments of the Fathers who decreed concerning such matters, but rather following their more humane determination.

The holy African synod says: “For penitents, according to the difference of their sins, the periods of penance are to be determined at the bishop’s discretion.” And Saint Leo, pontiff of the apostolic see, says: “For those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of impending danger, implore the remedy of penance and immediate reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied. For we can impose neither measures nor limits of time upon God’s mercy, with whom true confession suffers no delay in pardon,” as the Spirit of God says through the prophet: “When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved.” And elsewhere: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified.” And again: “With the Lord there is mercy, and abundant redemption with him.”

In distributing God’s gifts, therefore, we must not be difficult, nor disregard the groans and tears of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that the very disposition to repent is conceived through God’s inspiration. The Apostle says: “Perhaps God may grant them repentance, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will.” And Saint Gregory says in a homily on the Gospel: “Let the dead man come out”—that is, let the sinner confess his fault. “Let the disciples then release the man who comes out,” so that the pastors of the Church should remove the punishment deserved by the one who was not ashamed to confess what he had done.

11. After considering these matters, dearest brothers, if you find that the king whom we have said is beloved by us has been brought into conformity with the divine will and sacred authority, absolve him, according to the ministry entrusted to you by God and in our unity. But if not, do not in any way bind yourselves with him whom you cannot absolve; for neither before God nor in synod will you have us as authorities on the matter if, God forbid, you presume to act otherwise. You will have to give an account both in synod and before God for an invalid act.

And if he himself, which may God avert, repeats the acts concerning which we are now sending you to admonish him, let him know that he will return to have everything treated or cut away, both before God’s eyes and in ecclesiastical judgments, as a reopened wound. If anything has been presumed, secretly imposed, or extorted against sacred authority, it will prevail neither in divine examinations nor in divine laws.

Let that same glorious king not thereafter forget what Saint Gregory says: “It must be understood that whoever has committed nothing unlawful is rightly permitted to use what is lawful, and to perform works of mercy while not abandoning, if he does not wish to, the things of the world. But each person ought to cut away from himself that much of what is lawful in proportion as he remembers having committed unlawful things. For the fruit of a good work ought not to be equal in the case of one who has sinned less and one who has sinned more, nor in the case of one who has fallen into no crimes and one who has fallen into every kind of crime. Rather, each person should seek greater gains from good works through penance in proportion to the greater losses he has inflicted upon himself through guilt.”

Therefore let him be admonished by your voice—or rather, by God’s voice—that, repenting of the past and guarding against what threatens and what is yet to come, he should strive to serve God in the earthly kingdom in such a way that he may deserve to reign with Christ in the heavenly kingdom.

### What the Bishops Reported after Completing the Embassy

*(Year 859, June 4.)*

Concerning his indulgence, King Louis said to us on the day before the Nones of June at Worms: “I wish to ask you that, if I have offended your minds in anything, you forgive me for it, so that henceforth we may be able to speak with you securely.”

To this Hincmar, who stood first in rank on his left side, replied: “This matter can quickly come to its conclusion, because what we offer is what you ask.”

At the urging of Grimold [Note: [Col. 0657D] Abbot of Saint Gall and archchaplain.] and Bishop Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0657D] Of Minden.], Hincmar himself said again: “You have done nothing against me for which I should retain harmful resentment in my mind against you, because if I did so, I would not dare approach the altar to offer sacrifice to the Lord.”

When the same Grimold and Theodoric, together with Solomon [Note: [Col. 0658D] Of Constance.], urged him again, Theodoric himself saying, “Do as our senior asks; spare him,” Hincmar himself replied with these same words: “Whatever you have offended against me—that is, against my person—I have forgiven and do forgive. But concerning what has been done wrongly in the Church entrusted to me and among its people, I willingly give you counsel and, according to God, offer assistance, so that you may be safe from it, if you wish.”

The men mentioned above replied: “He speaks rightly.” And our other brothers both agreed with and followed these words. Such and so great an indulgence was granted to him, and no other, nor anything more.

As for the written document delivered to us after it had been confirmed, he himself asked us for nothing, nor did we say anything to him, since we had not yet entered into an accounting with him concerning such matters. After this and other things, however, he said that we had done what we had not done, taking his opportunity from the fact that Gunthar, speaking to him familiarly in order to instruct him and urge him to make satisfaction, reread the written document to him as follows:

“You sent us your letter with the chapters; you came with a case already constituted. We are only two or three here, having hurried here without the others. We cannot enter into those matters before discussing them with our fellow bishops; for, thanks be to God, I have done nothing without their counsel. Afterwards I shall answer concerning it.”

We were expecting him to ask us for counsel concerning his salvation, and then, according to that written document, we would give him counsel. He himself, however, replied in accordance with his rank that he would not enter into that written document before considering it with his own bishops. And so whatever he did concerning the general case of the Church and the people remained with him.

[Col. 0657]

## The Assembly of Charles II, Lothair II, and Their Brother Charles at Saponaria

*(Year 859, June 14.)* [Note: [Col. 0658] Of the proceedings of the assembly at Saponaria, there survive a memorandum presented by King Charles to the synod against Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, and the chapters promulgated there. Pithou published it among the *Contemporary Writers*, as did Goldast; Baronius published it twice in volume X from the manuscript of Antonius Augustinus; it was subsequently published by Sirmond and again, using the Beauvais manuscript, by Baluze.]

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0659A] Memorandum of complaint of Lord King Charles against Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, presented in person by the king’s own hand to the appointed judges Remigius, archbishop of Lyons; Eirard, archbishop of Tours; Wenilo, archbishop of Rouen; and Rodulf, archbishop of Bourges, in the holy synod of the twelve provinces at the parish of Toul, in the suburb of that city called Saponaria, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 859, seventh indiction, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July.

1. Since, as Saint Gregory says, and as you know from ancient custom, kings in the kingdom of the Franks arise from the royal line, the portion of the kingdom among my brother-kings was divinely assigned to me by the Lord and my father of pious memory, the emperor Louis Augustus.

At that time the metropolitan see of Sens lacked a shepherd. In accordance with the custom of my royal predecessors, I entrusted it for governance to Wenilo, then my cleric serving me in my chapel, who had commended himself to me according to the custom of a free cleric and had promised me fidelity by oath. With the consent of the holy bishops of that metropolitan see, I obtained from the bishops, insofar as it depended upon me, that they ordain him archbishop there.

2. After this, the well-known dispute arose concerning the division of the kingdom between me and my brothers. I therefore undertook to hold and govern my portion of the division with mutual oaths—namely, the oaths of ourselves and of our faithful men—just as the leading men of the whole kingdom had also established.

Wenilo swore to me with his own hand, as did the other bishops who were present, that I would henceforth substantially hold that division of the kingdom between me and my brothers. Wenilo also confirmed by oath peace and mutual assistance between me and the aforementioned brother, Louis.

3. After this, by his own election and that of the other bishops, and by the will, consent, and acclamation of the other faithful of our kingdom, Wenilo, together with the other archbishops and bishops, consecrated me as king according to ecclesiastical tradition in his diocese, at the city of Orléans, in the basilica of the Holy Cross. He anointed me with sacred chrism for the governance of the kingdom and raised me upon the royal throne with the diadem and royal scepter.

From that consecration and elevation to the kingship I ought not to have been overthrown or cast out by anyone, at least without the hearing and judgment of the bishops by whose ministry I was consecrated king, who are called the thrones of God, in whom God sits and through whom he gives his judgments. I was prepared, and now am prepared, to submit myself to their paternal corrections and disciplinary judgments.

4. Finally, when seditions in our kingdom began to multiply through irreverent men, with the consent of the bishops and of our other faithful men we wrote together a document setting out how I wished, with the Lord’s cooperation, to act toward them, and how those same faithful men of ours ought thereafter to bring me support through counsel and assistance.

Wenilo subscribed to that document with his own hand at the estate of Bajerna, as you can presently see.

5. Afterwards, when I set out with our faithful men against the pagans, by land and by ship, toward the island of the place called Oscellus, as you know, certain men who had defected from us fled. Wenilo, saying that because of his illness he could not go there, returned to his own see.

While we were ill and staying there in military readiness, our brother Louis, as you know, invaded our kingdom with an enemy force and seditious men from his kingdom. Wenilo went to meet him without my will or permission, and I recognized that he was my supplanter. No other bishop from our kingdom did this.

[Col. 0660B] 6. Thereafter, when I set out with God’s faithful and ours against my aforementioned brother and my enemies, the devastators of the Church and ravagers of the kingdom who were with him, Wenilo provided no assistance, either in person or through the proper support which my royal predecessors and I had been accustomed to receive from the Church entrusted to him—especially since I had devoutly requested it from him.

7. When necessity and the circumstances of the matter required me to withdraw from my aforementioned brother at the estate of Breona, and my brother Louis returned to my portion of the kingdom in order to seize my nephew from me, take my men away from me, and crush my faithful by devastation, Wenilo came to my aforementioned brother Louis, in opposition to me, with whatever assistance he could provide.

With him were the excommunicated men of this kingdom and the seditious men. Wenilo had received letters concerning their excommunication from their fellow bishops, yet he celebrated public Masses for my brother, with whom those seditious men were, in my palace at Attigny, and in the parish and province of another archbishop who was faithful to us, without that archbishop’s permission or the consent of his fellow bishops, celebrating with excommunicated persons or participants with the excommunicated.

He was also present in that council and deliberation in which it was arranged that my nephew Lothair would be taken away through lies, insofar as this depended on his seducers, and that the support and assistance due to me and promised by oath would be withdrawn from me.

8. In addition to the aforementioned counselors of my brother and the public and secret deliberations, Wenilo participated with his special associates and intimate companions in that gathering, together with the excommunicated men whom, as we have said, episcopal judgment and the judgment of the kingdom had condemned, so that my said brother might obtain the portion of the kingdom which he and Wenilo had sworn to me, and in which Wenilo had consecrated me king, while I would lose it.

9. Wenilo was involved in that council and deliberation so that the bishops who owed me the fidelity they had promised, and who ought to have brought me the counsel and assistance confirmed with their own hands, would defect and turn to the service and submission of my brother Louis.

10. From Louis, my brother, Wenilo obtained a grant concerning the abbey of Saint Columba and the property or honors of my kingdom, and secured letters to the envoys Echard and Theodoric ordering them to restore that same abbey.

But in those same letters to the aforementioned envoys, Wenilo obtained from my brother Louis the order that they should be permitted to take stones from the wall of the fortress of Melun, which belongs to the royal authority. From this it is clear that he was endeavoring to court and striving to retain him among the people of this kingdom which God had granted to me.

11. Wenilo was in that council and deliberation with the aforementioned excommunicated men, where it was arranged that those men who were faithful to me and had promised me fidelity by oath, whether willingly or unwillingly, should swear to my brother Louis that they would bring him assistance, so that he might obtain my kingdom against me.

Wenilo not only participated in the counsel, but himself gave this same counsel to my brother Louis against the fidelity to me which he had promised by oath.

12. Wenilo, both personally and through his associates—namely, the aforementioned excommunicated men—obtained from my brother Louis that the vacant bishopric, namely that of the city of Bayeux, should be given to his relative, my cleric Tortold, who had commended himself to me and promised me fidelity by oath.

With the consent of Louis, my brother, he accepted that bishopric in betrayal of me and against the fidelity he had promised me.

13. Finally, after God had given me the strength to recover myself through the support of my faithful against my brother, I went near the city of Wenilo. He knew that I was marching against my brother to recover my kingdom, yet he provided no assistance whatsoever, either personally, in accordance with the counsel he had promised and subscribed, or through the military force which customarily goes out from the Church entrusted to him.

### Chapters

The following matters were discussed, determined, and obtained in the synod of the twelve provinces held in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 859 [Note: [Col. 0661] 858, SIRM.], in the territory of Toul, under the princes Charles, Lothair, and the other Charles.

[Col. 0661D]

1. Let fraternal charity and the concord of peace be restored between the brothers—namely, our glorious princes, Kings Louis and Charles—so that the schism which recently arose in the Church may be reintegrated into the unity of benevolence; so that the condition of the Church, which has almost collapsed, may be restored; so that peace and justice may be secured among the Christian people; and so that those who have defected from the fidelity they owe may be saved through judgment and justice, by a proper reckoning and reasonable mercy, and turned from their perverse endeavor toward what is salutary.

2. Let the bishops, according to their ministry and sacred authority, be united, and [Note: [Col. 0661] Sirmond corrected this by hand to *ut*, as B.] through mutual counsel and assistance govern and correct in the Lord the kings, the leading men of the kingdoms, and the people entrusted to them. Let no one withdraw from mutual support; but [Note: [Col. 0661] Sirmond and the synodal text read *at*; B has *sed synodales* written by hand.] let them take care to attend synodal assemblies according to canonical command, so that the ecclesiastical order—which had already almost been obliterated because synods could not be held on account of the discord of the kings—may, through episcopal deliberation, be restored to its necessary and proper condition. For this reason they also obtained the consent they sought from the kings.

3. Nevertheless, our kings and princes Charles, Lothair, and the other Charles have, thanks be to God, been united according to God’s will, the condition of holy Church, their own salvation, and the salvation of the people, and have been strengthened in that same salutary unity.

4. It was brought before the assembly of the bishops that a certain deacon named Tortold had seized episcopal authority in the city of Bayeux and was troubling and soliciting many people by promises and threats. Therefore the holy synod determined that Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, whose deacon he had been, should, together with three others, summon and hear the aforesaid deacon and determine the matter concerning him according to canonical authority.

If he refuses their jurisdiction, he is to be compelled, with the support of the royal authority, to appear for a hearing. But if he avoids this as well, let him be struck with anathema.

5. Concerning a certain subdeacon, Anscarius, who, while the bishop of the city of Langres was alive and in possession of his office, invaded the episcopal see, a similar sentence was also determined. But when envoys of that same subdeacon intervened, a more lenient sentence was pronounced: namely, that he should confirm by oath that he would never again do anything of this kind through such presumption. We considered it worthy to append the wording of that oath to this chapter:

> I, Anscarius, subdeacon, confess before the Lord and his holy angels, and before the reverence of your holy fatherhood, that against God’s will and against canonical statutes I acted rashly toward Isaac, the venerable bishop, by usurping the see of the holy church of Langres entrusted to him, and by soliciting his clergy, vassals, and entire household. [Col. 0662D] Therefore, for the excess of so great a presumption, through the power which the Lord has granted you by the ministry of your sacred office, I humbly beseech you to grant forgiveness to me, the penitent. Henceforth I shall attempt no such presumption either against that bishop or against anyone else, either in that church or in any other; nor shall I cause him, or any of his clergy or laymen, any impediment in any matter on account of this affair, because I confess that I have sinned gravely. I shall lay no ambush of any disturbance for them, either through myself or through any of my relatives, or through any other person; rather, I shall be their helper, according to my strength and understanding, as he may wish. And those who are enemies of him for this very reason, whoever he wishes, I shall endeavor, if I can, to reconcile to him. [Note: Bellovacensis reads *conligare* (“to bind together”) instead of *conciliare* (“to reconcile”); Sirmondus reads *eidem* (“to him”).] So may God help me, and these holy relics of the saints.

The holy synod also decreed that he should never aspire to the same church of Langres, nor to that of Janua [Note: Bellovacensis reads *Januensem* (“of Genoa”).], which he had previously afflicted in the same manner. And if he should refuse to obey the episcopal commands as stated above, let him incur the sentence previously imposed upon the deacon.

6. Then the glorious king, lord Charles, presented to the holy synod a petition of appeal, the judgment of the electors between himself and Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, who had defected from him, and a document of complaint. [Col. 0663B] Accordingly, in accordance with sacred authority, a period of respite and a postponement of days were granted, and a definite accusation was communicated and granted to the aforesaid archbishop through the bishops and synodical letters, in accordance with the rules divinely promulgated.

7. A question was also raised concerning Atto, bishop of Verdun: namely, that he had been a regular oblate in the monastery of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, concerning which a petition had been presented there, and that, departing from it contrary to ecclesiastical rules, he had reached the episcopal order with less foresight than sacred authority teaches. Accordingly, it was also determined that permission should be given him to come to another synod, as sacred authority decrees.

8. To the bishops of the Britons, who are attempting to sever themselves from their metropolitan against authority, the synod sent a letter in accordance with sacred authority, so that they should return to their metropolitan church, submit to it by due right, and not separate themselves from canonical and episcopal communion. They should by no means communicate with the excommunicated, as the sacred rules decree; and they should admonish Solomon to observe the pledged faith which he promised to the glorious king Charles. Both he and the Britons, while communicating with the excommunicated, should not deprive themselves of sacred communion.

9. The holy synod also sent a letter to the aforementioned excommunicated persons and granted them time to correct themselves until the next forthcoming synod, admonishing them with ecclesiastical compassion to repent and live; for unless they correct themselves, at the future general synod they will be struck with a terrible anathema by unanimous consent. [Col. 0664A]

10. Finally, certain chapters were reread at the same synod, concerning which the opinions of certain brothers were found to disagree. Therefore the bishops agreed that, once peace and tranquility had been restored, God willing, they should meet together and, after bringing forward the judgments of the holy Scriptures and of Catholic teachers, follow by unanimous agreement those that were sounder.

11. At last the general synod humbly petitioned, prostrating itself to the ground before King Charles and Rodulf, archbishop of Bourges, beseeching and adjuring them by the cross and the blood of Christ to take care that the privilege of the monastery of Saint Benedict—which they had confirmed with the aforesaid king’s assent, and which the same Rodulf had subscribed, although he irregularly held the aforesaid abbey—be preserved ratified and unshaken. [Col. 0664B] [Note: Sirmondus reads *Quod si* (“But if”); manuscript B was corrected by hand to *Et si* (“And if”).] But if the negligent abbot, found by dispatched envoys to be incompatible with the sacred rules, should be removed by that fatherly authority, another who was found worthy should be substituted; and the authority of the regular privilege [Note: In the Bellovacensis manuscript, *status* (“condition/status”) is read. Sirmondus corrected it by hand to *auctoritas* (“authority”).] should not, on any pretext, be taken away from that monastery.

12. These were the principal matters decreed in that holy synod. In addition, particular matters concerning the various dioceses were defined as seemed appropriate, in accordance with ecclesiastical authority, and were entrusted to the bishops for execution in their own dioceses.

13. It pleased all those who, as is believed, had gathered by divine prompting for the universal council in the neighborhood of Toul, since they were suffering from the weariness of their calamities and sought somewhere where they might breathe for the sake of consolation. They therefore decreed that, for one another, as long as they lived, all should regularly offer prayers of this kind: namely, that each should celebrate Mass for all the others every week, on Wednesday. After the calling of any one of them, the survivors should arrange that, for the one who had died, seven Masses and an equal number of vigils be offered to the Lord at the sees, while the presbyters of the monasteries or villages should provide three Masses and an equal number of vigils. The death of each person in turn should be made known through pious letters as they circulated. The abbots who were present were also received into this highly beneficial fellowship and joined themselves under the same condition.

[Col. 0663]

# Synod of King Hlothar II at Aachen  
*(9 January 860)*

[Note: It appears in Hincmar’s book *On the Divorce of King Lothar and Queen Theutberga*, Paris edition of 1645, vol. I, pp. 573–574.]

[Col. 0663D] 1. After our lord, the most serene and glorious King Hlothar, with the consent and will of his faithful, joined the aforementioned Theutberga to himself in marriage according to royal custom, and complaints of discord began to arise between them, certain persons told that prince that the aforementioned Theutberga had committed some horrible and unspeakable crime and bore a hidden wound in soul or body, whereby she had grievously offended God; and for that reason she was neither worthy nor permitted, nor was it fitting for him, to have her any longer in marriage.

2. On the basis of the foregoing opinion, which was flying from mouth to mouth concerning her, the aforesaid king frequently spoke both privately and publicly in the presence of his faithful, and discussed the matter with them. A judgment was subsequently made by their counsel, but divine mercy, in its indulgence, did not wish to reveal the truth of the matter. Later, however, when he had reached Italy to visit his brother, the emperor Louis, the crime that had been committed was revealed to him more openly.

[Col. 0665B] 3. Therefore, so that this suspicion and most wicked report concerning the royal wife should not remain longer unexamined or unrefuted, and so that our lord might become more certain and secure about the matter and carry out more freely, according to royal custom, what had to be done, by order of that prince the following persons assembled: in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 860, in the fifth year of his reign, in the eighth indiction, on 9 January, at the palace of Aachen—Guntharius, chief chaplain and archbishop, Teotgaudus, archbishop; Adventius and Franco, bishops; Hegil and Odelingus, abbots; and other faithful men. Recounting to them everything inserted above, he instructed and admonished the aforesaid bishops and abbots, sending them to her to investigate from her the complete truth of the matter concerning the aforesaid report, just as they did. For she confessed to them before God and his angels everything that was in her, and the entire secret became fully apparent to them in accordance with the report that had arisen. On their return, they announced to the aforesaid king that he was not permitted to retain her as his wife.

[Col. 0666A] 4. Guntharius spoke first:

> She confessed to God and to us that she bore an inward wound, though not voluntarily, but inflicted upon her by force. For this reason she judged herself entirely unworthy to approach the royal or marital bed any further, and in no way could she, because of the aforesaid crime—which is shameful to mention—continue to live in marriage with him or with anyone else. Therefore she begged that permission be given her to exchange secular clothing and withdraw from sexual intercourse, without any fraud arising from anger or from any will that she might have against the same king, but so that, once she had withdrawn, he might find consolation in soul and body, and she herself might, through God’s mercy and the prayers of those same bishops, mourn what she had done wickedly.

5. Adventius said:

> This crime and deed has until now been hidden from me; and it is an abomination for you henceforth to come together in the manner of man and woman. Yet if, as before, she was dear and beloved to you, I would give you counsel according to the ministry entrusted to me and would strongly advise that she no longer be joined to your side as a wife, but that, in accordance with her petition, you permit her to receive the veil and change her habit.

6. Archbishop Teotgaudus spoke and agreed in the same way.

7. Abbot Egil, acting on behalf of Theutberga, advised that this should be done and requested that, since she had perpetrated the unspeakable deed not voluntarily but under force and oppression, she be granted the opportunity to receive the veil and a place where the wound that had been inflicted [Col. 0666C] might be healed. He stated that she requested this simply, with no fear weighing upon her and without any circumstance or desire, but for the love of God and the deliverance of her soul.

[Col. 0665]

# Second Synod of King Hlothar II at Aachen  
*(February 860)*

[Note: We have excerpted a fragment of its acts from Hincmar’s *On the Divorce of King Lothar and Queen Theutberga*, Paris edition of 1645, vol. I, pp. 573–575.]

[Col. 0665C] In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 860, in the eighth indiction, in the middle of February, when the glorious kings Louis, Charles, and the younger Hlothar had so decreed, a council of bishops was held at the palace of Aachen, in a general assembly of the nobles from the realm of the blessed Hlothar: Guntharius of Cologne, Teotgaudus of Trier, Wenilo of Rouen, Franco of Tongeren, Hatto of Verdun, Hildegarius of Meaux, and Hilduin of Avranches.

15. Concerning the passage about the woman at issue, we find the following written:

> Moreover, she, supported by no assurance that she could conceal or overcome this, first recounted to the king the sequence of the crime she had committed, as the report had stated. Then she explained the same matter in detail to certain bishops and laymen together. Later, at her own request, a written statement of her confession was drawn up, and in the presence of all of us and of many laymen she placed it in the hand of the glorious King Hlothar. Immediately afterward she spoke openly before everyone:
>
> “My lord king,” she said, “for God’s sake, and for the sake of your reward, I beg you to allow me to perform penance, since both by word and in writing I confess that I am unworthy of marital union. Therefore, prostrate, I humbly beg that from now on and hereafter you not deny me what can thereafter assist my salvation.”
>
> The text of that document therefore contained these words and this meaning:
>
> “I, Thietbrihc, whom the imprudence of the female sex and human frailty have deceived, and whom consciousness of guilt bites, for the hope of the salvation of my soul and for fidelity toward my senior, make this true confession before God and his holy angels, and before the venerable bishops and noble laymen, and confess as follows: my brother Hucbert, a cleric, corrupted me when I was a young girl and practiced and committed fornication upon my body contrary to natural usage. I testify to this, with my conscience as witness: I was persuaded neither by any malicious suggestion nor compelled by violent necessity, but of my own free will confessed the truth of the matter [Col. 0667A] as it is. So may the Lord help me, who came to save sinners and promised true forgiveness to those who confess their sins simply and truthfully, if I invent nothing, if I pronounce the truth with my own voice, and confirm the deed by the handwriting of this document. For it is more bearable for me, an imprudent and deceived woman, to confess my guilt simply before human beings than to blush before the tribunal of the Lord and suffer eternal woe.”

16. When this had been read aloud, horror and grief struck the minds of those present alike, and groans filled the hearts of the priests at the great license of diabolical deceit. But although her confession appeared credible, nevertheless, lest perhaps the woman, who had often said this, should be lying because of some deception or fear of someone, we addressed the aforementioned king again and pressed him with solemn entreaties to tell us whether he had compelled her by persuasion or threats to accuse herself falsely. In reply, he declared to us with the strongest assurances that he had persuaded her to confess only the truth of the matter, and that he had deliberately done nothing further in that affair.

He also related to us at that very time how, after he first heard of the unspeakable deed and believed it true, he had grieved over it, how deeply he had been displeased by this unexpected evil and wholly unwanted misfortune, and how, finally, he had wished to bear the foul matter patiently and, if the report had not already spread so far, to conceal it—and had done as much as he could. For this reason he knowingly accepted and endured a false judgment in place of a genuine investigation, so that, if possible, such incredible disgrace might appear and thus vanish from the world, and he himself might not remain before the world marked by so shameful a stain and ruinous offense.

But after the revealed infection could no longer remain hidden, and he himself could no longer bear the weight of so great a reproach—especially since, traveling through the regions of Burgundy and Italy, he recoiled from the disgrace, which had been excessively defamed and widely spread—he did not allow the matter to remain silent any longer without examination by the bishops. Indeed, he repeatedly declared, with many tearful sighs, that this had been impressed upon him concerning the aforesaid woman and affirmed by many people even in this kingdom, not without a groan.

17. We therefore approached the same woman again, first privately and then in the presence of laymen, and with divine adjuration exhorted her through many admonitions not to bring a false charge against herself in any way. We also sought to deter her from doing so by threats of eternal punishments. Again, with our counsel, assistance, protection, and defense, we assured her of security against every ambush or act of violence, asking only that she then confess to us confidently whether she had been persuaded or compelled to accuse herself.

At this she rebuked us with a harsh look:

> “Do you think,” she said, “that I would have wished to destroy myself in this way for anything in the world? As I confessed before, so I confess now, and so I shall confess.” [Col. 0668A]

She asked only, for the love of God, that we grant her at once the mercy she desired.

Then our concern asked whether, if her petition were granted, she intended thereafter to raise any complaint about the matter or ever to devise any ambush. Our unanimous response immediately addressed this obligation as follows:

> “Know, daughter, that if you await our judgment concerning you and your confession, so that the censure of divine and canonical authority may take hold of you and the unbreakable chain of the priests may begin to bind you, then whatever you may still recover—if indeed you can recover anything—you will not, as we judge, recover it thereafter.”

The laymen also admonished her at length, especially her own relatives and friends, who urged and reproached her with great force lest she deceive herself. Yet she remained unmoved in her confession, as though the secret of her conscience were visibly apparent to the eyes of those who observed it.

18. Why should we delay longer? Once every doubt had been removed and the truth of the matter discovered, this crime—new in its very hearing and horrifying because of its unspeakable pollution, especially since its stench had long been spread far and wide by innumerable reports—seemed not to be something to be treated with any light care or indulgence, lest it inflict a pestilential corruption upon those present and those yet to come unless it were uprooted more severely and diligently.

For there is no doubt that natural intercourse between brother and sister does not deserve temporary remission of honor; nothing remains but vengeance and penance. Nor does the condemnable crime have any opportunity to proceed further, since it immediately cuts off entirely from the transgressors many things that had been permitted. For this reason it has occurred all the more rarely in the world, since it is established that no one has presumed to take an example from it for himself, because it could never have been considered venial in the esteem of the world.

But whenever any persons have fallen into this misery, it did not happen through the example of another; rather, it was a recent and almost new fall through the ancient deceit of the devil and a similar impulse and precipitous weakness. This kind of contagion, which is now beginning to be new and was previously unknown to us, must be guarded against, lest it generate a diseased pestilence and incurable plague for the human race. The pernicious origin must therefore be eradicated completely, so that it leaves no example and no opportunity for the weak—lest, God forbid, such a custom take root by which someone avoids natural intercourse among blood relatives but grows accustomed more freely to fornication contrary to nature within his own kin, considering this a light evil.

19. Having therefore considered and carefully examined these matters, we decreed that the pollution of incest, mournful and breathed forth into public view, should be cleansed by the satisfaction of public penance.

[Col. 0669]

# Assembly of Louis, Charles, and Hlothar at the Basilica of Saint Castor at Confluentes

*(June 860)*

[Note: “In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 860, these are the chapters of the venerable kings Hlothar, Louis, and Charles, which they confirmed among themselves on 12 June in the district of Trecht, beside Trecht itself: ‘That all past evils,’ etc.” The middle portion is missing. “3, 3b, 3c.” The fact that these agreements were made not at Trecht but at Confluentes is clear from the annals of Rudolf and Prudentius and from the chapters issued by Charles after his return.]

[Note: The assembly of the kings in the church of Saint Castor at Confluentes is mentioned by Rudolf and Prudentius in their *Annals*; and Rudolf preserved the form of the oath sworn by King Louis. Nevertheless, the fuller acts of the assembly were first published by Baronius in his *Annals* under the year 860, found in a manuscript of Antonius Augustinus copied from an old exemplar of Muretus; that text, however, is clearly poorly copied in many places. Sirmondus presented Charles’s proclamation from manuscript 3b of Laon, Beauvais, and Metz; Baluzius, using manuscript 3c, the Palatine manuscript, reprinted Sirmondus’s edition. We have revised the text with the aid of manuscript 3, the Paris royal manuscript among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75 bis, and by using Baronius’s edition.
