Manuscripts 3, 3b, and 3c contain only the chapters to be observed by all, the names of the nobles, and the oath of King Louis. The chapters of King Charles that immediately follow, delivered to his envoys after his return from Confluentes, show how he carried out the Confluentes agreement; although they were also found in Baronius’s manuscript, they were first published by Sirmondus.]

## Proclamation of Lord Charles

[Note: This entire proclamation is absent from manuscripts 3, 3b, 3c, and from Baronius.]

[Col. 0669A]

You know how certain men, fearing God less than was necessary, persuaded our brother Louis this year, under a supposedly good intention, to come into our kingdom in the manner you yourselves know. In this matter God and your fidelity helped us as you also know well. Afterward, with the Lord’s help, this dearest nephew of ours labored so that peace might be made between us, as is right, and so that, at the bishops’ admonition, he might return to that charity and fraternal concord without which no Christian can be saved.

For this reason he sent his envoys to us and first conveyed to us a message that seemed impossible to us. Then, because we did not accept that message, his envoys delivered another message to us. Since this seems both salutary according to God and useful according to the world, we wish to tell it to you; and if it seems to you as it does to us, we wish to accept it with your counsel and bring to the necessary result whatever God grants. [Note: In what follows, the material before “Chapters” is placed below it in manuscripts 3, 3b, and 3c.]

These are the names of the bishops who, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 860, on 5 June, in the sacristy of the basilica of Saint Castor, considered with the noble and faithful laymen the compact which our glorious kings Louis, Charles, and Hlothar had made among themselves on 7 June in the same monastery, and who accepted these chapters as matters to be preserved by all.

[Note: “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 860” is absent from manuscripts 3, 3b, and 3c.]  
[Note: “and faithful laymen” is absent from Baronius.]  
[Note: Baronius reads “most glorious.”]  
[Note: Baronius reads “on 8 June.”]  
[Note: Baronius reads “to be observed.”]

Hincmar, Guntharius [Note: Baronius reads *Iuntherius*.], Altfrid, Solomon, Adventius [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Adventus*.], Hatto [Note: Baronius reads *Atto*.] [Note: “of Verdun.”], Franco [Note: Absent from manuscript 3 and from Baronius.] [Note: “of Tongeren.”], Theuderic [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Deodericus*.], Leutbert, Gebehard, Christian [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Cristianus*.] [Note: “of Auxerre.”], Abbot Vulfad [Note: “of Resbach” (*Resbacensis*).], Abbot Witgar [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Withgarius*.].

These are the names of the laymen:

Chuonrad [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Chonradus*; Baronius, *Conradus*.], Evrard [Note: Baronius reads *Euerardus*.], Adalard [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Adelardus*; absent from Baronius.], Arnust [Note: Absent from Baronius.], Warnar [Note: Baronius reads *Vicarnarius*.], Liutfrid [Note: The initials *l. hr.* are absent from Baronius.], Hruodulf [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Hrodulfus*.], Erkingar [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Erchingarius*; Baronius, *Exstangarius*.], Gislebert [Note: The initials *g. r.* are absent from Baronius.], Ratbod [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Rathbodo*.], Arnulf, Hugo [Note: The initials *h. i. ch.* are absent from Baronius.], also Chuonrad [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Conradus*.], Liuthar [Note: Baronius reads *D. L.*.], Berengar [Note: Baluzius reads *Beringarius*.], Matfrid [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Mathfridus*. Baronius omits *m. b. s. h.*.], Boso, Siger, Hartmann [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Harmannus*.], Liuthard [Note: Absent from manuscript 3; Baronius reads *Iuthardus*.], Richwin [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Richonius*. Baronius omits *r. w.*.], Wigrich, Hunfrid [Note: Baronius reads *Hunfriardus*.], Bernold [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Bernolfus*; absent from Baronius.], Hatto [Note: Absent from Baronius.], Adalbert [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Adelbertus*.], Burchard [Note: Baronius omits *b. ch.*.], Christian [Note: Baronius omits *b. ch.*; manuscript 3 reads *Cristianus*.], Leutulf [Note: Baronius gives the following expanded or differing sequence: *Leuthulphus, Hernodulphus, Adalardus, Luitfridus, Gislebertus, Huto, Matfridus, Boso, Rithuenus, Bernoldus, Burchardus, Hessi, Arnustus, Hynodulphus, Ratbotus, also Chuanradus, Siger, Harmainus, Wigricus, Atto, Christianus, Herimannus, Sigardus*.], Hessi, Herimann [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Eyrmannus*.], also Hruodulf [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Rodolfus*.], Sigehard [Note: Sirmondus reads *Sigeardus*.] [Col. 0670B].

## Oath of King Louis confirming the agreement

[Note: This is also found in Rudolf’s *Annals*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores* I, p. 373. The heading is absent from manuscript 3.]

From now on, and for as long as I live, I shall be a true helper, insofar as God grants me knowledge and ability, and insofar as they heed me and ask it of me, to this brother of mine, Charles, and to my nephews Louis, Hlothar, and Charles, for the will of God and the condition, honor, and defense of his holy church, for our common salvation and honor, for the safety and peace of the Christian people entrusted to us, and for the preservation of law, justice, and right reason.

I shall be a helper to maintain their kingdoms with sincere assistance and sound counsel, according to what is reasonably and salutarily possible for me; and neither in life [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *via*, “way.”] nor in limb nor in their kingdoms shall I give them evil counsel, provided that they make and maintain a similar promise toward me. [Note: This is where Rudolf’s text ends.] So may God help me, and these holy relics. [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *si*, “if.”]

## Chapters to be preserved by all

1. That the abolition of all past evils and hostilities, acts of betrayal, evil schemes, undertakings [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *monitionum* (“admonitions”) instead of *molitionum* (“undertakings”).], and injuries committed against one another should take place among us and with us [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *apud vos* (“with you”) instead of *apud nos* (“with us”).], and that all malice and resentment should be torn completely from our hearts, so that [Note: Baronius reads *et* (“and”) instead of *ut* (“so that”).] henceforth nothing may arise from it in our memory merely for the repayment of evil or hostility, reproach or insult [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *imperii et de* instead of *improperii*; the reading is uncertain].

2. That, with the Lord’s cooperation, the goodness of true charity should henceforth always remain among us, from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith, without deceit or pretense; that no one should covet or give evil counsel concerning the kingdom or faithful men of his equal [Note: Baronius reads “his brother.”], or anything pertaining to royal salvation, prosperity, or honor [Note: Baronius reads “the honor of the kings”]; and that no one should willingly accept fabricated lies or slanders through secret whisperers.

3. That each person should faithfully assist his equal [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “his equal”; Baronius reads “his brother”], wherever necessity requires and he is able, either personally or through his son or his faithful men, by counsel and aid, so that he may rightly obtain his kingdom, faithful men [Note: Baronius reads “a faithful man.”], prosperity, and royal honor. [Col. 0671C] Each person should truly demonstrate toward the other, with mutual zeal, that if adversity befalls his equal [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *pari* (“equal”); Baronius, “brother.”], he will grieve for him in a brotherly manner, and rejoice in his prosperity. And just as we have now confirmed that we shall preserve such fidelity among ourselves from this point forward, so each survivor shall preserve it for his brother’s children if that brother dies. [Note: Baronius omits “he who survives.”]

4. Since the peace and tranquility of the kingdom are often disturbed by wandering and disrespectful men who act according to tyrannical custom [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *et tyrannica consuetudine inreverentes*; Baronius reads “men who rush in” (*inruentes homines*) instead of *inreverentes homines*], we wish that, if such a person comes to any one of us so that he may evade account and justice for what he has done [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *ut de his quae egit rationem et justitiam*; it also omits *subterfugere possit*; Baronius reads *subterfugere non possit* (“may not be able to evade”).], none of us should receive or retain him for any other purpose [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *illum aliter* (“receive him otherwise”) and omits *vel retineat*] than to bring him to right account and due correction [Note: Manuscript 3 omits this phrase].

And if he evades a right accounting [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *si rationem rectam*], let us all together pursue him into whichever kingdom he has entered until he is brought to account or erased from the kingdom. [Note: Baronius reads “into whose kingdom he has come, let them pursue him.”]

[Col. 0672A] 5. The same must likewise be done concerning anyone who, because of some capital and public crime, is reproved or excommunicated by any bishop [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *corripitur vel*], or who, having committed a crime that incurs excommunication [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *aut de excommunicatione crimen faciens*], changes his kingdom and the administration of a king [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *regimen regis immutat* (“changes the king’s administration”) instead of *regnum et regis regimen mutat*] so that he may avoid undertaking the penance he owes [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *aut a suscipienda poenitentia*] or completing lawfully the penance he has undertaken. Sometimes, while fleeing, he also takes away with him an incestuous female relative [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *incertam* (“uncertain”) instead of *incestam* (“incestuous”)], or a nun, or a woman who has been abducted, or an adulteress whom he was not permitted to keep there [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *quam illic ei liceat habere* (“whom it is permitted for him to keep there”) instead of *quam illic ei non licebat habere*].

When such a man has been made known to us by the bishop to whose care he belongs [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *ad cujus curam pertinet* (“to whose care he pertains”)], he must be diligently sought out [Note: Manuscript 3 reads the plural *perquirantur* (“they must be sought out”)], so that he may find no place in the kingdom of any one of us where he can remain or hide [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *ne morandi vel latendi locum in regno alicujus nostrum inveniat*; Baronius reads “where he may hide”], and infect God’s faithful and ours with his disease [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *inficiant* (“they may infect”)]. Rather, he must be restrained by us or by the officers of the state, and compelled to return, together with the devilish spoil [Col. 0672B] that he took with him, to his own bishop, and to undertake the penance owed for whatever public crime he has committed [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *suscipere compellantur* (“they must be compelled to undertake it”); the intervening text is missing], or to complete lawfully the penance he has undertaken.

6. [Note: Chapters 6–9 had not been published at Marsna.] No bishop should exclude a sinful person from the church and Christian communion until he has admonished him, according to the evangelical precept, so that he may return to correction and penance. If the sinner [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *quia* (“because”) instead of *qui* (“who”).], after being admonished, remains disobedient and incorrigible and refuses to return to correction, then the bishop himself, or through his officers, should approach the royal or public authority, so that the sinner may be restrained and return to correction and penance. If he cannot in this way be brought to correction, then, in accordance with ecclesiastical laws, he should be separated from ecclesiastical communion by a medicinal separation.

[Col. 0672C] 7. To those men who, in disturbances such as occurred during these past years, have sinned against God, his holy church, and us, if they acknowledge themselves truthfully and ask forgiveness [Note: Baronius reads “ask pardon.”], and thereafter wish to be truly faithful to us, and remain peaceful and quiet in our kingdoms and obedient to laws and justice, reasonable mercy should be shown—not only in the forgiveness of what they have committed and the granting of their property, but also in the bestowal of honors according to our reasonable capacity.

8. Concerning robbery and plunder, conspiracies and seditions, and the abduction of women, the ecclesiastical and Christian laws and the chapters of our ancestors contain provisions; these provisions should be preserved in every respect and by everyone. [Note: Manuscript 3 reads the singular “let it be preserved.”]

[Col. 0672D] 9. Other chapters of those same ancestors of ours, concerning the honor, immunity, and preservation of the holy church, and also concerning royal honor and strength [Note: Baronius omits “and strength.”], and concerning the law and justice of the people entrusted to us, should likewise be preserved in every respect and by everyone.

[Col. 0673A] 10. That our faithful men, each in his own order and condition, should truly be secure concerning us, because from now on we shall neither condemn nor dishonor anyone contrary to law and justice, authority and right reason, nor oppress anyone or afflict anyone by unlawful schemes [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *et justitiam, vel auctoritatem ac justam rationem, aut* and *vel indebitis machinationibus adfligemus*].

Rather, with the common counsel of those who are truly faithful to us [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *illorum scilicet veraciter nobis fidelium*], and in accordance with God’s will and the common salvation [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *et commune salvamentum*], we shall give our assent to whatever pertains to the restoration of God’s holy church and the condition of the kingdom [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *et statum regni*], to royal honor, and to the peace of the people entrusted to us [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *populi commissi nobis*].

This is on the condition that they not only fail to contradict or resist us in carrying these matters out [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *in hoc* and *non solum non sint nobis contradicentes*], but also be our faithful and obedient men [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *sic sint nobis*], and true helpers and cooperators, with sound counsel and sincere assistance, in accomplishing the matters stated above [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *et cooperatores vero consilio et sincero auxilio* and the following words], just as, rightly, each person in his own order and condition ought to be toward his prince and his lord.

11. So that, being thus joined together—we brothers and our nephew with one another, we with our faithful men, our faithful men with us, and all of us together with God—we may be reunited, and, so that he may be gracious to us, may offer to him a devout gift. And let every one of us, without his own excuse or justification, acknowledge the matters in which, individually or collectively, we have acted or consented to act against his commandments and the decrees of his saints, in ecclesiastical order or in the condition of the kingdom, and let us bring each matter forward publicly. Let none of us spare, in secular matters, either himself, his friend, his relative, or his confederate—indeed, let him not spare even himself—so that he may be able to spare him spiritually and for his salvation. Rather, as we stated in the preceding chapter, let us strive with all our strength, by true counsel and sincere assistance, to correct these matters collectively and zealously, as soon as we can reasonably do so.

12. And if any one of the subjects, in whatever order or condition, withdraws from this agreement or removes himself from it, or contradicts this common decree, the senior rulers, together with their truly faithful men, shall carry out these provisions according to God’s will, law, and right reason, whether the man who resists and contradicts the divine counsel and decree and this agreement wishes it or not.

And if any one of the senior rulers withdraws from this agreement or removes himself from it, or—God forbid—contradicts this common decree, when several of our senior rulers’ faithful men and the leading men of the kingdoms have assembled, then, on the counsel of those senior rulers who have observed these provisions, and by the judgment and common consent of the bishops, the Lord shall determine what is to be done with the man who, after having been duly admonished, has persisted in being incorrigible.

And so that the chapters written above may be observed by us more resolutely and inviolably, with the Lord’s help, and so that we may be more certainly believed to observe them, we have confirmed them below with our own hands.

**Announcements of King Louis at Confluentes, in the Germanic language.**

[Note: [Col. 0673] S. and B. read “announcement.”]

[Note: [Col. 0673] S. and B. read “Confluentes.”]

[Note: [Col. 0673] S. and B. consistently read “Germanic.”]

1. You know what has happened in this kingdom. And therefore we have assembled here so that, with God’s help and the counsel of our faithful men, we may deliberate concerning God’s will and the condition of the holy Church, our common salvation and honor and yours, and the peace of the Christian people.

2. We laid this matter before the bishops and our other faithful men, so that they might discover how we could unite ourselves for carrying out the things we have mentioned. And we want you to know that, just as they discovered and showed us in writing, we have been united with one another, as brothers ought rightly to be, and we together with this nephew of ours, and he with us. We have also received his brothers, our nephews, together with us in this firm union, provided that they too establish and observe this bond of firmness toward us.

[Note: [Col. 0673] Bar. reads “reported” instead of “showed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0673] Bar. reads “his brothers and our nephews.”]

[Note: [Col. 0673] Bar. reads “provided that they establish.”]

3. And know that from now on we do not want anyone among us to convey any words except such as are pleasing to God and concern our common salvation and our honor, so that we may be toward one another as brothers, and as uncles with nephews and nephews with uncles ought to be. And if anyone attempts to do otherwise, let him be brought forward for account and punished in such a way that no one else will attempt to do anything similar.

[Note: [Col. 0673] Bar. reads “similarly.”]

4. And we want the churches and houses of God, the bishops and men of God, clerics, monks, and nuns to have such protection and honor as they had in the time of our predecessors.

[Note: [Col. 0673] Bar. lacks “and.”]

5. And we want you and our other faithful men to have such law, justice, and protection in our kingdoms as your predecessors had in the time of our predecessors; and we want to have among you, in our royal name, such honor and rightful authority as our predecessors had among your predecessors. Let justice and law be preserved for all; and let poor men have such defense as law and custom provided in the time of our predecessors, and as our faithful men here have unanimously agreed and shown us in writing. With their counsel we agree and jointly wish these provisions to be observed.

And if anyone wishes to disturb this arrangement, let none of us receive him except so that he may be brought either to a rightful hearing or to a reasonable grant of pardon.

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. lacks “they had” through “they had.”]

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. lacks “here.”]

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. lacks “and wish them to be observed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. lacks “either.”]

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. lacks “or to.”]

6. Moreover, concerning the robberies and depredations that many now customarily maintain almost as law, from this day forward we ban them under God’s ban and by our word, so that no one may presume to do such things any longer. Rather, let everyone remain within the country in peace and without oppression of the poor and of those dwelling around him. When coming to the army, to the assembly, or to the royal court, let him depart from his own property and household so provided that he can come in peace, remain with us, and return to his home.

Whoever transgresses this, we want the matter corrected in those transgressors according to the custom that existed in the time of our predecessors and according to what is contained in their chapters.

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. lacks “moreover.”]

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. lacks “under God’s ban.”]

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. lacks “by our word.”]

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. lacks “the custom.”]

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. reads *de suo scuvarintaes* (“provided from his own resources”); the marginal gloss is *guarni.* (“provided”).]

7. Likewise, concerning conspiracies and the abduction of women—widows, girls, and nuns alike—we ban such acts under God’s word and ours, so that no one may presume to commit them in our kingdoms. If anyone presumes to do so, he shall be compelled to make amends according to the law and as provided in the capitularies of our forefathers.

King Charles announced these same matters in the Roman language and recapitulated most of them in the Germanic language.

After this, Lord Louis said to his brother, Lord Charles, in the Roman language: “Now, if it pleases you, I wish to have your word concerning those men who have come over to my allegiance.”

And Lord Charles said in a louder voice, in the Roman language: “For the sake of God, of love for him, and of his favor, I wholly pardon those men who acted against me as you know and who came to my brother, for everything they did wrong against me. I grant them their allodial estates deriving from inheritance and acquisition, and what they held by gift of our senior ruler, except what came from my gift, provided that they give me a pledge of firmness that they will be peaceful in my kingdom and live there as Christians ought to live in a Christian kingdom.

“This is conditional upon my brother granting in the same way to my faithful men, who did nothing wrong against him and assisted me when I needed it, the allodial estates that they hold in his kingdom. As for the allodial estates they held by my gift, and also the honors, I shall deal with those who return to me voluntarily as I shall better determine with him.”

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. reads “what they did excessively” instead of “what they did wrong.”]

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. reads “who nevertheless acted” instead of “who did nothing wrong.”]

[Note: [Col. 0675] Bar. lacks “return to me.”]

And Lord Lothair said in the Germanic language that he consented to the chapters announced above and promised that he would observe them.

Then Lord Charles again spoke in the Roman language concerning peace, admonished them to go in health and safety by God’s grace, prayed that he might see them again safe and well, and brought the announcements to an end.

**Chapters of Charles, delivered to his envoys after his return from Confluentes.**

These are the instructions that Lord Charles, having returned from Confluentes, directed to be announced and observed throughout his kingdom with the counsel of his faithful men.

Let our envoys, traveling through the country, carry out the following:

1. In each of their circuits, let them make known the bond of firmness established between us and our dearest brother and our beloved nephews.

2. Let them also announce the chapters accepted by us and our common faithful men at Confluentes.

[Col. 0676C] 3. Let them also make known the chapters that we previously sent throughout our kingdom for observance, together with the episcopal chapters and those of our imperial forefathers; and let the announcement that we have now made at Confluentes be made known to all. From all who acted against us in the manner that is known, and concerning whom our dearest brother made a request, let them receive a pledge of firmness, provided that these men wish to hold allodial estates in our kingdom, as is written in our announcement.

This is nevertheless subject to the condition that, if the greater men wish, they shall come to us and make that pledge of firmness in our presence; their men, however, shall make the same pledge before our envoys.

[Note: [Col. 0675D] “That is, let them announce it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0676D] “The announcement.”]

4. Let our envoys return to those who have made the pledge of firmness their allodial estates—those which they held by inheritance or by an acquisition not deriving from our gift, and those which our senior ruler, the lord emperor, gave them—provided that they show his charters, to the extent that the relevant matter is contained in those charters.

5. Let them carefully record all who have made the pledge of firmness and to whom they have returned the allodial estates. If any refuse to make it, let them likewise record them and report them to us.

6. Concerning the robberies, acts of violence, and other injustices that they committed in our kingdom during these past years, after this disturbance arose, let our envoys endeavor to establish peace as far as they reasonably can. If pledges arising from that pacification come to our side, let them, by our authority, wholly pardon the offenses, as our dearest brother requested of us, on condition that they do not commit such acts thereafter.

7. Concerning the pacification of those who, while residing in our kingdom, committed robberies, acts of violence, and other injustices through their unjust presumption after God showed us his more gracious mercy: if pledges come over to our side, let our envoys record them and report them to us, so that we may determine what then seems appropriate to us.

8. Let them carefully ensure by every means that peace is observed throughout our kingdom in accordance with what we have made known and with the provisions of the chapters sent out by us. Let them diligently investigate how each person has observed it, without regard for any person, so that they may report the truth about it to us. Whatever they cannot carry out themselves of what we have commanded, let them refer to the senior envoys appointed over that circuit, so that with their counsel and assistance they may complete everything.

The pledge of firmness that our envoys are to receive from the men mentioned above is this:

> “From this day forward I will neither give evil counsel against nor wage war against the kingdom of Charles, son of Emperor Louis. So may God help me, and these holy relics.”

The confirmation of our senior rulers, the kings, made at Confluentes, is as follows:

“For God’s will, the condition, honor, and defense of his holy Church, their common salvation and honor, the protection and peace of the Christian people entrusted to them, and the preservation of laws, justice, and right reason, to the extent that God grants them knowledge and ability, they will be mutual helpers in maintaining their kingdoms, with true counsel and sincere assistance, according to what is reasonably and beneficially possible for them. None of them, whether in life, in limb, or in his kingdom, will give evil counsel against his equal.”

Their announcement is as follows:

1. They wish from now on to observe, and with the Lord’s help will observe, what is contained in the pledge of firmness stated above.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] See above, cols. 671–73, chapter 12.]

2. They do not want anyone among them to convey any words except those pleasing to God and pertaining to their common salvation and honor. If anyone presumes otherwise, let him be brought forward and punished in such a way that no one else will attempt to do anything similar.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Ibid., chapter 3.]

3. They want the churches and houses of God, the bishops and men of God, clerics, monks, and nuns to have such protection and honor as they had in the time of their predecessors.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Ibid., chapter 4.]

4. They want their faithful men to have such law, justice, and protection in their kingdoms as their predecessors had in the time of their predecessors; and they themselves, the kings, are to have such honor and rightful authority as their predecessors had. Let justice and law be preserved for all. If anyone wishes to disturb this arrangement, let none of them receive him except so that he may be brought either to a rightful hearing or to a reasonable grant of pardon.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Ibid., chapter 5.]

5. As for those men in this kingdom who acted contemptuously against their senior ruler, Lord Charles, if they acknowledge their fault, he wishes, for God’s sake and because of his brother’s entreaty, to pardon them whatever they did wrong against him. As prescribed above, he grants them their allodial estates deriving from inheritance and acquisition—provided that these did not come from his own gift—and also the allodial estates they held by gift of Lord Emperor Louis, if they make him the pledge of firmness specified above.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Ibid., at the end: Charles’s declaration.]

6. They have also firmly banned robberies and depredations, sworn associations and conspiracies, and the abduction of women—widows, girls, and nuns alike—so that from now on no one may presume to commit such acts. Whoever presumes to do so shall be compelled to make amends according to divine and human laws and according to the chapters of the emperors and their predecessors.

They also require that everyone remain within the country in peace and without oppression of the poor and those dwelling around him; and that, when coming to the army, the assembly, or the royal court, he depart from his own property and household so provided that he can come, remain, and return home in peace.

[Note: [Col. 0678D] Ibid., chapters 6 and 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0678D] Ibid., chapter 6.]

**Summary of the chapters accepted at Confluentes by our senior rulers, the kings, and their faithful men.**

1. Their concord, fraternal union, and mutual assistance, as contained in their announcement.

[Note: [Col. 0678D] Ibid., chapters 1–6.]

2. The pardon granted to those who acted contemptuously in this kingdom, if they acknowledge their fault, wish thereafter to guard against such acts, and wish to live peacefully in the kingdom, as contained in their announcement.

[Note: [Col. 0678D] Ibid., chapter 7.]

[Col. 0679A] 3. Law and justice are to be preserved for all, each person in his own condition and order.

[Note: [Col. 0679D] Cols. 671–73, chapters 9–10.]

4. Everyone is to guard against robberies, depredations, sworn associations, conspiracies, seditions, and the abduction of women. Whoever thereafter presumes to commit such acts shall, as contained in their announcement, be compelled to make amends according to ecclesiastical and secular laws and according to the chapters of the predecessor kings—through monetary compensation, through *harmiscara*, and through the penance to be received from the bishop of his diocese.

[Note: [Col. 0680D] Ibid., chapter 8.]

The chapters of the emperors, Lord Charles and Lord Louis, concerning such matters—of which we set down a few of the many here—are these:

*(BENED. II, 383.)* If anyone commits robbery within the kingdom, or forcibly takes anything from any of our faithful men or from one of their men, let him pay legal compensation in triple for whatever he took, and in addition pay us our ban, that is, sixty solidi. Afterwards let him be brought before us by the count and confined in prison until it pleases us, suffering punishment. If the act was public, let him perform public penance for it according to the sanction of the holy canons. If it was secret, let him perform penance for it on the counsel of the priests, for robbers, as the Apostle says, will not possess the kingdom of God unless they truly repent.

Whoever takes anything from church property shall be judged more severely, because the removal of sacred things is sacrilege, and one who takes or robs anything from them is called a sacrilegious person. Such persons are to be excluded from the thresholds of holy mother Church until they have made satisfaction to the Church they injured, and are to be firmly marked as such.

And likewise:

*(ANSEGIS. III, 65.)* If anyone in the army, within the kingdom and without the lord’s command, wishes by hostile force to plunder anything, take hay or grain, seize large or small livestock, break into houses, or burn them, we absolutely prohibit these acts. If anyone presumptuously does so, a free man shall be liable to sixty solidi and shall restore everything of the same kind, or clear himself by twelve witnesses. If a slave does this, he shall be subject to capital punishment, and his master shall restore everything of the same kind, because he neither corrected nor guarded his slave so that he would not commit such acts; for if we consume ourselves, we shall quickly perish. Nevertheless, let everyone guard his army so that no plundering occurs within the kingdom.

And likewise:

*(BENED. II, 382.)* If anyone breaks into another person’s house, whatever he forcibly takes, robs, or steals from it, he shall compensate the person whose house was broken into and plundered threefold according to the law, and shall additionally pay the lord’s ban. If a slave does this, let him receive the preceding sentence, and in addition let him pay compensation according to his own law. If anyone causes another person such damage that he is unable to make full compensation, let him endeavor to give himself as a pledge in place of a slave until he provides full compensation.

Of the chapters that we sent throughout our kingdom, the following extracts are relevant:

Every envoy is to take care in his circuit that, if any of our faithful men passes through his circuit, or resides or dwells there, and commits robberies or depredations, or does such unlawful things as ordinarily offend God and make the people groan under oppression, he investigate the matter carefully and truthfully, have it corrected according to law, and report it to us, so that we may arrange matters in such a way that neither he nor anyone else will take pleasure in doing such things.

And likewise: Let the envoys in their circuits take care that our men, or anyone else, do not plunder their neighbors, great or small, in summer, when they send their horses to pasture, or in winter, when they send their marshals to procure fodder. If they do so, let our envoys investigate this truthfully, as we have said, have it legally corrected, and report it to us, so that we may correct the senior ruler in such a way that he keeps his men under control, that they are content with what is owed to them, and that they do not unjustly desire what is not owed.

[Note: [Col. 0679] Baluzius prefixes this chapter with the following: “The two chapters that follow belong to the present title and are not repeated from the preceding material.”]

We also want our envoys to admonish everyone concerning destroyed benefices and forests sold off, whether from public property or ecclesiastical property, so that those who possess them thereafter may guard against such acts and endeavor, as far as they can, to correct what has been wrongly done, lest they be compelled to suffer vengeance according to the capitularies of our predecessors.

The chapters of divine and secular laws and of the emperors concerning the abduction of women, conspiracies, sworn associations, the breaking into churches, the dishonoring of clerics, and counts who act unjustly in their counties are not recorded here, because they are known and require greater rigor. We command all to be admonished concerning them and all to guard against them under God’s ban and ours. Meanwhile, let our envoys traveling through the country, with the counsel of the senior envoys, as we have stated, attend to these matters until, with the Lord’s help, we arrange throughout our kingdom for the complete body of chapters to be both announced and observed, for the common salvation and peace of us all.

[Col. 0679]

**Edict of Charles II concerning the Northmen’s tribute. (Year 861, May–June.)**

[Note: [Col. 0679] Hincmar mentions in his *Annals* an agreement by which Duke Weland promised, in return for a payment to be made to him by Charles, to drive the Northmen occupying the Seine out of the kingdom. We have decided that the edict issued concerning this payment, which in Sirmond and Baluzius is joined to a later edict under the year 877, should be placed here. It is worth noting that in the years 861 and 877 the amount of the payment—namely, 5,000 pounds of silver—and the method of imposing it were the same, whereas the contribution of the year 866, as reported by Hincmar, was distributed differently.]

**[Note.]**

[Col. 0679D] This levy was imposed on the Northmen who were on the Seine during the reign of King Charles, from his kingdom, so that they would withdraw from his kingdom.

Each bishop who has an abbey, or an abbot who likewise has an abbey, or a count who likewise has an abbey, shall take from his demesne mansus, and likewise from those of his vassals, twelve denarii from each demesne mansus; from each freeholder’s mansus, four denarii from the lord’s census and four from his own resources; from a servile mansus, two denarii from the census and two from his own resources.

From all churches, each bishop or abbot shall take only from his own authority: from priests, five solidi from whoever can pay the most, and from each according to what is possible—so that from the one who can pay the most there are five solidi, and from the one who can pay the least, four denarii.

As for the churches held by counts and royal vassals, whether by those who ought to travel with our senior ruler or by those who remain behind, the bishop in whose diocese they are located shall endeavor to collect according to the method prescribed above. From the empress’s churches the bishop shall likewise collect according to the prescribed method.

[Col. 0681]

**Edict of Charles II of Quierzy. (Year 861, July?)**

[Note: [Col. 0681] This constitution concerning coinage was published by Sirmond with the aid of the mutilated Laon and Beauvais manuscripts and reproduced by Baluzius.]

Lord Charles established this edict at Quierzy in the year 861 from the Lord’s incarnation.

[Col. 0681B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, by the grace of God king, to all the faithful of our kingdom.

It has come to our attention that, although we commended, in accordance with the custom of our predecessors and for the general utility of our kingdom, that fear should be instilled so that no one would dare reject a good denarius—that is, a pure coin of proper weight—certain envoys appointed to carry this out, misunderstanding the devotion of our intention and following the purpose of their own will, have introduced certain contrivances, which the Lord greatly detests, into the judicial proceedings and exactions.

When something is commanded and done for the utility of the kingdom, no private advantage contrary to the common utility, nor any shameful profit incompatible with the Christian religion, royal dignity, or the sincerity of faithful envoys, ought in any way to be mixed into it.

Therefore we have considered it necessary to have our instruction on this matter written down, to be retained according to custom in our palace by the chancellor and sent out from there by our envoys, so that no one may deviate from it through ignorance or deliberate ingenuity.

Accordingly, we wish it to be known that measured fear, merciful consideration, and restrained judgment are necessary in this instruction of ours on account of the poverty of the people. For in these times it was necessary to collect a contribution from them both for the fitting out of ships and, for the sake of the kingdom’s safety as circumstances require, in the matter of the Northmen, so that all may know that we seek not dishonorable profit but the public utility of the kingdom.

*(ANSEG. IV, 30.)* Without prejudice to the constitution that is to remain thereafter as the firmest law, which is written on this matter in the capitulary of our grandfather and our father, any Frankish man convicted of having rejected, after this ban of ours, a good denarius—that is, a pure coin of proper weight—shall pay half the Frankish ban.

As for colonists and slaves of any authority, if anyone is caught rejecting a denarius in cities or other markets, the public envoy shall take care that, if he does not find that the denarius is pure and of proper weight, he orders it exchanged for the merchant. If he finds that the denarius is good, he shall consider the person’s age, infirmity, and sex, since women too are accustomed to bargain hesitantly; and he shall punish the person who rejected the good denarius either with blows, as he deems appropriate, or with small rods, using reason and discretion, so that others may also be afraid and the person may not be punished cruelly.

Whoever, after this present ban, is found not to have been punished for such an offense, the public envoy in the cities and markets shall have marked in this fashion: once the person has been caught, he shall burn his forehead with a heated denarius, while preserving the veins, so that the man himself and others may be chastened, the man may not die, and he may show those who see him the mark of punishment.

Our envoys shall not summon poor colonists and slaves of any authority before the court or compel them to pay the Frankish ban. Rather, their advocate shall be subject to the court—not through any new contrivance, but because colonists or slaves under his advocacy rejected, contrary to our ban, a good denarius, that is, a pure coin of proper weight—as the law provides.

For all those under his advocacy, each advocate shall pay one complete ban if he cannot, by his oath, establish their innocence regarding this ban of ours. He shall agree that, together with the officials under his advocacy whom he finds to have acted contrary to this ban, he will punish them, as we have said above, with necessary and measured discretion.

If the case requires that an advocate be brought before the court on account of a single colonist or slave who acted contrary to our ban, we do not want—and it is not the law—that, as we have heard some attempt to arrange, the Frankish advocate should pay his own legal composition while the colonist or slave under his advocacy pays according to his law, unless perhaps he himself induced the person who acted contrary to our ban to do so.

We order this constitution of ours concerning the present time, without prejudice to the constitution of our predecessors that is to remain thereafter, as we have said, to be reread, announced, and observed in our palace, in our cities, in judicial assemblies, and in hearings or markets.

[Col. 0683]

**Synod of Charles II at Pîtres. (Year 862, at the beginning of June.)**

[Note: [Col. 0683] For the editions of Sirmond and Baluzius we used manuscripts 3) of the Royal Library of Paris, among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75, and 4) of the same library, no. 4761, Baluzius’s Dijon manuscript.]

[Col. 0683A] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, by the grace of God king, and the bishops, abbots also, counts, and the other faithful reborn in Christ, who have assembled from various provinces beside the River Seine, at a place called Pîtres, where, because our sins demanded it, the Northmen’s seat was for some time located, in the year 862 from the Lord’s incarnation,

[Note: [Col. 0683] Manuscripts 3 and 4 read 863.]

in the twenty-second year of the reign of our lord Charles, the glorious king,

[Note: [Col. 0683] Thus, before June 20. Manuscripts 3 and 4 read “twenty-third.”]

in the tenth indiction.

1. The kings and bishops who were before us, moved by love and fear of God, established many chapters with the counsel and consent of the other faithful of God, taking care that holy Church should possess her due standing and honor, and that the inhabitants of the kingdom, in every condition and order, should have law and justice. We too, according to the nature of circumstances and the suitability of the times, have added certain chapters appropriate to this matter. [Col. 0683B] But, with the devil striving and disturbances arising—miserably stirred up both by pagans and by those who are Christians in name only—the good beginnings failed, and evils increased in this kingdom to such an extent that we see and feel fulfilled in ourselves what was once foretold through the prophet:

> “Strangers devour your land in your presence, and it shall be as in a hostile devastation, and the sword has reached even to the soul.”

For strangers have risen up against us, and have sought our lives, and have not set God before their eyes. Against them we prepared a defense, but thus far we have not been aided by the help of that defense as was necessary. Therefore, compelled by sorrow of heart, we must cry out what the good king, troubled by the distress of siege, cried out, saying:

> “This day is a day of tribulation and blasphemy. The daughters have come as far as childbirth, but the woman in labor has no strength.”

We have seen, felt, and grieved over all these things. For when the enemies attacked, our defenders were ready, but they did not have the strength to carry out what they had prepared, because by evil works we drove away from ourselves that Holy Spirit who rested upon our helper in times of need and tribulation, Christ our Lord [Col. 0683: “the Lord,” d. 3], and whom we received through the laying on of the bishop’s hand in confirmation [Col. 0683: “and,” so 3, 4, or S.]. We drove away the Spirit of counsel and fortitude. Since we do not possess him as we needed to, we are therefore unable to stand manfully against our enemies and conquer courageously.

These two things are necessarily joined together, because neither strength without counsel nor counsel without strength can be useful. What good, then, are those things prepared through counsel, when one does not proceed to battle through strength? The daughters come as far as childbirth when suitable counsels advance as far as the desire to accomplish the work; but the woman in labor has no strength, because when someone weak conceives counsels, he does not bring them forth through the labor of action for any useful purpose.

We also see fulfilled what was formerly foretold by the Lord concerning a people acting against his will:

> “A curse is in your midst; you will not be able to stand before your enemies.”

But to those who are obedient he said, in contrast:

> “No one shall stand against you.”

For this reason also strangers devour our land in our presence: having driven away the grace of the Holy Spirit, we have received into our souls strangers from God, namely demons. Therefore our land is desolate as in a hostile devastation, because we have ravaged from the field of our hearts the flowers and fruits of faith, hope, charity, humility, chastity, sobriety, and the other virtues [Col. 0684B: “from the field,” so 3, 4; “from the altar,” S.], and in their place, while even laboring to act wickedly, we have deliberately caused the thorns of vices, the nettles of sins, and the hemlocks [Col. 0683: “all,” Met.] of vanity to grow and increase within us.

Therefore the inhabitants of the land have been killed and driven away, because we have killed ourselves with the sword of sin, and have turned to the pleasures of the flesh everything that the Lord bestowed upon us—whether natural understanding, instruction, wealth, honors, or relationships he granted us with those more powerful than ourselves. We have turned both ourselves and everything the Lord gave us away from his will, for the doing of which he gave those things to us.

Everyone can recognize this in himself if he considers, even concerning his individual bodily members, what he has done and what he is doing with what God gave him for working out his salvation. And just as he will discover this concerning the members of his body, so he can discover it concerning the members of his soul, which he scatters and destroys through spiritual vices, and whose spiritual virtues, bestowed upon him by God, he either drives away or tramples underfoot.

Therefore churches and estates have been burned, because the fire of avarice, rapacity, envy, adulteries, and other impurities has blazed and continues to blaze within us without repentance or remorse—not only through the natural sex, but also through that sex which is contrary to nature.

And because through pride, disobedience, and presumption we drove away from ourselves that Spirit who rests upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at his words, therefore the bodies of our saints and protectors have been dug out from the tombs of their repose.

And because we do not stand against the evil spirit who, by God’s permission, has received power and risen up against us [Col. 0684D: “by God’s just permission,” S.], so that he might flee from us, therefore the servants and handmaids of God have been driven from their places, and we have been expelled from the repose of the heavenly paradise and from fellowship with the heavenly Church—that is, with the holy angels—unless through worthy fruits of repentance we return to the things from which we have fallen.

And because we have made ourselves such as those concerning whom the Lord said through the prophet:

> “The case of the widow does not come before them,”

since justice has been made so saleable among us that no one can reach it unless gifts open the way for him, therefore the vows of the faithful and the prices of sins that had been presented to sacred places have, because of our sins, been entirely carried out of this kingdom. Those who sell justice and truth—and in these things Christ himself, who has been made justice for us by God and who said, “I am the truth”—unless they worthily repent, await eternal fires with Judas, the betrayer of Christ.

And because “blood has touched blood,” that is, because guilt has been joined to guilt, and, as it is written, adultery and murder, lying and theft, and perjury have overflowed, and our iniquities have surpassed our heads, therefore our nobles, both those of episcopal rank and those of other orders, have perished; and, having been captured with the greatest loss to both kingdom and Church, they have either been ransomed or killed.

And because through our sins we have become exiles from the land of the living, therefore, as it is written:

> “The prophet and the priest have gone into a land they did not know.”

And after all these things the merciful Father, by whose many compassions we have not been consumed—for his compassions have not failed—scourges us with maternal tenderness and awaits the time when this very affliction will give understanding to our hearing, because we refused to believe those things that, through the Scriptures, he promised to bring upon us if we did not do his will.

He shows us through outward devastations what we ought to understand concerning inward desolations, so that, having understood, we may return to him and believe, because he has again promised us this in many ways in Scripture. Among these promises, Truth himself truly said:

> “Return to me, and I will return to you”;  
> “Why will you die in your sins?”

And because we did not believe him when he promised, let us at last believe him even when he swears:

> “As I live,” says the Lord, “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

But unless we turn, as we already see, he has brandished his sword [Col. 0685: “he will brandish,” S.], stretched his bow—that is, his vengeance—and prepared to exercise a harsher vengeance. As it is likewise said concerning the reprobate:

> “Fire, sulfur, and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup.”

What we see and feel is also a portion of that vengeance; for greater, more numerous, and more grievous things will come upon us unless we turn, as it is written:

> “The whole world will fight on his behalf against the senseless.”

Therefore, as the Apostle says:

> “Just as we presented our members as weapons of iniquity for sin, to serve impurity and iniquity, so let us present our members to serve justice for sanctification.”

For the wages—that is, the repayment—of sin is death, but the grace of God, given to us for our works, is eternal life.

And just as, when we are accustomed to return from those frequent journeys to our lodgings, shorn and washed, with rags and worn-out footwear, we then refresh and restore ourselves, so let us now at least restore ourselves through a contrite and humbled heart, through confessions from a pure heart, through kindness of mind, and through concord with the will of God. For through discord we have both diminished and almost desolated this temporal kingdom, and lost the eternal kingdom.

For we cannot all be kings, nor can we endure having the king whom God has established over us, although, as it is written, “he has placed men over our heads.” We do not consider that, as the Apostle says:

> “There is no authority except from God, and whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God.”

For God, who in his essence is King of kings and Lord of lords, willed, through a participation in the name and divinity of God—that is, in his power—that there should be on earth, for his honor and in his place, a king who would both be called and be king and lord.

And just as the archangel who is now the devil fell from heaven with his followers because he refused to be subject to his Creator through humble submission and disdained to be the companion of his fellow angels through equality of charity, so those who refuse, for God’s sake and in God, to be subject to the authority established by God, and who cannot tolerate having peers or equals in the kingdom, are made subject to the devil and constituted enemies of God. Through that proper submission and equal fellowship they could have been God’s friends and companions of the angels.

Therefore it is written concerning the devil:

> “He is king over all the sons of pride.”

And to those subject to him the Lord, with whom there is no shadow of change, continually says in the Gospel, so long as they persist in that evil:

> “You are of your father the devil”—

not because they were made or begotten by the devil, but because they imitated the devil.

Let us therefore restore ourselves through repentance and confession, and through almsgiving, each according to his ability. To the extent that each person recognizes that he has become impoverished before God through his sins, to that extent let him drink the tears of his contrition.

Then the fortifications which we make in this water will avail [Col. 0685: “we have made,” Sirmondus’s manuscript; BAL] if through good works we rebuild the strongholds of the virtues that sins have destroyed within us [Col. 0685: Sirmondus wrote “if we rebuild”; BAL reads only “if we rebuild”; 3 reads “if we destroy the good things”]. They will also advance if each person first corrects, as far as he can, the evils he has committed—either by repaying what he has seized, by asking pardon, or by abolishing his other evils through worthy repentance.

And they will advance if thereafter he guards himself so that he does not defile himself with those things from which he has been cleansed, because it is written:

> “Wash yourselves; be clean. Remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes,” says the Lord. “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good.”

For whoever cleanses himself from sin through good works, tears, and prayers, and then again commits serious sins, is, as Saint Peter says, like a pig that washes itself [Col. 0687: “throws itself,” 3] in the mud, and like a dog that eats again its own vomit. He ought to fear that he will make those very tears unclean in the sight of God, through which he was able to be cleansed from sins.

We do not say this so that, if someone should again fall into sin after confession, he may lie despairingly in his sins, but so that he may guard himself from sins as much as he can. And if he falls through weakness, since it is written, “Will not one who falls continue to rise?”, let him say, “Now I have begun,” and through the changing of the right hand of the Most High let him continually rise again through repentance, lest the final day find him in his sins and he become lost without end.

2. Therefore, since physicians are accustomed, when a general illness or disease comes upon a land [Col. 0687: “kinds of illnesses,” 3; omitted in 4], to prepare a general medicine through which everyone may be healed, so now, with the Lord cooperating and mediating, we commonly establish this medicine for recovering and preserving our health, lest we be afflicted more grievously in this age and, in the age to come, when we depart from this body, be tortured by eternal punishments.

That is, let every bishop in his diocese, the royal envoys in their districts, and the counts in their counties take the greatest care and exercise the utmost diligence that all robbers and plunderers found there, whoever their men may be, be brought to account, so that they may make amends according to the law for the wrongs they have committed there, or pay according to the legal judgment [Col. 0687: “and pay,” written by Sirmondus; BAL], or obtain pardon for themselves through an act of clemency.

And let the bishops, according to the quality and quantity of the sins, without respect of persons, impose the laws of repentance upon robbers and those convicted of similar vices, with due regard to discretion and circumstance, as they see will be useful for each person’s salvation.

For the special execution of these matters, we have thought it fitting and necessary to set down here certain provisions from among the many chapters of our royal predecessors and of synods. We admonish bishops, envoys, and counts to recall and reread those chapters which were collected into one body in former years and which we gave to our bishops and envoys at Carisiacum [Col. 0687: “Paris,” 3] for execution throughout our kingdom, as well as those which we ordered to be made when we spoke with our brother Hlotharius, the glorious emperor, at Valentia, and which we commanded to be announced and observed by our faithful.

And because, for the sake of brevity, we have written only a few things here, whenever matters arise for correction in which they do not find chapters here applicable, let them endeavor to correct them by means of these and the other royal and synodal chapters which they judge ought to be corrected and ought to be applied.

But if, according to the devil’s cunning and human weakness, anything new should arise—for new kinds of illnesses seek new experiments in medicines—we shall, following the custom of our predecessors, enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, take care to administer medicinal antidotes against the devil’s poisons through Christ.

3. By common agreement we establish that, until the Mass of Saint Remigius—that is, the Kalends of October—those who during these times have committed these plunderings and other criminal and public wrongs shall have time to make peace concerning them both with God and with those whom they have wronged [Col. 0687: “concerning them,” omitted in 3].

Whoever does not do this shall pay our ban twice over. This means that [Col. 0687: “and,” 3, 4; “because,” omitted in 4], since, after we forbade those robberies [“those,” 3] and other wrongs at Carisiacum, and afterward at Confluentes with our beloved brother Hludowic, the glorious king, and our nephew Hlotharius, and after this ban had been established with everyone’s consent, they refused to correct those things as we had given them time to do, they shall be compelled to make legal compensation for everything they have committed and, through public repentance according to the sacred canons, make satisfaction to God and to the Church against which they have sinned.

If they refuse to obey, they shall either be brought before us by sureties, or everything they possess in our kingdom shall be placed under our ban, and by episcopal authority they shall be excluded from the common ecclesiastical fellowship and from the fellowship of all the faithful.

4. Concerning the honor of churches and the servants of God, and concerning robberies and other evils or acts of presumption that must be restrained from this day forward, we have thought it fitting and necessary to append here the chapters established in the times of our grandfather and father, and to command under our ban that they be observed in every respect.

For it is written in those chapters (Bened. II, 97):

> “If anyone within the kingdom commits robbery, or forcibly takes anything from any one of our faithful or from his man, let him make legal compensation threefold to the person from whom he took it, and in addition pay us our ban, namely sixty solidi. Afterward let him be brought before us by the count, so that, thrust into the bastonico or another prison, he may suffer punishment until it pleases us.
>
> “If it was done publicly, let him perform public penance for it, because, as the Apostle says, robbers, unless they truly repent, will not possess the kingdom of God.
>
> “Those who take anything from the property of churches shall be judged more severely for it, because the removal of sacred property is sacrilege, and one who takes or steals anything from it is called a sacrilegious person. Such persons are to be held as exiles from the thresholds of holy mother Church until they have made satisfaction to the Church whom they injured, and they are to be firmly marked as such.”

And Saint Paul, through whom Christ spoke, likewise says that neither the rapacious, nor murderers, nor adulterers shall possess the kingdom of God.

Again, if anyone is a fornicator, adulterer, robber, or murderer, a disciple of Christ—that is, a Christian—is not permitted to eat with such a person before satisfaction, that is, correction, amendment, and worthy repentance.

And the holy apostle John forbids greeting such a person or receiving him into one’s house.

The sacred canons, dictated through the Holy Spirit by those who reign with God in heaven and shine forth through miracles on earth, likewise established, saying:

> “If anyone of the powerful strips a cleric, any poor person, or a religious person of his possessions, and the bishop sends word to him that he should hear the case, but he despises it, let written communications immediately pass among all the bishops of the province whom they are able to reach, so that he may be held excommunicated until he hears the case and restores what belongs to another.”

And concerning ecclesiastical property and resources they say:

> “If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such duties have been entrusted, and refuses to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.”

Again, in the chapters of our grandfather and father it is written concerning those who take anyone with them in the army; and we wish this also to be observed within the kingdom. (ANSEG. II, 15.)

> “Henceforth we wish it to be announced to everyone, so that each person may know all who are in his service, whether they are his own men or another’s, and may know that he must render an account for their actions. Whatever they do wrong in violating the peace must concern his own danger.
>
> “The violator of the peace must first pay a fitting punishment according to the nature of his crime, either before us or before our envoy. The lord who took such a person with him, although he either would not or could not restrain him so that he observed our command, and who moreover did not fear to commit plunder in our kingdom, shall, for that negligence—if he did not warn him beforehand about these matters, and, after the negligence of the contemptuous person came to his knowledge, neglected to correct him as was proper—be deprived of his honor. Thus neither of them shall remain without just punishment.”

But you, bishops, by evangelical, apostolic, and episcopal authority, if a lord or any powerful person in the kingdom, after being admonished according to the evangelical command, refuses to correct himself and his men, and although he himself does not commit such acts, nevertheless, if his men or those remaining in his service do such things, he does not correct them, does not obtain amendment of what they do, and does not bring them to repentance, then let him be excommunicated according to the sacred canons until he brings his men back to amendment and repentance [Col. 0689: “You,” so 3; “We,” B.].

For we have judged it better that the person through whose power his men commit such things should be excommunicated than that all those who neither fear God nor respect bishops or royal envoys on account of his power should remain uncorrected when excommunicated and infect others with their disease. For, as the Apostle says, not only those who do such things but also those who consent to those who do them are worthy of death.

No one is free from consent who neglects to correct what he can correct; therefore he undoubtedly makes himself a participant in the sin.

But if the powerful person or lord satisfies the bishop and the royal envoys—because he cannot bring his men to amendment and repentance, but wishes either to show himself immune from such acts or to make worthy satisfaction, and to reject such evildoers from his service and pursue them as enemies of God—then let him either not be excommunicated or be released from excommunication.

Again, it is written in the chapters of the emperors (ANSEG. II, 23):

> “Let the counts become helpers of the ministers of the Church in their ministries, so that they may more fully obtain this both from our men, from themselves, and from their own men. Whoever, after being admonished by the count a first and second time concerning these matters, does not correct himself, we wish his negligence to be brought by that count to our attention, so that by our authority he may be compelled to undergo what is contained in our capitulary.”

Again (II, 14):

> “Concerning peace to be maintained on the army’s march as far as the frontier, we wish this to be made known to everyone: whoever knows by name the author of the damage inflicted upon him shall seek and receive justice from him.”

And again (BEN. I, 341):

> “If anyone in the army or within the kingdom, without the lord’s command, wishes by hostile force to plunder anything, or to take hay or grain, or large or small cattle [Col. 0689: alternatively ‘bodies,’ B.; ‘cattle,’ 3], or to break into or burn houses, we utterly forbid these things to be done.
>
> “If anyone presumptuously does so, let a free man be liable to sixty solidi, and let him restore everything of a similar kind, or clear himself by twelve witnesses. But if he is a slave, let him be subject to capital punishment, and let his lord restore everything of a similar kind, because he did not correct or guard his slave so that he would not commit such acts—for if we consume ourselves, we shall quickly perish.
>
> “Nevertheless, let each person guard his army, so that no plundering may occur within the kingdom.”

Likewise, the levies which the Theotisc language calls *herizuph* [variants: *herisub*, 3; *heriszup*, 4], as well as violations of immunities, burnings, assaults upon houses, conjurations, conspiracies, seditions, and the abduction of women, just as divine and human laws forbid them and our predecessor kings forbade them, we too firmly forbid under our ban.

We bishops likewise forbid these things by the authority of God and the sacred canons, just as the 630 holy pontiffs prohibited conspiracies at the Council of Chalcedon, and just as the other councils of bishops forbade such destructive acts [Col. 0690D]. Those who commit such acts are, by the judgment of those who now reign with God in heaven, separated both from the heavenly Church and from the fellowship of Christians, unless through worthy fruits of repentance they return to the point at which they can be reunited with holy Church.

Likewise, we command that these chapters written here, and all those collected and established in the places mentioned above—that is, at Carisiacum and at Valentia—be observed, and we all confirm them together.

But if anyone at all should prove disobedient, let the bishops, counts, and envoys take care to make this known to us with the greatest speed, so that we may order him to come into our presence as quickly as possible and undergo fitting punishment according to the judgment of our faithful.

And if, God forbid, someone should arise who sets aside the fear of God, despises ecclesiastical authority, and rejects royal power, whoever he may be should know that, according to canonical authority, he will be made alien both from the assembly of all Christians and from fellowship with holy Church, in heaven and on earth. By royal power and by the unanimous agreement of all the faithful of the kingdom, he will be pursued as an enemy of God and the Church and as a devastator of the kingdom until he is expelled from the kingdom.

And if there is a count who commits such acts in his county, permits them to increase there, fails to correct them himself, or fails to inform us so that our authority may correct them, he should know that he will suffer the same sentence for this as was customary in the time of our predecessors.

But if a bishop, according to the seventh chapter of the Council of Toledo, to whom those who commit such acts against God and the peace of the Church are known to belong, refuses through any gift, favor, or negligence to admonish them so that he may either receive them when they return or expel them from the Church when they persist in contempt, he shall be regarded as excommunicated from the college of the other bishops until a sentence of their amendment or condemnation has been issued by him.

For unless we struggle together so that justice is preserved for everyone in all things, neither the king, as father of the fatherland, nor the bishops, as those who show mercy and reconcile the people for eternal salvation, nor those who are called Christians through participation in Christ’s name, can be what we are called with the human mouth in the sight of the divine eyes.

But so that these things which we have written and named above as matters to be observed may now and hereafter be kept by us and our successors more certainly and explicitly, unshaken, we have decided by common consent to subscribe to them with our own hands. This condition is maintained: since all people in every order seek from royal authority that the legal rights appropriate to them be preserved, so too, with the Lord’s cooperation, let the law, the right due, and the honor owed to royal authority be preserved by everyone in every order, obediently and faithfully.

After all these things had been reread and approved, we decreed by common consent that if any man, on account of evil deeds which he refuses to correct both by law and by repentance, leaves his lord, or is expelled by him for these reasons, he shall not be received by another until he corrects the wrongs he committed, both through legal compensation and through the repentance of ecclesiastical satisfaction.

[Col. 0691]

**The Assembly of Hludowic, Karolus, and Hlotharius at Sablonaria.** (Year 802, November 3.) [Note: Baronius was the first to publish these acts from Augustine’s copy of the Muretian codex; we have revised them against earlier editions, using manuscript 3 of the Royal Library of Paris, among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75.]

**[Note.]**

[Col. 0691C]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 862, when Hludowic sent word to Karolus that he should receive both him and Hlotharius together for a kiss and conference, Karolus sent through him, and through the bishops Altfrid, Salomon, Adventius, and Hatto, the following chapters to Hlotharius, saying that, on account of these matters, he would not dare to communicate with him unless the matter were completed as written there.

When Hludowic and the bishops named above, on Hlotharius’s behalf, reported to Karolus and Hincmar, and likewise Hincmar, Hodo, and the bishop Christian reported, that Hlotharius had declared that he wished and intended to do so, Karolus and the bishops who were with him received him for a kiss and conference under this agreement [Col. 0691: “these words are lacking,” 3].

1. After, most recently, at Confluentes, with God’s assent [Col. 0691: “the Lord’s assent,” 3], we reconciled one another by mutual pardon, with the common counsel of our faithful, confirmed one another by oath concerning the peace to be observed between us and concerning the help we were to provide to each other, promised that we would observe the chapters dictated by our common faithful and reread to us, and publicly announced them to our common faithful, I do not wish to hold it against you, unique and dearest brother, that you have not thus far observed toward me the things we promised one another. Nor do I expect that you or anyone else could or would hold it against me that I have likewise failed to observe them toward you.

If anyone does so, I am prepared to render you a definite account of it and to make fitting satisfaction. And if anyone wishes to hold it against me that, insofar as it depends upon me, I have not observed toward our nephew Hlotharius the things I owe him, I am likewise prepared to render a definite account and make appropriate satisfaction.

But how he has observed toward me the things he promised me is known not only to me but also to many others.

2. But just as we then agreed there, that at the appointed time we would meet at the agreed place with the leading men of our kingdoms, so that there we might discuss whatever in our kingdoms required and deserved correction and was necessary for holy Church of God and for the salvation of ourselves and the people; so that we might correct ourselves toward our faithful and our faithful toward us; and so that we might establish what was to be observed thereafter—I was ready to carry this out both the first and the second time, and I have come together for this purpose even now, as you often sent word to me through our common faithful [Col. 0691: “that we should meet,” 3].

[Col. 0693A] 3. As for the reasons why I previously did not wish to speak with our aforementioned nephew before receiving counsel from you about them, I wish to indicate some here; others I shall afterward make known to you in a suitable place and in an appropriate manner.

4. When I came to Tusiacum on another occasion to discuss the matters I have mentioned, Boso brought me and the bishops of our kingdom certain letters from the lord apostolic, to be sent to our nephew and to the bishops of his kingdom. We transmitted these to them according to the command of the lord pope, while others were intended for us to read and observe. We have their text here also. In them [Col. 0693: “in which,” and “we found ourselves,” omitted in 3] we found ourselves reproved for permitting fornicators to remain in our kingdom, and for not excommunicating not only the woman herself but also all who supported her crime [Col. 0693: “all who committed it,” corrected to “those who consented,” 3] from the body and blood of the Lord until the woman herself returned to her husband.

And we know, as Saint Gregory says, that whoever fails to correct, if he can, what ought to be cut away, himself commits it [Col. 0693: reading uncertain: “if anyone the things and causes to be cut off, if…” in 3].

We have heard that the aforesaid woman remains in our nephew’s kingdom, and afterward we have not heard that this sentence has been changed. And since we are burdened by our own sins, we fear also communicating in the sins of others by communicating with excommunicated persons.

5. Our daughter Judith, a widow established under ecclesiastical protection and royal safeguard according to divine and worldly laws, Baldwin stole for himself as a wife. After a legal judgment, the bishops of our kingdom excommunicated him according to the sacred canons and the definition of Saint Gregory, pope, who says:

> “If anyone steals a widow as his wife, let both he and those who consent to him be anathema.”

We and the bishops of our kingdom made this known to our nephew Hlotharius both orally and in writing. We also, as you know, jointly confirmed by the counsel and consent of our faithful that none of us should receive such a man in his kingdom or permit him to remain there, but should compel him to return to render a proper account and perform repentance, as had been established.

But how our nephew Hlotharius has acted in this matter—not only toward us and our kindred, but also against God, sacred authority, and the common Christian community—I hope is not hidden from you, since it is known to very many.

And Saint Paul, through whom Christ spoke, says:

> “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death.”

6. You know the case concerning the wife of our nephew Hlothar, about which he sought and heard advice both from us and from the bishops of our realm, as well as from other bishops who were present with us; but he did not act on that advice. We also know that he sent to the apostolic lord concerning this matter and received letters from him about it. Nor do we wish to deny that we know what the apostolic lord instructed him and certain bishops concerning it; and we know—something we can neither deny nor wish to deny, since we ought not—that the apostolic lord’s recommendation in no respect conflicts with evangelical truth or with apostolic and canonical authority. Yet we have neither heard nor seen that his command concerning this matter has been carried out.

That holy and chief See throughout the whole world, through the divine Paul—the heavenly trumpet, who, having been caught up to the third heaven and to paradise, learned this from the Lord himself—continually cries out to us and to all Christians throughout the world that we are not to eat with such a person. And through blessed John the apostle, who, reclining at the supper upon the eternal and living fountain of Christ’s breast, when the sacraments of our redemption [Note: witness 3 reads “in redemptionis”] were celebrated and handed down, drank in what he poured out for all the redeemed, the apostolic See most explicitly forbids anyone to receive such a person into his house or to say “Hail” to him, because whoever says “Hail” to him shares in his evil works.

And through blessed Pope Gregory, in his Homilies on Ezekiel [Note: “Homilies on Ezekiel” is written as *omeliis jezechielis* in witness 3], it says that just as one who departs from God in faith is an apostate, so also one who departs from God in conduct is unquestionably an apostate.
