For, as the Apostle says, “Faith without works is dead.” And again, as another Apostle says: “There are those who profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds.” The Lord himself also says concerning one who, after being lawfully admonished once, twice, and three times [Note: witness 3 reads “excommunicated”], has not been corrected, that he is to be to us as a gentile and as one implicated in public crimes; and with such a person, as we have stated above, apostolic and canonical authority does not permit us to eat.

7. Therefore, only and dearest brother, accept counsel for yourselves [Note: “counsel” is absent in witness 3], give counsel to me, and give our nephew counsel for the sake of his salvation and honor; and offer him assistance. For I too am prepared to act toward this end together with you, insofar as the Lord grants me knowledge and ability, if he himself is willing to accept it.

8. As for the counsel that I have now recently received together with the bishops and our other faithful advisers—concerned for our common salvation and honor, that is, yours and mine, but also for the salvation and honor of our nephew, and for the common safety and preservation of all our faithful—I will state it to you, to whom I am prepared to deny no good thing but to share all my good things, if it pleases you and if it seems good to you [Note: witness 3 reads “thus”; witness B omits “thus”]; let us accept it jointly. And if you show us something better, consonant with reason and with divine and human authority and with our salvation and Christianity, I am prepared to accept it with complete devotion and, with God’s cooperation and with the counsel and assistance of our common faithful supporting us, most willingly to follow and carry it out together with you.

9. Since it is written—spoken by the good king, who nevertheless sinned as a man and acknowledged it as a blessed man, “I will confess to him of my own will”—let our nephew likewise profess before you and before the bishops who will be with you, and let him send word back to us through you and them, that he wishes, according to the counsel of the apostolic lord and of the bishops, or rather according to divine counsel, to meet at an assembly with the bishops and with the faithful, friends of God, of us, and of him; for this matter concerns all Christians. Let him either show that he has carried out what was done concerning his wife according to divine and human law as appropriate for Christians, or let him wish and be obliged, according to God’s counsel and the law befitting a Christian king, to correct this matter and the two matters mentioned above.

I am prepared to receive him with such affection and honor as a Christian king ought to receive a Christian king, and as a loving uncle ought to receive a beloved nephew; and, if he does this, to remain in his friendship for his salvation and honor. Let an appropriate time and a suitable place be established at which we may meet together peacefully and, treating this matter as though it concerned ourselves—for, as Scripture says, he is “our bone and our flesh” [Note: the phrase is absent in witness 3]—settle it for the common salvation and honor of ourselves and our faithful. Otherwise, although we ought to be an example of good conduct to our faithful and to all Christians, we shall be giving an example of destruction [Note: witness 3 omits “and”; the editor reads “let us give an example of destruction”], and although we ought to be correctors of evil, we shall become, God forbid, the head of evil.

Let us also discuss and establish those matters which, as we stated above, we promised at Confluentes to discuss and to set down for observance, so that we, who are being struck on every side because of our sins and because of the evil of discord that remains in our realms, may deserve, once God has been appeased, to obtain the consolation of his mercy.

Let it not be hard for our nephew to do this in his mind, for it is written: “He who is hard of mind will fall into evil.” But let him fear God and restrain this scandal [Note: witness 3 reads “that” scandal], which has been generated and spread throughout this Christianity on so great a scale and without any necessity, although through reason and authority it could have been brought to its proper conclusion; many people think that it has been carried out without full reason and due authority.

And since it is written, “Blessed is the person who is always fearful,” and the Lord says, “I love those who love me,” let him, for the love and fear of God, honor himself, his Christianity, and his royal name. Let him strip himself [Note: witness 3 reads “rescue himself”] and all of us of this calumny that follows him, and through him and because of him follows us, his relatives. Let him thereby honor God, knowing that the Lord says: “Those who honor me I will honor; and those who despise me shall be held of no account” [Note: witness 3 reads “shall be dishonored”].

10. And if he is unwilling to do this, let him do what he judges ought to be done. I desire to remain in your friendship and in the brotherhood that is owed, and to merit it by every due service. I do not seek what belongs to him, but him; yet if I cannot have him in a wholesome condition, I do not wish, for the sake of his friendship, to withdraw myself from God. Nor do I wish to offer assistance to anyone for evil, because we read in Scripture that the Lord said to a certain king: “You give assistance to the impious, and you join friendship with those who hate me; therefore you deserved the wrath” [Note: witness 3 abbreviates this as “that is, of the Lord”], “as is likewise written there in what follows.”

We also read that if any impious person turns from whatever impiety and says that he wishes to turn back from his heart [Note: absent in witness B], he is no longer counted among the impious; rather, he ought to be piously received by the pious and can be received for his salvation. Scripture says: “Turn the impious, and they shall be no more”—not that they shall cease to exist in essence, but that they shall no longer remain guilty of impiety.

We have said this, however, not because we wish our nephew to be counted among the impious, but because we desire that he be joined by the Lord to the number of the pious.

The announcements follow which the three kings were required to make at Sablonariae.

Announcement of the lord Hludowic.—

1. As you know, those of you who were present when, recently at Confluentes, with the Lord’s help, we joined together and established chapters to be observed by us and by our faithful, it was agreed that at an appropriate time and in a suitable place we should meet together again and, with God’s help and the counsel of our faithful, correct whatever needed correction in the condition of the holy Church, in ourselves, in our realms, and among our faithful, and establish that the corrected arrangements should thereafter be observed [Note: witness 3 reads “should be observed”].

For this purpose we have already agreed upon a time and place on three occasions; but circumstances arose for me, or for my brother, or for our common nephew, because of which we were unable to fulfill what we had agreed upon [Note: witness 3 reads “what we had said”].

2. In the meantime word reached me that my brother and our common nephew were not on such terms with one another as they had been when we met together. Therefore I came in order to act as a private mediator between them, so that they might be toward one another as they ought rightly to be.

Accordingly, through me, through our bishops, and through our nephew’s bishops, our brother sent our nephew both written and verbal instructions concerning matters because of which he was not toward him as a private friend [Note: “that is, as a familiar friend”] as he had formerly been. If he wished to correct these matters as he instructed him [Note: witness 3 reads “as he was correcting them”], our brother was willingly prepared to be toward him as a loving uncle toward a beloved nephew and as a Christian king ought rightly to be toward a Christian king.

Concerning these matters, we and the bishops who were with us on behalf of our nephew gave our brother and the bishops who were with him this reply: that he was prepared either to correct the matters he attributed to him or to give a definite account of them and make fitting satisfaction. Our brother and the bishops gladly received this reply; and, thanks be to God, our brother and nephew are now toward one another as they ought rightly to be.

3. We wish that, as has been agreed among us, faithful messengers should travel among us; that whatever needs correction in each of our realms should be corrected, after each of us has made it known to the other; that God’s churches, priests, and servants of God should have the law and honor owed to them; and that each of our faithful, in our realms, regardless of which of us he belongs to, should have law and justice both for himself and in his properties and honors, as they had in the time of our predecessors, as has now been agreed among us [Note: witness 3 reads “as it has been agreed among us”], and as was established in those chapters which our royal predecessors established [Note: witness B reads “intercessors” for “predecessors”], and as we confirmed at Marsna, and as we recently established at Confluentes.

This shall continue until, with God’s help, at an appropriate time and in a suitable place we meet together again and, together with the common counsel of our faithful, peacefully discuss and complete whatever has not been completed [Note: the remainder is absent in witness 3]. In this way we shall help one another, so that with God’s help we may save ourselves and our faithful and resist the oppressors of the holy Church.

We had this recognition written down by common agreement so that each of us might possess it and know more certainly what he must observe thereafter and in what manner; for it is not fitting that a king should deviate from his own declaration, just as it is not fitting that a bishop should disagree with his upright preaching.

Announcement of the lord Karolus.—

1. What our beloved brother recently said that we established at Confluentes, I have observed up to now, insofar as it depended on me, and I wish to continue observing it, if it has likewise been observed toward me. I do not wish to attribute to him that he has failed to observe these things toward me. Nor do I believe that he wishes, or that anyone else could attribute to me, that I have failed to observe them toward him. If anyone does so, I am prepared either to correct whatever needs correction or to give a definite account of what has been attributed to me.

2. And if our common nephew does what our brother and the bishops who acted as mediators between us, and who were with him, reported to me on his behalf, and what our brother has now said—if he is toward me as a private friend, friend, and helper, according to reasonable possibility, as a nephew ought rightly to be toward an uncle and a Christian king toward a Christian king—then I wish to be toward him as a private friend, friend, and helper, according to reasonable possibility, as a loving uncle ought to be toward a beloved nephew and as a Christian king ought rightly to be toward a Christian king.

3. As for faithful messengers traveling among us; correcting whatever needs correction in our realms; maintaining the condition and honor of churches, priests, and servants of God; preserving law and justice for each of our faithful in our realm, regardless of which of us he belongs to, both for himself and in his properties and honors; and observing the chapters—as our brother has now said, so too do I wish to observe all these things in every respect.

Announcement of Hlothar.—

1. Ever since this uncle of mine, Hludowic, in his goodness received me in the place of a son, he has continually dealt with me in his favor as was fitting for him and necessary for me. Therefore I am prepared to render him the service owed to him, as I rightly ought to do.

2. As for the matters that my uncle Karolus recently instructed me about, when we first met together, I wish to observe them as my uncle Hludowic and the bishops who acted as mediators between me and my uncle Karolus reported to him and to the bishops who were with him on my behalf.

And if he is toward me as a private friend, friend, and helper, according to reasonable possibility, as an uncle ought rightly to be toward a nephew and a Christian king toward a Christian king, then I too wish to be toward him a familiar friend, friend, and helper, according to reasonable possibility, as a loving nephew ought to be toward a beloved uncle and as a Christian king ought rightly to be toward a Christian king.

3. As for faithful messengers traveling among us; correcting whatever needs correction in our realms; maintaining the condition and honor of churches, priests, and servants of God; preserving law and justice for each of our faithful in our realm, regardless of which of us he belongs to, both for himself and in his properties and honors; and observing the chapters—as my uncles have now said, so too do I wish to observe all these things in every respect.

[NOTE.]

Since Hludowic and Hlothar, together with their followers, completely rejected the announcements above after they had been read aloud before all who were present—nearly two hundred advisers of the three kings, bishops as well as abbots and laymen—and did not allow them to be read to the people, so that the case of Hlothar might be entirely suppressed, the lord Karolus announced the following announcement in these very words that same evening at Sablonariae, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 862, indiction 11, on 3 November [Col. 0698D], in the very house where the preceding announcements had been read aloud. Few others entered it besides those who had been present earlier, since it was almost full of them.

Announcement of Karolus.—

As I instructed my nephew through my brother and through the bishops, by word and in writing, and as he reported back to me on his part, so I wish to be his friend and to save him, as an uncle ought rightly to save his nephew, if he saves me and mine as a nephew ought rightly to save his uncle.

[Col. 0699]

EDICT OF KAROLUS II AT PITAE. (Year 864, June 25.) [Note: We have reviewed this lengthy capitulary, published by Sirmond and Baluzius, with the aid of manuscript 3 of the Royal Library of Paris, among the Latin Supplements no. 75; nevertheless, we have retained Baluzius’s readings almost everywhere, because our manuscript—which is supported by 3b, Saint Vincent of Metz, and 3c, the Palatine manuscript—is to be regarded as representing another recension of the entire edict, somewhat shorter, namely. It is also found in a tenth-century manuscript of the Paris library, no. 5095, and in excerpts in manuscript no. 3878; but we did not have sufficient leisure to collate these completely with the printed editions.]

Announcement of the lord Karolus at Pistae.

[Col. 0699A]

1. We give you many thanks for your fidelity and for the good will that you have always shown toward us in every assistance and service, just as your predecessors showed it toward ours; and because you have observed, for the most part, the peace that three years ago we jointly confirmed here and had publicly acknowledged, according to the circumstances in which the matter lay in certain places—though not everywhere, as we desired; and because you have come to this assembly of ours in full number and peaceably.

2. Since we see and have experienced your good will in these matters and others, we admonish you with greater confidence to work manfully, without failing or tiring, both to preserve that peace and to continue the undertakings we have begun against the enemies common to God, his holy Church, and us—the Northmen.

You know how pleased we should have been if we had had these fortifications here when we jointly labored against them at Meaux in such distress as you experienced; from that distress God helped us, as it pleased his mercy, by a manifest sign of his clemency.

3. Since we have discovered that you willingly heard and accepted what we established here three years ago, together with the consent and counsel of our faithful, and had publicly announced to you, we now wish to make known to you in writing what we have established here, again with the consent and counsel of our faithful, for our common salvation, peace, and honor. In this way you may hear it more fully and, by referring to the document that we order to be issued, reread, and kept in each county, retain it more firmly and observe it more certainly. We also wish it to be delivered by the bishops or their ministers throughout each county, in plain speech, so that everyone may understand it.

Karolus, by the grace of God king. We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God and of ourselves that we have now established the following chapters at this assembly of ours, in the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 854, namely, in the twenty-fifth year of our reign, with his favor, in indiction 12 [Note: thus in Sirmond, Baluzius, and Paris manuscripts 5095 and 3878; witness 3 reads “the seventh day before the Kalends”], on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, at this place called Pistae, together with the consent and counsel of our faithful; and we command that they be observed throughout our realm without any resistance.

1. First, we considered the honor of churches, priests, and servants of God, and the immunity of ecclesiastical property, so that no one may presume to act against authority concerning those properties. Counts are to become assistants in every respect to bishops and the ministers of the Church in the exercise of their ministries, as is contained in the capitulary of our predecessors and ancestors, in the second book, chapter 23.

If any count or minister of public affairs neglects to observe these commands, and, after being admonished about them once and twice, does not correct himself, we wish the count’s negligence to be reported to our attention by the bishops and our messengers, and the negligence of others to be reported to our attention by the counts, so that by our authority they may be compelled to undergo what is prescribed in the capitulary of our predecessors.

2. Next, concerning the cases of orphans and widows; royal justice; and, above all, the abductors of girls, widows, and nuns; those who presume to flog priests; those who dare to expel priests from churches without the consent of the bishops, or to receive them; those who do not fear to exact a due from a mansus or from those properties that our lord and father granted to churches in his capitularies under immunity; and those who refuse to pay dues from ecclesiastical properties to the churches:

such persons are to be firmly investigated by our messengers and counts, severely constrained, and dealt with by full justice, according to what has been established in the capitularies of our grandfather and father. These despisers of laws—both divine and human—are to be brought lawfully into our presence, so that, with the advice of God’s faithful and our own, we may determine what is to be done concerning such men, who neither fear God nor dread acting against the holy canons or violating royal law and command; without prejudice to ecclesiastical censure and the penalty of episcopal penance.

3. So that law and justice may be preserved for everyone in every rank, and so that all may observe the peace that, with God as witness, we recently confirmed with our own hands by common agreement when we held our assembly here, let everyone take care to observe it both within the realm, when each person comes to the assembly and when he returns, and whenever necessity arises for us to announce our enemy, up to the appointed places, according to the custom and chapters of our predecessors.

If anyone, out of contempt, violates this confirmation, or neglects to correct as quickly as possible whatever has been done against it, we command that this be reported to us by our bishops, messengers, and counts, so that we may take care to correct such great contempt of God, of ourselves, and of all Christianity, according to what we find in divine and human laws, lest we ourselves, God forbid, be condemned by God in his judgment.

Our bishops, messengers, and counts must also see to it that, if anyone out of contempt acts against our common confirmation and refuses to make amends, we do not learn of this contempt through anyone other than those appointed for the purpose. For if we hear of it through someone other than them, as is not fitting, then, just as they will not be free from sin, so they will not be free from punishment.

4. We wish and expressly command our counts, as is contained in chapter 24 of the second book of the capitularies of our predecessors, that our vassals who serve us and our wife receive fitting honor from everyone, as our father and we have often admonished. And just as they wish to consider themselves honored by us, so they must show due honor to those who serve us, as was customary in the time of our predecessors.

5. We wish and expressly command our counts that our royal estates, as well as the estates of monasteries that we have granted and given to our wife and to our sons and daughters and that exist under immunity, remain within their counties with protection and due reverence. Further, our men and their men and women—who, without any distinction, are also ours [Note: witness 3 reads *nostris* for *nostri*]—may hold their possessions with protection and due honor.

Let our counts and messengers neither ignore nor forget that we know what the Lord of lords says concerning himself: “Those who honor me I will honor; and those who despise me shall be dishonored.”

6. Since human frailty is more inclined to act against justice [Note: witness 3 reads “to act toward injustice”] than to carry out justice, and since the devil is always striving to close the eyes of the human mind so that it may not see God’s chastisement and correct itself [Note: witness 3 reads “himself”], word has reached us that certain frivolous men from these counties devastated by the Northmen—men who had property, dependents, and houses there—now act as though they may do evil with impunity because they no longer have dependents and houses there.

They say that they have no means by which they can be brought to do justice [Note: absent in witness 3; witness 3 perhaps reads “because they do not have [them]”], and, since they have no houses to which they can legally be summoned and banned, they claim that they cannot be legally convicted or judged concerning a summons or ban.

Against these evil schemes, with the consent and counsel of our faithful, we have established that the count shall send his messenger to the land in which a man had his houses [Note: witness 3 reads “has his houses”] and order him to summon and ban him [Note: witness 3 reads “them”].

And since law is made by the consent of the people and by the king’s enactment, the Franks must swear [Note: witness 3 reads “ought to swear”] that, according to our royal command, he was summoned or banned by law [Note: witness 3 omits “our” and reads “legally”] to render or undergo justice. Thus those properties themselves are to be placed under a ban by the judgment of the *scabini*, and, if necessary, the man himself is to be placed under an extreme ban if he refuses to come to render justice.

[Note: Sirmond reads “who refused to come to render justice”; Baluzius proposed “because he did not wish to render justice.”]

The count who carried this out shall inform the other count, in whose county he has property and dependents, what has been done concerning the matter. In our name he shall command that count to constrain the man through the property he has in his county, so that he may return to his own county to render or undergo justice [Note: the words “to render or undergo justice” are absent in witness 3].

7. We have also heard that such frivolous men commit depredations and injustices in other counties and, after committing these wrongs in other counties, return to the county in which they reside, where they do not commit such misdeeds.

Therefore we expressly command our counts [Note: the preceding words are absent in witness 3] that the counts in whose counties such men commit acts subject to justice [Note: in witness 3 the text from “commit” to “one agreement” is absent] shall notify the counts in whose counties the men have refuge. With one mind, one agreement, and one effort, they are to rise up to apprehend such men and strive so that God’s churches and his ministers, the servants of God, and the people may have peace and quiet.

8. So that denarii from all mints, pure and of good weight, may not be rejected throughout our entire realm until the feast of Saint Martin, as is contained in the capitulary of our royal predecessors and ancestors, book four, chapter 32.

In all cities, boroughs, and villages throughout our realm—both our royal estates and those under immunity or belonging to counties and to our men, or belonging to anyone whatsoever—our judges and those to whom the estates belong, together with the ministers of public affairs and according to the size of the places and villages, are to appoint a sufficient number of inhabitants and residents there [Note: witness 3 reads “those residing there”] to take charge of this matter, so that good denarii are not rejected and only pure, well-weighted ones are accepted.

9. Those who are placed in charge of this matter are to swear an oath that, in accordance with what has been entrusted to them concerning it, they will faithfully observe it to the extent of their knowledge and ability. If they know of a man who rejects a pure and well-weighted denarius, they must not conceal him but must make him known to the ministers of public affairs.

Whoever is convicted of having perjured himself in this oath is to be punished as a perjurer according to secular law, as is contained in the capitulary of our predecessors and ancestors, at the end of chapter 10 of the third book [Col. 0703A], and according to ecclesiastical law [Note: witness 3 reads “holy law”], is to be subjected to public penance.

10. From the feast of Saint Martin onward, throughout our entire realm, only pure and well-weighted denarii of this new coinage of ours are to be accepted. Whoever from that day brings forward another denarius for the purpose of trade is to have it taken from him by the count and his ministers [Note: witness 3 reads “the merchandise is to be taken from him”; the remainder of the chapter is absent in witness 3], as is contained in the second book of the capitularies, chapter 18.

11. On the denarii of our new coinage, our name is to appear in a circle on one side, with our monogram in the center; on the other side, the name of the city, with a cross in the center.

12. Following the custom of our predecessors, as it is found in their capitularies, we establish that nowhere else [Note: witness 3 reads *a. I.*] in our entire realm is coin to be minted except at our palace; at Quentovic [Note: witness 3 consistently reads *Quantovico*] and Rouen [Note: witness 3 reads *Rotomagno*]—the mint at Quentovic belonging there by ancient custom; and at Reims, Sens, Paris, Orléans, Chalon [Note: witness 3 reads “Cavillonum”], Melle, and Narbonne [Note: witness 3 reads “Arbona.” This reading confirms my view through the reading of the Annals of Wolfenbüttel and Nazarius for the year 756 (*Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores I, p. 29)].

13. Those in whose power the mint shall henceforth remain are to set aside every favor, desire, and profit and choose faithful moneyers, if they wish to have God’s favor [Note: witness 3 reads “the favor of God and of the king”] and ours. The moneyers themselves shall swear that they will faithfully perform this office to the extent of their knowledge and ability.

They must neither mint nor consent to the minting of a debased denarius or one lighter than it ought to be [Note: witness 3 reads “nor allow other moneyers to mint it”]. Without any fraud or malicious intent toward those whose silver they have received for refining, they shall refine that silver and, without fraud either in weighing or in refining, exchange it for denarii.

If anyone is accused [Note: witness 3 reads “found”] of violating this oath, let him submit to God’s judgment [Note: witness 3 reads, corruptly and incompletely, *dei examinatus si comprobatus fuerit quia*—with *quia* corrected to *qui non*—*majorem*—corrected to *minorem*—*denarium minusque quam …*]. And when he has been convicted of acting against this provision—for he commits no greater fraud by minting a debased or underweight denarius [Note: witness 3 reads “by minting, weighing, and exchanging”] than by fraudulently cheating the public treasury of silver in the refining and exchange of silver, or the churches’ property, or the resources of the poor [Note: part of this phrase is absent in witness 3]—then, as has been established concerning false moneyers in book four of the capitularies, chapter 33, he shall lose his hand and, as a sacrilegious person and despoiler of the poor, be subjected to public penance by episcopal judgment.

In those regions where judgments are settled according to Roman law, he is to be judged culpable according to that law.

[Col. 0704A]

14. At the coming Kalends of July, during this twelfth indiction, each count in whose county we have ordered a mint to exist is to have at the city of Silvanectis his viscount together with two other men who possess property, dependents, or benefices in his county, and his moneyer with them [Note: witness 3 reads “they are to have”]. There they are to receive from our treasury, through their own hands, for the use of each moneyer, five pounds of pure silver by weight, so that he may have the means to begin minting.

The weight of silver that he receives from our treasury [Note: witness 3 reads “that they receive”] is to be returned by each moneyer through the hands by which he received it [Note: witness 3 reads “through those by whom he received it”], on the Saturday before the beginning of Lent, in minted denarii, at the aforesaid place, together with the same weight [Note: witness 3 reads “expense”] with which he had received the silver, to our treasury.

15. Let no one, as is customary, take this lightly for the sake of any profit or greed; rather, from the Kalends of July onward, let everyone have his silver exchanged at the designated mints, knowing that after the mass of Saint Martin no denarii other than those of this new coinage of ours will be accepted in our kingdom, and that from the Kalends of July these new denarii are to be accepted by everyone. Any free man [Note: [Col. 0703] “free man” is absent in 3.] who from that day rejects in our kingdom a pure denarius of our new coinage shall, as is contained in the aforesaid royal book and chapter, pay our bann, that is, sixty solidi.

But if ecclesiastical, comital, or vassal serfs should presume to do this, since the aforesaid capitulary provides that they are to be beaten with sixty blows—and because on this occasion indiscreet men [Note: [Col. 0703] 3 reads “among indiscreet men”.] were exceeding the proper measure in discipline—we establish, with the consent and counsel of our faithful [Note: [Col. 0703] “with consent and counsel” is absent in 3.], that the coloni and serfs of anyone who are convicted of this shall be beaten naked with rods, not with a heavy staff. In the cities [Note: [Col. 0703] 3 reads “counties”.] and in the villages or estates, let the bishop’s officials [Note: [Col. 0703] “let them carry out these same measures through their officials,” or half the passage is absent.] or priests, together with the officials of the public authority, take care that the measure of discipline is not exceeded in this matter either, but that it be carried out in such a way that people are corrected and those who impose discipline for the purpose or occasion of correction [Note: [Col. 0703] “and those who, on the pretext of correction, impose discipline”; the reading is uncertain.] do not incur sin, while those undergoing discipline do not become physically weaker [Note: [Col. 0703] this phrase is absent in 3.].

If anyone transgresses this order of ours, let it be reported to us by the bishops, so that he may be punished in such a way that henceforth no one will take pleasure in despising our order. And if any lord or master [Note: [Col. 0703] “lord or master” is absent in 3.] whatsoever [Note: [Col. 0703] 3, 3b, and 3c read “thus”; B, from Bellovacensis, reads “who is free”.], or the advocate of such men, prevents them from being handed over either to the count or to our envoy for undergoing discipline, or refuses to present them to our envoy when ordered to do so, he shall pay the aforesaid bann of sixty solidi, as is provided in the aforementioned capitulary.

16. If, from the next Kalends of July onward [Note: [Col. 0705] absent in 3.], anyone finds among this new coinage of ours a denarius that is mixed or weighs less than it ought, let him restrain the person who put that denarius into circulation, and let that person say from whom he received it. Thus let it pass from hand to hand until the author of the falsification is reached.

If the coiner of the mixed or underweight denarius is found, then in that land where judicial cases are concluded according to Roman law, let him be judged according to that law. In the land where judicial cases are not judged according to Roman law, let the moneyer, as we said above, lose his right hand for the false denarius, as is contained in the fourth book of the Capitularies, chapter 33. Whoever consented to this, if he is free, shall pay sixty solidi; if he is a serf or colonus, let him be beaten naked with rods [Note: [Col. 0705] 3 and 3b read “let him be beaten”.].

17. Let the counts and officials of the public authority diligently provide throughout their counties and offices [Note: [Col. 0705] absent in 3.] that no secret or fraudulent coinage can be produced anywhere. If anyone is found and proved to be striking fraudulent coinage [Note: [Col. 0705] the phrase “found to be striking fraudulent coinage” is absent in 3.], let his hand be amputated [Note: [Col. 0705] 3 and 3b read “let it be cut off”.], as has been established concerning a false moneyer in the aforesaid capitulary of our predecessors. Whoever consented to this, if he is free, shall pay sixty solidi; if he is a serf or colonus, let him be beaten naked with rods.

18. If a false moneyer—whether from those places in which we have ordered coinage to be made, or one secretly striking coinage, or one putting a false denarius of the new coinage into circulation—should take refuge in our fisc, in any immunity, or in the power or property of some powerful person [Note: [Col. 0705] “power or property” is absent in 3.], so that he cannot be restrained and punished as prescribed [Note: [Col. 0705] 3 reads “because he is in our fisc”], let him be demanded from our official if he has taken refuge in our fisc. If that official defends or conceals him, let it be reported to us, so that vengeance may be exacted upon him according to the royal capitulary, lest anyone else ever dare, by our authority or power, to consent to or defend a falsification [Note: [Col. 0705] 3 reads “conform to” instead of “consent to”.].

But if he has taken refuge in an immunity, or in the power or property of some powerful person, let the following be done concerning him, according to what is contained in Book Three of the Capitularies, chapter 26, concerning one who, after committing theft, homicide, or any other crime outside, has fled within an immunity:

“Let the count or official of the public authority order the bishop or abbot, or whoever holds the place of a bishop, abbot, or abbess, or the powerful person into whose power or property he has fled, to surrender the accused to him. If that person refuses and will not surrender him, let him be judged liable at the first refusal to fifteen solidi. If, upon a second demand, he refuses to surrender him, let him be judged liable to thirty solidi. If he is unwilling to comply even at the third demand, let the person who retains the accused within the immunity and refuses to surrender him be compelled to pay the entire amount of damage caused by the accused; and let the count, on coming, have permission to search for that man within the immunity wherever he may be able to find him.

“But if, at the first demand, the count is answered that the accused had indeed been within the immunity but had escaped, let the person swear that he had not caused him to flee in order to evade the justice due to anyone, and let that suffice as satisfaction in this matter.

“But if anyone attempts to resist the count, when he enters the immunity or the power or property of any person, with a gathered force, let the count refer this to the king or prince, and let judgment be rendered there. And just as the person who caused damage within an immunity must pay six hundred solidi, so let the one who has presumed to resist the count with a gathered force be judged liable to six hundred solidi.”

19. So that this provision concerning the non-rejection of sound denarii and concerning the safeguarding of false denarii may be observed more effectively and conveniently, we wish every count to have all the markets in his county recorded in a brief, and to be able to tell us which markets existed in the time of our grandfather, which began in the time of our lord and father, which were established by his authority, which were established without his authority, which began to function in our time, and which remain in their ancient locations; and, if they have been moved, by whose authority they were moved.

Each count shall bring this brief to our next assembly, so that we may decide that those markets which are necessary and useful and which exist by authority shall remain, while those that are superfluous shall be prohibited or restored to their proper places. Markets are not to be held anywhere on Sunday, as is provided in Book One of the Capitularies, chapter 136 [Note: [Col. 0705] Sirmond reads “145”; the correct reading is “139”. BAL.].

20. Let the count, the officials of the public authority, and our other faithful provide that in the cities, villages, and estates a just modius and an equal sextarius be used for buying and selling, according to Sacred Scripture and the capitularies of our predecessors. Let them receive the measure from our palace according to ancient custom, and on this account let no larger modius be demanded from the mansuarii or from those who owe a census, except as custom has required.

The men in the villages who, under oath, are responsible for supervision concerning the denarii shall also supervise the measure, so that it is not adulterated, as is contained in Book Three of the Capitularies, chapter 90.

If anyone is accused of adulterating the measure, of receiving grain or wine with a larger modius or sextarius, and of selling with a smaller measure, then, if he is a free man, let him either clear himself by oath according to his law, or, if he is proved to have done this, ordered it to be done [Note: [Col. 0707] “let him pay what, if he did it…”; the text is uncertain.], or consented to it, let the thing by which he adulterated the measure—that is, the wine and grain—be taken from him by the officials of the public authority; moreover, let him pay our bann, that is, sixty solidi.

If he is a colonus or serf and is accused in this matter, let him either undergo the judgment of God, or, if convicted, lose what he used to adulterate the measure, as we said above, and moreover be beaten naked with rods [Note: [Col. 0707] Sirmond prints “with the hand”; BAL corrects this to “with naked body” (*nudo corio*), the reading of the Bellovacensis and Palatine manuscripts.].

Whether the person convicted is free, a colonus, or a serf, after the legal compensation let him undergo episcopal judgment, because he acted against the Lord’s prohibition, which says: “He who has not given his money at interest”—thereby closing the kingdom of God to himself and opening hell to himself. This sin is counted among those capital sins of which the Apostle says that, when someone has committed them, a Christian may not even eat with such a person; and for this reason the sacred canons of Nicaea order clerics to lose their rank. From a matter of this kind, for which secular men lose their life, clerics lose their ecclesiastical rank.

Let the officials of the public authority carefully guard themselves, lest, led by greed on this pretext, they unjustly take anything from free men, coloni, or serfs by any evil device. If a complaint about this reaches us and they are convicted, they shall make compensation for this injustice in the same manner as those who commit extortion in their office.

In those regions where judicial cases are judged according to Roman law, let those who commit such acts be judged according to that law, since neither our predecessors established any capitulary above or against that law, nor have we established anything. Likewise, in the cities, villages, and markets, let the officials of the public authority provide that those who sell baked bread by the denarius or meat by the denarius, or wine by the sextarius, cannot adulterate or diminish their measures.

The number of measurable loaves that the officials of the bishop, abbot [Note: [Col. 0707] “bishop or abbot” is absent in 3.], or count [Note: [Col. 0707] 3 reads “of the count”.] receive from their bakers in each city from a just modius shall be the number of measurable loaves they require to be made from an equal modius by the bakers who sell bread. If those bakers are found to adulterate or reduce the measure, let them be judged liable according to the procedure stated above.

The men who are to supervise this matter, so that deficient measures are not made [Note: [Col. 0707] the phrase “who are to supervise this matter” is absent in BAL.], if they are convicted of perjury because they swore that they would not consent to this but did consent [Note: [Col. 0707] 3 reads “if they are proved to have consented to this, which they ought not to have done”.], shall be punished according to the law, as is contained at the end of chapter 10 of Book Three of the Capitularies; afterward they shall receive public penance from the bishop for their perjury.

21. Since for three years now we have pardoned the bann for rejecting sound denarii, we wish that from now on, according to the discretion we have commended to our envoys, the rewadiated or pledged payment (*rewadiatum*) be paid; and where it has not been pledged, let it be pledged and paid, so that, constrained both by this and by the discipline established, they may henceforth cease rejecting sound denarii.

Since we have heard that, taking advantage of the commutation of the bann, some have taken more from the poor than the bann requires, we wish our envoys to investigate this diligently. Whoever has taken more from them than we ordered shall be compelled to restore it to them, and our envoy shall bring them into our presence without any excuse, so that they may be punished by our harmiscara [Note: [Col. 0707] “armiscara” in 3.] in such a way that they will no longer take pleasure in oppressing the poor through such collusion [Note: [Col. 0707] 3 reads “concludium”.].

22. No other exaction is to be demanded from coloni who have already been flogged or are to be flogged for rejecting sound denarii [Note: [Col. 0707] “who have already been flogged or are to be flogged” is absent in 3.]. If anything has been taken from any of them on this account, our envoys shall compel its restoration.

Those who hold benefices or allods [Note: [Col. 0707] “allods” in 3.] in two, three, or four counties, but do not have enough in each county to pay the full bann [Note: [Col. 0707] the words from “to pay” through the repeated “to pay” are absent in 3.], or those who have an allod or benefices in only one county but do not possess enough there to pay the full bann, shall make this known to our envoys. Let the same envoys carefully record it in a brief and report it to us, so that by our discretion we may decide how both the punishment and the compensation are to be imposed, and so that people are not burdened beyond measure or unjustly.

For, as Sacred Scripture says, “we do not seek the gift, but the fruit”: that is, we do not seek dishonorable profit from it, but the benefit of the kingdom arising from correction. It is shameful or dishonorable profit, as Augustine explains, to gather any possessions dishonestly through various evasions and pretexts for the sake of gain [Note: [Col. 0707] the text from “It is shameful” through “gathered” is absent in 3.].

We wish this discretion to be observed not only toward the poorer but also toward the richer, the discretion that our predecessors, the kings, set forth in Book Four of the Capitularies, chapter 57 [Note: [Col. 0707] 3 reads “LVI”], decreeing:

“Concerning the debt,” they say, “that has been pledged for our purposes, such consideration shall be shown that the person who sinned unknowingly is not compelled to pay the full legal compensation, but only what seems possible. The person who sinned solely through evil intent, however, shall be compelled to pay the full legal compensation.”

23. Henceforth let no one presume to make or consent to the making of an admixture of gold or silver for sale. From the mass of Saint Remigius, that is, from the next Kalends of October, let no one bring gold or silver for selling or buying [Note: [Col. 0709] “for selling or buying” is absent in 3.] unless it has been purified.

If, after the aforesaid Kalends, anyone is found carrying gold or silver, or any object manufactured from gold or silver [Note: [Col. 0709] “from gold or silver” is absent in 3.], mixed for the purpose of selling or buying [Note: [Col. 0709] “for selling or buying” is absent in 3.], the object he carries shall be taken from him by the officials of the public authority. He shall be brought, with the gold or silver itself, before us through sureties if he has no land or dependents in that county, so that we may determine how he is to be judged liable. But if he has land, dependents, or movable property in that county by which he may legally be compelled, he shall be ordered to come before us according to the law.

If anyone is found carrying his own gold or silver, or any object manufactured from gold or silver, to a smith so that it may be purified, let the officials of the public authority take care that on this pretext they do not take from him what belongs to him. If they do so and a complaint about it reaches us, he shall be judged liable in our presence or in that of our faithful, like one who has committed extortion in his county or office.

If, after the aforesaid Kalends, a smith is proved to have adulterated or mixed gold or silver for selling or buying, then in those regions where judicial cases are concluded according to Roman law [Note: [Col. 0709] “Roman law” in 3.], let him be punished according to that law. In the other regions of our kingdom, let him lose his hand, like one who strikes false coin, according to the royal capitulary [Note: [Col. 0709] 3 reads “royal capitularies”.].

A free man who consented to this shall, as is contained in the aforesaid chapter, pay our bann, that is, sixty solidi. A colonus or serf shall be flogged naked with rods [Note: [Col. 0709] 3 reads “let them be flogged naked”.]. If he is a Jew, let him lose the object he brought in a mixed state, and let him pay our bann, as was customary in the time of our predecessors.

24. Throughout our kingdom, let no more than twelve pounds of silver in new and pure denarii be given for one pound of the purest fully refined gold. Gold that has indeed been refined but not to such a degree that gilding can be made from it [Note: [Col. 0709] absent in 3.] shall be sold at the rate of ten pounds of silver in new and pure denarii for one pound of gold.

Let both the counts and all the other officials of the public authority take every possible care that, by any addition or fraud, anything more is not sold under this pretext, as they wish to enjoy their offices. Whoever is found by any device to weaken, defraud, or otherwise alter this instruction of ours, if he is a free man, shall pay our bann, that is, sixty solidi; a colonus or serf shall be flogged naked with rods [Note: [Col. 0709] 3 reads “let them be flogged naked with rods”.].

25. Since the aforesaid capitularies contain, in Book Three, chapter 75 [Note: [Col. 0709] “Book Three” in 3.], that no one may presume, without royal permission, to give or sell armor or weapons to a foreigner, and since in the same book, chapter 6, the places in the kingdom are designated up to which merchants are to carry and sell armor and weapons, with the provision that if they are found carrying or selling them beyond those places, all their property is to be taken from them—the palace receiving one half and the other half being divided between the royal envoys and the discoverer—

because, as our sins demand, the Northmen have come into our vicinity [Note: [Col. 0709] 3 reads “have come”.], and our people give them armor, weapons, and horses [Note: [Col. 0709] “and horses” is absent in 3.] either for ransom or sell them out of greed for profit; and when these things are given for the ransom of one person or sold for a small price, this assistance is thereby provided to them against us [Note: [Col. 0709] 3 reads “is provided”.], causing the greatest harm to our kingdom, while many churches of God [Note: [Col. 0709] “churches and” in 3.] are destroyed, very many Christians are plundered, and the resources of the churches and the kingdom are exhausted; therefore, with the consent and counsel of our faithful, we establish that whoever, after the next Kalends of July of this twelfth indiction, gives armor, any weapons, or a horse to the Northmen by any device, whether for ransom or for any price, shall, as a traitor to his country and one who delivers Christianity to destruction at the hands of the heathen, pay with his life, without any reprieve or redemption. Let all these provisions be made known as quickly as possible to everyone by our envoys and counts [Col. 0710C], so that they cannot excuse themselves on the ground of ignorance.

[Note: [Col. 0710B] The following two paragraphs represent variant editions and should be read in parallel.]

[Col. 0710B] Christianity, and an assistant to heathen error. Therefore, for such a sale and reckless undertaking, we wish the seller to pay with his life and all his possessions to be confiscated. But if he is an ecclesiastic or a person consecrated to God, let him be condemned to perpetual exile. 3, 3b.

26. Let the Frankish pagenses who have or can have horses go with their counts to the army [Note: [Col. 0709] 3 and 3b read “with arms”.]; and let no one, by violence, by any evil device, or by any undue oppression [Note: [Col. 0709] 3 and 3b read “by any greed or oppression”.], take the property or horses of such Franks, so that they cannot perform military service or pay us the required relay-horses (*paraveredos*) according to ancient custom—neither the count nor any official of the public authority.

If any of them is proved to have done this, let him be compelled to pay compensation in the manner established in the royal capitularies for those who commit extortion in their county or office.

27. According to the royal capitulary that our lord and father established in the sixteenth year [Note: [Col. 0709] 3 reads “seventh year”.] of his reign, chapter 7 [Note: [Col. 0709] 3 reads “chapter 2”.], let our counts or envoys diligently inquire how many free men remain in each county who are able to perform military service on their own [Note: [Col. 0709] 3 reads *possint* rather than *possunt*, “may be able”.], how many there are among those in which one helps another, how many among those in which a third is helped or equipped by two [Note: [Col. 0709] this phrase is absent in 3.], and likewise among those in which a fourth is helped and equipped by three [Note: [Col. 0709] 3 reads “is equipped”.], or a fifth is helped and equipped by four, so that they may perform military service. Let them report their total to us.

Those who cannot go to war shall, according to ancient custom and the custom of other peoples, work on new cities, bridges, and marsh crossings [Note: [Col. 0711] absent in 3.], and keep watches in the city and in the march [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads “mark”.]. Let all come without any excuse for the defense of their country.

Those who fail to go to war shall pay the heribann according to the discretion contained in Book Three of the Capitularies of our ancestors, chapter 14 [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads “the discretion which”.]. Those who do not come to the defense of their country shall be judged according to ancient custom and the provisions of the capitularies.

28. Let those Franks who owe a census from their persons or property to the royal treasury not give themselves, without our permission, to the house of God or to the service of anyone else, so that the public authority does not lose what it ought to receive from them.

If they wish to give themselves or their property to the house of God or to the service of anyone else without our permission [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads “if they have given”], then, as is contained in our grandfather’s capitulary concerning those who wish to give themselves into service because of theft, let the counts or vicars not consent to this, but prohibit it by our bann. If they act against our bann, those who receive them shall pay our bann, that is, sixty solidi.

If they wish to retain them in their service, or to hold their property from which the census formerly went to the royal treasury [Note: [Col. 0711] the phrase concerning retaining their property is absent in 3.], let them pay to our royal treasury the census owed by those Franks [Note: [Col. 0711] the remainder of the sentence is absent in 3.] or customarily arising from their property [Note: [Col. 0711] absent in 3.], as is contained in the aforesaid third book of the Capitularies, chapters 15 and 86, and in Book Four, chapter 36.

Since, as is found in the sacred ecclesiastical regulations [Note: [Col. 0711] absent in 3.], the earlier observance was stricter, while the later one, circumstances requiring it, was more accommodating, the subsequent capitularies of our predecessors and ancestors did not prohibit such Franks, as we said above, from giving or selling their property to the house of God or to others, and from converting themselves to divine service if they wished, as is contained in Book One, chapters 132 [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads “134 and 136”.] and 134, in Book Two, chapter 31 [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads “32”.], and in Book Four [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads “Book Five”, chapter 18.], chapter 19.

If any such Frank wishes to give or sell his property, we do not prohibit him. Only let him not, without reason, lose the royal right that is owed to the king [Note: [Col. 0711] the phrase concerning the royal right is absent in 3.], since we do not wish to impose upon anyone unjust customs newly instituted, which we read were prohibited in Book Four of the same Capitularies, chapter 47 [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads “chapter 45”.]. Concerning those who live according to Roman law, we define nothing other than what is contained in those same laws.

29. Those coloni, both fiscal and ecclesiastical [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 has “fiscal and ecclesiastical coloni” in a different order.], who, as is contained in the polyptychs [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads *polipticis*.] and as they themselves do not deny [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads *denegent*, “should not deny”.], owe *carropera* and *manopera* according to ancient custom [Note: [Col. 0711] absent in 3.], refuse to carry marl [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 corrects *margila* to *argilla*, “clay”.] and any other things which they are ordered to carry when those things do not please them [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads, incompletely, “they do not refuse what pleases [them], although in those …”.].

Perhaps in those ancient times marl was not transported [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads “they would not have transported marl”.], whereas in many places it began to be transported in the time of our grandfather and of our lord and father [Note: [Col. 0711] absent in 3.], and they do not wish to do the manual work of threshing in the *scuria* (barn) [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads “it began”—with *debeat*, “ought,” in an erasure—“also to thresh in the *scuria*, and nevertheless they do not deny …”], although they do not deny that they owe *manopera* [Note: [Col. 0711] “*manopera*” is printed as a separate phrase in 3.].

Whatever they are ordered to carry as part of their *carropera* when they are required to perform it, let them carry without any distinction; and whatever they are ordered to do as part of their *manopera* when they are required to perform it, let them likewise do without any distinction [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads: “and let them perform every task whenever it is ordered, without any distinction.”].

30. Since in certain places coloni, both fiscal and belonging to the houses of God, sell their inheritances—that is, the mansi they hold—not only to their equals but also to canonical clerics, village priests, and any other persons, retaining only the dwelling-place, and since on this account the estates become so ruined that not only can the due census no longer be exacted from them, but even which lands belonged to each individual mansus can no longer be recognized, we establish that our officials and the ecclesiastical officials be ordered to ensure that this does not happen in any way henceforth, lest the estates become ruined and disordered.

Whatever has been sold from individual mansi by anyone without the permission of the lords or masters shall be recovered. It shall be restored to the individual mansi [Note: [Col. 0711] absent in 3.] from which the lands were sold and from which the census fell away [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads “ought to have fallen away”.] because of the inability of those who cannot serve their mansi [Note: [Col. 0711] much of this clause is absent in 3.]. After they have been restored, a census shall be exacted for the lord from each mansus according to the quality or quantity of the land or vineyards belonging to each mansus.

31. Concerning the displaced persons of this land, which has been devastated by the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0711] 3 reads “ravaged”.], we establish, as is contained in the capitulary of our grandfather, Emperor Charles, that each count shall have the names of those persons in his county recorded, together with the names of their lords [Note: [Col. 0711] absent in 3.], and that he shall permit those newcomers who have been living in their counties since the time of our grandfather and since the time of our lord and father [Note: [Col. 0711] absent in 3.] to remain there according to the custom that existed in their times.

But those who have recently fled from these regions to those regions because of the persecution of the Northmen shall be brought by the envoys of the bishops, together with the officials of the public authority, from those regions to these [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “from these regions to those”.], in such a way that they are not oppressed and that no census or any exaction is demanded from them. Let them have permission to entrust whatever they earned by their service in those regions or acquired by any legitimate means [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “whatever they may have acquired”.].

Those who do not expect any profit from work in the vineyards shall already have returned to their own place by the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “let each return, and let the one who…”.]. Whoever has earned profit from vineyards in those regions [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “expects profit”.] shall already have returned to these regions eight days after the mass of Saint Remigius [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “returned to his place”.], and shall make provision for himself in these regions for the future and serve his lord.

If it is necessary for him, let him return to those regions at the mass of Saint Martin for his contracted employment (*conductum*), and let him have permission to remain there until the Kalends of April [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “to reside”.]. From there let each return to the land of his birth and to his lord [Note: [Col. 0713] “senior” is printed in 3.], and let him remain there until mid-May for the sake of sowing [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “let them remain”.]. From there, if it is necessary for him, let him return to his contracted employment (*conductum*); and from there let each return to his own land for the harvest [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “let them return”.], and thereafter remain there [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “let them remain”.].

If a woman from these regions has taken a husband in those regions, or a husband a wife, let that marriage be dissolved, since it is neither lawful nor legitimate [Note: [Col. 0713] “lawful nor legitimate” is absent in 3.], as Leo demonstrates in his decretals and Saint Gregory in his letters. Whose slave the man or woman was, let that person receive his or her own slave and unite him or her to a person under his or her authority [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 and 3b read: “let him have the power to receive and join the person to himself or herself, and if…”.]. If children have been born from that union, let the children follow their mother according to the law [Col. 0713C] and ancient custom [Note: [Col. 0713] absent in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0713] “our” is absent in 3.]. In those regions that follow Roman law, we decree that this matter be handled according to that same law [Note: [Col. 0713] “according to that law” in 3; “from this matter” is absent in 3.].

32. Let neighboring and bordering counts, if possible, not hold their mallum on the same day [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “malum”; B reads “mallum”.], especially after the octave of Easter, on account of the Frankish men and advocates who cannot attend both mallum assemblies. Instead, let them send envoys to one another.

If one holds his mallum on Monday, let the other hold his on Thursday or on Monday of the following week. So that the one who has postponed his mallum is not burdened, whoever holds the mallum first in one year shall agree that the other hold it first in the following year.

If legal oaths are due to be sworn on the first Monday after Easter, or on other weekdays when he ought to have held the mallum [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “when he should have held it”.], let each count send his envoy to listen to those oaths [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads “the oath”.], lest those men be found to be *jectivi* [Note: [Col. 0713] the manuscript space is blank; 3 supplies *fugitivi*, “fugitives,” and 3b likewise.].

Let him hold his mallum in such a way that his *barigildi* and advocates, who have legal business in other counties, can attend his mallum [Note: [Col. 0713] 3 reads: “and his *barigildi* and advocates…can attend”; the text also contains a deletion before “can”.].

### 33.

And because legal oaths are received to be sworn after forty nights, and because it is found in the aforementioned capitularies of our predecessors and ancestors that, after the count and the country people have returned from any military expedition, from that day for forty nights the *bannus resisus* is in force—which in the German language is called *scastlegi*, that is, the laying down of arms—many disputes arise from this, and they bring suits against one another. For some wish to swear their oath on the fortieth day itself, on which they receive it; and they argue so insistently that, even if the fortieth day should fall within the forty-day period of the sacred fast, they maintain that they ought to swear their oath, and they bring suit against their opponents if they have not come to hear the matter. [Note: Column 0713: manuscripts 3, 3b, and 3c read *dies* (“days”) for *noctes* (“nights”); manuscript 3 has *teodisca* for *Theodisca*, *scastlei* for *scastlegi*, and *se inter* in an erased space, while *inter se* is absent. It reads *contendunt* (“they contend”) and *jectiscunt* (“they bring suits”) for the respective forms in the text, and omits the words “just as days are counted and nights are not counted.” It also reads *accusatores* (“accusers”) instead of *causatores* (“claimants”).]

For they count the days and do not count the nights with them, just as days are counted without nights from the Nativity of the Lord until the Purification of Saint Mary, and from the Resurrection of the Lord until the Ascension of the Lord. For on the fortieth day after the Nativity of the Lord the Purification of Saint Mary is celebrated, and on the fortieth day after the Resurrection of the Lord—which occurs on Sunday—the Ascension of the Lord is celebrated, which falls on the fifth feria, that is, Thursday. And concerning days counted without remembering the nights, the Lord says through the prophet Jonah: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.” But forty days together with nights are counted in the fast of the prophet Elijah, and of Moses [Note: Manuscript 3 spells the name *moisi*; it reads *noctis memoria*, “memory of the night,” for *memoria noctium*, “memory of the nights.”] when he received the law a second time, and in the Lord’s own fast.

In these periods six weeks—that is, forty-two days—are completed up to the Resurrection of the Lord, which takes place on Sunday, just as the beginning of Lent does. And these things do not happen without the mystery of God [Note: “ministry” instead of “mystery,” according to manuscript 3.], through whom the establishers of laws decree what is just. Therefore, as we have found to be more rightly observed in certain regions [Note: This is absent from manuscript 3.], with the agreement and counsel of our faithful [Note: This is absent from manuscript 3.], we have decreed that, from the very day on which the oath is received, after forty days and forty nights—that is, on the forty-second day, after the six weeks [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *de* (“after/from”) and reads *septimanas* in place of *septimanis*, both meaning “weeks.”]—the person who has received the legal oath shall swear it legally in the appointed places, on the same feria on which he received that oath, just as Easter itself takes place on the feria on which the beginning of Lent is observed [Note: Manuscript 3 reads: “if Easter falls on that same …”], and just as it is contained in the books of the capitularies of our deceased predecessors and ancestors. [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *accepit*, “received,” instead of *accipit*, “receives.”]

From now on, therefore, let no disagreement or retraction concerning this arise in our kingdom from anyone. If anyone should presume to disregard this command of ours, let him pay our fine, namely sixty solidi. And if that day should fall within the sacred fasts of Lent, let no one presume to swear during Lent the oath which he has received, because in this matter we have already seen and heard the manifest vengeance of God. [Note: Manuscript 3 omits “also.”] And if anyone [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “And whoever”] should presume to do so, let him likewise pay our fine, and thereafter do penance according to episcopal judgment.

We order that Lent itself be observed from Wednesday—that is, from the beginning of the fast, on the Wednesday when public penitents receive penance—until the holy Resurrection, according to ancient custom. But let the person who received an oath preserved until before Lent wait, if he has not had forty days and forty nights before that Lent [Note: Sirmondus reads *illud quadragesima*; the base text has *illam quadragesimam*], without any legal payment or bringing suit [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *ulla* (“any”) and reads *jectione* instead of *jectitione*], until the Monday after the octave of Easter [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *octabas*, “octaves”]; and then let him complete legally what he has received legally.

### 34.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God and of ours [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *quia* (“because”) for *quoniam* (“that”).] that certain of our counts consulted us concerning those Frankish men who owed the royal census for their persons and also for their small possessions [Note: Column 0715D: that is, small things; manuscript 3 has *et rescellis debeant*, corrected to *debent*, “and who owe for their small possessions”], and who, when famine compelled them by necessity, sold themselves into servitude. We therefore discussed with the bishops and the other faithful of God and of ours what ought to be done about this; and what we found and decreed with them concerning it [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “to establish”], we have now determined by this edict [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “because it is contained in the law”].

That is: since we have found nothing more explicitly expressed on this matter in the Salic Law [Note: Manuscript 3 reads: “because we have found nothing more explicitly contained in the Salic Law”], it is nevertheless contained in the third book of the capitularies, chapter 29, concerning a free man who has delivered himself, as a pledge, into another’s power, and who, after being placed there, has inflicted some injury on anyone: the person who received him as a pledge must either pay the compensation for the injury or lose the man produced before the court, at the same time losing the debt for which he received him as a pledge; and the person who committed the injury, once released, must be compelled to make amends according to the nature of the matter.

But if he has had a free woman, and while he was held in pledge they have had children, let them remain free. And in the law written by the finger of God we read that, if our brother has become impoverished and has delivered himself into servitude, he shall serve the man who bought him for six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free without payment. This sacred history both morally builds up those who observe it and enlightens those who understand it in a higher sense.

In the law also which our predecessors and the most renowned emperors established concerning those who, compelled by famine or some other necessity, sell their children, there are many chapters [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *hic*, “here.”] which we have not thought necessary to set down here. Yet we have thought it necessary to set down here that chapter which we have found to agree for the most part with the sacred ecclesiastical regulations [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *id*, “that,” instead of *hic*, “here”]. It says:

> “If any free persons sell their children—which we also wish to have observed concerning free men who sell themselves—when compelled by any necessity or in a time of famine, then, compelled by that necessity, if the buyer bought for five solidi, let him receive six; if for ten, let him likewise receive twelve solidi; or, if more, let him receive an increase in the price according to the rule written above.” [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *quod*, “that,” instead of *aut*, “or.”]

Saint Gregory too, concerning those who have been captured by pagans while free, says that, if someone redeems them, those who have been redeemed should arrange to give their redeemer as much money as they were redeemed for by him, and should remain in their freedom. But if the Church has redeemed them, let them become free without payment and without any compensation. [Note: Sirmondus reads: *Sanctus autem Gregorius, etiam de his*—“But Saint Gregory, concerning these also.”]

This too we order, by royal authority, to be observed throughout our kingdom, with the agreement and counsel of our faithful [Note: Both phrases are absent from manuscript 3]. And if anyone should say that he does not wish to pay the price for a free man, whether in a time of famine or because of some other necessity, since he ought not to keep him perpetually as a slave, let him attend to what the Lord says to him through his apostle: [Note: Manuscript 3 reads: “because I do not wish to give a price in a time of famine for a free man if I ought not always to have him as a slave.”]

> “Whoever has the substance of this world,” he says, “and sees his brother in need, and closes his heart against him, the love of God does not remain in him.” [Note: Manuscript 3 omits “the substance of this world.”]

And whoever does not possess this love—even if he gives himself over to martyrdom and to the fire—will not be able to obtain forgiveness of his sins without it, and will in no way enter the kingdom of God, because he refuses to give for God his money or his grain, which he received from God, although God gave himself and shed his blood for him on the cross, pierced with nails and a lance.

And because the minds of men who do not fear God, at the devil’s prompting, devise many evils, it may happen that those who receive such free men into servitude, compelled by necessity as we have said, transfer and sell them to other regions. Therefore, with the agreement and counsel of our faithful [Note: Both phrases are absent from manuscript 3], we have decreed what we found established in the ancient laws: if anyone should presume to transfer or sell such persons to foreign peoples or to lands overseas, the person who has presumed to act against these statutes shall pay the penalty of the royal fine.

And if such a man, previously free, has had children by a free woman while he has remained in such servitude, let those children remain free, just as is contained in the aforementioned chapter 29 of the third [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “fourth”] book of the capitularies of our predecessors and ancestors concerning the man who has committed himself, as a pledge, into another’s power—without prejudice to the provision of Roman law in the case of those who live according to it.

### 35.

And let our counts know that we shall send our envoys through each county, who shall inquire specifically into the matters we have now established: how they have striven to fulfill our command in these matters, as is contained in chapter 18 of the second book of the capitularies of our predecessors and ancestors.

And whoever is found negligent in this matter, we shall order to be summoned before our presence and to give an account whether he was unwilling or unable to do what we commanded; or, if some obstacle prevented him from doing it, why he did not report that impossibility to us in due time. For if he was unwilling to do this, or was unable because of his negligence, we wish to find someone who is willing or able to observe what we command.

### 36.

We wish that, just as is contained in chapter 24 of the second book of the capitularies of our deceased predecessors and ancestors, these capitularies which have now and at other times been established by us with the counsel of our faithful may be received from our chancellor by the archbishops and counts [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “our counts” instead of “their counts”] from their own cities, either personally or through their envoys.

Let each of them have them copied throughout his diocese for the other bishops, abbots, counts, or other faithful of ours [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “and other faithful”], and have them read aloud in their counties before everyone, so that our ordinance and will may become known to all. Our chancellor shall note the names of the bishops and counts who have taken care to receive them and shall bring those names to our attention, so that no one may presume to neglect this.

### 37.

And since our faithful are laboring at the works being carried out on the Seine and at other works, and since our military camp, which we ordered to be built here in the previous year, was destroyed by men coming from that side of the Seine to these regions and going from these regions to that side, under the pretext that they had begun to remain there contrary to due reverence—and since we have now had this military camp built only with labor and expense on the part of our faithful—we wish and expressly command that, just as no one may remain in our palace without our command, so no one may presume to remain in this military camp without our command [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “this military camp”], nor may anyone destroy it [Note: Manuscript 3 reads: “lest it be destroyed. If anyone …”].

If anyone should presume to do so, and this is reported to us by the guards whom we have appointed for this purpose, the offender shall not escape without due punishment. For we always wish to be ready, and we command you to be ready, so that in these regions and in any others where it may be necessary for us, against pagans and against any others, just as has been customary, and as your predecessors furnished assistance to our predecessors and you have provided due and necessary aid to us, so now and always we may all be ready together, according to the will of God, for the defense of God’s will, of the holy Church, and of this Christianity, and for securing and defending our common safety and peace, as far as God may deign to grant assistance. [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “always and in all things be ready, with such intention”; all the remaining words are absent.]

And after all this had been read:

### 1.

We admonish your fidelity to observe these things firmly and always to be ready, as beloved faithful of God and of ours, so that, if necessity should arise for us, whether against pagans or against any others, as soon as a messenger comes to each person, or he hears that we are in need, he may be prepared for military service without any delay, move out for the service of God and of us for the common benefit, and come to us without fail.

And we wish and expressly command that all those who in these times have constructed castles, fortifications, or hedges without our order have all such fortifications demolished by the Kalends of August, because the neighbors and those living around them suffer many acts of plunder and impediments as a result. And those who do not wish to demolish them shall have them demolished by the counts in whose counties they were built. If anyone should oppose them, let the counts take care to make this known to us in due time. If they neglect to fulfill this as we command, let them know that, just as is contained in these capitularies and in the capitularies of our predecessors, we shall seek out such counts and install others in their counties who are willing and able to carry out our command.

### 2.

The person who has been summoned to settle a case here must remain here until the matter for which he has been summoned has been settled. And whoever has need to remain here for his own case may remain with us for as long as necessity requires. Our vassals also shall remain and travel with us with as many men as is convenient for them.

### 3.
