But you others, as well as those who will remain with us, go with the grace of God and of us, whether traveling, remaining in your homeland, or returning to us, while observing the peace jointly confirmed by us. May God grant that we may soon, and for many years, see one another healthy and joyful, and rejoice in God’s mercy and grace over us.

[Column 0717]

## THE PACT OF HLUDOWICUS THE GERMAN AND CHARLES II AT TUSIACUM  
*(865, February 19)*

[Note: The Annals of Hincmar mention this agreement in February 865, and the Annals of Fulda also mention it, though they assign it to September 864. Sirmondus published it from the Laudun manuscript; Baluzius published it with the aid of the Rivipullensis manuscript.]

[Column 0717D]

In the year 865 of the Lord’s incarnation, on the Kalends of March, Hludowicus and Charles, kings, announced the following to the people at the estate of Tusiacum. [Note: The Rivipullian manuscript has only: “The Capitularies of King Charles and his brother Louis.”]

As we believe you and many others have heard, we proposed to assemble together a second and a third time during this period; but because various occupations impeded us, we have been unable to fulfill this until now. Now, because, thanks be to God, we have assembled together, we wish you to know that we have not assembled for anyone’s deception or condemnation, nor out of any unjust desire. We wish to make known to you the reasons for which, apart from the proper and fraternal desire to see one another in mutual affection, our assembly has taken place; and, with the help of God and with the counsel and aid of you and of our other common faithful, we wish immutably to uphold and usefully to increase whatever is pleasing to God and salutary and beneficial to us and to our faithful.

1. First, we fraternally and sincerely laid before one another the needs of ourselves, of the holy Church of God, and of the kingdom entrusted to us.

2. We carefully recalled those matters which were recently confirmed between us at Confluentes with the counsel of our faithful; with the Lord’s assistance, we shall preserve them inviolate.

3. As God sees this in our heart, we wish you also to know that, united—that is, made of one mind—with a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith, to the extent granted by him from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes, we have joined together for the will of God, for our common honor and safety, for the condition of the holy Church of God, for the due honor and strength of its priests and servants, and for restoring and preserving the stability of the kingdom entrusted to us by God.

Thus the Church and kingdom which God united in the hands of our ancestors and entrusted to us in his mercy may, in our time, possess the necessary defense and protection, honor, and stability.

4. Since, as Holy Scripture says, whoever does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever, we have considered and confirmed in our faith toward one another the matter of our wives and sons, who have been so faithfully subject and obedient to us as sons ought to be to their fathers and their lords: each of us shall hold the other’s sons as his own in true affection; and whichever of us survives the other shall provide the deceased man’s wife and sons with the due and necessary assistance agreed upon between us, and shall preserve faith toward them.

5. We have considered and established that our common faithful, by whose counsel and aid we must govern the holy Church of God and the kingdom entrusted to us, shall have due honor and safety. And let them, for the will of God, and so that our due honor, strength, and safety, the condition of the holy Church of God, and the stability and defense of the kingdom may be preserved, and so that the people in our kingdom may have law, justice, peace, and tranquility, be our helpers in all things with pure heart, good conscience, sincere faith, and faithful counsel and aid.

If anyone, which God forbid, should attempt to deviate from this, let us strive unanimously to turn him back to it. If he cannot be brought back to it, let us unanimously strive that he may at least harm himself alone and may not wickedly act against what we ought to preserve for the common good. And let all—both our friends and our opponents—hold this most certainly: whoever plots or contrives anything adverse against either of us shall have no place of familiarity or friendship with the other.

6. You know how our nephew Hlotharius, through his youth, through the agreement and encouragement of frivolous men, and also through the favor of those who ought to have saved him, has acted and is acting against that law which God first gave in paradise to the first human beings, and which he renewed and confirmed in the Gospel by dwelling among men in the presence of the flesh; that law applies to all people who use marriage lawfully according to God.

Therefore the universal Church of God is shaken, the priests are dishonored, and the Christian people are stained as though by the contagion of a serious disease. Because God said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” and because it is written, “He is our bone and our flesh,” and because the Church and kingdom entrusted to us and to him are one, and the people and Christianity are one, we have considered sending our envoys to him with such counsel as may enable him to be saved before God and honored before the world, so that the Church and kingdom entrusted to him for salvation may be firm, and so that God’s people may be safe and possess law, justice, peace, and tranquility.

7. Since he too sent his envoys to us as though seeking counsel, through our envoys we send him back a true and sincere counsel concerning the matters about which he instructed us, insofar as the Lord has granted us understanding; and through those same envoys we tell him that our will toward him is such as we have declared to you.

## THE CAPITULARIES OF CHARLES GIVEN TO HIS ENVOYS  
*(865, February)*

[Note.]

These capitularies follow the pact above in the Laudun manuscript, from which Sirmondus published them. Baluzius emended them with the aid of the manuscripts also used by us: 4) Royal Library of Paris, no. 4626, tenth century, formerly Bigotian; and 5) the same library, no. 4761, formerly Divionensis.

The following capitularies were sent by Lord King Charles to Burgundy to be carried out by Gauslenus [Note: Sirmondus has *Gauslinum*; Baluzius corrected it by hand to *Gaussenium*] and Fulco, and by Waltarius and Lantwinus [Note: Sirmondus has *Lantvinum*; Baluzius corrected it by hand to *Lantuvinum*], from Tusiacum, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: This phrase is absent from manuscripts 4 and 5].

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, by the grace of God king, to all bishops, abbots, abbesses, counts, and our vassals, and to all the faithful of God and of ours residing in the kingdom of Burgundy, greetings. We wish and expressly command that, in carrying out the matters set out below [Note: Manuscript 4 reads *subjecta*, “set beneath,” instead of *subjuncta*, “appended”], and in other matters which concern the will of God and the condition of the holy Church, our fidelity and honor, the stability of the kingdom, and the common safety of our faithful, each of you, according to what is appropriate to his order and person, be obedient and helpful in all things to these our envoys.

1. Just as our unfaithful subjects and common opponents have mutually bound themselves to oppose us, so that none of them reveals or betrays his equal concerning the matters they have considered, nor abandons the things they intend to carry out, so let our faithful bind themselves to the will of God and to our fidelity, to honor, to the condition of the holy Church, to the welfare of the kingdom, and to their common assistance and safety.

Let none of our faithful in any way join himself to any of our unfaithful subjects, favor him in anything, or spare him in any matter in which he could hinder him, unless that person immediately wishes to return to our fidelity. If he can know with certainty who has acted against this chapter, let him not conceal it from us. And if anyone hears that necessity has arisen or is about to arise for his faithful equal to resist our unfaithful subject, let him not wait for this to be commanded to him, but immediately be prepared, as a faithful man of God and of ours, to assist his equal in our fidelity, and hasten to go as far as he can.

2. Let all who have not yet promised us fidelity promise us fidelity, as is contained in the capitularies of our grandfather and father.

3. Let the property of those who promised us fidelity and, after that oath, joined themselves to our unfaithful subjects to our detriment be received into our royal domain until they come before us through sureties.

4. Let none of our unfaithful subjects who are free men be permitted to remain in our kingdom or possess property there unless he has promised us fidelity and becomes our man or the man of one of our faithful. [Note: Manuscript 4 reads *nulli fidelium*, “none of the faithful,” in place of *nullus infidelium*, “none of the unfaithful.”]

5. Let those unjust transfers which were made to women, mothers, or any persons, and which were prohibited by our predecessors and by us so that the transferors themselves might more freely carry out their infidelity toward us or might not render justice in the counties, be regarded as though they had not been made and counted as nothing.

And just as the transferors themselves had held those allods in their own hands, so let those allods be treated. If they cannot thereby be brought back to our fidelity or compelled to render justice, let those allods be received into our royal domain, and let a precise description of them be brought to us. Let those unfaithful subjects of ours not be permitted to have a place in our kingdom.

Let the same be done concerning commendations of any property or money. If they have had anything commended to a church, let the bishop or rector of the church where it was commended either return it in person, in the presence of our envoys, to those who commended it, or have it sealed before our envoys and kept under seal until those who commended it come and receive it before our envoys. Let them be constrained accordingly to return to our fidelity and to the peace of the Church and kingdom.

6. Concerning unjust exchanges made with churches without royal authority, let our envoys inquire and dissolve them [Note: Sirmondus reads “reclaim them, so that they may dissolve them”], as is contained in the capitularies of our grandfather and father.

If a mortmain arrangement or a royal order intervenes in these matters, let the envoys carefully and faithfully describe how they were made and report it to us. After the orders themselves have been sealed, let them be brought before us, as Roman law prescribes, just as is contained in the capitularies of our ancestors.

7. Since, as we have learned, many people requested allods from us and, having asked for little, received more from them, we wish our envoys to investigate and record this carefully, and have those men come before us with their orders.

8. Let our envoys inquire into all the censuses and *paraveredi* which Frankish men ought to pay to the royal power; wherever payment has been omitted through negligence, let them have it paid, carefully record everything from each county, and report it to us.

Let them do likewise concerning census-bearing lands [Note: Manuscript 4 reads *ceteris*, “other [things],” for *terris*, “lands.”] and concerning property given to churches from which a census has anciently been paid to the king’s share. If anyone produces any royal authority concerning this, let them have that authority brought before us.

9. *(Anseg. IV, chapter 48.)* Let our envoys, wherever necessary, carry out our authority concerning places for the cloisters of canons or monks, as is contained in the capitularies of our grandfather and father.

10. *(Chapter 49.)* Let our envoys carry out the matter of the nones and tithes to be paid to churches, as is contained in the aforementioned capitularies.

11. *(Chapter 85.)* Let no census or payment for the pasturing of horses be demanded by lords from priests for a single manse given to a church, as is contained in the aforementioned capitulary. Nor let such payment be demanded for small plots or little vineyards given to the same churches for a burial place, nor for tithes, as is contained in the canons and in the aforementioned capitularies.

*(Chapter 84.)* Wherever it is found by our envoys that lords eject priests from churches or install them in churches without the knowledge of the bishops, let our envoys act concerning this as is contained in the aforementioned capitularies. And let the bishops act concerning the clergy of our men as is contained in those same capitularies.

12. Let our envoys administer justice to all who need it, insofar as the nature of the time permits. Whatever they cannot now do because of the circumstances or brevity of the time, let them entrust to the counts, so that at a suitable time they may provide those people with law and justice.

Let them record in their memoranda which counts they have entrusted them to, so that, if those men again complain that they have been unable to obtain justice, we ourselves may investigate and determine why those counts have neglected this.

13. If our unfaithful subjects unite to ravage our kingdom, let our faithful—bishops, abbots, the men of abbesses, as well as the counts and our vassals, and all other faithful of God and of ours—arrange to assemble together from one *missaticum*. Let our envoys make provision within that *missaticum* concerning how each bishop, abbot, or abbess has sent his or her men there, with the full and necessary equipment for war and at the appointed time, together with a standard-bearer [Note: “Standard-bearer, commander,” according to Sirmondus] who shall render an account to our envoys on behalf of his equals [Note: Manuscript 4 reads *partibus*, “parts,” corrected to *paribus*, “equals,” in manuscript 5].

Let them report to us in writing how the counts and our vassals, and all the other faithful of God, have come to this assistance. If those from one *missaticum* are unable to prevail in this matter, let them quickly send their envoys to another *missaticum*, and let everyone from another *missaticum*, as we have said, come prepared to those who are in need.

If those two *missatica* are insufficient for this, let them report this to us in due time, explaining how we, or our son, or in whatever way we deem appropriate, should send them the necessary support, so that no unfaithful or hostile subject of ours may have an opportunity to harm anyone in our kingdom.

14. Since, as we have heard, certain men remain in their homes for as long as they can have peace and, when necessity arises, say that they will come into our service, we do not wish any of those who remain in that land and ought to defend it against our enemies to have this opportunity from now on. Rather, when necessity arises, let them come, as we have said, to our envoys and to their equals.

If we specifically order any one of them to come to us, or if he wishes to report to us some necessary matter concerning our fidelity, let him leave there the full body of his men [Note: Manuscript 5 reads “all his men”] to carry out our fidelity, and let him make this known to our envoys or to his equals. Otherwise, let him not go anywhere from that land except with the common counsel or commendation of our envoys or of the other faithful of ours who ought to defend that land [Note: Sirmondus reads “with the counsel and commendation”].

And let our envoys, together with the bishops, counts, and our vassals who live along the waters by which our unfaithful subjects cross into our kingdom, arrange how those ships are to be guarded, so that our unfaithful subjects cannot cross over to ravage our kingdom. If, through someone’s negligence, those ships are not afterward properly guarded, let this be reported to us, so that we may determine how that despiser of our command is to be treated, as a traitor to the fatherland.

15. If our envoys find in that land a case which they cannot bring to its proper conclusion either through these capitularies, through the capitularies of our ancestors, or through the legal capitularies, let them take care to send us a reasonable and truthful report, so that we may send them instructions concerning how they should act in the matter.

16. Let the counts’ officials in each county receive the provisions for our envoys which are to be supplied by anyone who must supply them, as is contained in our *tractoria*; and let them hand them over to the officials of our envoys. [Note: The reading *ministrorum nostrorum* (“of our officials”) was corrected by hand to *missorum nostrorum* (“of our envoys”), according to Sirmondus and Baluzius.] But let our envoys ensure that, on this account, the counts’ officials demand nothing more than what is contained in our *tractoria*. [Note: The remainder is absent from manuscripts 4 and 5.]

[Column 0723]

## THE OATH OF HLOTHARIUS II CONCERNING THE RECEPTION OF THEOTBERGA  
*(865, August 3)*

[Note: The oath, sworn by twelve men on Hlotharius’s behalf, is preserved in the Annals of Hincmar, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, vol. I, pp. 468–469, and in *Patrologia*, vol. CXV; for this reason we have thought it should be reproduced here.]

[Col. 0723C] I, so-and-so, swearing, promise by these four holy Gospels of Christ, which I touch with my hands, and by these relics of the saints, that my lord, King Hlothar, son of the late, piously remembered, most serene Emperor Hlothar, will henceforth and thereafter accept [Col. 0723D] Theodberga, his wife, as his lawful queen, [Col. 0724C] and will treat her in every respect as it is fitting for a king to treat his queenly wife. And because of the aforesaid disputes, she shall suffer no harm, either in her life or in her person, neither from my aforesaid lord Hlothar nor from any person, with him instigating, aiding, or even consenting; [Col. 0724D] rather, he shall treat her [Col. 0725A] as it is fitting for a king to treat a lawful wife. This is nevertheless on condition that she henceforth conduct herself as it is fitting for a wife in every respect to honor her lord. These are the names of those who swore this oath:

Of the counts: Milo, Ratharius, Erlandus, Theutmarus, Weremboldus, and Count Rocolfus.

Of the vassals: Erleboldus, Vulfridus, Eidulfus, Bertmundus, Nithardus, and Arnostus.

This oath was sworn upon the four Gospels of God, the most precious wood of the holy Cross of the Lord, and other relics of the saints, at the place called Vindonissa, on the third day of August, in the thirteenth indiction. This was done in the time of the lord, thrice most blessed and co-angelic, Nicholas the apostolic bishop, through the intervention and arrangement of Arsenius, venerable bishop, envoy and apocrisiary of the supreme holy Catholic [Col. 0725B] and Apostolic See, exercising apostolic authority and serving as legate of that same lord Nicholas the apostolic bishop.

The names of the bishops in whose presence [Col. 0726A] this took place and who were in attendance are these: Harduicus, archbishop of Besançon; Remedius, archbishop of Laon; Ado, archbishop of Vienne; Rodlandus, archbishop of Arles; Adventius, bishop of Metz; Atto, bishop of Verdun; Franco, bishop of Saint-Lambert; Rataldus, bishop of Strasbourg; and Fulcricus, chaplain and imperial envoy.

From King Charles’s kingdom: Isaac, bishop of Langres, and Erkanraus, bishop of Châlons. From their hands Theodberga the queen was received, on the part of King Charles, by Arsenius, venerable bishop and legate of the Apostolic See, together with the archbishops and bishops named above. Noblemen from various kingdoms were standing in the same place, along with a multitude of the people, publicly seeing and hearing these things; [Col. 0726B] we were not able to include all their names on this page.

[Col. 0725]

## Constitution of Emperor Louis II concerning the advance of the army to Benevento (866)

[Note: [Col. 0725] We present here again, in a more corrected form, the constitution edited by Camillo Peregrini in *Historia principum Langobardorum*, vol. I, pp. 99–101, from a single Casinensian manuscript, which we ourselves have again examined and corrected with the aid of manuscript no. 353, parchment, tenth century. Baluzius introduced the division into chapters, which is not found in the manuscript.]

Constitution concerning the advance of the army and the observance to be maintained in the districts of Benevento, under the fifteenth indiction.

[Col. 0725C]

1. Whoever possesses movable property worth his *widrigild* shall go on campaign. Whoever possesses half a *widrigild* shall join with another, the two together furnishing the requisite equipment, so that they may go properly. Poor persons, however, shall go to guard the coast or the homeland, namely, whoever has more than ten solidi in movable property shall go to that guard duty. Whoever has no more than ten solidi in movable property shall be required to do nothing.

If a father has one son, and the son is more capable than the father, the son, equipped by his father, shall go. If the father is more capable, he himself shall go. If he has two sons, whichever of them is more capable shall go, while the other shall remain with the father. If he has more sons, all the more capable shall go; only the one who is less capable shall remain.

Concerning undivided brothers, in accordance with the capitulary of our lord and father, we decree that if there are two, both shall go. If there are three, the one who appears less capable shall remain; the others shall go. If there are more, all who appear more capable shall go; one less capable shall remain.

We decree concerning this condition that no count, gastald, or their ministers shall, by command, advocacy, or any other pretext, have anyone excused, except that in each county the count shall leave one man to guard that place, and two with his wife. Bishops, however, shall leave no layman behind. For whoever presumes to remain contrary to this ordinance, we have ordered that his property be immediately taken by the envoys for our use, according to what we have set out below [Note: [Col. 0725] Read “according to what,” etc.], and that he be expelled.

2. We wish it to be known to all that, in accordance with this ordinance, properties had already been confiscated by our predecessors, but through mercy their owners deserved to recover them. Now, however, know with complete certainty that whoever’s property is confiscated will scarcely deserve its recovery from us.

3. From the river Po to the Trebbia, let Iotselmus be the envoy. Between the Po and the Ticino, Eriulfus. Between the Ticino and the Adda, Erembertus. Between the Adda and the Addaiza, Landebertus. From the Addaiza to the Forum Julii, Teodoldus.

[Col. 0726D] Bishops Peter and Arthemius, together with the envoys of the bishops and counts, shall oversee Pisa and Lucca; Teutmundus, Pistoia and Luni; Rodselmus, Florence, Volterra, and Arezzo; Andreas, Chiusi and Siena. In Wito’s ministry, Rimmo and John, bishop of Forcona. In Verengar’s ministry, Bishop Hiselmundus. On the Italian coast, Ermefridus, Macedo, and Vulfericus.

4. We wish these men to expel the population, provide for the guard, and make the people reside in the fortified places, and also to do so peacefully. If any envoy dares to fail to remove all the men [Note: [Col. 0725] I have corrected this to *qui nominibus*.] [Note: [Col. 0725D] That is, “the men.”] who have remained, let him immediately confiscate their property and expel them. And if the envoy himself is found to have remained behind, he shall lose his own property.

If a count leaves behind any excused person or his own vassal, apart from what we stated above, he shall lose his honor. Likewise, if their ministers dismiss anyone, they shall lose both their property and their office.

5. If any of our counts or vassals remain behind because they are detained by illness, or retain someone as excused, or if abbots or abbesses do not send out all their men in full, they themselves shall lose their honors, and their vassals shall lose both their property and their benefice. As for bishops, if any of their vassals remain behind, they shall lose both property and benefice.

6. If a bishop remains behind without manifest illness, he shall make such amends for this negligence that he must remain in that frontier district until the army goes there on another occasion.

7. And so that you may know with complete certainty that we intend to carry out this expedition in full, insofar as the Lord may have deigned to grant [Note: [Col. 0727] In the manuscripts: “insofar as the Lord may have deigned to grant him that we wish to complete this expedition fully,” etc. I have transposed the clauses.]—we decree that if a bishop, count, or our vassal is detained by an uncertain illness, the bishop through the better envoy he has, and the count and our vassals in person, shall affirm under oath that they would not have remained behind for any reason except that they were unable to act because of a completely certain illness.

8. We wish all of them to carry with them every kind of military equipment, so that when we have inspected it [Note: [Col. 0727] Another manuscript reads *prospexerimus*.] and caused it to be recorded, they may not appear negligent but may also deserve to have our favor.

9. Let them have clothing for one year, but provisions until the homeland itself can have new produce. Whoever causes a disturbance in a feud (*faida*) while going or returning shall incur the penalty of death [Note: [Col. 0727D] That is, *faida*.]

10. And because the appropriate season of Lent is also approaching, during which the commandments of God must be observed, we decree that whoever breaks into a church of God, commits adultery, or commits arson shall incur the penalty of death.

Whoever dares to take a horse, ox, *friskingas*, clothing, weapons, or other movable goods shall pay compensation threefold according to the law; and the free man shall be sent before us by his lords with an *armiscara*, that is, a saddle on his back [Note: [Col. 0727] Read *liber*, with *a*.], and shall endure this until we grant our pardon. Slaves, however, shall be flogged and beaten, and their masters shall restore what the slaves took. If a complaint reaches the lords and they do not correct such matters, then the lords of those men shall pay the compensation themselves and shall be compelled to provide the same *armiscara* for as long as we please.

11. We decree also that justice be maintained on both sides: namely, that our men, like their neighbors, shall buy what is necessary. The neighbors, however, shall in no way presume to sell at a higher price than they sell to their own neighbors.

12. Whoever commits homicide indiscriminately and presumptuously shall incur the penalty of death.

13. Our route will be through Ravenna, and then, in the middle of March, to Pescara; the entire Italian army will be with us. The Tuscans, together with the people who come from beyond, shall come through Rome to Ponte Curvo, thence to Capua, and through Benevento descend [Col. 0728C] to meet us at Luceria on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

[Col. 0727]

## Coronation of Queen Hermintrude, when she was consecrated in August 866 at the Synod of Soissons

[Note: [Col. 0727] We present here again the formula edited by Sirmond from a manuscript of Saint Lawrence of Liège.]

### Address of two bishops in the church of Saint Medard, when Hermintrude was consecrated as queen

[Col. 0727D]

We wish you to know, brothers, that our glorious lord and master, King Charles, asked the devotion of our humility that, by the authority of the ministry conferred upon us by God, just as he himself was anointed and consecrated king by episcopal authority, with sacred anointing and blessing—as we read in Scripture that the Lord commanded kings to be anointed and consecrated to royal power—we should likewise bless his wife, our lady, in the name of queen, just as we know this to have been done previously by the Apostolic See and by our predecessors for other women.

And so that you may not wonder why he makes this request, we hasten to give an account of it to your brotherhood. [Col. 0728D] Namely, as is known to many, Almighty God by his grace wonderfully united this kingdom in the hands of his predecessors. His predecessors governed it nobly, and their descendants have ruled it through successive generations down to the present time.

And God has given this lord of ours sons, as you know. In their nobility, his faithful subjects rejoiced to place their greatest hope in the holy Church and in the kingdom which God entrusted to him to govern. Of these sons he offered some to God, so that he might offer to God an offering from the fruit of his womb. Others God, while still immature in age, by his grace snatched from this world, lest, as it is written, wickedness should change their hearts. Upon others, as you are not unaware, he permitted by his judgment such suffering to come, [Col. 0729A] as his faithful are known to mourn.

Therefore he asks that episcopal blessing come upon his wife, so that the Lord may deign to grant him from her such offspring as may provide the holy Church with comfort, the kingdom with necessary defense, his faithful with the assistance they desire, and this Christian people with the tranquility, law, and justice it longs for; and so that, with the Lord’s approval and cooperation, these things may be possible through those whom he still has.

We have authority for this in the holy Scriptures. For just as the Lord said to Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed,” and, when he was already a hundred years old and his wife ninety, gave him Isaac as a son, so he also caused Isaac to take a barren wife, in order that in this, as in many other things, he might display the abundance of his mercy.

And Scripture says from this [Col. 0729B] that Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife because she was barren, and she conceived. Nor should you wonder why he did not do this earlier. For, as sacred Scripture says, at the beginning of the union of male and female the Lord said to Eve: “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.”

When Abraham and Sarah were already mature in character and advanced in age within lawful union, and, as Saint Peter says, Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord, the Lord said to Abraham something which we do not read that he had said either to him or to any other man previously: “Listen to Sarah in everything she says to you.”

For Abraham was now rightly called an old man, and Sarah’s feminine functions had ceased—that is, all her wantonness had ceased; and then they received [Col. 0729C] from the Lord the blessing of the blessed seed, in which all nations are blessed. Amen.

Supported, therefore, by these authorities in distributing God’s gifts—we who have been appointed by him as his ministers for this purpose—we ought not to be difficult or neglect the petitions of the devout, especially when we see that the petitions themselves have been conceived through evident signs by the inspiration of God.

For God’s manifold mercy has decreed to aid human salvation in such a way that salvation itself should chiefly be obtained through the supplications of priests. In this work, as we read in the sacred writings, the Savior himself intervenes and is never absent from those things which he entrusted to his ministers to accomplish, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days.”

And if, as Leo says, we fulfill anything through our ministry in good order and with a rejoicing disposition, let us not doubt that it has been given to us through the Holy Spirit.

And therefore, brothers, since this is so, and since our ministry for you and your united devotion toward us become one supplication before the Lord—as we read, priests were appointed for this purpose: first to pray for their own sins, then for those of the people—and since prayer was made without ceasing to God for Peter, that is, for the entire company of bishops, while we pray for our common need, indeed for the need and salvation of the whole Church and people, may your common prayer also carry forward the common vow before him who makes the united dwell in a house, and who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0730A] **Prayer.** Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who by the power of your might made all things from nothing, and, having ordered the beginnings of the universe, created for the human being made in your image an inseparable helpmate, and gave the female body its beginning from male flesh, teaching that what pleased you to establish from one person may not be separated by human beings: look favorably upon this your maidservant, joined in marital partnership, who seeks to be fortified by your protection.

May the yoke of love and peace be upon her. May she marry faithfully and chastely in Christ, and remain an imitator of holy women. May she be lovable to her husband like Rachel, wise like Rebecca, long-lived and faithful like Sarah. May no author of transgression usurp anything in her through her deeds. Bound to the commands of faith, may she remain; joined to one bed, may she avoid illicit contact. May she fortify her weakness with the strength of discipline. May she be grave in modesty, venerable in chastity, and instructed in heavenly teachings.

May she be fruitful in offspring pleasing to you; may she be approved and innocent. Through this sacred anointing of mercy, joy, and exultation, may she receive healing of mind, soundness of body, protection of salvation, security of hope, strengthening of faith, and fullness of charity.

Crown her, Lord, with the crown of justice; crown her with holy fruits and blessed works. May she be queen in merit, name, and virtue, standing in this world in right faith and good works, and in the future crowned with honor and glory at the king’s right hand, clothed in good works and surrounded by a diversity of virtues.

Grant that she may bear such offspring as may belong to the inheritance of your paradise. Grant, Lord, to this your maidservant such love, devotion to mercy, and increase of religion that she may continually deserve your help.

Drive away from her the poisons of the cunning serpent, and, clothed in the breastplate of faith, defend her with the shield of salvation. Correct her actions, improve her life, order her conduct, and deign to lead her in a good old age to the heavenly kingdoms. Through the same Lord our Lord.

May the Lord crown you with glory, honor, and everlasting protection. He who lives and reigns.

Almighty God, who blessed Adam and Eve, saying, “Increase and multiply,” and blessed the marriages of the patriarchs, and who sent his angel Raphael with Tobias, by whose ministry he drove the demon away [Col. 0730D] from Sarah, his wife, may he bless you and her, your future wife, so that, according to the Lord’s command, having become two in one flesh, what God joins together no human being may separate; and may he give you the blessing of the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth.

For we bless you in the name of the Lord: may he send his good angels to guard you always, drive away from you every apparition, wickedness, and deceit of all evil spirits and human beings, and protect, fortify, and defend you from every pollution of adultery and from every human and demonic ambush.

May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who continually pours his love and fear into your hearts, grant that you may grow old together in a good old age, see the children of your children flourishing according to the Lord’s will, and that peace may remain with you. Persevering in right faith, good works, good concord, sincere marital love, and the confession of the Holy Trinity and communion with the Catholic Church, may you reach eternal life.

May he himself deign to grant this, whose kingdom and dominion remain without end forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0731]

## The meeting of Louis and Charles at Metz (868)

[Note: [Col. 0731] Sirmond, apparently the first editor of this oath from a Laon manuscript, and Baluzius assigned it to the year 868. From the inscription, it must be placed after June 20, when Charles’s twenty-ninth year begins, and before the Kalends of September, when the first indiction ends. Hincmar did not mention this meeting. The meeting he reports under the year 867 appears not to have taken place at Metz, since he says that Charles, returning from Louis, came back through Hlothar, who was staying in the Ardennes, and that Hlothar then went from Metz to Frankfurt.]

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0731B] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 868, in the first indiction, in the city of Metz, at Saint Arnulf, these agreements were made between the glorious kings Louis and Charles, in the presence of the following: Hincmar, archbishop; Liutbert, archbishop; Altfrid, bishop; likewise Hincmar, bishop [Note: [Col. 0731D] Of Laon.]; Witgar, bishop [Note: [Col. 0731D] Of Augsburg.]; Odo, bishop [Note: [Col. 0732D] Of Beauvais.], in the twenty-ninth year of the reign of the glorious King Charles.

Henceforth and thereafter, for the will of God, for the restoration, honor, and defense of the holy Church, and for our common honor, safety, and advancement, and for the salvation and peace of the Christian people entrusted to us, I shall be a faithful helper to this brother of mine, Charles, in true brotherhood, with counsel and assistance, insofar as God grants me knowledge and ability.

And if God should further grant us something from the kingdoms of our nephews, both in acquiring and in dividing it, according as either we or the common faithful whom we choose by common agreement may find it more equitable, and in agreeing to that division, possessing it, preserving it, and defending it—both what we possess now and what the Lord may grant us from the aforesaid kingdoms—I shall be his sincere helper and fellow worker, without deceit, deception, or wrongful seizure, as a true brother ought rightly to be to a true brother; on the condition that he preserve the same toward me.

We shall likewise preserve jointly the protection and defense of the holy Roman Church, on the condition that the Roman pontiffs preserve the honor due to us, just as their predecessors preserved it for our predecessors. So may God help me and these saints.

[Col. 0732C] Charles likewise made the same promise to Louis.

[Col. 0731]

## The meeting of Charles II at Pîtres (869)

[Note: [Col. 0731] We reproduce the editions of Sirmond and Baluzius.]

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0731C] The following chapters were established by our lord, the glorious King Charles, with the counsel and consent of the bishops and the other faithful of God and of the king who were present at the place called Pîtres, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 869, in the thirtieth year of his reign and the second indiction. They were proclaimed by him, on his own behalf and that of all his faithful, as matters to be preserved inviolate according to each person’s order and status.

1. Concerning the honor and worship of God and the holy churches in our kingdom, we decree that, just as they were cultivated and honored in the time of our grandfather and father, and just as they have been or henceforth shall be honored and enriched by our generosity, subject to the requirements of equity, so they shall remain under immunity.

Archbishops and bishops, and the other priests, male servants, and female servants of God, each man and woman in the dignity of their order, shall have honor and immunity according to the sacred laws and canons.

2. Let the archbishops, bishops, and other faithful of ours exhibit to us, in all matters and by all persons, according to each one’s order, dignity, and ability, royal honor and power, due obedience, and assistance for maintaining and defending our kingdom, just as was customarily done justly and reasonably in the time of our predecessors.

3. We wish all our faithful truly to be secure concerning us: insofar as I know and can justly and reasonably do so, with the Lord’s help, I wish to honor and protect each person according to the dignity and status of his order, and to preserve each one honored and protected. I shall preserve for each one in his order, according to the laws applicable to him, both secular and ecclesiastical, [Col. 0732D] right reason and justice.

I shall neither condemn nor dishonor any of our faithful contrary to law and justice, or to authority and right reason; nor shall I oppress anyone or afflict anyone by improper schemes. And, as stated above, I pledge that I shall preserve for each person the law applicable to him, as his predecessors had it in the time of my predecessors, in every dignity and order, with the Lord’s help, provided that they are faithful and obedient to me, true helpers and fellow workers according to their office and status, offering counsel and assistance according to their knowledge and ability, and according to God and the world, as each person rightly ought to be in his order and station toward his king and lord.

And the chapters which our grandfather and father established for the condition and protection of the holy Church of God and its ministers, and for the peace and justice of the people and the tranquility of the kingdom; and those which we established jointly with our brother kings and our faithful and theirs; and also those which we decreed at various assemblies, with the counsel and consent of the bishops and the other faithful of God and of ourselves, to be preserved for the causes written above—we decree shall remain undisturbed.

4. Since, with the Lord’s help, our royal power wishes to carry this out in every respect, let the ministers of the kingdom, insofar as God grants them knowledge and ability, provide assistance to the bishops and the other priests, male servants, and female servants of God, so that they may fulfill their ministry, as established by our imperial and royal predecessors and by us.

Let them preserve and exhibit to the holy churches and to the priests and male and female servants of God, according to the sacred laws, both secular and ecclesiastical, and according to the chapters of our grandfather and father [Col. 0733C] and our own, the honor and immunity that are due, so that they may peacefully pray to the Lord for the stability of the kingdom, for our salvation, and for theirs.

5. Let the bishops show and preserve toward counts, envoys, and our vassals, as well as toward their own subjects, both clerical and lay, and toward the men of our counts and vassals, paternal kindness according to their ministry, and due honor, law, and justice, each according to his order and dignity, as the sacred laws, both secular and ecclesiastical, and the chapters of our grandfather and father decree; as has been established in the chapters by us and by our brother kings together with our common faithful; and as was the just and reasonable custom in the time of our grandfather and [Col. 0733D] father.

Likewise, let our counts, envoys, and vassals show due reverence to bishops and priests, and law, justice, and due honor to the bishops’ vassals, according to the laws, chapters, and custom stated above.

6. If bishops act unjustly toward their clerics, let those whose concern this is endeavor to correct the matter according to what the sacred canons and sacred laws, approved and observed by the Catholic Church, prescribe.

7. If bishops act unjustly toward their laymen, and those laymen appeal to us concerning it, let the archbishops and bishops obey our royal authority according to our ministry and theirs, so that they may take care to correct the matter according to the holy canons, the laws approved and observed by the Catholic Church, the chapters of our grandfather and father, and the just and reasonable custom of their time.

8. Let parish priests show their lords due reverence, appropriate honor, and obedience according to their ministry, as is contained in the sacred laws and in the chapters stated above, and as was the just and reasonable custom in the time of our grandfather and father.

If those priests fail to do this, let their lords endeavor to make the matter known to the bishops—not through pretext or malice, but by reason and truth. Let the bishops chastise the priests according to their ministry and the ecclesiastical laws in such a way that they may be pleased to correct them, so that, with the necessary kindly harmony, the priests may pray for their lords, and their lords may receive through them the sacred offices and divine mysteries with a pure heart.

9. If abbots or abbesses, or our counts or vassals, or other laymen, offer to bishops clerics of commendable life and learning to be canonically consecrated and installed in their churches, let the bishops or their ministers reject them on no pretext whatever.

Let the bishops ensure what honor priests ought to render to their lords for their churches. Let the bishops preserve parishes and tithes for the ancient churches, and let the lords preserve the immunity of the manse given to the church. Let priests neither be installed nor expelled in any church without the authority or consent of the bishops, as is contained in the first book of the chapters of our grandfather and father, and in the chapters made by our father in the sixteenth year of his empire.

Let this suffice for the lords of priests; let them not demand or exact anything more from priests through ingenious schemes, except as established in those same chapters of our grandfather, father, and ourselves, lest they offend God, lose their souls for earthly profit—which God forbid—and incur our displeasure, and, after due correction, suffer the worthy *armiscara* prescribed by us.

Let bishops guard both the lords of priests and the priests, and themselves as well, lest laymen through ignorance, priests through necessity, or the bishops themselves or their ministers through greed and avarice—which God forbid—fall into the heresy of simony.

For, as Saint Gregory says, whoever approaches or is promoted to holy orders through payment, favor, or improper supplication is judged a heretic by the Lord: both the one who is promoted, the one by whom he is so promoted, and the person through whose intervention he is so promoted.

Anyone who gives or accepts anything for such an unlawful ordination by any evil device—which cannot be hidden from God—or who acts as mediator, is condemned by God, as the canons composed by the Spirit of God demonstrate, through the judgment of those who reign with God in heaven and shine with miracles on earth.

Such wicked traffickers are indeed condemned in the present age and destined to be burned with everlasting fire. What they ought freely to give to those who have deserved well, they sell—justice, just as Judas sold Christ, who, as the Apostle says, was made for us by God as justice. Thus they sell God the almighty Father, Christ, that same justice, and the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with them, who is given to human beings through the laying on of priestly hands; for the holy Trinity has one nature, will, and operation.

Those who give or receive ecclesiastical orders for temporal advantage sell them. Those who give a price for them purchase sin and become heretics. Those who receive a reward for them, as the same holy Gregory demonstrates, having themselves become heretics, kill with the swords of their wickedness those whom they ought to have brought to life through the intercession of their prayers.

10. Let no bishop and no priest excommunicate anyone before the cause for which the ecclesiastical canons command this to be done has been proven, and before he has warned the person who sinned—whether he has confessed it voluntarily or has been openly convicted of it—according to the evangelical [Note: [Col. 0735] The Bigot manuscript reads “ecclesiastical.” Baluzius.] command, so that he may return to correction and penance.

If that sinner, after being warned concerning a certain and manifest cause to return to correction and discipline, remains disobedient and incorrigible, refuses to return to correction, and treats canonical excommunication concerning specified and manifest causes with contempt, let the bishop approach our royal or public authority, either personally, through his ministers, or by letter, so that the sinner may be compelled [Col. 0735C] to return to correction and penance.

Otherwise the Lord might say to us what we once read that he said to the ancient people: “Anathema is in your midst. You will not be able to stand before your enemies.”

But if that sinner wishes to come to penance for a manifest and proven cause, or one he has voluntarily confessed, but cannot undertake and carry out that penance peacefully because of a *faida*, let the bishop approach our royal or public authority, either personally, through his ministers, or by letter, so that the *faida* may be legally settled according to the constitution of our grandfather and father, or resolved according to the laws by which people live in other regions (ANSEG. IV, 25).

Then let the sinner receive and perform the medicine of penance according to the sacred canons, with pious and health-giving discernment and in accordance with the sacred rules, and receive reconciliation and communion, as is contained with the greatest discernment and mercy in those same sacred rules.

11. Let our counts, envoys, vassals, and ministers of the kingdom, each according to his order, dignity, and ability, establish peace and justice in their offices, and judge everyone justly under God’s scrutiny, remembering what the Lord says to all who judge: “With the judgment with which you judge, you shall be judged.” And: “Blessed are those who observe judgment and practice justice at all times.”

12. Let the bishops and abbots, and our counts and vassals, and all our faithful laymen, strive together with harmonious love and unanimous will, without envy, ill will, or improper contention, for the honor and stability of God, the holy Church, ourselves, and our kingdom, and for our common salvation, so that peace and justice, and true concord according to God’s will, may remain among us all and in our kingdom.

For, as holy Scripture says: “Justice exalts a nation; sin makes peoples wretched.” And where there is no true concord according to God’s will, God does not dwell there except for judgment—he who, as the psalm says, makes the united dwell in a house, that is, in the holy Church.

To those who faithfully remain in it he gives the spirit of charity. Because of his great charity with which he loved us, he handed himself over for us; and when we were dead in our sins, he made us alive together with himself, so that we might be holy and blameless in his sight in charity, and might be followers of good works. Persevering in these with right faith, may we all, with him going before us, helping us, and following after us, reach the kingdoms of heaven.

13. [Note: [Col. 0735] This chapter is absent from Sirmond’s edition; it was restored by Baluze from a single manuscript of Ripoll.] Let the bishops carefully guard the privileges of the Roman See and the charters of kings confirmed for their churches, so that they may thereby be defended with authoritative firmness. Let them receive the offerings and tithes which have been established, without anyone’s opposition. From the censual lands, the jurisdiction of his church, the demesne cultivated lands, the absitates, and the manufirmatae, let the greater church, which is the head of the bishopric, receive a tenth; likewise from a demesne ploughland [Note: [Col. 0735] *curte* instead of *carruca*. Baluze.] From hereditary holdings, let the parish priest receive a tenth, as has been established. And the greatest care must be taken lest contention arise over this.

## Proclamation of King Charles

1. We wish you to know that, following the custom of our predecessors, we have considered at this assembly, together with the bishops and our other faithful men, the honor of the holy Church and of the bishops and the other servants of God, so that they may receive the due honor which they had in the time of our predecessors. And for our faithful men, each in his own order, we shall preserve law and justice, as their predecessors had them in the time of our predecessors.

2. We wish and command that the vassals of bishops, abbots and abbesses, and likewise of counts and of our vassals, have such law and justice with their lords as their predecessors had with those lords in the time of our predecessors. And if any bishop, abbot, abbess, count, or our vassal acts against right and justice toward his man, and the man makes a complaint about it to us, let him know that we shall have the matter corrected, as reason, law, and justice require.

3. We wish and command that the bishops and abbots, our counts and vassals, strive with harmonious love and unanimous will for the honor and stability of God, of the holy Church, of us and our kingdom, and for our common salvation, so that peace, justice, and true concord according to God’s will may remain among all of us and in our kingdom. Let all always be so prepared that, should necessity arise for us, they may come without delay for the defense of the fatherland against pagans or against other enemies of God and of us, as was customary in the time of our predecessors, immediately upon receiving notification.

4. And we wish you to know that we commend each of you to undertake from his own work such a struggle as he knows to be necessary for the defense of this holy Church of God, according to our exhortation. We give you thanks because, faithfully and according to our exhortation, you have come into our service. Go, then, in God’s grace, safe and sound; and may God grant that we may again be joined together in health and joy, according to his will.

[Col. 0737]

# THE CORONATION OF CHARLES II IN THE KINGDOM OF LOTHAR (869, September 9)

[Note: [Col. 0737] We reproduce the editions of Sirmond and Baluze.]

[Note.]

[Col. 0737B] The order of how King Charles was crowned in the city of Metz in the year 869, in the month of September, on the fifth day before the Ides of September, which fell on a Friday, in the presence of these bishops: Hincmar the archbishop, Adventius, Hatto, Arnulf, Franco, Hincmar, and Odo; at the time when the former King Lothar, son of the Emperor Lothar, died in the city of Piacenza.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 869, in the second indiction, on the fifth day before the Ides of September, in the city of Metz, in the church of Saint Stephen the Martyr, Adventius, bishop of that city, publicly announced the following chapters, both in writing and orally, before the king, the bishops who were present, and the people.

1. You know, and it is known in many kingdoms, how many and what kinds of events we commonly endured during the time of our lord, whom until now we have had, for causes that are widely known; and with how great grief and anguish we have recently been struck in our hearts by his unfortunate death. Therefore, deprived and desolated of our king and prince, we have all judged that our one refuge and uniquely salutary counsel is to turn to him with fasts and prayers who is our helper in times of need and in tribulation, whose is counsel and whose is the kingdom, and who, as it is written, gives it to whomever he wills, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, and who makes the like-minded dwell in one house, removing the dividing wall and making the two one.

We beseech his mercy to give us a king and prince according to his heart, who according to his will might rule, save, and defend us in judgment and justice, in every order and condition; and that he might incline and unite all our hearts unanimously toward him whom, according to his mercy, he had foreknown, chosen, and predestined for our salvation and advancement.

2. Since, finally, by the will of God, who fulfills the desire of those who fear him and hears their prayers, we see in our harmonious unanimity that this man is the rightful heir of this kingdom, to whom we have voluntarily entrusted ourselves—namely, the present lord, our king and prince Charles—that he may preside over us and benefit us, it seems appropriate to us, if it pleases you, that, as we shall make clear to you after his speech, we should demonstrate by the surest sign that we believe him to have been chosen by God and given to us as prince, and that we should not prove ungrateful to God, the giver, for his benefits.

Rather, let us offer him thanksgiving and pray that he may preserve him for us longer, for the salvation and defense of his holy Church and for the help and advancement of us all, with salvation, peace, and tranquility; and that, as we serve him with faithful devotion and enjoy the salvation we desire, He may govern us under his administration in His service.

3. And if it pleases him, it seems worthy of him and necessary for us that we hear from his own mouth what a most Christian king ought to receive from a people faithful and unanimous in his service with a devoted mind from a people, each in his own order.

After this, King Charles himself publicly announced the following to all who were present in the same church:

Since, as these venerable bishops said through the voice of one of their number, and demonstrated by clear signs through your unanimity, and as you acclaimed, that I have come here by God’s election for your salvation, advancement, rule, and government, know that, with the Lord’s help, I wish to preserve the honor and worship of God and of the holy churches; and, according to the dignity of each one’s order and person, to the best of my knowledge and ability, to honor and save each of you, and to keep you honored and safe; and to preserve for each one, in his own order, law and justice according to the laws appropriate to him, both ecclesiastical and secular.

For this purpose, each of you, according to his order, dignity, and ability, must render to me the royal honor and authority, due obedience, and the assistance necessary to maintain and defend the kingdom given to me by God, as your predecessors faithfully, justly, and reasonably rendered them to my predecessors.

[Col. 0739A] After this, Hincmar, bishop of Reims, at the command and request of Adventius, bishop of that city, and of the other bishops of the province of Trier—namely Hatto, bishop of the church of Verdun; Arnulf, bishop of the city of Toul; and Franco, bishop of the city of Tongeren—the bishops of the province of Reims concurring, publicly announced the following chapters before the bishops, the king, and all who were publicly present in the same church.

1. Lest anyone should perhaps think it improper and presumptuous that I and the venerable fellow bishops of our province are involving ourselves in the ordination and affairs of this province, let him know that we are not acting against the sacred canons, since the churches of Reims and Trier, with the churches entrusted to them, are regarded in this Belgian region as sisters and fellow-provincial churches, as ecclesiastical authority and very ancient custom demonstrate.

Accordingly, by unanimous agreement they ought to exercise synodal judgments and concordantly preserve what has been established by the holy Fathers, subject to this privilege: that whichever of the bishops of Reims and Trier was ordained first should also be regarded as senior.

2. And the law inspired by God commands, saying: “If you pass through the harvest of your friend, gathering ears of grain, you shall rub them with your hand to eat; but you shall not put in the sickle, nor reap with the sickle.” The harvest is the people, as the Lord shows in the Gospel, saying: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.” For you ought to pray for us bishops, so that we may be able to speak words worthy of you.

The harvest belonging to a friend is the people in a province entrusted to another metropolitan. Therefore, by exhorting you—as though rubbing you with the hand of labor—we are able and ought to lead you across into obedience to God’s will and to your salvation, into the body of the unity of the Church. But we do not put the sickle of judgment upon the parishioners of provinces entrusted to other metropolitans, since neither is there a basis for doing so nor do we consider it to be our responsibility.

3. There is also another reason: these venerable lords and our fellow brothers, the bishops of this province, having no metropolitan bishop, command and urge our smallness, in fraternal charity, to act in their affairs just as in our own particular affairs. Is this so, brother lords? And those bishops replied: It is so.

4. In addition to what the lord bishop and our brother Adventius has said to you in his own voice and in the voice of his other brothers and ours, the venerable bishops, you may also observe in this that it is God’s will that the present lord and our king—who in that part of the kingdom which he has until now held and continues to hold has usefully ruled and continues to rule us, our churches, and the people entrusted to him, and has beneficially helped and continues to help us—has come from there to this place, led by the Lord; and that you too have flowed together here through his inspiration and have voluntarily commended yourselves to him.

By whose impulse all living creatures came together in Noah’s ark, signifying the unity of the Church, without anyone compelling them; because his father of holy memory, the lord Hludovicus, pious august emperor, descended from Hludowic, the illustrious king of the Franks, who was converted with his entire people through the Catholic preaching of blessed Remigius, apostle of the Franks, and who, together with three thousand Franks—apart from children and women—was baptized in the metropolitan church of Reims on the vigil of holy Easter, and, anointed with chrism received from heaven, of which we still possess some, and consecrated as king, sprang through blessed Arnulf, from whose flesh the same pious Augustus Hludovicus drew his bodily descent.

He was crowned emperor at Reims by Pope Stephen of Rome before the altar of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin. Later, deprived of earthly rule through the faction of certain men, he was restored to the aforesaid part of the kingdom through the unanimity of the bishops and the faithful people before the tomb of Saint Denis, the distinguished martyr, and in this house, before this altar of Stephen the protomartyr—whose name, when interpreted, means “crowned”—he was restored to the kingdom and imperial authority by the priests of the Lord, with the acclamation of the faithful people, as we who were present saw.

And since, as we read in sacred histories, when kings obtained kingdoms they placed the diadems of the individual kingdoms upon themselves, it does not seem improper to these venerable bishops, if it pleases your unanimity, that, in possession of the kingdom from which you have voluntarily come together to him and commended yourselves to him, he should be crowned by priestly ministry before this altar and consecrated to the Lord by sacred anointing. If this pleases you, let your voices agree in assent.

And when everyone had shouted assent, the same bishop said: “Let us therefore give thanks to God with one accord, singing, ‘We praise you, O God.’”

After this, the same king was crowned by the bishops with priestly blessing.

## BLESSINGS OVER KING CHARLES BEFORE MASS AND AT THE ALTAR OF SAINT STEPHEN

Adventius, bishop of Metz: God, who in your indulgence care for your peoples and in love rule over them, grant this servant of yours the spirit of wisdom, you who have given the governance of discipline; so that, devoted to you with his whole heart, he may always remain capable in the administration of the kingdom, and, persevering in good works, may reach the eternal kingdom with you as his guide. Through the Lord, etc.

Hatto of Verdun: We ask, Lord, that you grant this servant of yours the abundance of your grace, so that, following your commandments as you work within him, he may receive the consolation of the present life and of the life to come. Through the Lord, etc.

Arnulf of Toul: We ask, Lord, that you look favorably upon our times during the government of this servant of yours, so that, directed by your gift, our security and Christian devotion may be preserved. Through the Lord.

Franco of Tongeren: We ask, Lord, grant this servant of yours health of mind and body, so that, clinging to good works, he may always deserve to be defended by your power. Through the Lord.

Hincmar of Laon: May your blessing, Lord, be received by this servant of yours, so that, saved in body and mind, he may always render you acceptable service and always find the benefits of your favor. Through the Lord.

Odo of Beauvais: We ask, Lord, preserve this servant of yours, and mercifully cleanse him with the abundance of your blessings, so that he may always increase in your teachings and gifts. Through the Lord.

### Blessing of Hincmar the Archbishop

May the almighty Lord extend the right hand of his blessing, pour out upon you the gift of his favor, and surround you with the fortunate wall of the guardianship of his protection, through the interceding merits of holy Mary and all the saints. Amen.

May he forgive you all the evils you have committed and grant you the grace and mercy which you humbly ask of him; and may he free you from every adversity and from the snares of all visible and invisible enemies. Amen.

May he appoint his good angels always and everywhere for your protection, to go before you, accompany you, and follow after you; and may he by his power free you from sin, the sword, and every peril. Amen.

May he turn your enemies toward the kindness of peace and charity, and make you gracious and lovable to those who hate you. May he clothe those who persist in pursuing and hating you with salutary confusion. And may everlasting sanctification blossom over you. Amen.

[Col. 0741C] At the words “May the Lord crown you,” Archbishop Hincmar anointed him with chrism on the right ear, on the forehead from the right to the left ear, and on the head.

May the Lord crown you with a crown of glory in his mercy and compassion, and anoint you in the government of the kingdom with the oil of the grace of his Holy Spirit, with which he anointed priests, kings, prophets, and martyrs, who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced justice, and obtained the promises. By those same promises may you be made worthy through the grace of God, so that you may deserve to enjoy their fellowship in the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

May he always make you victorious and triumphant over visible and invisible enemies; may he continually pour into your heart both fear and love of his holy name; may he make you steadfast in right faith and good works; and, granting peace in your days, may he lead you with the palm of victory to the everlasting kingdom. Amen.

And may he who willed to establish you as king over his people grant that you be happy in the present age and a participant in eternal happiness. Amen.

[Col. 0742A] May he cause you to govern happily for many years, through his dispensation and your administration, the clergy and people whom he willed to subject to your authority through his assistance; so that, obeying the divine admonitions, free from every adversity, overflowing with every good, and serving you with faithful love through your ministry, they may enjoy the tranquility of peace in the present age and, together with you, deserve to obtain fellowship with the eternal citizens. May he himself deign to grant this.

At the words “May the Lord crown you,” those bishops placed a crown upon his head.

May the Lord crown you with a crown of glory and justice, so that with right faith and the abundant fruit of good works you may reach the crown of the everlasting kingdom, by the gift of him whose kingdom and empire endure for ever and ever.

At the words “May the Lord grant you the will,” they gave him the palm and the scepter.

May the Lord grant you the will and the ability to do what he commands, so that, advancing in the government of the kingdom according to his will, you may reach the palm of everlasting glory with the palm of enduring victory. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives…

### Prayers in the Mass

Grant us, almighty God, that the venerable solemnity of blessed Gorgonius, your martyr, may increase both our devotion and our salvation. Through the Lord.

We ask, almighty God, that your servant, who by your mercy has undertaken the governance of the kingdom, may also receive from you an increase of virtues; adorned suitably with these, may he be able to avoid the monsters of vices and graciously reach you, who are the way, the truth, and the life. You who live and reign with God.

### Over the Offerings

Look upon, Lord, the gifts of your people on this votive feast of the saints, and may the testimony of your truth advance us toward salvation. Through the Lord.

Sanctify, we ask, Lord, the gifts offered, so that they may become for us the body and blood of your Only-Begotten, and, by your gift, may they everywhere advance our king Charles toward the salvation of soul and body. Through the same Lord.

### After Communion

May the communion of your sacraments, Lord, which we have received, save us and confirm us in the light of your truth. Through the Lord.

May this saving communion, Lord, protect your servant from every adversity, so that he may obtain the tranquility of ecclesiastical peace and, when the course of this age is ended, reach the eternal inheritance. Through the Lord.

[Col. 0741]

# THE PACT OF AACHEN BETWEEN HLUDOWICUS THE GERMAN AND CHARLES II (870, March 6)

[Note: [Col. 0741] We publish it from Sirmond and Baluze; the same formula appears in Hincmar’s Annals, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, vol. I, p. 487.]

[Col. 0741D] In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 870, in the third indiction, on the day before the Nones of March, in the thirty-second year of the glorious King Charles, these agreements were made at the palace of Aachen between him and his brother, King Hludowicus.

Ingelramnus, count, on behalf of King Charles:

Thus I promise on behalf of my lord that my lord, King Charles, consents that his brother, King Hludowicus, should have such a portion of the kingdom of King Lothar as either they themselves or their common faithful men may find to be more just and more equitable. Nor will he deceive him or act against his interests in that portion, or in the kingdom which he previously held, through any fraud or underhanded action, provided that his brother Hludowicus preserves inviolate toward my lord, for as long as he lives, the same firmness and fidelity which I have promised him on my lord’s behalf.

Likewise Leutfridus, count, on behalf of King Hludowicus:

Thus I promise on behalf of my lord that my lord, King Hludowicus, consents that his brother, King Charles, should have such a portion of the kingdom of King Lothar as either they themselves or their common faithful men may find to be more just or more equitable. Nor will he deceive him or act against his interests in that portion, or in the kingdom which he previously held, through any fraud or underhanded action, provided that his brother Charles preserves inviolate toward my lord, for as long as he lives, the same firmness and fidelity which I have promised him on my lord’s behalf.

The same was pronounced by the third, Count Theodoric, on behalf of the glorious King Charles, and by the fourth, Count Radulf, on behalf of Hludowicus.

Those present were: Archbishop Leutbertus; Bishop Altfridus; Bishop Odo; Count Adalelmus; Count Ingelramnus; Count Liutfridus; Count Theodoricus; and Count Adalelmus again.

[Col. 0743]

# THE DIVISION OF THE KINGDOM OF LOTHAR BETWEEN HLUDOWICUS THE GERMAN AND CHARLES II (870, August 9)

[Note: [Col. 0743] Peter Pithoeus first published the formula of this division in *Scriptores coaetanei*, p. 488, in such a way that he presented Hludowicus’s portion from the Beauvais manuscript, while giving several readings from his own manuscript and Charles’s portion. We have a second edition in Aimoinus, vol. II of the *Corpus of Frankish History*, edited by Freher and Sirmond; a third in Hincmar’s Annals and in Baluze. For an explanation of the places, see *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, vol. I, pp. 488–490 (*Patrologia Latina*, vol. CXXV, cols. 1255 ff.).]

[Col. 0743B] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 870, in the thirty-third year of Charles’s reign, in the third indiction, on the sixth day before the Ides of August, this division of the kingdom was made between the glorious kings Charles and Hludowicus at Procaspis, on the river Meuse.

This is the portion which Hludowicus received for himself:

Cologne, Trier, Utrecht, Strasbourg, Basel; the abbeys of Susteren, Berch, Neumünster, Kastell, Inda, Saint Maximinus, Echternach, Horrea, Saint Gangulf, Faverniacum, Pollemniacum, Luxeuil, Lure, Balma, Offonis Villa, the monastery of Meien, Saint Deodatus, the monastery of Bodo, Stivagium, Mount Romericus, Morbach, Saint Gregory, the monastery of Maurus, Eberesheim, Hoinowa, the monastery of Mason, Hoinborch, Saint Stephen at Strasbourg, Erenstein, Saint Ursus at Solothurn, Grandval, Altenberg, Lusten, the Valley of Clus, Carnon Castle, Heribodesheim, the abbey of Aachen, Hohen Kirche, Augst Kirche.

The counties of Testrabant, Batua, Hattuaria, Lower Masau on this side; likewise Upper Masau on that side; Liugas on this side; the district of Aachen; the district of Utrecht; five counties in Ripuaria; Megen, Bedagowa, Nitachowa, Lower Sarachowa, Blesitchowa, Selme, Albechowa, Suentisium, Calmont, Upper Sarachowa, Odornense, which Bernard held; Solothurn, Basiniachum, Elischowe, Warasch, Scudingum, Emaus; two counties in Alsace at Basalchowa; two parts of Frisia of the kingdom which Lothar held.

For the preservation of peace and charity, we add this further provision to the division: the city of Metz, with the abbey of Saint Peter, the abbey of Saint Martin, and the county of Moselle, together with all the villages situated within it, both demesne villages and those of vassals; and of Ardennes, from where the river Ourthe rises between Bislane and Tumbas and flows into the Meuse, and as the straight road proceeds toward Bedensi, according to what our common envoys may determine more accurately—except for the part of Condroz that lies east of the Ourthe—and the abbeys of Prüm and Stavelot, together with all the demesne villages and those of vassals.

This is the division which Charles received for himself from the same kingdom:

Lyon, Besançon, Vienne, Tongeren, Toul, Verdun, Cambrai, Viviers, Uzès, Montfaucon, Saint Michael, the monastery of Gillinus, Saint Mary at Besançon, Saint Martin in the same place, Saint Augentius, Saint Marcellus, Saint Lawrence at Liège, Sens, the abbey of Neuilly, Molbure, Lobbes, Saint Gaugericus, Saint Salvius, Crispin, Fosses, Marilles, Hunulf Court, Saint Servatius, Mechelen, Ledi, Sunniacum, Antonius, Condé, Mesrebecchi, Tidivinni, Lutosa, Calmont, Saint Mary at Deomant, Eca, Andenne, Wasloi, Mont-Haut.

The counties of Texandria; four counties in Brabant; Cambrai, Hainaut, Lomme, and four counties in Hasbania; Upper Masau on this side of the Meuse; Lower Masau on this side; Liugas on this side of the Meuse, belonging to Visé; Scarponensis, Verdun, Dulmen, Arlon; two counties of Wavre; Mosminse, Castricium, Condroz; of Ardennes, from where the river Ourthe rises between Bislane and Tumbas and flows from this side into the Meuse, and as the straight road proceeds from this western side toward Bedensi, according to what our envoys may determine more accurately; Toul, the other Ordonense which Tetmar held, Bar, Port, Salmoringum, Lyon, Vienne, Viviers, Uccericium, and one-third of Frisia.

[Col. 0745]

# CHARLES II’S ASSEMBLY AT GUNDULF’S VILLA (872, September 9)

[Note: [Col. 0745] Hincmar speaks of this in his *Annals* under the year 872. The edition of Pithoeus in *Scriptores coaetanei*, p. 509, was taken up by the editions of Baronius, vol. X, and Sirmond, in which part of the title was supplied, while the general oath was omitted. Baluze, using both, produced a better text, which we have judged should be reproduced here.]

[Col. 0745A] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 872 [Note: [Col. 0745] 873, according to Pithoeus.], in the fifth indiction, on the fifth day before the Ides of September, at the general assembly at Gundulf’s villa—when Hludowicus had broken the oaths written above and had likewise joined himself to his namesake, the Emperor Hludowicus, and when Queen Ingilberga had ordered the oaths written above to be taken, with the legates of the Apostolic See, namely Formosus and Gadericus [Note: [Col. 0745] Hadericus, Sirmond.], present—in this pressing circumstance all the bishops from the kingdom of the glorious King Charles made the profession written below, and all the laymen likewise swore the oath written below.

### Profession of the Bishops

To the extent that I know and am able, with the Lord’s help, I shall be your faithful helper, according to my ministry, in counsel and assistance, so that you may have, obtain, and retain the kingdom which God has given or will give you, in accordance with his will and for the due honor of the holy Church and of your royal office, and for the salvation of you and your faithful people.

### Oath of the Laymen

To the extent that I know and am able, with the Lord’s help, I shall be your faithful helper and assist you, so that you may retain the kingdom which you possess according to God’s will, the honor of the holy Church and of yourself, and your salvation; and so that you may be able to acquire whatever God may still grant you and defend it against all men.

### General Oath of All the Faithful

Thus I promise that from this day forward, for as long as I live, I shall be faithful, obedient, and a helper to this my lord, to the fullest extent and as well as I know and am able; and in counsel and assistance, according to my ministry, I shall be present in all things, without fraud, evil intent, deceit, seduction, or deception, and without regard to any person.

Neither by myself, nor through an envoy, nor by letters, nor through a person sent out or introduced, nor in any manner or by any sign shall I plot, or consent to anyone plotting, against his honor or against the peace, tranquility, and stability of the holy Church and of the kingdom entrusted to him. Nor shall I ever provoke any scandal which could be contrary or harmful to his present or future salvation. So may God help me, and these holy relics.

[Col. 0745]

# CHARLES II’S CAPITULARY OF QUierzy (873, January 4)
