[Note: [Col. 0745] We reproduce again the editions of Sirmond and Baluze, accepting only the preferable title of the Laon manuscript; see also the beginning of Hincmar’s *Annals* for 873.]

[Note.]

[Col. 0745C] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 873, in the sixth indiction, on the day before the Nones of January, the lord King Charles decreed the following chapters at the palace of Quierzy, with the counsel of his faithful men, and commanded them to be proclaimed and observed throughout his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0745] Thus the Laon manuscript. The Beauvais manuscript, the manuscript of Antonio Agustín, and the editions of Baronius, Sirmond, and Baluze instead have: “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 873, and in the thirty-third year of the lord Charles’s reign, in the fifth indiction, the following chapters were established by the same king at the general assembly at Quierzy, with the will and consent of all, and were confirmed by the aforesaid king and by all who were present.”].

Since what has grown back in an evil form must be cut off again, we propose that the provisions of our predecessors and of ourselves, which were established in their chapters and ours, be firmly carried out by our envoys and counts, in order to cut away the evils that have again especially emerged. That is, whenever our envoys or counts have placed a robber, malefactor, or our unfaithful man under the ban, they are to notify us of this in our palace, and also notify the other envoys and counts, so that, if he comes to our court, we may do what is ours to do.

And if he flees from one district or county into another district or county, the envoy or count into whose district he has fled shall constrain him through sureties to return there, whether he wishes to or not, and there make amends for the evil which he committed. If he has no sureties, he shall keep him in custody until he can cause him to return to the count in whose county he was placed under the ban.

If he has an allod either in the county from which he fled or in the county to which he fled, the count shall receive that allod into the fisc. And anyone who receives such a man placed under the ban shall, according to what has been established in the capitularies of our grandfather and father in Book Three, swear with twelve similar Franks that he did not know him to be a robber or a man under the ban, even if he is his father, brother, or kinsman.

If he cannot swear this, or if he is convicted by another that he had received into his lodging a robber, malefactor, or our unfaithful man placed under the ban, he shall be judged as the man under the ban himself and as an unfaithful man.

2. Let our counts and envoys take the greatest care that the people in their counties and districts have justice and peace, and let them undertake the greatest effort to drive out robbers. If such a malefactor or unfaithful man of ours emerges, so that the count cannot himself apprehend him in his county, let him take men belonging both to us and to the bishops, abbots, or abbesses residing in his county, and pursue him in this way until he apprehends him.

Anyone summoned to seize such a malefactor who withdraws and fails to provide assistance for this purpose shall, if he is a free man, pay the royal ban; if he is a colonus, he shall receive sixty blows.

If such a malefactor is killed during that pursuit, the person who killed him shall pay no *leud* (compensatory payment) for it, and no one may presume to carry a feud against him on that account. If anyone presumes to do so, he shall be brought before our presence through reliable sureties.

3. Concerning those free men who are infamous or notorious for testejis [an uncertain offence-term], brigandage, rapacity or plundering, assaults, or disloyalty toward us, and who are not caught in the act of theft: if their lives have already been spared on account of some offense, let action be taken against them as is contained in the capitulary of our grandfather and father, book 3, chapter 47. If they have already been convicted of theft, let action be taken against them as against convicted persons. But if their lives have not yet been spared, and they have not been convicted, and they possess property, slaves, or movable goods, let action be taken against them as is stated in the fourth book of the Capitularies, chapter 29, when they come to the count’s court. If they do not come to the court, let them be placed under ban and constrained by their property, slaves, or movable goods [Note: [Col. 0747] “property, slaves, or movable goods” are absent in Sirmond], so that they come. If they still do not come, let action be taken against them as the capitulary prescribes. And if, after the count’s second summons, they are unwilling to come to the court, let them be compelled to come and render justice, their property having been placed under ban.

If there is such a man whom neither his relatives nor other people, because of a feud, are willing or dare to accuse, and he has not been caught in the offense and denies it, let him swear together with twelve such Franks whose testimony the public laws do not reject that he has committed no testejam [uncertain], brigandage, or robbery; and afterward let him swear by himself alone that henceforth he will commit no theft or robbery, nor consent to anyone committing it, and that, if he knows who has committed these things, he will not conceal it from our officials through whom such a case must be corrected.

Those who have no property, slaves, or movable goods by which they can be constrained to come to the court, and who there either clear themselves legally, as we have stated [Note: [Col. 0747] that is, “excuse themselves”], or, if they cannot clear themselves, legally make amends for what they have done wrong—if, after the count’s second summons, they do not come to the court, let them be arrested according to the aforesaid capitulary, book 3, chapter 56, which speaks of thieves who have a great reputation for evil. Whoever apprehends one of these men shall suffer no loss on that account.

Once apprehended, if he can provide sureties, let him be brought to the court through sureties. If he cannot provide sureties, let him be kept in custody by the count’s officials and brought to the court. If anyone accuses him, let action be taken against him according to the aforesaid chapter of the capitulary book. If no one accuses him, let him clear himself in the aforesaid manner and swear that henceforth he will commit no testejam [uncertain], brigandage, or robbery, nor consent to anyone committing it, and that, if he knows who commits this, he will not conceal it from the officials of the realm through whom such a case must be corrected.

But if such men cannot be brought to the court in the manner stated above, let them be placed under the ban of exclusion, and let the envoys or counts deal with them as we said above; and concerning those who receive such men, let action be taken as we prescribed.

If one of our fiscal tenants, being so infamous, flees into our fisc, or if a tenant flees from one immunity to another, let the count order our judge or the advocate of any house of God to present such an infamous man in his court. If he has presented him and someone wishes to prove the charge against him, let him do so. If no one wishes to prove it, nevertheless let him purge his infamy by the judgment of God, and by that judgment of God let him either be acquitted or condemned.

If our judge or the advocate of a house of God, having been notified, does not present such a notorious offender to the count in his court, let action be taken according to the capitulary, book 3, chapter 26.

If someone’s slave is so notorious, let the count admonish the slave’s master to present him in court; and once presented, if anyone wishes to prove the charge against him, let him do so. If no one wishes to prove it, let him submit himself to examination by the judgment of God in the aforesaid manner, and by that judgment of God let him either be acquitted or condemned. If the slave’s master is unwilling to present that slave of his to the count in court, let action be taken according to the capitulary, book 3, chapter 46.

4. Concerning those men who, together with Carloman, committed such great wrongs and such great crimes in our kingdom in past years: just as we then ordered by word and in writing, so let our counts and envoys carry out against them the order which we commanded, with the counsel of our faithful men, but which has not been carried out. That is, let them promise fidelity to us, as we then distributed [Note: [Col. 0748] “distributed” or “established”; the reading is uncertain] and as we gave in writing to our counts. Whatever they took from anyone, let them either make restitution or seek pardon and perform penance, as was then established. Those who do not have the lords whom we ordered them then to accept shall be brought to our presence through sureties; and the counts in whose counties they are shall receive their allods into the fisc.

5. Let each count in his county take care that those who have not yet promised us the fidelity that was required promise us fidelity, as is contained in the capitularies of our grandfather and father.

[Col. 0749A] 6. Let each count in his county take great care that no free man, whoever he may be, be permitted to remain in our kingdom or possess property unless he has promised us fidelity.

7. Since we have heard that wicked men and sorceresses are rising up in many places in our kingdom, and that by their evil arts many men have already been made ill [Note: [Col. 0749] another reading: “instructed”], while many others have died—for, as holy men of God have written, it is the duty of a king to destroy the impious from the land and not permit evil-doers and poisoners to live—we expressly command that each count in his county apply himself diligently so that such persons may be sought out and apprehended.

If males have already been convicted, or females convicted, let them be destroyed, as law and justice require. But if they have merely been named or suspected and have not yet been convicted, or cannot be convicted by truthful witnesses, let them be examined by the judgment of God; and by that judgment of God let them either be acquitted or condemned. And not only such authors of this evil, but also their accomplices and associates, whether male or female, shall be destroyed, so that together with them knowledge of so great an evil may perish from our land.

8. Since it is clear from writings, authority, and reason that there are two principal powers by which this world is governed—the royal power and pontifical authority—and since the book of the capitularies of our grandfather and father jointly provides that the property and slaves of churches are to be held in the same manner as property belonging to the royal fisc, it is just and reasonable that the same rule be applied uniformly and in one manner to the property and slaves that have been in royal and ecclesiastical possession (Benedict, final chapter).

Thus, whenever property or slaves that belonged to our grandfather’s and father’s royal possession, or to ours, are shown to be now held by others, it must be demonstrated how they left the royal possession of our grandfather, our father, or ourselves, since many have obtained some of them by lying and some have acquired more of them by fraud. Likewise, concerning property that belonged to the possession of churches and about which a dispute has arisen, it must be demonstrated by what authority anyone has acquired it as his property.

Since some people do not deny that the property and slaves they hold were in our possession, or that of our predecessors, or in the possession of the churches of God, but say that their fathers, when dying, left these things to them as an inheritance, they therefore do not wish to produce any authority for them, but only to prove their inheritance. Against them it is said that it can happen that someone appropriates something from the royal fisc or from church property, or obtains it by fraud, and that after his death his son or daughter wishes to hold those things as an inheritance.

Therefore, by the capitularies of our grandfather and father—which the Franks judged must be held as law, and which our faithful men decreed at our general assembly must be preserved—it must be determined with respect to what inheritance no documentary authority is to be demanded, but which may be approved as legitimate inheritance by anyone. For those capitularies show, where they speak of property belonging to others that was sold or given to someone by evil cunning, what constitutes legitimate inheritance for each person, when they say, among other things:

“Likewise, he shall be compelled to render an account of all jurisdictions belonging to him, except his legitimate inheritance, which ought lawfully to have come to him by succession from his parents.”

No documentary authority is to be required for this legitimate inheritance. But if a claim is made concerning it, the legitimate inheritance must be proved.

Since, however, documentary authority is required concerning property from the royal fisc and ecclesiastical property—which must be held, as those same capitularies state, in the same manner as property belonging to the royal fisc—the authority by which each person retains such things is demonstrated in those capitularies, where it says:

“Wherever exchanges have been made lawfully, reasonably, and beneficially to the churches of God, whether in our time or in the time of our father and grandfather, let them remain. But wherever exchanges have been made uselessly, disadvantageously, and unreasonably, let them be dissolved, and let each person receive what he gave. But wherever a dead hand intervenes, or any other cause is found that appears reasonable [Note: [Col. 0749] another reading: “rebellious”], let it be carefully described and brought to our attention.”

It also appears just and reasonable that, if the rulers of churches have negligently failed to cultivate property which they received in exchange, while those who made the exchanges have cultivated the property received in exchange, the cultivated and neglected lands should not be valued equally; rather, they should be valued as they were when the exchanges were made. Let the valuation therefore be brought to our attention, and let our judgment and that of our faithful men determine whether these exchanges should remain or be dissolved.

9. (Benedict, Additions IV, 105.) As is contained in the capitularies of our grandfather and father, let our envoys, wherever there are no good scabini, appoint good scabini; and wherever they find bad scabini, let them remove them and, with the consent of the whole people, elect good men in their place. Once elected, let them make the men swear that they will not knowingly judge unjustly.

10. (Capitularies, 107.) We wish that, according to the capitulary of our grandfather and father, whoever among the scabini is found to have judged unjustly because of gifts or friendship shall come through sureties to our presence. Let all the scabini also be warned that no one should presume to sell even a just judgment.

11. (Capitularies, 106.) We wish that, according to the capitulary of our grandfather and father, in every county our envoys choose for conducting investigations and discovering the truth of a case those who can be found to be the best and most truthful, so that they may assist the counts in carrying out justice.

12. (Ansegisus IV, 26.) We wish that, according to the capitularies of our grandfather, our father, and ourselves, courts be held neither in a church nor in its porticoes, nor in the church atrium, nor in the dwelling of a priest beside the church. For it is not fitting that men should be judged there for death, dismembered, or flogged, when, if they flee there, they ought according to another capitulary to have peace.

A house, however, as is contained in the capitularies of our grandfather and father, shall be built by the count in the place where he ought to hold the court, so that public business may not be neglected because of the heat of the sun or the rain. The count may hold lesser courts either within his own authority or wherever he can obtain permission, except in a church, its porticoes, the church atrium, or the priest’s dwelling, as is contained in those same capitularies.

[Col. 0751]

## The Assembly of Charles II at Attigny (A.D. 874, July 1)

[Note: [Col. 0751] Of the acts of this assembly there survives the council of the bishops concerning the complaint of the bishop of Barcelona, delivered to King Charles and published by Sirmond.]

[Note]

[Col. 0751B] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 874, the lord King Charles established the following capitularies at Attigny on the Kalends of July.

1. The bishop of Barcelona [Note: [Col. 0751] perhaps Frodoinus; Sirmond] complained that Tyrsus, a presbyter of Córdoba, while conducting a separate assembly in a church situated within the walls of that city, arrogates to himself almost two-thirds of the tithe of the city; that without the bishop’s permission he presumes to celebrate masses and baptisms in the same city; and that, even on the solemnities of Easter and the Nativity of the Lord, he calls back to himself those whom the bishop has summoned to the mother church and, despising the bishop, gives them communion.

The holy Council of Nicaea therefore says:

“Whoever rashly and dangerously, without keeping the fear of God before his eyes and without recognizing the rule of the churches, departs from the church—whether presbyter, deacon, or anyone who is subject to a rule—must by no means be received into another church. Rather, every necessity must be imposed upon him so that he may return to his own parishes. If he does not do so, he must be deprived of communion.”

This has been decreed concerning Tyrsus, who irregularly departed from his own city.

Concerning him and other despisers, the Council of Antioch says:

“If any presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, separates himself from the church, gathers people separately, and establishes an altar, and, when admonished by the bishop, does not yield, nor consent or obey when summoned once and again, he shall be condemned in every way and shall obtain no further remedy, because he cannot recover his dignity. If he persists in disturbing and troubling the church, let him be suppressed by secular powers as a seditious person.”

The canons of the province of Africa have also decreed this. But it is enough to have set forth this one chapter from the Council of Antioch.

Concerning basilicas and tithes, the holy canons have decreed that all basilicas which have been built in various places, or are built each day, must, according to the rule of the earlier canons, remain under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are situated.

And Saint Gelasius says in his decrees:

“Four portions, both from income and from the offerings of the faithful, according as the resources of each church permit, ought to be made, as was long ago reasonably decreed: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the building and repair of the churches. Just as it is the priest’s responsibility to pay the full amount mentioned to the ministers of the church, so the clergy must understand that they should not insolently demand anything beyond the sum assigned to them.

“The things assigned to ecclesiastical buildings must truly be shown by the evident restoration of the places to have been devoted to that work, for it is wicked if, while the sacred buildings are left destitute, the bishop converts to his own profit the resources designated for them.

“Likewise, although he may appear to demonstrate that he has distributed the portion assigned to the poor according to divine reckoning, nevertheless, in accordance with what is written—‘that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven’—it ought also to be proclaimed through present testimony and not be silenced by the praises of a good reputation.”

These decrees concern those revenues and offerings of the faithful that specifically belong to the bishops of the churches in those regions which do not abound in property but subsist only on the tithes and vows of the faithful.

Concerning rural parishes, however, how much a bishop in the regions of Septimania and Galicia ought to demand from presbyters is shown by the Council of Braga in its second chapter and by the Council of Toledo in its fourth chapter.

Concerning those who, contrary to the authority and will of the bishop of Barcelona, retain the presbyter Tyrsus in the church of the city of Barcelona, the capitulary of the Augusti, the lord Charles and the lord Louis, decrees as follows:

“Concerning those who establish presbyters in churches without the consent of the bishop, or remove them from churches, or who, when admonished by the bishop or by any royal envoy, refuse to obey: let them be compelled to pay our ban, and let them be ordered to come through sureties to our palace. Then let us decide whether it pleases us that they pay that ban or undergo another penalty.”

Since it is a lengthy matter to bring these men to the king’s presence, and dangerous to lead them farther from the frontier, the lord king will entrust to his margrave the manner in which he is to constrain and punish them.

Concerning the tithes which ought to be under the authority and disposition of the bishop, but which they withdraw from the mother church and give elsewhere according to their own pleasure, the same capitulary says:

“Whoever withdraws a tithe from the church to which it ought lawfully to be given and presumptuously gives it to another church, whether because of gifts, friendship, or any other pretext, shall be constrained by the count or by our envoy to restore the amount of that tithe together with its legal penalty.”

And again:

“Concerning those who for many years have neglected to give the ninth and the tithe, either in part or in full, we wish that they be compelled through our envoys to pay, according to the earlier capitulary, the ninth and tithe of one year together with the legal penalty, and in addition our ban. Let it also be announced to them that whoever repeats this negligence shall know that he will lose the benefice from which this ninth and tithe ought to have been paid.”

[Col. 0753B] 2. Concerning the complaint that the fortress of Terracina, subject to his authority, is obstructing his administration through the faction of Baio and the insolence of a presbyter: the decision of the aforesaid Council of Antioch concerning an insolent presbyter is to be followed.

Against the faction of Baio, however, the chapter of the Council of Carthage is to be followed, where it says:

“It has seemed good to all that defenders be requested from the emperors on account of the affliction of the poor, by whose troubles the church is continually wearied, so that defenders may be assigned to them against the power of the rich, with the provision of the bishops.”

The chapter quoted above from the capitulary of the Augusti is also to be followed, concerning those who establish presbyters in their churches without the consent of the bishop or remove them from churches.

3. Concerning the complaint that a certain Goth, Madascius, by fraud and stealth, obtained by royal grant the noble and ancient church of Saint Stephen, where, with the worship of God set aside, the conduct of the country people has become disgraceful; and likewise that Ricosindus the Goth, by fraud and stealth, obtained by royal grant the estate of Saint Eulalia: let the royal order command that this be diligently and truthfully investigated by faithful envoys, and let him ensure that the investigation itself, guarded by faithful men and sealed, be brought to his knowledge.

If it is found that the aforesaid church of Saint Stephen and the estate of Saint Eulalia were obtained by the aforesaid Goths through royal grants, let those grants be sealed according to law and brought together with the investigation to the royal presence, so that, according to the laws of the court, those who lied in their petitions may not benefit from what they obtained, may there be deprived of the benefit of the written instruments by which the rescripts were conveyed, and the royal magnificence may recover what belongs by right to the church of Barcelona.

[Col. 0753]

## Various Capitularies of Emperor Louis II (A.D. 875)

[Note: [Col. 0753] These capitularies survive in the Ambrosian manuscript, and some of them also in the Florentine, Vienna, Verona, and Este manuscripts. We owe the reading of the Ambrosian manuscript to our Blum, and in restoring the text we have followed it chiefly. They appear to have been promulgated in response to a certain consultation by the bishops; traces of this are found in chapter 29, in the words “concerning which it is necessary that Your Highness command the counts,” which survive from the bishops’ report to the emperor. We append two capitularies attributed in eleventh-century manuscripts to Emperor Louis II, although we have been unable to assign them with certainty to any particular year.]

Here begin the capitularies according to Louis the emperor [Note: [Col. 0753] the manuscript reads “of the emperor” with an abbreviation], son of Emperor Lothair [Note: [Col. 0753] the manuscript reads “emperor” with an abbreviation].

[Col. 0753C]

1. Concerning incestuous unions, we command here that henceforth no one shall take as his wife a female relative, nor one whom a male relative has had.

2. We wish that, with the utmost diligence and examination, according to the written law and by a just judgment, the use of oaths be prohibited to everyone for as long as this can be done, so that, with God’s help, the worst custom of perjury may be removed from the Christian people. Nevertheless, let these things altogether be done if all wish to consent to this [Note: [Col. 0753] the manuscript reads “let all in no way consent to this”; the editor thinks the sense should be: “if everyone wishes to consent to this”]. But if anyone is convicted of perjury, let him either lose his right hand [Note: [Col. 0753] another reading: “right”] or redeem it according to the written law, and let him never again be permitted to come to an oath in any court [Note: [Col. 0753] another reading: “to the oath”].

[Col. 0753D] 3. We have learned that those who, according to secular law, claim guardianship of widows and orphans not only neglect them but sometimes even oppress them. We judge that ecclesiastical concern must come to their aid. If such oppressors are willing to be corrected by episcopal admonition, this is to be welcomed. But if they persist in the impiety of obstinacy, it must be reported to the most merciful emperor, so that he himself may provide them with an effective guardian; thus they may receive a reward from God, and the priestly order may not be condemned for useless silence.

4 [Note: [Col. 0753] the chapter is supplied in the margin of the manuscript and has no number]. Let no ecclesiastical person presume to keep a woman with him. If he is a presbyter, deacon, or bishop, let him be deposed from his order. If he is a cleric, let him be flogged naked at the stake; and let the woman who consented to him likewise be flogged and have her head shaved [Note: [Col. 0753] an added word]. For thus says the Scripture of God: “Do not touch the members of Christ as though they were those of a prostitute.”

5. Concerning bishops, presbyters, deacons, and other persons, the great synod has prohibited this entirely: no presbyter, deacon, or cleric may have with him a woman who has been brought into his household, nor a maidservant, nor any other woman who remains under suspicion of adultery or is publicly accused of it, except perhaps his mother, sister, or aunt. Such a woman must not even be present in the same house where they live. Whoever dares to do this shall pay our ban on our behalf.

6. Let each presbyter leave to his own church the property which he acquires after the day of his consecration [Note: the manuscript omits “which”].

7. A man deprived of his status, if the person who deprives him has the legal means prepared to overcome him, shall obtain eight legitimate oath-helpers from the side from which he is being challenged, whether that side is paternal or maternal, and no fewer than four equally legitimate ones from elsewhere; and by swearing he shall vindicate his freedom. If the legal means are lacking, let him take twelve free men from anywhere and defend his free status by an oath.

8. It has pleased us that these chapters, which we have excerpted from the capitulary of our grandfather Charles and of our lord father, Emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 0755] a manuscript reading has “father” incorrectly written], be held and observed as law by all these men, by our faithful, and by those of the holy church residing in the kingdom of Italy. Whoever is found to be a despiser of these chapters shall pay sixty solidi.

[Note: [Col. 0755] In this place the manuscript contains a preface of Otto III, extending to the words “edict of the law,” in place of chapter VIII; it has been counted as part of this chapter, but the added gloss should not be written under this chapter, and the following chapter likewise bears the number VIII in the manuscript.]

9 [Note: [Col. 0755] This chapter is also found in the Vienna and Este manuscripts and in Muratori, chapter 1. In the Lombard collection it is attributed to Lothair]. It has been reported to us that in certain places the bishop and count receive pledges from incestuous persons and from those who do not pay tithes, and that they take pledges from certain negligent presbyters and divide the money among themselves [Note: [Col. 0755] another reading: “divide the money”]. We decree that this be entirely abolished, lest an opportunity for greed be given.

We establish that an incestuous person be punished with penance according to the canonical judgment. Whoever neglects to pay the tithe after three admonitions and the priests’ preaching shall be excommunicated. We do not wish him to be constrained by an oath, because of the danger of perjury.

10. We establish concerning tithes, about which we have already heard many disputes between the bishops or other priests, and the counts, vassals, and our other faithful men: if someone has the same tithe in his own property, as it has been established in the capitulary, we grant that the tithe from his cultivated estate be given to that same church. The priest ordained there shall distribute that tithe for lamps or for almsgiving.

We establish that the tithe of his tenants who reside in the same parish be given by the people. If they refuse, let them be publicly constrained, as we have established in our capitulary.

11. Concerning not taking female relatives in marriage: the wife’s kinship is to the husband as his own kinship is.

12. [Note: [Col. 0755] In the Vienna and Este manuscripts this is read as chapter 7 among the laws of Louis II; nevertheless, it is canon 16 of the Council of Paris of A.D. 829.] Let bishops beware of incurring reproach in disposing of church property for the benefit of their relatives, and let them maintain a proper measure of discretion.

For many bishops, out of love for their relatives, buy estates and slaves from the property entrusted to them, in their own name or in the name of one of their friends, and arrange that these things pass into the possession of their relatives. As a result, ecclesiastical rights are torn apart, the priestly ministry is clouded, and indeed it is withdrawn from and despised by those subject to it [Note: [Col. 0755] the Vienna and Este manuscripts read “diminished”].

Therefore it has pleased all of us that this form of greed be avoided henceforth. We have decreed that it be fixed and remain in force perpetually: a bishop may do whatever he wishes with property belonging to his own right which he acquired before the episcopate, or certainly during the episcopate by hereditary succession, according to canonical authority, and may grant it to whomever he wishes [Note: [Col. 0755] the Vienna manuscript adds “or confer it”].

But after he has become a bishop, whatever property from the resources of the church he acquires under any condition, whether in his own name or another’s, we decree that it pass not into the rights of his relatives but into the rights of the church over which he presides.

We establish the same concerning presbyters and deacons who buy estates and slaves from the property of the churches over which they preside in the same manner. For we have learned that many presbyters, by taking advantage of property acquired in this way, have damaged, offended, and stripped the churches over which they preside; have deviated from their ministry in many ways; have enslaved themselves to the devil; and, on this account, have caused many laymen to perish in the scandal of condemnation and destruction.

Therefore we must not be judged beforehand through suspicion, but must wait patiently until the truth itself becomes clear, whether we ought rather to be heard or condemned [Note: [Col. 0755] the Vienna and Este manuscripts read “whether it is true”].

13. No one shall dare to take in marriage a female cousin, niece, stepmother, brother’s wife, or any woman from his own kinship, or one whom a male relative has had.

14. If anyone enters into such a wicked marriage and remains in it, let him know that by episcopal authority he is bound by the bond of anathema, so that no priest may give him communion.

15. But if he turns back and separates himself from the illicit union, let him be subjected to appropriate penance, as the priest of the place shall determine.

16. We command that churches or any pious places lying destroyed be restored at the expense of those who, according to their established arrangement, are accustomed to receive income from them [Note: [Col. 0755] another reading: “which they are accustomed to receive”]. If the necessary resources are insufficient, let the people of the parish assist, so that the building may be seen to exist honorably [Note: [Col. 0755] another reading: “to be restored”].

[Col. 0757A] 17. No bishop may use immovable property from subject peoples [Note: [Col. 0757] another reading: “subject”] or from any other places for his own purposes, lest the greater become enriched and the lesser be found to have been made poorer by such an act [Note: [Col. 0757] another reading: “be found”]. Whoever acts contrary to this shall be restrained by canonical authority and desist.

18. A woman who has assumed religious dress or a veil under the pretext of religious devotion shall not be permitted to associate with powerful men [Note: [Col. 0757] the manuscript has a corrupt reading concerning “under the pretext of religiosity”]; rather, let her live regularly in a monastery, or observe in a household the habit she has assumed. If women of the contrary kind are found, let them be corrected by the bishop’s care.

19. A disputed possession may by no means be given or sold before the dispute has been settled.

20. Whoever is indebted to another and wishes to deny the debt, but is afterward convicted, shall pay the debt back double.

21. Likewise, a man who sells property and then draws up a charter for it, if he gives less than is written in the charter, shall restore double to the person who received it.

22 [Note: [Col. 0757] The Florentine manuscript, folio 104, places this chapter among the laws of Charlemagne]. After we have ordered this chapter to be recorded [Note: [Col. 0757] the Florentine manuscript reads “to record”], and after anyone in our kingdom has been entrusted by our command to anyone through our order [Note: [Col. 0757] the Florentine manuscript reads: “we have ordered that our pilgrim, entrusted to anyone by our command, …”; the remaining readings are corrupt], if he acts in any other way than what has pleased us and our faithful men, whoever has him under guard by our command shall pay our ban on our behalf [Note: [Col. 0757] the Florentine manuscript reads “our ban twice on our behalf”]. Afterward, let the accused himself appear before the holy synod [Note: [Col. 0757] the Florentine manuscript reads “the holy synod,” feminine], and let him be judged according to the canons.

[Col. 0757C] 23. It is established that everyone must observe that on the Lord’s Day no one dare carry out business or commercial transactions, except transactions involving food for travelers, so that they may be able to live [Note: [Col. 0757] another reading: “be able”]. On the Lord’s Day everyone ought, as far as possible, to hasten to church and devote himself solely to prayer to almighty God, so that those who are called by the Christian name may be seen to perform works.

24. Concerning a monastery or oratory built by its own lord solely for himself, we admonish that, once constructed by the lord, it not be taken away against the will of its builder. He may entrust it to whichever presbyter he wishes for sacred service—provided that the presbyter belongs to that diocese, is of good standing, has letters of dismissal with the consent of his bishop, and is not a bad man [Note: [Col. 0757] another reading: “of good authority and letters of dismissal”]—so that the priest obediently seeks the rightful approval of that bishop.

25. If anyone is proved to be an invader and says that he acted on behalf of the church, the invasion shall be undone from the private property belonging to him and to his heir [Note: [Col. 0757] another reading: “acted”]. If a priest is found guilty of such an offense, let him be canonically judged by his own bishop, so that the church entrusted to him may not suffer harm [Note: [Col. 0757] a manuscript reading has “the church entrusted to him”].

26. It is established in the sacred canons that tithes be distributed according to the proper disposition of the bishop. Some laymen, however, who have basilicas either on their own property or in their benefices, despising the bishop’s disposition, do not give their tithes to the church where they receive baptism, preaching, the laying on of hands, and the other sacraments of Christ [Note: [Col. 0757] another reading: “the other”], but give them according to their pleasure to their own basilicas or their own clerics [Note: [Col. 0757] the editor emends the manuscript, which reads “or their own …”]. This is plainly contrary in every way to divine law and the sacred canons. Therefore we await your authority to correct them.

27. Although a priest’s testimony is considered credible, priests are nevertheless not to be called upon to give testimony in secular affairs or to draw up documents, because it is not fitting for them to be involved in such matters.

28. But if, in the course of an investigation, they hear or see something in a place where no suitable secular persons are found, so that the truth may not be concealed and evil judged good, the matter shall lie within the providence of the proper bishop, so that they may bring the truth honorably before him, or before competent judges, or otherwise.

29. Since in many places there are parricides and other homicides, or persons implicated in other crimes, who refuse to perform public penance—and who are plainly useless to the interests of the commonwealth—it is necessary that Your Highness command the counts to give assistance to the bishops, so that they may be able to subject such persons to canonical penance.

30. Concerning the lawsuits of the churches of God, of widows, and of orphans and minors: in public courts they are not to be despised when they cry out, but are to be heard diligently.

31. Concerning homicides and other criminals who ought to die according to the laws: no one is to permit them to enter his church for the purpose of obtaining an excuse. If anyone enters there without the consent of the patron, then the person to whom that church belongs shall give him no food and shall not permit anyone else to give him any.

32. No one is to presume to appoint or bless another man’s slave as a minister of the church before he has been handed over by his master into the bishop’s hands, to remain in complete freedom for all his days. Nor may the master thereafter exercise any right of domination over him. Then, according to the master’s authority and will, let him approach the sacred order.

33. Let bishops, abbots, and priests divide the property of the church entrusted to them among their relatives and close kin no more than canonical permission has decreed, so that murmuring or detraction may be removed from the people entrusted to them, or from those who offer their property there.

34. Let free men render no service to counts or vicars—neither in the meadow nor in the harvest, neither at plowing nor in the vineyard—and let them not pay that transport-duty or residue, except to those who levy the *aribannum*, or to the royal messenger who conducts an embassy.

35. We decree concerning priests and deacons deprived of ecclesiastical dignity that they be reduced to penance, as the canons prescribe. And if a bishop or abbot has monasteries in his diocese, let them be sent there. The bishop himself shall then order that such persons be assigned there to the people from whom they come, so that, if they possess personal property, a patron may be chosen for them who will provide them food and clothing from that property. This, however, is to be so arranged that they have no permission to wander or roam about, whether to courts, to the palace, or to the very properties which they formerly possessed, without the permission of their bishop; and in the same place where they have been established they are to perform their penance continually. If they do not observe this, let them first be restrained by beatings; but if they do not correct themselves even then, let them be brought to such a place [the remainder is to be supplied from line 33, page 360].

[Col. 0759C] 36. [In the V. Vn. E. collection this appears among the laws of Louis II, chapter 2; in the Lombard collection it is assigned to Lothair.] Concerning widows, minors, orphans, the blind, and the lame: we command that they receive protection and assistance according to our ability and strength, as is contained in the lord king’s decree.

37. [In the V. Vn. E. collection this appears among the laws of Louis II, chapter 6. It is taken from Louis I, chapter 2 of the Worms capitulary above, p. 354.] We wish that every investigation concerning ecclesiastical property or property belonging to the right of our fisc—which must be carried out—be conducted not through witnesses who have been produced, but through the testimony of those who are recognized as the best and most truthful men in that county. According to what they testify, the property itself shall either remain in possession or be restored.

[Note: In chapter a. 829, the words “or property belonging to the right of our fisc” are absent.]

38. It has pleased us concerning orphans and poor persons who are said, rightly or wrongly, to have lost the inheritance belonging to them by paternal or maternal right: if any such persons are found anywhere whom their fathers or mothers have disinherited on account of their transfers, namely through the persuasion or petitions of others, or by some device, we entirely wish and decree that the matter be corrected insofar as it lies within us or our authority, according to the will of God and our own will, through holy admonition and consideration. Thus, if such a case should be found somewhere outside our official jurisdiction, our clemency may dare to admonish those concerned that it be corrected.

39. [See above, Louis I, chapter of 817, chapter 7; it is also present in the V. Vn. and Est. collections among the laws of Louis II, chapter 5.] It has been decreed that no ecclesiastical person shall henceforth presume to accept property from persons whose children or relatives could thereby be disinherited, without their knowledge, through the offering of their own property. If anyone thereafter attempts to do this, he shall in every way be struck by synodal and imperial judgment on account of it, and the property shall return to those who were disinherited.

40. If a free man is accused of theft and possesses property of his own, he shall give security in the court in the presence of the count. If he possesses no property, let him provide a surety who will give security for him and bring him to court. It shall be permitted to him, the first time, to prove himself suitable under the law by oath, if he can. If, on another occasion, two or three persons accuse him of theft, he may contend against one of them in the field with shield and staff. But if a slave is accused of theft, his master shall make compensation for him or excuse him by oath, unless he has committed such a theft that he ought to be handed over for punishment.

[Note: At this point the codex repeats chapter 39, with the opening words changed from “It has been decreed” to “We establish,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0760C] 41. It has been established that no one constituted under a canonical or regular institution shall henceforth persuade anyone to receive consecration in order to acquire property. Whoever attempts to do this shall in every way be struck by synodal or imperial judgment.

42. If several sureties have been given for one case, and one of those sureties dies, so that the principal does not thereby lose his case, let what he promised be paid by those among the sureties who are still alive.

43. It has been decreed concerning new villages and the churches newly established in them that the tithes from those villages be transferred to those same churches.

[Col. 0761]

## TWO CAPITULARIES OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS II (A.D. 875)

[Col. 0761A] We recall the judgment of a judge so frequently because we entirely wish to remove from judges the practice of judging unjustly. Let them judge only according to written law, so that they may in no way dare to judge according to their own discretion; rather, let them learn the written law fully. But concerning what is not written, let the matter be brought before our counsel.

[Note: In some manuscripts of the V. Vn. E. this reads “let it be dealt with according to our counsel.” We append the text of the London codex, in which this law is attributed to Lothair: “Concerning the custom of judgment: We wish entirely to remove from judges the custom of judging unjustly. Let them judge only according to writing, and let them in no way dare to judge otherwise according to their own discretion, unless the judgment is consonant with the laws. Let them learn the written law fully and thus judge. But matters that are not written shall be brought before our aid.”]

2. Concerning unions which, according to the canons or the edict, cannot be joined: it has pleased us that they be separated from one another.

[Note: In the Florentine codex, fol. 129, and in the V. Vn. E., chapter 8. One manuscript adds: “And whoever among our judges neglects to judge or constrain this case shall pay his *wergeld*.”]

[Col. 0761]

## THE ASSEMBLY OF CHARLES II AT PAVIA (A.D. 876, FEBRUARY)

[Note: When Charles was returning from Rome, an assembly was held at Pavia in February 876, at which the nobles of Lombardy subject to Charles met and certain capitularies were promulgated. Pithoeus published the edition preserved in the acts of the Council of Ponthion in *Scriptores coaetanei*, p. 506; Goldastus, Sirmond, and Baluzius also made it public. In the eighteenth century, an apograph and excerpts from a certain codex containing only the acts of the Pavia synod were found in the Ambrosian Library among Fontana’s papers and published in Muratori, *Scriptores*, vol. II, part II, pp. 145 ff. To Muratori we owe the formulas of the oaths sworn by the leading men of the kingdom and by Charles himself. Yet the readings of that sixteenth-century apograph, which assign Archbishop Anspert of Milan a unique position among all the nobles of the Italian kingdom, were such that I would have hesitated entirely to admit them into the text against the evidence of the document presented to the Council of Ponthion and of the Vienna codex. Fontana’s excerpts of the capitularies, likewise accepted by Muratori and Canciani, had also to be rejected, since the capitularies themselves survive. In editing them we used chiefly codex no. 106 of the Imperial Library at Vienna, among the canon-law books. Kopitar, aided by the distinguished scholar Stephan Endlicher, most kindly transmitted its readings from folios 117 and 118.]

[Col. 0761B] To the most glorious and God-crowned, great and peaceful emperor, our lord Charles, perpetual Augustus: we, all the bishops, abbots, counts, and the other nobles of the Italian kingdom who have assembled with us, whose names are generally inserted below, wish perpetual prosperity and peace.

Now, because divine mercy, through the intercession of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, by means of their vicar—namely, the lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and your spiritual father—has invited you to the advancement of the holy Church of God and of us all, and has raised you to the imperial summit by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, we unanimously choose you as protector, lord, and defender of us all. We rejoice to submit to you gladly with all the affection of our hearts, and we promise, with Christ’s consent, to observe with all our strength, in a harmonious spirit and ready will, everything that you shall decree and establish with us for the advancement of the entire holy Church of God and for the salvation of us all.

And those who were present in Italy signed.

Anspert, archbishop of the holy Milanese church, I have signed. John, humble bishop of the holy church of Arezzo, I have signed. John, bishop of the holy church of Pavia, I have signed. Benedict, bishop of Cremona, I have signed. Teudulf, bishop of Tortona, I have signed. Adalgaud, bishop of Vercelli, I have signed. Azo, bishop of Ivrea, I have signed. Gerard, the lowly bishop in the small church of Lodi, I have signed. Hilduin, bishop of the church of Asti, I have signed. Ratborn, bishop of the See of Augusta, I have signed. Leodoin, bishop of the church of Modena, I have signed. Hildrad, bishop of the church of Alba, I have signed. Bodo, humble bishop of the holy church of Acqui, I have signed. Sabbatinus, bishop of the church of Genoa, I have signed. Eilbert, bishop of Como, I have signed. Adelard, servant of the servants of God, bishop of Verona, I have signed. I, Paul, bishop of the holy church of Piacenza, have signed. I, Andreas, bishop of the holy church of Florence, have signed. Reginerius, abbot, I have signed.

The sign of Boso, illustrious duke, chief minister of the sacred palace, and imperial envoy. The sign of Count Richard. The sign of Count Walfrid. The sign of Count Liutfrid. The sign of Count Alberic. The sign of Count Suppo. The sign of Count Harding. The sign of Count Bodrad of the palace. The sign of Count Cunibert. The sign of Count Bernard. The sign of Count Airbol.

These acts were conducted in the palace at Pavia in the year of the Lord 876, in the reign of the lord Emperor Charles, son of Louis Augustus of pious memory, in France 36, in the first year of the empire, in the ninth indiction.

### Oath of Archbishop Anspert

Thus I promise, I, that from this day forward, for as long as I live, I shall be faithful, obedient, and an assistant to this lord of mine, insofar as I know and can, and I shall be his counselor and helper according to my office in all things, without fraud or evil intent, without any deceit, seduction, or deception, and without regard to any person. Neither by myself, nor through an envoy, nor by letters, nor through any person sent or introduced, nor by any method or sign, shall I plot against his honor, or against the peace, tranquility, and stability of his church and of the kingdom entrusted to him; nor shall I consent to anyone who plots such things. Nor shall I ever stir up any scandal that could be contrary or harmful to his present or future salvation. So may God and these holy patrons help me.

### What King Charles Swore [to Archbishop Anspert and] the Nobles of the Italian Kingdom

[The words in brackets are regarded as spurious.] And I, insofar as I know and can reasonably do so, with the Lord’s help, shall honor and preserve [you, most holy and most reverend archbishop, and] each one of you, according to his rank and person; and I shall preserve each of you, honored and safe, without any deceit, condemnation, or deception. I shall preserve for each person the law and justice appropriate to him, and to those who need it and ask reasonably I shall show reasonable mercy, just as a faithful king ought rightly to honor and preserve his faithful, to preserve for each person the law and justice appropriate to every rank, and to extend reasonable mercy to those in need who ask reasonably.

For no person shall I, insofar as human frailty permits, deviate from this through zeal, ill will, or anyone’s improper urging, to the extent that God grants me understanding and ability [the words “has granted” must be supplied]. And if, through frailty, anything contrary to this should secretly be taken from me, when I recognize it I shall willingly strive to correct it. So, and so forth.

## CAPITULARIES

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Here begin the capitularies which the lord Emperor Charles, son of Louis Augustus of pious memory, with the agreement and counsel of the venerable bishops and illustrious nobles and of his other faithful men, for the honor of the holy Church of God and for the peace and advancement of his entire empire, issued in the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 876 [the manuscripts and editions read 877], in the 36th year of his reign in France, in the first year of his empire, in the ninth indiction, in the month of February, in the palace at Pavia.

1. Since the holy Roman Church is the head of all churches, let it likewise be honored and venerated by all; and let no one presume to do anything unjustly against its right and authority. Rather, let it be permitted to maintain its due vigor, to exercise pastoral care on behalf of the universal Church, and to intercede with the Creator through the holy prayers of all on behalf of all.

2. Let the honor due to our lord and spiritual father John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, be preserved by all. Whatever he decrees by apostolic authority according to his sacred ministry shall be received by all with the utmost veneration, and due obedience to him shall be preserved in all things.

3. Although we wish this to be observed in every respect, we especially decree that within the territory of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul no one presume, while going or returning or remaining there, to commit any devastation or plundering. Nor may anyone presume, by any wicked contrivance and without the consent of that sacred pontiff, to claim for himself anything that belongs to the holy Church of God. If anyone does so, let him restore what he has wrongfully seized, pay the immunity-levy of that church, and pay our ban threefold.

4. Let ecclesiastical dignity and priestly and clerical reverence be embraced and preserved by all with the due and appropriate religious sincerity, just as the decrees of our grandfather and father admonish.

5. Let imperial dignity be faithfully observed by all; and no one may dare to violate with impunity what is commanded by it, whether by letter or through envoys.

6. Let bishops carry out their ministry according to the sacred canons promulgated by the Holy Spirit. Let them travel throughout their dioceses without anyone’s hindrance, preaching, correcting, and confirming. In doing this, no one in those dioceses may dare oppose them, contradict what pertains to their ministry, or inflict any trouble upon them on that account. Rather, every son of the Church shall be ready to assist when invited by the bishop, if the need arises, so that the bishops may inquire into, examine, and canonically judge criminal offenses and all other matters requiring correction. Whoever rashly and arrogantly presumes to violate this shall pay our law threefold and our ban threefold.

7. Let bishops, according to the sacred command of our Lord Jesus Christ, exercise preaching appropriately, either personally or through their own men, and ensure that their priests likewise do so. Let secular persons and faithful laymen who are in the cities attend the public stations on feast days; and let those who are in villages and estates hasten to the public service in the parish. No one may presume to celebrate secret offices of the Mass in his own home without the reasonable permission of his bishop.

8. Let bishops establish in their cities, near their churches, a cloister in which they themselves and their clergy may serve God according to the canonical rule. Let them compel their priests to do this, so that they do not abandon their churches and presume to live elsewhere. Let them also be subject to their own bishop according to canonical authority, and let them not defiantly break away from his power. Nor may they commend themselves for this purpose to secular authority, nor may anyone dare to receive them, so that they may in some manner be defended against the canonical laws and the bishop’s rightful authority. Let the bishop immediately subject such priests to ecclesiastical discipline. Nor is it lawful for bishops to neglect the care of all those with whom they have deemed it proper to share the sacred orders entrusted to them.

9. Let the residence of women be completely removed from the houses of priests, on account of the reputation for evil; nor may priests presume to enter their houses indiscriminately, lest—God forbid—the name of God be blasphemed through those by whom it ought piously and continually to be praised. Let no one of so sacred an order presume to practice hunting; nor dare anyone carry military weapons for any kind of disturbance, or assume any dress unbecoming the dignity of the priesthood.

10. No one may presume to invade or take away ecclesiastical property, movable or immovable. Whatever the rectors of churches appear to have lost up to now, through fear or favor, by fraudulent *libellary* or emphyteutic right and to the detriment of the church, shall return to its former right, so that those entrusted with its care may hold it in quiet and peaceful order, pray for us and for the kingdom entrusted to us by God, distribute the stipends due to the poor, and govern and administer the church’s household justly and reasonably. We command transgressors to restore what they have wrongfully seized and, as established above, to pay our law threefold and our ban threefold.

[Note: From this point the final page of the Vienna codex can scarcely be read because it has been worn away.]

11. Let the tithes of cultivated produce and animals be offered to the Lord, according to the sacred precepts, without fraud or any withholding. Let it remain in the bishop’s power to determine how they are to be distributed canonically by the priests. And let the baptismal churches, which are called parishes, be restored by the sons of the Church according to the ancient custom of the Church.

12. Let bishops love our counts and vassals who reside in their dioceses with paternal affection, according to ecclesiastical ministry. Let the counts and vassals, and all the rest of the people, honor and venerate those bishops as holy fathers, and strive to assist them wherever they can in carrying out their ministry. If—and may we never desire it—they are found to be hostile to the bishops, so that the bishops cannot perform the things of God, or if the counts themselves violate their duties contrary to the laws and trouble those whom they ought to venerate, let them make compensation according to the capitulary of our grandfather and father. Let the form of that capitulary teach them how they should honor priests and the other orders. The bishops themselves, nevertheless, each in his own bishopric, shall exercise the power and authority of our envoys.

13. Let bishops and counts residing in their jurisdictions remain in their own houses with their vassals, and let them not presume, on the pretext of lodging, to stay in the house of any poorer neighbor unless invited. For it is clear that devastations and quarrels have chiefly multiplied on this account. Let each of them also take care, according to his office, that plundering and devastation do not occur within his authority. If anyone attempts to do this, let them resist him with all their strength. If they cannot themselves compel such persons to make compensation, let them report the matter to our appointed envoys, so that by their judgment the offenders may make legal compensation according to the capitulary of our grandfather and father. If the envoys themselves cannot correct this, let them bring it to our attention.

14. Whenever divine judgment calls an ecclesiastical prelate from this world, let no one, to his own destruction, invade, plunder, or transfer to his own right the prelate’s possessions. Rather, let the distributors and almsgivers of the church, together with the steward appointed for that church, be free, according to canonical custom, to reserve what has been assigned justly and reasonably for the future successor, or to distribute it as appropriate for the prelate’s soul. Whoever presumes to transgress this through wicked greed shall be punished irrevocably, as stated above.

15. Let none of our faithful in any way conceal someone whom he knows to be unfaithful to us, nor attempt to provide him with any support, if he cannot bring him back to our fidelity. Whoever acts contrary to this shall experience the judgment of our predecessors and ancestors.

Anspert, archbishop, I have signed. John, humble bishop of the church of Arezzo, I have signed. Adalard, servant of the servants of God, bishop of the holy church of Verona, I have signed. Adalgaud, bishop of the church of Vercelli, I have signed. Azo, bishop of Ivrea, I have signed. Benedict, bishop of Cremona, I have signed. Hildrad, bishop of Alba, I have signed. Gerard, the lowly bishop of the church of Lodi, I have signed. John, humble bishop of the holy church of Pavia, I have signed. Teudulf, bishop of Tortona, I have signed. Hilduin, bishop of Asti, I have signed. Sabbatinus, humble bishop of the church of Genoa, I have signed.

The sign of Boso, duke and envoy of Italy, chief minister of the sacred palace. The sign of Count Bernard. The sign of Count Bodrad. The sign of Count Richard. The sign of Count Airbold. The sign of Count Cunibert. The sign of Count Suppo. The sign of Count Alberic. The sign, likewise, of Bernard. The sign of Count Harding. The sign of Count Berard.

[Note: All the subscriptions preceding this are absent in Sirmond; they were reported in his later *Opera varia* from the Beauvais codex.]

[Col. 0767]

## THE SYNOD OF CHARLES II AT PONTHION (A.D. 876, JUNE–JULY)

[Note: Hincmar recounts the history of this synod at greater length in the *Annals* (*Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores* I, pp. 499–500 [*Patrologia Latina* CXV]). Part of its acts survives: namely, the petition of Archbishop Hincmar against King Louis; the confirmation of the acts of the assembly at Pavia, issued on the day before the Kalends of July together with the formula of the oath sworn by all the nobles; the decision concerning the priest Adelgaud, issued on the day before the Ides of July; the capitularies read at the synod by Odo, bishop of Beauvais, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, but lacking authority, as Hincmar warned; and finally the authority of Leo, bishop of Sabina, and Peter, bishop of Fermo, envoys of Pope John for settling the affairs of Louis, king of Germany, and Charles. After the synod was dissolved, they hastened to Rome and entrusted their functions to John, bishop of Tusculum, and John, bishop of Arezzo. We present these materials here from Sirmond and Baluzius, though in the order in which they appear to have occurred.]

## PETITION OF THE CHURCH OF RHEIMS

[Col. 0767B]

We are instructed by the teachings of our fathers that, whenever greater matters or more important cases arise, they should always be referred to the apostolic see, as authority teaches and ancient custom has established. Therefore, because we rejoice that Your Imperial Excellence presides over the synod and that the vicars of the apostolic see are present among us, we make known to Your Serenity the calamities and miseries which our church and our sons have suffered this year at the hands of King Louis, and likewise of Louis his son and their accomplices: namely, slaughters, homicides, adulteries, fornications, robberies, sacrileges, and other crimes which no one could enumerate.

We beseech you, therefore, for the love of almighty God, for the innate kindness granted to you, and for the sake of the office imposed upon you, that, in accordance with the wisdom known to all, you both give counsel and bring aid to us, to our church, and to our sons, lest henceforth our church and the kingdom suffer such great evils as they have suffered until now.

## CONFIRMATION OF THE ACTS OF THE ASSEMBLY AT PAVIA

[Note.]

The synod which was held at the palace at Pavia in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 876, in the ninth indiction, in the month of February, was afterward confirmed at Ponthion, together with the envoys of the apostolic lord John and bishops from many other provinces. The election of the Emperor Charles was confirmed by the bishops of the Italian kingdom and the others.

To the most glorious, and so forth, as above, column 761, through “ninth indiction.”

### Confirmation by the Cisalpine Bishops

Just as the apostolic lord John, supreme and universal pope, first chose and established our lord Charles Augustus as emperor at Rome by sacred anointing, and all the bishops, abbots, counts, and all the others of the Italian kingdom who assembled with them chose our glorious lord Emperor Charles Augustus with unanimous devotion to be their protector and defender, so we also, who have assembled from France, Burgundy, Aquitaine, Septimania, Neustria, and Provence on the day before the Kalends of July at the place called Ponthion, in the thirty-seventh year in France and the first year of the empire, by order of that same lord and glorious Augustus, choose and confirm him by equal consent and harmonious devotion.

And all the Cisalpine bishops who were present signed; their names are written below together with the following capitularies, which they confirmed.

### Oath of Archbishop Hincmar and the Other Nobles

[Col. 0768C] Thus I promise, I, that from this day forward, for as long as I live, I shall be faithful, obedient, and an assistant to this lord of mine, insofar as I know and can, and I shall be his counselor and helper according to my office in all things, without fraud or evil intent, without any deceit, seduction, or deception, and without regard to any person. Neither by myself, nor through an envoy, nor by letters, nor through any person sent or introduced, nor by any method or sign, shall I plot against his honor, or against the peace, tranquility, and stability of himself, his church, and the kingdom entrusted to him; nor shall I consent to anyone who plots such things. Nor shall I ever stir up any scandal that could be contrary or harmful to his present or future salvation. So may God and these holy patrons help me.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and so forth, as above, column 763, through “the sign of Count Berard.”

Louis II, first capitulary. [Col. 0761] In V, Vn, and Est., and in Muratori, this is chapter 4; compare Charlemagne’s capitulary of 802, above p. 94, chapter 26 (*Patrologia*, vol. CXCVII). V and Vn read *offerre* for *auferre*; Est. has “our counsel.” Some V, Vn, and E manuscripts read *habeatur* (“let it be dealt with”) for *offeratur* (“let it be brought”). The London codex attributes the law to Lothair and reads: “Concerning the custom of judgment. We entirely wish to remove from judges the custom of judging unjustly. But let them judge only according to writing, and in no way dare otherwise to judge according to their own discretion, unless the judgment accords with the laws. Let them learn the written law fully and judge thus. But matters which are not written shall be brought before our aid.”

Louis II, chapter 2. [Col. 0761] In the Florentine manuscript, folio 129, and in V, Vn, and E, this is chapter 8. Est. adds: “And whoever among our judges neglects this case, either in judging it or in compelling its settlement, shall pay his *guidrigild* [wergeld].”

Pavia preamble. [Col. 0761] Muratori adds: “Ansbert, with all the bishops, abbots, counts, and the other nobles of the Italian kingdom who assembled with us.” Muratori reads *optamus* (“we wish”), *incitavit* (“has urged”), and omits “and your spiritual father”; Baluzius omits *nobiscum* (“with us”); Muratori reads *decernitis et sancitis* (“you decree and establish”).

Pavia subscriptions. [Col. 0761] Muratori reads *Theudulphus*, *Ratbonus*, *Januensis*, *Filbertus*, *Ragniensis*, *Ricardi*, *Walfredi*, and *Luitfredi*; Sirmond reads *Dertonensis*. Baluzius reads *Placentiae*.

Pavia dating formula. [Col. 0763] Muratori lacks the entire formula; in its place it prints the oaths of Anspert and Charles.

Charles’s oath. [Col. 0763] The words bracketed in the heading and oath are regarded as spurious. After “understanding and ability,” the text requires *dederit* (“has granted”).

Pavia capitularies, heading. [Col. 0763] Muratori omits *Hludowici augusti* (“of Louis Augustus”), adds “of the most reverend and most holy lord Anspert, archbishop of the holy Milanese church, as well as” after “counsel,” and adds “in the Italian kingdom” after “his faithful men.” The manuscripts and editions read A.D. 877.

Chapters 2–5. [Col. 0763] In chapter 2 the Vienna manuscript reads *decrevit [.....]*. In chapter 3 V reads *observare* and the editions omit “of God”; in chapter 4 V reads *ab* and omits the words from “just as” through “admonish”; in chapter 5 V reads *recipiuntur* and singular *audeat*.

Chapters 6–10. [Col. 0763–0765] In chapter 6 the editions read *in hoc*, V reads *corrigendo*, *triplicem*, and *exsolvat*. In chapter 7 V omits *per* and reads *plebem* and *licentiae*. In chapter 8 V omits “near their church” and “with their clergy,” reads *militant*, *dissilient*, *potestate*, and *epistolas*, adds *sed l.* after the clause concerning secular authority, and omits the final *subdat*. In chapter 9 the editions correct *a* to *ab omnibus*; V reads *abitum* and *sacerdotum*. In chapter 10 V preserves *amissae* (the editions read *amisisse*), reads *enfiteocario*, and the final Vienna page is scarcely legible because of abrasion.

Chapters 11–13. [Col. 0765] V reads *conlaborationem*; the editions read *retractatione* and omit *a* before *presbyteris*. In chapter 12 V reads *cominus* and omits “and, if they violate their duties contrary to the laws”; in chapter 13 V reads *omnis*. After “capitulary of our grandfather and” everything remaining is absent from the Vienna manuscript.

Final subscriptions. [Col. 0767] All the preceding subscriptions are absent from Sirmond and were reported in his later *Opera varia* from the Beauvais codex.

Pontignon synod, editorial note. Hincmar narrates this synod more fully in the *Annals* (*Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores* I, pp. 499–500 [*Patrologia* CXV]). What survives includes Hincmar’s petition against King Louis; the confirmation of the Pavia proceedings, issued 30 June with the oath formula; the decision concerning the priest Adelgaud, issued 14 July; capitularies read by Odo of Beauvais on 16 July but, as Hincmar warned, lacking authority; and the commission of Leo of Sabina and Peter of Fermo, papal envoys charged with the affairs of Louis, king of Germany, and Charles, who, when the synod ended and they hastened to Rome, delegated their functions to John of Tusculum and John of Arezzo. These materials are printed from Sirmond and Baluzius, in their apparent chronological order.

The confirmation note identifies the Pavia synod of February 876, ninth indiction, as later confirmed at Pontignon with envoys of Pope John and bishops of many provinces; it also records confirmation of Charles’s election by the Italian bishops and others.

## DECISION CONCERNING THE PRIEST ADALGAUDUS

On the day before the Ides of July, at the place called Pontigonis, the following decision concerning the priest Adalgaudus was reached by the legates of the apostolic see—Leo, apocrisiarius of the holy Roman see; Peter; John; and likewise John, legates of the aforesaid [Col. 0770B] holy see—and by Ansegisus, vicar of that same holy see, together with the entire council: his own church shall be restored to him, and, beginning from the aforesaid Kalends, a delay of four months shall be granted to him to clear his reputation. If after four months he is unable to clear himself canonically, thereafter his plea shall be heard no more at all.

## ARTICLES PROPOSED BY ODO

The holy synod, which was assembled in the name of the Lord at the summons of the lord John, thrice-blessed and universal pope, and by order of the lord Charles, perpetual emperor, at the place called Pontigonis, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 876, in the ninth indiction, in the thirty-seventh year of the reign of the aforesaid invincible emperor, and in the first year of his empire, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, enacted the following articles, set out below. [Col. 0770C]

1. When Louis, who governed the rights of the Roman Empire, died, the lord John, thrice-blessed pope, invited the lord Charles, then king, through Gadericus, bishop of Velletri; Formosus, bishop of Porto; and John, bishop of Arezzo, venerable bishops, to the threshold of the blessed apostles. He chose him as defender and protector of that Church and crowned him with the imperial diadem, choosing him, before all others, as the sole and special one to hold the scepters of the Roman Empire. Obeying his sacred institutions as duty requires, we institute what he instituted, and, with equal consent, we all confirm what he confirmed.

2. After the holy synod had therefore been assembled in the city of Rome, [Col. 0770D] before the arrival of the aforesaid lord emperor, it sent, with the consent of all, letters to King Louis, and also to his sons, archbishops, bishops, abbots, and the other leading men of his kingdom, admonishing them with apostolic authority and in paternal fashion to preserve what belongs to peace, so that they would not rashly attempt any incursion into the kingdom of the aforesaid emperor until they should come together for mutual discussion, and until he himself should jointly decide and determine among them matters concerning the preservation of peace and the rights of the kingdoms, according to the ministry entrusted to him by God. They utterly refused to receive these letters, sent to them through Odo, venerable bishop of Beauvais, [Col. 0771A] even after they had been delivered twice.

3. He himself, however, disregarding the apostolic and paternal admonitions and breaking the bonds of brotherhood, invaded his brother’s kingdom with a hostile force, in tyrannical fashion devastating it; his authority enabled those responsible to perpetrate murders, sexual crimes, adulteries, sacrileges, and countless evils that cannot be enumerated.

4. When the thrice-blessed pope heard that these evils had been perpetrated in the kingdom of his spiritual son, the lord Charles, ever august, he was touched with anguish of heart and hastened to send his legates, namely John and John, venerable bishops, with other letters of his, wishing to admonish him to repent of the past evil and finally to cease invading his brother’s kingdom. Though admonished a second time, he still did not wish to receive their embassy. [Col. 0771B]

5. After these, finally, he sent other legates: namely Leo, most holy bishop of Gabii and envoy and apocrisiarius of the holy Roman Church, and likewise Peter, venerable bishop of Fossombrone, who pleaded, admonished, and protested these same matters. Whether he wishes to receive their admonitions remains uncertain.

6. But because the aforesaid Leo, most reverend bishop of Gabii and envoy and apocrisiarius of the holy Roman Church, and Peter, bishop of Fossombrone, are unable to remain here longer on account of certain ecclesiastical necessities, and because it is not fitting to weary bishops who have come from afar for any longer, they have decided that John of Tuscany and John [Col. 0771C] of Arezzo, venerable bishops, should undertake the embassy of the aforesaid men together with the earlier embassy. Whatever they decide, in the name of all the bishops, concerning summoning a synod or striking those who show contempt, they shall freely define with apostolic authority, together with the other bishops whom they choose by common consent to carry out these matters. Whatever they deliberate, the apostolic lord, together with the entire holy Roman Church, shall determine, establish as enduring forever, and confirm.

7. Just as the lord Pope John decreed—with the assent, consent, and joint decision of the lord and most glorious Charles, emperor, ever august—that the venerable bishop Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens, should exercise his authority, and conferred upon him primacy over Gaul and [Col. 0772A] Germany for summoning a synod and canonically deciding whatever necessities might arise, and so that he might report more serious matters to the pope’s knowledge, we unanimously commend this with all devotion; and we decree and sanction that he shall thus hold the primacy over Gaul and Germany.

8. The synod that the lord John, apostolic and universal pope, recently instituted concerning the deposition of certain men—namely Formosus, bishop of Porto; Gregory, the nomenclator; Stephen, the secundicerius; George, the vestiarius; and their other accomplices—as is contained in his letter sent to us: in accordance with his command, and dissenting from its head in nothing, we unanimously consent to and decree it; and, obeying all his apostolic sanctions in every respect, as is proper, [Col. 0772B] we submit to them.

9. The sentence that the apostolic lord established and confirmed concerning the most unspeakable acts of King Louis and his accomplices, unless they come to their senses and render due obedience to the apostolic see, we—all who have assembled for the present synod—unanimously decree and confirm.

## AUTHORITY OF THE LEGATES LEO AND PETER
