[Col. 0772C] Because our lord John, most holy and thrice-blessed pope, sent us—namely me, Leo, bishop of Gabii and envoy and apocrisiarius of the holy Roman Church, and Peter, venerable bishop of Fossombrone—to these regions for the purpose that, just as he had previously ordered through the venerable bishops John and John, when your holiness had assembled, we should determine the matters that had arisen this year between the two brothers; but because we cannot remain longer on account of certain necessities of the holy Roman Church, and do not wish to weary your blessedness any further, we have decided that these brothers of ours, namely John of Tuscany and John of Arezzo, venerable bishops, should remain with you until the matter under consideration reaches its desired conclusion by the favor of divine grace. Whatever they decide concerning summoning a synod, defining its decisions, or striking those who show contempt, they shall freely define with apostolic authority; and whatever they deliberate, the apostolic lord, together with the entire holy Roman Church, shall determine, establish as enduring forever, [Col. 0772D] and confirm.

[Col. 0771]

## EDICT OF THE EMPEROR CHARLES II CONCERNING THE NORMAN TRIBUTE

*(Year 877, 7 May; at Compiègne.)*

[Note: Hincmar, reporting the edict, places it at Quierzy in June; but from its heading we publish it as promulgated at Compiègne, following Sirmond and Baluze. It agrees with what Hincmar reports in the *Annals* concerning the amount of the individual payments.]

[Col. 0771D] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 877, on the Nones of May, at the palace of Compiègne, the following levy was established from part, but not the whole, of the kingdom that the lord Emperor Charles possessed before the younger Lothair had died: it was to be paid to the Normans who were on the Seine, so that they would withdraw from his kingdom.

Bishops, abbots, counts, and the lord’s vassals shall give from their honors twelve denarii from each demesne mansus; [Col. 0772D] from a free mansus, four denarii from the demesne due and four from the resources of the holder of the mansus; but from a servile mansus, two denarii from the non-demesne due and two from the resources of the holder of the mansus. From all churches, each bishop from his diocese, or each abbot from his own abbey alone, wherever they may lie in the parish of another bishop, shall receive, together with the envoy of the bishop in whose parish [Col. 0773A] they are, from the priests according to their ability five solidi, or four, or three, or two, or one solidus. From the one who can contribute the most, five solidi; from the one who can contribute the least, four denarii. [Col. 0774A] From the churches of the emperor, the empress, the counts, and the imperial vassals—both those who will travel with the emperor and those who will remain—the bishop in whose parish they are situated shall collect the levy according to the aforesaid arrangement. From merchants, however, and from those who live in cities, the levy shall be exacted according to their ability and according to the resources they possess.

[Col. 0773]

## THE ASSEMBLY OF EMPEROR CHARLES II AT QUIERZY

*(Year 877, 14 June.)*

[Note: We publish the articles proposed by the emperor and the responses of the assembly, following Sirmond and Baluze, and then the promulgated articles, collated with manuscript no. 4761 of the Royal Library of Paris, tenth century.]

[Col. 0773A] These articles were established by the lord Charles, glorious emperor, with the consent of his faithful at Quierzy, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 877, [Col. 0773B] in the thirty-seventh year of his reign and the second of his empire, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the tenth indiction. Some he determined himself, and concerning others he ordered his faithful to respond.

## ARTICLES PROPOSED WITH THE RESPONSES OF THE ASSEMBLY

1. Concerning the honor and worship of God and of the holy churches which, by God’s providence, stand under the authority and protection of our government, with the Lord’s help we decree that, just as they were cultivated, honored, and enlarged in their possessions in the time of our lord and father of blessed memory, and just as those honored and enriched by our generosity have been, so henceforth they shall be preserved in their entirety. Priests and servants of God shall receive ecclesiastical authority and their due privileges according to venerable authority; and [Col. 0773C] the chief power, the vigor of illustrious men, and the administrators of public affairs shall all cooperate with them reasonably and justly, so that they may competently carry out their ministry. And our son likewise, with God’s help, shall preserve the foregoing.

**Response.** Concerning the first article, just as you have decreed under God’s inspiration, we all praise it and wish to preserve it.

2. Concerning the monastery built by us at Compiègne in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God: it shall be honored by our son and our faithful in the manner in which we began; its privilege, confirmed by the lord pope and by all the bishops, and also its imperial decree, shall be most benevolently and inviolably preserved by all the faithful for the love of God and of us, and shall be confirmed by our son. [Col. 0773D]

**Response.** Concerning the second, we respond likewise.

3. Let such men be chosen by you, except those whom we have entrusted to you, whose special counsel and assistance we shall use on the present journey.

**Response.** Concerning the third, you have arranged, as you have seen best under God’s inspiration, for the defense and protection of your kingdom and for the custody of your son through your faithful—bishops, abbots, and counts alike—and we recognize that this is necessary. We cannot and ought not disrupt that arrangement, nor do we know how we could arrange it better.

4. How can we be secure, until we return here by God’s gift, that no one will disturb our kingdom, insofar as God may wish to assist you and insofar as you are able; and how can we be secure concerning our son and concerning you, and you concerning our son, and he concerning you, so that you may be able to trust one another? [Col. 0774A]

**Response.** [Col. 0774B] Concerning the fourth, where it is written how you may be secure concerning your son, we answer that, thanks be to God, you both fathered and raised that same son, and under your nurture God has brought him to this age. None of us can, ought, or knows how to preserve him more than you can; and after God and his saints, his salvation and honor rest upon your counsel, assistance, and arrangement concerning him. How you may be secure concerning him for the will of God, the benefit of the holy Church, and the welfare of your kingdom remains in your hands.

Concerning what is written there about how you may be secure concerning us, namely how, until you return here by God’s gift, your kingdom may not be disturbed [Col. 0774C] by anyone insofar as God may wish to help us and insofar as we are able, we answer: there are the oaths that we have sworn to you; there is the declaration that clergy and laymen made and subscribed to you at Quierzy; there is the pardon that your lordship both granted and subscribed for us, your faithful; and there are the declaration and oath that we made to you at Gundulf’s estate concerning the new matters arising from the death of Lothair and from the mission of the apostolic lord Hadrian and the mission of Louis, your nephew.

There is also the declaration that we made at Reims concerning our fidelity to you, the arrangement and defense of your kingdom, your wife, and the son whom you have, and, if God should give you another, that son also. We have preserved and are preserving all these things up to now, [Col. 0774D] and, with God’s help, we wish to preserve them until the end of our lives. Therefore you can truly and certainly believe us.

If anyone has deviated from the aforesaid oaths or declarations, let him correct this according to reason, authority, and custom, and preserve them henceforth. If any of your faithful has not made these declarations, let him do so if necessary and preserve them thereafter.

Your faithful also came to you after the death of your brother. What oath they swore to you, you know. Whoever among them has preserved that oath until now should preserve it henceforth. If anyone has deviated from that oath, let him correct this according to reason, authority, and custom, and preserve it thereafter.

Concerning what is written there about how we may be secure concerning your son, [Col. 0775A] we answer that, concerning your son—whom, by God’s grace and through your arrangement, we wish to have as our future lord after you—we seek no other guarantee than what you established and decreed in your capitulary: that he preserve each of us in our own order and person.

Concerning what is written there about how he may be secure concerning us, we answer what we also answered at Reims: if God and you raise him to the government of the kingdom and designate him for the specified portion, we wish to be faithful to him just as, rightly, we ought to be faithful to our lord. [Note: At Reims, as Hincmar testifies, provision was made in the presence of the magnates of the kingdom—except Abbot Hugh and Count Bernard of Auvergne—for Louis’s succession to the kingdom after his father’s death. Sirmond.]

Concerning what is written there, and what you told us verbally, so that we may trust one another, we have faithfully confirmed one another by word, so that, for the will of God, your fidelity and [Col. 0775B] honor, the benefit of the holy Church and your kingdom, and the safety of your faithful, we may remain united, with God’s assistance, insofar as each of us, in his own order and person, has knowledge and ability by God’s grace, so that we may trust and assist one another.

5. Our son shall confirm beforehand the things that, by grants of our generosity, we have permitted our beloved wife to hold as her own. From everything that we have granted or shall grant to her by beneficiary right, if our death should occur and she survive us, how may we be secure that our son and our faithful will strive to preserve her and all her possessions with due honor?

**Response.** Concerning the fifth article, which concerns the honor and protection of your beloved wife, our lady, the preservation of the possessions that you have given or will give her, and the confirmation that your son is to make concerning them: your son is prepared to do this as you command, and we too shall be prepared to do so insofar as we know and can.

6. Concerning our daughters: with what honor, according to God’s will, and with what protection or assistance should they live? Whatever we have given our little daughter, or may henceforth give her, with what security may she hold it? And if God grants her to reach mature age, let her remain under her mother’s authority; let no one, against her will, give her to a husband or impose upon her the sacred veil.

**Response.** [Col. 0775D] Likewise concerning your daughters, and also concerning your little daughter, as your article provides: your son is prepared to preserve these things, and we shall offer assistance toward preserving them insofar as we know and can.

7. Concerning the arranging of the military forces, and, if our nephews, following their father’s footsteps, should wish to contrive some evil against us or our kingdom, either on the journey or after we have reached the appointed place under God’s guidance, how may they be fully resisted with God’s help?

**Response.** Concerning the forces to be arranged, and concerning assistance if any of your nephews should wish to cause you some hindrance either on the road or in Italy, it will be in your hands to determine who should remain in this kingdom and who should travel after you to your assistance. [Col. 0776A]

8. If, before we return, any offices should meanwhile become vacant, consideration must be given to what is to be done in consequence.

**Response.** If, before you return with the Lord’s help, an archbishop should die, the neighboring bishop of his diocese, together with the count, shall oversee that see until the archbishop’s death has been reported to you. If a bishop should die in the meantime, the archbishop shall appoint a visitor to that see according to the sacred canons; together with the count, he shall guard that church against plunder until the bishop’s death has been reported to you. If an abbot or abbess should die, the bishop in whose parish that monastery lies, together with the count, shall guard the monastery until your command concerning it is issued. [Col. 0776B]

9. If a count should die whose son is with us, our son, together with our other faithful, shall arrange for one of those who were most closely associated and related to him to oversee that county with the county officials and the bishop in whose parish it lies, until the matter is reported to us. If he has a young son, that same person, together with the county officials and the bishop in whose parish it lies, shall oversee that county [Col. 0776C] until the matter comes to our knowledge. If he has no son, our son, together with our other faithful, shall arrange for someone to oversee that county with the county officials and the bishop until our order concerning it is issued. No one should become angry on this account if we give that county to another whom we prefer rather than to the man who has overseen it until now.

The same is to be done concerning our vassals. We wish and expressly command that bishops, abbots, counts, and all our other faithful likewise strive to preserve their own men. As for bishoprics and abbeys, the neighboring bishop and count shall oversee them, so that no one may plunder ecclesiastical property or resources and no one may hinder them from giving alms. If anyone should presume to do so, let him make compensation according to human laws, satisfy the church he has harmed according to ecclesiastical laws, and endure our royal penalty according to the measure of his fault and as we see fit. [Col. 0776D]

**Response.** The remaining articles require no response, since they have been arranged and defined by your wisdom.

10. If, after our death, any of our faithful, moved by love of God and of us, should wish to renounce the world, and should have a son or such a close relative as could benefit the state, let him be able to commend his honors to him as he best wishes. If he wishes to live peacefully on his allod, let no one presume to cause him any hindrance, nor demand anything else from him except that he go to the defense of the country.

[Col. 0777A] 11. If, on any account, news of our death should be reported to our son or to our faithful, let it not readily be believed. Rather, let our faithful assemble together and, reasonably and according to God’s will, arrange everything that we have ordered.

12. If death should overtake us in the service of God and his saints, our almoners shall administer our almsgiving according to what we have entrusted to them. Our books, which are in our treasury, shall be distributed by them, as we have arranged, among Saint Denis, Saint Mary at Compiègne, and our son. They are: Hincmar, venerable archbishop; Franco, bishop; Odo, bishop; Gauzlinus, abbot; Arnulfus, count; Bernardus, count; Chuonradus, count; and Adalelmus [Col. 0777B] count. They shall act similarly concerning the things belonging to the alms of our wife, if she should die. Whatever remains shall be safeguarded by them until, God granting it, we make our inquiry.

13. It must be determined what portion of the empire our son should expect to be assigned to him if our death occurs, and what portion that other son should have if God should meanwhile grant us another son. If one of our nephews should show himself worthy of this, or if he should not do so, the matter shall be decided according to what seems right to us then and to whomever we please.

14. Our son must prepare himself in such a manner that, when we return with God’s help, he may be able to go to Rome and there serve God and the holy apostles for as long as necessary, [Col. 0777C] and, with God’s assistance, be crowned king there.

15. How and in what order our son is to remain in this kingdom; who are to be the men whose assistance he uses and who are to take turns being with him. Namely, among the bishops, Ingilwinus, Reinelmus, Odo, or Hildeboldus shall always be with him. Among the abbots, unless another necessity arises, Welpho, Gauzlinus, and Folco shall always be with him. Among the counts, Teudericus, Balduinus, Chuonradus, or Adalelmus shall remain with him in turn; and Boso and Bernardus shall do so as often as they can for our benefit.

If he travels toward the Meuse, Franco the bishop, John the bishop, Arnulfus the count, Gislebertus, Letardus, [Col. 0777D] Matfridus, Widricus, Gotbertus, Adalbertus, Ingelgerus, and Rainerus shall be with him, together with the men named above. If he travels beyond the Seine, Hugo the abbot, Waltherus the bishop, Wala the bishop, Gislebertus the bishop, and our other faithful from that region shall be with him, together with the men named above. The same applies to our other faithful, according to what is necessary in each part of the kingdom.

16. If an emergency should suddenly arise in some part of the kingdom, it seems to us that, since our son is young, thanks be to God, he should not make all our faithful labor equally. Rather, as we ourselves have very often done with God’s help, he should take with him capable men from among our faithful, fall unexpectedly upon our enemies, and terrify them manfully. Those who cannot go with him should send selected men with him, as necessity requires. [Col. 0778A]

17. Adalardus, count of the palace, shall remain with him with the seal. If he is absent because of some necessity, Gerardus, Fredricus, or one of those who are his military commanders shall administer justice. He himself shall administer justice one day each week, and wherever they may be, they shall oversee the preservation of peace.

18. Counts shall also, throughout their counties, oversee the suppression of robbers and evil men, so that peace may be established, and shall hold the courts. They shall notify all who owe military service so that they are ready, in case of necessity, to go into the service of God and of us. Our envoys, who have been appointed throughout our entire kingdom, must not neglect to carry out our mission as opportunity requires. [Col. 0778B]

19. If war should arise in the kingdom that the count cannot suppress by himself, our son, together with our faithful, shall strive to suppress it as quickly as possible, before the evil can grow in our kingdom.

20. Our son, together with our faithful, shall remain in that part of the kingdom where the need is greatest. No one shall take lodging dues in our villages or in the villages of our wife; no one shall dare to plunder our men or others; and the benefices and villages of those who travel with us shall remain under immunity. If anyone should presume otherwise, he shall pay threefold compensation, like one who commits an offense within the lord’s protection. Those who plunder the villages of bishops, abbots, or our other faithful shall make compensation according to what is contained in the capitularies of our predecessors and in our own. [Col. 0778C]

21. No one shall disregard letters sealed with our authority, or in our son’s name, or in the name of those whom we leave with him in this kingdom; nor shall anyone disobey what has been commanded to him. If anyone should presume to do so, he shall be fined as provided in the capitulary of our grandfather and lord and father.

22. It must also be advised and urged that none of our faithful who remain with our son should prove slow in counsel. Rather, each should speak as seems best to him, and after everyone has spoken, they should choose what seems best.

[Col. 0778D] 23. How the kingdom that had once been confirmed to the Bretons by oath, since none of those to whom it was confirmed survives, is to be received by our faithful.

24. Concerning the kingdom of Aquitaine.

25. After us, with the things that must be carried for us, Willebertus the bishop shall go first, then Arnoldus the bishop, and then Wala the bishop. Our son and our other faithful shall strive to ensure that nothing new or evil arises in this kingdom that we do not learn of through horsemen or foot couriers, because we shall always be as concerned for your prosperity as for our own. If our nephews, the sons of our brother, following their father’s example, should wish to travel after us and rise up against us, do not wait for us to command our faithful to come to our aid. As soon as they learn of this, let them come to our assistance as quickly and as fully as they can, and let all always be warned for this purpose. [Col. 0779A]

26. The fortress at Compiègne, begun by us, shall be completed for love of us and in honor of you, as a testimony to your affection for our benevolence.

27. Concerning the city of Paris and the fortresses on both sides of the Seine and the Loire: how and by whom they are to be restored, and especially the fortress of Saint Denis.

[Col. 0779B] 28. Concerning Vulframnus, Gauzmarus, and Hadebertus the goldsmith: they shall remain as we have decreed.

29. Concerning the mints.

30. How the payment that is to be given to the Normans from the levy is to be completed and brought to fulfillment.

31. Concerning the honors of Boso, Bernardus, Wido, and the other men of those regions. And concerning the circumcised—that is, Jews [Note: i.e. the circumcised, Jews.]—and the other merchants: namely, that Jews should pay a tenth, as Christian merchants an eleventh.

32. In which of our palaces our son is not to stay, unless necessity requires it, and in which forests he is not to hunt. Quierzy is entirely excluded, together with its forests. Silvacus likewise, together with the whole of Laon. Compiègne likewise, together with Causia. Salmonciacus likewise. At the estate of Audreia [Note: Audriaca villa, between Amiens and Arras. S.] he is not to take pigs; and he is not to hunt there except while passing through. [Col. 0779C] At Attigny he is to hunt little. At Verne [reading uncertain], he may take pigs only. The Ardennes is entirely excluded, except while passing through. The estates assigned to our service are likewise excluded. At Ligurio he may take pigs and wild animals. Aristallium, together with its forest, is entirely excluded. At Lens, Wara, and Astenido he may take both wild animals and pigs. At Rugitusit, at Scadebolt, and at Launif, only while passing through and as little as possible. The same applies at Crisiacus. At Lisga he may take pigs only. [Note: It should perhaps be read: “he may take pigs at Rugitusit, and likewise at Scadebolt; at Launif, only while passing through,” etc.]

33. Adelelmus shall carefully ascertain how many pigs and wild animals have been hunted by our son in each place.

## CAPITULARY

*Year 877, 16 June*

[NOTE]

[Col. 0779D] On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of the aforesaid month, after the lord Emperor Charles had generally announced to the people his journey to Rome; that he had arranged how his son was to remain in this kingdom, whose counsel he was to use and whose assistance he was to receive in particular and general matters; that he had arranged how the Normans were to be expelled from this kingdom and thereafter defended against; and that, if war should arise in any part of this kingdom, it was to be suppressed or defended against; and because he had arranged general and particular articles concerning general and particular matters, which he had given to his son and to his faithful who were remaining in this kingdom and was carrying with him, he said that he had extracted certain articles from those capitularies which he wished to have read aloud to the knowledge of them all. He then ordered Gauzlinus the chancellor to recite the following articles to the people. [Col. 0780A]

The lord Emperor Charles composed these articles and most recently ordered them to be announced at Quierzy.

1. Concerning the honor and worship of God and of the holy churches which, by God’s agency, remain under the authority and protection of our rule, we decree, with the Lord’s help, that just as they were cultivated, honored, and enlarged in their resources in the time of our lord and father of blessed memory, and as they have been honored and endowed through our generosity, so henceforth they shall be preserved in the entirety of their rights; and that priests and servants of God shall obtain ecclesiastical vigor and their due privileges according to revered authority [Note: [Col. 0779] “optineant” in 4761.]; and that the principal authority, the energy of illustrious [Note: [Col. 0779] “inlustrium” in 4761.] men, and the administrators of public affairs shall all contribute to them, reasonably and justly in every respect, so that they may competently [Note: [Col. 0779] “conpetentur” in 4761.] carry out their ministry. And may our son likewise, with God’s help [Note: [Col. 0779] “adjuvante” in 4761.], preserve the matters stated above.

2. We wish all our faithful to be truly secure concerning us: namely, that, insofar as we are able and insofar as we know what is just and reasonable, we wish to honor and protect each person according to the dignity of his order and person, and to preserve him honored and protected. And for each of them, in his own order and according to the laws appropriate to him [Note: [Col. 0779] “conpetentes” in 4761.], both ecclesiastical and secular, we shall preserve right reason and justice; and none of our faithful shall we condemn, dishonor, oppress, or afflict by improper machinations contrary to law, justice, authority, or right reason. And, as we have said, we pledge to preserve for each person the law appropriate to him, just as his predecessors held it in the time of our predecessors, in every dignity and order, with the Lord’s help—namely, for those who are faithful and obedient to us and who, according to their ministry and person, are our helpers and fellow workers in counsel and aid, according to their knowledge and ability and according to God and the world, just as by right each person in his own order and status ought to be toward his emperor and his lord [Note: [Col. 0779] “sui” in 4761.].

And the capitularies which our grandfather and father established for the status and protection of the holy Church of God and its ministers, and for the peace and justice of the people and the tranquility of the kingdom; and those which we established jointly with our brothers, the kings, and with our own faithful and theirs; and also those which, with the counsel and consent of the bishops and [Note: [Col. 0779] “et” in 4761.] the other [Col. 0781A] faithful of God and of ours, we decreed at our various assemblies should be preserved for the matters written above—we decree that they remain unshaken, and likewise we wish and command our son to preserve them unshaken [Note: [Col. 0781] The remainder is lacking in 4761.].

3. If a count of this kingdom should die whose son is with us, our son, together with our other faithful, shall arrange that those who were most closely connected and related to that count, together with the officials of that county and the bishop in whose diocese that county lies, oversee the county until the matter is reported to us, so that we may honor the son of the man who is with us with his honors. If, however, he has a young son, that son, together with the officials of the county and the bishop in whose diocese it lies, shall oversee the same county until the death of the aforesaid count comes to our knowledge, and that son shall, by our grant, be honored with his father’s honors. If he has no son, our son, together with our other faithful, shall arrange who, along with the officials of the county and its own bishop, is to oversee the county until our order concerning it is issued. And let the man who has overseen that county not be angry if we give the same county to someone else whom we prefer rather than to the one who has overseen it until then. The same is to be done concerning our vassals. And we wish and command that bishops, abbots, counts, and all our other faithful strive to preserve this practice with regard to their own men.

4. We also wish and expressly command that, if any bishop, abbot, abbess, count, or our vassal should die, no one shall plunder ecclesiastical property or resources, nor presume to invade or usurp the property or resources of a count, our vassal, or any other deceased person, nor inflict any violence upon the wives or sons of deceased laymen; and no one shall hinder their almoners from making alms on their behalf. If anyone should presume to do so, let him make satisfaction for it according to secular laws under our ban, and, according to ecclesiastical laws, let him make satisfaction to the church which he has injured. In addition, let him suffer our *harmiscarum*, according to the measure of his fault and as we see fit.

After these capitularies had been read, he gave everyone permission, with God’s grace and his own, to return to his own home, except those whom he specifically ordered to remain with him for several days in order to consider particular matters or to release gifts.

[Col. 0781]

## THE CORONATION OF HLUDOWICUS II, SON OF KARLUS. (A.D. 877, November 30–December 8.)

[Note: [Col. 0781] The following material, except the coronation rite itself, is found in Hincmar’s *Annals*; the petition of the bishops and the king’s promise are preserved in Paris manuscript no. 4761; Sirmond published the rite from the manuscript of Saint-Laurent of Liège.]

### Commendation of the Magnates

The commendation of Bishop Ansegisus and the other bishops who were present at Compiegne when they blessed Hludowicus, son of Emperor Karlus.

[Col. 0781C]

“I commend myself and the church entrusted to me to you, for the preservation of due law and justice and for the provision of protection, just as a king ought, by right judgment, to preserve and protect the bishops of his church.”

### Their Profession

“I, the same person, make this profession: from this day forward, to this lord and my king, Hludowicus, son of Karlus and Hermentrudis, according to my knowledge and ability and my ministry, I shall be faithful and shall be his helper in counsel and aid, just as a bishop is rightly bound to his lord, in my faith and in my priesthood.”

In response to the petition of the bishops written above, King Hludowicus made the following profession to the bishops, and at Compiegne, on the second day before the Kalends of December, he gave them this very written pledge of pardon with his own hand.

### The Promise of King Hludowicus

[Col. 0782C]

“I, Hludowicus, established king by the mercy of our Lord God and by the election of the people, promise, with the Church of God as witness, to all orders—namely, bishops, priests, canons, monks, and nuns—that from this time forward I shall preserve for them in their entirety the rules written by the Fathers and confirmed by apostolic testimonies. I also promise to preserve the laws and statutes for the people who, by God’s mercy, are entrusted to me to govern, through the common counsel of our faithful, according to what my predecessors, the emperors and kings, inserted into their deeds and decreed must be held and observed altogether inviolably. Therefore I, Hludowicus, rereading this spontaneous promise of mine out of love for rectitude and justice, have confirmed it with my own hand.”

### Coronation

The rite by which King Hludowicus was crowned in the palace at Compiegne by Archbishop Hincmar, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 877, on the sixth day before the Ides of December; at that time the following petitions were made by the bishops to the king, and promises were made by him to the bishops.

[Col. 0782D]

[Col. 0783A]

### Petition of the Bishops

“We ask you to pardon us in this matter: that for each one of us and for the churches entrusted to us, according to the first capitulary which most recently at Carisiac your lord father the emperor announced that he would preserve, both on his own behalf and on yours, with his faithful, yours, and the legates of the Apostolic See consenting, while Gauzlenus was reading it, you preserve canonical privilege and due law and justice, and provide protection, just as a king ought by right to provide these things in his kingdom for each bishop and the church entrusted to him.”

### The King’s Promise

“I promise and pledge to you that, for each one of you and for the churches entrusted to you, according to the first capitulary which most recently at Carisiac my lord father the emperor announced that he would preserve, both on his own behalf and on mine, with his faithful, ours, and the legates of the Apostolic See consenting, while Gauzlenus was reading it, I shall preserve canonical privilege and due law and justice, and, insofar as I am able, with the Lord’s help, I shall provide protection, just as a king ought by right to provide these things in his kingdom for each bishop and the church entrusted to him.”

This is the capitulary referred to here.

Concerning honor as well, see above, columns 773 and 780, through the words “may he preserve.”

### Blessings Pronounced over King Hludowicus

“O God, who by your power guide your peoples and rule them through love, [Col. 0783C] grant this servant of yours the spirit of wisdom together with disciplined government, so that, devoted to you with his whole heart, he may always remain capable in the governance of the kingdom, and so that, by your gift, in his days the security of the Church may be directed and Christian devotion may remain in tranquility. Through the Lord.”

### Pouring of the Sacred Oil

“Almighty and everlasting God, creator and governor of heaven and earth, maker and disposer of angels and human beings, who caused your servant Abraham to triumph over his enemies, who granted manifold victory to Moses and Joshua, leaders of your people, who raised your humble servant David to the height of kingship, and delivered him from the lion’s mouth, from the hand of the beast and of Goliath, and also from the evil sword of Saul and all his enemies, and who enriched Solomon with the ineffable gift of wisdom and peace, [Col. 0783D] look, we beseech you, upon the prayers of our humility, and adorn this servant of yours with the virtues with which you adorned those faithful servants of yours, through a manifold blessing of honor; exalt him in the governance of the kingdom; and anoint him with the oil of the grace of your Holy Spirit, with which you anointed priests, kings, prophets, and martyrs, who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced justice, and obtained the promises.

“May this most sacred anointing flow down upon his head, descend into his inmost being, and penetrate the depths of his heart; and may he be made worthy by your grace of the promises obtained by the most victorious kings, so that in this present age he may reign happily, and may reach their fellowship in the heavenly kingdom. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, who by the power of the cross battled the powers of the air, destroyed Tartarus, overcame the kingdom of the devil, and ascended victoriously to heaven. In his hand are all victory, glory, and power; and with you he lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

### Placing of the Crown

“May the Lord crown you with a crown of glory and justice, with honor and the work of strength, so that, through the ministry of our blessing, with right faith and the manifold fruit of good works, you may reach the crown of the everlasting kingdom, by the gift of him whose kingdom and rule remain throughout the ages of ages. [Col. 0784B] Amen.”

### Delivery of the Sceptre

“Receive the sceptre, the emblem of royal power, namely the straight rod of the kingdom, the rod of strength, by which you may govern yourself well; defend with royal strength the holy Church, that is, the Christian people entrusted to you by God, from the wicked; correct the perverse; and guide the upright with your assistance, so that they may be able to keep to the straight path. Thus may you pass from the temporal kingdom to the eternal kingdom, with the help of him whose kingdom and rule remain without end throughout the ages of ages. Amen.”

### Blessings

“May the Lord God almighty, who said to Moses his servant, ‘Speak to Aaron your brother and to his sons, saying: Thus shall you bless my people, and I shall bless them,’ bless you and guard you. Amen.

“May he make his face shine upon you and have mercy on you. Amen.

“May he turn his face toward you and grant you peace. Amen.

“May he extend the right hand of his blessing and pour out upon you the gift of his reconciliation, and surround you with the happy wall of the protection of his guardianship, through the intercession of the merits of holy Mary and all the saints. Amen.

“May he forgive you all the evils you have committed, grant you the grace and mercy which you humbly ask of him, and free you from every adversity and from all the snares of visible enemies. Amen.

[Col. 0784D] “May he multiply in you the abundance of his blessing and confirm you in the hope of the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

“May he correct your actions, amend your life, regulate your conduct, and lead you to the inheritance of the heavenly paradise. Amen.

“May you be filled with such an intention as will please him forever. Amen.

“May he set his good angels always and everywhere to guard you—angels who go before you, accompany you, and follow after you—and may he free you by his power from sin, from the sword, and from every danger. Amen.

“May he turn your enemies toward the kindness of peace and charity, and make you gracious and beloved to those who hate you. [Col. 0785A] May he also clothe those who persist in pursuing and hating you with salutary confusion. And may everlasting sanctification blossom over you. Amen.

“May the Lord always make you victorious and triumphant over visible and invisible enemies; may he continually pour into your heart both fear and love of his holy name; may he make you steadfast in right faith and good works; and, granting peace in your days, may he lead you with the crown of victory to the everlasting kingdom. Amen.

“And may he who wished to establish you as king over his people grant that you be happy in this present age and a participant in eternal happiness. Amen.

“May he cause you, through his dispensation and your administration, to govern happily for long ages the clergy and people whom he wished, through his assistance, to subject to your rule; so that, obeying the divine commands, free from every adversity, overflowing with every good, and serving your ministry with faithful love, they may enjoy the tranquility of peace in this present age and may deserve, together with you, to obtain fellowship with the eternal citizens. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this.”

[Col. 0785]

## THE ASSEMBLY OF HLUDOWICUS THE YOUNGER AND HLUDOWICUS, SON OF KARLUS, AT FURONIS. (A.D. 878, November 1.)

[Note]

[Col. 0785B] The agreement made between the glorious kings, Hludowicus, son of Emperor Karlus, and likewise Hludowicus, son of King Hludowicus, at the place called Furonis, on the Kalends of November, with the favor and consent of both kings and their common faithful, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 879, indiction II, King Hludowicus, son of Karlus, speaking:

“Just as the kingdom of Lotharius was divided between my father Karlus and your father Hludowicus, we wish it to remain so. And if any of our faithful holds by seizure anything from the kingdom of his equal, let him relinquish it at our command.

“But concerning the kingdom which Emperor Hludowicus possessed in Italy: since no division has yet been made from it, whoever now holds it shall hold it in this way until, God willing, we come together again and, with our common [Col. 0785C] faithful, determine and define what seems to us better and more just concerning it.

“Concerning the kingdom of Italy, since at present no accounting can be made, let everyone know that we have both demanded and do demand our portion of that kingdom, and, with the Lord’s help, shall demand it.”

### Capitularies

The following provisions were established on the next day.

1. Since the firmness of our friendship and union has now, because of certain obstructing circumstances, not been possible until that assembly which we have arranged to attend together, nevertheless, with the Lord’s help, such friendship shall remain between us, from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith, that neither of us shall desire or secretly plot against his equal’s life, kingdom, faithful, or anything that pertains to the safety, prosperity, or honor of the kingdom.

2. If pagans or pseudo-Christians rise up in the kingdom of either of us, each of us shall truly help his equal wherever it is necessary and he is reasonably able, either personally or through his faithful, with counsel and aid, as he can best do.

3. If I outlive you, I shall help your son Hludowicus, who is still a child, and your other sons whom the Lord may grant you, with counsel and aid, as best I can, so that they may peacefully hold their father’s kingdom by hereditary right. If you outlive me, I ask you likewise to help my sons Hludowicus [Col. 0786B] and Karlomannus, and any others whom divine mercy may wish to grant me, with counsel and aid, as best you can, so that they may peacefully hold their father’s kingdom.

4. If any whisperers and slanderers, who envy our peace and do not allow the kingdom to remain tranquil, wish to sow quarrels, disputes, and discord between us, neither of us shall admit or willingly accept this, unless perhaps he wishes to bring the matter to a hearing before both of us and our common faithful. If he does not wish to do so, let him have no association with either of us; rather, let us all jointly reject him as a liar and falsifier who wishes to sow discord between brothers, so that no one thereafter may dare to insert such lies into our ears.

5. Let us jointly, as soon as we can, send our messengers to Karlomannus and Karlus, the glorious kings, to invite them to the assembly which we have arranged for the eighth day before the Ides of February, and to beg them not to delay coming in any way. If they are willing to come as we desire, then, with the Lord’s cooperation, let us join together for the will of God, the salvation of the holy Church, our common honor and advancement, and the safety of the entire Christian people entrusted to us, so that thereafter, in him who is one, we may be one and may desire one thing; and, according to the Apostle, may we all say and do the same, and may there be no schisms among us.

6. If, however, summoned and invited by our entreaty, they delay coming to the aforesaid assembly, let us not fail in any way to come there, as we have arranged, and to join ourselves according to God’s will, unless perhaps an unavoidable necessity arises that makes this wholly impossible. If this should happen, let each of us notify his equal of it in due time; and on that account let our friendship neither diminish nor change, until, at the Lord’s command, it is perfectly confirmed at a suitable time.

7. Wherever ecclesiastical property lies within the kingdom of either of us—whether belonging to bishoprics or abbeys—let the rulers of those churches possess it without any contradiction. And if anyone has done anything wrong there, in whichever kingdom that property lies, let the ruler cause him to render justice there according to law.

8. Since the peace and tranquility of the kingdom are usually disturbed by wandering and irreverent men who live according to tyrannical custom, we wish that, if such a person comes to either of us in order to evade accountability and justice for what he has done, neither of us receive or retain him for any other purpose than to bring him to a proper accounting and due correction. If he evades a proper accounting, let us all jointly pursue him in the kingdom to which he has come until either he is brought to account or he is expelled from the kingdom or destroyed.

9. We wish those who have deservedly lost their property in our kingdom to be judged according to what was found to be the practice in the times of our predecessors. But those who say that they unjustly lost their property shall come into our presence; let judgment be given to them as justice requires, and let them receive back their own.

[Col. 0787]

## THE ELECTION OF BOSO AS KING. (A.D. 879, October 15.)

[Note: [Col. 0787] First published by Paradinus in the *Annals of Burgundy* as the acts of the assembly at Mantaille; Sirmond published it in volume III of the *Councils*, adding the subscriptions of the bishops from Paradinus’s account; and Bouquet republished it in volume IX, p. 304.]

### Election of Boso as King

[Col. 0787B]

When the holy fathers had assembled in the name of the Lord our Savior to hold an assembly at Mantaille [Note: [Col. 0787] Now a village of the territory of Vienne in the Allobroges, situated between Vienne and Valence, called Callice Mantaille. BOUQ.], in order to deliberate on many matters of the Church and to enter the sanctuary of holy concern, many circumstances arising and compelling them by their own consideration, the priestly affection infused from ancient times into the hearts of the Fathers plainly dictated that care should be taken for a person by whose assistance the people might be provided with worthy government, as had customarily been done both in the Old Testament and in the New.

And since for a long time both those very fathers whom divine grace permitted to be called bishops, and the princes and the entire common people, had been deprived of the protection of that person and lacked the assistance of any compassionate support—especially since, after the king had been taken by common death, no one had extended his inward affection toward them through the generosity of charity—they were compelled to great anxiety, because they seemed to be utterly ruined not only inwardly by the invisible enemy, but also openly by visible enemies, even by some of those whom the holy mother Church of Christ herself had brought forth.

Therefore, as they turned the focus of their minds in every direction and, together with the nobles, considered suitable persons for removing this necessity, they found no one willing to respond to their deliberation, since everyone was negligent about undertaking so great a labor for the honor of God, his saints, and Mother Church. All, inflamed with zeal, earnestly besought God, the ruler of all, concerning this distress, asking that he who has singular care for mortals, and whose ordering directs the courses of all ages, grant right counsel and bring forth a clear indication of his counsel.

Finally, he to whom every heart and every will is open, seeing the wearied spirits of great and small, caused a certain consolation to become clear and in a certain manner presented an answer. Indeed, when all were of one mind and, through divine visitation, were indivisibly seeking the same thing, there was brought before their hearts a man who had long ago been the necessary defender and helper in the principate of the lord Karlus; after him, the son of that emperor, seeing his outstanding prudence, had chosen to exalt him—namely, the lord King Ludowicus.

He also shone forth not only in Gaul but in Italy, so that the lord Pope John of Rome, embracing him as a son, praised his sincerity with many encomiums and, on returning to his own see, chose him for his protection.

Therefore, by God’s will, through the votes of the saints, because of the pressing need, and because they had found in him a desirable usefulness and very prudent and far-sighted intelligence, with a common mind, equal vote, and one [Col. 0788C] agreement, they requested and unanimously elected the illustrious prince, Lord Boso, under Christ’s guidance, for this royal office.

Although he initially refused and renounced it out of consideration for so great a labor, setting against it the things belonging to God and his Church, at length he obediently submitted his neck by promising obedience. The man elected was set before God; prayers were offered, and the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ—which had preceded them in willing—was earnestly sought as certainly and perfectly efficacious.

And so that this election might become more certainly known to present and future generations, the subscription of all the bishops makes it clearer than light. Done publicly at Mantaille, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 879, on the Ides of October.

The bishops subscribed: Ottramnus, archbishop of Vienne; Aurelianus, archbishop of Lyon; [Col. 0788D] Teutrannus, archbishop of Tarentaise; Rotbertus, archbishop of Aix; Radbertus, bishop of Valence; Bernarius, bishop of Grenoble; Helias, bishop of Vaison; Hemico, bishop of Die; Adalbertus, bishop of Maurienne; Biraco, bishop of Wapicensis; Eustorgius, bishop of Toulon; Girbaldus, bishop of Chalon; Hieronymus, bishop of Lausanne; Richardus, bishop of [Col. 0789A] Agde [Note: [Col. 0789] Correction: Apt. And certainly at that time Alaricus was bishop of Agde, nor did Boso ever reign in Septimania. BOUQ.]; Guntardus, bishop of Mâcon; Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles; Theodericus, archbishop of Besançon; Aetherius, bishop of Viviers; Leodoinus, bishop of Marseille; Germardus, bishop of Orange; Ratfridus, bishop of Avignon; Walefridus, bishop of Uzès; Edoldus, bishop of Riez.

### Embassy of the Synod to Boso, the Designated King

“The holy synod of Mantaille in the territory of Vienne, assembled in the name of our Lord together with the leading men, under the inspiration of the divine majesty, approaches your prudence, most illustrious prince, with sincere devotion, asking to learn from your most certain reply what sort of ruler you wish to show yourself to all in the principate to which we hope, by divine mercy, to see you raised. [Col. 0789B]

“Specifically, whether you will truly seek the honor of almighty God and love within the Catholic faith, and exalt his Church to the best of your ability; whether, like the good princes who preceded you, whose character you know from writings and reputation, you wish to grant and preserve law, justice, and right for all; whether you will maintain humility, which is the foundation of the virtues, together with patience and a serene, most humble spirit, unprepared to condemn, but stable and firm in all just promises, well prepared and adorned by God’s grace, and made gracious by suitable sobriety.

“May you be accessible to all who offer right advice and intercede for others, seeking rather to benefit than to rule; following the footsteps of holy princes and trampling underfoot anger, savagery, [Col. 0789C] harshness, avarice, greed, indignation, and pride; appearing as a just patrician to your greater and lesser subjects; preferring truth in word and deed; willingly hearing wholesome counsel; avoiding and pursuing the monsters of vices; loving the virtues; and providing each person with protection and guardianship (*mamburgium*) [Note: [Col. 0789] *mundeburdium*.].

“Thus neither this holy synod nor your leading men who share its judgment may now be cursed or slandered concerning you for your goodness, or in the future, nor may your sacred principate, which we believe will benefit us, justly be diminished. Rather, may there be peace and truth, through the suffrages of the saints and by divine grace, for rulers and subjects, for priests and the leading men entrusted to them, when you have agreed to and observed evangelical and apostolic authority together with just human law, so that God may be blessed in every respect and in all things.

“The priestly and lay faithful also ask that your prudence cause each person in your household to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor.”

### Response of Boso, the Elected King, to the Synod

“To the most sacred synod and to all our faithful leading men, Boso, the humble servant of Christ.

“First, I return thanks with heart and mouth to your most sincere devotion, because, although undeserving, I clearly perceive that through your benevolence alone and the unchanging grace of God you embrace me with your innermost affection. Likewise, I perceive that the fervor of your charity divinely desires to advance me to that office, so that my littleness may strive, for an immortal reward, on behalf of my mother, who is the Church of the living God.

“But I, conscious of my condition and fragile creation, judging myself unequal to so great a task, would have refused in every way, unless I had perceived that, by God’s will, you had been given one heart and one soul in a single agreement. Therefore, knowing with certainty that I must obey priests and our friends and faithful who have been inspired by God, I do not resist, nor do I dare resist, your commands.

“As for what you asked—what sort of person I wished to show myself to be when, by God’s mercy, I should undertake the future government—and as you also displayed the standard and instructed me in sacred teaching, I most willingly accept it.

“I embrace the Catholic faith in which I was nourished, which I hold with a most pure heart and profess with a most truthful mouth; for it I am prepared to be spent and to spend myself beyond measure, if this pleases the Lord our God. With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, I shall strive to restore and preserve the privileges of the churches, and I shall administer justice through your common counsel.

“As you have admonished me, I shall preserve and strive to provide for all, with God’s help, law, justice, right, and guardianship. Following the footsteps of the good princes who preceded me, I shall strive to care both for the sacred orders and for you, our faithful, while preserving equity.

“As for my conduct, although I know that I am a sinner above all others, I truly declare that this is my will: to show myself in every respect well behaved among the good and in no respect among the wicked. If, since I am human, I should in spirit go astray against anyone, I shall strive to correct myself according to your counsel.

“In this matter I reverently ask you to honor yourselves in me by appropriately suggesting, according to time and place, whatever you find to be more just and reasonable; for I too, if any one of you should offend against me, shall reasonably await correction after making myself accessible.

“I shall follow evangelical and apostolic authority together with just human law, so that, with him as guide and companion, God may be blessed in every respect and in all things.

“Concerning our household, as you have admonished me, since God dwells among the holy, I shall take care, and shall make every effort to ensure that each person conducts himself properly.

“Therefore, my lords, most holy pontiffs, prelates of the Church of our most high God, and all of you, our faithful, leading men and lesser leading men: trusting in God’s grace and help, through the suffrages of his saints, and because I favor your commands, I ask and beseech you that, through him and with him, with those who piously intercede with him, you assist my need and humility in undertaking so great a labor, and that you also strive to support me with human means and aid as far as you are able.

“If anyone is displeased and holds another view in his heart, I ask him to state it openly and not deceive himself in any way with us.

“Likewise, through the charity with which you burn, I ask you, favoring the common good, solemnly to beseech our Lord God for three days with the peoples entrusted to you, so that, because of my sins or my light-mindedness, he may not allow you or me to err into the deception of his people, but may mercifully reveal his will through this.”

[Col. 0781]

## THE PROMISE OF KARLOMANNUS, SON OF HLUDOWICUS II, KING OF GAUL, AT CARISIAC. (A.D. 882, September 9.)

[Note: [Col. 0791] Baluzius first published this capitulary from the Rivipullensis manuscript, “when, after the death of his brother Ludowicus, he obtained the whole kingdom in the year 882, in the month of September.” The month was missing from the manuscript, but Baluzius, observing that Karlomannus had been summoned by the nobles of his brother, who had died in August, and had remained in his brother’s portion in September, conjectured that he had also been crowned in his brother’s kingdom in that month.]

### Petition of the Bishops to Lord King Karlomannus, When They Commended Themselves to Him at Carisiac on the Fifth Day before the Ides of September, in the Year 882

[Col. 0791B]

“We ask you to pardon us in this matter: that for each one of us and for the churches entrusted to us, according to the first capitulary which most recently at Carisiac your lord grandfather the emperor announced that he would preserve, both on his own behalf and on that of your father, with his faithful, your father’s faithful, and the legates of the Apostolic See consenting, while Gauzlenus was reading it, you preserve canonical privilege and due law and justice, and provide protection, just as a king ought by right to provide these things in his kingdom for each person, both for each bishop and for the church entrusted to him; and just as is contained in the document which you pledged at the monastery of Ferrières before the altar of Saint Peter and confirmed with your own hand together with your brother.”

### The Promise of Lord King Karlomannus in Response to the Petition Above

[Col. 0792B]

“I promise and pledge to you that, for each one of you and for the churches entrusted to you, according to the first capitulary which most recently at Carisiac my lord grandfather the emperor announced that he would preserve, both on his own behalf and on that of my father, with his faithful, my father’s faithful, and the legates of the Apostolic See consenting, while Gauzlenus was reading it, I shall preserve canonical privilege and due law and justice, and, insofar as I am able, with the Lord’s help, I shall provide protection, just as a king ought by right to provide these things in his kingdom for each bishop and the church entrusted to him; and just as is contained in the document which I pledged at the monastery of Ferrières before the altar of Saint Peter.

“In this matter, may you be faithful helpers to me, both in counsel and in aid, according to God and according to the world, just as your good predecessors were to my excellent predecessors, according to your knowledge and ability.”

[Col. 0791]

## THE CAPITULARIES OF KARLOMANNUS AT THE ORCHARD OF COMPIEGNE. (A.D. 883, February 22.)

[Note: [Col. 0791] We reproduce the editions of Sirmond and Baluzius.]

[Note]

[Col. 0791C] The following capitularies were promulgated by the glorious lord King Karlomannus in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 883, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, a Friday, in the first year of his reign in Gaul, in the orchard of the palace at Compiegne, concerning plunder.

1. We have established, with the common counsel of our faithful, that from now on no one shall commit plunder or consent to anyone committing it.

2. That the robbery committed previously be remedied with all diligence, and that the one who committed it suffer a fitting *harmscar* [penalty] for it.

[Col. 0792C] 3. If anyone is found committing a robbery after this assembly and our ban, let the person whose man committed it bring him before us for legal compensation. If he cannot bring him, let him make compensation for him according to the provisions of the laws. Let everyone know that the one who flees justice is outlawed, so that no one may receive him except in order to present him [to justice].

[Col. 0791]

## THE CAPITULARIES OF KARLOMANN AT THE PALACE OF VERNIS. (A.D. 884, March.)

[Note: [Col. 0791] The capitularies were published by Sirmond from manuscript 3b) of Saint Vincent at Metz, and collated by Baluze from Palatine manuscript 3c); we now publish them for the third time with the aid of manuscript 3) of the Royal Library at Paris, among the Latin supplementary manuscripts, no. 75, of the tenth century.]

[Col. 0791D] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Karlomannus, by the grace of God king, to all venerable bishops, abbots, counts, judges, and all faithful men of the holy Church of God and of ours.

When we had assembled at the palace of Vernis in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 884, in the fifth year of our reign, in the second indiction, in the month of March, and some of our faithful were with us, it pleased us that certain statutes of the sacred canons, as well as certain capitularies of our predecessors, should be renewed; for we grievously and painfully bear that, because sins obstruct and the wickedness of perverse men abounds, they have become excessively disregarded and almost abolished—especially those promulgated by the holy fathers against the evil of robbery and plunder, and confirmed by royal authority by most Christian kings.

Indeed, this poison has been so widely diffused and scattered everywhere that all who have been infected and corrupted in body and soul by this most wicked and deadly disease now abuse it almost openly, giving no thought to what Paul says—or rather, what almighty God says through him: “The rapacious shall not possess the kingdom of God.” Nor do they heed what the Apostle says elsewhere [Col. 0793B]: if we devour and consume one another—that is, plunder one another—we shall soon perish.

Thus there is fulfilled in us, indeed through us, what almighty God reproaches us with through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “Each one shall devour the flesh of his own arm,” that is, he shall seize his brother’s property. He devours the flesh of his own arm and drinks the blood of his own arm who takes away his neighbor’s property, by which the flesh ought to have been sustained.

It is no wonder that pagans and foreign nations rule over us and take away our temporal goods, when each person violently takes from his neighbor what he ought to live by. Therefore what almighty God threatens through the prophet Isaiah rightly applies to us: “Woe to you who plunder—will you not yourself be plundered?” We plunder our brothers, and [Col. 0793C] therefore the pagans justly plunder us and our property.

How, then, can we proceed confidently against the enemies of the holy Church of God and our own enemies, when the poor man’s plunder is shut up in our house? Indeed, it is not merely locked away at home; it often happens that certain men set out against the enemy with their bellies full of plunder. And how shall we be able to defeat our enemies when the blood of our brothers drips from our mouths, our hands are full of blood, our arms are weighed down by the burden of misery and robbery, and all the strength of mind and body is weakened?

Our prayers are not received by God, because the cries, wailings, and deep sighs of the poor, orphans, minors, and widows seize and precede our prayers [Col. 0793D], which, burdened with the raw flesh of our brothers, have become hoarse and possess no resonance of virtue.

There are also many who appear to give alms from the very proceeds of robbery, not understanding what Isaiah says of such people: “Whoever offers the Lord an offering from plunder is like one who slaughters a son before his father.”

There are some who seek counsel and penance for murders, adulteries, perjuries, and arson, yet regard the evil of robbery as nothing. They do not understand that however many poor people someone strips and causes to be endangered by hunger and nakedness, so many murders he commits: for he kills his neighbor when he takes from him what he must live by.

And we know, as the Apostle Paul says, that no murderer has life in the kingdom of God, and that God will judge murderers and adulterers. Since, therefore, the rapacious shall not possess the kingdom of God unless they restore what they have taken and moreover perform penance, let us flee this one evil from which so many and such great evils proceed, and let us love our neighbors as ourselves, fulfilling the law which says: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property, nor anything that is his.” Otherwise we shall be able neither to resist our enemies nor to possess the kingdom of God.

1. We therefore wish our palace, following the custom of our predecessors, to be established in the worship of God, royal dignity, the practice of religion, harmonious concord, and the order of peace; and that the peace preserved in that palace by the enactments of our predecessors be promulgated for observance throughout our entire kingdom.

2. We decree, therefore, that all who reside in our palace or come to it from every direction shall live peacefully. If anyone, after the peace has been violated, commits robbery, let him be brought before the palace court by our royal authority and at the command of our envoy, so that, according to what is contained in the capitularies of our predecessors, he may be punished by legal judgment, after making threefold compensation together with the royal ban.

3. If someone without a lord, living either within the palace or near it, does the same, let our envoy approach him and order him, in our name, to come to the palace. If he rashly refuses to come, let him be brought by force into our presence and subjected to the enactments of our predecessors.

If he disregards both us and our envoy, refuses to come to us, and is killed there while defending himself, and one of his relatives or friends wishes to carry a feud from that killing against our faithful men who killed him, we shall make him swear it by compurgation, and we shall assist our faithful men in the matter by royal authority.

4. It has also pleased us and our faithful men that whoever within our kingdom robs or plunders anything shall make threefold compensation for everything, pay the royal ban, and additionally perform public penance for it, as is contained in the capitulary of our predecessors [Col. 0794D].

If he is a peasant or a slave, let him likewise make threefold compensation for everything, or let his lord receive sixty well-delivered blows in his place, and let him additionally perform public penance for it. Its measure shall be determined by the bishop, according to the extent of the deed, because fornications, adulteries, murders, arsons, drunkenness, and many other vices arise from it.

If anyone denies the deed, and he is not convicted, let him clear himself by oath with his own hand [Note: [Col. 0793] “let him conceal himself,” in 3.]. Excepted are our royal vassals, for whom their better men shall provide the oath [Col. 0795A]. This shall be arranged with the utmost diligence in the following manner.

5. The bishop in whose parish someone residing there has committed a plunder shall once, twice, and a third time if necessary, summon him through his priest, by his admonition and canonically, to make compensation [or to make settlement; [Note: [Col. 0795] “or to make settlement” is added by 3c, as well as by Regino and Burchard; it is absent from 3 and 3b.] and to perform penance, so that he may satisfy God and the church whom he has injured.

If he despises and disregards the bishop’s admonition [Note: [Col. 0795] absent in 3.] and most salutary invitation, let him be struck with the pastoral rod—that is, with the sentence of excommunication—so that he may be separated from communion with the holy Church and all Christians until suitable satisfaction and [a fitting [Note: [Col. 0795] added by the same witnesses; absent in 3 and 3b.]] compensation have been made.

The same bishop must make this excommunication known to his lord and to all his fellow bishops, so that they do not receive him until [a fitting [Note: [Col. 0795] added by the same witnesses; absent in 3 and 3b.]] satisfaction has been made.

6. As for those who possess neither benefices nor allod within the parish, but belong to another bishop’s parish, and who, while going to a court or traveling from one place to another, commit robberies and plunder within the parish, it has pleased us that, if they are near enough to the bishop for their plunder to be brought to his notice before they leave his parish, he should send a vigorous and prudent priest who, in his place, shall reasonably summon them to make compensation.

The foregoing procedure for settlement and compensation shall be observed if, once summoned, they refuse to come. But if they arrogantly despise the bishop’s summons and admonition, let them be struck with the same sentence of excommunication as those who possess property or benefices within the parish; and, in addition, let them be excommunicated so that they may not leave the parish before fulfilling the provisions stated above.

Their excommunication must be reported to their lord and to their own bishop, so that they do not receive them before they return to the place where they committed the robbery and make full compensation there.

7. Since bishops, who are occupied with the needs of ourselves, of themselves, and with the common needs of the Church and the entire kingdom, are unable by themselves to oversee everything committed within the boundaries of their parishes [Note: [Col. 0795] “for themselves,” 3b; S.], we decree that whenever bishops depart from their own city, each shall leave in his city such assistants as will carry out all these matters there with the greatest prudence, and so that the poor redeemed by Christ’s blood may always find someone present in the city from whom they can receive an answer and consolation.

In the districts and villages far removed from the city, each bishop shall appoint respected and cautious priests, tempered by moral prudence [Note: [Col. 0795] “of morals” is added by 3c and Regino; absent from 3 and 3b.] [Col. 0796A], who shall modestly carry out the provisions stated above [“modestly” is added in brackets] in his place, and to whom other, younger, and less cautious priests may refer their cases.

8. It has pleased us [and our faithful men [Note: [Col. 0795] “and our faithful men” is added by 3c and Regino; absent from 3 and 3b.]], for the common good and pressing necessity, that no bishop should take offense if another bishop excommunicates one of his parishioners for such a matter of plunder.

9. Since, for the complete eradication and removal of so great an evil [“and removal” is found in brackets in one copy, 3c] and the planting [and establishment] of so great a good, episcopal authority needs to be assisted by judicial power, it has pleased us and our faithful men jointly that the royal envoys should faithfully assist them in their localities in this matter.

Let the count order his viscount, his [vicars and] centenarii, and his other public officials, as well as the Frankish men trained in the principles of secular law, to assist from now on, for love of almighty God, for the peace of the holy Church, and for our fidelity, as best they can [both by themselves and together with the ministers of the Church [Note: [Col. 0795D] The words in brackets here and below occur in one copy, 3c.]], whenever the bishops, their ministers, or even the poor themselves appeal to them [on this matter]. Thus the ministers of the Church shall have the authority of their bishop, and the count’s ministers shall have our authority and that of their count.

10. We wish that if anyone, living in a county or traveling through it, rashly disregards episcopal or [also royal authority [Note: [Col. 0795] “also royal authority,” 3c.]] authority as worthless, refuses to make legal compensation for something he has unjustly taken, and, while resisting, is killed there [Col. 0796C], none of our faithful men who killed him shall incur a feud on that account or make any compensation for his death.

If one of his relatives [or friends] wishes to carry a feud from the killing, we shall make him swear it by compurgation, and we shall assist our faithful men in the matter by royal authority.

11. Concerning our royal vassals also, we order that if any one of them has carried out a raid, the count under whose authority he falls shall summon him to make compensation. If he refuses to heed the count or his envoy, he shall be compelled by force to make compensation, as the law directs and as is expressly contained in the capitularies of the [kings who were] our predecessors, in the very place where the raid was committed.

If he declares that he wishes to be summoned before our presence rather than before the count [Col. 0796D], he shall be permitted to come before us through credible sureties or on the oath of a better man, so that the matter may there receive its conclusion.

For we grant our royal vassals this privilege: they are not to swear an oath with their own hands like the rest, but their better and more credible man must not delay in performing it [Col. 0797A].

If they disregard what we have stated above, refuse in any way to make compensation, and, remaining in contempt, are killed there, we shall never hold anger against those who kill them.

If one of their relatives [or friends] wishes to carry a feud from the killing, [we shall make him swear it by compurgation, as stated above, and] we shall assist him in the matter by our royal authority [Note: [Col. 0797] “our voice” has been supplied from 3.]. If they say that the count did not proceed against them according to law but did so because of some [Note: [Col. 0797] 3 has “thus”; Baluze has “some.”] anger [or envy] that he previously held against them, [and did this], the count shall satisfy them before us [according to what pleases us], since it was done for no other reason than robbery.

12. To remove every opportunity for robbery, we wish [Col. 0797B] priests, who ought to display a good example of [charity] to everyone, to be hospitable, as the Apostle says: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.” [Col. 0798A] Let them provide this [Note: [Col. 0798] 3c has “and hospitality.”] to travelers, because through that hospitality [Note: [Col. 0798] 3c has “through hospitality.”] some have pleased God by receiving angels as guests [Note: [Col. 0797] 3c has “received” instead of “welcomed as guests.”].

13. It has pleased us [and our faithful men] that priests admonish their parishioners to be hospitable themselves and to deny lodging to no traveler.

To remove every opportunity for robbery, let them sell nothing to travelers at a higher price [Note: [Col. 0797] 3c and Regino read “let them sell” instead of “let them sell at a higher price.”] than they receive in the market [Note: [Col. 0798] 3c and Regino read “unless at the price at which they can sell in the market.”]. If they wish to sell at a higher price, let the travelers report this to the priest, and, at his command, let them sell to them humanely.

14. We wish priests and the count’s ministers to order the villagers not to make the levy commonly called a *gelda* [Note: [Col. 0797] 3 corrects *geldeam* to *geldam.] against those who have committed a robbery. Instead, let them refer their case to the priest who has been sent by the bishop [Col. 0798B], and to those who in those places serve as the count’s ministers in this matter, so that everything may be corrected prudently and reasonably.

[Col. 0797]

## THE ELECTION OF KING ODO. (A.D. 888, December, or 889, January.)

[Note: [Col. 0797] Of his acts there survives only the king’s promise, published by Baluze, vol. II, p. 291, under the title: “The capitulary of King Odo when he was anointed by Walter, archbishop of Sens, in the year 888.”]

[Col. 0797B] I promise and grant to each of you and to the churches entrusted to you that I shall preserve canonical privilege, due law, and justice, and that I shall provide, insofar as God grants me the ability, according to my office, protection against the plunderers and oppressors of your churches [Col. 0797C] and of the property belonging to them.

I shall preserve ecclesiastical right and canonical law for you in such a way, and I shall permit the property of your churches, whether bestowed by kings or emperors or by other faithful servants of God, to remain whole and immune, without any dishonor, which your churches now lawfully and legally retain.

I shall strive to increase and exalt them according to the due service of each, insofar as God shall reasonably grant me knowledge and ability and time shall allow, just as my predecessors, who observed this well and reasonably, did for your predecessors [Col. 0798B].

I shall restore, with the help of divine mercy, whatever has previously been corrupted by evil intent to a better and original condition, with the counsel and assistance of you and my other faithful men [Col. 0798C], so that you may be faithful helpers to me, before God and in this world, in counsel and assistance, just as your good predecessors were to my better predecessors, according to their knowledge and ability.

Confirmation of King Odo.

[Col. 0797]

## THE ELECTION OF KING WIDO. (At the end of A.D. 888 or the beginning of 889.)

[Note: [Col. 0797] Muratori published his acts from a contemporary parchment preserved in the celebrated monastery of Bobbio, first in *SS. Ital.*, vol. II, pp. 416 ff., and then, with several readings corrected, in *Antiquities of Italy*, vol. I. According to the few charters of Wido that survive and the annals of his time, the date falls either in the final months of 888 or in January or the first days of February, before the twenty-first day of that month in 889.]

### CAPITULARIES OF THE ELECTION

[Col. 0797D]

After the dreadful wars and most heinous disasters that befell this province because of the deserts of our crimes, while our illustrious king and lord Wido was arranging the laws of this kingdom in tranquility and its enemies had been quieted, we humble bishops, gathered at the palace of Ticinum from different parts of Pavia, assembled in a single college with the assent of that same ruler, for the recovery of our churches and the salvation of all Christianity, which had already almost inclined toward destruction and desolation [Col. 0798D].

Our purpose was that those through whom murders, sacrileges, robberies, and other crimes had been committed should, after being withdrawn from their evil undertaking, be imposed a fitting penance for obtaining salvation through true confession, with God’s help; and, so that such wickedness might not grow further or gain strength, we resolved that it should be restrained by pastoral oversight and royal assistance.

[Col. 0799A] 1. First, we pray, desire, and work that our holy mother, the Roman Church, be held, maintained, and perpetually preserved unharmed in her status and honor, with all her privileges and authorities, just as she has been exalted by ancient and modern emperors and kings.

For it is wicked that she, who is the head of the whole body of the Church and the refuge and relief of the weak, should be rashly repelled or harassed by anyone, especially since her health is the welfare of all of us.
