The supreme pontiff himself must always be venerated by all rulers and worshipers of the Christian name with worthy honor and must surpass them in due reverence.

2. Let the churches of each bishop, with their privileges and possessions, both within and outside, remain undisturbed and unimpaired, without any diminution of their rights or unjust harassment by wicked men, as their charters granted by kings and emperors provide.

Let their rectors freely exercise episcopal authority, both in arranging ecclesiastical affairs and in restraining all violators of God’s law.

3. We also decree that no violence or burden of a new condition be imposed either in bishoprics, abbeys, hospitals, or any places consecrated to God, but that, according to ancient custom, all should remain perpetually in their own status and privilege.

4. Let every priest and minister of Christ [Col. 0799C] be venerated with fitting honor and reverence in his own order, and, together with all ecclesiastical property and dependents belonging to him, remain peacefully and securely under the authority of his own bishop, with ecclesiastical discipline preserved.

5. Let the common people and all the sons of the Church freely use their own laws. Nothing beyond what the laws prescribe shall be exacted from them by public authority, nor shall they be violently oppressed.

If this is done, let it be legally corrected by the count of that place, if he thereafter wishes to retain his office. If he himself neglects or commits it, or consents to one who commits it [Note: [Col. 0799] “or gives approval to the one committing it,” SS.], let him be regarded as excommunicated by the bishop of the place until [Note: [Col. 0799] absent in SS.; present in *Antiquities*.] suitable satisfaction has been made.

6. Let the palace officials who remain in royal service serve the king peacefully and without plunder, content with their stipends.

7. Those who assemble from different regions at the time of a court session shall commit no robbery while passing through villages or cities, but shall purchase what they need at a fitting price according to ancient custom.

8. Whoever, coming from foreign provinces, presumes to commit plunder and robbery within this kingdom: let those with whom they reside either bring them before the court or make compensation for them, and let them no longer dare to defend such enterprises by their authority. If they do so, let them be regarded as excommunicated until they repent.

9. Moreover, since the glorious King Wido has deigned to promise us that he will preserve the capitularies set out above, which were composed in a matter of no small necessity, and the provisions contained in them, taking thought, under divine inspiration, for his salvation and ours, as he already demonstrates by clear indications, it has therefore pleased all of us to elect him as king, lord, and defender.

Thus, from now on and thereafter, while he governs us according to the royal office, each of us shall, in his own order, be obedient and, as far as possible, an assistant to him for his salvation and that of his kingdom [Col. 0800B].

### DECREE OF THE ELECTION

After the death of the lord Charles, glorious emperor and our lord, whose memory is worthy of remembrance, no tongue can recount and no pen can explain how many and how great dangers have come upon this Italian kingdom up to the present time.

Finally, in those very days, as though summoned by a sure signal, certain men appeared who, for the sake of this kingdom, secretly and deceitfully drew us in, entangling us by various threats and persuasions so that, willingly or unwillingly, we might assent to them [Note: [Col. 0799] *inlectos* in *Antiquities*; *inretitos* in SS.].

But when the illustrious prince Wido appeared, they had already twice fled and vanished like smoke, leaving us in uncertainty like sheep without a shepherd. We therefore considered it necessary to assemble at Pavia in the royal palace for mutual discussion.

There, carefully considering the common salvation and condition of this kingdom, we resolved with one mind and one judgment to elect the aforesaid magnanimous prince Wido as our king and lord, to protect and govern us royally, and, by God’s mercy, to set him at the summit of the kingdom.

We did so because that magnificent king, protected, as we believe, by divine aid, had powerfully triumphed over his enemies and wisely attributed this not to his own strength [Note: [Col. 0799] SS. reads “his own virtue”] but wholly to the providence of divine mercy [Note: [Col. 0799] SS. reads “the mercy of God”].

Moreover, he professed before God that he loved and exalted the holy Roman Church from his heart, observed ecclesiastical rights in all things, granted each person under his rule his own laws, would utterly root out robberies from his kingdom, and wished to restore and preserve peace [Col. 0800D].

For these and many other signs of his good will, we admitted him, as stated above, to the government of this kingdom, adhered to him with all the strength of our minds, and, by equal consent, appointed him from this time forward and thereafter as our most pious lord and most excellent king.

[Col. 0801]

## THE LAWS OF KING WIDO. (A.D. 889, May 1.)

[Note: [Col. 0801] We have reviewed the capitularies published in the editions of the Lombard laws, using the Ambrosian, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Este manuscripts, and have assigned them to their proper year.]

[NOTA.]

[Col. 0801A] Here begin [Note: [Col. 0801] This inscription occurs only in the Ambrosian and London manuscripts. The Vienna, Veronese, and Este manuscripts instead have: “The royal proclamation of Gido commands these things to good men.” Goldastus has: “Given at Pavia on the Kalends of May, in the first year of our empire.”] the capitularies which the lord Wido, emperor, added on the Kalends of May in the city of Ticinum, in the first year of his empire, in the seventh indiction [Note: [Col. 0801] A has “fourth.”].

1. It pleased us also to decree with the greatest urgency [Note: [Col. 0801] A. reads “with the greatest urgency also.”] that bishops and counts should be united in their parishes and counties for peace and the salvation of all the people living in their jurisdictions and honors [Note: [Col. 0801] A. omits “in their honors”; V. and Vn. read “in their own honors.”], so that they permit no robber, ravager, or incestuous person to remain in their seats or granted jurisdictions.

If they learn [Note: [Col. 0801] L. reads “if they understand that”] that foreigners intend or ought to pass through their borders from any direction for the devastation of this kingdom, let them send against them envoys bearing a summons, so that they may pass peacefully through their land without plunder.

Let them arrange for what is necessary to be sold to the foreigners, not at a higher price [Note: [Col. 0801] L. reads “not more expensively”], but according to the practice and custom of the land.

If they refuse to comply but commit plunder and robbery, whatever they have robbed from another, let them be compelled by the bishop and count of that place to make legal compensation together with our ban.

If they refuse to carry this out, let them immediately be excommunicated by the bishop.

Afterward, if it happens that the count of the place and the people of the land come against those robbers, hinder them, and they are killed, we decree that no feud shall grow from this, nor shall compensation ever be demanded for those who fall there.

If the count of that place neglects to fulfill this, let him be deprived of his own office.

If it is necessary for the count to call upon a neighboring count for assistance, and that man withdraws himself [Note: [Col. 0801] V. and Vn. read “a neighboring count”], let him likewise be deprived of his office and additionally pay thirty pounds of silver to the count [Note: [Col. 0801] The text of A. omits this; an interlinear gloss reads: “to the count to whom he denied assistance, that is, to the one.”].

[Col. 0801C] 2. Therefore, whoever among the lay order—whether free men or slaves—residing in the county, if warned by his own count or by the public authority, that is, by those who administer public affairs, withdraws from assisting his own count and does not help him within that county against invading robbers, shall, if free, make compensation from his movable property to the amount of one third; slaves, however, shall receive sixty blows—provided it has been proved that this was announced to them.

3. No count, his deputy appointed in his place [Note: [Col. 0801] V., Vn., and E. omit this phrase; L. deletes it.], or *sculdasius* shall exact anything by force from his *arimanni*, beyond what is established by the laws.

Nor shall he, by his own force, lodge at the dwelling of his *arimannus* [Note: [Col. 0801] A. reads “enlarge”; an interlinear Ambrosian gloss explains: “that is, provide lodging.” *Applicare* means “to turn aside” or “to lodge”], hold a court, or commit any violence.

If any of the aforesaid public officials makes this void, let him be deprived of his office or ministry and make legal compensation [Note: [Col. 0801] V., Vn., and E. read “compensate for what he did to him.”].

4. If, on the emperor’s command, the count of the place orders his *arimanni* to hasten in a hostile manner to the defense of their homeland, either personally or through his envoy, and any of them remains behind—except those whom the bishop chooses to retain because of necessity or whom the count wishes to release, unless someone is detained by illness or other impediments contained in the laws—let him pay his *widrigild*.

No count or public official [Note: [Col. 0801] I have supplied the word “official”; V., Vn., and E. use another correction.] shall have authority to exact this, except together with an envoy from the emperor’s palace.

5. Concerning charters, we forbid anyone presumptuously to invade another’s property on the basis of a document made by someone who is known to have invaded it without possessing lawful vesture [Note: [Col. 0801] A London gloss explains: “that is, the man himself makes that charter.”].

If someone has become an acquirer, let him not presume to invade the property of another, whether of a church or of any free man, before the author of the charter has claimed it by lawful and judicial determination; only then shall he have the free power to hand it over to whomever he wishes.

If anyone invades those possessions without legal authority, let him not only lose the possessions themselves [Note: [Col. 0801] L. omits “themselves.”], but also pay our ban.

[Col. 0802C] 6. [Note: [Col. 0801] This chapter is absent in Herold.] Concerning charters and any writings that certain persons call false, we decree that, if the notary and the witnesses are still alive, the same notary, together with twelve lawful oath-helpers and the witnesses whose names are written in that charter, shall establish that charter as genuine [Note: [Col. 0801] V. and Vn. add “and valid.”].

Likewise, the presenter of the charter, with twelve oath-helpers, may lawfully swear and establish the charter as genuine and valid.

The claimant, however, must first swear that, to his knowledge, he seeks nothing other than what is wholly true and just.

If the notary withdraws and is entirely unable to authenticate the charter written in his name [Col. 0803A] [Note: [Col. 0803] L. reads “the charter subscribed with his signature”], no redemption shall be granted to him, but he shall lose his own hand; and the presenter of the charter, after losing the property, shall pay his *widrigild* [Note: [Col. 0803] E. adds: “And if the presenter has no relatives, he nevertheless must not lose his case, but shall swear with the other oath-helpers. If the notary has never previously written a charter and this is his first, comparison shall also be made with another writing of his, as it is read in the *Novels*. The same is understood of a charter of freedom, and if the presenter does not pay the *widrigild*.”].

If the notary is unavailable [Note: [Col. 0803] L. reads “But if the notary…”] and the witnesses survive, the presenter of the charter, together with those witnesses and twelve oath-helpers—six of his relatives, including himself as the seventh, and five other suitable men—after first producing two other charters copied by the same notary and compared by handwriting [Note: [Col. 0803] A. reads “of a collection”; L. reads “of a comparison”], shall establish by oath that the third charter is genuine and valid [Note: [Col. 0803] E. adds: “If the notary is absent or prevented from appearing in court for any reason, let the presenter bring what he must produce; this is also to be done if the notary is dead.”].

[Note: [Col. 0803] At the end of this chapter, manuscripts V. and Vn., and at the end of the ninth chapter in the London manuscript, write the substance of this chapter as a legal heading: “Concerning charters which certain persons call false, we establish that, if the witnesses are dead and the notary survives, he shall establish the charter as genuine and valid with twelve swearers.” Manuscripts V. and Vn. read: “so that … he shall establish it; let him swear.”]

7. We further wish and decree that if any free man [Note: [Col. 0803] V., Vn., and E. read “any Lombard free man”] gives his lawful wife, while he lives [Note: [Col. 0803] that is, while the wife lives, L.], his property in writing for usufruct, and has two or more children, and one or two of them die leaving sons [Note: [Col. 0803] V., Vn., and E. read “legitimate sons”] or daughters, the deceased children shall divide equally with their paternal uncles the property which the aforesaid wife holds in usufruct, just as the rest of the inheritance, and shall likewise divide the usufruct [Note: [Col. 0803] L., V., Vn., and E. read “the usufruct itself.”].

8. We also grant that, just as Lombard women [Note: [Col. 0803] V., Vn., and E. read “Lombard women”] can sell and give their property together with their husbands, so they may also exchange it and make their household free.

9. If anyone brings threats or even insults against our judges while they are sitting in judgment, and dishonors them shamefully by word or deed, let him pay the *widrigild* to the one whom he has injured.

But if one of those judges, in connection with that judgment itself, renders a false judgment, or kills any man because of that litigation and cause [Note: [Col. 0803] L. reads “or another cause”], let him pay fifty pounds of the finest gold: half first to the heirs of the slain judge and the other half to our treasury.

The Ambrosian Codex adds in the margin:

“If a Lombard woman has a husband, she cannot make any instrument concerning inheritance without consulting her relatives; but if she has no husband, she may make one with the consent of her *munduald*, without consulting her relatives; and if she is Roman and has no husband, she may make one alone.”

[Col. 0803]

# Election of Louis, King of Arles  
*(Year 890, toward the end of August.)*

[Note: [Col. 0803] His acts were first published in the *Annals of Burgundy* by Paradinus, then reprinted by Anesius, vol. II, p. 530, and Bouquet, vol. IX, p. 315. That it was promulgated in the middle or toward the end of August is established by the indiction and by a diploma of Louis for Isaac, bishop of Grenoble, dated 11 August 894, indiction XII, in the fourth year of his reign, published in Bouquet, vol. IX, p. 675.]

[Col. 0803C] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 890, indiction VIII, the religious and most venerable Bernoinus, archbishop of the holy see of Vienne, having approached the Apostolic See on account of certain necessities of his own church and of the kingdom as a whole, reported, with the advice of the apostolic lord himself, whose care and solicitude extend to all the churches, and in a manner worthy of his account, how this kingdom, after the death of the most glorious emperor Charles, having for some time existed without a king and ruler, was being grievously afflicted on every side—not only by its own inhabitants, whom no rod of authority restrained, but also by pagans. For on one side the Northmen persisted in utterly devastating everything, while on the other the Saracens, laying waste Provence, were reducing the land to desolation.

[Col. 0803D] After hearing these and other matters of this kind from him, the reverend lord Stephen, the apostolic bishop, was moved even to tears. By letters and words addressed generally to all the archbishops and other venerable bishops of Cisalpine Gaul, he exhorted them with his most holy admonition [Col. 0804C] that, unanimously and harmoniously consenting in Louis, nephew of the late glorious emperor Louis, they should establish him as king over the people of God.

Therefore, when we had carefully learned that the assent of our holy catholic and apostolic mother favored this election, we assembled together in the city of Valence: namely, the lord Aurelianus, archbishop of the see of Lyons; the lord Rostagnus, archbishop of the city of Arles; the venerable Arnaldus, archbishop of Embrun; and Bernoinus himself, archbishop of Vienne. From his report we reverently received the will of the apostolic lord, and, together with several other fellow bishops, we deliberated and investigated, seeking according to God’s will to determine whether, in accordance with the admonitions of the apostolic lord, whose letters were in our hands, we ought rightly and reasonably to establish this man as king over us.

The assent of all was therefore that no one ought more properly to become king than he who, sprung from imperial lineage, was already maturing as a boy of good character. Although his age seemed insufficient to restrain the savagery of the barbarians [Col. 0805A], nevertheless, with the counsel and courage of the noble princes of this kingdom, whose number is not small, they would, with God’s help, be suppressed.

This would be administered most suitably according to the fear of God, especially with the support of the illustrious Richard, duke and outstanding prince, and indeed of the most glorious lady Queen Ermengard, endowed with the exceptionally keen and profound wisdom given her by God for the welfare of the kingdom, together with the worthy exhortation of the bishops mentioned above and the counsel of the nobles of the entire kingdom.

Finally, relying upon and strengthened by so great a confidence, by God’s will, as we believe, we elected the aforementioned Louis, son of the most excellent King Boso, and decreed that he should be anointed king [Col. 0806A]. We judged him worthy of this, since the most distinguished emperor Charles had already granted him royal dignity; and Arnulf, who succeeded him, through his scepter and through his most discerning envoys—namely, Bishop Reoculfus and Count Bertaldus—has shown himself in every respect to be a supporter and promoter of the kingdom.

Supported by such great and such authoritative license, we all came by common agreement to the aforesaid city and decreed that this royal document should be drawn up. We further ratified it with our own hands, desiring that it should endure happily for all time, and each of us subscribed it.

[Note: [Col. 0805] The subscriptions are lacking.]

[Col. 0805]

# Council of Arnulf at Tribur  
*(Year 895, May.)*

[Note: [Col. 0805] From the acts of the Council of Tribur, first published in 1524 by Cochlaeus from the Brixen manuscript, we have judged that only the general letter, the king’s constitution concerning excommunicated persons, preserved as chapter 3, and the subscriptions of the bishops—corrected with the aid of the Imperial Viennese manuscript among the canon-law books, no. 99, parchment, eleventh century—should be presented.]

[Col. 0805B] Since it is evident to all who treat of divine law that, after the Gospels and the clear streams of the New Testament, the canons established by the blessed apostles and by the holy fathers assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia, as well as the decrees of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See of Rome, have sufficiently confronted, resisted, and opposed heretics, schismatics, and all who attack the true faith; nevertheless, the ancient serpent, called the devil and Satan, the enemy of the human race, does not cease to mix the new poisons of his malice into the sweet cup of the Holy Spirit and to sow the weeds of his depravity and profane iniquity among the good seed of the holy Gospel.

As it is written in Matthew, when weeds had been inserted into the good crop: “An enemy has done this.” And concerning his followers, under the appearance of scales, it is said in Job: “One is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them.” Therefore it is necessary to oppose his most perverse machinations and the attacks of his followers by authentic authority, and to set against them a new model of true affirmation.

For this reason, the King of kings, whose kingdom, as the Psalmist sings, is the kingdom of all ages, has deigned to place before all the orders of ecclesiastical rank, as well as the dignities of secular power, the new prince Arnulf as king in a peaceful order of perpetual tranquility.

He wished to inflame his heart with the ardor of the Holy Spirit and kindle it with zeal for divine love, so that the whole world might know that he had been chosen not by man, nor through man, but by the Lord himself.

For that most wise king, considering with the insight of his profound mind the abundant grace of the Holy Spirit within him—for those whom the Spirit fills with ardor, he also makes speak of himself—came in the year of the incarnation of Jesus Christ our Lord 895, in the eighth year of his reign, indiction XIII, in the month of May, prompted by that same Holy Spirit and with the counsel of his leading men, to the royal estate called Tribur, situated in the land of the Franks [Col. 0806B], together with the bishops written below, abbots, counts, and all the princes of his kingdom, as well as countless throngs of ecclesiastical and secular persons who had assembled.

This was so that, with tireless perseverance, divine and human matters might be discussed and emerging evils suppressed, so that the holy Church of God might more freely enjoy her honor.

When the most wise king had decided that the sacred council should continue, it pleased him and the entire clergy that, after a three-day fast, they should invite by litanies and prayers the assistance promised from heaven: just as the Savior himself, ascending into heaven, promised his disciples, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.” Thus future councils might begin in him and end through him, who is the beginning and the end and the fulfillment of the law, as the Apostle says in writing to the Romans: “For Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes.”

When this had been completed, he proceeded to the palace and sat upon the royal throne. Clothed in the most splendid garment, woven by wisdom, he was filled with prudence, uplifted by power, and surrounded by a multitude appropriate to his greatness. In practical terms he discussed the condition of the kingdom; in theoretical terms, the order and stability of the churches of Christ; and how the good might live in peace and the wicked might not sin with impunity.

Meanwhile, after the common prayers and supplications had been completed, the sacred assembly of bishops in the basilica of the aforesaid estate, most honorably vested and supported by episcopal seats, their minds serene and endowed with prudence, entered the holy synodal conference [Col. 0806D].

Among the matters they were to discuss, divine and human alike, by common vote and equal agreement they sent knowledgeable and suitable mediators from the college of holy priests to the aforesaid pious king. They asked with what zeal and what kindness, according to the wisdom and ability granted him by God, he would deign to defend the Church of Christ—which had been entrusted to him through royal power and to them through priestly eminence—and to enlarge and exalt their ministry [Col. 0807A].

They set before him the proper excellence of a king: that mercy and moderation should surpass all else; that he should not judge according to persons; and that, in accordance with Solomon, he should love justice, judgment, and equity.

They further added examples from the sacred writings, in which Wisdom, instructing her pupils trained through their labors, says:

“Counsel is mine, and equity; mine is prudence, mine is strength. Through me kings reign, and legislators decree what is just; through me princes rule, and the powerful decree justice.”

And again:

“A king who judges in truth—his throne shall be established forever.”

They also placed before him the instructions of Bishop Martin to King Miron, by which he instructed him, in an orderly and rational manner, in uprightness of life and piety of conduct, saying:

“It is characteristic of the prudent to examine counsels”; and he added: “If your mind is prudent, let it be apportioned among three times. Set the present in order, foresee the future, remember the past. And let your speech not be empty, but let it either persuade, advise, console, or command.”

While they were expounding theology to the king as though from above, he, revealing the secret of his mystery from the august seat of his mind—for, as Wisdom says, “The heart of kings is unsearchable”—burst forth in these words:

“O shepherds of the churches of Christ, and brightest lights of the world, carry out the pastoral care entrusted to you. And, in accordance with the Apostle, ‘Be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and instruction,’ so that through vigilant care and constant admonition you may deserve to lead the sheep of Christ into the folds of eternal life.

“You have in me a most determined warrior against all who oppose the Church of Christ and resist your priestly ministry. For, as the Apostle wrote to the Romans, ‘In all these things we conquer through him who loved us.’ And again: ‘If God is for us, who is against us?’

“For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither things present nor things to come, nor any creature will be able to separate us from the love of God and from holy unanimity, most blessed fathers.”

The blessed priests who had been sent rejoiced. After certain nobles had been dispatched from the king’s throne to the holy synod on a mission of justice and true unanimity, they returned to those who had sent them [Col. 0807D].

They proceeded through the assembly, entered the sacred gathering, and gladdened the church assembled there with their consoling reply. Then they fell silent and began quietly to await what they would do next.

The most reverend fathers then rose from their seats, together with the clergy standing by. Crying out three and four times and beseeching the divine majesty, they said: “Hear, O Christ: life to the great king Arnulf!”

When the bells sounded and all sang together, they praised and glorified Jesus Christ, who comforts through his servants and who had deigned, for the honor of his name, to grant his holy Church so pious and gentle a comforter and so vigorous a helper.

After their prayers to the divine majesty had been completed, they bowed before the envoys of the pious ruler who were standing there, expressed their gratitude, and offered the great prince the praises due to him. Then they sat down in proper order and, with the Holy Spirit preceding them, subscribed certain chapters of greatest necessity from the canonical constitutions.

They corrected errors, cut away what was superfluous, and brought what was right into the narrow royal way.

After this, the most prudent king took part in the sacred mysteries of divine religion, and the holy fathers in the secret chambers of the palace. There was harmony in everything, to the praise of Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be praise and glory for endless ages of ages . . . .

## Chapter 3

Therefore, since the care of the kingdom and the solicitude of the churches of Christ have been entrusted to us, we cannot rightly govern and administer the kingdom and empire according to ecclesiastical law unless we persecute with the zeal of faith those who disturb the Church of Christ, which, as the Apostle says, has neither spot nor wrinkle.

Concerning this, King David bears witness: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away because of your enemies? With perfect hatred I hate them; they have become enemies to me.”

And when the Gospel was being read, we heard: “If he does not hear you, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector.” And elsewhere: “He who strikes down the wicked because they are wicked is the minister of the Lord.”

Therefore, not displaying power but exercising justice, we command and by our authority enjoin all the counts of our kingdom that, after such persons have been struck by the bishops with the anathema of excommunication, yet have not been inclined to repent, they are to be seized by those counts and brought before us [Col. 0808C], so that those who do not fear divine judgments may be struck by a human sentence.

Hence it was said by a certain wise man: “A king who sits upon the throne of judgment scatters all evil with his gaze.”

If they should prove so rebellious that they attempt to resist those who seize them, and if they are killed in such recklessness, then, by the judgment of the bishops, no penance is to be imposed upon their killers; and by our command no composition in weregeld is to be exacted from them.

Their relatives and kinsmen, moreover, are to be bound by oath not to avenge them, but to maintain peace and harmony with them . . . .

In this holy and universal council, with the pious prince Arnulf, most glorious king, presiding over and assisting it, the holy fathers and venerable shepherds of the churches who had assembled sat together. What they promulgated in the catholic faith they confirmed by a common profession and subscribed unanimously.

Hattho, archbishop of the holy church of Mainz: I have subscribed.

Herimannus, archbishop of the holy church of Agrippina, also called Cologne: I have subscribed.

Ratbotus, archbishop of the church of Trier: I have subscribed.

Waldo, bishop of the church of Freising: I have subscribed.

Erchanbaldus, bishop of the church of Eichstätt: I have subscribed.

Tuto, bishop of Regensburg.

Adalpero, bishop of Augsburg.

Salomon, bishop of Constance.

Theodulfus, bishop of Chur.

Iringus, bishop of Basel.

Baldrammus, bishop of Strasbourg.

[Col. 0809A] Cothethancus, bishop of Speyer.

Theotelaus, bishop of Worms.

Adalgarius, bishop of Bremen [Note: [Col. 0809] *brumensis* in manuscript C.].

Dado, bishop of Verdun.

Wigbertus, bishop of Hildesheim.

Ruodulfus, bishop of Würzburg.

Sigimundus, bishop of Halberstadt [Note: [Col. 0809] *haluarastanensis* in manuscript C.].

Ruodbertus, bishop of Metz.

Druogo, bishop of Minden.

Biso, bishop of Paderborn.

Engilmarus, bishop of Osnabrück.

[Col. 0809]

# Coronation of Emperor Arnulf  
*(Year 896, April 18.)*

[Note: [Col. 0809] Since Arnulf remained in Rome for only fifteen days, our Boehmer observed in the *Regesta of the Carolingians* that the date must have been either 18 or 25 April. I favor the former, because the *Annals of Fulda* immediately report the city’s capture and also preserve the formula of the oath sworn by the Romans.]

## Oath of the Romans

[Col. 0809B]

I swear by all these mysteries of God that, without prejudice to my honor, law, and loyalty to the lord Pope Formosus, I am and shall be faithful every day of my life to Emperor Arnulf, and that I shall never join myself to anyone in treachery against him.

I shall never provide assistance for secular honor to Lambert, son of Agiltrude, or to his mother herself; and I shall not hand over this city of Rome to Lambert himself, to his mother Agiltrude, or to their men by any device or stratagem.

[Col. 0809]

# Assembly of Emperor Lambert at Ravenna  
*(Year 898, October?)*

[Note: [Col. 0809] The acts of this assembly, held in the presence of Pope John IX, were first published by Baronius from a copy made by Muretus from the manuscript of Antonio Agostino, and he assigned them to the year 904. Since this seemed inappropriate, as Lambert was by then no longer alive, Goldast, in the third volume of his *Constitutions*, assigned the chapters promulgated by the emperor to Berengar.

Baluzius, however, warned in the preface to the *Capitularies*, vol. I, p. 15, that this industrious man had been mistaken in the matter. He stated that excerpts were preserved in an old manuscript of the Thuane Library, bearing the heading: “Likewise, from the Roman laws promulgated by the lord Lambert, emperor, chapter XI, first chapter concerning the petition to be presented to the emperor: If anyone [concerning] the rules of the holy Fathers, etc.”; and chapter nine of the secular laws: “That every tithe,” etc.

Canciani thought that both laws belonged to the year 898, but he did not observe that they were not the acts of one and the same assembly. This seems to follow from the chapters cited above and from the short interval preceding Lambert’s death. For since John IX began his pontificate in July 898, while Lambert died in October or at the beginning of November of that same year, it is scarcely credible that, besides the Roman council and the assembly at Ravenna, a third assembly was held in so short a time. We present the text from Baronius, corrected in several places as the matter seemed to require.]

## Synodal Chapters

[Col. 0809C]

### Preface of the Pontiff

Because, by the inspiration of divine mercy, your fraternity has joined with us, so that, by the will of the Holy Spirit, who is never absent from his faithful, and by the common counsel of you all, dearest brothers, we may strive, together with our spiritual son, namely the most glorious Emperor Lambert, and with your holy college, to address the matters we have foreseen as necessary for the holy Church of God, and to uproot with the canonical hoe whatever was attempting to sprout as a harmful shoot in the field of the holy Church, let the matters noted chapter by chapter be read before everyone, if they please all, and let them be examined; once examined, let them be confirmed by the hands of all for future remembrance.

Thus no one may ever be permitted to violate them without endangering his own status, but they may remain forever ratified and firm, for the order and protection of the holy Church of God and for the salvation of all the faithful, by the mercy of God.

### Response

We offer immense praises to God our Savior, who has placed you over his Church in such a way that you may determine what is timely for her, and may strive to uproot all weeds from her, as is openly demonstrated to all peoples by the evident signs in this holy synod.

If it pleases your piety, let the chapters also be read that have been written for the general security of all, for the strength and protection of the holy Church, so that through them we may all be taught what we ought to observe and what we ought to avoid, lest we be found in any respect to have departed from the rules of the holy fathers—God forbid.

### Petition of the Synod

1. If anyone has despised the rules of the holy fathers and has not observed what the most glorious emperors—namely, the emperor Charles the Great, Louis, and Lothar, as well as his son Louis—established and sanctioned in their capitularies concerning ecclesiastical tithes, then both the one who gives and the one who receives shall be subject to excommunication by the authority of the holy Apostolic See and by the sanction of the holy synod.

2. If any Roman, whatever his rank—whether of the clergy, the senate, or any other order—should wish to come freely to the imperial majesty, or, compelled by necessity, should wish to bring a complaint before [you] [Note: [Col. 0809] Here and below the words enclosed in brackets have been corrected as follows: the printed edition has *our . . . us . . . our . . . our . . . us . . . our . . . our* instead of *your . . . you . . . your . . . your . . . you . . . your . . . your*.], no one shall dare oppose them; nor shall anyone dare invade or plunder any of their property, or disturb their persons while they are going, returning, or staying, until the imperial authority has been able to deliberate concerning their cases or persons, or through [your] envoys.

Whoever attempts to disturb them while they are going, returning, or staying, or takes away any of their property, shall, after they have lodged their complaint through [your] mercy, incur the indignation of imperial vengeance.

3. Let the privilege of the holy Roman Church, established and confirmed from ancient times by the most pious emperors, now be confirmed by [you] as well, and let it be preserved unaltered throughout [your] days, as is fitting. Let the holy Roman Church, our mother, be exalted, protected, and defended for as long as the empire belongs to [you].

4. Let the synod held in your time in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, for the eradication of certain evils and especially on account of the case of the lord Formosus, most holy pope, be strengthened by your imperial consent and by that of your venerable bishops and nobles, and let it be preserved as permanently established. It was carried out canonically, not from the zeal of envy, but for the sake of righteousness.

5. Let those great impieties on account of which we have come to you, and which we have also witnessed throughout our territories in legal proceedings, plundering, arson, robbery, and violence, be most diligently investigated by you and, as necessary, legally corrected.

For we have been struck by such great sorrow at seeing these things that we would rather have died than have seen such acts in our days [Note: [Col. 0811] Baronius alternatively reads “than have seen such things increase.”]. If they are not corrected, you and we shall be separately called to account for them by the supreme Judge.

Therefore we ask, and adjure you by Christ the Lord, not to leave such things unpunished.

6. Let the pact made by your father of blessed memory, the lord Wido [Note: [Col. 0811] The printed editions read “lord.”], and by you, most pious emperors, in accordance with the preceding custom, now be restored and preserved inviolate.

7. As for the places and possessions contained in that same pact, certain unlawful grants have been made there. We ask that these be settled in the same synod, and that the grants which were not properly made be annulled.

8. We ask that the patrimonies, suburbs, estates, and tenant holdings, as well as the cities that have been granted contrary to reason, as though by official charters, be returned [Col. 0811D], and that the same . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0811] Some words have fallen out.]

9. Your majesty is certainly not unaware that Romans and Lombards, and likewise Franks, have dared to make unlawful unions in the territories of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, contrary to apostolic and imperial will.

We ask that, just as your imperial predecessors prohibited such unions from being made in any way, so from now on they be altogether prohibited by your august decree, and that it be firmly established and confirmed synodally and perpetually that no attempt be made to form them hereafter.

10. Above all, we grieve over this: having been raised by Christ’s grace to so great an apostolic height, when we saw the Church of the Lord Savior called the Constantinian Church destroyed, we sent men to cut beams for some restoration of it. But those whom we sent were entirely unable to do what was necessary because of the harassment of wicked men.

Concerning all these matters, dearest son, see together with us, and consider from the depths of your heart how indecent this is and how much violence the holy mother Roman Church has suffered. Work, as her most beloved son and most exalted emperor, so that from now on and thereafter, through your imperial care, she may be brought to the desired strength.

But we wish you to know that the holy Roman Church has been reduced to such utter nothingness that even the alms formerly distributed to the poor for the safety of your empire, as well as the stipends of her clergy and servants, have been entirely exhausted.

For this reason, it is all the more necessary for you to deliberate prudently with your faithful concerning the stability of your empire, so that, as we have said, you may devote yourselves to restoring her, who has been afflicted beyond measure.

After these matters had been read, the pope addressed the bishops and concluded as follows:

Because all your fraternity professes with one voice that the matters we have set forth, inspired by the grace of Christ our God, are pleasing to you, we exhort you to strive, each of you according to the solicitude owed, to care for the Church entrusted to him by God, and to instruct the flock [Col. 0812C] redeemed by the blood of Christ through good examples and salutary teachings.

Always keep before your eyes that fearsome Judge who poured out his most sacred blood for all, so that, when you stand before his tribunal, he may say to each of you:

“Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord.”

When, with God’s help, you have returned to your own places, proclaim a fast and celebrate a litany, asking and beseeching the pious and merciful Lord to mitigate his fury, avert his anger from the people, grant peace, suppress schisms and seditions, remove discord, wipe away past sins, and mercifully abolish them.

Thus, with all offenses forgiven, may he grant mercy to those who ask, preserve our spiritual son, the most excellent Emperor Lambert, for the protection and exaltation of his holy Church, and subject to him the necks of proud nations by his powerful right hand—Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# Capitular of Emperor Lambert

1. Let the count subject the plundering of the army, among his honors, to the law.

2. Let the imperial men hurrying to the emperor’s assembly or service be content with their own allowances.

3. Let no count grant freemen of the army (*arimanni*) as benefices to his own men.

4. Let the counts’ men in no way reside in the houses of the *arimanni*, but let them restore the public houses and reside there.

5. Let public scribes in no way be forbidden to copy the property of the *arimanni* whenever it is necessary for them to do so. But if, to avoid military service or a court hearing, such property has been sold and they have ceased to pay for it, let both sums be exacted from them, just as before the transcription.

6. Let the *arimanni* themselves not be compelled to go to court more often than the law has established, either by the counts or by the *sculdaisii*.

7. Let the imperial envoys exact only the ban of the imperial army.

8. Let the emperor’s provisions be paid by the bishops and counts according to ancient custom. But if, in recent times, the comital fisc has been converted into ecclesiastical ownership, let the imperial allowance from the Church be increased in proportion to the reduction of the public property.

9. Let every tithe be supplied by the bishops or by those whom they have appointed; let no one transfer it to his own chapel unless perhaps by concession of the bishop [Col. 0814A].

If it should happen that anyone does so, let him first be subjected to human laws; afterward, bound by the excommunication of the people, let the chapel itself—which provides more contention than any benefit—be destroyed.

10. Let the parishes of the Church in no way be granted as benefices to counts, to the vassals of bishops, or to any laymen.

11. Let neither an envoy, nor a count, nor a judge claim, as though by custom, a court hearing or hospitality in the houses of the churches. Instead, let them establish houses in public villages, where they may hold court and receive hospitality according to ancient custom.

12. Let each parish have an archpriest. Therefore, for the constant care of the people of God, we wish archpriests to preside over each parish. They are not only to take responsibility for the uneducated populace, but also to watch continually over the lives of the priests who live in the smaller titular churches, and to report to their bishop with what diligence each one performs the divine work.

Let no bishop claim that a parish has no need of an archpriest. Even if he himself is able to govern it because he is highly suitable, it is nevertheless fitting that he share his burdens. Just as he presides over the mother church, so priests should preside over the parishes, so that ecclesiastical solicitude may not falter in any respect.

Nevertheless, let them refer everything to the bishop and not presume to arrange anything contrary to his decree.

[Col. 0813]

# Chapters of Charles III Concerning the Bishopric of Tongeren  
*(Year 920.)*

[Note: [Col. 0813] Sirmond published these from the manuscript of Saint Mary of Verdun. We read the sequence of events in the *Annals* of Flodoard, and a somewhat fuller account in Book I of Richer’s *Histories*.]

[Col. 0813C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, illustrious man, by the gracious favor of divine clemency king of the Franks, to all archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom entrusted to us by God: peace and salvation from that same eternal God.

1. Since we are entirely unable to enumerate the benefits of divine favor that we have experienced from him from our earliest childhood, therefore my mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord, and shall bless his holy name forever and ever.

Since, moreover, because of our many failings, we have often endured various adversities, we believe that this was permitted not as a punishment merited by our damnation, but as a grace of his reconciliation with us, so that, instructed by his scourges, we may learn to avoid what is perverse and obey his will in all things.

As many of you know, long ago certain of our faithful, departing from the fidelity they owed us, attempted to deprive us of life and kingdom. They went over to our enemies, attached themselves closely to them, and desired that possessions and bishoprics of our kingdom should be given to them by those enemies.

To say nothing of many others, we shall reveal to your holiness one man who infused the venom of a serpent into our own vitals—namely, Hilduinus. He acted against royal power and also against the words of the Apostle, where it is said: “Fear God, honor the king”; and: “There is no authority except from God”; and: “He who resists authority resists the ordinance of God” [Col. 0814C].

“For there is no authority except from God.” He also acted against the words of David the harpist, who says to the Lord: “You have set men over our heads.”

He went beyond the Rhine to our enemies, entirely forgetting the oaths he had promised us and casting them behind his back. He sought from our enemy Henry the bishopric of the Church of Tongeren and, to his own damnation, usurped it contrary to all the statutes of both the holy fathers and our royal predecessors.

Concerning such persons, the capitulary Book of Kings says:

“If anyone presumes to take a dignity from a prince or just lord which he has not deserved, let him be considered sacrilegious.”

And blessed Gregory says:

“Just as one who, when invited, refuses, and when sought, withdraws, is to be brought to the sacred altars, so one who seeks office voluntarily or thrusts himself forward importunately must undoubtedly be rejected. For he who strives to reach higher things—what does he do except diminish himself by increasing? Why does he not consider that the blessing is turned into a curse for the one who is promoted for the purpose of becoming a heretic?”

2. When certain destructive men, as we have mentioned above, departed from our fidelity, we summoned sixteen archbishop-princes of our kingdom, as well as certain nobles, margraves, counts, and leading men, so that with their counsel, authority, and strength we might resist such great madness.

It was determined that, just as new kinds of humps are cut away and healed by new remedies [Col. 0815A], so these men should be expelled from the fellowship and society of Christians by episcopal authority and the constitution of the sacred canons.

Inflated by their presumption and wicked tyranny, Hilduinus not only knowingly took part with them after giving Henry and his nobles considerable weights of gold and silver, but also, from the treasures of the Church of Tongeren—which he had seized or stolen at the devil’s instigation—used threats and terrors to force Herimannus, archbishop of the city of Agrippina, to consecrate him bishop through the violence of Henry and his faithful.

For, as that venerable archbishop himself later reported to us in the presence of many, if he had not done so, they would have taken his life and ecclesiastical possessions, slaughtered his entire household, and plundered their property [Col. 0815B].

Therefore he consecrated him without the authority of his legitimate predecessors, as he himself still testifies, but compelled by such great terrors and dreadful cruelties.

Hence the following is found in the Council of Nicaea:

“If anyone from the clergy is discovered communicating with excommunicated persons, let him himself also be deprived of communion, as one who confounds the rules.”

Such provisions concerning excommunicated persons are found extensively in various councils and in the capitularies of kings.

### 3.

The same Hilduin also invaded, plundered, and carried away at will the property of our kingdom from the aforesaid bishopric, acting against the decrees of Pope Anacletus, where it is said:

“Saint Anacletus, who was ordained a presbyter by the apostle Peter himself and later became his successor as bishop in the Roman see, judged together with the priests of the whole world. Whoever, he says, takes anything from his father or mother is a participant in homicide. Our father is undoubtedly God; our mother, however, is the Church, which regenerated us in baptism. Therefore whoever robs, removes, or defrauds Christ and the Church of money is a murderer, and shall be reckoned a murderer in the presence of the just Judge. Whoever robs his neighbor’s money acts wickedly. But whoever removes the Church’s money or property commits sacrilege and must be judged as a sacrilegious person.”

### 4.

Finally, the aforesaid Hilduin, driven by greedy covetousness, seized the treasures of the Church of Tongeren and of the palace at Aachen, placed in a certain chest beside the body of the blessed martyr Lambert; he gave them to our enemies—namely, to his own supporters—and removed them from the Church. Concerning such matters, the sacred canons decree as follows:

“If anyone is found to have sold or removed anything from the Church’s sacred vessels or furnishings, he has committed sacrilege. It has been decided that he is not to remain in the ecclesiastical order.”

Accordingly, blessed Augustine says in Homily 47 on the Gospel of John:

“Behold, Judas is among the saints; behold, Judas is a thief. And lest you despise him, this thief is sacrilegious—not a thief of just any places, but of the Lord’s places; not of just any places, but of sacred places.”

And shortly afterward:

“Whoever removes or defrauds anything from the Church is compared with Judas the betrayer.”

### 5.

He gave these treasures of the Church to bishops, counts, and supporters as payment for his ordination, having no regard for the decrees of the African Council, which prescribe that no one is to be ordained for money, stating:

“If any bishop has obtained his dignity through money, let him be deposed and rejected in every way, just as Simon Magus was cut off by Peter.”

Likewise, in the Council of Chalcedon:

“If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon wishes to obtain the grace of the Holy Spirit at a price, he shall be subject to the peril of his own rank; and nothing from this ordination or promotion, which has been carried out through commercial dealing, shall benefit him. Rather, let him be anathematized.”

### 6.

The aforementioned Hilduin, to increase the measure of his condemnation, came into the presence of the venerable Herimann and wickedly swore upon the sacred objects that I, Charles, had given the bishopric of Tongeren. He also compelled certain clerics and laymen to swear the same.

[Note: That this was indeed the case is clear from Flodoard and Richer.]

How absurd and how deserving of avoidance this was is confirmed by testimonies scattered throughout the holy Scriptures.

### 7.

Moreover, the aforementioned Hilduin, summoned three times to the synod by Lord Bishop Herimann so that he might answer the charges brought against him—if he had a just defense, or, if he could not, might be struck by the darts of the canons—delayed coming. He thus incurred the sentence of Pope Boniface, who says:

“He proves that the things spoken against him are true who is entirely unwilling to be present to refute them. And let him not doubt that the guilty person evades judgment in this way, just as the innocent person seeks to be acquitted.”

And shortly afterward:

“For whoever thinks that he can evade judgment by delays confesses everything.”

Again, the same pope says:

“If he wishes to be present, let him answer the charges in person, if he has confidence. But if he neglects to appear, let him not gain a postponement of the sentence by his absence.”

### 8.

All the clerics and laypeople of the aforesaid Church, coming to our eminence, made known in mournful voices that the aforementioned Hilduin, together with his robbers, had plundered their possessions and taken away all their property and household goods, leaving them nothing from which they could provide even the necessities of life.

They also added in their petitions that action should be taken more quickly on your advice, lest they continue to suffer plunder and devastation; and that we should give them as bishop Richer, whom they had unanimously elected.

Concerning all these matters, inserted here point by point, we beseech your pontifical authority, for God’s sake and on account of the fidelity that you promised us, to help us henceforth with all your strength, so that our honor may not further diminish in affairs of this kind and the condition of God’s holy Church may be established.

[Col. 0817]

## THE ASSEMBLY OF HENRY I AND CHARLES AT KOBLENZ  
*(A.D. 922.)*

[Note: The acts of this assembly, mentioned by Burchard, were published from a royal Munich manuscript in volume IV of the Historical Writings and Documents of the distinguished M. Liberius Baron of Freyberg, prefect of the royal Munich archives. We therefore thought that they should be reproduced, together with a fragment copied by Schannat from Vatican Library Codex no. 4227 and published by Harzheim in volume II, p. 600.]

[Col. 0817A]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 922, by order of the venerable and most reverend princes—namely, Kings Charles and Henry—eight bishops assembled at Koblenz: Herimann, archbishop of Cologne; Heriger, archbishop of Mainz; Thiado, bishop of Würzburg;

[Note: The word *episcopus* is absent here and below in the Freising manuscript copied for our use once more by the distinguished Föringer. It is present, however, as the distinguished scholar reports, in the Collection of Canons of the Bavarians added in a tenth-century manuscript from the end of the tenth or beginning of the eleventh century, Codex Tegernseensis Cimel. IV. 3. There, fol. 24, Book VIII, chapter 94, the opening and chapter 1 of this council are found. The same manuscript has: *Wirziburgensis, Mindanensis, Doto Osnebrugensis, Rigouuo, Rihuuînus Padebrunensis*. It omits Heriger, archbishop of Mainz.]

Liuthar, bishop of Minden; Dodo, bishop of Osnabrück; Richgauwo, bishop of Worms; Rihwin, bishop of Strasbourg; Unwan, bishop of Paderborn; together with very many abbots and other men of the sacred order.

[Note: Preface and apparatus 3, 6, 7, 8. See Burchard, VII.30; III.240; VI.49; III.241, chapter 9 in the Palatine manuscript; IV.131, in Theiner at the cited place.]

### 1.

With the Lord Christ cooperating and confirming their decisions, they sat in synodal assembly and, deliberating with the most salutary counsel on many matters useful and beneficial to God’s holy Church, firmly established among other things that the incest of kinship—which, alas, is exceedingly common in the present age through abuse—must be avoided with the utmost care. That is, no Christian shall presume to contract marriage within the fifth generation.

[Note: The Tegernsee manuscript has “sixth.”]

### 2.

It was likewise decreed that, as is confirmed by the decisions of the fathers who preceded us, no one should take his own son or daughter from the baptismal font, nor marry his goddaughter or his spiritual mother, nor the woman whose son or daughter he has brought to confirmation. Wherever this has occurred, the parties shall separate.

### 3.

Concerning the number of persons who may approach to receive an infant from baptism: no more than one, whether man or woman. The same shall also be observed at confirmations.

### 4.  
*(Council of Tribur, canon 51.)*

If a woman, while her lawful husband is alive, has perhaps been adulterated against what is right by another man, it shall not be permitted for that adulterer, if her lawful husband should later die, to join in lawful marriage with the adulteress whom he previously violated. But if they do this, they shall separate and undergo penance.

### 5.

Judgments concerning ecclesiastical matters shall belong exclusively to the bishops.

### 6.

It has also been decreed that the churches of any monks located in the several parishes shall, as is proper, be divinely subjected to the governance of the bishops, and that they shall diligently render them the due obedience required in carrying out the affairs of ecclesiastical care.

The monks themselves shall undoubtedly obey their bishops in all matters.

[Note: The later hand has *oboediant* instead of *obediant*.]

### 7.

It was also asked what should be done with someone who has sold a Christian person. Everyone answered that he thereby incurs the guilt of homicide against that person.

### 8.

If any layman or cleric, or any person of either sex, assigns by gift places or property belonging to him somewhere else, he shall have no authority to withdraw from them the income from tithes lawfully assigned to the former church. If he attempts to do so, such a transfer shall be considered entirely invalid, and he himself shall be compelled to make amends by ecclesiastical censure.

### 9.

It was also reported to the same holy synod that certain secular persons had irrationally entrusted their churches to particular presbyters and, whenever they wished, removed them according to their own pleasure. Therefore it was unanimously agreed that no presbyter should henceforth accept a church except in the presence of the bishop or his vicars, and that no layman should have any authority to remove it without the judgment of the bishop or his archpresbyters.

For if that presbyter should be found, on grounds of justice, to have administered it carelessly in the performance of ecclesiastical duties, he shall be removed from it. Otherwise, he shall enjoy the benefit of his labor without injury.

When he has died, the lord of the church shall claim no ownership over the possessions of his estate. Rather, two parts shall be distributed as alms for his soul, while the third part shall be left for the benefit of the church in whose service he was engaged. Whoever acts contrary to these provisions shall be subject to ecclesiastical correction.

[Note: The Theiner manuscript has *conferendi* (“of transferring”) instead of *auferendi* (“of removing”).]

[Note: The Theiner manuscript has *dominum* (“lord”) instead of *dominium* (“ownership”).]

### 10.

It has also been decreed that no presbyter shall presume to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass unless two others are present and respond to him, so that he himself is the third. Since he says in the plural, “The Lord be with you,” and in the Secret, “Pray for me,” it is most appropriate that his greeting also be answered in the plural.

[Note: Harzheim added this chapter on p. 600, according to the report of the distinguished Föringer concerning the distinguished Kanstmann. Theiner found it in the royal Munich manuscript, among the canons in the Ratisbon collection of St. Emmeram, G. XII, eleventh century. From that source we now present a more accurate text:

“From the council—or councils, as the Emmeram manuscript reads—held at Koblenz, which Henry and Charles attended. Immunity is redeemed with six hundred solidi and nine chapters. Sacrilege shall be compounded for with nine times nine [*novigeldis*]. Or, if anyone wishes to deny it, let him swear upon the altar with twenty-four named and chosen witnesses; or let him swear upon the altar with seventy-two free men, unnamed nevertheless. [A slave or ignoble person shall swear by red-hot iron,” according to the Emmeram manuscript.]]

[Col. 0819]

1. Concerning Bishops Einhard and Benedict.

## THE ASSEMBLY OF HENRY I AT ERFURT  
*(A.D. 932, June 1.)*

[Note: We present the chapters, corruptly published by Baronius in volume XI, pp. 803–804, corrected through the work of the distinguished Föringer from a royal Munich manuscript.]

[Col. 0819A]

In the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 932,

[Note: The diplomas of Henry issued at Erfurt give the same year and day; hence it is clear that the Annals of Hildesheim and the Continuator of Regino were mistaken in reporting the years 935 and 936. Chapters 2, 3, and 5 are found in Burchard XIII.21, 28, and 27.]

and likewise in the fourteenth year of the reign of the most Christian King Henry, in the fifth indiction, on the Kalends of June, a holy and universal synod was convened at Erfurt, as the most wise king decreed with the counsel of his chief men, through the inspiration of the mercy of the Savior of all, for the welfare and stability of holy mother Church.

[Note: Baronius reads “of the king.”]

The diligence of the most prudent man, Archbishop Hiltibert, directed this undertaking.

[Note: The word *studium* is absent in manuscript B.]

[Note: Manuscript B reads “governs the council.”]

The most religious priests were seated there: namely, Ruopert, archbishop of the holy see of Trier;

[Note: Manuscript B has the abbreviation “R.”]

[Note: Manuscript B repeatedly has “of the holy Church of Trier.”]

Unni, archbishop of the holy Church of Hamburg;

[Note: Manuscript B has “bishop.”]

Adalward, bishop of the see of Verdun;

[Note: The manuscript’s *adaluuarto* has been corrected to *adaluuardo*; manuscript B has *adalguardo*.]

Riquin, bishop of the city of Strasbourg;

[Note: Manuscript B has *ricuino*.]

Noting, bishop of the Church of Constance;

[Note: Manuscript B has *nodtingo*.]

[Note: Manuscript B has *Constantiae* (“of Constance”).]

Unwan, bishop of the see of Paderborn; Uodalrich, bishop of the Church of Autun;

[Note: The manuscript reads *augustitudunensis*, without deleting *ti*. Manuscript B writes *Othilrico A.*, followed immediately by *ecclesiae* in the next place.]

Bernhard, bishop of the see of Halberstadt; Burchard, bishop of the Church of Würzburg; Tuoto, bishop of the see of Osnabrück;

[Note: Manuscript B has *Duodone*.]

Rumald, bishop of the Church of Minden;

[Note: Manuscript B has *memigernafurdensis*.]

Eberiso, bishop of the Church of Minden;

[Note: Manuscript B has *eburgiso mimidonensis*.]

and also abbots and other men of the sacred order. Moreover, with their unanimity and, above all, with God’s favor, the chapters written below were collected both for our correction and for that of the Christian people.

[Note: The words *tam pro nostra* are absent in manuscript B.]

### Chapter 1

Henceforth let the feast days of the twelve apostles be solemnly celebrated with the highest reverence. We also decree that the vows of fasting on the vigils established in ancient times and observed until now by our predecessors be fulfilled with every diligence. For we do not doubt that those whom we know to possess higher merit from heaven must also be honored by us with the greater dignity of honor.

[Col. 0820A]

### 2.

We do not wish secular lawsuits to be conducted on Sundays or other feast days, or even on those days

[Note: The words are absent in manuscript B.]

on which the lawful fasts are observed, in accordance with canonical institution.

Moreover, the most glorious king, for the advancement of the Christian religion, granted that no judicial authority should have permission, on its own authority, to summon Christians before a court under penalty of the ban during the seven days before the Nativity of the Lord, from Quinquagesima until the octave of Easter, and during the seven days before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, so that they might have greater freedom to visit the church and devote themselves to prayer.

### 3.

For we prescribe that no Christian, while seeking a church out of reverence, remaining there, or returning from it, shall be constrained there by the ban of any public authority, lest, while hastening to church for the sake of prayer,

[Note: Manuscript B has *orationum* (“of prayers”).]

he be hindered by the ban from devoutly attending to the salvation of his soul.

### 4.

If any presbyter or deacon, negligent in his way of life, has allowed evil to be suspected of him, and his infamy is canonically reported before the bishop, the bishop shall admonish him once, twice, and a third time, so that either by revealing his guilt he may acknowledge himself culpable and receive the sentence of just correction, or, bringing his colleagues with him, prove himself innocent by purging himself under oath.

### 5.

We entirely forbid anyone, unless his own bishop or the bishop’s representative consents, to impose upon himself a fast under the pretext of religion, selecting one day in preference to the others.

[Note: The manuscript has *opteptu*, an apparent scribal error for *optentu*.]

[Note: The words “one day” are absent in manuscript B.]

We disapprove of this when it has been done, and prohibit it from being done in the future, because it is recognized as serving more as a means of divination

[Note: Manuscript B reads *cognoscitur* (“is recognized”) instead of *dinoscitur*.]

than as an addition to Catholic law.

## ECCLESIASTICAL CONSTITUTIONS OF THE THREE OTTOS

*(Monumenta Germaniae historica, Pertz.)*

## CONSTITUTIONS OF OTTO THE GREAT

[Col. 0821]

## THE SYNOD OF INGELHEIM  
*(A.D. 948.)*

[Note: The monk Richer described at great length the causes and history of the assembly of Kings Otto and Louis held in the palace at Ingelheim; consequently, the abbot Trithemius of Sponheim transcribed much of it into his History of Hirsau. Flodoard inserted a concise account of what occurred there in his Annals under the year 948 and in his History of Reims. The acts were published in Canisius’s *Readings* from a poorly transcribed manuscript of the Weingarten library. I attempted, though unsuccessfully, to investigate its traces in the royal libraries of Stuttgart and Fulda, which divided the Weingarten manuscripts between them, as well as in the royal library of Paris, with the assistance of the distinguished scholars D. Moser, Hauck, and Guérard. Finally, I found the series of bishops in a manuscript of the Imperial Library at Vienna, in the canon-law catalogue no. 99, fol. 87, parchment, tenth century. We report here those elements that appear to express the acts themselves. Richer, an author from the end of the ninth century, seems to have had the extensive acts of the assembly before his eyes, but they differ from those reported by Flodoard and the Weingarten manuscript. Thus, since Otto’s charters are silent on the matter, it is genuinely uncertain whose testimony should be trusted in determining the date of the assembly.]

### Address of Rotbert, Metropolitan of Trier, at the Synod

[Col. 0821A]

There are many matters, reverend Fathers, on account of which we have been compelled to assemble and sit here before the most serene kings. There are also very many matters that appear to require ordering through your integrity.

It is evident that the commonwealth of almost the whole of Gaul has been thrown into confusion by the recklessness of wicked men and is subject to great dangers. Consequently, divine and human laws alike are indiscriminately despised by evildoers, while the one to whom the rights of kingdoms are owed, and to whom the power of ruling was entrusted through paternal succession, has been seized by the persecution of his own people, brutally thrust into prison, and is still being attacked by their swords. The metropolis of Reims, too, is being savagely harassed by thieves while lacking a shepherd; divine worship is held cheap, and canonical religion is treated as worthless.

Therefore, Fathers, I believe that we must press these matters most vigorously and strive with great diligence—we who have come together here through the grace of the Holy Spirit—so that affairs previously thrown into disorder may return to harmony in such a way that the power of ruling may be restored freely to our lord, the serene king, and through him the honor due to the Church of Reims may likewise be restored.

### Response of Marinus, Legate of the Roman See

Brother and fellow bishop Rotbert has set out the sequence of events excellently and usefully. Indeed, since he himself recognizes that divine laws must be placed before human laws, he nevertheless, having considered the circumstances, rightly stated that the authority of the royal dominion must first be restored, so that, once its strength has been secured and its power usefully restored, the honor of God’s churches may afterward grow correspondingly through his generosity, with his patronage restoring strength to every good person.

If this can be accomplished with God’s assent, it appears that the cause of our lord, the serene king, must first be heard and most vigorously arranged, if this too is permitted by the judgment of your authority.

**The Synod said:** “Let it be heard.”

### Complaint of King Louis before King Otto and the Synod of the Realm

How much I am compelled to complain because of Hugh’s instigation and urging is witnessed by Him through whose grace you were shortly before said to have assembled here.

To begin at the beginning: his father, envying the kingdom of my father, although he owed him service at home and in war, brutally deprived him of the kingdom and caused him to be confined in prison until the end of his life. He compelled me, while still a small child hidden by my own people in a bundle of miscellaneous goods, to flee to foreign regions and almost as far as the Riphæan Mountains.

After my father’s death and my deportation into exile, this man, remembering his own father, who had been killed because of his arrogance, feared to assume responsibility for the kingdom and promoted Rudolf. But the divine power, determining his fate as it does everything else, brought his reign to an end when it wished.

When the kingdom was again vacant, he recalled me, an exile in foreign lands, by the counsel of good men and, with everyone’s consent, raised me to the kingdom, leaving me nothing except Laon. When, after being promoted, I tried to reclaim what appeared to belong to royal right, he bore this with the greatest envy. Thus secretly becoming my adversary, he undermined with money whatever friends I had and stirred my enemies to greater hatred.

At last, driven by envy, he arranged with pirates that I should be captured by them through deceit, supposing that the kingdom could be transferred to himself if this happened. Nor did the plot fail of its result. I was captured and consigned to prison.

He, however, while pretending that he wished to rescue me, demanded that my sons be handed over under the law of hostages. When all those who were bound to me by loyalty protested that they should all be given, he received me back from the pirates after releasing one of them.

Already hoping for freedom, I wanted to go wherever my mind urged me. But it is clear that matters turned out otherwise. For he immediately threw me, once captured, into chains and consigned me to imprisonment for a year.

When he noticed that my enraged relatives and friends were preparing to attack him, he promised me freedom if he received Laon. For this alone I was kept confined; on this condition alone I was received with my wife and children. What could I do? I preferred life to the fortress; in exchange for the fortress I obtained freedom.

And now, deprived of everything, I ask for everyone’s aid. If the duke dares to oppose this, let us confront him alone in this matter.

### Rotbert’s Speech on Behalf of Louis

Since we have received, as I believe, the complaint of our lord, the serene king, set out sufficiently briefly and clearly, it seems appropriate that we determine his cause insofar as is lawful.

Since the duke has transferred almost all the rights of the kingdom to himself, and we are unable to resist him by force, I believe that this must be attempted more gently: the man who fears neither God nor respects man must, through much reasoning and careful consideration of the circumstances, be brought back to proper order with God’s help.

Therefore, in accordance with the decrees of the Fathers and the rule of the canons, he must first be fraternally admonished to make satisfaction and very modestly recalled to this course by persuasive words. But if, after a gentle admonition recalling him, he refuses to come to his senses, let him be struck by the anathema of all. We have this support: he has already been corrected by our lord the pope and ordered to cease persecuting his lord.

### Response of Marinus the Legate on the Same Matter

I remember that, before this past year, our lord the pope sent an anathema against those guilty persons who were persecuting this lord and king of the Franks. He also sent them a persuasive letter, entrusted to good men, urging them not to abandon him, and a written complaint concerning the same matter was likewise entrusted to those of sounder judgment.

Therefore I believe that it has been most justly stated: since he was previously summoned and corrected by the pope, he must now also be recalled through charity and admonished with the most diligent persuasion to cease from his evil actions. Afterward, he must be condemned by the anathema of all.

And not only he, but all who favored and continue to favor him in his evil actions.

But this is the only aid he will receive from us. Will he really receive any aid from someone else? His complaint, in its conclusion, asks for everyone’s help. But if we come to his aid, what will he receive from Lord King Otto?

The holy decretals also proclaim that, after the bishops have imposed upon tyrants the anathema of condemnation, good and powerful men must likewise use force against them, so that, if they refuse to return to proper order through ecclesiastical correction, they may at least be compelled to return to the good by the vigorous violence of the powerful, so that goodness may be provided even to those unwilling to receive it.

### Speech of King Otto on the Same Matter

There are many benefits, Fathers, that can usefully be extended by you to our lord, the serene King Louis. For if you attack his persecutors with divine weapons, then either they will quickly collapse when defeated in the tumult, or, if anything remains to be dealt with, it will more easily be weakened by our weapons.

Therefore, at the command of our lord the pope’s legate, bring forth the instruments of your order and pierce the adversaries of so great a king with the sword of anathema.

If afterward they dare to raise their necks against this and do not fear to resist the Lord’s prohibitions, it will then be our responsibility—we who have been entrusted with defending God’s holy Church in this part of the world—to take up arms against such men and defeat them.

And if necessity presses, let us rage with drawn swords even to the most savage slaughter of the utterly wicked, having the most just cause for indignation against them: they undertake unlawful actions and, although warned concerning their unlawfulness, do not correct themselves.

Therefore, apply yourselves only to your own task; after your moderation, our strength will follow.

### Letter Sent by the Synod to Hugh

The holy synod, properly held in the palace of Ingelheim under the lordly and orthodox kings Louis and Otto, to Duke Hugh.

Everyone’s lips speak of how many evils and how much persecution you have inflicted upon that venerable metropolis of Reims, and of how cruelly you have raged against your lord, the king; the matter is discussed everywhere.

[Col. 0824C]

How criminal and destructive this is, the divine and human laws reveal in the fullest manner. Therefore, sympathizing with you, we admonish you to cease from such actions and urge you to return as quickly as possible to your lord with great humility and gentleness.

But if you despise this warning, before we are carried into different courses, we shall undoubtedly bind you with anathema until either you make satisfaction or go to Rome to give an account before our lord the pope. You have already been warned twice by his letters and forbidden to commit so great a crime. Therefore, following him, we now recall you for the third time to correction.

## ARTOLD’S BOOKLET PRESENTED TO THE SYNOD
To the holy Roman and apostolic see’s vicar, Lord Marinus, and to the entire holy synod assembled at [Col. 0824D] Engulenheim, Artoldus, by the propitious mercy of God bishop of Reims.

Lord Pope Agapitus sent letters to us and to the other fellow bishops of our diocese, in which he instructed us to make every effort to convene at this council of your holiness, so instructed concerning all matters that the truth of the affair, and the sufferings of our see which we endure, might be made manifest before your holiness. Accordingly, we have thought it useful to disclose to your wisdom how the matter that began this dispute originated—a dispute that is still being most miserably contested between me and Hugh.

After Archbishop Heriveus had died, we elected to the episcopate of that same see Seulf, who at that time held the office of archdeacon of our city. Once ordained bishop, he took up hostility against the relatives of his predecessor. Since he could not drive them away from the place by himself, he formed a plan with certain laymen, namely his advisers, and sought the friendship of Count Heribert. Through those same advisers, he obtained it by oath, on these terms: after his death, the soldiers of the church were in no way to seek the election of a bishop without the counsel of Heribert himself; and the count, for his part, was to exclude the brother and nephews of Bishop Heriveus from participation in the possessions of the bishopric of Reims.
