After these arrangements had been made, those relatives of Bishop Heriveus were accused by Bishop Seulf’s advisers of disloyalty to their lord. Count Heribert was summoned with many of his men, and they were ordered to appear before them to give an account. Because they refused to meet in single combat those by whom they had been accused, their possessions, which they held from the bishopric, were taken away; they were arrested and led by Count Heribert to King Robert, who kept them in custody until his death.

Finally, in the third year of his episcopate, Bishop Seulf died, as many assert, after drinking poison administered by Heribert’s associates. Immediately afterward Count Heribert went to the city of Reims, and compelled the soldiers of the church, as well as certain clerics, to attend to his counsel regarding the election of a ruler, as had been sworn. He went with them to King Rudolf in Burgundy, and obtained from him the commission of that bishopric, on the condition that he grant and preserve the due honor of both clerics and laymen, do no one an injustice, and govern the bishopric according to equal right until he could present to the king a cleric capable of being duly ordained to carry out the episcopal ministry.

When the count returned to the same city, he divided the possessions of the bishopric among his supporters as he pleased, deprived the others of theirs, and, without any judgment or law, stripped whomever he wished of their property or expelled them from the city. Finally, receiving Bishop Odalric of Aachen in that city, he ordered him to celebrate the episcopal ministry there.

Thus for six years and more he claimed the same bishopric as his own dominion, treating it according to his personal will; he himself and his wife sat in the bishop’s seat until, in the seventh year, certain disputes arose between him and King Rudolf, as well as Count Hugh. Then King Rudolf, together with Hugh and his brother Boso and many others, both bishops and counts, besieged the city of Reims. The bishops were angered at him and complained against him because, contrary to the authorities of divine law, he had allowed this city to remain without a shepherd for so long.

Moved by their complaints, the king urged the clergy and people to elect a shepherd, granting them the freedom to do so [Col. 0826A] for the honor of God and their fidelity to him. Thus, with all in agreement—both the clerics and laymen who were outside the siege, and with many of those enclosed within also favoring the same course—the person of our humility was elected to undertake this burden rather than an honor.

At last, when both the soldiers and citizens opened the city gates to King Rudolf, and the eighteen bishops who were present conferred episcopal blessing upon me, and the entire clergy and the remaining citizens received our humility, I was enthroned there by the bishops of our diocese. I administered the ministry entrusted to me, as God granted, for nearly nine years, ordaining throughout the diocese eight bishops and, in the bishopric, many clerics as seemed appropriate.

Then, in the ninth year afterward, after I had blessed King Louis, with Hugh’s support and that of all the kingdom’s leading men, and had also blessed Queen Gerberga and anointed her with sacred chrism, Count Hugh, provoked by anger because I had been unwilling to consent or join him in the disloyalty toward that king, laid siege to the city of Reims with Count Heribert and William, prince of the Normans, whom he had brought with him.

The siege did not last long: on the sixth day of the siege, I was deserted by almost the entire body of the lay soldiery. Thus abandoned by them, I was compelled to go out to Hugh and Heribert. Constrained and terrified by them, I was forced to renounce the administration of the bishopric; and, driving me away in this manner, they arranged for me to live in the monastery of Saint Basolus. But they brought into the city Hugh, the son of Heribert, who had been ordained deacon at Auxerre, and took possession of the city.

King Louis, returning from Burgundy, found me at Saint Basolus. Taking me with him, together with my relatives whose possessions Count Heribert had taken away, he led us to Laon, which Heribert and Hugh were then besieging. When the siege was lifted, we entered the town, and lodgings were assigned for us there.

Meanwhile, our clerics of the place, as well as certain laymen, were treated most harshly by Heribert. Some of the clerics were thrust into prison; their possessions were taken away and plundered; and robberies were openly committed throughout the entire city.

In the meantime, the bishops of our diocese were summoned by Hugh and Heribert, who were diligently questioning them concerning the ordination of Hugh, the son of Heribert. They assembled at Soissons and sent Bishop Hildegarius to me at Laon with certain other envoys, instructing me to come to them—in order, that is, to consent to the perversity of this ordination.

I sent them word that it was not fitting for me to go to them where my adversaries and enemies had gathered with them. But if they wished to speak with me, they should come to a place where I could approach them without danger.

When they came to a place chosen by them, I went to them. On arriving, I prostrated myself before them, begging them, for the love and honor of God, to make every effort to give both me and themselves suitable counsel.

They began to question me concerning the aforesaid ordination of Hugh, and in every way to persuade me to give my consent to this ordination, promising that they would obtain for me certain possessions of the bishopric.

But after I had delayed my response for a long time, seeing that they all persisted in the plan they had undertaken, I rose and forbade it. In the hearing of everyone, I excommunicated them openly by the authority of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, declaring that none of them should participate in that ordination, nor, while I lived, lay hands on anyone for episcopal office; nor should anyone presume to receive that blessing. If it should nevertheless be done, I appealed against them to the apostolic see.

When they raged at this and I wished to leave their midst and return to Laon, I moderated my response, saying that they should send someone with me who could report to them what counsel I might be able to find concerning this matter from my lady the queen [Col. 0827B] and her faithful men, since the king was absent.

They sent Bishop Deroldus for this purpose, thinking that I would change my decision. When he arrived and questioned me about the matter before my lady the queen and her faithful men, I rose again and hurled the aforesaid form of excommunication against those same bishops. I also took care to repeat the appeal to the apostolic see. I excommunicated Deroldus himself, instructing him not to conceal this from them at all, but to proclaim it openly to everyone.

After these things had occurred, they disregarded our excommunication, went to Reims, and some of them laid hands upon the man for this ordination, while others are known to have withdrawn.

I, meanwhile, remained with the king and endured with him the distresses that he is known to have suffered. When Hugh and Heribert attacked him in war, I was with him and barely escaped the danger of death.

Thus, having escaped from the midst of my enemies with the help and protection of God, I wandered as a fugitive and exile through every trackless place and forest, not daring to settle anywhere securely.

Counts Hugh and Heribert, addressing certain of our friends who were subject to them, persuaded them to search for me and lead me to them, promising that they would do me good and enrich me with whatever possessions I might request from them.

Our friends therefore searched for me, found me wandering in various places, and I was led by my brothers and friends to the aforesaid counts. After they saw me in their power, they began to demand that I surrender the pallium conferred upon me by the Roman see and renounce entirely my priestly ministry. I testified that I would do this under no circumstances, not even for the love [Col. 0827D] of this present life.

Thus kept under constraint and severe pressure by them, I was finally compelled to renounce the possessions of the bishopric. Once again I was led to Saint Basolus, as though vacant, to live there.

I remained in that monastery for a few days. Then, after learning through reliable messengers from among Count Heribert’s household that he was plotting my destruction, I was again and again frightened and driven on by such messages. I left the place once more, returned as a wanderer to the hidden recesses of the forests, and, during the silent hours of the night, by a circuitous route, went back to Laon. There I was received by the king and appointed to remain with him.

I stayed there with him and his faithful men, awaiting and imploring God’s mercy, until he deigned to put it into the heart of Lord King Otto to hasten into Francia to aid my lord King Louis and us.

Finally, after our lady the queen had left Laon for the absolution of Lord King Louis, I departed from there with my lord King Louis and went to Lord King Otto; together we came to Reims.

The city was then surrounded by armies, and the bishops who were present judged that I should be restored to our see. Lord King Otto therefore ordered Hugh to leave and abandon the city he had seized.

For some time Hugh hesitated and resisted as best he could. But when he saw that he was wholly unable to hold out against the resistance, and that the support of his friends could not assist him, he decided that he must leave, asking to be allowed to depart freely with his men.

He was therefore permitted to leave unharmed, with all who wished to accompany him; and he carried away whatever he wished to take with him, without anyone objecting.

Thus, when I entered the city with the kings, I was ordered to be restored to my place and honor. I was received by the lords Archbishop Robert of Trier and Archbishop Frederick of Mainz, with the others accompanying and congratulating me, as well as by the clerics of our church and the remaining citizens; and by them I was restored to the episcopal chair.

After Hugh left Reims, he occupied the fortress of Mouzon with his men, fortified it, and held it against the faithful of our lord king.

A conference was finally arranged between the kings—namely my lord King Louis and Lord Otto—on the river Chiers. We both attended it: I, and Hugh himself with his ordainers.

There the bishops heard the case in dispute. Hugh produced letters [Col. 0828C] to the Roman see, supposedly written in my name, offering an excuse for my conduct, as though I were requesting release from the administration of our bishopric. I declared, and still declare, that I had never dictated them, nor in any way confirmed them by subscribing them.

Because a synod had not then been convened, our dispute could not be resolved, since Hugh’s supporters raised that objection. A synod was announced for the middle of November at Verdun, with the bishops of both parties agreeing. In the meantime, it was decided that I should govern the see of Reims, while Hugh was permitted to remain at Mouzon.

Not long afterward, when the season of the vintage was approaching, our rival Hugh, taking with him Theobald, an enemy of the king and of our kingdom, together with many other evildoers, came to the villages of the bishopric of Reims adjoining the city. He gathered almost all the wine from them and had it carried off to various districts.

Many evils were then perpetrated there; men of our church were taken captive and carried away, and various tortures were inflicted upon them to force them to pay ransom.

The synod announced for the middle of the month was held at Verdun, under the presidency of Robert, bishop of Trier, by command of the lord Roman pope. Lord Bruno was also present, together with several bishops and abbots.

The aforesaid Hugh was summoned to it, and two bishops, Adalbero and Gozlin, were sent to bring him. He nevertheless refused to come.

The entire synod decided that I should govern the bishopric of Reims. Another synod was then announced for the day [Col. 0829A] of the Ides of January. As announced, it assembled in the church of Saint Peter, before the fortress of Mouzon, under Lord Robert, with the other bishops of the diocese of Trier and some of those of Reims also attending.

Our rival Hugh came there and spoke with Lord Robert, but refused to enter the synod. Instead, through his cleric, who was said to have brought them from Rome, he sent the bishops letters supposedly issued in the name of the lord pope. They contained no canonical authority, but only commanded that the bishopric of Reims be restored to Hugh.

After these letters had been read, the bishops took counsel with the abbots and the other wise men present. They replied that it was neither worthy nor appropriate for Archbishop Robert to abandon the mandate of the apostolic legation, which he had formerly received before the kings and bishops of both Gaul and Germany, delivered by Archbishop Frederick of Mainz, and part of whose instructions he had already carried out, on account of the letters produced by our plotter.

Rather, they unanimously judged that what had been regularly begun should be handled canonically. The nineteenth chapter of the Council of Carthage, concerning the accused and the accuser, was ordered to be read.

After it had been read, judgment was given according to the definition of that chapter: since I retained communion and the parish of Reims, Hugh—who had already refused to attend two synods to which he had been summoned—was to abstain from communion and from governing the bishopric of Reims until he presented himself at the universal synod that had been announced, either to clear himself or to render an account [Col. 0829C].

They then had that chapter written out on a sheet in the presence of the bishops, appended this decision of their own, and sent it to Hugh. The following day Hugh returned the same document to Bishop Robert, sending back this reply: he would in no way obey their judgment.

The council was thus concluded. Hugh retained Mouzon, contrary to the commands of the kings and bishops. I returned to Reims and sent the complaints of my protest to the Roman see through envoys of Lord King Otto, awaiting the commands of that holy see and prepared to obey its decrees and the judgments of your universal holy council.

## Acts of the Synod from the Weingarten Codex

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, in the year 948 from the incarnation of the Lord, in the sixth indiction, on the seventh day before the Ides of January. In the thirteenth year of the most serene King Otto, while he himself also remained present together with the illustrious King Louis, a holy and general synod was assembled at Engilenheim, in the church of Saint Remigius, confessor of Christ, in the district called Nagau, under the presidency of the apostolic legate of Lord Pope Agapitus, the venerable bishop of the church of Polymartium, Marinus [Note: [Col. 0829] “apocrifario” in C. The Vienna imperial codex, Juris canonici N. 99, after prefacing it with Michael (of Regensburg) and Starchand of Rubiloco, gives these names of bishops: Marinus; Frideric of Mainz and Wichfred of Cologne; Robert of Trier; Adaltag of Hamburg; Herold; the archbishops Conrad of Constance, Paldric of Tournai, and Trajectensis; Tuoto of Osnabrück; Rihhardus, corrected to Wichard, of Basel; Adalbert of Passau; Diothard of Hildesheim; Peringar of Verdun; Reginzo of Speyer, superscribed “of Nemetum”; Tuto of Paderborn; Pernhard of Halberstadt; Rihgouo of Worms; Artolfus, corrected to Artoldus, of Reims; Hiberis of Minden; Poppo of Würzburg; Adalpero of Metz; Gozlin of Toul; Hiltipald of Mimigerneford; Uaperi, Varabert of Liège; Lioptacus of Ribe; Horat of Schleswig; Fulpert of Cambrai; Reginprant of Arusi (Arusiensis); and Rudolf of Laon; and these fragments: “This excommunication was enacted at Ingelheim by the bishops written below. I, Marinus, bishop, vicar of my lord, the most blessed and apostolic pope Agapitus of the universal Church of the city of Rome, presiding over the synod, consented to and subscribed this decree.” Then in another hand: “But if the whole line of descent has failed, the bishop shall make canonical inquiry of the older, more venerable, and more truthful persons to whom the same law or kinship is known; and if kinship is found, they shall be separated.”].

The archbishops sitting with him were: Wichfredus, archbishop of the holy church of Cologne; Frithuricus, archbishop of the holy see of Mainz; Rhotbertus, archbishop of the holy church of Trier; Ardoldus, bishop of the holy church of Reims; Adaldagus [Note: [Col. 0829] “adalgago” in C.], archbishop of the holy church of Hamburg [Note: [Col. 0829] “hainmeburgensis” in C.]; Richgawone, archbishop of the church of Wangion; [Col. 0830B] Heroldus, archbishop of the holy church of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 0829] “keroldo s. juvanensis” in C.]; Udalricus, bishop of the church of Augsburg; Bernardus, bishop of the church of Halberstadt [Note: [Col. 0829] “habalrestensis” in C.]; Thiedhardus [Note: [Col. 0829] “thiedardo” in C.], bishop of the church of Hildesheim; Dudo, bishop of the church of Paderborn; Cuonradus, bishop of the church of Constance; Starcand, bishop of the church of Eichstätt; Reginbaldus, bishop of the church of Speyer; Bobbo, bishop of the church of Würzburg; Adalbero, bishop of the church of Metz; Gozlinus [Note: [Col. 0829] “Gochlino” in C.], bishop of the church of Toul; Berengarus, bishop of the church of Verdun; Baldericus, bishop of the church of Utrecht; Wichardus, bishop of the church of Basel; Duodo, bishop of the church of Osnabrück; Eberiso, bishop of the church of Minden; Hildibaldus, bishop of the church of Minden [Mimigardeford]; [Col. 0830C] Varabertus, bishop of the church of Tongeren; Volgbertus, bishop of the church of Cambrai; Rudolfus, bishop of the church of Lyon; Michael, bishop of the church of Regensburg; Adalbertus, bishop of the church of Lorch; Liopdagus, bishop of the church of Ribe; Oredo, bishop of the church of Schleswig [Note: [Col. 0829] “sueuuicensis” in C.]; Reginbrandus, bishop of the church of Arusi; together with a company of abbots, canons, and monks, fervent with the love of one spirit, so that, aided from heaven, the tares sown by an enemy’s hand in the field of divine worship might be uprooted root and branch by the hoes of canonical judgments.

First, the Gospel was read, prayer was completed, and the many precepts of the holy canons were opened before them as keys of knowledge. Then the envoy honorably produced the document of the apostolic see setting out his legation. In it they were admonished, as a gift of due reverence to be offered to the Roman pontiff, that the ship of the universal Church might safely reach the harbor of the desired tranquility, and no longer fear being battered by the stormy whirlwind of tribulations.

The purport of the same reading further declared that the aforesaid Bishop Marinus had been sent to our regions by the universal pope himself on these terms: as his vicar in every investigation of ecclesiastical laws, he was to bind by apostolic authority whatever required binding and to loose with equal power whatever appeared to require loosing.

Without doubt, the glorious kings named above, together with the bishops and the entire clergy, rejoicing in so salutary a message from the legate, declared, as was fitting, that they consented and would obey in all things. With the apostolic legate authorizing and confirming them, they established the following chapters.

Then the illustrious King Louis rose from his place in the session and, before the most serene King Otto and the entire holy council, presented a complaint with many tears: namely, that he had been deprived of royal power by a certain prince named Hugh, formerly subject to him. The holy fathers, united in spiritual unity and sharing his distress and manifold complaint, pronounced the following judgment concerning the matter.

### 1. Complaint of Louis: how Count Hugh deprived him of his kingdom

Henceforth no one shall presume to ravage royal power or deceitfully incur for himself any stain of treachery. For, in carrying out the judgment of the Council of Toledo, we have decreed that Hugh, invader and usurper of the kingdom of King Louis, shall be struck by the sword of excommunication—unless he comes at the appointed time to the synodal council and, by making satisfaction, turns back from such wicked insolence.

### 2. Complaint of Bishop Ardoldus: how the pseudo-bishop Hugh unlawfully invaded his see

Ardoldus, archbishop of the church of Reims, expelled from his own see, has been enthroned again in his former honor by canonical authority. Hugh, however, who has usurped his see contrary to law, has been struck by the sword [Col. 0832A] of anathema. His ordainers, and those ordained by him, unless they come to Trier on the sixth day before the Ides of September and there undergo worthy penance by making satisfaction for their errors, shall suffer the same sentence of excommunication.

### 3. Complaint of Rudolf, bishop of the church of Lyon

Concerning the aforementioned Count Hugh, who expelled Rudolf, bishop of the church of Lyon, from his own see—not on account of any crime, but because of his loyalty to the aforesaid King Louis, his rightful lord—we have decreed in the holy synod that he is to be excommunicated for this matter, as in the preceding case, unless he comes and makes satisfaction.

### 4.

Laymen shall not presume, without episcopal permission, to give or remove churches from priests.

### 5.

No layman shall dare to harass or fatigue a priest [Note: [Col. 0831] “to flog?”], or inflict any injury upon him.

### 6.

The entire week of Easter shall be celebrated festively; and on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday of Pentecost, those days shall be solemnly honored no less than Sunday.

### 7.

On the Greater Litany, a fast shall be observed, as during the Rogation days before the Lord’s Ascension.

### 8.

The offerings of the faithful shall be brought to the altar four times [Note: [Col. 0831] “which?”]. They shall in no way belong to lay power, since Scripture says: “Those who serve at the altar shall partake of the altar.”

### 9.

If the tithes that the Lord commands to be brought into his granary are not returned to the churches of God, but are retained by secular persons through that wicked greed which burns more fiercely than the fires of Etna, no secular judgments shall be exercised concerning this matter, nor shall it be investigated in civil courts. Rather, in the holy synod, the priests themselves, for whose uses they have been assigned, shall determine by definite decrees what must be done concerning them [Col. 0832C].

### 10.

By the authority of the Gospel and the institution of the sacred canons [Note: [Col. 0831] something is missing here] … and penalties shall be proposed by divine judgment, so that our conscience may be absolved and their intention may render an account to God on its own behalf. For it must be guarded against, as the blessed apostle Paul testifies concerning their morals and actions. We omit explaining this more fully, lest the unstable sex appear to be not so much deterred as admonished.

## Frankfort Constitution (951)

[Note: [Col. 0831] Baluzius published it from a tenth- or eleventh-century codex of the Oratory of Paris, in the appendix to Regino, *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines*, I, chapter 53; Eccardus in *Laws of the Franks*, p. 198, from the Gotha codex of the eleventh century, fol. 1451; and Harzheimius in *Councils of Germany* II, p. 621, from Schannat’s copy of the parchment codex Palatinus-Vaticanus no. 583. We have prepared a new edition by collating the Gotha codex with the editions of Baluzius and Harzheimius.]

In the year 951 from the incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0831] the codex, the Appendix, and Harzheim read 952; I have corrected this, since both the ninth indiction and the fifteenth year of the reign fall in the year 951, in which Otto also stayed at Frankfort in January. Harzheim printed the tenth indiction, but this appears to be a correction rather than the reading of the codex, since the same regnal year is given], in the ninth indiction [Note: [Col. 0831] Harzheim reads tenth], a decree was established at Frankfort by the most glorious King Otto, in the fifteenth year of his reign, with the consent of bishops, counts, and many other faithful men, with the authority of the canons and holy fathers, as well as the statutes of earlier kings’ capitularies, set before them: that no one should oppress virgins or widows or carry them off; and that those who carry them away under the pretext of living together, and those who cooperate with or connive at the abductors [Note: [Col. 0833] thus the Appendix; “convenientes” in Gotha and Harzheim], if they are clerics, shall fall from their proper rank; but if they are laymen, they shall be anathematized. The abductors shall remain perpetually without hope of marriage [Note: [Col. 0833] “shall remain” in the Appendix]. If afterward they presume to unite themselves, both parties shall be anathematized.

### 2.

It was also established by the aforesaid king that no abbey which has an election of its own may be given either to a monastery or to anyone as private property. Those, however, which lack an election may, by the king’s donation and privilege, be transferred to another monastery [Note: [Col. 0833] “that monastery” in Gotha and Harzheim] which stands under his protection [Note: [Col. 0833] “may be” in Harzheim].

## Augsburg Assembly (952, August 7)

[Note: [Col. 0833] Of this assembly, at which, according to the testimony of Regino’s continuator, the case of Berengar and Adalbert, kings of Italy, was treated, only the ecclesiastical chapters have been preserved. We owe them to the now-lost Weingarten codex, and therefore its first edition must be sought in Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*.]

When the most excellent and most pious King Otto, drawn by heavenly mercy, resolved to deal no less with spiritual affairs than with the condition of the Christian empire [Note: [Col. 0833] a word appears to have dropped out here; it is absent in Canisius], he first relied upon the common counsel of the bishops and his other leading men. In the year 952 from the incarnation, in the tenth indiction, and in the sixteenth year of his reign, on the seventh day before the Ides of August, he decreed that a session and synodal assembly should be held at Augsburg, so that, through united diligence, the progress of the holy clergy and people toward the stability of the Church, as well as the interests of all Christianity, might be discussed.

He decided that the administration of this divine undertaking should be directed chiefly through the industry of the most reverend and prudent Frithuricus, archbishop of the see of Mainz.

The following bishops also devoted their attention to this deliberation: Heroldus, archbishop of the church of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 0833] I have corrected this to “Salzburg”; Canisius reads “Juvavensis”]; Manasse, archbishop of the church of Milan; Peter, archbishop of Ravenna; and the other bishops of Italy, Gaul, and Germany listed below:

Udalricus, bishop of the church of Augsburg; Anno, bishop of the church of Wangion; Starcand, bishop of the church of Eichstätt [Note: [Col. 0833] I have corrected this; C. reads “eibstensis”]; Cunradus, bishop of the church of Constance; Poppo, bishop of the church of Würzburg; Godefridus, bishop of the church of Speyer; Harbertus, bishop of the church of Chur; Uodo [Note: [Col. 0833] “Vudo” in C.], bishop of the church of Strasbourg; Lantbertus, bishop of the church of Freising; Hugo, bishop of the church of Brixen [Note: [Col. 0833] I have corrected this; C. reads “Aritiensis,” but here it is plainly not the Italian bishop of Atri who is meant, but the bishop of Brixen. The suffragans of the church of Mainz begin with Augsburg; those of Salzburg with Freising; those of Milan with Pavia]; Michael, bishop of the church of Regensburg [Note: [Col. 0833] “Ratisbonensis” in C.]; Adelbertus, bishop of the church of Passau [Note: [Col. 0833] “Patavensis” in C.]; Luidfridus, bishop of the church of Pavia [Note: [Col. 0833] “Picinensis” in C.]; Gisibrandus, bishop of the church of Tortona; Antonius, bishop of the church of Brescia; Waldo, bishop of Como [Note: [Col. 0833] I have corrected this; C. reads “Vultoni”]; Deodatus, bishop of the church of Parma; Witto, bishop of Modena; Adelhardus, bishop of Reggio; Sigolfus, bishop of Piacenza; Adalgisus, bishop of Acqui [Note: [Col. 0833] “Aquenensis” in C.].

As all these men diligently devoted their united efforts to this ecclesiastical affair, everyone considered it appropriate to ask the prince of the kingdom, a devoted son of the blessed mother Church, to deign to attend there while they discussed divine matters.

On the appointed day he came there. Received honorably by all with the sweet and harmonious delight of musical melodies, as befitted royal dignity [Note: [Col. 0833] “received” perhaps?], and after the celebration of Mass had ended [Note: [Col. 0833] “celebrated” in C.], he entered the synod with a distinguished private retinue in response to the bishops’ petition.

Meanwhile, the venerable archbishop of the see of Mainz, Frithuricus, rose from his seat and delivered, humbly and energetically, a speech appropriate to the regular discipline. He then declared all that had been discussed concerning ecclesiastical law according to canonical authority and the decrees of the holy fathers that ought to be imitated, and asked that in all these matters necessary for the undertaking the king should consider himself its common protector.

The king, inflamed by the fire of heavenly love [Col. 0834C] and animated by zeal for divine love, assured them by promising that he would be an eager helper and defender of ecclesiastical affairs, with all the effort of mind and body.

After this royal promise had been heard, the aforementioned archbishop resumed his seat and, with the common consent of the others, ordered the following chapters to be recorded.

### 1.

If any bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon takes a wife, he is to be removed from the office entrusted to him, as is laid down in chapter 25 of the Council of Carthage.

### 2.

Bishops, priests, and any member of the clergy may not keep hunting dogs or hawks for the love of hunting, as is read in chapter 10 of the Council of Toledo. Whoever, being one of such persons, delights in this pleasure [Col. 0834D] [Note: [Col. 0833] I have corrected this; C. reads “denadatus”] shall, for as long as he remains attached to that detestable pleasure, cease from every ecclesiastical office.

### 3.

If a bishop, priest, or deacon devotes himself to dice and refuses to cease from this forbidden activity, he is to be deposed, as is laid down in chapter 42 of the Apostolic Canons.

### 4.

No one remaining in clerical office shall permit a woman brought into his household to live with him [Col. 0835A]. If any woman, marked by suspicion, attempts to act contrary to this rule, she shall be beaten with rods and have her hair cut off by the bishop or his envoy. If secular power prevents this from being done, the woman shall be compelled by royal power to submit to the sentence just stated.

### 5.

Those who flee the various affairs of secular life and undertake the rule of monastic discipline may not go outside the cloister without the permission of their own abbot. They are to devote themselves only to fasting and prayer, remaining in the places where they have renounced the world, as is commanded by the Council of Chalcedon.

### 6.

The bishop in whose diocese a monastery is situated must also exercise care for the monks. If he finds anything deserving correction, he shall hasten to correct it.

### 7.

Clerics who desire to follow the monastic habit and, rejecting secular things in expectation of divine reward, wish to enter a stricter life shall in no way be denied entry by the bishop. Rather, he should try to exhort them to persevere in such a way of life, as is laid down in chapter 50 of the Council of Toledo.

### 8.

If a nun, of her own free will, wishes to bind herself to a stricter purpose of life, the bishop shall not prevent her, for any reason whatsoever, from carrying out what she has resolved upon with good intention.

### 9.

Laymen shall not presume to expel priests from churches canonically entrusted to them without the knowledge and consent of their own bishop, nor install others in their place. For just as priests are ordained by bishops, so they must receive from them the churches that they are to administer, as is laid down in chapter 4 of the Council of Arles.

### 10.

Every tithe shall be under the authority of the bishop; and if it has been neglected, whatever must be corrected concerning it shall be put right before the bishop or his envoy.

### 11.

Bishops, priests, deacons, and subdeacons, as has been established in many councils, shall abstain from wives, because they handle the divine ministries. The other clerics, when they reach a more mature age, shall be compelled to continence, even if unwilling.

# Roman Coronation (February 2, 962)

[Note: [Col. 0835] I have transcribed the oaths made on Otto’s behalf before the coronation from: (1) Codex C. n. 47 membr., from the end of the tenth or beginning of the eleventh century, in the public library of Bamberg, containing the canons of Isidore Mercator; (2) Vatican Library Codex n. 3833, in folio, 1391, from the beginning of the twelfth century, containing Cardinal Deusdedit’s collection of canons. In the margin of folio 1391 one reads: “The writer of this book found this oath in Saxony, in the monastery called Lüneburg.” I transcribed Otto’s oath itself from (3) two codices of Cencius Camerarius’s work on the revenues of the Roman Church preserved in the more secret Vatican archive: namely, the Codex of Sant’Angelo, fourteenth century, fol. 360, and the Avignon Codex, early fifteenth century, fol. 278, where it is inserted into a concise account of the history of Pope John XII. It is also found in Cencius’s Vatican codex and in Gratian, Distinction 63, chapter 33; Baronius observed this under the year 960.]

## The Oath Which Otto Caused His Own Followers to Take Before He Went to Rome

[Col. 0835C]

“To you, Lord Pope John, I, King Otto, cause it to be promised and sworn, by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, by this wood of the life-giving cross, and by these relics of the saints: if, with God’s permission, I come to Rome, I will exalt the holy Roman Church and you as its ruler to the best of my ability; and I will never, by my will, consent, counsel, or exhortation, cause you to lose your life, your limbs, or the very honor that you now possess and will possess through me. In Rome I will make no legal settlement or appointment concerning anything that pertains to you or to your Romans without your counsel. Whatever from the land of Saint Peter comes into our power, I will return to you. Whoever I entrust with the Italian kingdom, I will make him swear to you that he will be your helper, to the best of his ability, in defending the land of Saint Peter.”

## The Oath of the Future Emperor

“To Lord John, Pope of Rome, King Otto sends this oath through us [Note: [Col. 0835] eight codices], and swears by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, by this wood of the life-giving cross, and by these relics of the saints [Col. 0836C], that, if with God’s permission he comes to Rome, he will exalt the holy Roman Church and that same Lord John, Pope and its ruler, to the best of his ability, if he finds him alive. If not, he will exalt the one who lawfully succeeds him. He will never, either by his will, consent, counsel, or exhortation, cause to be lost the life, limbs, or honor that he possesses or that his successor will possess; neither he nor any of his successors. In Rome he will make no legal settlement or appointment concerning anything that pertains to the pope and the Romans without the counsel of the Lord Pope [Note: [Col. 0835] I have corrected *nullum*; the codex reads *romanum*.]. Whatever from the land of Saint Peter has come or will come into his power, he will restore to the Roman Church. Whoever he entrusts with the Italian kingdom, he will make him swear that he will be a helper to the Lord Pope and his successors in defending the land of Saint Peter, to the best of his ability. Thus may God and these holy Gospels and these most sacred sanctuaries help the same Lord King Otto.”

## The Oath Physically Administered

“To you, Lord Pope John, I, King Otto, promise and swear by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, by this wood of the life-giving cross, and by these relics of the saints [Col. 0837A], that, if with God’s permission I come to Rome, I will exalt the holy Roman Church and you as its ruler to the best of my ability, and I will never, by my will, consent, or exhortation, cause you to lose your life, limbs, or the honor that you possess. In Rome [Note: [Col. 0837] so both codices] I will make no legal settlement or appointment [Col. 0838A] concerning anything that pertains to you or to the Romans without your counsel; and whatever from the land of Saint Peter comes into our power, I will return to you. Whoever I entrust with the Italian kingdom, I will make him swear that he will be your helper in defending the land of Saint Peter, to the best of his ability.”

# Otto the Great’s Pact with John XII

[Note: [Col. 0837B] Fredegar, Chronicle, chapter 110.]  
(February 13, 962)

[Note: [Col. 0837] The defense of the Roman Church, offered by hereditary right to the Carolingian line through the pact concluded by Charles the Mayor of the Palace with Gregory III, and assumed by him under the title of patriciate or consulship, bound the patrician and the pope equally by mutual oaths [ [Col. 0837B] Life of Hadrian I, chapter 39]. What later centuries thought of this pact is shown both by the constitution of Leo VIII and by the passage in the third book of the Tripartite Collection of Canons, written in the time of Urban II. This passage also passed into Ivo’s *Decretum*, book VIII, chapter 134, and into the *Chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux* under the year 774. Here we present it, transcribed by our copyist from Ivo’s imperial Viennese codex among the Salzburg manuscripts, no. 323, fol. 104, from the end of the eleventh or beginning of the twelfth century:

“Pope Hadrian asked King Charles to come to Rome to defend the Church’s possessions. Charles therefore came to Rome [Note: [Col. 0837] read “Italy”] and besieged Pavia. Leaving his army there, he was honorably received by Pope Hadrian in Rome on the holy Resurrection. After the holy Resurrection he returned to Pavia and captured King Desiderius. Then, returning to Rome, he held a synod there with Pope Hadrian in the patriarchate [Note: [Col. 0837] one codex reads “patriarch”] of the Lateran, in the church of Saint Saviour. This synod was celebrated by 153 religious bishops and abbots. Pope Hadrian, together with the whole synod, gave Charles the right and power to elect the pope and to regulate the apostolic see, and granted him the dignity of patrician [Note: [Col. 0837] one codex reads “patriarchate”]. Moreover, they decreed that archbishops and bishops in each province should receive investiture from him, and that no one should consecrate a bishop unless he had been commended and invested by the king. Whoever acted against this decree they bound with the bond of anathema, and, unless he repented, they ordered his goods to be confiscated.”

See also Theoderic of Niem, *De privilegiis et juribus*, in Schardius, *Syntagma*, pp. 248–249.]

The defense of the pope and the Church, supreme authority, highest jurisdiction, and the right to participate in the election of the pope belonged to the patrician. But after assuming the imperial dignity, Charlemagne and his heirs bound the pope, as well as the other Romans and the inhabitants of the patrimony of Saint Peter, to themselves by an oath of fidelity; nevertheless, the duty of defense and the Church’s possessions, just as those of the other churches of the empire, remained intact.

I believe that this oath was first sworn in the presence of Charles in the year 800, when, after returning to Francia, the emperor required it also from the other peoples of his kingdom. That Rome was counted first among the metropolises of the empire is clear from Charles’s testament. From that time, therefore, the kings of the Franks, having acquired by hereditary right not only the patriciate, as previously, but now also the empire and patriciate, received the Roman crown either in Francia [Note: [Col. 0838B] Louis I in 813 at Aachen, and again in 816 from Stephen IV at Rheims] or at Rome. Conversely, the pope, elected according to ancient custom [Note: [Col. 0838B] a custom already prevailing under the Constantinopolitan emperors] by the Roman clergy and people, was to be ordained only after his election had been examined and approved by the emperor or his envoy.

After assuming the empire or the pontificate, the pope, together with the whole Roman people, swore an oath of fidelity to the emperor; the emperor confirmed the pact of his predecessors with earlier pontiffs and the privileges of the Roman Church. That this was so may be gathered from historians of the ninth and tenth centuries [Note: [Col. 0838B] On the oath of the pope, cardinals, nobles, and the whole clergy and Roman people, see Thegan under 816; the constitution of Lothair and the oath of the Romans under 824; the Life of Sergius II, no. 15, under 844; the oath of the Romans under 896; and the Roman synods under 963 and 964 in Liutprand. On the manner of electing the pope, see the *Annals of Einhard* under 817; the constitution of Lothair and the oath of the Romans under 824; the *Annals of Einhard* under 827; the *Annals of Prudentius* under 844; the *Annals of Fulda* under 885; and the constitution of John IX at the Roman council, chapters 10 and 36, under 898. The spurious privilege of Louis concerning confirmation of the election is silent, although Paschal himself, to whom it is falsely said to have been granted, had sent Louis an apologetic letter concerning his consecration before he had been confirmed, according to Einhard’s *Annals*.]

The charters preserved in the Vatican archive would also provide confirmation, if all those preceding the eleventh or twelfth century had not perished. For neither the charters granted by Louis I to Stephen IV in 816 [Note: [Col. 0838C] Ermoldus, Book II, pp. 485–486] and to Paschal I in 817 [Note: [Col. 0838C] *Annals of Einhard], nor the charter apparently granted by Charles II in 876 [Note: [Col. 0838C] Council of Pavia; Benedict of Saint Andrew in the appendix to Eutropius; and Letter 9 of John VIII. See also letters 119 and 216], nor those granted by Wido and Lambert in 888 [Note: [Col. 0838C] *Monumenta Germaniae*, vol. III], by Lambert in 898 [Note: [Col. 0838C] ibid., p. 563, chapters 3 and 6], or by Berengar in 916 [Note: [Col. 0838C] *Panegyricus in Berengarium*, Book IV], nor those which we may confidently infer were issued by the other emperors, survive any longer.

Nevertheless, it seems quite probable that those charters expressed both the duty of defense assumed by the emperor and each of the Roman Church’s possessions, as these were contained in the donations of Pippin and Charles and in the Pact of Quierzy, perhaps with the addition, from the year 824 onward, of the principal provisions of the constitution of Lothair I, which we see preserved even in the twelfth- and thirteenth-century laws of the Lombards.

There still exists in the Vatican archive a purple-colored parchment written in golden letters, difficult to access and denied to me, in which Otto I’s confirmation promised to John XII in 962 is said to be written [Note: [Col. 0838C] See Liutprand, Book VII]. Whether regarded as an original or as a contemporary copy, it was printed again by V. M. Marini, prefect of the Vatican archive, in the book cited above, pp. 111–120 [Col. 0839], and supplied with a commentary. Previously it had more rarely been published from the original than from copies of later centuries, and had been extensively discussed by learned opponents and defenders, especially Muratori and Borgia.

I found the oldest copies of it, together with copies of the charters of Louis and Henry II, in Vatican codices nos. 1984 and 3833, written at the beginning of the twelfth century. I also observed that they had been transcribed into the census book of Cencius Camerarius [Note: [Col. 0839C] See our *Annales*, *Archiv.*, etc., vol. V, pp. 84, 88, 94].

The principal second part of the pact confirms the chapters of Lothair’s constitution of 824 together with the formula of the oath of the Romans. The first part, however, contains confirmation of the possessions of the Roman Church: those which it claimed by ancient right, through the donations of Pippin and Charles, through the Pact of Quierzy, and through the right confirmed to Charlemagne; as well as those which, as we stated above, the pontiffs had claimed south of the line extending from Luni to Monte Silicis but had been unable to establish, with the addition of the church of Saint Christina near Pavia; and finally other possessions which we read almost nowhere except here and in the fictitious diploma of Louis and Henry.

Although the appendix to Eutropius’s history, published by Flacius Illyricus—which I believe should be attributed to Benedict, a monk of Sant’Andrea al Soratte—says that Charles II, after renewing the pact with the Romans, that is, with the Roman Church, granted it the monasteries of the Saviour, the Blessed Mary, and Saint Andrew at Soratte, together with the territories of Sannia (Samnium) and Calabria and all the cities of Benevento; moreover, the whole duchy of Spoleto with the two Tuscan cities of Arezzo and Chiusi [Note: [Col. 0839C] This agrees with Peter Mallius’s statement that he read both cities inscribed in silver letters on the donation at the gate of the basilica of Saint Peter]; and although John VIII mentions in his ninth letter that Capua was entrusted by Charles to the jurisdiction and power of the Roman Church, it is self-evident that such a donation, if it really occurred, did not last beyond the presence of Charles II the usurper, nor was it recognized by the legitimate successors to the crown.

For it is agreed among all who know the antiquity of Germany that the German emperors and kings, even legitimate ones, possessed the right to grant the goods and possessions of the empire or kingdom only for the duration of their own lives, so that upon the death of the donor the property reverted by that very law to the state. Still more certainly did the acts of a usurper become void once his power had collapsed.

That Emperor Otto III held this view is demonstrated by the charter of the donation of eight counties granted by him to Sylvester II. Although the charter was still preserved in the Vatican archive in the sixteenth century [Note: [Col. 0840C] *Index scripturarum archivi arcis S. Angeli*, in Aretin’s *Beyträge*, vol. II, fasc. 2, p. 80, no. 158], Baronius inserted it into his *Annals* under 1191, p. 847, after it had been transcribed in 1339, by authority of Pope Benedict XII, from Otto’s original, secured by a leaden bull of the kind of which several remain in our royal archive. We have therefore thought it appropriate to reproduce it especially here.]

[Col. 0839A]

> “In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Otto, servant of the apostles and, by the will of God the Saviour, august emperor of the Romans.
>
> “We profess Rome to be the head of the world, and we bear witness that the Roman Church is the mother of all churches; but through the negligence and ignorance of the pontiffs she has greatly obscured the titles of her own glory. For they have not only sold what seemed to lie outside the City and alienated it from the household of Saint Peter through various corrupt bargains, but—what we cannot say without grief—whatever they possessed in this our royal City, so that they might wander about with greater license, they gave away indiscriminately for money exacted by force. They stripped Saint Peter and Saint Paul, and the very altars themselves, and always regarded restoration as a source of confusion.
>
> “But when the papal laws had been thrown into confusion and the Roman Church had already been cast aside, some pontiffs went so far that they joined the greater part of our empire to their apostolate. They no longer sought to recover what and how much they had lost through their own crimes; they did not care how much they had squandered through voluntary folly. Abandoning their own possessions, which they themselves had dissipated, as though turning their guilt back upon our empire, they migrated to what belonged to others—that is, chiefly to our possessions and those of our empire.
>
> “These are the inventions discovered by those same men, for which John the Deacon, nicknamed ‘the mutilated one of the fingers,’ wrote an imperial command in letters of gold and fabricated a long period of falsehood under the name of the great Constantine. These are also the inventions by which they say that a certain Charles [Note: [Col. 0839] Charles the Bald] granted our public property to Saint Peter.
>
> [Col. 0839C] “But to this we reply that Charles himself could not legally give anything, since he had already been driven out by the better Charles [Note: [Col. 0839] Charles the Fat], had already been deprived of the empire, and had already been abandoned and annulled. Therefore he gave what he did not possess; he gave as one who could indeed give, since he had acquired it wrongfully and did not hope to possess it for long.
>
> [Col. 0840A] “Therefore, rejecting fictitious commands and imaginary writings, from our own generosity we donate to Saint Peter what is ours, rather than bestowing upon him as ours what is his. Just as, for love of Saint Peter, we elected our master Pope Sylvester and, God willing, solemnly appointed and created him, so, for love of that Lord Pope Sylvester, we grant gifts from our public property to Saint Peter, so that our master may have something to offer to our prince Peter on behalf of his disciple.
>
> “Therefore, for love of our master, Lord Pope Sylvester, we offer and donate eight counties to Saint Peter [Col. 0840B], so that, for the honor of God and Saint Peter and for the salvation of both him and us, he may possess and hold them and administer them for the increase of his apostolate and of our empire. We grant these to him to administer: Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia, Ancona, Fossombrone, Cagli, Jesi, and Osimo, so that no one may ever dare to cause any disturbance to him or to Saint Peter or harass him by any device. Whoever presumes to do so shall lose everything he possesses, and Saint Peter shall recover what belongs to him.
>
> “So that this may be preserved by all forever, with the Lord’s help we have confirmed this command with our own hand, which shall live long, and have ordered it to be marked with our seal, so that it may benefit him and his successors.”

[Col. 0840C]

> “The sign of Lord Otto, the unconquered august emperor of the Romans.”

## Note

[Col. 0841]

This charter professes that the donation of Charles the Bald was reduced to nothing by the victory of Charles the Fat. It should not be attacked either because of the imperial title or because of its formulas; it is illuminated by other letters of Otto to Gerbert. The emperor writes, in letter 158 of Chesne, p. 826, as he was about to leave Italy and seek Germany:

“We leave the leading men of Italy to you, with your comfort and assistance. Hugh of Tuscany, wholly faithful to you, and S., count set over the Spoletans and Camerines, to whom, for love of you, we have granted the eight counties that are under dispute, and whom we have presently appointed as our legate over them, so that they may have a governor and, through his agency, render you the services owed to you.”

I believe that this was written at Rome in the year 999, around November.

Since the donation of Charles II was therefore regarded as invalid by later emperors, the judgment of Benedict of Sant’Andrea, who copied out the very words of Otto’s donation, cannot stand when he maintains that the power of the emperors was diminished by Charles II’s donation [Note: [Col. 0841B]:

> “He granted them everything they wished, just as things are given which are neither rightly acquired nor expected to be possessed. Thus, after this Charles had been driven out through fear of the other Charles who was coming, he was weakened before he left the Italian kingdom. For scarcely had he departed when he died. From that day onward no emperor and no king acquired the honorable customs of royal dignity, because either strength was lacking or knowledge, amid the many contests for the kingdom and its continual divisions.”

Nor is this all. We learn from another charter of Otto that, at the end of the tenth century, false imperial donation charters, forged by a certain John and written in golden letters, were being kept at Rome.

Although it can scarcely be doubted that Otto I, like his predecessors and all emperors from Charlemagne onward, renewed the pact and privileges of the Roman Church, we nevertheless acknowledge that the charter now preserved in the Vatican archive under his name is touched by serious suspicion in one portion, namely from the words “in the parts of Campania, Sora, Arces, etc.” to “Gaeta and Fundi with all their dependencies.” Concerning the other portion, beginning “Moreover we offer you, blessed Peter,” and extending to Terracina with its dependencies, we cannot reach a definite conclusion, since we read only in general terms that Otto promised Pope John the restoration of Saint Peter’s territory.

Apart from these points, if this charter presents Otto’s pact, it nevertheless departs in several respects from the genuine form. It calls Pippin “emperor”; gives the twenty-seventh year of Otto’s empire instead of the twenty-sixth year of his reign and the first year of his empire; and inserts other minor matters, including the cross of the emperor: “The sign of Lord Otto, most serene emperor, and of his bishops, abbots, and counts.” Since this is followed by the individual signs of the bishops and other witnesses, these features reveal not an authentic diploma but a copy of uncertain authority.

Someone might also wonder why the emperor says that the pontiff should not be consecrated before making a promise of the kind which “our lord and venerable spiritual father Leo” is known to have made voluntarily, since it is neither established that Leo VII made any promise to Otto nor possible to doubt that Leo VIII was later than John XII. Unless we wish to suppose that these words were repeated from Louis I’s pact with Stephen IV and fixed in the pacts of subsequent emperors, they would otherwise seem quite out of place.

To conclude in a word: I believe that this charter reports the genuine pact of Otto and John XII, but corrupted by an added donation and not entirely sincere in form. It is known to all that from the end of the eleventh century onward it was passed off as genuine, transcribed into the Vatican codices, and gradually gained the confidence of the peoples; from the dispute among the emperors Philip, Otto IV, and Frederick II onward it was also believed by the emperors, and was finally confirmed by Rudolf I and his successors.

Here is the text presented by the illustrious Marini:

[Col. 0841A]

> “In the name of the Lord God Almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Otto, by the grace of God august emperor, together with Otto, our glorious son and king, by the ordering of divine providence, pledge and promise by this pact of our confirmation to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, and through you to your vicar, Lord John XII, supreme pontiff and universal pope:
>
> “Just as your predecessors have held and governed down to the present in their power and jurisdiction, so we confirm to you the city of Rome with its duchy and suburbs, and all its villages and territories, both mountainous and maritime, its shores and ports, as well as all the cities, castles, towns, and villages in the regions of Tuscany—that is, Porto, Centumcellae, Caere, Blera, Marturianum, [Col. 0841B] Sutri, Nepi, Castel Sant’Elia, Gallese, Orte, Polimartium, Amelia, Todi, Perugia with its three islands, the Greater, the Lesser, and Pulvensis, Narni, and Otricoli—with all the boundaries and territories belonging to the cities written above.
>
> “Likewise, the Exarchate of Ravenna in its entirety, with its cities, towns, and castles, which the lords Pippin and Charles, of blessed memory, our most excellent emperors and predecessors, long ago granted by written donation to the blessed apostle Peter and your predecessors: namely, the city of Ravenna, Emilia, Bobbio, Cesena, Forlimpopoli, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Bologna, Ferrara, Comacchio, and Adria and Gabello, with all the boundaries, territories, and islands belonging by land and sea to the cities mentioned above.
>
> “Likewise the Pentapolis, namely Rimini, Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia, Ancona, Osimo, Humana, Jesi, Fossombrone, Montefeltro, Urbino [Note: [Col. 0841] Marini reads “Urbanum”], and the territory of Bagnoregio, Cagli, Lucioli, and Gubbio, with all the boundaries and territories belonging to those same cities.
>
> “In the same way the Sabine territory, [Col. 0842B] just as it was granted in its entirety to the blessed apostle Peter by a written donation of our predecessor, the lord Emperor Charles [Note: [Col. 0841] ‘that is, likewise,’ in the codices].
>
> “In the regions of Tuscia Langobardorum: Castellum Felicitatis, Urbs Vetus, Bagno Regio, Ferento, Viterbo, Orte, the March, Tuscania, Sovana, Populonia, and Roselle, with all their suburbs and villages, territories, maritime districts, towns, villages, and boundaries [Col. 0843A].
>
> “Likewise from Luni, with the island of Corsica; then to Suriano; then to Mount Bardonis; then to Berteto; from there to Parma; then to Reggio; from there to Mantua; then to Monte Silicis and to the province of Venice and Istria.
>
> “Likewise the whole duchy of Spoleto and Benevento, together with the church of Saint Christina situated near Pavia beside the Po, four miles away.
>
> “In the parts of Campania: Sora, Arces, Aquino, Arpino, Teano, and Capua; and also the patrimonies belonging to your power and jurisdiction, such as the patrimony of Benevento, the Neapolitan patrimony, and the patrimonies of Upper and Lower Calabria.
>
> “As for the city of Naples, with its castles, territories, boundaries, and islands belonging to it, as they appear to pertain to those same lands [Col. 0843B], and the patrimony of Sicily, if God delivers it into our hands, likewise the cities of Gaeta and Fundi with all their dependencies.
>
> “Moreover, for the salvation of our soul and those of our son and our parents, we offer to you, blessed Peter the apostle, and to your vicar, Lord Pope John, and his successors, from our own kingdom, cities and towns with their fisheries: namely Rieti, Amiternum, Forcone, Norcia, Balva, and Marsia, and elsewhere the city of Terracina with its dependencies.
>
> “All these provinces, cities, towns, castles, villages, territories, and patrimonies written above, for the salvation of our soul and that of our son, our parents, and our successors, and for the whole people of the Franks preserved and to be preserved by God [Col. 0843C], we confirm to your aforesaid Church, blessed Peter the apostle, and through you to your vicar, our spiritual father, Lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and to his successors to the end of the age, in such a way that they may hold them in their own right, principate, and jurisdiction.
>
> “In the same way, by this pact of our grant, we confirm the donations which the lord King Pippin of blessed memory, and afterward the lord Charles, most excellent emperor, voluntarily granted to the blessed apostle Peter; also the tribute, payments, and other gifts which used annually to be brought to the palace of the kings of the Lombards, whether from Tuscany or from the duchy of Spoleto [Col. 0843D], as is contained in the donations written above and was agreed between Pope Hadrian of holy memory and the lord Emperor Charles, when that pontiff confirmed for him, by his own authority, the grant concerning the duchies mentioned above, namely Tuscany and Spoleto—specifically, that each year the aforesaid tribute should be paid to the church of the blessed apostle Peter, while our dominion over those duchies in every respect, and their subjection to us and to our son, remain intact.
>
> “Furthermore, as we have said, we strengthen by this pact of our confirmation everything named above [Col. 0844A], so that it remains in your right, principate, and jurisdiction, and so that neither by us nor by our successors, through any device or contrivance, may your power in any part be diminished, nor anything be taken from you concerning the provinces, cities, towns, castles, villages, islands, territories, patrimonies, payments, and tributes written above. Thus neither shall we do these things nor consent to anyone wishing to do them. Rather, we declare ourselves, insofar as we are able, defenders of everything written above—the provinces, cities, towns, castles, territories, patrimonies, islands, tributes, and payments—for the church of the blessed apostle Peter and the pontiffs residing in his most sacred see, so that these possessions may firmly remain in his jurisdiction, for use, enjoyment, and administration; while our power, and that of our son and our descendants, remains intact, according to what is contained in the pact, confirmation, and binding promise of Pope Eugenius and his successors.
>
> “That is [Note: [Col. 0843] Marini reads ‘the same’]: the whole clergy and all the nobility of the Roman people shall bind themselves by oath, so that, in order to restrain the various necessities and unreasonable harshness of the pontiffs toward the people subject to them, the future election of pontiffs may, insofar as each person understands, be conducted canonically and justly.
>
> “And the man who is elected to this holy and apostolic government shall not be made pontiff, with anyone’s consent, until he has made, in the presence of our envoys or of our son and the whole community, a promise for the satisfaction of all and for future preservation, of the kind which our lord and venerable spiritual father Leo is known to have made voluntarily.
>
> “Furthermore, we have deemed it necessary to insert other, lesser provisions into this instrument: namely, that at the election of pontiffs neither free man nor slave may presume to come forward to cause any impediment to those Romans whom the ancient custom established by the constitution of the holy fathers has admitted to this election. If anyone presumes to act against this institution of ours, he shall be sent into exile.
>
> “Moreover, we prohibit any of our envoys [Note: [Col. 0843] Marini reads ‘our envoy’] from daring to devise any pretext for interference in the aforesaid election. For we have also decided to establish this in every respect: those once received under the special protection of the apostolic lord or of us shall enjoy the protection lawfully obtained. If anyone presumes to violate it against any of those who have earned it, let him know that he will incur danger to his life.
>
> “We also confirm that they shall render the apostolic lord just obedience in all things, and likewise his dukes and judges, for the administration of justice.
>
> “We have judged it necessary to attach this provision to the institution: envoys of the apostolic lord or of us shall always be appointed, who may report annually to us or to our son how each duke and judge administers justice to the people and how they observe this imperial constitution.
>
> “We decree that these envoys shall first bring to the attention of the apostolic lord all complaints found through the negligence of dukes or judges. He shall choose one of two courses: either the needs themselves shall immediately be remedied through those same envoys, or, after our envoy has reported to us, they shall be remedied by our envoys sent by us.
>
> “So that all the faithful of God’s holy Church and our own may believe this to be firm, we have strengthened this pact of our confirmation with the mark of our own hand and the subscriptions of our noble magnates, and have ordered it to be affixed with the impression of our seal.

> “The sign of Lord Otto, most serene emperor, and of his bishops, abbots, and counts.

# Roman Synod

[Note: [Col. 0845] Its acts, otherwise lost, were inserted by Liutprand in Book VII of his history. We have drawn out those portions that appeared to preserve the authentic form and corrected them with the aid of the former Spanheim Codex, now Brussels.]

## Letter of the Synod to Pope John XII

[Col. 0845C]

“To the supreme pontiff and universal pope, Lord John: Otto, august emperor by the favor of divine clemency, together with the archbishops of Liguria, Tuscany, Saxony, and Francia, sends greetings in the Lord.

“When we came to Rome in the service of God and questioned your sons—the Roman bishops, cardinals, priests, and deacons, and also the whole people—about your absence and about the reason why you did not wish to see us, the defenders of your church and of yourself, they made statements about you so shameful and obscene that, if they had been made about actors, they would have caused us embarrassment.

“So that none of this may remain hidden from Your Majesty, we briefly set down some of it for you. If we wished to state everything individually, one day would not suffice for us. Know, therefore, that you have been accused, not by a few but by all, both of our own order and of the other order, of murder, perjury, sacrilege, incest with your own kin, and incest with two sisters.

“They also report something horrible even to hear: that you drank wine in the love of the devil and that, at the game of dice, you called upon the aid of Jupiter, Venus, and the other demons.

“We therefore earnestly beseech Your Paternity not to refuse to come to Rome and purge yourself of all these charges. If perhaps you fear the violence of the rash multitude, we assure you by oath that nothing will be done beyond the sanction of the holy canons.

“Given on the eighth day before the Ides of November.”

## Pope John’s Apologia
Joannes, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops. We have heard it said that you wish to make another pope. If you do this, I excommunicate you by Almighty God, so that you shall not have the authority to ordain anyone or celebrate Mass.

## Synodal Rescript to the Pope

### [Col. 0846C]

To the supreme pontiff and universal pope, the lord Joannes: Otto, by the favor of divine clemency august emperor, and likewise the holy synod assembled at Rome for the service of God, greetings in the Lord.

At the preceding synod, which was celebrated on 8 November, we sent you a letter in which the words of your accusers and the grounds of the accusation were set forth. In that letter we also urged Your Greatness, as is just, to come to Rome and clear yourself of the charges brought against you.

We received a letter from you—not one demanded by the character of the time, but by the frivolity of ill-advised men. Failure to come to the synod ought not to have been excused on reasonable grounds. Moreover, the envoys of Your Greatness ought to have been present, so that they might explain that you had avoided the holy synod because of illness or, at any rate, because of some difficulty. There is also something else written in your letter which it would be fitting for a child, not a bishop, to write. For you excommunicated everyone, so that they would not have the authority to sing Masses or make ecclesiastical appointments if we established another bishop for the Roman see. For thus it was written: “you shall not have the authority to ordain anyone.” Until now we have supposed—or rather, we truly believe—that two negatives make one affirmative, unless your authority should invalidate the opinions of the ancient authors.

We, however, respond to your intention, not to your words. If you do not delay coming to the synod and clearing yourself of the charges, we shall without doubt obey your authority. But if, God forbid, you neglect to come and clear yourself of the capital crimes alleged against you, especially since nothing prevents you from coming—not the crossing of the sea, not bodily illness, not the length of the journey—then we shall regard your excommunication as of little account and shall rather turn it back upon you, since we can justly do so.

Judas, the betrayer—or rather the seller—of our Lord Jesus Christ, had earlier received from his master, together with the others, the power of binding and loosing in these words: “Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” As long as he was good among his fellow disciples, he was able to bind and loose. But after he became a murderer through greed and wished to destroy the life of all, whom could he afterward loose when bound, or bind when loosed, except himself—the man whom he strangled with a most wretched noose?

Given on 10 Kalends of December [22 November], and sent through Adrian, cardinal priest, and Benedict, cardinal deacon.

## Otto’s Address to the Synod

We awaited his arrival so that, in his presence, we might complain of what he had done to us. But since we know for certain that he will not be present, we earnestly implore you again and again to recognize carefully how treacherously he has acted toward us.

We therefore make known to you, archbishops, bishops [Note: [Col. 0847] I have supplied the word.], priests, deacons, and the rest of the clergy, as well as counts, judges, and all the people, that this same Pope Joannes, oppressed by Berengarius and Adalbert, our rebels, sent messengers to us in Saxony, asking us to come to Italy for the love of God and free the Church of Saint Peter and himself from their clutches.

With God’s help, how much we accomplished need not be stated, as you see here and now. After he had been rescued by my efforts from their hands and restored to the honor due to him, he forgot the oath and the loyalty which he had promised me over the body of Saint Peter. He caused that same Adalbert to come to Rome, defended him against me, fomented seditions, and, before our soldiers, having become a military leader, put on a coat of mail and a helmet.

Let the holy synod declare what it decrees concerning this.

## Synod’s Response

An unheard-of wound must be cauterized with an unheard-of cautery. If he harmed only himself through his corrupt morals, and not everyone, he might in some way be tolerated. How many previously chaste persons have become incestuous through imitation of this man? How many upright people have become reprobate by following his way of life?

We therefore ask Your Imperial Greatness to drive that monster—redeemed by no virtue from his vices—from the holy Church, and to appoint another in his place, one able to preside over us by the example of a good way of life and to benefit himself: let him live rightly and offer us an example of living well.

## Otto’s Consent

What you say is pleasing to us, and nothing could be more welcome than that a man might be found to be placed over this holy and universal see.

## Election of Pope Leo

We choose Leo, a venerable protoscriniarius of the holy Roman Church, an approved man, as our pastor for the highest degree of the priesthood, so that he may be supreme and universal pope of the Roman Church, while Joannes the apostate is rejected on account of his shameful morals.

### [Col. 0847]

# Edict of the Emperors Otto I and Otto II, King  
*(A.D. 967, 29 October)*

[Note: After earlier editions, this text has been revised here with the aid of the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Estense manuscripts in Muratori, and restored to its author and its period.]

### [Col. 0847C]

Here begin the chapters which the most glorious lord Otto, emperor, and likewise his son Otto, glorious king, instituted together with the highest princes—that is, bishops, abbots, and judges—and with all the people.

[Note: This heading appears only in L.]

[Note: Textual apparatus for the preface and chapters, keyed by lemma. *Antiquis*: the preface is absent in A; Fl reads *Antiquitus* (“in ancient times”). *inscriptio*: V reads *inascriptio*, Vn *adscriptio*. *jure*: deleted in L. *Deum*: L reads *dominum* (“the Lord”). *residente*: V and E read *residentis*; Vn, *residens*. *summo*: L, V, Vn, and E read *summa*; *papa*: V, Vn, and E read *papae*; *domno*: L, *donne*; Vn, *donni*; E, *domni*; *Johanne*: V and E, *johannis*; Vn has *johanne*, corrected to *johannis*. *anima*: L reads *anime*; V, Vn, and E read *anima periret et pauper* (“the soul should perish and [he should be] poor”). *Judicio*: L reads *Judicium*. The Ravenna synod was held in March or April 967. *quod*: V, Vn, and E read *quo*. The long L reading is corrected to: “the most glorious Augustus Otto, King Otto, his glorious son.” V and Vn gloss the preceding Otto as “the first.” *convenientibus vel*: V, Vn, and E read *cunctis et consentientibus* (“with all assembled and consenting”). The closing citation is variously headed “Otto the Second” (V), or, in V and Vn, “The greatest King Otto enriches [men] with the gift of war.”]

[Note: Chapter 1: L glosses *praedia* as *alodum* (“allod”); Vn reads *descriptionibus* (“descriptions”) for *scriptionibus*; A reads *et*, Vn *ad*, for *per* (“by”) combat. Chapter 4: A and V omit *ut* (“so that”); A omits *veritas* (“the truth”). Chapter 6: A reads *scasco* for *scacho*; L and V omit *ut* (“so that”). Chapter 7: L reads *supra* (“above”) for *super*, *aut* (“or”) for *et*, and *haec* (“these things”) for *hoc*. Chapter 9: L reads *servare* as *servari* (“to be observed”). Chapter 10: A reads *De ecclesias* for *Aecclesiae*.]

[Note: In the dating clause, L reads *urbem* for *urbe* and omits *in*; it also omits the words from the first *Ottonis* through the second occurrence of *Ottonis*.]

In ancient times it was established that, if an adversary declared false a document whose inscription concerned estates, its presenter proved it genuine by touching the most holy Gospels, and thus claimed the estate for himself by the judgment of the judges.

From this there grew up in Italy a detestable custom, wicked and not to be imitated: under the appearance of law, a person acquired property by swearing an oath, although he did not fear God and was wholly unafraid to commit perjury.

Therefore, at the time when the most pious King Otto received the anointing of the empire at Rome, while the supreme and universal pope, the lord Joannes, was presiding in synod, in his thirteenth year, the nobles of Italy acclaimed that the holy emperor should change the law and destroy this unworthy practice, by which a person might become rich in body while his soul perished and remained poor forever.

[Note: The manuscript reading at this point is corrupt and cannot be restored with the aid of the codices. In A.D. 962 Joannes XII had occupied the see for seven years, whereas in A.D. 967 the pope was Joannes XIII. Muratori conjectures that one should read “Joannes XII, in the first year,” namely the first year of the reign of Otto the Great. This is nevertheless contradicted by the fact that the author of this preface does not distinguish Joannes XII and XIII below, but seems to assign both Otto’s coronation and the synod of Ravenna to Joannes XIII.]

The judgment of the lord pope and of the most pious Augustus was therefore awaited until the synod which, after a short interval, was held at Ravenna.

When a complaint concerning the same matter was renewed there, it was postponed because certain nobles were absent, until the time when the glorious Augusti—King Otto, glorious son of Otto the Great, and King Conrad of Burgundy—hastening toward Italy, held a conference at Verona with all the nobles of Italy.

There, when all were assailing the imperial ears with great cries, asking that by a change of the law he remove this dreadful fraud from Italy, and when everyone had assembled and consented, he promulgated the following law according to the chapters below.

[Note: The manuscripts read variously: “Otto the Second”; “Wealthy through the gift of war, King Otto”; and similar forms.]

1. If a dispute should arise concerning estates [Note: “Allod” is supplied as a gloss in L.], and both parties, or one of them, should wish to claim the estate for himself by charters or writings [Note: So A, L, V, and E; Vn reads “descriptions”], if the person who has called the charter false wishes to establish this by combat, let the matter be decided accordingly. Otherwise, we decree that it be determined according to the preceding chapters.

[Note: This chapter is cited, with respect to its substance, in the proceedings held at Rome on 2 December A.D. 999 before Otto III and Sylvester, in Muratori, *Scriptores*, vol. II, part II, p. 501, though not in the precise words used.]

2. Concerning the property of churches, we likewise order that the matter be conducted through advocates.

3. If there is a dispute concerning the investiture of an estate, we decree likewise that it be decided by combat.

4. [Note: The London manuscript places this chapter after the following one.] If anyone should deposit something with another person, either personally or through his messenger, and, overcome by greed, should deny the deposit [Note: L reads “if, having been convicted, he should deny it”], if its value is twenty solidi, we order that the truth be decided by combat.

[Note: A and V omit “so that.” A omits “the truth.”]

5. [Note: The Florentine manuscript places this chapter after the following one.] If anyone should say that he made a charter for someone concerning an estate under compulsion [Note: A reads “to make”; V “should make”; Vn “had made”], we decree that the truth be decided by combat.

6. In a case of theft or fraud [Note: A reads “theft” in a different form], if the value exceeds six solidi, we likewise order that the truth be discovered by combat.

### [Col. 0850A]

7. If anyone should find his horse, other animal, or property in someone’s possession, and that person should say that he will provide a guarantor, let him immediately swear that he will lead him to a specific guarantor, and let him not proceed beyond a third guarantor and a third county [Note: L reads “above”; “or”]. If he refuses to do this [Note: L reads “these things”], let him lose the property and make compensation according to law.
