8. Among laymen, we permit no one, except counts [Note: L reads “a count”; Vn abbreviates “count,” with the correction “count”; E reads “count”], to have any advocate in purely ecclesiastical matters.

9. Whatever law a man may live under throughout the Italian kingdom, even Roman law, we order him to observe all these provisions which we have decreed in these chapters to be decided by combat. This condition applies, however: if youth, extreme old age, or illness prevents one of them from fighting, he may appoint a champion in his place, and the other may do likewise [Note: V and E add: “If there is doubt concerning the illness, let him swear that he has such an illness that he is unable to fight.” Vn adds in the margin: “through customary practice”].

10. Churches, counts, and widows shall settle by combat, through similar advocates [Note: L originally read “advocates,” corrected to “advocates”; V, Vn, and E read “advocates”], their lawsuits concerning matters contained in the chapters written above [Note: A reads “those matters”]. All other naturally free men shall answer and determine matters themselves, according to the former law.

11. We absolutely prohibit the sons of deacons, priests, and bishops, as well as notaries, *sculdasii* [Note: A reads *sculdaxii*; V, Vn read *sculdascii*, with c inserted], counts, and judges from becoming [such officials].

Enacted [Note: These words occur only in the Florentine and London manuscripts, though the latter places them before the chapters] beneath the city of Verona, in the place called the Island of Saint Zeno, on 4 Kalends of November [29 October], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 967 [Note: The Florentine manuscript reads 968], in the sixth year of the empire of the lord Otto, most serene emperor augustus [Note: L omits “of Otto” up to the second occurrence of the name], and in the sixth year of the reign of his son, the lord Otto, in the eleventh indiction.

### [Col. 0849]

# Mandate of Otto the Great Concerning the Enthronement of the Archbishop of Magdeburg  
*(A.D. 968, October–November)*

[Note: From the acts establishing the archbishopric of Magdeburg, published by Sagittarius—see Boysen, *Historisches Magazin*, fascicle I—and compared by our Boehmer with the authentic documents and with a thirteenth-century cartulary, we select the emperor’s letter to the nobles of Saxony concerning the enthronement of Adalbert, the first archbishop of Magdeburg, assigning it the place given to the other documents among the charters. The original is preserved in the royal archives at Berlin. It was issued after Adalbert’s consecration, which took place at Rome on 18 October. A hand of the same period has written the heading: “How Adalbert the archbishop was first enthroned in the episcopal see.”]

### [Col. 0849C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Otto, by the favor of divine clemency emperor augustus, to all our faithful, namely bishops, counts, and the other men of our province: eternal salvation in the Lord and every good thing.

### [Col. 0850C]

Because we believe the increase of divine worship to be the salvation and stability of our kingdom and empire, we therefore strive and desire in every way available to us to enlarge it.

Accordingly, since—as all your charity knows—we desire the city of Magdeburg to become an archiepiscopal see, and since we now find a suitable time for carrying this out, with the counsel of the venerable Archbishop Hatto [Note: Of Mainz] and Bishop Hildeward [Note: Of Halberstadt], and of our other faithful men, we have jointly decided and chosen that the venerable Bishop Adalbert, formerly appointed and sent as a preacher to the Rugi, should become archbishop and metropolitan of the entire people of the Slavs beyond the Elbe and Saale, now converted or yet to be converted to God. We have also sent him to Rome to receive the pallium from the lord pope.

To make this election of ours firmer and more secure, we send him to your charity, and we desire in every way that, having been elected by all of you through acclamation and the raising of hands, he should be enthroned in his see.

But lest his election or enthronement should, God forbid, be troubled in future by anyone’s envy, we wish three bishops to be ordained by him—one for Merseburg, another for Zeitz [Note: Hugh], and a third for Meissen [Note: Burchard]—in the presence of the lord pope’s legates and of you, so that this same presence of yours may in the sight of God and his saints bear future witness to our intention.

And because the venerable man Boso has already labored greatly among that people of the Slavs who are to be converted to God, let him have his choice between the churches of Merseburg and Zeitz. The other church, according to our arrangement, shall fall under the disposition of our archbishop.

You, however, our margraves—namely Wigbert, Wigger, and Gunther—we exhort and admonish, by the fidelity you owe us, not to allow anything in this ordination to oppose our archbishop among you. Let everything be done according to our arrangement and according to his, as he shall tell you. Whatever you hear from him, know that we desire it.

But lest those same bishops who are to be ordained be considered poor and like peasants, we ask you to take care, with the advice of the archbishop and of the bishops and counts who will be with him at the Nativity of the Lord, to discover how they may be supported. For whatever is expended on them is offered to God for our salvation, and by this your reward with God will not be diminished.

Moreover, we wish the lords Bishop Dudo [Note: Of Havelberg] and Doudelinus [Note: Of Brandenburg] to subscribe to the election of our archbishop and to promise him faith and submission.

And so that this election of ours and yours may afterward remain firm and stable, we ordered this charter or record to be written, to remain perpetually in the church of Magdeburg and to be an enduring witness to what we have stated above. We have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

Sign of the lord Otto the Great and most invincible emperor augustus. (L. M.) (L. S.)

### [Col. 0851]

# Council of Pavia  
*(A.D. 971)*

[Note: We possess its sole trace in an eleventh-century manuscript of the *Institutions* in the Bamberg Library, published by the distinguished Rosshirt in his book *Beiträge zum Römischen Recht*, I, 7. In substance it seems scarcely to differ from the first chapter of the year 967.]

### [Col. 0851B]

Chapter of Otto the Great, Roman emperor augustus, issued at Pavia in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 971.

If there is a dispute or conflict between churches and other free or independent men, or between a church and a man, concerning estates, let it be decided by combat. If he does not dare [to fight], let his property be confiscated, and let his property be returned to the church or the man to whom justice belongs.

# Works of Otto II

### [Col. 0851]

# Peace of Emperor Otto II with the Venetians  
*(A.D. 983, 7 June, Verona)*

[Note: I transcribed this from (1) the *Libro Blanco*, compiled about 1340 by Andrea Dandolo, doge of Venice, now preserved with (2) a sixteenth-century Trevisan manuscript in the imperial archives at Vienna.]

## The Pacification and Confirmation of Otto with the Venetians

### [Col. 0851D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Otto, by the favor of divine clemency emperor augustus.

We wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that a disagreement arose between us and the Venetians. Therefore, moved by divine mercy, and softened by the intervention of our most serene mother, the lady Empress Adelaide, and of Theophanu, our beloved wife and consort of our empire, and appeased by the prayers of the poor of that people, we made peace and a treaty between us on these terms: neither we nor our heirs shall henceforth inflict trouble or disturbance arising from this disagreement upon any man of that people, and neither they nor their heirs shall afterward suffer a similar disagreement from us or our heirs without a judgment, as is contained in the pact which we have established with them [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *habuimus* (“we possessed”) for *hujus*; the word *non* (“not”) has been supplied by the editor.]. Rather, unharmed and secure, free from the molestation of all men, they shall remain forever.

And so that this may be more truly believed and more carefully observed by all, we ordered it to be confirmed by the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Otto II, emperor and most invincible augustus. (L. M.)

I, Adalbert, chancellor, acting in place of Peter, bishop and archchancellor, have reviewed and written this.

## Security Granted to the Venetians by Emperor Otto

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *prestitam* rather than *prestita* (“granted”).]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 983, in the eleventh indiction, in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of Otto II, and the sixteenth of his empire, on 7 June.

While there were present with Otto, the most pious emperor and most invincible augustus, his mother Adelaide, his wife Theophanu, and the transalpine and Italian princes—Willigis, archbishop of Mainz; Gislar, archbishop of Magdeburg [Note: The manuscripts read “Magiburg”]; Ecbert, archbishop of Trier; the bishops Peter of Pavia [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *Ucinensi* for *Ticinensi*; the exact place-name is uncertain], Peter of Como, Dietrich of Metz, and Albin of Brescia; Ezzo, duke of the Bavarians; the counts Otto and William [Note: The manuscripts read *uuielmo*]—and many other noblemen of higher and lower rank, the Venetians approached the imperial majesty.

They displayed the charters and confirmations which their predecessors had received from kings and emperors, asking that the imperial dignity establish through an imperial document peace and treaties so firm and valid that they might live free and secure, without any injury, throughout the emperor’s realm.

For this reason all the ecclesiastical and secular men advised that, for the love of God and in recompense for the heavenly kingdom, it would be fitting to do what those Venetians requested.

Therefore the majesty of the empire ordered this document [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *hujus*; manuscript 2, *hujusce*] to be written and, with its confirmation by his own hand, strengthened it by the impression of his seal, so that henceforth such a disagreement might never arise between him and them, or their heirs, and so that the greater and lesser people of that Venetian homeland might travel freely and securely throughout his empire, toward the east, south, west, and north.

# Works of Otto III

### [Col. 0853]

# Edict of Emperor Otto III  
*(A.D. 996? May)*

[Note: Revised with the aid of the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Estense manuscripts in Muratori, we have assigned it to the first assembly of the emperor Otto III, when, after being crowned at Rome, he gathered Romans, Franks, Bavarians, Saxons, Alsatians, Swabians, and Lotharingians around him.]

### [Col. 0853C]

Here begins the chapter of the lord Otto III, most pious emperor augustus.

[Note: L reads: “Here begin the chapters of Emperor Otto III.” L also adds the verse *hic Romae syndonico rex invidet tercius Otto* (“here at Rome King Otto III is hostile to the syndicus” [uncertain]); Estense reads *Romae sindonico rex tertius invidet otto*; Vienna and Verona, *Festorum placito rex tertius invidet Otto* (“At the assembly of the festivals King Otto III is hostile”). The Ambrosian manuscript appears to count this as chapter XII of the constitutions of 967.]

Every day men act against the laws; every day evil men do not hesitate to do evil [Note: L reads “evil things”; V and Vn read “evil”]. Therefore, by this law, which by God’s favor shall remain valid for all time, we decree [Note: One manuscript explains: “that is, so that”] that throughout the entire year judges may hear cases, settle lawsuits, and bring the disturbances of legal inquiries to an end and decide them, so that those who offend against the laws every day may every day be struck by the sentence of the law [Note: Some manuscripts read “the law”].

For those who have not ceased to sin at any time should not evade the edict of the law during the seasons of harvest [Note: L reads *messis* (“harvest”); A has a corrupt reading at *qui* (“who”); L reads *desierint* (“have ceased”)] or vintage. To do good, speak the truth, love justice, and judge rightly [Note: L, V, and Vn read *recte* (“rightly”)] is permitted at every time and will always be permitted, because we have learned in accordance with Catholic teaching, and have continually maintained, that one must never rest from good works but always rest from evil works. With God as author and the imperial majesty as guarantor, we have decreed this.

King and prophet David says: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice justice at all times.”

But on the Nativity of the Lord, on the Epiphany [Note: Some editions add: “and on the appointed days of fasting, on the days of Lent”; V and Vn read: “on the days of Lent”], on Easter, on the Ascension of the Lord [Note: L omits this], at Pentecost, on Sundays and the principal feasts [Note: L reads “chief feasts,”] and on the appointed days of fasting, we utterly prohibit legal proceedings from being carried out and public inquiries from being pursued, so that the solemnities of Christians may be celebrated with complete vigilance [Note: A reads *solennitates quod christianorum* (“the solemnities which [are] of Christians”); V, Vn, and E read *solennitas quod christiana est* (“the solemnity which is Christian”).].

[Note: The Vienna, Vn, and Estense codices add: “These are the principal festivals in the year, which must be honored in every respect: the Nativity of the Lord; Saint Stephen; Saint John the Evangelist; the Holy Innocents; the octave of the Lord; the octave of the Epiphany; the Purification of Saint Mary; the eight days of Easter; the greater litany; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; Saint John the Baptist; the octave of the Apostles, especially Saints Peter and Paul; the dedication of Saint Michael the Archangel; Saint Martin; and the Assumption of Saint Mary.”]

### [Col. 0853]

# Constitution of Otto III at Pavia  
*(A.D. 998, 20 September)*

[Note: Holstenius, Labbe, and Muratori published it after inserting it into the *Chronicon Farfense*, in *Scriptores rerum Italicarum*, vol. II, p. 207, and vol. II, pp. 496–497; for this reason we present it again. We do not deny, however, that it contains certain things—for example, the phrase “whether they are priests” and the year of the pontiff—which may raise some suspicion concerning the text’s complete authenticity.]

### [Col. 0855A]

Here begins the constitution of the sacred law decreed by the lord Otto, most pious emperor.

Otto, by the grace of God Roman emperor augustus, to the consuls [Note: The words “of the senate and Roman people” are absent in Labbe], the senate and people of Rome [Note: The reading is “to the senate and Roman people according to law”], archbishops [Note: “Bishops” has certainly fallen out], abbots, margraves, counts, and all judges established within Italy, forever.

We have learned that the bishops and abbots of the churches abuse their possessions and grant them to any persons whatsoever by written instruments, not for the benefit of the churches but for reasons of money, kinship, and friendship.

When their successors are admonished to restore the houses of God, to fulfill the duties of the commonwealth and our service, they claim that the estates of their churches are held by others and thereby demonstrate that they are unable to carry out what has been commanded.

Therefore, because the condition of God’s churches is being destroyed, and because our imperial majesty likewise suffers no small injury when our subjects are unable to render the services they owe us [Note: This phrase is absent in Muratori, II, b.], we establish and confirm by imperial edict that every written instrument—whether issued under the name of a lease or of an emphyteusis—which has been made concerning the churches of God, or which in any way cannot be brought into effect, shall expire when its author dies, and that the sole person who shall suffer loss is the one who bound and obligated himself by that document. The aforesaid losses shall in no way affect the person who succeeded him in the administration.

Rather, his successor shall have full freedom to recall to the church’s own right everything alienated by leases or by any other written instruments, and to arrange matters so that he may be able to render the service owed to God and to us.

For if kings and emperors are not permitted to give away what belongs to the kingdom and empire except to those who serve them during their lifetimes—churches being excepted—how can abbots and bishops be permitted to distribute the property of churches throughout the terms of their successors? [Note: Muratori II, p. 207 reads *se viventibus*; Muratori II, b, *servientibus* (“those serving [them]”).]

Every right—whether law, any written instrument, or any custom—if it is contrary to the benefit of the church, must be annulled. Nor should matters be confirmed by our authority when they are proved to have been introduced against the founder and propagator of the empire.

Therefore let this single document be held as law in such cases: whatever benefits the church of God and can in no way harm it.

If anyone should attempt to act against this constitution of ours, let him be judged a rebel, and let him be subject to anathema *maranatha*, unless he repents, by all the bishops who have subscribed to or given their consent to this edict of our empire, whether they are priests. Amen.

Enacted [Note: “At Pavia” has fallen out; Muratori] on 12 Kalends of October [20 September], in the twelfth indiction, in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Gregory V, promulgated by the hand of Gerbert, archbishop of the holy church of Ravenna, in that synod in which the papacy was taken away from Arnulf, bishop of Milan, in the basilica of blessed Peter called the Golden Heaven; and all the bishops who were present subscribed.

# Liturgical Monuments

## Gallican Masses

# A Critical Inquiry into the Eleven Gallican Masses Discovered by the Distinguished Mone

By Heinrich Denzinger, professor of theology at the University of Würzburg

Recently, when the highly accomplished diplomatist Franciscus Josephus Mone, prefect of the archives of the Grand Duke of Baden, was examining a palimpsest manuscript from the Reichenau Library in Karlsruhe [Note: Codex 253], he discovered eleven very ancient Gallican Masses, concealed beneath the script of Jerome’s commentary on Matthew. He also made them public, adding liturgical and palaeographical investigations and other fragments of liturgies which he had collected elsewhere [Note: *Latin and Greek Masses from the Second to the Sixth Century*, edited by Fr. J. Mone, archival director at Karlsruhe. Frankfurt: C. B. Lizius, 1850].

It would indeed have been appropriate to concede to this learned man the honor due to him: since by discovering this monument, certainly one of no small importance, he rendered an excellent service to Catholic scholarship, he might also have been the first to publish it in this collection. Nevertheless, since his conclusions concerning the date of the Masses, being less versed in theology, have not been equally accepted by scholars, and since it would not be useful to insert here longer treatises less relevant to our present purpose, we have undertaken to reconsider the entire question, using everything written on the subject either by the distinguished Mone himself or by others [Note: H. Denzinger, *Würzburger Quartalschrift*, 1850, third issue; J. G. Müller, *Theologische Monatsschrift von Hildesheim*, 1850, fourth issue].

The sacred remains which we owe to this most deserving man consist of forty-five leaves of Gallican Masses, though none of them survives complete. The leaves are in what is called small quarto, so that the codex may properly be called a little book, just as Gregory of Tours commonly calls the Gallican sacramentaries serving the sacrifice of the Mass *libelli*.

[Note: Zaccaria, *Bibliotheca Ritualis* I, 75, was the first to indicate this meaning of the word. Compare Gregory of Tours, *On the Lives of the Fathers*, 16: “One Sunday he was invited to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass, and he said to the brothers: ‘Now my eyes are covered with darkness, and I cannot look at the little book.’” — *History of the Franks* II, 22: “After the little book by which he had been accustomed to perform the sacred solemnities had been wickedly taken away from him, he nevertheless, having prepared himself, completed the entire office of the festival from memory, so that everyone marveled.” These are the words of the distinguished Mone.]

Our Masses belong among those which, under the headings of daily and Sunday Masses, are added to the others in the Gallican sacramentaries. Of their complete sequence, only two are missing, since the third bears the number V in the manuscript, and the fourth the superscript number VI.

Mone was mistaken when he concluded from this that, apart from the two missing Masses, our sacramentary contained no more than the eleven surviving Masses. The final Mass, that of Saint Germanus, bears the number VII, corresponding to the number III of the seventh Mass, so that other losses also appear to have occurred.

The eighth Mass is metrical; the ninth and eleventh refer to saints. It can scarcely be established by argument that one of them should be classified among Masses for the dead, as Mone maintains.

It follows that the Roman Canon was not yet in use, since the very short prayer after the *Sanctus* proceeds directly to the words “who, on the day before,” just as may also be seen in Mabillon’s Gothic-Gallican Missal.

In general, our Masses must be assigned to that purer and more ancient Gallican rite which Mabillon called Gothic-Gallican. The language in which they were written is the rustic language of Gaul, with many distinctive features, on which Mone has discussed the matter with great excellence [Note: In chapter 4 of his work, p. 39 and following].

As for the date, this copy of the sacramentary should certainly not be assigned later than the seventh century. For the beginning of the commentary written above it is copied in a script which appears to belong to the end of the seventh century. It may therefore be presumed to have been brought here from its homeland in Austrasia by Saint Germinius himself, the founder of the Reichenau monastery [Note: Pirminius built the monastery at Reichenau around the year 724 and departed to heaven in 754].

This is also confirmed by the fact that, at the end of the commentary, these words were added in a more recent hand: “May God bless Bishop John and our congregation.” This John was the second bishop of Constance of that name, and was also abbot of Reichenau; he presided over that church from the year 760 until 781.

Nevertheless, we must ascend much farther back in time. The final leaf of the sacramentary contains two prayers written in sixth-century Merovingian script, concerning the hostile invasion of foreign peoples. Our Masses therefore reach back to those times—or rather, they surpass them, since the Masses themselves must considerably predate the prayers appended to them.

Moreover, a Mass for Saint Germanus of Auxerre is found added to the Masses themselves. It was written in a somewhat more recent hand than the one that had originally formed the little book of Masses. This can be explained only by supposing that, after the primary codex had been completed, a more recent liturgy bearing the name of that saint was added as devotion to him grew.

Since that blessed man ascended to the heavenly realms in the year of Christ 448, the first ten Masses must have been transcribed not long after his death.

Finally, the liturgy seems scarcely assignable to a date later than the time of the Council of Chalcedon. Although it served the orthodox, it nevertheless speaks of the person of Christ in the manner found in ours. Thus, in the second *contestatio* of the sixth Mass, the Word is said to have been sent from heaven, “which, having been conjoined and solidified with human flesh, healed the ruined regions of the world and its ancient wounds.” It is scarcely possible to imagine that, after the anathemas pronounced against Eutyches, such a formula was not removed from the public liturgy, since it appears to favor the errors of that heresiarch [Note: The orthodox Fathers, too, used a term of this kind, although less precisely, as may be seen in Petavius, *De Incarnatione*, book III, chapter 2, no. 8 ff.].

We therefore have a latest limit to which we may descend: the middle of the fifth century. The question is where we should begin in establishing the earliest limit of the booklet’s period. If we follow the distinguished Mone, we must ascend to the time following that celebrated persecution of the Churches of Lyons and Vienne. Let the documents be produced and the arguments weighed! The eminent scholar says that his Masses contain passages suggesting that the persecutions were still raging and that they specifically, though not obscurely, point to that most ancient persecution. In the prayer of the fourth Mass, he says, these words are sung before the names: “Grant that we may truly believe in you, confess you rationally, and, if temptation arises, not deny you.” In the preface of the seventh: “May he deign to hear those afflicted by punishments and vexations …” Above all, he cites the following words of the fifth Mass’s *contestatio*:

“Indeed, no harps yet resound for us: your saints, who, by persevering harmony of virtues, conquered the beast of this age. [Here, he says, a word is missing, or the particle *qui* is superfluous.] No song of Moses belongs to us, who are still tossed amid the waves of this age. No voice of the angels—unless perhaps they can praise us [here he thinks *possumus*, ‘we can,’ should be read]—when we consecrate the body and blood of your most beloved Son; but a devout concern for the people, a holy prayer for the salvation of the congregation, and a mind intent upon divine worship, although it cannot explain the majesty of so great a work, nevertheless strives to practice frequently the use of the gift granted.”

From these words he concludes with the utmost certainty that, when the liturgy was composed, the persecutions were still in force; that Christians were being treated like the Jews detained in Babylonian or Egyptian captivity; and that the faithful could neither explain the majesty of divine worship—that is, publicly devote themselves to sacred rites—nor praise the God of the angels—that is, in a loud voice.

Yet neither we nor others have seen in the words cited what this otherwise most deserving scholar thought he had discovered; nor can we see it unless we wish to hunt out subtleties and do violence to the texts. The Babylonian and Egyptian captivities are here merely figures of the present life, in which we are not granted to praise God as we shall in that most blessed rest of the age to come. Nevertheless, the liturgy urges us to strive to offer at least what we can.

“Our harps”—namely, those of the heavenly Jerusalem—do not yet resound for us; nor do the saints yet sing the song of Moses for us, since we are still tossed by the waves [Col. 0859] of this life. The saints occupy the place of Moses here; and, since the people have not yet crossed the sea of this age or escaped its dangers, they cannot sing a triumphal hymn over us. Nor, the *contestatio* continues, are the heavenly voices of the angels yet heard praising us for the victory won—unless perhaps the angels who stand beside the sacred sacrifice can praise us on account of the extraordinary and wholly divine work in which we are engaged. Therefore we cannot perform the work of God worthily, nor explain—that is, set forth in words and exalt—the majesty of so great a sacrifice; nevertheless, we ought to strive to practice frequently the use of the gift granted, lest worship be lacking to God or grace to the people. This is plainly the meaning of the passage.

As for the other two points, it must be admitted that the passage looks back to persecutions and to the danger of corruption arising from them, especially since in the preface of the seventh Mass, among the various orders for whom the priest implores God, no mention is yet made of Christian rulers. Nothing follows from this, however, except that certain parts of the liturgy are extremely ancient and were composed during the time of persecutions. It cannot legitimately be concluded from this that this complete form of the liturgy, as presented by the Reichenau manuscript, must be assigned to such a period. Similar passages are found in both of Mabillon’s Masses [Note: *Liturgia Gallicana*, book III, pp. 243–244; *Patrologia* vol. LXXII, col. 27 A, “Prayer for Exiles”; *Musaeum Italicum*, vol. I, p. 320; *Patrologia* vol. LXXII, col. 497 C, “Prayer for Those Who, Detained in Prison Bonds and Captivity, Cannot Attend Easter.”], although the period of those Masses must certainly be placed much later. Finally, the fifth century likewise did not lack persecutions stirred up by Arian barbarians, nor the danger of corruption arising from them.

Once these points have been established, it will scarcely be worthwhile to treat at greater length the considerations by which Mone specifically attempted to refer the cited words to the first and most celebrated calamity of the Church in Gaul. There is scarcely anything in them that did not occur in every persecution, or that cannot be bent to the editor’s interpretation only by altered readings and twisted explanations. Finally, there are so many documents from a later age, and so unmistakable, that it is inappropriate to linger over this matter any longer.

Above all, we have formulas of doctrine that differ from those of the second or third century—not, I say, in teaching, but in their manner of expression. The word *Triad* or *Trinity* occurs on almost every page, whereas its use was exceedingly rare in the third century of the Church: the first instance is found in Theophilus of Antioch, and afterward in Tertullian.

The collect of the third Mass presents the Nicene *ὁμοούσιον*—“consubstantial”—in these words: “The Son, with the Father who has always existed, ruling all the ages consubstantially and equally.” The *contestatio* of the same Mass says that the Holy Spirit “subsists through a mystical procession from the Father and the Son.” This addition was made to the creed at the time when invading barbarians devoted to the Arian faction were devastating Gaul and Spain, so that the divinity of the Holy Spirit might be defined against their error. The Council of Galicia in 447 was the first of all to employ such an addition. Accordingly, such a controversy can scarcely have arisen in Gaul before the beginning of the fifth century, and such a formula can scarcely have been used in the public liturgy. Indeed, it will later appear that perhaps the earliest monument of such a formula is found in our Masses.

Unless we are mistaken, we seem to have detected another indication in certain words of the *contestatio* of the fifth Mass, from which it follows clearly enough that our liturgy was not composed before the beginning of the fifth century. The liturgist says that man, being clay, is indeed unworthy to praise God, but that God himself breathed an immortal mind into this clay, gave it the law and the prophets, and caused the Savior to triumph on the cross through this clay. Finally, he adds:

“What shall I say? Incorporeal powers are tormented at the ashes of your martyrs: this clay burns those whom no flame touches; dust torments those whom the punishment of claws does not reach; a groan is heard whose tortures we do not see.”

These words certainly seem to refer to some highly remarkable events that preceded the period of the liturgy. For after those general statements by which he had exalted the dignity of man, the author of the liturgy would scarcely have related so specific an event unless it had been something that, shortly before the liturgy was written, had struck everyone’s minds.

Now we find something similar in Gregory of Tours. In book II, chapter 30, of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, while discussing the miracles of the most holy martyr Julian, he relates the following:

“When the possessed come, they often utter insults against the saint of God, asking why he summons other saints to his festivals. They confess by name the virtues and merits of those saints. For they say: ‘Let it be enough for you, Julian, to torment us by your own power. Why do you challenge the others? Why do you invite strangers? Behold Martin of Pannonia, our perpetual enemy, who drove three dead men from our caves. Here is Privatus of Gévaudan, who refused to hand over his sheep to the barbarians, although they had been stirred up by our instigation. Here is Ferreolus, your colleague from Vienne, who sent us punishment in you and protection to the inhabitants. Why do you summon Symphorianus of Autun, or Saturninus of Toulouse? You have assembled a council to inflict infernal torment upon us.’ When they say these and similar things, they represent the saints of God to human minds in such a way that no one doubts that they are present there. Yet many who are ill are healed by them and depart restored.”

He also relates that a possessed man, before Julian’s relics, “striking his hands together, began to rave and cry out that he was being burned by the power of the martyr Julian” [Note: Chapter 44.], but was afterward freed by touching the sacred relic. Moreover, when Julian’s relics were carried to the basilica constructed in his honor, the possessed man complained that Martin had joined himself to Julian [Note: Chapter 34.].

How frequently such events occurred may be inferred from the words with which Gregory concluded his account:

“From that time onward, as the years passed, so many possessed persons, sufferers from chills, and people afflicted by various diseases were healed by the martyr’s power that neither their names could be retained nor their number counted.”

Julian himself suffered martyrdom under Diocletian. All these events took place in his basilica at Brioude, which, as may be inferred from Gregory himself [Note: Chapters 7 and 9.], was built at the time when the Burgundians had scarcely yet invaded Gaul—that is, at the beginning of the fifth century.

These considerations themselves prevent us from assigning our liturgy to the latter part of the fourth century, as did the distinguished J. G. Mueller, professor at Hildesheim, although in other respects he admirably corrects Mone’s errors, using almost the same arguments as we do. Both the events we have reported from Julian’s Life and the statements concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit exclude a date for such a booklet in the fourth century. Finally, there is the character of the manuscript, which the distinguished Mone, a competent judge in this matter, proved to belong to the first half of the fifth century. The added Mass of Saint Germanus is written in nearly the same script as the Darmstadt manuscript of the canons from the year 535, and cannot be later, since manuscripts of a later age already differ in many respects. The script of the ten Masses could belong to the fourth century, were it not that the letter *d* occurred less frequently; hence he rightly judges that it must be assigned to the first part of the fifth century.

[Col. 0861] 1–4. From the first ten Masses. — 5, 6. From the Mass of Saint Germanus of Auxerre. — 7. Prayers added at the beginning of the sixth century. — 14–18. From the ten Masses.

[Col. 0863] Once this has been established, it follows that our Masses, apart perhaps from a few very minor exceptions, are the oldest monument of the Gallican liturgy. For the Gothic-Gallican Mass published by the blessed Cardinal Giovanni Maria Thomasius [Note: *Codices sacramentorum*, Rome 1680, p. 263; *Patrologia* vol. LXXII.] must be assigned to after the year 687, since it commemorates Saint Leodegar, who died in that year, and appears to belong to the beginning of the eighth century. The other Gothic-Gallican Sacramentary, which Mabillon included in his *Musaeum Italicum* [Note: *Mus. Ital.*, vol. I, p. 278.], belongs to the end of the sixth or the beginning of the seventh century, since it lists Martin and Benedict in the canon and celebrates Blessed Sigismund, who was killed by the Arians in 523.

Apart from its venerable antiquity, the monuments of ecclesiastical tradition contained in this liturgy deserve celebration; from what has been said, they must be assigned to the first part of the fifth century. Here we have the sacrifice of the Mass [Note: Mass 2, prayers at the peace, after the mystery; Mass 4, collect; Mass 5, after the secret prayer.], a prayer for the dead [Note: In the prayers after the names of Masses 2, 3, 4, 5, and 8.], the veneration of the saints [Note: Masses 9 and 11.] and of relics [Note: Mass 5, in the *contestatio*.], the sacrament of penance [Note: Mass 4, second *contestatio*.], and the benefit of the Mass for the dead [Note: Mass 8, prayer after the names.].

What must especially be noted is the remarkable evidence for transubstantiation. The third Mass calls upon God “to grant the sanctification of his power, so that this offering, converted into the body and blood of Christ, may bring benefit”; and further, “to pour the Spirit of sanctification upon these creatures placed upon your altar, so that, through the outpouring of the heavenly and invisible sacrament, this bread, changed into flesh, and this chalice, transferred into blood, may be grace for all,” and so forth. Finally, the fourth Mass prays “that it may become for us a legitimate Eucharist through the transformation of the body and blood of the Lord.”

This word “transformation” should certainly not be interpreted, as is customary among us, as referring merely to a change of some external form. For *forma*, μορφή, meant among the ancients the same as οὐσία, “essence,” following the Apostle, who says in Philippians 2:6 that Christ, being in the form of God, took the form of a servant. Accordingly, the Fathers often designated both natures in Christ by the term “forms” [Note:

Petavius, book VII *On the Incarnation*, chapter 8, nos. 3 and 9; book IV *On the Trinity*, chapter 3, no. 2:

“To what the most celebrated author has brought together, one may add Ovid, who at the beginning of his work indicates that he understands *metamorphosis* in no other way than as a change of essence:

> My mind impels me to tell of bodies changed  
> into new forms.

“This appeared so strange to interpreters ignorant of ancient usage that Scaliger called the opening exceedingly unfortunate, while Vossius admitted a *hypallage*. The Gallican interpreter of Ovid, de Saint-Ange, suspected the matter more perceptively. (*Oeuvres de Saint-Ange*, vol. II, Paris, 1823, p. 148.)

“Also relevant is Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 22. To show that the Word was not changed after assuming humanity, he says:

‘It is necessary to believe God immutable and without form, just as he is eternal. Transformation, however, is the destruction of what previously existed. For whatever is transformed into something else ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not … But the Word is God, and the Word of the Lord remains forever, obviously by persevering in his own form … for if the Word became flesh through a transformation and alteration of substance, Jesus would now be one substance formed from two.’”]

Hence Psellus says: “Substance, form, and nature are one in the Logos.”

Finally, concerning the method by which the distinguished Mone had the text printed, the following points should be prefaced; he himself drew attention to them. He rendered the ancient comma, which resembles the numeral J, by the modern sign. He retained the punctuation of the manuscript; since this differs astonishingly from ours, the signs seem to indicate musical phrasing rather than divisions of sense. He himself enclosed the number of the Mass in parentheses and printed it in italics; likewise, he added the names of the prayers, following the example of Mabillon’s Gothic Sacramentary. The titles of the prayers and the numbers of the Masses that survive in the manuscript are reproduced in larger, upright type. The number of each manuscript folio is added in the margin, and the end of each folio is indicated by a vertical line. We have retained Mone’s notes wherever possible and added a few of our own.

[Col. 0863]

## ELEVEN GALLICAN MASSES DISCOVERED BY F. J. MONE, DIRECTOR OF THE ARCHIVES OF THE GRAND DUKE OF BADEN

(*Lateinische und Griechische Messen aus den zweiten bis sechsten Jahrhundert herausgegeben von Franz Joseph Mone, Archivdirector zu Karlsruhe.*) (C)

## MASS I

[Col. 0863]

### Before the Lord’s Prayer

… may command them to be freed in his holy name, and let us now assist them with our prayers—those who, still ignorant of the true path, are held by the devil in the errors of the world—so that he may enlighten all by the knowledge [Col. 0864] of his majesty, through Jesus Christ our Lord, whose commandments we retain [Note: At Mabillon, p. 202: “retaining the precepts.”], and we pray and say:

### After the Lord’s Prayer

Deliver us, Lord, deliver us from every evil, and establish us in every good work [Col. 0865A] [Note: Mabillon, p. 192: “Deliver us from every evil, and guard us in every good work.” P. 189: “Deliver us from evil and guard us in goodness.” Compare pp. 294 and 297, *Apostolic Constitutions* VIII, 8: “Let us pray that, having turned away from every unlawful work, they may be joined to every good deed.” *Missa of Saint Basil*, in Goar, *Ritus Graecorum*, p. 148: “Turn us away from every evil work, and join us to every good work.” From the Epistle to Titus 3:1.]—you who live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

### After Communion

Having been refreshed by spiritual food and drink [Note: Mabillon, p. 190: “refreshed by heavenly food and drink.” P. 203: “restored by spiritual food and refreshed by a heavenly cup.” P. 296: “fed at spiritual banquets.”], let us venerate God the almighty Father with the fitting thanksgiving, through our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, who lives and remains with him together with the Holy Spirit for eternal ages, for ever and ever. Amen.

### Collect

Hear us, God the almighty Father, and grant what we ask through the Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives [Note: The present tense, as also in *vives*, according to the manner of rustic speech.] and reigns, God, for ever and ever [Note: The same prayer occurs in Mass 6.].

### Blessing

May your worthy mercy, Lord, regard with compassion the voice of those who ask, and not reject anyone in particular [Note: That is, *cunctos*], making this vow on our behalf: that we may receive what you know to be necessary, so that our intemperance may not desire to ask for anything other than what your power knows to be fitting. Through the same Lord.

## MASS II

### Collect

Beloved brothers, let us unanimously beseech the God who saves the faithful and preserves believers, the eternal God, the author of immortality, that by the gift of his spiritual mercy he may unceasingly grant us his compassion. Through the same Lord.

### Collect before the Names

God, who according to your greatness are poured out throughout all things, and yet are wholly present everywhere [Note: A scribal error. Read *ubique*, “everywhere.”], discerning the qualities of every will according to places, times, and persons, capable of receiving every vow, graciously hear us. Since you look upon all things, sustain them, and have mercy upon all. Through the same Lord.

[Col. 0865C]

### After the Names

After the names have been recited, may the Lord bless them, and may this offering be acceptable to the Lord; may intercession, received with our prayers, support us; and may the spirits of our dear ones rest in joyful dwelling places and attain the joys of the first resurrection [Note: “Of the first,” as at Mabillon, p. 292, “in the first resurrection with your saints and elect”; p. 299, “in the first resurrection,” Revelation 20:5; 1 Thessalonians 4:16.]. Through our Lord.

### At the Peace

Hear us, our saving God [Note: That is, *salutaris*.], and graciously admit us to the fellowship of divine sacrifices. In your kindness grant us this peace. Through the same Lord.

### Contestatio

It is worthy and just. It is truly fitting and just that we should venerate you, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, in every place and at every time, at every moment; that we should be suppliants before you and offer you our prayers [Note: That is, *preces*]; that we should adore you with our whole devotion and affections [Note: *Affectibus*]. O God, who are beyond all virtues [Note: *Omnes*, “all”;], beyond every power, God, judge of the universe and of hidden things, whom heaven and earth, whom angels and archangels, whom thrones and dominions, whom cherubim and seraphim proclaim with unceasing voice, saying: Holy, holy, holy.

### Contestatio

It is worthy and just that we give thanks to you, Lord God, through Christ Jesus your Son, who, although he was the eternal God, deigned to become man for our salvation.

O unique and singular, yet manifold mystery of our Savior! For one and the same person is both the supreme God and perfect man, the highest priest and the most sacred sacrifice. According to divine power he created all things; according to human condition he liberated man [Note: The perfect tense, as also below, *explebit*.]; according to the power of sacrifice he atoned for the defiled [Note: Accusative plural, as also *offensus*.]; according to priestly right he reconciled the one who had been offended.

O unique mystery of redemption, singular mystery, in which that ancient wounds were healed by the Lord’s new medicine, and the first man’s prejudicial sentence was cut away by the privileges of our salvation. The former, driven by the goads of desire, stretched out his hands intemperately toward the tree; the latter, fastened by the nails of obedience, patiently attached himself to the cross. The former, enticed by pleasure, satisfied the desire to taste; the latter was afflicted with undeserved sufferings of pain [Note: That is, *doloris*, “of pain,” as *debitores* below should be read]. Therefore, deservedly, punishment became the release of innocence, and debtors were justly discharged. For the guilty are dismissed from debts [Col. 0866C] which the one who owed nothing abolished on their behalf.

This singular mystery is venerated not only by human beings on earth but also by the angels in heaven. To him …

[Note: The entire concluding clause is also found in Mabillon, pp. 195–200.]

### After the Sanctus

Truly holy, truly blessed is our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son [Note: After the Sanctus, the *Apostolic Constitutions* VIII, 12, has a similar prayer, beginning: “For truly you are holy—your Son, our Lord and God, Jesus Christ.” Compare the Mass of Saint Basil in Goar, *Ritus Graecorum*, p. 142, and the Liturgy of Saint James in Renaudot, vol. II, p. 31.], who on the day before …

### After the Mystery

Let us beseech the glory of our eternal Lord and God, praying [Note: Nominative plural.] that you may drench this sacrifice with your blessing, blessedness, and the dew of your Holy Spirit, so that for all who receive it, it may be a legitimate Eucharist [Note: “A legitimate Eucharist” also occurs in Mabillon, pp. 202, 251, and 296. So too in Mass 4 and Mass 5, with the predicates “true,” “pure,” and “legitimate.”] through Jesus Christ your Son, our God, Lord, preserver, and savior. To him [Col. 0867A] with you, Lord, together with the Holy Spirit [Note: In place of the ablative.] belongs an everlasting kingdom and perpetual divinity for ever and ever. Amen.

[Note: This Mass is not complete, for the prayers after the consecration are missing. It has, moreover, a double preface, like the Masses that follow.]

## MASS III

### Collect

Let us beseech the almighty God, the venerable Father subsisting in the Trinity, author of divinity; the Son, with the Father who has always existed, ruling all the ages consubstantially and equally [Note: Several accusatives follow here in place of ablatives.], beloved brothers, with the fullness of love, so that our senses, separated from earthly actions, may be joined inseparably to him from whom they understand that they have received the life they possess. When the devout mind, humbling itself before its author, has submitted itself, may our Restorer exalt those who have been bowed down by the power of the majesty of him who redeemed them. Through the same Lord.

[Note: In the manuscript I have *F KI*. This form of address occurs in the most ancient Sacramentaries and Homiliaries. Compare Mabillon, pp. 190, 204, and 283. The Frankish Missal often uses the formula *dilectissimi fratres*, “most beloved brothers,” which also occurs in our Masses. Roman epitaphs likewise use this spelling, *karissimus*, and this is the so-called lapidary form.]

### Before the Names

God, who are an overflowing fountain of mercy, slow to vengeance [Note: *Vindictam*, “vengeance.” The abbreviation sign is missing.] and swift to pardon, whom the ignorance of our sins does not turn back, but whom patience mercifully awaits: graciously forgive us. Grant us understanding, love what is loved, and imitate it blamelessly, so that, while avoiding what causes death, we may be able to approach you, going before us, through whom we may live. Through our Lord.

[Note: The passage from here to the end is corrupt.]

### After the Names

Beloved brothers, let us reverently and humbly beseech the propitiator for our crimes, that, after the names of the dead have been recited [Note: Mabillon, p. 218: “after the series of the names of the dead has been recited.”], he may graciously regard the gifts of those who offer them; that, having bestowed the sanctification of his power [Note: In place of the ablative.], this offering, converted into the body and blood of Christ, may bring benefit; that it may become rest for the dead, reward for those who offer, and salvation for those who receive. Through our Lord.

### At the Peace

God, ruler and creator of every creature [Note: *Dominator*, “ruler.”], whom to acknowledge is light, whom to worship is salvation, and whom to desire is a crown: willingly receive our humility and graciously grant the gifts of your divinity, so that we who offer the gifts of your honor may not suffer the debts due for our guilt. We beseech you that all who are joined in the kiss may be more deeply united in affection, and may hold in this heart what is expressed by the mouth. Through the same Lord Jesus Christ.

### Contestatio

It is worthy and just. It is truly fitting and just that we give thanks to you, almighty and eternal God, Father, only-begotten Son, and Holy Spirit, subsisting by a mystical procession from the Father and the Son: one and the same substance of the three persons in the holy Trinity, coeternal, and not divided by discord; equal in power, united in will, remaining itself in itself, before all times and ages, possessing nothing beyond itself and knowing nothing within itself that is not itself, surpassing all things and filling all things, containing places and exceeding places, needing nothing and filling everything, ineffable in speech, effective in power, and, although not contained by voice, creating heaven, earth, and seas, with their forms and kinds, by the sole command of your power.

But among the other living creatures you created man more particularly for your praise, in the image and likeness of the most blessed Trinity [Note: *Ut*, “so that.”], so that, placed in the sweetness of paradise and serving the Creator, he might rule over the other creatures, and, faithfully serving you, might hold dominion over the other kinds of beings. But when the guilt of transgression had been admitted [Note: *Culpae*, “of guilt.”], man was cast out. Death succeeded the life of paradise, punishment succeeded sin, and he lay in darkness, despising the commands of your light. In this condition there was no one to show light to the blind, to extend a hand to the fallen [Note: “Having fallen, he extended a hand.”], or to restore a homeland to the exile and the gifts of life to the buried.

But you, merciful and compassionate Creator, grieving that sin had prevailed over your human creature, so that the one who lay fallen might be able to rise, descended with power inclined toward him. For in this way the person of the only-begotten Son absolved human flesh [Note: *Persona*, “person.”; *humanae*, “human.”], and what the almighty had given, the humble one restored by his mercy in forms. Therefore, let the one who is unworthy rightly proclaim what divine mercy bestowed upon the unworthy: that divinity might be wonderfully united, and that eternity might be granted to humanity through God [Note: Prayers of this kind, treating of the creation and end of man, Adam’s sin, and redemption, frequently occur before the consecration in the liturgies of the Eastern churches. Compare *Apostolic Constitutions* VII, 35–36; the Coptic Liturgies of Saint Basil, Saint Gregory, and others in Renaudot.]. To him …

### Contestatio

It is worthy and just. It is truly fitting and just, and holy, that we give thanks to you, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God; that we pour forth prayer to you, confess you, and glory in your praises. You command every word through wisdom, arrange wisdom by power [Note: *Virtute*, “by power,” as *ratione* follows.], and confirm reason. Therefore it is worthy and just to praise you, whom all the angels praise together, the stars marvel at, the seas bless, the earth venerates, and the underworld receives [Note: A scribal error for *inferna*, “the underworld”]. To you cherubim and seraphim never cease to cry out, saying:

### After the Sanctus

Blessed is God, who by a merciful purpose, to eradicate [Note: *Eradicandis*, “to eradicate,” rather than *erudiendis*, “to instruct.”] the crimes of our mortality, the only-begotten Son himself, in that part by which he became flesh, became mortal [Col. 0869A], voluntarily submitting himself to mockery. The pillar of his body supported the ruins of our love, and, crushing the weapons of his enemies beneath the weight of his fall [Note: *Pondere*, “weight,” rather than *rubore*, “redness”], he raises the church with a stronger strength [Note: *Robore*, “strength,” rather than *rubore*, “redness.”] than the one by which we destroy it [Note: Something appears to be missing here.]. Through the same Lord. Who on the day before …

### After the Secret Prayer

Therefore, remembering and observing the commands of the only-begotten [Note: Mabillon has “we remember the Passion,” p. 192 and p. 222; “therefore, observing these commands,” p. 227.], we beseech you, almighty Father, that you pour the Spirit of sanctification upon these creatures placed upon your altar, so that, through the outpouring of the heavenly and invisible sacrament, this bread may be changed into flesh [Note: In place of the accusative, as below *sanguine*, “into blood.”], and this chalice transferred into blood [Note: The invocation of the Holy Spirit is likewise used in the Eastern liturgies to change the elements.], and may be grace for all and medicine for those who receive it. Through the same Lord.

## MASS IV

[Col. 0869B]

### After the Prophecy

[Note: Mabillon sometimes has this title as well, p. 190 and p. 251. In Masses of this kind the following prayer is said after the prayers. It should also be noted that the number V occurs after this prayer. Hence it may be concluded that the prayer after the prophecy was not present in every Mass; otherwise it would have had to be added to the preceding section. Mone rather ineptly concluded from this that no other Mass had preceded in the Missal.]

While the prophetic words have been proclaimed, let us accompany them with the services of our devotion, return thanks for the blessing, and repay the obligation for the visitation; because the almighty has raised up a horn for his people in the house of David, assigning joy after the passage of ages, fulfilling the prophecies of the prophets, directing our steps and the way of peace, and bringing salvation. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

### VI

[Note: From this number it must be concluded that two Masses are missing from this sequence. From this Mone rather ineptly concluded that no other Masses had previously stood in the Missal. D.]

### Preface

[Note: This prayer occurs frequently in the Gothic Missal, but without a title. It seems doubtful whether it should be called a preface or assigned to the ordinary collect.]

Having confessed one God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, with the names of the persons distinguished but the divinity undivided, beloved brothers, let us beseech him with our whole minds that, in every place and time, all may possess right faith and an innocent life; may acknowledge the author of their created nature [Note: *Conditionis*, “of created nature.” The scribe’s dialect used the genitive singular of third-declension nouns in *-es*. He sometimes thought the form in *-is* was a plural dative and changed it to *-ibus*, as at the end of this Mass, where *benedictionibus* occurs in the place of the dative *benedictionis*.], recognize their redemption, understand that they will rise again, and know that they will be judged according to their works. And because, through the corruption of nature, once the fragility of our will has been touched, it is wounded, may the piety of his goodness, which he has granted, make it pleasing. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

### Before the Names

God, whose goodness is as immense as your power, grant that we may receive what you promise to the just, escape what you threaten to the guilty, truly believe in you, confess you rationally, live in a wholesome manner [Note: Mabillon, p. 219: “live in a wholesome manner”], may rest and delight be found in worshipping you; may they not deny you if temptation arises; may they abound in the necessities of temporal life and not lack eternal joys. Through the same Lord.

### After the Names

Sanctify, almighty God, what has been ordained by you; graciously and willingly receive what we offer, and mercifully forgive what we have done. May the glorious merits of your saints excuse us, so that we do not come into punishment [Note: Accusative, *poenam*, “punishment.”]. May the souls of the faithful departed, who rejoice in blessedness [Note: In place of the ablative.], help us; may those who need consolation be absolved through the prayers of the Church; and may the offering of those whose names are recited before your altar [Note: *Altare*, “altar.”] be pleasing in your eyes, so that it may be abundant for them in benefits. Through our Lord.

### At the Peace

Give us, Lord our God, your gift of peace, to guard and preserve; and grant that we may follow in your name as you yourself command [Note: *Ipse*, “he himself.”] and bestow through charity, so that in every circumstance we may know how to hate our faults, not persons; desire an end to crime, not to salvation; and, if there is concord among all, may love prevail, so that no one may be permitted either to inflict discord or to return it. Through the same Lord.

## (Contestatio)

It is fitting and just, almighty Father, always to give thanks to you, to love you above all things, and to praise you for everything. Your gifts are these: through your image, dignity is granted to all human beings; in nature, the capacity for eternity is graciously bestowed; in the soul, freedom of choice is provided; in life, the blessedness of baptism is offered; in grace, the inheritance of heaven is promised; in innocence, the usefulness of the remedy is preserved; in repentance, pardon through goodness is proposed; and for iniquity, punishment is set forth. Thus God’s mercy may abound all the more toward all human beings: that those whom he created may not degenerate in warfare; that those whom he taught may not perish in ignorance; that those whom he loves may not remain in punishment; and that those whom he redeemed may not depart from the kingdom. Before whose sight all the angels do not cease to cry out, saying: Holy, holy, holy.

[Note: Col. 0870D: *munere*, “by/through a gift,” is read for *munera*, “gifts.”]

[Note: Col. 0870D: accusative *veniam*, “pardon,” is used where nominative *venia* is required.]

[Note: *degenerare*, “to degenerate,” should be read.]

[Note: “before whose sight” is in the place of the accusative.]

## Another Contestatio

It is fitting and just that we always give thanks to you, God the Trinity: your power created us through the Word; through our merit it condemned us when we offended; through the Son your mercy freed us; through baptism and repentance it called us to the heavens. To whom, with all [the angels], Holy, holy, holy.

[Note: *pro* is printed in place of *per*, “through.”]

[Note: *filium*, “Son,” should be read.]

## After the Sanctus: Say

O God, who wishest a heavenly hymn to be offered to thee by us—[a hymn] both fitting and sacred—that we may attain both the places and the songs of the angels: let us take up the harmony of the heavenly powers in thy praise; let us also take up, through correction, the disposition of the higher life. Let us say those words of our Lord Jesus Christ which he handed down in remembrance of his Passion:

Through the Lord. Who, on the day before [his Passion]...

[Note: Col. 0871D: accusative *praedicationem*, “proclamation/praise,” is used in place of the ablative *praedicatione*.]

[Note: *memoriam*, “memorial,” should be read.]

## Collect

God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from your heavens look favorably and kindly upon this sacrifice of ours; pursue it with your most indulgent mercy. Let the fullness of your majesty, divinity, mercy, power, blessings, and glory descend, Lord, upon this bread and upon this chalice. Let it become for us the legitimate Eucharist in the transformation of the body and blood of the Lord, so that whenever and as often as we taste this bread and this chalice, we may receive for ourselves a memorial of sincere love, tranquil hope of resurrection, and eternal immortality in you and in your Son. This...

[Note: *benedictionibus*, “blessings,” is in place of *benedictionis*, “blessing.”]

[Note: Concerning this word, see our Prolegomena. D.]

[Note: Col. 0871D: *tranquilla*, “tranquil,” is used in place of accusative *tranquillam*, agreeing with *spem*, “hope.”]

## (Mass V)

### (Contestatio)

We are debtors of grace; by continual repetition [of the celebration of the most holy sacrifice] we venerate you, whether we consecrate the altars with a public sacred prayer, or whether, in the secret recesses of our hearts, we silently cherish with quiet affection those ineffable words that you have spoken, judging them worthy. For the voice says: “Just are your ways, O King of the nations; who will not fear and glorify your name?”

[Note: Read *viae*, “ways.” Mueller.]

Indeed, no lyres of your saints yet sound for us—those who, while persevering in harmony of virtues, conquered the beast of this age. We have no song of Moses, since we are still tossed amid the waves of this age. No voice of the angels—unless perhaps those who could be present with us are able to praise us when we consecrate the body and blood of your most beloved Son. Yet the devout care of prayer for the people, the holy prayer for the salvation of the congregation, and the mind intent upon divine worship—although it cannot fully explain the majesty of so great a work—nevertheless strives to frequent the use of the gift granted.

For who could pass over your divine gifts with a negligent understanding? You deigned to breathe the spirit of life into corruptible clay and dissolvable mud; you made the human being from what was mud. You vivified mortal matter according to your image and likeness with the spiritual vigor of nature, so that fiery vigor might animate the sluggish earth and dull clay within, and agile movement might give life to our flesh through the veins’ warm current.

What are we, and how much do we owe to this clay? To this clay the laws and the prophets’ oracles ministered;

[Note: Mab., p. 190 reads *oracula vatum*, “the oracles of the seers.”] to this clay the angelic ministries served. Upon this clay the Lord Jesus himself, pitying human labors, triumphed by the cross of his body.

What shall I say? At the ashes of your martyrs, incorporeal powers are tortured. This clay burns those whom flame does not touch; this dust torments those whom the punishment of claws does not reach. The groaning of those whose torments we do not see is heard. And how great are the rewards of this small labor: unhappy pleasure, which the wretched flesh expels! Why does it begrudge itself? It draws itself back from heaven and returns itself to the mud. Nor is this surprising, if earth outweighs it.

But because you, Lord God, almighty Father, in the body of your only-begotten Son lifted us up, and commanded heaven to separate us [the text is corrupt], I beg you: do not allow me to perish by violence. Let your mercy toward us be enough—that the soul enclosed in the body passes into wretched foreign laws, and that the punishment common to the race is paid for the error of one. Even if we have lost the privilege of nature, let us certainly not lose the grace of your redemption.

Therefore, Lord, preserve for yourself your purchase, which you acquired for yourself through the body of your most beloved Son. We owe nothing to this flesh and blood, and the command of the Lord’s redemption is that, as it is written, we should belong to him who rose from the dead. Rightly [we say this] to you.

[Note: The passage means, evidently, that we are debtors through the repeated celebration of the most holy sacrifice. The following words concern the Secret and therefore also the Canon of the Mass; from this one may conclude that it too was then recited in a subdued voice: “The ineffable words of the institution of the Eucharist have been spoken.” Mone. Perhaps *dictu* should be read. D.]

[Note: “they conquered” refers to your saints who triumphed over their persecutors and the devil. Mab., p. 198.]

[Note: *spiritu*, “spirit,” is in the place of the accusative. The abbreviation mark is missing.]

[Note: *erimus*, “we shall be,” is apparently intended.]

[Note: Cf. Romans 8:12.]

[Note: The text appears corrupt.]

### Another Contestatio

It is fitting and just; it is right and just that we give thanks to you, holy Father, almighty God. Although we are unable to reach the merit of your greatness in worthy speech, we nevertheless most willingly confess the debt of praise. Your unconquered name rules heaven, earth, and seas; and although all things are from you, you are found in all things.

You are so exalted that you possess the heights; so worthy of reverence that you do not abandon earthly things; and so compassionate that you are not absent even from the underworld. For although you are wholly and always everywhere, the clemency of your majesty—made known to the stars, disclosed to earthly things, and manifested among the dead—has shone forth.

By the mercy in which you abound, you nourish the faith of believers, so that the Holy Spirit has always worked through this very abundant number of prophets. They do not disagree, one with another; rather, every prophecy bears witness with harmonious voice to the one God and the gifts of God. Thus our faith becomes evident, and the intention of belief will possess greater increase because it is attested more abundantly by the number and testimony of the prophets.

When the members of faith were brought together from both sides, the fullness of the body was found. Nor are these things announced to us through the ages without reason: clearly, it was so that the heavenly gift would not come upon the unsuspecting, and that ignorance would not find it difficult to believe what enlightened faith ought immediately to receive.

Accordingly, after the ordinances of the law had been handed down and the voices of the prophets inspired, the signs proceeded, so that, when we rejoiced in the heavenly gift, we might also confess its author. Reverencing the mercy of God, we saw each of these things prefigured in Christ: how the signs previously announced immediately displayed an indication of the future Passion, so that the triumph of the Passion might overcome the captivity of the human race, when our God destroyed the adversary of death, who had held the power of death. To whom rightly [be praise].

[Note: *numero*, “by the number,” is printed in place of *numeri*, “of the number.”]

[Note: Mab., p. 280: “He enclosed it within the wall of faith.” The sentence is incomplete in the source.]

### Post Sanctus Prayer

This Christ, our Lord and our God, who willingly became like mortals throughout this entire age, displayed to you an unstained body and offered a pure and undefiled soul as an adequate expiation for the ancient offense. If it should again become stained, blood would wash it clean.

Having finally abolished the law of dying, he raised the lost body in heaven to the right hand of the Father. Through the Lord our God. Who, on the day before [his Passion]...

[Note: “similar” is read in one witness; *ad* is superfluous.]

[Note: *omnem*, “the whole,” is in the place of *omne*, “all.”]

[Note: Something appears to be missing here. Mone. Or at least the passage is obscure and corrupt. Its sense seems to be that the words “soul” and “body” should be taken generically, both of the soul and body of Christ and of those of other human beings. Christ therefore showed this soul unstained in himself to the Father, so that, if it should again become stained in human beings, it might again be washed by his blood. D.]

### After the Secret

He also adds this command: whenever his body is received and the blood is received, let there be a commemoration of the Lord’s Passion. Because of this action of Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord and God, we always proclaim glory. We ask that you bless this sacrifice with your blessing and pour upon it the dew of the Holy Spirit, so that for all who receive it, it may be a pure, true, and legitimate Eucharist, through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord and God, who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

### Another Prayer

Let us pray to our God that the offering which...

## (Mass VI)

### (Prayer before the Names)

...for the people. Be present [the printed *adsto* is corrupt; read *adesto*] to the one discharging the commanded services; let there at least be obedience. Because conscience is polluted through merit or desert [the construction is corrupt], let confession sought through guilt obtain pardon, since sinful conduct has lost glory. What wanton fault contracted in us through fleshly goads, let sighs cleanse through sorrow—what flesh is known to have committed through pleasure. Through the Lord.

[Note: The reading *adsto* appears corrupt; it should probably be *adesto*, as in Mabill., p. 210: “Be present to your people.”]

### After the Names

The naming of the offerers, and the making known also of the givers and of the persons to be received, has shown by the designation of the words that we should return to the chosen duties of prayer [the printed syntax is corrupt]. We hope in the immense power of the Trinity that it may confirm the vows of the living and loosen the prisons of the dead; grant grace alike to the living and the buried; hear those people when they invoke it; and not condemn those who invoked it formerly. Through the Lord.

[Note: *dilecta*, “beloved,” is apparently intended in place of *delicta*, “offense.”]

[Note: *hos*, “them,” is intended in place of *illos*, “him.”]

### At Peace

Hear us, almighty God the Father, and grant what we ask. Through the Lord. May the peace of the Lord be [with you].

### (Contestatio)

It is fitting and just to praise you, God the Trinity: you made your human being from a lump of clay, shaped and bound together by the twisting of the thread, and formed according to the likeness of your image through the work of harmonious limbs by a natural process. You made him heavenly from earth, everlasting from dust.

For when you immediately infused your spirit through the shameful limbs, blood grew warm in the veins, vigor in the nerves, and, at the command of the heavenly Creator, earth at once received soul, soul spirit, and spirit reason. Entrusting all the elements of your work to him, just as you had formed him superior in his limbs, so you willed him to be higher in merits also.

But, inflamed by the alluring pleasure of miserable flesh, he lost what had been granted while desiring what was forbidden. While he strove through forbidden foods to become unlike [himself—or, according to another reading, “like the gods”], he immediately received mortality in place of eternity, fasting in place of gluttony, punishment in place of presumption, and through guilt became subject to the condition common to all mortals: he deserved by guilt what he had not received by nature.

Yet you pitied the image of your form. You grieved that what you had made should perish, although he did not know that he had lost what you had given. Therefore, although he himself did not know the captivity of the chain, you appointed the manner of redemption: to send us your only-begotten Son, our Lord and God Jesus Christ, who would release in himself and through himself the bonds of our debts; who would overthrow our death by his death; and who, washed with the blood and water flowing from his wounds, would cleanse us and crown us with baptism and martyrdom.

He became for us the guide in paradise, the Redeemer in Tartarus, the Teacher in the world, and the inviter into heaven. To whom rightly [be praise].

[Note: *martyrii*, “of martyrdom,” is intended.]

[Note: Mone reads *dissimiles*, “unlike”; the distinguished Mueller correctly observed that *diis* should be read: “like the gods.”]

[Note: *confertim*, “in abundance,” is printed in place of *confestim*, “immediately.”]

### Another Contestatio

It is fitting and just; it is right and just that here and everywhere we give thanks to you, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God. You tore us away from perpetual death and the deepest darkness of the underworld, and you gave mortal matter, gathered from dissolvable clay, to your Son and to eternity.

Who could be a grateful narrator of your praises? Who could be an abundant advocate of your works? Every tongue marvels at you; all priests proclaim your glory. To chaos, the confused beginnings, and the perpetual darkness of things, you added wondrous forms, while the elements stood amazed, when the tender world blushed with the fires of the sun and the unformed earth marvelled at the commerce of the moon.

But lest no inhabitant adorn all these things and the globe stretch over empty objects alone, a figure was made from clay by your hands, more excellent than the sacred fire within could animate. Through its parts the sluggish soul became alive, agile.

It is not permitted, Father, to investigate the inner mysteries; the majesty of your work is known to you alone. What is that within the human being which, while the limbs tremble, makes earth alive; in which enclosed blood flows through the veins; by which the loosened forms of bodies are gathered together by rigid nerves; and in which, amid earthly entrails alone, the bones give off their scent?

But from where comes so great a blessing for the wretched, that we should be fashioned like your Son and like you, and that something from earth should be eternal? We lost the commands of your blessed majesty and, once more immersed as mortals in the earth from which we had come, we mourned the loss of the eternal consolations of your gift.

But your manifold goodness and immeasurable majesty sent the saving Word from heaven. Formed through mixture with a human body, it would heal the ruined parts of the age and the ancient wounds. Therefore all the angels, together with the numerous throng of the saints, praise him with unceasing voice, saying: Holy, holy, holy.

[Note: The passage after “darkness of things” appears corrupt.]

[Note: “tender world” is found in Proba Falconia, verse 130: “the tender globe of the world.”]

### After the Sanctus

Your mercy willed that this praise of your glory, resounding in the voice of heavenly creatures, should also become known to us, your servants. These gifts, celebrated in the starry seats, have appeared not only to be known by your servants but also to be imitated. Who, on the day before [his Passion]...

[Note: *imitandam*, “to be imitated,” is intended in place of *himetandam*, “to be hymned.”]

### After the Secret

Look, therefore, most merciful Father, upon the mysteries of the Son instituted for believers, the gifts offered by those who supplicate and to be distributed to those who plead. Through the Lord our God.

### Before the Lord’s Prayer

We are indeed unworthy, almighty God, of the name of sons. Yet, because you command us through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, although trembling, nevertheless obedient, we pray with humble mind and say:

[Note: *jubente*, “commanding,” is intended in place of *iouente*.]

[Note: *te*, “you,” is superfluous. Mone suggests reading *te et*, “you and.”]

### After the Lord’s Prayer

Our freedom liberates us from evil, because it is yours alone to increase merits and remit sins. Empty us of vices and fill us with virtues, so that, sanctified and increased, it may sanctify hearts while it is believed and erase sins while it is received, so that here and forever we may deserve to be saved. Through the Lord our God.

### After Communion

Refreshed by heavenly food and restored by the Lord’s cup, let us return praises and thanks to God the almighty Father. Through the Lord.

[Note: *refecti*, “refreshed,” is intended in place of *refesti*.]

### Blessing

Hear us, Lord, and grant what we ask of you. Give us your perfect peace from heaven today, and grant this day and the remaining days of our life to be peaceful. Through the Lord our God.

[Note: Mone thinks that two numerals are missing, namely VI, so that this Mass would be ninth in order. If, however, one counts backward from Mass VII of Saint Germanus, number III agrees with VII, so that this appears to be another order of Masses, from which some Masses are missing.]

## (Mass VII)

### Preface
