May this water and this oil be blessed and full of glory, and may they be holy, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, for the thanksgiving of your people and of all who have offered their children, your servants, to you, for the glory and honor of your holy Son. Receive them as a holy and heavenly sacrifice, as a sweet fragrance to your heavenly greatness, through the prayers of your holy angels and archangels.

Lord, deliver your people and [Col. 0948B] bless your inheritance; preserve and exalt it forever. Amen. Preserve it in the rightness of faith throughout all the time of its life, and let it abide in love, which surpasses all peace, through the prayers of all the saints and the intercession of the Virgin Mary, full of grace, mother of God, who is holy in all things, and of Saint John the martyr and Baptist, forerunner and guide of life, and of all the saints whom you chose from the beginning, through the grace of your only Son, with whom, together with the Holy Spirit, glory belongs to you forever and ever. Amen.

Then the priest says the Gospel prayer, namely:

Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us today our daily food [Col. 0948C]; forgive us our offenses and our errors, and grant that we also may forgive the offenses committed against us; and do not lead us, Lord, into temptation, but redeem and deliver us from every evil. For yours is the kingdom, the honor, and the glory, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

Afterward he says the prayer of the laying on of hands over those who are to be baptized.

Then he takes the cross and traces the water three times in the form of a cross, crying out three times:

Holy, holy, holy, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

Afterward he descends into the font and pours balsam [Col. 0948D] into it in the figure of a cross, saying:

Blessed is God the Father. Amen. +

Blessed is the only Son, Jesus Christ. Amen. +

Blessed is the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete. Amen. +

Then he says in a loud voice, “Alleluia,” while mixing the water with the balsam; with his right hand he says Psalm 131: “For the Lord has chosen Zion as his dwelling.”

And Psalm 28: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of glory has thundered.” And Psalm 33: “Draw near to him, and he will enlighten you.” And Psalm 65: “He has brought us through fire and water.” And Psalm 50: “You will sprinkle me, Lord, with myrtle, and I shall be cleansed,” up to the verse: “Do not cast me away from your presence.” Then he says: “Glory to the Father, and [Col. 0949A] to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.”

Afterward he says: “Honor be given here to all the saints. Blessed be God, who enlightens throughout all ages. Amen.”

Then the deacon leads those who are to be baptized toward the west and makes them enter toward the east; the priest receives them and wipes them, saying:

I BAPTIZE YOU IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER, AND OF THE SON, AND OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, THE PARACLETE. AMEN.

When this has been completed, he says the following prayer, for the absolution or restoration of the water to its first nature:

Lord, O Lord, good Father, our almighty God, who created all things from what does not exist, and from [Col. 0949B] nothing through your true wisdom, you are the one who gathered [Col. 0950A] the waters together into one mass at the beginning and established all things from the foundation of the world by the greatness of your power and your imperceptible understanding. You are the one, Lord, who made this water cleansing through the grace of your Christ over it, and made it, for these baptized servants of yours, a washing of regeneration and a renewal from their former error, so that they may repent of it and be enlightened by your light. We ask and beseech you, O good one and lover of humankind, to change it back to its first order and first nature upon the earth; but let it be for us a help and deliverance, so that we may always glorify the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and render you honor, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

# Various Monuments Pertaining to the Celebration of the Sacraments and to Ecclesiastical Offices of Every Kind

*(In Gerbert, Monuments of the Ancient Alemannic Liturgy.)*

[Col. 0949]

# Order of Baptism

*[From codex theol. 685, Imperial Library of Vienna, tenth century.]*

**[Note: [Col. 0949C]** Nothing is prefaced here concerning scrutinies or the appointed times of baptism. Indeed, the beginning itself immediately indicates something else. This codex was certainly written before the fixed seasons for solemn baptism were gradually abolished, roughly from the middle of the twelfth century onward. Yet this order is not of the kind that is commonly found in older sacramentaries, including those reported in our preceding volume, intended for use in an emergency—namely, when illness and the danger of death press urgently.

This is what Saint Augustine says in *On Faith and Works*, chapter 6: “When the final day perhaps presses upon someone, so that he may believe through a very few words, in which nevertheless everything is contained, and receive the sacrament, so that, if he departs from this life, he may go forth freed from the guilt of all his former sins.” Saint Cyprian had said earlier: “Let them hear also,” he says in letter 13, “that if any have been overtaken by danger and are at the point of death, your vigilance must not be lacking.”

Severus, however, together with other Fathers, had been severe toward the Novatians and other “clinic” Christians, who postponed baptism and sometimes deferred it until the very end [Col. 0949D] of life. The holy Fathers often denounce them, among them Saint John Chrysostom, in his commentary on John, volume VIII of his works, pages 104 and 147, and at greater length in homily 1 on chapter 1 of Acts, volume IX, pages 11 and following. There he places the gravest danger before their eyes, concluding on page 13: “How greatly do you think I am tormented when I hear that someone has died uninitiated, and I consider those intolerable punishments and that unavoidable torment?”

The holy Father considered that these matters should be pressed more seriously upon the leading men of the empire and upon the emperors themselves at Constantinople, moved by examples of the past. Saint Ambrose, however, in his funeral speech on the death of the emperor Valentinian, judged more gently concerning this pious prince, who had desired to be baptized by Saint Ambrose but was killed before he could obtain it. Thus, when the people of Milan were anxious about his salvation, Ambrose consoled them, saying: “I have heard that you grieve because he did not receive the sacraments of baptism. Tell me, what else is there in us except willingness, except petition? Indeed, he had this desire long before: that, before he came into Italy, he might be initiated; and recently he indicated that he wished to be baptized by me,” and so forth.

At that time, moreover, the appointed seasons were prescribed by the canons, outside which—except in a case of necessity—it was not permitted to baptize. Conversely, once the discipline had been changed, baptism was forbidden to be deferred for more than a month in the case of infants. See Launoius, *On the Ancient and Solemn Times of Baptism*, vol. II of his works, part II, p. 731.]**

First, before the doors of the church, the priest begins the sacrament of baptism by saying:

Do you renounce Satan?  
**R.** I renounce him.

And all his works?  
**R.** I renounce them.

And all his pomps?  
**R.** I renounce them.

Then blow three times into the catechumen’s face and say:

“Depart, devil, rebuked by him from this image of God, and make way for the Holy Spirit.”

Then make the sign of the cross on the forehead, saying:

“I place the sign of the holy cross of our Lord Jesus Christ upon your forehead.”

Likewise make the sign of the cross on the breast, saying:

“I place the sign of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, upon your breast.”

Then place your hand upon the child’s head, saying this prayer:

“Receive the sign of the cross of Christ both upon your forehead and in your heart. Take the faith of the heavenly commandments. Let your conduct be such that you may already be able to be the temple of God. Having entered the church of God, joyfully acknowledge that you have escaped the snares of death. Shudder at idols, reject images; worship God the almighty Father and Jesus Christ, his Son, who lives and reigns with the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”

## Another

“I beseech you, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, Lord, to command that the way of your truth and knowledge be shown to this servant of yours, who wanders uncertain and doubtful in the night of this age, so that, with the eyes of his heart opened, he may recognize you, the one God, the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father with the Holy Spirit, and may deserve to receive here and in the age to come the fruit of this confession. Through him.”

## Another

“We beseech you, Lord, mercifully hear our prayers and guard this chosen one of yours by the power of the Lord’s cross, with whose impression we mark him, so that, preserving the beginnings of your greatness, he may deserve to attain the glory of regeneration through the keeping of your commandments. Through him.”

## Another

“Receive the sign of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Immediately afterward, for the same little catechumen—that is, to make him instructed—the following prayer follows:

“Let us pray. Almighty and eternal God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, deign to look upon him,” etc.

“Let us pray. I exorcize you, creature of salt, in the name of God the almighty Father,” etc.

When this prayer has been completed, ask the names of each one and place some of the salt in the infants’ mouths, saying:

“Receive the salt of wisdom, having been reconciled, unto eternal life. Peace be with you.”

## Blessing after the giving of salt, for males and females alike

“Let us pray. God of our fathers, God, creator of the whole truth,” etc.

Here again, making the sign of the cross on the infants’ foreheads, let the priest immediately say the following prayers.

Here is the prayer over a male:

“Let us pray. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, God who [—] your servant Moses,” etc.

“Therefore, accursed one,” etc.

## Prayer over females, likewise making the sign of the cross on their foreheads

“Let us pray. God of heaven, God of earth, God of angels, God of archangels,” etc.

## The devil is driven away from both males and females alike

Therefore, accursed devil, acknowledge your sentence and give honor to the living and true God; give honor to Jesus Christ, his Son, and to the Holy Spirit, and depart from this servant (or this handmaid) of God, because God and our Lord Jesus Christ has deigned to call this one to his holy grace and blessing and to the font of baptism by this sign [Col. 0952A] of the holy cross that we place upon his or her forehead. You, accursed devil, must never dare to violate it.

## Likewise over males

“Let us pray. Hear, accursed Satan: adjured by the name of the eternal God and of our Savior, his Son, overcome by your envy, depart trembling and groaning. Let nothing be shared between you and the servant of God, who is now thinking of heavenly things, who will renounce you and your world, and who will live for blessed immortality.

“Therefore give honor to the Holy Spirit who is coming. Descending from the highest citadel of heaven, may he confound your deceptions, cleanse the breast by the divine font, make it a temple sanctified to God and a dwelling place, and, once entirely freed from all the harms of former sins, may the servant of God give thanks to the eternal God always and bless his holy name [Col. 0952B] forever and ever. Amen. Therefore, accursed one,” etc.

## Prayer over females

“Let us pray. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob,” etc.

## Likewise, prayer over a male

“Let us pray. I exorcize you, unclean spirit,” etc.

## This prayer over females

“Let us pray. I exorcize you, unclean spirit, through the Fa+ther, and the So+n, and the Holy + Spirit,” etc.

## Likewise, the prayer to be said immediately afterward

“Let us pray. I beseech you, Lord, for your eternal and most just mercy,” etc.

Here afterward the deacon reads the Gospel over the infants:

“The Lord be with you.”  
“The continuation of the holy Gospel according to Matthew.”

At that time infants were brought to Jesus, so that he might lay his hands on them and pray. But the disciples rebuked them. Jesus, however, said to them: “Let the little children come, and do not prevent them from coming to me. Amen, I say to you, the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.” And when he had laid his hands upon them, he departed from there.

After this, the priest, holding his hand over the infant’s head, silently sings the Creed, which is “I believe in God,” and the Lord’s Prayer, which is “Our Father.” When these have been read, the following prayer is said publicly for the catechizing of the infants:

“Let us pray. Do not be unaware, Satan, that punishments threaten you,” etc.

Here spit from your mouth onto the first two fingers—that is, the thumb and index finger—and, taking hold of the little lobe of the right ear, say:

“Ephphatha,” which means “to open.”

Then, taking hold of the infants’ nostrils, say:

“For a fragrance of sweetness.”

Then, holding the lobe of the left ear, say:

“But you, depart, devil, for the judgment of God will draw near.”

When all this has been completed, before the church the priest orders the little children to be brought into the church.

# Blessing of the Font

**[Note: [Col. 0951D]** We showed above that consecrated water was carried home by the faithful. You have this in the rubric of this baptismal order, as follows: “Here let blessed water be sprinkled over those standing around, and let anyone who wishes take some away to sprinkle wherever he wishes.” After this, “take the chrism with its vessel and pour it in the form of a cross over the baptismal water itself, mixing it together,” and so forth.

This is precisely what we noted in *Liturgical Investigations*, p. 436, from de Moleon’s *Liturgical Journey*: the faithful drew the consecrated water before the holy oil was mixed with it—a custom that still continues in our regions. Nor does the fact that in former times, as later and even now, water was always preserved throughout the year for administering baptism on days other than the appointed ones prove that the present order of baptizing outside the appointed seasons is late; nevertheless, the consecration of the baptismal water immediately precedes the baptism here.]**

Then the priest, saying “The Lord be with you”—which he must never say beforehand—reads the following prayer over the font:

“Let us pray. Almighty and eternal God, be present at the mysteries of your great mercy,” etc.

Thereafter the priest delivers the following blessing by singing, according to canonical authority:

“O God, whose Spirit was borne over the waters at the very beginning of the world,” etc.

Here he touches the water with his hand in the form of a cross.

Here he touches it with his hand as above.

“Let this holy and innocent creature be free from every assault of its attacker and cleansed by the departure of every wickedness. “Therefore I bless you, creature of water, through the living God, through the holy God, who in the beginning separated you by his word from the dry land, who caused you to flow from paradise—”

Here he divides the water into four parts with his hand in this manner: +

“—and into four rivers,” etc.

Here he changes the tone of the chant, as though reading a lesson.

Here he places a burning candle in the water and, bending over the font, says this word:

After this he breathes over the font three times in this manner: Ψ

“—and let him make the whole substance of this water fruitful for regeneration.”

Here he removes the candle from the water and immediately adds the following:

“Here let the stains of all sins be erased,” etc.

Here blessed water is sprinkled over those standing around, and anyone who wishes takes some away to sprinkle wherever he wishes.

After this, take the chrism with its vessel and pour it in the form of a cross over the baptismal water itself, mixing it together, saying:

“The pouring in of the chrism of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Paraclete, in the name of the holy Trinity. Amen.”

And in another form:

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, let this font be sanctified and made fruitful. Amen.”

When this has been completed, let the infants be presented in order before the priest, being held in the arms of those who are to receive them from baptism. Then at last the priest asks each one individually, [Note: [Col. 0953D] The customary renunciations of Satan and the profession of faith, such as are commonly read in ancient Latin in baptismal orders of this kind, are missing here. They are found in volume I of the *German Councils*, p. 51, in these words:

“Forsachistu Diobolae?” (“Do you renounce the devil?”) And the response: “Ec forsacho Diobolae.” (“I renounce the devil.”)

“En allum diobol gelde?” (“And all devil-worship?”) Response: “End ec forsacho allum diobol galde.” (“And I renounce all devil-worship.”)

“End allum Dioboles wercum?” (“And all the devil’s works?”) Response: “End ec forsacho allum Dioboles wercum, und wordum thuna eren de woden ende Saxnote, ende albam them unholdum, the hira genotas sint.” (“And I renounce all the devil’s works and words: Thunear, Woden, and Saxnot, and all the fiends who are their companions.”)

“Gelobistu in Got almehtigan Fadaer?” (“Do you believe in God the almighty Father?”) Response: “Ec gelobo in Got almahtigan Fadaer.” (“I believe in God the almighty Father.”)

“Gelobistu in Christ Godes Suno?” (“Do you believe in Christ, God’s Son?”) Response: “Ec gelobo in Christ Gotes Suno.” (“I believe in Christ, God’s Son.”)

“Gelobistu in halogan Gast?” (“Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?”) Response: “Ec gelobo in halogon Gast.” (“I believe in the Holy Spirit.”)

Eccard supplies more material in his *German Catechesis*, §13, preface.]**

having first named him or her, [Col. 0955A] so that they may firmly hold the Creed in God, in these words of belief:

And the sponsor responds below:

“I believe.”

**R.** “I believe.”

The priest:

“Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life?”

**R.** “I believe.”

After such a response from the little children, the priest makes the sign of the cross with exorcized oil upon the breast and between the infants’ shoulders, naming them, and says:

“And I anoint you with the oil of salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord, unto eternal life. Amen.”

When this order has been completed, the priest receives the infants from their parents, as is proper, and, at their request, baptizes them under a triple immersion—first the males and afterward the females—naming each one and using these words:

“N., do you wish to be baptized?”  
**R.** “I do.”

“I baptize you in the name of the Father.” And he immerses him once.

“And of the Son.” And he immerses him a second time.

“And of the Holy Spirit.” And he immerses him a third time.

But remember also to do this in the form of a cross. First carry the infant toward the eastern region, with his feet extended toward the western region. Second, toward the right, which is toward the southern region. Third, toward the left, which is toward the northern region.

When the infants have been lifted from the font, the sponsor of each one receives him and holds him within the *cuba*, while the infant’s feet still remain in the water until the priest, having asked for the chrism, brings it forward. Meanwhile he says:

“God the almighty Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who regenerated you from water and the Holy Spirit, and who gave you forgiveness of all sins.”

Here the priest makes the sign of the cross with chrism on the crown of the infant’s head, naming him, and says:

“He himself anoints you with the chrism of salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord, unto eternal life. Amen.”

After this, placing a cap over his head and naming him, he says:

“Receive a holy, white, and undefiled garment, which you are to present before the tribunal of Christ, in the name of the holy Trinity. [Col. 0956A] Amen.”

At last the infant is taken out of the *cuballa*, and on that same day they remain in the church until Mass has been celebrated, however many of them there may be. After Mass, before they receive the body and blood of the Lord, the following prayers are said over the newly Christian infants:

“Let us pray. Almighty and eternal God, who regenerated your servant from water and the Holy Spirit, grant him continual health, so that he may recognize the truth of your unity. Through him.”

## Another

“Almighty and eternal God, we humbly beseech your majesty to deign to present this servant of yours before your serene countenance, and to grant long-lasting health to the one to whom you have given the sacrament of baptism.”

After these prayers, the Eucharist is given to them, saying:

“May the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve you unto eternal life. Amen.”

When this has been completed, let them return home in peace; and every day from that day until the seven days have been completed, at the time of the anticipated [Note: [Col. 0955D] The same is found in Martène, vol. I, *On the Rites*, p. 203, in the fourteenth order of the monastery of Gladbach. Yet a mistake seems to have entered the text, and it should be read “also at the time of the evening Mass.” Perhaps scribes of a later age altered the text because they were ignorant of the ancient meaning of *missa* as a synaxis or collective service, as we demonstrated in vol. I of the *Liturgical Investigations*, book IV, chapter 1, on the authority, among other sources, of the Council of Agde in 506, whose canon 30 establishes:

“At the conclusion of the morning or evening Masses, after the hymns, little chapters from the psalms are to be said, and the people are to be dismissed toward evening with a collective prayer [Col. 0956C] and a blessing.”

That an evening synaxis was celebrated throughout the entire Easter week we learn from the Council of Mâcon in 585, whose canon 11 decreed concerning Easter week:

“During those six most holy days, no one should dare to perform servile work; rather, all gathered together, devoting themselves to the Easter hymns, should show our perseverance especially through our daily sacrifices, praising our Creator and Regenerator in the evening, morning, and midday.”

Mabillon, in *Gallican Liturgy*, book I, chapter 5, noted other synaxes or evening sacrifices from the same council. These are said in canon 9 to be celebrated according to the Lenten order, and at the Council of Vaison in 529, canon 3, they are called Lenten observances; the Second Council of Braga, canon 9, assigns them to the ninth or tenth hour. The Third Council of Orléans, chapter 29, decrees: “As for the morning sacrifices of the Masses, or the evening ones, let no one attend with weapons belonging to the use of war.” Whatever their precise character, the following certainly belongs to the earlier reckoning: in canon 14 of the same council, concerning the celebration of Masses on the principal solemnities, it is established that the celebration of Mass should begin at the third hour, so that people might more easily gather at the appropriate hours for the evening offices, that is, in the evening.] Mass, let them visit the church.

**The sacred order of baptism ends here.**

If a sick infant comes to be baptized, let the order written above be performed, and add the prayer “I beseech your eternal and most just mercy.”

“I beseech your healing, holy Father,” etc.

He says the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer and catechizes him:

“Nor should it be unknown to you, Satan, that punishments threaten you, that Gehenna threatens you, that the day of judgment threatens you, the day of punishment, the day that will come like a fiery furnace, in which eternal destruction will come upon you and all your angels. Therefore, devil, give honor to the living and true God and to Jesus Christ, his Son, who will come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

“In his name and power I adjure you, whoever you are, unclean spirit established in the body of this one who lies here: come out and depart from him, and let him become a clean vessel for the Spirit who is now coming into him. “I exorcize you, creature of water, in the name of God the almighty Father, and in the love of Jesus Christ, his Son, and of the Holy Spirit. I exorcize you, every power of the adversary, every assault of Satan, and every phantom: be rooted out and driven away from this creature of water, so that it may become a spring of water leaping up into eternal life. And whoever is baptized from it, let him become a temple of the living God, and let the Holy Spirit dwell in him for the forgiveness of all sins. Through him.”

[Col. 0957B] **The book of baptism ends here.** [Note: [Col. 0957D] In some places it is simply called the *baptistery* or the *order of the baptistery*. Charlemagne established the following in his capitularies concerning various matters, in 789, chapter 7: “Let the bishops hear the baptistery of the priests, so that they may baptize according to Roman custom.”]

In the celebrated sacramentary of the monastery of Reichenau, preserved in the Imperial Library of Vienna and catalogued by Lambecius, the following prayer for baptizing a sick person is found:

“I beseech your healing, holy Lord, almighty and eternal God, who comes to the aid of those in danger, who moderates the scourges while you chastise. Therefore we humbly beseech you to rescue this servant of yours from this illness, so that the enemy may not prevail even to the temptation of his soul. As with Job, set a limit for him, lest the enemy begin to triumph over this soul without the redemption of baptism. Delay, Lord, the departure of death and extend the span of life; raise up the one whom you may lead to the grace of your baptism. Through him.”

[Col. 0957C] **Prayer over the water for baptizing a sick person.** After you have catechized him, bless the water with these words:

“I exorcize you, creature of water, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, and of the Holy Spirit. If there is any phantom, any power of the enemy, any assault of the devil, be rooted out and driven away from this creature of water, so that it may become a spring leaping up into eternal life. And when this servant of the Lord has been baptized, may he become a temple of the living God for the forgiveness of all sins, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. Amen.”

“You baptize and anoint him on the brain.” And you say:

“N., such-and-such, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Afterward you touch him on the head with chrism and say this prayer:

“Almighty God,” etc.

You give him communion and confirm him.

[Col. 0957D]

# Order of Confirmation
When the infants have been lifted from the font, let those who are to receive them be ready, [Col. 0958A] with linens in their hands; and let them receive them from the bishop, and from the priests or deacons who baptize them. The bishop, however, should return from the font to the sacristy, where he has arranged a seat—or to whatever place in the church he wishes—and sit there, so that, when the infants have been clothed, he may confirm them. Once clothed, let them be arranged in order, as they are listed, around him. The infants are to be held in the right arms; the older ones, however, should place their right foot upon the right foot of their sponsor.

Then the bishop, coming to the infants [Note: [Col. 0957D] In the order of the sacrament of confirmation, infants are here, as elsewhere, mentioned indiscriminately, although shortly before there is also discussion of older persons. The same applies to those reborn from the baptismal font, so that, according to 2 Peter 2, they may be like newborn infants. Thus Saint Zeno addresses the newly baptized in Sermon 1: “You who differed in age, differed in nation, suddenly emerged as brothers, suddenly as only-begotten infants.” Likewise, in Invitation 3 to the fonts, he alludes to the passage in Saint Peter: “Come now, why do you stand there, brothers, whom the generative water has conceived in faith and already brings forth through the sacraments? The solemn hymn is already being sung; behold, soon the sweet cry of infants is heard; behold, from the womb that gives birth in one day a most glorious crowd proceeds.” Paul Paciaudi cites these words in *On the Sacred Baths of Christians*, chapter 12, to remove the common error concerning a passage of Saint Isidore of Seville about the washing of the head, as though this service had been performed only for infants, in Book 1 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*; it is also cited by Rabanus Maurus and by an anonymous writer under the commonly circulated name of Alcuin. The passage is as follows: “The common people call this day the day of head-washing, because it was then customary to wash the heads of infants who were to be anointed, lest they should come to the anointing without observing the forty-day period.” He rightly observes that, if the heads of those to be baptized were washed when dirty after the observance of the forty days, this ought much more to have occurred with adults, who were capable of fasting.], while the archdeacon holds the chrism, wrapped around his shoulders and arms in linen cloth, and, with his hand raised and arranged over the heads of all, gives this prayer over them, invoking the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit:

“May the Holy Spirit come upon you, and may the power of the Most High keep you without sin. Almighty and everlasting [Col. 0958B] God, who have deigned to regenerate these your male and female servants from water and the Holy Spirit, and who have given them remission of all sins, send upon them your sevenfold Spirit, the Paraclete, from heaven. Amen. The Spirit of wisdom and piety. Amen. The Spirit of wisdom and piety. Amen. Fill them with the Spirit of your fear, and, being propitious, mark them with the sign of the cross of Christ unto eternal life. Amen.”

P. When the prayer has been completed, the deacons ask the name of each person, and the bishop, having dipped his thumb in the chrism, makes the sign of the cross upon each person’s forehead, saying:

“I confirm you and mark you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

“Peace be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

After all have again been confirmed, let him say these verses:

“Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord. May the Lord bless you from Zion, so that you may see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life. May the Lord preserve you in his most holy fear, he who lives and reigns as God for ever and ever. Amen.”

“Peace be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

Prayer:

“O God, who gave your Holy Spirit to your apostles and willed that through them and their successors it should be handed on to the other faithful, look favorably upon the service of our humility, and grant that the same Holy Spirit, coming upon the hearts of those whose foreheads we have anointed with sacred chrism, may graciously perfect them by dwelling within them as the temple of your glory. Through him who is with you.”

Let the deacon say:

“Bow down for the blessing.”

“Thanks be to God.”

“May almighty God bless you, who created all things from nothing and, in baptism through the Holy Spirit, granted you remission of all sins. May he who gave the same Holy Spirit to the disciples in tongues of fire, by his illumination enlighten your hearts and continually kindle them with his love. Amen. Thus, cleansed from all vices by his gift and defended from every adversity by his assistance, may we deserve to become his temple. May he himself deign to grant this.”

From the Codex of San Blas, ninth century.

For confirming children, let the bishop say:

“Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

Assistants: “From this time forth and for evermore.”

Bishop: “Our help is in the name of the Lord.”

Assistants: “Who made heaven and earth.”

Let us pray.

“Almighty and everlasting God, who have deigned to regenerate this male servant and this female servant of yours from water and the Holy Spirit, and who have given them [Col. 0959B] remission of all sins, send upon them your sevenfold Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, from heaven. Amen. The Spirit of wisdom and understanding. Amen. The Spirit of counsel and fortitude. Amen. The Spirit of knowledge and piety. Amen. Fill them with the Spirit of your fear, and, being propitious, mark them with the sign of the cross of Christ unto eternal life. Through Christ our Lord.”

Then, after asking each person’s name and dipping his thumb in the chrism, let him make the sign of the cross on each person’s forehead, saying:

“I mark you with the sign of the cross and confirm you with the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

When all have therefore been marked with the holy chrism, let him say:

“Peace be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

“Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord. May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life. Glory be to the Father, etc. Peace be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

Let us pray.

“O God, who gave your Holy Spirit to your apostles and willed that through them and their successors it should be handed on to the other faithful, look favorably upon the service of our humility, and grant that, when we have anointed with sacred chrism and marked with the sign of the cross the forehead of this person, the same Holy Spirit, coming upon this person, may graciously perfect the person as the temple of his glory by dwelling within him. Through our Lord.”

Concerning this rite, it should be noted that, if the bishop cannot say the foregoing prayers as often as people successively and individually come to seek confirmation, he should nevertheless not fail to say them at least at the end of the day, that is, after Compline.

(From Codex Vindobonensis Theologicus 277, twelfth or thirteenth century.)

Blessings over those confirmed [Note: [Col. 0959D] This is how the order of confirmation is entitled; it agrees almost entirely with the rite in use today and corresponds to what Tertullian, the most ancient of the Latin Fathers, explains clearly concerning this sacrament in chapter 8 of *On Baptism*. Furthermore, Edmond Martène, in Book 1, chapter 2, article 4, of *On the Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*, among various rites of confirmation, cites this one—“bowing down for the blessing”—from the Sacramentary of Moissac, and so forth. In the Roman Pontifical it is still prescribed in section 9: “Let no one who has been confirmed depart without having received the blessing, which the bishop shall give after confirming everyone.” This is widely neglected.]

“May the Holy Spirit come upon you, and may the power of the Most High keep you without sin. Amen.”

Another:

“Almighty and everlasting God, who reign, etc.”

And the bishop says:

“I confirm you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

“Peace be with you, and with your spirit.”

“The sign of Christ unto eternal life. Amen.”

“Peace be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

“O God, who gave your Holy Spirit to your apostles, etc.”

Then the deacon announces:

“Bow down for the blessing.”

“Thanks be to God.”

And the bishop gives the blessing:

“Almighty God, who caused you to be reborn through the water of baptism, may he himself strengthen you by the sevenfold gift of the Spirit, the Paraclete; for thus shall everyone who fears the Lord be blessed, so that he may obtain entrance into the heavenly kingdom. Amen.”

Another:

“May he bless you from Zion, so that you may see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of our life, and so that in all things you may take up the shield of faith, that you may deserve to be enrolled in the army of the eternal King.”

Another:

“May he preserve you in his most holy fear, and grant you unity of peace and triumphant victory over all enemies, so that you may preserve undefiled to the end the seal of faith that you bear. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and is glorified as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

“May the blessing of God the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit descend.”

Another blessing over those confirmed:

“May he bless you, etc., as above.”

Another:

“The blessing of God the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. And may the peace of the Lord always be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

“Go in peace.”

“Thanks be to God.”

[Col. 0959]

JUDGMENT OF THE PENITENT

(From the most ancient sacramentary of Rheinau in Alemannia, circa the year 1000.)

[Col. 0959D] The diversity [Note: [Col. 0960D] This preface is found in full in the ancient collection of penitential canons (in Martène, *Thesaurus novus anecdotorum*, vol. 4, col. 53), with the heading: “Here begins [the section] on various evils”; from this it is possible to correct the errors of our codex. At the very beginning, one should indeed read: “The diversity of faults.”] of faults produces a diversity of penances; for physicians of the body also prepare different medicines according to their kinds. They treat wounds in one way, disease in another, swellings in another, and putrefactions in another [Col. 0960D] [Note: [Col. 0960D] The same place adds: “and darknesses in another, fractures in another, burns in another.”]. Thus spiritual physicians also ought, by different kinds of treatment, to heal the wounds, diseases, faults, pains, sicknesses, and infirmities of souls [Note: [Col. 0960D] In the *Book of Penitence* from the archives of the Roman Church, in Canisius, vol. 2, p. 129, Basel edition of Basnage, we read as follows: “Thus spiritual physicians also ought, by different kinds of treatment, to heal the wounds of souls. But because it belongs to few to know, treat, heal, and restore all things completely to the state of salvation, therefore we earnestly admonish every learned priest of Christ to arrange everything not according to his own judgment but according to the statutes of the canons and the traditions of the Fathers; and to examine the condition of either sex, age, persons, poverty, cause, status of each penitent, and the very heart of the penitent; and according to these matters, as it seems good to him, let him, like a wise physician, judge each case.”]. But because these matters belong to few—namely, to know all things thoroughly, treat them, and restore them to the complete state of salvation [Col. 0961A] [Note: [Col. 0961D] Read: “to which they ought to restore them to the complete state of salvation.”]—therefore, according to the traditions of our elders, or at least a few things according to our partial understanding [Note: [Col. 0961D] Added: “and according to.”]; for in part we prophesy and in part we know, let us set forth certain matters pertaining to the remedy of the soul. We shall speak of remedies for wounds according to the definitions of the former Fathers; but first, most faithful brother, let us communicate to you the medicines of sacred discourse in abbreviated form [Note: [Col. 0961D] From this the most obscure passages in Martène may be corrected.].

The first is remission, by which we baptize [Note: [Col. 0961D] Read: “by which we are baptized.”] in water, according to the saying: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

The second is the effect of charity, as in the saying: “Because he loved the world” (Luke 7:4).

The third is the fruit of almsgiving, according to this: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” [Note: [Col. 0961D] In the Vulgate, Ecclesiasticus 3:33 reads: “Water extinguishes a burning fire, and almsgiving resists sins.”].

The fourth is the pouring forth of tears, as the Lord says: “Because he wept in my sight and walked sadly before me, I will not bring evil in his days” [Note: [Col. 0961D] The anonymous author appears to have had in mind 2 Kings 22:19–20, where it is said to King Josiah of Judah: “Your heart was terrified, and you humbled yourself before the Lord … and you wept before me, and I heard you, says the Lord. Therefore I will gather you to your fathers … so that your eyes may not see all the evils that I will bring upon this place.” Certainly the words quoted here do not occur elsewhere in Holy Scripture.].

The fifth is confession of crimes, as the Psalmist testifies: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustices against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm 31:5).

The sixth is affliction of heart and body, as the Apostle consoles us: “I have handed such a man over to the destruction of the flesh of Satan, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 5:5).

The seventh is amendment of conduct, that is, renunciation [Col. 0961C] of vices, as the Evangelist testifies: “Behold, you are now well; do not sin any longer, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14).

The eighth is the intercession of the saints, as in this passage: “If anyone is sick, let him call for the priests of the church; and let them pray over him, and the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power with God” (James 5:14).

The ninth is mercy and the merit of faith, as in this: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7).

The tenth is the conversion and salvation of others, as James bears witness: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:20); but it is better for you [Note: [Col. 0962D] Added: “that.”] to be weak and lead a solitary life than to perish with the many [Note: [Col. 0962D] From this it is easy to conclude that the present collection of penitential canons was addressed to a monk.].

The eleventh is our indulgence and forgiveness, as the Truth promises and says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37).

The twelfth is the passion of martyrdom, granting the sole hope of salvation, as God answered the crucified thief: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Having thus brought forward these matters on the authority of the canons, it is also fitting for you to investigate the definitions of the Fathers and the statutes handed down from the Lord’s mouth, according to the saying: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deuteronomy 32:7).

Again [Note: [Col. 0962D] The ancient collection cited above has: “again.”], let the matter be referred to them. They therefore decree that the eight principal vices opposed to human salvation are healed by these eight contrary remedies. For whoever has freely committed unlawful acts must restrain himself from lawful acts [Note: [Col. 0962D] “Let *licet* be deleted.”].

In another place: “But this must be carefully introduced into every penance: how long someone has remained in his offenses; with what instruction he has been imbued; by what passion he has been assailed [Note: [Col. 0962D] The same source reads: “by what passion he is assailed.”]; with what strength he exists; by what tearfulness he seems to be afflicted; by what burden he has been compelled to sin. For almighty God, who knows the hearts of all and has implanted different natures [Note: [Col. 0962D] The same source reads: “and has implanted different natures.”], has weighed sins so that penance may not be equal for all [Note: [Col. 0962D] The same source reads: “not an equality of penance,” and so forth—that is, not equal penance for all sins, but different penance for different sins: greater for greater sins, lesser for lesser sins, and suitable penance for each, as becomes clear from what follows.],” according to the prophetic saying:

“For the threshing sledge will not thresh the *gith* [Note: [Col. 0962D] “Saws.”], nor will the cartwheel turn over the *cumin* [Col. 0962C], but the *gith* and the *cumin* will be beaten out with a rod; and bread grain will be crushed with a staff,” as it is said: “The powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wisdom 6:7).

Therefore a certain wise man says: “To whom more is entrusted, from him more is required” [Note: [Col. 0962D] Saint Benedict, *Rule*, chapter 2.].

Let the priests of the Lord, therefore, who preside over churches, learn that their portion is given to them together with those whose offenses they have reconciled. What does it mean to reconcile an offense, except that, when you have taken the sinner in hand and, by admonishing, exhorting, and teaching, have led him to penance, corrected him from error, and amended him from vices, if you have made him such a convert that God is favorable toward him, you are said to have reconciled the offense? [Note: [Col. 0963C] In the edition: “And if you have made him such that God is favorably disposed toward him after such conversion”?] Since, therefore, you are such a priest and such is your teaching [Note: [Col. 0963D] The edition adds: “and your discourse.”], a portion is given to you among those whom you have corrected, so that their merit may be your reward and their salvation your everlasting glory.

Here begins an excerpt concerning several other penances and canons regarding the vices of gluttony, drunkenness, or vomiting, and concerning the distinction of foods found to be clean and unclean.

If a bishop or another ordained person habitually suffers from the vice of drunkenness, let him either cease or be deposed. If a monk vomits because of drunkenness, let him do penance for thirty days. If a priest or deacon, let him do penance for forty days. But if it was because of illness, or because he had abstained for a long time and was not accustomed to drinking or eating much, or because he did so out of joy at Christmas, Easter, or the commemoration of one of the saints [Note: [Col. 0963D] In the *Book of Remedies for Sins* in Martène, *Thesaurus novus anecdotorum*, vol. 4, col. 21, it reads: “or because.”], and then he did not take more than was decreed by the elders [Note: [Col. 0963D] Same source: “And then.”], it does him no harm. If a bishop ordered it, it does no harm, unless he himself did the same.

If a faithful layman vomits because of drunkenness, let him do penance for twelve days. A priest who becomes drunk through ignorance: seven days of penance. If through contempt: let him do penance for forty days. A deacon and monk: four weeks. A subdeacon: three. Clerics: two. Laymen: let them do penance for one week [Note: [Col. 0963D] Read: “one week.” For a layman, a seven-day penance for the same offense is imposed in the ancient collection cited above.].

Whoever compels a person to become drunk out of misplaced kindness, let him do penance as a drunkard; if out of hatred, let him be judged as a murderer [Note: [Col. 0963D] In excerpts from David’s book among the Irish canons, at the same place, col. 10: “But whoever, out of hatred or lust, in order to disgrace or mock someone, compels others to drunkenness—if he has not done sufficient penance, let him do penance as a murderer of souls.”].

Whoever cannot chant the psalms, being stunned and tongue-tied [Note: [Col. 0963D] “Tongue-tied.”], should undertake a *superpositio* [Note: [Col. 0963D] That is, let him fast. Thus Gildas, canon 6 on penance, in Martène, same place, col. 7: “If a monk, because of an overflowing stomach, vomits the sacrifice during the day, let him not presume to eat his evening meal. And if it was not because of illness, let him erase the fault by seven fasts; if because of illness and not gluttony, by four fasts,” etc. And immediately, canon 7: “But if anyone cannot chant because of drunkenness, being stunned and tongue-tied, he is deprived of his evening meal.”].

Whoever anticipates the canonical prayer and takes a more agreeable food than the others merely for the sake of gluttony should abstain from the evening meal, or spend two days on bread and water. Whoever feels pain from excessive distension of the stomach and satiety: one day. But if he vomits without illness: seven days. If he vomits the sacrament, let him do penance for forty days; if because of illness, seven days. If he threw it into the fire, let him sing one hundred psalms. But if a dog licks such vomit, let the person who vomited do penance for one hundred days.

Whoever steals food shall do penance for forty days; if he does it again, three forty-day periods; if a third time, let him do penance for a year; but if a fourth time, let him do penance in perpetual exile under another abbot.

Whoever eats unclean, carrion, or beast-torn meat [Col. 0964A] shall do penance for forty days. If necessity compels him, there is no offense. If out of necessity he eats an animal that appears unclean, whether bird or beast, it does no harm. If someone accidentally touches food with an unclean hand, or a dog, a *pilax* [Note: [Col. 0964D] In the *Book of Remedies for Sins* this canon is reported from Theodore of Canterbury as follows: “But if someone accidentally touches food with an unclean hand, or a dog, or a *pilax*, or a mouse, or an unclean animal that has drunk blood, it does no harm.” But even in this canon the first word should be in the fourth case: “a dog,” etc. Martène identifies *pilax* as a cat that catches mice.], or an unclean animal eats blood, it does no harm.

Whoever is polluted by blood [Note: [Col. 0964D] Read: “by blood.”] or by anything unclean, if he does not know it and eats it, incurs no penalty; but if he knows, let him do penance according to the degree of the pollution. Whoever drinks blood or semen shall do penance for three years.

If birds defecate in any liquid, let the dung be removed from it, and let the water be sanctified; the food will then be clean. If a mouse falls into a liquid, let it be taken out, and let the drink be sprinkled with sanctified water and consumed if the mouse is alive. If it is found dead, let it be thrown out and the vessel cleansed.

Animals torn by wolves or dogs must not be eaten by human beings, unless perhaps they are first killed by people while still alive; instead, let them be given to pigs and dogs. Neither a deer nor a goat, if dead, may be eaten. Birds and other animals strangled in nets are not to be eaten by human beings; nor may animals killed by a hawk be eaten if they are found dead, because four chapters of the Acts of the Apostles command abstention from fornication, blood, what has been strangled, and idolatry. Fish may be eaten, because they are of another nature. The horse is not prohibited, although it is not customary. The hare may be eaten.

If bees kill a person, they too [lacuna] promptly [Note: [Col. 0964D] Theodore of Canterbury’s canon among the Irish: “They must be killed immediately.”]; nevertheless, their honey may be eaten.

If pigs or hens accidentally eat human blood, we do not think that they need to be discarded [Col. 0964C], but they may be eaten. But if they have eaten while tearing apart the corpses of the dead, it is not lawful to eat their flesh until they have been emaciated, and not until a year has passed.

Animals polluted by intercourse with human beings are to be killed, and their flesh thrown to the dogs; but what they have brought forth may be used, and their hides taken [Note: [Col. 0964D] More clearly in the ancient collection of penitential canons, in Martène, same place, col. 41, beginning: “But their hides may be taken.”]. Where there is doubt, however, they are not to be killed.

The sick may take food and drink at any hour, whenever they desire or are able. If circumstances prevent them from eating at the proper time [Note: [Col. 0964D] Supply: “from eating.”], whoever eats any liquid in which a weasel [Note: [Col. 0964D] “A weasel.”] has been mutilated or found dead shall do penance by three *superpositiones* [Note: [Col. 0964D] “Fastings.”].

If little creatures are found in flour, or in some dried food, or in porridge, coagulated food, or milk, whatever is around their bodies should be thrown out [Note: [Col. 0965C] In the Roman penitential of Halitgarius, in Canisius, *Lect. antiqu.*, vol. 2, part 2, Basel edition of Basnage, p. 138, there is a similar canon, but in a better form: “What is around their bodies should be thrown away.”]; all the remainder may be consumed with a sound conscience.

If someone drinks blood involuntarily from his teeth—that is, together with saliva—it is not a sin.

If anyone practices any kind of hunting, let a cleric do penance for one year, a deacon for two, and a priest for three.

Catechumens must not eat with the baptized, nor Gentiles.

A wife who tastes her husband’s blood as a remedy [Note: [Col. 0965D] In the ancient collection, same place, col. 52: “as a remedy.”] shall do penance for forty days. Likewise, a woman who mixes her husband’s semen into food so that she may receive more of his love [Note: [Col. 0965D] Read: “so that she may receive more of his love.”] shall do penance for three years.

Whoever, despising an imposed fast in the Church and acting contrary to the decrees of the elders, does so outside the forty-day period shall do penance for forty days. But if during the forty-day period, let him do penance for a year. If he does it frequently and has made it a habit, he shall be expelled from the Church, the Lord saying: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble,” and the rest, etc. If it occurs within the forty-day period, let him do penance for a year.

Whoever eats skin from his own body, or scabs, or the little worm called a louse [Note: [Col. 0965D] “Lice.”], and likewise drinks his own urine or eats excrement, shall, with the laying on of the bishop’s hands, do penance for a full year on bread and water.

Concerning fornication and the remaining inborn forms of lust, or unclean acts involving children.

Bishops, priests, and deacons who commit fornication ought to be degraded and do penance; nevertheless, by the judgment of the bishop, they may receive communion.

For sodomites: bishops shall do penance for thirteen years, priests twelve, deacons eight, subdeacons three [Col. 0965C], clerics six, and laymen five years; and they must never sleep with another.

A brother who commits natural fornication with his natural brother through sexual intercourse shall do penance for fifteen years and abstain from all flesh. If he has put semen into the other’s mouth, let him do penance for seven years; others say, until the end of his life.

Men who fornicate between the thighs shall first do penance for a year. If they repeat it, those who fornicate between the legs, if they are boys, shall do penance for two years; if men, for three. But if they make it habitual, the measure of the penance is to be increased according to the judgment of the priest [Note: [Col. 0965D] “Of the priest.”].

A man who pollutes himself shall first do penance for one hundred days, and, if he repeats it, for a year. If he is in an ordained rank, let forty days be added to the penance for each of twelve years [The wording is corrupt; the Latin literally reads: “if he is with rank, let the penance be added by forty days of twelve years.”].

Whoever desires to fornicate with you [Note: [Col. 0965D] Instead of “with you,” the *Book of Remedies for Sins* reads more aptly “in his mind.”] but was unable to do so shall do penance for a year, especially in three forty-day periods.

Whoever has been polluted through obscene speech or by sight, although he did not wish to fornicate bodily, shall do penance for twenty or forty days. But if he has been polluted by violent thoughts [Note: [Col. 0965D] That is, through an intense imagination. In the ancient collection this canon is reported as follows: “Whoever has been violently polluted by an assault of the mind shall do penance for seven days, or until the thought is overcome.”], let him do penance for seven days.

Whoever is long tormented by a thought, resisting it lukewarmly, for three, two, or many days, shall do penance for as long as the thought has persisted [Note: [Col. 0965D] That is, whoever has spent that much time in penance without overcoming the temptation should do penance for as long as he is attacked by the shameful thought, as is stated in the canon just cited.].

Boys who fornicate among themselves are to be punished, according to the judgment [Note: [Col. 0965D] Perhaps supply: “the canon judges.”]—perhaps beaten [Note: [Col. 0966C] “Be beaten.”]. Boys who merely converse together and transgress the statutes of the elders shall make amends by three fasts; those who give a simple kiss shall make amends by six fasts. A seductive kiss without pollution requires eight fasts; with pollution but without an embrace, ten fasts [Note: [Col. 0966D] The complete passage in the Roman penitential described by Halitgarius, bishop of Cambrai, title 9, on minor causes, reads: “Boys merely conversing together and transgressing the institutions of the elders shall be corrected by three fasts. Those who give a simple kiss: seven fasts [read: fastings]. A seductive kiss without pollution: eight fastings; but with pollution, whether or not accompanied by an embrace, let them be corrected by fifteen fastings.” See Morinus, *On Penance*, p. 567, Venetian edition, 1702.].

After the age of twenty, that is, when they are adults, those who commit the same offense shall spend forty days separated from the table and excluded from the Church, with bread and water [Col. 0966B]. But the youngest, who imitate fornication with one another [Note: [Col. 0966D] Read: “who imitate fornication upon one another.”], but are not polluted, shall do penance for twenty days because of their immaturity. If it happens frequently, forty days.

Boys under twenty who pollute one another with their hands, and confess before receiving communion, shall do penance for twenty days. If they repeat it after penance, one hundred days. But if more frequently, let them be separated and do penance for a year.

A boy assaulted by an older person, if under ten years of age, shall fast for a week. The consenting party shall do penance for forty days.

The effeminate shall do penance for one year.

Whoever is polluted voluntarily in sleep should rise and, kneeling, chant the seven penitential psalms the next day on bread and water; or let him kneel and chant thirty psalms, saying “Glory be to the Father” at the end of each. Whoever wishes to sin as though in sleep, or is polluted involuntarily, shall chant twelve psalms, [Col. 0966C] saying three times after each psalm, “O God, come to my assistance.”

Whoever emits semen while sleeping in a church shall fast for three days. One who sins but is not polluted shall chant twenty-four psalms.

A bishop who commits fornication must be degraded; alternatively, he shall do penance for seven or twelve years.

A priest or deacon who commits natural fornication [Note: [Col. 0966D] Gildas adds in his preface on penance, no. 1: “or sodomy.”], before taking the monastic vow [Note: [Col. 0966D] Read: “vow.”], shall do penance for three years and ask forgiveness at every hour. He shall fast once each week, except during the periods of fifty days [Note: [Col. 0966D] Gildas has: “except for the days after the Passion.”]. After the fast he may use bread without measure and a dish somewhat thickened with butter, that is, one quarter-measure; and on Sunday let him live in this way. On the other days, let him have the prescribed measure of bread and a small amount of thickened food, garden vegetables [Col. 0967A] [Note: [Col. 0967C] Gildas, same place: “and a small dish thickened with garden vegetables, a few eggs, and a little British cheese. A Roman *hemina* of milk, because of the bodily weakness of this age. For the thirsty, a Roman *sextarius* of thin milk or buttermilk and a little water, if he is a laborer. Let him have a bed supplied with little hay. For three additional forty-day periods let him add something according as his strength permits. Let him always grieve his fault from the depths of his heart. Let him willingly accept obedience in all things. Afterwards, etc.”], a few eggs, cheese, a small measure of milk because of bodily weakness, thin milk or buttermilk, a *sextarius* of milk to relieve thirst, and water as a drink if he is a laborer; and let his bed be supplied with little hay.

For three years of forty-day periods, let him add something according as his strength permits; let him always grieve his fault from the depths of his heart, and let him most willingly accept obedience, which is required of everyone. After a year and a half, let him receive the Eucharist and come to peace; let him chant the psalms with the brothers, lest his soul perish, deprived for so long of heavenly medicine [Note: [Col. 0967C] “Of medicine.”]. [Note: [Col. 0967C] Gildas, same place, no. 2: “If a monk of a lower rank does penance for three years, let the measure of bread not be burdensome. If he is a laborer, let him take a Roman *sextarius* of milk, another of thin milk or buttermilk, and as much water as suffices for the heat of thirst.”]

If someone was previously a monk of lower rank, let him indeed do penance for three years, but let the measure of bread not be burdensome. If he is a laborer, let him take a *sextarius* of Roman milk, another of thin milk or buttermilk, and as much water as suffices for the heat of thirst.

But if a priest or deacon without a monastic vow has sinned, let him do penance like a monk without rank, and afterward let him regain his orders [Note: [Col. 0967D] These words—“and afterward let him regain his orders”—do not appear in Gildas. It is therefore clear that around the eighth or ninth century, when this codex was written, from which we have extracted these penitential canons, there were people who held that clerics who had fallen into carnal sin might return to their former orders after completing their penance. The eminent Cardinal de Aguirre undertook to prove that the contrary discipline then prevailed generally in an extensive dissertation on the Tenth Council of Toledo, recently reprinted in our press together with the learned works of other distinguished men concerning the administration of the sacrament of penance. Perhaps in England or Ireland, whose peoples were converted to the faith later than those of other kingdoms, a different discipline prevailed, with bishops relaxing something of the ancient severity? It is evident from the notes added here and there by us that the penitential canons we publish here were for the most part drawn from the councils of England and Ireland [Col. 0968C]. The codex containing them belongs to the abbey of Rheinau and may have been brought there by Saint Findan, who, after the beginning of the ninth century, set out from the province of Leinster in Ireland, visited Saint Martin at Tours, traveled through France and Alemannia, and then went to Italy, where he visited the thresholds of the blessed apostles and the sacred places of the city. On his return he finally withdrew to Rheinau, later than Mabillon believes (*Annals*, Book 26, vol. 2, p. 351). The sacramentary prefixed to this penitential, however, was compiled for the use of the Frankish kingdom and written by a single hand in characters approaching the Merovingian style. In our Germany, it may be doubted whether in the eighth century hope of returning to their former rank was preserved for fallen clerics; for in the canonical letter of Gregory II to Saint Boniface of Mainz, chapter 3, we read that a priest accused but not convicted of a crime may remain in his own rank. And in a certain council of Germany held in 742 by the authority of that same Saint Boniface, canon 6, clerics and monks who had fallen into the crime of fornication are condemned to severe penance, although no indication appears that they were restored to their former rank.].

But if, after such a sin, a priest or deacon wishes to become a monk, let him do penance for one year and a half under a strict rule. Nevertheless, the abbot has the power to moderate this matter if his obedience is pleasing to God and to his abbot.

Concerning adultery, abduction, incest, and dismissed wives; unlawful times for marrying, or intercourse with animals; and those who, after having vowed themselves to God, returned to the world—foolish vows.

If anyone commits adultery—that is, has intercourse with another man’s wife, or corrupts a betrothed woman or virgin, or a nun or woman dedicated to God—laymen shall do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water; clerics [Col. 0967C] for five, two on bread and water; deacons and monks for seven, three on bread and water; priests for ten; bishops for twelve [Col. 0968A], five of them on bread and water. If a cleric of a higher order, who has had a wife, has intercourse with her again after his confession or after receiving clerical office, let him know that he has committed adultery, and let each do penance according to his order, as in the preceding ruling.

If anyone desires another man’s wife but is unable to sin with her, or the woman does not wish to receive him, a layman shall do penance for forty days; a cleric or monk for one year, half of it on bread and water; a deacon for two years; a priest for three.

If any cleric or monk, after having dedicated himself [Note: [Col. 0968D] The ancient collection cited has “after having dedicated himself to God.”] to God, returns again to secular clothing or takes a wife, let him do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water. He shall never afterward be joined in marriage. If he refuses, the holy synod or the apostolic see shall separate them from communion [Col. 0968B] and from the fellowship of Catholics. Likewise, a woman who, after dedicating herself to God, commits such crimes shall be subject to the same ruling.

If a priest or deacon takes a foreign wife, he shall be deposed publicly before the people. If he commits adultery with her, and the matter becomes publicly known, he shall be deposed, expelled from the church, and do penance among the laity for as long as he lives.

If anyone fornicates with his mother, let him do penance for twelve years, and let him never change [his place of penance] except on the Lord’s Day. Whoever does so with his sister shall fast in the same manner for twelve years.

## The Canons of Ancyra

[Note: [Col. 0968D] L[atinus], “On the canons of Ancyra.”]

### On Incest

[Note: [Col. 0968D] The fuller heading is found in the ancient collection of penitential canons (vol. I of Luc d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 525, new edition, folio), namely: “On those who fornicate unnaturally, that is, who mate with animals, or who join themselves to relatives, or who pollute themselves with males.” In the canon itself, at the cited place, nothing is prescribed either about incest or about sodomy. [Col. 0969C] To lessen the obscurity in which the canon of our manuscript is enveloped, and to fill the gaps opened by the copyist’s carelessness, it seemed useful to insert here the interpretation of Isidore Mercator, who rendered canon 15—canon 16 in his version—of the Council of Ancyra as follows:

“Therefore, all who committed such a crime before their twentieth year shall, after completing fifteen years in penance, begin to share only in the prayer; and, remaining for another five years in the communion of prayer alone, they shall afterward, once past the twentieth year, be admitted to communion with the offering. Their life during the time of penance must also be examined, and according to this they shall receive leniency. But if anyone has persisted more obstinately in this crime, let him undertake a longer period, twenty years of penance. Those, however, who, having reached the age of twenty and having wives, fell into this crime shall, after completing twenty-five years of penance, be admitted to the communion of prayers. Remaining in that communion of prayers for another five years, they shall be admitted to full communion with the offering. But if some, while having wives and being over fifty years of age, have fallen into this crime, let them be deemed worthy of communion only at the end of life.”]

If anyone has, like animals, entered into incestuous intercourse with a blood relative before the twentieth year of his age, let him afterward do penance for ten years [Col. 0968C]. When these have been completed, let them begin to communicate only in prayer; after twenty years, let them be received into communion with the offering. Let their life during the time of penance also be examined [Col. 0969A], and let them receive this leniency accordingly. But if they have engaged in this crime, [the text is defective] let them undergo a longer period. If, at the age of twenty, while having wives, they have fallen into this crime, let them do penance for twenty-five years; when the penance has been completed, let them be admitted to the communion of prayers. Then, after another five years, let them be received into full communion with the offering. But if any, while having wives, have fallen into this sin after the [unspecified] year of their age, let them be deemed worthy of communion only at the end of life.

If anyone marries his wife from behind, let him first do penance for forty days; or, if he marries her in the rear, let him do penance as for intercourse with an animal.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] The complete canon in the ancient collection of Martène, at the cited place, column 52, reads: “If a man has intercourse with his wife from behind, let him do penance as for intercourse with animals—that is, if it has become customary, for three years. But if he has intercourse in the rear, and it has become customary, let him do penance for seven years.”]

If anyone has intercourse with a woman during her menstrual period, let him do penance for forty days. Women during their menstrual period shall not enter the church or communicate; neither nuns [Col. 0969B] nor laywomen [shall do so] if they presume to enter; let them do penance for three weeks.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Martène’s codex has *Letatae*, in place of which the learned man thought *velatae* should be read. But this is canon 36 among the chapters of Theodore of Canterbury, vol. I of the *Spicilegium*, folio edition, p. 487. It is therefore restored as follows: “nor laywomen … Likewise let those who enter the church before the cleansing of the blood after childbirth do penance, that is, for forty days.”]

Likewise, let the one who enters the church before the cleansing of the blood after childbirth do penance for forty days.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Supplied from Martène, cited work, column 53: “who enters.”]

Whoever marries during these periods shall do penance for twenty days.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] The mutilated canon should be restored as follows: “Let a woman abstain from a man for three months when she has conceived, before she gives birth, and for forty days after childbirth. Whoever has intercourse during these days shall do penance for forty days, or thirty or twenty.” See Martène, cited work, column 52.]

Whoever marries on the Lord’s Day shall do penance for three days.

[Note: [Col. 0970C] Theodore of Canterbury: “Whoever marries on Sunday should ask forgiveness from God and do penance for two or three days.” Here “to marry” must, as the context suggests, be understood not of the wedding ceremonies but of marital intercourse.]

A married person shall abstain during the Lents of the year, and on Saturday nights and Sunday nights, and on many days—especially for three days before communicating—and, from the time of conception until the blood has been consumed, must practice continence during the menstrual period.

[Note: [Col. 0970C] He would have to be an Oedipus to extract sound meaning from this canon. It nevertheless seems to be the same text which, in the ancient collection apud Martène, at the cited place, column 52, reads: “Those who are married shall abstain during the three Lents, on Sunday night, on Saturday, and on the fourth and sixth ferial days, which are customary, and they shall abstain for three nights before they communicate.” It is added there: “Whoever in Lent before Easter has intercourse with his wife shall do penance for one year.” The latter part of our canon, concerning avoidance of intimacy with a menstruating woman, is expressed at the cited place in the book *On Remedies for Sins*, column 24, in these words: “Whoever has intercourse during the menstrual period shall do penance for twenty days.”]

A bigamist shall do penance for one year. On Wednesday and Friday, and during the three Lents, he shall abstain from meat, but he shall not dismiss his wife. A trigamist shall do as above, that is, in the fourth or fifth [Note: [Col. 0970D] Or “sixth.”] or later [marriage], and shall do penance for seven years; on Wednesday and Friday, and during the Lents, he shall abstain from meat, but they shall not separate.

Basinus judged this; but in the canons [the period is] four years. In the fifth degree of kinship they may marry; if the fourth is discovered, they shall not separate. In the third degree of kinship, however, it is not permitted to take a wife after the death of the former wife.

[Note: [Col. 0970D] Whatever the origin of this canon, it is at least clearly older than those cited by Gratian, *C.* XXXV, *Q.* II, where canons 16, 17, 18, 19, and 21 establish consanguinity in more remote degrees as a diriment impediment to marriage.]

A man may equally marry women who are related to him by blood, and women related by blood to his wife after his wife’s death. Two brothers may also marry two sisters, and a father and son may marry a mother and daughter.

If a layman fornicates with a widow, let him do penance for two years, after paying her parents the price of humiliation; if he has no wife, and if her parents consent, let her become his wife, and let both do penance for five years.

If a layman fornicates with an animal, let him do penance for two years if he has a wife, and for one year if he does not. A cleric shall do penance for two years, a deacon for three, and a priest for five, two of those years on bread and water. If a cleric fornicates once, let him do penance for one year on bread and water. If he begets a son, let him do penance for seven years in exile; the same applies to a virgin.

Whoever dismisses his wife and joins himself to another shall do penance for seven years with hardship, or twelve years more lightly. If someone’s wife leaves him and afterward returns, he shall receive her, and he shall do penance for one year with bread and water; the same applies if he himself has taken another wife.

If anyone goes in to his own female slave, let him sell her and do penance for one year. If he begets a son by her, let him free her.

[Note: [Col. 0970D] Read: “let him make her free.”]

An adulterous woman shall do penance for four years. But a woman who has intercourse with herself shall do penance for three years.

[Note: [Col. 0970D] The ancient collection adds “with a man.”]

Women who fornicate and kill their offspring, and those who do something to themselves in order to expel what has been conceived in the womb, shall do penance for ten years.

[Note: [Col. 0970D] The complete Ancyran canon, which is Isidore’s twenty-first, reads in his interpretation as follows: “Regarding women who fornicate and kill their offspring, and also those who do something to themselves in order to expel what has been conceived in the womb, the ancient rule was that they should be removed from the Church until the end of life. But now we decree more humanely that a period of ten years of penance be assigned to them.”]

If a woman has intercourse with a woman, let her do penance for three years.

[Note: [Col. 0971C] The ancient collection reads: “If a woman has intercourse with a woman, three years—that is, if a woman joins herself to another in the manner of a fornicator, let her do penance for three years as a fornicator.”]

If a husband, or a woman, having made a vow of virginity, joins himself or herself in marriage, let the marriage not afterward be dissolved, but let the person do penance for three [Note: [Col. 0971D] The ancient collection reads “four.”] years. Foolish vows must be broken, for they are burdensome. A woman may not make a vow without her husband’s permission; but if she wishes, she may be dismissed, and let her do penance according to the priest’s judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0971D] The ancient collection reads “if she makes the vow.”]

[Note: [Col. 0971D] The following words—“Foolish vows must be broken, for they are burdensome … and let her do penance according to the priest’s judgment”—are entirely absent from Martène.]

If a priest kisses a woman out of desire, let him do penance for twenty days; if he is defiled through a kiss or by touching, let him do penance for forty days. If he emits semen through thought, let him do penance for seven days.

If a woman marries two brothers, she ought to be cast out until the day of her death, but she should be reconciled at the end of life; if she should recover, however, she shall be admitted to penance after the marriage has been dissolved. If such a woman dies while remaining in this union, the penance of the survivor shall be difficult. This ruling must be observed by both men and women.

[Note: [Col. 0971D] Canon 2 of the Council of Neocaesarea, in Isidore’s interpretation, reads: “If a woman marries two brothers, let her be cast out until the day of her death. But because of humaneness, she ought to be reconciled at the end of life in the sacraments; if she should recover, however, let her be admitted to penance after the marriage has been dissolved. But if the woman dies while remaining in such a union, the penance of the survivor shall be difficult. This ruling must be observed by both men and women.”]

Girls who, not compelled by the authority of their parents but by their own free decision, have adopted the purpose and habit of virginity, if afterward they desire marriage, are transgressors even if consecration has not followed; they would not, however, have been deprived of that gift if they had remained in their purpose.

## On Theft, Arson, Violators of Tombs, Those Who Expel Their Father, Booty Taken from the Enemy and Captivity, and Those Who Strip a Martyr

Money belonging to the church, whether stolen or seized, shall be repaid fourfold; popular property, twofold.

If anyone steals something from the sacred church vessels or neglects them, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and [Col. 0971C] water, and let him restore in full what he took.
