If anyone commits theft, a child shall do penance for forty days, according to age and the quality of his education; a layman for one year; a cleric for two; a subdeacon for three; a deacon for four; a priest for five; and a bishop for six years.

If a layman commits theft once, let him restore what he stole and do penance during the Lents with bread and water. If he does so repeatedly and has nothing with which to make restitution, let him do penance for two years on bread and water and during the other Lents, and afterward let him be reconciled at Easter.

[Col. 0972A] Whoever frequently commits theft shall do penance for seven years, or according to the priest’s judgment, in proportion to what can be made good to those whom he harmed. He must always reconcile the person whom he offended and make restitution according to the harm he caused; afterward his penance will greatly benefit him. But if he refuses or is unable fully to carry out the prescribed period,

[Note: [Col. 0971D] Add from the ancient collection: “let him himself increase the penance.” Thus the cited ancient collection, column 42: “Whoever commits theft and does not make compensation to those whom he harmed … must restore his own property to them or make compensation. But if he has no substance with which he can make compensation, or does not know whom he harmed, let him increase his penance still further.”]

a ten-year-old child who eats [Note: [Col. 0972C] Read “commits.”] something stolen shall do penance for seven days.

Whoever steals food shall do penance for forty days; if again, three Lents; if a third time, one year; if a fourth time, let him do penance in perpetual exile under another abbot.

If a layman carries off a monk by theft [Note: [Col. 0972C] Read “carries away by theft.”], let him either enter a monastery to serve God or undergo human servitude.

If anyone, by any device, takes a slave or any other person into captivity, or sends him there, let him do penance for three years on bread and [Col. 0972B] water.

If anyone expels his father or mother, he is to be judged impious or sacrilegious, and shall do penance for as long as he remained in that impiety.

[Note: [Col. 0972C] Read “for as long as he remained in impiety.”]

Those who provide guides to barbarians, if they burn basilicas, kill good and innocent clerics or nuns, or drag innocent persons from the church, shall do penance for fourteen years.

[Note: [Col. 0972D] This canon is divided into two chapters by Luc d’Achery (*Spicilegium*, vol. I, folio edition, among the selected Irish canonical chapters, book LVII, p. 506), and reads as follows:

“Chapter II, On the Penance of Those Who Lead Barbarians. The Irish Synod says: Whoever provides a guide to barbarians shall do penance for fourteen years; a barbarian, that is, an outsider. Who is an outsider except one who, with cruel and savage custom, lays all men low?

Chapter III, On the Law by Which the Senators Judge: Fourteen Years of Penance for Those Who Are Led. The Irish Synod says: The senators have decreed fourteen years for this reason, if they burn the basilicas of bishops, or kill or strike down a religious man or a nun, or remove innocent persons from the church; the guide shall do penance for seven years on his own account and seven additional years on account of those whom he led.”]

If money has been taken as booty from the enemy in a foreign province—that is, after another king has been defeated—one third shall be given to the church or to the poor, as the king’s command required, and the offender shall do penance for forty days.

If anyone burns down another person’s house or property by fire, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water.

## On Perjury, False Testimony, and Lying

If anyone commits perjury, a layman shall do penance for three years; a cleric [Col. 0972C] for five; a subdeacon for six; a deacon for seven; a priest for ten; and a bishop for twelve.

[Note: [Col. 0972D] The same is found in the Roman Penitential, in Halitgar’s section “On Perjury,” with only the words transposed.]

Whoever commits perjury in church shall do penance for eleven years. If he lies by the hand of a bishop, priest, or deacon, or at an altar or upon a consecrated cross, let him do penance for three years.

[Note: [Col. 0972D] The ancient collection of Martène, cited work, column 42, adds “and has lied.”]

If upon an unconsecrated cross, let him do penance for one year.

If a layman swears falsely out of greed, let him sell all his possessions and give them to the poor, and, having entered a monastery, serve God until death. But if he did not do so out of greed,

[Col. 0973A] and incurred the danger of death, let him do penance for three years as an unarmed exile on bread and water; let him abstain from wine and meat for two years; let him free a male or female slave on his behalf; let him give alms for two years; and after four years let him communicate according to the priest’s judgment. Whoever was led into perjury in ignorance and afterward recognizes it shall do penance for one year. Whoever suspects that he is being led into perjury but nevertheless swears with consent shall do penance for two years. For false testimony, a layman shall do penance for one year; a cleric for two; a subdeacon for three; a deacon for four; a priest for five; and a bishop for six years.

One who speaks false testimony shall make satisfaction to his neighbor. As he imposed upon his brother, so let him be condemned by the priest’s judgment.

A liar through ignorance who has caused no harm shall confess to the person to whom he lied and to the priest; he shall be sentenced to silence, or shall recite twelve psalms. But if he lied deliberately, let him keep silence for three days, or for thirty if he is able.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] In Martène’s *On Remedies for Sins*, cited work, column 25, the complete text reads: “But if he did not lie through ignorance, let him keep silence for two days, or, if he presides, sing thirty psalms, for prelates cannot keep silent.”]

A liar through greed shall make satisfaction by generosity to the person whom he defrauded.

## On Homicide and Bloodshed without Death; Those Who Suffocate Infants Who Die Unbaptized; Abortion; Those Who Cut Off Their Own Limbs; and Those Who Provide Guides to Barbarians

### The Canons of Ancyra

[Note: [Col. 0973D] Read “of Ancyra.”]

Those who commit voluntary homicide shall continually submit themselves to penance; near the end of life, however, they shall be considered worthy of communion.

Whoever commits homicide not deliberately but by accident shall do penance for five years.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] In the edition based on Isidore’s interpretation, canon 22 of the Council of Ancyra reads: “Those who commit homicide not deliberately but by accident were formerly admitted to communion after seven years of penance, according to the established degrees. But this more humane ruling assigns a period of five years.”]

Women who fornicate and kill their offspring, and those who act to expel what has been conceived in the womb, were formerly assigned by the ancient Fathers to exclusion until the end of life; now, more humanely, it has been determined that they shall do penance for ten years.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] See above, p. …]

If anyone kills a monk or cleric, let him lay down his weapons and serve God, or do penance for seven years. Whoever kills a bishop or priest is subject to the king’s judgment.

If a layman kills another out of hatred,

[Note: [Col. 0973D] Martène’s ancient collection, column 41, adds: “or to possess his inheritance.”]

and does not wish to lay down his weapons, let him do penance for seven years without meat and wine.

Whoever kills a man shall abstain from the church for forty days and afterward perform the penance prescribed above.

Whoever kills a man at the command of his lord shall do penance for forty days. Whoever kills a man in a public war, together with the king, shall do penance for forty days. If he kills by poison or by some evil art, let him do penance for seven years [Col. 0973D] or more.

If a mother kills her son, let her do penance for twelve [Note: [Col. 0973D] Martène’s text has fifteen years.] years, and never change [her place of penance] except on the Lord’s Day.

A very poor woman shall do penance for four years.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] The cited text reads: “If a poor woman kills her son, let her do penance for seven years.”]

If a woman kills her son in the womb before forty days, let her do penance for one year; but if it is after forty days from conception, let her do penance as a murderer for three years.

If a cleric commits homicide, let him do penance for ten years in exile, three of them on bread and water. If anyone commits homicide by accident and without intending it, let him do penance for five years, three of them on bread and water. If he consented to homicide and it was carried out, let him do penance for seven years. If he wished it but could not accomplish it, let him do penance for three years.

If anyone commits homicide, a layman shall do penance for three years; a cleric for five; a subdeacon for six; a deacon for seven; a priest for ten; and a bishop for twelve years.

If a layman kills his neighbor, let him do penance for five years in exile.

If anyone strikes another and sheds blood, let him do penance for ten days on bread and water; if, I say, it is seven months, a priest shall do penance for one year.

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Martène’s ancient collection, column 41: “If anyone strikes another in any other way and sheds blood, let him do penance for forty days and make restitution for the wound. If he is a deacon, let him do penance for six months; if a priest, one year.”]

If someone’s infant dies through negligence without baptism, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water.

[Note: [Col. 0974D] The cited text, column 42: “If an infant dies without baptism, the father and mother, having a three-year-old child [text corrupt], shall do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water.”]

If laypeople suffocate their infants, let them do penance for one year on bread and water, abstain from wine and meat for two years, and abstain from their wives during the time of penance.

If a woman voluntarily aborts, let her do penance for three years on bread and water.

Whoever, in a quarrel, by a blow makes a person disabled or deformed shall pay the medical expenses and restore him from his illness, and do penance for half a year on bread and water. If he has nothing with which to make restitution, let him do penance for one year.

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Read “the expenses of medical treatment.” In the book *On Remedies for Sins*, Martène, cited work, column 26: “He shall pay the expenses of the physicians, the price of the injury, and restore the work until he is healed”—that is, as much as the injured person could have earned by his labor—and shall do penance for half a year.]

If a layman sheds blood through a public disturbance, let him repay as much as he caused in harm. If he has nothing with which to make restitution, let him repay through the labor of his neighbor for as long as that person is ill, and let him do penance for forty days on bread and water.

Whoever strikes his neighbor without harming him shall do penance for one, two, or three Lents on bread and water. If he is a cleric, for one year or half a year.

If anyone voluntarily cuts off any limb, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water. Small children who strike one another shall do penance for seven days; adolescents, however, for forty days.

If anyone kills a man in vengeance for his brother [Note: [Col. 0974D] Read “in vengeance for his brother”], let him do penance for three years if he makes compensation to his relatives within half the period.

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Read “within half the period.”]

Those who provide guides to barbarians shall do penance for three years.

Whoever does not receive guests into his house, as the Lord commanded and promised the kingdom of heaven when he said, “Come, you blessed,” [Col. 0974D] and the rest—let him do penance on bread and water for as long as he failed to receive guests, fulfill the evangelical commandments, wash their feet, or give alms, unless he reforms.

Whoever persists in greed shall be separated, hoarding surplus possessions for the future. If this is through ignorance, let him give those possessions to the poor; but if it is through contempt of those who rebuke him, let him give alms and fast according to the priest’s judgment. Whoever persists in greed shall be separated.

[Note: [Col. 0975D] That is, excommunicated.]

Whoever reclaims what is his from one who takes it away, contrary to the prohibition

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Supply “of the Lord,” from Theodore of Canterbury.]

shall give to the needy what he has reclaimed.

A cleric who has surplus possessions shall give them to the poor; otherwise, let him be excommunicated.

[Note: [Col. 0975D] This penalty was never inflicted except upon those guilty of serious crimes. Therefore our anonymous author did not regard as innocent those clerics who treated surplus goods as their own.]

But if, after the period of penance during which he lives in opposition, he continues to live removed from penance [the text is corrupt].

If anyone is greedy, avaricious, proud, drunken, or hates his brother,

[Col. 0975B] or commits other similar things too numerous to list, let him do penance for three years and give alms according to his means.

## On Anger, Sorrow, Hatred, Cursing, Slander, Envy, Informing, Evil Thoughts, and Heresy

Whoever speaks harsh words in anger, though not insulting, shall make satisfaction to his brother and be assigned additional penance. But if, with pallor, blushing, or trembling, he curses, let him make satisfaction to the one whom he cursed and do penance for seven days, separated from others with bread and water.

Whoever hates his brother shall remain on bread and water for as long as he does not drive away the hatred, and shall be compelled to join himself to the one whom he hated with sincere charity.

Whoever slanders out of envy, or willingly listens to a slanderer, shall be separated for four days on bread and water. But if he slanders one who presides, let him do penance for four days and willingly serve him for the remainder.

Lay slanderers shall do penance for six days; clerics for two weeks; subdeacons for three; deacons for four; priests for five; and bishops for six.

If anyone holds anger against another in his heart, let him be judged a murderer. If he does not wish to be reconciled to the brother whom he hates, let him do penance on bread and water until he is reconciled to him.

Whoever conceals from his brother a deadly sin shall rebuke him confidently; for as long as he concealed it, so long shall he live on bread and water. If he concealed a minor sin, he shall indeed rebuke him, but shall do penance through psalms or according to the priest’s judgment.

Whoever attributes an imputable sin to his brother before rebuking him privately shall make satisfaction to him and do penance for three days on bread and water.

If a monk speaks alone with a woman alone, or remains under the same roof with her, let him go without supper. But if he does so after the prohibition, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water.

If anyone makes denunciations [Note: [Col. 0975D] Read “detestable.”], which are detestable, let him do penance for three years on bread and water.

If a layman, through ignorance, communicates with heretics, let him stand among the catechumens—that is, separated from the church—for forty days, and do penance for another forty days at the end; thus let him expiate his fault. But if, after the priest has preached that he should not communicate with a heretic, he does so again, let him do penance for one year and three Lents, and abstain from wine and meat for three years.

If anyone has been ordained by a heretic, he must be ordained again.

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Ecclesiastical history sufficiently shows that the same discipline was not observed with regard to all heretics.]

If he is liable to censure [*prehensibilis*]; otherwise, he ought to be deposed.

If anyone has passed from the Catholic Church to heresy and afterward returned, he cannot be ordained again except after prolonged abstinence or in a great emergency. Pope Innocent asserts, on the authority of the canons, that such a person may not become a cleric even after penance.

If anyone abandons the faith of God without any necessity and afterward accepts penance with his whole heart, let him spend three years outside the church, that is, among the hearers, according to the Council of Nicaea; seven years in the church among the penitents; and two further years outside communion.

## On Repeated Baptism

Those who have been baptized twice in ignorance need not do penance for this, except that according to the canons they may not be ordained except in a great emergency.

But those who, knowingly, have been baptized again have crucified Christ again, as it were; let them do penance for seven years, fasting on Wednesday and Friday and during the three Lents.

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Supply “let them fast,” from the canon “Those baptized twice,” canon 117, distinction 4, *On Consecration*.]

If it was done because of some fault,

[Note: [Col. 0976D] Supply from the same canon of Gratian: “likewise.”]

but if they thought it lawful for the sake of purity, let them do penance for three years.

## On the Ministry of the Church, Rebuilding, Masses, Various Negligences, and the Holy Sacrifice

A church may be moved to another place if necessary, and it ought not to be consecrated again; the priest need only sprinkle it with water, and a cross must be set up in the place of the altar.

[Note: [Col. 0976D] This same canon is published among the chapters of Theodore of Canterbury, no. 15, except for the final words, “and a cross must be set up in the place of the altar,” which are absent there. D. de La Barre further notes that the earlier edition read: “And then the sacrifice must again be offered, not merely sprinkled with holy water.” This reading agrees with canons 9 and 24 of distinction 1, *On Consecration*, where, after the altar has been moved and the church restored, a new consecration is prescribed.]

The wood of a church must not be put to another use except for another church, or burned in a fire, or used in the monastery to benefit the brothers; it is permitted to cook bread with it. Such materials must not be used for secular works.

The sacrifice must not be received from the hand of a priest who cannot perform the prayers or readings according to the rite. We must offer for good rulers, but in no way for evil ones.

[Col. 0976D]

Priests, however, are not prohibited from offering for bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0976D] Gildas, canon 17: “Priests are not prohibited from offering for bishops.”]

Whoever knowingly communicates with one excommunicated from the church shall do penance for forty days.

Before the completion of penance, penitents ought not, according to the canons, to communicate.

[Note: [Col. 0977C] In chapter 21 of Theodore, the following words are inserted: “Theodore says.” Hence we infer that this canon belongs to some English council attended by Theodore.]

But out of mercy we grant permission after one year or six months.

Whoever has committed many evils—that is, homicide, adultery, intercourse with four-footed animals, or many thefts—shall go to a monastery and do penance until death.

If a priest denies penance to the dying, he shall be guilty concerning their souls, because the Lord says: “On whatever day the sinner is converted, he shall live and shall not die.” True conversion can occur at the final hour, because the Lord is an observer not only of time but also of the heart, just as the thief in a single moment deserved to be in paradise, as a confessor in a single moment.

[Note: [Col. 0977C] This canon, “If a priest …,” is taken in substance from a letter of Pope Celestine I to the bishops of Gaul.]

For a deceased monk, Masses shall be celebrated on the day of his burial, on the third day, and afterward as much as the abbot wishes.

For a good layman, fasting may be performed for penance on the third or seventh day, for thirty or seven days; and his relatives ought to fast on the seventh day and offer an oblation at the altar, as is read in Jesus son of Sirach. The Israelites fasted for Saul; afterward, as much as the priest wishes.

[Note: [Col. 0977D] In Theodore’s chapters, no. 34: “For a good layman, on the third or sixth day, after fasting; for a penitent, on the thirtieth or seventh day; and his relatives ought to fast for five days and offer an oblation,” and so forth.]

Masses for secular dead shall be celebrated three times a year: on the third day, the ninth day, and the thirtieth day, because the Lord rose on the third day, gave up his spirit at the ninth hour, and on the thirtieth day the children of Israel mourned Moses.

Women may receive the sacrifice under a black veil; Saint Basil judged this to be so.

## On the Holy Sacrifice
[Col. 0977C] Whoever who is not in communion shall approach neither for the peace nor for the kiss; and whoever has eaten beforehand is not permitted the kiss. Whoever receives the sacrament after a meal shall do penance for seven days. But if a monk has neglected to receive the sacrament and has not asked about it, and no excusable reason has existed, an additional penalty shall be imposed. Whoever receives the sacrament while polluted by a nocturnal emission shall likewise do penance. If the sacrament falls to the ground through negligence, an additional penalty shall be imposed. Whoever loses the sacrament, leaving it to be devoured by beasts, shall do penance for three Lents if the loss was excusable, but otherwise for one year.

Whoever has not carefully guarded [Col. 0978A] the sacrament, and a mouse has eaten it, shall do penance for forty days. Whoever loses it in the church, or a portion falls and is not found, shall do penance for twenty days. Whoever loses his chrism, or merely the sacrament, in any place, and it is not found, shall do penance for three Lents or one year.

If anything is poured from the chalice onto the altar when the linen cloth is removed, he shall do penance for seven days; or, if a greater quantity has been spilled, he shall do penance for seven additional penalties. If the chalice drips onto the altar, the minister shall suck up the drop and do penance for three days. If it passes through the linens onto other things, he shall do penance for seven days; if as far as the third linen, for nine days; if as far as the fourth, for twelve days. The linens touched by the drop shall be washed three times, with the dregs of the chalice placed beneath them, and the water used for washing shall be consumed.

But if, through negligence, something from the chalice drips onto the ground, it shall be licked up with the tongue, the board shall be scraped, [Col. 0978B] and, if there is no board, he shall put down something so that it will not be trampled, and it shall be consumed by fire.

[Note: [Col. 0977D] Read: “so that it will not be trampled, the place shall be scraped out and consumed by fire, and the ashes shall be placed inside the altar, and the priest shall do penance for forty days,” as in Gratian’s *Decretum*, Distinction I, *De Consecratione*, canon 27, taken from Theodore’s penitential. In the first penitential from the Roman Church Treasury, published by Canisius, vol. II, part II, ed. Basnage, p. 126, we read: “If something from the chalice drips onto the ground through negligence, it shall be licked up with the tongue, the board shall be scraped, it shall be burned with fire, and he shall do penance for fifty days.” In the other, copied by Halitgar and printed in the same place, p. 138, only forty days of penance are assigned, as in Gratian. The especially obscure words “if there is no board, he shall put down something” are clarified by canon 46 of the penitential published by Mabillon, vol. I of the *Museum Italicum*, p. 394, where it reads: “If there is a board, scrape it; if there is none, put down a board, so that the blood of Christ will not be trampled.”]

As above, the priest shall do penance for fifty days if the chalice drips while it is being washed. The first time, he shall sing twelve psalms.

Whoever submerges the sacrament in a river shall immediately drink the water in which the chrism was; he shall receive the sacrament and make amends for the fault alone for ten days.

[Note: [Col. 0978C] A fragment of a penitential book exists in Martène, *De antiquis Ecclesiae ritibus*, book I, chapter 5, [Col. 0978D] from a manuscript of the Colbert Library, which Martène already in his own day judged to be eight hundred years old. There this canon is reported as follows: “Whoever submerges the sacrament shall immediately drink the water that was in the chrismal; he shall receive the sacrament and make amends for the fault alone for ten days.” Here *chrismal* or *chrismale* means a small vessel in which the Eucharist was kept or carried to the sick. In this sense the preface of the chrismal is found in the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory; in the Roman Ordo it is the preface of the vessel in which the Eucharist is stored. See Du Cange. “Alone,” that is, as a solitary person withdrawn from human company, means that the offending priest is ordered to amend his fault in solitude.]

Whoever has been negligent regarding the sacrament, so that, when it dries out, it is consumed by worms and reduced to nothing, shall do penance for three Lents with bread and water. If it is found intact, it shall be burned with fire and the ashes hidden beneath the altar; whoever was negligent shall expiate his negligence for forty days.

If the sacrament becomes discolored through loss of its proper taste, a fast shall be completed for twenty days; if it has become clotted, for seven days. If the sacrament falls from the hands of the one offering it onto the ground and is not found, whatever is found shall be burned in the place where it fell, and the ashes shall be hidden as above; thereafter the priest shall be sentenced to penance for half a year.

If the sacrament that fell from the hands of the one offering it is found, the place shall be cleaned with brooms and [Note: [Col. 0978D] Read: “and straw.” Martène, from the cited Colbert manuscript.] straw; or whatever is found there shall be burned as above, and the priest shall do penance for twenty days. If it has fallen as far as the altar, an additional penalty shall be imposed.

[Note: [Col. 0978D] That is, the priest shall be punished with a fast.]

Whoever through ignorance communicates with someone who has committed a capital crime shall do penance for seven days. Whoever vomits the sacrament, and a dog consumes it, shall do penance for one year; otherwise, for forty days.

If, on the day on which he communicated, he vomits the sacrament, then, if before midnight, he shall perform three additional penalties; if after midnight, two; if after Matins, one. If he vomits the sacrament because of illness, he shall do penance for seven days. If he throws it into the fire, he shall sing one hundred psalms. But if dogs lick such vomit, the one who vomited shall do penance for one hundred days.

## Concerning reconciliation and various and many evils

Whoever has committed many evils—that is, homicide, adultery with a woman and with an animal, and theft—shall go to a monastery and do penance until death.

The Greeks communicate every Sunday, clergy and laity alike; and whoever does not communicate on three Sundays is excommunicated, as the canons also prescribe. [Col. 0979B] The Romans likewise communicate if they wish; those who do not wish to do so are not excommunicated. Greeks and Romans alike abstain from women for three days, as it is written in the law, before the offering of the bread.

[Note: [Col. 0979C] Read “before the offering of the showbreads,” as in Martène, vol. IV of the *Thesaurus*, col. 46.]

Before the completion of penance, penitents according to the canons ought not to communicate. But we, out of mercy, grant permission after one year and six months. Whoever can fulfill what is written in the penitential does well; and for one who cannot do it, we give the following counsel:

[Note: [Col. 0979C] The passage is given in full in the Roman Penitential, in Canisius, vol. II, part II, p. 129: “Whoever can fast and fulfill what is written in the Penitential does well and should give thanks to God. But whoever cannot, by the mercy of God we give this counsel, so that neither he nor anyone else need perish or despair. For one day that he ought to fast on bread and water, let him sing fifty psalms on bended knees, if this can be done, in a church or another suitable place, and feed one poor person. Or, if he cannot remain on bended knees for so long, let him sing seventy psalms standing and feed a poor person. Or let him ask pardon one hundred times on bended knees.” Thereafter there is no agreement between the Roman penitential and ours. In the frequently cited collection of ancient penitential canons, Martène, at the place cited, col. 55, several canons concerning the redemption of penances occur under the name, naturally, of Theodore of Canterbury; for the most part they agree with ours. Thus, after the words “does well,” Theodore continues: “And this is the order of the psalmody for penance, for one day—that is, when he ought to do penance on bread and water. These are the psalms: fifty on bended knees, or seventy without bending the knees, in the church; let him sing them in order in one place. For a week, when he ought to do penance on bread and water, let him sing three hundred psalms in order on bended knees in the church or in one place, or four hundred and twenty without bending the knees. And for one month, when he ought to do penance on bread and water, let him sing twelve hundred psalms on bended knees, or one thousand six hundred and eighty without bending the knees,” and so forth.]

For one day on bread and water, let him sing fifty psalms on bended knees, or seventy without bending the knees, in the church, or let him sing them in order in one place. For one month, during which he ought to do penance on bread and water, let him sing one thousand two hundred and thirty psalms. Afterward, on all days, let him take nourishment at the sixth hour, except on Wednesday and Friday, when he shall fast until the ninth hour.

He shall abstain from meat and wine; after singing the psalms, he shall take whatever other food [Note: [Col. 0980C] Theodore, at the place cited, adds: “which he has been given.”] has been given to him [Note: [Col. 0980C] In the same place: “let him sing.”]. Whoever does not know the psalms [Note: [Col. 0980C] The same source adds: “And thus he ought to do penance, and cannot fast.”] shall distribute for each day in alms the value of a denarius.

[Note: [Col. 0980C] Theodore’s wording is equally obscure: “For each day let him distribute among the poor a redemption worth a denarius,” that is, let him distribute a coin worth one denarius as redemption for the penance that ought to be performed. Much more follows in Theodore, either absent here or transposed.]

For one year on bread and water, let him give twenty-six solidi in alms; each week he shall fast one day until the ninth hour and another until evening; and during the three Lents he shall calculate how much he consumes and give half of it in alms.

In the second year [Note: [Col. 0980C] Theodore: “In the second year the remission of penance is from Christmas,” and so forth.] the penance is lighter from Christmas until Epiphany and from Easter until Pentecost. Whoever cannot do penance in this way [Note: [Col. 0980C] Supplied from Theodore: “perform penance.”] shall, for one year [Note: [Col. 0980C] Theodore: “in the first year.”], give twenty-six solidi in alms; for two [Note: [Col. 0980C] Theodore: “and in the second year,”] twenty; for three [Note: [Col. 0980D] Theodore: “and in the third, eighteen; that is, sixty-four solidi.”] eighteen.

Those who are able shall make restitution for criminal offenses as Zacchaeus said: “Lord, I give half of all my goods to the poor, and if I have taken anything unjustly, I will restore fourfold.” If the person from whom he took it is not present, or if they are unable, let him give in silver half of what his conscience assesses, and in alms [Note: [Col. 0980D] Theodore’s text is no clearer, though it is longer; at this point in our manuscript the page has been completely cut away.]

## ORDER FOR IMPOSING PENANCE

[Note: [Col. 0980D] In an ancient Sicilian order, which elsewhere generally agrees with this one, the following rubric is prefixed, as frequently elsewhere, in Morinus’s appendix to *De poenitentia*: “According to the customary practice, when someone comes to the priest to confess his sins, the priest should tell him to wait a little until he enters his room to pray. But if he has no room, he should first say privately in his heart this prayer: ‘Lord God almighty, be merciful,’” and so forth. All this, like the order itself, indicates private penance, distinct from that which was proclaimed and performed publicly at the beginning of the fast.]

(From the manuscript of the Imperial and Royal Library at Vienna, Theology no. 685, tenth century.)

[Col. 0980B]

The priest asks, saying:

“Do you believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit?”

**Response:** “I believe.”

“Do you believe that these three persons whom we have just named—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are three persons and one God?”

**Response:** “I believe.”

“Do you believe that in the flesh in which you now are, you will rise again in it on the day of judgment and receive either good or evil according to what you have done?”

**Response:** “I believe.”

“Do you wish to forgive whatever sins they have committed against you, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: **‘If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins’?**”

And question him carefully whether he is involved in incest; and if he does not wish to renounce that incest, you cannot give him penance. But if he wishes to renounce it, say the psalm, “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.” Then say this prayer:

[Note: [Col. 0980D] In the Sicilian manuscript used by Morinus, it reads: “God, whose forgiveness,” and so forth.]

“Whose forgiveness all people need. Let us pray.

“Remember your servant N., who has been stripped bare by the fragile slipperiness of the earthly body; we ask that you grant forgiveness to the one who confesses. Spare the suppliant, so that we, who are accused by our merits, may be saved by your mercy. Through.”

Then say the psalm “Bless the Lord, O my soul,” up to “it shall be renewed.” And say this prayer:

“Let us pray.

“God, beneath whose eyes every heart trembles and every conscience quakes, be merciful to the groans of all and heal the wounds of everyone. Just as none of us is free from guilt, so may no one be excluded from forgiveness. Through.”

Then say the fiftieth psalm, “Have mercy on me, O God,” up to “blot out all my iniquities.” Then say this prayer:

“Let us pray.

“I beseech you, O Lord, by the majesty of your clemency and mercy, that you would deign to release forgiveness to your servant N., who confesses his sins and crimes, and pardon the guilt of his past offenses. You brought back the lost sheep upon your shoulders; you heard with favor the publican’s prayers when he confessed. Be favorable also to this servant of yours, O Lord. Look kindly upon his prayers, so that his weeping may remain acceptable in confession, and that his request may swiftly obtain perpetual clemency. Restored to the holy altars and sanctuaries, may he again be devoted to eternal hope and heavenly glory. Through.”

Ask him whether he has already confessed; and for this reason ask whether he has anything arising from evil intent, or theft, or any unjust matter against the law. If he confesses that he has such a thing, instruct him that he is not permitted to receive judgment concerning other sins before he has returned or removed that evil.

Afterward, if he has done so, ask him whether he harbors anger against anyone. If he confesses it, admonish him that it is written that his abstinence is of no benefit. If he is such a person, ask him whether he is a fugitive, because he may not do penance before he has been reconciled.

Then make him confess all his sins, saying as follows:

“Have you committed homicide, whether accidentally, unwillingly, for vengeance upon your parents, by the command of your lord, in a public war, or because you wished to do so but were unable?”

Five or three years, or forty days.

**Response:** “I have.”

“Have you committed perjury through worldly greed, under compulsion, from necessity, for the life of your parents, unknowingly, or by knowingly leading others into perjury?”

Seven years, or three years and forty days.

**Response:** “I have.”

“Have you committed theft—that is, burglary, theft of four-footed animals, or another more serious offense worth forty or one hundred solidi?”

Seven or five years.

**Response:** “I have.”

“And for lesser thefts: one year, or three Lents, or forty days.”

**Response:** “I have.”

“Have you committed adultery with another man’s wife or with a betrothed woman? Or have you violated a virgin, or a holy nun, or a woman dedicated to God?”

Five or three years.

**Question:** “Have you had intercourse with your wife from behind, or with a slave woman?”

Eleven days.

**Question:** “Have you committed fornication as the Sodomites did, or with a brother or mother, or with animals, or by any other means?”

Fifteen, twelve, or seven years, or one year.

**Question:** “Have you given false testimony through greed, knowingly or unknowingly?”

Three, two, or one year.

**Question:** “Have you struck a person so that blood came from him, or have you broken his bones?”

One year or forty days.

[Col. 0982A]

**Question:** “Have you cut off any of his limbs out of anger?”

Three years.

**Question:** “Have you hated your brother?”

For as long as you were in that hatred, so long shall you do penance on bread and water.

**Question:** “Have you taken anything from the service of the church? Have you slandered anyone, whether an elder or parents, out of envy?”

One year or forty days.

**Question:** “Have you had intercourse with your wife or another woman within forty days before or after childbirth?”

Do penance for forty days.

**Question:** “Have you married on a Sunday?”

One day or three days.

**Question:** “Have you violated tombs for the sake of theft?”

Three or two years.

**Question:** “Have you committed any negligence regarding the sacrament?”

One hundred or forty days.

**Question:** “Have you practiced usury?”

Five or three years.

**Question:** “Have you taken another person’s property unjustly through evil intent?”

Three years.

**Question:** “Have you committed sacrilege—that is, practiced what haruspices, augurs, and diviners do; or have you made vows at trees, springs, or enclosures, or by any other means; cast lots; or performed an aversion ritual?”

Five or four years.

**Question:** “Have you abducted a virgin or a widow?”

Do penance for three years.

**Question:** “Have you taken money in a church unjustly?”

Three years, or restore it fourfold.

**Question:** “Have you betrayed some matter through an unjust delay?”

Do penance for three years.

**Question:** “Have you led away or transferred, by any means, your slave or another Christian person into captivity?”

Do penance for five or three years.

**Question:** “Have you burned a house or a farmyard?”

Three years.

**Question:** “Have you vomited because of drunkenness?”

Fifteen days; if through a quarrel, forty days; if unknowingly, seven days.

[Col. 0982C]

**Question:** “Have you forced anyone to drink so that he became drunk, or have you done this out of hatred?”

One hundred days.

**Question:** “Have you drunk blood, or eaten from any animal or human being?”

Do penance for three years.

“I took another person’s treasure, for which I did not fulfill the prayers that were owed.”

**Question:** “Have you eaten carrion or flesh torn apart by beasts?”

Forty days.

**Question:** “Have you drunk from a liquid in which a mouse or weasel had been found dead?”

**Question:** “Have you despised a fast proclaimed in the church, or acted against the decrees of the elders?”

Forty days.

**Question:** “And if it was during the four seasons of the year or Lent?”

One year.

**Question:** “Have you suffocated your child or another child so that it died?”

Seven, five, or three years.

**Question:** “Have you drunk any magical potion—that is, herbs or other substances—to prevent yourself from having children; or given such a thing to someone else; or wished to kill a person by means of a potion; or, using blood or your husband’s semen, so that he would love you more, have you tasted it or drunk urine?”

Do penance for seven, five, or three years.

“You killed your offspring.”

Do penance for ten years.

**Question:** “And if you killed a son or daughter?”

Do penance for twelve years.

**Question:** “And if it was in the womb before conception?”

One year.

**Question:** “If after conception?”

Three years.

**Question:** “If an infant died through negligence without baptism?”

One year, and never without some form of penance.

**Question:** “Have you performed other pagan practices, such as those performed at the Kalends of January, in *cervulus* or *vagula* [terms uncertain]?”

Do penance for three years.

**Question:** “Have you placed your child on a roof or in a furnace for the sake of some healing?”

Do penance for five years.

Finally, the penitent is to be told:

“Many are my sins, in deeds, in words, and in thoughts.”

**Response:** “Do you have faith confessed before God and the priest, so that your sins may be forgiven?”

**Response:** “I do.”

**Question:** “Do you believe this?”

**Response:** “I believe.”

**Question:** “Do you have the will to amend what you have done against God’s commandments?”

**Response:** “That is my will.”

**Question:** “For what you have confessed, do you wish to receive judgment and observe it faithfully, renounce every device of the devil, and believe in the Trinity?”

**Response:** “I do.”

Say to him:

“May the Lord be your helper and protector, and may he grant forgiveness for your past, present, and future sins.”

Then impose penance upon him and judge according to the measure of his crimes. After penance has been imposed, say the psalm “O God, save me by your name.” Then say these prayers over him.

**Collect:**

“Hear, O Lord, our prayers, and spare the sins of those who confess to you, so that those whom the guilt of conscience accuses may be released by the forgiveness of your mercy. Through.”

**Another:**

“Grant, O Lord, to this servant of yours N. worthy fruits of penance, so that, having obtained forgiveness for his offenses, he may be restored harmless to your holy Church, from whose integrity he had departed by sinning. Through.”

**Another:**

“May the cleansing of crimes and the granting of forgiveness to sinners precede this servant of yours N., you who have said that you prefer the repentance of sinners to their death. Grant, therefore, O Lord, that he may celebrate the vigils of penance for you and, having corrected his deeds, rejoice that before the eternal joys he has been granted forgiveness. Through.”

**Another:**

“Be present, O Lord, to our supplications, and mercifully hear me, who also am the first to need your mercy, so that, although you have appointed me to be the minister of this work not by merit of election but by the gift of your grace, you may give me confidence to carry out your commission; and work through our ministry what belongs to your goodness. Through.”

## ORDER FOR RECONCILING PENITENTS

[Note: [Col. 0983D] The same order that we publish separately here from the Vienna manuscript occurs in its proper place, on Holy Thursday, in another manuscript from which we shall publish book III of the order of the divine office throughout the year. That this was done on the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper is shown to have been the custom of the Roman Church by Innocent I in his letter to Decentius of Gubbio. It is also noted in book VII, chapter 73, of the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings* in these words: “All public penitents shall assemble on the Thursday before Easter, which is the Lord’s Supper, at the city, in ashes and sackcloth, with faces prostrate in the presence of the bishop; and there they shall be reconciled and judged by the bishop canonically and properly, as is contained in the Sacramentary and the Roman Ordo.” In the church of Milan, however, it was done on Friday, as is gathered from the twentieth letter of Saint Ambrose to his sister Marcellina, no. 20, and also from book V of the *Hexameron*, the final sermon. It is clear from canon 6 of the Fourth Council of Toledo that the same rite prevailed in Spain; Martène also reports that it was practiced in some places in Gaul, book I of *The Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 6, article 5, no. 10.]

From the manuscript of the Imperial and Royal Library at Vienna, tenth or eleventh century, Theology no. 359.

While the pontiff sits before the doors of the church, the penitents stand at a distance in the church atrium with the archdeacon, awaiting his command. Before presenting them, the archdeacon asks in these words: “The venerable pontiff is present,” and so forth.

Then the pontiff says: “Come.”

And the deacon, on behalf of the penitents: “Let us bend our knees.”

Then all those standing bend their knees, as do the penitents. When this has been done, the deacon, on behalf of the pontiff, says: “Rise.”

The same is done a second time, with the bishop repeating: “Come, come.” The deacon follows: “Let us bend our knees,” as before. Thus they come on the ground as far as the middle of the atrium floor.

When, however, for the third time the lord bishop announces the antiphon, “Come, come, come,” the deacon continues: “Let us bend our knees.” Immediately the penitents fall with the deacon at the feet of the bishop and remain prostrate until the lord bishop rises and signals to another deacon, who continues: “Rise.” The clergy then sing the antiphon: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. I will bless the Lord in all things,” and continue to the end.

While the clergy sing the psalm with the antiphon “Come, children,” the penitents are continually presented by hand by the archdeacon [the transmitted wording is corrupt], are handed over by the archdeacon to the bishop, and are restored by the bishop to the bosom of the Church, remaining prostrate on the ground throughout.

Then the bishop begins the antiphon: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.” Psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God.”

When it is finished, the bishop prostrates himself together with the penitents in the oratory, while the clergy perform the litany. When it has been completed and “Kyrie eleison” has been said, he rises from the ground and says:

“Our Father.”

And the prayers:

“Save your servants, O Lord, my God, who hope in you.”

“Turn, O Lord—how long? And be gracious toward your servants.”

“Send them, O Lord, help from the sanctuary, and protect them from Zion.”

“Make your face shine upon your servants; save them, O Lord, and do not put them to shame.”

“O Lord, see my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my offenses.”

“Hear me, O Lord, for your mercy is kind, according to the abundance of your mercies.”

“Do not remember our ancient iniquities; let them quickly precede us.”

[Col. 0984C]

“Help us, O God our Savior, and for the glory of your name, O Lord, deliver us.”

“O Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.”

**Prayer:** “Be present, O Lord, to our supplications,” and so forth.

**Another:** “Hear, O Lord, our prayers,” and so forth.

**Another:** “May these servants,” and so forth.

**Another:** “God of infinite mercy and immeasurable truth, be gracious toward our iniquities and heal all the sicknesses of our souls, so that, having received the forgiveness of your mercies, we may always rejoice in your blessing. Through.”

**Another:** “God, beneath whose eyes every heart trembles and every conscience is afraid, be merciful to the groans of all and heal the wounds of everyone, so that, just as none of us is free from guilt, so no one may be excluded from forgiveness. Through.”

**Another:** “Grant, we ask, O Lord, to these servants of yours worthy fruits of penance,” and so forth.

“Almighty everlasting God, to those who confess to you,” and so forth.

[Col. 0985A]

“Almighty and merciful God, who [grant] forgiveness of sins.”

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, look down favorably,” and so forth.

“Merciful God, gracious God, who according to the abundance of your mercies blot out the sins of penitents,” and so forth.

**Another:** “We ask, O Lord, your majesty,” and so forth.

**Another:** “We ask you, O Lord, to deliver your servants from your anger,” and so forth.

**Another:** “God, who purifies the hearts of those who confess to you and releases those who accuse their consciences from every bond of iniquity, grant forgiveness to the guilty and provide medicine to the wounded, so that, having received remission of all sins, they may thereafter remain in your sacraments with sincere devotion and suffer no loss of eternal redemption. Through.”

**Another:** “Most gracious creator and most merciful restorer of the human race, who, in the reconciliation of the fallen, also willed that I, who am the first to need mercy, should serve the effects of your grace through the priestly ministry, so that, when the merit of the suppliant ceases, the indulgence of the one who forgives may become more wondrous.

“God, who always temper justice according to the law by multiplying mercy, while you apply penance to offenders, while you do not withdraw the gifts of your providence even from the wicked, and while by moderating vengeance you hold it back.

“God, who redeemed by the blood of your only Son the human being cast down from eternity through the envy of the devil, give life to these servants of yours, whom you by no means desire to die, and whom you have not abandoned though they went astray; receive them once corrected.

“May this weeping of your mourners move your mercy; heal their wounds. Extend your kind hand to those lying prostrate. Do not allow your Church to be dishonored by being deprived of any portion of its body. Do not let your flock suffer loss. Do not let the enemy rejoice at the loss of your household. Do not let a second death seize souls reborn through saving tears.

“To you, therefore, we all humble ourselves. To you, O Lord, we pour out our suppliant prayers. To you we offer the weeping of our heart. Spare those who confess, so that, through your mercy, they may not fall under the punishments that threaten or the sentence of the future judgment. Let them not know what terrifies in darkness, what crackles in flames; and, having now returned from the path of error to the way of justice, may they never again be wounded by new injuries.

“Be gracious, therefore, O Lord, toward those who tremble and supplicate under the expectation of your judgment. Extend the right hand of salvation to raise up those lying prostrate in humility.

“To us also, your servants, whom you have appointed ministers of the apostolic key and priestly office not by merit of election but by the gift of your grace, give confidence to carry out so great a commission. And work through our ministry what belongs to your power.

“Most merciful shepherd, recognize the sheep of your redemption, bound by the chains of sins, and, entreated by the prayers of your Church, release them. Let them return to the unity of your Church; and, returning after the bitter hunger of their wretched exile, adorned in splendid clothing, let them rejoice that they have been received again at their father’s banquet. Let them lose nothing of the honor of adoption, nothing of the portion of their inheritance; but let what your grace has bestowed and your mercy has restored remain whole and perpetual for them.”

## Absolution by a priest

“Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned to say to your disciples: ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be loosed in heaven’—of whose number, although unworthy and bound by the chains of sins, he willed by his condescension that I should be—may he himself, by the abundant gift of his goodness and through the ministry of my own depravity, deign to absolve you from all the excesses of your human frailty, contracted inwardly and outwardly. Amen.

“And just as he deigned to cleanse the sins of the whole world by his surrender and the pouring out of his spotless blood, so may he mercifully not disdain to cleanse the stains of your sins also, through the intercession of that same holy blood, which was poured out for the forgiveness of sins. Amen.

“With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, may he also deign henceforth to strengthen your devotion by the help of his grace, so that in this world you may be able to escape the snares of sins that creep upon you, and in the world to come possess without end the eternal life obtained through Christ’s blood. Amen.

“With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who made us when we did not exist and redeemed us when we were lost, to the praise and glory of his name for ever and ever. Amen.”

## Signed absolution

“As the principal sentence declares: **‘Because we all offend in the world,’** and therefore we groan, so we are consoled by the principal sentence: **‘For if we confess our sins, Jesus Christ our creator, redeemer, and savior is faithful and just. We have him as a just advocate with the Father, and he is the propitiation for our sins. He faithfully intercedes for us who confess, forgives us our sins, and cleanses us from every iniquity.’**

“Therefore, our brother, since you have confessed your sins to me, by the authority of the Church that our Lord Jesus Christ entrusted to his disciples and apostles when he said: **‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them,’** and through those same apostles to their successors, whose place we, although unworthy, occupy; although not by merit, nevertheless in name and by the assumption of office he granted the same authority, and he said to the one who faithfully believes in him: **‘Let it be done for you according to your faith.’**

“By his grace and power, through the power of the Holy Spirit, who is the remission of all sins, may he forgive you all your sins, free you from every evil, preserve you in every good work, lead you into eternal life, and bring you to the company of the saints, the citizens of heaven. Amen.”

**Prayer:** “Grant, we ask, O Lord, to these servants of yours, according to your most merciful compassion and according to their desire, the fruit of the absolution of their sins, so that they may be a worthy temple of your dwelling and may thereafter deserve to remain absolved from every stain of crime, standing before you with the righteous and the saints. Through Jesus Christ.”

**Another:** “We too, according to the authority entrusted by God to us unworthy servants, absolve you from the bond of your offenses, so that you may deserve to have eternal life. Through him who lives.”

## Another signed absolution

“Brother N., the Lord Jesus Christ, who said to his disciples: **‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose shall be loosed in heaven,’** of whose number he willed that we, although unworthy, should be, may he himself through our ministry absolve you from all your sins, whatever you have negligently committed in thought, delusion, and deed, and, once absolved from the bonds of sins, may he deign to lead you to the kingdom of heaven. Amen.”

## Another

“Brother N., may you deserve to receive the absolution and remission of your sins through the invocation of the name of God and through our ministry, here and for ever. Amen.”

Here he sprinkles them with blessed water and then says:

**“Rise, you who sleep; rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.”**

After this the penitents rise, and the bishop admonishes them not to restore by repetition what they have washed away through penance.

The order continues as above.

## PRAYERS FOR VISITING THE SICK

(Manuscript Cod. Th. V, 683, tenth century.)

“God, who granted your servant Hezekiah fifteen additional years of life, by your power likewise raise your servant from the bed of sickness to health. Through.”

**Another:** “Look, O Lord, upon your servant laboring under the illness of his body, and revive the soul which you created, so that, corrected by chastisements, he may immediately feel himself saved by your healing. Through.”

[Col. 0987C]

**Another:** “Almighty and merciful God, whose immense goodness we ask you to show by deigning to visit beneficially, in your name, this servant of yours lying exhausted in his dwelling, just as you visited Tobias, O Lord, and Sarah, Peter’s mother-in-law, and the centurion’s boy; so may you also deign to visit this man with his former health. Through.”

## OTHER PRAYERS

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who strengthen the frailty of our condition by the infusion of your gracious power, so that our bodies and limbs may be invigorated by the saving remedies of your goodness, look favorably upon this servant of yours, so that, every bodily necessity of sickness having been removed, the grace of his former health may be perfectly restored in him. Through.”

[Col. 0987D]

**Another:** “God, who always rule your creation with devoted affection, incline your ear to our supplications, and look favorably upon your servant N., who is suffering from adverse bodily health; visit him with your salvation and grant him the medicine of heavenly grace. Through.”

**Another:** “God, who have granted the human race both the remedy of salvation and the gifts of eternal life, preserve your servant in the gifts of your virtues, and grant that he may feel your healing not only in body but also in soul.”

**Another:** “God of the heavenly powers, who by the authority of your command drive every sickness and every infirmity from human bodies, be graciously present to this servant of yours N., so that, when his infirmities have been driven away and his rights restored, he may immediately bless your holy name with renewed health. Through.”

[Col. 0988A]

**Another:** “God, who sent your apostle Saint Peter to your servant Tabitha so that she might be raised to life through his prayers, hear us on behalf of your servant N., whom our frailty visits in your name, so that your healing, having been entreated, may come to his aid. Through.”

**Another:** “Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who are the way, the truth, and the life, hear and preserve your servant, whom you brought to life by redeeming him at a great price through the sacred blood of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. Who…”

## Blessing over the sick person
God the Father Almighty, who created you, heal you; and may there be no pain in your head or in your hair, nor in your eyes, nor in your breasts, nor in your mind, [Col. 0988B] nor in your ears, nor in your whole body. Rise, rise, Lord; make the devil flee, and cast him out from the head, from the hair, from the forehead, from the eyes, from the tongue, from beneath the tongue, from the mouth, from the throat, from the heart, from the shoulders, from the belly, and from all the limbs of this person. Through him. The blessing of God the Father.

Almighty eternal God, who drive away the illnesses of souls, display the power of your aid upon this sick person, so that, having recovered complete health, he may render thanks to you in your Church. Through him.

Another. Almighty and merciful God, who come to the aid of those laboring in dangers and who temper scourges, we beseech you: by your holy visitation raise up your servant N. from this illness by which he is held, [Col. 0988C] and present him sound to your holy Church, for the praise and glory of your name. Through him.

## Blessing over one person

May the God of heaven bless you; may Christ, the Son of God, help you; may he deign to guard and preserve your body in your service. Through him.

Another. May he enlighten your mind and guard your understanding; may he extend his grace to you for the advancement of your soul; may he free you from every evil; may he defend you with his right hand. And may he who always helps his saints himself help you and lead you to the heavenly kingdoms. He who lives and reigns, God.

Another. Lord God eternal, who mercifully redeemed both sexes from the destruction of everlasting death through Jesus Christ your Son, born of the Virgin Mary, may you deign to bless this servant of yours, who serves you with devoted mind, with every spiritual blessing, so that he may possess faith amid grace and always persevere in the commandments of your law; may he despise earthly and transitory things, love eternal and invisible things with attentive meditation, and, remaining among the number of your saints, confidently meet the heavenly Bridegroom with the lamps of good works. Amen.

Another. May God bless you, who in the beginning created all things. May God the Son bless you, who descended from the heavenly seats as Savior for us. May the Holy Spirit bless you, who rested in Christ in the likeness of a dove in the river Jordan; may he himself sanctify you in the Trinity—he whom all nations await as coming [Col. 0989A] for judgment, who with the Father lives and reigns, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Another. May God the Father bless you; may Jesus Christ guard you; may the Holy Spirit enlighten you all the days of your life. May the power of Christ strengthen you. May the Lord forgive you all your offenses, he who lives and reigns in perfect Trinity, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Another. May that almighty God, the Father from heaven, bless you—he who through his glorious birth, his marvelous resurrection, his venerable cross, his most holy Mother, and the outpouring of his precious blood came to redeem us from the earth. Amen.

May God the Father bless you; may God the Son heal you; [Col. 0989B] may God the Holy Spirit enlighten you; may he save your body, guard your soul, illumine your heart, direct your understanding, and lead you to the life above. Amen.

Another. May the Lord Jesus Christ be with you, to refresh you; may he be around you, to lead you; may he be above all things, to bless you; may he be for you, to intercede for you. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Another. May he bless, protect, and defend you all the days of your life, and lead you to the kingdom of his glory—he whom all nations await as the coming judge. Amen.

Another. O God, who do not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn and live: forgive this servant of yours, who has turned to you with his whole [Col. 0989C] heart, his sins, and grant him the grace of everlasting life. Through him.

Here let a more private place be provided for the sick to confess.

I confess to the Lord and to all his saints, and to you, priest of Christ, that I have sinned greatly throughout my life: in thought, in speech, in deed, in eating, in gluttony, in drunkenness, in the cares of this world, in the desire of the flesh, in avarice, in lust, in uncleanness, in pollution, in pride, in vainglory, in arrogance, in boasting, in concealment, in disobedience, in stubbornness, in hardness of mind, in contradiction, in murmuring, in indignation, in contempt, in detraction, in wandering, in hatred, in envy, in cursing, in obstinacy, in fornication, [Col. 0989D] in whispering, in muttering, in perjury, in lying, in theft, in negligence, in the sadness of this age, in vain joy, in speaking, in keeping silent, in rebuking immoderately, in forgiving carelessly, in vain affection, in harshness, in pretense, in laughter, in joking, in vulgarity, in discord, [Col. 0990A] in sowing discord, in false peace, in feigned friendship, in cowardice, in sluggishness, in hearing, in taste, in touch, in sight, in smell, in giving, in receiving, in contention, in receiving interest.

### Another confession of sins

[Note: In the library of Caesar, Lambecius’s hand records that this was written in this manuscript under Otto I. From the celebrated Codex Augiensis of the same imperial library, Theol. 149, he published an even older Germanic confession in book II, chapter 5, p. 318, of the Imperial Library. Diedericus von Stade repeats it in *Specimen lectionum antiquarum Francicarum*, p. 20 and following. Sebastian Münster published a similar confession in the vernacular speech still used among us, called Old Franconian; Grupenius, in *Formulis veterum confessionum*, notes many Anglo-Saxon features in it. There follows the shorter confession which, after Achil. Gassarus, Goldast, vol. III of *Rerum Alemannicarum*, p. 145, Eccard, *Francia Orientalis*, p. 930, and Schilter, *Thesaurus*, vol. I, p. 87, published with various versions and variant readings from Brower, *Antiquitates Fuldenses*, book II, chapter 14, transcribed from a manuscript of St. Gall. Grupenius added, in third place, the Lambecian confession of the likewise Alemannic Codex Augiensis, and finally an Anglo-Saxon confession from the canons of the year 967 under King Edgar, Hanover, 1767.]

#### Old High German confession

*Ih. gihun. gode. almahdigen unde allen godes engilon unde allen godes heilegon unde dir godes boden allero minero sundino unde uuili dero bigihdig uuerdan.*

I confess to almighty God, to all God’s angels, to all God’s saints, and to you, God’s messenger, all my sins, and I wish to confess them.

*So sochsegi uremidi so uuaz soih unrehdes gisahrode, unrehdes gihanedi, unrehtero uuordo, unrehtero uuerco, unrehtero gidanco, ubilero lusto, ubiles uuillen, fluochonnes, liogannes, bisprachidu, unrehtes stadales, unrehdes sedales.*

Whatever evil I saw wrongfully, whatever I heard wrongfully, wrongful words, wrongful works, wrongful thoughts, evil desire, evil will, cursing, lying, slander, wrongful standing, wrongful sitting—

*In uncidin sclaphun, uncidin uuachun, in uncidigimo mazze, uncidigimo dranche, thaz unmezzon uehonti, minero spiungu, huores, thiubu, manslahdu, meinero eido, minero fastu, ferbrocheneru mina chirichun.*

I sinned in improper sleeping, in improper waking, in improper food, in improper drink, in excessive hunting, in spying, in fornication, in theft, in manslaughter, in my oaths, and in broken fasts.

*So nisuohda, so ih solda, sunnon daga unde andere beilega daga, so ne ereda noh ne begienc, so ih solta heilegan uuizzuht, so ne gihielt, so ih solta minan curs, ne iruulta, so ih solta ghorsam ni uuas.*

I did not attend my churches as I ought; I neither honored nor observed Sundays and other holy days as I ought; I did not keep holy discipline as I ought; I did not fulfill my course as I ought; I was not obedient as I ought.

*Thurphtigun nint phiec, so ih solta alamuosa nigab, so ih solta ana urlaub gab unde na dazih nisolta.*

I did not care for the needy as I ought; I did not give alms as I ought; I gave, and took, without permission what I ought not.

*Zuene nibesuonda, so ih solta sunda ni uerliez, thien ih solta mine nahiston so ni minnota so ih solta thes alles unde anderes manages thes ih uuidar got sculdic si.*

I did not reconcile two people; I did not abandon the sin I ought to have abandoned; I did not love my neighbor as I ought; and I did not love much else that I ought to have loved—all this and many other things for which I am guilty before God.

*Thes ih in minero cristanheidi gehiezi unde ih daz beminen menisgin ferliezzi unde bemineru chindesgi geburidi so mir iz slafanti geburiti so uuachandi so ih iz selbo gefremidi oder anderemo gehancti oder anderen gespuoni.*

Whatever I promised in my Christianity and then neglected; whatever I incurred through my humanity and through the birth of my child; whatever befell me while sleeping or awake; whatever I myself did, or laid upon another, or prompted others to do—

*So ih es gehuge so ni gehuge, so ih es gedahte oder gesahi oder ih iz gedadi oder gesprachi, so uuirdon ih es alles bigihdig gode almahdigen unde allen godes heiligon unde thir godesmanne.*

whether I remember it or do not remember it, whether I thought it, saw it, did it, or spoke it—I confess all of it to almighty God, to all God’s saints, and to you, man of God.

When someone comes to a priest to confess his sins, he is first questioned in this manner.

**Question.** Do you believe in God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

**Response.** I believe.

**Question.** Do you believe that these three persons, as we have said—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are three persons and one God?

**Response.** I believe.

**Question.** Do you believe that in the very flesh in which you now are, you must receive either good or evil, whatever you have done?

**Response.** I believe.

**Question.** Are you willing to forgive those who have sinned against you, so that God may forgive your sins, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “FORGIVE, AND YOU WILL BE FORGIVEN. BUT IF YOU DO NOT FORGIVE PEOPLE THEIR SINS, NEITHER WILL YOUR HEAVENLY FATHER FORGIVE YOU YOUR SINS”?

And the priest should bless him, pray, and say to him:

Almighty God, who said, “WHOEVER CONFESSES ME BEFORE PEOPLE, I TOO WILL CONFESS HIM BEFORE MY FATHER,” may he bless you, guard you, and grant you remission of all your sins and crimes. Amen.

May almighty God have mercy on you and forgive you all your sins. Amen.

May he free you from every evil and preserve you in every good. Amen.

May he grant you true humility and true repentance, sobriety and endurance, good perseverance and a good end, and lead you into eternal life. [Col. 0991B] Amen.

May the Lord forgive you all your sins, past, present, and future. Amen.

May the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, enlighten you. Amen.

May the Lord save you, his servant. Amen.

May the Lord guard you from every evil. Amen.

May the Lord bless you from Zion. Amen.

May the Lord send you help from the sanctuary. Amen.

May the Lord preserve you, and may Christ, the Son of God, Savior of the world, give you life. Amen.

May almighty God be favorable to you, here and forever. Amen.

Then, after the penance and explicit profession of faith have been received, the visitors should return. They then begin to sing the psalm with the antiphon, “In your strength hear me, O Lord.” Psalm: “O Lord, hear my prayer.” The Lord’s Prayer follows, with these versicles:

Save your servant.

**Response.** My God, who hopes in you.

Send him, O Lord, help from the sanctuary.

**Response.** And from Zion protect him.

May the enemy accomplish nothing against him.

**Response.** And the son of iniquity—

May the Lord preserve him and give him life.

**Response.** And make him blessed.

May the Lord bring him help upon his sickbed.

**Response.** You will transform his entire bed.

Rise, O Lord, my God, and exalt—

**Response.** Do not forget the poor.

To you, O Lord, the poor man is abandoned.

**Response.** You will be a helper to the orphan.

You have heard the desire of the poor.

**Response.** The preparation—

Make your mercies marvelous.

**Response.** You who save those who hope in you.

But you dwell in the holy place.

**Response.** The praise of Israel.

In you our fathers hoped.

**Response.** They hoped and you delivered them.

To you they cried out and were saved.

**Response.** In you they hoped and were not put to shame.

Many are the tribulations of the righteous.

**Response.** And from all these—

The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants.

**Response.** And none of them—

Do not hand over the souls of those who confess you to beasts.

**Response.** The souls of the poor.

Rise, O Lord; help us.

**Response.** And deliver us for the sake of—

## Prayers

[Col. 0992A]

Grant, we ask, O Lord, to this servant of yours a worthy fruit of repentance, so that, having obtained forgiveness for his offenses, he may be restored innocent to your Church, from whose integrity he had strayed by sinning. Through him.

Another. May your mercy, we ask, O Lord, go before this servant of yours, and may all his iniquities be erased by your swift forgiveness. Through him.

Another. Hear, O Lord, the prayers of those who beseech you, and spare the sins of those who confess to you, so that those whom the guilt of conscience accuses may be absolved by the indulgence of your mercy. Through him.

### Another

Almighty everlasting God, in your goodness forgive this servant of yours who confesses his sins, so that the guilt of conscience may not harm him more toward punishment than the indulgence of your goodness benefits him toward forgiveness. Through him.

After this, the sick person is anointed with consecrated oil, making crosses at five places of the body, and this is said to him:

N. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, receive healing.

I anoint your forehead with holy oil in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, for the remission of all sins, so that this anointing with oil of sanctification may be for you the purification of mind and body, and so that the unclean spirit may not remain hidden in you, neither in your limbs nor in your marrow nor in any joining of your members, but that the power of Christ Most High and of the Holy Spirit may dwell in you. Amen.

The antiphon follows, with the psalms to be sung:

Heal, O Lord, this sick person whose bones are troubled and whose spirit is troubled. Turn, O Lord, and heal him.

Psalm: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.”

First psalm: “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up.”

Psalm: “Blessed are they whose…”

Psalm: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.”

Second psalm: “Blessed is he who understands.”

Psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God.”

First psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God.”

Third psalm: “May God have mercy on us.”

Psalm: “O God, attend to my help.”

Psalm: “Incline, O Lord.”

Psalm: “O Lord, hear.”

First psalm: “Out of the depths.”

Psalm: “O Lord, hear.”

Second psalm, with the litany, until the anointing is finished.

Afterward he makes a cross at the ears, saying:

N. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, receive healing.

I anoint these ears also with the liquid of holy oil in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, so that whatever harmful sin has been admitted through the pleasure of hearing may be removed by spiritual medicine. Amen.

Then, making a cross over the eyes, he says:

N. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, receive healing.

I anoint your eyes with sanctified oil in the name of the Holy Trinity, so that whatever you have sinned through illicit sight may be expiated by the anointing of this oil.

Then the nostrils are anointed:

N. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, receive healing.

I anoint these nostrils with holy oil in the name of the Holy Trinity, so that this anointing may cleanse whatever harmful thing has been contracted through excessive smell.

Then the lips are anointed:

N. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, receive healing.

I anoint these lips with the remedy of consecrated oil in the name of the Holy Trinity, so that whatever you have sinned through idle or even criminal speech may, by divine clemency, be cleansed through this anointing.

Afterward the breast is anointed. [Note: [Col. 0993D] This part of the body ceased to be anointed; Mabillon had already observed, in the preface to the sixth Benedictine century from Christ’s true birth, from the life of Saint Augendus, that it had formerly been the only part likewise anointed: when he was lying at the point of death, he called one of the brothers to him—the very man whom he had once specially charged with the task of anointing the sick—and secretly asked that his little breast also be anointed, as was customary.]

N. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, receive healing.

I anoint your breast with holy oil in the name of the Holy Trinity, so that by the protection of this anointing you may be able to fight bravely against the aerial hosts.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father—

Then he makes a cross between the shoulder blades and in the middle of the shoulders:

N. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, receive healing.

I anoint these shoulders, or the middle of the shoulders, with sacred oil, so that, fortified on every side by spiritual protection, you may be able courageously to despise the darts of the devil’s assault and repel them far away with the strength of assistance.

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Afterward he makes a cross on the palms:

N. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, receive healing.

I anoint these hands also, in the name of the Holy Trinity, with consecrated oil, so that whatever they have done in an illicit or harmful work may be removed through this anointing.

Then the feet are anointed, saying:

N. In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk.

I anoint these feet with blessed oil in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that this anointing may erase whatever they have committed through excessive or harmful walking, and so that, strengthened by this anointing, you may be able to overcome the aerial hosts.

## Prayer

Almighty God, who through the mouth of your blessed apostle James commanded this ministry to be performed for all the sick, preserve in your servant N. the gifts of your virtues, and grant that he may receive your healing not only [Col. 0993C] in body but also in mind. Through him.

Another. Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who are the way, the truth, and the life, hear and preserve this servant of yours, whom, redeeming him at a great price, you have given life through the sacred blood of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with you.

Here he is to receive Communion. [Note: [Col. 0994D] See Launoi’s book entitled *The Ancient Tradition of the Church Explained concerning the Eucharist Given to the Sick after Anointing*. From it I thought it necessary to say a few things about this rite, which prevailed everywhere, in Part II, investigation V, chapter 3, no. 3, p. 486.]

May the peace and sharing of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul unto eternal life. Amen.

## Other prayers

Let us pray, brothers, to our Lord for our brother, whom a harsh illness grievously afflicts at present, that the Lord’s goodness may deign to heal him with heavenly medicines, so that he who gave life may give health. Through him.
