# BLESSING OF CANDLES

3 February. Hypapante (the Meeting [of the Lord]). [Note: [Col. 1053D] Joseph Beleth, who lived in the twelfth century, mentions this celebration in his explanation of the divine offices. This feast, also called Candlemas, is recalled as deriving from the most ancient custom of the Romans of purifying the city at the beginning of February by going around or walking through it with burning candles in their hands; hence the feast was also called Amburbale.] At Saint Mary’s.

*(From Codex Vindobonensis theol. no. 685, tenth century.)*

[Col. 1053A] Lord God almighty, Creator of heaven and earth, King of kings and Lord of lords, hear us, your servants, crying out and praying to you. We beseech you, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who created all things from nothing, and by your command caused this liquid, through the work of bees, to come to the perfection of wax, and who on this day fulfilled the request of the righteous Simeon: we humbly beseech you to b+less and sancti+fy these can+dles for human use and for the health of bodies and souls, whether on land or on water, through the invocation of your holy name, through the intercession of holy Mary, your mother, whose feast we devoutly celebrate today, and through the prayers of all your saints. May this people of yours, carrying them honorably in their hands, singing to you [Col. 1053B] and praising you, be heard by you from your holy heaven and from the seat of your majesty. Be favorable to all who cry out to you, whom you redeemed with your precious blood, you who live and reign throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

The Lord be with you. And with your spirit. Lift up your hearts. We have them with the Lord. Let us give thanks to the Lord our God. It is right and just. It is truly right and just, fitting and saving. For through the most serene and most tranquil star, your mother, whose most sacred name, because of her ineffable and unspeakable merit, is interpreted as “star of the sea,” you have deigned to illuminate the human race. For this greatest joy, exulting today and reverently carrying these candles in our hands, and crying out with an unceasing voice, we ask that, for the sake of the sweetest love and most merciful intercession of your worthy mother, ever-virgin, you may mercifully grant that we, unworthy yet redeemed by your precious blood, may enjoy the eternal and true light. Through.

Let us pray. Almighty and everlasting God, who on this day presented your Only-Begotten Son to be received in the holy temple in the arms of holy Simeon, we humbly implore your clemency: deign to b+less and sancti+fy these can+dles, which we, your servants, receiving in the magnificence of your name, desire to carry, and to kindle them with the light of heavenly blessing, so that, offering them to you, Lord our God, we may be found worthy to be presented in the holy temple of your glory, kindled by the holy fire of your sweetest charity. Through.

[Col. 1054A] Then let the candles be distributed to each person and lit. While all remain standing in the same place, let this antiphon be sung:

Antiphon. Hail, full of grace, virgin Mother of God, for from you has arisen the Sun of justice, illuminating those who are in darkness. And rejoice, righteous elder, receiving in your arms the liberator of our souls, who grants us resurrection.

Prayer. Hear us, we ask you, Lord, your people, and grant that what you have given them to venerate outwardly with annual devotion, they may attain inwardly through the light of your grace. Through.

Then, going out from there for the first time, let them proceed as far as the cross while singing:

Antiphon. Simeon received an answer from the Holy Spirit: he would not see death unless he had seen Christ the Lord. And when they brought the child into the temple, he took him in his arms, blessed God, and said: “Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace.”

Versicles.

He who was offered without sin upon the altar of the temple.

May he, in mercy, remove every crime from us.

What the venerable choir of prophets once sang, filled with the Holy Spirit, is shown to have been accomplished in Mary, the Mother of God: he who was without sin.

This virgin conceived the God and Lord of heaven and earth, and, having given birth as a virgin, deserved to remain inviolate after childbirth. He who was without sin.

The righteous elder Simeon joyfully took him in his arms in the house of the Lord; for this reason he saw with his own eyes the Christ whom he had desired. He who was without sin.

Kindly favor, we ask, the prayers of your suppliant, O Mother of the eternal King, radiant one who holds the kingdoms of lofty Olympus. He who was without sin.

To our God be glory and power. May there be perpetual salvation and everlasting honor to him who, three and one, sits in the highest citadel of heaven. He who was without sin.

Prayer. Illuminate your people, Lord, we ask, and always kindle their heart with the splendor of your glory, so that they may continually recognize and truly grasp their Savior. Through the same.

Then, proceeding from there, let them come to the altar of Saint Mary while singing:

Antiphon. Adorn your bridal chamber, Zion, and receive Christ the King. Embrace Mary, who is the heavenly gate, for she herself carries the King of glory. The virgin of the new light comes forward, bringing her Son in her hands before the morning star. Receiving him in [Col. 1054D] his arms, Simeon proclaimed to the peoples that he was Lord of life and death and Savior of the world.

Prayer. Let us pray. Grant, we ask, Lord, to your people an unshakable firmness of faith, so that those who confess your Only-Begotten, eternal with you in your glory, truly born in our bodily nature from a virgin mother, may be freed from present adversities and admitted to lasting joys. Through.

Then, with the cantor beginning the antiphon “When they brought the child,” Psalm “Blessed,” let us pray.

Complete your grace in us, we ask, Lord, who fulfilled the expectation of the righteous Simeon, so that, just as he did not see death before he was found worthy to see Christ the Lord, so we too may obtain eternal life. Through the same.

[Note: [Col. 1055D] Most of the prayers and antiphons of this festive rite agree with modern Roman usage; concerning its antiquity we have spoken in Part III, Investigation IX, chapter 2, no. 12. Nowhere, however, in our liturgical monuments does anything occur concerning the blessing of a new fire struck from flint, from which the candles were to be lit. Saint Bernard mentions this at the beginning of Sermon 1, On the Purification, as do various ritual books cited by Martène.]

*(From the Rhenaug manuscript, approximately eleventh century.)*

[Col. 1055B] Hail, full of grace. Verse: We have received, etc. The Lord be with you.

Let us pray:

Teach your people, we ask, Lord; and grant that what you give them to venerate outwardly with annual devotion, they may attain inwardly through the light of your grace. Through our Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1056D] Roman Missal: “Hear,” etc.]

Lord God, Creator of heaven and earth, King of kings and Lord of lords, hear your unworthy servants, crying out and praying to you. We beseech you, etc.

God the almighty Father, unfailing light, Creator of all lights: hear us and b+less this light, which we offer while asking that it be sanctified and blessed by you, so that we may be kindled and illuminated by the fire of your brightness. And just as you illuminated Moses by fire, so, we ask, illuminate our hearts and senses, and deign to send your holy angel Raphael, so that he who tore away and drove off the deadly demon afflicting Sarah and Tobias may crush and destroy him from all the dwellings of those who worship the Lord: from basilicas, houses, corners, beds, dining rooms, and every place in which those serving the Lord live and rest, sleep, keep watch, walk, or stand. May he no longer be able to trouble them or inflict terrors upon those whom the anointing of your holy chrism has made secure.

I b+less you, wax, in the name of the holy Trinity, so that you may be the destruction of the devil and of all his companions. Through him who lives and reigns, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1055D] Be present to our supplications, almighty God, and permeate these candles with your b+lessing, [Col. 1056A] so that the faithful people, carrying them in their hands, may rejoice not only in outward light, but, with blindness of heart driven away, may grasp the light that shines in darkness, so that they may never stray from the way of truth. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages. Amen.

The Lord be with you, etc. Lift up your hearts, etc. Let us give thanks to the Lord, etc. It is truly right, etc., eternal God.

Source and origin of all light, who illuminated the world with the light of your brightness by sending us your Only-Begotten through the womb of the undefiled Virgin, and whom you promised long beforehand through the oracles of the prophets, you sent in the last times as light to peoples sitting in darkness; in the region of the shadow of death, brightness arose for them in him. You too, by your blessing, deign to bless these candles prepared for your name; you who transferred us from the power of darkness into the light and kingdom of your beloved Son, through whom light has arisen in darkness for the upright in heart, and the joy of eternal salvation.

And you who filled the righteous Simeon with faithful expectation, so that he would not see death before he saw Christ the Lord clothed in flesh, the light and salvation of the whole world: may you yourself so fill us with the light of your brightness that you drive away from us every darkness of unbelief. And just as today you dismissed your servant in peace, so may you deign to guide us in the peace of your holy Church, so that we may be able to enter the harbor of eternal rest, and, drenched in rays of light [Note: [Col. 1056D] Read: “of your light.”], may there, on the day of righteous Judgment, joyfully behold, with the hymn-singing choirs of angels, the face of the unfailing sun. Through the same, our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages. Amen.

Then let them be sprinkled, incensed, and distributed.

Antiphon. A light for revelation, etc. Verse: Simeon, taking the child in his hands, gave thanks and blessed the Lord.

Almighty and everlasting God, who sent your Only-Begotten, begotten from you before all ages but incarnate in time from the Virgin Mary, as the true and unfailing light to drive away the darkness of the human race and kindle the light of faith and truth in the world: mercifully grant that, just as we deserve to be illumined outwardly by bodily light, so also inwardly by spiritual light. Through the same Christ.

[Col. 1055]

# BLESSING OF ASHES

[Col. 1055D] The Lord be with you. Let us pray.

God, who are moved by humility and appeased by satisfaction, incline the ear of your mercy to our prayers, [Col. 1056D] and mercifully pour out the grace of your blessing upon the heads of your servants through the sprinkling and touching of these new ashes [Note: [Col. 1056D] Read: “having been touched.”], [Col. 1057A] so that you may fill them with the spirit of compunction, effectively grant what they rightly ask, [Col. 1058A] and decree that what has been granted remain untouched with perpetual stability. Through.

[Note: [Col. 1057B] I found this one prayer, which is also contained in the Roman Missal, in the manuscript Rhenaug. 600, approximately six hundred years old, for the blessing of ashes; it seems that the monks first imitated it on this day, according to the discipline of penance, with the imposition of ashes. It is useful here to describe in due order a distinctive rite from the manuscript *Work of God* of the fourteenth century, which remained in use in the monastery of Saint Blasius until the sixteenth century:

On Wednesday at the beginning of the fast, let the exposition of the Gospel “When you fast” be read, though it is not to be proclaimed by the deacon. At all the hours, let chapters on fasting and a collect for sins be said.

The order of the procession on that day is to be carried out as follows. At the customary general hour, after the prayer has been made, let the antiphon “Arise, O Lord” be sung with the verse “God, with our ears”; on that day, however, without “Glory,” while two bells sound meanwhile. After it: the chapter “Not according to our sins,” Lord, have mercy, Our Father, Psalm “God, have mercy,” the chapter “Do not remember,” The Lord be with you, and the prayer “Hear us.”

Then the priest, wearing a stole over an alb, rises and comes before the altar with the lay brothers who are to hold the cross and the ashes, and he stands in the middle, so that the lay brother holding the cross is on his left and the one holding the ashes on his right. No one is to hold holy water in his hands there.

Then the priest, standing barefoot, says the chapter “Help us, God our Savior.” After it he adds this prayer: “God, who are justly angry.” Then follows the blessing over the ashes, while the others remain at prayer in their places. This prayer is not to be said solemnly, but plainly, as are the preceding ones: “Almighty and everlasting God.”]

[Column 1058B] Then, when all rise together, let the cantor impose the antiphon “Let us be changed,” with the verse “God have mercy.” Then, without the Gloria, let the antiphon be repeated. [Column 1058C] Let them go barefoot with fear and reverence, while all meanwhile receive ashes upon their heads, bending their knees before each person takes them for himself. The secretary must have these ashes burned and ready in the morning before Terce, from the olive branches that the elders had offered into the priest’s hands in the preceding year on Palm Sunday. He must also have them thoroughly sifted through such a vessel as is used for sifting flour. Then, when those carrying the holy objects leave the church—first, namely, the holy water, then the cross, and afterward the priest—let the priest sing the antiphon “Be gracious,” with the verse “Help us, O God.” Likewise, near the vestibule, and thus with the aforesaid antiphon, let them enter the chapel of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Afterward the priest says the chapter “Hear us”; then he solemnly adds this prayer: “The Lord be with you. Let us pray: Grant us, O Lord, the defenses of Christian warfare.” Then the prayer of the Blessed Virgin Mary. When it is finished, let them prostrate themselves and pray in silence. After this, when the sign has been given, let them rise, sign themselves, make the sign before and behind, and begin the litanies. With these they return to the mother church, proceeding around it, as is customary. On the first day of the fast, moreover, the cantor shall announce at the chapter, on a written sheet, the daily mandate concerning what must be done for the poor; and on that day let it begin according to what has been ordained (or announced), as the customary book teaches. On the same day let a procession be made, and let this same practice be observed every Wednesday and Friday until Easter.]

.

[Column 1057]

# BLESSINGS OF PALMS

## + BLESSING OVER PALM BRANCHES

*(From the most ancient Sacramentary of Rheinau.)*

[Column 1057A]

Good Lord, our Redeemer, who of your own will draw near to the passion of our redemption, while the road is strewn before you in eager rivalry with branches of trees and you are met with victorious palms and the voice of praise: we beseech your divine Majesty that you may gladly receive the confession of our mouths and of our bodies in the humiliation of fasting, and grant us to bear the fruit of our greenness, so that, just as those people went out to meet you with branches of trees, so we may joyfully deserve to meet you when you return at your second coming with the palms of victory. Through the Lord.

## BLESSING OF PALM AND OLIVE BRANCHES

[Column 1057B]

Almighty and merciful God, extend your mercy toward us, so that what we ask of you in hope we may, by your gift, deserve to obtain. Through.

Another. We ask you, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, that you would deign to look upon this creation of the olive, etc.

Another. Almighty and eternal God, who gather what is scattered, etc.

Another. God, who sent your Son Jesus Christ our Lord into the world for our salvation, etc.

(+) Among the other commandments of your wonders, to praise + and bless you, who gave Noah, the just offspring of Lamech, [Column 1058A] to whom you revealed through the Spirit the waters of the Flood, knowing what was to come; whose ark bore witness to the mother Church for our salvation; from it the dove, flying spiritually (or specially), brought back a fruitful shoot of the olive, which Noah joyfully received when it returned to him; which, returning to him with spiritual (or special) fruit, he gladly received. From the anointing of its branch Jacob, the chosen one, erected a title to the Lord, vowed a vow, and poured oil over it.

This is the sign of that branch flowing from the heavens with grace and filling the vessels of the people. This is the grace that also blessed the widow through oil. This is the sign of that branch planted beside streams of water, whose leaf does not wither; through it the Church is daily brought forth by the washing of baptism, [Column 1058B] and our sins are wiped away. This is your planting, O Lord, very good indeed; and you are the life and resurrection of the dead, who raised Lazarus, dead for four days, from the dead. Therefore the crowd, coming to meet you with palm branches, cried out: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” Therefore we ask your clemency, O Lord, that you may rescue us, your servants, who have received the grace and faith of this reality, from the mouth of hell; and that by the help of your grace you may deign to grant us that, living justly, piously, and holily, you may cause us to share fellowship with your Elect and Saints. Through Christ.

## BLESSING OF PALMS

*(From Codex Vindobonensis theol. 149, formerly from Reichenau, ninth century.)*

[Column 1059A]

Almighty God, who for the salvation of the human race descended from heaven to earth, and, as the hour of your passion approached, came to Jerusalem upon a donkey, and willed to be called King and praised by the crowds: deign to bestow your bene+diction upon these branches of palms and of other foliage, so that all who receive them may be so filled with the gift of your blessing that in this age they may overcome the temptations of the ancient enemy, and in the future may be able to appear before you with the palm of victory and the fruit of good works. Through our Lord.

### Another Blessing

Almighty and eternal God, who in the Flood showed your servant Noah, by the sending forth through the mouth of the dove bearing [Column 1059B] an olive branch, that peace had been restored to the earth: we humbly beseech you that your truth may sancti+fy this creation which we offer before the sight of your glory, so that the devout people, receiving it, may deserve to obtain the grace of your blessing. Through.

Another. Almighty and eternal God, creator and redeemer of the world, who for the sake of our liberation and salvation deigned to descend from the highest citadel of heaven, assume flesh, and undergo passion; and who, of your own will, as that passion approached, willed to be blessed and praised by the crowds meeting you with palm branches, and to be called with raised voice the blessed King who comes in the name of the Lord: now deign to accept the confession of our praise and to bestow bene+diction and sancti+fication upon these palm and flower branches, so that whoever thereafter carries anything of them in the service of your worship may be sancti+fied by heavenly blessing and may deserve to receive the remission of sins and the rewards of eternal life, through you, Savior of the world, who live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.

[Column 1059C]

### Other Prayers on Palm Sunday for Blessing Flowers or Palms

God, who sent your Son Jesus Christ our Lord into this world for our salvation, etc.

### Another Prayer

Almighty and eternal God, who deigned to descend from heaven to earth and willed to come to the passion of your will, so that you might free the human race through your precious blood; who on the Mount of Olives sent your disciples and commanded them to bring with them [Column 1059D] a she-ass and its colt, because you, God, deigned to mount it; and the Hebrew children came to meet you with palm branches, praising you and saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel! Hosanna in the highest!”

You who guided Noah in the ark over the waves of the Flood, and he sent a dove from it to survey the world; when it returned to him, it brought an olive branch in its mouth, and from it anointing arose. Therefore Jacob erected a stone as a title, and poured blessed oil from olive branches upon the top of the title; from it you anointed your kings and prophets with oil.

Therefore we ask you, almighty God, to bless these olive branches which your servants are about to receive [Column 1060A] in their hands; and, coming to meet you, blessing you and saying, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel, Savior of the world,” who live and reign for ever and ever.

Another. God, who gather what is scattered and restore what has been gathered, who [to] your peoples, etc.

Another. We ask you again, holy Lord Father, that you would deign to look upon this creation of the olive or of trees, which you commanded to be produced from the substance of wood, which the returning dove carried in its own beak to the ark; deign to bless and sancti+fy it, so that whoever receives anything from it may receive it for the defense of soul and body. Let it be for us, O Lord, a remedy of salvation through the sacrament of your grace. Through our Lord.

# PALM SUNDAY AT SAINT JOHN IN THE LATERAN

*(From Codex Vindobonensis theol. 685, tenth century.)*

[Column 1060B]

First the Gospel according to Matthew is read: “At that time, when they had drawn near to Jerusalem …” Then follows the blessing of palms or other foliage:

God, whose Son descended from heaven to earth for the salvation of the human race, and, as the hour of his passion approached, willed to come to Jerusalem upon a donkey and to be called and praised as King by the crowds: deign to bestow your bene+diction upon these branches of palms and other foliage, so that all who are going to carry them may, here and in the future, be able to appear with the palm of victory and the fruit of good works. Through the same Lord.

Another. God, who commanded peace to be announced to the earth through an olive branch, grant, we beseech you, etc.

[Column 1060C] Another. Almighty and eternal God, who on this day caused our Lord Jesus Christ to sit upon the colt of a donkey, etc.

## Exorcism of the Foliage

I exorcize you, every creation of leaves (read: flowers) or foliage, in the name of the [omni+potentis: almighty] Father, and in the name of Jesus [Chri+sti: Christ], his Son. May every power of the adversary, every army of the devil, every spirit of the enemy, and every attack of demons be uprooted and torn out from this creation, so that you may not presume to disturb or mock those who carry it and hasten toward the grace of God. I forbid you by our Lord Jesus Christ, who comes …

Let us pray. God, who deigned to send your only-begotten Son for our redemption, so that you might recall your people, submerged from the beginning in the depths of sin, from death to life, and, after the deadly bond had been erased by the blood of your Son, renew the kingdom for the nations. God, who gather what is scattered and preserve what has been gathered, who blessed the peoples carrying branches to meet Christ: bestow bene+diction also upon these branches of palms and trees, which your servants faithfully receive for the blessing of your name, so that wherever they are brought they may obtain your blessing, and, every adverse illness having been driven away, your right hand may protect those whom it has redeemed. Through the same Lord.

The Lord be with you. And with your spirit. Lift up your hearts. We have them with the Lord. Let us give thanks to the Lord our God. It is fitting and right.

### Preface

It is truly fitting and right, equitable and salutary, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God. Creator of the world and wondrous disposer of all creatures, etc.

While the ministers distribute the branches among the people, let the clergy sing:

Antiphon: “A great crowd,” with Psalm 95, “Sing to the Lord,” first verse, and the Gloria Patri.

[Column 1061A]

## Prayer in Choir after Receiving the Branches

Help, O Lord, the weakness of your people, so that, through the intercession of your blessed martyr Alban, it may return, being guided bodily toward the fulfillment of the great solemn festival, and may reach eternal life through your mercy. Through.

[Note: [Column 1061B] In the margin of the codex one reads here: “With the blessed Mother of God, Mary,” to whom the monastery of Saint Margaret of the Order of Saint Benedict at Waldkirch was dedicated. We think that this Codex theol. 685, Imperial Library, from which we report many transcriptions, came there from the monastery of Saint Alban outside the walls of Mainz. In it the Mass of Saint Margaret, written by the same hand, is placed separately and out of order; the names of Saints Scholastica and Margaret are added in the canon after the consecration to Anastasia and Euphemia. Before the consecration, after the words “Cosmas and Damian,” are added Alban, [Column 1061C] Sergius and Bacchus, Dionysius and Boniface, Martin, Benedict; also, “and of all those saints whose solemnity is celebrated today in the sight of your majesty, O Lord our God, throughout the whole world, and of all the saints,” etc. After the Lord’s Prayer, in the prayer “Deliver us,” etc., after Saint Andrew is added: “But also to your holy martyrs Alban and Sergius, Cyriacus, Pancratius, Vincent; and to your holy confessors Martin, Bothard, Benedict, with all the saints, mercifully grant peace,” etc. Thus in the final litanies of the Rogations: “O Bothard the confessor, and Martin likewise, help us by your prayers with the confessors.” And shortly before: “Martyr of Christ Theodolus, and Alban as patron,” etc. In the same order, in the first litanies, Saints Theodolus and Alban are listed separately; the latter occurs most frequently of all in the litanies, sometimes even with the name Alban distinguished in uncial letters and marked with a sign for repetition. Saint Margaret also occurs twice, finally among the virgins. The following words are also noteworthy: “That the Lord may preserve King Otto and his army.” And: “We pray that our king Otto and his army may be kept safe on every side; Christ, hear us.” “That the raging sword and the pagan people may be driven away from us,” etc. This concerns the Hungarians of the tenth century, who continually invaded Alemannia and other regions and ravaged monasteries everywhere.]

## For the Procession

Antiphon: “The crowds come to meet him.”

Another antiphon: “Five days before the solemn Passover.”

Another: “When the people had heard.”

Another: “The chief priests gathered together.”

“One of them.”

Another: “When he had drawn near.”

Versicles: “Glory and praise.” [Column 1061B] (approximately as in the Roman Missal.)

Then follows the children’s greeting to the cross.

Antiphon: “The Hebrew children.”

Response: “As the Lord entered.”

Verse: “When they had heard …”

[Note: [Column 1061D]

These rites are reported as having been performed with especially great solemnity by Saint Ulrich of Augsburg in our Alemannia. On Palm Sunday he went very early in the morning to the church of Saint Afra, where he sang a Mass of the Trinity and performed the blessing of the branches. Accompanied by the clergy and people, he carried them, together with the Gospel, cross, banners, and an image representing our Lord Jesus Christ upon a donkey, to a certain place. There the choir of canons and a great crowd of people met him; they spread branches or garments upon the road.

The manner of the monks’ processions, divided and meeting one another, is explained as follows [Column 1062B] by the order of the Work of God, a fourteenth-century manuscript that was still observed in the sixteenth century at the monastery of Saint Blasius: After the morning Mass, let them prepare holy water; then let a procession be made through the cloister. Meanwhile let them sing Terce, and let all be vested in albs without other sacred vestments. After Terce let the deacon read the Gospel, “When he had drawn near”; then let the priest begin the blessing over the palms. When it is completed, let him sprinkle the palms with holy water; then, after incense has been offered upon the altar and afterward over the palms, let the cantor begin the antiphon “The Hebrew children.” [Column 1062C] Then let the secretary give palms to each person. When all have received their palms, let them make the procession in this manner: first the holy water, then the thurible and two candelabra, afterward the cross, then the Gospel book, and the entire choir. Let them proceed around the cloister to the monastery gates, and there let them make a station.

Likewise, after the elders have left the choir, let some of the schola remain there, who shall also have the procession arranged as written above. Let them also leave the choir and make a station behind the image of Christ. When the antiphons of the procession have been finished by the elders, let the boys begin “Glory and praise” and sing the entire verse; then let the elders repeat “Glory and praise.” Then the boys: “You are Israel, the King”; likewise the elders, “to whom belongs the child’s praise.” Let them proceed in this way to the end of the hymn “Glory and praise.” Afterward let the smaller procession return to the larger procession, each person in his order and place.

Then let the cantor begin “The crowds come to meet him.” Afterward let the lord abbot offer a palm to the Redeemer on bended knees, [Column 1062D] singing the antiphon “Shining forth”; likewise, “They began.” At the entrance, “As he entered,” then “The chief priests gathered together.” Meanwhile let two men with strong voices sing at the steps: verse, “One of them”; response, “The choir,” lest they come.

At Mass: “O Lord, do not be far away.” Let two brothers sing the Gradual; let three sing the first verse of the Tract before the steps, the right choir the second, the left choir the third, and the aforesaid three the fourth. Thus let the entire Tract be sung alternately. Let the final verse be said by everyone. While the right choir sings its verse, let the left choir sit; while the left choir sings, let the right choir sit. While they are singing at the steps, either choir may sit.

And note that, after the meal on this day, the brothers are to go to the dormitory and rest. When the time comes, let the brothers be awakened by a small bell, and afterward let the bell be rung for None.

This custom is to be begun again on Saint Easter’s Day and observed throughout the entire summer.]

.

Through the same Lord, [Column 1063B] etc.

Through, etc.

Bestow bene+diction, O Lord, we beseech you, upon these branches of palms and also of olives. We also beseech you, O Lord, to deign so to sancti+fy the aforesaid shoots of trees that the places to which they are carried may be made holy, so that every iniquity or deception of demons may depart and your right hand may always deign to protect us. [Column 1064A]

The Lord be with you. | And with your spirit. |

Lift up your hearts. | We have them with the Lord. |

Let us give thanks, etc. | It is fitting, etc. |

It is truly fitting and right, etc., eternal God. Creator of the world and wondrous disposer of all creatures, who at the very beginning of the world, when you created all things from nothing, also commanded the earth to produce fruit-bearing trees suited to various uses; and after the curse of the forbidden tree, you converted all things for us into blessing through the obedience of your only-begotten Son: bestow bene+diction also upon these branches of trees of many kinds, among which the olive tree especially excels in richness. Through it, too, when the sins of the world were once purged by the Flood poured out, the dove, carrying its branch, announced that peace had been restored to the earth. Moreover, the innocent crowd, inspired by the Holy Spirit and running to meet your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who was about to suffer for the salvation of the whole world, cut branches of palms and of this tree and spread them beneath his feet, already displaying him as though triumphant over the prince of death.

We humbly beseech you, O Lord, that we who, with annual devotion, strive to anticipate the most sacred passion of this same Redeemer may, with his help, holding the palm of victory and inwardly shining with the oil of mercy, deserve to receive, at his holy resurrection, the reward of life and the crown of immortality. Through the same Lord. Amen.

[Column 1063]

# BLESSING OF OIL

## ON HOLY THURSDAY

*(From Codex theol. 359 of the Imperial Library at Vienna, tenth or eleventh century.)*

[Column 1063C]

On that day let the bells be rung for Mass and for the other hours, as is customary on solemn days, so that everyone may come to the church in which the chrism is customarily consecrated; and then let them remain silent until Holy Saturday.

At Terce, let the priests and the other clergy put on solemn vestments; let the deacons wear dalmatics, and let the subdeacons be clothed in white silks. Let them stand in their proper order, each awaiting in the church until the lord Pontiff comes with the full procession for Mass, as is customary on solemn days, with seven deacons, an equal number of subdeacons and candle-bearers, seven candle-stands, and two thuribles with incense.

As soon as he has been ordered to do so, let the cantor and schola begin the Introit for Mass: “But we shall glory,” with the psalm, the Gloria, the verse, and the Kyrie eleison.

Then let the pontiff say: “Glory to God in the highest.” When this is finished, let him say the complete prayer, as on other days: “Peace be with you.” Response: “And with your spirit.” Prayer: “O God, from whom Judas the traitor …”

Then let the Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians be read: “Brothers, when you come together as a group …” through “so that he may not be condemned with the world.” Gradual: “Christ became obedient.” Verse: “For this reason God …”

Before the Gospel, let candles and incense be carried in, as is customary. Let the Gospel according to John be read: “At that time, before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come …” through “as I have done to you, so you also should do.”

When the Gospel has been read, after preaching to the people, let the pontiff say: “The Lord be with you.” “And with your spirit.” “Let us pray.” Then let the Offertory be sung: “The right hand of the Lord.” When the priests and others who wish have offered, let the Secret be said: “To you, Lord,” etc. (as in volume I of the *Monumenta*, p. 72).

Then follows the Preface. Let the pontiff say the *Te igitur* in its proper order, until the words “celebrating the most sacred day on which our Lord Jesus Christ was handed over for us,” but also “venerating the memory.” Then follows:

“This offering, therefore, of our service and of your entire household, which we offer to you on the day on which our Lord Jesus Christ handed over to his disciples the mysteries of his body and blood to be celebrated, we ask you graciously to accept,” and the remainder through “Who, on the day before he suffered, [Column 1065A] for the salvation of us all—that is, today—took bread into his holy and venerable hands.”

Then oil is offered to the pontiff from the vessels that the people bring for anointing both the sick and the possessed. At the end, before the words “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things,” let both the pontiff himself and all the priests present exorcize and bless it, so that it may be heard by those standing around.

## EXORCISM OF OIL

I exorcize you, most unclean spirit, and every attack of Satan and every phantom, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that you may depart from this oil, that it may become a spiritual anointing for strengthening the temple of the living God, so that the Holy Spirit may dwell in it, through the name of God the almighty Father and through the name of his most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. And the conclusion is not to be made.

Another. Send forth, O Lord, your Paraclete Spirit from heaven into this richness of the olive, which you deigned to produce from green wood for the refreshment of the body, so that by your holy blessing it may be a health-giving ointment and heavenly medicine for everyone who touches it, a protection of mind and body, for removing all pains, all infirmities, and every sickness of mind and body, with which you anointed priests, kings, prophets, and martyrs. May your perfect chrism, O Lord, blessed by you for us, remain within our innermost being. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: [Column 1065D]

In Codex Vindobonensis theol. 277, twelfth or thirteenth century, the following are added.

“And the conclusion is not to be made.” Likewise, the blessing of the same oil:

“Lord, who in your concern for human salvation endowed your creatures with the power of blessing, so that the usefulness of the sanctification of our souls might also be granted to our salvation in these times through the ministry of bodily creatures: pour your sanctification into this oil, so that the limbs it anoints may, through the expulsion of the snares of the hostile power and through the reception of the Holy Spirit’s saving grace in this present oil, drive away weakness and confer complete health, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

And the conclusion is not to be made.

Likewise, the blessing of the same oil for every sickness, at whatever time; and no conclusion is to be said in this blessing of the oil before the following is added:

“Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things. In your name, God the almighty Father, and of Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, by the sign and power of the Holy Spirit, we exorcize this creation of oil.”

Here let it be said: “Through whom,” etc.]

.

Then let it be said: “Through whom you always create all these good things,” etc. “Instructed by saving precepts and formed by divine instruction, we dare to say: Our Father.” Let the oil be carried back and kept in its proper place. Let the Mass proceed in its proper order until the episcopal blessings have been completed.

Then let the pontiff alone communicate before the altar. Let the deacon offer him the chalice, and let him not break the offerings except the one from which the pontiff communicates, on that day alone. After he has communicated, let the deacon place the chalice upon the altar. Then, having received the paten from the subdeacon, let him place it beside the chalice, on the left side of the altar. Immediately, let two deacons cover both vessels with a clean cloth, which they had previously prepared at the edge of the altar, opposite the spread corporal.

Then let the lord bishop go to his seat with the deacons and wait.

# ON THE CONSECRATION OF THE PRINCIPAL CHRISM

While the pontiff waits at his seat, let twelve priests and as many other clergy as are needed come to the sacristy to carry, with every mark of honor, the chrism oil and the oil of the catechumens and neophytes into the church before the bishop. Let the same priests be prepared, and with them the other clergy, in chasubles and solemn vestments.

[Column 1066A]

Then let two acolytes take two vessels, one to be consecrated for the chrism and the other for the oil of the catechumens, and proceed. Let those priests and the aforesaid clergy arrange themselves properly and in due order, so that first two acolytes walk with candle-stands and burning candles. Then let two crosses be carried, with the chrism oil between them. After these let the Gospel be carried, so that every good thing may be fulfilled. Afterward let the twelve priests, witnesses and fellow-workers of this most holy mystery of the chrism, follow in pairs. Then let the boys follow, singing these verses in praise of the same mystery:

Hear, Judge of the dead, one hope of mortals.  
Hear the voices of those bringing forth the gift that precedes peace.

Verse: O Redeemer, receive the song of those singing to you.

Verse: The tree, fruitful in gracious light, has brought forth this thing to be consecrated. The present crowd, bowed down, bears it to the Savior of the world.

O Redeemer.

Verse: The mitred pontiff, standing at the altar and deeply suppliant, fulfills every due rite with the consecrated chrism.

O Redeemer.

Verse: Deign to consecrate this olive oil, King of everlasting glory; make this living sign a protection against demons.

O Redeemer.

Verse: So that every sex may be renewed by the anointing of chrism, and the glory of dignity, wounded, may be healed.

O Redeemer.

Verse: With the mind washed in the sacred font, crimes are driven away; when anointed in the font, let sacred gifts flow in.

O Redeemer.

Born from the heart of the Father, filling the Virgin’s womb: grant light and shut out death for those who share in the chrism.

O Redeemer.

May this day be festive for us through the ages of ages. May it be consecrated and worthy of praise, and may it not grow old with time.

O Redeemer.

When they have come into the choir in the same order and stand facing east, and when the verses have been completed, let the lectors, doorkeepers, acolytes, and subdeacons arrange themselves from time to time and stand in their proper order according to their rank, where one ascends to the altar, so that the subdeacon is sixth in the more elevated place, and next to him the archdeacon who was reading. In this way, let them receive the wrapped vessel in order as it ascends. When it has reached the archdeacon, let him carry it, still wrapped, before the pontiff. [Column 1066D] Meanwhile, one subdeacon carries a small vessel with balsam to another deacon, and that deacon carries it to the pontiff.

Then let the same candle-stands, crosses, thuribles, and Gospel be arranged on both sides around the bishop. Likewise, let the aforesaid twelve priests, witnesses and assistants of the same mystery, stand there, so that the deacons stand behind the bishop’s back, and the priests to his right and left. The crosses and other objects are to be placed between them on either side.

When these arrangements have been made, let the bishop—or the person whom he has ordered—turn both toward the clergy and toward the people and deliver a sermon appropriate to the making of the chrism. Then let him turn toward the east and begin the consecration of the principal chrism. First let him mix the balsam with the oil; then let him breathe three times over that vessel and say in a low voice:

I exorcize you, creation of oil, through God the almighty Father, etc. (as in volume I of the *Monumenta*, p. 74).

For ever and ever. Amen.

The Lord be with you. And with your spirit.

Lift up your hearts. We have them with the Lord.

Let us give thanks to the Lord our God. It is fitting and right.

[Column 1067B] It is truly fitting and right, equitable and salutary, that we should always and everywhere give you thanks, etc. (there, p. 76).

When the blessing has been completed, let the lord bishop and the ministers who are beside him salute the uncovered chrism. Then let it descend again in order, as it ascended. While the acolyte holds the vessel, let it be carried, covered, to everyone for salutation in order, so that it is seen uncovered by no one. When this has been done, let it be handled with the highest honor until the other vessel ascends and descends again, so that both may honorably return to their proper place.

## EXORCISM OF OIL

When the vessel containing the chrism has descended, immediately let another vessel containing the covered oil of the catechumens ascend, as the first did, until it reaches the bishop. Let him breathe over it three times as over the first, but silently, in the order in which it was carried above. [Column 1067C] First let him perform the exorcism over it, and bless it as though reading a lesson.

I exorcize you, creation of oil, in the name of God the almighty Father, etc. (Volume I of the *Monumenta*, p. 74, column 1).

Then let him say: “The Lord be with you.” “God of increase,” etc. (there, p. 75).

Then let the lord bishop and those who are beside him salute it, and let it descend in order as the other did. Let it be carried to everyone for salutation. When these things have been done, let both vessels return to the sacristy in the same order and with the same dignity with which they had ascended into the church.

Then let the pontiff wash his hands. Let the deacons go to the altar and uncover the holy vessels. The pontiff, coming to the altar, shall divide the offerings for breaking, and let all the people communicate in their proper order. Let them take whole offerings from these to keep until the morning of Good Friday, and let them communicate from them without the Lord’s blood; but let the blood itself be entirely consumed on that same day.

Let the schola say the “Lamb of God” without the kiss and communion: “The Lord Jesus,” with the psalm and the Gloria. When the offerings have been broken, let the priests communicate first, then the deacons, and afterward all the others. Thus let the Mass be completed in its proper order.

At Compline: “Refreshed with life-giving nourishment.”

Over the people: “Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, that what we have received …”

Then let the pontiff descend into the sacristy, giving the priests whatever instructions he wishes. Let the new chrism be mixed with the old, if anything remains; likewise the oil. Then let it be divided among the priests. And these things are finished.

At Vespers on the Lord’s Supper. “O God, come to my assistance” is not said [Col. 1068A], but the antiphon “The cup of salvation.” Psalm: “I believed because of …” Antiphon: “With those who hate.” Psalm: “To the Lord.” Antiphon: “From unjust men.” Psalm: “Rescue me.” Antiphon: “Guard me from the snare.” Psalm: “Lord, I have cried.” Antiphon: “I looked to the right.” Psalm: “With my voice.” No reading or verse is said, but the antiphon “But when they were striving.” Psalm: “My soul magnifies the Lord.”

Prayer at Vespers:

O God, whose most sacred Supper we venerate, so that we may be found worthy of it, cleanse us, we beseech you, from the filth of sins. You graciously deigned to wash the feet of your disciples, to impress upon us an example of humility; you who, with God the Father—

When the schola first says the antiphon “The cup of salvation,” two acolytes, prepared and wearing black chasubles, immediately begin to strip the altars, continuing until Vespers is finished; afterward they are removed. From Vespers of this day the altars remain bare until the morning of Holy Saturday [Col. 1068B].

When everything has been completed, the lord Bishop proceeds with all eagerness, together with the priests and clergy, if he wishes, either before or after the meal, to the place where he intends to perform the Mandatum. One of the subdeacons, carrying the Gospel, and attendants carrying a cross, two burning candles, and incense, proceed with the archdeacon to the place where the brothers assemble for the Mandatum.

First of all, the Gospel according to John is read: “Before the feast of Passover.” Then, while the brothers wash one another’s feet, the antiphons for the Lord’s Supper are sung:

“After the supper Jesus said.” Psalm: “Have mercy on me.” Antiphon: “After he had risen.” Psalm: “May God have mercy on us.” Antiphon: “If I, the Lord and Master.” Psalm: “How lovely.” Antiphon: “By this they will know.” Psalm: “Lord, hear.” Antiphon: “After the Lord.” Psalm: “Blessed are the undefiled.” Antiphon: “Let us love one another” [Col. 1068C]. Psalm: “Behold, how good.” Antiphon: “A new commandment.” Antiphon: “In those days.” Antiphon: “Before the feast.” Antiphon: “You call me Master.” Antiphon: “Lord, do you wash my feet?”

Prayer after the Mandatum:

After the washing of the feet and after the breaking of the bread, the lord Bishop or priest pronounces these verses:

“We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple. You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly. You washed the feet of your disciples. Do not despise the works of your hands, O Lord, forever.”

Be present, O Lord, to the duties of our service, since you deigned to wash the feet of your disciples. Do not despise the works of your hands, which you commanded us to preserve, so that, just as external impurities are washed away here, so the sins within all of us may be cleansed by you. May you deign to grant this, who live, and so forth.

Another:

O God, who, in washing the feet of your disciples, gave them an example through devoted love and gave them a commandment: mercifully grant that, through obedience to your commandments and by their intercession, we may rejoice in your presence. May you grant this, and so forth.

Another:

Merciful God, grant that we who, by violating the divine commandments, have fallen from the happiness of paradise may return to the attainment of eternal blessedness through the keeping of your commandments. May you grant this, and so forth.

THURSDAY: THE LORD’S SUPPER

One must rise at midnight, and the signal is sounded; after this it is not sounded again until the night of Holy Easter at Matins. The church, however, is adorned with every light [Col. 1069A]. As usual, “O God, come to my assistance” is not said, nor the Gloria, nor the Invitatory. Instead, the cantor begins the antiphon in the psalms, as it is contained in the antiphoner. The priest does not complete the prayer at the end, but one must rise silently, and the lector asks for a blessing. When he has finished, he does not say “But you, Lord”; rather, he is instructed to conclude with the words of the lessons.

Three lessons are read from the Lamentations of the prophet Jeremiah, beginning where it says, “How solitary sits the city,” and ending at “The Lord has resolved to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion.” Three are read from Saint Augustine’s first treatise on the psalm “Hear, O God, my prayer.” Three are read from the Apostle, where he says, in 1 Corinthians, chapter 11: “I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you.” Nine psalms, nine lessons, and nine responsories, together with the antiphons [Col. 1069B], are all to be completed.

Matins follows. When Matins has been completed, neither “Kyrie eleison” nor “And lead us not into temptation” is said.

At the third hour they enter the sacristy. Both the pontiff and all the deacons put on dalmatics, or the full vesture. While the pontiff sits in his chair, two ampullae containing oil are prepared. The better one is brought to the pontiff, so that, after receiving balsam and mixing it with the oil, he may fill it with his own hand; the other is held full by the ministers. Having washed his hands, the pontiff proceeds with seven candle-stands to the Masses [Note: [Col. 1069] The whole Mass is in M. R.; the prayers that follow are likewise read in the Pontifical of R.].

After the entrance antiphon has been said, “But it is right for us to glory,” the Gloria in excelsis Deo follows.

He says the prayer:

“O God, from whom Judas [received] the punishment of his guilt and of confession …,” and so forth.

The apostolic lesson is read: “Brothers, when you come together in one place,” ending at “so that we may not be condemned with this world.”

The Gradual follows: “Christ was made obedient for us,” ending “unto death.”

The Gospel according to John, chapter 13, is read: “At that time, knowing that his hour had come,” ending “as I have done for you, so you also should do.”

The Offertory is sung: “The right hand of the Lord.”

The prayer over the offerings follows: “May he himself, we beseech you, O Lord.” The pontiff says the Eucharistic prayer in its proper order up to the words: “Celebrating the most sacred day on which our Lord Jesus Christ was handed over for us; and also commemorating—”

The following is then said:

“Therefore, O Lord, we beseech you, graciously accept this offering of our service and of your entire family, which we offer to you for the day on which our Lord Jesus Christ delivered to his disciples the mysteries of his body and blood to be celebrated. He, on the day before he suffered for the salvation of us all—that is, today—took bread into his holy and venerable…”

Likewise, at the end, before “Through him, O Lord, you always create all these good things,” the ampullae from which they offer to the people are lifted; both the lord pope and all the priests bless them [Col. 1069D].

BLESSING OF THE OIL FOR THE SICK

“Send forth, O Lord, we beseech you, your Holy Spirit,” and so forth.

“Through him, O Lord, you always create all these good things” follows. When this has been completed, the bishop alone receives Communion before the altar, and the deacon assists him with the chalice. On that day only, after he has communicated, he places the chalice upon the altar.

Then, having received the paten from the subdeacon, he places it beside the chalice on the left side. Immediately two deacons cover both vessels with a clean linen cloth, which they had previously prepared at the edge of the altar opposite the pontiff, after the corporal had been spread.

At once two acolytes hold the wrapped ampullae, visible beneath a white silk cloth. They hold them at the middle with the left arm, the cloths thrown over the left shoulder so that they reach the right shoulder, allowing them to retain the hanging ends. The subdeacon comes from where they stand beneath the shoulder, receives the ampulla containing the mixture together with its cloth, and gives it to the archdeacon. The archdeacon carries it before the pontiff at the altar.

Then the pontiff, facing east, with the deacon holding before him the ampulla wrapped in the cloth on his left arm, as we have said, says:

“Lift up your hearts.”

Response: “We have them lifted to the Lord.”

“Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.”

Response: “It is worthy and just.”

He enters into the consecration of the chrism in a loud voice; but before it is blessed, he breathes three times into the ampulla.

“It is truly worthy and just, right and salutary, that we should always and everywhere give thanks to you, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God; who in the beginning, and among other things,” and so forth.

EXORCISM OF THE OIL

“O God of increase and spiritual progress,” and so forth.

When this has been completed, he blesses the ampulla of oil that was brought in the order described above, and likewise breathes into it silently. The ampulla containing the chrism, however, as soon as it has been blessed [Col. 1070C], is covered so that it may appear like a naked soul; while an acolyte holds it, everyone venerates it in order. The Bishop and the deacons first venerate it uncovered.

After this has been completed, the Pontiff washes his hands, comes before the altar, and the entire people communicate in their proper order. They preserve some of the consecrated sacrament until the following day.

TO BE COMPLETED

“Refreshed with life-giving nourishment, we beseech you, Lord our God, that what we perform in the time of mortality we may attain through the gift of your immortality. Through…”

On that day, at the ninth hour, he ordered fire to be struck from a stone in a place outside the basilica; if there was an oratory there, they struck it at the doorway; otherwise, in the place he had designated. First, so that a candle could be lit from it. This candle is to be placed on a reed and kept by the church’s mansionary, or in the place where the lamp is lit, until Holy Saturday, to light the paschal candle that is to be blessed on that same day according to the order contained in the sacramentary.

On that day everyone sings the daily office together. From Vespers of this day the altars are to remain bare until the morning of Saturday.

FRIDAY IN PARASCEVE

One must rise at midnight. Nine psalms are said with responsories. Three lessons are read from the Lamentations of the prophet Jeremiah, beginning where he says, “The Lord has resolved to destroy,” and ending at “The mercies of the Lord are many.” Three are from Saint Augustine’s treatise on Psalm 63. Three are from the Apostle, where he says in Hebrews, chapter 5: “Let us hasten, therefore, to go forth” [Col. 1071A].

Matins follows. The lamps are extinguished. The light of the church begins to be extinguished from the beginning of the nocturnal chant, in this order: it begins at the entrance of the church and is gradually diminished. Thus, for example, when the first nocturn has been completed, one third of the lights should appear extinguished; after the middle nocturn, another third; and when the third has been completed, no light should remain except for seven lamps.

These too are extinguished during Matins in the following manner. At the beginning of the first psalm, a custodian is always ready in the place on the right side of the church, near the lamps. When he hears the antiphon, holding a reed in his hand, he extinguishes one lamp. At the end of that psalm he extinguishes another on the left side. Thus, one on one side and another on the other are extinguished until the Gospel. During the Gospel, the lamp in the church is extinguished [Col. 1071B].

At the third hour the Pontiff, or the one who holds his place, proceeds in the designated church within the city, though not in the principal church. When he has come from the sacristy and proceeded before the altar to pray at the oratory, as is customary, as soon as he rises he ascends silently to the seat. When he is seated, the subdeacon immediately ascends to read.

After the lesson the canticle “Lord, I have heard” is sung with its verses. The Pontiff says, “Let us pray,” and the Deacon says, “Let us bend our knees.” He prays at length, then says, “Arise,” and says the prayers—perhaps the prayers are intended here—which, when he has finished, everyone silently goes outside.

The priests of the churches, whether from the city or from the suburbs, go through their own churches so that they may do everything in this order until Vespers. They change only this: where the Pontiff mentions the apostolic [one], they name their own bishop [Col. 1071C].

After the prayers, the cross is prepared before the altar, with a space left between it and the altar, and is supported on either side by two acolytes. An oratory is placed before it. The Pontiff comes, venerates the cross, and kisses it; afterward the bishops, priests, deacons, and the others in order, and then the people. The Pontiff remains seated until everyone has venerated it.

As soon as the first two priests have venerated it, they enter the sacristy—or wherever the body of the Lord has been placed—which had remained from the previous day. They place it on a paten, while one subdeacon holds before them a chalice with unconsecrated wine and another subdeacon holds the paten with the Lord’s body. While they hold these, one priest takes the paten and the other the chalice, and they carry them onto the bare altar.

The Pontiff remains seated while the people venerate the cross. Whenever the Pontiff or the people venerate the cross, the antiphon is always sung:

“Behold the wood of the cross, on which hung the salvation of the world; come, let us adore.”

Psalm 118 is said.

When the cross has been venerated and returned to its place, the Pontiff descends before the altar and says:

“Let us pray. Instructed by saving precepts and formed by divine institution, we dare to say: Our Father, who are in heaven.”

The following is said:

“Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord, from all evils.”

When they have said “Amen,” he takes a portion of the consecrated sacrament and places it in the chalice, saying nothing. Everyone communicates in silence. When all has been completed, the Pontiff says:

“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, peace be with you.”

Response: “And with your spirit.”

After a short while, each person says Vespers privately, and thus they go to the meal.

HOLY SATURDAY

One must rise at midnight. Nine psalms are said with responsories. Three lessons are read from the Lamentations of Jeremiah, beginning where it says, “The mercies of the Lord are many,” and continuing to the end. Then homilies of the holy Fathers appropriate to that day are read. The lighting and extinguishing of the candles is done as stated above [Col. 1072B].

After the third hour on Saturday, those who are to be baptized proceed to the church. They are arranged in order as they are listed: males on the right, females on the left. The priest makes the sign of the cross on the forehead of each.

Afterward, having placed his hand upon each person’s head, he says:

When this has been completed, he touches each person’s nostrils and ears with spittle and says:

“Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened,” for the fragrance of sweetness. “But you, devil, flee, for the judgment of God is drawing near.”

Afterward he touches the shoulders and breast with holy oil and says:

“Do you renounce Satan?”

Response: “I renounce [him]; and all his pomps?”

Response: “And all his works?”

Response: “And I anoint you with the oil of salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord, propitiated unto eternal life. Peace be with you” [Col. 1072C].

When this has been completed, he walks around, placing his hand upon their heads and chanting in a loud voice: “I believe in God.” He then turns to the women and does likewise.

Afterward the archdeacon says to them:

“Pray, elect ones; bend your knees.”

After a short while he says:

“Arise; complete your prayer together and say, ‘Amen.’”

They all respond, “Amen.”

Again they are admonished by the archdeacon in these words:

“Catechumens, depart. If anyone is a catechumen, let him depart. Let all catechumens go outside.”

Again the deacon says:

“Most beloved children, return to your places, awaiting the hour at which God’s grace may work baptism in you.”

At the ninth hour the priests and levites enter the sacristy and put on the vestments in which they are to celebrate the vigil. After the candle has been lit, they all proceed together from the sacristy into the church in silence, singing nothing. The candle is placed in a candlestick before the altar. One deacon asks one of the priests or levites who are standing there vested to pray for him. When he has risen, the deacon himself says:

“The Lord be with you.”

Response: “And with your spirit.”

He says this prayer:

[Col. 1071]

VARIOUS BLESSINGS

BLESSING OF THE CANDLE

[Col. 1071D]

When the lessons have been completed, a minister immediately comes, holding the ampullae in his hands and standing at the right corner of the altar [Col. 1072D]. Then he goes ahead of the pontiff to the fonts. Afterward the schola descends to the fonts to perform the litany, waiting there prepared for the pontiff.

The second member of the schola holds a golden vessel in his left hand over the chasuble, from which the pontiff is to pour chrism into the font. At the command, they perform the threefold litany.

Then the pontiff proceeds with all due solemnity, supported by two deacons. The two candle-stands that had earlier been lit always proceed before him until everything has been completed.

When the litany is finished, the pontiff says:

“The Lord be with you.”

Response: “And with your spirit.”

He says:

“Let us pray,”

and gives the prayer.

BLESSING OF THE FONT

“Almighty and everlasting God, be present,” and so forth.

CONSECRATION OF THE FONT

“The Lord be with you.”

Response: “And with your spirit.”

“Lift up your hearts.”

Response: “We have them lifted to the Lord.”

“Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.”

Response: “It is worthy and just.”

[Col. 1073B]

“It is truly worthy and just, right and salutary; O God, who by invisible power,” and so forth.

“Therefore I bless you, creature of water, through the living God, through the true God,” and so forth.

“Mark them; come forward for the blessing.”

The godfathers or godmothers mark the infants on their foreheads with their thumbs, saying:

“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

Then an acolyte again makes the sign of the cross on each forehead, saying:

“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

He places his hand upon them and gives the prayer in a loud voice, in these words:

“God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob,” and so forth.

“Therefore, accursed devil, acknowledge your sentence,” and so forth.

The deacon announces, saying:

“Pray, elect ones; bend your knees,”

and the rest as before. The godfathers or godmothers mark them as before. Then another acolyte follows, makes the sign of the cross over the males as the preceding one did, places his hand upon them, and says:

“Hear, accursed Satan. You are adjured through the name of the eternal God and of our Savior, the Son of God. Defeated by your envy, depart trembling and groaning. Have nothing in common with the servants of God, who already contemplate heavenly things, renounce you from this age, and are destined to live in blessed immortality.

“Therefore give honor to the Holy Spirit who is coming. Descending from the highest citadel of heaven, may he, for your confused deceptions, accursed one, cleanse their hearts through the divine font, sanctify them, and perfect them as a temple and dwelling. May the servants of God, completely freed from every stain of former crimes, always give thanks to the eternal God and bless his holy name forever and ever. Through…”

“God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob,” and so forth.

“Therefore, accursed devil,” as above.

The deacon likewise says:

“Pray, elect ones,”

and the rest as above. The godfathers or godmothers mark them as before.

Then a third acolyte makes the sign of the cross on the boys’ foreheads as the preceding one did, places his hand upon their heads, and says:

“I exorcise you, unclean spirit,” and so forth.

Likewise, making the sign of the cross over the females as above, he places his hand upon their heads and says:

“I exorcise you, unclean spirit, through the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, so that you may depart and withdraw from these maidservants of God. For he commands you, accursed and condemned one, who opened the eyes of the man born blind and raised Lazarus, four days dead, from the tomb. Therefore, accursed one”—as above [Col. 1074A].

“Your eternal and most just mercy,” and so forth.

The exorcism follows.

“I exorcise you, creature of water, in the name of God the almighty Father, and in the name of Jesus Christ his Son, and of the Holy Spirit. May every power of the adversary, every assault of the devil, every phantom, and every power of the enemy be uprooted and driven away from this creature of water.

“Therefore I exorcise you, creature of water, through the true God, through the living God, through the holy God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, so that you may become holy water, blessed water. Wherever you are poured or sprinkled, whether in a house or in a field, may you drive away every phantom and every power of the enemy. May the Holy Spirit dwell in this house. Through…”

Salt and ashes are mixed in, and with them he makes the sign of the cross three times over the water. Then he pours wine mixed with that blessed water into it and says this prayer:

“Creator and preserver of the human race, giver of spiritual grace, bestower of eternal salvation: you, Lord, send your Spirit upon the wine mixed with water, so that, armed with the power of heavenly protection, they may be effective for the consecration of this church or altar. Through our Lord.”

Then, with his finger, he makes the sign of the cross with that water on the right side, over the four corners of the altar. From there he sprinkles the sides seven times with hyssop, singing the antiphon:

“You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall become whiter than snow.”

Psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to”—[Col. 1074C].

Going around the altar, he then sprinkles the right-hand walls of the church until he comes before the altar, sprinkling again above and around the altar or church while singing the antiphon:

“Let God arise and let his enemies be scattered.”

Psalm: “He himself,” and so forth.

He continues until he comes again before the altar, sprinkling above and around the church while singing the antiphon:

“He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High shall abide under the protection of the God of heaven.”

Psalm: “He himself,” and so forth.

He sends two or three ministers or clerics outside the church, who sprinkle it together once while singing psalms.

Again the pontiff goes from that altar to sprinkle through the length and breadth of the church, making the sign of the cross in the same manner, or sprinkling the entire pavement, with the antiphon:

“My house shall be called a house of prayer” [Col. 1074D].

Verse: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will praise you.”

And Gloria.

When he comes into the middle of the church, he says:

“Let us pray.”

The deacon says:

“Let us bend our knees.”

“Arise.”

He says this prayer:

“O God, who sanctify places dedicated to your name, pour out your grace upon this house of prayer, so that all who invoke you here may experience the help of your mercy. Through…”

Again he says:

“Let us pray.”

The deacon says:

“Let us bend our knees.”

“Arise.”

The following prayer:

“Almighty ruler of sanctifications, whose mercy is perceived without end; O God, who embrace heavenly and earthly things together, preserving your mercy for your people who walk before the sight of your glory: hear the prayers of your servants, so that your eyes may be open over this house day and night.

“And mercifully dedicate and graciously illumine this basilica, established in honor of Saint N., for the sacred mysteries; glorify it with your own splendor. Graciously admit every person who comes to adore in this place. Deign to look upon them favorably, and for the sake of your great name, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, willingly protect those who plead in this dwelling, graciously hear them, and preserve them with eternal defense, so that they may always be happy, always rejoicing in your worship, and steadfastly persevere in the catholic faith of the holy Trinity. Through our Lord.”

“Having entered into regeneration, may he be reborn in the new infancy of true innocence. Through.”

When all this has been completed, he pours chrism from the vessel into the font over the water in the form of a cross. With his hand he mixes the chrism into the water and sprinkles it over the entire font or over the entire people.

After this, all the people who wish may receive a blessing in their vessels from that water, before the children are baptized there, to sprinkle it in their houses, vineyards, fields, and among their crops.

Then the priest, or the deacon if necessary, and the acolytes, barefoot and wearing other clean or white garments, enter the font and go into the water. First the males are baptized, then the females, under this interrogation:

“May this font be sanctified and made fruitful in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

“Do you believe in God the almighty Father, creator of heaven and earth?”

Response: “I believe.”

“Do you also believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, born and having suffered?”

Response: “I believe.”

“Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit; the holy catholic Church; the forgiveness of sins; the resurrection of the flesh; and eternal life?”

Response: “I believe.”

The infants are received from their parents and baptized under a threefold immersion, invoking the holy Trinity only once, in this manner:

“I baptize you in the name of the Father”—and he immerses him once—

“and of the Son”—and he immerses him again—

“and of the Holy Spirit”—and he immerses him a third time.

After lifting the infants in their hands, they offer them to a priest. The priest makes a cross of chrism with his thumb on the crown of their heads, invoking the holy Trinity, and says:

“Almighty God,” and so forth [Col. 1075C].

Those who are to receive them are prepared with linens in their hands. They receive them from the priests or deacons who baptized them.

The Pontiff comes out from the font and has a seat arranged for himself in the church wherever he wishes; he sits upon it. The infants are brought before him, and he gives each a stole, chasuble, chrismal, and ten siliquae, and they are clothed.

When clothed, they are arranged in order around him as they are listed. The Pontiff gives a prayer over them, making a cross with chrism on their foreheads while invoking the holy Trinity, and confers upon them the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Prayer for Confirmation

“Almighty and everlasting God, who causes rebirth…”

“Receive the sign of the cross of Christ for eternal life, reconciled through his favor” [Col. 1076A].

He says:

“Peace be with you.”

Response: “And with your spirit.”

“Behold, thus shall every person who fears the Lord be blessed. May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things that are in Jerusalem all the days of your life.”

Then he says:

“The Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit confirm you, so that you may have eternal life and live forever and ever.”

Amen.

Taking every precaution in all this so that these things are not neglected, for then all are confirmed with the legitimate name of Christianity through baptism.

Meanwhile, at the command, the schola performs the litany before the altar: first sevenfold, then, after an interval, fivefold, and again, after an interval, threefold. When it says “Lamb of God,” the master of the schola says, “Light them”; then the church is illuminated.

The Pontiff proceeds from the sacristy, with the two candle-stands mentioned above standing as before on the right and left sides of the altar.

When the litany is complete, the Pontiff says the Gloria in excelsis Deo and the prayer. Then the Apostle is read. The Alleluia follows: “Give thanks to the Lord.” The tract follows: “Praise the Lord, all nations.” The Gospel follows.

On the evening of Saturday, before the Gospel, they do not carry a light during that night, but only incense. They do not sing the Offertory, the Agnus Dei, or the Communion, but celebrate the Mass in its proper order.

Provision must be made concerning the infants: after they have been baptized, they are to receive no food and are not to be nursed before they have communicated in the sacrament of Christ’s body. On every day of Easter week they are to proceed to the Masses, and offerings are to be made for them, and all are to communicate.

The order of baptism written above is to be celebrated in every respect on the Saturday of Pentecost just as on this Saturday of Easter.

On that day they sing the daily office separately.

On that night, after cockcrow, when Matins breaks the darkness with the light, they rise and come into the church, kissing one another with mutual charity, and say:

“O God, come to my assistance.”

The Invitatory follows with Alleluia.

Three psalms follow with antiphons:

“Blessed is the man.”

“Why do the nations rage?”

“O Lord, how they have multiplied.”

Then three lessons follow with responsories. The first lesson is from the Acts of the Apostles. The second and third follow from homilies of Saint Augustine. Matins follows with Alleluia.

During the Easter Octave, over “Come,” the antiphon is:

“The Lord has truly risen,” with Alleluia.

Three psalms are appointed for each nocturn on each night until the octave of Easter, namely:

Monday:

“When I called.”

“My words.”

“O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.”

Tuesday:

“O Lord my God, in you I have hoped.”

“O Lord, our Lord.”

“In the Lord I trust.”

Wednesday:

“Save me, O Lord.”

“How long, O Lord?”

“The fool has said.”

Thursday:

“O Lord, who shall dwell?”

“Preserve me, O Lord.”

“Hear, O Lord, my justice.”

Friday:

“The heavens declare.”

“May God hear you.”

“O Lord, in your strength.”

Saturday:

“The earth is the Lord’s.”

“To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.”

“Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence.”
