See how you are to present this woman consecrated to God immaculate before the tribunal of our Lord.

# Blessing and Prayer for Making Nuns

Deign, Lord, we beseech you, to open the doors of your grace to your servants—your servant—who renounce worldly pomp, who, having scorned the devil, flee beneath the title of Christ. Receive them as they come to you with serene countenance, lest the enemy prevail in triumphing over them. Grant them the tireless arm of your help; surround their minds with the breastplate of faith, so that, enclosed within a fortunate wall, they may rejoice that they have escaped the world. Through [Christ our Lord].

## Another

Most merciful God, we invoke your compassion: we beseech you concerning these servants of yours, whom you have deigned to call from the world, after their conversion, into the number of your saints, that they may worthily preserve the faith of their conversion and obtain whatever they ask for the salvation of their souls. May their lives be approved; may they be wise and humble; learned in truth; distinguished in obedience; harmonious in teaching; unshaken in rebukes; dignified in seriousness; most devout in suffering; cautious in action; diligent in administration; strong in temptation; patient under injuries; steadfast in peace; prompt in almsgiving; frequent in prayer; effective in mercy. May they not forget that they are to be judged by your judgment.

We beseech you, Lord, graciously to receive their offerings and mercifully to grant whatever they ask of you. Through [Christ our Lord].

Almighty and merciful God, source of all holy religion and salvation for everyone who professes you, receive the profession of your servants who flee to you from the vanity of this world. We beseech you: with your help may they be stripped of all the noise of secular affairs, rescued from the snares of the ancient enemy, dead to this world, and removed from every restraint of the wicked.

Teach them, Lord, to despise all the prosperity of this life, not to fear adversity, not to inflict injuries but to endure them with equanimity, to love their enemies, and humbly to pray for their persecutors and slanderers. May they desire nothing carnally; may pride not inflate them, the heat of greed not kindle them, the incitements of luxury not inflame them, vain glory not shamefully boast through them, gluttony or drunkenness not impede them, empty ambition not hurl them headlong, the heat of spirited contention not harass them, and the desire for human opinion not exalt them. May the devil, author of destruction, neither wound nor destroy them, but may the right hand of your compassion, most merciful God, rescue them from every evil and protect, govern, and guide them in the age to come.

May they fear you, imitate you, and love you. Open their understanding, so that through devotion to the divine writings they may read you with their heart, meditate on you with mouth and deed, understand you, and serve you day and night. May they savor heavenly and eternal things and reject earthly and transitory things. May they be obedient and instructed; may they love and cherish friends and enemies for love of your name; may they hold and practice humility and usefulness. May they preserve chastity and modesty in heart and body. May they take up and guard patience and long-suffering. May they pursue and love fasting and abstinence; may they desire sighing and prayer and watch over them. May they continually accuse and wash away their sins with tears and sighs. May they carry the almighty God in heart, mouth, and deed.

Receive, we beseech you, holy Father almighty, these servants of yours whom you have rescued from the shipwrecks and dangers of this world and have deigned to call to the grace of monastic life. Graciously grant that they may continually love and follow the narrow and difficult way which they have professed, so that they may deserve to attain the eternal glory which you have deigned to promise to those who persevere in you. Through the Lord.

# Regular Profession

I, Sister N., from this day forward, being a nun, promise stability in this life, conversion of my conduct, and obedience according to the rule of Saint Benedict the abbot, insofar as human frailty permits me, before God and his saints and in the presence of the abbot. [EIBIKA: reading and meaning uncertain.]

Then let them prostrate themselves before the altar and say this verse:

Receive me, Lord, according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation.

Let it be repeated three times by all. They then add, “Glory be to the Father,” and, while they lie prostrate, let the litany and prayers follow:

Save your servants, Lord my God.

May the Lord guard them from every evil.

Send them help, Lord, from the holy place.

May the enemy accomplish nothing against them. And the Son.

Be for them, Lord, a tower of strength. From the face.

Arise, Lord; help …

Then let their clothing be sprinkled with holy water, and let this prayer follow:

Hear, we beseech you, almighty God, our prayers, and drench these garments, which your servants ask for their covering, with the shower of your most abundant blessing, just as you drenched the edges of Aaron’s garments with the blessing flowing from the head down to the beard; and just as you blessed the garments of all religious persons who please you in every way, so deign to bless these. Grant, we beseech you, Lord, that for the servants mentioned above these garments may be a saving protection, a recognition of religion, the beginning of holiness, and a strong defense against every weapon of the enemy. Through [Christ our Lord].

God, who promised your faithful a saving garment and clothing of eternal joy, we humbly entreat you: graciously bless these garments signifying mortification, humility of heart, and contempt of the world, by which your servants are invisibly to be formed for the holy purpose; and may they preserve, under your protection, the habit of monastic religion which they have received at your inspiration. Through [Christ our Lord].

## Another

God, giver of good virtues and generous pourer-out of every blessing, hear our prayers and deign to bless and sanctify these garments which your servants ask to put on as a sign that they will preserve the rule. [Through.]

## Another

Be present, Lord, to our supplications and deign to bless these servants of yours, upon whom we place the habit of holy religion in your holy name, so that, by your generosity, they may deserve to remain devoutly in the monastery and receive life. Through [Christ our Lord].

Grant, Lord, we beseech you, forgiveness of their sins to your servants, so that, persevering in regular practice in the present life, they may deserve to receive eternal pardon for all that they have done against the rectitude of your commandments through bodily pleasure, thought of the mind, or the vain ambition of this world. Through [Christ our Lord].

Then let them remove their own garments and be clothed in the things of the monastery, and let this be said:

May the Lord strip you of the old human being with his deeds and clothe you with the new human being, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth.

Then let all answer: Amen. Let them offer the offering.

# Mass on the Same Day for Them

Almighty and eternal God, who commanded us to undertake the narrow and difficult way, graciously receive your servants who flee to you from the dangers of this world; mercifully break the punishment of sins by which they feel themselves bound, and grant perseverance in good works and eternal rewards. Through [Christ our Lord].

## Preface

Truly it is worthy … Eternal God, we implore your clemency: protect your servants whom on this day you have deigned to draw away from worldly contagion and call to the profession of monastic religion. You gave them the beginning of good will; grant them perseverance in right action and the reward of eternal blessedness. Through [Christ our Lord].

## At Communion

May this reception of the divine sacrament, we beseech you, Lord, cleanse us from our offenses and mercifully rescue your servants from worldly wickedness and from the pleasures of every carnal tumult. Through [Christ our Lord].

## Another

May your protection, Lord, cleanse and fortify your servants, so that the purpose of holy virginity which they have undertaken in mind they may preserve unharmed forever under your protection. Through [Christ our Lord].

## Another

May your right hand bless your servants, we beseech you, Lord, and lead them, blameless, to eternal life. Through [Christ our Lord].

# Appointment of an Abbot

From the Canon of Theodore.

(From Codex Vindobonensis theol. 359, tenth or eleventh century.)

At the appointment of an abbot, the bishop ought to celebrate Mass and bless him with bowed head, together with two or three of his brothers, and give him the staff and sandals. After the antiphon at the Introit and the prayer has been given, the bishop announces to the people, saying an address:

Dearest brothers of our Church, the elected father is present to receive his office. Therefore we judge that he must first be examined by apostolic authority: whether he wishes to observe his purpose and the rule of Saint Benedict, and diligently to instruct those subject to him to do the same; also, to gather together, insofar as he can, the property of the church that has hitherto been unjustly dispersed in various places, and to preserve it for the use of the church, the poor brothers, and pilgrims; and thus to show himself worthy to enter upon the office.

When he has professed that he will fulfill these things to the best of his ability, let the bishop and the abbot, clothed in sacred vestments, prostrate themselves before the altar. Let the litanies be made there. Then follow the Lord’s Prayer and the prayers:

Save your servant, Lord my God, who hopes in you.

May the Lord preserve him and give him life, and make him blessed.

May the Lord guard your coming in and your going out. From now.

May the Lord guard you from every evil; may he guard your soul.

May he send you help from the holy place, and protect you from Zion.

May the enemy accomplish nothing against him, nor the son of iniquity.

Be for him, Lord, a tower of strength, against the face of the enemy.

Arise, Lord; help him and redeem him.

Lord, hear my prayer.

And let my cry come to you.

## The prayer follows

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that the desire of our heart may receive the effect of your mercy, and accompany your servant N., whom we have chosen for the governance of souls, with the gift of your grace, so that, by your generosity, we may please you through our election itself. Through [Christ our Lord].

Then let him give him the rule, saying:

Receive the rule handed down to us by the holy Fathers, for governing and guarding the flock entrusted to you by God, insofar as God himself strengthens you and human frailty permits. Through [Christ our Lord].

Then let him give him the staff, saying:

Receive the pastoral staff, which you are to bear before the company entrusted to you, as an example of just severity and correction.

# Consecration

## When an abbot or abbess is appointed in the monastery

Institutor of all good works, and so forth. Then let him place his hand upon his head, saying this prayer in the manner of a preface.

[Note: [Col. 1109D] See what we noted shortly before concerning this imposition of hands and the word “appointment” in the blessing of an abbess. This word is used according to the practice of the rule of Saint Benedict when the blessing of an abbess or abbot is under discussion. Saint Anselm mentions such a rite performed by bishops for abbots in the eleventh century, *Book II, Letter 42*, p. 358, and *Letter 52*, p. 261 [Col. 1110D].]

Almighty and eternal God, abundant Spirit, and so forth.

God, shepherd and ruler of all the faithful, look graciously upon your servant whom you have willed to preside over your Church. Grant him, we beseech you, by word and example, to advance those over whom he presides, so that together with the flock entrusted to him he may attain eternal life. Through [Christ our Lord].

## Prayer after the attainment of the dignity

Fountain of all good things, Lord, and so forth. God, whom every power serves, and so forth.

Then let the *Te Deum laudamus* be sung, with the people acclaiming, “Kyrie eleison.” Afterward he says the prayer:

Eternal God, inventor of light, we beseech your omnipotence with humble prayer: accompany your servant N., whom we have chosen for the governance of souls, with the gift of your grace, so that, by your generosity, we may please you through our election itself; through your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom and with the Holy Spirit you are one and true God, living and reigning forever and ever.

# Mass for an Abbot

“Our protector, look upon us, O God.” Psalm: “How lovely are your tabernacles.”

Mass. [Note: Here “Mass” is used uniquely for the collect or prayer.]

Grant, we beseech you, Lord, to your servant the abbot that, by preaching and practicing what is right, he may instruct the minds of his subjects by the example of good works and receive from you, the most loving shepherd, the reward of eternal recompense. Through [Christ our Lord].

## Secret

Receive our offerings, we beseech you, Lord, with favor, and mercifully protect your servant N. always and everywhere. Through [Christ our Lord].

## Blessings

May the God of heaven bless you; may Christ, the Son of God, help you; may he deign to guard and preserve your body in his service. Amen.

May he illumine your mind, guard your understanding, and extend his grace to you for the advancement of your soul. Amen.

May he free you from every evil, defend you with his right hand, and may he who always helps his saints himself help you and lead you to the heavenly kingdoms. Amen.

## At the conclusion

May this communion, Lord, cleanse us from guilt and preserve your servant through kindly compassion. Through [Christ our Lord].

# Order for Blessing a King

## Here begins the order for blessing a king, when a new king is raised to the kingdom by clergy and people

(From Codex Vindobonensis theol. 277, twelfth or thirteenth century.)

First, as he comes out of the bedchamber, one of the bishops gives a prayer:

Almighty and eternal God, who have deigned to raise your servant to the summit of royal power, grant him, we beseech you, that in the course of this age he may order all things for the common salvation of all, so that he may not depart from the path of your truth. Through [Christ our Lord].

Afterward two bishops, honorably vested and wearing relics of the saints around their necks, receive him on his right and left. The other *phaphones*—as they were once called in German, *Phaphen*—are adorned in chasubles.

[Note: Thus they were formerly called in German. In the vernacular charter of foundation of the monastery of Weingarten, dated 1090: “Welf, duke of Nornegau by God’s grace, sends greetings to all princes, counts, and free *phaphen* [priests].” This word, our *Pfaff*, seems to derive from the Greek *papa* (“father, pope”), through the Germans’ harsher pronunciation and a kind of contraction, just as we say *Kyrch* from Greek κυριακὸν (“the Lord’s [house], church”), and *priester* from πρεσβύτερος (“elder, presbyter”). These are among other ecclesiastical words of Greek origin which show that the first seed of faith among us was sown by Greeks, as we demonstrated in vol. I, Disquisition 1. This passage shows that *phaphones* were the more honored clergy, although the name *pfaff* is now commonly taken as a term of reproach. [Col. 1111D–1112D]] With the holy Gospel preceding, and with two crosses and incense of good fragrance, they lead him to the church while singing this antiphon in loud voices: “Behold, I send an Angel,” with the verse, “Israel, if you will hear me.”

At the church door let the clergy stop, and let the archbishop give the following prayer:

God, who know that the human race cannot endure by any virtue of its own, graciously grant that your servant, whom you have willed to be placed over your people, may be so supported by your help that he may be able to benefit those over whom he has been able to preside.

As they enter, let the clergy who go before sing the antiphon, “Lord, save the king,” as far as the entrance of the choir. Then let the metropolitan bishop say the prayer:

Almighty and eternal God, ruler of heavenly and earthly things, who have deigned to raise your servant to the summit of royal power, grant, we beseech you, that, freed from every adversity, he may be fortified by the gift of ecclesiastical peace and, by your gift, may deserve to attain the joys of eternal peace. Through [Christ our Lord].

There, before the choir, let the designated prince lay aside his cloak and weapons. Led between the hands of the bishops, let him proceed into the choir as far as the steps of the altar. When the whole floor has been covered with carpets and small rugs, let him lie there humbly, prostrate in the form of a cross, together with the bishops and priests prostrate on either side, while the others in the choir briefly sing the litany—that is, of the twelve apostles and an equal number of martyrs, confessors, and virgins.

Among the other petitions, let these be included:

That you may deign to choose this servant of yours, N., as king. We ask you, hear us.

That you may deign to bless and exalt him. We ask you.

That you may deign to lead him to the summit of imperial power. We ask you.

Then the prince, raised up, is questioned by the metropolitan bishop in this way:

Do you wish to hold the holy faith handed down to you by Catholic men and to observe it in righteous works?

Response: I do.

Do you wish to be guardian and defender of the holy churches and their ministers?

Response: I do.

Do you wish to govern and defend the kingdom granted to you by God according to the justice of your fathers?

Response: I do. I do, and, insofar as I shall be able, supported by divine help and the assistance of all who belong to me, I promise that I shall act faithfully in all things.

Then the metropolitan lord himself addresses the people in these words:

Do you wish to submit to such a prince and ruler, strengthen his kingdom and establish it with firm faith, and obey his commands, according to the Apostle: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers,” and to the king as to one who is preeminent?

Response: I do.

Then let the clergy standing around and the people say unanimously: “Let it be so. Let it be so. Amen.”

Afterward, with him devoutly bowing his head, let one of the bishops say:

Bless, Lord, this king of ours, you who govern all kingdoms from age to age, and glorify him with such a blessing that he may hold the scepter of David’s exalted dignity and, once glorified, may immediately be received into David’s merit.

Grant him, Lord, by your inspiration, to govern the people with gentleness just as Solomon obtained a peaceful kingdom. May he always be subject to you with fear and serve you peacefully. May he be protected by your shield together with the nobles, and may he everywhere be victorious through your grace.

Honor him above all the kings of the nations. May he rule over peoples in happiness, and may nations happily adorn him. May he live magnanimously among the throngs of nations; may he be distinguished in judgments of equity. May your exceedingly rich right hand enrich him; may he possess a fruitful homeland, and grant his children what will benefit them.

Grant him length of life through the years. In his days may righteousness arise, and may he hold a strong throne of government. May he rejoice eternally in his kingdom with gladness and joy. Through [Christ our Lord].

## Prayer

[Note: [Col. 1113D] In the Roman pontifical this prayer is shorter than here. In the ancient Roman Order, in the Codex of Ratoldus and elsewhere, it is entitled “Consecration of a King,” since the king was to be anointed for it. The cited Menardus notes more concerning the same prayer, p. 401 and following [Col. 1114D].]

Almighty and eternal God, creator of all things, emperor of angels, king of kings and Lord of lords, who caused your faithful servant Abraham to triumph over his enemies, granted manifold victory to Moses and Joshua, placed over the people, exalted your humble servant David to the summit of royal power, and enriched Solomon with the ineffable gift of wisdom and peace: look, we beseech you, upon the prayers of our humility, and multiply the gifts of your blessings upon this servant of yours, N., whom we have chosen as king with humble devotion. Always and everywhere surround him with the right hand of your power, so that, strengthened by the faithfulness of the aforementioned Abraham, relying upon the gentleness of Moses, fortified by the courage of Joshua, exalted by the humility of David, and adorned with the wisdom of Solomon, he may please you in all things and always walk with an unoffending step along the path of justice.

May he henceforth nourish, teach, fortify, and instruct your Church together with the peoples joined to it. Against all visible and invisible enemies, may he powerfully and royally administer to it the governance of your strength, and with your help restore their minds to the harmony of true faith and peace, so that, supported by the due submission of these peoples and glorified by worthy love, he may by your mercy deserve fittingly to ascend his ancestral throne.

Therefore, armed with the helmet of your protection, continually defended by an unconquerable shield, and surrounded with heavenly weapons, may he happily win the triumph of desirable victory, spread terror of his power among the unbelieving, and joyfully bring peace to those who serve you; through our Lord, who by the power of the holy cross destroyed Tartarus and, after overcoming the kingdom of the devil, ascended victoriously to heaven. In him is established every power and the victory of kings; he is the glory and life and salvation of the humble and of peoples. Who with you …

Then let another bishop say this prayer:

Ineffable God, author of the world, creator of the human race, governor of empire, confirmer of kingdoms, who from the womb of your faithful friend, our patriarch Abraham, chose beforehand kings destined to benefit the ages: now enrich this king and his army with abundant blessing through the intercession of all the saints, and bind him securely to the throne of the kingdom with firm stability.

Visit him as you visited Moses in the bush, Joshua son of Nun in battle, Gideon in the field, and Samuel in the temple. Drench him with that star-like blessing and with the dew of your wisdom, which David received in the Psalter and Solomon, his son, received from heaven through your gift.

Be his battle line against enemies, his breastplate in adversity, his helmet in prosperity, his patience in protection, and his everlasting shield. Grant that the nations keep faith with him (*illi*; variant *illius*, “his”), that his nobles have peace, love charity, abstain from greed, speak justice, and guard truth.

And thus may this people under his rule flourish, united [the text reads *coaluus*, with the note “or *coalitus*?”], through the blessing of eternity, so that they may always remain victorious, rejoicing in peace. May he himself deign to grant this, who lives with you.

Then let the metropolitan bishop anoint the hands with consecrated oil.

“Let these hands be anointed with consecrated oil, with which kings and prophets were anointed; and just as Samuel anointed David as king, so may you be blessed and established as king in this kingdom over this people, whom the Lord your God has given you to rule and govern.” What he himself may grant.

Look favorably, almighty God, upon this glorious king [*ill.*; the abbreviation is uncertain] with serene eyes; and just as you blessed Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, so deign to water and pour over him, with abundant blessings of spiritual grace, the fullness of your power. Grant him, O Lord, from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth an abundance of grain, wine, and oil, and of all crops in their seasons, so that while he reigns there may be health of bodies in the fatherland [*patria*; the manuscript has *pata*], inviolable peace in the kingdom, and the glorious dignity of the royal palace may shine before the eyes of all with the greatest splendor of royal power, gleam with the clearest light, and appear suffused with the greatest brilliance, as though drenched in the most splendid radiance.

Grant him, almighty God, to be the strongest protector of his country and, with the greatest piety of royal munificence, a consoler of churches and holy monasteries; and grant that he may be the strongest of kings, a triumphant conqueror of enemies, for crushing rebellious and pagan nations. Let him also be exceedingly terrible to his enemies through the greatest royal strength, but magnificent, beloved, and compassionate toward the nobles, the eminent men, the magnates, and the faithful of his kingdom, so that he may be feared and loved by all. May kings, too, proceed from his loins through the successions of future ages, to rule this entire kingdom; and may he deserve, after the glorious and happy joys of this present life, to possess eternal joys in perpetual blessedness. What he himself may grant.

Afterward the metropolitan prelate shall anoint the head, breast, and both shoulder joints with consecrated oil.

“I anoint you king with consecrated oil, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

[Note: This rite of anointing agrees here with the ancient Roman Order, from which the Roman Pontifical differs: in the latter, anointing is prescribed only on the right arm, between the joints of the hand and elbow, and between the shoulders.]

“May the grace of the Holy Spirit descend abundantly upon you through the ministry of our humility, so that, just as you are externally made rich by being smeared with material oil by our unworthy hands, so may you deserve to be inwardly enriched by being touched with its invisible anointing. May you always be perfectly imbued with its spiritual unction, and learn or be enabled with your whole mind to avoid and reject unlawful things, and continually be able to think about, desire, and do what is useful for your soul, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father…”

Then the following prayer is said:

“God, who are the glory of the righteous and the mercy of sinners, who sent your Son to redeem the human race with his most precious blood; who crush wars and are the defender of all who hope in you; under whose authority the power of all kingdoms is held: we humbly beseech you to bless in your mercy this present servant of yours, N., confessing you in the present royal seat, and graciously deign to be present with him, so that he who seeks to be defended by your protection may be stronger than all his enemies.

“Make him, O Lord, blessed and victorious over his enemies. Crown him with the crown of justice and piety, so that, believing in you with his whole mind, he may serve you, defend and exalt your holy Church, and rule justly the people entrusted to him by you. Let no one turn him toward injustice through evil ambushes. Kindle his heart, O Lord, to love your grace through this oil of anointing, with which you anointed kings and prophets, so that, loving justice, leading the people along the familiar path of righteousness, he may deserve, after completing the years appointed by you in royal excellence, to arrive at eternal joys. Through him.”

Another.

“May God’s Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, who was anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions, through the present infusion of sacred anointing pour upon your head the blessing of the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, and make it penetrate into the innermost depths of your heart. Thus, by this visible and tangible gift, may you perceive invisible things, and, having administered the temporal kingdom with just governance [the text reads *exsecutio*, perhaps *exsecuto* or *exsecutus*], may you deserve to reign eternally with him who alone, without sin, lives and is glorified as King of kings with God the Father in the unity of the Spirit, throughout all ages.”

Afterward he shall receive the sword from the bishops, and with the sword he shall understand that the entire kingdom has been faithfully entrusted to him to govern according to the words stated above, while the metropolitan prelate says:

“Receive this sword, imposed upon you royally through the hands of the bishops—though unworthy, yet consecrated in the place and authority of the holy apostles—and divinely ordained through the ministry of our blessing for the defense of the holy Church of God. Remember him of whom the Psalmist prophesied, saying: ‘Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one,’ so that by it you may exercise the power of equity, mightily destroy the mass of iniquity, and defend and protect the holy Church of God and its faithful. No less abhor and destroy those falsely professing the faith than the enemies of the Christian name. Mercifully assist and defend widows and orphans; restore what has been desolated; preserve what has been restored; avenge wrongs; and confirm what has been rightly established. Thus, glorious in the triumph of virtue through these deeds and an outstanding cultivator of justice, may you deserve to reign without end with the world’s Savior, whose likeness you bear in name. He who with God…”

[Note: We have supplied this phrase from the Roman Pontifical, in which the same formula for girding the king is described still more explicitly.]

When he has been girded with the sword, he shall likewise receive from them the armlets, mantle, and ring, while they say:

“Receive the ring of dignity, and through it recognize in yourself the sign of the Catholic faith, because just as today you are appointed head and prince of the kingdom and people, so may you remain an enduring author and establisher of Christianity and the Christian faith. Thus, may you be happy in deed and rich in faith, and glory with the King of kings, through him to whom belong honor and glory forever.”

Afterward he shall receive the scepter and staff, while the metropolitan says to him:

“Receive the rod of strength and equity, by which you may understand how to soothe the pious and terrify the reprobate, open a way for those who have gone astray, extend a hand to those who have fallen, destroy the proud, and raise up the humble. May the Lord Jesus Christ, our God, open the door to you; for he said of himself: ‘I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved’; and he is the Key of David and the Scepter of the house of Israel, who opens and no one closes, who closes and no one opens.

“May he be the author who leads the captive out of the prison house, and the one sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. May you deserve to follow him in all things, of whom the prophet David sang: ‘Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom.’ By imitating him, may you love justice and hate iniquity, because for this reason God, your God, anointed you, after the example of him whom, before the ages, he had anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions: Jesus Christ.”

Then the metropolitan reverently places the crown upon the king’s head, saying:

“Receive the crown of the kingdom, which, although from unworthy hands, is nevertheless placed upon your head by the hands of bishops. Understand that through it the glory of holiness, honor, and the work of strength are expressly signified, and do not fail to recognize through it that you share in our ministry. Just as we understand ourselves to be pastors and rulers of souls in inward matters, so may you always appear in outward matters as a true worshiper of God, a vigorous defender of the Church of Christ against every adversity, and a useful executor and profitable ruler of the kingdom given to you by God and entrusted to your government through the ministry of our blessing in the place of all the apostles and saints. Thus, adorned among the glorious athletes with the jewels of virtues and crowned with the reward of everlasting happiness, may you glory without end with the Redeemer and Savior Jesus Christ, whose name and office you are believed to bear. He lives and reigns, God with God the Father, forever and ever.”

Response: Amen.

[Note: Up to this point the rite agrees with the Roman Pontifical. The following blessing, consisting of three prayers, is absent there. These resemble the ancient episcopal blessings customarily given at Mass, differing according to the variety of days and feasts, as may be seen in volume I of the *Monumenta*, p. 331. Soon afterward another blessing follows here in its proper place in the celebration of Mass, before “The peace of the Lord,” and so forth.]

Immediately afterward a prayer or blessing shall be said over him, which is also to be said at the time of the synod:

“May the Lord bless you and guard you; and just as he willed you to be king over his people, so may he grant you, in the present age, to share in eternal happiness.”

Response: Amen.

“May he cause the clergy and people, whom he has willed to be gathered together under your sanction with his assistance, to be governed happily for long ages through his dispensation and your administration.”

Response: Amen.

“So that, obeying the divine commands, free from adversities, abounding in every good thing, and serving your rule with faithful love, they may enjoy tranquility in the present age and, with you, deserve to possess the fellowship of the eternal citizens.”

Amen. What he himself may grant.

Then the crowned king is honorably led by the bishops from the altar through the choir to the throne, while the clergy sing the responsory *Desiderium animae* (“The desire of the soul”).

Then the metropolitan says to him:

“Stand and retain from now on the place which until now, by paternal succession and hereditary right, has been assigned to you through the authority of almighty God and through our present transmission—that is, through the transmission of all the apostles and the other servants of God. And remember that, the closer to the sacred altars you see the clergy, the greater the honor you must accord them in their appropriate places. Thus may the Mediator of God and human beings establish you as mediator between clergy and people.”

(At this point the metropolitan causes him to sit, saying:)

“May Jesus Christ, our Lord, King of kings and Lord of lords, confirm you in this royal throne and cause you to reign with him in the eternal kingdom. He who with God the Father…”

Then let him give them the kiss of peace.

The entire company of clergy, rejoicing in that ruler, shall sing this hymn in a loud voice, with resounding hymns: *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”).

Then the metropolitan bishop shall celebrate Mass with the full procession.

“God, who dispose all things in wondrous order and govern them ineffably, grant, we beseech you, that your servant N. may determine to fulfill these things in the course of this age, so that he may prevail in pleasing you forever. Through him.”

[Col. 1118B]

### Secret

“Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, being pleased by these saving sacrifices, that your servant N. may always be found suitable for carrying out the office of royal dignity and may be made acceptable to the heavenly homeland. Through him.”

### Episcopal Blessing

“Almighty God, who willed you to be the ruler of his people: sanctifying you with heavenly blessing, may he make you a sharer in the eternal kingdom.”

### Prayer

“May he grant you triumphant victory over all visible and invisible enemies of the Christian faith, and make you for himself, far and wide, a most fortunate founder of ecclesiastical peace and tranquility. Amen.

“So that, while you hold the reins of the kingdom, the people subject to you, guarding the laws of the Christian religion, may enjoy secure and tranquil peace on every side; and when you have been placed in the council of the blessed, may they deserve to rejoice there with you in eternal happiness. What he himself may grant.”

### For the Completion

“May this reception of the saving sacrifice, O Lord, cleanse the stains of the sins of your servant N., so that it may make him fit to rule the people according to your will; and through this saving mystery may he be rendered invincible against visible and invisible enemies, by which the world was redeemed through divine providence. Through him.”

[Col. 1117]

## BLESSING OF THE QUEEN

[Col. 1117D]

At the entrance into the church the bishop shall say the prayer:

“Almighty and eternal God, source and origin of all goodness, who do not reject or turn away from the frailty of the female sex, but rather graciously approve and choose it; who, by choosing the weak things of the world, have taught us to confound all the strong; who also once willed to place in the hand of Judith, a woman, the triumph of your glory and virtue over the fiercest enemy for the salvation of the Jewish people: look, we beseech you, upon the prayers of our humility, and multiply the gifts of your blessings upon this servant of yours, N., whom with humble devotion we choose as queen.

“Surround her always and everywhere with the right hand of your power, so that, firmly protected on every side by the rampart of your defense, she may triumphantly overcome the wickedness of visible and invisible enemies. Together with Sarah, Rebecca, Leah, and Rachel, those blessed and venerable women, may she deserve to be made fruitful—or to rejoice—in the fruit of her womb, for the adornment of the entire kingdom and for governing and protecting the state of the holy Church of God.

“Through Christ our Lord, who deigned to be born from the undefiled womb of the blessed virgin Mary, to visit and renew this world, who lives with you…”

[Note: Here and before the following prayer, space for a rubric is left blank.]

“God, who alone possess immortality and dwell in inaccessible light, whose providence is not deceived in its ordering of things; who made what was to be and called things that are not as though they were; who by equitable governance cast down the proud from authority and graciously raised the humble to an exalted place: we humbly implore your ineffable mercy.

“Just as you caused Queen Esther of Israel, for the sake of salvation, to pass from the fetters of her captivity into the chamber of King Ahasuerus and into a share in his kingdom, so mercifully grant that this servant of yours, through the blessing of our humility, may pass, for the grace of salvation of the Christian people, into a worthy and exalted union with our king and into a share in his kingdom.

“And grant that, remaining always in the covenant of royal marriage, she may preserve the palm of chastity, close to virginity; that she may continually desire to please you, the living and true God, in all things and above all things; and that, with you inspiring her, she may accomplish with her whole heart whatever pleases you. Through him.”

“May the grace of the Holy Spirit descend abundantly upon you through the ministry of our humility, so that, just as you are externally made rich by being smeared with material oil by our unworthy hands, so may you deserve to be inwardly enriched by being touched with its invisible anointing. May you always be perfectly imbued with its spiritual unction, and learn or be enabled with your whole mind to avoid and reject unlawful things, and continually be able to think about, desire, and do what is useful for your soul, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Spirit lives and reigns, God, throughout all ages. Amen.”

[Note: The litanies that follow are to be referred to this same celebration of royal inauguration. Since Goldast has already published litanies of this kind in volume II of the *Antiquitates Alemannicae*, p. 147, I have judged it preferable to place here another version, one that pertains to nearby Bavaria in Alemannia, rather than reprint those already published. I have taken it from the Vienna manuscript. In Goldast, an invocation is made for Nicholas P. The same purpose is found separately in Augustine Patricius, in the *Roman Ceremonial*, for the emperor; here they are read together with the praises customarily sung for the pontiff.]

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Hear us, O Christ.

For Silvester, supreme pontiff and universal pope: life and victory.

Savior of the world: help him.

Holy Peter: help him.

Holy Paul: help him.

Saint Andrew: help him.

Saint Clement: help him.

Saint Sixtus: help him.

Saint Cyriacus: help him.

Hear us, O Christ.

For Henry, crowned by God, the great and peaceful king: life and victory.

[Note: In Goldast, the name is Louis. The same formula is recorded as having been used at the coronation of Charlemagne at Rome in the year 800, when he was inaugurated emperor on the Nativity of the Lord, as may be read in Einhard and Ademar, in their *Lives of Charlemagne*. P. Harzheim, in the *Critical Historical Catalogue of the Manuscripts of the Metropolitan Church of Cologne*, notes the litany sung on that occasion, with the rubric: “After the prayer has been completed by the pontiff, before the lector ascends the ambo.”]

Redeemer of the world: help him.

Saint Mary: help him.

Saint Michael: help him.

Saint Gabriel: help him.

Saint Raphael: help him.

Saint John: help him.

Saint Stephen: help him.

Saint Linus: help him.

Hear us, O Christ.

For the bishop chosen by God: life and victory.

Saint Felicity: help him.

Saint Perpetua: help him.

Saint Agatha: help him.

Saint Lucy: help him.

Saint Cecilia: help him.

Saint Petronilla: help him.

Hear us, O Christ.

For all the clergy of the church of Passau: life and victory.

Saint Apollinaris: help him.

Saint Lawrence: help him.

Saint Nazarius: help him.

Saint Silvester: help him.

Saint Leo: help him.

Saint Anastasius: help him.

Hear us, O Christ.

For all faithful judges and the entire army of Christians: life and victory.

Saint Maurice: help them.

Saint Dionysius: help them.

Saint Willibald: help them.

Saint Gregory: help them.

Saint Alban: help them.

Saint Martin: help them.

Saint Ambrose: help them.

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Our hope.

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Our glory.

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Our strength.

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Our mercy.

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Our help.

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Our deliverance and redemption.

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Our victory.

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Our unconquerable weapons.

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Our impregnable wall.

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Our defense and exaltation.

Christ conquers. Christ reigns. Christ commands. Our light and our life.

To him alone be glory and power throughout immortal ages of ages. Amen.

To him alone be honor, praise, and jubilation throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

To him alone be strength, fortitude, and victory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

O Christ, hear us. Three times.

Lord, have mercy. Three times.

O Christ, have mercy. Three times.

Lord, have mercy.

[Col. 1121]

## BLESSING OF ARMS

## BLESSING OF THE BANNER

[Note: The formulas for the blessing of arms and the sword, and for the presentation of the military banner, are found in Part II of the *Roman Pontifical*, titles 22, 23, and 24. A sword, helmet, or rose is sometimes sent to the pontiff by distinguished military leaders and princes. On this subject there is an exposition by Cardinal Pole in Joseph Catalanus, *Commentary on the Roman Pontifical*, volume II, p. 388, where, among other things, a brief of Clement XI sent to Prince Eugene of Savoy for this purpose, along with other examples, may be read.]

(From Vienna Codex Theol. 277, twelfth or thirteenth century, as in the *Roman Pontifical*.)

[Col. 1121A]

“Almighty and eternal God, who are the blessing of all and the strength of those who triumph, look graciously upon the prayers of our humility, and sanctify with heavenly blessing this banner, which has been prepared for military use, so that it may be strong against hostile and rebellious nations and surrounded by your protection. Let it be terrifying to the enemies of the Christian people and a firm support and sure confidence of victory for those who trust in you. For you are God who crushes wars and grants the help of heavenly protection to those who hope in you. Through him.”

## BLESSING OF THE SWORD

[Note: The following corresponds to material found in Ed. Martene, book II, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 12, taken from the manuscript Pontifical of William Durand, concerning the blessing of a new knight, in these words, volume II, p. 667: “In the blessing of a new knight, the procedure is as follows. Before the Gospel is said, the pontiff blesses his sword: ‘Hear, we beseech you, O Lord, our prayers, and this sword,’ and so forth. Another blessing: ‘Bless, O Lord, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, through the invocation…’” Martene had previously said that, since the Church abhors bloodshed, he had nowhere found a blessing of a new knight in the ancient pontifical books which he had examined with the greatest diligence and in great number. For the blessing printed at the end of the Roman Order seemed to him to have been taken, outside the proper order, from some more recent codex. Nevertheless, that bishops had blessed soldiers more than five hundred years earlier is proved by a letter of Cardinal William, in Chesne, *History of France*, volume IV, p. 765, and by others. P. Joseph Bianchini noted this and Joseph Catalanus reports it in his appendix to volume I of the *Roman Pontifical*, p. 427: from a Vallicellian manuscript of about the year 800 he gives a blessing of the banner and sword almost identical to the one we present, as well as two orders for blessing a new knight from Vatican codices nos. 4744 and 4748. The latter is the order describing how someone is made a knight in the sacred basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in the city.]

“Hear, we beseech you, O Lord, our prayers, and deign to bless with the right hand of your majesty this sword with which this servant of yours, N., desires to be girded, so that it may be the defense and protection of churches, widows, orphans, and all who serve you against the cruelty of pagans, and may be dread, terror, and fear to other plotters.”

[Col. 1121C]

Another.

“May your mercy, O Lord, protect your servant N., so that, with your help, he may keep unharmed this sword which, inspired by you, he desires to receive. Through the Lord.”

Another blessing.

“Bless, O holy Father, almighty Lord, through the invocation of your holy name, through the coming of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and through the gift of the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, this sword, so that he who today, by your mercy, is girded with it may trample visible enemies under his feet and, through victory, always remain unharmed in all things. Through him.”

The antiphon follows:

“Beautiful beyond the sons of men, grace has been poured upon your lips. Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one.”

Another.

“Almighty and eternal God, who commanded your servant N. to be girded with a prominent blade, arm him against all adversity with heavenly defenses, so that he may not be disturbed here or forever by any storms of war. Through him.”

## BLESSING OF SATCHELS AND STAFFS

[Note: The staffs and satchels mentioned here are the staffs and bags of pilgrims, such as were also blessed and given, together with swords, to those marked with the cross for the recovery of the Holy Land. Concerning this, Conrad, abbot of Ursperg, says in his *Chronicle*, p. 232: “When crowds of people, flocking together beyond belief to the churches, were running everywhere, the priestly blessing, in a new rite, distributed swords together with staffs and satchels.” See Ed. Martene, book II, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 25, at the end. But this formula of ours was composed for those traveling to Rome, to the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul.]

And over all who are about to seek the thresholds and intercession of the saints.

(From Vienna manuscript Theol. 277, twelfth or thirteenth century.)

“Lord Jesus Christ, Redeemer and Creator of the world, who commanded your blessed apostles, when they went forth to preach, to take nothing but staffs: we beseech you with humble devotion to deign to bless these satchels and these staffs, so that those who receive them as a sign of pilgrimage and for the support of their bodies may receive the fullness of your heavenly grace, and may be able to receive in them the protection of your blessing.

“Just as the rod of Aaron, flowering in the temple of the Lord, was rightly joined to its own stock from among the number of the rebellious Jews, so may you absolve from all sins those who are to be adorned with the sign of Saint Peter, so that, separated from the impious on the day of judgment, they may be crowned on the right hand. Through him.”

When the satchels and staffs are given, he says:

“Receive these satchels and these staffs, and go to the thresholds of the apostles in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Through the intercession of blessed Mary, Mother of God, and of all the apostles and all the saints, may you deserve in this age to receive the remission of all sins, and in the future the fellowship of all the blessed. Through the Lord.”

Another.

“Almighty and eternal God, reformer and creator of the human race, who commanded your servant Abraham to go out from the land of his birth and come into the promised land, which you had promised to give him; and who also caused the Israelite people to come through the desert by many wonders in order to worship you: we beseech you to rescue these people, who are going to pray at the thresholds of the blessed Peter and Paul, from every danger and release them from the bonds of sins.

“And you, who are the true way for those who trust in you, order their journey well, so that amid all the disturbances of this age they may be protected by your help. Send them, O Lord, your angel, whom you gave as a companion to your servant Tobias, so that wherever they stay he may be their defender against the snares of all visible and invisible enemies, and so that they may be able to return to us again joyful and unharmed. Through him.”

[Col. 1123]

## ORDER OF EXCOMMUNICATION

## THE ORDER OF EXCOMMUNICATION: HOW EACH INCORRIGIBLE PERSON OUGHT TO BE ANATHEMATIZED

(From Vienna Codex Theol. 277, twelfth or thirteenth century.)

[Col. 1123B]

When a bishop has determined to excommunicate or anathematize someone for certain and manifest crimes, after the reading of the Gospel he should address the clergy and people as follows:

“Let your charity know, my brothers, that a certain man named N., at the prompting of the devil, setting aside the Christian promise which he professed in baptism, has turned through apostasy after Satan, whom he renounced, and all his works. He does not fear to devastate and plunder Christ’s vineyard, that is, his Church, violently oppressing, killing, and seizing the goods of Christ’s poor, whom he redeemed with his precious blood.

“Although he ought to have been a son of this Church of ours, over which by God’s authority we preside—for in it he was reborn through water and the Holy Spirit and numbered among God’s adopted sons—he is now, by imitating the devil, a son of the devil. We are concerned lest, through pastoral negligence, any of the sheep entrusted to us should perish, for their account we shall be compelled to render before our shepherd and Lord Jesus Christ at the dreadful judgment, according to his own terrifying warning: ‘If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I shall require his blood at your hand.’

“Accordingly, we sent to him our priest and admonitory letters once, twice, and three times, canonically inviting him to amendment and satisfaction and penance, and correcting him with paternal affection. But he—alas!—with the devil hardening his heart, despised the saving admonitions and, persisting in the evil he had begun, disdainfully refused to satisfy the Church of God, which he had injured, being puffed up by the spirit of pride.

“Concerning such transgressors and violators of the holy religion and peace which Christ gave and left to his disciples, we have the Lord’s and the apostles’ commands, by which we are instructed how we ought to act toward such offenders. For the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘If your brother sins against you, rebuke him.’

“A brother sins against each one of us. For if the holy Church is one body, whose head is Christ, and if we individually are members of one another, then, when one member suffers, all the members suffer. Without doubt, therefore, the person who injures our members sins against us.

“The Lord therefore commands that a brother—that is, a Christian—who sins against us should first be rebuked privately, then reproved with witnesses, and finally confronted publicly in the assembly of the Church. But if he despises these three admonitions and charitable corrections and scorns to make satisfaction, then afterward let him be to you as a heathen and a publican, that is, as a gentile and pagan; let him no longer be regarded as a Christian but as a pagan.

“And elsewhere the Lord commands that a member which is separated from its joint, divided from the bond of charity, and causes the whole body to stumble should be cut off and cast away, saying: ‘If your eye, hand, or foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it away from you.’

“And the Apostle says: ‘Remove the evil from among you.’ Again: ‘If someone is named a brother and is a fornicator, adulterer, murderer, or robber, you must not even eat with such a person.’ And John, beloved above the other disciples of Christ, forbids greeting such a wicked person, saying: ‘Do not say “Hail” to him, nor receive him into your house. For whoever says “Hail” to him shares in his evil works.’

“Therefore, fulfilling the Lord’s and the apostles’ commands, let us cut off from the body of the Church with the sword of excommunication the rotten and incurable member that does not receive medicine, lest the remaining members of the body be infected like poison by so deadly a disease. Through him.”

### The Anathematization Itself

“Therefore, because he despises our admonitions and repeated exhortations; because, summoned a third time according to the Lord’s command to amendment and penance, he has refused to come; because he has not yet recognized or confessed his fault, nor, having sent us an embassy, sought pardon concerning the case which we investigate because he is our parishioner [the printed text is corrupt: *quam causam, qua causam*]; because, with the devil hardening his heart, he persists in the evil he has begun and, as the Apostle says, according to his hardness and impenitent heart stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath: for this reason, with all his accomplices, associates, and supporters, by the judgment of almighty God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and of all the saints; and by the authority and power of our mediocrity, divinely conferred upon us to bind and loose in heaven and on earth, we exclude and excommunicate him, declare him anathematized, and judge him condemned with the devil, his angels, and all the reprobate in eternal fire—unless he should recover from the snares of the devil, return to amendment and penance, and make satisfaction to the Church of God, which he has injured.”

And let everyone answer three times: “Amen,” or “Fiat, fiat,” or “Let him be anathema.”

[Note: Most of this is still read word for word in the present Roman Pontifical. The following rite of extinguishing and casting down the candles is absent, however. An early example of it is found in the synod of Limoges under Pope Benedict IX, in Labbe, volume IX of the *Councils*, p. 891, and volume X, p. 406, in the council of Quedlinburg, chapter 13. Berthold of Constance, under the year 1085, says concerning this matter: “At the end of the synod the sentence of anathema was pronounced against Guibert, the heresiarch and invader of the apostolic see, with burning candles.” Saint Peter Damian mentions it in his synodal dispute with the royal advocate: “Gerard, count of Galeria, was excommunicated by the full synod of Nicholas II and condemned under perpetual anathema after the lights had been extinguished.” Romuald of Salerno, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1177, gives the formula used in the peace made by Alexander III with Frederick I, under the penalty of anathema against anyone who violated it: “As these candles are extinguished, so may the souls of those who violate the peace be deprived of the light and splendor of eternal vision.” This rite is frequently mentioned in the diaries of the Roman *Ceremonial*.]

Twelve priests must stand around the bishop and hold burning candles in their hands, which at the conclusion of the anathema or excommunication they must throw upon the ground and trample underfoot.

After this the bishop must explain the excommunication to the people in ordinary words, so that all may understand how terribly the person has been condemned and know that from that hour onward he is to be regarded not as a Christian but as a pagan. Whoever communicates with him as though he were a Christian, drinks with him, kisses him, holds familiar conversation with him, receives him into his house, or prays with him—unless perhaps he is making an effort to summon him to satisfaction and penance—shall without doubt likewise be excommunicated.

Then letters are to be sent to the priests throughout the parishes, containing the form of the excommunication. They are to be instructed to announce the excommunication publicly to the people entrusted to them on Sundays after the reading of the Gospel, so that no one may through ignorance associate with the excommunicated person.

For the Council of Toledo commanded that written notices should immediately circulate among all the bishops of the province whom they could reach, and that the excommunicated person should be heard.

The excommunication itself must also be made known to his lord.

## SATISFACTION, AMENDMENT, AND RECONCILIATION OF THE ANATHEMATIZED PERSON
When someone who has been excommunicated or anathematized, moved by repentance, asks forgiveness and promises amendment, the bishop who excommunicated him must come before the doors of the church, accompanied by twelve priests, who are to stand around him on either side. Those against whom injury or damage was inflicted must also be present there. There, according to the divine laws, the damage committed ought to be repaired [Col. 1125D], or, if it has already been repaired, this must be confirmed by their testimony. Then the bishop should ask whether he is willing to undertake repentance for the crimes committed, in accordance with what the canons prescribe. And if, prostrate on the ground, he asks forgiveness, confesses his fault, implores repentance, and promises to take precautions for the future, then the bishop, taking him by his right hand, should lead him into the church, restore to him Communion and Christian fellowship, and recite with him the seven penitential psalms together with these prayers:

“Kyrie eleison” [Lord, have mercy]. “Christe eleison” [Christ, have mercy]. “Kyrie eleison” [Lord, have mercy]. “Our Father.” “And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil. Save your servant, O Lord. My God, who hopes in you. Send him help, O Lord, from the sanctuary. And defend him from Zion. Let not the enemy prevail against him. And let not the son of iniquity prevail. Be for him, O Lord, a tower of strength. Against the face of the enemy. O Lord, hear my prayer. And let my cry come to you. Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, to this servant of yours N. a worthy fruit of repentance, so that he may be restored to your holy Church [Col. 1126B], from which …”

“Merciful God, gracious God, who according to the multitude of your mercies blot out the sins of the penitent.” Seek this on the Thursday of Holy Week, that is, on the Lord’s Supper, in the reconciliation of the fallen.

After this, he should impose repentance upon him according to the measure of his fault. He should also send letters throughout the parishes, so that all may know that he has been received into Christian fellowship; he should likewise inform the other bishops. No bishop, however, should presume to excommunicate or reconcile another bishop’s parishioner without the knowledge or consent of his own bishop.

Leo, bishop [Note: [Col. 1126D] Attached immediately in the cited manuscript I found what follows here under the counterfeit name of the Vicar of Christ, fabricated by someone who, while stitching together these curses, shook off the law of Christ from his mind.], servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual greeting to his most beloved brothers and sons, the archbishops, their suffragans, abbots, and the communities of monks residing in Francia.

It has been reported to us, dearest sons, that in your regions the perversity of wicked men has increased, so that they desire to convert your possessions to their own evil uses. Therefore, by the authority of God the almighty Father, and of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, and in the place of blessed Peter the apostle, as well as of blessed Mary, the mother of the Lord, and by the blessed angels, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins, we excommunicate and curse those who seize and wrongly invade the possessions of the servants of Saint Martin and whatever belongs to them.

May their portion be with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive because of their pride, and with Judas the betrayer, who sold the Lord for a price. Amen.

“May their sons become orphans, and their wives widows. May their sons be driven away wandering and beg. May they be cast out from their dwellings. May the moneylender search out all their substance.” And again:

“All who have said, ‘Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance’—my God, make them like a wheel and like stubble before the face of the wind. Amen. As fire consumes the forest and as flame burns up the mountains, so may you pursue them in your tempest and fill their faces with disgrace, so that they may be ashamed, confounded, and perish.”

May those curses which the Lord proclaimed through Moses against the children of Israel be upon those who plunder the goods and estates of Saint Martin. May they be cursed in the city, cursed in the field, and in every place. Amen. Cursed be their storehouses; cursed be the fruit of their womb and the fruit of their land. Amen. Cursed be everything that belongs to them, and cursed be those who go out and those who return. Amen. May the Lord swiftly destroy them from the earth. Amen. May the Lord swiftly strike them from the earth. Amen. May the Lord strike them with hunger and thirst, poverty, cold, and fever, until they perish. May the Lord hand them over, falling before their enemies, and may their corpses become food for all the birds of heaven and the beasts of the field. May the Lord strike them with a most evil ulcer, with scabies and itching, madness and blindness. Amen. May they grope at midday, as a blind man is accustomed to grope in darkness. Amen.

And just as the Lord gave blessed Peter the apostle and his successors—whose place we occupy, although unworthy—the power that whatever they bound on earth would be bound in heaven, so, if these men refuse to amend, we close heaven against them and deny them the earth for burial. May they be cast into the lowest hell and pay without end for what they have done. Amen.

But if they come to repentance and amendment, and, according to the name of their fault, produce worthy fruits of repentance, may God turn all these evils away from them, and we are ready to receive them and pray for them. But if they refuse to come to amendment, let them be struck with perpetual anathema: let them not enter the church of God, let them have no peace with Christians, nor take part in any participation. Let them not receive the body and blood of the Lord even on the day of death; but, delivered over to eternal oblivion, let them become like dust before the face of the wind, and let them be handed over with the devil and his angels to everlasting fires. And as this lamp is extinguished, so may their souls be extinguished in the stench of hell. Amen.

[Col. 1127]

## PROOFS BY WATER, GLOWING PLOUGHSHARES, ETC.

## BLESSING OF THE JUDICIAL IRON

[Note: [Col. 1127C] This belongs to what was commonly called the ordinary, canonical purgation, or judgment of God. We discussed the matter in *Disquis.* 6, chapter 3, part II, pp. 553 ff., where we explained the various kinds of such proofs and their use and fortunes in the Church, until they were completely abolished, since they readily deviated into superstition through excessively frequent and indiscriminate use without legitimate authority and discernment. This also caused their varieties to multiply over time, after the earlier forms had been abolished. At first this was indeed done through the prudent caution of the Church, lest people be misled by more uncertain indications—for example, in the various kinds of lots, of which the most ancient examples are known. When consulted by Januarius, Saint Augustine responds in Letter 55, no. 37, concerning lots by means of the divine books, and he relates his own example in Book VIII of the *Confessions*, chapter 12; but in a doubtful matter he refers approval to the tomb of Saint Felix of Nola, Letter 78. Not long afterward, however, every sort of lot of the saints was forbidden in various councils: at Vienne, still in the fifth century; at Agde, in 506, canon 42; at Orléans I, in 511, canon 20; at Auxerre, in 578, canon 4; and also in the capitulary of Charlemagne, in 789, vol. I, p. 243. See also Saint Gregory the Great, *Homily 32 on the Gospels*, vol. I, p. 1591, on purgation by oath; specifically concerning the tomb of Saint Peter, vol. II of his works, p. 1219. Gregory of Tours frequently mentions such proofs, including oaths and duels sanctioned by ancient laws and examples—for instance, by Gondebald, the Arian king of the Burgundians, at the end of the fifth century. The *Gundobad Law*, or *Law of the Burgundians*, still remained in force under Saint Sigismund, Gondebald’s son. Agobard wrote against the Gundobad Law and the impious contests carried on under it. See also the *Capitula of Ansegisus*, Book IV, chapter 13. Concerning the judgment of the cross permitted by Charlemagne, see Grets., *On the Cross*. Saint Augustine lamented that, both then and now, malicious people abused this most holy sign and the most sacred name of Christ for superstitions, *Tractate VII on John*, chapter 1, p. 344.]  

(From Codex Vindobonensis Theologicus 149, formerly Augiensis, ninth century.)

[Col. 1127B]

Bless, O Lord, through the invocation of your most holy name, this kind of metal for the manifestation of your judgment, so that, with every deception of demons driven far away, the truth of your true judgment may be made manifest to your faithful. Through the Lord.

[Col. 1128B]

May the blessing of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit descend upon this iron, for discerning the judgment of God. Amen.

## BLESSING OF FIRE AND IRON, OR OF WATER

[Note: [Col. 1128C] At the beginning of the fifth century, Saint Bricius of Tours is said to have purged himself by the judgment of glowing iron. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 1, p. 43, reports this, and Father Peter Brunius, a priest of the Oratory, asserts that the first authentic testimony is found in the same Gregory, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 76, concerning Saint Simplicius, bishop of Autun, in his French work *A Critical History of Superstitious Practices that Have Misled the Peoples and Ensnared the Learned, Together with the Method and Principles for Distinguishing Natural Effects from Those That Are Not*. He shows that the indiscriminate use of such proofs makes them superstitious, vol. II, p. 221 ff., since they arose from paganism and were authorized neither by pontiffs nor by councils, p. 236 ff. Their extensive use is likewise established by the Salic, Ripuarian, and Lombard laws, as well as by the capitularies of the Frankish kings from the eighth century onward into the tenth, and especially from the end of the sixth century, as Brunius has already demonstrated from both volumes of Baluzius’s *Capitularies*. He also does not deny that certain and authentic facts concerning these proofs occurred, and he presents various examples in vol. II. Collected examples and authorities are found in Hildebert of Le Mans and Ivo, who also discusses the matter in several letters and admits in Letter 74 that the proof had deceived him. Hincmar dealt with this matter much earlier in a special treatise on behalf of Thietberga, the wife of Lothar. A treatise against the damnable opinion of those who think that the truth of divine judgment is revealed through fire, water, or armed combat was published by Baluzius among the works of Agobard. Agobard wrote this toward the end of the ninth century. Nevertheless, at its close, in 895, the rite was permitted in canon 1 and 22 of the Council of Tribur; authority for it in the succeeding centuries is likewise found in the acts of councils, in Labbe, vol. IX, pp. 587 and 1022. As regards England, where Emma’s example is mentioned in *Monastic England*, p. 34, Brunius shows, vol. II, pp. 196 ff., that it also spread into the East. The rite for investigating truth, or the judgment of the red-hot iron, which the Hungarian people once used in settling disputes, was reprinted after the Claudiopolitan edition of 1550 with extensive notes by Matthew Belius in his apparatus to the *History of Hungary*, vol. I, p. 191. From the monuments of the liturgy of Alemannia I provide a few examples relevant to the subject.]  

(From Codex Theologicus Vindobonensis 685, tenth or eleventh century.)

[Col. 1128C]

O God, just, strong, and patient judge, author of peace and judge of equity, look upon our supplication [Col. 1129A] and direct our judgment, for you are just and your judgment is right. You look upon the earth and make it tremble; through the coming of your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, or through his Passion, you saved the world and redeemed the human race. Sanctify this water or iron heated by fire. Just as you saved the three young men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, sent at the command of the king of Babylon into a burning furnace, unharmed, and sent your angel to lead them out, and rescued Susanna from false testimony, so, most merciful ruler, we ask and beseech you that whoever is innocent of the aforementioned crime and puts his hand into this water or carries the iron may bring it out sound and unharmed, through you, the Savior and Redeemer of the whole world. You who are to come to judge …

[Col. 1129B]

Another. Almighty, eternal God, guardian of hidden hearts, we humbly beseech you: if this man is guilty concerning the matters stated above and, with the devil pressing upon him, presumes in his heart to put his hand into this water heated by fire or upon the glowing iron, may your most just truth reveal it, and manifest your truth in this work, so that through manifest repentance his soul may be saved at the final judgment. But if he wishes to conceal and hide this sin by herbs or by any magical means, may your holy right hand deign to undo it, through your only-begotten Lord Jesus Christ, who is to come to judge the living and the dead.

## JUDGMENT OF COLD WATER

[Note: [Col. 1129D] The Wertinensis manuscript of the eleventh century agrees for the most part; it contains the *Order of Ecclesiastical Rites* of Berno, abbot of Augia [Reichenau]. See Eccard, vol. II of *Frankish Affairs*, p. 923.]

(From Codex Theologicus Vindobonensis 511, tenth or eleventh century.)

[Col. 1129C]

When you wish to put a person into water for examination, you must do the following. Take those people whom you intend to put into the water [Note: [Col. 1130C] Brunius discusses this type of proof extensively throughout Book VI of vol. II. He has numerous testimonies on the matter, beyond doubt, including some more recent ones, especially concerning women accused of witchcraft who were condemned by this judgment. Wier is cited on this subject, *On the Illusions of Demons*, Book VI, chapter 7. There is also Scribonius’s letter *On the Purgation of Witches over Cold Water*, in which he refutes Nevald’s explanation of the purgation or examination of witches over cold water. Godelman, however, refutes Scribonius’s refutation in *On Recognizing and Punishing Magi, Sorcerers, and Witches*, Frankfurt, 1591. Brunius refutes Scribonius’s system. He shows in chapters 3 and 4 how this proof was disseminated in Gaul; then, in chapter 5, he investigates whether its effects were produced by good or evil angels, and rightly judges in section 2, p. 312, that even if an effect was sometimes produced, it would be rash to repeat the same procedure. See also *The Washing of Women*, which they call purgation by cold water; likewise the common opinion concerning the power of witches, both of which are contrary to God, nature, every law, and approved custom. By Conrad ab Anten, Doctor of Both Laws, Lübeck, 1590. Brunius, in turn, cites Rickius’s *Defense of the So-called Proof by Cold Water*, which most judges now use in the examination of sorceresses—namely, still in the sixteenth century. The author lived and the book appeared at Cologne toward the end of that century.] and lead them into the church, and before everyone let the priest sing Mass. When they have come to Communion, before they receive it, let the priest question them with this adjuration, saying:

“I adjure you, men, by the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the Holy Trinity, and by the invocation of the only-begotten Son, and by the Christianity which you have received, and by the holy Gospel, and by these relics which are in this church, that you presume in no way to receive Communion or approach the altar if you have done this, consented to it, or know who did it.”

But if they all remain silent and no one declares this, let the priest approach the altar and give Communion to those whom he intends to put into the water. When they receive Communion, the priest should say to each one:

“May the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ be for you today as a proof.”

This is the celebration of Mass for the judgment either of water or of iron.

“You are just, O Lord.” “Blessed are the undefiled.” “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we may so merit your grace [Col. 1130B] that we may correct our transgressions, and so forgive the sin of those who confess that we may restrain those who persist in their wickedness.” Through …

When Mass has been completed, let the priest prepare holy water and go to the place where the people are to be tested. When they have been tested, let them all drink from the holy water; and when he gives it, let him say to each one:

“May this water be for you today as a proof.”

Then let the priest turn toward the water into which he is putting them and first conjure it with the following words, saying:

“God, come to my assistance.” Three times, with the Gloria. “Kyrie eleison. Christe eleison.” Three times, and the litany. When the names of the saints have been recited in it, let him say these verses:

“For the nature of this matter, we ask you: hear us.”

V. “That iniquity may not rule over justice, but falsehood may be subjected to truth.” We ask you: hear us. Three times.

When this has been completed, let the priest sing “Our Father.” “I believe in God.” And let him say, “The Lord be with you.” And with your spirit.

“I adjure you, water, in the name of God the almighty Father, who created you in the beginning and commanded you to serve human needs, who also commanded you to be separated from the waters above. I adjure you also by the ineffable name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of almighty God, beneath whose feet the sea, the element of waters, offered itself to be trodden; who also willed to be baptized in the element of waters; and by the undivided Trinity, by whose will the element of waters was divided and the Israelite people passed over it with dry feet.

“At whose invocation Elijah also caused the iron that had fallen from its handle to float upon the water. In no way, therefore, are you to receive this man if he is guilty in any respect of the matter laid against him—whether through action, consent, knowledge, or any device. Rather, make him float upon you, and let there be no cause or deception against you capable of concealing what has been done.”

After you have been adjured by the name of Christ, we command you to obey through his name, for every creature serves him. The Cherubim and Seraphim praise him, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts,” who also reigns and rules through endless ages of ages. Amen.

Another. God, who, serving the greatest sacraments … [lacuna], may divine grace take effect for exposing the devil’s deceptions, dissolving their fabrications and arguments, and destroying their manifold arts. Let all the ambushes of the hidden enemy depart from here, so that the truth concerning those things which, unknown to us in divine understanding and to the minds of others, are required from us may shine forth, sought by your judgment through the invocation of your holy name. And let no innocent person be unjustly condemned because of what we seek; nor let the guilty, before you, who are the true light, from whom darkness is not hidden and who illumine our darkness, be able to deceive with impunity those seeking the truth, since you reveal what is hidden and your power, which knows secrets, declares it. Thus may knowledge of the truth be made manifest to us who believe in you.

Another. Almighty God, who commanded baptism to be performed in water and granted human beings the remission of sins through it, you, the just judge, discern a right judgment in this water, so that if this man is guilty of the stated cause, the water which received him in baptism may now not receive him. But if he is innocent, may it now receive him within itself, and may no magic overcome the truth of your examination or alter it in this judgment. Rather, resisting every demonic illusion, let the guilty person be compelled, through the merits of Saint John the Baptist, to worthy fruits of repentance. Through …

Another.
