Afterward let the Gospel according to Luke be read. The Lord be with you. And with your spirit. At that time. Jesus rose from the synagogue.

In the name of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, who is to come to judge the living and the dead.

God, who for the salvation of the human race … As above.

I exorcise you, creature of salt and water, by the living God, by the true God, so that every power of the adversary, every army of the devil, every attack, and every phantom may be uprooted and driven away from this creature of water or salt. When your servant has been sprinkled with it or tasted it, may he be protected by this creature of water, Lord, from every attack of diabolical power and be kept free from it. Through.

Therefore, may you, as an exorcised substance, become effective against every phantom of the enemy, and may you uproot and eradicate the enemy himself, in the name of Jesus Christ, who is to come in the Holy Spirit to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. Amen.

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who according to the great dispensation of your incarnation willed to die upon the wood [Col. 1157C] of the cross, so that by your death you might free the human race from perpetual death: grant, through the invocation of your name, that this water, sanctified by contact with that holy cross, may benefit the bodily and spiritual health of your servant N., whom a burning fever grievously torments. May you yourself deign to grant this, who with God the Father and the Spirit …

Another. God, to whom all creatures obey, and who made all things in your word with wisdom, we suppliantly ask your ineffable clemency: you who deigned by the wood of the holy cross of your Son’s pious blood to redeem us, and who are the tree of life and the restorer of paradise, extinguish for all who believe in you the deadly poisons of the serpent, and through the grace of the Holy Spirit continually pour out the cup of salvation. Almighty God, Father, and Christ Jesus, Son of God, and Holy Spirit: I ask you to deign to send your blessing upon this creature of salt and water, or of fruit or cheese, so that they may benefit all to whom they are given, bringing them health in the mouth, nostrils, eyes, forehead, crown, neck, [Col. 1158A] chest, heart, belly, arms, hands, feet, and all the limbs of the body; so that chills and fevers may neither overcome nor harm them, whether in sight, hearing, walking, tasting food, or drinking. But may the perfect God, who is the Savior of all, save this human being N. from every danger—the redeemer of the world, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

# Office for the Dying

## Here begins the Office for the Dying

*(From Codex Vindobonensis theologicus 685, tenth century.)*

[Col. 1159D]

When someone has drawn near to death, a litany is first performed, and before the soul leaves the body the priest says this prayer:

**Let us pray.** Merciful and gracious God, who by the multitude of your pardons are confined by no law of time, but open the door of your mercy to those who knock, and do not reject penitents even at the very end of this life: look favorably upon this servant of yours, who with a full confession of heart asks you for forgiveness of all his sins. Renew in him, most merciful

[Col. 1160D]

Father, whatever has been corrupted by the devil’s deceit in deed, in word, and finally even in thought; and join him to the unity of the body of the Church, among the members of your redemption. Have mercy on his groans; have mercy on his tears; and admit him, who has confidence in nothing except your mercy, to the sacrament of reconciliation. Through…

After the excised page, the following words of the holy Gospel according to John are read: “The Jews were therefore disputing…” and so forth.

**Offertory.** Lord, turn.

**Secret.** Be gracious, we ask, Lord, to the soul of your servant, for whom we offer you sacrifices of reconciliation; and because he remained in the faith of the Catholic Church in this light, may a reward

[Col. 1161A]

be granted him in the life to come. Through…

**Preface.** Truly it is fitting… through Christ our Lord. At whose coming, when you command the genuine people to stand before you, command that your servant be separated from the number of the wicked; grant that he may escape the flames of eternal punishment and rather attain the rewards of the just life. Command that strength be restored after death has been conquered, and that he may always possess an unquenchable breath of light. Deign to grant him everlasting life in a glorious body, where night does not defend its dark shadows; secure in salvation, may he rejoice peacefully in honor, destined to live forever and always to be in the light, through Christ.

**Within the Canon.** We ask, Lord, that you may graciously accept this offering which we present to you for the repose of the soul of your servant, and in your kindness grant that, freed from the bonds of mortality, he may deserve to be numbered among

[Col. 1161B]

your faithful. Through…

We beseech you, O God.

**At Compline.** We ask you, almighty God, that you cause the soul of your servant, received by the angels, to be led into the prepared dwellings of the blessed.

**Another.** Grant us, Lord, that the soul of your servant may deserve to receive the forgiveness of sins which it has always desired. Through…

Before the body itself is lifted, the priest says the prayer.

**Let us pray.** Let us beseech the mercy of almighty God, by whose judgment we are either born or brought to an end, that eternal rest may receive the spirit of our brother [or sister], whom the Lord’s mercy has commanded to pass from the dwelling-place of this world; that he may be restored at the blessed resurrection and may deserve to be placed in the bosoms of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, through him who is to come to judge the living and the dead.

Then the cantor begins the responsory.

**R.** Come to his aid,

[Col. 1161C]

Saints of God.

**V.** May [he] receive you.

Here all say together three times: “Lord, have mercy.”

The prayer follows.

**Let us pray.** Let us beseech God, judge of the universe, God of the heavenly, earthly, and infernal realms, for the spirit of our dear one, that the Lord may deign to place him in rest and raise him in the portion of the first resurrection, he who is to come.

**R.** Before I was born…

**V.** My transgressions…

And they say together: “Lord, have mercy.”

The prayer follows.

**Let us pray.** God, creator and maker of all things, who, being the blessedness of the saints, grant to us who ask that you cause the spirit of our brother, freed from the bonds of the body, to be presented at the resurrection of your saints. Through…

After it has been lifted, this antiphon is sung:

**A.** Into paradise.

**Ps.** To you, Lord, I have lifted up…

**Prayer.** Incline your ear, Lord, to our prayers, by which we humbly beseech your mercy, so that you may establish the soul of your servant, whom you have commanded to depart from this world, in the region of peace and light, and command that he be a companion of your saints. Through…

**Prayer before the grave, before he is buried.**

**Let us pray.** We implore your mercy, eternal and almighty God, who deigned to create humankind in your image: receive gently and mercifully the spirit and soul of your servant, whom on this day you have commanded to be taken from human affairs and summoned to yourself. May the shadows of death not rule over him, nor chaos and the darkness of shadows touch him; but, stripped of every stain of crime and placed in the bosom of Abraham, may he rejoice that he has attained a place of light and refreshment. And when the day of judgment has come, command that he be raised with your saints and elect. Through…

Open to him.

**Ps.** Give thanks to the Lord.

The prayer follows.

God, with whom the bodies of the dead live, and in whom the souls of the elect, having laid aside the burden of the flesh, rejoice in complete happiness: hear the prayers (or, read: “grant”), of us your suppliants, that the soul of your servant, which through the temporal body lacked the sight of this light, may enjoy the comfort of that eternal light. May torments not touch him; may the pain of a dreadful vision not infect him; may penal fear not torture him; may the neighboring chain of the guilty not bind him. Rather, with forgiveness granted for all offenses, may he attain the joys promised to those who have obtained rest.

Here let him be placed in the grave, and let the priest say:

**Ant.** I shall go forth.

**Ps.** As…

**Let us pray, dearest brothers,** for the spirit of our dear one, whom the Lord has deigned to free from the snare of this world, whose little body is today handed over to burial:

[Col. 1162B] that the Lord’s mercy may deign to place him in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and, when the day of judgment has come, may raise him to be placed among his saints and elect at the right hand. Through the favor of our Lord.

**Ant.** From earth you fashioned me.

**Ps.** Lord, you have searched me.

The prayer follows.

**Let us pray.** God, who are always present to righteous supplications and deign to regard devout prayers, grant your servant, for whom today we perform the duties of burial as human beings, a portion of blessedness with your saints and faithful. Through him who is to come.

This is my rest.

**Ps.** Remember, Lord.

**Another prayer.** As we fulfill, according to the custom of the faithful, the due duty of burying a human body, let us faithfully beseech God, to whom all things live, that he may raise this body of our dear one, buried by us in weakness, in the order of his saints, and command that his spirit be joined to the saints and faithful, with whom he may deserve to enjoy indescribable glory and everlasting happiness. Through…

**Ant.** Eternal rest.

**Ps.** Have mercy on me, O God.

**Another prayer.** It is indeed an act of boldness, Lord, for a human being to dare to commend a human being, a mortal a dead person, ashes to ashes, to you, Lord our God. But because earth has received earth and dust is turned into dust until all flesh is reduced to its origin, therefore, most merciful Father God, we tearfully ask your kindness: receive into the bosom of your friend Abraham the soul of this servant of yours, whom you are leading from the abyss of this world to the homeland, and sprinkle it with the dew of refreshment.

[Col. 1162D]

May it be separated from the harsh burning fire of scorching Gehenna and, by your gift, joined to blessed rest. And if he has any sins, Lord, deserving of torments, forgive them through the grace of your gentlest kindness. May he not receive the due of sin, but may he experience the gracious goodness of your forgiveness. And when, at the end of the world, the kingdom above has shone upon all, may he be joined to the assemblies of all the saints and rise with the elect, to be crowned at the right hand. Through…

**Another.** To you, Lord, we commend the soul of your servant, so that, dead to the world, he may live for you; and if he committed any sins through the frailty of worldly conduct, wipe them away by the forgiveness of your most merciful kindness. Through…

**Another.** We ask, Lord, that the souls of all your male and female servants

[Col. 1163A]

who rest in Christ may find the fellowship of eternal light—those who, placed in this light, attained your sacrament.

**Another.** Multiply, Lord, your mercy over the souls of your male and female servants; and to those to whom you granted the sacrament of baptism, give the fullness of eternal joys. Through…

**Another.** May he obtain a share in the blessed resurrection, and may they deserve eternal life in heaven. Through you, Jesus Christ.

In the same codex of the Imperial Library at Vienna, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Margaret in the Black Forest, under the title *Agenda of the Dead*, there is an office for the dead entirely as it is observed today, except that the ninth lesson is not from Job but is a reading from the epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Thessalonians.

[Col. 1164A]

“Brothers, we do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep…” [lacuna] “therefore comfort one another with these words.”

**R.** Deliver me, Lord, from the ways of hell.

At the morning Lauds:

**Ps.** Have mercy [on me, O God].

**Ant.** Grant them eternal rest, Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them.

**Ant.** Do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord.

**Ps.** Lord, hear my prayer.

**Second antiphon.** Your right hand has received me, Lord.

**Ps.** God, my God.

**Ant.** You have rescued my soul, Lord, so that it might not perish.

**Ps.** I said…

**Ant.** Let every spirit praise the Lord.

**Ps.** Praise [the Lord]…

**V.** Eternal rest.

In the Gospel:

**Ant.** I am the resurrection and the life… and so forth.

[Col. 1163]

# Exposition on the Mass

*(From a tenth-century manuscript of the monastery of Einsiedeln, approximately.)*

[Col. 1163B]

**The Lord be with you.** The priest greets the people and prays that the Lord may be with them.

**And with your spirit.** The response of the people, and a prayer that, just as the priest prayed that the Lord might be with the people, so the people also pray that the Lord may be with the spirit of the priest.

When the priest says, “Let us pray,” he asks everyone to pray that his prayer may be heard by the Lord.

And when he says, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son,” the priest prays to the Lord Father that the prayer may be brought to completion through his Son, who is our Lord and is equal to the Father.

When he says, “Who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” he wishes the people to believe and understand that the Son lives and reigns with the Father without beginning and without end, and that he is God as the Father is God. He is God, and the Holy Spirit has one power with the Father and the Son, one substance, and in all things the unity of the Godhead.

**For ever and ever,** that is, so that the Son with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, just as he lived and existed in the Godhead before all ages, is likewise to be believed to live in the present age and in the future, where the just will remain with the holy angels and the unjust will be tormented with the demons, equally with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and to be enclosed by no end.

**Amen.** This is the confirmation of the prayer by the people. In our language it can be understood as though everyone were saying, “May it happen just as the priest has prayed.” Its proper interpretation, however, is “truly” or “faithfully.”

**Lift up your hearts.** The priest admonishes the people to raise their hearts upward—that is, above themselves—to the almighty Lord, and to pray faithfully that help may come to them from above, from the heavenly God by whom they were created.

**We have them with the Lord.** This is the response of the people: just as the priest commanded them to hold their hearts above, so they profess that they hold them.

**Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.** The priest gives thanks to God according to the profession of the people, because the people have confessed that they are intent upon the Lord.

**It is fitting and just.** The people, together with the priest, give thanks to the Lord, because it is right and fitting to give thanks to God, since we have received every good thing from him.

**It is truly fitting and just, right and salutary.** The priest confirms the profession of the people and says that it is truly fitting and just to give thanks to God for all things, and that it is right—that is, proper or equitable—and salutary, that is, full of salvation, to give thanks to him who gave us eternal salvation.

**To give you thanks always and everywhere.** After the profession of the people, the priest turns toward the Lord and speaks as though to one present, because we are always in the presence of the Lord, and he sees our thoughts. The priest says this both of himself and of the people: “To give you thanks always,” that is, at every time, “and everywhere,” that is, in every place.

**Holy.** You are holy, and through you all things are holy, because you created what is good and holy.

**Father.** In Greek, *Pater*; in Latin, *genitor*, because he himself begot the Son without any defilement or corruption. In Latin, *Pater* is said to derive from *patrando*, that is, from *perpetrando*, which means “completing” or “helping,” because he completed all things that were made and willed us to become his adopted sons through sanctification, since he sanctified us.

**Almighty.** Since he can do all things, he is therefore called almighty; and no word is impossible with God.

**Eternal God.** This distinguishes the eternal from the temporal and the everlasting. Eternal is that which had no beginning and will have no end, but always was, is, and will be. Everlasting is that which began to exist but will not have an end. Temporal is that which had a beginning and will have an end. Therefore he is called “eternal God,” because God alone is eternal. He is eternal: he did not begin to be and does not cease to be, but always is.

God is said to derive from *diligendo*, “loving,” because he loves and governs all that he created. Alternatively, God is said to derive from *divinitas*, “divinity,” because he is divine and divides all things as he wills.

**Through Christ our Lord.** *Christus* is Greek; in Latin it is called “anointed.” This Christ was ineffably begotten before all beginnings; he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. In the Old Testament, priests and kings were also anointed, and therefore were called “Christs,” because they were anointed with a temporal anointing. This Christ, through whom we give thanks to the Father, is eternally Christ; with the eternal Father he is God; through him we have been redeemed; and he is our Lord because he rules us.

**Through whom the angels praise your majesty.** Through that Christ, through whom we give thanks to the Father, the angels praise the majesty of the Father, who is himself equal to the Father in divinity. Majesty is as if to say “greater power,” because the power of God is greater than that of human beings. The angels praise God’s majesty through Christ because Christ, together with the Father, created the angels.

*Angel* is Greek; in Latin it is interpreted as “messenger.” Angel is the name of an office, not of a nature, because the angel announces, but by nature he is spirit.

**The Dominions adore.** Through the Son they praise and adore the majesty of God the Father. Dominions are an order of angels. There were ten orders of angels. The tenth order fell and through pride was changed into the devil. Nine, however, remained in their holiness. These are their names: Angels, Archangels, Virtues, Principalities and Powers, Thrones, Dominions, Cherubim, Seraphim.

The names of the last two are not Latin. *Cherubim* is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge”; *Seraphim* means “burning.” The names of the other orders mentioned are Latin, except those of Angels and Archangels. Angels are called messengers; Archangels, exalted messengers.

Pope Gregory the Roman, in his homily on the Gospel reading, “There were approaching Jesus tax collectors and sinners to hear him,” explained these orders at great length. Let us return to our subject.

**The Powers tremble.** He speaks of the orders mentioned above. He did not say this because the orders mentioned above are bodily, but he speaks according to our custom, because we usually tremble and fear before our lords. He says that they tremble so that we may understand that all heavenly, earthly, and infernal things tremble and fear before the sight of the divine majesty.

**The heavens and the Virtues of the heavens.** The heavens themselves obey the divine command, because they do not have the power to show themselves either clear or cloudy. The Virtues of the heavens are the angelic orders mentioned above, as the blessed Gregory testifies in his homily on the Gospel reading, “There will be signs in the sun, the moon, and the stars.”

**And the blessed Seraphim.** Concerning the Seraphim, the foregoing has been said.

**Celebrate together with shared exultation.** All the orders mentioned above celebrate the majesty of God the Father through Christ with united exultation and equally.

**With whom we ask you to command that our voices also be admitted.** This is our supplication with them: that the heavenly Father himself, through his Son Christ, through whom we give him thanks for all things, may deign to admit our voices and join them to the voices of the angelic orders mentioned above.

**Saying with humble confession,** that is, with humble acknowledgment. What is humbler than to commend ourselves to the eternal Father through the eternal Son, to presume nothing from our own conscience or goodness, and, in accord with the voices of the angels, always to believe and proclaim him essentially holy, saying:

## Holy, Holy, Holy

John the Evangelist wrote in the book of the Apocalypse that he saw before the throne of God and of the Lamb twenty-four living creatures standing and continually saying, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” and so forth.

It is said “holy” three times so that the holy Father, holy Son, and holy Spirit of the Father and Son may be signified. Although “holy” is thus said threefold, it is not said in the plural, “holies,” so that one holiness and one eternity may be understood in these three persons.

**Lord God of Sabaoth.** Many customarily interpret this as “almighty.” Others interpret it as “of hosts,” so that he is himself Lord God and himself disposes all the hosts of angels and human beings.

**The heavens and earth are full of your glory.** That is, the heavens and earth are governed by his glory, and those who are in heaven and on earth glorify and honor his holy name.

**Hosanna in the highest.** As it is now said in corrupted form, *Hosanna*, it was formerly said *Osianna*. *Anna* is an interjection used by one praising or magnifying. *Osi* means sacrifices. But it is corruptly said *Hosanna*, and it can be understood as “save” or “grant salvation in the highest,” that is, in the heights.

**Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.** When Christ came to Jerusalem and descended from the Mount of Olives, the children of Israel cried out, saying, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” But what does that coming of Christ to Jerusalem signify except the future resurrection, when he was to come to judge the living and the dead and appear to us in the same flesh in which he suffered for us? Then, in the name of the Lord Jesus, every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bows. And the rest—the things that the Apostle said.

**You, therefore, most merciful Father.** “You, therefore,” that is, certainly, most merciful Father. *Clemens* is said as if from *clara mens*, “a bright mind,” or from abundance; and *clementissime*, “most merciful,” as if from “most bright in mind” or “most abundant,” because he is most bright in mind and most merciful in heart, the Father.

We do not call him gracious and merciful because he is composed of bodily members, or of a heart or mind, as a human being is; rather, we cry out that he is gracious and merciful so that we may experience that graciousness and mercy from him and understand from where we ought to be saved.

**Through Jesus Christ your Son.** *Jesus* is Greek; in Latin, “Savior,” because he saves his people from their sins. He saves from sins because he has the power to forgive sins. He is called “salutary” because he gave us salvation, so that, if we keep his commandments, we may be able to attain eternal life.

**Your Son, our Lord.** His only-begotten Son, because he is the only-begotten one from the substance of the Father. We, however, are adopted sons through him, who proceeds as the only-begotten one from the Father.

**Coeternal with the Father.** Therefore we ought to ask the Father through him, saying humbly:

**We humbly beseech and ask you.** “Humbly,” that is, in a lowly manner.

**That you accept and bless these gifts, these offerings, these holy and unblemished sacrifices.** Gifts are what are given voluntarily; offerings are what are presented for the sake of some gift or reward, as we offer them to God so that our sins may be forgiven. Sacrifices are what are already consecrated with prayers. “Unblemished,” that is, immaculate and free from every stain of malice. Gifts and sacrifices are unblemished when they are offered without the stains of scandals and have been acquired through just labor. It is not as many err who say that “unblemished” means “not dedicated.” Read the seven Conferences of the Fathers; in the ninth section of the second Conference of Theonas you will find what “unblemished” means.

**First, those which we offer to you.** This indicates for whom they are offered. First they ought to be offered for your holy Catholic Church. *Church* is Greek; in Latin it is called “assembly,” or “convocation.” *Catholic* means universal, because all who believe in God ought to be in one congregation.

**Which may you deign to pacify, guard, unite, and govern throughout the whole world.** We offer this first of all so that you may deign to preserve your congregation, mentioned above, pacified and united throughout the whole world.

**Together with your servant N.,** that is, together with him who occupies the apostolic see, because the church in which Peter, prince of the Apostles, sat is the head of all Catholic churches. Therefore Christ said to Peter, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church,” and so forth. On account of this statement, we ought all to pray for the one who presides over that same church.

**And our bishop N.,** that is, for the bishop in whose diocese we are; we ought to pray for him because he is our shepherd and preacher.

**Remember, Lord, your male and female servants and all who are present.** The priest has already prayed for the apostolic bishop and his own bishop. If a bishop celebrates Mass, he should not say “our bishop.” Prayer has already been offered for the elders. Afterwards prayer is to be offered for the people, when the priest says, “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants.” He beseeches the Lord Father to deign to remember all the men and women who come to the service of the Mass; and when he says “those present,” these are the men and women who stand around.

The priest has now prayed for all who came to hear Mass; then at last he prays for those who offer their offerings.

**Who offer you this sacrifice of praise.** He says that they offer first for the praise of God, and afterwards for themselves and all who belong to them.

**For the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and well-being, they pay their vows to you, eternal, living, and true God.** They offer because the faith of all those present, whether offering or not offering, is known to and recognized by the living and true God of all, and their devotion is known; all pay their vows. Vows are what are promised willingly, because we ought willingly and gladly to make and fulfill vows to God.

**In communion and venerating the memory, first, of the glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of your blessed Apostles and Martyrs.** To communicate means to share; to venerate a memory means to hold something reverently in memory: that the holy Virgin Mary, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, became the mother of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God and human, through whom we beseech the Father. We ought to share this faith and believe that, when the Holy Spirit came, the Son of God was born from her and her virginity was not violated.

**And also of your blessed Apostles and Martyrs.** *Apostle* is called in our language “one sent.” *Martyr* means “witness.” The Apostles are so called because they were sent by Christ. Martyrs are so called because they are witnesses that Christ suffered for us—and that they themselves suffered for Christ.

**Therefore, this offering of our service, and also of your entire household, we ask you, Lord, to accept graciously.** The priest commends his offering, and that of all who serve the Lord—that is, who are servants of the Lord—so that it may please the Lord and he may be favorable to us.

**And dispose our days in your peace; rescue us from eternal damnation; and command that we be numbered among your elect through Christ our Lord.** On account of what the priest offers, the people ought to pray that the priest may be heard, that everyone’s days may be ordered in peace, and that we may be rescued from eternal damnation, concerning which the Lord Christ will say to the wicked at the end of the world: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire,” and so forth. And may we deserve to be numbered by the holy angels among the flock of his elect, to whom he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom,” and so forth.

**This offering, which you, O God, we ask, deign in every respect to make blessed, enrolled, valid, rational, and acceptable.** The priest entreats that almighty Father may deign to accept as blessed the offering that he himself makes for himself and for the people, and to have it enrolled—that is, assigned—so that it may please him.

**Valid,** that is, approved, so that he may judge it worthy to be offered in his sight.

**Rational,** that is, may he deign to make it full of right reason. For it is acceptable to him when we who believe rightly offer it according to right reason.

It is right to ask that the offering which we rationally offer may be sanctified by the almighty Father and made for us the Body and Blood of his most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. The Son is beloved by the Father, as the Father himself testified from heaven, saying, “This is my beloved Son,” and so forth. And we ought to love him, because he first loved us and suffered for us.

The day before he suffered, he took bread into his holy and venerable hands, and, with his eyes lifted toward heaven, to you, God the almighty Father, giving you thanks, he blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying:

“Take and eat of this, all of you, for this is my body.”

In like manner, after supper had ended, taking also this excellent Chalice into his holy and venerable hands, likewise giving you thanks, he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying:

“Take and drink from it, all of you, for this is the Chalice of my Blood, of the new and eternal covenant, the mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Whenever you do this, you will do it in remembrance of me.”

“What we have omitted”—namely, “the day before he suffered,” that is, the day before he himself suffered for us—“he wished to hand over to his disciples the mystery of his Body and Blood, so that they might hand it over to us.”

Who would ever believe that bread could be changed into flesh, or wine into blood, unless the Savior himself said so—he who created bread and wine and made all things from nothing? It is easier to make something from something than to create everything from nothing.

The Savior himself wished to assume a human body and unite humanity to God, so that he might become the one mediator between God and human beings. Christ Jesus, the man, himself wished bread and wine to be offered to him by us, to be consecrated divinely by him, and the faithful people to believe that the mystery he handed on to his disciples was true, when he said: “Take and eat of this, all of you.” Likewise, concerning the Chalice he said: “Take and drink from it, all of you.”

And when he lifted his eyes toward heaven and gave thanks to the Father, he taught us that we ought always to entreat the Father, that he may deign to accomplish so great a Sacrament through our hands. And when he said, “Whenever you do this, you will do it in remembrance of me,” he commanded us to remember that Passion and how much he endured for us.

Whenever we celebrate this Sacrament, we must remember him, and place our trust in his mercy, not in our own goodness. Therefore also: “We remember, Lord, we your servants, and also your holy people”; and we priests profess that we remember Christ, your Son, the Lord our God; and we testify that the people remember Christ, your Son, the Lord our God.

For this reason priests must faithfully remember, because they celebrate the Mass and offer the sacrifice, instructed by Christ’s example. Those who celebrate must also know that a petition is foolish if one does not know what one is asking for.

The holy people must therefore remember because Christ suffered not only for the priests but also for the people. It is called “holy” because, having received the faith and baptism of Christ, it has been sanctified. He now indicates what they must remember: namely, that blessed Passion, as well as the Resurrection from the dead and the glorious Ascension into heaven of Christ, the Son of God.

We must remember the Passion because righteous souls were freed from the underworld through his Resurrection. We must remember his glorious Ascension because the human body that he had assumed, bound to divinity without anyone’s assistance, ascended—so that it may be understood that he ascended into heaven by no vehicle of human beings, angels, or any creature, but was lifted up by the Father in majesty. Of this he himself said in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one.”

[Col. 1170A] We offer to your splendid majesty, from your own gifts and things bestowed by you, a pure Sacrifice, a holy Sacrifice, an immaculate Sacrifice, the holy Bread of eternal life, and the Chalice of everlasting salvation.

“Lord of all, remembering your aforementioned goodness, we offer to your majesty a pure Sacrifice”—that is, with a pure heart, because your body, which we believe is made from this bread, is pure.

“A holy Sacrifice,” because you sanctified your body when you assumed humanity into God; and now sanctify this bread also, so that it may become your body.

“An immaculate Sacrifice,” because you suffered for us without the stain of sin.

“The holy Bread of eternal life,” because you are the living Bread who descended from heaven, and you wished us to receive your body in this bread sanctified by you; and through the Chalice of your Passion you wished us to receive your blood.

Sanctify this Sacrifice, so that it may become for us your body and your blood.

Above these gifts we beg you to look with a propitious and serene countenance. We ask that the holy Father may deign to look upon the gifts offered by us with a gracious, kindly, and radiant countenance—that is, to see them—and to regard them as acceptable, just as you deigned to regard as acceptable the gifts of your righteous servant Abel, the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and what your chief priest Melchizedek offered to you: a holy sacrifice, an immaculate Sacrifice.

The Lord regarded Abel’s gifts as acceptable because whatever he found to be best, he offered to the Lord; and we ought to offer just and pure gifts to God with a pure heart. Abraham did not spare his son Isaac, but, obedient to the Lord’s command, wished to offer him. Melchizedek, the first priest, offered bread and wine to the Lord. Therefore it is written in the Psalm: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

For just as Melchizedek offered bread and wine, so also Christ in his Passion offered his Body and Blood to God the Father for us; and in bread and wine he wished us to imitate the mystery of his Passion when, giving bread and the Chalice to his disciples, he said: “This is my Body, and this is the Chalice of my Blood.” We too ought to pray that, just as the gifts of the aforementioned Fathers were acceptable to God, so also our gifts may become acceptable.

We humbly beg you, almighty God, command that these gifts be carried by the hands of your Angel to your sublime altar in the presence of your divine Majesty.

We humbly ask that the heavenly Father command our gifts—which can be seen as offered upon this altar—to be carried by the hand of his Angel to that lofty altar before his divine majesty, which our eyes cannot see, because it is not material but spiritual.

And just as we ought not to investigate the divine majesty of the Father, but rather to believe, so may all who have received the most holy Body and Blood of your Son from participation in this altar be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace, through Christ our Lord.

We ought to pray to the heavenly Father that everyone who has received from that altar of his—upon which we offer to God the Father, in remembrance of your Son, the Lord our God, the Body and Blood of the aforesaid Son—may merit to receive every heavenly blessing through that same Christ our Lord.

[Col. 1171A] Grant also to us sinners, your servants, who hope in the abundance of your mercies, some portion or fellowship with your holy Apostles and Martyrs, and with all the Saints.

All these sacrifices are offered by both priest and people so that almighty God may not count our sins against us, but may grant us a portion with his saints. Among their fellowship admit us, we ask, not as one who assesses merit, but as the giver of forgiveness.

This is what we ask, as he himself said: “On whatever day the sinner turns back and does penance, all his sins will be forgotten before me.” Let him not assess the recompense due for sins, but let him himself be the giver of forgiveness, and let him send us into the fellowship of the saints, through Christ our Lord.

Through him he created all these gifts; may he sanctify and bless them, and grant us that through Christ—through whom all things were made, in Christ—in whom all things were made, and with Christ—with whom all things were made, because he is coeternal with the Father—we may always give thanks to the Father, forever and ever. Amen.

## Instructed by the saving commandments

We have been admonished, commanded, and formed by the commandments of Christ, which are full of salvation, because he is eternal salvation. That is, we have received from Christ our Lord a form and example, and we have dared to pray as he taught his disciples. We believe that our Father is in heaven, the one who created us, and we say:

“Our Father, who are in heaven.”

After his Resurrection Christ said: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father.” He called him his Father in one way, and our Father in another. He is his Father because he is the proper Son: the Son is begotten of the Father’s substance before all times and is coeternal with the Father.

He is our Father because he created us in time, and we are his adopted sons. We ought to possess the heavenly inheritance of our heavenly Father if we fulfill by our works what we have promised by receiving the faith.

“Heaven” (*coelum*) is said from *celare*, “to conceal,” because it conceals divine secrets. Alternatively, heaven is named from height (*celsitudo*), because it is higher than earthly things. We say, “Our Father, who are in heaven,” so that we may show that we believe in the heavenly Father and, like sons desiring to fulfill the commandments of their Father, may always strive toward heaven.

“May your name be sanctified”: that is, may we be worthy to hold his holy name in our hearts, so that, just as the holy angels who are in heaven know and understand the holiness of his name, so we who are on earth, with his help, may merit to recognize his holiness, so that his name may be sanctified in earth as it is in heaven.

“May your kingdom come”: that is, may we merit to know his kingdom and his power, and may the devil no longer reign over us because of our sins, but may his kingdom come, as it is written in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you.”

“May your will be done, as in heaven so on earth”: that is, may we who are on earth do his will just as those who are in heaven do it.

“Earth” (*terra*) is said from *terere*, “to wear down,” because it is worn down by feet.

“Give us today our daily bread.”

Among the Greeks, *pan* is interpreted in our language as “all,” and we pray that the almighty Father may deign to grant us every kind of spiritual and bodily nourishment at all times.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

No one does anything unjustly who demands a debt owed to him. No one will be found without a debt. Therefore we ought to forgive the debts of our debtors, so that almighty God may forgive ours, because he said: “If each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins.” And elsewhere: “All scandals will be removed from his kingdom.” And again: “The sacrifice is not accepted if it is offered with scandal; rather, it is commanded to be left before the altar until one has been reconciled to one’s brother, and then to be offered with a pure heart.”

“And do not lead us into temptation”: that is, may we not enter that temptation in which the devil tempts us, nor consent to him, but may the Lord himself defend us, so that we are not led into diabolical temptation.

For if God abandons us, we are immediately brought into the devil’s snare. Therefore we ask him to free us from evil—that is, from every diabolical assault.

“Deliver us, we ask, from all evils, past, present, and future”: that is, we ask him who created us good and pure, in whom there is no evil, to free us from all evils.

Past evils are those which we committed earlier, while sinning, and for which we endure scourges. Present evils are those which we commit daily. Future evils are those which, with the devil’s persuasion, may still come upon us. Therefore we pray to be freed from all of them, because before the sight of God there are neither past nor future things, but everything is present.

With the blessed and glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and with your blessed Apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew interceding for us.

We invoke for our assistance the Mother of God, who was a virgin before giving birth, a virgin in giving birth, and a virgin after giving birth; and the blessed Apostles, who handed down to us the celebration of these mysteries, so that they may intercede for us. For we ourselves are not worthy to merit forgiveness for past and present things, nor prudence concerning future things, unless this is granted to us through their prayers.

We have already prayed to be freed from evils; now we pray that, with the aforementioned saints intervening, he who is powerful to free us from evil may graciously grant peace in our days.

Peace from the devil’s temptation, so that we may not be led into it. Peace from evil people, so that we may not suffer their scourges. And, aided by your mercy—that is, helped by God’s assistance—may we always be free from sin and secure from every disturbance: that is, with our sins forgiven, may we not again be disturbed in the present age while praying, nor suffer eternal disturbance on the day of judgment, through Christ our Lord.

“May the peace of the Lord be always with you.”

Christ is eternal peace. Through his Passion he reconciled us to the Father, so that we would not be held in the underworld because of the sin of the first human being.

The priest prays that this peace may remain with the people and make everyone harmonious, so that, having been made peaceful with Christ, we may merit to reign in heaven. Therefore we make peace before receiving the Lord’s Body and Blood, to show that we have harmony among ourselves and may receive the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ into our bodies in harmony.

Without harmony we are not worthy to receive holy Communion, because, if we have discord with our neighbors, our gifts are not accepted by God before we have been reconciled.

Then the clergy pray by singing:

“Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.”

He is called a lamb because of his innocence, since he harms neither human beings nor beasts. When he is led to the slaughter, he does not injure the one killing him, but after his own slaughter he refreshes his killer.

So also Christ harmed no one, as the Apostle said: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.” But after his Passion he refreshed many of his converted persecutors through the holy Communion of his Body and Blood, and made them believers.

He took away the sins of the world when he gave us forgiveness of sins. Before his Passion, righteous and sinful people alike descended into the underworld, and in the Old Testament we nowhere read of forgiveness of sins. But Christ promised us through repentance not only forgiveness of sins but also angelic joy, saying: “There will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”

We ask that Christ himself, the innocent Lamb of God who suffered for the salvation of the world, have mercy on us, saying:

“Have mercy on us.”

[Col. 1173D]

**Note:** In many manuscripts, including Alemannic ones, this is also added:

“This exposition came from the monastery of Saint-Denis. Saint Fulrad, its abbot, united to it by testament various cells founded by him in Alsace. In the eighth century he was the famous archchaplain of Pepin and Charlemagne, and at the same time the pope’s envoy, employed in the most important affairs of Church and empire.

“At the Council of Verberie in the year 853, the bishops say: ‘When, among other ecclesiastical matters, we were arranging the orderly administration of the monastery of Saint-Denis, the monks of that holy monastery came into the presence of the venerable synod, bringing documents—namely, the testament which Fulrad, of holy memory, the abbot, had made concerning the monastery of Lebbraha, where Saint Alexander the Martyr lies buried, and concerning the cell called Saint-Hippolytus, as well as concerning other possessions which the same venerable abbot had bestowed upon Saint-Denis through that testament.’”

That testament is preserved in Mabillon, *Saeculum III of the Order of Saint Benedict*, volume II, p. 341. It was drawn up in the year 777, seven years before Fulrad’s death, which occurred in 784. It is therefore easy to understand how this exposition passed from monasteries subject to Saint-Denis into other monasteries of Alemannia.

For in the Old Testament also the Lamb, Christ, offered himself to God the Father, so that through his Passion he might free the human race from sin. Therefore “Lamb of God” is sung when the Body and Blood of the Lord are received, so that we may all believe that the Body and Blood of that Lamb are then received—the Lamb who took away the sins of the world by dying and gave us eternal life by rising again: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

When the Mass has ended, the Deacon says to the people: “Go, the Mass is ended.”

*Deacon* is called in Greek, and in Latin means “minister.” He announces to the people that the prayers are finished, because no one ought to leave the church before this has been announced by the minister.

And all respond: “Thanks be to God.”

## The Order of the Mass

First, the Antiphon at the Introit is sung in the Order of the Mass. For *antiphon* is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “reciprocal voice.” In this kind of singing, two choirs alternate melodies by responding to one another in turn; or the voice of one person, turning back, answers and responds to the other.

*Introit* is named from entering (*introitus*). Through this chant one enters upon the duties of sacred melody; and at that time the assembly of the Christian religion, entering the church of God, prepares itself for the other praises of the offices.

For just as *Invitatory* is named from inviting when the beginning of the night office is initiated and “Come” is said, so *Introit* is named from entering when the night office begins.

Pope Celestine, a Campanian by nation, established the Antiphon at the Introit in Rome, so that it would be celebrated before the sacrifice. This was not done previously; only Paul’s Epistle and the holy Gospel were recited.

Then *Kyrie eleison* is said, which is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “Lord, have mercy.” Likewise *Christe eleison* means “Christ, have mercy.”

The angelic hymn, “Glory to God in the highest,” was sung by the angels when the Lord was born. Pope Telesphorus, a Greek by nation, also established that it should be sung before the sacrifice. He further established that Masses should be celebrated through the night on the Lord’s Nativity.

Next Paul’s Epistle is read. It is known to everyone that Paul was the Teacher of the Gentiles. And because he merited to be the Lord’s chosen vessel, he taught certain peoples for a time by writing while he remained in the body. Therefore, when it is now read daily, it strengthens the minds of all the faithful with the solidity of firm faith.

After the responsory, the Gradual is sung. It is called a *responsory* because, when one stops, another responds with the same thing. It is called a *Gradual* from the distinction of those responsories, because this one is sung on the steps.

The rest is done wherever the clergy may wish.

Then the Alleluia is sung, which is interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as “praise of God.” This single name is composed of two Hebrew expressions. Among the Hebrews God is called by ten names, one of which is *ia*, which is said here.

These things have otherwise been placed in the service of melody by holy founders so that the people, intent upon the praises of God, may approach the words of the holy Gospel, and may be more attentive and watchful for the other duties of the sacred mystery.

After this praise, the reading of the holy Gospel is given. For *Gospel* is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “good news.” No message can be better than the one that announces the salvation of the whole world and promises the rewards of the eternal kingdom to the blessed.

It is fitting that immediately after this praise of melody—which is properly contained in the name of God—his most holy words should be read, so that the people’s spirit may first be formed by the sweetness of song. Afterwards, the hearer, eager for the good message—that is, the Gospel—may be comforted by joyful gladness.

The ecclesiastical book, in which the Offertories sung in honor of the sacrifices are recorded, shows that the ancients were accustomed to sing when victims were sacrificed, as it says:

“The Priest extended his hand over the libations, poured a libation from the blood of the grape, and poured it upon the foundation of the altar as a fragrance for the divine and exalted ruler. Then the sons of Aaron cried out on their extended trumpets, sounded them, and made a great voice heard as a memorial before the Lord.”

In the same way, now also, by the sound of the trumpet—that is, by the proclamation of the voice—we kindle song. At the same time, proclaiming praises to the Lord in heart and deed, we rejoice aloud in the high place, namely in the true sacrifice by whose blood the world was saved.

Then, after the prayer, the Priest says secretly: “The Lord be with you.”

The Priest prays while greeting the people on behalf of the clergy and the people; and the clergy and the people, praying in turn that they may likewise be participants with the Lord, respond: “And with your spirit.” That is, may our mind and spirit be one, according to the Apostle: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind.” He prays for them, and they for him, because the Apostle teaches us to pray for one another so that we may be saved.

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, if two or three agree concerning any matter on earth, whatever they ask will be done for them by my Father, who is in heaven.”

Again the Priest says: “Lift up your hearts.”

Here he not only exhorts the people to raise their hearts to the Lord, but also, desiring to share his own heart with them, entreats them. Just as he wishes them to have their hearts above and to think about heavenly things, as the Apostle says, “Our citizenship is in heaven,” and again, “Seek the things that are above, not the things that are on earth,” so he too, leaving earthly things behind, may strive with them in mind toward heavenly things, according to the Psalmist: “I lifted up my eyes,” and, “To you I lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven.”

Then the clergy, strengthened by the Priest’s exhortation, answer: “We have them toward the Lord,” as though saying: “Just as you exhort us to raise our hearts, so, following your exhortation, we profess that we have them directed toward the Lord.”

“Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.”

The Priest commands us, while desiring that we give thanks to God, to whom we have already professed that we are attentive. The people respond:

“It is worthy and just.”

For what is more worthy than that we should give unceasing thanks to God for the immense gift of his condescension, by which he has deigned to adopt us as his children in mind? Hence in what follows he permits himself to be called our Father. This response of the people increases and piles up their act of thanksgiving.

## PREFACE

“It is truly worthy, just, right, and salutary.”

The Priest firmly and truthfully confirms the people’s profession: namely, that it is worthy to give thanks to God, who grants eternal salvation to us, the unworthy.

“Worthy,” that is, meritorious; “just,” that is, standing and established by right and reason; “right,” that is, straight and equal; and “salutary,” that is, health-giving, full of every kind of salvation, and healing.

“To give you thanks always and everywhere.”

After the people have professed that they have their hearts intent upon the Lord, the Priest turns his voice and mind, as though speaking directly to him, saying: “To give you thanks always and everywhere.”

Thanks are then worthily celebrated to God if they are always and everywhere offered by all the faithful of the human race.

“Always,” according to the Psalmist: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth.” And again: “I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing to my God as long as I exist.” And the Apostle: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in everything,” and so forth.

“And everywhere,” as the Psalmist says: “In every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, my soul.”

And because God is everywhere, we ought therefore to give thanks to him everywhere.

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God.”

*Lord* (*Dominus*) is said from *dominating* (*dominari*), for this name properly belongs to him who by his power rules over all creatures. In this name every knee bends—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

Just as *Lord* is derived from *dominating*, so *holy* is derived from *sanctifying*, because all things are sanctified by him.

“Father”: we do not say this by our own merit, but solely through the generosity of his granting. When we were slaves of sin and, according to the Apostle, children of wrath, we were made free for righteousness. Loving him and at his command, we call him Father.

“Through Christ our Lord.” For *Christ* is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “anointed.” Hence in the Psalm: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

“Through Christ our Lord”: all the faithful give thanks to God the Father through the mediator and redeemer of the world, by whom all created and perishing things have been restored, not through our merits but solely through his mercy.

And fittingly, just as through him he created the nine orders of angels, distinguished by their names, saying, “Let there be light,” and there was light, so also through him the Father’s majesty is rightly praised in reciprocal order by the Angels—that is, by the messengers—and the Archangels—that is, the princes of the angels—because *archon* in Greek means “prince” in Latin.

And by the Dominions—that is, by those who rule over the aforementioned orders—he is worshiped. Through the one Word, that is, the Son, the Powers tremble before the Father’s divinity.

The heavens and the virtues of the heavens—that is, those possessing power and strength over the lower orders—and the blessed Seraphim also praise him.

*Seraphim* is interpreted as “burning” and “kindling,” because of their nearness to the most holy fire of divinity, since “our God is a consuming fire.” Therefore the Father is rightly celebrated by them with united exultation through the one Word.

With these aforementioned orders of angels, and with our voices—that is, the voices of human beings—we ask you to command that our voices be admitted.

For *ammittere*, with two *m*’s, and *admittere*, with a *d*, mean “to receive.” But *amittere*, with one *m* and without a *d*, means “to dismiss.”

Here the lower part of the strings is joined to the upper in the harmony of the heavenly lyre—that is, of the harmonious Church. She makes a spiritual and new sound, resounding in tuneful modulation to the eternal King.

Hence John says: “And I heard a voice like the voice of harpists playing on their harps, and they sing a new song.”

God created two creatures—namely, angels and human beings—to render him the service and fitting worship owed to him, so that they might offer him worthy praise and fulfill his pleasing will perceptibly with praises and thanksgivings.

Through his only-begotten Son, through whom all these orders continually praise, worship, and tremble before his divine power, they celebrate him with humble confession, saying—that is, with prayerful and humble praise.

Hence Cassiodorus says:

“For in the divine Scriptures the name ‘confession’ is understood in two ways. Sometimes it pertains to satisfaction and to a public and healing disclosure through repentance, as the Apostle says: ‘Confess your sins to one another, so that you may be saved.’ At other times it pertains to thanksgiving, as in the Gospel: ‘I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth.’

“Hence Cassiodorus says again: Those who lament their sins confess; and those who give thanks to the Lord also confess. But the one is in tears, the other in joy; the one in affliction, the other in the liveliness of a holy mind; the one in sadness, the other in exultation; the one in labor, the other in rest; the one in fear, the other in love; the one in mourning, the other in gladness; the one in filthiness, the other in beauty. The one comes to rest in forgiveness; the other remains here and in the future. Human beings who are sinners confess the one, while holy human beings and angels confess the other with rejoicing and praise.”

From this it is understood, as has been said, that the name “confession” is understood in two ways: sometimes confession is made as satisfaction for salvation and for mourning sins; at other times it is made as thanksgiving, by giving thanks to God and worthily praising his name. Hence it is said in the Psalms: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good,” and so forth.

Here, however, we can understand the present passage in this way: while the saints live in this transitory age, before they are joined to the heavenly choirs in inseparable fellowship, they praise the Lord in divided and various ways.

Hence Augustine says:

“All his angels praise him worthily. Their food is eternal; they live by his life, and by his eternity and goodness they always live blessedly. Let us praise our Lord, who redeemed and made us. They praise him fittingly; let us also praise him in obedience. They praise by seeing; we by believing. They by enjoying; we by asking. They by receiving; we by seeking. They by entering; we by knocking.”

## Holy, holy, holy

This name is rightly and reasonably sung three times to the divine majesty, because the Father is holy, as the Son says to him: “Holy Father, sanctify them in truth, whom you have given to me, because you are holy.”

Concerning the Son, the angel says to Mary: “And the one who will be born from you will be called holy.”

The Son himself speaks of the Spirit of the Father and of the Son to his disciples: “Receive the Holy Spirit,” and so forth.

Although the name “holy” is applied to each Person, there are not three holy beings in the plural, but one holy God. Under the threefold repetition, holiness in the three Persons is shown as one.

Hence Isaiah says:

“I saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty and elevated throne, and the things beneath him filled the temple. And Seraphim stood above it; each had six wings, and one cried to another and said: ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.’”

John the Evangelist likewise writes in the book of Revelation that he saw before the throne of God and of the Lamb twenty-four living creatures standing and incessantly saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth,” and so forth.

*Sabaoth* is also interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as “of hosts” or “of powers,” because he himself is the creator and God of all, who works through the Son, together with the Holy Spirit, all things in all.

“Full are the heavens”: that is, the heavenly orders in which God is said to dwell most fully.

“And the earth”: that is, the faithful who still live on earth in hope of future blessedness.

“Of your glory”: the heavens and earth are full of that glory which, when the Lord was born, the multitude of angels is said to have sung: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

## Hosanna in the highest

*Hosanna* cannot be transferred completely into the interpretation of another language, because *osi* is interpreted as “save.” *Anna*, however, is an interjection signifying a movement of the mind under the emotion of one who is asking.

*Osianna* is properly the complete form; but we say *Hosanna* with the middle vowel altered and elided, as happens in verses when we scan them. For the first letter of the following word, when it comes upon the last letter of the preceding word, excludes it.

It is said in Hebrew, *Hosanna*, which is interpreted as “save,” with the implied words: “your people,” or “the whole world.”

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

As Jesus approached Jerusalem, the children of the Hebrews took branches of olive trees and went out to meet him, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.”

Even now, without interruption, his name ought to be pronounced by the faithful in his holy Church, because by him the spiritual are filled with spiritual blessing. Concerning this the Apostle testifies:

“Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

Therefore, most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord. God is rightly entreated through Jesus Christ [Col. 1178D] and now as Father, because through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made. And because through him we have been saved, it is fitting that through him we should also implore the Father, from whom he was begotten.

We humbly beseech and ask—that is, we ask as the lowly—that you regard these as acceptable; that is, that you receive them favorably, and bless these gifts, these offerings, these holy, undefiled sacrifices. The gift (*donum*) belongs to the giver, while the offering (*munus*) belongs to the recipient, because the former is named from giving (*dare*), the latter from providing (*munire*). Properly speaking, however, gifts are what are given to God. Offerings belong to human beings, because they are given and received by hand. In this passage, nevertheless, both gifts and offerings are offered to God.

“Sacrifices” means “sacred things made,” because they are consecrated by mystical prayer [Col. 1179A] in memory of the Lord’s Passion suffered for us. Hence, at his command, we call it his body and blood. When this is done, it is sanctified from the fruits of the earth and becomes a sacrament, through the invisible working of the Spirit of God. The Greeks call the sacrament of this bread and cup *eucharistia*—Greek *εὐχαριστία*, “thanksgiving”—which in Latin is interpreted as “good grace.” And what is better than the Body and Blood of Christ?

“Undefiled” means uncontaminated and free from every impurity. Sacrifices are undefiled, then, if they are given from one’s own possessions with a pure heart and acquired by honest labor.

“Especially those which we offer to you for your holy catholic Church.” First of all, we ought to offer for the holy Church with a pure mind and with the whole worthy affection of devotion, so that it may always be enlarged and, strengthened by Christ’s protection, remain steadfast in peace. “Catholic” means universal, because in Greek *catholicon* means “universality” in Latin. We pray that it may be pacified—that is, that it may remain in concord—as it is said: “Because he made the two into one new man in himself, making peace.” “Peace to those who are far away, and peace to those who are near.”

We pray that God may guard it, because he is its guardian, just as the one who keeps watch by night is a guardian; and unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain. We pray that he may unite it—that is, make it one through faith—because “one is the dove,” that is, one is the Church. Although seven churches are written of in the Apocalypse, it is nevertheless one Church, filled with the sevenfold Spirit.

For Solomon says: “Wisdom built herself a house; she cut out seven columns.” The Apostle calls these seven one Church of the living God, which is “the pillar and foundation of truth.” And we pray that you may deign to rule it—that is, strengthen it by your protection and governance [Col. 1179C] throughout the whole world, together with your servant, our Pope N.

Because he is the head of the Church in apostolic succession, he is named first in this prayer. “And our bishop.” A bishop (*antistes*) is so called because he stands before others, since he presides over the remaining orders. It is fitting that the priests should pray for him by name, since they are governed in his parish and under his direction.

“Remember, Lord, your servants, men and women.” Servants (*famuli*) are named from serving (*famulari*), because they render service to anyone. “And all who stand around.” Some think that prayer is not being offered at that moment for those who happen to sit, perhaps because of illness or some intervening necessity. Rather, they say that “those standing around” means those who are at present standing firm and remaining in faith and hope, as the Apostle says [Col. 1179D]: “Be watchful, and stand firm in the faith, and be steadfast and immovable.”

“Their faith is known to you, and their devotion is recognized.” Nothing is unknown to God, because he searches the hearts: “For the Lord knows the thoughts of human beings.” “They offer you this sacrifice of praise,” according to the Apostle: “Whatever you ought to do, do everything to the praise of God, so that God may also be praised in you.”

“For themselves and all their own”—that is, both for themselves and for all who belong to them. “For the redemption of their souls”: for the hope of their salvation and well-being. Through the offering of that sacrifice, souls are redeemed from vices and saved through the hope of eternal salvation.

“They render their vows to you.” Vows are things freely given; hence the Psalmist says: “Vow and repay to the Lord your God, all you who in his presence offer offerings” [Col. 1180A].

“To the eternal, living, and true God.” He is eternal because he had neither a beginning nor will he be enclosed by an end. He is called the living God because he himself is life, and all things will be made alive by him. He is true because he is truthful and does not deceive.

“Sharing together”—that is, participating together. “And reverently commemorating”—that is, holding the memory with reverence.

“Especially of the glorious ever-virgin Mary.” The priest commemorates her first, because through her salvation came to us all. He calls her “ever-virgin” because the blessed Virgin Mary remained undefiled: a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth.

“Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ.” By these two titles, “God” and “Lord,” he shows that blessed Mary gave birth to both God and man [Col. 1180B].

“And also of your blessed Apostles and Martyrs.” After commemorating the Mother of God, he commemorates these saints, who were the first rulers of the Church entrusted to Peter; after them he names all the rest, saying, “and all your saints,” and so forth. We do not deserve God’s assistance through our own prayers and merits, but through the intercessions of the saints, provided that our offering has been worthily made. And this occurs only through Christ our Lord, from whom all things come and through whom all things were made.

“Therefore, this offering of our service, and also of your whole household.” The priests call this the offering of their service because everything belonging to the celebration of this mystery is administered through their ministry. He says not only “of our service” but also “of your whole household” [Col. 1180C], because although the celebration takes place through their ministry, the sacrifice is offered not only for them but also for the entire household of God.

“We beseech you, Lord”—that is, we pray that you receive it favorably; that is, that you do not consider the guilt of our offenses, but mercifully grant forgiveness.

“Order our days in your peace.” This was not said originally, but was later added by Pope Gregory, a most learned man. We ought all to ask this continually: that, as long as we journey through this world, our days may be governed by God. For what else is it for him to order our days in peace than to rescue us from eternal condemnation, to join us to the assembly of his elect, and to do this through him by whom and from whom all things were made with the Father?

“Which offering, O God, we beseech you, deign to make blessed in every respect” [Col. 1180D]—confirmed by spiritual blessing; “inscribed,” assigned to the heavenly table; “approved,” firmly established for you; “reasonable” and acceptable. A thing is reasonable when it is done with reason. Thus, if an offering is made reasonably and worthily, it is considered acceptable to God.

“So that it may become for us the Body and Blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.” This means that we may become his body and that, by divine power, he may provide us in the ministry of divine grace with the bread that descended from heaven. Just as the body is nourished by visible bread and drink, so may our invisible soul be refreshed and given drink, lest it grow weary on the journey through this wilderness.

Why did the Lord wish to transform his body into bread and wine? It is because bread is made from many grains, and wine is pressed from many clusters of grapes. So too the Church, which is the Body of Christ, is gathered from many ranks, ages, persons, and languages into one faith [Col. 1181A]. The Lord revealed himself through these same elements when he said: “I am the living bread.” And further: “I am the true vine.” Therefore he transformed his body into the same elements by which the human heart is strengthened and gladdened, as the Psalmist says: “Bread strengthens the human heart, and wine gladdens it.”

The Lord transformed his body so that, as long as we receive it, we may remain joyful and strong, and so that he himself may remain in us, as he promises: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

He is called the “most beloved Son” because, although there are many sons by grace, not by nature [Col. 1181B], he alone is Son by nature, as the Father testifies, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

“Lord God,” because he alone, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, exercises lordship and is worshiped with divine worship.

“Christ Jesus.” These names express his divine grace. One is Hebrew, namely Jesus, which is interpreted as “Savior.” Hence it is said: “He will save his people from their sins.” The other is Greek, namely Christ, concerning which we have already spoken above.

“Who, on the day before he suffered.” “The day before” (*pridie*) is as though one said “before the day” (*prae die*), that is, before the day on which he would be killed through his Passion.

“He took bread into his holy and venerable hands.” In this bread, who else is signified except that living bread which descended from heaven?

“And with eyes raised to heaven, to you, his almighty Lord and Father [Col. 1181C].” He raised his eyes to heaven to show us that in everything we do we should seek nothing earthly, and so that we may know that every good thing comes to us from there.

“Giving you thanks, he blessed it.” He gave us an example, so that in everything good that we do we may always give thanks to God.

“He broke it and gave it to his disciples.” What else does the breaking of this bread signify except that he provided us with his body as food?

“In like manner, after supper”—that is, after the lamb of the Old Testament had been eaten. When he says “in like manner,” this means nothing other than that just as he first acted with the bread, so in every respect he acted also with the cup. Just as he blessed the bread with thanksgiving, breaking it to be eaten, so he blessed the cup and handed it to his disciples to drink, saying: “Take and drink from it, all of you; for this is the cup of the Blood of my new [Col. 1181D] and eternal covenant.”

When it is called “the cup of the new covenant,” this is said to distinguish it from the old law, as Moses says: “This is the blood which the Lord has commanded for us.”

“The mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you.” For it is said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have eternal life.”

“Whenever you do this, you will do it in memory of me.” Hence the Apostle says: “Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.”

“Therefore, remembering, Lord, we your servants, and also your holy people, of Christ your Son, our Lord and God.” Here the priests, instructed by Christ’s admonition [Col. 1182A], profess that they remember him, because the celebration of this sacrifice has been entrusted to them for consecration.

Then it adds, “and also your people,” so that we may understand that it is fitting not only for priests to reverence the memory of Christ, but also for all generally who are called Christ’s people, because Christ died and rose for everyone and ascended victoriously into heaven. This people is called holy because it has been cleansed through the mystery of holy baptism. The word “your” is rightly added because it was redeemed by the very blood of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

“We remember his blessed Passion, and also his resurrection from the dead, and his glorious ascension into heaven.” We remember all these things because we believe that through them we have been saved.

“And therefore we offer to your glorious majesty from your gifts and grants” [Col. 1182B]—a pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim; the holy bread of eternal life and the cup of everlasting salvation.

Among the ancients, victims were called sacrifices that were made before they went against the enemy. But now, Lord, we offer to your majesty with a pure heart a pure victim—that is, one free from every ferment of malice and wickedness. For just as they believed that they would obtain your help for victory, so we believe that through the Body of your Son, who is the true victim, we shall merit the salvation of our souls.

“A holy victim”—that is, sanctified by the heavenly gift through the assumption of the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“An immaculate victim,” because he himself, born from the Virgin Mary without the stain of sin and suspended on the cross, ascended again into heaven.

“We offer the holy bread of eternal life” [Col. 1182C] because all who receive him will receive unending life; for he himself is the living bread.

“And the cup of everlasting salvation.” If we receive the Lord’s cup worthily, we shall always possess salvation that endures.

“Upon these”—the word “gifts” is understood—“deign to look with a favorable and serene countenance”; that is, receive them mercifully and with a clear regard. “And accept them, just as you deigned to accept the offerings of your righteous servant Abel, and the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and that which your high priest Melchizedek offered to you, a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim.”

Abel brought whatever he regarded as best from the firstborn, and from the fat portions of his flock, acquired by honest labor. He offered this to God with the inmost love of his heart and with complete devotion of mind [Col. 1182D]. Therefore God looked upon his offerings with a serene countenance.

Abraham, obeying the Lord’s voice, did not spare his son for the Lord’s sake but wished to sacrifice him; therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness.

Melchizedek, the high priest, first offered bread and wine symbolically to the Lord. Christ, who is the true priest forever, later fulfilled that figure by offering his body and blood to God the Father. For, giving bread and the cup to his disciples, he said: “This is my Body; and this is the Cup of my Blood, which will be poured out for the redemption of many.”

With complete purity of mind, therefore, we ought to implore almighty God that, just as he was appeased by the offerings of these three and looked upon them [Col. 1183A], so he may also, through his mercy, deign to look upon our offering.

“We humbly ask you, almighty God, command these things to be carried by the hands of your angel to your sublime altar, in the presence of your divine majesty.” We must ask this continually and with the greatest humility: that the sacrifices offered by us on this bodily altar and consecrated through the hands of priests may be received by the holy angel who is present, and through his holy hands carried to God’s sublime altar.

May they be brought into the presence of the Father’s majesty, which “no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.” So may all of us who have received the most holy Body and Blood of your Son through participation in the altar be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace [Col. 1183B], through Christ our Lord.

We ought always to entreat God the Father that all of us who faithfully receive his own Body and Blood in memory of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, may recognize that, filled with his blessing and grace, we are to be saved by his heavenly and abundant goodness, not by our merits.

“And to us also, sinners, your servants, who hope in the multitude of your mercies, deign to grant some part and fellowship.” Here it is requested that he grant us, though unworthy, glory together with his saints and elect. They are called “mercies” because he knows how to have compassion on our wounds and gives medicine.
