V Ides of September. At Nicomedia, the passion of the holy martyrs Dorotheus and Gorgonius. On the same day, [the feast] of Audomarus, bishop of Terouanne. At Rome, the feast of Saint Sergius the pope.

IV Ides of September. The deposition of Saint Hilary the pope. In Africa, [Col. 1242A] the feast of ten holy confessors whose glorious acts are preserved. At Chalcedon, the feast of Saints Sosthenes and Victor, who, after various tortures, devoted themselves to prayer; called from heaven and having given one another the kiss of peace, they gave up their spirits.

Louis, the most serene king, son of Charles, died.

III Ides of September. At Rome, in the cemetery of Basilla, the feast of the holy martyrs Protus and Hyacinth, who were eunuchs of Saint Eugenia the virgin. At Lyon in Gaul, the deposition of Saint Patientius, bishop and confessor.

II Ides of September. At Ticinum, [lacuna], called Pia, the feast of the holy confessors Syrus and Juventius, who rested in peace after a glorious end. And in Sicily, in the city of Catania, Saint Euplus and blessed Serapion the bishop. At Autun, in the city, Saint Evantius, bishop and confessor.

[Col. 1242B] Ides of September. In Egypt, in the city of Alexandria, blessed Philip, bishop and martyr, father of Saint Eugenia the virgin. On the same day, Saint Amatus, priest and abbot of the monastery of Romeric. At Angers, the deposition of Saint Maurilius, bishop. At Autun, blessed Nectarius, bishop.

XVIII Kalends of October. The Exaltation of the Holy Cross, when the emperor Heraclius brought it back from Persia to Jerusalem. At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus, the feast of Saint Cornelius, pope and martyr. Twenty-three men suffered with him. In Africa, blessed Cyprian, bishop and martyr, whose most sacred bones, together with the head of Saint Pantaleon and the members of blessed Speratus the martyr, were brought to Lyon in the time of Charlemagne and honorably buried. The following are also said to have suffered with him [Col. 1242C]: Crescentianus, Victor, Rosula, and Generalis.

XVII Kalends of October. The feast of Saint Nicomedes, priest and martyr. In the territory of Chalon, at the fortress of Tournus, Saint Valerian the martyr. At Lyon in Gaul, blessed Albinus, bishop. At Toul, the feast of Saint Aper, bishop and confessor.

Dadoenus and Alfaldus, priests, died; they gave their estate at the villa of Montiniacum to the brothers.

XVI Kalends of October. In the city of Chalcedon, the feast of Saint Euphemia the virgin and martyr with forty-nine others. At Rome, the feast of Saint Lucia, widow and martyr. Likewise at Rome, blessed Geminianus the martyr with seventy-five others.

Gofridus died, renowned for counsel, a friend of peace and piety, a bishop worthy of being remembered by his own church [Col. 1242D] with tears and blessings. Guibertus the soldier also died; with the consent of his wife, his two sons, and his daughter, he placed in the hand of Bishop Humbaud the church at the villa of Acolacum.

XV Kalends of October. In Britain, the feast of the holy Socrates and Stephen. On the same day, the feast of Saint Lambert, bishop of Tongeren and martyr. At Córdoba, the holy martyrs Emilianus the deacon and Jeremiah, whose bodies, after their heads had been cut off, were consumed by fire.

XIV Kalends of October. The feast of blessed Methodius of Olympus in Lycia and afterward bishop of Tyre, who, as Jerome writes, was crowned with martyrdom at Chalcis in Greece under Diocletian. At Milan, the feast of Saturus, brother [Col. 1243A] of Saint Ambrose, bishop. At Alexandria, the feast of Saint Trophimus.

XIII Kalends of October. At Naples in Campania, the feast of the holy martyrs Januarius, bishop of Benevento, with eight others. In Palestine, the feast of the holy martyrs Pilius and Nilius, bishops. At Nuceria, the feast of Saint Felix the martyr and blessed Constantia the martyr. In the territory of Langres, at the monastery of Segester, the deposition of Saint Secuanus, priest and monk; and elsewhere, Saint Potitus the martyr. In Gaul, in the city of Vienne, the feast of Saint Ferreolus the martyr.

XII Kalends of October. At Cyzicus, the feast of the holy martyrs Fausta the virgin and Evilasius, who, mangled by unheard-of and manifold tortures, were called from heaven and gave back their souls.

[Col. 1243B] XI Kalends of October. The feast of blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist, who first wrote the Gospel of Christ in Judea in the Hebrew language. Later, while preaching in Ethiopia, he suffered martyrdom. On the same day, the feast of Saint Alexander the martyr, for whom Pope Damasus made a fitting crypt and transferred him there on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, when he also dedicated his feast.

X Kalends of October. In Gaul, in the city of Sion, at the place of Agaunum or Octodurum, the feast of the holy Theban martyrs Maurice, Exuperius, Candidus, Victor, Innocent, and Vitalis with their companions, six thousand six hundred sixty-six in number. At Auxerre, the arrival—or reception—of the body of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor, from Italy. At the monastery of Réomé, the translation of the body [Col. 1243C] of Saint John, our most blessed father and confessor. In the province of Bavaria, the feast of Saint Emeramnus, martyr and bishop.

IX Kalends of October. In Campania, the feast of Saint Sosius, martyr and deacon of the city of Misenum. While he was reading a certain Gospel in the church of that city, in the presence of blessed Januarius, the same bishop suddenly saw a flame rising from his head—though no one else saw it—and declared that he would become a martyr. The truth of this prediction was later confirmed by his martyrdom, as well as by that of five other ministers of the same bishop. On the same day, the feast of Saint Thecla, virgin, who rests at Seleucia and who was instructed by the blessed apostle Paul from the city of Iconium.

[Col. 1243D] VIII Kalends of October. The Conception of Saint John the Baptist. In the territory of the Aedui, at a village called Sedelocus, the feast of the holy martyrs Andochius, Thyrsus, and Felix, who were sent from the East to teach Gaul and were crowned with the glory of martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian. Elsewhere, that of the holy Julian, Christopher, and Lawrence. In the territory of Bourges, at the fortress of Mediolanum, the feast of Saint Genesius, martyr.

VII Kalends of October. The feast of Blessed Cleopas, who was one of the Seventy disciples of Christ. They relate that he was killed by the Jews in that same city, and in that very house where he had prepared a table for the Lord as though for a traveler. At Lyon, Saint Lupus, bishop, formerly an anchorite. In the city of Amiens, the feast of Saint Firminus, bishop and martyr. [Col. 1244A] At Auxerre, the burial and translation of Saint Aunarius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the feast of Saint Herculianus, martyr.

Eldaldus, archbishop of Sens, died. On the same day Abbo, levite and perfector, died.

VI Kalends of October. The feast of the holy martyrs Cyprian, bishop and outstanding teacher, and the blessed Justina, who became the occasion of salvation for the aforementioned bishop. Their bodies were carried to the city of Rome and buried there with reverence. Also at Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus, the burial of Saint Eusebius, bishop. At Clermont, Saint Apollinaris, bishop and confessor.

V Kalends of October. At Aegea, the feast of the holy Cosmas and Damian. In the city of Córdoba, the holy martyrs Adulfus and John, brothers. In the territory of Autun, [Col. 1244B] the passion of the holy Florentinus and Hilary.

IV Kalends of October. In Spain, in the city of Córdoba, the feast of the holy martyrs Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis. At Rome, at Guttas, the feast of Saint Sterteus. At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Alodius, bishop and confessor.

III Kalends of October. On Mount Garganus, the venerable memory of Saint Michael the archangel, where God has displayed many miracles. At Rome, the dedication of the oratory of Saint Michael, which the venerable pontiff Boniface dedicated at the summit of the circus, raised very high with marvelous workmanship. At Auxerre, the passion of Saint Fraternus, whom they relate to have been killed on the same day on which he was ordained bishop.

Walterius, bishop of Autun, died.

[Col. 1244C] The day before the Kalends of October. In Gaul, at the fortress of Solodorum, which lies above the river Arola, the passion of the holy Victor and Ursus, from the glorious Theban Legion. On the same day, at Bethlehem in Judea, the burial of Saint Jerome, confessor and eminent teacher, who completed his books over 56 years and rested in peace in the ninety-eighth year of his age, on the day before the Kalends of October. In the city of Piacenza, the holy Antonius, Gastus, and Desiderius.

Teubertus, a layman, died. He gave his estate to the canons of Saint Stephen in the territory of Auxerre, in the vicariate of Baugiacum, at the village of Matriacum, for the salvation of his soul and the preservation of his memory.

OCTOBER.

[Col. 1244D]

The Kalends of October. At Auxerre, the burial of the most sacred body of the blessed Germanus, bishop and confessor, who had happily died at Ravenna on the day before the Kalends of August and was finally returned to his own city on the Kalends of October and honorably committed to burial. On the same day, the translation of the bodies of the holy confessors Remigius, bishop of Reims, and Vedastus of Arras. In the district of Medenentum, the feast of Saint Patroclus, martyr. At Portus Ganto, the feast of Saint Bavo, confessor.

VI Nones of October. At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Eleutherius, martyr. In the village of Syricinium in the territory of Arras, the passion of Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun. At Rome, Saint Eusebius, pope, during whose time the cross was discovered. And elsewhere, that of Serenus, confessor.

V Nones of October. The feast of Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop and martyr of Athens; and elsewhere, the feast of the holy priests Ewald and Ewald, who came with Saint Willibrord, crossed into Germany to the Saxons, and, when they had begun preaching Christ there, were seized and killed by the pagans. At Auxerre, the dedication of the crypts of the most blessed Stephen, protomartyr.

Adhebaldus, priest and master of this church, died.

IV Nones of October. The feast of the holy Crispus and Gaius, whom the blessed apostle himself remembers having baptized among the Corinthians. In Egypt, the feast of the holy martyrs Marius and Marcianus, brothers, and with them countless others who suffered. At Rome, on the Appian Way, Saint Balbina, virgin, and Marcellus, bishop. At Auxerre, Saint Marsus, priest and confessor. At Paris, Saint Aurea, virgin.

III Nones of October. In Gaul, in the city of Valence, the feast of Saint Apollinaris, bishop and confessor. At Auxerre, the burial of the holy siblings Firmatus, deacon, and Flaviana, consecrated to God as a virgin. At Eumeneia, Blessed Thraseas, bishop and martyr.

The day before the Nones of October. At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Romanus, bishop, who, after ruling the church entrusted to him for three years and fifteen days, finally, as is reported, ended his life in martyrdom. At Laodicea, Blessed Sagaris, bishop and martyr. In the city of Agen, the feast of Saint Faith, [Col. 1245C] virgin and martyr.

Charles, emperor, and Guido, abbot, died. On the same day Aginulfus, subdeacon, died; he gave the brothers his allod together with a small dwelling and five arpents of vineyard.

The Nones of October. At Rome, the feast of Saint Mark, pope. Also at Rome, that of the holy martyrs Marcellus and Apuleius. In the province now called Augusta Euphratesia, the holy martyrs Sergius and Bacchus, under the emperor Maximian.

VIII Ides of October. In the city of Cortina, Blessed Philip, bishop. At Thessalonica, the feast of Saint Demetrius, martyr. On the same day, near the Mount of Olives, the burial of Saint Pelagia, who is called “the sinner.” In the district of Laon, the feast of Saint Benedicta, virgin and martyr. At Auxerre, Saint Palladia, virgin. At Sens, Saint Porcaria, virgin.

Arnaldus, subdeacon, died. He gave the brothers his estate in the district of Sens, at a village called Vallis Diaconi, and eight arpents of vineyard in the village of Aganon.

VII Ides of October. The death of Abraham, patriarch. At Paris, the feast of the holy martyrs Dionysius, bishop, Eleutherius, priest, and Rusticus, deacon. The blessed bishop had been sent into Gaul by Saint Clement because of his preaching ministry, and there he was martyred. At Cologne Agrippina, the feast of Saint Gereon, martyr, with 308 others, who are said to have been Thebans. Near Julia, on the Claudian Way, the passion of Saint Domninus.

[Col. 1246A] VI Ides of October. In Crete, Blessed Pinytus, one of the most illustrious bishops, who left in his writings, as in a kind of mirror, a living image of himself. At the city of Agrippina, the feast of the holy martyrs Mallosus and Victor. In Britain, the feast of Saint Paulinus, bishop of York.

Trutbertus, a layman, died. He gave the brothers his small dwelling together with vineyards and fields in the district of Sens, at the village of Caciacum.

V Ides of October. At Acervum in Sicily, Saint Zenas, priest. At Tarsus, the metropolis of Cilicia, the holy martyrs Tharacus, Probus, and Andronicus. At Tours, the burial of Saint Venantius, abbot and confessor.

On the same day Ato, archpriest and canon, a simple and upright man who feared God, became a monk and gave up his spirit to Christ. He gave his fellow canons a house with its appurtenances, which he had bought from Hugh of Gurgiacum, and a vineyard that he had planted at Billiacum, as well as another that he had bought at Curtus Canis. He also gave eight coins from the rent.

IV Ides of October. At Ravenna, on the Laurentian Way, the feast of Saint Hedistus, martyr. In Africa, that of 4,976 martyrs. At Bourges, Saint Opilio, priest.

Taganboldus, priest, died. He gave the brothers his estate together with a small dwelling, vineyards, and fields at a village called Pradilis. On the same day Hugh, of blessed memory, bishop of Auxerre, an ornament among bishops and the model of all religious life, who loved peace during his life, rested in good peace. Among the other things with which he enriched his bishopric, he acquired, with the greatest labor and diligence, the right to use the forest of Tullum, which the canons had lost for many years without hope of recovering it. He also gave the church excellent priestly vestments and a gilded chalice. Moreover, he assigned thirty solidi at Lindriacum, so that on the anniversary of his death a meal might be provided each year for the canons. He also left the church of Lindriacum to the canons after Anselm’s death or resignation. Meanwhile, Stephen the provost will pay ten solidi to provide the meal.

III Ides of October. At Troas, the feast of blessed Carpus, disciple of the apostle Paul. At Antioch, blessed Theophilus, [Col. 1246D] bishop. At Alexandria, Athanasius, bishop and confessor.

Rudovicus, levite, died. Through his diligence, a small dwelling with a vineyard in the village situated opposite Saint Julian’s was acquired for the brothers, together with what belonged to it.

The day before the Ides of October. At Rome, the feast of Saint Callistus, pope and martyr. At Lyon in Gaul, the passing of Saint Justus, bishop.

The Ides of October. In Gaul, at Cologne Agrippina, the feast of the holy martyrs called the Mauri, fifty soldiers from that sacred Theban Legion, buried in a basilica adorned, as it were, with gilded mosaic; hence they are also called the holy Aurei. [Col. 1247A] At Lyon, blessed Antiochus, bishop. In the territory of Reims, the feast of Saint Basolus, priest and confessor. At the monastery of Fontenelle, Saint Wilfrid, archbishop.

Henry, margrave of Burgundy, died.

XVII Kalends of November. In Africa, 270 holy martyrs crowned together, and the holy martyrs Martianus and Satrianus with their two brothers, and the outstanding handmaid of Christ, Maxima, virgin and martyr. At Bourges, the feast of Saint Ambrose, bishop and confessor.

Gaufridus, a knight, died. He returned the land that he held securely at Artadisvilla.

XVI Kalends of November. The feast of Blessed Aristion, who was one of the seventy disciples of Christ. On the same day, [Col. 1247B] the feast of Blessed Heron, bishop. In the city of Orange, Saint Florentius, bishop.

Seuvinus, archbishop of Sens, died.

XV Kalends of November. The feast of Saint Luke the evangelist, who died in Bithynia; but his sacred bones were later carried to Constantinople. At Antioch, the feast of Saint Asclepiades, bishop and confessor. At Rome, Saint Trophonia, wife of Caesar Decius. In the territory of Beauvais, the passion of Saint Justus, martyr, whose head rests in the basilica of Saint Amator.

XIV Kalends of November. At Alexandria, the feast of the precious holy martyrs Ptolemy and Lucius. In Antioch of Syria, the feast of the holy Pelagius, Veronica, and Pelagia.

On the same day Gauzo, priest and dean, died. He gave to the canons of Saint Stephen his estate with male and female servants, everything he possessed in the village of Crevennum.

XIII Kalends of November. In Gaul, in the city of Agen, the feast of Saint Caprasius, martyr. In the province of Avienne, the feast of Blessed Maximus, levite and martyr.

On the same day Humbaldus, a bishop of humility and kindness, died. Together with many buildings and ornaments by which he adorned the church inside and out, he gave the church of Acolacum and the church of Crevennum, with their tithes and the *pareda* [a term for the brothers’ provisions or support]. After peace had first been restored among the brothers, he went to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer; and, returning from there, while making holy confession to God by singing psalms, he merited a precious burial in the sea.

XII Kalends of November. At Nicomedia, the feast of the holy martyrs Dasius and Soticus with twelve soldiers. On the same day, that of our holy father Hilarion, whose life Saint Jerome wrote as full of virtues. In the city of Ostia, the feast of Saint Asterius, priest. On the same day, the passing of Saint Viator, lector. In the wilderness, Saint Justus, count.

Arnulfus, a layman, died. Together with his brothers Norgaudus and Walgaudus, he gave the brothers the estate that they possessed in the village of Crevennum.

XI Kalends of November. At Jerusalem, the feast of Saint [Col. 1248A] Mark, bishop and martyr. At Adrianople in Thrace, the feast of the holy Philip, bishop, Eusebius, and Hermes. In the city of Oea, the holy virgins Mulinion and Helodia. In the city of Langres, at Portus Bucinus, the passion of Saint Valerius, martyr and levite.

X Kalends of November. At Antioch in Syria, the feast of Saint Theoderic, priest and martyr. In Spain, the feast of the holy martyrs Servandus and Germanus. At Cologne, Saint Severinus, bishop.

Herifredus, bishop of this house, a most devout father, died. He gave half of Malliacum to provide meals for the brothers. On the day of his ordination he also gave the brothers the village of Artadum, one mansus at Lindriacum, another mansus at Capiliacum, and a mill below the wall. On the Nativity of Saint [Col. 1248B] Mary he gave the church of Bacerna, Lindriacum, and Lupinum, as well as Logniacum; but Gimiliacum on the feast of Saint Clement.

IX Kalends of November. In the city of Venusia in Apulia, the feast of the holy martyrs Felix, bishop; Audactus and Januarius, priests; and Fortunatus and Septimus, lectors.

VIII Kalends of November. In Gaul, in the city of Soissons, the feast of the holy martyrs Crispin and Crispinian. On the same day, in the city of Périgueux, the feast of Saint Fronto, bishop, who by God’s power, having received the staff of the apostle Peter, restored his companion, the priest Gregory, from death. At Rome, the holy 46 soldier-martyrs. Also at Rome, Boniface, pope. In the city of Javols, the burial of Saint Hilary, [Col. 1248C] a bishop renowned for life and miracles. In the territory of Tours, the feast of Saint Spanus, martyr.

VII Kalends of November. In Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Rogatianus, priest, and Felicissimus. At Ephesus, Saint Polycrates, an outstanding bishop and most distinguished man.

VI Kalends of November. At Rome, Euvcharistus, pope and martyr. At Auxerre, the burial of blessed Desiderius, bishop. In the district of Poitiers, the feast of Saint Florentius, priest and monk. In Spain, in the city of Helbora, the feast of the holy martyrs Vincentius, Sabina, and Christea.

V Kalends of November. The feast of the blessed apostles Simon the Cananaean, also written “the Zealot,” and Thaddaeus, who is also read as Judas of James and elsewhere called Lebbaeus. Thaddaeus is said to have preached in Mesopotamia, while Simon preached in Egypt. From there they entered Persia together; after gathering an innumerable multitude to Christ, they were martyred. At Rome, Saint Cyrilla, martyr, daughter of the emperor Decius. In the city of Meaux, Saint Faro, bishop and confessor. At Paris, the translation of Saint Genevieve, virgin.

IV Kalends of November. The feast of blessed Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, a man praiseworthy for holiness, endurance, and faith. When three witnesses had sworn a false accusation against him, they called down curses upon themselves: the first, that he should be consumed by fire if he were not telling the truth; the second, that he should be afflicted with a royal disease; [Col. 1249A] the third, that he should be deprived of his sight. This happened to each of them immediately after the perjury. At Sindon, the feast of Saint Zebaeus, priest and martyr.

III Kalends of November. In the city of Tingis, the passion of Saint Marcellus, centurion. In Africa, 220 holy martyrs. At Antioch, blessed Serapion, bishop and confessor.

Andreas, priest, died. He gave the brothers his small dwelling with the adjoining vineyard in the village of Ferreolus, and likewise in the village of Garrica. Bernardus, priest, also died; he gave the brothers his small dwelling with a garden and vineyard in the village of Vendonsa.

The day before the Kalends of November. At Rome, Blessed Nemesius, deacon and martyr, and his daughter Lucilla. He was beheaded on the eighth day before the Kalends of September and was honorably translated on the day before the Kalends of November. In Gaul, in the territory of Vermandois, Saint Quintinus, martyr.

On the same day Robertus, provost, died. He gave the brothers his vineyards, so that each year on the day of his death a common meal might be provided for the canons.

NOVEMBER.

The Kalends of November. The feast of All Saints. At the fortress of Dijon, the feast of Saint Benignus, priest and martyr. On the same day, the feast of the holy martyrs Caesarius, deacon, and Julianus, priest. At Paris, Saint Marcellus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the feast of Saint Severinus, a monk from the city of Tibur. Elsewhere, the feast of Saint Mary, virgin and martyr. In the territory of Bourges, at a place called Dolus, Saint Lusor, confessor.

IV Nones of November. At Rome, the passion of Saint Eustace with his wife and two sons. On the same day, the feast of Saint Victorinus, martyr and bishop of Poitiers. At Laodicea, Blessed Theodotus, bishop, an excellent man. At the monastery of Agaunum, the feast of Saint Ambrose, abbot.

III Nones of November. The feast of Saint Quartus, disciple of the apostles. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of the holy martyrs Germanus, Theophilus, Caesarius, and Vitalis. In the district of Vexin, Saint Clarus, priest and martyr.

II Nones of November. At Alexandria, Blessed Iterius, priest, a man of God. In the territory of Rouen, [Col. 1249D] Saint Amantius, bishop and confessor. At Autun, the feast of Saint Patroclus, bishop and confessor.

On the same day Hugh, an ornament among bishops, gave up his spirit.

The Nones of November. The death of Zachariah, prophet and father of John the Baptist. In the city of Terracina in Campania, the feast of the holy martyrs Felix, priest, and Eusebius, monk. In the city of Capua, the feast of Saint Quartus, confessor.

VIII Ides of November. At Thoniza in Africa, the feast of Saint Felix, whose martyrdom blessed Augustine wondrously expounds in a certain psalm. In the East, in the city of Theopolis, the ten holy martyrs who are said to have suffered under the Saracens. At Rennes, Saint Melanius, bishop and confessor.

VII Ides of November. At Alexandria, blessed Achillas, bishop, a man of God. At the city of Albiga, the feast of Saint Amaranthus, martyr. Near Perugia in Italy, the feast of Saint Herculanus, bishop and martyr, whose body, after the severing of his head, was found on the fortieth day joined together in such a way, as Pope Gregory recalls, as though no cut of iron had touched it. In Frisia, the feast of Saint Willibrord, bishop, whose deeds Bede the priest describes in his *Ecclesiastical History of the English*.

Teodaldus, a young man, died. He gave the canons of Saint Stephen part of his patronage and inheritance, for love of the heavenly homeland and the remission of his sins. These properties lie in a village called Cormedus, with its chapel and appurtenances, bondservants, vineyards, fields, and houses, so that his memory might be commemorated.

VI Ides of November. At Rome, the feast of the five martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Simphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius. On the same day, near their bodies, the feast of the four holy crowned martyrs Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus.

Hunencus, priest and dean of Saint Mammes, died.

V Ides of November. The feast of Saint Theodore, martyr, crowned after various torments. At Bourges, Saint Ursicinus, bishop and confessor. *(By another hand: In the city of Berytus in Syria, the passion of the holy and glorious image of the Lord Savior.)*

Ademarus, priest and provost, died.

IV Ides of November. In the territory of Agde, at Cessario, the feast of the holy martyrs Tiberius, Modestus, and Florence. At Antioch, the feast of the holy Demetrius, bishop, Anianus, deacon, Eustasius, and twenty others. At Orléans, Saint Monitor, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the feast of Saint Martin, pope and martyr.

III Ides of November. In Gaul, in the city of Tours, the feast of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor, whose glorious deeds are preserved, spread far and wide. In Scythia, in the metropolis of Phrygia Salutaris, the passion of Saint Menas, crowned after various torments. At Lyon, the passion of Saint Veranus, bishop.

[Col. 1250D] Stephen, bishop of Chalon, died.

The day before the Ides of November. In Africa, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Arcadius, Paschasius, Probus, Eutychianus, and the boy Paulillus. In the province of Tarraconensis, in the city of Tarazona, Blessed Emilianus, priest and confessor.

Ingelboldus died. He rebuilt the villages of Saint Stephen—Crevennum, Acolacum, and Villanova—and donated five hundred solidi from his own property to arrange the brothers’ houses.

The Ides of November. At Ravenna, the feast of the holy martyrs Valentinus, Solutor, and Victor. At Toledo, the burial of Blessed Eugenius, bishop. At Tours, the feast of Saint Brictius, bishop and confessor. At Auxerre, the reception of the body of Saint Alexander and Saint Chrysantus, martyr. At Sens, Saint Paternus, martyr.

Aldulfus, bishop, died. He established that on this day a meal should be prepared for the brothers at the hospital from his own resources.

XVIII Kalends of December. At Heraclea in Thrace, the feast of the holy martyrs Clementinus, Theodotus, and Philomenus. At Alexandria, blessed Serapion, a most renowned martyr. At Laodicea, Saint Anatolius, bishop.

Velfo, abbot, died.

XVII Kalends of December. The feast of Saint Felix, bishop and martyr, martyred together with thirty others. On the same day, Saint Eugenius, who, after completing the course of martyrdom in the district of Paris, received from the Lord the crown of blessed suffering.

[Col. 1251B] Waltherius, archbishop of Sens, and Gratianus, abbot, died.

XVI Kalends of December. At Lyon in Gaul, the feast of Saint Eucherius, a man of admirable faith, life, and teaching. In Africa, the holy Nereus, Paulus, and Adrianus.

XV Kalends of December. At Alexandria, Blessed Dionysius, bishop, a man of great holiness. At Pontus, the feast of blessed Gregory, bishop and martyr of Neocaesarea. At Orléans, Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor, whose death is attested before the Lord by frequent miracles. On the same day, at Córdoba in Spain, the holy martyrs Acisclus and Victoria, where roses are divinely gathered on that same day in commemoration of their precious death. At Tours, Saint Gregory, bishop and worker of miracles.

Milo, a boy who was a canon and acolyte, died. He gave the brothers fifteen arpents of vineyard at Monteium.

XIV Kalends of December. At Antioch, the feast of Saint Romanus, monk and martyr. On the same day, in the same city, the feast of Saint Sychus, martyr. At Auxerre, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Germanus, bishop, together with the upper crypts. On the same day, the translation of the body of blessed Stephen, protomartyr, from Jerusalem to Byzantium.

XIII Kalends of December. At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of Saint Maximus, priest and martyr.

At Vienne, the holy martyrs Severinus, Exuperius, and Felicianus. On the same day, Saint Faustus, martyr. At Autun, the feast of Saint Simplicius, bishop and [Col. 1251D] martyr. On that day also, blessed Crispinus, martyr. Also at Rome, Gelasius, pope.

Lantbertus, priest, died. He gave the brothers his allod in a village called Stabulis and in the surrounding places. Lanfredus, priest, also died; he gave the brothers his patrimony in the village of Gratiacum.

XII Kalends of December. At Rome, the feast of Saint Pontius, pope and martyr. In Sicily, in the city of Messina, the holy Ampelius and Gaius. At Chalon, Saint Silvester, bishop and confessor.

Iterus of Porta died. To obtain pardon for his sins, he gave the canons of Saint Stephen [Col. 1252A] two men at Crevennum, with their wives and children.

XI Kalends of December. The feast of the most blessed Rufus, concerning whom the apostle Paul writes to the Romans: “Greet Rufus, chosen, and his mother and mine.” At Antioch, the holy Basil, Auxentius, and Zephyrinus.

Otardus died. For the love of God and the remission of his sins, he gave the brothers excellent properties of his own in the county of Tonnerre, at a village called Malorum and in the surrounding places, with small dwellings, vineyards, fields, and houses.

X Kalends of November. At Rome, Saint Cecilia, virgin and martyr. Also at Rome, Saint Maurus, martyr. [Col. 1252B] At Caesarea, the feast of Saint Longinus, soldier and martyr, who pierced the Lord’s side with a lance.

Christianus, bishop, died. He gave the brothers the village of Albaris, so that his memory might be commemorated. On the same day Clemens, radiant with the light of all wisdom, died.

IX Kalends of December. The feast of Saint Clement, pope and martyr. On the same day, the feast of Saint Felicity, mother of the seven martyr-sons whom the emperor Antoninus ordered to die by various punishments; their mother was finally beheaded for Christ. In Italy, at the monastery of Bobbio, the feast of Saint Columbanus, abbot. In the district of Asbania, the feast of Saint Trudo, priest and confessor.

VIII Kalends of December. At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Chrysogonus and Crescentianus. At the fortress of Blavia, Saint Romanus, priest and confessor, whose proclamation of holiness is demonstrated by the glory of his miracles. In the city of Córdoba, the holy virgins Flora and Maria, who, after prolonged imprisonment, were killed by the sword for Christ.

Hictarius, of blessed memory, died. He gave his brothers the vineyards he had acquired around the city. On the same day, the anniversary of Atto, canon, who gave the brothers thirty pounds, as well as male and female servants, three arpents of vineyard at Montetensum, and the plots situated beside the chapel of Saint Stephen, together with one plot lying before the house of the poor. He set out for Jerusalem and, on that journey, died through Christ’s mercy.

VII Kalends of December. The feast of Saint Peter of Alexandria, [Col. 1252D] bishop and martyr, outstanding among the foremost. After various struggles for the faith of Christ, the Lord appeared to him one night, clothed in a garment—a very white linen *colobium*—torn from top to bottom. With both hands he was clasping it about his breast, in a way covering his nakedness. Peter said to him: “What is this, Lord, that I see—your garment torn?” The Lord replied: “Arius has done this, he who separated from me the people purchased with my blood. I now command and warn you not to receive him into communion,” and so forth. Some 660 bishops from Egypt, together with clerics and laypeople, suffered martyrdom with him.

[Col. 1253A] Milo, a layman, died. He gave the brothers his allod, which lies in the village of Colonicas above the river Senodus. On the same day Goscelinus, canon and dean of this church, died. For the remedy of his soul, he gave his house with its vineyards to the canons, so that on the day of his anniversary they might dine in the refectory. [Note: [Col. 1253D] Goscelinus, dean, whose death is recorded on this day, was alive in 1133 and 1137, when the common life still flourished among the canons of Auxerre, as is clear from this passage. [Col. 1254D]]

He appointed his own priest to celebrate Masses for the dead at Saint Clement, together with two arpents of vineyard, and established him in the oversight and custody of the chapter. He also gave the aforementioned church a priestly vestment, an excellent missal with a gradual, a silver chalice with silver tubes, and left the church so furnished.

VI Kalends of December. The feast of Saint Linus, pope and martyr, [Col. 1253B] who governed the Roman church for twelve years, three months, and twelve days after blessed Peter; he was crowned with martyrdom and buried in the Vatican. At Alexandria, the feast of the holy martyrs Faustus, priest, Dius, and Ammonius. On the same day, blessed Alexander, martyr and bishop. In the district of Avala, the feast of Saint Magnentia, virgin. At Autun, the feast of Saint Amator, bishop and confessor.

V Kalends of December. At Bologna in Italy, the feast of the holy martyrs Vitalis and Agricola, crucified after various torments. In Gaul, in the city of Reims, the feast of Saint Maximinus, bishop and confessor.

On the same day John, priest and canon of this church, its outstanding cantor, died. From his books he gave our church one missal, an antiphonary, [Col. 1253C] a gradual, a hymnary, and an excellent prosary. At the village of Acolacum he gave the brothers his houses and whatever property he appeared to possess, for the commemoration of his memory.

IV Kalends of December. The feast of Saint Sosthenes, disciple of the apostles. On the same day, Saint Rufus, martyr. On that day also, the bishops Papinus and Mansuetus with many others who suffered at that time. At Rome, Saint Gregory III, pope, who governed the church for ten years. At Auxerre, the translation of Saint Vigilius, bishop and martyr.

III Kalends of December. The vigil of Saint Andrew the apostle. At Rome, the feast of Saint Saturninus, martyr, and the deacons and martyrs Sisinius and Sisinnius. On the same day, at Toulouse, the feast of Saint Saturninus, bishop and martyr.

[Col. 1253D] The day before the Kalends of December. In the city of Patras in the province of Achaea, the feast of blessed Andrew the apostle, who also preached in Scythia. At Saintes, Saint Trojanus, bishop, a man of great virtue and holiness. At Rome, in the cemetery at Guttas, Saint Castulus.

DECEMBER.

The Kalends of December. At Rome, the passion of the holy Chrysantus and Daria, virgin. In Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Papinus and Mansuetus, bishops. At the city of Mainz, blessed Albanus, martyr. On the same day, Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon. At Byzantium-Nicomedia, [Col. 1254A] the feast of Saint Natalia, wife of Saint Adrian, martyr.

Teutgarius, deacon, died. He gave us a vineyard in the village of Sigliniacum. On the same day, the ordination of Lord Gaufridus, bishop. On the same day Vitalis, dean of the church of Auxerre, entered upon the way of all flesh.

IV Nones of December. The feast of Saint Viviana, martyr, and the holy martyrs Faustus and Daphrosa, his daughter. On that day also, the passion of the holy Verus and Secura, who were crowned with martyrdom in Africa.

III Nones of December. At Tingis, the metropolis of Mauretania Tingitana, the feast of Saint Cassianus, martyr. On the same day, the holy martyrs Claudius, tribune, his wife Hilaria, their sons Jason and Maurus, and seventy soldiers, all of whom came to believe in Christ through the preaching of Saint Chrysantus.

Abbo, bishop, died.

II Nones of December. At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Symphronius and Olympius under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. In Africa, Armogastes, Archinimus, and Satyrus, who, though they were shining members of the church of Christ, endured many severe punishments and insults from the Arians for confessing the truth and completed the course of their glorious contest. And at Laodicea, the metropolis, Saint Felix.

On that day Stephen, provost and priest of Saint Stephen, an outstanding man and an excellent teacher of the divine Scriptures, died.

[Col. 1254C] The Nones of December. In Africa, at the colony of Theveste, the feast of Saint Crispina, martyr. On the same day, in Italy, the feast of Dalmatius, martyr. At Trier, Saint Nicetius, bishop and confessor.

Ermenbertus, provost and levite, and Arnaldus, viscount, died.

VIII Ides of December. The feast of blessed Nicholas, bishop of Myra in Lycia. In Africa, the holy Dionysia, Davita, Leontius, and Emilianus the physician, and the religious men Noetercius, Boniface, Servus, Victrix, and Majoricus the young man. All of them, tortured by innumerable punishments, were deemed worthy to be numbered among Christ’s confessors.

VII Ides of December. At Alexandria, blessed Agathon, martyr, under the emperor Decius. At Saintes, blessed Martin, abbot, disciple of blessed Martin, bishop of the city of Tours, who rests in peace in the monastery that he himself built. On the same day, in the city of Spoleto, Saint Sabinus, bishop and martyr. In the district of Meaux, Saint Fara, virgin.

VI Ides of December. At Rome, the feast of Saint Eutychianus, pope and martyr, who himself buried 342 martyrs with his own hand in various places. At Alexandria, Saint Macarius, martyr. In the territory of Dunum, the burial of Saint Leonard, an outstanding confessor.

V Ides of December. The feast of Saint Leocadia, virgin, who, imprisoned at Toledo, heard of the sufferings of blessed Eulalia and the other martyrs who were then being killed. Kneeling in prayer, she gave her undefiled spirit to Christ. On the same day, blessed Cyprian, abbot of Périgueux.

IV Ides of December. At Rome, Melchiades, pope. At Mérida in Spain, the feast of Saint Eulalia, virgin and martyr. On the same day, in the aforementioned city, the passion of Saint Julia, virgin, who was a companion in virginity of blessed Eulalia. In the city of Seville, the holy martyrs Carpophorus, priest, and Abundius, deacon.

Wadimirus, chorepiscopus, died. On the same day Amalricus, levite, died. He gave the brothers his acquired estate in a village called Castriacum and, on its boundaries, seven arpents of vineyard, for love of eternal life and the commemoration of his memory. On the same day Reinaldus, archpriest and canon, died. He gave the brothers an excellent vineyard, twenty *modii* of wine, one female servant, and one hundred solidi toward the construction of the cloister.

III Ides of December. At Rome, Saint Damasus, pope, and the feast of the holy martyrs Pontianus, Praetextatus, and Thrason. In Gaul, in the city of Amiens, the feast of the holy martyrs Victoricus, Fuscianus, and Gentianus, who adorned the most glorious confession of their faith with the blood of their passion. In Spain, the feast of Saint Eutychius, whose deeds are preserved.

Gerberga, countess and wife of Duke Henry, died. On the same day Gozfridus, priest and dean [Col. 1255C] of the city of Sens, died.

II Ides of December. The feast of the holy Hermogenes, Donatus, and twenty-two others. At Alexandria, the blessed martyrs Epimachus and Alexander. In the city of Narbonne in Septimania, the burial of blessed Paul, bishop and confessor. In the district of Vimeu, the feast of Saint Walericus, confessor, who led an eremitical life beside the river Somme.

The Ides of December. At Syracuse in Sicily, the feast of Saint Lucy, virgin and martyr.

On that day Matilda, countess and wife of Landricus, died. On the same day Hermengardis, abbess, died.

XIX Kalends of January. In Cyprus, the feast of Saint Spyridon, bishop and confessor. At Reims, Saint Nicasius, bishop and martyr, who was beheaded by the Vandals inside the church building for the faith of Christ. At Auxerre, the dedication of the altar of the upper church, carried out by Pope Callistus II; the same pope also established that we should celebrate it solemnly each year.

XVIII Kalends of January. In Africa, the feast of Saint Valerian, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Orléans, the blessed Maximinus, a presbyter and man of venerable holiness.

Aclevertus, priest and dean, died.

XVII Kalends of January. The Three Boys—Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael—whose bodies have been placed near Babylon in a certain cavern. On the same day, the feast of the blessed martyrs Rufus and Zosimus. In Tuscany, Saint Barbara, virgin and martyr. In Pontus, Saint Meletius, bishop and confessor.

XVI Kalends of January. At Antioch, the translation and burial of the body of Saint Ignatius, bishop and martyr, who suffered at Rome on the Kalends of February. On the same day, the blessed Lazarus, whom the Lord Jesus is read to have raised from the dead in the Gospel. Also the blessed Martha, his sister. In the East, at the city of Eleutheropolis, fifty holy martyrs who suffered under the Saracens.

XV Kalends of January. In Africa, the feast of Saint Moses, martyr. On the same day, Saint Anatolia, virgin and martyr. At Tours, Saint Gatianus, first bishop of that city.

Eldegarius, a layman, died. He gave all his estate to the brothers in the county of Tournêtre, in the village of Madriacum: vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated lands and meadows, woods, houses, and all their appurtenances, for the absolution of his sins.

XIV Kalends of January. At Auxerre, the burial of the blessed Gregory, who sat as bishop for twelve years, seven months, and three days. He was buried in the church of Saint Germanus. In Egypt, the blessed martyr Nemesius. At Alexandria, the blessed Clement, presbyter.

XIII Kalends of January. The most blessed martyrs Ammon, Zeno, Ptolemy, Ingenius, and Theophilus.

Eliseus, archdeacon, died. He gave to the brothers nine arpents of vineyards from his property in the village called Gratiacum, for the remedy of his sins and for the perpetuation of his memory.

[Col. 1256C] XII Kalends of January. The feast of the blessed apostle Thomas, who, preaching the Gospel to the Parthians and Medes, suffered in India on the fifth day before the Nones of July. His body was transferred on the XII Kalends of January to the city which the Syrians call Edessa, and there buried with due honor.

The election of Lord Gerannus as bishop. He gave the brothers the estate of Logniacum and Solium, from which a measure of oil is owed for the lamps of the churches of Saint Mary, Saint Stephen, and Saint John, and one pound of denarii to the brothers who hold that land. On the same day Agnes of Longavilla died. She gave to the church of the protomartyr, the blessed Stephen, a costly curtain decorated in various colors.

XI Kalends of January. At Rome, on the Lavican Way between the Two Laurels, the feast of thirty martyrs, all crowned on one day during the persecution of Diocletian. At Alexandria, the blessed martyr Schyrion. On that day also, many other martyrs who, wandering in the deserts and mountains of Egypt, were consumed by hunger, thirst, cold, illness, robbers, and beasts. On the same day, Theodosia, virgin and martyr, and Saint Didymus, a monk and most learned man.

X Kalends of January. At Rome, the feast of Saint Victoria, virgin and martyr. At Nicomedia, twenty holy martyrs. Also at Rome, the blessed Servulus, of whom Saint Gregory writes: “Poor in worldly goods but rich in merits,” and the other wonderful things he says about him. On the same day, the feast of Saint Evaristus, pope and martyr. At Auxerre, the dedication of the church of Saint John the Baptist.

Ablenus, deacon, died. He gave the brothers his property in the village called Saint Maurice and in the village called Antonus, in order to obtain forgiveness of his sins and to have his memory celebrated.

IX Kalends of January. The vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. On the same day at Syrian Antioch, the feast of forty holy virgins, who completed their martyrdom through various tortures. At Spoleto, the feast of Saint Gregory, presbyter and martyr, who, after being repeatedly stretched on the rack and subjected to various tortures, was crowned.

VIII Kalends of January. At Bethlehem, the Nativity according to the flesh of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. On the same day, the feast of Saint Anastasia, virgin and martyr, who followed from Rome the saints being led to martyrdom. At Rome, in the cemetery of Apronianus, the suffering of Saint Eugenia, virgin.

VII Kalends of January. At Jerusalem, the suffering of Saint Stephen, protomartyr and deacon. Not long after the Lord’s Ascension, when he was full of faith and the Holy Spirit, he was ordained deacon by the apostles; in the same year in which Christ suffered, he was stoned by the Jews. On the same day, the feast of Saint Marinus, a most distinguished man, who received the reward of martyrdom at Rome under the emperor Marcian.

Ingelboldus, a soldier, died.

VI Kalends of January. At Ephesus, the feast of Saint John, apostle and evangelist, beloved of the Lord. After his exile and banishment, after the divine revelation of the Apocalypse, and after composing the Gospel, he died, worn out by old age, sixty-eight years after the Lord’s Passion, at the age of ninety-nine. In the region of Aquileia, the feast of Saint Zoilus, presbyter and confessor.

V Kalends of January. At Bethlehem, the feast of the Holy Innocents, whom Herod ordered killed in the thirty-fifth year of his reign after learning of Christ’s birth through the Magi. In the thirty-sixth year he died miserably and deservedly of dropsy, his whole body teeming with worms.

Sigradus died. He gave the brothers his demesne holding with all its appurtenances in the county of Tournêtre, in the village of Cidernacum: [a number of] arpents of vineyards, [a number of] measures of land, to be given to the brothers as a rent.

IV Kalends of January. At Jerusalem, the burial of King David. At Arles, the feast of Saint Trophimus, bishop, of whom the Apostle writes to Timothy: “I left Trophimus ill at Miletus.” Ordained bishop by the apostles at Rome, he was sent first to the city of Arles in Gaul to preach Christ’s Gospel. From his fountain, as blessed Pope Zosimus writes, all Gaul received the streams of its faith. In the county of Ouche, the feast of Saint Ebrulfus, confessor, whose deeds are recorded. At Auxerre, the dedication of the church of Saint Michael and Saint Clement.

III Kalends of January. At Spoleto, the suffering of Saint Sabinus, bishop; Exuperantius and Marcellus, deacons; and Venustianus with his wife and children, martyred together under the emperor Maximian. At Tours, the feast of Saint Perpetuus, bishop and confessor.

II Kalends of January. At Rome, the feast of Saint Silvester, pope and confessor, whose deeds are well known. He was the thirty-fifth after the blessed Peter among the apostles. He occupied the episcopal office for twenty-three years, five months, and eleven days. Full of virtues, he died in peace and was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, on the day before the Kalends of January. At Sens, the blessed Sabinus, bishop, and Potentianus, who, sent by the blessed apostles to preach, made that city illustrious by the confession of their martyrdom. Also at Sens, the suffering of Saint Columba, virgin, who, after overcoming the fire, was struck with the sword.

Anseisus, bishop of Troyes, died.

[Col. 1257]

## Mantuan Calendar

January has 31 days and 30 lunar days.

[Col. 1257D]

A. Kalends of January: the Circumcision of the Lord; Pope Boniface.  
B. the fourth day before the Nones: the Octave of Stephen.  
C. the third day: the Octave of John.  
D. the second day: the Octave of the Innocents.  
E. the Nones, vigil.  
F. the eighth day before the Ides: the Epiphany of the Lord.  
G. the seventh day before the Ides.

A. the sixth day before the Ides.  
B. the fifth day before the Ides.  
C. the fourth day before the Ides.  
D. Paul, first hermit.  
E. Pope Agatho, on the third day.  
F. Pope Hyginus and martyr, on the second day.  
G. the Ides: the Epiphany.

[Col. 1258D] G. the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February: Felix, presbyter.  
A. the eighteenth day: Maurus, abbot.  
B. the seventeenth day: Marcellus, pope and martyr.  
C. the sixteenth day: Sabinus, bishop, and Antony.  
D. the fifteenth day: Prisca, virgin.  
E. the fourteenth day: Bassianus, bishop.  
F. the thirteenth day: Fabian, pope, and Sebastian, martyr.  
G. the twelfth day: Agnes, virgin.  
A. the eleventh day: Vincent and Anastasius, martyrs.  
B. the tenth day.  
C. the ninth day: Timothy, apostle.  
D. the eighth day: the Conversion of Saint Paul.  
E. the seventh day: Paula, abbess.  
F. the sixth day: Vitalianus, pope.  
G. the fifth day: Agnes for the second time.  
A. the fourth day.  
B. the third day.  
C. the second day: Geminianus, bishop.

February has 28 days and 30 lunar days.

D. Kalends of February: Severus, bishop; Brigid, virgin.  
E. the fourth day before the Nones: the Presentation of the Lord.  
F. the third day: Blaise, bishop and martyr.  
G. the second day.  
A. the Nones: Agatha, virgin.  
B. the eighth day before the Ides.  
C. the seventh day: Pelagius, pope.  
D. the sixth day.  
E. the fifth day.  
F. the fourth day: Scholastica, virgin.  
G. the third day.  
A. the second day.  
B. the Ides: Gregory, pope.  
C. the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March: Valerian, bishop and martyr.  
D. the fifteenth day: Faustinus and Jovita, martyrs.  
E. the fourteenth day.  
F. Thursday: Fra… died in the year of the Lord 1200…  
G. the thirteenth day.  
A. the twelfth day.  
B. the eleventh day.  
C. the tenth day.  
D. the ninth day: Siricius, pope.  
E. the eighth day: the Chair of Saint Peter.  
F. the seventh day: Matthias, apostle; Sabinianus, pope.  
G. the sixth day.  
A. the fifth day.  
B. the fourth day.  
C. the third day.  
D. the second day.

March has 31 days and 30 lunar days.

D. Kalends of March: Simplicius, pope.  
E. the sixth day before the Nones.  
F. the fifth day.  
G. the fourth day.  
A. the third day.  
B. the second day.  
C. the Nones: Perpetua and Felicity; Thomas Aquinas.  
D. the eighth day before the Ides.  
E. the seventh day.  
F. the sixth day.  
G. the fifth day.  
A. the fourth day: Pope Gregory and the discovery of the Blood of the Lord.  
B. the third day.  
C. the second day: Pope Zacharias.  
D. the Ides.  
E. the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April.  
F. the sixteenth day.  
G. the fifteenth day: Anselm, bishop.  
A. the fourteenth day: + Ioxep.  
B. the thirteenth day.  
C. the twelfth day: the Passing of Saint Benedict.  
D. the eleventh day.  
E. the tenth day.  
F. the ninth day.  
G. the eighth day: the Annunciation of Saint Mary.  
A. the seventh day.  
B. the sixth day: the Resurrection of the Lord.  
C. the fifth day.  
D. the fourth day.  
E. the third day.  
F. the second day.

April has 30 days and 29 lunar days.

G. Kalends of April.  
A. the fourth day before the Nones.  
B. the third day.  
C. the second day.  
D. the Nones: Ambrose, archbishop.  
E. the eighth day before the Ides.  
F. the seventh day: Celestine, pope.  
G. the sixth day.  
A. the fifth day.  
B. the fourth day: Donus, pope.  
C. the third day: Leo, pope.  
D. the second day: Julius, pope; Benno, bishop.  
E. the Ides.  
F. the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May: Tiburtius and Valerian, martyrs.  
G. the seventeenth day.  
A. the sixteenth day.  
B. the fifteenth day: Anicetus, pope and martyr.  
C. the fourteenth day.  
D. the thirteenth day: Leo, pope.  
E. the twelfth day.  
F. the eleventh day.  
G. the tenth day: Soter, pope and martyr; Gaius, pope and martyr.  
A. the ninth day.  
B. the eighth day: George, martyr, and Adalbert; Benedict, pope.  
C. the seventh day: Mark, Evangelist, and the Greater Litany.  
D. the sixth day.  
E. the fifth day: Anastasius, pope.  
F. the fourth day: Vitalis, martyr.  
G. the third day: Peter, martyr, of the Order of Preachers.  
A. the second day.

May has 31 days and 30 lunar days.

B. Kalends of May: Philip and James, apostles.

Third day: the Octave of Saint John.  
Second day: the Octave of the Innocents.  
Nones.  
Eighth day before the Ides: the Epiphany of the Lord.

Third day: Paul, first hermit.

## Fragment of a Lucanian Calendar

November has 30 days, while the moon has 30. The night has 16 hours, the day …

VIII.

HERE BEGINS BEDE’S MARTYROLOGY

[Note: [Col. 1293D] This is the very ancient Martyrology of Bede—as it is entitled in the manuscript—which we print here. I would judge it to be neither a martyrology nor Bede’s, but a calendar, since it contains only the bare names of saints; yet perhaps it was extracted from Bede’s Martyrology and enlarged and supplemented here and there. The codex from which we publish it exists in the celebrated Laurentian Library, shelf XVI, no. 6. It appears that the Missal belongs to the eleventh century, as does also Bede’s Martyrology, which is written at its beginning. I noticed, however, both in this and in the other calendars, quite a few additions inserted by later hands. It was therefore my concern to distinguish these appropriately from the original exemplar. Accordingly, I prefixed a certain asterisk to these additions, and to those that are altogether more recent than the others, two asterisks. I also ordered that the feast days, which in manuscript codices are for the most part marked in red characters, should here be displayed in a different type. For I understood that to students of such delicacies none of these observations would be useless or unwelcome.]

[MASS IN LATIN.]

[Col. 1301]

NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING MASS AND FRAGMENT OF A MASS, BY JOHN BONA, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Bernard at the Baths, of the Holy Roman Church, of the Cistercian Order.

(*Liturgical Matters*, Book I, p. 108.)

[Col. 1301C] Matthias Flacius Illyricus, leader of the Magdeburg Centuriators and of the rigid Lutherans, had a Latin Mass found in an ancient manuscript codex printed at Strasbourg in the year 1557, and prefixed to it this title: “The Latin Mass which was formerly in use before the Roman [Mass], about the seven-hundredth year of the Lord, faithfully transcribed from an ancient and authentic codex.” In a prefatory letter to the Elector Palatine of the Rhine, he also claims that it was in use in the West, especially in Gaul and Germany, before the Roman manner of celebrating Mass was received everywhere.

It lacks the Introit, Collects, Epistle, Gradual, Gospel, Offertory, Preface, Postcommunion, and certain other elements that are named only in general, without any specific assignment, because the variety of days and feasts requires different Introits, different Prayers, Epistles, and the other things peculiar to individual Masses. This destroys the false opinion of Illyricus, who believed that formerly there had been one single way of celebrating Mass, without any distinction of seasons or feasts.

By publishing this Mass, the wicked man believed that he would cause great harm to the Catholic Church, as though it had improperly innovated the ancient rites of the sacrifice; but his own malice blinded him. For, on the contrary, the doctrines of orthodox faith and the received rites of the Church are repeatedly confirmed by it—namely, the invocation of the saints and of the Blessed Virgin, the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, auricular confession, prayer for the living and the dead, and many other things of the same kind.

When Luther’s followers immediately noticed this, they gathered together and promptly burned every published copy they could find. Hence that codex is extremely rare; neither Cassander nor Pamelius saw it, although they lived at that time and were most diligent in searching out books relating to the sacred rites. Menardus did see it: he examines this Mass and compares it with another similar Mass published by him in the notes to Saint Gregory’s *Book of Sacraments*, p. 380 and following. William Peyratius also saw it; he gives a synopsis of it in his treatise *On the Rights and Antiquities of the Chapel of the Kings of France*, Book II, chapter 13, from p. 561 onward.

After seeking it for a long time, in Rome and elsewhere, but in vain, I finally found it at Vienna, in the emperor’s very well-stocked library, through the care and diligence of Charles Veterani, a musician, who transcribed it from the printed codex; the distinguished prefect of that library, Peter Lambecius, most willingly made the codex available to him. Later, an erudite work came into my hands, *Annals of the Frankish Church*, by Charles Le Cointe, into which it had been inserted in volume II, under the year 601, no. 20, with various notes and observations.

So that nothing might be lacking here that contributes to the elucidation of the Latin Mass, I am having it reprinted here, together with a fragment of another similar Mass that has not yet been published.

II. Moreover, although the aforementioned William, followed by Charles, knew well enough what trust could be placed in a most obstinate heretic, they were nevertheless distracted by other studies from considering the matter more carefully. They readily believed his unsupported assertion—based on mere suspicion and devoid of every foundation—that this was the Mass used in the Gallican churches before they received the Roman Mass, and they attempted to support it with certain conjectures.

But how far this Mass is from the ancient Gallican Mass, and how false and misguided a judgment Illyricus formed concerning it, I shall first demonstrate here; afterward I shall propose my conjectures concerning the true Gallican Mass and submit them to the judgment of the skilled and learned men with whom Gaul abounds.

First, I ask where Illyricus knows that the Mass he published preceded the reign of Pippin, or by what witness or argument he proves it. Will he thrust upon us that Pythagorean formula, “He himself said it”? I, however, have learned to believe no mortal unless he gives an account of what he says.

I prefer to believe the most learned Hugh Menardus, who in the passage cited demonstrates by arguments not to be despised that it is not as ancient as the sectarian attributed to it, but later by two or three centuries.

Who, moreover, taught him that it is older than the Roman Mass and different from it? For, even with Homeric eyes closed—or, to use Tertullian’s phrase, even in total blindness—it is clear that this is a pure and simple Roman Mass, interpolated with various prayers.

George Wicelius, at first a disciple of Luther and afterward a Catholic, noted this in his *Defense of the Ecclesiastical Liturgy* as soon as he fixed his eyes upon it. “Illyricus,” he says, “published the Latin Mass he had found, yet he did not triumph over Catholics as though he had discovered so great a treasure, since even a blind man can see that he published the whole thing against the sects of Luther and Calvin; rather, he did us Catholics a very welcome service. For what does he defend there, unknowingly and unwittingly, except the Latin Mass that is now in general use? He is so far from attacking it according to the custom of himself and his sect that the opposite is true. It is indeed richer and contains more prayers, but nevertheless it is altogether the same as the customary Mass; it follows everywhere all of its words and actions, so that no one would dare assert that it is different.”

Charles Le Cointe quotes and praises these words of Wicelius under the year mentioned above, no. 21. He agrees with him, acknowledging that this is the pure Roman Mass now in use, although more prayers have been inserted into it. Nevertheless, he says that this Mass, enlarged by these prayers, was Gallican—as though one should believe that the Gallican churches, abandoning their own rites at that time, adopted the Roman order at Pippin’s command, and that, after rejecting the prayers added to Illyricus’s Mass, they began to use the pure Roman Mass. This would plainly be absurd.

Just as a naked man and that same man clothed in different garments are one and the same man, so the Roman Mass is always Roman, even if more prayers are mixed into it.

Moreover, Illyricus’s Mass bears no resemblance or correspondence to what the authors whom we shall soon cite have transmitted concerning the ancient Gallican Mass. For they say that in the Gallican Masses the sufferings of the martyrs were described, whereas in Illyricus’s Mass there is not even the slightest trace of this. They say that the ancient order of the Mass was entirely different from the usage of the Roman Church; but Illyricus’s Mass does not differ from the Roman Mass—indeed, it is the same, though interpolated.

Finally, I observe that no mention of this Illyrician Mass is found among the ancient Fathers or ecclesiastical writers, nor is there any approval of it in councils or in the decrees of the supreme pontiffs. From this it follows that, by the private institution of some bishop, so many prayers were added to the common Roman Mass that the priest would be occupied in reciting them while he celebrated the Mass solemnly, especially at the time when the choir was singing the Introit, Gradual, Creed, and other such things.

Exactly the same must be said of the two similar Masses that Hugh Menardus published from ancient codices in an appendix to Saint Gregory’s *Book of Sacraments*: they were instituted by some bishop out of particular devotion, and are therefore very far from having once been common to all Gaul.

Although so many councils were held in those regions, and so many men outstanding in learning and ecclesiastical scholarship flourished there, whose writings are still read, no trace whatever of these liturgical prayers appears in them. This is certainly of great importance for rejecting Illyricus’s fiction that his Mass was commonly used throughout Gaul.

III. Another argument may be added for overturning Illyricus’s false conviction. A certain other Mass, interpolated in the same way for the use of a church in a Roman diocese, has been found; I happened to see it while examining Illyricus’s Mass.

It exists in the manuscript codex of the library of the eminent Cardinal Chigi, no. 1521, written in Lombard script. Some leaves are missing at the beginning and many more at the end. First, it contains aspirations to God skillfully composed from psalms, together with other prayers and litanies; second, it contains the order of the Mass only up to the Gospel, for the remainder is either torn away by an impious hand or missing through human carelessness, to the great detriment of ecclesiastical scholarship.

I am making this hitherto unpublished fragment public after Illyricus’s Mass, so that it may not wholly perish. It agrees with that Mass in almost every respect, although the added prayers are often different.

This had nothing whatsoever to do with Gaul, for it uses the Italian version of the Psalms, which was long in use not only in the City but also in all the suburban churches and in other regions, except Gaul, which immediately received the version corrected by Saint Jerome and which was therefore called the Gallican version.

Since, then, a Roman Mass with many added prayers, like the one Illyricus claimed to have been the ancient Gallican Mass, was also used in Italy and was common to other churches, it follows clearly enough that this rite was not peculiar to any kingdom or province, but was granted to one church alone, or to a few churches, by the private authority of their own bishop, without the approval of any synod or of the Apostolic See.

In the manuscript Missal of the Vatican Library, no. 3807, there is likewise the prayer “Supreme Priest,” to be recited at the celebrant’s discretion while the choir sings the Kyrie or Gloria. The same prayer is prescribed in the Missal of the Church of Seville and in that of the Order of Preachers.

From all this, and from the two Masses published by Menardus, it may also be deduced that these interpolations had a place only in solemn Masses, so that both the priest and the ministers, while the choir sang, might be occupied in reciting them either in full or in part.

From the silence of the ancient writers, who mention none of these Masses, and from the rarity of the codices in which they have been found, I infer, not implausibly, either that they were not accepted by the churches to which they had been handed down, or that they perished immediately together with their authors.

For most people recoil from prolixity, and those who are more religious are reluctant to consent to novelties; nor are prayers readily admitted into the public functions of the Church unless they have been approved by synodal or apostolic authority in accordance with the decree of the Council of Milevis and other ecclesiastical sanctions.

I judge that Masses of this kind began near the end of the tenth century or at the beginning of the eleventh, as Menardus asserts concerning his own; he does not consider the Illyrician Mass older than these. The Chigi codex likewise belongs to the tenth century, for the learned men whom I consulted affirm that the Lombard script in which it was written came to an end at the close of that century.

The same conclusion follows from the saints listed in the litanies in the first part of the little book. Although all the holy monks are invoked individually, those who flourished around the year 1000 and afterward are not included. The musical notes prefixed in the order of the Mass to the *Gloria in excelsis* and *Dominus vobiscum* are also those that were in use before Guido of Arezzo.

All these considerations, if properly weighed, refute Illyricus’s fiction. Without probable testimony, he dared to publish the Mass he had found under the name of the ancient Gallican Mass.

[Col. 1305]

LATIN MASS

[Col. 1305A] Here begins the Order of the Sacraments: first, how the priest ought to celebrate the Apologetic prayers before proceeding to the celebration of Mass. Immediately, before putting on the priestly vestments, if circumstances permit and time allows, kneeling before the altar, let him sing the Seven Penitential Psalms with the litany. When it is finished, let him say: “Our Father.” “I believe in God, the Father almighty.” After these prayers:

Arise, O Lord; help us, and redeem us for the sake of your name.

Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are the Lord my Savior, and I have waited for you all day.

Remember your mercies, O Lord, and your compassions, which are from of old.

Do not remember the sins of my youth and my acts of ignorance, O Lord.

According to your mercy, remember me, because of your goodness, O Lord.

For the sake of your name, O Lord, you will be gracious to my sin, for it is great.

Do not abandon me, O Lord my God; do not depart from me.

Be pleased, O Lord, to deliver me; O Lord, hasten to help me.

Give me, O Lord, a sign of goodness, so that those who hate me may see it and be confounded, for you, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me.

Your hands, O Lord, made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments.

I am your servant; give me understanding, that I may know [Col. 1305B] [Col. 1305C] your testimonies.

Go forth, O Lord, for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Anointed One.

Restore us, O God our Savior, and turn away your anger from us.

Deign, O Lord, on this day to keep us without sin.

Have mercy on us, O Lord; have mercy on us.

Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, just as we have hoped in you.

We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly and committed iniquity, O Lord.

O Lord, do not remember our ancient iniquities; may your mercies quickly come before us, for we have become exceedingly poor.

Help us, O God our Savior; for the glory [Col. 1305D] of your name, O Lord, deliver us, and be gracious to our sins for the sake of your name.

O Lord, do not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities.

Do not remember, O Lord, our sins or those of our parents; do not take vengeance for our sins. [Col. 1306A]

Deliver us, O God, by your wonders, and give glory to your name.

Stretch out your arm, O Lord, and deliver our souls, lest we perish.

Remember us, O Lord, in the favor shown to your people; visit us with your salvation.

Remember your congregation, O Lord, which you possessed from the beginning.

Guard us, O Lord, as the apple of the eye; protect us under the shadow of your wings.

Protect us, O Lord, from the face of the wicked who have afflicted us.

Be for us, O Lord, a protecting God and a house of refuge, so that you may save us.

[Col. 1306B] Be for us, O Lord, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy.

Give us help, O Lord, in tribulation, for the salvation of man is vain.

In the Lord we shall do valiantly, and he himself will bring those who trouble us to nothing.

Let there be peace within your stronghold and abundance within your towers.

O God, when you turn toward us, you will revive us, and your people will rejoice in you.

Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.

Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your holy ones rejoice.

O Lord God of hosts, restore us; show [Col. 1306C] your face, and we shall be saved.

O Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.

When these prayers have been completed, let the priest say these Prayers:

The Lord be with you. Let us pray.

Almighty and most gentle God, look favorably upon my prayers, and free my heart from the temptation of evil thoughts, so that I may deserve to become a worthy dwelling place of the Holy Spirit.

O God, whose proper work is always to have mercy and to spare, receive our supplication, and by the mercy of your kindness release what the chain of sins binds.

Hear, we beseech you, Lord, the prayers of those who supplicate you, and spare the sins of those who confess to you, so that, in your kindness, you may grant us both pardon and peace.

Almighty and everlasting God, show your mercy to us who supplicate you, so that we who distrust the quality of our merits may experience not judgment but indulgence.

Almighty God, appeased, bestow your mercy upon us, so that we who, by despising you, incurred guilt may, by confessing, obtain pardon.

Afterward, rising to put on the priestly vestments, he should first say:

With all your saints and elect intervening for us, we beseech you, Lord, both to go before our actions by your inspiration and to accompany them by your help, so that every prayer and all our activity may always begin from you and, begun through you, be brought to completion.

Then he should wash his hands, saying this verse:

“I shall wash among the innocent.”

Let us pray.

Almighty God, grant generously to our senses that, just as the impurities of the hands are washed away externally here, so the pollutions of our minds may be cleansed inwardly by you, and that the increase of holy virtues may grow within us.

When he has removed his ordinary garments, he should say:

[Col. 1307B] “You have torn my sackcloth, Lord, and clothed me with saving gladness.”

Meanwhile, while the bishop is being prepared, the clerics standing around should sing these psalms:

“How lovely are your tabernacles,” etc.; “You blessed the earth, Lord,” etc.; “Incline your ear, Lord,” etc.; “Its foundations are upon the mountains,” etc.; “Lord God of my salvation”; “I believed, therefore I spoke”; “Remember, Lord.”

For putting on the ephod or amice:

Cover my shoulders, Lord, with the grace of the Holy Spirit, and, with all vices driven out, gird my loins for sacrificing to you who live and reign forever and ever.

[Col. 1307C] For the alb:

Surround me, Lord, with the arms of faith, so that, delivered from the arrows of iniquities, I may be able to guard equity and justice.

Prayer for the alb:

Almighty and everlasting God, I earnestly beseech you that, stripped of every deceit by which I have been darkened and clothed in a white garment, I may be worthy to follow you to the kingdoms where true joys are found.

For the girdle:

Gird my loins, Lord, with the belt of justice, and circumcise the vices of my heart and body.

For the cincture:

Gird me, Lord, with strength, and set my path blameless.

[Col. 1307D] For the stole:

Surround my neck, Lord, with the stole of justice, and purify my mind from every corruption of sin.

Prayer for the stole:

Break, Lord, the bonds of my sins, so that, supported by the yoke of your service, I may be able to serve you with fear and reverence.

For the tunicle:

Clothe me, Lord, with the garment of salvation, and surround me with the breastplate of strength.

For the dalmatic:

Clothed in this symbolic garment, woven in the manner of a cross with purple bands according to the rite of the ancient fathers, I humbly ask that, through the remembrance of your Passion, I may become continually pleasing to you, Lord Jesus Christ, who live, etc.

For the chasuble:

Clothe me, Lord, in priestly justice, so that I may be worthy to be led into the everlasting tabernacles.

Prayer for the chasuble:

Clothe me, Lord, with the adornment of humility and charity, and grant me protection against the enemy who lies in wait, so that I may praise your holy name with a pure heart and a chaste body forever and ever. Amen.

When he has received the maniple:

By the wearing of this maniple I earnestly beseech you, Lord, that I may so act in my temporal life that, following the example of the former fathers, I may hereafter be worthy to rejoice eternally. Through all things, etc.

When he has put on the maniple:

Grant strength to my hands, Lord, for wiping away every unclean stain, so that without pollution of mind or body I may be able to serve you. Amen.

For putting on the gloves:

Creator of every creature, deign to clothe me, your unworthy servant, in the garments of justice and gladness, so that, with pure minds, I may be worthy to stand clean before your presence.

For the ring:

Surround my fingers, Lord, with strength, and adorn them with the sacrificial rite.

[Col. 1308C] For the rationale:

Grant us, Lord, firmly to retain your truth and worthily to open the teaching of truth to your people.

After he has been mitred, he should say this prayer:

I ask you, most high Sabaoth, holy Father, to deign to gird me with the tunic of chastity, to encircle my loins with the belt of your love, and to burn the loins of my heart and body with the fire of charity, so that I may be able worthily to intercede for my sins, obtain pardon for the sins of the people standing by, and offer peaceful sacrifices for each person. Do not permit me, Lord, as I approach you boldly, to perish; rather, deign to cleanse, wash, adorn, and gently and kindly receive me, most holy Father, who, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, live and reign as God forever and ever. [Col. 1308D] Amen.

Then follows the individual confession.

Almighty Lord God, who are three and one and present everywhere, I confess to you all my sins. Even if I did not confess them, they could not remain hidden from you, because I have sinned greatly in thoughts, in words, and in various evil deeds, and many of them. And because I, wretched and pitiable, Lord, on account of the hardness and wickedness of my heart, remain in the very death of my sins unless you help me, therefore, for your sake, have mercy on me, who live and reign.

When all these things have been duly performed, the bishop should say these prayers:

“Rise up, Lord, help us, and redeem us for your name’s sake.”

[Col. 1309A] “Let your mercy, Lord, be upon us, just as we have hoped in you.”

“God, when you turn to us, you will revive us, and your people will rejoice in you.”

“Show us, Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.”

“Do not enter into judgment with your servants, Lord, for no living person will be justified in your sight.”

“Lord, do not remember our former iniquities. May your mercies quickly go before us, for we have become exceedingly poor.”

“Be favorable to our sins, Lord, for your name’s sake, Lord.”

“Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.”

The prayers follow. Let us pray.

Make me, I beseech you, almighty God, so to be clothed in justice that I may be worthy to rejoice in the exultation of your saints, and, cleansed from every filth of sin, may attain fellowship with the priests who please you. May your mercy also strip me of every vice, me whom the guilt of my own conscience weighs down. Who, etc.

Another.

Most gentle God, incline the ears of your mercy to my prayers, and illumine my heart with the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that I may be worthy to minister worthily at your mysteries and to love you with everlasting charity. Through, etc.

For placing on the incense:

[Col. 1309C] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, may this incense be blessed as a sweet fragrance to the Lord and for the remission of all our sins. Amen.

For kissing the Gospel:

May the peace of Christ remain in our inward being.

When the bishop goes out from the sacristy, he should say:

Lead me, Lord, in your way, and let me enter into your truth; let my heart rejoice, so that it may fear your name. I will sacrifice to you willingly, and I will confess your name, Lord, for it is good.

Entering the church, he should say:

“I shall enter your house, Lord, and I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear.”

Lord, lead me in your justice because of my enemies; direct your way before me.

Turn my eyes away, Lord, so that they may not see vanity; revive me in your way. God, be merciful to me, a sinner.

Meanwhile, as he goes out in procession, he should sing this psalm for himself with those leading him, at the steps:

“The Lord is my shepherd, and I shall lack nothing,” etc.

With the verse:

“Your rod and your staff,” etc.

When this is finished, he should add this prayer:

The Lord be with you.

And with your spirit.

Let us pray.
