For Peter, John, Matthew, and Paul and the others thereafter, together with their followers, proclaimed all the prophetic writings just as the interpretation of the Elders contains them.’

“For this reason it was always held in great veneration among Christians. But when it was later corrupted through the fault of copyists, as the holy Fathers Justin Martyr in the Dialogue with Trypho, Augustine in The City of God, book 15, chapter 13, and Jerome in letter 108 complain, it was cleansed of errors first by Origen, then by Lucian the martyr, afterward by Hesychius, and finally by Jerome.

“Whether Origen saw the original exemplar—which Tertullian, in the cited place of the Apology, believed still existed intact at Alexandria in his own time—and when it perished is uncertain. Nor is it my purpose or leisure to linger over the investigation of this matter.

“Since, then, this Greek translation had such authority among all, all the Latin versions made after the Lord Christ’s ascension into heaven and thereafter in those earliest times, before Saint Jerome, were not rendered immediately from Hebrew sources but were taken from the Greek text of the Seventy. These versions were innumerable, because, as Saint Augustine writes in book 2, chapter 11, of On Christian Doctrine, ‘Anyone who seemed to himself to possess even a little ability in both the Greek and Latin languages ventured to forge a new translation.’

“Among all of them, however, the most excellent and commonly and universally received was the one called the Itala, as Augustine himself testifies in the cited book, chapter 15: ‘Among the translations themselves, let the Itala be preferred to the others, for it is more faithful to the words while preserving clarity of meaning.’ Since in Saint Jerome’s time it was marked by the names ‘Vulgate’ and ‘Ancient,’ it follows that it was older than the others and possessed greater authority among them.

“It was also called Roman because the Roman Church received it from the beginning. Perhaps it was the first translation made from the Greek text, by some disciple of the apostles, and seen and approved by the first founders of the Church; these handed it down to their successors together with the deposit of faith. Not only did the Apostolic See, which never at any time lacked a Latin translation, use it, but so did the other Western Churches, although some changes crept into it, either through the boldness or negligence of copyists, or through the license of bishops who adapted certain words or sentences to the idioms of their own regions.

“Moreover, the complete body of this version exists nowhere; only the Psalter remains, together with the canticles recited in the divine offices. Some fragments of it are also found in the expositions of the holy Fathers. Since Saint Jerome’s version, as Isidore writes in book 6, chapter 3, of the Etymologies, was considered better than the others and more consonant with Hebrew truth, and therefore began to be read in churches, cited in councils, and expounded in commentaries, that ancient version, as though it were now scarcely necessary, gradually began to be neglected, until finally it wholly perished and was buried in perpetual oblivion.

“I suspect that this occurred two hundred or more years after Jerome. For in the time of Gregory the Great both versions—the old and the new—were in use, as he himself indicates at the end of the dedicatory letter of his exposition of Job to Saint Leander, bishop. There he says that he is expounding the new version, namely Jerome’s, and that whenever the reason for confirmation requires it he takes up now the new, now the old: ‘Since,’ he says, ‘the Apostolic See, over which by God’s authority I preside, uses both, my labor of study too should be supported by both.’

“Only the Psalter of that most ancient version, which had nourished the faith of the nascent Church in the Western regions, escaped this grievous shipwreck. Since the faithful used it in chanting the divine offices and had committed it to memory through long practice, they could not be persuaded to learn a new translation and abandon the old one to which they were accustomed.

“This, then, is the Psalter on whose account I have digressed to these matters, the Psalter from which Gregory excerpted the Introits and the rest contained in his Antiphoner.”] and proper to the Roman Church, which we discussed in book 2, chapter 3.

“You blessed.”  
“Bend down, Lord.”  
“Our Father.”  
Verse: “Rise up, Lord, help us.”  
“Let your mercy, Lord, be upon us.”  
“O God, you have turned and revived us.”  
“Show us, Lord, your mercy.”  
“Do not enter into judgment with your servant.”  
“Be favorable, Lord, to our sins.”  
“Lord, hear my prayer.”

Let us pray.

“Most merciful God, incline the ears of your compassion to my prayers, and enlighten my heart by the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that I may deserve to minister worthily in your mysteries and love you with everlasting charity. Through our Lord, etc.”

Then let him say privately:

“I ask you, most high God of Sabaoth, holy Father, to deign to gird me with the tunic of chastity, surround my loins with the belt of your love, and burn the kidneys of my body with the fire of charity, so that I may worthily intercede with you, my Lord, for my sins, obtain from you the forgiveness of the sins of the people standing here, and offer to you the peaceful sacrifices of each person.

“Allow me, unworthy as I am, though I approach you boldly, to perish; rather, deign in your compassion to cleanse me, wash me, adorn me, and make me a suitable and worthy minister for you. Receive me gently and kindly. Grant me this, almighty Father, through your only-begotten Son, our Lord, who lives with you, etc.”

“Make me, I ask, almighty God, so clothed in righteousness that I may deserve to rejoice in the exultation of your saints, so that, cleansed from all the filth of sins, I may obtain fellowship with the priests pleasing to you, and that your mercy may strip me of every vice, for I am weighed down by the guilt of my own conscience. Through Christ, etc.”

Then, when the clergy have begun the Gloria after the Introit, let him proceed, with the deacon before him, the subdeacon before the deacon carrying the Gospel book, and an acolyte before the subdeacon carrying incense. Before that acolyte let two other acolytes go with candelabra and lights. Thus, in ordered procession, let them leave the sacristy with the Antiphon, “Redeem me and have mercy on me, that I may bless you, O God of Israel,” and with the Psalm, “Judge me, Lord, for I have entered in my innocence.” When they have reached the altar, let them begin the Psalm with the Antiphon, “I will go in to the altar of God,” “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause,” with the Gloria Patri, and let the Antiphon be repeated.

Then, bowing, let them make confession, with the deacon standing at the priest’s right together with the acolyte, and the subdeacon on his left holding the Gospel book opposite his face.

The confession follows.

“I confess to almighty God, to these saints, to all his saints, and to you, brothers, that I, wretched, have sinned exceedingly against the law of my God in thought, word, and deed, through pollution of mind and body, and through all the evils by which human frailty can be defiled. Therefore I ask you to pray for me, a wretched sinner.”

“By the prayers and merits of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary and of all her saints, may the almighty Lord have mercy on you and forgive you all your past, present, and future sins; may he free you from every evil, preserve you in every good work, and may Christ, the Son of the living God, lead us together into eternal life. Amen.”

“May almighty, gracious, and merciful Lord grant us, through the intercession of all his saints, indulgence, absolution, and remission of all our sins, and a period for true repentance. Amen.”

Verse: “Turn us, O God our Savior.”  
Response: “And turn away your anger from us.”

“Deign, Lord, to keep us this day without sin.”

“Let your mercy, Lord, be upon us, as we have hoped in you.”

“Lord, hear my prayer.”  
“And let my cry come to you.”

Let us pray.

“Take away our iniquities, we ask, Lord, so that with pure minds we may deserve to enter the Holy of Holies. Hear, we ask, Lord, the prayers of those who implore you, and spare the sins of those who confess to you, so that in your kindness you may grant us together indulgence and peace. Through the Lord, etc.”

When these things have been completed, let the subdeacon present the open book for the priest to kiss. After he has kissed the Gospel which is to be read that day, let him say:

“May the peace of Christ, which he handed down to us through his Gospel, preserve and strengthen our hearts and bodies unto eternal life. Amen.”

The subdeacon, closing the book, should place it on the altar at the left corner. When they have begun the Kyrie eleison in the choir, let the acolytes set down the candelabra on the pavement.

The deacon should take the thurible from the hand of the acolyte and, approaching, kiss the altar. The priest follows him and, bowing, first prays as follows:

“To you, my Maker, my Redeemer, my Savior, I, your most wretched servant, flee with devotion of heart. Because you are compassionate, have mercy on me and receive my confession, you who are the one hope of my salvation, my Lord and my God.

“For daily, without interruption, I serve and delight in the vices of gluttony, drunkenness, and excess. From almost childhood I have been corrupted by the filth of fornication, pollution, and lust; I have been stained inwardly and outwardly by every impurity and uncleanness of lust.

“I am ruined by sadness, sloth, drowsiness, anger, desire, craving, greed, envy, malice, hatred, detraction, suspicion, hypocrisy, perjury, falsehood, lying, negligence, disobedience, vainglory, frivolity, and pride; and I am destroyed by every evil thought, word, or deed, and by all evils and iniquities.

“But you, who justify the ungodly and give life to the dead, justify me and raise me up, Lord my God.”

Then let him rise and kiss the altar, saying:

“Almighty and everlasting God, who have willed that I, a sinner, stand at the sacred altars and praise the power of your holy name, grant, we ask, through the mystery of this sacrament, forgiveness of my sins, so that I may deserve to minister worthily to your majesty. Through, etc.”

Then, having received the thurible from the deacon’s hand, let him incense the altar and return it to the same deacon, giving him a kiss. The deacon should incense around the altar and, returning, present the fragrance to the priest. Having returned the thurible to the acolyte, let him stand behind the priest, and the subdeacon behind him.

When the Kyrie eleison in the choir has ended, if the time is appropriate, let the priest say “Glory to God in the highest.” Then, turned toward the people, with whom the deacon must also turn, let him say “The Lord be with you” and the prayer. After it has been said, let the subdeacon read the Epistle facing the altar. When he begins, the priest and deacon should sit in their seats on the right side of the altar, and the subdeacon should sit beside them after reading the Epistle.

Then the Gradual, Alleluia, Tract, or Sequence is sung. Meanwhile, the priest or ministers should say these prayers.

Prayer.

“Most kind and most merciful, most serene and most gracious God, whom every angelic power serves and to whom everything holy and clean renders service: before the sight of your divine majesty I stand guilty, a most unworthy usurper of the most holy mystery. Indeed, I am not fit even to invoke your holy and venerable name, since I am weighed down by innumerable offenses, inflated by pride, swollen with vainglory, destroyed by envy, tormented by sloth, rotten with lust, loosened by wantonness, goaded by anger, grown old in hatred, ruined by detraction, puffed up by insolence, immoderate in the gluttony of the belly and the appetite of the throat, filled with deceit, stained by uncleanness, held too tightly by love of the world, entangled in greed, lifted up by boasting, crafty through hypocrisy, most obstinate in contention, treacherous through discord, exceedingly ready for whispering, afflicted by resentment of heart and faintheartedness, sluggish through torpor, thoughtless in swearing, constant in buffoonery, devoted to idle, superfluous, and criminal words, gravely polluted by both spiritual and bodily fornication, and most wretchedly plunged into every pleasure in which human frailty can fall.

“In every vice and offense whatsoever, through which one can sin by thinking, speaking, or acting, I recognize and confess that I have sinned gravely and am guilty before the tribunal of your equity.

“But you, most merciful and compassionate God, do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person shall be justified in your sight, since he is withered grass and corruptible flesh, tending every day altogether toward nonbeing.

“Who, then, can make what was conceived from an unclean seed clean, except you, who alone are God? For we are like a menstruous cloth, unclean before the majesty of your glory, Lord. In your sight even the heavens themselves are not clean—how much less are we, created in corruptible flesh, earthly and unclean human beings?

“For what can a mortal worthily offer to the immortal, the corruptible to the incorruptible, the changeable to the unchangeable? Yet, so that this might be possible, you were incarnate for us, Son of God, remaining clean and incorruptible as you are. You also handed on to your elect the sacrament of your body and blood, through which we might be made clean from unclean, holy from sinners, chaste from the unchaste, and bright from filth, and through which we might appear splendid before the majesty of your glory.

“Therefore, Lord, you supreme priest, sanctifier and sanctification of the priesthood, have mercy on me, a sinful man; spare an unworthy priest; forgive one who handles the secrets of your mystery; and do not judge unworthy of your mercy the one whom you permit to pray for others. Although you recognize in me no testimony of a good work, at least do not refuse the duty of the stewardship entrusted to me.

“May this frequent celebration of the most holy mystery become for me an absolving propitiation for all my crimes, Savior of the world. You who live, etc.”

Another prayer.

“O God of mercy and truth, I humbly implore your clemency, etc.” This appears above in the Mass of Illyricus.

Another prayer.

“O God, who desire not the death but the repentance of sinners.” As above in the Mass of Illyricus.

## The Litany follows.

Christ, hear us. God the Father of heaven, have mercy on us. God the Son, Redeemer of the world, have mercy on us. God the Holy Spirit, have mercy on us. Holy Trinity, one God, have mercy on us. Holy God of gods, have mercy on us. Holy Mary, pray for us. Holy Mother of God, [Col. 1342A] Holy Mother of the Lord, Holy Virgin of Virgins. Holy Queen of heaven. Holy Mother of mercy. Holy Michael. Holy Gabriel. Holy Raphael. All holy Angels and Archangels. Holy John the Baptist. All holy Patriarchs and Prophets. Holy Peter. Holy Paul. Holy Andrew. Holy James. Holy John. [Col. 1342B] Holy James. Holy Philip. Holy Bartholomew. Holy Matthew. All holy Apostles and Evangelists. Holy Dionysius. Holy Stephen. Holy Cornelius. Holy Cyprian. Holy Sebastian. Holy Chrysanthus. Holy George. Holy Aurelius. Holy Processus. Holy Januarius. [Col. 1342C] Holy Hermes. Holy Vitus. Holy Mercury. Holy Caesarius. Holy Pancratius. Holy Adalbert. Holy Cyriacus. Holy Evaticus. Holy Phocas. Saints John and Paul. Saints Tiburtius and Valerian. Saints Faustinus and Jovita. Saints Primus and Felician. Saints Sergius and Bacchus. Saints Nazarius and Celsus. [Col. 1342D] Saints Felicissimus and Agapitus. Saints Nicander and Marcian. Saints Valentine and Hilary. Saints Quirinus and Maximus. The Forty Holy Martyrs. Holy Fortunatus, with your companions. All holy Martyrs. Holy Gregory. Holy Martin. Holy Ambrose. Holy Paulinus. Holy Maximus. Holy Felix. Holy Nicholas. [Col. 1343A] Holy Remigius. All holy Bishops and Confessors. Holy Benedict. Holy Maurus. Holy Placid. Holy Severinus. Holy Romanus. All holy Monks and Hermits. Holy Scholastica. Holy Cecilia. Holy Daria. Holy Catherine. All holy Virgins. All holy men and women of God. Be merciful, spare us, O Lord. [Col. 1343B] From the snares of demons, deliver us, O Lord. From the danger of death, deliver us. From unclean thoughts. From the domination of all vices. From blindness of heart. From every evil. We sinners beg you: hear us. That you may spare us, we beg you. That you may grant us a sure hope. That you may bestow a right faith. That you may confer perfect charity. That you may put to death in us the monsters of every vice. That you may bring us to life through the prerogative of every virtue. That through your incarnation you may open for us an entrance into the Holy of Holies. [Col. 1343C] That through this most holy mystery you may renew our souls and bodies. That through it you may purify our consciences. That you may not allow this fearful mystery to become judgment for us. That we may handle this ineffable sacrament with clean hands. That we may receive it with pure minds. That through it we may obtain pardon for all sins. That through it we may always be able to cling to you. That through it both you may deign to remain in us and we in you. That you may deign to pour the grace of the Holy Spirit into our hearts. [Col. 1343D] That you may deign to preserve the entire Christian people redeemed by your most precious blood. That you may grant us a place for repentance.

Our Father.

**Versicles.** Convert us, O God our salvation. Deign, O Lord, on this day. Have mercy on us, O Lord. Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us. The sins of my youth and my ignorances. Help us, O God our salvation. Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord. Do not deal with us according to our sins, O Lord. [Col. 1344A] Not to us, O Lord, not to us. Arise, O Lord; help us. O Lord, hear my prayer.

### The following prayer

Help us, O Lord our God, through the prayers of your saints, so that at the opportune time we sinners and unworthy servants may experience the help we desire and need from all the blessed Angels, Archangels, and all the heavenly spirits; from the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, Evangelists, Martyrs, Confessors, Priests, Levites, Monks, Virgins, Widows, Innocents, and all the faithful who minister to you in heaven and on earth, whose feasts are celebrated today throughout the whole world. Through you, Jesus Christ, [Col. 1344B] Savior of the world, who live, etc.

### Another prayer

With a trembling conscience, almighty God, I approach your altar; but if I withdraw, I fear being condemned for disobedience. Therefore spare me, O Lord, your unworthy servant; and although I am always found unworthy to celebrate such great mysteries, nevertheless I retain confidence in your mercy. For this reason, almighty God, deign in fatherly kindness and with a peaceful countenance to look upon me, to cleanse the inner places of my heart; and although I am guilty by reason of my own fault, nevertheless, through the intercession of the blessed and glorious ever-Virgin Mary and of all your saints, may my ministries in all things be pleasing to you. You who live, etc.

### Another prayer

[Col. 1344C] Lord God almighty, who are three and one, present everywhere and wholly present everywhere, I confess to you all my sins. Even if I did not confess them, they could not remain hidden from you, O Lord, whom secret things do not deceive: for I have sinned exceedingly in thoughts, words, and various evil and numerous deeds. And because I, wretched and pitiable, would remain in the very death of my sins unless you helped me, therefore I beg you: have mercy on me. You who live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.

### Another

God, who make the worthy from the unworthy, the clean from the unclean, and the righteous from sinners, cleanse my heart and my body from every filth and contagion of sin, [Col. 1344D] and make me a worthy minister at your holy altars. Mercifully grant that upon this altar, to which I, unworthy, approach to minister, I may offer acceptable and propitiatory sacrifices to your goodness for all my sins and offenses, for my innumerable daily transgressions, and for all who have commended themselves to my unworthy prayers; also for all faithful Christians, for all who stand here, for all who are joined to me by friendship or blood, and also for all who remember me in their prayers. And through him may my vow and sacrifice be acceptable to you, God the Father, who offered himself to you as a sacrifice: Jesus Christ our Lord. Who with you, etc.

[Col. 1345A] ### Another

I confess, O Lord, that I am unworthy of your sacred things, since I am daily defiled by innumerable sins. It appears in exactly the same words in the preceding Mass of Illyricus.

### Another

Most High God, forgive me, etc. It also appears above, with several words added and altered.

[Col. 1346A] ### Another

The duty of ministering impels me to offer the saving sacrifice for the people’s offense, but the conscience of an unmerited priesthood terrifies me, etc. It is likewise found in the preceding Mass.

The remainder is missing.

# Monastic Monuments

[Col. 1345]

## Concerning the meal of the monks: how it is customary in monasteries established in the Roman Church

(Gerbert, *Ancient Alemannic Liturgical Monuments*, from the ninth-century manuscript of St Gall.) (C)

[Col. 1345B] When they approach the meal, the prior says the prayer with the brothers, namely, “The eyes of all”; the whole prayer is said at length, followed by the *Gloria Patri*, and afterward “Alleluia” is sung at the end. The priest says the prayer in such a voice that all may hear and respond, “Amen”: “May your gifts, O Lord, be blessed for us.” There are also many other prayers assigned to this meal.

Then all sit in their places. Near the abbot’s table there is a raised chair, with a reading stand, on which the book is placed when they read. As soon as the ministers set out the first food and the signal sounds for the food to be blessed before eating, all respond, “Thanks be to God.” The prior, or the presbyter, or whoever has been ordered to do so, blesses it in such a voice that everyone hears, and they respond, “Amen.”

At the very beginning of the meal a reader is ready. He immediately asks for a blessing, saying, “Command, lord, a blessing.” The senior says, “May the Lord save us,” and all respond, “Amen.” The reader then goes in to read and reads for as long as they eat that food. Afterward, if the meal has been long and they are to sit longer, or if another serving is to be provided, the prior touches the table so that the reader may be silent for a little while. If there are fish or birds, they eat them when they are served. When the signal sounds for them to be blessed, all respond, “Thanks be to God,” and the prior, or whoever has been ordered, gives the blessing, saying, “May the Lord, Creator of all, bless his creature”; and all respond, “Amen,” and the food is eaten.

If there is another kind of food, he says this prayer: “Through the prayers of holy Mary, Mother of God, may Christ, the Son of God, bless both us and his gifts”; all respond, “Amen.”

[Col. 1345C] For another serving the reader again reads until the abbot orders him to finish. Or, if he has found an appropriate conclusion, when the blessing is heard at the end of the reading he repeats the same passage a second time at length. All respond, “Thanks be to God,” and he descends. If the reading has been long and he has brought the discourse to a good conclusion, he repeats it, [Col. 1345D] and afterward says, “But you, O Lord, have mercy on us”; all respond, “Amen.”

The same custom applies at the night offices, at the collect, or wherever a divine command is read: whenever the reader begins, having asked for a blessing, he says, “Command, lord, a blessing”; when the reader has finished the reading, they respond, “Thanks be to God.” As he descends, he goes before the abbot’s table and receives from him the blessing from which he eats and drinks.

When the brothers rise, they say quietly, “Let them give thanks to you, O Lord,” adding the *Gloria Patri* and singing “Alleluia” at the end. If they have had a more substantial meal and anything remains afterward, the prior, or the person entrusted with this care, says the prayer: “The fragments that have remained for his servants, Christ the Son of God has multiplied; may he bless them and make them abound, who is blessed for ever and ever.” All respond, “Amen.” They go to the oratory to pray, giving thanks to the Lord, and there, after the prayer has ended, they say, “He scattered; he gave,” the food-service having been completed.

[Col. 1346B] Likewise, in the evening, when they have entered the place where they are refreshed, they say without delay the prayer “The poor shall eat,” adding the *Gloria Patri* and singing “Alleluia” at the end. The senior says a prayer in such a way that all hear and respond, “Amen,” namely: “You, O Lord, ...”; or there are many others according to the season.

While sitting in their seats, they do likewise as at the daytime meal. If it happens that night arrives while they are eating and it is necessary to light a lamp, the brother who brings the light, as soon as he enters the room near the seniors, says in such a voice that all hear, “The light of Christ”; and all say, “Thanks be to God.” Then, bowing, he again says, “Command, lord, a blessing.” The senior says, “In the name of the Lord, may it be”; all respond, “Amen.” He then puts the light in its place, so that it may shine for everyone in the room.

If the brothers have been ordered to mix a drink for themselves, the minister goes to the serving place and touches the cup with his finger. All respond, “Thanks be to God”; he blesses it, and all respond, “Amen.” Thus they drink with a blessing. If the Lord has given them fruit, the senior says this prayer: “May the almighty Lord bless his fruits”; all respond, “Amen.” Thus it is done with every serving.

[Col. 1346C] When the meal has been completed, the signal is given for them to rise. The brother who is assigned for the week to the kitchen, whenever the brothers eat, always serves at the table of the seniors or brothers together with the other ministers. When they rise from the table, this brother kneels facing east and asks them to pray for him, saying, “Lords, pray for me.” The senior says, “May the Lord save us.” The brother rises and says in a loud voice, “Thanks be to God.”

Immediately all the brothers begin to sing, “Always give thanks to you, O Lord.” When this is finished, the prior with the brothers says, “Merciful and compassionate God,” at length with the *Gloria*, adding “Alleluia” at the end. Or: “He who gives food to all flesh, give thanks to the Lord of heaven, for he is good, for his mercy is everlasting.” The priest says the prayer, namely, “You have satisfied us, O Lord.” When it is finished, all respond, “Amen.” Thus they go to prayer and pray as written above.

The weekly kitchen-server who enters the kitchen [Col. 1346D] enters or leaves on Sunday according to what is written in the Rule of Saint Benedict. When Matins has ended, the one who is leaving immediately asks for prayer in the oratory, saying, “Lords, pray for me.” The senior says, “Save your servant.” Then he says with all the brothers, “Blessed are you, O Lord God,” repeating this three times. Having received the blessing, he leaves.

The one who is entering immediately says, “O God, attend to my help”; this prayer is repeated three times with all the brothers. Having received the blessing, he enters to serve his brothers.

Likewise in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, the presbyter serves for a week; or the custodians who guard the light or adornment of that church, on Saturday at the third hour, hand over their duties to their equals. Thus they descend and go to their homes, while the others serve with the presbyter or their equals until the following Saturday and do likewise. Thus, in all offices, they are preserved for God honorably and in due order.

And if perhaps anyone should dislike these things, of which I have written a few from many, [Col. 1347A] let him not be lazy but show prudence. Other priests, Fathers, and devout monks who desire to live and preserve their way of life in right order and with divine authority practice them in this manner. Wherever they go, they carry this sacred teaching for their own benefit, for that of their associates, and for the edification of many, with great labor, so that hereafter or in the future they may rejoice and be glad perpetually in the presence of God, his angels, and all his saints.

Let such a person go to Rome himself; or, if he is reluctant, let him send a faithful representative in his place and inquire diligently whether what we have written briefly from many sources is so or not. Or, if it is not celebrated there in this manner, let him inquire with holy intention and devotion whether he can find something better, by which he may advance in the work of God a hundredfold more. Only afterward should he perhaps presume to hear, despise, disparage, or oppose such and so great holy Fathers who established this sacred norm.

First, the blessed Pope Damasus, with the assistance of the presbyter Saint Jerome, instituted and ordered the [Col. 1347B] ecclesiastical order described and transmitted from Jerusalem with the permission of Saint Damasus himself. After him, the most blessed Pope Leo instituted the entire annual chant and published exceptionally brilliant little works in canonical instruction; if anyone does not receive or venerate them down to a single jot, let him be anathema.

Then the blessed Pope Gelasius (Zelasius) likewise wrote out with honor and the greatest diligence the entire annual chant and the canonical decrees, after holding an assembly of many priests at the see of the blessed apostle Peter. After him Pope Symmachus likewise published his annual chant. Again after him Pope John likewise wrote out the chant of the yearly cycle and its whole order.

After him Pope Boniface, inspired by the Holy Spirit, wrote the rule and arranged the singing of the yearly cycle. After these, the blessed Pope Gregory, to whom the Lord, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, granted great and exceedingly high grace, illuminated the *Moralia* on the Book of Blessed Job [Col. 1347C]—with the corrupt or uncertain reading “diptycha”/“tibica”—by a threefold investigation and a sevenfold exposition. He also expounded the first and final parts of the prophet Ezekiel with a most brilliant explanation.

What he did concerning the Gospels in an exposition of forty homilies is known to all Christians, and how beautifully he explained them. What he arranged in certain books through the work of the Holy Spirit, and what he interpreted from many other sacred Scriptures, has been revealed to Christians living in the world. He also published the noble chant of the annual cycle.

After these, Abbot Catalenus, serving there at the tomb of Saint Peter, likewise published the chant of the yearly cycle with the greatest diligence. After him Abbot Maurianus, serving the same holy apostle Peter, likewise nobly arranged his annual chant. After him, the good abbot Domnus Vir arranged the entire chant of the yearly cycle magnificently.

If anyone, after learning these things, [Col. 1347D] neglects to preserve or celebrate them insofar as he is able with God’s command, or perhaps boasts that he knows or has received a better example elsewhere, there is no doubt that he deceives himself and unhappily plunges himself into the darkness of error. He has dared to despise or disparage such and so great holy Fathers and authors.

I do not know with what face or presumption they have dared, in a presumptuous spirit, to oppose the blessed Hilary and Martin, or Germanus and Ambrose, or the many other saints of God whom we know to have been sent into this western land from the holy Roman see by the successors of the blessed apostle Peter, and to have shone through virtues and miracles. We know that they deviated in no respect from the holy Roman see, from the synod of the three hundred and eighteen Catholic Fathers assembled at Nicaea, or from the other three principal synods in communion with the Holy Spirit. Everything is known to exist together with this holy canonical instruction.

How, then, do they dare to cite such men as witnesses, saying, “As those men held and observed, so we too appear to hold and observe,” [Col. 1348A] when their life, conduct, works, and merit seem to be as far removed from those just mentioned as heaven is from earth? We know that these illustrious Confessors of Christ, whom we named above, frequently traveled to Rome, held conversations with the blessed Popes and with Christian emperors, and often corrected those who deviated from the holy Roman see. This is manifest among us.

Let those who profess to have these men as authorities inquire into their books and deeds: if they hold and act in this way, as those men acted and held, we too agree with them in complete devotion and reverence. But if this is not so, they must diligently inquire, imitate, and preserve their practice, just as the holy Roman Church preserves it, so that they too may hold the unity of the Catholic faith. Amen.

Otherwise, while investigating and following foreign customs, they may become entangled or fall away from the faith, lest what the excellent preacher foretold come upon them: “In the last [Col. 1348B] days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves,” bringing every understanding into captivity, speaking no truth, and accepting none.

And this also: “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and they will indeed turn away their hearing from the truth, but will turn to fables.”

And this also: “I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge or the tradition that they received from us. For, being ignorant of God’s knowledge and seeking their own, they established their own righteousness rather than submitting their righteousness to the righteousness of God.”

Who are those who “established” it? Those who abandon true authority and follow their own judgment or will. Christians ought not to do this, but should rather search the divine Scriptures daily and investigate and imitate the teachings of the holy Fathers, who always pleased the Lord in all things and were approved by men [Col. 1348C] in this world. They must not be shown to be schismatics or contradictors against the holy see of the Roman Church.

Nor should they perhaps appear to be little branches that are members of that seventh seal—that is, the seventh heresy, which is to rise at the end—as Holy Scripture attests: “For it is near at the doors,” or “before the gates.” This is according to the words of the blessed apostle John, who was commanded by the Lord to write in the Apocalypse to the seven churches and saw a book sealed with seven seals, according to the mystery of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

On the opposing side, seven evil spirits are contrary to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the seven seals signify seven heresies. Six have already arisen in the world from the eastern region against the holy Roman Church; but, with the help of Christ’s grace, the holy see of the blessed apostle Peter has broken and overcome all those heresies.

The seventh still remains. Thus the elders, wise men, and Doctors [Col. 1348D] of the holy Roman Church teach: it is to arise from this western region, or from the north. A dark power has been given to them; they destroy themselves and lead others into error. Those whom they cannot seduce through enticements, they attempt to slaughter and extinguish by force, tortures, or the sword of the Church of God.

But God’s foundation stands firm and steadfast. In the Gospel the Lord himself deigned to promise this, saying to the blessed apostle Peter: “Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”

The faithful of the Roman see may indeed be afflicted by tortures and tribulations or may die, but their faith and belief can in no way be overcome or broken.

Let us pray to the merciful Lord, watch constantly, be sober, and not sleep as those who have no hope, so that [Col. 1349A] he may deign to rescue and deliver us from all this evil that is soon to come upon the whole world. May he grant us to possess and preserve the unity of the Catholic faith to the end, and may our entrance be through the gates into the city of God, which is the heavenly Jerusalem, so that we may deserve to enjoy and rejoice forever with the saints of God in the tree of life, [Col. 1350A] through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Finished. Thanks be to God.

[Col. 1349]

# Fragment of the Statutes of the Canons of Tours when they lived in common

(*Library of the Holy and Metropolitan Church of Tours, abridged and systematically arranged; or, Catalogue of the Manuscript Books Preserved in That Library, etc. By the study and work of D. D. G. Joüan, chief archdeacon, and V. d’Avanne, canon of the same church, in the notes at the end, pp. 61, 62, 63, and 64, note i.*)

[Col. 1349B] If any brother established in the canonical community neglects to attend the canonical hours; enters the church not reverently but pompously or disorderly; performs the work of God negligently; delays coming to the conference; refuses to carry out the obedience imposed upon him by his superiors; fails, according to his ability, to show diligence in reading, singing, or the other ecclesiastical disciplines; comes late to the table not from necessity but through fault; leaves the cloisters without permission; after leaving with permission, lingers outside beyond the time appointed for him; attempts to walk in the streets or sit at crossroads; commits anything indecent or dishonorable by words or deeds in the dormitory; presumes to sleep anywhere except in the dormitory with the others without unavoidable cause; neglects obediently to serve the brothers in the duty of charity; sows discord among the brothers, which, as Scripture says, the soul of God detests; is obstinate, proud, murmuring, or in any way contrary to this institution; [Col. 1349C] or attempts to do anything else of this kind—let him first, according to the Lord’s command, be admonished not only once, twice, or three times, but even more frequently.

If he does not yield to these admonitions, let him be corrected by public admonition. If he resists even this, [Col. 1350B] let him be forbidden all food except bread until he has made worthy satisfaction, and let him use water.

If he still does not correct himself, let him be separated from the table and removed from the company of the brothers singing in the choir. Let him be compelled to stand apart in a place appointed by the superiors for negligent persons of this kind, so that at least he may be corrected by the shame of separation.

Then, if after being corrected by these methods he proves incorrigible, and if his age permits—for, in the words of Solomon, “A fool is not corrected by words”—let a suitable chastisement of blows be applied to him, so that he may be beaten as a son, in accordance with the judgment of blessed Gregory: “Those who do not heed the words of one commanding are to be admonished with blows, so that punishment may draw them toward good desires when rewards do not invite them.”

But if he is someone whom either age or the quality of his person does not permit to be beaten, let him be corrected by public rebuke and separation of this kind until he obtains pardon through worthy penitential satisfaction.

If, however, both the one who is beaten and the one whom age or personal condition prevents from being beaten still prove incorrigible, let there be within the canons’ cloister a place—such as is known to exist in many places—to which they may be confined for a time and chastised according to the measure of their fault, so that, according to the Apostle, “having been handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”
